units.la: Reverendo, Clarissimoque Viro, LUDOVICO CAPELLO, Euangelii Ministro, Theologia & Ebraearum litterarum in Salmurienfi Schola Profeffori eximio, JOANNES DALLÆUS S. P. D.

units.la: QUANTA fit antiquitatis apud homines vis atque auctoritas, CAPELLE præstantissime, vel hinc discimus, quod eam, etiam qui oppugnant ac delent, simulant tamen & præ se ferunt, omnemque dant operam, ut quæ instituta fovent, ea tametsi recentia, & pene mustea sint, antiqua fuisse videantur. Id in Christiana inprimis religione accidisse comperimus, cui cum ab hominum ingenio plurima omnibus fere temporibus præter optimi maximi auctoris mentem addita fuerint, ea qui sectati sunt ita semper & ipsi habuerunt, & ab aliis haberi voluerunt, quasi non nuper inventa, sed jam inde ab Euangelii initio constituta, & Ecclesiæ à Domini Christi Apostolis tradita essent. Mihi vero ab hoc fonte duo quædam gravissima incommoda & primum exorta, & latissime deinceps cum magna rerum Sacrarum pernicie pervagata manasse videntur; quorum prius hoc fuit, quod homines vera ac genuina vetustissimorum Christianorum monumenta, ne ex iis suæ disciplinæ à veteri diversitas proderetur, vel immani socordia absumi, atque intercidere siverunt, vel ipsi etiam fortasse data opera aboleverunt. Alterum vero multo etiam nocentius huc accessit, quod impostores, eodem præsentium rerum studio pereiti, sua ipsi opera antiquiftiquissimis, ac facile principibus litterarum Christiana-rum scriptoribus affingere non dubitarunt, in quibus eas novitiam Ecclesiasticæ doctrinæ, ac disciplinæ formam commendare ac confirmare pro sua libidine faciunt. Sce-leratissima utrorumque fraude effectum est, ut antiquis-simorum rei Christianæ Scriptorum monumentis, & veris sincerisque ac genuinis plerisque careamus, & falsis, supposititiisque, atque commentitiis abundemus. Ac verorum quidem jacturam deflere licet; sarcire vero, & quæ semel perierunt, revocare non licet. Itaque hoc unum superest, ut à supposititiis caveamus, eorumque fraudes ac venena pro virili nostra aperiamus, ac detegamus: quo in genere nullius fuit imposturæ major impudentia, quam ejus, quæ ipsis Sanctissimorum Apostolorum nominibus illudere ausa est. Ac cætera quidem ab hæreticis in hac proprie specie olim conficta, sed jam tum ab omnibus Catholicis mature explosa, nunc vero plane intermortua, solisque titulis nota mitto. Diataxes vero & Canones, spurium malefepиati alicujus Græculi fœtum, cum impune volitare, & à Romanis Theologis magna veritatis fraude usurpari, ac nostris identidem obje&tari cernerem; cœpi universum opus paulo diligentius inspicere ac rimari, cumque veris tum Apostolorum, tum Ecclesiasticorum auctorum dogmatis, atque monumentis comparare, magnamque hinc emicantium argumentorum copiam annotare, ac colligere, quæ (quantum quidem ego judico) clarissime demonstrant, validissimeque conficiunt, neque Apostolum, neque Apostolici sæculi virum fuisse, vel Constitutionum, vel Canonum parentem. Totam de his disputationem, quam in libros tres digestam amicorum consilio atque auctoritate compulsi nunc edimus, tibi (Frater ac conserve in Domino Christo observandissime) ideo inscribere placuit, tum ut constantem nostri in te amoris, cultus atque obsequii fidem testemur; tum ut tibi pro eximio, quo nos pridem beasti dono aliquam grati animi significationem rependamus. Cum enim tua
units.tr: How great is the power and authority of antiquity among men, most excellent Capellus, we may learn even from this: that those who attack and destroy it nevertheless pretend to it and display it, and take every pains to make what they favour appear ancient, even though it is recent and nearly mouldy. We find that this has happened especially in the Christian religion, to which, at almost all times, a great deal has been added by human ingenuity apart from the mind of the best and greatest Author. Those who followed these additions have always so regarded them, and wished others to regard them, as if they were not newly invented but had been established from the very beginning of the Gospel and handed down to the Church by the Apostles of the Lord Christ. From this source, it seems to me, two very grave evils arose at first and then spread widely, with great ruin to sacred things. The first was that men either allowed the true and genuine monuments of the most ancient Christians to be consumed and perish through monstrous negligence, lest by them the difference of their own discipline from the old one should be revealed, or perhaps even destroyed them deliberately. The second, far more harmful, followed: impostors, equally driven by a passion for the present, did not hesitate to ascribe their own works to the most ancient and, as it were, chief writers of Christian literature, in which they commend and confirm, as they pleased, this new form of ecclesiastical doctrine and discipline. By the most wicked fraud of both, it has come about that we lack the most ancient monuments of Christian antiquity, true, sincere and genuine for the most part, and abound in false, supposititious and fabricated ones. We may indeed lament the loss of the true ones, but we cannot repair them or recall what has once perished. So this alone remains: that we guard against the supposititious works and, as far as we can, expose and uncover their frauds and poisons. In this kind, no imposture has shown greater impudence than the one that dared to mock the very names of the most holy Apostles. As for the rest, I pass over those things that heretics once fabricated in this particular class, which were early and thoroughly rejected by all Catholics, and are now quite dead, known only by their titles. But when I saw that the Diataxes and the Canons, the spurious offspring of some wretched little Greek, were flying about with impunity and being wrongfully used by Roman theologians, and were constantly thrown in our faces, I began to examine and search the whole work somewhat more diligently, to compare it with the true doctrines and monuments of the Apostles and of the ecclesiastical writers, and to note and collect the great abundance of arguments that stood out from this comparison, which (as far as I judge) most clearly demonstrate and most forcefully establish that the work is the product neither of an Apostle nor of a man of the Apostolic age, neither of the Constitutions nor of the Canons. I have decided to dedicate the whole discussion, which I now publish, digested into three books, at the urging and by the authority of my friends, to you, brother and most esteemed fellow-servant in the Lord Christ: partly to bear witness to the constant faith of our love, respect and deference towards you, and partly to offer you some token of a grateful mind for the outstanding gift with which you blessed us some time ago. units.la: & pietas atque eruditio singularis, & industria in Christi negotio ante nos haud vulgari cum laude versata exposceret ; adhæc autem & tuorum in nos meritorum magnitudo flagitaret , ut ego tecum hoc officii genere prior certarem, tu tamen quæ tua in nos fuit benevolentia , atque humanitas , hunc mihi locum jamdudum præripuisti , cum ante annos octodecim chronologicæ Apostolorum historiæ , summo à te judicio, parique fide ex divinis libris accuratissime atque eruditissime contextæ, nomen meum honorifice præscribere dignatus es. Quod ergo tibi munusculum multis jam ante nominibus prior debebam , id vel nunc tandem liberalitate tua provocatus exsolvo. Sed & præter ipsam officii rationem , nonnulla me quoque mei cum tuo operis similitudo invitavit , ut hanc potissimum disputationem ad te mitterem. Commune enim utriusque lucubrationis argumentum , Apostoli ; quorum tu veros actus asseris , ego falsa fictitiaque scripta revinco , ac refello. Fateor in cæteris magnum esse discrimen , nostraque cum tuis , non aliter , quam ut vitrum cum gemma , conferri posse. Sed inter amicos etiam καλλεια ξενσίων ἀμει-βισθαι fas est ; quod à Glauco (ut Porphyrius * interpretatur) magnanimo, & à Diomede olim factum apud summum Poëtam legimus. Hoc ego jure atque exemplo fretus, tibi pro libello aureo tenuem hunc exigui pretii commentarium reddere non dubito. Tu vero, CAPPELLE amicissime , facilis , sat scio, accipies ; neque tam nostrum ex munusculo animum , quam ex animo munusculum æstimabis. Ita te Dominus JESUS familiæ, amicis , & Ecclesiæ diu incolumem , ac florentem servet. VALE.
units.tr: Both your singular piety and learning, and your diligence in the affairs of Christ, which have been held in no common esteem among us, would demand it of me; and besides, the greatness of your services to us would press me to contend with you first in this kind of duty. Yet your goodwill and kindness toward us have long since snatched this place from me, when eighteen years ago you deigned to prefix my name, with honour, to your chronological history of the Apostles, most accurately and learnedly woven together from the divine books with your great judgment and equal fidelity. Therefore I now at last, prompted by your generosity, pay this little gift which I owed you earlier under many other names. Yet beyond the reason of duty itself, the similarity of my work to yours also invited me to send this treatise to you in particular. For the subject of both our labours is the same: the Apostles. You vindicate their true acts; I expose and refute false and fictitious writings. I admit that in other respects there is a great difference, and that ours can be compared with yours only as glass with a gem. But between friends it is permitted to exchange gifts of beauty [καλλεια ξενσίων ἀμείβισθαι]; as we read was done long ago by the magnanimous Glaucus (as Porphyry interprets it) and by Diomedes, in the works of the greatest poet. Relying on this right and this example, I do not hesitate to give you in return for your golden little book this slight commentary of small worth. And you, my most friendly CAPPELLUS, I know, will receive it easily; and you will value not so much our mind from the little gift as the little gift from the mind. So may the Lord JESUS keep you, your family, your friends and the Church long safe and flourishing. FAREWELL.

units.tr: To the most excellent man, JOHN DALLÆUS.

units.la: QUID si ipsum audires Lector, sua verba tonantem, Cum jacit æterno fulmina digna Deo; Attonitosque trahit populos, & pectora mulcet, Eloquioque potens regnat, & astra quatit?
units.tr: What if you, reader, could hear the man himself thundering his own words, as he hurls lightning worthy of the eternal God, drags astonished peoples along, soothes hearts, reigns powerful in eloquence, and shakes the stars?

units.la: DALLÆUM nemo, DALLÆI, dicere posses, Vox superat calamum, solaque Lingua manum.
units.tr: No one could speak of Dallæus, Dallæus; the voice surpasses the pen, and the tongue alone surpasses the hand.

units.la: Attamen hoc præsto, Genium non defore chartis, Quæ de DALLÆI nomine nomen habent.
units.tr: Yet this much is at hand: that genius is not lacking in the pages which take their name from the name of Dallæus.

units.la: Maxima pars isto vel amœna effundimus ævo, Vel gravia & nullo tincta lepore damus:
units.tr: Most of what we pour out in this age is either pleasant, or we produce things that are grave and tinged with no charm.

units.la: Pagina DALLÆI quovis sub judice punctum Omne tulit, lepidum seu grave quæris opus;
units.tr: Before any judge, the page of Dallæus has carried every point, whether you seek a witty work or a serious one.

units.la: Hic lepor occurrit, qualem decet esse virorum, Qualis & Angelico fulget in ore lepor:
units.tr: Here wit meets us, such as befits men, such as also shines on angelic lips.

units.la: Hic gravitas lato incedit perfusa sereno, Cœlesti gravitas convenit illa choro.
units.tr: Here gravity advances, bathed in a broad serenity; that gravity suits the heavenly choir.

units.la: Triste supercilium procul hinc, procul omnis & horror, Barbariesque ipso pœnè superba situ:
units.tr: Far from here is the gloomy frown, far is every harshness, and the barbarism that is almost proud of its own rough style.

units.la: Mollities tamen omnis abest, & luxus inermis
units.tr: Yet all softness is absent, and so is a feeble luxury

units.la: Frangens in teneros languida verba sonos.
units.tr: breaking its languid words into tender sounds.

units.la: Quicquid habet docti schola, quicquid Roma decôri,
units.tr: Whatever the school of the learned has, whatever Rome has of grace,

units.la: Hoc Pietas uno junxit utrumque libro:
units.tr: Piety has joined both together in this one book:

units.la: Pulveris at Schola quicquid habet, vel Roma veneni,
units.tr: But whatever the school has of dust, or Rome of poison,

units.la: Hoc Bona mens toto pellit utrumque libro.
units.tr: A good mind drives out of both by this whole book.

units.la: Cerne vices rerum! fidei quondam inclyta famâ Roma fuit, quæ nunc destruit ecce fidem:
units.tr: Behold the changes of things! Rome was once famed for its renowned faith, and behold, now it destroys faith:

units.la: Nec non & pariter quo Roma vetusta superbit Eloquio liber hic destruit ecce novam.
units.tr: And likewise, by the same eloquence in which ancient Rome takes its pride, this book behold destroys a new one.

units.la: LIB. I.
units.tr: BOOK I.

units.la: Quo demonstratur ex rebus ipsis libros 8. Constitutionum Apostolicarum apocryphos esse, & Apostolis falso & impudenter suppositos.
units.tr: Showing from the things themselves that the eight books of the Apostolic Constitutions are apocryphal and were falsely and shamelessly ascribed to the Apostles.

units.la: CAP. I. Latinorum, & recentium (ut Bellarmini, Baronii, Perronii, Petavii &c.) & veterum, (ut Honorii Augustod. Humberti, Gelasii &c.) de Constitut. judicia, apocryphas esse consentientium. 1
units.tr: Chapter I. The judgments of Latin writers, both recent (such as Bellarmine, Baronius, Perron, Petavius, etc.) and ancient (such as Honorius of Autun, Humbert, Gelasius, etc.), agreeing that the Constitutions are apocryphal. 1

units.la: Cap. II. Æthiopum de Constit. error, eas divinis libris æquiparantium. Græcorum de iisdem judicia. Memoratas ab Epiphanio Constit. neque nostras esse, neque ab Apostolis conditas. 22
units.tr: Chapter II. The error of the Ethiopians about the Constitutions, who put them on a level with the divine books. The judgments of the Greeks on the same. The Constitutions mentioned by Epiphanius are neither ours nor composed by the Apostles. 22

units.la: Cap. III. Falli Bovium, qui Constit. Cyrillo Hierosol. cognitas fuisse putat. Cyrillum, quæ de phœnice tradit, ea ex Clementis ad Corinthios epistola habere, non autem ex Constitutionibus. 50
units.tr: Chapter III. Bovius is mistaken in thinking that the Constitutions were known to Cyril of Jerusalem. Cyril, in what he says about the phoenix, took it from the Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, and not from the Constitutions. 50

units.la: Cap. IV. Frustra pro Constit. afferri Eusebii & Athanasii testimonium. Demonstratur eorum loca nihil ad Constitutiones pertinere. Quid sit ἡ διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων. 56
units.tr: Chapter IV. The testimonies of Eusebius and Athanasius, cited in vain in support of the Constitutions, are shown to have nothing to do with them. What the "Teaching of the Apostles" [ἡ διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων] is. 56

units.la: Cap. V. Constitutionum antiquitas multis arg. evertitur. 1. arg. quod ea neque à Græca, neque à Latina Ecclesia vel olim, vel nuper, fuerint in divinorum librorum canonem relatæ, quod necesse erat fieri, si ea pro Apostolicis litteris essent agnita. Bovii temeritas arguitur. 76
units.tr: Chapter V. The antiquity of the Constitutions is overturned by many arguments. First argument: they were never placed in the canon of divine books, either by the Greek or by the Latin Church, either formerly or recently, which would have had to happen if they had been recognised as Apostolic writings. The rashness of Bovius is exposed. 76

units.la: Cap. VI. Arg. 2. quod Constitutionum sermo, qua à vocibus, qua à vocum συνπάξει ab Apostolico
units.tr: Chapter VI. Second argument: the language of the Constitutions, both in its words and in the combination of its words, is far removed from the Apostolic manner, and contains much that is foreign to the Apostles. 87

units.la: lico charaƫere abhorreat, multaque contineat ab Apostolis aliena. 87
units.tr: Chapter VII. Third argument: they are out of harmony with the Apostolic truth, since the Constitutions keep speculating about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. The quibbling of Bovius is refuted. 97

units.la: Cap. VII. Arg. 3. quod ab Apostolica veri- tate aliena sint, quæ Constitutiones de Dei Filio, deque. Sp. S. identidem philosophantur. Bovii ca- villatio refellitur. 97
units.tr: Chapter VIII. Fourth argument: not a few things in the Constitutions are foreign to the Apostolic doctrine, such as those about marriage and about a master's fornication with a female servant. The rather dishonourable defence of Bovius is refuted. 106

units.la: Cap. VIII. Arg. 4. ab aliis non paucis, quæ Constit. habent ab Apostolico dogmate aliena, ut de conjugio, de heri cum ancilla fornicatione. Re- futatur parum honesta Bovii defensio. 106
units.tr: Chapter IX. Fifth argument: the Constitutions deny that those are truly ministers who labour under ignorance or wickedness. The empty defence of Bovius. Sixth argument: the same decree that baptism conferred by a heretic is void. 110

units.la: Cap. IX. Arg. 5. Negant Constitut. vere mi- nistros esse, qui inscitia, vel improbitate laborant. Inanis Bovii defensio. arg. 6. Eadem baptismum ab hæretico collatum irritum decernunt. 110
units.tr: Chapter X. Seventh argument: the Constitutions add to the rite of baptism certain things unknown to the Apostles. Eighth argument: they give the Eucharist to infants. Ninth argument: concerning ministers, they teach some things differently and some contrary to what the Apostles taught. 117

units.la: Cap. X. Arg. 7. Constit. baptismi ritui ad- dunt quædam Apostolis ignota. arg. 8. Euchari- stiam infantibus communicant. Arg. 9. De mini- stris quædam aliter, quædam contra quam Apost. docent. 117
units.tr: Chapter XI. Tenth argument: the Constitutions command all the faithful to pay tithes. Eleventh argument: they lay down a strange law of sacred celibacy. Twelfth argument: they establish new feasts and fasts, which arose after the Apostolic age. 133

units.la: Cap. XI. Arg. 10. Constit. Decimarum so- lutionem fidelibus omnibus præcipiunt. arg. 11. le- gem sacri cœlibatus miram statuant. arg. 12. fe- sta & jejunia nova & infra Apostolicos orta, sta- tuunt. 133
units.tr: Chapter XII. Thirteenth argument: the Constitutions condemn tax collectors outright, etc. Fourteenth argument: they philosophise wrongly about the law of sacrifices once given by God, and falsely attribute certain things to Moses. 143

units.la: Cap. XII. Arg. 13. Constit. publicanos sim- pliciter damnant &c. arg. 14. de sacrificiorum le- ge olim à Deo lata male philosophantur, & quæ- dam Moysi falso assingunt. 143
units.tr: Chapter XIII. Fifteenth argument: the discipline of the Constitutions, in the administration of baptism, the Eucharist and repentance, in the age of the bishop, and in the building of churches, is foreign to the age of the Apostles. 152

units.la: Cap. XIII. Arg. 15. Quod Constitutionum disciplina in baptismi, & Eucharistiæ, & pœni- tentiæ administratione, in Episcopi ætate, & basi- licarum structura ab Apostolor. ævo aliena est. 152
units.tr: Chapter XIV. Sixteenth argument: the Constitutions put forward many things foreign to the truth of Apostolic history: for example, that Stephen lived when Paul was called to the apostleship, that James the son of Zebedee lived after his death, and that the other Apostles survived, although Clement was made bishop of Rome and sermons were delivered on the feasts with them. 163

units.la: Cap. XIV. Arg. 16. Constit. multa ponere ab historiæ Apostolicæ veritate aliena; ut Stepha- num vixisse Paulo in Apostolatum alleƫo, Jaco- bum Zebedæi post suam mortem vixisse, & cæteros Apostolos superfuisse, cum Clemens Romæ episcopus factus
units.tr: Chapter XIV. Argument 16. The Constitutions set down many things alien to the truth of apostolic history: for example, that Stephen lived before Paul was admitted to the apostolate, that James the son of Zebedee lived on after his death, and that the other apostles survived, when Clement was made bishop of Rome

units.la: factus est, & cum iis dicta sunt festa. 163
units.tr: was made bishop, and feasts are named along with them. 163

units.la: Cap. XV. Arg. 17. Constitutiones Ebionaeos, & alios haereticos post Apostol. mortem exortos. Apostolis coaevos; Clementem vero Petro vivo Romae sedisse Episcopum, & alia fabulantur. 171
units.tr: Chapter XV. Argument 17. The Constitutions claim that the Ebionites and other heretics, who arose after the death of the apostles, were contemporaries of the apostles, and that Clement was made bishop of Rome while Peter was still alive, and they invent other fables. 171

units.la: Cap. XVI. Arg. 18. Constitutiones Sibyllinos versus, post Apost. mortem factos, citant, & Romanos Principes Apostol. tempore Christianos fingunt. Refelluntur Bovii & Turriani cavillationes. 177
units.tr: Chapter XVI. Argument 18. The Constitutions cite Sibylline verses, which were written after the death of the apostles, and they pretend that Roman rulers were Christians in the apostles' time. The quibbles of Bovius and Turrianus are refuted. 177

units.la: Cap. XVII. Arg. 19. Constitutiones pnoeus ex libris N. T. citant, praeter Apost. morem apocrypha V. T. laudant; Israelis etymon absurdum ponunt; Philippum Apostolum, Ioannem non Apostolum mentiuntur; Mariam Lazari a Magdalena distinguunt; Moysem & alias scripturas falso citant. 186
units.tr: Chapter XVII. Argument 19. The Constitutions cite the Pseudo-Clementine... the Constitutions quote the books of the New Testament in a way that is contrary to apostolic custom; they cite apocryphal books of the Old Testament; they give an absurd etymology of "Israel"; they falsely make Philip an apostle and John a non-apostle; they distinguish Mary of Lazarus from Magdalene; and they cite Moses and other Scriptures falsely. 186

units.la: Cap. XVII. Refelluntur Bovii & Turriani ἀσ-φὰ Φαξμανκ, quibus frustra student Constitutiones absurdis liberare, quandam sermonis ideam comminiscentes, in qua vera falsaque, vetera & recentia permiscere, fabulari denique ac mentiri sine flagitio liceat. 204
units.tr: Chapter XVII. The "safe" [ἀσφὰ Φαξμανκ] devices of Bovius and Turrianus are refuted, by which they labour in vain to free the Constitutions from absurdities, inventing a certain notion of speech in which it is permitted to mix true with false, old with new, and in short to tell fables and lie without disgrace. 204

units.la: Cap. XIX. Contra Bov. & Turrian. probatur non esse Clem. R. Constitutionum scriptorem. 223
units.tr: Chapter XIX. Against Bovius and Turrianus it is proved that Clement of Rome is not the author of the Constitutions. 223

units.la: LIB. II.
units.tr: BOOK II.

units.la: Constitutiones refellit ex earum cum libris & dogmatis Ecclesiasticis comparatione,
units.tr: He refutes the Constitutions by comparing them with the books and the ecclesiastical doctrines.

units.la: CAp. I. Arg. 1. Constitutiones a nullo veterum, qui primis Christianismi saeculis floruerunt, memorari. arg. 2. Constitutiones ipsi Clementi, qui earum auctor fuisse fingitur, ignotas fuisse. 231
units.tr: Chapter I. Argument 1. That the Constitutions are not mentioned by any of the ancients who flourished in the first centuries of Christianity. Argument 2. That the Constitutions were unknown to Clement himself, whom they are pretended to have as their author. 231

units.la: Cap. II. Arg. 3. Constitutiones Justino a.D. 163, mortuo; arg. 4. Et Athenagorae ignotas fuisse. 244
units.tr: Chapter II. Argument 3. That the Constitutions were unknown to Justin, who died in A.D. 163. Argument 4. And to Athenagoras. 244

units.la: Cap. III. Arg. 5. Irenaeum a. D. 197. mortuum, Constitutiones nescivisse. Id fuse ex veris ejus libris prob.
units.tr: Chapter III. Argument 5. That Irenaeus, who died in A.D. 197, knew nothing of the Constitutions. This he proves at length from his genuine books.

units.la: CAPITUM
units.tr: CHAPTERS

units.la: Cap. IV. Arg. 6. ex apocrypha Barnabæ epistola ostenditur Constitutiones impostoris opus esse. 265
units.tr: Chapter IV. Arg. 6. From the apocryphal Epistle of Barnabas it is shown that the Constitutions are the work of an impostor. 265

units.la: Cap. V. Arg. 7. Constitutiones Clementi Alex. Arg. 8. & Tertulliano omnique ejus seculi Ecclesiæ plane penitusque ignotas fuisse : quod fuse ex Tertulliani veris demonstratur. 267
units.tr: Chapter V. Arg. 7. The Constitutions were wholly and utterly unknown to Clement of Alexandria (Arg. 8), to Tertullian, and to the whole Church of their age. This is shown at length from Tertullian's genuine works. 267

units.la: Cap. VI. Arg. 9. Constitutiones nondum extitisse Origenis temporib. (arg. 10) neque Cypriani, (arg. 11) neque Dionysii, (arg. 12) neque Petri Alexandrini. 298
units.tr: Chapter VI. Arg. 9. The Constitutions did not yet exist in the time of Origen (Arg. 10), nor of Cyprian (Arg. 11), nor of Dionysius (Arg. 12), nor of Peter of Alexandria. 298

units.la: Cap. VII. Arg. 13. Constitutiones ignotas fuisse Patribus Eliberitanis, & Nicænis; adeoque nondum quarto ineunte seculo extitisse. arg. 14. à decimis. arg. 15. ab Episcoporum judiciali tribunali. arg. 16. à Paschatis ritu apud Antioch. ante Synod. Nicænam. 316
units.tr: Chapter VII. Arg. 13. The Constitutions were unknown to the Fathers of Elvira and of Nicaea, and so had not yet come into existence at the beginning of the fourth century. Arg. 14. From the tithes. Arg. 15. From the judicial tribunal of the bishops. Arg. 16. From the rite of Easter at Antioch before the Nicene Synod. 316

units.la: Cap. VIII. Arg. 17. Et Arriani, & Catholici quarti seculi Constitutiones nesciverunt; & (arg. 18) Laodiceni Patres; & (arg. 19.) Basilius Cæsar. Arcudii stropha excutitur & solvitur. 322
units.tr: Chapter VIII. Arg. 17. Both the Arians and the Catholics of the fourth century did not know the Constitutions; and (Arg. 18) neither did the Laodicene Fathers; and (Arg. 19) Basil of Caesarea. Arcudius's trick is shaken off and solved. 322

units.la: Cap. IX. Arg. 20. Constitutiones Christianis quinti seculi ineuntis ignotos: quod probatur ex eo, quod sabbato (nisi uno) jejunari severissime vetant. 339
units.tr: Chapter IX. Arg. 20. The Constitutions were unknown to Christians at the beginning of the fifth century. This is proved from the fact that they strictly forbid fasting on the Sabbath (except one). 339

units.la: Cap. X. Arg. 21. Constitutiones vel nesciverunt, vel nihili fecerunt Hieronymus, Victor Ant. Augusti, Socrates, Nicephor. Berno, Chrysost. Cassian. Isidor. Raban.. omnis Latinorum Ecclesia; idque ex jejuniorum ratione certissime deprehenditur. 343
units.tr: Chapter X. Arg. 21. The Constitutions were either unknown or disregarded by Jerome, Victor of Antioch, Socrates, Nicephorus, Berno, Chrysostom, Cassian, Isidore, Rabanus, and the whole Latin Church. This is most certainly detected from the rationale of the fasts. 343

units.la: Cap, XI. Arg. 22. Idem probatur ex ea festorum ratione, quam ponunt Constitutiones 352
units.tr: Chapter XI. Arg. 22. The same is proved from the rationale of the festivals which the Constitutions set out. 352

units.la: Cap. XII. Arg. 23. Constitutiones in omni Græca, Latinaque Ecclesia spretæ; quod probatur ex baptismo à laicis administrato. (arg. 24.) ex episcopatus à presbyterio discrimine (arg. 25) ex mediatione Pastorum: ex Judæ communione; ex Magdalenæ à Maria Laz. diversitate. 357
units.tr: Chapter XII. Arg. 23. The Constitutions were rejected in the whole Greek and Latin Church. This is proved from baptism administered by laymen; (Arg. 24) from the difference between bishop and presbytery; (Arg. 25) from the mediation of the ministers; from Judas's communion; and from the difference between Magdalene and Mary of Lazarus. 357

units.la: Cap. XIII. Arg 26. Constitutiones vel ignotæ, vel spreta Gregorio Romano, & Augustino Angl. Apost. & Beda, & pæne omnibus Liturgicorum interpretibus, etiam infimorum temporum. 366
units.tr: Chapter XIII. Arg. 26. The Constitutions were either unknown or disregarded by Gregory of Rome, Augustine the Apostle of the English, Bede, and almost all interpreters of the liturgies, even those of the lowest times. 366

units.la: Cap. XIV. Arg. 27. Constitut. Valafrido Straboni ignota: imo & toti (arg. 28) Latinorum Ecclesia, qua duo earum de Exorcistarum, & inferiorum ministrorum ordinatione decreta jampridem constanter negligit. 373
units.tr: Chapter XIV. Arg. 27. The Constitutions were unknown to Walafrid Strabo; indeed, also to the whole Latin Church (Arg. 28), which for a long time has consistently neglected the two decrees of them concerning the ordination of exorcists and of the lower ministers. 373

units.la: Cap. XV. Refellitur frivola, putidaque Trullanorum Patrum, & multorum recentium exceptio, Constitution. hæreticorum dolo & manu vitiatas fuisse causificantium. 376
units.tr: Chapter XV. The frivolous and foul excuse of the Trullan Fathers, and of many recent writers, is refuted: that the Constitutions were corrupted by the trickery and hand of heretics, as those who argue the case maintain. 376

units.la: Cap. XVI. Excutitur ac confutatur inanis atque absurda Albaspinæi de Constitutionibus conjectura, sive potius deliratio. 316
units.tr: Chapter XVI. The empty and absurd conjecture, or rather delirium, of Albaspinaeus concerning the Constitutions is examined and refuted. 316

units.la: Cap. XVII. De vero Constitutionum & auctore & tempore, parum liquere. Nihil cogere, ut ante Syn. Nic. multa suadere, ut diu post eam editas, publicatasque putemus. Conclusio disputationis. 392
units.tr: Chapter XVII. Little is clear about the true author and time of the Constitutions. Nothing compels us to think they were published before the Nicene Synod, while much suggests that they were published and made public long after it. Conclusion of the disputation. 392

units.la: LIB. III.
units.tr: BOOK III.

units.la: De Canonibus Apostolicis, tum 85. Græc. tum 9. Turriani Antiochenis.
units.tr: On the Apostolic Canons: the 85 Greek canons and the 9 Antiochene canons of Turrianus.

units.la: CAP. I. De Canonibus, qui dicuntur Apostolici, seorsum disputandum esse. Diversa de iis Latinorum recentiorum judicia; Bellarm. 50. tantum admittentis, Baronii præter hos, 33. alios probantis; Turriani omnes 85. cum Græcis schismaticis defendentis.
units.tr: CHAP. I. That the canons called Apostolic must be discussed separately. The differing judgments of recent Latin writers on them: Bellarmine admits only the first 50; Baronius, apart from these, approves 33 others; Turrianus defends all 85 together with the Greek schismatics.

units.la: Cap. II. Græcorum de Canonibus sententia in Trullana Synodo promulgata, omnes 85. can. vere Apostolicos esse. Latinos veteres ab a. D. 520. plerosque admisisse quidem 50. priores canones, sic tamen tamen ut eos non plane haberent pro authenti-cis.
units.tr: Chap. II. The view of the Greeks on the canons, promulgated in the Trullan Synod, that all 85 canons are truly Apostolic. The older Latins, from the year 520 A.D., mostly admitted the first 50 canons, yet in such a way that they did not hold them to be fully authentic.

units.la: Cap. III. Celasium E. R. cum Romana Synodo a. D. 494. omnes omnino Apostolor. canones apocryphos censuisse. Isidor. Hisp. a. D. 620. idem senssisse. Bell. Baronii, & Turriani diversa ad Gelasii decretum glossa fuse refelluntur. 436
units.tr: Chap. III. That Gelasius, Bishop of Rome, with the Roman Synod in the year 494 A.D., judged all the canons of the Apostles to be altogether apocryphal. That Isidore of Spain in the year 620 A.D. thought the same. The contrary glosses of Bellarmine, Baronius and Turrianus on the decree of Gelasius are refuted at length. 436

units.la: Cap. IV. Solvuntur, qua Turrianus Gelasiana sententia objicit, quibusque probare frustra nititur ipsum Gelasium Canones pro vere Apostolicis agnovisse. 471
units.tr: Chap. IV. The objections Turrianus raises against the opinion of Gelasius are answered, and the arguments by which he vainly strives to prove that Gelasius himself acknowledged the canons as truly Apostolic. 471

units.la: Cap.V. Solvuntur, qua pro 50. Canon. Apostolicis contra Gelasii decretum ex Tertulliano, Athanasio, & Damasceno attulit Bellarminus. 483
units.tr: Chap. V. The arguments Bellarmine brought from Tertullian, Athanasius and John of Damascus for the 50 Apostolic canons against the decree of Gelasius are answered. 483

units.la: Cap. VI. Solvuntur, qua pro Canon. ex Paulo contra decretum Gel. attulit Turrianus. 489
units.tr: Chap. VI. The arguments from Paul that Turrianus brought for the canons against the decree of Gelasius are answered. 489

units.la: Cap. VII. Defenditur Gelasii decretum contra alias Turriani ex Patribus objectiones. Ac primo rejiciuntur, qua ille ex apocryphis adduxit; ut ex Anacleti, Alexandri, Iulii, &c. urbis Episcoporum stramineis epistolis; item ex Nican. Canon. Arabicis, ex fictitia Hieronymi ad Damas. epistola, & ex Pseudo-Dionysio Areop. 492
units.tr: Chap. VII. The decree of Gelasius is defended against the other objections of Turrianus drawn from the Fathers. First, those he drew from apocryphal writings are rejected: from the straw-stuffed letters of the bishops of the city, Anacletus, Alexander, Julius, etc.; likewise from the Nicene canons in Arabic, from the spurious letter of Jerome to Damasus, and from the pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. 492

units.la: Cap. VIII. Quam stulta & absurda sit omnis Turriani ex veteribus hac in causa disputatio. Expenduntur ac refelluntur sigillatim, qua ille ex Orig. & Cypr. & ex Synodis Nic. Ant. & Gangr. attulit; & ostenditur quis sit locorum sensus. 499
units.tr: Chap. VIII. How foolish and absurd is all of Turrianus' argument from the ancients in this matter. The passages he drew from Origen, Cyprian, and the Synods of Nicaea, Antioch and Gangra are weighed and refuted one by one, and the sense of the passages is shown. 499

units.la: Cap. IX. Diluuntur, qua Turr. ex Africanis Synodis; item ex Athan. Basil. & Epiphan. pro suis Can. stulte & inverecunde obtrudit. 519
units.tr: Chap. IX. The arguments Turrianus foolishly and shamelessly forces from the African Synods, and likewise from Athanasius, Basil and Epiphanius, in support of his canons, are dissolved. 519

units.la: Cap. X. Expenduntur, qua non minori impudentia ex quinto saeculo Innoc. 1. item ex Ephes. & Chalcedon. Synodis, adhac ex Cyrillo & Leone Turrianus objicit. 526
units.tr: Chap. X. Those arguments are examined which Turrianus raises with no less impudence from the fifth century, from Innocent I, and likewise from the Synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and further from Cyril and Leo. 526

units.la: Cap. XI. Asseritur & constituitur Gelasii de Can. decretum. Disputationis partes 3. Pars 1. qua ostenditur
units.tr: Chap. XI. The decree of Gelasius on the canons is asserted and established. The disputation has three parts. Part 1 shows

units.la: estenditur 35. Canones ex 85. postremos non esse Apostolicos. 1. arg. ex omnium (uno dempto Turriano) Latinorum testimonio dudum. 549
units.tr: It is shown 35. canons of the 85 last ones are not Apostolic. 1. argument from the testimony of all the Latins (Turrianus alone excepted) from of old. 549

units.la: Cap. XII. Arg. 2. ex 1. can. dudum. arg. 3. 4. & 5. ex canonibus 9. 12. & 15. qui explicantur, & à Turriani cavillationibus vindicantur. 555
units.tr: Chap. XII. Argument 2 from the 1st canon of old. Arguments 3, 4 and 5 from canons 9, 12 and 15, which are explained and vindicated from the cavils of Turrianus. 555

units.la: Cap. XIII. Arg. 6. ex iis, quæ de quadragesima, & aliis jejuniis decernit c. 18. Turriani objecta & glossa refelluntur, aperiturque insignis ejus de Psychicis Tertull. hallucinatio. arg. 7. 8. 9. 10. ex C. 21. 22. 30. 34. Immanis c. 34. absurditas: & par Turriani in eo defendendo impudentia. Concluditur. 1. pars disputationis contra 35. Can. postremos. 575
units.tr: Chap. XIII. Argument 6 from those things which canon 18 decrees about Lent and other fasts. Turrianus' objections and gloss are refuted, and his notable error about the "psychici" in Tertullian is laid open. Arguments 7, 8, 9 and 10 from canons 21, 22, 30 and 34. The monstrous absurdity of canon 34, and Turrianus' shamelessness in defending it. The first part of the disputation against the last 35 canons is concluded. 575

units.la: Cap. XIV. Altera pars disputationis contra 50. priores Canon. Demonstratur eos quoque falsos, atque apocryphos esse. Arg. 1. ex Isidori Hisp. & aliorum Latinorum veterum, nominatim Hincmari, testimonio. Arg. 2. ex. c. 1. de Episcopis. Arg. 3. ex C. 4. Arg. 4. ex C. 3. de incenso. 594
units.tr: Chap. XIV. The second part of the disputation against the first 50 canons. It is shown that these too are false and apocryphal. Argument 1 from the testimony of Isidore of Spain and other older Latins, especially Hincmar. Argument 2 from canon 1, on bishops. Argument 3 from canon 4. Argument 4 from canon 3, on incense. 594

units.la: Cap. XV. Arg. 5. ex C. 7. de non celebrando cum Judæis paschate. arg. 6. ex c. 8. de clericis, & ex 9. (arg. 7.) de fidelibus post oblationem non communicantibus. Refelluntur Bellarmini & Binii cavillationes. 601
units.tr: Chap. XV. Argument 5 from canon 7, on not celebrating Passover with the Jews. Argument 6 from canon 8, on clerics, and from canon 9 (argument 7), on the faithful who do not communicate after the oblation. The cavils of Bellarmine and Binius are refuted. 601

units.la: Cap. XVI. Arg. 8. ex can. 16. de clerico concubinario. Refelluntur Turriani ineptiæ. 612
units.tr: Chap. XVI. Argument 8 from canon 16, on the clergyman who keeps a concubine. The silly arguments of Turrianus are refuted. 612

units.la: Cap. XVII. Arg. 9. ex can. 21. 22. 23. de iis, qui se ipsos abscindunt. arg. 10. ex c. 26. 29. de iis, qui Ecclesiæ dignitates potestatis sæcularis favore invadunt. arg. 11. ex c. 33. de Metropolitanis. arg. 12. ex c. 49. de trina in baptismo mersione. adversar. cavillationes refutantur. 617
units.tr: Chap. XVII. Argument 9 from canons 21, 22 and 23, on those who mutilate themselves. Argument 10 from canons 26 and 29, on those who seize church dignities by the favour of the secular power. Argument 11 from canon 33, on metropolitans. Argument 12 from canon 49, on threefold immersion in baptism. The objections of the opponents are refuted. 617

units.la: Cap. XVIII. 3. pars disputationis qua communibus in utramque partem argumentis evertitur tota Can. Apostolicorum 85. Syllogę, arg. 1. ex ipsius sermonis, quo scripti sunt Canones, idea, ab Apostolorum oratione aliena. arg. 2. ab Episcopi & presbyteri diversitate Apostolis ignota. Arg. 3. à reprobato collato ab hæreticis baptismo. Profligantur Binii vitilitigationes. 632
units.tr: Chap. XVIII. The third part of the disputation, in which the whole of the 85 Apostolic canons is overturned by arguments common to both sides, a syllogism. Argument 1 from the very style in which the canons are written, alien to the speech of the Apostles. Argument 2 from the difference between bishop and presbyter, unknown to the Apostles. Argument 3 from baptism conferred by heretics, which is rejected. The trifling quarrels of Binius are demolished. 632

units.la: Cap. XIX. Arg. 4. inde ductum, quod Syllogae non fuerit à veteri Ecclesia in Apostolicarum scripturarum canonem relata. arg. 5. ex eo sumptum, quod non fuerunt isti Canones Ecclesiastico Canonum codici inserti à veteribus. Universalis Ecclesiæ codex vetus. 642 Cap. XX. Arg. 6. inde ductum, quod omnes isti Canones omnibus priorum quatuor saeculorum Christianis ignoti fuerint; ut ex eo apparet, quod à nullo istorum temporum scriptore memorati uspiam reperiantur. Concluditur tota contra hos can. disputatio. 658 Cap. XXI. Expenditur ac refellitur mustea Albaspinei de Canonibus hariolatio, somniantis eos diversis quidem temporibus conditos, sed sensim alios aliis adjectos, excrevisse tandem in eam, quam hodie habemus, syllogen. Eam videri quinto, sed adulto, saeculo factam. 667 Cap. XXII. Altera quaestio de aliis novem Canonibus, quos velut ab Apostolis in Antiocheno nescio quo Concilio factos obtrudit Turrianus, & ex eo Baron. & Binius. Totam horum Can. molem una Turriani fide niti, qua quam sublesta sit, ostenditur. 687 Cap. XXIII. Probatur istos 9. can. falsos esse & apocryphos, 1. ex eo ipso Pamphilo Martyre, qui eorum testis à Turr. laudatur, librum quem scripsisse fingitur, contra di fertum Eusebii testimonium negantis eum quicquam scripsisse. 2. ex Eusebii de iis silentio. 3. ex eo, quod clarissime deprehenditur, eos & Origeni, in cujus tamen bibliotheca fuisse fingun-tur, plane ignotos fuisse. 4. ex eo quod Synodus illa Apostolo-
units.tr: Chapter XIX. Argument 4: drawn from the fact that the Syllogē was not received by the ancient Church into the canon of the apostolic Scriptures. Argument 5: taken from the fact that these Canons were not inserted by the ancients into the ecclesiastical code of Canons. The old code of the universal Church. 642 Chapter XX. Argument 6: drawn from the fact that all these Canons were unknown to all Christians of the first four centuries, as appears from the fact that no writer of those times is found to mention them anywhere. The whole disputation against these canons is concluded. 658 Chapter XXI. The idle conjecture of Albaspinaeus about the Canons is examined and refuted. He dreams that they were indeed composed at different times, but that others were gradually added to them by others, until they grew at last into the Syllogē we have today. This seems to have been made in the fifth, though already mature, century. 667 Chapter XXII. The second question concerns the other nine Canons, which Turrian thrusts forward as if they were made by the Apostles at some council at Antioch, I know not which, and which Baronius and Binius follow him in. It is shown that the whole mass of these canons rests on Turrian's word alone, and how shaky that word is. 687 Chapter XXIII. It is proved that these nine canons are false and apocryphal: 1. from Pamphilus the Martyr himself, who is cited by Turrian as their witness, and whom they pretend wrote the book, although Eusebius' testimony denies that he wrote anything at all. 2. from Eusebius' silence about them. 3. from the fact that it is most clearly evident that they were entirely unknown even to Origen, in whose library they are pretended to have been. 4. from the fact that that synod of the Apostles-

units.la: INDEX.
units.tr: INDEX.

units.la: Apostolorum Antiochena in omni retro Ecclesia inaudita & incognita fuit. Insignis Hincmari locus. Objectus pro ea Synodo ex Innocent. ep. 18. à Baronio locus, mendosus. Emendatur & explicatur. Gregorii Pisinuntensis pro eadem testimonium, velut merito suspectum, rejicitur. Pessima Patrum Synodi 7. fides notatur. 695
units.tr: The Antiochene Canons of the Apostles were unheard of and unknown in the whole Church in all earlier times. A notable passage of Hincmar. A passage from Innocent's letter 18, cited by Baronius in defence of that Synod, is faulty. It is corrected and explained. The testimony of Gregory of Pisinum for the same, as deservedly suspect, is rejected. The very bad faith of the Fathers of the Seventh Synod is noted. 695

units.la: Cap. XXIV. Expenduntur ipsi Canones a Turr. editi. C. 1. notata in lectione diversitas, ejusque, quod ibi decernitur, absurditas. C. 2. ineptia, circumcisionem superflue vetantis. C. 9. prodigiosa ineptia, immanisque in scriptura depraedicanda impudentia. c. itidem 3. ineptum & ridicule Apostolis affictum esse. 712
units.tr: Chapter XXIV. The canons themselves, as published by Turrianus, are weighed. Chapter 1: the variation in the reading is noted, and the absurdity of what is decreed there. Chapter 2: the foolishness of forbidding circumcision needlessly. Chapter 9: a monstrous foolishness, and a vast impudence in praising Scripture. Likewise chapter 3: that it has been foolishly and ridiculously fastened upon the Apostles. 712

units.la: Cap. XXV. Ostenditur, quam falsus, vanusque sit octavus canon. 1. ex triplici lectionis diversitate. 2. ex vere Apostolica doctrina. 3. ex vetustissimorum Patrum fide, & dogmate. 4. ex ipsius Synodi 7. totiusque Graeca Ecclesiae de imaginibus sententia, & praxi. Binii in voce στήλη fraus detegitur; cujus etymon, verusque ex eo sensus explicatur, & asseritur. Tota de Apostolicis pseudepigraphis disputatio concluditur. 722
units.tr: Chapter XXV. It is shown how false and empty the eighth canon is. (1) From a threefold variation in the reading. (2) From true Apostolic doctrine. (3) From the faith and teaching of the most ancient Fathers. (4) From the view and practice of the Seventh Synod itself and of the whole Greek Church concerning images. The fraud of Binius in the word stele [στήλη] is exposed; its etymology and true sense are explained and maintained. The whole discussion of the Apostolic pseudepigrapha is concluded. 722

units.la: JOANNIS DALLÆI DE PSEUDEPIGRAPHIS APOSTOLICIS LIBER I. CAP. I.
units.tr: John Daillé, On the Apostolic Pseudepigrapha, Book I, Chapter I

units.la: Latinorum, & recentium, ut Bellarmini, Baronii, Perronii, Petavii, &c. Et veterum, ut Honorii, Humberti, Gelasii &c. de Constitutionibus judicia, opus adulterinum & apocryphum esse consentientium.
units.tr: Latin writers and recent ones, such as Bellarmine, Baronius, Perron, Petavius, and others, and ancient ones, such as Honorius, Humbert, Gelasius, and others, agree in judging the Constitutions to be a spurious and apocryphal work.

units.la: CONSTITUTIONES Apostolorum octo libris comprehensas è Græco in Latinum sermonem transtulit Carolus Bovius Episcopus Ostunensis, & anno 1563. edidit. Eandem Iesuita nobilis, Franciscus Turrianus, homo apocryphorum avidissimus, Latinè quoque est interpretatus. Habetur opus & seorsim sæpius, & una cum Conciliis à Surio & Binio in primis Conciliorum editionibus, & una cum canonicis Zonaræ commentariis conjunctim Græcè Latinéq; publicatum. De eo opere quid senserint veteres ac recentiores Christianorum Theologi, ac utrum Clementis, cujus nomen præfert, vere sit, operæ pretium est investigare.
units.tr: Charles Bovius, bishop of Ostuni, translated the Constitutions of the Apostles, comprised in eight books, from Greek into Latin and published it in 1563. Francis Turrianus, a noble Jesuit and a man most eager for apocrypha, also translated it into Latin. The work is found both on its own, often, and together with the Councils, as published in Greek and Latin by Surius and Binius in the first editions of the Councils, and jointly with the canonical commentaries of Zonaras. It is worth investigating what the ancient and more recent Christian theologians have thought of this work, and whether it truly is Clement's, whose name it bears.

units.la: Ac nostri quidem ad unum omnes spu‑rium ac adulterinum esse fœtum conten‑dunt ; multis post Clementis Romani dor‑mitionem annis natum,idque haud segniter validis argumentis probant. Ex adversariis pauci, quos Romanæ adversum nos caussæ studium egit præcipites, reclamant ; ut Bo‑vius, Turrianus, Stapletonus, qui eo usque progressus est , ut librum hunc scripserit a Spiritu Apostolico plenissimum esse;& alibi definierit b,nullam rationem obstare,quin si præsens Ecclesia referret has Constitutiones Apostolicas, à Clemente editas , in canonem Sacræ Scripturæ ; nos eas pro canonicis admittere debeamus æque atque epistolam Iacobi.Paria de iis jactant minutiores quoque non pauci earundem partium Scriptores. Quorum vero nunc præcipua fertur ex adversariorum Theologis eruditio,ac fama, ii fere omnes in nostrorum sententiam pedibus eunt.
units.tr: Our own writers almost all contend that it is a spurious and adulterated offspring, born many years after the death of Clement of Rome, and they prove this not feebly, with strong arguments. Among our opponents, a few, whom zeal for the Roman cause has driven headlong, cry out against this, such as Bovius, Turrianus, and Stapleton, who went so far as to write that this book is full of the Apostolic Spirit; and elsewhere he declared that there is no reason why, if the present Church were to receive these Apostolic Constitutions, published by Clement, into the canon of Holy Scripture, we should not admit them as canonical just as we admit the Epistle of James. Not a few of the lesser writers of the same party boast similar things about them. But those whose learning and reputation are chiefly reported among the opponents' theologians almost all come over on foot to our view.

units.la: Bellarminus c quidem cum dixisset, se probabile existimare, non esse Clementis, quæ ejus nomine circumferuntur, Recogni‑tiones, easque idem opus esse cum eo, quod Itinerarium , vel Circuitus Petri dicitur , quodque apocryphum esse constat; cum illa inquam, dixisset, continenter hæc subjicit: De libris Constitutionum Apostolicarum, quæ Clementi authori tribuuntur , idem fere judicium dicium fieri debet, ac de libris Recognitionum. Ergo & has perinde ac Recognitiones apocryphas esse vult, Clementisque nomen mentiri. Tum ait, eas in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen habere, ipsosque etiam posteriores Graecos in Concilio Trullano can.2. improbare has Constitutiones, ut ab haereticis depravatas. Denique notat plura, quae in iis libris occurrunt, peccata, quaeque satis arguunt, quam falsum id sit, quod titulus praefert, haec vel ab Apostolis tradita, vel a Clemente Romano, studiosissimo ac fidelissimo eorum discipulo, conscripta.
units.tr: Bellarmine indeed, having said that he considers it probable that the Recognitions attributed to Clement are not Clement's, and that they are the same work as the one called the Itinerary or Circuits of Peter, which is known to be apocryphal, then immediately continues with these words: Concerning the books of the Apostolic Constitutions, which are attributed to Clement as author, almost the same judgment must be made as concerning the books of the Recognitions. So he wants these too to be apocryphal, just like the Recognitions, and the name of Clement to be falsely claimed. Then he says that in the Latin Church they have almost no reputation at all, and that even the later Greeks themselves, in the Council in Trullo, canon 2, disapprove these Constitutions as corrupted by heretics. Finally he notes many errors which occur in those books, and which sufficiently show how false it is that the title declares them to have been either handed down by the Apostles or written by Clement of Rome, their most zealous and faithful disciple.

units.la: Baronii quin eadem fuerit de his Constitutionibus sententia, dubitandum non videtur. Cum enim quaedam ex hoc volumine sibi ipsi de Mariae Magdalenae a Maria Lazari sorore diversitate objecisset, Sed uno verbo (inquit a) his liberari possemus, si apocryphu esse librum exciperemus. Sane quidem si haec dicta sunt a Clemente, quomodo ea latere potuerunt tot antiquos Patres, qui de ea re scripserunt? cum praesertim tanti authoris praecipua fuerit authoritas in Ecclesia: adeo ut licet ejus epistola ad Corinthios scripta penitus exciderit; tamen quod saepius citata reperiatur, bene revivisccat integra in fragmentis. Haec ille; clarissime ex eo, quod veteribus ignotus fuerit Constitutionum liber, conficiens falsum, & ab homine Clementis
units.tr: There seems to be no doubt that Baronius held the same opinion about these Constitutions. For when he had objected to himself certain things from this volume about the difference between Mary Magdalene and Mary the sister of Lazarus, he says (a): But we could be freed from these by a single word, if we excepted that the book is apocryphal. Indeed, if these things were said by Clement, how could they have escaped so many ancient Fathers who wrote about that matter, especially since the chief authority of so great an author was in the Church, so much so that although his letter to the Corinthians has utterly perished, yet, because it is found cited quite often, it revives well intact in fragments. Thus he, concluding most clearly from the fact that the book of the Constitutions was unknown to the ancients that it is false, and was forged by a man of a later age than Clement's.

units.la: a Tom.1. ann. Dom.32. §.18. mentis ævo recentiore confictum esse. Mox illud a de apocryphi exceptione, quo sibi uti licuisse dixerat confugium honestum vocat. Sed & in alia operis ejus parte Clementis constitutiones memorans, eas Clementis nomine ita indigetat, ut & Apocryphas esse obiter moneat; Putarunt aliqui (inquit b) eandem sententiam ex ejusdem Clementis Constitutionibus, sed apocryphis roborari. Idem alibi Athanasio, & Epiphanio, aliisque veteribus visas fatetur; sed inter apocrypha ab omnibus adnumeratas. Tum, Sicut aliqua (inquit c) quæ in eis sunt, hæretici sunt perperam interpretati; ita etiam ab iisdem multa fuisse corrupta, canon nomine sexta Synodi testari videtur. Aliqua insuper in eas ex Græcorum fontibus effluxisse, mihi facile persuadeo. Hæc ille; & librum per se apocryphum esse, adhæc ab hæreticis & schismaticis corruptum, atque adulteratum difertissime censens.
units.tr: Soon after, he calls that exception, that it is apocryphal, which he had said he was allowed to use, an honorable refuge. But also in another part of his work, mentioning Clement's Constitutions, he designates them by Clement's name in such a way that he also remarks in passing that they are apocryphal: Some (he says) have thought that the same opinion is confirmed by the Constitutions of that same Clement, but apocryphal ones. He admits elsewhere that these seemed so to Athanasius, Epiphanius, and other ancients, but reckoned among the apocrypha by all. Then: As some things in them (he says) heretics have wrongly interpreted, so also many things were corrupted by the same heretics, as the canon under the name of the Sixth Synod seems to testify. I can easily be persuaded that some things also flowed into them from Greek sources. Thus he, judging most plainly that the book is apocryphal in itself, and moreover that it was corrupted and adulterated by heretics and schismatics.

units.la: Margarinus de la Bigne, qui Bibliothecam Patrum edidit, idem Constitutionum opus in apocryphorum censum liquido refert, dum hanc ex iis desumptam apud Anastasium Nicænum sententiam d, Episcopus ignorantia, aut mala mente oppressus, non est amplius Episcopus, hac in margine appositā annotatione, velut obelo confodit; Caute lege ita ex apocrypho libro accepta. Nam Episcopus malus, aut imperitus, verus Episcopus est.
units.tr: Margarin de la Bigne, who edited the Bibliotheca Patrum, also plainly lists the same work of Constitutions among the apocrypha, when he pierces, as with an obelus, this opinion taken from them in Anastasius of Nicaea, a bishop oppressed by ignorance or an evil mind is no longer a bishop, with this annotation placed in the margin: Read this cautiously, as things taken from an apocryphal book. For a bad or unskilled bishop is a true bishop.

units.la: Iacobus Davius Perronius Cardinalis, cujus nomine nullum fere est apud adversarios illustrius, de his Constitutionibus ita loquitur in grandi de Eucharistia volumine a: Hoc opus (inquit) à multis gravibus authoribus veteris ac recentis memoriæ in dubium vocatur. Epiphanius * libri meminit id nomen præferentis, aitq; multos suo tempore eum in dubium revocare; se verò eum nequaquam rejicere. Synodus Constantinopoli in Trullo, multis post Epiphanium temporibus sub Iustiniano Rhinotmeto habita, opus condemnat. Photius b vero Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, ipsa illa synodo recentior, vix Arianismo purgari posse ait; quod suspicari cogit librum hunc vel non eundem esse cum eo qui Epiphanii temporibus hoc nomine censebatur, vel certè ab Arianis postea corruptum, adulteratumque fuisse. Sanè multa apud veteres inde descripta reperiuntur, quæ cum iis, quæ nunc circumferuntur, exemplaribus non congruunt. Cardinalis Bessario c Marco Ephesio, quendam ex his Constitutionibus locum objectanti, respondet opus esse apocryphum. Hactenus Perronius. Idem in alio opere d; Quæ (inquit) Clementis nomine Apostolica Constitutiones circumferuntur, non sunt ejus fidei, ut ut in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus authoritatem habeant decisivam. Sive enim jam ab initio Clementis nomine suppositus, sive ab haereticis postea interpolatus, atque adulteratus fuerit hic liber, constat, suspectam esse ejus authoritatem. Memorat Epiphanius a librum istius nominis, quem ait suo tempore a multis in dubium vocari, a se nequaquam rejici. Synodus quidem Trullana, diu post Epiphanium Constantinopoli habita, eum damnat; & caetera omnino cum iis, quae nuper ex alio ejusdem Peronii opere descripsimus, eadem.
units.tr: James Davy Perron, the Cardinal, whose name is almost the most illustrious of all among the opponents, speaks of these Constitutions thus in his large volume on the Eucharist: This work (he says) has been called in doubt by many grave authors of both ancient and recent memory. Epiphanius mentions a book bearing that name and says that many in his time called it into doubt, but he himself by no means rejected it. The Synod of Constantinople in Trullo, held many years after Epiphanius under Justinian Rhinotmetus, condemns the work. But Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, even later than that synod, says it can hardly be purged of Arianism, which forces one to suspect that this book either is not the same as the one which in Epiphanius's time was counted under this name, or certainly was afterwards corrupted and adulterated by the Arians. Indeed, many things are found described from it among the ancients which do not agree with the copies that now circulate. Cardinal Bessarion, when Mark of Ephesus objected a certain passage from these Constitutions, replied that the work is apocryphal. Thus far Perron. The same author, in another work: The Apostolic Constitutions which circulate under Clement's name are not of such trustworthiness that they have decisive authority in matters pertaining to religion. For whether this book was from the beginning falsely ascribed to Clement, or later interpolated and adulterated by heretics, it is certain that its authority is suspect. Epiphanius mentions a book of that name, which he says in his time was called in doubt by many, but which he by no means rejects. The Trullan Synod, held at Constantinople long after Epiphanius, condemns it; and the rest is entirely the same as what we lately transcribed from another work of the same Perron.

units.la: Gabriel Albaspineus, Aurelianensis Episcopus, non tantum hos libros dubios atque apocryphos censet, sed & eos, qui aliter de iis sentiunt, imperitia palam arguit, Turrianum, & Bovium, & Stapletonum, ni fallor, tacite perstringens ac sugillans; Certe si quis esset (inquit b) qui canones Apostolorum, & Divi Clementis Constitutiones, Apostolorum authoritate sancitas publicataque certo affirmaret, imperitus censeretur. Nam qui antiquarum consuetudinum gnari, quo quidque tempore, aut loco observari desitum sit, aut mutari coeptum norunt, de iis ne dubitare quidem possunt. Et vero, quae mox dicam, ita clara sunt, ea ut revinci a nullo possint. Haec ille. Quae autem his se subjecturum profitetur, ea nos postea suo loco, ubi de re ipsa dicendum erit, affere-mus.
units.tr: Gabriel Albaspine, bishop of Orléans, judges not only these books doubtful and apocryphal, but also openly charges with ignorance those who think otherwise, tacitly striking at and sneering at Turrianus, Bovius, and Stapleton, unless I am mistaken: Certainly, if anyone were to affirm firmly that the Canons of the Apostles and the Constitutions of the divine Clement were sanctioned and published by the authority of the Apostles, he would be judged unskilled. For those who know the ancient customs, and at what time or place each practice ceased or began to be changed, cannot even doubt about these things. Indeed, what I shall say presently is so clear that it can be refuted by no one. Thus he. What he promises to add to these, we will set forth afterwards in its place, where the matter itself must be discussed.

units.la: Dionysius Petavius, quo nemo hodie vivit in ea, quam falso vocant, Iesu societate, eruditionis ac doctrinae nominibus clarior, ad locum Epiphanii, in quo is Constitutionum Apostolicarum meminit, deque iis jam tum a nonnullis dubitatum fuisse scribit, Eodem (inquit) nomine circumferuntur hodie in VIII libros distincta; qua a prioribus illis ac nihilominus dubiis, quarum meminit Epiphanius, diversa videntur. Etenim V. ex illis sententia hoc & sequenti numero citantur, quae in vulgatis nusquam reperiuntur; imo vero contraria quaedam in iis leguntur. Id vero exsecutus ita concludit; Apparet igitur, aliud fuisse Constitutionum genus, quam quibus hodie Clementis nomen inscribitur. Atque ex his liquet Petavium tantum ab eo abesse, ut eas, quas nunc habemus Constitutiones, vere vel Apostolorum, vel Clementis esse putet; ut ne eas quidem existimet easdem cum illis esse, quae Epiphanii temporibus hoc nomine circumferebantur, dubiae tamen ipsae incertaeque, ac eo ipso tempore controversae fidei. Idem alibi a, De Diaconissis (inquit) nugatur Pseudodiataxis Clementis L. II. c. XXVI. quaeque inde refert, ea γραώδη, id est anilia, vocat; & quidem merito,
units.tr: Dionysius Petavius, whom no one alive today in that so-called Society of Jesus surpasses in fame for learning and scholarship, in his note on the passage of Epiphanius where Epiphanius mentions the Constitutions of the Apostles, writes that even then some had doubts about them: They (he says) circulate today under the same name, divided into eight books; but they appear to differ from those earlier and nonetheless doubtful Constitutions which Epiphanius mentions. For in them, in his opinion, the fifth and the following numbers are cited, which are nowhere found in the printed texts; indeed, certain contrary things are read in them. Having pursued this, he concludes: It appears, therefore, that there was a different kind of Constitutions from those which today bear the name of Clement. From this it is clear that Petavius is so far from thinking that the Constitutions we now have are truly by the Apostles or by Clement, that he does not even think they are the same as those which were circulated under this name in the time of Epiphanius, themselves doubtful and uncertain, and disputed in that very age as to their faith. Elsewhere the same man says: Pseudodiataxis of Clement, Book II, chapter 26, trifles about deaconesses, and what he reports from it he calls γραώδη, that is, old-wives' tales; and rightly so,

units.la: a Ibid. ad expositionem fidei, p. 349. merito, ut mox suo loco demonstrabimus. Sed & postea in eodem opere, quod in istis Constitutionibus de Sabbato decernitur, id Petavius idem pronunciat (& quidem verè meritoque) nunquam ab Apostolis toti Ecclesiae fuisse praescriptum, approbare consensum sanctissimorum Patrum. Mox quod in iisdem Constitutionum libris habetur de sabbato feriando decretum refigens ac refutans Petavius, & ab Apostolis manasse (sane verissimè) negans, hoc opus non Διαταξεις, qui ei vulgo titulus praescribitur, sed Pseudodiataxes Apostolicas nominat . Sed idem in novissimo de Theologicis dogmatis opere, quid de Constitutionibus sentiat, alicubi clare quoque professus est, ubi post recitata Athenagorae, Tatiani, Theophili, Irenaei quaedam loca; Poterat (inquit ) ante omnes illos, quorum hactenus memini, vetustatis unus nomine commemorari (Clemens Romanus); siquidem germana essent, quae illius inscripta nomine circumferuntur. Sed non sunt. Hic igitur in Constitutionibus Apostolicis ridiculum nescio quid, & haereticum de Trinitate posuit. Id autem quid sit, postea suo loco explicabimus. Vides ut rotundè neget Clementis esse, quae ejus nomine habentur Constitutiones, caeteraque ejusdem & tituli & ingenii opera.
units.tr: a Ibid., on the exposition of the faith, p. 349. Rightly, as we shall show in its proper place shortly. But also later in the same work, where the Constitutions prescribe the keeping of the Sabbath, Petavius pronounces the same thing (and indeed truly and rightly): that it was never prescribed by the Apostles for the whole Church, and that the consensus of the most holy Fathers does not approve it. Next, when he refutes and rejects what is laid down in the same books of the Constitutions about the observance of the Sabbath as a day of rest, and denies that it came from the Apostles (certainly most truly), he calls this work not Διαταξεις, which is the title commonly prefixed to it, but Apostolic Pseudodiataxes. But in his last work on theological dogmas, he also clearly declared somewhere what he thinks of the Constitutions, where, after quoting some passages of Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus and Irenaeus, he says: Among all those whom I have so far mentioned, one of the most ancient could have been named (Clement of Rome), if what is circulated under his name were genuine. But it is not. Here, then, in the Apostolic Constitutions he has put something ridiculous and heretical about the Trinity. What that is, we shall explain later in its place. You see how flatly he denies that the Constitutions which bear Clement's name, and his other works both in title and in character, are his.

units.la: Atque haec quidem de recentioribus ad-versaversariorum Theologis satis sunt; quibus nihil est in istorum partibus, quod jure opponi aut exæquari possit. Nam sive eruditionem, sive dignitatem, aut famam, nominisque celebritatem spectes, quid nostra parentumque ætas apud Romanam communionem tulit cum Bellarmino, Baronio, la Bigne, Perronio, Albaspineo, & Petavio comparandum? Horum autem, ut liquet, concors est sententia, Constitutiones Apostolicas, Clementis nomine vulgatas, dubias, incertas, apocryphas, falsas, corruptas, adulteratas, nullius in religionis rebus fidei vel authoritatis esse. De iis in superioribus quidem, sed tamen nostro proprioribus sæculis, vel nulla, vel admodum rara, tenuisque occurrit apud Romanos hominess mentio;, ut verissime à Bellarmino scriptum sit, eas in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen habere: quod ipsum invicto argumento est, falsas esse & supposititias. Nam si verè Clementis (id est primi, vel certe primo proximi Romanorum Episcopi) hoc esset opus; si vere sacram doctrinam ὁμόστοιχον τοῖς ἐνδόξοις φθογγαῖς τῆς Σωτῆ-ρος. Salvatoris, gloriosis vocibus æquiparan-dam (ut reddit Bovius) si sancitam omnium Apostolorum voce atque authoritate disciplinam contineret; quis Ecclesiam Latinam, caterarum omnium (si ipsi credimus) ma-gistram, gistram, ac ducem, id per tot sæcula adeo contemptim habituram fuisse crediderit,ut toto eo tempore nullius fere apud ipsam nominis extiterit? Repertum recenti tandem memoria sive Bovium, sive Turrianum, qui tantum scilicet thesaurum de contemptus (ut sic dicam) pulvere ac situ, in quo tandiu jacuerat, erutum ac vindicatum, suæ dignitati, suoque nitori postlimi-nio restitueret? Certè Honorius Augusto-dunensis,qui ante quingentos annos in no-stra Gallia vixit, circa a. D. 1120. omnia, quæ Clementi Romano tribuuntur (adeoque & Constitutiones) inter apocrypha re-jicit; excepta una ad Corinthios epistola. Hæc autem sunt ejus in opere de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis verba, pene omnia ex Hieronymo desumpta; Clemens (inquit) cujus Apostolus ad Philippenses meminit, quartus post Petrum Apostolum Romæ Episcopus (siquidem secundus Linus, tertius Anacletus fuit) scripsit Epistolam ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, valde utilem; & Itinerarium Petri; & disputationem Petri & Appionis, & MULTA alia, quæ inter apocrypha recensentur. Sed & 150. ante Honorium annis,quod esset Latinæ Ecclesiæ de his Constitutionibus judicium exsertè aperteque docuerat Humbertus Cardinalis, Episcopus Sylvæ Candidæ, à Leone nono legatus Constantinopolim missus, vir fui saeculi longe doctissimus (vixit autem anno Domini 1054. ante annos sexcentos) qui Nicetæ Pectorato Constitutionum Apostolicarum, itemque Canonum, qui Apostolici dicuntur, loca quaedam contra Sabbati jejunium objectanti, his verbis respondit, Nos (inquit) reprehendens, cur jejunemus Sabbatis, dicis, quarta & sexta feria jugiter jejunandum; una propter traditionem, altera propter passionem Domini: sabbato autem nunquam, nisi uno; & hoc afferre conaris ex apocryphis libris & Canonibus pari sententia sanctorum Patrum repudiatis. Nam Clementis librum, id est Itinerarium Petri Apostoli, & canones Apostolorum numeravere inter Apocrypha, exceptis capitulis quinquaginta, quae decreverunt regulis orthodoxia adjungenda. Unde nos quoque omne apocryphon b abjicientes, dedignamur audire eorum fabulosas traditiones, quia non sunt ut lex Domini. Hactenus Humbertus. Neque quenquam moveat quod librum illum Clementis dicat esse Itinerarium Petri. Omnino id Clementis opus intelligit, quod Constitutionum Apostolicarum titulum praefert; ut liquet, siquis rem attente consideret. Nam imprimis observandum est, Nicetam, cui respondet, nullum ex eo volumine, quod Petri Itinera-
units.tr: And so much for the more recent theologians on the opposing side; none of them has anything on their side that can rightly be set against them or matched with them. For whether you look at learning, dignity, reputation or the fame of the name, what has our age or that of our fathers produced in the Roman communion that can be compared with Bellarmine, Baronius, La Bigne, Perron, Albaspinaeus and Petavius? Their opinion, as is clear, agrees: that the Apostolic Constitutions, circulated under Clement's name, are doubtful, uncertain, apocryphal, false, corrupt and adulterated, and of no authority in matters of religion or faith. In earlier centuries, though still in ours, almost no mention, or only a very rare and slight one, of them occurs among Roman men; so Bellarmine truly wrote that they have almost no reputation in the Latin Church. This itself is an unanswerable argument that they are false and spurious. For if this work were truly Clement's (that is, of the first, or at least of the bishop of Rome closest to the first); if it truly contained a sacred doctrine ὁμόστοιχον τοῖς ἐνδόξοις φθογγαῖς τῆς Σωτῆρος, to be matched with the glorious words of the Saviour (as Bovius renders it), if it contained a discipline sanctioned by the voice and authority of all the Apostles; who would believe that the Latin Church, which (if we believe them) is the teacher and leader of all the rest, would have held it in such contempt for so many centuries that almost no one in it ever knew its name? Was it only in recent memory that Bovius or Turrianus found it, and drew out and vindicated this treasure from the dust and mould of contempt, in which it had lain so long, and restored its dignity and its lustre after long neglect? Certainly Honorius of Autun, who lived in our Gaul about five hundred years ago, around the year of our Lord 1120, rejects among the apocrypha everything attributed to Clement of Rome (and so the Constitutions too), with one exception, the letter to the Corinthians. These are his words in his work on ecclesiastical writers, almost all taken from Jerome: Clement (he says), whom the Apostle mentions in his letter to the Philippians, was the fourth bishop of Rome after the Apostle Peter (for Linus was second and Anacletus third). He wrote a very useful letter to the church of the Corinthians, and the Itinerary of Peter, and a disputation of Peter and Apion, and MANY other things, which are counted among the apocrypha. But also one hundred and fifty years before Honorius, Humbert, Cardinal and Bishop of Silva Candida, sent as legate by Leo IX to Constantinople, a man by far the most learned of his age (he lived in the year of the Lord 1054, six hundred years ago), had expressly and openly taught the Latin Church's judgment on these Constitutions. When Nicetas Pectoratus objected to him certain passages of the Apostolic Constitutions, and likewise of the Canons which are called Apostolic, against the fasting on the Sabbath, he answered in these words: Reproaching us (he says) for fasting on Sabbaths, you say that we should fast continually on Wednesday and Friday, the one because of the betrayal, the other because of the Lord's passion; but on the Sabbath never, except one; and you try to bring this from apocryphal books and Canons, rejected by the equal judgment of the holy Fathers. For they have counted among the Apocrypha the book of Clement, that is, the Itinerary of the Apostle Peter, and the Canons of the Apostles, except fifty chapters, which they decreed should be added to the rules of orthodoxy. Hence we too, rejecting every apocryphal writing, disdain to hear their fabulous traditions, because they are not as the law of the Lord. So far Humbert. Nor should anyone be disturbed that he calls that book of Clement the Itinerary of Peter. He clearly means the same work of Clement which bears the title Apostolic Constitutions, as is clear to anyone who considers the matter carefully. For first it must be observed that Nicetas, whom he answers, produced no passage from that volume which is properly called the Itinera-

units.la: a Contr: Nicet.Pectror. T.4. Bib.Patr. part. 2 p. 243. a.b. & in append. T. II. ann. Bar.
units.tr: a Against Nicetas Pectoratus, Bibliotheca Patrum vol. 4, part 2, pp. 243 a–b; and in the appendix to vol. 2, under the year (Baronius).

units.la: b Bar. omnē apocryphum. nerarium proprie dicitur, locum pro sua(id est Græcorum) sententia attulisse: sed duntaxat ex Constitutionibus & Canonibus Apostolicis. Sic enim habet a ; Apostolorum vertices in quinto quidem libro ordinationum, qui de martyribus inscribitur, juxta Clementem, Quartam feriam & sextam præcepit b nobis jejunare Dominus : unam quidem propter traditionem, alteram propter passionem. Ipsum autem sabbatum non tradidit jejunare, quoniam non oportet, præter illud solum omnium, quo c Creator sub terra fuit. Unde juxta calcem ejusdem libri iterum sic loquitur, Omne quidem sabbatum & omnem Dominicum celebrandum esse dicimus. Gaudere enim oportet in his,& non lugere.Septimo quidem libro earum Constitutionum juxta vicesimum d caput hoc inquiunt;Sabbatum namque & Dominicam celebramus; quia illud quidem divinæ operationis est memoria e; hic vero tantum Sabbatum custodiendum est in toto anno sepulturæ Domini,quo jejunare oportet. Quando enim Christus in sepulchro jacuit, discipuli potentiorem circa eum fletum habebant,quam gaudium ex memoria divinæ operationis. Hæc Nicetas ex quinto & septimo Ordinationum, sive Constitutionum (id est Διαταξεων) Apostolicarum libris : quæ & in nostris codicibus totidem pene verbis habentur. Prima enim sententia extat in Græcis exemplaribus.l.5. c. 14. a in Bovii vero editione l. 5. c. 16. b τετρᾶδα δὲ ἡμῖν παρασκευὴν προσέταξεν ἡμῖν νηστεύειν. τῷ μὲν σαββάτῳ τῷ προσαββάτῳ, τῷ ὃ δὲ τῷ σαββάτῳ. Tum; αὐτὸ ὃ νηστεύσαι τὸ σάββατον, οὐχ ὅτι δεῖ τὸ σάββατον νηστεύειν, κατάπαυσιν δημιουργίας ὑπάρχον, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐκεῖνο μόνον χρὴ νηστεύειν, τῆ δημιουργῷ ἐν αὐτῷ ἔτι ὑπὸ τῷ γὴν ὄντι. Quæ sic reddidit Bovius: In quarta feria & parasceve nobis jejunium indixit; in illa ob proditionem, in hac ob passionem, &c. Iussit in ipso sabbato jejunare, non quod oporteat in sabbato jejunium servare, cum in eo cessatio conditi operis (id est creationis) sit, sed quod in illo tantum jejunare oportet, in quo opifex ipse subtus terram mansit. Secundam vero sententiam, in eodem libro quinto, & quidem extremo, quod monet Nicetas, nostri quoque codices exhibent c; πᾶν μὲν τοι σάββατον, ἄνευ τῆς ἑνὸς, ἐπὶ πᾶσαν νυκτὸς ἐπιτελοῦντες σωσθῆς εὐφραίνεσθε, &c. εὐ- φραινθῆναι γὰρ δεῖ ἐν αὐταῖς, ἀλλ' ὁ πνευθῆσαι. Sic etiam apud Bovium d; In omni Sabbato (excepto uno) atque die Dominico convenitus celebrantes exhilaramini, &c. Per hos enim dies exhilarari oportet, non lugere. Tertia denique sententia ipsa quoque in nostris codicibus legitur, libro septimo,
units.tr: b Baronius reads "every apocryphal book." -nerarium is properly so called; but he brought forward a passage in support of his (that is, the Greeks') opinion only from the Apostolic Constitutions and Canons. For thus it reads: In the fifth book of the Ordinances, which is entitled concerning martyrs, the Apostles, according to Clement, commanded us to fast on the fourth day and the sixth, the Lord having given it to us: the one on account of the betrayal, the other on account of the passion. But he did not hand down that we should fast on the Sabbath itself, since it is not right, except that one alone of all, on which the Creator was under the earth. Hence, near the end of the same book, he again speaks thus: We say that every Sabbath and every Lord's Day should be celebrated. For it is fitting to rejoice in them and not to mourn. In the seventh book of those Constitutions, near the twentieth chapter, they say this: For we celebrate both the Sabbath and the Lord's Day; because the one is the memory of the divine work, while the other is the memory of the resurrection. Only one Sabbath is to be kept by us in the whole year, that of the Lord's burial, on which it is fitting to fast. For when Christ lay in the tomb, the disciples had a grief over him more powerful than their joy in the memory of the divine work. These are Nicetas's words from the fifth and seventh books of the Ordinances, or Constitutions (that is, the Διαταξεων) of the Apostles; and they are found in our manuscripts in nearly the same words. For the first statement is found in the Greek copies, book 5, chapter 14, and in Bovius's edition book 5, chapter 16: τετρᾶδα δὲ ἡμῖν παρασκευὴν προσέταξεν ἡμῖν νηστεύειν [the fourth day and the preparation day he commanded us to fast]. Then: αὐτὸ ὃ νηστεῦσαι τὸ σάββατον, οὐχ ὅτι δεῖ τὸ σάββατον νηστεύειν [he did not command fasting on the Sabbath because the Sabbath must be fasted, being the rest of the creation, but because that alone must be fasted, on which the Creator remained under the earth]. Bovius rendered these thus: He indicated a fast for us on the fourth day and on the preparation day; on the one because of the betrayal, on the other because of the passion, etc. He commanded fasting on the Sabbath itself, not because one must keep a fast on the Sabbath, since in it there is a cessation of the created work (that is, of creation), but because one must fast only on that day on which the maker himself remained under the earth. The second statement, in the same fifth book, and indeed at its end, which Nicetas warns of, our manuscripts also present: On every Sabbath (except the one) and on the Lord's Day, as you celebrate assemblies, rejoice, etc. For on these days it is fitting to rejoice, not to mourn. So also in Bovius: On every Sabbath (except one) and on the Lord's Day, assembling and celebrating, you should be cheerful, etc. For on these days one must rejoice, not mourn. Finally, the third statement is also read in our manuscripts, in the seventh book,

units.la: unde eam citat Nicetas,cap. 24. Τὸ σάβ- βαλον μέντοι ᾗ τῶν κυριακῶν ἑορτάζετε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν δημιουργίας ἐστιν ὑπόμνημα. ἡ δὲ ἀνάστασεως. ἐν ᾗ μόνον σάββατον ἡμῖν φυλακτέον ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ ἐνιαυτῷ, τὸ τῆς τῦ Κυρίυ ταφῆς, ὅπερ νηστεύειν προσῆκεν, ἀλλ' οὐχ ἑορτάζειν. ἐν ὅσῳ γὰρ ὁ δημιουργὸς ὑπὸ γῆν τυγχάνει, ἰσχυρότερον τὸ περὶ αὐτὸν πένθος τῆς καλῆς τῶν δημιουργίαν χαρᾶς.Sabbatum & Dominicum diem festum agite, quoniam illud quidem natura condita est monimentum, sive recordiatio, hic vero resurrectionis.
