Unum vero tantummodo sabbatum nobis toto anno observandum est, sabbatum scilicet sepultura Christi; quo quidem jejunare deceat, non autem celebrare festum. Dum enim author mundi sub terra est, validior est de eo luctus, quam de mundo condito laetitia. Hactenus nostri Clementis codices.
units.tr: Hence Nicetas cites it at chap. 24: [Greek: Keep the Sabbath, and celebrate the Lord's day, since the one is a memorial of creation and the other of the resurrection. Only one Sabbath must be kept by us throughout the whole year, the Sabbath of the Lord's burial, on which it is fitting to fast, not to hold a festival. For while the Author of the world lies under the earth, grief for him is stronger than joy at the fair creation.] Keep the Sabbath and the Lord's day as a festival, since the one is a memorial of creation, the other of the resurrection. Only one Sabbath must be observed by us throughout the whole year, the Sabbath of the Lord's burial, on which we ought to fast, not celebrate a festival. For while the Author of the world is under the earth, our grief for him is greater than our joy in the fair creation. So far the codices of our Clement. [Greek: Τὸ σάββατον μέντοι καὶ τὴν κυριακὴν ἑορτάζετε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν δημιουργίας ἐστιν ὑπόμνημα, ἡ δὲ ἀναστάσεως. ἓν δὲ σάββατον μόνον ἡμῖν φυλακτέον ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ ἐνιαυτῷ, τὸ τῆς τοῦ Κυρίου ταφῆς, ὅπερ νηστεύειν προσῆκεν, ἀλλ' οὐχ ἑορτάζειν. ἐν ᾧ γὰρ ὁ δημιουργὸς ὑπὸ γῆν τυγχάνει, ἰσχυρότερον τὸ περὶ αὐτὸν πένθος τῆς περὶ τὸν κόσμον καλῆς δημιουργίας χαρᾶς.]

units.la: Cum hæc ergo ex Clementis Apostolicis sive Ordinationibus sive Constitutionibus afferentem Nicetam Humbertus dicat disputare, suaque afferere ex Apocryphis libris, sententia sanctorum Patrum repudiatis; respondeatque, se omne apocryphon abjicientem dedignari audire eorum fabulosas traditiones; clarum est, eum ipsas illas Clementis Constitutiones, quæ tum apud Græcos in pretio habebantur, nunc vero etiam apud nos circumferuntur, inter apocrypha, crypha, sententia Patrum repudiata, ac inter fabulosas Graecorum traditiones censuisse; putasseque nullam earum in Christianae vel fidei vel disciplinae rebus habendam esse rationem. Quae cum ita sentiat, ac scribat, non imperitus aliquis de plebis faece, sed vir sui saeculi maximus, ac doctissimus, adhaec Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalis Episcopus, Pontificisque Romani Legatus; dubitandum non est, quin eadem tum de his libris & Romani Pontificis, & totius Romanae Ecclesiae fuerit sententia. Vide ergo quantum ab his veris, germanisque Romanis degenerarint Turrianus, & Bovius, & alii siqui sint hodierni Romulidae, qui apocryphas istas, a suis majoribus damnatas ac rejectas pseudodiataxes in coelum tollant.
units.tr: Since Humbert says that Nicetas, in citing these words from the Apostolic Clementines, or the Ordinances or Constitutions, is arguing, and maintaining his views from apocryphal books, which the judgement of the holy Fathers has rejected; and since he replies that he, who rejects every apocryphal work, disdains to listen to their fabulous traditions; it is clear that he judged those very Clementine Constitutions, which were then held in high regard among the Greeks and are now circulated among us too, to be apocrypha, a thing the judgement of the Fathers has rejected, and among the fabulous traditions of the Greeks, and that he thought no account should be taken of them in matters of Christian faith or discipline. Since he thinks and writes thus, he is no unlearned man from the dregs of the common people, but the greatest and most learned man of his age, moreover a Bishop Cardinal of the Roman Church and Legate of the Roman Pontiff. There can be no doubt that at that time the view of the Roman Pontiff and of the whole Roman Church about these books was the same. See then how far Turrianus and Bovius, and any other Romulidae of today, have degenerated from these true and genuine Romans, who extol those apocryphal pseudo-diataxes, which their forebears condemned and rejected, to the heavens.

units.la: Jam vero quod ait Humbertus, Clementis librum illum a Niceta laudatum, esse itinerarium Petri; id fateor mirum iis visum iri, qui Itinerarium Petri volumen esse putant ejusdem quidem Clementis, sed tamen ab Apostolicis Constitutionibus diversum; quorum in numero est Bellarminus, qui Recognitionum & Itenerarii idem esse opus censet. Sed utcunque se res ipsa vere habeat, illud quidem liquet, non Recognitionum, sed Constitutionum opus Humberto idem visum fuisse cum Petri Itineraria rio. Neque enim dubitandum est, quin id ipsum Clementis opus intelligat, quod & nunc passim censetur,& à Niceta olim censebatur Constitutionum nomine. Itaque Papæ Gelasii decretum, quo Itinerarium nomine Petri Apostoli, quod appellatur Sancti Clementis libri octo, in apocrypha refertur, omnino de Constitutionibus accepit Humbertus: non ut Bellarminus de Recognitionibus. Certe Humberto favet librorum numerus. Recognitionum enim libros decem esse constat; Constitutionum vero non plures quam octo.
units.tr: Now as for Humbert's statement that the book of Clement cited by Nicetas is the Itinerary of Peter, I admit this will seem strange to those who think the Itinerary of Peter is a volume by the same Clement but different from the Apostolic Constitutions; among them is Bellarmine, who holds that the Recognitions and the Itinerary are the same work. But however the matter truly stands, this much is clear: Humbert took the work he meant to be not the Recognitions but the Constitutions, identical with Peter's Itinerary. Indeed there is no doubt that he means that very work of Clement which is still commonly reckoned, and was once reckoned by Nicetas, under the name of Constitutions. So the decree of Pope Gelasius, in which the Itinerary under the name of the Apostle Peter, which is called the eight books of St Clement, is listed among the apocrypha, Humbert understood entirely of the Constitutions, not, as Bellarmine does, of the Recognitions. The number of books certainly favours Humbert: the Recognitions are known to be ten books, but the Constitutions are no more than eight.

units.la: Ex quibus liquet Humberti, adeoque Latinæ, quæ tum erat, Ecclesiæ judicio, jam anno Christi 494. à Gelasio urbis Episcopo, totaque Romana Synodo, à 70. Episcopis præside Gelasio habita, damnatas, rejectasque in apocryphorum censum fuisse Clementis nomine vulgatas, & in octo libros digestas Apostolorum Constitutiones, eo canone, qui his verbis expressus habetur a: Item Itinerarium nomine Petri Apostoli, quod appellatur S. Clementis libri octo, apocryphum. Non de aliis quam de Constitutionum octo libris hæc intellexit Humbertus, omninoque huc respexit, cum libros, e quibus sua afferebat Nicetas, pari sententia Sanctorum Patrum repudiatos fuisse scripsit. Nimirum illo de Apocryphis decreto
units.tr: From these points it is clear that, by the judgement of Humbert and therefore of the Latin Church of that time, the Apostolic Constitutions, published under Clement's name and arranged in eight books, were already condemned and rejected into the class of apocrypha in the year of Christ 494 by Gelasius, Bishop of the city, and by the whole Roman Synod, held under Gelasius with seventy bishops presiding, by that canon which is expressed in these words: Likewise the Itinerary under the name of the Apostle Peter, which is called the eight books of St Clement, is apocryphal. Humbert understood these words of nothing other than the eight books of the Constitutions, and he certainly had them in mind when he wrote that the books from which Nicetas drew his citations had been rejected by the same judgement of the holy Fathers. Indeed, by that decree on the Apocrypha,

units.la: a Syn. Rom. I. Sub Gel. I. notitia libror. a. par. T. 3. Conc. p. 662. col. a. E. decreto à Gelasio, & septuaginta aliis Episcopis damnatum est utrumque illud volumen, è quo sua defendebat Nicetas: prius quidem Constitutionum, iis verbis, quæ modo descripsimus; posterius vero Canonum, his, quæ ibidem post multa leguntur a ; Liber Canonum Apostolicorum apocryphus.
units.tr: a Roman Synod I, under Gelasius I, list of books; Tom. 3 of the Councils, p. 662, col. a. E. By the decree of Gelasius and seventy other bishops, both volumes from which Nicetas was defending his views were condemned: first the Constitutions, in the words we have just quoted; and secondly the Canons, in those words which are read there after much else: The Book of the Apostolic Canons is apocryphal.

units.la: Hinc in ulteriora secula sursum ascendentibus, nulla, quod sciam, occurrit Constitutionum Clementinarum apud Latinos mentio. Hieronymus quidem in libro de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis illius Epistolæ, quam ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam ex persona Romanæ Ecclesiæ Clemens scripsit, magna cum laude meminit, eamque tradit nonnullis locis etiam publice lectam fuisse; sed tacitis, altoque silentio transmissis Constitutionibus, hæc tantum de Clemente addit; Fertur & secunda ex ejus nomine Epistola, quæ à Veteribus reprobatur. Et disputatio Petri & Appionis, longo sermone conscripta, quam Eusebius in tertio historia Ecclesiastica volumine coarguit. Obiit tertio Trajani anno, & nominis ejus memoriam usque hodie Romæ extructa Ecclesia custodit. Unde nemo non videt, vel nullas plane tum extitisse apud Latinos Apostolicas Clementis Constitutiones; vel certe nullo in pretio, nulloque in usu fuisse, sed inter
units.tr: Ascending from here to later centuries, no mention of the Clementine Constitutions among the Latins occurs that I know of. Jerome, indeed, in his book on ecclesiastical writers, speaks with great praise of the Epistle which Clement wrote to the Church of Corinth in the name of the Roman Church, and says it was even read publicly in some places; but passing over the Constitutions in deep silence, he adds only this about Clement: There is also a second Epistle under his name, which is rejected by the ancients. And a disputation of Peter and Apion, written at great length, which Eusebius refutes in the third volume of his Ecclesiastical History. He died in the third year of Trajan, and the church built at Rome keeps the memory of his name to this day. Hence everyone can see that either there were no Apostolic Clementine Constitutions among the Latins at that time at all, or certainly that they were held in no esteem and had no use, but lay among the empty and fabulous things of the apocrypha.

units.la: a Ibid. p. 663. col. 1. d. inter apocryphorum vana ac fabulosa jacuisse. Librum enim tanti viri, tantisque de rebus scriptum (si quidem verus ac legitimus fuisset, imo si vel in mediocri usu fuisset) Hieronymo Latinorum scriptorum eruditissimo ac florentissimo ignotum, vel indictum futurum fuisse, quis sanae mentis putaverit? Unde satis refellitur frigida Bovii, Turrianique conjectura , qui hos ipsos Constitutionum libros ab Hieronymo Latine olim converses fuisse suspicantur. Atqui ne notos quidem ei fuisse, vel pro Ecclesiasticis habitos, hinc clarum est. Cur enim Clementis opera vel vera, vel etiam notha in libro de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis tradens, nobilissimum ejus auctoris (si iis credimus) opus omitteret, si quidem id ei notum, ac pro Ecclesiastico habitum fuisset? Sed Hieronymus (inquiunt) Latinam Origenis in Epistolam ad Romanos interpretationem suam concludens, testatur se in convertendis Clementis operibus versari: Quae autem Clementis circumferebantur apocrypha, cum a Ruffino iam fuissent Latine edita, nihil erat quod in iis Hieronymus insudaret. Itaque verisimile est, libros, quos ille a se converti ait, has ipsas esse Apostolorum Constitutiones. Verba autem illa, quae citant, habentur in peroratione translatoris Commenta-
units.tr: a Ibid. p. 663, col. 1, d. For who of sound mind would suppose that a book written by so great a man, on such great matters (if it had been true and genuine, or even if it had been in moderate use), would have remained unknown or unmentioned to Jerome, the most learned and flourishing of Latin writers? Thus the cold conjecture of Bovius and Turrianus is sufficiently refuted, who suspect that these very books of the Constitutions were once translated into Latin by Jerome. Indeed, that they were not even known to him, or regarded as ecclesiastical, is clear from this. For why, when handing down Clement's works, true or even spurious, in his book on ecclesiastical writers, would he omit the most noble work of that author (if we believe them), had it been known to him and regarded as ecclesiastical? But Jerome (they say), concluding his Latin version of Origen's commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, testifies that he is busy translating the works of Clement. But since the apocryphal writings circulating under Clement's name had already been published in Latin by Rufinus, there was nothing in them for Jerome to labour over. It is therefore likely that the books he says he translated are these very Apostolic Constitutions. The words they cite, however, are found in the closing address of the translator of the Origenian commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans,

units.la: a Prefat. in Constit. mentariorum Origenicorum in Epistolam ad Romanos; in qua iste, quisquis est, profitetur, se Clementina Latine editurum: Post hoc sane (inquita) vocat nos opus, quod olim quidem injunctum est, sed nunc à B. Gaudentio episcopo vehementius perurgetur, Clementis scilicet Romani Episcopi, Apostolorum comitis, quorum ut successoribus darem cognitionem, libri à nobis in Latinum vertuntur. In quo opere bene novi, quod laborem labor multiplicat, si fortem suscipiat. Satisfaciam sane in eo amicis meis. Dabo titulo nomen meum, authoris nihilominus vocabulo permanente. Nam Hieronymi ne putetur, Clemens scribetur. Idem paulo ante; Ajunt mihi (inquit) In his quae scribis, quoniam plurima in eis tui operis habentur, da titulum nominis tui, & scribe, Hieronymi (verbi gratia) in Epistolam ad Romanos explanationum libri. Hæc Bovio, Turrianoque imposuerunt, ut Latinam Origenis in epistolam ad Romanos interpretationem, Hieronymi esse putarent. Sed jampridem monuerat, variisque argumentis evicerat Erasmus, eam Ruffini esseb; Librarios vero magnifice perfricuisse frontem & in praefatione & in peroratione pro Ruffino Hieronymum supponentes; quod hujus scilicet gratiosum, illius invidiosum nomen esset. Ipse sane Hiero-
units.tr: a Preface to the Constitutions. In which this man, whoever he is, declares that he will publish the Clementines in Latin: Moreover (he saysa) a work calls us, which was indeed enjoined long ago, but is now more urgently pressed by the blessed Bishop Gaudentius: that of Clement, Bishop of Rome, companion of the Apostles, whose books we are translating into Latin, so that the successors might have knowledge of them. In this work I well know that labour is multiplied by labour, if one undertakes it with strength. I will certainly satisfy my friends in this. I will give my name to the title, while the author's name remains in the wording. For lest it be thought to be Jerome's, it will be written under Clement's name. The same man a little earlier: They say to me (he says) among the things you write, since many of your own work are contained in them, give your name to the title, and write, for example, Books of Explanations of Jerome on the Epistle to the Romans. These words deceived Bovius and Turrianus into thinking that the Latin version of Origen's commentary on the Epistle to the Romans was by Jerome. But Erasmus had long ago warned, and proved by various arguments, that it is by Rufinusb: the copyists had brazenly shamelessly put Jerome's name in the preface and closing address in place of Rufinus's, obviously because his name was popular and the other's unpopular. Jerome himself, indeed-

units.la: a T. 2. Orig. p. 634.
units.tr: a T. 2. Orig. p. 634.

units.la: b Censura Orig. de hom. in gen. & de comm. in ep. ad Rom.
units.tr: b Censura Orig. de hom. in gen. & de comm. in ep. ad Rom.

units.la: Hieronymus, sua in libro de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis opera a. D. 392. recensens, profitetur a se homilias in Hieremiam & Ezechielem Origenis XXVIII de Graeco in Latinum vertisse; commentarios ejusdem in epistolam ad Romanos nullus memorat.
units.tr: Jerome, in his book on ecclesiastical writers, listing his own works in the year 392, professes that he translated twenty-eight homilies of Origen on Jeremiah and Ezekiel from Greek into Latin. No one mentions a commentary by Origen on the Epistle to the Romans.

units.la: Huc accedit, quod hujus operis translator in praefatione non dissimulat, sibi consilium esse, quae in Graeco Origenis codice deerant, ea ex suo ingenio supplere, & ingens commentariorum corpus abbreviare, & ad media si fieri potest spatia coarctare; quam in alienis operibus immutandis, ac pro libidine abbreviandis, ac producendis temeritatem Ruffini quidem singularem fuisse, omnes norunt: ab Hieronymo viro longe doctissimo ac gravissimo usurpatam, nemo sanus dixerit. Ad haec Hieronymum quicquam ex Clemente transtulisse, non ipse, non quisquam alius prodidit: Ruffinum Recognitionum Clementis Romani libros Latine interpretatum esse atque edidisse, & Gennadius b, & Honorius Augustodunensis, & caeteri testantur, & opus ipsum fatetur, quod etiam hodie extat cum praefatione ad ipsum illum Gaudentium, cujus in peroratione Origenicorum in Paulinam epistolam commentariorum meminit. Vana ergo, falsaque est omnis Bovii hariolatio: cum & author illius perorationis,
units.tr: In addition, the translator of that work does not conceal in his preface that it was his intention to supply from his own talent what was missing in the Greek copy of Origen, and to shorten the vast body of commentaries and compress it into moderate lengths where possible. Everyone knows that Rufinus was singularly reckless in altering, shortening and lengthening the works of others. That Jerome, a man far more learned and serious, adopted the same recklessness, no sane person would say. Moreover, neither Jerome himself nor anyone else reports that he translated anything from Clement. That Rufinus translated and published the Recognitions of Clement of Rome in Latin, Gennadius b and Honorius Augustodunensis and the others attest, and the work itself confesses, as it still does today, with its preface addressed to that same Gaudentius whose Origenian commentaries on the Pauline epistle it mentions in its closing address. Therefore all of Bovius's guesswork is empty and false, since the author of that closing address is Rufinus, not Jerome,

units.la: b Gennadius, de viris illustribus. orationis Ruffinus sit, non Hieronymus; & Clementis, ad quod convertendum se iste accingebat, opus Recognitionum volumen sit, non Constitutionum: nulli Latinorum istis quidem seculis viventium memoratum. Jam ulteriora supra Hieronymum nihil necesse est persequi; cum omnes confiteantur, totis quatuor saeculis, quae a Christi natalibus ad Hieronymi mortem fluxerunt, nullam plane extare apud Latinae Ecclesiae scriptores Constitutionum istarum Clementinarum mentionem. Quod unum, si bene reputes, argumentum satis est ad abrogandam omnem istius voluminis fidem: quod si vere Clementis esset, nuspiam majori in pretio atque authoritate fuisset, quam Romae, cujus ille scilicet Ecclesiam vel statim, vel certe proxime post Apostolos rexit. Vides ex Hieronymo, quanta fuerit in authoritate ejusdem viri vera ad Corinthios epistola; ut etiam publice apud Christianae plebis collectas legeretur. Quis dubitaverit, quin & alterius operis, si agnitum, ac pro ejusdem parentis foetu habitum esset, eandem quoque futuram fuisse apud veteres, praesertim Latinos, gratiam, atque dignitatem? maxime cum Apostolos ipsos scriptor iste loquentes, omnemque Christianae religionis fidem ac disciplinam ore sacro cro exponentes ac definientes inducat ? Apage Turriani & Bovii, hominum nudiustertius natorum, adhæc ingenio fabularum ac quisquiliarum avidissimo, nupera musteaque judicia. Quasi vero duobus istis heroibus hanc felicitatem fata servaverint, ut quæ omnis Latinorum Ecclesia totis quindecim sæculis vel plane penitusque nescivit, vel certe cognita contempsit ac nihili fecit, isti ultimis demum his temporibus inusitata spiritus copia perfusi, vera genuinaque Apostolorum dictata esse agnoverint, ac orbi Occidentali manifestarint. Nobis satis sunt, quæ ab initio toti Ecclesiæ tradita, toti agnita, Apostolorum monumenta in publica apud Occidentem æquè ac apud Orientem luce extiterunt. Ista tam sero ab hominibus novis, & quidem merito suspectis, revelata, apocrypha, ut fuerant hactenus, ita quoque deinceps sunto.
units.tr: b Gennadius, On Illustrious Men. and the work of Clement that he was preparing to translate is the volume of the Recognitions, not the Constitutions, a work mentioned by no Latin writer living in those centuries. There is no need to pursue later writers beyond Jerome, since everyone agrees that throughout the four centuries that passed from the birth of Christ to the death of Jerome, there is plainly no mention of these Clementine Constitutions among the writers of the Latin Church. If you consider it carefully, this one point is enough to abolish all credit for that volume. For if it were truly Clement's, it would nowhere have been held in greater esteem and authority than at Rome, whose Church he governed, certainly at once or very soon after the Apostles. You see from Jerome how great was the authority of Clement's genuine letter to the Corinthians, so that it was even read publicly at the collections of the Christian people. Who could doubt that, if another work of his had been recognised and regarded as the offspring of the same father, it too would have enjoyed the same favour and dignity among the ancients, especially the Latins, particularly since this writer introduces the Apostles themselves speaking and, with sacred mouth, setting out and defining the whole faith and discipline of the Christian religion? Away with the recent and new-minted judgments of Turrianus and Bovius, men born only the day before yesterday, and moreover men most greedy for fables and trifles. As if fate had reserved this happiness for those two heroes: that what the whole Latin Church either entirely failed to know over fifteen centuries, or knew and despised and held as worthless, these men, drenched in an unusual abundance of spirit in these last times, should recognise as the true and genuine dictates of the Apostles and reveal to the Western world! We are content with the monuments of the Apostles that from the beginning were handed down to the whole Church, acknowledged by the whole Church, and stood in public light in the West as well as in the East. Those things, revealed so late by new men, and rightly suspected, are apocryphal, and as they have been until now, so let them remain henceforth.

units.la: CAP. II. Æthiopum de Constitutionibus error, eas divinis libris æquiparantium. Græcorum de iis judicia, Epiphanio memoratas Constitutiones, neque nostras fuisse, neque vere ab Apostolis conditas.
units.tr: CAP. II. The Ethiopians' error concerning the Constitutions, in equating them with the divine books. The judgments of the Greeks about them. That the Constitutions mentioned by Epiphanius are neither ours nor truly composed by the Apostles.

units.la: ÆC de Latinis hactenus. Nunc cæteras Ecclesiæ Christianæ partes videamus. Idem ille Bellarminus, aus, qui Constitutiones nullum fere nomen apud Latinos habuisse fatetur, ait a eas a {a}Græcis veteribus magni fieri: tum audire se addit, Æthiopes his uti, ut vere Apostolicis. Ego vero de Æthiopibus quidem fateor, quibus facile fuit in summa rerum, ac temporum Ecclesiæ ignorantia versantibus, veteris impostoris ludos pro Apostolorum statutis obtrudere. Certe in suo de rebus Abyssinis libro {b}narrat Alvares, Abyssinos sive Æthiopes habere librum in octo partes divisum, quem ab universis Apostolis Hierosolymæ congregatis scriptum ferunt, quemque ipsi vulgo Manda & Abetilis vocant. Clarum est, Clementinas Constitutiones intelligi; quæ & in 8 libros, ut notum est, divisæ sunt, & velut ab Apostolis una congregatis dictatæ finguntur. Hos autem octo libros, aliosque ejusdem farinæ non paucos, ut Canones fortasse Apostolorum, & similes, eodem, quo sacros veteris novique Instrumenti codices, loco & numero censere Æthiopes, ex eo liquet, quod iidem apud Alvarem {c}jactant se veteris ac novi fœderis libros habere LXXXI. qui numerus (quod nemo nescit) verorum ac legitimorum & a Spiritu Sancto inspiratorum librorum numerum haud modice superat. Tam crassi autem erroris hanc habent Æthiopes ab ipso Bellarmino {d} observatam, mercedem, quod circa
units.tr: So much for the Latins. Now let us look at the other parts of the Christian Church. That same Bellarmine, who admits that the Constitutions had almost no reputation among the Latins, says that they were held in high esteem by the ancient Greeks; then he adds that he had heard that the Ethiopians use them as truly apostolic. For my part, I confess about the Ethiopians that, living in great ignorance of the affairs and times of the Church, it was easy for them to foist upon Apostolic ordinances the tricks of an old impostor. Certainly in his book on the affairs of Abyssinia, Alvares reports that the Abyssinians or Ethiopians have a book divided into eight parts, which they say was written by all the Apostles gathered at Jerusalem, and which they commonly call Manda and Abetilis. It is clear that the Clementine Constitutions are meant, which, as is well known, are also divided into eight books and are feigned to have been dictated by the Apostles gathered together. That the Ethiopians count these eight books, and not a few others of the same kind, such as perhaps the Canons of the Apostles and similar things, in the same place and number as the sacred codices of the Old and New Testament, is clear from the fact that they boast, in Alvares, that they have eighty-one books of the Old and New Covenant, a number which (as nobody is unaware) far exceeds the number of the true and lawful books inspired by the Holy Spirit. Yet the Ethiopians have this error, so gross, noted by Bellarmine himself, as their reward, that about
