units.la: d 1. De script. Eccl. in Clem. circa cultum Sabbati & diei dominica et circa ministrum baptismi, & in aliis quibusdam dogmatibus, graviter hallucinantur; caecum scilicet caeci ducem sequuti.
units.tr: d 1. On ecclesiastical writers, under Clement. they go badly wrong about the observance of the Sabbath and the Lord's day, and about the minister of baptism, and about certain other doctrines; following, of course, the blind leader of the blind.

units.la: Sed Æthiopes quidem mittamus, quorum non nisi recentissima novimus; antiqua plane ignoramus; tum ob rara & difficilia nostrorum hominum cum remotissima ac paene inaccessa gente commercia, tu etiam ob veterum apud eam monumentorum penuriam. Ad Græcos veniamus; quibus neq; recentioribus neque prisccis, in pretio fuisse istas Constitutiones, clarum esse videtur; & miror, quod Bellarminus aliud senserit. Hieremias ex recentissimis Constantinopoleos Patriarchis anno superioris seculi 76. ad Virtenbergenses scribens fatetur γενοθεὶν ∆αι τὰς Κλημεντείας διατάξεις, adulteratas fuisse Clementinas Constitutiones. Balsamon, qui an. D. 1191. floruisse perhibetur, in Canonem, ut vocant, Apostolorum LXXXV. b Σὺ γινώσκε (inquit) ὡς εἰ καὶ γι-γνώσκεται ἐντεῦθεν ἀναγινώσκειν ἡμᾶς τὰς διαταγὰς τῶν Κλημεντίνων, πλὴν μὴ δημοτιεύειν αὐτὰς, ἀλλ' ὁ β' κανὼν τῆς ἐκτῆς συνόδου ἀπηγορεύσε τῶν τῶν ἀναγνωσμὸν, ἐξ τὸ γενέσθαι ἀπαρωμοίωσιν ἐν αὐταῖς. Tu autem intelligas, quod etsi hic scriptum est, Constitutiones (clementis legi a nobis, sed non devulgari debere, secundus tamen sexta Synodi canon earum lectionem lectionem prohibuit, quod in eis adulteratio facta sit. Zonaras de iisdem Clementis Constitutionibus a, Αὐτὰ (inquit) παρὰ πολλῶν τινῶν, ἐνοθεύτησάν τε τὴν παράδοσιν, ἀπηγόρευσεν. Ab heterodoxis et sectariis quibusdam adulterata et corrupta fuerunt. Quapropter istas omnino legi vetuit Oecumenica sexta Synodus c. 2. Similia habet Alexius Aristenus, interpres ineditus, à Rev. Vsserio b allata: ὁ Ἀλέξιος ... Secundus canon Synodi sextae in Trullo habita Constitutiones hasce omnino rejicit, propterea quod iis nonnulla adulterina ab heterodoxis adjecta fuerint, atque à pietate aliena.
units.tr: But let us leave the Ethiopians, of whom we know only the most recent things and are entirely ignorant of the ancient; partly because of the rare and difficult commerce of our people with a most remote and almost inaccessible nation, and partly because of the scarcity of ancient monuments among them. Let us come to the Greeks, among whom it seems clear that these Constitutions were held in esteem neither by the more recent nor by the earlier writers; and I wonder that Bellarmine thought otherwise. Jeremiah, one of the most recent Patriarchs of Constantinople, writing in the year 1576 to the Württembergers, admits that the Clementine ordinances have been adulterated [γεγονέναι τὰς Κλημεντείας διατάξεις]. Balsamon, who is said to have flourished in the year of our Lord 1191, on the Canon of the Apostles, as it is called, LXXXV, says: b [Σὺ γινώσκε ὡς εἰ καὶ γινώσκεται ἐντεῦθεν ἀναγινώσκειν ἡμᾶς τὰς διαταγὰς τῶν Κλημεντίνων, πλὴν μὴ δημοσιεύειν αὐτὰς, ἀλλ' ὁ β' κανὼν τῆς ἕκτης συνόδου ἀπηγόρευσε τὸν τούτων ἀναγνωσμὸν, ἐπειδὴ γεγονέναι ἀπαρωμοίωσιν ἐν αὐταῖς] You should know, he says, that although it is stated from this that we may read the ordinances of the Clementines, they must not be made public; but the second canon of the sixth Synod forbade their reading, because a falsification has been made in them. Zonaras, speaking of the same Clementine Constitutions, says: "They were adulterated and corrupted by many heterodox and sectarian persons; for which reason the ecumenical sixth Synod, canon 2, forbade them to be read at all." Alexius Aristenus, an unpublished commentator cited by the Reverend Ussher, has similar words: "The second canon of the sixth Synod held in Trullo rejects these Constitutions entirely, on the ground that some adulterous additions were made to them by heterodox persons, and are alien to piety."

units.la: Ergo si quis ex Graecis recentioribus, ut Nicetas, Constitutionum authoritate utitur, vel eas in pretio habet, id praeter communem suae gentis sententiam facit, causae fortassis adversus Latinos studio abreptus; quod non pauca sint in istis Constitutionibus, quae Graecis evidenter favent. Neque veteriorum, qui plurimi apud eos eruditione celebres fuerunt, alia de his sententia fuisse videtur. Photius C P. episcopus, vir omnium Graecorum sui saeculi longe eruditissimus (floruit autem anno 859. vixe-
units.tr: So if any of the more recent Greeks, like Nicetas, uses the authority of the Constitutions, or holds them in esteem, he does so apart from the common opinion of his nation, perhaps carried away by zeal against the Latins, since there are not a few things in those Constitutions which plainly favour the Greeks. Nor does the opinion of the older writers, of whom there were very many famous for learning among them, seem to have been different on this matter. Photius, bishop of Constantinople, a man by far the most learned of all the Greeks of his age (he flourished in the year 859 and ceased to live in 889), writes thus about these Apostolic Constitutions, in the place where he reviews the works of Clement that he had read:

units.la: a Ibid. re desiit anno 889) de his Apostolorum Constitutionibus ita scribit, quo loco Clementis opera a se lecta recensetᵃ: Ai δἀγι διαταγαὶ τῇσι μόνοις δοκιμον ἐν ἐχεθαγ᾽ κακο-ταλασίαν ἡ χαλκῖτον ἀποσκευάσασθαι. καὶ ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀνλεγονομίαν ὑβρεὶς τινὰς ἐπαφῖνσιν, ὡς καὶ ῥᾷον διαλύσασθαι. καὶ ἔτι ἀρειαυισμῶς, ὅπερ αὐτὶς ἕ βιαίως διαγρύσαιτο. ἡ μὲν τοί γε τῶν ταρᾶξεων βιέλ@τῷ τε λαμπρῷ ἕ τῇ σεμ-νότητι. ἕ ἔτι τῷ καθαρῷ ἕ σωτόνῳ ἕ τῇ ἄλλῃ ἀρετῇ τε λόγω καὶ πολυμαθεία τοσοῦτον ἔχει πρὸς τὰς διαταγὰς τὸ παράλλακτον, ὡς μηδὲ συγκεῖσει τὴ κατὰ τὰς λόγως πρὸς ἀλλήλας παραβάλλεσθαι τὰς βίβλως. Hactenus Photius: quem vera, ut liquet, videntem, & argumenta, quibus horum librorum falsitas ac vanitas deprehenditur, animadverten-tem, causæ ut videtur adversus Latinos suæ studium transversum egit, ut scriberet, duo priora facile, tertium ægre quidem, sed tamen & ipsum quoque solvi ac dilui posse. Nos infra singula expendemus, & quæ sit eorum vis dispiciemus.
units.tr: a Ibid. re desiit anno 889) concerning these Apostolic Constitutions writes thus, in the passage where he reviews Clement's works: "The holy Constitutions are approved only in this respect: that they [...] (they put forth some insolent things according to the [...], so that they might easily be dissolved); and moreover some [...] which [...] violently [...]. But the [author] of the [...], in lustre and gravity, in purity and other virtue, in word and learning, is so far superior to the Constitutions that they cannot even be set side by side in their words." [Αἱ δὲ ἅγιαι διαταγαὶ τῇσι μόνοις δοκιμον ἐν ἐχεθαγ᾽ κακο-ταλασίαν ἡ χαλκῖτον ἀποσκευάσασθαι. καὶ ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀνλεγονομίαν ὑβρεὶς τινὰς ἐπαφῖνσιν, ὡς καὶ ῥᾷον διαλύσασθαι. καὶ ἔτι ἀρειαυισμῶς, ὅπερ αὐτὶς ἕ βιαίως διαγρύσαιτο. ἡ μὲν τοί γε τῶν ταρᾶξεων βιέλ@τῷ τε λαμπρῷ ἕ τῇ σεμνότητι. ἕ ἔτι τῷ καθαρῷ ἕ σωτόνῳ ἕ τῇ ἄλλῃ ἀρετῇ τε λόγω καὶ πολυμαθεία τοσοῦτον ἔχει πρὸς τὰς διαταγὰς τὸ παράλλακτον, ὡς μηδὲ συγκεῖσει τὴ κατὰ τὰς λόγως πρὸς ἀλλήλας παραβάλλεσθαι τὰς βίβλως.] Thus far Photius, who, as is clear, saw the truth and noticed the arguments by which the falsity and emptiness of these books is detected; yet, as it seems, his zeal against the Latins led him astray, so that he wrote that the first two could be solved easily and the third with difficulty, but still could be solved and refuted as well. We shall examine each point below and see what force they have.

units.la: Qui vero annis ante Photii Episcopatum 170. vixerunt, Græcę Ecclesię Patres, a. D. 692. in Trullo congregati, exserte liquido-que adulteratas ab hæreticis Constitutiones agnoscunt, & ab Ecclesiasticorum librorum censu rejectas, abdicant atque explodunt his verbis ᵇ, Ταῖς τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων ᾽ΗΚλήμιντ@
units.tr: But the Greek Fathers who lived about 170 years before Photius's episcopate, gathered at Trullo in the year 692, expressly and plainly acknowledge that the Constitutions were adulterated by heretics, and they reject and explode them from the list of ecclesiastical books, in these words: [Ταῖς τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων

units.la: ᵃ Bibli Ath. cod. 113. p. 156.
units.tr: a Bibl. Ath. cod. 113, p. 156.

units.la: ᵇ Trull. Can. 2. T. 5. Cancil. p. 320.
units.tr: b Trull. Can. 2, T. 5, Concil. p. 320.

units.la: Κλήμεντος διαλάξεις πάλαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἑτεροδόξων ἐν λύμῃ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας νόθα τινὰ ἢ ξένα τῆς ἐυσεβείας παρεισηχθέντα, τὸ ἐυαρεστες καλλίῳ τῶν θείων δογμάτων ἡμῖν ἀμαυρώσαντα, τῶν τοιούτων διατάξεων προσφόρως ἀποβολῇ πεποιήμεθα πρὸς τὴν τε χριστιανικωτάτην σαιμυίαν οἰκονομίαν καὶ ἀσφάλειαν, ἐδαμῶς ἐγκείνοντες τὰ τῆς αἱρετικῆς ψευδολογίας κυήματα, ἢ τὴν γνῶσιν τῶν ἀποστόλων ὁ ὁλοκλήρῳ διδαχῇ παρεισφέροντες. His Apostolorum per Clementem Constitutionibus jam olim ab iis qui à fide aliena sentiunt, ad Labem Ecclesiæ aspergendam, adulterina quadam & à pietate aliena introducta sunt, quæ divinorum nobis decretorum elegantem at decoram speciem obscurarunt, has Constitutiones ad Christianissimi gregis ædificationem ac securitatem conducibiliter REIECIMVS, hæretica falsitatis fœtus nequaquam admittentes, & germanæ ac integræ Apostolorum doctrinæ inserentes. En, ut à veteribus Græcis magnifiant hæ Pseudodiataxes: qui eas exsertè rejiciunt, & extra Ecclesiasticorum Scriptorum ordinem esse jubent! Hic vero mirari subit Nicetæ Pectorati; & aliorum siqui sint ex recentibus Græcis, temeritatem atque impudentiam: qui quas ipsorum Patres in celeberrima hac & apud eos receptissima Synodo Trullana, tam aperte rejiciunt
units.tr: Κλήμεντος διαλάξεις πάλαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἑτεροδόξων ἐν λύμῃ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας νόθα τινὰ ἢ ξένα τῆς ἐυσεβείας παρεισηχθέντα, τὸ ἐυαρεστες καλλίῳ τῶν θείων δογμάτων ἡμῖν ἀμαυρώσαντα, τῶν τοιούτων διατάξεων προσφόρως ἀποβολῇ πεποιήμεθα πρὸς τὴν τε χριστιανικωτάτην σαιμυίαν οἰκονομίαν καὶ ἀσφάλειαν, ἐδαμῶς ἐγκείνοντες τὰ τῆς αἱρετικῆς ψευδολογίας κυήματα, ἢ τὴν γνῶσιν τῶν ἀποστόλων ὁ ὁλοκλήρῳ διδαχῇ παρεισφέροντες.] These Constitutions of the Apostles, attributed to Clement, were long ago introduced by men of other opinions to the defiling of the Church, as something spurious and foreign to piety, and they have obscured for us the pleasing and fair appearance of the divine decrees. We have fittingly rejected such Constitutions, for the building up and security of the most Christian flock, in no way admitting the offspring of heretical falsehood, and not inserting them into the whole and genuine teaching of the Apostles. Behold how highly the Greeks of old speak of these pseudo-diataxes: they expressly reject them and order that they be placed outside the order of ecclesiastical writers! Here, indeed, one is struck with wonder at Nicetas Pectoratus, and at any others among the recent Greeks, for their rashness and shamelessness: they praise and kiss

units.la: jiciunt Clementis Constitutiones,ipsi lau-dant, atque exosculantur, & Latinis velut legitima ac Canonica Apostolorum opera objectare non verentur. Nimirum unum causæ adversus Latinos studium eorum animos sic excæcavit, ut Patrum alioqui scitis addictissimi, hic ea secure negligant; & quæcunque sors obtulit, ea nullo discrimine in adversarios mittant. Hæc Humbertus Nicetæ Diataxes sibi objectanti reponere poterat; & fecisset haud dubie, si disputanti hic Trullanæ Synodi canon in mentem venijset.
units.tr: the Constitutions of Clement, which their own Fathers so openly reject in this most famous synod, so highly regarded among them, and they do not hesitate to throw them at the Latins as the lawful and canonical works of the Apostles. Surely the single zeal against the Latins has so blinded their minds that these men, otherwise most devoted to the opinions of the Fathers, here carelessly neglect them, and send whatever lot offers against their adversaries without distinction. Humbert could have answered this to Nicetas, who objected his Diataxis to him; and he would undoubtedly have done so, had the canon of the Trullan Synod come to mind while he was disputing.

units.la: Jam totis tribus sæculis, quæ a quarto sæculo jam affecto ad Trullanam Synodum fluxere, nemo Græcorum Patrum occurrit, qui Clementinas illas Constitutiones aliquacum laude vel nominaverit, si unum Epiphanium, qui a. D. 375. scripsisse perhibetur, exceperis. Is sane hujus operis aliquoties meminit. Nam hæresi xlv. hæc habet a: Αλλά γὰρ οἱ Ἀποστολοι φασὶν ἐν τῇ Διαταξέι τῇ καλουμένῃ, ὅτι φυλεία Θεοῦ ἡ ἀμπελων ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία. Quin & Apostoli in eo libro, qui Διάταξις, hoc est Constitutio vocatur, Dei stirpem ac vineam esse Catholicam Ecclesiam produnt. Hæc autem verba etiam in nostris, hoc est nostro tempore vulgatis Constitutionibus, in ipso operis limine occur-
units.tr: Now throughout the whole three centuries that ran from the fourth century, already spent, to the Trullan Synod, no Greek Father appears who named those Clementine Constitutions with any praise, if you except Epiphanius alone, who is said to have written in 375. He indeed mentions this work several times. For in heresy 45 he has: [Αλλά γὰρ οἱ Ἀποστολοι φασὶν ἐν τῇ Διαταξέι τῇ καλουμένῃ, ὅτι φυλεία Θεοῦ ἡ ἀμπελων ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία.] Indeed the Apostles, in that book which is called Diataxis, that is Constitution, declare that the Catholic Church is the stock of God and his vineyard. These words also occur in our present, that is, our present-day published Constitutions, at the very beginning of the work

units.la: a §.2. p. 390. a. occurrunt a ; Θεᾶ φυλεία ἡ καθολικὴ Ἐκκλη-σία & ἀμπιλὼν αὐτῆ ἐκλεκτὸς. Meminit & alibi contra Messalianos disputans b ; ἀλλὰ μὲν ἓν τῇ ἡμέᾳ (inquit) ἐν ᾗ Διαλάξει τῶν Ἀποςτόλων φάσκει ὁ Θεῖος λόγος καὶ ἡ ςι-σκαλία, μὴ φθείρειν· τετέςι μὴ τέμνειν τρίχας γενείς, μηδὲ ἐταιρισμῷ καταςκοσμεῖ-σθαι, μηδὲ ὑπηρεσίας ὑπόδειγμα δικαιο-σύνης τὸ προςέλυσιν ἔχειν. Atqui quod ad barbam attinet, in Apostolorum Constitu-tionibus divino sermone ac dogmate prae-scribitur, ne ea corrumpatur; hoc est, ne barba ponatur neve meretricius cultus & ornatus usurpetur; ac ne per arrogantiam & fastum affectata quaedam justitiae species in congressu, ac consuetudine praeferatur. Hæc Epiphanius; quorum aliquid simile etiam hodie in vulgatis Constitutionibus legitur; quo loco postquam nimium capillorum cultum, totiusque vestis impen-siorem ornatum viris author ille prohibuit, eaque omnia ἐταιρισμῷ τιμωρεία ὑπάρχειν, meretricia consuetudinis indicia esse dixit c, mox hæc quoque de barba adjicit; ἀγὴ ὃ ἀδὲ γενείς τρίχα διαφθείρειν, καὶ τὸν μορφὴν τῆς ἀνθρώπου προς φύσιν ἐξαλλάττειν. Sed neque barbam corrumpere decet, neque formam hominis contra naturam immutare. Alibi contra Aerium de Pascha te disputans a ; Εἰ ὃ ἐξ ἀγὴ (inquit) τὸ τῆς διατάξεως τάξεως. {a} Har. 75. §.6. p.910. b.c
units.tr: (a §2, p. 390 a) [Θεᾶ φυλεία ἡ καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία & ἀμπιλὼν αὐτῆ ἐκλεκτὸς]. He mentions it also elsewhere, when disputing against the Messalians: [ἀλλὰ μὲν ἓν τῇ ἡμέᾳ ἐν ᾗ Διαλάξει τῶν Ἀποςτόλων φάσκει ὁ Θεῖος λόγος καὶ ἡ ςισκαλία, μὴ φθείρειν· τετέςι μὴ τέμνειν τρίχας γενείς, μηδὲ ἐταιρισμῷ καταςκοσμεῖσθαι, μηδὲ ὑπηρεσίας ὑπόδειγμα δικαιοσύνης τὸ προςέλυσιν ἔχειν.] But as for the beard, in the Constitutions of the Apostles the divine word and doctrine prescribe that it must not be corrupted; that is, that the beard must not be cut, nor adorned with meretricious ornament, nor the appearance of righteousness, affected through arrogance and pride, be displayed in company and intercourse. These are the words of Epiphanius. Something similar is read today also in the Constitutions in circulation, where, after the author has forbidden men an excessive care of the hair and a costly ornament of the whole dress, and has said that all these are signs of harlot-like habit, he adds this also about the beard: [ἀγὴ ὃ ἀδὲ γενείς τρίχα διαφθείρειν, καὶ τὸν μορφὴν τῆς ἀνθρώπου προς φύσιν ἐξαλλάττειν.] But neither is it fitting to corrupt the beard, nor to change the form of the man contrary to nature. Elsewhere, disputing against Aerius about Easter, he says: [Εἰ ὃ ἐξ ἀγὴ (inquit) τὸ τῆς διατάξεως τάξεως.] (a Haer. 75, §6, p. 910 b, c)

units.la: τάξεως τῶν Ἀποστόλων λέγειν, πως ἐκεῖ ᾠκεί- ζοιτο τετράδα, ἢ προσάδεσθαι ὑπηρεσίαν ὁμ- ταυλὸς, χωρὶς Πεντηκοστῆς· καὶ περὶ τῶν ἐξ ἡμέρων τὸ Πάσχα, πως παραγγέλλεσι, μὴ- δὲν ὅλως λαμβάνειν, ἡ ἄρτε, καὶ ἁλὸς, καὶ ὕδατ᾽ ; ποιάντε ἡμέραν ἄγειν, πως τε ἀπο- λύειν ἐς ἐπιφώσκουσαν κυριακὴν, φανερὸν ἐστι.
units.tr: [τάξεως τῶν Ἀποστόλων λέγειν, πως ἐκεῖ οἰκείζοιτο τετράδα, ἢ προσάδεσθαι ὑπηρεσίαν ὁμταυλὸς, χωρὶς Πεντηκοστῆς· καὶ περὶ τῶν ἐξ ἡμέρων τὸ Πάσχα, πως παραγγέλλεσι, μηδὲν ὅλως λαμβάνειν, ἢ ἄρτε, καὶ ἁλὸς, καὶ ὕδατ᾽· ποιάντε ἡμέραν ἄγειν, πως τε ἀπολύειν ἐς ἐπιφώσκουσαν κυριακὴν, φανερὸν ἐστι.] That is: if, as they say, the order of the Apostles, how is it there that the fourth day is kept, or that a common service is adopted apart from Pentecost; and concerning the six days of Easter, how do they command taking nothing at all but bread, salt and water; and how they keep the day and dismiss it into the dawning Lord's day, it is clear.

units.la: Quod si ex Apostolorum Constitutione repetenda nobis authoritas est, cur illis quarta sextaque feria jejunium perpetua lege sancitur, excepta Pentecoste? Cur sex Paschatis diebus nihil omnino ad cibum praeter panem, salem & aquam adhibendum definiunt? Quamnam vero celebrari diem, & in illucescentem Dominicam dimittere praecipiant, nemini esse potest obscurum. Haec autem de quartae sextaeque feriarum jejunio, deque Paschatis hebdomadis Xerophagjis decreta, etiam in nostris hodie Constitutionibus leguntur libro quinto, capitibus xiv & xviii.
units.tr: But if we must draw authority from the Apostles' Constitution, why is fasting on the fourth and sixth days enjoined by perpetual law there, Pentecost excepted? Why do they prescribe that on the six days of Easter nothing whatever is to be taken for food except bread, salt and water? What day is to be kept, and that it is to be dismissed into the dawning Lord's day, can be obscure to no one. These decrees about the fasting on the fourth and sixth days, and about the xerophagy in Easter week, are also read in our present Constitutions, in book five, chapters 14 and 18.

units.la: Sed insignis praeceteris est Epiphanii de Constitutionibus locus in haeresi Audianorum, quos ait suum de Paschate cum Judaeis celebrando errorem ex Apostolorum Constitutionibus confirmasse: Εἰς τοῦτο ὁ (inquit*) οἱ αὐτοὶ Audiani voi παραφέρεσι πῶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων διατάξιν, ὕσαν μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐν ἀμφιλέκτῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἀδήλιμον. πᾶσα γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ κανονικὴ τάξις ἐμφέρεταί, καὶ ὑδὲν παρακεχαραγμένον τῆς πίστεως.
units.tr: But Epiphanius's passage about the Constitutions in the heresy of the Audians is especially notable. He says that they confirmed their error of celebrating Easter with the Jews from the Apostles' Constitutions: [Εἰς τοῦτο ὁ (inquit) οἱ αὐτοὶ Audiani οἱ παραφέρεσι πῶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων διατάξιν, ὕσαν μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐν ἀμφιλέκτῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἀδήλιμον. πᾶσα γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ κανονικὴ τάξις ἐμφέρεταί, καὶ ὑδὲν παρακεχαραγμένον τῆς πίστεως.] To this end, the same Audians, he says, bring forward a passage of the Apostles' Constitution, which is indeed disputed by many, but not obscure. For the whole canonical order is contained in it, and nothing in it is corrupted of the faith.

units.la: * Apud Bovium 16. & 19. πίστεως, καὶ τῆς ὁμολογίας, καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς διοικήσεως, ἐκ κανόνων, καὶ πίστεως, τὸ ὃ ῥητὸν ἀφ᾽ ὧν λαμβάνοντες περὶ τὰ πάσχα κακῶς παρεξεμπνεύσαν οἱ προειρημένοι, ἐκ ἀγνοοῦντες ἑτέρως ὑπολαμβάνουσιν. Ὁρίζων γὰρ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ διατάξει οἱ Ἀπόστολοι, ὅτι ὑμεῖς μὴ ψηφίζητε, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖτε ὅταν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ὑμῶν οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς, μετ᾽ αὐτῶν ἅμα ποιεῖτε. Audiani vero ad institutum sunm quandam ex Apostolorum Constitutione authoritatem accommodant; qui liber tametsi dubia apud multos (τοῖς πολλοῖς, non apud nonnullos, quod habet Petavius) fidei sit, non est tamen improbandus. Nam in eo quae ad disciplinam Ecclesiae attinent omnia comprehenduntur; neque quicquam aut in fide ac Catholica professione depravatum, aut Ecclesiae administrationi, ac decretis contrarium continent. Sed quod ad locum illum attinet, unde suam de Paschate sententiam affirmare conantur, hunc illi perperam interpretantur, & ad alienum sensum per iscitiam traducunt. Etenim Apostoli in illa Constitutione ita definiunt; Vos, inquiunt, temporum rationes ne subducite; sed eo tempore celebrate, quo fratres vestri, qui ex Circumcisione prodierunt. Cum iis itaque Pascha peragite. Tum narrat Epiphanius post illam Apostolorum de Paschate Constitutionem, quindecim sedisse disse Hierosolymis è Circumcisione Episcopos; quorum authoritatem omnis (inquit) Christianus orbis sequi, & cum illis celebrare Pascha debuit; una ut omnium concordia, una professio, una celebritatis obeunda ratio ac consuetudo firmaretur. Quin & ait, Apostolos ipsos in illa sua Constitutione praecepisse, ut etiam errantes in Paschatis celebratione Hierosolymitanos caeteri Christiani nihilosecius sequerentur: ὅτι κἂν τε πλανῶνται (inquiunt) μηδὲν ὑμῖν μηλέτω, quamvis aberrent ipsi, nihil id vos commoveat. Nunc ex his Epiphanianis duo sunt observanda, quorum hoc quidem prius est, eas, quae Apostolorum nomine tunc extabant, Constitutiones, diversas ab iis fuisse, & quae nunc circumferuntur, & quae Trullanorum Patrum tempore prostabant. Illae enim Epiphanianae Apostolorum Constitutiones, nihil aut in fide, ac Catholica professione, depravatum, aut Ecclesiae administrationi ac decretis contrarium continebant. Contra vero, iis, quae sua memoria vulgo habebantur, Constitutionibus Trullani Patres affirmant, jam olim ab heterodoxis adulterina quaedam & a pietate aliena inducta esse, quae divinorum decretorum elegantem ac decoram speciem obscurarent. Photius vero eas itidem, quas legerat, Constitutiones Arianismi nisi purgari vix, ac ne vix quidem, posse, confitetur: quæ omnia iis quoque, quæ nunc circumferuntur, convenire, & liquet, & nos postea demonstrabimus: ut eas verisimillimum sit plane easdem cum illis esse, quas & Photius, & ante ipsum, Trullani Patres viderant; Utrasque autem ab Epiphanianis diversas esse, ex his, ut omnes intelligunt, necesse est. Sed & alio argumento, quod tum à Cardinali Perronio, tum etiam à Dionysio Petavio observatum est, clarissime probatur, nostras ab iis, quæ ab Epiphanio commemorantur, diversas esse. Nimirum quæ ex suis laudat, ac describit hoc loco Epiphanius, ea nusquam in nostris occurrunt; Imo vero (inquit Petavius) contraria quaedam in iis leguntur. Duas jam ex Epiphanio contra Audianos Constitutionum sententias exhibuimus; Apud eundem & hoc & sequenti numero hæ quoq; velut ex iisdem allatæ leguntur; hæc quidem τὸω ἀζυμιτῶν φέρειν μεταζόντων τῶν ἀζύμων, medio azymorum tempore perviligia obeunda. Numero vero sequenti, a hæ; Ὅταν ἐκεῖνοι (οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι) ἐυωχῶνται, ὑμεῖς νηστεύοντες ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν πινθέντε, ὅτι ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἑορτῆς τὸν Χειςὸν ἐςαύρωσαν. ἡμεῖς ὅταν αὐτοὶ πινθῶσι τὰ ἄζυμα ἐδιόντες ἐν πιπείσιν, ὑμεῖς ἐυωχεῖσθε. Dum epulantur illi (Iudæi) vos jejunantes C pro iis lugete, quoniam festo illo die Christum in crucem sustulerunt. Cumque illi lugentes azymis, & lactucis agrestibus vescantur, vos epulamini. Mox & hęc ex Diataxi affert Epiphanius: ὅτι ὁ κακῶν ἑαυτὸν τῷ ψυχῷ ἐν Κυριακῇ, ἐπικαταράτος ἐστὶ τῷ Θεῷ, Qui afflixerit animam suam Dominica die, maledictus est Deo. Hæ ergo quinq; sententiæ, quæ in Epiphanianis Constitutionibus extabant, nusquam in nostris hodie leguntur: imò vero quædam in iis leguntur, quæ cum prima & secunda ex illis sententiis obversa fronte pugnare videntur. Statuebant enim duæ illæ sententiæ, cum iis Christianis, qui ex circumcisione Hierosolymis erant, pascha celebrandum, adeoque cum Judæis, quorum illi diem celebrabant. Atqui plane contra scriscunt hodiernæ Constitutiones : Μηκέτι ὁ παγατηρούμενοι μετ' Ἰουδαίων ἑορτάζειν· ἐσχήκαμεν γὰρ κοινωνίαν ἡμῖν νῦν πρὸς αὐτούς. Neque amplius cum Judæis tempus celebrandi Pascha observetis. Nulla enim nobis nunc cum eis communio est. Hæc si in antiquis illis Constitutionibus legebantur, mirum est (inquit Petavius) hoc tam præsenti ac diserto testimonio usum non esse contra Audianos Epiphanium; qui Judæorum more celebrandum Pascha iisdem ex Constitutionibus affirmabant. Ex quibus concludit, aliud tum fuisse ConstiConstitutionum genus, quam quibus hodie Clementis nomen inscribitur. Unde porro manifestum est, nihil ad hodiernas Constitutiones ea pertinere, quae de suis illis Constitutionibus hic ait Epiphanius: quae scilicet aliae, quam nostrae erant; frustraque esse Bovium , qui hunc unum fere Epiphanii locum omnibus iis objicit, quae contra Constitutionum authoritatem afferuntur.
units.tr: * In Bovius, 16 and 19: [πίστεως, καὶ τῆς ὁμολογίας, καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς διοικήσεως, ἐκ κανόνων, καὶ πίστεως, τὸ ὃ ῥητὸν ἀφ᾽ ὧν λαμβάνοντες περὶ τὰ πάσχα κακῶς παρεξεμπνεύσαν οἱ προειρημένοι, ἐκ ἀγνοοῦντες ἑτέρως ὑπολαμβάνουσιν.] For the Apostles, ordaining in the same constitution, say: "You should not calculate, but act when your brethren of the circumcision act; do it together with them" [Ὁρίζων γὰρ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ διατάξει οἱ Ἀπόστολοι, ὅτι ὑμεῖς μὴ ψηφίζητε, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖτε ὅταν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ὑμῶν οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς, μετ᾽ αὐτῶν ἅμα ποιεῖτε]. The Audians, however, adapt to their own position an authority drawn from the Constitution of the Apostles. This book, although of doubtful faith to many (to the many, not to some, as Petavius has it), is nevertheless not to be rejected. For it contains everything that pertains to the discipline of the Church, and it contains nothing either corrupted in the faith and Catholic profession or contrary to the administration and decrees of the Church. But as for that passage from which they try to affirm their opinion about the Passover, they interpret it wrongly and, through ignorance, twist it to a meaning not its own. For the Apostles define as follows in that Constitution: "You," they say, "do not reckon the times; but celebrate at the time when your brethren who came out of the Circumcision celebrate. Therefore keep the Passover with them." Then Epiphanius relates that after that apostolic Constitution about the Passover, fifteen bishops from the Circumcision sat at Jerusalem. Whose authority (he says) the whole Christian world ought to follow, and with them to celebrate the Passover, so that one agreement, one profession, and one manner and custom of observing the festival might be established. Indeed he also says that the Apostles themselves, in that Constitution, commanded that the other Christians should follow the Jerusalemites even when they err in the celebration of the Passover: "Even if they err (they say), let nothing trouble you; although they go astray, let that not move you." Now from these words of Epiphanius two things are to be noted. The first is that the Constitutions which then went under the name of the Apostles were different both from those now in circulation and from those which existed in the time of the Trullan Fathers. For those Constitutions of Epiphanius contained nothing corrupted in the faith and Catholic profession, nothing contrary to the administration and decrees of the Church. On the other hand, the Trullan Fathers affirm that the Constitutions commonly held in their own time had long before been introduced by heterodox men, some of them adulterated and alien to piety, which obscured the elegant and proper appearance of the divine decrees. Photius likewise confesses that the Constitutions he had read were scarcely, if at all, purged of Arianism. It is clear, and we shall show later, that all these things apply also to those now in circulation. So it is very likely that they are plainly the same as those which both Photius and, before him, the Trullan Fathers had seen. And it is necessary, as everyone understands, that both sets be different from those of Epiphanius. But also by another argument, which has been noticed both by Cardinal Perron and by Denys Petavius, it is most clearly proved that our Constitutions differ from those which Epiphanius cites. Namely, the things Epiphanius quotes and describes from his own copies in this passage are nowhere found in ours. "Indeed," (says Petavius) "some contrary things are read in them." We have already set out two statements from the Constitutions against the Audians, taken from Epiphanius. In the same place, in this and the following section, these also are read as if taken from the same source: the first is to be observed with the unleavened bread during the middle of the days of unleavened bread (the vigils to be kept); the second, from the following section: "When those (the Jews) feast, you, fasting on their behalf, lament, because on that festival day they hanged Christ on the cross. And while they, lamenting, eat unleavened bread and wild lettuce, you feast." Epiphanius then also brings forward this from the Diataxis: "He who afflicts his soul on the Lord's day is accursed of God." These five statements, which stood in the Constitutions of Epiphanius, are nowhere read today in ours. Indeed, some things are read in them which seem to clash flatly with the first and second of those statements. For those two statements required that the Passover be celebrated with those Christians who were at Jerusalem from the circumcision, and so with the Jews, whose day they kept. Yet our present Constitutions write quite the contrary: "Do not observe the feast any longer with the Jews; for now we have no communion with them." If these things were read in those ancient Constitutions, it is strange (says Petavius) that Epiphanius did not use so clear and explicit a testimony against the Audians, who affirmed from those same Constitutions that the Passover was to be celebrated in the manner of the Jews. From this he concludes that the kind of Constitutions then in use was different from those which today bear the name of Clement. Hence it is further evident that those things which Epiphanius says here about his Constitutions have nothing to do with our present Constitutions, since they were plainly other than ours; and that Bovius is wrong in almost alone objecting this one passage of Epiphanius to all the arguments brought against the authority of the Constitutions.

units.la: Praeterea Apostolicae Epiphanii Διαταγαί quarta, sextaque feria, & Dominica Synaxes fieri praecipiebant. Tradit enim Epiphanius primo quidem in genere de quarta sextaque feria accurate in eo opere scripsisse Apostolos; tum alibi haec diserte habet; σωσάξεις ὁ (inquit c) ἐπιλελυμέναι τάξεις εἰσὶν ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, τετράδι, καὶ παρασκευῇ, καὶ Κυριακῇ. Sacri porro conventus & Synaxes ab Apostolis instituti sunt his diebus, quarta, sextaque feria, & Dominica. Nostrae vero, id est Bovianae Constitutiones, nihil hujusmodi continent; Dominicam quidem una cum istis sacris synaxibus dicant; caetera vero omnia diversa sunt. Nam conventibus Ecclesiasticis sabbatum consecrant d (de quo nihil Epiphaniani Apostoli) & quam hi in eum usum destinabant, quartam sextamque feriam, illi utramque jejunio determinant e; de synaxibus utraque illa feria faciendis, ne unum
units.tr: Moreover, Epiphanius's Apostolic Diataxeis ordered that synaxes be held on the fourth day, the sixth day, and the Lord's day. For Epiphanius first says in general that the Apostles wrote accurately about the fourth and sixth day in that work, and then states it clearly in another place: "The assemblies and synaxes which are appointed by the Apostles fall on these days: the fourth day, the sixth day, and the Lord's day." [σύναξεις... ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, τετράδι, καὶ παρασκευῇ, καὶ Κυριακῇ.] Our Constitutions, that is those of Bovius, contain nothing of this kind. They do name the Lord's day together with these sacred synaxes, but everything else is different. For they consecrate the Sabbath to ecclesiastical assemblies (about which the Apostles of Epiphanius say nothing), and they set apart both the fourth and sixth days, which the Epiphanian Apostles had appointed for that purpose, as days of fasting. As for the synaxes to be held on both those days, they do not write even one word about them.

units.la: unum quidem μυ̃ scribunt. Unde liquet (ut hoc obiter dicam) quam falso,quamq; inverecunde scripserit Turrianus a, tales habere nostram ætatem Apostolorum Constitutiones, sanas scilicet & incorruptas, quales Epiphanii ætas habuit. Sed & illud secundo observandum est, ne ipsas quidem Epiphanianas Diataxes hinc effici veras fuisse, vel pro Apostolicis ab illorum temporum Ecclesia habitas; nedum ut nostrarum, quæ ab illis omnino diversæ sunt, authoritas ex hoc loco constitui possit. Fatetur ipse Epiphanius, diserteque testatur, hanc à se memoratam, ab Audianis usurpatam Διάταξιν, id est, interprete Petavio, constitutionis, sive Constitutionum librum, fuisse τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐν ἀμφιλέκτῳ, dubiā apud multos fidei, controversæque authoritatis. Ergo vel ex ipso constat, non fuisse à Græca illius temporis (hoc est sæculi à Christo in terris nato quarti jam adulti) Ecclesia publice receptam Constitutionum istarum, qualescunque de cætero fuerint, scripturam; sed contra vulgo, & à compluribus rejectam, tanquam dubiam & incertam. Quod vel unum satis est ad convellendam omnem istius operis in rebus ad fidem pertinentibus authoritatem. Quis enim pro veris ac genuinis Apostolorum libris nunc sibi obtrudi trudi patiatur, quos multos quidem quarti sæculi Christianos in Ecclesia Græca velut spurios & supposititios abjecisse constat? Ullos pro veris habuisse non constat? Epiphanium quidem eos tribus quatuorve locis usurpasse concedo; eo fieri, ut pro vere Apostolicis habuerit, nego. Hoc quidem contra Audianos loco, qui omnium est luculentissimus, Constitutionum opus negat esse ἀδόκιμον, reprobum, sive reprobatum, hoc est, ut ego quidem interpretor, publico Ecclesiæ decreto rejectum & explosum. Laudat item, quod in eo contineretur omnis ordo canonicus, nihil inesset vel à fide vel à disciplina Ecclesiæ alienum. At non ideo fit, ut libros à Clemente vere scriptos, vereque ab Apostolis instituta dictataque, quæcunque in illis narrantur, fuisse crediderit. Multis enim libris nihil inest vel à fide, vel à disciplina Ecclesiæ alienum, quos non idcirco dixeris vel Clementinos, vel Apostolicos. Omnino videtur Epiphanius sensisse, illas Apostolorum nomine tum vulgatas Diataxes boni & Catholici viri opus esse non inutile; iisque sincere explicatam esse Ecclesiæ fidem, ac disciplinam; Ut à Clemente scriptas, & ab ipsis Apostolis dictatas crediderit, nihil sane cogit. Contrarium suadet, quod idem alibi de hujus, quem citaverat, libri authoribus,
units.tr: They do not write even one word. From this it is clear (to say this in passing) how falsely and how shamelessly Turrianus wrote that our age has such Apostolic Constitutions, sound and uncorrupted, as the age of Epiphanius had. But it must also be noted in the second place that not even the Epiphanian Diataxeis can be shown from this passage to have been genuine, or to have been held as Apostolic by the Church of those times; much less can the authority of ours, which are wholly different from those, be established from this passage. Epiphanius himself admits and plainly testifies that this Diataxis which he mentions, used by the Audians (that is, as Petavius interprets, the book of Constitutions), was among many of doubtful faith and of disputed authority. So it is clear from this very fact that the Greek Church of that time (that is, of the fourth century now grown up since Christ was born on earth) did not publicly receive that writing of Constitutions, whatever it may have been otherwise, but on the contrary was generally, and by many, rejected as doubtful and uncertain. This alone is enough to overthrow the entire authority of that work in matters pertaining to faith. For who would allow himself now to be forced to accept as true and genuine books of the Apostles those which many Christians of the fourth century in the Greek Church are known to have cast aside as spurious and supposititious? That they ever held any of them to be true is not established. I grant that Epiphanius used them in three or four places; but that he held them to be truly Apostolic, I deny. In this passage against the Audians, which is the clearest of all, he says that the work of the Constitutions is not reprobatum (rejected), that is, as I understand it, cast out and rejected by a public decree of the Church. He also praises it because all the canonical order is contained in it, and there is nothing in it alien either to faith or to the discipline of the Church. But it does not follow from this that he believed the books to have been truly written by Clement, and that whatever is narrated in them was truly instituted and dictated by the Apostles themselves. For many books contain nothing alien either to faith or to the discipline of the Church, and yet one would not for that reason call them Clementine or Apostolic. Epiphanius seems to have judged that those Diataxeis, then circulating under the name of the Apostles, were the work of a good and Catholic man, not useless, and that the faith and discipline of the Church were sincerely set out in them. That he believed them written by Clement and dictated by the Apostles themselves he certainly does not force us to think. What he says elsewhere about the authors of this book which he had cited points the other way, since he speaks of them as apparently

units.la: ribus,ut videtur, loquens, eos ait {a} ait, πρὸ ἡ-μῶν μαρτυρας γενομένας, ἔχοντας πρὸ ἡμῶν ἐν παραδόσιν ἐν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τούτους παρειληφότας ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν πατέρων, τῶν τε αὐτῶν πατέρων πάλιν μεταδηκότων ἐκ τῶν πρὸ αὐτῶν γεγονότων,ante nos testes extitisse, habentes ante nos traditionem in Ecclesia, quam & ipsi à parentibus suis acceperant, & ipsorum parentes à majoribus suis didicerant. Hæc profecto neque Apostolis, neque Clementi ipsi conveniunt; qui quæ in Ecclesia instituerunt, non à parentibus, vel ab avis, sed Apostoli quidem à Christo, Clemens vero ab Apostolis, acceperant. Sed concedamus tamen, vel certe donemus, fuisse in ea sententia Epiphanium, ut existimaverit, suarum illarum Diataxeon verè authores, scriptoresque fuisse Apostolos, quorum nomen præferebant; non ideo consecteris, vel id verum esse, vel saltem idem sensisse Græcam illius temporis Ecclesiam. Ipse tradit, multos de illo Constitutionum opere dubitasse. Si authores numeres, iniquum est unum multis præferri. Si sententias expendas, haud obscurum est, illos plures merito de hoc opere dubitasse; Epiphanium sequiora hic, ut sæpe alibi secutum; sive judicii infirmitate, quadamque naturæ simplicitate, ac facilitate, sive rerum veterum ignoratione decedeceptum, sive denique, quod rem minus attente, neq; ea qua par erat diligentia considerasset; quod illi haud paucis locis accidit. Quæso enim ea ipsa quæ ille ex istis, quæ tum circumferebantur, Constitutionibus attulit, paulisper intueamur, ac expendamus, an talia sint, quæ Apostolorum nomen tueri & sustinere possint. Facile deprehendemus, nihil pæne in iis ipsis reperiri, quod non Epiphanium fraudis monere debuerit; docereque, nunquam ista ab Apostolis, quorum nomen mentiebantur, fuisse profecta. Quale est, verbi gratia, quod iste Audianis concedit, fuisse ab Apostolis ex isto Diataxeon volumine decretum, ac constitutum de Paschate cum iis, qui ex circumcisione erant, celebrando? Audi Petavium de eo ipso cum Epiphanio suo haud sane timide, sed ut solet, libere ac fortiter litigantem; Falsum est (inquit a) de-crevisse unquam Apostolos, ut Judaico ritu Pascha celebraretur; aut cum iis etiam Christianis, atque Episcopis, qui Judaice, ac minime legitimo tempore fungerentur. Qua enim est ista ratio: aut quid in mentem Epiphanio venit, ut ab Apostolis constitutum istud assereret; oportere Christianos omnes ac τ πάντα κόσμον cum recutitis Pascha facere? Nimis hoc absurdum decretum fuisset. Non negamus aliquot saltem Apostolos
units.tr: ...the witnesses who came before us, having before us the tradition in the Church, and having received it from their own fathers, and those fathers having in turn handed it down from those who came before them [ἀρχὴ ἡ-μῶν μαρτυρας γενομένας, ἔχοντας πρὸ ἡμῶν ἐν παραδόσιν ἐν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τούτους παρειληφότας ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν πατέρων, τῶν τε αὐτῶν πατέρων πάλιν μεταδηκότων ἐκ τῶν πρὸ αὐτῶν γεγονότων]: they had witnesses before us, had the tradition in the Church before us, which they themselves had received from their parents, and which their parents had learned from their ancestors. These words do not really suit the Apostles or Clement himself, who received what they established in the Church not from parents or grandparents, but the Apostles from Christ and Clement from the Apostles. But let us concede, or at least grant, that Epiphanius held the view that those Constitutions bearing the name of the Apostles were truly the work of the Apostles whose name they carried. Even so, you should not infer from this that the claim is true, or at least that the Greek Church of that time held the same view. He himself tells us that many doubted the authenticity of that work of the Constitutions. If you count authorities, it is unfair to set one man against many. If you weigh their judgments, it is plain that those many had good reason to doubt this work. Here Epiphanius, as he often does elsewhere, followed the weaker view, whether through weakness of judgment and a certain simplicity and credulity of nature, or through ignorance of ancient affairs, or finally because he treated the matter carelessly and did not give it the attention it deserved, as happened to him in not a few places. Let us now look briefly at the very things he drew from those Constitutions that were then in circulation, and weigh whether they are the sort of thing that could uphold and sustain the Apostles' name. We will easily find that almost nothing in them can be found that should not have warned Epiphanius of a fraud, and shown him that these things never came from the Apostles whose name they falsely bore. Take, for example, what he grants to Audianus: that the Apostles in that volume of Constitutions decreed and laid down that the Passover was to be celebrated with those who were of the circumcision. Hear Petavius, who disputes with his Epiphanius on this very point, not timidly but, as is his habit, freely and boldly: It is false (says he, a) that the Apostles ever decreed that the Passover be celebrated in the Jewish manner, or with those Christians and bishops who acted in a Jewish way and at a wholly improper time. For what kind of reasoning is this? Or what came into Epiphanius's mind, that he would assert that this was established by the Apostles, that all Christians throughout the world should keep the Passover with the circumcised? That decree would have been far too absurd. We do not deny that at least some of the Apostles at first accommodated themselves to the Jews' time. Polycarp, John, and Polycrates, and all the Asians, used to plead this against the Roman bishops, as Eusebius and other ancient writers attest. But we deny altogether that this was settled by any constitution of the Apostles. Indeed, the opposite is clearly what was handed down by those same Apostles. Eusebius mentions this tradition in book 5, chapter 23 of his History. For after saying that the Asians, from an ancient tradition, kept the Passover in the Jewish manner on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it fell on, he adds shortly after that in all the other churches throughout the world the custom was contrary, [ἐξ Αποστολικῆς παραδόσεως] from Apostolic tradition. So far Petavius. If you believe him, this single constitution about the Passover, wholly and utterly foreign to the Apostles, ought to have convinced Epiphanius that the book which laid down such absurd laws, abhorrent to all truth, was anything but Apostolic. And I, indeed, gladly agree with the most learned Jesuit that the Lord Christ's Apostles never decreed or commanded that Christians should keep the Passover together with the Jews. For this is strongly at odds both with the character of the Gospel and with the whole history of the first Church. As for his further claim that the Apostles handed down that Christians should celebrate the Passover otherwise, namely in that manner and rite which Victor, bishop of Rome, wished to enforce, and which was afterwards widely received on the authority of the Council of Nicaea, I, for my part, would not easily be persuaded of this, nor would anyone else. I should rather agree with Socrates and Nicephorus that neither Christ nor the Apostles laid down any law about this feast [τούτης νομοθετῆσαι τῆς ἑορτῆς], this festival; that people took up its observance of their own accord, as they did with the other feasts, and gradually strengthened it by custom; and that it came about that it was celebrated differently by different people. From this arose that serious controversy between the Asians and the rest, while each side kept the custom it had received from its own people and thought it should be preferred to the other's rite. In this sense that phrase in Eusebius, "ancient and Apostolic tradition" [ἀρχαίας & Ἀποστολικῆς παραδόσεως], must be interpreted, according to the mind of the contenders and not the truth of the matter itself. Clearly the Asians called their own tradition "ancient," and the others called theirs "Apostolic." It seems the Asians also boasted of their own tradition as Apostolic, just as the others did. Certainly Polycrates, who pleads the Asians' cause in Eusebius, relies on the examples of the Apostles too, namely Philip and John. But this is by the way. I return to Epiphanius, who, had he applied his mind and paid somewhat closer attention to the events in the Church before his time, could not have doubted that the Constitution which Audianus praised under the Apostles' name was utterly spurious, false, and counterfeit [ἀδόκιμος].

units.la: a Not. ad hær. 70. ad num. 10. p. 291. stolos initio ad Iudæorum se tempus accommodasse: quod de Ioanne Polycarpus, & Polycrates, Asiaticique omnes contra Romanos Pontifices excipere solebant; ut Eusebius, aliique veteres testantur. Verum id nulla Constitutione definitum ab Apostolis, negamus omnino. Quin potius contrarium ab iisdem illis constat fuisse traditum. Cujus παραδόσεως meminit Eusebius L. V. hist. C. XXIII. Nam cum dixisset Asianos ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀρχαίας XIV luna Iudaico more Pascha peregisse, οποίᾳ ἂν ἡ-μέρᾳ τῆς ἐβδομάδος περιλυγχάνοι, Subdit mox, in cæteris omnibus per orbem Ecclesiis ἐξ Αποστολικῆς παραδόσεως contrariam suis-se consuetudinem. Hactenus Petavius: cui si credis, vel una hæc de Paschate Constitutio, plane penitusque ab Apostolis aliena, persuadere debuit Epiphanio, nihil minus quam Apostolicum esse eum codicem, qui leges ferret adeo absurdas, & à veritate omni abhorrentes. Atque ego quidem doctissimo Iesuitæ libens assentior, nunquam decretum præceptumve fuisse à Domini Christi Apostolis, ut Pascha Christiani una cum Iudæis celebrarent; Id enim & ab Euangelii ingenio, & ab omni primæ Ecclesiæ historia vehementer alienum est. Illud quod addit traditum fuisse ab Apostolis, ut aliter Christiani Pascha celebrarent, eo nimirum nimirum more rituque: quem Victor Romæ Episcopus obtinere voluit, quique diu postea ex Nicenæ Synodi authoritate pene apud omnes receptus est; id, inquam, neque ipse sane, neq; quisquam alius facile mihi persuaserit. Verius cum Socrate & Nicephoro putaverim, neque Christum, neque Apostolos quicquam τούτης νομοθετῆσαι τῆς ἑορτῆς, de hoc festo lege constituisse: ejus ut cæterorum festorum observationem homines sponte sumpsisse, usuque suo paulatim confirmasse; eoque factum esse, ut diversa apud diversos ejus celebratio esset: unde porro exorta est gravis illa inter Asiaticos, & cæteros, controversia, dum quisque morem à suis acceptum retinet, & diverso aliorum ritui præferendum putat. Quo sensu interpretanda est illa & ἀρχαίας & Ἀποστολικῆς παραδόσεως vox apud Eusebium, ex contendentium mente, non ex rei ipsius veritate. Nimirum & suam Asiatici veterem, & suam alii Αποστολικὴν traditionem vocabant; & videntur Asiatici suam Apostolicam quoque, perinde ut alii, jactasse. Certe qui eorum causam apud Eusebium agit Polycrates, Apostolorum quoque exemplis nititur, Philippi scilicet & Joannis. Sed hæc obiter. Redeo ad Epiphanium, qui si mentem intendere, & ad res ante se in Ecclesia gestas
units.tr: a Not. ad hær. 70. ad num. 10. p. 291. The Apostles at first accommodated themselves to the time of the Jews. This is what Polycarp and Polycrates, and all the Asians, used to allege against the Roman bishops, as Eusebius and other ancient writers attest. But that this was ever prescribed by any ordinance of the Apostles I deny altogether. Rather, the contrary is plainly recorded as having been handed down by those same Apostles. Eusebius mentions this tradition in Book V, chapter 23 of his History. When he has said that the Asians, from an ancient tradition [ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀρχαίας], kept the Passover in the Jewish manner on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it fell on, he adds straightway that in all the other churches throughout the world their custom was the opposite, [handed down] from the apostolic tradition [ἐξ Ἀποστολικῆς παραδόσεως]. So far Petavius. If you believe him, this one ordinance about the Passover, utterly and entirely foreign to the Apostles, ought to have convinced Epiphanius that the code which laid down such absurd laws, so far removed from the truth, was by no means apostolic. For my part I gladly agree with that most learned Jesuit that the Lord Christ's Apostles never decreed or commanded that Christians should keep the Passover together with the Jews. For this is wholly alien both to the spirit of the Gospel and to the whole history of the earliest Church. As for what he adds, that the Apostles handed down that Christians should keep the Passover in another way, namely in that manner and rite which Victor, bishop of Rome, wished to enforce, and which for a long time afterwards was almost universally received on the authority of the Synod of Nicaea: this, I say, neither he himself nor anyone else will easily persuade me. I would rather think, with Socrates and Nicephorus, that neither Christ nor the Apostles laid down any law [τούτης νομοθετῆσαι τῆς ἑορτῆς] about this feast; that people took up the observance of it of their own accord, as of the other feasts, and gradually confirmed it by their practice; and that it came about that its celebration differed among different people. From this there further arose that serious controversy between the Asians and the rest, while each party kept the custom received from its own people and thought it should be preferred to the rite of the others. In this sense that phrase "ancient and apostolic tradition" [ἀρχαίας & Ἀποστολικῆς παραδόσεως] in Eusebius must be interpreted, according to the mind of the disputants, not according to the truth of the matter itself. Clearly the Asians called their own practice "ancient" (veterem), and the others called theirs "apostolic" [Ἀποστολικὴν]; and the Asians seem to have boasted of their own tradition as apostolic too, just as the others did. Certainly Polycrates, who pleads their cause in Eusebius, relies also on the examples of the Apostles, namely Philip and John. But this in passing. I return to Epiphanius, who, if he had been willing to attend more carefully to the intention and to what had been done in the Church before his time, could not have doubted that the constitution which the Audians praised under the name of the Apostles was plainly spurious, false and counterfeit.

units.la: a hist. l. 5. c. 22. b l. 12. c. 32. extr. gestas animum paulo diligentius advertere voluisset, dubitare non potuit, quin plane ἀδόκιμος, falsa ac adulterina esset illa Constitutio, quæ ab Audianis Apostolorum nomine laudabatur. Is enim ignorare non potuit, quod est in veteri primæ Ecclesiæ historia testatissimum, Pascha aliter, atque aliter celebrasse vetustissimos secundi sæculi Christianos; Asianos quidem cum Iudæis, quarta decima luna, in quamcunque hebdomadis feriam incideret; aliter cæteros, qui alia quam Dominica die solvere jejunia absurdum & indecorum putabant. Neque inter plebes, aut plebeios tantum, verum etiam inter spectatissimos, probatissimosque Episcopos, id observationis discrimen locum habuisse; quales, verbi gratia, fuere Polycarpus & Anicetus, ille Smyrnæ, hic Romæ Episcopus. Cum enim Polycarpus Romam venisset, & Anicetum, qui tum urbis Ecclesiæ præerat, officii causa invisisset circa secundi à Christo nato sæculi annum 60 (præfuit enim Anicetus circiter hæc tempora) amantissimus quidem, ac suavissimus, Christianæque charitatis plenus fuit summorum præstantissimorumque virorum congressus; cæterum neque Anicetus Polycarpo persuadere potuit, ut à servato hactenus Asiaticorum in Pascha celebrando usu discedere. cederet ; neque Polycarpus Aniceto, ut acceptam à suis decessoribus consuetudinem mutaret. Sed omnis illa contentio intra verba stetit, & quidem amicissima; neutro se à fratris communione ob hanc ritus diversitatem abrumpente, aut reji-ciente,ut est ab Eusebio a ex praeclara qua- dam Irenaei ad Victorem urbis Episcopum epistola traditum. Neque tu hos solos fuisse putes qui dissenserint. Utrumque & viri sanctissimi, & Ecclesiae multae magnaque magno studio sequebantur. Iam dic mihi, Epiphani, si quod tu vis, Apostoli totam hanc litem suo decreto ab ipsis Christianismi incunabulis definiverant; si legem qua quid esset agendum, clare exsertequae edixerant, vel Clemens, vel ipsi in publicas tabulas relatam Ecclesiae tradiderant; putas-ne fieri potuisse, ut eam viri excellentissimi, aevo Apostolico proximi, adhuc incomparabilis in rem Christianam zeli, & quidem hujusmodi, qui plerique martyrio postea functi sunt, vel ignoraverant, vel cognitam negligerent? Anicetus scilicet, & Irenaeus, & omnes, quod ait Eusebius, praeter Asiaticos, Christiani vel quid statuissent Apostoli, nuper e terris ad superos translati, nescierunt; vel quod ab iis decretum sciebant, contemserunt! Sed Epiphanius, multo etiam in Victorem, quam in cæteros, contumeliosior est; quem fingit Apostolicæ legis usq; adeo vel ignarû, vel despectorem fuisse, ut non modo eam ipse, quod majores quoque peccaverant, calcare & negligere auderet; sed ultra etiam provectus, Asiaticos, quod eam accurate arcteque servarent, pulsandos & excommunicandos putaret. Scilicet Apostolicus præsul, vir spiritus in martyrium suffecturi, fratres Apostolis obsequentes ferre non potuit! & summa apud Ecclesias pœna dignos censuit, qui legem ab Apostolis latam, à suo Clemente scriptam ac publicatam, religiose servassent! Sed ut Victorem impium; ita & Polycarpum, & Polycratem, aliosque Asiaticos stultos ac bardos facit hæc Epiphanii hypothesis. Nam si, quod hic statuit, Apostolorum lex scripta extabat, diversis verbis edicens Pascha cum Iudæis celebrandum; illos sane stultissimos fuisse necesse est, qui de hoc à Romanis pulsati non suum illis Clementem statim regessèrunt, Apostolorumque traditas ab eo leges in medium attulerunt. Obvia hæc erat, facilis, ac expedita istorum defensio, Se id sequi, quod Apostoli, uni nostræ disciplinæ duces, non modo fecerant, sed & aliis lata lege faciendum edixerant, quodque ipse Clemens Romanorum antiquissimus ac laudatissimus Episcopus, ab Apostolis stolis præceptum testaretur; se adeo insontes, qui legi Apostolicæ obsequantur; Romanos, qui accusant, reos manifestosq; gravis criminis esse, qui & ab Apostolis latam, & a suo authore descriptam legem spernant. Atqui his, quæ etiam infans ad Asiaticorum causam defendendam dicturus fuit, non Polycarpus apud Anicetum, non Polycrates apud Victorem usus fuit. Uterque Ioannem & alios Apostolos ita observasse ait: neuter lege lata præcepisse memorat. Utriusq; enim extat apud Irenæum defensio; in qua Polycarpus simpliciter ac in genere casatur, se Pascha ita observare a, μετὰ Ιωάννε τὸ μαθητὴ τε Κυρίε ἡμῶν, & τῶν λοιπῶν Ἀποστόλων, οἷς συνδιέτριψεν, cum Ioanne Domini nostri discipulo, & reliquis Apostolis, quibuscum conversatus erat. Polycrates b vero, Ephesi Episcopus, eadem latius exsequitur; Ut ipse & Asiatici observabant, ita quoque Philippum observasse, unum ex duodecim; ita observasse tres Philippi filias virgines, singularis sanctimoniæ fœminas: ita observasse & Ioan. Apostolum, & Polycarpum Smyrnæ Episcopū, Christi martyrē, & Thraseam de Eumenia Episcopum itidem & Martyrem, & Sagarim ejusdem dignitatis ac gloriæ virum, & beatum Papyrium, & Melitonem Sardensem: quæ apud Hieronymum quoque habentur
units.tr: a hist. l. 5. c. 22. b l. 12. c. 32. extr. For he could not have been ignorant of what is most abundantly attested in the old history of the earliest Church: that the very ancient Christians of the second century did not keep the Passover in one way. The Asians kept it with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it fell on; the others, who thought it absurd and improper to end their fasts on any day other than the Lord's Day, kept it differently. Nor was this difference of observance confined to the common people or to ordinary persons; it was found also among the most distinguished and most approved bishops, such as, for example, Polycarp and Anicetus, the one at Smyrna, the other at Rome. For when Polycarp came to Rome, and visited Anicetus, who then presided over the church of the city, out of duty, about the year 60 of the second century after Christ's birth (for Anicetus flourished about that time), the meeting of these most eminent and outstanding men was full of the warmest affection and the sweetest Christian charity. Yet Anicetus could not persuade Polycarp to give up the custom of the Asians, which had been kept until then in keeping the Passover; nor could Polycarp persuade Anicetus to change the custom he had received from his predecessors. But the whole dispute stayed within words, and indeed on the most friendly terms: neither broke off fellowship with the other or rejected him over this difference of rite. This is recorded by Eusebius from a notable letter of Irenaeus to Victor, bishop of the city. Nor should you think that these were the only ones who differed. Both sides were followed by most holy men and by many and great churches with great zeal. Now tell me, Epiphanius: if the Apostles had settled this whole quarrel by their decree from the very beginnings of Christianity; if they had clearly and expressly issued a law stating what was to be done, and either Clement or the Apostles themselves had handed it down to the Church, written into the public records; do you think it could have happened that such excellent men, close to the Apostolic age, still of unmatched zeal for the Christian cause, most of whom afterwards suffered martyrdom, either did not know of it or knew of it and neglected it? Surely Anicetus, and Irenaeus, and all the Christians except the Asians, as Eusebius says, either did not know what the Apostles, lately translated from earth to heaven, had decreed, or, knowing what had been decreed by them, despised it! But Epiphanius is much more insulting towards Victor than towards the others. He imagines that Victor was so ignorant of, or so contemptuous of, the apostolic law that he not only dared to trample on it and neglect it himself, as his predecessors had also sinned, but went further and thought the Asians, because they observed it carefully and strictly, should be struck and excommunicated. Clearly the apostolic bishop, a man of the spirit destined for martyrdom, could not bear brethren who obeyed the Apostles! And he judged those who religiously kept a law issued by the Apostles and written and published by his own Clement worthy of the severest punishment in the churches! But this hypothesis of Epiphanius makes not only Victor impious, but also Polycarp, Polycrates and the other Asians foolish and stupid. For if, as he holds, a written law of the Apostles existed, ordering in different words that the Passover be kept with the Jews, then those men must surely have been most foolish who, when pressed by the Romans on this matter, did not at once throw back to them their own Clement and bring forward the laws handed down by him from the Apostles. Their defence was ready to hand, easy and simple: "We follow what the Apostles, the sole leaders of our discipline, not only did but also commanded others to do by a law they issued; and what Clement himself, the most ancient and most praised bishop of the Romans, testifies was enjoined by the Apostles. Thus we are blameless, since we obey the apostolic law; and it is you Romans who accuse us who are manifestly guilty of a grave crime, since you despise a law issued by the Apostles and written down by your own author." Yet neither Polycarp before Anicetus nor Polycrates before Victor used any such argument, which even an infant could have put forward in defence of the Asian cause. Each says that John and the other Apostles observed it in this way; neither records that a law had been laid down ordering it. For Polycarp's defence survives in Irenaeus, in which he simply and in general states that he observes Easter in this way, "[with John the disciple of our Lord, and the rest of the Apostles, with whom he associated]" [μετὰ Ἰωάννου τοῦ μαθητοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν Ἀποστόλων, οἷς συνδιέτριψεν]. But Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, sets out the same things more fully: that, as he and the Asians observed it, so Philip, one of the twelve, had observed it too; that three virgin daughters of Philip, women of singular holiness, had observed it; that the apostle John, Polycarp bishop of Smyrna, a martyr of Christ, Thraseas bishop and martyr of Eumenia likewise, Sagaris, a man of the same dignity and glory, the blessed Papirius, and Melito of Sardis had observed it as well. These things are also found in Jerome.

units.la: bentur a. Horum omnium Asiani usum, nullius scriptam legem afferunt. Ergo nulla fuit quam afferrent, quam utique non erant omissuri, si fuisset aliqua. Ergo non Apostolorum, quod Epiphanius temere credidisse videtur, sed impostorum fuit illa ab Audianis objecta pro suo errore Διάταξις. Quid illam alteram dicam, quam ibidé paulo post recitat Epiphanius b, Qui afflixerit animam suam, hoc est, qui jejunaverit Dominica die, maledictus est Deo? Ego vero miror, ac, ut mihi quidem videtur, merito indignor, putasse Epiphanium tam stultam, tamque ab Evangelicae doctrinae genio alienam vocem sanctissimis Christi Apostolis excidere potuisse. Illine, qui passim dierum discrimina, planetariamque istam omnem certis temporibus affixorum rituum religionem sustulerunt, nunc repente mutati diris devovent, qui una ex hebdomadis feriis jejunaverit? Absit, ut cordatissimos viros tam puerililiter, mitissimos ac mansuetissimos tam atrociter ac immaniter de hominum factis judicasse, credamus. Atqui (siqua Hieronymo, viro & doctissimo, & Epiphanii amicissimo fides c) etiam Apostolus Paulus, & cum eo credentes, diebus Pentecostes, & die Dominico jejunarunt; idque in Actibus Apostolorum, haud paulo graviori libro,
units.tr: bentur a. The Asians allege the observance of all these things, but none of them cite any written law. So there was none they could cite, and they would certainly not have omitted it had there been one. Therefore that Diataxis [Διάταξις] which the Audians put forward for their error was not the work of the Apostles, as Epiphanius seems rashly to have believed, but of impostors. What shall I say of that other saying, which Epiphanius quotes a little later in the same place, Whoever afflicts his soul, that is, whoever fasts on the Lord's day, is accursed of God? I truly wonder, and as it seems to me rightly feel indignant, that Epiphanius could have thought such a foolish saying, so alien to the spirit of the gospel doctrine, could have fallen from the most holy Apostles of Christ. Did they, who everywhere removed the distinction of days and all that planetary superstition of rites attached to fixed times, suddenly change and curse with dire imprecations whoever fasted on one of the weekdays? Far be it that we should believe that they judged such upright men so childishly, and such gentle and meek men so savagely and monstrously for their deeds. And yet (if any credit is due to Jerome, a man both most learned and a very close friend of Epiphanius c) even the Apostle Paul, and those who believed with him, fasted on the days of Pentecost, and on the Lord's day; and this is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, a book by no means less weighty

units.la: c Ep. 28. ad Lucin. Baet. T. 1. sol. 69. b. bro, quam Constitutionum, legitur. Ergo-ne Paulus, ergo-ne ejus comites & discipuli ἐπικαλάςῳτοι Ἰωσ Θεῳ; Sane, si valet Epiphaniana Constitutio. Pereat vero quantumcunque est Clementinarum Constitutionum, potius quam tantum nefas vel in mentem vel in aures admittamus. Non devoverunt, non damnarunt Christi Apostoli quod fecit Paulus; quod fecerunt Pauli exemplo ejus comites. Hi autem die Dominico jejunarunt. Non ergo vere Dominici, sed straminei, fictitiique Apostoli sunt, qui maledictum Deo pronunciant, siquis die Dominica jejunaverit. Certe ne Bellarminus a quidem, quantumvis alioqui & Lunæ & Soli & diebus & elementis cum suis affixus, docet, nefas esse Dominico jejunare; sed quæ à Patribus in hunc sensum dicta videri possunt, ea ipse emollit, variisque adhibitis distinctionibus, ac cautionibus, interpretatur. Itaque vel ex hoc absurdo, ridiculoque decreto & nos discimus, & discere potuit Epiphanius, non fuisse Apostolicas illas, quæ ab Audianis obtrudebantur, Διαλάξεις Ejusdem est farinæ, quod alibi, ut supra diximus, recitat ex eodem codice decretum b, quo quarta sextaque feria jejunium perpetua lege sancitur, excepta Pentecoste. Item illud aliud, quo definitur sex Pascha-
units.tr: c Ep. 28. ad Lucin. Baet. T. 1. sol. 69. b. than the Constitutions. Then did Paul, and his companions and disciples, become accursed of God [ἐπικατάρατοι τῷ Θεῷ]? Certainly, if the Epiphanian Constitution holds, they did. But let the whole of the Clementine Constitutions perish rather than we admit so great an impiety either into our minds or into our ears. The Apostles of Christ did not condemn or curse what Paul did; his companions, following Paul's example, did it too. And they fasted on the Lord's day. Therefore those who pronounce a curse on whoever fasts on the Lord's day are not true Apostles of the Lord, but straw-men and fictitious ones. Certainly not even Bellarmine a, however much he is otherwise bound to the Moon, the Sun, the days and the elements, teaches that it is wrong to fast on the Lord's day; but the things the Fathers may seem to have said to this effect, he softens himself, and explains them by applying various distinctions and cautions. So from this absurd and ridiculous decree both we have learned, and Epiphanius could have learned, that those Apostolic Diataxeis which the Audians thrust upon them were not Apostolic. Of the same stamp is another decree, which he elsewhere, as we said above, quotes from the same code b, by which fasting on Wednesday and Friday is established by perpetual law, except at Pentecost. Likewise that other one, by which it is defined that six Pascha-

units.la: Paschatis diebus nihil omnino ad cibum praeter panem salem & aquam adhibendum. Scio, libensque confiteor, hos jejuniorum & Xerophagiarum per illos dies ritus veteres fuisse, & multis ante Epiphanium annis receptos : ab Apostolis fuisse traditos, vel, quod gravius etiam est, certa & inviolabili, eaque scripta lege praeceptos, ne hodierni quidem Romanae communionis Theologi dixerint; apud quos neque quartae feriae jejunium, neque severa illa antepaschalis hebdomadis Xerophagia vel omnibus praecipitur, vel in publico, communive multorum usu est; ut ipsos fateri necesse sit, vel spuriam falsamque esse hanc, quae ita praecipit, Epiphanianam Διάξιν, vel certe se suosque Pontifices a multis jam saeculis spretae violataeque Apostolicae disciplinae reos. Sed illi quidem viderint. Certe ex primaevo atque Apostolis proximo Ecclesiae monumentis discere, exploratequo ac certo cognoscere & nobis nunc licet, & Epiphanio olim eo etiam facilius, quam nobis, licuit, quo propius a veri fontibus abfuit, nihil unquam hujusmodi praecepisse Apostolos; falsam proinde, & Apostolis impudenter affictam esse eam, quae ista edicit, Constitutionem. Quod, quia eadem leges in nostris quoque Constitutionibus habentur, infra, cum de iis dicendum erit, clarissime elarissimè demonstraturos nos confidimus; ut nihil nunc quidem necesse sit in eo pro-bando immorari. Postremò ultimam il-lam, quam ab Epiphanio Apostolis quoque tribui diximus, de triplici totidem dierum (quartæ, sextæque feriæ, & Dominicæ) synaxi, Constitutionem, ne ipse quidem Petavius veram esse credit; Haud scio (inquit) an ea satis certo constare queat. Nam primis Ecclesia temporibus unus duntaxat Dominicus dies ad eam rem observatus videtur; ut ex Apostolo. 1. Cor. 16. colligitur. Quin etiam Iustinus Martyr. Apol. 2. cum de Christianorum conventibus agit, solius Dominica meminit. Quare magis id ex privato Ecclesiæ cujusque ritu, quam ex communi Apostolorum præscripto, derivatum existimo, ut quarta sextave feria, aut etiam sabbato, synaxes, conventusque fierent. Quam in rem egregius est Augustini locus ep. 118. qui mihi hic adscribendus videtur. Alia vero (inquit) quæ per loca terrarum regionesque variantur; sicuti est, quod alii jejunant sabbato, alii verò non; alii quotidie communicant corpori, & sanguini Domini; alii certis diebus accipiunt; alibi nullus dies intermittitur, quo non offeratur; alibi sabbato tantum & Dominico; alibi tantum Dominico; & siquid aliud hujusmodi animadverti potest, totum hoc genus rerum liberas habet observatio‐nes. Hactenus Petavius, Epiphanianorum Apostolorum de triplici synaxi Διάταξιν, & merito sane, repudians, & egregie ex Augustino confutans. Itaque cum & ex iis, quæ hactenus diximus, satis constet, & ex iis porro quæ infra adjiciemus, clarius futurum sit, Epiphanianas ipsas Constitutiones falsas, & Apostolis affictas fuisse; apparet, nihil ex eo Scriptore præsidii iis Constitutionibus quæri posse, quæ nunc circumferuntur; etiamsi verum esset (quod supra salsissimum esse demonstravimus) illas plane easdem esse cum Epiphanianis. Sed jam cætera pertexamus.
units.tr: on the days of the Passover nothing at all is to be taken for food except bread, salt and water. I know, and gladly confess, that these rites of fasting and dry diet on those days are ancient, and were received many years before Epiphanius; that they were handed down by the Apostles, or (what is more serious still) commanded by a fixed and inviolable and written law, not even the present theologians of the Roman communion have said; among whom neither the fast on Wednesday, nor that severe dry diet of the week before Easter, is enjoined on all, or is in public and common use among many; so that they themselves must admit either that this Epiphanian Diataxis, which so commands, is spurious and false, or at least that they and their Pontiffs have for many centuries been guilty of despising and violating Apostolic discipline. But let them see to that. Certainly we too may now learn from the earliest monuments of the Church, nearest to the Apostles, and know for certain and clearly; and Epiphanius, who was then even more easily able to do so than we are, since he was further from the sources of truth, could have known that the Apostles never prescribed anything of this kind; therefore the Constitution which decrees these things is false, and shamelessly fabricated in the name of the Apostles. Since the same laws are also found in our own Constitutions, we trust that we shall demonstrate this most clearly below, when we come to speak of them; so there is no need now to linger on proving it. Lastly, that final Constitution which we said Epiphanius attributes also to the Apostles, concerning the triple synaxis of three days (Wednesday, Friday and the Lord's day), not even Petavius himself believes it to be genuine; I do not know (he says) whether it can be established with sufficient certainty. For in the first times of the Church only the Lord's day seems to have been observed for that purpose; as is gathered from the Apostle, 1 Cor. 16. Moreover Justin Martyr, Apol. 2, when he treats of the assemblies of Christians, mentions only the Lord's day. Wherefore I judge that this practice arose from the private custom of each Church rather than from a common command of the Apostles, namely that gatherings and assemblies should be held on Wednesday or Friday, or even on the Sabbath. An excellent passage of Augustine on this matter, in Letter 118, seems to me worth quoting here. But (he says) there are other things which vary from place to place and region; such as that some fast on the Sabbath and others not; some communicate daily in the body and blood of the Lord, others on certain days; in some places no day is omitted on which it is offered, in others only on the Sabbath and the Lord's day, in others only on the Lord's day; and whatever else of this kind can be noted, the observance of all this sort of thing is left free. So far Petavius, rightly rejecting the Epiphanian Apostolic Diataxis on the triple synaxis, and well refuting it from Augustine. Therefore, since it is sufficiently established both from what we have said so far and from what we shall add below, and it will become clearer still, that the Epiphanian Constitutions themselves are false and fabricated in the name of the Apostles, it is evident that no support can be sought from that writer for those Constitutions which are now in circulation; even if it were true (which we have shown above to be most false) that they are plainly the same as the Epiphanian ones. But let us now proceed with the rest.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Falso putasse Bovium suas Constitutiones Cyrillo Hierosolymitano fuisse cognitas. Ratio, quam is erroris suo obtendit, solvitur. Cyrillum, qui habet de phœnice, ea ex Clementis Epistola ad Corinthios habere.
units.tr: On the false supposition that Bovius's Constitutions were known to Cyril of Jerusalem. The reason he offers for his error is refuted. That Cyril, who writes about the phoenix, took it from Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians.

units.la: BOVIVS suo Clementi testem etiam citat Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum, Epiphanio paucis annis vetustiorem. Is enim in quadam Catechesi mirabilem avis phœnicis historiam ex Clemente ita narrat * ; Τῆς (ὀρνέου) ὡς γεγραφεῖ Κλήμης, καὶ ἱστορῶσι πλεῖ-
units.tr: BOVIUS also cites Cyril of Jerusalem as a witness for his Clement. Cyril was a few years older than Epiphanius. In one of his Catecheses he relates the wonderful history of the phoenix from Clement, as follows: "Of the bird, as Clement has written, and as many relate" [Τῆς (ὀρνέου) ὡς γεγραφεῖ Κλήμης, καὶ ἱστορῶσι πλείονες]*.

units.la: a Catech. 18. p. 213. d. πλείονες, μονογενὴς ὑπάρχον ἐν τῇ Αἰγυ- πτίων χώρᾳ, ἐν πεδιάσοις πεντακοσίων ἐτῶν ἐχόμενον, δείκνυσι τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἐν ἐν ἐρήμοις τόποις, ἵνα μὴ ἀγνοηθῇ τὸ μυστή- ριον γινόμενον, ἀλλ' ἐν φανερᾷ πόλει παρα- γενόμενον, ἵνα φηλαφηθῇ τὸ ἀπιστούμενον· φησὶν γὰρ ἑαυτῷ ποιῆσαν ἐκ λιβάνου & σμύρ- νης καὶ λοιπῶν ἀρωμάτων, & ἐν τῇ συμπλη- ρώσει τῶν ἐτῶν εἰς τοσοῦτον εἰσελθὸν, τελευ- τᾷ φανερῶς καὶ σήπεται· εἶτα καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς τῆς σαρκὸς τὰ τελευτήσαντος, σκώληξ τις γεννᾶται, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ αὐξηθεὶς εἰς ὄρνεον μορ- φῶταί. Hæc avis, ut scribit Clemens, & alii complures idem referunt, cum sit una tantum & sola, in terram Ægypti in spa- tio quingentorum annorum venire solet, atque demonstrare resurrectionem; non in lo- cis desertis, ne mysterium id ignoretur, sed in aperta (vel potius clara & nobili) civi- tate consistit, ut contrectetur, quod non creditur. Loculum enim sibi facit e thure, & myrrha, caterisque aromatibus, & com- pletis annis eo devenit. Moritur aperte & putrescit; deinde ex putrefacta carne mortua, vermis quidam generatur, & hic deinceps in avem efformatur. Hæc Cyril- lus; quæ, quia in quinto Constitutionum libro consimilia de Phœnice narrantur, bo- nus Bovius a eo avidissime retulit, inde- que conficit suarum Constitutionum codi-cem
units.tr: a Catech. 18. p. 213. d. "The bird, being the only one of its kind, lives in the land of Egypt for about five hundred years, and it shows forth the resurrection. It does not appear in deserted places, lest the mystery go unknown, but comes into a notable city in the open, so that what is disbelieved may be touched. For it makes for itself a nest of frankincense, myrrh and other spices, and when the years are complete it enters into it. It dies openly and rots. Then from the decaying flesh of the dead body a certain worm is generated, and this, growing, is shaped into a bird." [ἐν πεδιάσι πεντακοσίων ἐτῶν ἐχόμενον, δείκνυσι τὴν ἀνάστασιν, ἐν ἐρήμοις τόποις... φηλαφηθῇ τὸ ἀπιστούμενον· φησὶν γὰρ ἑαυτῷ ποιῆσαν ἐκ λιβάνου καὶ σμύρνης καὶ λοιπῶν ἀρωμάτων...]. Hear what Clement writes, and what many others relate: this bird, being single and alone, comes into the land of Egypt about every five hundred years and is wont to show forth the resurrection. Cyril says this. Since in the fifth book of the Constitutions a similar account of the phoenix is given, the good Bovius most eagerly reported it from him and from this concludes that the Constitutions are the true and genuine offspring of Clement, held to be such by that bishop of Jerusalem.

units.la: a c. 6.
