units.la: Bov. 8. cem pro vero ac genuino Clementis fœtu ab Hierosolymitano illo antistite habitum. Ego vero fateor quidem, phœnicis historiam in Constitutionibus legi: inde eam Cyrillum hausisse; vel hoc opus, dum Clementem laudat, intelligere, nequaquam concedo. Extabat enim ejus tempore aliud Clementis opus, & quidem longe nobilissimum, & apud Christi Ecclesias adeo receptum, ut in multis etiam publice legeretur, in quo eadem illa de phœnice narratio continebatur, nimirum Epistola illa ad Corinthios, de qua in superioribus & Hieronymum, & Honorium Augustodunensem insigne testimonium perhibuisse diximus. In ea quippe Epistola memoratam fuisse a Clemente phœnicis historiam, & ex Photio pridem didicimus, qui eam dum a se lectam recenset, inter cætera,-reprehensioni, ut ipse putat, obnoxia, & hoc ponit ; ὅτι, ὡς πανταλνθέστα- τῷ τῷ κ̣ῳ τ φοίνικα τὸ ὄρνεον ὑποδείγματι νέχρηται, quod phœnicis avis exemplo usus est, tanquam verissimo; & ex ipsa illa Epistola multo nunc clarius perspicimus, Oxonii ante aliquot annos a Patricio Junio ex manuscripto codice edita, Constantinopoli ad Regem magnæ Britanniæ misso atque allato. Sic enim in eo exemplari de phœnice narrat Clemens b ; ὄρνεον γάς
units.tr: Bov. 8. This bird, as Clement writes and many others relate the same, since there is only one and it is alone, is wont to come into the land of Egypt at the span of five hundred years, and to demonstrate the resurrection. It does not stay in deserted places, lest the mystery be unknown, but in an open (or rather, a clear and noble) city, so that what is not believed may be touched. For it makes a little tomb for itself of incense and myrrh and other aromatics, and when the years are complete it goes into it and dies. Then, from the corrupted flesh of the dead body, a certain worm is generated, and this one, growing, is formed into a bird. Cyril: these things, because in the fifth book of the Constitutions similar things are told about the phoenix, the good Bovius eagerly reported from him, and from that he concludes that the codex of his Constitutions was held by that Jerusalem bishop to be the true and genuine offspring of Clement. I indeed admit that the history of the phoenix is read in the Constitutions, and that Cyril drew it from there; but that he understood this work when he praised Clement, I by no means concede. For at his time there was another work of Clement's, and indeed a far more noble one, and so widely received among the churches of Christ that in many places it was even read publicly, in which that same narrative of the phoenix was contained: namely, that Epistle to the Corinthians, of which we have said above that both Jerome and Honorius of Autun gave a notable testimony. Indeed, that the history of the phoenix was mentioned by Clement in that Epistle we learned long ago from Photius, who, while recounting that he had read it, among other things (which he thinks open to blame) states this: "that, as the most wise Clement used the phoenix bird as an example, as most true," [ὅτι, ὡς πανταλνθέστατος Κλήμης τῷ φοίνικα τὸ ὄρνεον ὑποδείγματι κέχρηται]; and from that very Epistle we now see much more clearly, since it was published at Oxford some years ago by Patricius Junius from a manuscript codex, sent to and brought from Constantinople to the King of Great Britain. For in that copy Clement tells of the phoenix thus: "For the bird which is called the phoenix, which is unique, lives five hundred years; and when it, now aged, is near to its end and to dying, it makes for itself a tomb of frankincense and myrrh and other spices, into which, when the time is fulfilled, it enters and dies; and from the putrefied flesh a certain worm is born," etc., which it is unnecessary to describe.

Avis est, qua Phœnix vocatur; hæc sui generis sola & solitaria existens annos quingentos vivit, & cum morti vicinam se sentit, è thure, myrrha, & reliquis aromatibus, loculum sibi struit, quem completo annorum spatio ingreditur, & vitam deponit; ex carne vero ejus putrefacta vermis quidam nascitur, &c.
units.tr: b Pp. 34, 35. [illegible, about 8 letters] "It is a bird which is called the phoenix; this, being sole of its kind and solitary, lives five hundred years, and when it feels itself near to death, it builds for itself a tomb from frankincense, myrrh and the remaining aromatics, into which, when the span of time is fulfilled, it enters and lays down its life; and from its putrefied flesh a certain worm is born," etc. [ὄρνεον γάρ ... ὁ προσονομάζεται φοῖνιξ.]

units.la: Ex his jam ipse Bovius, si revivisceret, haud dubiè intelligeret, nihil necesse esse, ad Constitutiones confugere, quo hæc Cyrillus dici possit ex Clemente referre; cum non rem modo ipsam, sed verba etiam pleraque ex hoc Clementinæ ad Corinthios Epistolæ loco mutuatus sit; qualia sunt ista, exempli gratia, μονογενὲς ὑπάρχον, σηκὸν ἑαυτῷ ποιήσαν ἐκ λιβάνου, σμύρνης, καὶ λοιπῶν ἀρωμάτων. Item, εἰς τοσοῦτον εἰσελθὸν τελευτᾷ, καὶ σήπεται. Denique, ἡ τῆς σαπείσης σαρκὸς σκώληξ τις γεννᾶται quæ in Epistola quidè leguntur fere totidem apicibus; in Constitutionibus pleraque non leguntur; nequid de rerum ipsarum diversitate tate dicam. Nam verus Clemens phœni-cem in Arabia mori facit; hinc avem redi-divam nidum, e quo efflorpit, una cum reliquiis sublatum Heliopolim in Ægyptum portare, advolantemque interdiu omnibus inspectantibus super solis altare collocare, atque ita eò, unde venerat, reverti. Con-stitutionum vero architectus plane aliter. Fingit a enim avem primū venire in Ægyptum, ad eam aram quæ vocatur solis, cinnamomi, cassiæ, & xylobalsami magnam copiam ferentem; stantemque ad orientem, precari solem, & sponte incendi, atque in cinerem redigi: ex cinere autem vermem renasci, atque ex eo tepefacto formari novam avem, & cum facta est volucris, ferri in Arabiam, ἴνπερ ἐςὶ πεqαιτέqω τῆ Αἰγυπτιακῆ νόμῳ, quæ est ultra Nomum Ægypti. Mitto ineptias fabulatoris, ut quod ait, locum Ægypti, quo venit Phœnix, vocari aram Solis, cum Heliopolim, Solis non aram, sed civitatem dici, & verus Clemens, & cæteri authores tradant: tum quod fingit avem ὡς ἡλίῳ προσευχέσθαι, soli supplicare, eumque precari; quasi novus Æsopus, mutis animalibus nostros & mores, & sensus, nostra etiam scelera, id est, idololatriam tribuens; denique quod ait Arabiam esse ultra Ægyptiacum Nomum. Quis enim, quæso, est Ægyptiacus iste Nomus?
units.tr: From these things Bovius himself, if he were to come back to life, would undoubtedly understand that there is no need to flee to the Constitutions in order to suppose that Cyril reported these things from Clement; since he has borrowed not only the matter itself but also most of the words from this passage of Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians, such as these, for example: "being unique, making a tomb for itself of frankincense, myrrh and other spices," likewise "entering into so great a span, it dies and rots," and finally "from the putrefied flesh a certain worm is born." These are indeed read in the Epistle almost word for word; in the Constitutions most of them are not read at all, not to mention the difference in the things themselves. For the true Clement makes the phoenix die in Arabia; from there the bird, carrying away its nest, together with the remains, brings them to Heliopolis in Egypt, and flying in by day, in full view of all, places them upon the altar of the sun, and so returns to the place whence it came. But the architect of the Constitutions is quite different. For he invents that the bird first comes into Egypt, to that altar which is called the altar of the sun, bearing a great quantity of cinnamon, cassia and xylobalsamum; and standing toward the east it prays to the sun, and spontaneously catches fire and is reduced to ashes; then from the ashes a worm is reborn, and from it, warmed, a new bird is formed, and when it has become a bird it is carried into Arabia, [ἵνα περ ἐστὶ πεπαιτέρω τῇ Αἰγυπτιακῇ νόμῳ], which is beyond the Egyptian nome. I pass over the silliness of the fabulist: that he says the place in Egypt to which the phoenix came is called the altar of the sun, whereas Heliopolis is said, both by the true Clement and by other authors, to be a city of the sun and not an altar; and that he invents that the bird "prays to the sun, supplicating it" [ὡς ἡλίῳ προσεύχεσθαι]; like a new Aesop, giving to dumb animals our customs, feelings and even our sins, that is, idolatry; and finally that he says Arabia lies beyond the Egyptian nome. For what, I ask, is this Egyptian nome?

units.la: Nomus mus? Ægyptus ipsa in Nomos plures dividebatur, ut Tanitem, Pharbaitem, Bubastitem, Heliopolitem, &c. qui omnes ε Ægypti, vel ε Ægyptiaci Nomi erant. Qui unus singulariter ε Ægyptiacus Nomus diceretur, equidem non memini. Sed hæc, inquam, mitto. Illud unum nunc observo, id esse duarum istarum de phœnice narrationum discrimen, ut utraque unius ejusdemque hominis esse non posset. At quæ in Epistola habetur, ea vere Clementis est. Non igitur Clementis, quæ in Constitutionibus legitur. Atque ita nobis Phœnix, præter Bovii spes & vota, Διαλάξεων codici non vitam & ornamentum, sed cladem & perniciem attulit. Id vidit, & ad Tertullianum observavit Clariss. doctissimusque Rigaltius: Etsi autem (inquit) ejusdem phœnicis historia exemplum reperiatur etiam in Constitutionibus supra citatis, tamen ex earum cum epistola Clementis comparatione hoc videmur assequi, vix esse, ut ejusdem authoris utrumque opus censeri debeat.
units.tr: Egypt itself was divided into several nomes, such as Tanis, Pharbaitis, Bubastis, Heliopolis, etc., all of which were nomes of Egypt or of the Egyptian nome. I do not remember that any single one was called simply "the Egyptian nome." But these things, I say, I pass over. This alone I now note: that the difference between these two accounts of the phoenix is such that both cannot be the work of one and the same man. But what is contained in the Epistle is truly Clement's. Therefore what is read in the Constitutions is not Clement's. And thus the phoenix, contrary to Bovius's hopes and wishes, has brought to his Diataxeis not life and ornament but ruin and destruction. The most distinguished and most learned Rigaltius saw this, and noted it in connection with Tertullian: "Although (he says) the history of the same phoenix is found also in the Constitutions cited above, nevertheless from comparing them with Clement's Epistle we seem to gather that it is hardly possible that both works should be considered to belong to the same author."

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Frustra pro Constitutionibus afferri Athanasii & Eusebii testimonium. Utriusque loca explicantur, quae ad Constitutiones nostras nihil pertinere, demonstratur. Διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων quid fuerit.
units.tr: The testimony of Athanasius and Eusebius is wrongly cited in support of the Constitutions. The passages are explained, and it is shown that they have nothing to do with our Constitutions. What the Teaching of the Apostles was.

units.la: QUID, quod etiam ex anterioribus temporibus Bovius suarum Constitutionum volumini praesidium petere ausus est, Athanasiumque & Eusebium inter earum patronos edere? Athanasius (inquit) cujus testimonium gravissimum esse debet, horum librorum mentionem facit, & de iis praeclare sentit. Videamus ergo, quod sit de his tanti illius viri testimonium. Id vero mox recitat Bovius, ex epistola (ut ipse quidem ait) ad Ammum Monachum, sed quod in nostris codicibus extat in fragmento epistolae heortasticę 39. in hęc verba a; Ἀλλ᾽ ἔνεκά γε πλείονος ἀκριβείας προσ-ίθημι, ἡ ἴδιος γράφων ἀναγκαίως· ὡς ὅτι ὅσ᾽ ἡ ἑτέρα βίβλια τούτων ἐξωθεν, ἃ κανονιζόμενα μὲν, τετυπωμένα δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν πατέρων ἀναγινώσκειν τοῖς ἄρτι προσερχομένοις, καὶ βουλομένοις κατηχεῖσθαι τὸν τῆς εὐσεβείας λόγον· Σοφία Σολομῶνος, καὶ Σοφία Σιρὰχ, καὶ Ἐσθήρ, καὶ Ἰουδὶθ, καὶ Τωβίας, καὶ Διδαχὴ καλουμένη τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ ὁ Ποιμὴν.
units.tr: What of the fact that Bovius has even dared to seek support for his volume of Constitutions from earlier times, and to name Athanasius and Eusebius among their patrons? Athanasius, he says, whose testimony ought to be most weighty, mentions these books and thinks highly of them. Let us see, then, what the testimony of that great man on these books actually is. Bovius quotes it straight away, from a letter (as he himself says) to the monk Ammon. But in our copies it is found in a fragment of the Festal Letter 39, in these words a: "But for the sake of greater accuracy I add also this, since I write of necessity: that besides these books there are others outside the canon, which are not canonized but are laid down by the Fathers to be read by those newly coming forward and wishing to be instructed in the word of godliness: the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the so-called Teaching of the Apostles [Διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων], and the Shepherd."

units.la: † T. z. Ath. p. 39. d. μλω. Καὶ ὅμως ἀγαπητοὶ, ἀκεὶνων κανονι- ζομένων, καὶ τύτων ἀναγινωσκομένων ὠφελιμῶ̃ ἔ ἀπολυφων μνήμη. ἀλλὰ ἀιρετικῶν ὄξιν ἐ- πινοια, χαφόντων μὲν ὅτε θέλουσιν αὐτὰ, χα- ειζομένων ὁ καὶ προσιθέντων αὐτὰις χρόνες. Caterum majoris & exactioris disciplina caussa addo & illud scribens necessario, praeter superiores (utriusque scilicet Testamenti nuper recensitos) libros esse alios, non quidem in canonem relatos, sed veterum authoritate illis, qui pietatis elementis imbuendi essent, propositos: Sapientiam nempe Salomonis, Sapientiam Sirach, Esther, Judith, & Tobiam, Doctrinam etiam, ut vocatur, Apostolorum, & Pastorem. Verumtamen dilecti, cum & illi in canonem relati sint, & hi legantur, nusquam est apocryphorum memoria; quae sunt haereticorum inventum, ea quidem, quando lubet, scribentium; iis vero tempora largientium, ac addentium. Quae in his ab Athanasio memoratur Διδαχὴ καλυμένη τῶν Αποςόλων, eam Bovius scisciit suum esse Constitutionum Clementinarum codicem; quae ejus suspicio novissimae Athanasii editionis authoribus a usq; adeo placuit, ut eam non in libri margine, quo loco ascribi nulla e- rat invidia, sed in ipso authoris, ut loquun- tur, textu, velut Athanasii ipsius voces, omnino ridicule legi voluerint his verbis expresexpressam; Videtur intelligere Apostolo-rum Constitutiones, qua nomine Clementis nunc habentur. Sed antequam hunc locum expendo, alter ei jungendus est ejusdem scriptoris, sed ex alio opere a: Τῆς νέας; (inquit) Διαθήκης ἀντιλεγόμενα ταῦτα. Πέτρου, Πέτρου, Ἰωάννου, Θωμᾶ, Εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Θωμᾶ, Διδαχὴ Ἀποστόλων, Κλημέντια· ἐξ ὧν μετεφράσθησαν ἐκλεγέντα τὰ ἀληθέστερα, Θεόπνευστα, ταῦτα τὰ ἀναγινωσκόμενα. Novi Testamenti quibus contradicitur, sunt hi, Circuitus Petri; (Circuitus Ioannis, Circuitus Thomae, Evangelium Thomae, Doctrina Apostolorum, Clementina. Ex his veriora quaedam, & spiritus Dei instinctum respientia transsumpta, & ut legantur selecta sunt. His & ista, observatu digna, continenter subjicit; Ταῦτα πάντα ἐξετάσθησαν μὲν, ὅσον πρὸς εἰσῆν· παραγεγραμμένα ἢ εἰσὶ πάντως ξ νόθα, καὶ ἀπόβλητα, καὶ ἐδὲν τῶν τῶν Ἀπορρύφων μάλιστα ἐγκριτῶν, ἢ ἐπωφελές, ἐξαιρέτως τῆς νέας Διαθήκης· ἀλλὰ πάντα, ςίχα τῶν ἀνωλέγω ςιαλνφθέντων ἐγκεθέντων ἀλλὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς σοφοῖς ἢ παλαίσιν, ἀποκρυφῆς μᾶλλον, ἢ ἀναςνώσεως, ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄξια. Hi omnes (libri scilicet) cognitionis quidem gratia expositi sunt; caeterum omnino perverse & falso scripti sunt, & nothi, ac reprobi; nihilque istorum, maxime apocryphorum, approbatum aut utile est, prasertim novi Testamen-ti; sed omnia (exceptis iis quæ supra digesta sunt & à vetustis sapientibus, ac Patribus approbata, sive in canonem relata) revera dignæ sunt, quæ abscondantur potius, quam ut legantur. Hactenus Athanasius : qui quam præclarè de his libris senserit, illa postrema nos docent ; nothos esse scilicet & ἀποβλήτως, & παρασυνεγραμμένους, id est, rejectaneos, spurios & adulterinos, dignioresque qui abscondantur, quam qui legantur. Hoc quidem nos Athanasii de his judicium gravissimum esse libentes Bovio assentimur. Sed ut omnis ejus in hoc Athanasii testimonio ad suum pseudoclementem inflectendo, vel fraus, vel inscitia patesiat; tum etiam, ut solvatur quædam, quæ inter duo ista Athanasii de eodem libro dicta videtur existere, contradictio, utrumq; diligentius est explicandum. Imprimis observandum, quam desperata sit Bovii causa, qui suarum Constitutionum decus in eo loco quærit, qui iis indelebilem ignominiæ notam inurit. Esto enim, quod ille vehementer, quanquam falso & inique ac nulla ratione, cupit, hæc ab Athanasio memorata Apostolorum doctrina, ipse ille Constitutionum codex, qui nunc nobis obtruditur. Quid inde fiet, nisi falsum & ementitum esse hunc librum, eoque, quem ipse sibi tribuit, loco ac numero (ex Athanasii quidem & Patrum judicio) indignum? Nam Constitutionum quidem Boviana- rum author in ipso statim operis limine a suam doctrinam audiri vult, velut divinam, & æquiparandam gloriosis Christi vocibus; eam omnem, velut sacro Apostolorum ore dictatam, proponit; proque scriptura canonica hos, quibus ea continetur, libros haberi cupit. Ac ne esset obscura ejus mens, diserte in ultimo Apostolorum canone b (quod opus ejusdem plane est cum Constitutionibus furfuris) decernitur, ut omnibus clericis & laicis venerandæ & sanctæ sint aj Διαλαγαj, ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπισκόποις (inquit) δὲ ἐμοῦ Κλήμεντ̀ ἐν ὀκτὼ βιβλίοις προσπεφωνημέναι, vobis Episcopus per me Clementem in octo libris edita: quæ ideo in hoc ipso loco libris Euangelicis & Apostolicis accensentur, & in sacro eorum canone collocantur. Athanasius contra commemoratam à se Apostolorum doctrinam locat extra libros Novi Testamenti à se recensitos, ἐξωθεν λόγων, inquit, extra hos: tum diserte addit, ὃ κανονιζομένων, non pertinere ad canonem sacrum; à Patribus scilicet receptum. Ergo, tum Athanasius, tum illi Patres, si per hunc Apostolica doctrina librum Constitutiones Bovianas intellexerunt, mentitum earum scriptorem putarunt; runt; mentitum Canonem illum inter Apostolicos ultimum, existimarunt, qui scilicet quem hi Apostolis librum tribuunt, quem Christi vocibus æquiparari volunt, quem inter Novi Testamenti canonica censuerunt, ipsi eum ex hoc loco deturbatum in aliam classem amandarunt. Nam, si has Apostolorum veré voces esse, scriptori essent assensi; si id de iis & Apostolorum & Clementis judicium esse, sibi persuasissent; nunquam eum librum extra Novi Testamenti canonem posuissent. Itaque qui aliter instituunt, eos necesse est, & ipsius Constitutionum scriptoris, & canonis eas commendantis, sidem fluxam vanamque censuisse: omnino perinde ac nos, qui librum hunc totum, non ab Apostolis, non à Clemente, non à verace ullo authore, sed ab impostore, Apostolorum sibi & Clementis nomen impudentissimè assingente, scriptum & consarcinatum fuisse, putamus. Ea qualem Bovius naƐtus sit Constitutionum suarum patronum! qui scilicet liquido diserteque testatur, earum parentem hominem esse vanum, ac in toto opere splendide mentitum! Huc secundò accedit, quod, etiamsi de Apostolorum Constitutionibus intelligatur Athanasiana ἡ τῶν Ἀποστόλων καλυμένη Διδαχή, Apostolorum dicta doctrina, quicquid de ea dicit
units.tr: And yet, beloved, though those books are received as canonical and these are read, there is nowhere any memory of the apocrypha. These are the invention of heretics, who write them whenever they please and who add to them as time allows. As for the Teaching of the Apostles, which Athanasius mentions here, Bovius has claimed that it is his codex of the Clementine Constitutions. This guess has so pleased the authors of the latest edition of Athanasius that they wished it to be read, absurdly, not in the margin of the book, where there was no harm in adding it, but in the very text of the author, as if they were Athanasius's own words, expressed in these terms: "It seems to mean the Constitutions of the Apostles, which are now found under the name of Clement." But before I weigh this passage, another passage of the same writer, from a different work, must be set beside it: "Of the New Testament these are disputed: the Circuits of Peter, the Circuits of John, the Circuits of Thomas, the Gospel of Thomas, the Teaching of the Apostles, the Clementines. From these, certain truer things, which agree with the inspiration of God, have been translated and selected to be read; these are the things read." To these he continually adds other remarks worth noting: "All these have been examined so far as concerns their antiquity; but they are wholly spurious, false and to be rejected, and none of them, especially of the apocrypha, is approved or useful, least of all for the New Testament. All of them, however, excepting those which have been set out above and approved by the ancient wise men and Fathers, or received into the canon, are truly worthy to be hidden rather than read." So far Athanasius. His final words teach us how highly he thought of these books: namely, that they are spurious, rejected, and counterfeit [νόθα, ἀπόβλητα, παρασυνεγραμμένα], and more worthy to be hidden than to be read. We, then, agree with Bovius that this is a most weighty judgment of Athanasius on these books. But so that the whole of Bovius's fraud or ignorance in bending this testimony of Athanasius toward his own pseudo-Clement may be made plain, and so that a certain apparent contradiction between these two statements of Athanasius about the same book may be resolved, each point must be explained more carefully. First, we must observe how desperate Bovius's cause is, since he seeks the glory of his Constitutions in a passage which brands them with an indelible mark of disgrace. Suppose that the teaching of the Apostles which Athanasius mentions were, as Bovius vehemently wishes (though falsely, unfairly and without any reason), that very codex of Constitutions which is now thrust upon us. What then follows, unless that this book is false and fabricated, and, by the judgment of Athanasius and the Fathers, unworthy of the place and rank which its author gives it? For the author of the Bovian Constitutions, at the very threshold of his work, wants his doctrine to be heard as divine, and to be equated with the glorious words of Christ. He sets it all forth as if dictated by the sacred mouth of the Apostles, and wishes these books, in which it is contained, to be held as canonical Scripture. Lest his meaning be unclear, it is expressly decreed in the final canon of the Apostles (a work plainly by the same hand as the Constitutions), that all clergy and laity should hold these in reverence and as holy: "For to you, bishops," it says, "I, Clement, have addressed these eight books," vobis Episcopus per me Clementem in octo libris edita. These, therefore, are counted in this very passage among the Gospel and Apostolic books and placed in their sacred canon. Athanasius, on the contrary, places the teaching of the Apostles which he mentions outside the books of the New Testament which he lists, outside these, he says, and expressly adds that they do not belong to the sacred canon, that is, the canon received by the Fathers. Therefore, if Athanasius and those Fathers understood this teaching of the Apostles to be the Bovian Constitutions, they judged that its writer was a liar, and they judged that the canon of the Apostles which places it last was a liar. Indeed, the book which they assign to the Apostles, which they want equated with the words of Christ, and which they counted among the canonical books of the New Testament, they would have thrust out of that place and into another class. For if these were truly the words of the Apostles, they would have agreed with the writer; if they held the same judgment as the Apostles and Clement, they would have been fully persuaded of it, and they would never have placed that book outside the canon of the New Testament. So those who take another view must have judged the faith of the author of the Constitutions, and of the canon that commends them, to be unstable and empty. We are exactly in the same position: we think that this whole book was written and patched together not by the Apostles, not by Clement, not by any true author, but by an impostor who most shamelessly ascribed to himself the names of the Apostles and of Clement. What a patron Bovius has found for his Constitutions! He plainly and clearly testifies that their parent is a vain man, who has lied splendidly throughout the work! Here is a second point: even if the teaching of the Apostles, as Athanasius named it, is taken to mean the Constitutions of the Apostles, whatever Athanasius says of it will apply to the Constitutions which existed under this name in his own time, if any did exist, and not especially to the Bovian ones.

units.la: —— — dicit Athanasius ad Constitutiones eas pertinebit, quae ipsius tempore hoc nomine si forte extabant, non adeo ad Bovianas. Cum enim, siquae extabant Athanasii tempore Apostolorum dictae Constitutiones, ex aliae esse non potuerint, quam quas Epiphanius commemoravit, Athanasio quidem junior, sed tamen ejusdem cum eo saeculi, quique eum & viderat, & cum eo collocutus, ac versatus erat; profecto nihil ad Bovianas, quae Athanasius de iis dixit, quas nos supra liquido deprehendimus alias fuisse a Bovianis. Sed quid ego in his haereo? Palam est, & a reverendissimo, clarissimoque viro Iacobo Usserio a Armachano praesule, perspicue demonstratum, non esse hanc Apostolorum ab Athanasio commemoratam Διδαχὴ, Apostolicarum Constitutionum codicem; quicquid contra senserint & Bovius & Turrianus, & Baronius {b}, & Graecorum etiam, referente Zonara, nonnulli, cujus hanc φησιν ex manuscripto quodam libro descripsit Usserius; τῶν Ἀποστόλων τινὲς λέγουσιν εἶναι τὰς διδαχὰς τῆς Κλήμεντος γραφείσας Διαθήκης ὡς ἡ λεγομένη ἐντὸς σωσθῆναι ἀναγινώσκειν ὡς συγχωρεῖ, ὡς νοθευθείσας ἢ παραφθαρείσας ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν. Doctrinam Apostolorum quidam dicunt esse Constitutiones per Clementem scriptas; quas sexta quae dicitur Synodus legi non conconcedit, velut ab hæreticis corruptas, & adulteratas. Istorum, inquam, & adversariorum eadem sequentium errorem tribus rationibus refellit Rev. Usserius, quas hic ipsius descriptis verbis recitabo. Hanc opinionem refellit, Primo (inquit) ipsius Athanasii authoritas; qui in eodem loco Διδαχλὼ hanc inter eos libros numerat, qui Catechumenis & nuper ad fidem accedentibus legendi essent; cum isti (Constitutionum libri Episcopis sint dicati, resque ad Ecclesiæ regimen spectantes tractent;) & alia quadam μυστικώτερα, qua idcirco Canonis Apostolorum 85 a consarcinator in vulgus efferenda esse vetuit. Altera R. Usserii ratio ab exiguo ducentorum versiculorum numero, quibus illam Διδαχλὼ definiunt ac concludunt, tum ipse Nicephorus CP. Patriarcha in Στιχομετρία, quo loco eam inter scripta Novi Testamenti apocrypha recenset. Διδαχὴ Αποστόλων (inquit) στίχων σ. tum Nicephori interpres Anastasius Bibliothecarius, in latina ejusdem στιχομετρίας interpretatione. Eo enim ostenditur, illius Διδαχῆς libellum Cantico Canticorum minorem fuisse, quod 280. ejusdem generis στίχας, sive versiculos, habuisse ibidem legimus. Quis tam brevem libellum pro Constitutionum volumine haberi posse putet, quas octo libris constare & quidem
units.tr: ... Athanasius refers to the Constitutions that were then circulating under that name, if any did, and not to Bovius' Constitutions. For if any books called the Apostolic Constitutions existed in Athanasius' time, they can have been none other than those Epiphanius mentioned. Epiphanius was younger than Athanasius but of the same century, and he had both seen him and conversed and lived with him. So what Athanasius said about them has nothing to do with Bovius' work, which we have already shown above to be a different book from the one Athanasius knew. But why do I linger over these points? It is plain, and the most reverend and distinguished James Ussher, archbishop of Armagh, has clearly demonstrated, that the Teaching of the Apostles that Athanasius mentions (Διδαχὴ) is not the codex of the Apostolic Constitutions. Whatever Bovius, Turrianus and Baronius have held to the contrary, and some of the Greeks too, as Zonaras reports (Ussher copied his words from a certain manuscript book), φησιν [says]: "Some say that the teachings of the Apostles are the Clementine writings of the Covenant, which, as the so-called Holy Synod (the sixth) allows to be read, were corrupted and adulterated by heretics" [τῶν Ἀποστόλων τινὲς λέγουσιν εἶναι τὰς διδαχὰς τῆς Κλήμεντος γραφείσας Διαθήκης ὡς ἡ λεγομένη ἐντὸς σωσθῆναι ἀναγινώσκειν ὡς συγχωρεῖ, ὡς νοθευθείσας ἢ παραφθαρείσας ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν]. Ussher refutes the error of these people, and of the adversaries who follow them, with three arguments, which I will recite here in his own words. He refutes this opinion: First (he says), by the authority of Athanasius himself, who in the same place counts this Διδαχὴ among those books which are to be read by catechumens and by those newly come to the faith, since the books of the Constitutions are dedicated to bishops and deal with matters concerning the government of the Church, and also with other more mystical things, which for that reason the compiler of Apostolic Canon 85 forbade to be published among the people. The second argument of Ussher is drawn from the small number of two hundred verses by which that Διδαχὴ is defined and concluded, and from Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, who in his Stichometry lists it among the apocryphal writings of the New Testament: "Teaching of the Apostles, 200 verses" (Διδαχὴ Ἀποστόλων στίχων σ). So too does Nicephorus' translator, Anastasius the Librarian, in his Latin version of the same Stichometry. It is thereby shown that this little book of the Teaching was smaller than the Song of Songs, since we read that it had 280 verses of the same kind. Who would think so short a book could be taken for a volume of Constitutions, which, as is well known, consist of eight books, and rather lengthy ones?

units.la: a can. A-post. 35. dem satis prolixis, notum est? Tertio, inquit R. Usserius, nos movet indiculus librorum canonicorum & apocryphorum, quem Anastasii Nicæni quaestionibus subjectum in publica Oxoniensis Academia Bibliotheca invenimus: ubi Διδαχαὶ τῶν Αποστόλων, καὶ Διδασκαλία Κλήμεντος, ut distincta opera recensentur, & in scriptorum Apocryphorum censu pariter reponuntur. Illas vero Apostolorum Διαταγαὶς in graeco quodam vetusto exemplari manuscripto Διδασκαλίας titulo prænotatas se reperisse, F. Turrianus indicat; indeque utrumque se conjunxisse, & ex utroque inscriptionem hanc, quae in ipsius editione Constitutionum legitur, contexuisse; Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Αποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος τῆς Ρωμαίων ἐκκλησίας τε & πολίτης, Catholica Διδασκαλία. Constitutiones sanctorum Apostolorum, authore Clemente, episcopo & cive Romano, Catholica Doctrina. Quem Διδασκαλίας titulum confirmant etiam illa in ipso corpore Constitutionum l. 1. c. 1. Ἀνύσατε Διδασκαλίαν ἱερὰν, &c. l. 2. c. 39. Ἐγὼ Ματθαῖος, εἰς τῶν ἐν τῇδε τῇ Διδασκαλία λαλούντων ὑμῖν, εἰμὶ Αποστόλος. l. 6. c. 14. ἐγχάραμεν ὑμῖν τῷ Καθολικῷ ταύτην Διδασκαλίαν, Et c. 18. καταλιπόντες ὑμῖν τήνδε τῷ Καθολικῷ ταύτην Διδασκαλίαν.
units.tr: Third, Ussher says, we are moved by the list of canonical and apocryphal books that we found in the public Bibliotheca of the University of Oxford, appended to the questions of Anastasius of Nicaea: there the Teachings of the Apostles and the Teaching of Clement are listed as separate works, and likewise placed in the census of apocryphal writings. Turrianus indicates that he found those Ordinances of the Apostles in an old Greek manuscript copy marked with the title Διδασκαλία [Teaching], and from this he joined the two together and composed from both the title that is read in his edition of the Constitutions: Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος τῆς Ρωμαίων ἐκκλησίας τε καὶ πολίτης, Καθολικὴ Διδασκαλία [Ordinances of the holy Apostles, through Clement, bishop and citizen of the Roman Church; Catholic Teaching]. Latin: The Constitutions of the holy Apostles, by Clement, bishop and citizen of Rome, Catholic Teaching. This title Διδασκαλία is also confirmed by passages in the body of the Constitutions itself: book 1, chapter 1, "Ἀνύσατε Διδασκαλίαν ἱερὰν" [Hasten to the holy teaching], etc.; book 2, chapter 39, "Ἐγὼ Ματθαῖος, εἰς τῶν ἐν τῇδε τῇ Διδασκαλία λαλούντων ὑμῖν, εἰμὶ Ἀπόστολος" [I, Matthew, one of those speaking to you in this Teaching, am an apostle]; book 6, chapter 14, "ἐγχάραμεν ὑμῖν τῷ Καθολικῷ ταύτην Διδασκαλίαν" [we have engraved this Catholic Teaching for you]; and chapter 18, "καταλιπόντες ὑμῖν τήνδε τῷ Καθολικῷ ταύτην Διδασκαλίαν" [leaving you this Catholic Teaching].

units.la: quibus addi poterit & illa Epiphanii a citatio,
units.tr: To these may be added also that citation of Epiphanius,

units.la: a Har. 8o. adverf. Messal. tio, ἐν ταῖς Διατάξεσι τῶν Ἀποστόλων φάσι· καὶ ὁ Θεῖος λόγος, ἕ ἢ Διδασκαλία. Ha- ctenus R. Usserius: cujus argumentis tri-bus nos & hoc quartum addimus, ex altero nuper descripto Athanasii in Synopsi loco ductum. Ibi enim inter τὰ τῆς γέας διαθήκης ἀντιλεγόμενα recensentur velut diversi libri, Διδαχὴ Ἀποστόλων, Κλημέντια, Doctrina Apostolorum, Clementina; ut distinguit & Graecus codex, & Latina interpretatio. Ergo Clementina, sive Clementis nomine dicta & vulgata, alia ab Apostolorum doctrina. Nimirum Clementina Athanasius intelligit, quae tum circumferebantur Clementis nomine, Petri & Appionis Dialogos, vel Recognitionem, id est ἀναγνωρισμόν, & alia apud Latinos a Rufino exeunte quarto, quo vixit Athanasius, Christianismi saeculo, postea ex Graeco interpretata ac vulgata. At si Doctrina Apostolorum codex Constitutionum revera erat, non fuit liber a Clementinis sejungendus. Liquet enim Constitutiones Clementis nomen praeferre; in quibus fictitii illi, qui loquentes inducuntur Apostoli se doctrinam illam suam διὰ τῶ συλλέγτως- γῶ Κλήμεντι διαπέμψαδαι, per commi-nistrum suum Clementem misisse profitentur. Itaque & a Trullanis Patribus τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος διατάξεις vocantur, E tur, & à Photio a in Clementis operibus recensentur. Ex quibus apparet Διδαχὴ illam Apostolorum Athanasianam, quæ alia est à Clementinis, eadem quoque ratione à Constitutionibus, quæ, si fuerunt tum ullæ, Clementinorum nomine & censu necessario continebantur, plane diversam fuisse. Ergo nihil ad Apostolicas Bovii Constitutiones hic Athanasii locus; neque ejus de Doctrina Apostolica judicium hanc causam quicquam juvat. Iam vero quod ad illud enantiophanes pertinet, quod inter duo Athanasii de libro cui nomen erat Apostolorum Doctrina, dicta intercedere diximus; ego quidem non nego, sanctissimum virum longe mitius de illo opere in epistola heortastica censere, quam in synopsi. Illic enim ex librorum quidem divinorum canone eum submovet; legi tamen ex Patrum præscripto à Catechumenis, & ab iis qui nuper accedentes in pietatis negotio erudiri ac instituì cupiunt, & cum Ecclesiastico, ac Syrachide, Esthere, Judith & Tobia recenset, apocryphis quidem illis, sed tamen utilibus libris, & qui cum fructu legi possunt. In synopsi vero aliter, ut videtur. Locat enim illam Apostolorum doctrinam una cum Petri, Ioannis & Thomæ πράξεις sive itinerariis; quæ deterrimi apocryphorum rum generis indubie & sunt, & fuerunt semper. Itaque mox ait, ista omnia esse παραγεγραμμένα, περὶ νόθα, περὶ ἀπόβλητα, ἀποκρυφῆς μᾶλλον, ἢ ἀναγνώσεως ἄξια. Ad hunc solvendum nodum imprimis observandum arbitror, quod Athanasius in Synopsi post commemorata illa, Διδαχὴ Ἀποστόλων, & Clementina, statim addit, ex his veriora quaedam electa esse, quae & leguntur. Hinc enim haud absurde quis, ut mihi quidem videtur, conjecerit & Doctrinae Apostolorum, & Clementinorum codicem a veteribus defloratum fuisse, & ex utroque opere, missis falsis, noxiis, aut inutilibus, excerpta & selecta quae alicujus esse visa sunt ad piorum hominum aedificationem usus. Ac opera quidem ipsa integra plane reprobata fuisse, & in ultimam apocryphorum classem, veluti fictitia, abjecta; has vero ex iis factas utilium sententiarum collectiones non quidem in canonem relatas (quod solis divinis libris convenit) sed tamen hominibus Christianis in usu atque lectione relictas, ac concessas. Quae si vera sunt, ut videntur, equidem putaverim, Athanasium in epistola per illam Apostolorum doctrinam, quam legi a catechumenis ait, collectionem hujusmodi ex apochrypho illo libro factam intelligere; in Synopsi vero, ipsum illud spurium, unde facta erat, opus significare; indeque ortum esse, ut de Doctrina Apostolorum priori loco mitius, posteriori acerbius loquutus sit. Utcunque sit, illud quidem satis constat, Doctrinam, quae dicitur Apostolorum, ab omnibus, qui ejus meminerunt, extra canonicorum censum poni; relegarique ab uno quidem Athanasio inter τὰ ἀναγινωσκόμενα, ut ille vocat; à caeteris omnibus vel inter τὰ νόθα, ut ab Eusebio a; vel inter τὰ ἀπόκρυφα, ut à Nicephoro CP. Patriarcha, & ab authore Indiculi, quem se R. Usseriūs Anastasii Nicaeni quaestionibus subjectum reperisse testatur.
units.tr: in the Ordinances of the Apostles, Epiphanius says: "And the divine word, or Teaching" [ἐν ταῖς Διατάξεσι τῶν Ἀποστόλων φάσι· καὶ ὁ Θεῖος λόγος, ἢ Διδασκαλία] (Haer. 80, against the Messalians). So far Ussher, to whose three arguments I add this fourth, drawn from the other passage of Athanasius, recently noted, in the Synopsis. There, among the disputed books of the New Covenant (τὰ τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης ἀντιλεγόμενα), are listed as separate books the Teaching of the Apostles and the Clementina (Διδαχὴ Ἀποστόλων, Κλημέντια), as both the Greek manuscript and the Latin translation distinguish: Doctrina Apostolorum, Clementina. Therefore the Clementina, that is, the works given and circulated under Clement's name, are different from the Doctrine of the Apostles. Certainly Athanasius means by the Clementina those writings then circulating under Clement's name: the Dialogues of Peter and Apion, or the Recognitions (ἀναγνωρισμός), and others which, in Latin, were translated from the Greek and published by Rufinus at the end of the fourth century, in which Athanasius lived, the century of Christianity. But if the Doctrine of the Apostles really was the codex of the Constitutions, it could not have been separated from the Clementine works. For it is clear that the Constitutions bear Clement's name, and in them the fictitious Apostles who are introduced as speaking profess that they sent that teaching of theirs through their fellow-minister Clement (διὰ τῶ συλλειτουργῶ Κλήμεντι διαπέμψασθαι). So too the Trullan Fathers call them "the ordinances of the holy Apostles through Clement" (τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος διατάξεις), and Photius counts them among the works of Clement. From this it appears that the Athanasian Apostolic Teaching, which is different from the Clementine works, was on the same reasoning plainly different from the Constitutions, which, if there were any such then, were necessarily included under Clement's name and in the same category. Therefore this passage of Athanasius has nothing to do with Bovius' Apostolic Constitutions, and his judgment about the Apostolic Doctrine does nothing to help this case. Now, as for the apparent contradiction, which I said lies between the two statements of Athanasius about the book called the Doctrine of the Apostles: I do not deny that the most holy man judges that book much more mildly in his festal letter than in his Synopsis. For there he indeed removes it from the canon of the divine books, yet allows it to be read by catechumens, and by those who recently come forward and wish to be instructed in the matter of piety, and he lists it with Ecclesiasticus, Sirach, Esther, Judith and Tobit, apocryphal indeed, but useful books that can be read with profit. In the Synopsis, however, he seems to speak differently, for there he places that Doctrine of the Apostles together with the Acts (πράξεις), or itineraries, of Peter, John and Thomas, which undoubtedly belong to the worst kind of apocrypha and always have. Hence he soon says that all these are "forged, spurious, to be rejected, fit for concealment rather than for reading" (παραγεγραμμένα, νόθα, ἀπόβλητα, ἀποκρυφῆς μᾶλλον ἢ ἀναγνώσεως ἄξια). To loosen this knot, I think it should be noted above all that in the Synopsis, after mentioning those two, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Clementina, Athanasius at once adds that certain truer selections from these are also read. From this one might reasonably conjecture, as it seems to me, that both the codex of the Doctrine of the Apostles and that of the Clementine works were culled by the ancients, and that from both works, the false, harmful or useless parts having been set aside, certain passages thought fit for the edification of pious people were excerpted and selected. The works themselves were entirely rejected and cast into the last class of apocrypha as fictitious, but the collections of useful sayings made from them were not indeed placed in the canon (which belongs to the divine books alone), yet were left to Christians for use and reading, and permitted. If this is true, as it seems, I would suppose that in the letter, by that Doctrine of the Apostles which he says is read by catechumens, Athanasius means a collection of this kind made from that apocryphal book, while in the Synopsis he means the spurious work itself from which the collection was made. And hence it came about that he speaks more mildly of the Doctrine of the Apostles in the former place and more harshly in the latter. However that may be, it is quite certain that the book called the Doctrine of the Apostles is placed outside the canonical list by all who mention it: Athanasius alone relegates it among "the things to be read" (τὰ ἀναγινωσκόμενα), as he calls them, while all the others put it either among the spurious (τὰ νόθα), as Eusebius does, or among the hidden (τὰ ἀπόκρυφα), as Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, and the author of the Index that Ussher testifies he found appended to the questions of Anastasius of Nicaea, do.

units.la: Atque ex his quidem, quae de Athanasii testimonio disputavimus, patet, quam nullius sint momenti quae Bovius ex Eusebio profert. Athanasii (inquit) judicium secutus Eusebius, neque in eis Scripturis hos libros numeravit, quae pro Canonicis ab omnibus Ecclesiis receptae erant, neque in apocryphis, sed in eis, quas non omnes Ecclesiae agnoscebant. In quibus illud primo parum belle dictum videtur, quod ait Bovius, Eusebium Athanasii judicium secutum. Nam cum ille annis non paucis hoc fuerit vetustior, neque fortassis ullum ejus librum legerit; nescio unde habere posset Bovius, quod hic temere, nullaque veri specie affirmat, Eusebium Athanasii in his judicium secusecutum. Sed verba ipsa Eusebii recitemus, quæ non in primo, quod idem quoque Bovius per errorem ait, sed in tertio libro historiæ, habentur. Istic ergo, enumeratis publice ab omnibus receptis Novi Testamenti Scripturis, sic pergit a: Τῶν δ' ἀντιλεγομένων, γνωείμων δ' ὢν ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς ἡ λεγομένη Ἰακώβε φέρεται, ἡ ἡ Ἰούδα, ἥτε Πέτρου δευτέρα ἐπιστολή, ἡ ἡ ὀνομαζομένη δευτέρα ἡ τρίτη Ἰωάννου, εἴτε τῆς Εὐαγγελιστῆς τυγχάνουσαι, εἴτε ἡ ἑτέρα ὁμωνύμως ἐκείνῳ. Ἐν νόθοις καταταξάχθω ἡ τῶν Πάυλε πράξεων ἡ γραφή, ὁ τε λεγόμενος Ποιμήν, ἡ ἡ Ἀποκάλυψις Πέτρου· ἡ πρὸς τούτοις ἡ φερομένη Βαρνάβα ἐπιστολή, καὶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων λεγόμεναι Διδαχαί. Ἔτι δὲ, ὡς ἔφην, ἡ Ἰωάννου Ἀποκάλυψις, εἰ φανείη, ἢν τινες, ὡς ἔφλω, ἀθετοῦσιν, ἑτέροι δ' ἐγκεῖνται τοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις. Hæc Eusebius; quæ latine ita vertit Christophorsonus b: Ex illis, quæ in dubitationem quidem vocantur, sunt tamen a plerisque recepta, est Epistola quæ Iacobi dicitur, & Iudæ, & secunda Petri, & secunda & tertia quæ Ioannis nomine inscribuntur, sive illa ab Euangelista, sive ab quopiam eodem nomine appellato, perscriptæ sunt. Inter scripturas autem, quæ falso inscriptæ, minimeque germanæ dicuntur, Pauli acta numerantur, & liber, qui vocatur Pastor, & Apocalypsis Petri: porro epistola nomine Barna-
units.tr: And from what we have argued about the testimony of Athanasius, it is clear how worthless are the things Bovius brings forward from Eusebius. Following the judgment of Athanasius, Eusebius (he says) did not number these books either among those Scriptures which all churches received as canonical, or among the apocrypha, but among those which not all the churches acknowledged. Here the first point is that Bovius's statement, that Eusebius followed the judgment of Athanasius, is put rather clumsily. Eusebius was some years older than Athanasius and perhaps never read any of his books, so I do not see where Bovius got the idea, which he asserts rashly and with no appearance of truth, that Eusebius followed Athanasius in these matters. But let us quote Eusebius's own words, which are found not in the first book (as Bovius also mistakenly says) but in the third book of the History. There, after listing the New Testament Scriptures publicly received by all, he goes on thus: "Of the disputed books, which are nevertheless known and read by most, there are the epistle said to be of James, and that of Jude, and the second epistle of Peter, and the so-called second and third of John, whether they are by the Evangelist or by another of the same name. Among the spurious books let the Acts of Paul be placed, and the writing called the Shepherd, and the Apocalypse of Peter; and besides these the epistle said to be of Barnabas, and the so-called Teachings of the Apostles. Also, as I said, the Apocalypse of John, if it seems fit, which some reject, while others count it among the acknowledged books." [Τῶν δὲ ἀντιλεγομένων, γνώριμων δ' ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἡ λεγομένη Ἰακώβου φέρεται, καὶ ἡ Ἰούδα, ἥτε Πέτρου δευτέρα ἐπιστολή, καὶ ἡ ὀνομαζομένη δευτέρα καὶ τρίτη Ἰωάννου, εἴτε τοῦ εὐαγγελιστοῦ τυγχάνουσαι, εἴτε ἕτερου τοῦ ὁμωνύμου ἐκείνῳ. Ἐν τοῖς νόθοις καταταχθήτω ἡ Παύλου πράξεων γραφή, ὅ τε λεγόμενος Ποιμήν, καὶ ἡ Ἀποκάλυψις Πέτρου· ἡ πρὸς τούτοις ἡ φερομένη Βαρνάβα ἐπιστολή, καὶ αἱ Ἀποστόλων λεγόμεναι Διδαχαί. Ἔτι δὲ, ὡς ἔφην, ἡ Ἰωάννου Ἀποκάλυψις, εἰ φανείη, ἣν τινες μὲν ἀθετοῦσιν, ἕτεροι δ' ἐγκεῖνται τοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις.] Eusebius says this, and Christophorsonus translates it into Latin thus: Of those books which are called in dispute, yet are accepted by most, there is the epistle said to be James's, and Jude's, and the second of Peter, and the second and third which are inscribed with John's name, whether they were written by the Evangelist or by someone else of the same name. Among the writings that are falsely inscribed and said to be by no means genuine, the Acts of Paul are numbered, and the book called the Shepherd, and the Apocalypse of Peter; further, the epistle under the name of Barnabas.

units.la: b. Christophorsono c. 19. Barnabæ edita, & quæ dicitur Doctrina Apostolorum. Adde his, si videtur, Joannis (ut dixi) Apocalypsin: quam nonnulli, ut docui, penitus antiquare contenderunt; alii tamen eam in Scripturis maxime approbatis collocandam judicant. Ex his liquet, Bovium, primo, quas ait Eusebius Ἀποστόλων λεγομένας διδαχάς, perperam, &, ut videtur, malo animo, Institutiones Apostolorum dixisse; inflexo ad Constitutiones suas nomine, ut lectori fucum faceret. Ruffinus, quasi quod apud Athanasium extat, hic quoque legisset ἡ Ἀποστόλων λεγομένη Διδαχή, in singulari numero vertit, doctrina quæ dicitur Apostolorum. Ergo Eusebius non alium librum intelligit, quam hunc ipsum, quem Athanasius duobus locis, & alii non pauci Doctrinam Apostolorum vocant; quem cum nuper demonstraverimus à Bovianis Constitutionibus diversum esse, nihil ad hanc quidem causam facit iste Eusebii locus. Sane qui de Clementis scriptis duobus locis, & quidem posteriori accuratissime, verba facit Eusebius, si quæ tum extitissent ejus nomine vel Constitutiones, vel etiam Doctrina Apostolorum, eas haud dubie non erat omissurus. Nam in priori quidem loco, Romanum Clementis episcopatum narrans; Ταῦτα δὴ (inquit a) οὖν ὁμολογούμενα μία ἐπιστολὴ φέρεῖ, μεγάλη τε ἡ θαυμασία, ἥν ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥωμαίων Ἐκκλησίας τῆς Κορινθίων ἐτυπώσαλο, ςάσεως ἴνvικάςὲ καὶ Κόεινθον γενομένης. τάυτλῳ ὃ καὶ ἐν πλείςαις ἐκκλησίαις ὅπ τε κοινῇ ςιδηµοσιευμένῳ πάλαι τε καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς αὐτὰς ἐγνωμεν. Hujus vero Clementis una fertur Epistola, omnium judicio approbata, illustris illa quidem & digna plane admiratione; quam tanquam ex Ecclesia Romana persona ad Corinthiorum Ecclesiam tum quidem exaravit, cum jam Corinthi gravis esset inflata seditio. Hanc sane cum veterum, tum nostra ipsorum memoria, plurimis in Ecclesiis publice lectam, usurpatamque cognovimus. Cur qui hujus epistolæ meminit, neque Διαλέξεων, neque Διδαχῆς Apostolorum meminit? Quia neque illas, neque has Clementis ullas noverat. Sed en tibi alium locum ex eodem Eusebii volumine, ab Hieronymo supra citatum, in quo de Clementis Romani operibus velut ex professo agit; ac imprimis eandem illam ex Romanæ Ecclesiæ persona ad Corinthios Διαλελυπωμένην Epistolam memorat; observatque, quod & ex Hieronymo in superioribus audivimus, multos in ea reperiri sensus, quædam etiam verba, quæ cum iis congruunt, quæ in Epistola ad Hebræos leguntur. Tum alteram Epistolam Iam, quæ à quibusdam Clementis esse dicebatur, refellit : ἃ μὲν ἐξ ὁμοίως τὴν προ- τέρα καὶ ταύτλω γνώσιμον ἐπισάμενα· ὅτι μηδὲ τὰς ἀρχαίας αὐτῆς κεχρημένας ἴσμεν. Verum eam non perinde ut priorem approbatam cognoscimus: propterea quod non animadvertimus, veteres illius testimonia suis aliquando scriptis intexuisse. Quibus dictis tandem hæc adjicit: ἡδὴ ὁ ἢ ἑτέρα προ- λυτίπη καὶ μακρὰ συγγράμματα, ὡς τὸ αὐ- τὸ χθὲς ἐ πρώην τινὲς προῄγαγον, Πέτρου δὴ καὶ Ἀππίωνος διαλόγους πεπείχοντα, ὧν ἐδ' ὅλως μνήμην τις τοῖς παλαιοῖς φέρει. ὁ- ὁ γὰρ καθαρὸν τῆς Ἀποστολικῆς ὀρθοδοξίας ἀ- ποσωζει τ χαρακτῆρα. Iam vero quidam alia item opera, verbosa illa quidem & prolixa, heri prope & nudiusTertius perinde quasi illius essent, introduxerunt, quæ quidem disputationes Petri & Appionis continent; quorum apud veteres nulla omnino fit mentio; nam puram illam & sinceram Apostolicæ orthodoxaque doctrinæ notam minime retinent. Atque ita denique totum hunc locum concludit : Ἡ μὲν ἂν τῷ Κλήμεντι ὁμολογουμένη γραφὴ πρόδηλός ἐστιν. Atque ita quidem manifesta est, quæ apud omnes in confesso est, Clementis Scriptura. Obsecro tuam fidem: Illas Apostolorum dictas doctrinas, si eæ Clementis nomen seu vere seu falso præferebant ferebant, cur hoc loco omisit Eusebius, quo Clementis opera & vera affirmat, & notha refellit, sive, ut loquitur Hieronymus, coarguit ? Ergo & hoc ex Eusebii silentio ductum argumentum ad ea quintum accedat, quibus Reverendissimi Usserii sententiam nuper probavimus. Eo enim liquido conficitur, non fuisse Clementis nomine scriptam illam Apostolorum dictam doctrinam: proinde neque eä esse, quod vult Bovius, Apostolicarum Constitutionum codicem; quæ scilicet Clementis, sive Διὰ Κλήμεντος, per Clementem, esse dicuntur. Itaque frustra laborat Bovius, qui quæ Eusebius de Apostolorum doctrinis, sive, ut habet Ruffinus, doctrina dicit, ea non modo nulla ratione, sed etiam contra manifestam rationem, ad suas Pseudo-Clementinas Diataxes torquet. Huc accedit, quod ne ipsam illam quidem Apostolorum dictam doctrinam valde commendat Eusebius. Eam enim non modo, quod concedit Bovius, τοῖς ἀντιλεγομένοις, sed etiam τοῖς νόθοις accenset. Disserta sunt verba, ἐν τοῖς νόθοις κατατετάχθω, In nothis sive spuriis reponatur, καὶ τῶν Παύλου πράξεων ἢ γραφὴ, ὅ τι λεγόμενον Ποιμὴν, ἡ Ἀποκάλυψις Πέτρου, & Pauli actuum scriptura, & qui dicitur Pastor, & Petri Revelatio. καὶ πρὸς τέτοις ἡ Φιλο- μένη μὲν Barnabæ ἐπιστολὴ, & τῶν Ἀποστόλων τᾶ λεγομένας Διδαχὴ, Apostolorum doctrinam eodem locari, censerique quo Pauli actus & Petri Revelationem. Itaque si (quod facit Bovius) rectum est ex eorum librorum ingenio, quibuscum hic collocatur Doctrina Apostolorum dicta, de ejus apud Ecclesiam censu argumentari, consequens est, eam nullo tum in pretio fuisse; cum liqueat illos, quibus accensetur, Actuum Pauli, & Revelationis Petri libros, vel Bellarmino teste, omnino apocryphos, imo spurios & Suppositititios & esse, & habitos apud veteres fuisse. Sed ludit Bovius. Planum enim est, Eusebium promiscue hic τὰ ἀντιλεγόμενα recensere, sive iis jure ac merito, sive inique falso contradiceretur. Prioris generis sunt illi Pauli Actus, Petrique Apocalypsis, & Barnabæ epistolæ, & Apostolorum doctrina: posterioris Apocalypsis Ioannis, & duæ ejusdem posteriores epistolæ. Ille vero, tametsi tanto abse invicem discrimine separata simul recensét, quod nihil esset istorum cui non aliqui tunc contradicerent; licet alioqui diversa esset contradicentium causa ac ratio. Itaque nullum hinc quidem in alterutram partem, de istorum librorum sive falsitate sive veritate, certum duci potest argumentum. Unde denique consequitur, si vel concederemus (quod su-
units.tr: b Christophorsonus, ch. 19. The epistle of Barnabas, and what is called the Teaching of the Apostles. Add to these, if you think fit, the Apocalypse of John (as I said), which some have strongly tried to set aside entirely, while others judge it should be placed among the most approved Scriptures. From these things it is clear that Bovius, first, wrongly and, it seems, with bad intent, called the Teachings of the Apostles (which Eusebius calls αἱ Ἀποστόλων λεγόμεναι διδαχαί) Institutions of the Apostles, bending the name toward his own Constitutions so as to deceive the reader. Rufinus, as if he had read here too what is found in Athanasius, ἡ Ἀποστόλων λεγομένη Διδαχή, rendered it in the singular, the doctrine which is called the Apostles'. So Eusebius means no other book than this very one, which Athanasius in two places, and many others, call the Doctrine of the Apostles. Since we have just shown that it differs from Bovius's Constitutions, this passage of Eusebius contributes nothing to the present question. Indeed, Eusebius speaks of Clement's writings in two places, the second most carefully, and if any writings under Clement's name then existed, either Constitutions or even Doctrine of the Apostles, he would undoubtedly not have omitted them. In the first place, narrating the Roman episcopate of Clement, he says: "These things, then, are acknowledged; one epistle of Clement is extant, great and admirable, which he wrote in the name of the Roman Church to the Church of Corinth when a sedition had broken out at Corinth. This we know to have been publicly read in many churches both in ancient times and in our own." [Ταῦτα δὴ οὖν ὁμολογούμενα· μία φέρεται ἐπιστολή, μεγάλη τε καὶ θαυμασία, ἣν ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥωμαίων Ἐκκλησίας τῇ τῶν Κορινθίων ἐξετύπωσεν, στάσεως ἐν Κορίνθῳ γενομένης.] Of this Clement one epistle is said to be extant, acknowledged by all, illustrious and truly admirable, which he wrote in the name of the Roman Church to the Church of the Corinthians, when a serious sedition had arisen at Corinth. This we know, both from ancient and from our own memory, to have been publicly read and used in very many churches. Why does he who mentions this epistle say nothing of the Disputations or the Teaching of the Apostles? Because he knew neither those nor any others of Clement's. But see another passage from the same volume of Eusebius, cited above by Jerome, in which he treats of Clement of Rome's works as if professedly; there he mentions that same epistle written in the person of the Roman Church to the Corinthians, and observes, as we heard from Jerome above, that many senses are found in it, and even some words which agree with those read in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Then he refutes the second epistle, which some said was Clement's: "We do not know it to be approved in the same way as the first, because we have not noticed that the ancients ever used its testimonies in their writings." [Ἃ μὲν ἐξ ὁμοίως τὴν προτέραν καὶ ταύτην γνώσιμον ἐπίσταμαι· ὅτι μηδὲ τὰς ἀρχαίας αὐτῆς κεχρημένας ἴσμεν.] Having said these things, he at last adds: "Now certain others have brought forward other works, verbose and long, as if they were Clement's, namely the Disputations of Peter and Apion, of which the ancients make no mention at all, for they do not keep the pure mark of apostolic orthodoxy." [Ἤδη δέ τινες ἕτερα προήγαγον, πολυλόγα καὶ μακρὰ συγγράμματα, ὡς τὰ αὐτοῦ, χθὲς ἢ πρώην τινές προῆγαγον, Πέτρου δὴ καὶ Ἀππίωνος διαλόγους πεπλασμένους, ὧν ἐδ' ὅλως μνήμην τις τοῖς παλαιοῖς φέρει· οὐ γὰρ τὸν καθαρὸν τῆς ἀποστολικῆς ὀρθοδοξίας ἀπόσωζει χαρακτῆρα.] And so he finally concludes this whole passage: "Thus indeed Clement's writing is manifest, which all agree upon." [Ἡ μὲν οὖν τῷ Κλήμεντι ὁμολογουμένη γραφὴ πρόδηλός ἐστιν.] Thus Clement's writing is clear, which is acknowledged by all. I beg you to consider: if those so-called doctrines of the Apostles bore Clement's name, whether truly or falsely, why did Eusebius omit them in this place, where he affirms Clement's genuine works and refutes the spurious ones, or, as Jerome puts it, exposes them? So let this argument from Eusebius's silence be added to the five others by which we lately confirmed the judgment of the most reverend Ussher. For it is plainly established from it that the doctrine called the Apostles' was not written under Clement's name, and therefore it is not, as Bovius wants, the code of the Apostolic Constitutions, which are said to be of Clement, or through Clement (Διὰ Κλήμεντος, per Clementem). Bovius therefore labours in vain, since he bends what Eusebius says about the doctrines of the Apostles, or, as Rufinus has it, doctrine, not only without any reason but even against its plain sense, to his own Pseudo-Clementine Diataxes. Moreover, Eusebius does not commend even that so-called doctrine of the Apostles very highly. For he reckons it not only among the disputed books (which Bovius concedes) but also among the spurious: the words are, "let it be placed among the spurious" (ἐν τοῖς νόθοις κατατετάχθω), "the Acts of Paul, and the so-called Shepherd, and the Apocalypse of Peter", "and besides these the epistle said to be of Barnabas and the so-called Teachings of the Apostles." So the Doctrine of the Apostles is placed in the same company as the Acts of Paul and the Revelation of Peter. Therefore, if (as Bovius does) it is right to judge its standing in the Church from the character of the books with which it is ranked here, it follows that it was of no account at that time, since it is clear that the books with which it is grouped, the Acts of Paul and the Revelation of Peter, are, even by Bellarmine's testimony, altogether apocryphal, indeed spurious and supposititious, and were so regarded by the ancients. But Bovius is playing games. For it is plain that Eusebius here lists the disputed books indiscriminately, whether they were rightly and justly contradicted or unjustly and falsely. Of the first kind are the Acts of Paul, the Apocalypse of Peter, the epistle of Barnabas, and the Doctrine of the Apostles; of the second kind are the Apocalypse of John and the two later epistles of the same John. Though he lists them together, separated by such a great difference, because none of them was not contradicted by someone at that time, yet the reasons for contradicting them were otherwise different. Hence no certain argument can be drawn from this passage in either direction, about the falsity or truth of these books. From this it finally follows that even if we were to grant (which I have refuted elsewhere) that those Teachings of the Apostles mentioned by Eusebius are really the Constitutions which are called the Apostles', no one, neither Bovius nor Turrianus, will find in this passage of Eusebius any support for his delusion, by which they dream that their own (which

units.la: a De Scriptor. Eccles. in Petro. {ꝑ}ra refutavimus) illas ab Eusebio memoratas Ἀποστόλων Διδαχαὶ vere eas esse Constitutiones, quę Apostolorum dictæ sunt, nullum tamen vel Bovium vel Turrianum in hoc Eusebii loco sui delirii præsidium habituros, quo somniant suas illas Constitutiones verum ac genuinum esse vel Apostolorum, vel Clementis Romani fœtum.
units.tr: In my book On the Writers of the Church, under Peter, where I refuted it. Even if we granted (which I have refuted there) that the Teachings of the Apostles (Ἀποστόλων Διδαχαί) mentioned by Eusebius are truly the work called the Constitutions of the Apostles [Ἀποστόλων Διδαχαί], neither Bovius nor Turrianus would have any support for his folly in this passage of Eusebius, by which they dream that their Constitutions are a true and genuine work either of the Apostles or of Clement of Rome.

units.la: Hæc de Eusebio hactenus, qui a. D. 315. Cæsareæ in Palæstina ordinatus Episcopus an. 330. Historiæ suæ opus composuit, ad a. D. 340. vitam produxit. Totis, quæ supra ejus Episcopatum fluxerant, tribus Christianismi sæculis nulla usquam apud Græcos Patres Constitutionum vel levis umbra, aut mentio licet eorum temporum multi, & quidem eruditissimi extent; ut Origines, ejusque præceptor Clemens Alexandrinus, Irenæus, & Iustinus, & alii.
units.tr: So much for Eusebius. He was ordained bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in A.D. 315, wrote his Church History in about 330, and brought his life down to A.D. 340. Throughout the three centuries of Christianity that preceded his episcopate, there is no trace or even faint shadow of the Constitutions among the Greek Fathers, though many writers of those times survive, and very learned ones too, such as Origen, his teacher Clement of Alexandria, Irenaeus, Justin, and others.

units.la: Ergo non in Græca magis, quam in Latina veteri Ecclesia, notæ fuerunt, vel pro veris habitæ illæ quæ nunc nobis a Bovio obtruduntur, Constitutiones. Itaque jure ac merito & nostri, & ex adversariis doctissimi celeberrimiq; Theologi Baronius, Bellarminus, Perronius, purpurati, Albaspineus Episcopus, la Bigne Sorbonicus, Petavius Iesuita, de obscuro, ignobilique libro dubitarunt, ejusque velut apocryphi in rebus fidei authoritatem nullam esse putarunt.
units.tr: Therefore these Constitutions, which Bovius now thrusts upon us, were unknown to the ancient Greek Church, and no more known to the ancient Latin Church, nor were they regarded as genuine in either. Accordingly, and rightly, both our own theologians and the most learned and celebrated of our opponents, Baronius, Bellarmine, Perron (a cardinal), Albaspinaeus, the bishop, la Bigne of the Sorbonne, and Petavius the Jesuit, have doubted this obscure and undistinguished book, and have judged that its authority in matters of faith, as that of an apocryphal work, is nothing.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Constitutionum authoritas multis argumentis evertitur. I°. inde sumpto, quod ea neque à Græca, neque à Latina Ecclesia, vel olim, vel nuper, fuerint in canonem Scripturarum divinarum relata; quod omnino necesse erat fieri, si ea pro vere Apostolicis libris essent agnita. Bovii temeritas & impudentia castigatur.
units.tr: The authority of the Constitutions is overthrown by many arguments. First, it is drawn from the fact that these works have been received into the canon of the divine Scriptures neither by the Greek Church nor by the Latin Church, either formerly or recently; which would certainly have had to happen if they had been acknowledged as truly apostolic books. The rashness and impudence of Bovius is rebuked.

units.la: SEd ne solis eorum nominibus niti videamur, age rem ipsam nunc totam perspiciamus, expendamusq; accuratius; quamq; firmis fundamentis stet doctissimorum virorum sententia, paulo diligentius ac fusius ostendamus. Principio illud ante omnia statuendum est, has, quæ nunc circumferuntur, Diataxes, siquidem eæ veræ sunt, ab ipsis Domini Iesu Apostolis simul congregatis dictatas, ordinatas, conscriptas, ac denique ad Ecclesiarum præpositos missas fuisse; non secus ac quæ Pauli habentur epistolæ eæ à beatissimo illo Apostolo scriptæ, missæque sunt. Non jam urgeo libri titulum Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, Constitutiones sanctorum Apostolorum; quem fateor etiam iis convenire, quæ licet non ab ipsis Apostolis scriptæ, missæque, ab iisdem tamen quacunque alia ratione traditæ ac præceptæ sunt. Sed ipsum opus totum tum à capite ad calcem Apostolos authores praefert. Ab his verbis ordiuntur a; οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι πᾶσι τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν πιστεύσασιν εἰς τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη. Apostoli & Presbyteri omnibus qui ex Gentibus in Dominum Iesum Christum crediderunt, gratia vobis & pax. Alibi b ; Ἡμεῖς νῦν ὅτι τὸ αὐτὸ γινόμενοι Πέτρος καὶ Ἀνδρέας, Ἰάκωβος καὶ Ἰωάννης υἱοὶ Ζεβεδαίου· Φίλιππος καὶ Βαρθολομαῖος· Θωμᾶς καὶ Ματθαῖος· Ἰάκωβος Ἀλφαῖου, καὶ Λεββαῖος ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς Θαδδαῖος, καὶ Σίμων ὁ Καναναῖτης, καὶ Ματθίας ὁ αντὶ Ἰούδα καταψηφισθεὶς ἡμῖν· Ἰάκωβος τε ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδελφὸς, καὶ Ἱεροσολύμων ἐπίσκοπος· καὶ Παῦλος ὁ τῶν ἐθνῶν διδάσκαλος, τὸ σὺν ἐκλογῆς, ἅμα πάντες, καὶ ὅτι τὸ αὐτὸ γινόμενοι, ἐγράψαμεν ὑμῖν τῷ καθολικῷ ταύτῳ διδασκαλίαν εἰς ἐπισκέψεγμὸν τῆς τοῦ καθόλου ἐπισκοπῆς πεπιστευμένων. Ipsi nunc in unum congregati Petrus, & Andreas, Iacobus & Ioannes Zebedaei filii, Philippus & Bartholomaeus, Thomas & Matthaeus, Iacobus Alphaei, & Lebbaeus cognomento Thaddaeus, Simon Cananaeus, & Matthias qui loco Iudae electus nobis cooptatus est, & Iacobus frater Domini, idemque Hierosolymitanus Episcopus, item Paulus Doctor gentium, vas electionis: omnes una, & in unum congregati scripsimus mus vobis Catholicam hanc doctrinam, ad fulciendum, ac confirmandum vos, quibus universalis episcopatus creditus est. Sic etiam libro octavo a; Ἀμαλόινω ὑπάρχοντες ἡμεῖς οἱ ἁγιασμένοι τῶ Κυρίῳ Ἀπόστολοι τάσσε τὰς θείας ἡμῶν ἐντολὰς διατάξεις περὶ παντὸς ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ τύπου, συμπαραχόν-των ἡμῖν, καὶ τῆς ἐκλογῆς σκεύους Παύλου τοῦ συναποστόλου ἡμῶν, ἐξ Ἰακώβου τοῦ ἐπισκόπου, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν πρεσβυτέρων, ἐκ τῆς ἑπτὰ διακόνων.
units.tr: But so that we do not seem to rest only on their names, let us now look at the whole matter itself, weigh it more carefully, and show more fully how firmly the opinion of these learned men stands. First of all, this must be laid down: these Ordinances now in circulation, if they are genuine, were dictated, arranged, written, and finally sent to the leaders of the churches by the Apostles of the Lord Jesus themselves, gathered together, just as the Epistles of Paul which bear his name were written and sent by that most blessed Apostle. I do not press the title of the book, Ordinances of the Holy Apostles (Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων) [Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων], Constitutions of the holy Apostles, which I grant may also fit those things which, though not written and sent by the Apostles themselves, were nevertheless handed down and taught by them in some other way. But the work as a whole, from beginning to end, presents the Apostles as its authors. It opens with these words: "The Apostles and the elders to all who from the Gentiles have believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, grace to you and peace" [Οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι πᾶσι τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν πιστεύσασιν εἰς τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη]. Elsewhere: "We, now gathered together, Peter and Andrew, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus called Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean, and Matthias who was chosen by lot in place of Judas, and James the brother of the Lord, who is also bishop of Jerusalem, and Paul the teacher of the Gentiles, all together and with one accord, have written to you this Catholic teaching, to strengthen and confirm you, to whom the universal episcopate has been entrusted" [Ἡμεῖς νῦν ... ἐγράψαμεν ὑμῖν τῷ καθολικῷ ταύτῳ διδασκαλίαν εἰς ἐπισκέψεγμὸν τῆς τοῦ καθόλου ἐπισκοπῆς πεπιστευμένων]. So also in the eighth book: "We, the Apostles sanctified to the Lord, being gathered together, set down our divine ordinances concerning every ecclesiastical form, with the presence of us, and of Paul, the chosen vessel, our fellow apostle, and of James the bishop, and the other elders, and of the seven deacons" [Ἀθροισθέντες ἡμεῖς οἱ ἡγιασμένοι τῷ Κυρίῳ Ἀπόστολοι τάσσομεν τὰς θείας ἡμῶν ἐντολὰς διατάξεις περὶ παντὸς ἐκκλησιαστικοῦ τύπου, συμπαρόντων ἡμῖν, καὶ τῆς ἐκλογῆς σκεύους Παύλου τοῦ συναποστόλου ἡμῶν, ἔκ τε Ἰακώβου τοῦ ἐπισκόπου, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ τῶν ἑπτὰ διακόνων].

units.la: Nos igitur duodecim Apostoli, una consistentes divinas has nostras de omni Ecclesiastica forma constitutiones vobis praecipimus; nobiscum quoque praesentibus & vasa electionis Paulo coapostolo nostro, & Iacobo Episcopo, ac reliquis Presbiteris, & septem Diaconis. In ultimo vero operis capite b, post multa in superioribus singulorum Apostolorum nomine constituta; ἐκεῖνο ὁ κοινὴ πάντες παραγγέλλομεν· Illud vero (inquiunt) omnes communiter praecipimus. Mox causam, sive occasionem scriptionis afferunt, quod scilicet multi disciplinam a se traditam negligerent, & ordines confunderent, & ordinationem cujusque movere auderent, dignitates rapiendo minime sibi collatas, ac per vim potestatem sibi sumendo ea dandi aliis, qua dare non possunt:
units.tr: We therefore, the twelve Apostles, standing together, command you these our divine constitutions concerning every ecclesiastical order; with us also being present Paul, the vessel of election and our fellow apostle, and James the bishop, and the rest of the elders, and the seven deacons. In the last chapter of the work, after many things laid down in the earlier chapters in the name of individual Apostles, they say: "This, however, we all command in common" [ἐκεῖνο ὃ κοινῇ πάντες παραγγέλλομεν]. Soon afterwards they give the cause or occasion of the writing, namely that many neglected the discipline handed down by themselves, and confused the orders, and dared to disturb the ordination of each, seizing dignities not conferred on them, and by force assuming a power to give to others what they cannot give.

units.la: εἰκότως (inquiunt c) τὴν ἐπηρτημένον κίνδυνον τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα πράττουσι προειδόμενοι δὲ τὸ εἰς τὰς Θυσίας καὶ εὐχαριστίας ἀμέλειαν ἐκ τῶν ὑφ᾽ ὧν μὴ χρὴ προσαγομένας ἀσεβῶς, παιδίαν ἡγουμένων τὴν ἀρχιερατικὴν τιμὴν, ἥτις μίμησιν πεπέιχει τῆς μεγάλης ἀρχιερέως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ βασιλέως ἡμῶν, ἀνάγκλω ἰσχομεν κῆ τοῦτο παραινέσαι. Idcirco necessitate compulsi sumus, ut de hoc etiam moneremus, quia iis, qui talia committunt, periculum, ut par est, impendere providemus, neglegi etiam sacrificia & eucharistias, quod ab illis adhibeantur, quibus non est fas, qui ludicrum & jocularem putant honorem Pontificalem, qui imitationem continet magni Pontificis Jesu Christi nostri Regis. Sed & isti Διαλογεῖς Apostolorum ut nomina, ita & gesta, actusque omnes sibi constanter tribuunt; se partim piscatores, partim publicanos, partim tabernaculorum contextores a fuisse profitentur: se à Christo vocatos esse; ei, qua nocte captus est, adfuisse, hymnum de more cecinisse b; à resuscitato missos cum mandato docendi omnes gentes, & baptizandi eos in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti c: se cum Christo resuscitato quadraginta dies versatos esse d; Eundem ante oculos suos in coelum sublatum e: se missum ab eo Spiritum die Pentecostes accepisse, repletosque esse ejus operatione, & novis linguis locutos f: Se à Cajapha & Alexandro & Anna saepius pro Christo plagas
units.tr: "Rightly," they say, "foreseeing the danger hanging over those who do such things, and foreseeing that negligence in sacrifices and eucharists would follow from the impious offering of them by those who ought not to offer them, who regard the high-priestly honour as a game, though it contains the imitation of the great High Priest Jesus Christ our King, we are constrained by necessity to exhort on this point also" [εἰκότως ... ἀνάγκῃ ἰσχομεν ... τοῦτο παραινέσαι]. But these men also claim for themselves, constantly and as a matter of course, the names and deeds and all the actions of the Apostles. They profess that they were partly fishermen, partly tax-collectors, partly tentmakers a. They say that they were called by Christ; that they were present on the night he was taken, and sang the hymn in the usual way b; that after his resurrection they were sent with the command to teach all nations and to baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit c; that they spent forty days with the risen Christ d; that they saw him taken up into heaven before their eyes e; that they received the Spirit sent by him on the day of Pentecost, were filled with his working, and spoke in new tongues f.
