units.la: f l.5.c. 20. plagas accepisse g : sibi à Simone Mago oblatas fuisse pecunias h; suos denique esse qui à Luca perscripti in Ecclesiis leguntur actus; sua, suorumque discipulorum quatuor Christi Euangelia i; ut cætera mittam Apostolu, quæ isti passim sibi vendicant k Itaque si vera sunt, quæ isti narrant, dubitandum non est, quin ipsi Domini Christi Apostoli fuerint. Non esse autem istos, qui sic in Constitutionibus loquuntur, veros Domini Apostolos, sole meridiano clarius est. Nam ut hinc ordiar, si isti revera fuissent ii, quos se esse profitentur Domini Iesu Apostolos; agnovisset eos Ecclesia maxime vetus ac Christianismi initiis proxima, proque Apostolis habuisset. Non agnovise autem eos pro Apostolis Ecclesiam Christianam, vel Latinam vel Græcam, vel veterem vel recentem, inde clarissime intelligitur, quod has istorum diataxes certum est à neutra unquam Ecclesia in sacrorum ac divinorum librorum canonem fuisse relatas. Extat earum Scripturarum, quæ sub Novo Testamento editæ sunt, canon à multis Græcis Latinisque sive Theologis, sive etiam Synodis, descriptus; ut apud veteres ab Origene, ab Athanasio, à Gregorio Nazianzeno, ab Amphilochio, ab Hieronymo, ab Innocentio; à Synodis Laodicena, & Carthaginensi tertia; apud recen-
units.tr: f l.5.c. 20. They say that they were often struck for Christ by Caiaphas, Alexander, and Annas g; that money was offered to them by Simon Magus h; and that the Acts which Luke wrote down and which are read in the Churches are theirs, as are the four Gospels of Christ, written by them and their disciples i; not to mention the other writings which these men claim for themselves everywhere k. Therefore, if what these men relate is true, there is no doubt that they were the Apostles of the Lord Christ. But that those who speak in the Constitutions in this way are not the true Apostles of the Lord is clearer than midday sun. For to begin with this: if they were really those whom they profess to be, the Lord Jesus' Apostles, the Church, very ancient and closest to the beginnings of Christianity, would have recognized them and held them as Apostles. That the Christian Church, whether Latin or Greek, ancient or recent, did not recognize them as Apostles is most clearly understood from the fact that it is certain that these ordinances of theirs were never included by any Church in the canon of the sacred and divine books. There exists a canon of those Scriptures which were published under the New Testament, drawn up by many Greek and Latin writers, or even by Synods: among the ancients by Origen, by Athanasius, by Gregory Nazianzen, by Amphilochius, by Jerome, by Innocent; by the Synods of Laodicea and the Third Council of Carthage; and among recent writers...

units.la: {g} l. 5. c. 2. & l. 4. c. 6. & i l. 2. c. 57. d. & k Vide si placet l. 2. c. 1. & c. 14. & c. 24. & c. 55. L. 3. c. 6. & c. 9. & c. 19. L. 6. c. 7. & c. 8. & c. 12. & L. 8. c. 1. & c. 15. & c. 46. recentiores, ut reliquos taceam, à Tridentino Concilio; Atqui nullum est istorum monumentorum, in quo Diataxes inter libros canonicos recensitæ deprehendantur. Ipse, eas qui obtrudit, ac tantopore commendat Bovius , fatetur, nunquam obtinuisse ut in canonem sacrarum scripturarum referrentur; & homo verecundus negat, se iis tantam authoritatem tribuere velle.
units.tr: {g} l. 5. c. 2. & l. 4. c. 6. & i l. 2. c. 57. d. & k See, if you please, l. 2. c. 1. & c. 14. & c. 24. & c. 55. L. 3. c. 6. & c. 9. & c. 19. L. 6. c. 7. & c. 8. & c. 12. & L. 8. c. 1. & c. 15. & c. 46. More recent writers, to say nothing of the rest, have done so since the Council of Trent. And yet there is no monument of these where the Diataxes are found listed among the canonical books. Bovius himself, who presses these works and recommends them so strongly, admits that they never obtained that they should be counted in the canon of the sacred Scriptures; and this modest man denies that he wishes to grant them so great an authority.

units.la: Quæ dum ita agit, causam ipse suam prodit atque evertit imprudens. Ea enim est librorum istorum conditio, ut eos vel summo, vel nullo loco esse necesse sit. Nihil est medium, quo se de prima sede dejecti recipere possint. Nam qui Apostolorum sibi nomen arrogant, eos vel summæ dignitatis atque authoritatis inter canonicos censeri decet; vel si hoc, quod confitetur Bovius, consequi neque possunt, neque debent, omnino relinquitur, ut veluti falsi ac mendaces, inusta ultimæ impudentiæ nota, inter ficta, fabulosaque, ac plane apocrypha relegentur. Quale enim, quæso, istud est, quod velle videtur Bovius, ut qui liber Apostolicum se esse profitetur ac contendit, is fide dignus, ac verax habeatur, neque tamen in Ecclesiæ canonem referatur? Ullum-ne unquam opus pro Apostolico agnovit Ecclesia, quod non statim in suarum Scripturarum canonem retulerit? Eorumne, qui sibi à Christo fidei magistri, ac duces dati sunt, librum aliquem summo hoc honore indignum censuit? Fateor quosdam fuisse olim, qui posteriores Joannis & Petri epistolas in canone non habherent: nimirum, quod dubitarent, an eorum Apostolorum, quorum praescripta nomina praefe-rebant, vere essent. Qui quem librum Apostoli alicujus vere fuisse censeret, eundem scripturarum canone excluderet, Christianus, quod sciam, nemo, hactenus fuit. Bellarminus quidem hoc ipso argumento probat, non fuisse à Domino Christo scriptam eam epistolam, quae ejus nomine ad Abgarum Edessae Regem, jam olim Eusebianis ipsis temporibus circumfe-rebatur; Ea (inquit a) nunquam fuit admissa ab Ecclesia inter scripturas canonicas, inter quas sine dubio admissa fuisset, si ab ipso Domino scriptam fuisse constaret. Cum ergo ipsa teste Bovio, Diataxes nunquam fuerint admissae ab Ecclesia inter Scripturas Canonicas; omnino necesse est, nunquam constitisse eas ab Apostolis scriptas esse: id optime vidit impostor, qui Apostolorum nomine, canones immani impudentia procudere ausus est, is enim Diataxes cum vellet pro vere Apostolicis haberi, in canonem scripturarum audacter retulit; gnarus nimirum pro veris agnoscI eas non posse, nisi iis statim
units.tr: While he argues thus, he unwittingly betrays and overturns his own cause. For the condition of these books is such that they must stand either in the highest place or in none at all. There is no middle position to which they can retreat once driven from the first seat. Those who claim the name of Apostles for themselves ought to be counted among the canonical books of the highest dignity and authority; or, if they cannot and must not obtain what Bovius confesses, it follows entirely that, as false and lying works, branded with the mark of utter shamelessness, they must be relegated among the fictitious, fabulous and plainly apocryphal writings. For what, I ask you, is that which Bovius seems to want, namely that a book which professes and claims to be Apostolic should be held trustworthy and truthful, and yet not be placed in the canon of the Church? Has the Church ever acknowledged any work as Apostolic which it did not at once place in the canon of its Scriptures? Has it ever judged any book unworthy of this highest honour among those who were given by Christ as teachers and leaders of the faith? I grant that there were once some who did not include the later epistles of John and Peter in the canon, doubtless because they doubted whether they were truly by the Apostles whose names they bore. But so far as I know, no Christian has ever yet existed who thought a book truly belonged to some Apostle and yet excluded it from the canon of Scripture. Bellarmine indeed proves by this very argument that the letter which was circulated under the name of Christ to Abgar, king of Edessa, and which was already current in the time of Eusebius, was not written by the Lord Christ. "It (he says) was never admitted by the Church among the canonical Scriptures, among which it would undoubtedly have been admitted, if it were established that it had been written by the Lord himself." Since, therefore, by Bovius' own testimony, the Diataxes were never admitted by the Church among the canonical Scriptures, it must follow entirely that it was never established that they were written by the Apostles. The impostor saw this well, he who dared with monstrous impudence to forge canons under the names of the Apostles. For when he wished these Diataxes to be held truly Apostolic, he boldly placed them in the canon of Scripture, well aware that they could not be recognised as genuine unless at once this honour was also conferred on them.

units.la: a De scri. Eccles. in Petro. init. statim & hic canonis honos decernatur: ἀξιῶ ὑμῖν παῖ πλησίοις λαϊκοῖς βιβλία σπάσματα καὶ ἁγία τ μὴ παλαιᾶς διαθήκης Μωσέως πέντε, &c. ἡμέτερα ὅ, τυτέςι τ καινῆς διαθήκης Εὐαγγέλια τέσσαρα, &c. Κλήμεντ@ ἐπιςολαὶ δύο. Ϛ αἱ Διαταγαὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπισκόποις, δὲ ἐμὸς Κλήμεντ@ ἐν ὀκτὼ βιβλίοις προσπεφωνημέναι, ὡς ἡ χρὴ δημοσιεύειν ὑπὸ πάντων, διὰ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς μυστικά, ἡ αἱ πράξεις ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποςτόλων. Sint autem vobis omnibus Clericis & Laicis venerabiles & sancti libri veteris quidem Testamenti, Moysis quinque &c. Nostri vero, hoc est novi Testamenti Euangelia quatuor, &c. Clementis epistola dua; Et constitutiones vobis Episcopis per me Clementem in octo libris nuncupata; quas apud omnes publicare non decet, ob arcana in ipsis; Et nostra, idest Apostolorum Acta. Vides, ut Diataxes inter Canonicas novi Testamenti Scripturas, & quidem ante Actus Apostolorum, recenseat. Merito sane, qui eas scilicet pro vere Apostolicis haberi voluit; haberi autem pro Apostolicis non posse judicavit, nisi & in Scripturarum canonem referrentur. Quo loco praetermittere non possum singularem Bovii inverecundiam. Is enim hunc ipsum Canonem & quidem primo statim loco attulit, ut suarum nobis Constitutionum authori-
units.tr: a On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Peter, at the beginning. [Greek] I wish you, both clergy and laity, to hold as venerable and holy the books of the Old Testament, the five books of Moses, etc.; and ours, that is, the four Gospels of the New Testament, etc.; the two epistles of Clement; and the constitutions addressed to you bishops by me, Clement, in eight books, which it is not fitting to publish to all, on account of the mysteries in them; and our Acts, that is, of the Apostles. You see how the Diataxes are listed among the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament, and indeed before the Acts of the Apostles. Rightly so, since he wished them to be held truly Apostolic, and judged that they could not be held Apostolic unless they were also referred to the canon of the Scriptures. At this point I cannot pass over Bovius' singular shamelessness. For he cites this very canon, and indeed in the first place, in order to affirm and prove the authority of his own Constitutions. units.la: a Can. Apost. 85. authoritatem affirmaret, ac probaret. {a}Primi (inquit a) prodeant Canones Apostolorum, perpetuo constantique omnium Gracorum, multorum Latinorum Patrum consensu, atque approbatione recepti, in quorum ultimo inter eos libros, qui in Ecclesiis veluti sacrosancti habendi sunt, numerantur octo libri de Constitutionibus, authore Clemente, scripti Episcopis. Hactenus Bovius. Non jam urgeo, quanti sit flagitii hominem Latinum, & quidem Episcopum, eorum canonum authoritate niti, qui cum apud Latinas Ecclesiae scriptores ante annum 494. ne nominati quidem uspiam reperiantur, ipso illo anno a Gelasio urbis Episcopo, totaque Romana Synodo, velut apocryphi; rejecti ac repudiati sunt: qui ab Humberto Cardinale anno 1050. cum eos ipsi objiceret Nicetas, eodem nomine refutati sunt: qui ab omnibus Latinis ad hunc diem constantissimo spreti, ac damnati sunt, ut videre est apud Bellarminum {b}Baronium {c}, & alios; Neque enim is de quo agitur canon, ex illis quinquaginta unus est, quos recentiores Ecclesiae Romanae homines probant, sed eorum triginta quinque ultimus, quos etiam nunc isti pro additiciis & spuriis habent. Non exagito, quod insigni temeritate mentitur Bovius, istos Canones perpetuo, constantiq omnium Graco-
units.tr: a Canons of the Apostles 85. "First (he says) let the canons of the Apostles come forward, received and approved by the constant and perpetual consensus of all the Greeks and of many Latin Fathers, in the last of which are numbered, among those books which are to be held as it were most sacred in the Churches, the eight books of the Constitutions, written by Clement, to the bishops." Thus far Bovius. I do not now press how great a disgrace it is for a Latin, and indeed a bishop, to rest on the authority of those canons which, though they are nowhere named among the Latin Church writers before the year 494, were in that very year rejected and repudiated as apocryphal by Gelasius, bishop of the city, and the whole Roman Synod; which were refuted under the same name by Cardinal Humbert in 1050, when Nicetas objected them to him; which have been despised and condemned by all Latins to this day with the greatest constancy, as may be seen in Bellarmine, Baronius and others. For the canon in question is not one of those fifty-one which modern men of the Roman Church approve, but the last of the thirty-five which they still regard as supplementary and spurious. I do not dwell on the fact that Bovius lies with remarkable rashness when he claims that these canons were received by the constant and perpetual consensus of all Greeks and many Latin Fathers.

units.la: b De script. Eccl. a. 92. Clem. Rom. c Ann. l. 2. a. D. 102. §. 15. Græcorum, multorum Latinorum Patrum, consensu atque approbatione receptos; qui, si urgeatur, è Græcis Latinisque quatuor primorum sæculorum scriptoribus ne unum quidem proferre poterit, qui eos recipiat, è sequentibus duobus paucissimos: ex Latinorum vero omni ad annum 1500 memoria, prorsus neminem, qui ex Apostolicis illis 85. canonibus, triginta quinque postremos approbet, è quorum numero suum hunc attulit Bovius. Ista, inquam, & alia ejusdem generis mitto, seorsim in proprio opere exsequenda. Nunc te, Bovi, non ex tuorum hominum placitis, ac decretis, sed ex tuis ipsius sensibus atque sententiis convenio. Tu nobis Græcum illum à tuis omnibus rejectum canonem objectas, tu ex eo Constitutiones tuas constituere satagis. Tametsi id, ut dixi, flagitiosum sit, teram tamen, si tu, quem laudas canonem, probas ipse, ac sequeris. Nunc quis non videt, quanta sit, quamque intolerabilis, tuę frontis inverecundia, qui authores nobis affers, iisque niti nos jubes, à quibus ipse apertissime dissentis? Illi quidem tuas Constitutiones inter sacrosanctos (ut ais) Ecclesiarum libros numerant, hoc est, ut nos ex ipsis audivimus, in Scripturarum novi Testamenti canone post Euangelia & Epistolas, ante ApostoloApostolorum actus locant. Tu vero, Bo-vi, quid censes? Nunquam (inquis) obti-nuerunt,ut in Canonem sacrarum Scriptu-rarum referrentur; neq; nos eis tantam au-thoritatem tribuere volumus. Ergo, in-quam, tuo ipsius judicio, straminei sunt, vel lutei, aut (ut verius dicam) nulli tui il-li Apostoli, quos nuper Constitutionum opus in canone Scripturarum collocantes ostentabas, quos tu scilicet si vere Aposto-los, si eorum decretum ab omni Ecclesia perpetuo constantique consensu receptum putares, nunquam dixisses Constitutiones, quod iis in illo decreto defertur, id nun-quam obtinuisse; neque tu iis id authori-tatis negasses. Apage ergo, quem tu re-sigis, canonem. Absit, ut cujus tu ipse authoritatem tam secure contemnis, ac proculcas, eum nos aliquo loco ac nume-ro habeamus. Sed quam in illius authore, licet impostore, laudamus prudentiam at-que constantiam, in te sane desideramus. Ille enim, qui quas pro Apostolicis habet Constitutiones, eas in scripturarum cano-nem refert, sibi quidem hactenus constat, & suæ hypothesi consentanea loquitur. Id-que etiam faciunt Æthiopes, qui hoc idem opus, ut pro Apostolico habent, ita & in Scripturarum canone censent. Tu, non modo cum vero, sed etiam tecum ipse pu-gnas gnas, qui quas velut vere Apostolicas nobis venditas, eas tamen Constitutiones in Sacrarum Scripturarum canonem referri non vis. Eas ergo vel canonicas cum Apostolis illis tuis assere, si vere Apostolicas esse defendis; vel certe nobiscum Apostolicas nega, si canone eas sacro merito excludi fateris. Non potes utrumque tenere, ut & Apostolicae sint, & extra canonem sint. Itaque cum (exceptis modo novitiis Abyssinis, & tuis illis stramineis Apostolis, canonis 85. conditoribus) omnis eas Ecclesia extra canonem Scripturarum, vel te ipso fatente, habuerit, necessario relinquitur, ut concedas, ne Apostolicas quidem esse Constitutiones tuas.
units.tr: b On Ecclesiastical Writers, a. 92. Clement of Rome; c Annals, l. 2, a.D. 102, §15. Which, if pressed, he will be unable to produce even one of the Greek and Latin writers of the first four centuries who accepts them, and from the following two centuries very few. Indeed, from the whole memory of the Latins down to the year 1500, there is absolutely no one who approves the last thirty-five of those Apostolic eighty-five canons, from whose number Bovius brought forward his own. These things, I say, and others of the same kind I leave to be pursued separately in a work of their own. Now, Bovius, I address you not from the opinions and decrees of your men, but from your own feelings and judgements. You object to us that canon which all your people have rejected, and you labour to base your Constitutions upon it. Although, as I have said, this is shameful, I will nevertheless go on, if you yourself approve and follow the canon which you praise. Now who does not see how great and how intolerable is the shamelessness of your brow, you who bring forward authors for us and bid us rely on them, while you openly dissent from them? Indeed they count your Constitutions among the sacred books of the Churches (as you say), that is, as we have heard from them, they place them in the canon of the New Testament Scriptures after the Gospels and Epistles, and before the Acts of the Apostles. But you, Bovius, what do you think? They never (you say) obtained that they be referred to the canon of the sacred Scriptures; nor do we wish to grant them so great an authority. Therefore, I say, by your own judgement, those Apostles of yours are of straw, or of mud, or (to speak more truly) are nothing at all; those Apostles whom you lately displayed as placing the work of the Constitutions in the canon of Scripture. If you really thought they were true Apostles, and that their decree was received by every Church with constant and perpetual consensus, you would never have said that what is granted to them in that decree had never been obtained by the Constitutions, nor would you have denied them this authority. Away, then, with the canon you bring back! Far be it from us to hold any place or number for that canon whose authority you yourself so confidently despise and trample underfoot. But the prudence and constancy with which we praise its author, though he was an impostor, we surely miss in you. For he who holds the Constitutions to be Apostolic and refers them to the canon of Scripture is at least consistent with himself, and speaks in agreement with his own hypothesis. The Ethiopians also do the same, who hold this same work to be Apostolic and likewise count it in the canon of Scripture. You contend not only with the truth but with yourself, since you want the Constitutions, which you sell to us as truly Apostolic, not to be referred to the canon of the sacred Scriptures. Either, then, assert them to be canonical along with those Apostles of yours, if you maintain that they are truly Apostolic; or certainly deny with us that they are Apostolic, if you admit that they are rightly excluded from the sacred canon. You cannot hold both, that they are Apostolic and that they are outside the canon. Therefore, since (leaving aside only the novel Abyssinians and your straw Apostles, the authors of the eighty-five canons) the whole Church, even by your own confession, has held them outside the canon of Scripture, it necessarily follows that you must concede that your Constitutions are not even Apostolic.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: Argumentum II. contra constitutiones, quod totus eorum sermo, qua a vocibus, qua a vocum συνθέσει ab Apostolico charactere abhorreat, multaque contineat ab Apostolis aliena.
units.tr: The second argument against the Constitutions: their whole style, both in its individual words and in how those words are put together, is alien to the apostolic character, and the work contains much that is foreign to the Apostles.

units.la: PSÆ vero, etiam sepositio hoc totius Ecclesiae de iis judicio, satis per se loquuntur ac clamant, se non fuisse ab Apostolis scriptas; & hoc quod in quadam operis parte mentiuntur, in aliis fortiter, ac ineluctabiliter refellunt. Nimirum id mendacii fatum est, ut nunpunquam sibi constare queat. Tam multa vero sunt in istis Constitutionibus, quae authorem Apostolis eas impudenter affingentem, mendacii coarguunt, ut, ne nimium prolixi simus, pluribus missis, pauca tantum de hoc genere prolaturi simus. Sermo ipse imprimis Apostolos esse, qui loquuntur, negat; & vocibus scatens ab eorum usu alienis, & non eo more, modoque compositus, qui plurimum ab omni virorum divinorum charactere abhorret. Voces quidem innumerabiles, in Constitutionibus occurrunt nihil minus, quam Apostolicae; ut exempli gratia, νεοφώτιςῳ a pro recens baptizato, μύησις, pro baptismo, μυηθεὶς vel μεμυημένῳ, pro baptizato, ἀμύητῳ a pro baptismi experte, b χειμαζόμενῳ, pro daemoniaco, κατηχούμενῳ, & in eodem sensu ἀκροωμένῳ c, catechumenus & audiens, θυσία sacrificium, & θυσία ἀναιμακτὴ pro Eucharistia, ἀρχιερεὺς d Pontifex pro Episcopo; ἱερεῖς e sacerdotes, pro Episcopis & presbyteris, ἀρχιερατικὴ ἀξία pro Episcopatu, ἱερατικὸς καταλογῷ f, sacerdotum catalogus, θυσιαστήριον g, altare, pro mensa Domini, Ecclesia καθολικὴ, οἰκουμενικὴ, Αποστολικὴ, catholica, oecumenica, Apostolica, διδασκαλία καθολικὴ h, doctrina Catholica. Has voces, quae apud Constitutionum authorem
units.tr: Indeed, the fact that the whole Church has set these books apart and judged them spurious speaks plainly enough for itself and cries out that they were not written by the Apostles. What the author lies about in one part of the work, he refutes strongly and unavoidably in another. Lying always has this fate: it can never be consistent with itself. There are so many things in these Constitutions that convict their author, who shamelessly attributes them to the Apostles, of lying that, so as not to be too long, I will pass over many and bring forward only a few of this kind. The style itself declares that the Apostles are not the ones speaking. It is full of words foreign to their usage and composed in a manner that is far removed from the whole character of inspired men. Countless words occur in the Constitutions that are anything but apostolic. For example: νεοφώτιστος [neophotistos] for a newly baptized person; μύησις [mysis] for baptism; μυηθείς or μεμυημένος [mythes, memyemenos] for one who is baptized; ἀμύητος [amyētos] for one without experience of baptism; χειμαζόμενος [cheimazomenos] for a demoniac; κατηχούμενος [katēchoumenos], and in the same sense ἀκροώμενος [akroōmenos], for catechumen and hearer; θυσία [thusia], sacrifice, and θυσία ἀναιμακτός [thusia anaimaktos], unbloody sacrifice, for the Eucharist; ἀρχιερεύς [archiereus], high priest, for bishop; ἱερεῖς [hiereis], priests, for bishops and presbyters; ἀρχιερατικὴ ἀξία [archieratikē axia], high-priestly dignity, for the episcopate; ἱερατικὸς καταλόγος [hieratikos katalogos], the catalogue of priests; θυσιαστήριον [thusiastērion], altar, for the Lord's table; Ἐκκλησία καθολικὴ, οἰκουμενικὴ, ἀποστολικὴ [Ekklēsia katholikē, oikoumenikē, apostolikē], the catholic, ecumenical, apostolic Church; διδασκαλία καθολικὴ [didaskalia katholikē], catholic doctrine.

units.la: a l. 2. c. 10. & b l.7. c. 26. extr. c l.8. c.7. & 12. in. d l.8. c. 12. e l.8. c. 13. extr. & paff. l.8. c.46. f l.3. c. 15. b. l.7. c. 42. b. l.8. c.7. & c.12. init. g l.8. c. 12. p. 1046. & alibi passim. h l.6. c. 14. c. tem : crebro occurrunt, quasque in iis quos dixi, sensibus Ecclesiæ sequentium temporum familiares fuisse confiteor, nusquam à Scriptoribus divinis sic usurpatas fuisse ex iis, quæ supersunt veris & indubitatis illorum monumentis satis constat. Tale etiam est ἐνσωματώσεως a incorporationis vocabulum, pro quo Græci ἐνσάρκωσιν & ἐναν-θρώπησιν crebrius postea dixerunt : Item μονα-ρχίας pro unius Dei imperio, Gentilium & hæreticorum πολυθεΐτηλι opposito. Mitto μαχοσύμξυλος b, & πασοφοείας c, non tantum Apostolis, sed etiam vetustissimis omnibus Christianismi Scriptoribus ignota. Huc quoque illud pertinet, quod nostri Διαταγεῖς episcopi & presbyteri vocabula, semper velut sensu, ac significatione distincta, seorsim, nunquam promiscuè usurpant; quin & diserte monent, esse inter hæc nomina differentiam, & quidem hujusmodi, quæ rerum iis significatarum differentiam ostendat, eaque ratione se iis usos esse: ἵς·ε γὰρ πάντως (inquiunt d) ἐπισκόπης παρ' ἡμῶν ὀνομαζόμενος καὶ πρεσβυτέρως καὶ διακόνως εὐχὴ καὶ χειρῶν ἐπιθέσει, τὴν διαφορὰν τῆς ὀνομάτων καὶ τῶν διαφορὰν τῆς πραγμάτων δηλοῦντες. Scitis enim plane eos, qui à nobis per orationem, & manuum impositionem Episcopi, presbyteri & diaconi nominati sunt, differentia nominum dif- serénferentiam rerum declarare. Atqui & jam pridem monuerunt veteres non pauci, & confitentur hodie poene omnes, & vero res ipsa clarissime docet episcopi,presbyterique nomina ab Apostolis nullo discrimine usurpari; ut videre est in eorum & actis a & epistolis, praecipue Paulinis. Huc etiam illud refero, quod nostri Διαθηκης pro Eucharistia interdum dicunt τα αντιτυπα σωματος και αιματος, antitypa regii corporis & sanguinis: interdum vero simpliciter το σωμα και το αιμα corpus & sanguinem b, (Domini scilicet) quae utraque Eucharistiae nomenclatura, ut ut sequentibus temporibus apud Patres frequens, nusquam in libris vere Apostolicis occurrit. De priori nulla est controversia. Sed neque de posteriori esse debet. Narrant (fateor) Apostoli, Christum de pane Eucharistico dixisse c, hoc est corpus meum; adjunt ipsi hunc panem esse participationem corporis Domini; adeoque quicunque panem hunc manducaverit indigne, eum corporis Domini reum fore, non dijudicantem corpus Domini, judicium sibi manducare. Nomen ipsum corporis Domini nunquam pro Eucharistia ponunt.
units.tr: (The notes to this passage are as printed: a l. 2. c. 10; b l. 7. c. 26, end; c l. 8. c. 7 and 12, beginning; d l. 8. c. 12; e l. 8. c. 13, end, and passim; l. 8. c. 46; f l. 3. c. 15; b l. 7. c. 42; b l. 8. c. 7 and c. 12, beginning; g l. 8. c. 12, p. 1046, and passim elsewhere; h l. 6. c. 14.) These words, which occur often in the author of the Constitutions, and which I admit were familiar to the Church of later ages in the senses I have mentioned, are nowhere so used by the divine writers, as is sufficiently clear from what survives of their true and undoubted writings. Similar is the word ἐνσωμάτωσις [ensōmatōsis], incorporation, for which the Greeks later more often said ἐνσάρκωσις [ensarkōsis] and ἐνανθρώπησις [enanthrōpēsis]. Likewise μοναρχία [monarchia], the rule of the one God, set against the polytheism [πολυθεΐα] of Gentiles and heretics. I pass over μαχοσύμξυλος [machosymxylos] and πασοφοεία [pasophoeia], words unknown not only to the Apostles but to all the very earliest writers of Christianity. To this also belongs the fact that our authors [Διαταγαί] always use the terms bishop and presbyter separately, as though they had distinct meanings, and never use them interchangeably. Indeed they expressly warn that there is a difference between these names, and of such a kind as shows a difference in the things signified, and say that they used them on that basis: "For of those who are called by us bishop, presbyter and deacon by prayer and the laying on of hands, we surely know..." [ἴσασι γὰρ πάντως...]. You know full well that those who are named bishop, presbyter and deacon by us through prayer and the laying on of hands declare by the difference of names the difference of things. Yet many of the ancients have long since pointed this out, almost all now admit it, and the matter itself teaches very clearly that the names bishop and presbyter were used by the Apostles without any distinction, as can be seen in their Acts and letters, especially Paul's. To this I also refer the fact that our authors sometimes call the Eucharist τὰ ἀντίτυπα σώματος καὶ αἵματος [ta antitypa sōmatos kai haimatos], antitypes of the Lord's body and blood, and sometimes simply τὸ σῶμα καὶ τὸ αἷμα [to sōma kai to haima], the body and blood (of the Lord, of course). Both of these names for the Eucharist, though frequent among the Fathers of later times, nowhere occur in the books that are truly apostolic. There is no dispute about the first. Nor should there be about the second. The Apostles do relate (I admit) that Christ said of the Eucharistic bread this is my body; they add that this bread is a participation in the body of the Lord; and that whoever eats this bread unworthily will be guilty of the body of the Lord, not discerning the body of the Lord, eating judgment to himself. But they never use the phrase body of the Lord itself as a name for the Eucharist.

units.la: Atque haec de singulis vocibus. Jam si earum Syntaxin, & dispositionem, & totam, quae inde exurgit, orationis ideam spectes, species, immanem reperies τὴν Διαφωνίαν ab Apostolis discrepantiam. Horum enim oratio simplex est, inerudita, neque solum plebeia, sed pœne etiam rusticana; & à rhetoricis ornamentis usque adeo aliena, ut vix Grammaticam paulo severiorem ferat; Ebraïsmis, & aliis barbarismis scatens, sola rerum quas eloquitur dignitate, cœlestique quadam & apud homines inusitata venustatis specie majestatem suam tuetur. Nostri vero Διαφωνίας multo purius, & ad linguæ Græcanicæ genium & canones rectius, atque accuratius loquuntur: quia & ad rhetoricum cultum sæpiusculè assurgunt, & elegantiam præferunt etiam sæculari eruditione non indignam. Multa observari possunt: ego unum & alterum exemplum dabo. In precatione quadam liturgica de Christi incarnatione sic loquuntur a: εὐδόκησεν αὐτὸς γνώμῃ σὴ ὁ δημιουργὸς ἀνθρώπῳ γενέσθαι, ὁ νομοθέτης ὑπὸ νόμως· ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἱερεῖον, ὁ ποιμὴν προβάτων. Quæso te, quid istis cultius, ac venustius dicere potuit vel Basilius, vel Gregorius, vel Chrysostomus, vel de eruditissimorum grege quivis? Quid illa dicam, quæ paulo post de eodem argumento sequuntur b? γέγονεν ἐν μήτρᾳ παρθένου ὁ ἁπλάστων πάντως τῆς γινωμένης· ἐσαρκώθη ὁ ἀσαρκῷ, ὁ ἀχρόνως γεννηθεὶς, ἐν χρόνῳ γεγέννηται. Tum mox ; προφῆς καὶ ποτὲ ἐ̂ ὕπνῳ μεταλαβὼν ὁ τρίφων πάντας τὰς χρόνους προφῆς, Et illa què continuo de Christo subjiciuntur, sane pulcherrima ; τῷ ἁγνοίαν ἐφυγάδευσε, τῷ ἐυσέβειαν ἀντιζωπύρωσε· τὸ θέλημά σε ἐπλήρωσε· τὸ ἔργον, ὁ ἐδωκας ἀπῶ, ἐτελείωσε.
units.tr: So much for individual words. Now if you look at their syntax, their arrangement, and the whole idea of style that arises from it, you will find a huge discrepancy [διαφωνία] from the Apostles. The Apostles' style is simple and unlettered, not only plebeian but almost rustic, so far removed from rhetorical ornament that it can hardly bear even a moderately strict grammar. It is full of Hebraisms and other barbarisms, and it keeps its majesty only through the dignity of what it says and a certain heavenly kind of beauty unusual among men. Our authors, by contrast, speak much more purely, and more correctly and accurately according to the genius and rules of the Greek language. They often rise to rhetorical polish and display an elegance not unworthy even of secular learning. Many examples could be noted; I will give one or two. In a certain liturgical prayer about the incarnation of Christ they speak thus: "Of your own will, O Creator, you were pleased to become man, the lawgiver under the law, the high priest and the sacrifice, the shepherd of the sheep" [εὐδόκησεν αὐτὸς γνώμῃ σῇ ὁ δημιουργὸς ἀνθρώπῳ γενέσθαι, ὁ νομοθέτης ὑπὸ νόμον, ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἱερεῖον, ὁ ποιμὴν προβάτων]. I ask you, could Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, or any of that most learned company have said anything more polished and graceful than this? What shall I say of the words that follow shortly on the same theme? "He who is beyond all creation came to be in the womb of a virgin; the incorporeal was made flesh; he who was born outside time was born in time." Then soon after: "The prophet who once, taking part in sleep, foretold all the times..." Then the things said of Christ immediately after are indeed most beautiful: "He banished ignorance, rekindled piety, fulfilled your will, and completed the work you gave him" [τὴν ἀγνοίαν ἐφυγάδευσε, τὴν εὐσέβειαν ἀντεζωπύρησε, τὸ θέλημά σου ἐπλήρωσε, τὸ ἔργον ὃ ἔδωκας αὐτῷ ἐτελείωσε].

units.la: Neque inferiora sunt, quę sequuntur : κρινθεὶς ὁ κρίτης, καὶ κατακεληθεὶς ὁ σωτὴρ σαυρῷ προσηλώθη ὁ ἀπαδής· καὶ ἀπέθανεν ὁ τῇ φύσει ἀθάνατος· καὶ ἐτάφη ὁ ζωοποιός.
units.tr: No less fine are the words that follow: "The Judge was judged, and the Saviour, condemned, was nailed to the cross, he who is impassible; and he who is immortal by nature died; and the Life-giver was buried" [κριθεὶς ὁ κριτής, καὶ κατακριθεὶς ὁ σωτήρ σταυρῷ προσηλώθη ὁ ἀπαθής, καὶ ἀπέθανεν ὁ τῇ φύσει ἀθάνατος, καὶ ἐτάφη ὁ ζωοποιός].

units.la: Hęc vero etiam suavissima ; εὐχαεεςὑμέν σοι Θεὲ παντοκράτορ, ὑχ ὅσον ὀφείλομεν, ἀλλ' ὅσον δυναμεθα. Sed & illa de Deo alibi quam magnifica c! ὁ παντοχρὴ ὢν, καὶ τοῖς πᾶσι παρῶν, ἐ̂ ἐν ὑσὶνὶ ὡς ἑνόντι ὑπάρχων, ὁ τόποις μὲν περιγραφόμενος, ὁ αἰῶσι μὴ περατούμενος, ὁ λόγοις μὴ χωρούμενος, ὁ ὑρίσει μὴ ὑποκείμενος, ὁ φυλακῆς μὴ δεόμενος, ὁ φθορᾶς ἀνώτερος, ὁ τροπῆς ἀνεπίδεκτος, ὁ φύσει ἀναλλοίωτος. Hæ & alię id genus Græcanicæ sermonis deliciæ passim in Constitutionibus obviæ satis produnt, qui sic loquuntur, eos nihil minus esse, quam veros Christi Apostolos, ab hujusmodi orationis ornamentis alienissimos.
units.tr: These are also most pleasing: "We give you thanks, Almighty God, not as much as we owe, but as much as we are able" [εὐχαριστοῦμέν σοι, Θεὲ παντοκράτορ, οὐχ ὅσον ὀφείλομεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅσον δυνάμεθα]. And the passage elsewhere about God is equally splendid: "You who are everywhere and present to all, who are in one place as in a place, yet are bounded by no place; not limited by ages; not contained by words; not subject to definition; not in need of protection; superior to corruption; not susceptible of change; unalterable by nature" [ὁ παντοχρὴς ὢν καὶ τοῖς πᾶσι παρών, ὁ ἐν τόπῳ ὡς ἐν τόπῳ ὑπάρχων, ὁ τόποις μὲν περιγραφόμενος, αἰῶσι μὴ περατούμενος, λόγοις μὴ χωρούμενος, ὁρισμῷ μὴ ὑποκείμενος, φυλακῆς μὴ δεόμενος, φθορᾶς ἀνώτερος, τροπῆς ἀνεπίδεκτος, φύσει ἀναλλοίωτος]. These and other such delights of Greek speech, found everywhere in the Constitutions, make it plain enough that those who speak in this way are anything but true Apostles of Christ, being very far removed from such ornaments of style.

units.la: Istos Διαλαξεις loquela manifestos facit. Merito quoque, ut mihi quidem videtur, dubitaveris, an sit Apostolorum gravitate ac simplicitate digna ille sane lepida, sed tamen frigida, ac pœne puerilis nostrorum Διαλαξεων de vagis & avaris, ac per alienas domos discurfantibus viduis,paronomafia a, ἀλλὰ πήρας αὐτὰς ὑπάρχειν ἑτοίμως εἰς τὸ λαμβάνειν. Sunt & quædam in Constitutionum sermone inepta, quæ vix ad sensum probabilem revocaveris; quale illud est, quod in primo libro occurrit sane ioculare; quo loco Διαταγὴς, postquam e lege hæc verba descripserunt, ἐκ ἀπομα- δαρώσητε τὰς πώγωνας ὑμῶν, Non radetis barbas vestras, τοῦτο γὰρ (inquiunt b) γυναι- ξιν ὑπηρέτης ὁ κτίσας ἐποίησε θεὸς· ἀνδράσι ὃ ἀναρμόστιον ἰδιαίωσε. Hoc enim (nimirum barbas radere) mulieribus quidem decorum fecit; viris vero indecorum ac inhonestum constituit Creator Deus. Quasi scilicet barbas etiam sequior sexus habeat. Sed & interdum boni illi Διαταγῆς assumtæ personæ obliti, omnino sic loquuntur, ut loqui eos decet, qui post Apostolorum tempora vivunt. Verbi gratia, quodam loco ita loquentes inducuntur Apostoli c; ἐν γὰρ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν ἡμετέρων χειρῶν ἐδίδοτο πνεῦμα ἅγιον τοῖς πιστεύουσι. Siquidem per impositionem manuum nostrarum dabatur Spiritus Sanctus credentibus. Cur dicunt dabatur? quasi tum cum loquerentur dari desiisset? Cur non dicunt datur? cū constet, Apostolos, quandiu vixerunt, spiritum per manuum impositionem dedisse? Nimirum im-
units.tr: Their own speech makes this manifest. You may also rightly doubt whether that rather witty but cold and almost childish pun of our authors, about wandering and greedy widows who run through other people's houses, "but rather let them be ready to have wallets for receiving" [ἀλλὰ πήρας αὐτὰς ὑπάρχειν ἑτοίμως εἰς τὸ λαμβάνειν], is worthy of the gravity and simplicity of the Apostles. There are also things in the Constitutions' language so silly that you could hardly bring them to any plausible sense. An example is what occurs in the first book, quite jocular, where the Constitutions, after citing these words of the law, "You shall not mar the corners of your beards" [οὐ ἀπομαδαρώσετε τοὺς πώγωνας ὑμῶν], add: "For God the Creator made this for women as a servant, but for men he appointed what is unfitting: for shaving the beard is decorous for women, but for men the Creator God has made it indecorous and dishonourable." As though the weaker sex had beards! At other times, too, those good Constitutions, forgetting the persona they have assumed, speak altogether as those living after the time of the Apostles would speak. For example, the Apostles are introduced speaking thus: "For through the imposition of our hands the Holy Spirit was given to believers" [ἐν γὰρ ἐπιθέσει τῶν ἡμετέρων χειρῶν ἐδίδοτο πνεῦμα ἅγιον τοῖς πιστεύουσι]. Why do they say "was given"? As if the giving had ceased by the time they spoke? Why not "is given," since it is certain that the Apostles, as long as they lived, gave the Spirit through the laying on of hands? Certainly the im-

units.la: c l. 2. c. 41. pag. 865. d. postor artis suæ immemor, non quod falsæ, id est assumptæ, sed quod veræ, id est suæ personæ conveniebat, id dixit imprudens; eo scilicet tempore vivitis, quo extinctis jam pridem Apostolis, vigerein Ecclesia desierat illud Apostolicum spiritus per manuum impositionem conferendi donum. Ideo dixit dabatur; veluti de re, quæ olim quidem fuerat, nunc vero desierat; non dixit datur; quod procul dubio dixissent Apostoli, si ipsi veré hæc essent loquuti. Hujus loci alter ille geminus est, in quo impostor Apostolos de sua in examinandis iis, quos Ecclesiæ ministros ordinabant, diligentia sic facit loqui; ὢ γὰρ ὁ βούλόμενος παρ ἡμῖν ἐπλήρωσε τὴν χεῖρα, ὥσπερ ἡ πιβδῄλε ψαμάλεων ἡ τῶ Ἱερόβοαμ παραινεσομένης ἱερωσύνης, ἀλλ' ὁ καλύμενος ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Neq; enim quicunque volebat, apud nos manum implebat, ut in illo falso, & adulterino sacerdotio vitularum, rege Hieroboam, sed qui vocabatur à Deo. Nemo non videt, istos si vere Apostoli essent, dicturos fuisse, non qui vult apud nos manum implet; sed qui à Deo vocatur. Impostorem ipsa rerum veritas invitum, ac repugnantem à fabulæ suæ instituto abduxit, & quod suo non dramati sed sæculo congruebat, id dicere coegit, non quicunque volebat, apud nos manum num implebat ; quod , ut liquet, de re tan-tum praeterita, ac desita sic dicitur; non au-tem de ea, quae nunc quoque fit & viget.
units.tr: c l. 2. c. 41. pag. 865. d. The impostor, forgetful of his own craft, said this without thinking. What fit his assumed character, which was not false but was in fact his own person, was this: "You live at a time when the Apostles have long been dead and the Church has ceased to flourish with that Apostolic gift of conferring the Spirit by the laying on of hands." So he said was given, as of a thing that once existed but has now ceased; he did not say is given, as the Apostles would undoubtedly have said if they had really spoken these words. There is another passage like this, in which the impostor, out of his care in examining those whom the Church ordained as ministers, makes the Apostles speak thus: "ὢ γὰρ ὁ βούλόμενος παρ ἡμῖν ἐπλήρωσε τὴν χεῖρα, ὥσπερ ἡ πιβδῄλε ψαμάλεων ἡ τῶ Ἱερόβοαμ παραινεσομένης ἱερωσύνης, ἀλλ' ὁ καλύμενος ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ" [ὢ γὰρ ὁ βούλόμενος παρ ἡμῖν ἐπλήρωσε τὴν χεῖρα, ὥσπερ ἡ πιβδῄλε ψαμάλεων ἡ τῶ Ἱερόβοαμ παραινεσομένης ἱερωσύνης, ἀλλ' ὁ καλύμενος ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ]: For it was not whoever wished who filled the hand among us, as in that false and adulterous priesthood of the calves under King Jeroboam, but he who was called by God. No one fails to see that if these men were truly Apostles, they would have said, not whoever wishes fills the hand among us, but he who is called by God. The truth of the matter, against the impostor's will and in spite of himself, drew him away from the plan of his fiction, and forced him to say what suited his own age rather than his drama: not whoever wished filled the hand among us. As is clear, this is said of a thing only past and ceased, not of what is still done and flourishes now.

units.la: Ejusdem commatis est , quod ubi de Pa-schate post vernum æquinoctium celebran-do præcipiunt, suam ipsi novitatem pro-dunt,ita loquentes a ; μηκέτι ὁ πασχατηςζμέ-νοι μὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων, non amplius cum Iudaïs observantes , Pascha scilicet. Haec verba hominum sunt post ea tempora viventium, quibus tametsi perperam , usitatum tamen fuerat apud Christianos Pascha cum Iudeis celebrare ; id autem secundo tertioque saeculis apud omnes Asianos solenne usita-tumque fuisse omnes sciunt : Ergo his ver-bis nostri Διαζυγεῖς imprudentes fatentur, se post illa tempora vixisse ; eademque adeo opera negant se esse Apostolos , qui scili-cet non post , sed ante utrumque illud saeculum vixerunt. Alibi nostri Διαζυγεῖς de haereticis Iudaïzantibus verba facientes, de iis perinde loquuntur , quasi qui antehac fuerint b ; ἕτεροι ὁ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἔλεγον μόνῳ δεῖν φάσκοντες χρεία ἀπέχεσθαι· τὰ δὲ νόμον κατὰ θεῖα ἱδίειν· καὶ περιτέμνεσθαι νομίμως. Alii vero ex illis dicebant sola suilla abstinere oportere; iis vero vesci, quae secundum legem pura sunt, & ex lege circumcidi. Tum de aliis multo impudentioribus ; ἄλλοι ὁ (inquit) ἀναίδην ἐκπογύνειν καὶ παραχρῆ-σθαι
units.tr: Of the same kind is what they say when they instruct that the Passover be kept after the vernal equinox, which reveals their own novelty. They speak thus: "μηκέτι ὁ πασχατηςζμέ-νοι μὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων" [μηκέτι ὁ πασχατηςζμένοι μὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων]: no longer keeping the feast with the Jews, that is, the Passover. These are the words of men living after those times, when, although it was wrongly done, it had nonetheless become customary among Christians to celebrate the Passover with the Jews. Everyone knows that in the second and third centuries this was the established and customary practice among all the Asians. Therefore, in these words our authors [Διαζυγεῖς] unwittingly confess that they lived after those times, and by the same act they deny that they are Apostles, who of course lived not after but before both of those centuries. Elsewhere our authors [Διαζυγεῖς], speaking of Judaizing heretics, talk about them as though they had existed some time earlier: "ἕτεροι ὁ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἔλεγον μόνῳ δεῖν φάσκοντες χρεία ἀπέχεσθαι· τὰ δὲ νόμον κατὰ θεῖα ἱδίειν· καὶ περιτέμνεσθαι νομίμως" [ἕτεροι ὁ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἔλεγον μόνῳ δεῖν φάσκοντες χρεία ἀπέχεσθαι· τὰ δὲ νόμον κατὰ θεῖα ἱδίειν· καὶ περιτέμνεσθαι νομίμως]: Others of them said that one must abstain only from swine's flesh; but they should eat what is clean according to the law, and be circumcised according to the law. Then, of others far more shameless, he says: "ἄλλοι ὁ (inquit) ἀναίδην ἐκπογύνειν καὶ παραχρῆ-σθαι"

units.la: a l.5.c. 16.init. Sic. b l.6.c. 10.c. Αλλοι τὴν σαρκὶ ἐιθίαστον. Alii docebant sine ullo pudore scortandum & carne abstendum. Nimirum, iis temporibus vixit impostor, quibus utrique illi haeretici apud Christianos esse desierant. Itaque scenae suae oblitus, velut de re praeterita loquitur, dicebant, docebant; non quod fabulae conveniebat, velut de praesenti, dicunt, docent. Unde certo certius deprehenditur, impostorem, non modo Apostolico saeculo non vixisse, sed etiam multis post id temporibus extitisse; cum constet, illas, quas memorat haereses, non nisi post Apostolorum mortem extinctas fuisse. Omnem vero stultitiam superat, quod in sequenti volumine occurrit a: ἀλλὰ ὁ τῶν ἡμῶν χειροτονηθέντων ἐπισκόπων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν. De Episcopis vero, qui a nobis dum viximus, vel, in vita nostra, ordinati sunt, certiores vos facimus. Clamat hic locus, istos, qui haec loquuntur, vixisse; eaque post mortem, vel certe in ipso mortis limine loquentes induci. Nam si tum adhuc vivebant, ac valebant; si in unum e diversis orbis partibus locum convenerant; quid opus fuit ista ab iis addi ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ, in vita nostra, vel, dum viximus?
units.tr: a l.5.c. 16.init. Sic. b l.6.c. 10.c. "Αλλοι τὴν σαρκὶ ἐιθίαστον" [Ἄλλοι τὴν σαρκὶ ἐιθίαστον]: Others taught that one must fornicate without any shame and abstain from flesh. Clearly, the impostor lived in times when both of those heretics had ceased to exist among Christians. So, forgetful of his role, he speaks as of a past matter: they said, they taught; whereas it suited his fiction to speak as of the present: they say, they teach. Hence it is more certainly than certain that the impostor not only did not live in the Apostolic age but existed many times after it, since it is agreed that the heresies he mentions were extinguished only after the death of the Apostles. Yet what occurs in the following volume surpasses all folly: "ἀλλὰ ὁ τῶν ἡμῶν χειροτονηθέντων ἐπισκόπων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν" [ἀλλὰ ὁ τῶν ἡμῶν χειροτονηθέντων ἐπισκόπων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν]: But concerning the bishops who were ordained by us, while we lived, or in our lifetime, we make you aware. This passage cries out that those who speak these words lived, and that they are introduced as speaking after their death, or at least on the very threshold of death. For if they were still alive and in health at that time, and had gathered in one place from the different parts of the world, what need was there for them to add in our life, in our lifetime?

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: Argumenta contra Constitutiones à rebus ipsis petita; ut arg. III. quod ab Apostolica veritate aliena sint, qua Constitutiones de Dei Filio, deque Spiritu Sancto identidem philosophantur. Bovii ad hanc objectionem inanus cavillatio refellitur.
units.tr: Arguments against the Constitutions drawn from the matters themselves: such as the third argument, that they are foreign to apostolic truth, since they repeatedly philosophize about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. Bovius's empty quibble against this objection is refuted.

units.la: SED haec è sermone petita falsi-moniae argumenta, tametsi perse gravia, tamen quod præ iis, quæ sequuntur, levia videri possunt, non urgebimus nos quidem acrius. Ad res ipsas veniamus, in quibus multa sunt, ac propemodum innumerabilia, quæ hos Constitutionum libros certissime demonstrant aliorum quorumvis potius esse, quam Apostolorum. Nos quædam libabimus; ac ut disputatio certo ordine procedat, argumenta ad tria capita revocabimus; quorum primum ea continebit, quæ ad dogmata pertinent; alterum, quæ ad disciplinam; tertium, quæ ad historiam.
units.tr: But although these arguments of falsehood, taken from the style, are weighty in themselves, they may seem slight beside those that follow, so we shall not press them too hard. Let us come to the matters themselves, in which there are many, almost countless, things that most certainly show these books of the Constitutions to belong to anyone rather than to the Apostles. We shall touch on some of them. So that the discussion may proceed in good order, we shall reduce the arguments to three heads: the first will contain those that pertain to doctrines; the second, those that pertain to discipline; the third, those that pertain to history.

units.la: In dogmatis primum illud longe sane gravissimum notetur, quod cum veri Apostoli Dominum Christum esse affirment ὑπὲρ πάντων θεὸν εὐλογητὸν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, Deum super omnia benedictum in saecula, id nostri Διαταγὰς præfracte negant, & haereticis exserte tribuunt a; ἕτεροι ὃ ἐξ αὐτῶν αὐτὸν τὸν.
units.tr: Under doctrine, let the first and by far the most serious point be noted. The true Apostles affirm that the Lord Christ is "God over all, blessed for ever" [Rom. 9.5], God over all, blessed for ever, but our author of the Diatagai stubbornly denies this and openly attributes the denial to heretics [a]; some of them, he says, suspect that Jesus himself is God over all.

units.la: a l.6. c. 25. d. — reference in the right margin. τ Ἰησᾶν τ' Θν πάντων Θεὸν Χριστὸν ὁμολογοῦντα. Alii ex iis (haereticis) suspicantur ipsum Iesum esse Deum super omnia. Haereticus ergo, si iis credimus, Paulus; haeretica omnis Ecclesia, quae id ipsum, quod illi nunc haeretico-rum esse defendunt, constantissime contra Arianos, Photinianos & Ebionaeos asseruit; Christum scilicet summū esse Deum. Neque vero audiendi, qui Διαθηκας excusant; quasi haec eorum verba Sabellianos, & alios Filii personam una cum Patris persona impie miscentes ac confundentes pulsarent. Acciperent excusationem, si de aliis doctoribus ageretur: quos scio in hac causa interdum ita peccasse, ut Dionysium Alexandrinum, verbi gratia, qui dum totus in Sabellium, quem oppugnabat, incumberet, ad Arium, quem non videbat, incautus delatus videtur. Nunc cum de Apostolis quaeratur, quos certum est medium constanter tenuisse, neque ita unquam unum errorem oppugnasse, ut alteri oppositio faverent, nihil valet haec istorum caussificatio. Eo ipso non fuisse istos Apostolos liquet, quod sic incaute & temere loquantur; Ariique furori aperte faveant. Neque sane in veris ac indubitatis Apostolorum scriptis periculosas id genus locutiones, aut sententias reperire est, quales interdum in Patrum, aliorumque orthodoxorum libris occurrunt. Nimirum rum hi humano, illi vero divino spiritu regente sua scribebant. Itaque venia, atque excusatione his quidem nunquam, illis vero aliquando opus est. Non sunt faniora, quae alibi quoque de Filio philosophantur οἱ Διαλαγεῖς, quę fingunt a, ὑπηρετούμενον Ϊῳ θεῶ αὐτῶ ᾱ̃χρ̣ .. ministrantem Deo suo, ac Patri ad rerum omnium creationem. Quorum ista in ultimo operis volumine similia sunt, Dominus noster, ac Deus Iesus Christus ἐις πάντα ὑπηρετησάμενος σοι τῷ Θεῷ αὐτῷ, εἰς τὴν δημιουργίαν διάφορον, καὶ προνοίαν καλὰ λήλον, ὑπεικεῖς τὸ γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀπολλύμενον, tibi Deo suo, & Patri per omnia inservens, tum in varia creatione rerum, tum in providentia cujusque earum accommodata, genus hominum periens non despexit. Eodem & haec pertinent in alia Constitutionum parte, ubi de creatore loquentes pseudo-διαλαγεῖς, γινώσκομεν (inquiunt) ὅτι οὐχ ὕλης ἦν ἐνδεής, ἀλλὰ βουλήσει μόνη, ἃ προστάξει ὁ Χριστὸς, ταῦτα καὶ ἐπαγγέλλει. Scimus non indigniffe illum materia, sed sola voluntate effecisse, quae Christus jussus est facere. Sic alibi diaconum Christo, episcopum Patri more suo comparantes, ὅσα ὁ δημιουργὸς (inquiunt d) ἐνδωσίτω δὲ ἑαυτῷ, λαβὼν τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν τῶν ἐξουσιῶν, ὡς ὁ Κύριος τὴν πατρὸς τὸ δημιουργεῖν. Verum quacunque potest, falsa ab Episcopo potestate, moderetur per se, diaconus, sicut Christus potestatem creandi a Patre accepit. Hæ vero sunt, non Apostolorum, sed Arianorum voces; qui, ut notum est, Christum in mundo creando Patris ministrum ac instrumentum fuisse volebant; ut merito his locis censoriam notam in antiquissimo codice appo-suerit vetus ille Criticus, de quo est apud Turrianum. Atque ad ultimum quidem locum, hæc ejus erant, Turriano referente, verba, βλάσφημον· γυμνὸς γὰρ σαρκὸς ὢ προσ-τάχθη ὁ υἱός, Blasphemum. Filius enim carnis expers (id est, antequam carnem indueret) nihil jussus est. Duo vero loca superiora similibus insuflis stigmatis conpunxerat; priorem locum ita sugillans, Οὐ διέχομαι ὑπηρε-τῆσαί πῶ Θεῷ ἀλλ' ἀλλὰ σὺν αὐτῷ πάντα ποιῆσαι. Non admitto Deo & Patri ministravisse Filium, sed una cum ipso omnia perfecisse. Posteriorem denique locum hac animadversione castigarat; μὴ ψ σαρκωσιν, εἴποι ἄν τις τῷ ὑπηρεσίαν δὲ αὐλὸν, ὁ μὲν πρὸ τ' σαρκώσεως. Post incarnationem quidem ministerium quis per eum dixerit, ante incarnationem nequaquam. Sed neq; videntur Ariana labe vacare, quæ iidem Διαθήκης de Filii generatione non semel effutiunt; nimirum Patrem genuisse Filium ante sæcula, βουλήσει & δυνάμει & ἀγαθό-τητι, τῆτι a, voluntate, & potentia, & bonitate; vel, ut iidem alibi loquuntur b, τῇ εὐδοκίᾳ, beneplacito suo: quæ profecto durissima sunt, & ab Apostolicæ doctrinæ charactere aliena; quæ non voluntaria & temporali, sed æterno & naturali actu, genitum fuisse Filium tradit.
units.tr: a Book 6, ch. 25 (d): reference in the right margin. [Ἰησοῦν... Θεὸν πάντων Χριστὸν ὁμολογοῦντα] Some of them (the heretics) suspect that Jesus himself is God over all. The heretic, then, if we believe these writers, is Paul; and the whole Church is heretical, which most steadfastly maintained, against the Arians, the Photinians and the Ebionites, the very thing that these men now claim is the heresy of others: namely, that Christ is the supreme God. Nor should those who excuse the Diathekai be heard, as if these words struck at the Sabellians and others who impiously mix and confuse the person of the Son with the person of the Father. They would have a point if the discussion concerned other teachers, some of whom I know to have erred in this matter in such a way as Dionysius of Alexandria, for example, who, while wholly bent on Sabellius, whom he was attacking, seems to have been carried unwarily toward Arius, whom he did not see. But since we are speaking of the Apostles, who are certain to have held the middle course constantly, and never to have opposed one error in such a way as to favour its opposite, this excuse of theirs is worth nothing. The very fact that these men speak so carelessly and rashly, and openly favour the madness of Arius, shows that they were not Apostles. Indeed, one does not find in the genuine and undoubted writings of the Apostles such dangerous expressions or statements of this kind as sometimes occur in the books of the Fathers and other orthodox writers. Obviously, those wrote under the guidance of the human spirit, while the Apostles wrote under the guidance of the divine Spirit. Hence those men sometimes need pardon and excuse, but the Apostles never do. No less absurd are the things that the pseudo-Diatagai philosophize elsewhere about the Son, which they feign: serving God his own, and the Father, in the creation of all things. Similar to these, in the last volume of the work, are the words: Our Lord and God Jesus Christ, [serving in all things his own God and Father, in the creation of diverse things, and in the providence of each suited to the other, did not despise the perishing race of men]; serving in all things thy God and Father, both in the various creation of things and in the providence fitted to each, did not despise the perishing race of men. To the same effect is what the pseudo-Diatagai say in another part of the Constitutions, speaking of the Creator: "We know," they say, "that he was not in need of matter, but by will alone did what Christ commanded him to do." We know that he did not need matter, but by his will alone effected what Christ was bidden to do. Likewise, elsewhere, comparing the deacon with Christ and the bishop with the Father in their own way, they say: "Whatever the Creator [does], (they say) let him yield to himself, having received the oversight of the powers, as the Lord received from the Father the power to create. But whatever he can, let the deacon, removed from the bishop's power, govern by himself, just as Christ received from the Father the power of creating." These are not the words of the Apostles but of the Arians, who, as is well known, wished Christ to have been the minister and instrument of the Father in creating the world. Therefore that ancient critic, of whom Turrianus speaks, rightly placed a mark of censure on these passages in a very old codex. As to the last passage, these, according to Turrianus, were his words: blasphemous; for the Son was not commanded anything apart from the flesh. Filius enim carnis expers (that is, before he put on flesh) was commanded nothing. The two earlier passages he had marked with similar brands of censure: he rebuked the first with the words, I do not allow that the Son ministered to God and the Father, but that he did all things together with him. Finally, he had reproved the last passage with this comment: After the incarnation one might speak of his ministry through him, but before the incarnation by no means. But they do not seem to be free of Arian stain, these same Diathekai, who more than once blurt out concerning the generation of the Son that the Father begat the Son before the ages by will and power and goodness, [voluntate, et potentia, et bonitate]; or, as they say elsewhere, by his good pleasure [beneplacito suo]. These things are indeed very harsh and alien to the character of apostolic doctrine, which teaches that the Son was begotten not by a voluntary and temporal act but by an eternal and natural one.

units.la: Non sunt istis meliora, imo multo etiam absurdiora, quæ de Spiritus Sancti Theologia apud Diataxes reperiuntur; quæ Jesuita Petavius, ut supra me dixisse memini, γραώδη merito sane vocat: idemque alibi de hoc eodem Constitutionum loco verba faciens, ait, istum Clementem ridiculum nescio quid, & haereticum de Trinitate posuisse. Nam Episcopum (inquit c) in Ecclesia esse instar Dei Patris ait; Diaconum itidem, ut Christum qui Patri assistit, & in omnibus ministrat. Qua, si Christus ut homo esset consideretur, non improbe dicta videri possunt. (Filio autem etiam, qua Deus est, tribuia fictitio Clemente τῷ ὑπηρέτῃ, ex iis quæ nuper attulimus, liquido patet.) Pergit Petavius; Sed (inquit) pestilens est, quod addit, Diaconissam figuram habere Spiritus Sancti, quæ nihil sine Diacono facere debeat, aut loqui; quemadmodum neque Paracletus a se ipso aliquid loquitur, aut facit; sed Christum glorificans voluntatem illius expectat.
units.tr: These are no better, but far more absurd still, are the things found in the Diataxes about the theology of the Holy Spirit. The Jesuit Petavius, as I recall saying above, rightly calls them γραώδη (old wives' tales). Discussing this same passage of the Constitutions elsewhere, he says that this Clement has put forward some ridiculous and heretical notion about the Trinity. For he says (he writes) that the bishop in the Church is in the place of God the Father, and the deacon likewise as Christ, who stands beside the Father and ministers to him in all things. If Christ is considered as man, these words may seem not wrongly said. (That the forged Clement attributes to the servant to the Son, insofar as he is God, is clear from the passages we quoted recently.) Petavius goes on: But (he says) it is pestilential that he adds that the deaconess has the figure of the Holy Spirit, who ought to do or say nothing without the deacon, just as the Paraclete does not speak or act of himself, but, glorifying Christ, waits for his will.

units.la: a l.8. c. 12. p. 101 5. a. b l. 7. c. 42. Quod quidem Macedonianum pus, ac venenum sapit. Verba Constitutionum hæc sunt a; ὁ δὲ διάκονος τὰτῳ παρεισάδω, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς τῷ πατρὶ, καὶ λειτουργείτω αὐτῷ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀμέμπτως, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ποιῶν ὅσα ἓν, τὰ ἀρεστὰ ποιεῖ τῷ πατρὶ πάντοτε· ἢ ὁ διάκονος εἰς τύπον τῆς ἁγίας πνεύματος τετιμήσω ὑμῖν, μηδὲν ἄνευ τοῦ διακόνου πρᾶττεσθαι ἢ φθεγγόμενον, ὡς ὁ παράκλητος ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ τι λαλεῖ, ἢ ποιεῖ, ἀλλὰ δοξάζων τὸν Χριστὸν περιμένει τὸ ἐκείνου Θέλημα. Hæc & Macedonianæ pravitatis, & ridiculæ ineptiæ plena, nemo, nisi delirans, Apostolis tribuerit. Neque alibi magnificentius de Spiritu Sancto loquuntur ut Διδάσκαλοι cum eum à Christo doceri dicunt , nosque in eum, non tanquam in Dominum Deum, quod rectum erat, sed tantum velut in testem, novo & inaudito dogmate, baptizari affirmant: Mandatum (inquiunt ) à Christo accepimus βαπτίσαι εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τῶν Θεῶν... quod est... in mortem ejus in authoritate Dei universorum, qui est ejus Pater; & in testimonio Spiritus Sancti, qui est Paracletus; Quasi vero vel non universorum quoque Deus una cum Patre sit Spiritus Sanctus, vel non ejus æque ac Patris, ἀνθρωπίας baptizemur, qui in nomine
units.tr: a Book 8, ch. 12, p. 101, sec. 5, a. b Book 7, ch. 42. This indeed Macedonian smacks of pus and poison. The words of the Constitutions are these: "And let the deacon stand beside him as Christ beside the Father, and let him minister to him in all things blamelessly, as Christ, doing of himself whatever he does, always does the things pleasing to the Father; or let the deacon be honoured by you as a type of the Holy Spirit, nothing being done or spoken without the deacon, as the Paraclete does not speak or act of himself, but, glorifying Christ, waits for his will" [ὁ δὲ διάκονος τοῦτον παρεισάγω, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς τὸν πατέρα, καὶ λειτουργείτω αὐτῷ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀμέμπτως, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ποιῶν ὅσα ἓν, τὰ ἀρεστὰ ποιεῖ τῷ πατρὶ πάντοτε· ἢ ὁ διάκονος εἰς τύπον τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος τετιμήσω ὑμῖν, μηδὲν ἄνευ τοῦ διακόνου πρᾶττεσθαι ἢ φθεγγόμενον, ὡς ὁ παράκλητος ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ τι λαλεῖ, ἢ ποιεῖ, ἀλλὰ δοξάζων τὸν Χριστὸν περιμένει τὸ ἐκείνου θέλημα]. No one but a madman would attribute these things, full of Macedonian perversity and ridiculous silliness, to the Apostles. Nor do they speak more grandly of the Holy Spirit elsewhere, where, as teachers they say that he is taught by Christ, and affirm that we are baptized into him, not as into the Lord God, which would have been right, but merely as into a witness, by a new and unheard-of doctrine: "We have received a command from Christ to baptize into the name of the God [βαπτίσαι εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ]... which is... into his death, by the authority of God of all, who is his Father, and into the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who is the Paraclete." As if the Holy Spirit were not also God of all together with the Father, or as if we were not baptized equally into him as into the Father, in the name of...

units.la: a Constit. Apost. l.1 c.26.
units.tr: a Constitutions of the Apostles, book 1, ch. 26.

units.la: b Ibid. l.3 c.17.
units.tr: b Ibid., book 3, ch. 17.

units.la: c Ibid. l.5 c.6. mine unius Dei, Patris, Filii, ac Spiritus Sancti baptizamur. Eodem pertinent, quæ iidem alibi de baptismo habent a; τῆ πατρὸς ἢ μνήμῃ ὡς αἰτίᾳ ἐξ ἀποςολέως, ἢ πνεύματος ἢ συμπαρᾶλήψις, ὡς μάρτυς. Fit patris commemoratio, tanquam causa & emissoris; Spiritus coassumptio, ut testis.
units.tr: c Ibid., book 5, ch. 6. We are baptized into the one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. To the same purpose belong the things the same writers say elsewhere about baptism: "the commemoration of the Father as cause and sender [τῆ πατρὸς ἢ μνήμῃ ὡς αἰτίᾳ ἐξ ἀποςολέως], and the co-assumption of the Spirit as witness [πνεύματος ἢ συμπαρᾶλήψις, ὡς μάρτυς]." The commemoration of the Father is made as cause and sender; the co-assumption of the Spirit as witness.

units.la: Deniq; Patrem alio loco ajunt b leges Ecclesiæ dedisse per adventum Christi in carne τὸ μάςλυεα τῆς παρακλήτῳ, Sub teste Paracleto; quasi Spiritus in Filii œconomia & Ecclesiæ ædificatione non aliæ fuerint, quam testis partes. Quo & illud pertinet, quod Patrem in ultimo operis libro c Spiritus Dominum vocant; πρὸ πάντων Ante omnia Deus ac Pater Filii, Dominus Spiritus. Ita & alibi prædicant d ἐνὰ θεὸν ἑνὸς υἱὸς παλέρα, ὁ τῆς πνεύματος Κύριος, ἑνα Θεὸν ἑνὸς υἱὸς παλέρα, ἡ πλειόνων. ἑνὸς παρακλήτος Χριστοῦ τῶν ἄλλων ταγμάτων ποιητὴν, unum Deum unius Filii, ac non plurium Patrem, unius Paracleti per Christum, aliorum ordinum effectorem; quæ vix aliter interpretari licet, nisi Patrem statuas Spiritus Sancti per Christum vel ποιητὴν, vel certe πατέρα, quod utrumque est ab omni Apostolorum & doctrina & sermone alienum. Atque ex his patet, quam vere Arianum huic Scriptori crimen jam inde à Photii temporibus objectum sit, quamque frustra
units.tr: Finally, in another place they say that the Father gave the laws of the Church through the coming of Christ in the flesh "under the Paraclete as witness" [τὸ μάρτυρα τῆς παρακλήτῳ, Sub teste Paracleto]. As if the Spirit in the economy of the Son and in the building up of the Church had any other part than that of witness! To this belongs also their calling the Father, in the last book of the work, "Lord of the Spirit" [Spiritus Dominum]; "before all things, God and Father of the Son, Lord of the Spirit" [πρὸ πάντων]. So they also declare elsewhere "one God, Father of one Son and not of many, maker of the one Paraclete through Christ and of the other orders" [ἑνὰ θεὸν ἑνὸς υἱὸς παλέρα, ὁ τῆς πνεύματος Κύριος, ἑνα Θεὸν ἑνὸς υἱὸς παλέρα, ἡ πλειόνων. ἑνὸς παρακλήτος Χριστοῦ τῶν ἄλλων ταγμάτων ποιητὴν]. These words can hardly be interpreted otherwise, unless you make the Father the maker [ποιητήν] or certainly the Father [πατέρα] of the Holy Spirit through Christ, and each of these is wholly foreign to the teaching and language of all the Apostles. And from this it is plain how truly the charge of Arianism was brought against this writer already in the time of Photius, and how vainly Photius hoped that it could be removed.

units.la: a Ex Scriptura lib. I.
units.tr: a From Scripture, book 1.

units.la: frustra sit Photii a spes, qui hanc ab eo criminatione tametsi ægre, ac nonnihil βιαίως, depelli tamen posse censet. Ipse certe Bovius, cujus magnę sunt hę Diataxes delicię, fateri cogitur b, videri aliquando earum authorem de Spiritu Sanƈto exiliter loqui, de Verbo queque duriores quasdam interdum voces fundere. Ac ille quidem ista defendi omnia posse putat, suamque propriam habere rationem, atque sententiam. Mihi vero, quanquam fortasse haud difficile futurum sit σοφα istius φάρμακα diluere, & quęcunque ad suos Διαταγὰς excusandos comminiscitur, ea refutare, tamen non libet in caussa ab ipso Petavio aperte damnata diutius immorari. Unum libet à Bovio quærere, (ut alios concedamus, quanquam orthodoxos, vel animi aliquo affectu, vel alicujus caussæ studio abreptos aliter nonnunquam loqui, quam decet) an Apostolorum sit, qui nihil nisi ex Spiritus Sancti afflatu, ac dictamine scripserunt, de primis ac maximis Euangelii mysteriis vel exiliter, vel dure loqui? Absit vero, ut de fidei nostræ ducibus, ac magistris tam abjecte, tamque (quod iste ait) exiliter sentiamus. Tertullianum, & Athenagoram, & Iustinum, & Dionysium Alexandrinum, & alios non paucos, antequam Arii certaminibus excitatæ Ecclesia accuratissime hanc Theologiæ giæ partem excussisset, multa incautius dixisse non nego ; neque in iis explicandis, ac molliendis Bovii & aliorum operam aspernor: qua in re luculentum suæ in Dionysium caritatis exemplum posteris reliquit Athanasius. Ut idem Apostolis quoque contigerit, vel contingere potuerit ! ut quorum oratio fidem nostram constituit, ii veniam, & excusationem nostram desiderent, ac poscant; non equidem concedo ; non quisquam, ut opinor, dederit Christianus. Quod ergo Διαθηκῶν voces dura sunt, quod exiles, & infra rerum majestatem dejectæ; quod mendicata Bovii aut Turriani industria, vel Photii βιαίοις commentis egent adhoc, ne Arianæ, ac Macedoniane videantur; id ipsum, inquam, magnum & ideoneum argumentum est, ad id quod defendimus, confirmandum, non esse scilicet Christi Apostolos illos Bovii ac Turriani Διαθήκας. Sed ad cætera nunc pergamus! in quibus palam est istos ab Apostolis dissentire, quæ neque pauca, neque levia sunt.
units.tr: Photius hoped that this accusation, though with difficulty and somewhat forcibly βιαίως, could nevertheless be removed. Bovius himself, in whose eyes these Diataxes are a delight, is forced to admit that their author sometimes seems to speak meagrely of the Holy Spirit, and to pour out rather harsh expressions about the Word. He thinks that all these things can be defended, and that he has his own reasoning and opinion. For my part, although it would perhaps not be difficult to refute the clever remedies φάρμακα of that man and to rebut whatever he contrives to excuse his Diataxes Διαταγὰς, I do not wish to linger long over a cause that Petavius himself has openly condemned. I would like to ask Bovius one thing (granting, for the sake of argument, that orthodox writers, carried away by some emotion or zeal for some cause, sometimes speak otherwise than they ought): are the men who wrote nothing except under the inspiration and dictation of the Holy Spirit to be said to speak meagrely or harshly about the first and greatest mysteries of the Gospel? Far be it from us to think so meanly and (as he says) meagrely of the leaders and teachers of our faith. I do not deny that Tertullian, Athenagoras, Justin, Dionysius of Alexandria, and not a few others spoke too carelessly in many places, before the Church, roused by the Arian controversies, had examined this part of theology with the greatest care; nor do I scorn the labour of Bovius and others in explaining and softening such passages. In this matter Athanasius left to posterity a splendid example of his charity towards Dionysius. But that the same should have happened, or could have happened, to the Apostles, so that those whose teaching establishes our faith should need pardon and excuse from us and beg for it, I do not concede; I think no Christian would have granted it. Therefore, that the expressions of the Διαθηκῶν are harsh, that they are meagre and fallen below the dignity of the matters, that they need the borrowed ingenuity of Bovius or Turrianus, or the forcible βιαίοις inventions of Photius, lest they seem Arian or Macedonian: this very thing, I say, is a great and fitting argument to confirm what we defend, namely that those Apostles of Christ are not the Διαθήκας of Bovius and Turrianus. But let us now go on to other matters, in which it is clear that these men differ from the Apostles, and the differences are neither few nor slight.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Arg. I V. ab aliis non paucis, quae habent Constitutiones ab Apostolico dogmate alienas: ut, de conjugio, quod parum honestè tractant; de hac cum ancilla fornicatione, quam culpa liberant. Parum honesta Bovii defensio refutatur.
units.tr: Argument IV: that many other things in the Constitutions are alien to apostolic doctrine, for example concerning marriage, which they handle dishonourably, and concerning fornication with a female slave, which they excuse from blame. Bovius's dishonourable defence is refuted.

units.la: VERBI gratia, cum veri Christi Apostoli doceant a, liberam esse quamcunque mulierem, cujus vir dormiit, & modo in Domino, nubere ei cui voluerit licere; Item b, Si fuerit mortuus vir ejus, liberatam esse a lege viri, ut non sit adultera, si fuerit cum alio viro; denique d, honorabile esse conjugium in omnibus, & thorum immaculatum; Boviani contra Apostoli conjugium infamant, ac novo nescio quo spiritu perciti decernunt, τὸ πεῖραμα ἀκαθαρσίας σημεῖον εἶναι, τὸ δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν πεῖραμα προφανῆ πορνείαν, ἀσέλγειαν ἀναμφιβόλον, tertium conjugium intemperantiae signum esse, quartum vero conjugium & deinceps, manifestam esse scortationem, & indubitatam impudicitiam. Ista vero non tantum falso, sed etiam impudenter, ac praeter disertam Pauli sententiam dicta sunt; quae quam ille mulierem adulterii clarissime absolvit, eam inverecundissime scortationis ac impudicitiae damnant.
units.tr: For instance, when the true Apostles of Christ teach that a "a woman whose husband has died is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord"; likewise b "if her husband has died, she is released from the law of the husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man"; and finally d "marriage is honourable in all things, and the bed undefiled"; the Bovian Apostles, on the other hand, slander marriage and, roused by I know not what new spirit, decree that "the first trial is a sign of impurity, the second trial clearly fornication, and the third an undoubted lewdness" [τὸ πεῖραμα ἀκαθαρσίας σημεῖον εἶναι, τὸ δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν πεῖραμα προφανῆ πορνείαν, ἀσέλγειαν ἀναμφιβόλον]; that is, "a third marriage is a sign of intemperance, but a fourth marriage and any beyond it are manifest fornication and undoubted impudicity." These statements are not only false but also shameless, and they contradict the plain sentence of Paul, who most clearly acquits a woman of adultery and yet most shamelessly condemns her as a fornicator and an impudent woman.

units.la: Sed neque de secundis nuptiis multo honestius sensisse videntur; qui unius uxoris conjugium Dei in creatione legi consentaneum probant; secundas nuptias per dispensationem quandam tolerant magis, quam probant. Postquam enim ea, quae recitavimus dixerant, continenter haec subjiciunt; ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς μίαν γυναῖκα ἐν ἀνδρὶ ποιῆσαι ἐν τῇ δημιουργίᾳ. ἔσονται γὰρ οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν· νεωτέρας ὁ μὲν τῷ τὸ πρῶτον τελευτῆσαι συγχωρηθῆναι καὶ ὁ δεύτερος, ἵνα μὴ εἰς κρίμα τῆς διαβολῆς ἐμπέσωσι. Deus enim unam uxorem dedit viro, Erunt, inquit, duo in carnem unam. Adolescentioribus vero mor(tuo) primo marito secundus conceditur, ne in judicium diaboli incidant. Vides istos secundas nuptias, non ut per se legitimas, ac honestas, constituere, sed ferre ut minus noxias quam scortationem; & eos hactenus tantum junioribus viduis concedere ac indulgere, ne in crimina graviora labantur.
units.tr: Yet they do not seem to have held second marriages in much higher regard, since, while they approve marriage to one wife as consistent with God's law at creation, they tolerate second marriages by a certain dispensation rather than approve them. After saying what we have quoted, they add at once: "For God made one wife for one man in creation" [ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς μίαν γυναῖκα ἐν ἀνδρὶ ποιῆσαι ἐν τῇ δημιουργίᾳ]. "For the two shall be one flesh" [ἔσονται γὰρ οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν]. "To the younger widows, when the first husband has died, a second is allowed, lest they fall into the judgement of the devil" [νεωτέρας ... συγχωρηθῆναι ... ἵνα μὴ εἰς κρίμα τῆς διαβολῆς ἐμπέσωσι]. You see that they do not set up second marriages as lawful and honourable in themselves, but permit them as less harmful than fornication; and that they grant and indulge this only to younger widows, so that they do not slip into graver sins.

units.la: Sed qui sunt in conjugium, rem honestissimam, severi ac contumeliosi, iidem alibi in fornicationem praeter modum mites, ac indulgentes, ancillis concedunt, ut heris infidelibus, modo solis, morigerentur a; πάλαι καὶ τινῶν ἀπίστων ἄλλη, ἐκείνῳ μόνῳ σχολάζεσθαι, προσδέχεσθω· εἰ δ᾽ ἡ γυνὴ πρὸς ἄλλας ἀσελγαίνει, ἀποβαλλέσθω. Pellex, infidelis delis ancilla, foli Domino obsequens reci-piatur. Si cum aliis intemperans fuerit, re-jiciatur. Haec scilicet Paulus decrevit? has ille leges tulit? qui & quorumvis fornicatio-nem passim in veris libris abominatur, & cuivis fornicatori judicium a Deo minatur. Atque haec ipsa Bellarminus quidem, ut dignum erat, in istis Constitutionibus denotavit. Bovii vero me pudet, usque adeo inverecundi, ut in suorum Διαθηκῶν gratiam hoc libidinis decretum tueri, ac defendere non dubitet; (cum (inquit) ancilla sui corporis potestatem non habeat, merito culpa non in eam, sed in dominum est rejicienda. Plane dignus suis Apostolis Bovius, qui ancillas heris, etiam ad flagitia, ac libidines, morigeras esse vult. Ille vero hac lege etiam turpiora servis adolescentibus pati concedet; modo non alii quam hero obsequantur. Non enim hi magis, quam ancillae, corporis sui potestatem habent. Severior vero est Christi, quam Bovii, & Bovianorum Apostolorum Lex: ex illius enim disciplina, nemini neque libero neque servo, corpus, quod Dei & Spiritus Sancti est, libidinibus polluere licet. Hanc ille suis omnibus libertatem dedit, ut cujusvis, quantumcunque praecellentis, libidini adversentur; eique & in Dei offensionem, & in suae carnis contumeliam, morem, rem, gerere detrectent. Hoc sibi jus, hoc fas esse intellexit jam olim Iosephus; cui ex Boviano jure licebat herae suae furiis succumbere; erat enim ejus servus; & culpam flagitii in dominam merito rejecisset; ex Bovio quidem. Decernit enim cum suis Apostolis bonus, ac sane humanus Episcopus, carnis servilis jus penes Dominorum libidinem esse. Si ancillam, nulla sua voluntate, sed una heri vi oppressam flagitii absolveret, non equidem repugnarem. Neque enim decet qui per vim invití ac reluctantes aliquid patiuntur, iis suam miseriam fraudi esse, aut in crimen verti. Sed longe aliud est, quod volunt Boviani Apostoli. Ajunt enim, non, Si pellex vim ab hero passa fuerit, Sed, Si ei soli [illegible, ~4 letters] obsequitur, vel dat operam, quod significat eam non plane nolentem viro non suo morigerari. Huc accedit, quod si mulierem vi compressam intelligerent, tam eam admitterent, cui a pluribus vis allata est, quam cui ab uno hero; Atqui aliter instituunt. Admittunt enim eam, quae cum uno hero rem habet; eam rejiciunt, quae cum aliis, praeter herum. Ergo eam intelligunt, quae volens hero obsequitur. Et tamen mulierem hujusmodi nostri Διαθηκεῖς in Christi Ecclesiam admittunt; hoc est, pellicem & concubinam. Quid Paulus? Ille vero, qui omnes semel fornicarios regno Dei excludit, ne dubites, quin & hanc pellicem fuerit rejecturus. Ergo quicquid affirmet cum suis Apostolis Bovius, non est hic Ἀιαζ&-γὴς Paulus.
units.tr: But these same men, who are severe and abusive about marriage, which is a most honourable state, are elsewhere far too lenient about fornication and indulgent toward slave-women, allowing them to submit to unbelieving masters, provided it is only to them. "Let a concubine, an unbelieving slave-woman, be received if she serves the Lord alone" [πάλαι καὶ τινῶν ἀπίστων ἄλλη, ἐκείνῳ μόνῳ σχολάζεσθαι, προσδέχεσθω]; "but if the woman plays the wanton with others, let her be cast off" [εἰ δ᾽ ἡ γυνὴ πρὸς ἄλλας ἀσελγαίνει, ἀποβαλλέσθω]. Did Paul really decree this? Did he enact these laws, he who everywhere condemns the fornication of every kind in the true books and threatens every fornicator with the judgement of God? Bellarmine, to be sure, rightly marked these Constitutions with censure. As for Bovius, I am ashamed of him, so shameless that he does not hesitate to defend and uphold this decree of lust for the sake of his Testaments: "since (he says) a slave-woman does not have power over her own body, the blame is rightly to be laid not on her but on the master." Truly Bovius is worthy of his Apostles, who wants slave-women to comply with their masters even in crimes and lusts. Under this rule he would also allow young male slaves to suffer things even more shameful, provided they obey no one but their master. For these men no more have power over their bodies than the slave-women do. But the law of Christ is stricter than that of Bovius and of the Bovian Apostles: under his discipline no one, free or slave, may pollute with lusts the body which belongs to God and the Holy Spirit. He gave all his people this liberty, to resist the lust of anyone, however eminent, and to refuse to obey him to the offence of God and the disgrace of their own flesh. Joseph long ago understood that this right and this lawfulness were his; by Bovius's law he would have had to yield to the frenzy of his mistress, for he was her slave, and he could rightly have laid the guilt of the crime upon his mistress. Good and indeed humane Bishop Bovius, with his Apostles, decrees that the right over a servant's body lies in the lust of the masters. If he had acquitted a slave-woman of the crime, when she was overpowered by the violence of her master and not by her own will, I would not have objected.
