For it is not right that those who suffer something against their will and under violence should have their misery turned to their loss or into a crime. But what the Bovian Apostles want is something quite different. For they say not "if the concubine has been forced by her master," but "if she obeys him alone," or "takes pains to please him alone," which means that she submits to a man who is not her husband not wholly against her will. Moreover, if they meant a woman violated by force, they would admit the one who had been forced by several masters as readily as the one forced by a single master. But they do otherwise. For they admit her who has relations with one master, and reject her who is with others besides her master. So they mean the woman who willingly obeys her master. And yet our so-called Testament-men [Διαθηκεῖς] admit such a woman, a concubine, into the Church of Christ. What does Paul say? He who excludes all fornicators from the kingdom of God once and for all, you may be sure, would have rejected this concubine too. Therefore, whatever Bovius affirms along with his Apostles, this is not the Paul of the true Scriptures.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Arg. V. Negant Constitutiones vere ministros esse, qui vel improbitate vel insciitia laborant. Refelluntur Bovii inanes apologia. Arg. VI. Constitutiones baptismum haereticorum valere negant, adeoque rebaptizant ab haereticis quibusvis tinctos.
units.tr: Arg. V. The Constitutions deny that those who labour under wickedness or ignorance are truly ministers. The empty apologies of Bovius are refuted. Arg. VI. The Constitutions deny that the baptism of heretics is valid, and so rebaptize all who have been baptized by any heretics.

units.la: ED & illud cum Apostolico dogmate pugnat, quod in Constitutionibus legitur a, & ab authore operis in Matthaeum b imperfecti ex canonum Apostolorum (sic enim loquitur) libro octavo citatur: ὥτε ἐ-πίστοπ& ἀγνοίᾳ ἢ κακονοίᾳ πεπεισμένος ἐ-πίστοπός ἔστιν, ἀλλὰ ψευδώνυμος, ὁ τῶν Θεῶν, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προβληθείς. Neque Episcopus ignorantia, aut malo animo oppletus Episcopus est, sed falsus Episcopus, non a Deo, sed ab hominibus promotus. At constans est Ecclesiae Catholicae, Apostolicis scripturis consentanea sententia, etiam improbum hominem, legitime vocatum, vere tamen ministrum esse. Bellarminus hunc
units.tr: And this also conflicts with the apostolic doctrine: what is read in the Constitutions, and is cited by the author of the work on Matthew, which is falsely attributed to Hilary, from the eighth book of the Canons of the Apostles (for so he calls them): "Therefore a bishop who is persuaded by ignorance or ill will is not a bishop, but a bishop in name only, one put forward not by God but by men" [ὥστε ἐπίσκοπος ἀγνοίᾳ ἢ κακονοίᾳ πεπεισμένος ἐπίσκοπός ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ ψευδώνυμος, ὁ οὐ τῶν θεῶν, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προβληθείς]. But it is the settled view of the Catholic Church, agreeing with the apostolic Scriptures, that even a wicked man, if lawfully called, is truly a minister. Bellarmine clearly noted this error in the Constitutions.

units.la: b Hom. 53. hunc in Constitutionibus errorem diserte notavit a: Jubent (inquit) rebaptizari eos, qui baptizantur ab haereticis, ea de causa quia haeretici non sunt sacerdotes. Bovius vero respondet, non hanc suorum Διαῤῥέων mentem esse, ut velint ignaros, vel improbos sacerdotis amittere potestatem, quam in ordinatione acceperunt, sed eos (inquit b) negant esse Episcopos, quatenus officia ac munera, quibus funguntur, non sunt grata atque accepta Deo, imo neque electio ipsorum ei tribuitur, sed hominibus. Sunt igitur hi Episcopi quo ad potestatem; non sunt Episcopi, quo ad Deum attinet, quia institutiones ipsorum atque officia, quae postea exercent, non sunt probata Deo. Sed Bovium palam est ingenio suo abuti, & lectoribus fucum facere. Primo enim pravum, aut ignarum Episcopum potestate muneris carere, eo clare significant οἱ Διαῤῥέων, tum quod illum Episcopum esse negant, qui si potestatem Episcopalem haberet, vere Episcopus esset: tum quod ajunt, eum esse ψευδώνυμον, hoc est falsi nominis Episcopum, revera autem nequaquam Episcopum. Qui vere Rex est, potestatemque regiam vere habet, eum nemo vel negaverit Regem esse, vel ψευδώνυμον, hoc est, nominis falsi regem esse dixerit. Sed & illud falsum sum est quod addit Bovius, electionem im-proborum ministrorum Deo minime tribui: Quorum enim electio legitima est, & ex Ecclesiasticis canonibus rite institua, nihil eos prohibet dici a Deo ad ministerium electos; quantumvis alioqui τῆ κακονοιᾳ laborent. Christus sane Judae, quo nemo fuit sceleftior, electionem ad Apostolatum, sibi ipsi diserte tribuit; Nonne ego vos (inquit) duodecim elegi; & ex vobis unus diabolus est? Officia vero episcopatus, quae hujusmodi ministri exercent, per se ac seorsim spectata, ut bona sunt, ita & hactenus Deo grata, ac probata, licet vitium, quo episcopi animus ea inficit, Deo summopere displiceat. Ista enim sunt a se invicem diligenter distinguenda, teste ac authore Paulo; qui cum nonnulli Christum praedicarent, malo animo propter invidiam, & contentionem, eorum quidem vitiosos affectus, ut par est, damnat, atque abominatur; opus ipsum, scilicet, Dominicam praedicationem, probat atque exosculatur. Quid enim? (inquit) dum omni modo, sive per occasionem, sive per veritatem, Christus annuncietur, & in hoc gaudeo, sed & gaudebo. Facessant ergo Bovii glossae. Manifestissime pugnant ejus διαδοχῆς cum Apostolorum & Ecclesiae doctrina, dum negant Episcopum esse, qui
units.tr: b Hom. 53. Bellarmine clearly noted this error in the Constitutions: "They order those who are baptized by heretics to be rebaptized, for this reason, that heretics are not priests." Bovius, however, replies that this is not the mind of his Διαταγή authors, that they wish to take away from ignorant or wicked priests "the power they received at ordination," but that they deny that such men are bishops (he says) "insofar as the offices and functions they perform are not pleasing and acceptable to God; indeed their election is not ascribed to God but to men. These men are therefore bishops as regards the power; they are not bishops as regards God, because their institutions and the offices they afterwards exercise are not approved by God." But it is plain that Bovius abuses his cleverness and tries to deceive his readers. For first, the Constitutions clearly indicate by the words of their authors that a wicked or ignorant bishop lacks the power of his office: they deny that he is a bishop at all, and they say he is a bishop in name only, that is, a bishop of a false name, but in fact not a bishop. One who is truly king, and truly holds royal power, no one would deny to be king, or would call a king of false name. Also false is what Bovius adds, that "the election of wicked ministers is in no way ascribed to God." For those whose election is lawful, and duly instituted according to ecclesiastical canons, nothing prevents them from being said to be chosen by God for the ministry, however much they may otherwise labour under wickedness [τῇ κακονοίᾳ]. Certainly Christ openly ascribed to himself the choice of Judas to the apostolate, than whom no one was more wicked: "Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" [John 6. 71]. But the offices of the episcopate which such ministers exercise, considered in themselves and separately, are good in themselves, and so far pleasing and approved to God, although the vice by which the bishop's mind taints them is highly displeasing to God. For these things must be carefully distinguished from one another, as Paul bears witness and teaches. When some preached Christ with a bad mind, "out of envy and strife," he indeed condemns and abhors their vicious affections, as is right, but approves and embraces the work itself, namely the preaching of the Lord: "What then? Only that in every way, whether by pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and will rejoice" [Phil. 1. 17–18]. Let Bovius's glosses therefore go away. His διαδοχή plainly conflicts with the doctrine of the Apostles and the Church, while it denies that he is a bishop "who is" [b Phil. 1. 17–18] filled with ignorance or an evil mind.

units.la: a Ioan.6. 71.
units.tr: a John 6. 71.

units.la: b Phil.1. 17.18. qui ignorantia , aut malo animo oppletus est.
units.tr: b Phil. 1. 17–18. who is filled with ignorance or an evil mind.

units.la: Atque hanc , quam dixi , vere istorum mentem esse , præter diserta eorum verba, evincit alius ipsorum error, ex hoc necessario consequens, ac manans ; qui & ipse quoque à Bellarmino notatus est. Jubent enim rebaptizari eos, qui ab hæreticis baptizati sunt ; stultè, ac nequicquam, si putarunt, quod vult Bovius , etiam ἀγνοίᾳ vel κακονοίᾳ laborantes episcopos legitimam muneris potestatem nihilo secius retinere. Valent enim actus ab iis exerciti, qui potestate prediti sunt. Quam autem dixi Διατάγμα de rebaptizandis iis , qui ab impiis & hæreticis baptizati sunt, legem,ea sic habet b ; ὁμοίως καὶ βαπτίσματι ἐνὶ ἀρξαμένῳ μόνῳ τῷ εἰς τὸ τῆς Κυρίου θάνατον ἀποδομένῳ , ἢ τῷ ἀπὸ τῆς συσωνύμων αἱρετικῶν , ἀλλὰ τῷ ἁμαρτίαις . τῆς ἀμέμπτων ἱερέων ἀποδομένῳ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς , καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ , καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος· μήτε ὁ τῷ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀσεβῶν ἑκατὸν ὑμῖν ἔγω , μήτε τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ὁσίων ἀνυσάτῳ εἰς ἑκατόν. Mox : οἱ ὁ ἀπὸ ἀσεβῶν ἐκχόμενοι μόλυσμα κοινωνοὶ τῆς γνώμης αὐτῶν γεννήσουσι. ἡ γὰρ εἰσὶν ἐκεῖνοι ἱερεῖς. &c. ὅτε μὲν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπ' αὐτῶν μεμύνηνται, ἀλλὰ μεμολυσμένοι ὑπάρχουσιν. Similiter docemus, oportere contentos esse uno baptismo, qui in mortem Domini datus est, non non illo baptismo, qui ab infamibus hære‐ticis, sed qui à probatis sacerdotibus tribui‐tur in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Itaq; neque ab impiis datus bapti‐smus vobis probetur; neque à Sanctis mini‐stratus, per secundum irritus fiat, &c. Qui vero ab impiis accipiunt inquinamentum, erunt quoque participes animi eorum. Illi enim Sacerdotes non sunt, &c. Quare qui ab istis baptizati sunt, non baptismo initia‐ti, sed inquinati sunt. Hæc illi; quæ Bovius a non de omnium hereticorum, sed de eorum tantum baptismo accipi vult, qui sinceram sacramenti formam immutabant, quales Paulianistæ fuerant: quorum idcir‐co baptisma Nicæna Synodus b pro irrito habet, jubens rebaptizari, qui ab iis tincti fuerant. Sed Bovium hic fugit ratio. Cla‐rum enim est, Διαζάγεας omnium omnino hæreticorum baptisma reprobare, iteran‐dumque scisicere. Primo enim non tantum rejiciunt τὸ παρὰ τῶν ἀσωνυμῶν αἱρετικῶν βάπ‐τισμα, sed insuper addunt, id tantum bap‐tisma suscipiendum, ac pro sacramento habendum, quod παρὰ τῶν ἀμιάντων ἱερέων, ab inculpatis, sive irreprehensibilibus sacer‐dotibus ministratum est. Ergo hæreticos hic omnes in genere intelligunt, non cer‐tum eorum genus, ut verbi gratia Paulia‐nistarum: nisi forte Bovius solos Pauliani‐stas,
units.tr: And that this, as I have said, is truly their mind, apart from their plain words, is proved by another error of theirs, which necessarily follows from it and flows out of it, and which Bellarmine has also noted. For they order that those who were baptized by heretics be rebaptized. Foolishly and to no purpose, if they thought, as Bovius wishes, that bishops labouring under ignorance or ill will nonetheless retain the lawful power of their office. For acts performed by those who are endowed with power are valid. Now the law concerning the rebaptism of those who were baptized by the impious and heretics, which I have mentioned, reads as follows: "Likewise, a baptism begun by one alone who was given over to the death of the Lord, or by one of the heretics who are companions of the impious, but by sinners, is not to be received by you; nor let the baptism of the impious be approved by you, nor let what is administered by the holy be rendered void by a second baptism," etc. Soon after: "Those who receive pollution from the impious will also become partakers of their mind; for those are not priests," etc. "Therefore those who have been baptized by them are not initiated, but are defiled." We teach similarly that one ought to be content with the one baptism which was given into the death of the Lord, not that baptism which is given by infamous heretics, but that which is given by approved priests in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore let neither the baptism given by the impious be approved by you, nor, when administered by the holy, be made void by a second baptism. "But those who receive pollution from the impious will also be partakers of their mind. For those are not priests." Therefore those who have been baptized by them are not initiated but defiled. These are their words, which Bovius wishes to be understood not of the baptism of all heretics, but only of those who altered the pure form of the sacrament, as the Paulianists did. For this reason the Synod of Nicaea also holds their baptism void, ordering those baptized by them to be rebaptized. But Bovius's reasoning fails him here. For it is clear that the Διαταγή authors reject the baptism of all heretics without exception, and require it to be repeated. For first they not only reject the baptism given by impious heretics, but add that only that baptism is to be received and regarded as a sacrament which is administered by unstained priests, that is, by blameless or irreproachable priests. So here they understand all heretics in general, not some particular kind, such as the Paulianists. Unless perhaps Bovius denies that only the Paulianists and those like them are blameless priests, and concedes that the priests of the other heretics are blameless.

units.la: a in l. 6. c. 16. stas, eorumque similes, neget esse ἀμίμ-ητος ἱερέως, caeterorum haereticorum sacerdotes inculpatos esse concedat. Valere negant baptismum ab aliis, quam ab inculpatis ministris datum; Ergo neque ab ullo cujuscumq; haereseos ministro datum probant; cum constet, nullum, nisi orthodoxum, inculpatum ministrum vel esse, vel dici posse. Idem probant, quae statim subjiciunt, neque ἅγιον esse baptismum τὸν τῆς ἀσεβῶν, neque reprobandum τὸν τῆς ὁσίων. Atqui omnis a quovis haeretico datus baptismus & est τῆς ἀσεβῶν, & τῆς ὁσίων nequaquam est, nisi forte Bovius aliquos haereticos norit, qui sancti sint, impii non sint. Denique addita in Constitutionibus ratio hoc ipsum invicte demonstrat. Non enim, quod pro nullo habent haereticorum baptisma, ideo id reprobant, quod legitima ac sincera sacramenti forma careat; (quae ratio, ut quivis videt, afferenda erat, si istorum ea mens fuisset, quam Bovius esse vult) sed quod ii, a quibus id est administratum, sacerdotes non sint; ὁ γὰρ εἶπν (inquit) ἐκεῖνοι ἱερεῖς. Nulla autem ratio est, cur quorundam haereticorum ministri vere sacerdotes sint; aliorum vero non sint. Et quem ad id probandum afferunt οἱ Διαθήκης Scripturae locum, is siquid valet, conficit, nullos omnino esse haere-
units.tr: They deny that baptism given by any ministers other than blameless ones is valid. Therefore they also prove that baptism given by any minister of any heresy is not valid, since it is established that no one except an orthodox minister can be or be called blameless. The same is proved by what they add immediately: that baptism is neither holy when it is of the impious, nor to be rejected when it is of the holy. But every baptism given by any heretic is both of the impious and by no means of the holy, unless perhaps Bovius knows of some heretics who are holy and not impious. Finally, the reason added in the Constitutions proves this very point invincibly. For they do not reject the baptism of heretics on the ground that it lacks the lawful and pure form of the sacrament (which reason, as anyone can see, ought to have been given if their mind had been that which Bovius wishes it to be), but because those by whom it was administered are not priests; "for those," they say, "are not priests." But there is no reason why the ministers of some heretics should truly be priests while those of others are not. And the passage of Scripture which they cite in support of this, if it proves anything, proves that there are altogether no heretical ministers who are priests. Thus they prove the point: "Those are not priests; for God says to them, Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you from serving as my priest."

units.la: hæreticorum ministros, qui sacerdotes sint. Itaenim isti institutum probant : ὑπ' εἰσὶν ἐκεῖνοι ἱερεῖς· λέγει γὰρ πρὸς αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς, ἐπεὶ σὺ ἀπώσω γνῶσιν, ἀπωσόμαι σε κἀγὼ ἱερατεύειν μοι. Non sunt illi sacerdotes. Dicit enim ad eos Deus; Quoniam rejecisti, vel repulisti cognitionem, & ego rejiciam te ne fungaris mihi sacerdotio. Nullus est hæreticus, qui non rejiciat cognitionem. Ergo nullum isti hæreticum sacerdotem esse censuerunt; qui hinc eos sacerdotes esse negant, quod cognitionem rejiciant. Nimirum isti, quod nuper demonstravimus, neminem pro sacerdote habuerunt, qui vel ἀγνοίᾳ, vel κακονοίᾳ laboraret. Unde consequens est, ut, cum baptismum nisi a vero sacerdote administrari nefas existimaverint, eum, non tantum qui a Paulianistis, sed etiam qui a quibusvis hæreticis administratur, pro nullo planeque irrito habuerint. Quod quam sit ab Apostolica fide alienum, & ipse Bovius, & omnes cum eo adversarii vident, ac confitentur.
units.tr: the heretics' ministers, who are priests. For these men approve this principle: "Those are not priests; for God says to them: 'Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, that you should not serve me as priest'" [ὑπ' εἰσὶν ἐκεῖνοι ἱερεῖς· λέγει γὰρ πρὸς αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς, ἐπεὶ σὺ ἀπώσω γνῶσιν, ἀπωσόμαι σε κἀγὼ ἱερατεύειν μοι]. Those men are not priests. For God says to them: "Because you have rejected or cast off knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve me in the priesthood." No heretic exists who does not reject knowledge. Therefore these men have judged that no heretic is a priest; they deny that heretics are priests on the ground that they reject knowledge. Indeed, as we have just shown, these men have regarded as a priest no one who labours under ignorance or ill will. Hence it follows that, since they have thought it wrong for baptism to be administered except by a true priest, they have held that baptism administered not only by the Paulianists but also by any heretics whatever is null and utterly void. How far this is alien to the Apostolic faith, both Bovius himself and all his adversaries with him see and confess.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Arg. VII. Constitutiones baptismi ritui addere non pauca Apostolis ignota. VIII. Constitutiones Eucharistiam infantibus communicandam decernere, quod est ab Apostolica doctrina alienum. IX. De Ministris plurima aliter, quaedam plane contra, quam Apostoli, docere.
units.tr: Arg. VII. The Constitutions add to the rite of baptism not a few things unknown to the Apostles. VIII. The Constitutions decree that the Eucharist is to be given to infants, which is alien to Apostolic doctrine. IX. Concerning ministers, they teach many things differently, and some things plainly contrary to what the Apostles taught.

units.la: TAM & illud ab Apostolorum doctrina alienum est, quod baptizandos oleo, eosdemque postquam baptizati sunt, unguento sive chrismate inungi praecipiunt; neque, nisi ubi olei & unguenti copia nulla est, aliter homines baptizari concedunt. Ab Apostolis vero, & aliis eorundem temporum Christi discipulis solam aquam in baptismo adhibitam ex toto novo Testamento constat; idque vel Aethiopis a Philippo baptizati, quae apud Lucam extat, historia abunde testatur. Is enim narrat, cum ii ad aquam quandam venissent, dixisset que Eunuchus, Ecce aqua, quid prohibet me baptizari? respondisse Philippum, Si credis ex toto corde, licet; & exemplo hominem suam in Christum fidem professum baptizasse. Ille vero duplicis unctionis ritus, post Apostolici saeculi simplicitatem, ab aliis in Ecclesiam invectus est.
units.tr: It is also alien to the teaching of the Apostles that they order those to be baptized to be anointed with oil, and afterwards, once baptized, to be anointed with unguent or chrism; and they allow people to be baptized in any other way only where there is no supply of oil or unguent. Yet the whole of the New Testament shows that the Apostles and the other disciples of Christ of that same time used only water in baptism. The history of the Ethiopian baptized by Philip, found in Luke, bears ample witness to this. For he relates that when they came to a certain water, the eunuch said, "See, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?" and Philip replied, "If you believe with all your heart, you may" [Acts 8:36-37]; and by this example he baptized a man who professed his faith in Christ. But that rite of double anointing was introduced into the Church by others, after the simplicity of the Apostolic age.

units.la: Quid quod nostri Διαβαγεὶς & aquæ, & unguenti illius sui mysticam per preces sacerdotales sanctificationem tanti faciant, ut sine ea baptismum pro re inani ac ludicra habere videantur? Certe, postquam eas preces recitarunt, quibus & aquam & chrisma sanctificari abepiscopo decernunt, continuo hæc addunt ἀ;ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν ἐπικλήσεις γίνηται ... τὸ εὐσεβὲς ἐπ- εἰ-ως τοιαύτη τις, εἰς ὕδωρ μόνον καταβαίνει ὁ βαπτιζόμενος, ὡς Ἰουδαῖοι· καὶ ἀποτίθεται μόνον τὸ ῥύπον τοῦ σώματος, οὐ τὸν ῥύπον τῆς ψυχῆς.
units.tr: What of the fact that our men set such store by the mystical sanctification, by sacerdotal prayers, both of the water and of that unguent of theirs, that without it they seem to regard baptism as an empty and frivolous thing? Certainly, after they have recited those prayers by which the bishop decrees that both the water and the chrism are to be sanctified, they immediately add that if such an invocation is not made over each of them, the one being baptized goes down only into the water, like the Jews, and puts off only the filth of the body, not the filth of the soul. Those are their words.

units.la: Nisi enim unicuique horum aliqua hujusmodi à pio sacerdote adhibeatur invocatio, qui baptizatur in solam aquam descendit, ut Iudæi; & corporis tantum, non autem animæ sordes deponit. Hæc illi; quibus non video quid vel in sanctissimum Christi baptisma contumeliosius dici possit, vel à constanti Apostolorum doctrina magis alienum. Ipse Bovius lectorem monet, ut in his verbis sit cautus; fateturque sanctificationem materiæ baptismi magis requiri præcepti, quam sacramenti necessitate. Quæ si vera sunt, apparet, etiam eum, qui aqua nulla prece sanctificata baptizatur, animæ tamen sordes, contra quæ censent οἱ Διαβαγεῖς, deponere, cū hęc sit divini sacramenti vis, ut animam abluat. Nequid jam de unguento dicam, quod iidem, & quidem mystica stica invocatione sanctificatum, ad hoc necessarium putant, ut baptizati peccata deleantur. Quod vero negat Bovius istorum dictis adversari, ut quis non adhibita ad baptismum aqua sanctificata, vere sit baptizatus, & si absit contemptus vel negligentia, sacramenti fructum consequatur; id, inquam, nimis inverecundum est. Nam Διαθηκης exserte negant, sordes animæ ab eo deponi, qui vel aqua tingitur, vel chrismate inungitur nulla sacerdotis invocatione sanctificantis. Qui vero sordes animam non deponit; eum constat nullum sacramenti fructum consequi. Neque isti de contemptu vel negligentia, sed de una omissione suæ consecrationis loquuntur. Quanquam neque illud satis assequor, cur istis id juris tribuat Bovius, ut quod ipsi præter Apostolica instituta huic sacramento nulla ratione infulciant, id nemo sine salutis æternæ jactura negligere possit, vel contemnere. Nobis satis est, quod hæc istorum mysteriorum decantata in Constitutionibus ad baptismum necessitas, ea procul est à verorum Christi Apostolorum disciplina, qui præter aquam nihil ad hoc sacramentum aliud requirunt.
units.tr: For unless some invocation of this kind is made over each of these by a pious priest, the one who is baptized goes down only into water, like the Jews, and puts off only the filth of the body, not of the soul. What could be said more insulting to the most holy baptism of Christ, or more alien to the constant doctrine of the Apostles, I do not see. Bovius himself warns the reader to be careful in these words, and he admits that the sanctification of the matter of baptism is required more by precept than by the necessity of the sacrament. If this is true, it follows that even one who is baptized with water not sanctified by any prayer still puts off the filth of the soul, against what the authors of the Constitutions think; since this is the power of the divine sacrament, that it cleanses the soul. Not to mention the unguent, which the same men, sanctified by a mystical invocation, judge necessary so that the sins of the baptized may be blotted out. But when Bovius denies that these men's words oppose the view that a person may be truly baptized without water sanctified for baptism, and that if there is no contempt or negligence he obtains the fruit of the sacrament, this, I say, is far too shameless. For the Constitutions plainly deny that the filth of the soul is put off by one who is dipped in water or anointed with chrism without the invocation of a priest who sanctifies it. And whoever does not put off the filth of the soul, it is plain that he obtains no fruit of the sacrament. Nor do these men speak of "contempt or negligence," but of a single omission of their consecration. Yet I also do not quite see why Bovius grants them this right, that what they themselves, contrary to Apostolic institution, stuff into this sacrament without any reason, no one can neglect or despise without loss of eternal salvation. It is enough for us that this necessity, so loudly proclaimed in the Constitutions' mysteries concerning baptism, is far removed from the discipline of the true Apostles of Christ, who require nothing else for this sacrament but water.

units.la: Jam quod Eucharistiam τοῖς παισίοις pueris & infantibus communicandam, & quidem ante populum, decernunt, id dogma fuit(fateor)plerorumque quidem Christianorum, qui tertio & sequentibus deinceps Christianismi saeculis vixerunt; Apostolorum tamen non fuit; qui cum neminem ad sacram Christi mensam admittant, nisi a qui se ipsum probaverit, eo ipso infantes, nondum hujus probationis per aetatem capaces, ab Eucharistiae participatione excludunt, quod & nos & universi communionis Romanae Christiani nunc magno consensu sequimur. Qui ergo aliter instituunt Διαθῆκαι, ii non sunt Christi, quod mentiuntur, Apostoli; sed sequentium saeculorum, quibus diversus ab Apostolico usus obtinuit, homines.
units.tr: Now, as to their decree that the Eucharist be given to children and infants, and indeed before the people, I grant that this was the doctrine of most Christians who lived in the third and following centuries of Christianity; but it was not the Apostles' doctrine. The Apostles admit no one to the holy table of Christ unless he has examined himself; by that very fact they exclude infants, who are not yet capable of such examination by reason of their age, from participation in the Eucharist. This we, and all Christians of the Roman communion, now follow with great agreement. Therefore those who establish the Constitutions otherwise are not Christ's apostles, as they falsely claim, but men of later centuries, among whom a usage different from the Apostolic one prevailed.

units.la: Venio ad Ministros, de quibus isti multa aliter, non pauca contra, quam Apostoli docent. In primis cum Apostoli nullos alios in Ecclesia ministros, praeter presbyteros (quos & Episcopos appellant)& diaconos memorent; constanterque a rerum Ecclesiasticarum peritis concessum sit, quod ab ipso Scholae Romanae magistro diserte perscriptum est b, hos solos ministrorum duos ordines Ecclesiam primitivam habuisse, & de his solis praeceptum Apostoli nos habere; isti Boviani & Turrianici Apostoli c subdiaconos, & acoluthos, exorcistas, lectores, & ostiarios in ore passim habent, ac de eorum, non minus, quam de presbyteris rum, & diaconorum institutione, munere & officiis præcipiunt. Ergo necesse est, istos quiqui de cætero sint, neque Apostolos fuisse, neque Apostolicis temporibus vixis- se, sed iis, quibus postea subdiaconos, & acoluthos, cæterosque inferioris ordinis ministros Ecclesia sibi constituit, ut ait Magister sententiarum.
units.tr: I come to the ministers, about whom these men teach many things differently and not a few things contrary to what the Apostles teach. First of all, since the Apostles mention no other ministers in the Church apart from elders (whom they also call bishops) and deacons; and since it is generally conceded by those skilled in church affairs, as the very master of the Roman school has expressly written, that the primitive Church had only these two orders of ministers, and that we have the Apostles' precept concerning these alone; these Constitutions, Bovian and Turrian apostles, constantly have subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers and doorkeepers on their lips, and they give precepts about their institution, office and duties no less than about the presbyters and deacons. Therefore it is necessary that whoever these men are, they were neither Apostles nor lived in Apostolic times, but belonged to the period in which the Church later established for itself subdeacons, acolytes, and the other ministers of lower order, as the Master of the Sentences says.

units.la: Sed & hoc ab Apostolorum dogmate alienum est, quod isti magnum & manifestum faciunt presbyteri ab episcopo discriminem; omnino quale secutis post Apostolos temporibus, tertio, quartoque sæculis cernitur. Episcopum enim volunt esse b ἀρχιερέα, principem sacerdotum, & Pontificem; presbyterum vero ἱερέα; illum instar Christi, presbyteros instar Apostolorum c, ὡς συμβούλους τῶν ἐπισκόπων & τῆς ἐκκλησίας ςεφα-νον, καὶ συνέδριον, ut consiliarios Episcopi, & Ecclesia coronam, synedrium, & senatum. Tum omnem ordinandi, etiam minimos ministros, ut ostiarios, potestatem presbyteris ereptam, solis Episcopis tribuunt d; ac ne nos ista minus attentos fugerent, diserte etiam monent, se diversis episcoporum, presbyterorum, ac Diaconorum nominibus rerum ipsarum, sive munerum & ordinum differentiam declarasse, ajuntque nos fortasse hæc non ignorare apud se alia. τὰ δ' ἐφ' ἡμῶν ἴσως ἂν ἀγ-
units.tr: But it is also alien to the Apostles' doctrine that these men make a great and manifest distinction between the presbyter and the bishop, such as is seen in the times after the Apostles, in the third and fourth centuries. For they want the bishop to be a high priest, the chief of priests and a Pontiff, and the presbyter a priest; the one in the place of Christ, the presbyters in the place of the Apostles, "as counsellors of the bishops and the crown of the Church, and the senate, and the council" [Greek]. Then they take away from presbyters all power of ordaining, even of the very lowest ministers such as doorkeepers, and give it to bishops alone. And lest we, not paying close attention, should miss these things, they also expressly warn that by the different names of bishop, presbyter and deacon they have declared the difference of the things themselves, that is, of offices and orders; and they add that perhaps we do not know these other things among ourselves. [Greek: "but the things among us you would perhaps understand otherwise"]

units.la: a Vt supra. b l. 2. c. 25. extr. c l. 2. c. 28. d l. 3. c. 11. 20. e l. 8. c. 28. & c. 46. νοεῖτε· ἴςε γὰρ πάντως ἐπισκόπως παρὰ ἡμῶν ὁ-νομαςδίνςες καὶ πρεσβυτέρες ἐ διακόνες ἐυχῆ χεῖρῶν ἐπιθέσει τῇ διαφορᾷ τῶν ὀνομάτων, ἐ τῶν διαφορᾷν τῶν πραγμάτων ἀπινδυονζες. Omnia à veris Christi Apostolis aliena; qui neque episcopi & presbyteri nominibus differenter, sed promiscue nulloque discrimine utuntur a (quod & nos jam supra diximus, & omnes pæne veteres recentioresque confitentur) neque ullum ufpiam ministerium Ecclesiasticum inter diaconos & episcopos medium agnoscunt; neque χειροθεσίαν b, hoc est, manuum impositionem, episcoporum tantum esse scisci unt, sed eam ipsis quoque presbyteris diserte tribuunt; ut ex Paulo constat c, qui Timotheo datam ait fuisse gratiam per impositionem manuum presbyterii: neque unum tantum insingulis Ecclesiis episcopum esse statuunt, sed plures etiam in una Ecclesia Episcopos diserte nominant; ut in Ecclesia Ephesiorum d & Philippensium. Ex quibus ruit omnis illa Διαζυγίων falsa ratiocinatio; εἰ μὴ γὰρ (inquiunt e) μὴ θεσμὸς τις ἦν ἐ τάξεων διαφορὰ, ἥρκει ἂν δι' ἑνὸς ὀνόματος καὶ ὅλα τελείσθαι. ἀλλ' ὑπὸ τῶν Κυρίων διδαχθέντες ἀνολυσίαν πραγμάτων, τοῖς μὲν ἐπισκόποις καὶ τῆς ἀρχιερωσύνης ἐνείμαμεν, τοῖς δὲ πρεσβυτέροις καὶ τῆς ἱερωσύνης, τοῖς δὲ διακόνοις τὰ τῆς πρὸς ἀμφοτέρας διακονίας. Etenim si non esset aliqua liqua lex posita, & aliquod discrimen ordinum, satis erat, uno nomine asseętos omnia ista ministeria perficere. Verum a Domino rerum consequentiam edoƈti, episcopis quidem quæ sunt Pontificatus, tribuimus; presbyteris vero, quæ sunt sacerdotii; diaconis deinde, quæ ad ministrandum utrisque pertinent. Fateor procedere argumentū de presbyteris & diaconis, quorū ut res, ita & nomina clarissime sunt ab Apostolis inter se distinƈta; sic ut nusquam, qui diaconus est, is presbyteri nomine donatus in divinis litteris reperiatur; ac de episcopis & presbyteris idem quoque concederem, si eorum nomina itidem quoque ab Apostolis distinƈta ex veris & sinceris eorum monumentis constaret. Nunc plane aliter est. Constat enim ex iis, & qui sunt presbyteri, eos nulla invidia episcopos a, & qui sunt episcopi, eos vice versa presbyteros b quoque ab Apostolis vocatos fuisse. Cum ergo nomina, tametsi per se diversa, unius ejusdemque rei communia, nullam in re significata differentiam constituant; apparet, frustra nominum episcopi & presbyteri diversitatem à Constitutionum scriptore urgeri; quæ, ut ex superioribus liquet, nullo discrimine ab Apostolis usurpantur. Potius inde collegerim, ut unus idemque Apostolis est & presbyter, & episcopus; unum quoque eundem iis esse, & presbyteratum & episcopatum: qui cum Διάκονοι non sit unus, idemque, profecto necesse est, istos alios fuisse, quam Apostolos. Sed hoc quidem, tametsi certissimum, & validissimum imposturæ in Constitutionum libris argumentum, accuratius tamen in præsentia persequi, neque libet, quod ea res longiorem disputationem requirat; neque necesse est, cum reverendus ac doctissimus vir David Blondellus, frater ac collega in Domino carissimus, fusè nuper, ac, ut solet, enucliatè demonstraverit, episcopatum ista sic a presbyteratu, ut hodie fit, & jam olim a tertio Christianismi sæculo factum est, distinctum, rem esse, non Apostolicæ, sed Ecclesiasticæ, adeoque humanæ institutionis.
units.tr: a As above. b Book 2, ch. 25, end. c Book 2, ch. 28. d Book 3, chs. 11 and 20. e Book 8, chs. 28 and 46. [Greek continued: "For by us, they are all named bishops and presbyters and deacons, by prayer and the laying on of hands, not distinguishing the differences of the things by the difference of the names."] These things are all foreign to the true Apostles of Christ, who do not use the names "bishops" and "presbyters" as different, but interchangeably and without any distinction (as we have already said above, and nearly all the ancient and more recent writers acknowledge). Nor do they recognise any ecclesiastical ministry intermediate between deacons and bishops. Nor do they hold that the laying on of hands, that is, the imposition of hands [Greek: cheirothesia], belongs to bishops alone; they expressly grant it to presbyters as well, as is clear from Paul, who says that the grace given to Timothy was given "through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery" [1 Tim. 4:14]. Nor do they hold that there is only one bishop in each Church; they expressly name several bishops in one Church, as in the Church of the Ephesians and of the Philippians [Acts 20:17, 28; Phil. 1:1]. From these premises that whole false reasoning of the Constitutions collapses; for they say: "For if there were no law and no distinction of orders, it would have been enough to accomplish all these things under one name. But, taught by the Lord the proper order of things, we have assigned to bishops what belongs to the high priesthood, to presbyters what belongs to the priesthood, and to deacons what pertains to the service of both." I admit that the argument proceeds concerning presbyters and deacons, whose things and names alike the Apostles have most clearly distinguished from one another, so that nowhere is one who is a deacon found in Scripture as having been given the name of presbyter. And I would concede the same concerning bishops and presbyters, if their names too had been distinguished by the Apostles, as is evident from their true and genuine records. But now it is quite otherwise. For it is clear from the texts that those who are called presbyters were without any objection also called bishops by the Apostles, and conversely, those who are bishops were also called presbyters. Therefore, since names, though different in themselves, when common to one and the same thing establish no difference in the thing signified, it is evident that the author of the Constitutions insists in vain on a difference of names between bishop and presbyter, which, as is clear from what has gone before, the Apostles use without any distinction. Rather I would infer from this that the same person was for the Apostles both presbyter and bishop; and that the presbyterate and the episcopate were the same for them too. And since the deacon is not the same as these, it must surely follow that these men were other than the Apostles. But this argument, though most certain and a very strong proof of the imposture in the books of the Constitutions, I do not, for the present, wish to pursue more closely, since the matter would require a longer discussion; nor is it necessary, since the reverend and most learned man David Blondel, my dearest brother and colleague in the Lord, has lately demonstrated it at length and, as is his custom, with clarity: that the episcopate, as distinguished from the presbyterate as it is today, and as it has been since the third century of Christianity, is a matter not of Apostolic but of ecclesiastical, and so of human, institution.

units.la: Illud quidem certe nemo, quod reor, sanus negaverit, omnino a veris Apostolis aliena esse, quæ nostri Διάκονοι in suos passim episcopos sine ullo pudore, aut modo, magna cum pompa congerunt dignitatis & potestatis elogia; adeo ea sunt invidiosa, & typhi fastusque sæcularis plena.
units.tr: Certainly no sane person, I think, would deny that the titles of dignity and power which our deacons [Διάκονοι] heap upon their bishops everywhere, without any shame or restraint and with great pomp, are entirely foreign to the true Apostles. They are so odious and so full of worldly pride and arrogance.

units.tr: They say that the bishop has the image of God among men, since he rules over and presides over all men: priests, kings, magistrates, parents, sons, and all subjects alike. Soon after: Judge, then, O bishop, with authority, as God does. [Κρίνε ἂν, ὧ ἐπίσκοπε μὴ ἐξουσίας, ὡς ὁ Θεὸς.] Elsewhere: You ought to rule over your subjects, not they over you. [ἀρχειν τε χρὴ τῶν ὑπηκόων, ὃ μὲν καὶ ὑπ' αὐτῶν ἄρχεσθαι.] They bid the laity honour, love and fear the bishop as Lord, as Master, as High Priest of God [ὡς Κύριον, ὡς Δεσπότην, ὡς Ἀρχιερέα Θεοῦ]. Turning the speech to the bishops elsewhere, they say: "You are to your laity prophets, princes, leaders and kings, mediators between God and his faithful" [Ὑμεῖς τοῖς ἐν ὑμῖν λαϊκοῖς ἐστε προφῆται, ἄρχοντες, καὶ ἡγούμενοι, βασιλεῖς, μεσῖται Θεοῦ καὶ τῶν πιστῶν αὐτοῦ]. You are to your laity prophets, princes, leaders and kings, mediators between God and his faithful. And, lest the laity should fail to know this great mystery, they thought they should be told it plainly in these words: "The bishop, they say, is your ruler and leader; he is not your king or lord; he is not an earthly god, not God, who ought to enjoy honour from you" [ὁ ἐπίσκοπος ἄρχων καὶ ἡγεμὼν ὑμῶν· οὐ βασιλεὺς ὑμῶν ἢ δυνάστης· οὐχ ὑμῶν ἐπίγειος Θεὸς μὴ Θεὸν]. But indeed the same thing God said of such men as well: "I have said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High" [Ἀλλὰ γὰρ τότε καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων αὐτὸ ὁ Θεὸς ἔλεγεν, Ἐγὼ εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες]. This one is your Prince and Leader; this one your King and Lord; this one, after

units.la: e l. 2. c. 26. init. post Deum Deus terrenus; qui honore à vobis exhibito fruì debet. De hoc enim & ei similibus ajebat Deus, Ego dixi, Dii estis, & filii altissimi omnes. Et, Diis populi tui non detrahes. Episcopus igitur vobis praesideat, ut Dei dignitate cohonestatus, qua clero dominatur, & toti populo imperat. Satin' magnifice? Audi vero & alia. Suum hunc beatum monarcham laïcos jubent accuratissima veneratione colere, reverentesque habere, neque temere in tantae majestatis arcanum irrumpere, ejusve delicias, ac curas turbare; μὴ φαδῶς δὲ (inquiunt a) ἐνοχλεῖτωσαν τῇ ἀρχοντι ἀλλὰ δὲ τὴν ὑπηρέτων, ἃ βελοντ​αι συμπαι-​νέτωσαν, τουτέστι δὲ τὴν διακόνων, πρὸς ὃς πλέον παρρησιαζέτωσαν. Caveant vero, ne facile Principi suo obstrepant; quia potius quae volent, per ministros, id est, per diaconos, significent, cum quibus audacius ac fidentius agant. Obsecro, nonne isti videntur aliquem vel veterum Persarum, vel hodiernorum Abyssinorum Regem, vel barbarici supercilii satrapam, potius quam Christianum Episcopum effingere, à cujus limine ita diligenter omnem turbam summovent? in cujus conspectum nullos de plebe pios per se venire patiuntur? cum quo quemquam nisi per interpretem, ac mediatorem colloqui nefas putant? ac si totus Dei populus plane profanum sit vul-gus, episcopali numine, ac obtutu indi-gnum? Sed ne tantum homuncionibus de-ferri indigneris, cavent, & suæ hujus legis rationem addunt, sane bellam, ac commo-dam, & quam nemo dubitaverit ex Apo-stolorum animo, atque ore manasse: ὑσὶ ψὶ (inquiunt) τῶ παντοκρατόρι θεῶ προσελ-θεῖν ἐςιν, ἐὰν μὴ διὰ τῆ Χρισ̃ͅ ὕτως ἂν ἐ οἱ λαϊκοὶ πάντες, ὅσα βέλου̃, διὰ τ διακόνυ̃ φανερὰ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ποιεῖτωσαν, ἐ ὅτω χ̃ͅ τὸ ἀρχ̃ͅ ἐκείνῳ ἐπιτελείτωσαν. Neque enim ad omnipotentem Deum accedere licet, nisi per Christum. Ad hunc ergo modum quæcunque volunt laici, per Diaconum Episcopo indicent, atque ita ut ei videbitur agant, Hæc vero quis patienter audiat? nefas esse Episcopum nisi per Diaconum convenire, quod neque Deus adiri, nisi per Christum possit? Quasi scilicet vel Diaconus Christus. Atqui licebit hoc exemplo concludere, & episcopatum & diaconum, perquem aditur, utrumque adorandum esse; qui honos scilicet & Deo & Christo habetur. Quæ si placent, (placere autem debent, si sunt Apostolica) nullus erit Episcopus, qui non & Papa quoque sit apud suos. Sed ecce in proximo hunc ipsum suis Episcopis cultum tantum non poscentes Διαξγίας. Allato enim Moysis exemplo, qui & Aaronis Prophetes, & Pharaonis Deus dictus est; (inquiunt a) μὴ γὰρ ὑμεῖς τὰς μεσίτας ὑμῶν τ λόγυ πρ-οφήτας εἶναι νομίσαντε, καὶ ὡς θεὺς σεβασθῆσ-θε; (Cur vos internuncios sermonis vestri non habetis in Prophetis, & Episcopos tanquam Deos colitis? Tum illa subjiciunt aurea, ac plane Apostolica b; Νῦν γὰρ ὑμῶν μὲν ὁ Ἀαρὼν ἕστιν ὁ διάκονος, Μωϋσῆς ὁ ἐπίσκοπος. εἰ γὰρ ἐρρέθη Μωϋσῆς ὑπὸ Κυρίου Θεὸς, καὶ ὑμῖν ὁ ἐπίσκοπος εἰς Θεὸν τετιμῆται· ὁ δὲ διάκονος ὡς προφήτης αὐτοῦ. Nunc enim vester Aaron est diaconus, Episcopus vero Moyses vester. Si igitur Moyses a Domino appellatus est Deus, Episcopus a vobis in Deum honorator; & Diaconus ut Propheta ejus. Quis jam dubitet istos fuisse Apostolos, qui sic nullo negotio diaconos in Aaronem, Episcopos in Moysem transformant? Neque saniora sunt quae alibi habent. Nam ne putes iis nuda honorifici cultus signa satis esse, ecce, suis Episcopis tributa pendi, non secus ac saeculi Principibus jubent. Τὰς ἐπισκόπους (inquiunt c) ἀρχοντας ὑμῶν ἢ βασιλέας ἡγεῖσθαι νομίζετε, καὶ Δασμὸς ὡς βασιλεύσι προσφέρετε. Mox; ὡς Σαμουὴλ διετάξατο πρὸς τὸν λαὸν περὶ τ βασιλέως, ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ τ Βασιλειῶν, καὶ Μωσῆς περὶ τ ἱερέων ἐν τῷ Λευιτι-κῷ· ἔτω δὲ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν περὶ τ ἐπισκόπων διατα-ταξότασσόμεθα. Tum paulo post; ἐὰ ὃ δεῖ κρὶ τι προσδεῖναι τῷ λόγῳ, πλεῖον ἢ τῷ (ἐπίσκο- πῷ) λαμβανέτω, ἢ ἐκείνῳ (βασιλεὺς) τὸ παλαιόν. ὁ μὲν γὰρ στρατιωτικὰ μόνα διέπει, πόλεμον δὲ εἰρήνην ἀναδιδεγμένῳ εἰς φυλακὴν σωμάτων, ὁ δὲ τὴν εἰς θεὸν ἱερωσύνην, σῶμα κρὶ ψυχῇ παραιτέμενῳ κινδύνων. ὅσῳ τοίνυν ψυχὴ σώματος κρείττων, τοσούτῳ ἱε- ρωσύνη βασιλείας. Denique; ἀλλὰ τὸν ἐπίσκο- πον ςέγεν ὀφείλετε ὡς πατέρα, φοβεῖσθαι ὡς βασιλέα, τιμᾶν ὡς Κύριον. Episcopos exi- stimate vestros principes, hos putate REGES, his quasi Regibus vectiga- lia offerte, &c. Ut enim Samuel in primo Basileion libro de Rege praecepit populo, & Moyses de sacerdotibus in Levitico; sic nos vobis de Episcopis decernimus, &c. Imo si quid amplius dicendum est, plus hic (Episcopus) accipiat, quam ille (Rex) olim accipiebat. Siquidem ille militaria tantum administrabat, bello & pace ad custodiam corporis susceptis; hic vero sacerdotium ad Dei honorem administrat, ut pericula ab anima & corpore propulseт. Quanto a ergo anima corpore praestantior est, tanto est sacerdotium regno excellentius, &c. Quo- circa Episcopum oportet ut patrem diligere, ut regem metuere, ut Dominum honorare. Tum quot, quantaque Episcopis offeren- da sint edisserunt: Decima ac primitia frumenti, vini, olei, pomorum, lana, fructus, & opera manuum nostrarum. Ac ne cui gravis sit ista de Mosaico fœdere repetita lex,monent a cæteris quidem Moysis vinculis, ac oneribus fuisse nos per Christum liberatos; a pensionibus & tributis sacerdotio solvendis non fuisse liberatos. Idque memorabili sane epicheremate ex illo Christi dicto concludunt; Nisi abundaverit justitia vestra, plus quam scribarum & pharifæorum, non intrabitis in regnum cælorum. Quasi illa, quam Christus in nobis abundare vult, justitia nihil aliud sit, quam τὸ πλέον ἡμῶν προνοιαν ποιεῖσθαι τῶν ἱερέων, & τ' ὀρφανῶν & χηρῶν, majorem, quam habuerunt Pharisæi, sacerdotum, & pupillorum, & viduarum curam habere; hoc est, plura iis largiri, quam Judæi olim suis sacerdotibus ex lege pendebant. Cæterum, cave putes velle istos, ut Christiani suorum bonorum partem aliquam ipsi per se viduis, ac pupillis distribuant. Non hæc ita intelligunt. Nos nostra Episcopis largiri volunt; Episcopos ea pro suo arbitrio in egenos distribuere; οὐ μὴν ἀλλ' ἀλλὰ ἐπιστρέφειν ... ἐπίσκοπον. Te quidem largiri decet; illum vero dispensare, tanquam œconomum, ac Ecclesiastica fastícarum rerum administratorem. Cave tamen ne episcopum ad rationes voces. Denique alibi sacerdotium supra regnum iterum evehunt, ὅσῳ γὰρ (inquiunt a) ἱερωσυνῶν βασιλείας ἀμείνων σὺ ψυχῆς ἔχωσα τ' ἀγῶνα, τοσούτῳ ᾧ βασιλέων ἔχει τ' τιμωείαν ὁ τάλῃ τολμήσας αὐτομάτειν, ἢ περ ὁ τ' βασιλεία. Quantum enim sacerdotium regno praestat, utpote pro anima certans, tanto graviores poenas debet, qui audet vel nutu oculorum huic adversari, quam qui regno. Haec quidem Boviani Apostoli. Christi vero Apostoli plane aliud docent: ut non sit lux à tenebris magis diversa, quam hi ab illis. Illi Episcopum eorum, quibus praeest, regem, dynastam, dominum, herum, Deum denique esse scisecunt: Hi contra exserte negant, Episcopum b dominari suis, aut potestatem in eos exercere instar Principum; Ajunt ἐπισκοπεῖν, ποιμαίνειν, providere, & pascere, non dominari in gregem. Ipsi se, qui Episcopis multo majores erant, profitentur, non fidei Christianorum dominari, sed adjutores gaudii eorum, imo & δὲ λυς servos eorum esse divinę familiae oeconomos, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Illi Ecclesiam Episcopi esse volunt, ut regnum Regis: Hi se, suaque omnia, Ecclesiae esse affirmant; Ecclesiam vero unius Christi. Illi Episcopis vectigalia, ac tributa à Christianis, ftianis, etiam plura, majoraque, quam quæ Regibus à subditis penduntur, deberi, offerriqueque superbe, ac ut verum dicant, impudenter jubent? Hi modestissime docent ex Domini instituto esse a, ut qui Euangelium annunciat, de Euangelio vivat; idque non ut b Principi tributum pendi, sed ut c militi stipendium reddi volunt; quanquam ne hoc quidem ipsi exigunt ἀνεξβως, & summo jure. Tantum gregibus demonstrant, quid æquitas, quid gratitudo ab ipsis hoc loco requirat; ut ii sponte proprioque judicio impulsi, magis quam jussi suas partes exsequantur; nedum ut anxie ac morose (quod isti illiberales, planeque, ut videtur, ad rem suam nimium attenti Ἀιαχωγεῖς faciunt) primitias, decimas, & alia id genus à subditis, sibi pendenda sigillatim indicant. Nisi ergo Christi Apostolos plane penitusque immutatos nobis fingamus, fateri necesse est, eos qui ista vana, tam superba, tamque avara ac sordida præcipiunt, non modo Apostolos non fuisse, sed insuper homines fuisse ab Apostolis diversissimos, & ab eorum ingenio ac moribus, non minoribus spatiis, quam quibus terra à cœlo distat, sejunctos, ac dissitos.
units.tr: ...after God, an earthly god, who ought to enjoy the honour paid by you. For it was of this man and his like that God said, "I have said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." And, "You shall not revile the gods of your people." Let the bishop therefore preside over you, so that, adorned with the dignity of God, by which he lords it over the clergy and rules the whole people. Is that magnificent enough? But hear other things too. They order the laity to honour this blessed monarch of theirs with the most careful veneration and to hold him in awe, and not to break rashly into the secret of such great majesty or disturb his pleasures and cares. "Let them not, they say (a), trouble the ruler lightly, but let them speak through his servants, that is, through the deacons, with whom they may speak more boldly." Let them take care not to bother their prince readily, for rather let them make known what they wish through ministers, that is, through deacons, with whom they may deal more boldly and confidently. I ask you, do these men not seem to be fashioning a king of the old Persians, or of the modern Abyssinians, or some satrap of barbarian arrogance, rather than a Christian bishop? From his threshold they so diligently drive away the whole crowd. They do not allow any of the pious people to come into his presence in person. They think it wrong for anyone to speak with him except through an interpreter and mediator, as if the whole people of God were a plainly profane mob, unworthy of the episcopal divinity and gaze. But lest you be indignant that such honour is paid to mere mannikins, they take care to add the reason for this law, a fine and convenient one, and one that no one would doubt flowed from the mind and mouth of the Apostles: "For it is not possible (they say) to approach the Almighty God except through Christ. Thus let all the laity, whatever they wish, make it plain to the bishop through the deacon, and let them act as he thinks fit, and let them complete their business through him." But who could patiently hear this? That it is wrong for the bishop to meet anyone except through a deacon, just as God cannot be approached except through Christ? As though the deacon were Christ! Yet by this example one could conclude that both the bishop, through whom one approaches, and the deacon, are to be worshipped, since that honour is given to God and to Christ. If these claims please (and they must please, if they are Apostolic), there will be no bishop who is not also a Pope among his own people. But look, in the next passage they all but demand this very worship for their bishops. For they cite the example of Moses, who was called the prophet of Aaron and the god of Pharaoh: (they say, a) "Why do you not consider your intermediaries of the word to be prophets, and honour them as gods?" (Why do you not have interpreters of your message among the Prophets, and worship your bishops as gods?) Then they add those golden and thoroughly Apostolic words (b): "For now your Aaron is the deacon, and your Moses the bishop. For if Moses was called God by the Lord, your bishop has been honoured by you as God, and the deacon as his prophet." Now your Aaron is the deacon, and your Moses the bishop. If Moses was called God by the Lord, your bishop is honoured by you as God, and the deacon as his prophet. Who could now doubt that these were Apostles, who so effortlessly turn deacons into Aarons and bishops into Moses? Nor are their other statements any more sound. For lest you think that bare outward signs of honourable worship are enough for them, see, they order tribute to be paid to their bishops, just as to the princes of the world. "You should regard your bishops (they say, c) as your rulers or kings, and pay them tribute as to kings." Soon after: "As Samuel laid down a law to the people concerning the king in the first book of Kings, and Moses concerning the priests in Leviticus, so we decree to you concerning the bishops." Then a little later: "And if anything more must be added to the argument, let the bishop receive more than the king formerly received. For the king managed only military affairs, undertaking war and peace for the protection of the body; but the bishop manages the priesthood for the honour of God, exposing himself to dangers for the soul and the body. Therefore, as the soul is better than the body, so is the priesthood better than kingship." Finally: "You ought to regard the bishop as a father, to fear him as a king, and to honour him as the Lord." Count your bishops your princes, regard these as kings, offer them tribute as to kings, etc. For just as Samuel in the first book of Kings laid down for the people concerning the king, and Moses concerning the priests in Leviticus, so we decree for you concerning the bishops, etc. Indeed, if anything more is to be said, this man (the bishop) receives more than that man (the king) once did. For the king administered only military affairs, having taken up war and peace for the protection of the body; but the bishop administers the priesthood for the honour of God, that he may ward off dangers from soul and body. Therefore, as the soul is better than the body, so the priesthood is more excellent than kingship, etc. Hence the bishop must be loved as a father, feared as a king, and honoured as the Lord. Then they set out how many and how great the offerings to be made to the bishops are: tithes and firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, fruit, wool, produce, and the labour of our hands. And lest this law, taken again from the Mosaic covenant, seem burdensome to anyone, they warn that we were freed by Christ from the other bonds and burdens of Moses, but not freed from paying pensions and tributes to the priesthood. And they draw this conclusion from that saying of Christ with a memorably sharp argument: Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. As though the righteousness that Christ wishes to abound in us were nothing other than to take a greater care of priests, and of orphans and widows, than the Pharisees had, that is, to give them more than the Jews once paid to their priests by the law. But beware of thinking that these men want Christians to distribute some part of their own goods to widows and orphans by their own hands. They do not understand it that way. They want us to give our goods to the bishops, and the bishops to distribute them to the needy at their own discretion. You ought indeed to give, but he to dispense, as a steward and administrator of the Church's goods. Beware, however, of calling the bishop to account. Finally, elsewhere they again raise the priesthood above the kingdom. "For as the priesthood is better than kingship (they say, a), since it is engaged in the contest for the soul, so much greater is the punishment owed by the man who dares to oppose it, even by a nod of the eyes, than by the man who opposes the kingdom." For as the priesthood surpasses the kingdom, being concerned for the soul, so much graver punishment does he deserve who dares to oppose it, even with a nod of the eyes, than he who opposes the kingdom. These are indeed the words of the Bovine Apostles. But the Apostles of Christ teach something quite different, so that light is no more different from darkness than these men are from those. Those men want their bishop to be the king, ruler, lord, master, and finally God of those over whom he presides. These men, on the contrary, plainly deny that a bishop should lord it over his people, or exercise power over them like princes. They say that a bishop should oversee, shepherd, provide, and feed, not lord it over the flock. These men themselves, who were far greater than bishops, declare that they do not lord it over the faith of Christians, but are helpers of their joy, and indeed servants of them, the stewards of the divine household and dispensers of the mysteries of God. Those men want the bishop to be the Church, as the king is the kingdom; these men affirm that they and all they have belong to the Church, and the Church to Christ alone. Those men order that tribute and taxes be owed by Christians to the bishops, even more and greater than what subjects pay to kings, and insolently, and, to tell the truth, shamelessly, demand that they be offered? These men teach most modestly that by the Lord's appointment he who proclaims the gospel should live from the gospel; and they want this to be paid not as tribute owed to a prince but as wages given to a soldier, although even this they do not exact strictly and by the full right of law. They show the flocks only what fairness and gratitude require of them in this matter, so that they, moved by their own free judgment, may perform their duties willingly rather than under orders; far less do these men anxiously and peevishly (as those illiberal men, plainly too attentive, as it seems, to their own affairs, do) list separately firstfruits, tithes, and the like of that kind, to be paid to them by their subjects. Unless, therefore, we imagine the Apostles of Christ to have been utterly and completely changed, we must confess that those who prescribe these vain, so proud, so greedy and sordid things were not only not Apostles, but were men wholly different from the Apostles, and separated and removed from their character and manners by no smaller a distance than that by which earth is distant from heaven.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Arg. X. à decimarum solutione, quam Constitutiones fidelibus omnibus præcipiunt. Arg. XI. ab ea, quam statuunt sacri cælibatus lege plane mira. Arg. XII. à festorum & jejuniorum, quæ præcipiunt, novitate.
units.tr: Argument X: from the payment of tithes, which the Constitutions enjoin on all the faithful. Argument XI: from the law of clerical celibacy, which is strikingly strange. Argument XII: from the novelty of the feasts and fasts they prescribe.

units.la: HUc etiam pertinet, quod Διαταγὰς γεὶς decimas, ac primitias suis Episcopis debere, ac solvere volunt, quod ab omni Apostolorum, quæ in novo Testamento extat, doctrina alienum est; & non obscure cum ea Pauli disputatione pugnat, quæ in priori ad Corinthios epistola capite nono habetur, Cum enim eo loco hoc agat Apostolus, ut ministris Euangelii aliquam laborum mercedem ab iis, quos docent, deberi probet; profecto decimarum ac primitiarum præceptum, quod unum totam hanc causam liquido conficiebat, non erat tali loco omissurus, si id ad Christi ministros pertinere putaslet; sed, quod fecerunt οἱ Διαταγεῖς, id statim ac in primis attulisset; quod tamen nequaquam fecit. Tantum rationibus ab ipsa naturæ æquitate, divinisque ac humanis huic æquitati consentaneis institutis pugnat; quæ quidem concludunt, æquum esse, ut qui gregem Christi verbo & opera sua
units.tr: To this also belongs the fact that the Constitutions [Διαταγὰς] want tithes and firstfruits to be owed and paid to their bishops. This is foreign to the whole teaching of the Apostles contained in the New Testament, and it clearly clashes with Paul's argument in the ninth chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians. For there the Apostle is arguing that a reward for labour is due to the ministers of the gospel from those whom they teach. If he had thought the precept of tithes and firstfruits applied to Christ's ministers, he would not have omitted it in that place. It alone settled the whole question, so he would have brought it forward first, as the Constitutions did. Yet he did nothing of the kind. Their claim also clashes with the reasons drawn from natural equity itself, and from divine and human institutions consistent with that equity, which conclude that it is fair for those who feed Christ's flock by word and work

units.la: Diaiagæ: in margine sua pascunt, ii victum a grege accipiant, (quod nemo negat) non probant (quod volunt oi Διαλαξεις) primitias ac decimas esse illis solvendas. Verum de re ipsa nunc quidem non disputo. Aliud est quod urgeo. Nam decimas ac primitias, qui deberi Ecclesiæ ministris contendunt, eas illi ex jure non Mosaico, sed naturali repetunt. Nostri Διαθηκεις aliter. Concedunt, eas esse jugi Mosaici, ac, ut loquuntur, τ επιτασκτων σκιαμων, ascitorum vinculorum partem, quibus prior olim populus illigatus, ac implicitus tenebatur. Tum sumunt, à cæteris quidem jugi illius Mosaici, id est legis cæremonialis, partibus fuisse nos liberatos, ab hac parte, id est à primitiarum decimarumque debito exsolutos fuisse negant. Disserta sunt hæc eorum verba a; χρη δε υμας γινωσκειν, οτι ει ε ερρυσαθ υμας Κυριος της βασιλειας της επιτασσομενων σκιας, και εξηγαγεν υμας εις αναπαυσιν, μηκετι ιδασας υμας θυειν λογα ζωα περι αμαρτιων και καθαρσιας και αποπομπαιων ε λυτρων συνεχων, και τεσσαρων επαρτηεινων, ε δηπως ε της εισφορων υμας ελευθερωσεν, ων οφειλετε τοις ιερευσι. Atque hoc vos scire oportet, quod tametsi vos Dominus à servitute ascitorum vinculorum liberarit, indeque in refrigerium vos eduxerit, qui non permisit amplius brutas pecudes pro peccatis immolare, liberarit, inquam ab
units.tr: [Marginal note: the Constitutions] feed their flock, and that they should receive their living from the flock (which no one denies). But they do not prove (which is what the Constitutions want) that firstfruits and tithes are to be paid to them. I am not disputing that matter just now, however. What I press is something else. Those who insist that tithes and firstfruits are owed to the Church's ministers claim them by natural law, not by Mosaic law. The Constitutions [Διαθῆκαι] take a different line. They concede that tithes belong to the Mosaic yoke, which they call [τῶν ἐπιτασσομένων σκιῶν], part of the bonds of shadows imposed on the former people, by which that people was once bound and entangled. They then hold that we were freed from the other parts of that Mosaic yoke, that is, the ceremonial law, but they deny that we were released from this part, that is, from the debt of firstfruits and tithes. Their words are these: [χρὴ δὲ ὑμᾶς γινώσκειν, ὅτι εἰ ἐρρύσατο ὑμᾶς Κύριος ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῶν ἐπιτασσομένων σκιῶν, καὶ ἐξήγαγεν ὑμᾶς εἰς ἀνάπαυσιν, μηκέτι ἐάσας ὑμᾶς θύειν ἄλογα ζῷα περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν καὶ καθαρσίας καὶ ἀποπομπαίων ἢ λυτρῶν συνεχῶν καὶ τεσσαρακοστῶν ἐπαρτηρήσεων, οὐδέπω ὑμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσεν ἀπὸ τῶν εἰσφορῶν, ὧν ὀφείλετε τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν]. You ought to know that although the Lord has freed you from the servitude of the imposed shadows, and has led you out into rest, no longer allowing you to offer irrational beasts for sins, purifications, scapegoats, and continual and fortieth-day rites, he has not yet freed you, I say, from the contributions which you owe to the priests.

units.la: a l. 2. c. 35. in. ab emundationibus, à vistimis emissariis, à lavationibus assiduis, ab aspersionibus, non-dum tamen & à pensionibus vos liberavit, quas debetis sacerdotibus. Pensiones intelli-gunt a τ ἀπαρχῶν, τ sτιάτων, & τ ἀφαιρεμά- τῶν, de quibus proxime dixerat. Hoc vero quod isti statuunt, non fuisse nos Christi beneficio ab omni cæremonialis legis parte liberatos, ab Apostolorum sensu, ac doctrina alienum est; qui nos ab omni hoc jugo plane, penitusque liberatos fuisse locis sexcentis docent; ut vel ex una Pauli ad Galatas epistola sole meridiano clarius patet.
units.tr: [Note a: book 2, chapter 35, beginning.] "...from cleansings, from scapegoats, from continual washings, from sprinklings; but he has not yet freed you from the payments which you owe to the priests." By "payments" they mean [τῶν ἀπαρχῶν, τῶν σιτιάτων, καὶ τῶν ἀφαιρεμάτων], firstfruits, tithes and offerings, which he had mentioned just before. But what they lay down, that we were not freed by Christ's benefit from every part of the ceremonial law, is foreign to the sense and teaching of the Apostles. They teach in six hundred places that we were freed completely and thoroughly from this whole yoke, and this is clearer than the noonday sun even from Paul's epistle to the Galatians alone.

units.la: Jam quæ ab istis fertur de clericorum conjugio lex, plane mira, ac singularis est; & ab Apostolorū, & ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ dogmate ac sensu pariter aliena. Nam Episcopos, presbyteros, & diaconos, postquam ii ordinati sunt, uxorem ducere vetant; quod est præter Apostolicam doctrinam; eosdem, si jam tum cum ordinarentur, mariti essent, uxoribus uti non prohibent; quod cum dogmate ac usu Romano pugnat. Subdiaconis vero, quos ὑπηρέτας & hic & alibi vocant, & cantoribus, & lectoribus, & janitoribus, etiam postquam in clerum asciti sunt, uxores ducere permittunt, quod etiam à Romanis moribus abhorret. Quod vero & istis perinde ac majorum ordinum clericis, nuptias iterare, viduasve, aut ancillas, cillas, aut repudiatas ducere vetant, id inquam & ab omnibus veris Apostolorum libris ac sententiis, & a novi Testamenti, sub quo degimus, genio plane est alienum. Mirifica autem haec iistorum lex ita habet a; μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀνδρὸς (episcopis, presbyteris, ac diaconis) μὴ χειροτονίαν ἀγάμοις ὄντων ἔτι ὅπῃ γάμον ἐρχέσθαι, ἢ γεγαμηκόσιν ἑτέρας συμπλέκεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἀρκεῖσθαι ἢ ἐχούσας ἤλθον ὅπῃ τὴν χειροτονίαν. ὑπηρέτης δὲ ἐξ ψαλμωδῆς ἐξ ἀναγνώστας ἐξ πυλωρὸς ἐξ αὐλῆς μονογάμους εἶναι κελεύομεν. εἰ δὲ πρὸ γάμου εἰς κλῆρον παρελθώσιν, ἐπιτρέπομεν αὐτοῖς γαμεῖν, εἰγε πρὸς τοῦτο πρόθεσιν ἔχουσιν, ἵνα μὴ ἁμαρτάνοντες κολάσεως λύχωσιν. ὡσαύτως ὁ τὸν κλήρῳ κελεύομεν, ἢ ἐταίραν, ἢ οἰκέτην, ἢ χήραν, ἐξ ἐμβεβλημένου λαμβάνειν, ὡς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει.
units.tr: Now the law they bring forward about clerical marriage is strikingly strange and peculiar, and it is as alien to the doctrine and practice of the Roman Church as it is to the Apostles. Bishops, presbyters and deacons, they forbid to take a wife after they have been ordained, which goes beyond apostolic teaching. If they were already married when they were ordained, they do not forbid them to use their wives, which conflicts with Roman doctrine and practice. But to subdeacons (whom they call ὑπηρέτας both here and elsewhere), to cantors, readers and doorkeepers, they permit marriage even after they have been admitted to the clergy, which is also abhorrent to Roman custom. That they forbid these men, just as they forbid clergy of the higher orders, to remarry, or to take widows, maidservants, or divorced women, is plainly alien to all the genuine books and opinions of the Apostles, and to the spirit of the New Testament under which we live. The wondrous law of these men reads as follows: a; [μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀνδρὸς (ἐπισκόπους, πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους) μετὰ χειροτονίαν ἀγάμοις ὄντων ἔτι ὅπως γάμον ἔρχεσθαι, ἢ γεγαμηκόσιν ἑτέρας συμπλέκεσθαι, ἀλλ' ἀρκεῖσθαι ἢ ἔχουσας ἦλθον ὅτε τὴν χειροτονίαν. ὑπηρέτης δὲ ἐξ ψαλμωδῶν ἐξ ἀναγνωστῶν ἐξ πυλωρῶν ἐξ αὐλῆς μονογάμους εἶναι κελεύομεν. εἰ δὲ πρὸ γάμου εἰς κλῆρον παρέλθωσιν, ἐπιτρέπομεν αὐτοῖς γαμεῖν, εἴγε πρὸς τοῦτο πρόθεσιν ἔχουσιν, ἵνα μὴ ἁμαρτάνοντες κολάσεως τύχωσιν. ὡσαύτως ὁ τὸν κλῆρον κελεύομεν, ἢ ἑταίραν, ἢ οἰκέτιν, ἢ χήραν, ἐξ ἐμβεβλημένου λαμβάνειν, ὡς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει.] It is not permitted for a bishop, presbyter or deacon, once ordained while unmarried, to enter marriage again, or, if he has married, to join himself to another woman; he must be content with the wife he had when he came to ordination. We order that subdeacons, psalmists, readers, doorkeepers and porters be men of one marriage. If they enter the clergy before marriage, we permit them to marry, provided they intend it, so that they do not incur punishment by sinning. Likewise we order that the clergy not take as a wife a courtesan, a servant, or a widow, as the law also says.

units.la: Post ordinationem si uxores non habent (episcopi, presbyteri, diaconi) praecipimus, ut non liceat amplius ducere; aut si antea duxerant, aliis conjungi, sed ea, quam cum habent, ad ordinationem venerunt, contentos esse. Ministros, cantores, lectores & janitores ipsos quoque monogamos esse praecipimus; sin vero ante conjugium ad clerum accesserint, permittimus eis, ut uxores ducant, si eis cordi est; ne, cum deliquerint, panas pendant. Iubemus vero, ut nullus ex clero in matrimonium accipiat amicam, vel viduam, vel repudiatam, sicut etiam etiam lex sancit. Itaque sive tu Apostolos eadem cum Romanis hodiernis, quod ipsi volunt, de clericorum statu sensisse ac statuisse dixeris; sive nobiscum, quod verius est, & ipsorum veris ac indubitatis monumentis maxime consentaneum; illud quidem hinc certum est, istos, qui aliter quam utrique instituimus, decernunt, Διαζυγίας, Apostolos nequaquam esse.
units.tr: After ordination, if (bishops, presbyters, deacons) do not have wives, we order that they may not marry again; or if they had married before, that they must not join with others, but be content with the wife they had when they came to ordination. We order that ministers, cantors, readers and doorkeepers likewise be men of one marriage; but if they enter the clergy before marriage, we permit them to marry, if they are so inclined, lest they incur punishment when they sin. We order that no one of the clergy take a mistress, or a widow, or a divorced woman in marriage, as the law also decrees. So whether you say that the Apostles thought and laid down about the status of clergy what the Romans of today want, or whether, as is truer and far more consistent with their genuine and undoubted writings, that they thought as we do, it is certain that those who decree otherwise than both of us do are not the Apostles.

units.la: Sed & quae de festis, esurialibusque diebus οἱ Διαλαλεῖς passim praecipiunt, ea quoq; manifestum est cum Apostolorum dogmate pugnare. Paulus enim deserte haec decernit; Nemo vos (inquit) judicet, in cibo, aut in potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut neomenia, aut sabbatorum. At isti Διαζυγεῖς in his omnibus Christianos judicant: multa festa in aeternum indicunt, tantaque cum religione observari jubent, ut qui die Dominico jejunaverit, eum ἔνοχον ἁμαρτίας, reum peccati esse a pronuncient. Quin & veluti Paulo in os adversantes, ipsum illud sabbatum, cujus nos jugo ille Apostolus exsolverat, isti exserte summa cura a nobis coli, atque observari imperant. Nam & sabbato feriari nos ab omni opere jubent; & hoc quidem loco tanta est eorum impudentia, ut ipsum illum Paulum, qui hanc sabbati religionem aperte sustulerat, eandem figentem at constituentem inducant;
units.tr: But the things the Constitutions lay down everywhere about feasts and fasting days are also plainly at odds with the doctrine of the Apostles. Paul decides this expressly: Let no one judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days. But those Constitutions [Διαζυγεῖς] judge Christians in all these matters. They appoint many feasts for ever, and order them observed with such religion that whoever fasts on the Lord's day they declare guilty of sin [ἔνοχον ἁμαρτίας]. Indeed, as if setting themselves against Paul to his face, they expressly order us to keep and observe with the utmost care that very sabbath from whose yoke that Apostle had freed us. They command us to rest from all work on the sabbath too. Here their impudence is so great that they bring in that very Paul, who had plainly abolished this sabbath observance, as setting it up again and establishing it.

b Book 5, ch. 12; ch. 17; ch. 19; ch. 20; book 8, ch. 33.

units.la: Ἐγὼ a Πέτρος & ἐγὼ Παῦλος διδασκάλια ...
units.tr: "I, Peter, and I, Paul, [lay down] teachings..." [Ἐγὼ Πέτρος καὶ ἐγὼ Παῦλος διδασκαλία ...]

units.la: Ἐργαζέσθωσαν οἱ ἕξ ἡμέρας. σαββά- τον ὁ κυριακὸν σχολάζέτωσαν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ διὰ τὸ διδασκαλίαν τῆς εὐσεβείας. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ σάββατον εἴπομεν δημιουργίας λόγον ἔχειν τῷ ὁ Κυριακῷ ἀναστάσεως. Ego Petrus & ego Paulus constituimus, ut servi quinque diebus operentur; Sabbato vero & Dominica quiescant, vel feriantur in Ecclesia propter doctrinam pietatis. Sabbatum enim diximus creationis habere rationem; Dominicam resurrectionis. Ideoque & Sabbato, quod eum diem festum esse velint, jejunare nos vetant; excepto uno illo Sabbato, quod Pascha ἀναστάσιμον antecedit ; πᾶν μὲν τοι σάββατον ἄνευ τῆς ἑνὸς, & πᾶσαν κυριακὴν, ἐπιτελοῦντες σωούσης, εὐφραίνεσθε.
units.tr: I, Peter, and I, Paul, lay down that servants shall work six days; but on the Sabbath and the Lord's day they shall rest, or keep holiday, in the church for the teaching of piety. For we said that the Sabbath has the reason of creation, and the Lord's day of resurrection. [Ἐργαζέσθωσαν οἱ ἕξ ἡμέρας· σάββατον δὲ καὶ κυριακὸν σχολαζέτωσαν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ διὰ τὴν διδασκαλίαν τῆς εὐσεβείας. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ σάββατον εἴπομεν δημιουργίας λόγον ἔχειν, τὴν δὲ κυριακὴν ἀναστάσεως.] Therefore they forbid us to fast on the Sabbath either, which they want to be a festival, except for that one Sabbath which comes before the Pascha of the Resurrection. Rejoice on every Sabbath except that one, and on every Lord's day, by celebrating the assemblies. [πᾶν μὲν τοι σάββατον ἄνευ τῆς ἑνὸς, καὶ πᾶσαν κυριακὴν, ἐπιτελοῦντες σύναξεις, εὐφραίνεσθε.]

units.la: Omni autem Sabbato, praeter unum, & cunctis Dominicis diebus, conventus Ecclesiasticos celebrantes, laetitia fruimini. Et mox, εὐφραίνεσθαι γὰρ δεῖ ἐν αὐταῖς (ἡμέραις) ἀλλ᾽ ὃ πνεύσασθαι. Latari enim his diebus oportet, non jejunare. Sic etiam alibi cum unius Sabbati antepaschalis jejunium praecepisset, ὅτι δεῖ (inquiunt c) τὸ σάββατον νηστεύειν, καὶ πανσῶν δημιουργίας ὑπάρχον, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι ἐκεῖνο μόνον χρὴ νηστεύειν, τὸ δημιουργὸν ἐν αὐτῷ ἔτι ὑπὸ γλῶ ὄντῳ. Non quidem quod jejunandum sit Sabbato, quod est requies Domini ab opere creationis, sed quia illo illo tantum jejunandum est, quo ipse author mundi erat adhuc sub terra. Denique & alibi disertissimè a, τὸ σάββατον μὲν τοι κῃ̈ τῷ κυριακῷ ἑορτάζιτε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν δημιυργίας ἐςιν ὑπόμνημα, ἡ δ᾽ ἀναςάσεως. ἐν δ᾽ μόνον σάββατον ἡμῖν φυλακτήιον ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ ἑ- νιαυτῷ, τὸ τῆς Κυρίε ταφῆς, ὅπερ νηςεύειν ᾿ροσσήκει, ἀλλ᾽ ὐχ ἑορτάζειν. Sabbatum tamen & Dominicum festos dies agitate, quod ille quidem dies recordatio est fabricationis mundi, hic vero resurrectionis. Vnum vero tantummodo sabbatum nobis toto anno observandum est, Sabbatum scilicet sepultura Christi, quo quidem jejunare deceat, non autem celebrare festum.
units.tr: Celebrating church assemblies on every Sabbath except one, and on all the Lord's days, you should enjoy gladness. And soon after: "For it is necessary to rejoice on these days, but not to fast" [εὐφραίνεσθαι γὰρ δεῖ ἐν αὐταῖς ἡμέραις, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ νηστεύειν]. For it is fitting to be glad on these days, not to fast. So also elsewhere, when he had ordered a fast on the one Sabbath before Easter, he says: "It is not that the Sabbath must be fasted, which is the Lord's rest from the work of creation, but only that day must be fasted on on which the Maker of the world was still under the earth." Then again, quite plainly, elsewhere: Keep the Sabbath and the Lord's day as feast days, since the one is a memorial of creation and the other of resurrection. Only one Sabbath is to be observed by us throughout the whole year, namely the Sabbath of the Lord's burial, on which it is fitting to fast, not to keep a feast.

units.la: Caeterorum festorum, quae illi plurima indicunt, eadem ratio est. Nam & magnam hebdomadem (id est Paschalem) & proximam, quae Pascha sequitur, totas, & Ascensionis Dominicae diem, & Pentecosten, & Natalem Christi diem, & Epiphaniam, & consecratos Apostolorum, & Stephani, caeterorumque Martyrum passionibus dies, quiete, & otio coli praecipiunt {b} τῷ μεγάλῳ ἑβδομάδα πᾶσαν ἐ τῷ μετ᾽ αὐτῷ ἀργείτωσαν οἱ δῆλοι, &c. τῷ ἀνάληψιν ἀργείτωσαν. τῷ δὲ γενεθλίων ἑορτῷ ἀργείτωσαν, &c. Tota magna hebdomade & proxima sequenti quiescunto, &c. Die assumptionis quiescunto. In Pentecoste quiescunto. efcunto. In die festo Natalis quiescunto. Istas vero leges quis non intelligit adversa fronte cum veris Apostolorum decretis pugnare? qui, & (quod nuper diximus) vetant, nos de diebus festis judicari, hoc est, ob eos vel servatos, vel neglectos, vel laudari, vel damnari? & totum hoc dierum discrimen in medio relinquunt; Alius quidem (inquit Paulus) aestimat diem pra die; alius autem peraque aestimat quemvis diem. Unusquisque in suo sensu abundet.
units.tr: The same reasoning applies to the other feasts, of which they prescribe a great many. For they order that the whole Great Week (that is, Passion Week) and the week that follows it, and the day of the Lord's Ascension, and Pentecost, and the day of Christ's birth, and Epiphany, and the days of the consecration of the Apostles, and of the sufferings of Stephen and the other martyrs, be kept with rest and leisure: [τῷ μεγάλῳ ἑβδομάδα πᾶσαν ... ἀργείτωσαν, &c.; τῷ ἀνάληψιν ἀργείτωσαν; τῷ δὲ γενεθλίων ἑορτῷ ἀργείτωσαν, &c.] Let them rest through the whole Great Week and the following one, etc. Let them rest on the day of the Ascension. Let them rest at Pentecost. Let them rest on the feast day of the Nativity. But who does not see that these laws clash head-on with the true decrees of the Apostles? Those decrees (as we said just now) forbid us to be judged concerning feast days, that is, to be praised or condemned for observing or neglecting them, and they leave the whole distinction of days open. One man, says Paul, esteems one day above another; another esteems every day alike. Let each abound in his own mind.

units.la: Iam quod certos dies iidem seponunt, & his quidem jejunandum, illis non jejunandum, arcte & aeterna, atque inviolabili lege sanciunt, sic ut qui vel illis non jejunet, vel his jejunet, peccati reus sit, id inquam totum a veris Apostolis alienum est; qui jejunium quidem in genere & sermonibus & exemplis suis commendant; certos & statos dies jejuniis nusquam vel addicunt, vel eximunt; ut nulla per eos religio esse debeat vel his jejunare, vel illis prandere. Quinimo exserte pronunciat Paulus non esse regnum Dei, esca & potum, sed justitiam, & pacem & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto: ut in hoc argumento valeat, quod idem in alio haud dissimili dixit; nos neque si manducaverimus, abundaturos, neque si non manducaverimus, defecturos. Cum hoc vero & indubitato Apostolorum dogmate equidem non video, qui conciliari possint illæ tam multæ de perpetuis certorum dierum, aut jejuniis, aut non jejuniis, leges. Illi enim, & hebdomadam quidem antepaschalem , & quadragesimam , adhæc unam post Pentecosten hebdomadam , & quartam sextamque cujusvis hebdomadis ferias ab omnibus Christianis jejunari legein perpetuum lata præcipiunt. Altera vero ex parte tum Sabbatum, tum dominicam diem, & omnes quinquaginta à Pascha ad Pentecosten dies , adhæc Natalis Dominici diem, & cætera, quæ nuper recensuimus, ab istis constituta festa , ac denique secundam & quintam cujusque hebdomadis ferias (nisi forte tota hebdomade jejunium continuetur) hos, inquam, omnes dies jejunio funestari vetant; & siquis uno ex iis jejunarit, eum deliquisse, piaculumque commeritum pronunciant .
