units.tr: That these same men set apart certain days, on some of which fasting is required and on others forbidden, and enact this with a strict, eternal and inviolable law, so that whoever fasts on the former or does not fast on the latter is guilty of sin: all this, I say, is alien to the true Apostles. They commend fasting in general, both in their words and by their examples, but nowhere do they bind or release us to particular fixed days, so that there should be no religious obligation either to fast on these or to feast on those. Indeed Paul plainly declares that the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, and in another, not dissimilar, passage he said the same thing: if we eat we shall not abound, and if we do not eat we shall not be lacking. I cannot see how those many laws about perpetual fasting or not fasting on certain fixed days can be reconciled with this clear and undoubted doctrine of the Apostles. For these men prescribe as a perpetual law that the week before Easter, and Lent, and in addition one week after Pentecost, and the fourth and sixth days of every week, be fasted by all Christians. On the other hand they forbid all these days to be made sad by fasting: the Sabbath, the Lord's day, all fifty days from Easter to Pentecost, the day of the Lord's Nativity and the other feasts recently listed as instituted by them, and finally the second and fifth days of every week (unless perhaps fasting is continued through the whole week). And if anyone fasts on any one of these, they declare him to have sinned and to have incurred a penalty.

units.la: Ἐνοχος ἁμαρτίας ἔσται ὁ τῆ Κυριακῇ νηστεύων ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεως ὄσαν, ἢ τῇ Πεντηκοστῇ, ἢ ὅλως ἡμέραν ἑορτῆς Κυρίου καταφρῶν.
units.tr: He who fasts on the Lord's day, the day of the resurrection, or on Pentecost, or generally despises a day of the Lord's feast, shall be guilty of sin. [Ἔνοχος ἁμαρτίας ἔσται ὁ τῇ Κυριακῇ νηστεύων ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεως οὖσαν, ἢ τῇ Πεντηκοστῇ, ἢ ὅλως ἡμέραν ἑορτῆς Κυρίου καταφρονῶν.]

units.la: Reus peccati erit, qui dominico die jejunaverit, cum sit dies resurrectionis, aut qui Pentecosten, aut denique ullum diem Domini festum in mæstitia egerit. Mitto rei ipsius absurditatem, atque ineptiam; mitto pleraque harum Legum ab ipsa Ecclesia Romana pro sua libidine vel retenta, vel spreta. Hoc unum dico, nihil minus istos esse, quam Christi Apostolos, qui omnem fere totius anni diem vel jejunii moerori, vel prandii laetitiae addicunt, ac mancipant; cum Apostoli plane contra doceant,nullum omnino esse non ab utraque illa religione solutum ac liberum; ut nobis quolibet per eorum disciplinam liceat, pro rerum ac personarum, quibuscum versamur, ratione, vel jejunare, vel prandere, vel operari, vel quiescere.
units.tr: He will be guilty of sin who fasts on the Lord's day, since it is the day of resurrection, or who spends Pentecost, or indeed any feast day of the Lord, in mourning. I pass over the absurdity and silliness of the thing itself, and I pass over the fact that the Roman Church itself has kept or rejected many of these laws as it pleased. I say only this: these men are nothing less than Apostles of Christ, who assign almost every day of the whole year either to the mourning of fasting or to the joy of feasting. The Apostles, on the contrary, plainly teach that there is no day at all that is not released and free from both of those observances, so that under their discipline we may, according to the circumstances of the things and persons with whom we have to do, either fast or feast, work or rest.

units.la: Qua in parte id quoque Apostolicam doctrinam aperte pulsat, quod sciscunt oi Διάδαγεις de antepaschalis hebdomadis diegta: ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἓν τῷ πάσχα νηστεύετε, ἀρχόμενοι ἀπὸ δεύτερας μέχρι τῆς παρασκευῆς, καὶ σαββάτῳ, ἐξ ἡμέρας μόνῳ χρώμενοι ἀρτῳ, καὶ ἁλί, ἀ λαχάνοις, καὶ ποτῷ ὕδατι. οἶνος ἢ κρέατων ἀπέχεσθε ἐν ἰδίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ ἡμέραι γὰρ εἰσὶ πένθους, ἀλλ' οὐχ ἑορτῆς.
units.tr: In this respect the Didascalia also openly contradicts the Apostolic doctrine, when it lays down the rule about the days of the week before Easter: [ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐν τῷ πάσχα νηστεύετε, ἀρχόμενοι ἀπὸ δευτέρας μέχρι τῆς παρασκευῆς, καὶ σαββάτῳ, ἐξ ἡμέρας μόνῳ χρώμενοι ἄρτῳ καὶ ἁλί, καὶ λαχάνοις, καὶ ποτῷ ὕδατι. οἶνος ἢ κρέατα ἀπέχεσθε ἐν ἰδίᾳ ἡμέρᾳ· ἡμέραι γάρ εἰσι πένθους, ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ ἑορτῆς.] That is: "Fast on the days of the Passover, beginning from Monday until Friday and on the Sabbath, living on bread, salt, vegetables and water alone for one day. Abstain from wine and meat on those days, for they are days of mourning, not of feast."

units.la: Jejunate igitur diebus Paschae, incipientes a secunda feria usque ad sextam, & sabbatum, sex diebus pane tantum, sale, oleribus, & aqua mensa adhibitis. Abstinete his diebus vino & carne. Dies enim hi non festi, sed luctus sunt. Hoc quidem si vere Apostolicum decretum est, nemo hodie (nisi apud Abyssinos fortasse, aut apud superstitiosos Graeculos) ex Apostolica disciplina vivit. Romana quidem Ecclesia, taetricam istam ac severam Xerophagiam phagiam à nullo suorum exigit; & vinum, & maris ac fluviorum copias omnibus bona mater indulget. Sed absit, ut ista Montani inventa, Apostolorum fuisse putemus, qui salvis modo sobrietatis ac castimoniæ Christianæ rationibus nobis semel in totum macellum admissis omni cibo potuque impune cum gratiarum actione, uti fruique licere non semel decreverunt.
units.tr: Fast therefore on the days of Passover, beginning from the second day until the sixth, and on the Sabbath, taking only bread, salt, vegetables and water as food. Abstain from wine and meat on these days, for these days are not festal but days of mourning. If this really is an Apostolic decree, then no one today lives by Apostolic discipline, except perhaps among the Abyssinians or the superstitious Greeklings. The Roman Church certainly demands no such grim and severe xerophagy from any of its members, and the good mother indulges all of them with wine and with the abundance of sea and river fish. But far be it from us to think that these inventions of Montanus were the work of the Apostles, who, provided only the rules of Christian sobriety and chastity are kept, once and for all admitted us to the whole meat market and decreed that we may freely eat and drink of all food, with thanksgiving, and that it is permitted to use and enjoy it.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAP. XII.

units.la: Arg. XIII. quod Constitutiones publicanos simpliciter damnant; Et ex natura jure uxorem adulteram necessario dimittendam putant. Arg. XIV. Constitutiones de sacrificiorum lege olim à Deo lata male philosophantur, & Moysi quadam falso ac temere affingunt.
units.tr: Arg. XIII. That the Constitutions simply condemn tax-collectors; and that by the nature of the case an adulterous wife must necessarily be dismissed. Arg. XIV. That the Constitutions, philosophizing badly, misrepresent the law of sacrifices once given by God and rashly attribute certain false things to Moses.

units.la: PRÆTEREA id etiam ab Apostolica doctrina discedit, quod Boviani Δισλυγεῖς publicanos simpliciter ab Ecclesiæ communione rejiciunt; Vitabis quoq; (inquiunt a, Episcopo præcipientes) deceptores, & Rhetores injuriam defendentes, idolorum artifices, fures, injustos, publicanos, pondera & mensuras fraudantes, militem calumniatorem, &c. Aliter nostri Apostoli, apud quos Joannes Baptistes publicanos quidem monet, ne quid amplius, quam quod iis conconstitutum est, exigant a; caeterum si id praestent, minime eos a baptismo repellit. Est enim ipsum per se publicani munus (ut omnes fatentur) honestum, & in omni republica necessarium; solae sordes ac rapinae hominum, qui id exercent, iniquae ac fugiendae sunt. Id (ut suspicor) Turrianus vidit; suosque ideo Διαξυγίας cautius loqui facit, quam suos Bovius; & publicanos, non, ut apud hunc, omnes & simpliciter, sed injustos duntaxat, excommunicare. Sic enim habet hic locus apud Turrianum; παρὰ τὰ ὀρθῶς ... ὁ ἡμῖν βασιλεύς, &c. ἐξ ἀλλήλων, ἡμῖν τελῶναι ἀδικοι; Vitabis etiam falsarios, &c. fures, & publicanos injustos. An autem haec, ita ut exhibet, in manuscriptis codicibus invenerit, an vero, cum eadem, quae Bovius, invenisset, ipse in suorum Διαξ-γίων gratiam, ita immutarit, novit Deus. Ego qui codices non vidi, nihil habeo quod in alterutram partem pro certo dicam. Illud quidem quod eodem loco in utriusque (id est, tam Turriani, quam Bovii) editione τὸν δῆμον eodem numero habent, quo φορέα, simpliciterque adeo hominem excommunicant, id & ab Apostolorum doctrina (qui nullius, quantumvis infimi status, aut loci hominem reiiciunt, modo fidelem) & ab ipsa Ecclesiae Romanae praxi alienum videtur.
units.tr: Besides, this also departs from apostolic doctrine: the Bovians, or Diazygians [Διαζυγεῖς], simply reject tax-collectors from the communion of the Church. You shall also avoid deceivers, and rhetoricians who defend wrong, makers of idols, thieves, unjust men, tax-collectors, those who cheat with weights and measures, the soldier who calumniates, etc. Our Apostles, however, take a different line. Among them John the Baptist warns tax-collectors not to exact anything more than what has been appointed for them, but if they do that, he does not at all exclude them from baptism. For the office of tax-collector is in itself honourable (as everyone admits) and necessary in every commonwealth; only the greed and robbery of the men who carry it out are wrong and to be shunned. I suspect Turrianus saw this. That is why he makes his Diazygians speak more cautiously than Bovius does, and excommunicates tax-collectors not as a whole and without qualification, as Bovius does, but only unjust ones. For this passage in Turrianus reads: beside what is right ... our king, etc. ... from one another, unjust tax-collectors for us [παρὰ τὰ ὀρθῶς ... ὁ ἡμῖν βασιλεύς, &c. ἐξ ἀλλήλων, ἡμῖν τελῶναι ἀδικοι]; you shall also avoid forgers, etc., thieves, and unjust tax-collectors. Whether he found this in the manuscripts as he gives it, or whether, having found the same text as Bovius, he changed it thus to favour his own Diazygians, God knows. I have not seen the manuscripts, so I have nothing certain to say either way. But this much seems foreign both to apostolic doctrine (which rejects no one of whatever rank or station, provided he is a believer) and to the actual practice of the Roman Church: in the same passage, in the edition of both Turrianus and Bovius, they put the people on the same footing as the bearer, and so excommunicate a man simply, without qualification.

units.la: a Luc. 3. 13. Neque illud sane video, qui verum, adeoque Apostolicum esse possit, quod iidem violatæ legis naturalis eum virum damnant, qui uxore adulterio corruptam non dimittit: ὡσαύτως ὁ κατέχων τὴν διαφθαρεῖσαν, φύσεως δίκης παράνομος, Similiter, qui corruptam retinet, natura legem ac institutum violat. Is quidem ejus dimittendæ à lege concesso jure non utitur, fateor. Ut ideo legem violare dicatur, nulla ratio est. Aliud enim est legem violare; quod facit παράνομος, aliud id, quod tibi per leges licet, non usurpare; quod etiam boni interdum faciunt.
units.tr: a Luc. 3. 13. Nor indeed do I see how it can be true, and therefore Apostolic, that the same men condemn as a violator of the natural law the man who does not put away a wife corrupted by adultery. Likewise, he who keeps the corrupted one is, by the justice of nature, a transgressor of the law [ὡσαύτως ὁ κατέχων τὴν διαφθαρεῖσαν, φύσεως δίκης παράνομος]. Similarly, he who keeps the corrupted woman violates nature's law and ordinance. I admit that he does not use the right of dismissal that the law grants him. But there is no reason to say that he therefore violates the law. For it is one thing to violate the law, which is what the lawless man [παράνομος] does, and another not to make use of what the law allows you, which good men also sometimes do.

units.la: Sed & Photius testatur suo jam sæculo (id est nono adulto) Constitutionum operi objectam fuisse ὅτι τὴν ἐν συλλεγομένῳ ὕβρεις τινὰς ἐπαφίησιν, quod quadam contumeliosa contra Deuteronomium emittat; sed ea ait facillimum esse dissolvere, ῥᾳστον διαλύσασθαι. His autem verbis ne putes accusatos fuisse Διαθηγέας, quasi librum Deuteronomii ex Scripturarum canone ejicerent, aut aliquid contumeliosum in eam Scripturæ partem jacerent. Non est ista Photii, non Διαθηγῶν mens. Neque item Judaïcas deuteroses, id est, traditiones à veteribus Magistris disciplinæ Mosaicæ adjectas Deuteronomii nomine intellexerunt, vel Διαθηγεῖς, vel eorum criminatores. Planum num est ex multis Constitutionum locis Deuteronomium, sive Δευτερώσεις illis in hoc argumento nihil aliud esse quam eam legis Mosaicae partem, quae ritus, & sacrificia, omnemque caerimoniarum umbratilium disciplinam continet. Legem enim duplicem statuunt; unam quae in decalogo tradita, ipsiusque Dei ore e monte Sina pronunciata verae sanctitatis, justitiaeque praecepta explicat; alteram, quae est de carnalibus sacrificiis, purificationibusque & lotionibus, & aliis id genus Mosaicis ritibus. Illam νόμον φυσικὸν, legem naturalem a; hanc νόμον ἐπισταντὸν, legem ascitam, vel τὰ ἀφ' Δευτερώσεως ἐπισταντ..., ea quae per deuterosim ascita sunt b: illam interdum νόμον simpliciter, hanc Δευτερω-σιν c, Illam νόμον πιστῶν, legem fidelium, hanc Δεσμὰ ἀπίστων c, vincula infidelium, & alibi Δεσμὰ μάταια d, vana vincula; Illam denique alibi νόμον, hanc Δεσμὰ e simpliciter vocant. Qua in nomenclatura omnino abusi videntur Δευτερώσεως vocabulo; quod & olim habuit, & nunc etiam habet hunc sensum, ut significet Judaicas traditiones non scriptas, quas Hebraei מִשְׁנָיוֹת misnajot vocant. Unde & Δευτεραὶ חכמים Tannaim vocantur earum vel authores, vel doctores. Qui deuterosim pro lege caerimoniali dixerit, neminem praeter istos Διαδοχίας, authorem memini. Sed vocem quidem mittamus. Illi ergo statuunt Christum priorem quidem illam legem adeo non sustulisse, ut etiam impleverit, ac perfecerit; posteriorem vero, si nontotam, maxima certe ex parte abolevisse, ἐκ ἀνελῶν τ φυσικὸν νόμον, ἀλλὰ πα-ραὶς τὰ δῆ. τῆς ἀντιτρωσεως ἐπισαγεῖ, εἰ μὴ ἐπ-αντᾶ. Legem quidem naturalem nequaquam sustulit, illa vero, tametsi non omnia, abrogavit, quae fuerant per deuterosim ascita. Quibus & ista similia sunt, quae initio ejusdem capitis occurrunt, Χριστὸς τὸν νόμον κυρώσας ἐπλήρωσε, τὰ ἐπισαγκτὰ πα-ρειλεν, εἰ γὰρ μὴ πάντα, ἀλλά τὰ βαρύ-τερα, τ μὴ βεβαιώσας, τὰ ὁ παύσας. Christus legem & ratam habuit, & implevit: ascita vero sustulit, tametsi non omnia, ea tamen quae graviora erant; illam confirmans, haec vero abrogans. Eadem non semel alibi repetunt c; in quibus nihil aliud ego quidem reprehenderim, nisi id quod tam affirmate statuunt non fuisse omnes Mosaicae legis caerimonias à Christo nostro abrogatas; quod (ut supra diximus) recta cum Apostolis pugnat. Sed istos sane suarum decimarum ac primitiarum amor coegit partem aliquam veterum rituum ab interitu excipere; quos si omnes à Christo abrogatos una cum Apostolis dicerent, illorum lorum sibi redituum jacturam faciendam vi-debant; quibus novorum suorum Regum, suorum in terris Deorum (hoc est Episcoporum) rem ac dignitatem fulciendam firmandamque censuerunt. Nam cum decimarum primitiarumque religionis ministris pendendarum ritum ad Mosaicas caerimonias pertinere, & liqueat, & vero ipsi confiteantur, illas profecto tueri, ac conservare haud aliter potuerunt, quam id, quod affirmant veri Apostoli, negando, omnibus omnino Moysis caerimoniis solutum, liberatumque esse Christi populum. Sed reliqua eorum τ theoremata persequamur. Statuunt ergo illi decalogum quidem, quo lex (ut loquuntur) naturalis continetur, primo ac per se datum fuisse Israelitis: illa vero hoc est caerimonialia, non per se, sed per accidens & ex occasione tantum fuisse iis imposita ob admissam in vitulo conflatili idololatriam; Deum enim hoc eorum scelere provocatum, cum plane ingratos & beneficiorum immemores videret, tum demum conflrinxisse eos vinculis insolubilibus, & compressione oneris, ac asperitate jugi, jussisseque ut ara fieret, & sacrificia assidue offerrentur, & ciborum genera distinxisse, separationes, purgationes, crebras lotiones, aspersiones, purificationes, variasq; αγνίας ἁγνίας a labore vacationes, instituisse ; ut in his perpetuo occupati presfiq; velut obtorto collo ab idolorum quidem servitute abducerentur, divinorum autem mandatorum vel inviti recordarentur. Hæc est de cærimoniali lege Διαλαγέων sententia; pluribus quidem locis expressa, fuse vero ac perspicue libro sexto operis, capiteque vicesimo explicata. De his ἐπεισακτοῖς ca-piunt a præcepta illa non bona, quæ Deus apud Ezechielem b profitetur se Israelitis dedisse; eodemque referunt c, quod negat apud Hieremiam d Dominus se de verbo holocautomatum & victimarum præcepisse Israelitis, qua die eduxit eos de terra Ægypti. Scio eadem tradere alicubi Chrysostomum e ; & esse aliorum Patrum, quin & ex ipsis Judæis Moysis Majemonidis haud absimilem de cærimoniali νομοθεσία sententiam, quæ nunc quidem persequi nihil necesse est. Illud unum observasse satis est, quicunque cetera fuerint qui hæc ita ut explicavimus docent Διαλεγεῖς, Apostolos certe eos non esse. Primo quidem, quod Apostoli de ritibus & cærimoniis aliud sentiunt. Docet enim non uno in loco Paulus ista cærimonialia non per accidens propter Israelitarum μοχθοποιίαν, sed certo definitoque consilio instituta esse tum ad Christianæ disciplinæ adumbranda mysteria,
units.tr: But Photius also testifies that in his own age (that is, in the full ninth century) it was objected against the work of the Constitutions that in the collection it lets fly certain insults [ὅτι τὴν ἐν συλλεγομένῳ ὕβρεις τινὰς ἐπαφίησιν] against Deuteronomy, and he says that this is very easy to dissolve [ῥᾳστον διαλύσασθαι]. Do not, however, suppose from these words that the Constitutionists [Διαθηγέας] were accused of rejecting the book of Deuteronomy from the canon of Scripture, or of hurling anything insulting at that part of Scripture. This is not Photius's meaning, nor the mind of the Constitutionists [Διαθηγῶν]. Nor did they understand by the Jewish deuteroses, that is, the traditions added to the discipline of Moses by the ancient masters, under the name of Deuteronomy, either the Constitutionists [Διαθηγεῖς] themselves or their accusers. It is clear from many passages of the Constitutions that in this matter Deuteronomy, or the Deuteroseis, means nothing other than that part of the Mosaic law which contains the rites and sacrifices and the whole discipline of the shadowy ceremonies. For they posit a twofold law: one, delivered in the decalogue, and proclaimed by God's own mouth from Mount Sinai, which sets forth the precepts of true holiness and justice; the other, concerning fleshly sacrifices, purifications and washings, and other Mosaic rites of this kind. The former they call the natural law [νόμον φυσικὸν]; the latter the added law [νόμον ἐπισταντὸν], or those things added by deuterosis [ea quae per deuterosim ascita sunt]. Sometimes they call the former simply "law," and the latter "deuterosis." The former they call the law of the faithful [νόμον πιστῶν], the latter the bonds of the unfaithful [Δεσμὰ ἀπίστων], and elsewhere empty bonds [Δεσμὰ μάταια]. Finally, elsewhere they call the former simply "law" and the latter simply "bonds" [Δεσμὰ]. In this nomenclature they seem to have wholly misused the word deuterosis, which both formerly had, and now also has, the sense of signifying the unwritten Jewish traditions that the Hebrews call misnajot [מִשְׁנָיוֹת]. Hence those who handed them down, or their teachers, are called the Deuterai, the Tannaim [חכמים]. I do not recall anyone, apart from these Successors [Διαδοχίας], who used deuterosis for the ceremonial law. But let us leave the terminology aside. They hold, then, that Christ did not so much abolish the former law as fulfil and perfect it; but the latter, if not wholly, at least for the most part, he abolished: [Greek: not abolishing the natural law, but ... the things added by deuterosis, if not all]. He indeed by no means abolished the natural law, but abrogated those things which had been added by deuterosis, though not all of them. Similar to these are the statements at the beginning of the same chapter: [Greek: Christ, confirming the law, fulfilled it; he abrogated the added things, if not all, at least the heavier ones, confirming the one and abolishing the others]. Christ both held the law valid and fulfilled it; but he removed the added things, though not all, yet those that were heavier; confirming the one, abrogating the other. They repeat the same things more than once elsewhere. In these I would find nothing to reprove, except that they so confidently assert that not all the ceremonies of the Mosaic law were abrogated by our Christ, which (as we said above) is directly contrary to the Apostles. But the love of their own tithes and firstfruits certainly compelled them to save some part of the ancient rites from perishing. If they had said that all of them had been abrogated by Christ, together with the Apostles, they saw that they would be making a loss of that revenue for themselves; and they judged that by these they should support and confirm the position and dignity of their new kings, their gods on earth (that is, the bishops). For since both the fact and the truth are that the rite of paying tithes and firstfruits to the ministers of religion belongs to the Mosaic ceremonies, and since they themselves confess this, they could in no way defend and preserve those things except by denying what the true Apostles affirm: that the people of Christ have been wholly released and freed from all the ceremonies of Moses. But let us follow through the rest of their theorems. They hold, then, that the decalogue, in which the so-called natural law is contained, was given to the Israelites first and in itself; but the ceremonial law was imposed on them not in itself, but only by accident and on occasion, because of the idolatry they committed in the molten calf. For God, provoked by this wickedness, seeing that they were plainly ungrateful and forgetful of benefits, at last bound them with indissoluble chains, with the pressure of a burden and the harshness of a yoke; and he commanded that an altar be made and sacrifices be offered continually, and he distinguished kinds of foods, separations, purgations, frequent washings, sprinklings, purifications, and various ritual abstentions from labour [ἁγνίας]; so that, perpetually occupied with these and as though pulled by a twisted neck, they might be drawn away from the servitude of idols, and might unwillingly be reminded of the divine commands. This is the opinion of the Constitutionists about the ceremonial law; it is expressed in many places, but set out at length and clearly in the sixth book of the work and in its twentieth chapter. To these added precepts they refer those "not good precepts" which God, in Ezekiel, professes he gave to the Israelites; and they also refer to them what the Lord, in Jeremiah, denies he commanded the Israelites concerning burnt offerings and victims on the day he led them out of the land of Egypt. I know that Chrysostom also teaches the same thing somewhere, and that there are other Fathers of this view; and even among the Jews, Moses Maimonides holds a not dissimilar opinion about the ceremonial legislation, though there is no need to pursue it now. It is enough to have noted this one thing: whatever else those Constitutionists were who teach these things as we have explained, they were certainly not Apostles. First, because the Apostles think otherwise about rites and ceremonies. For Paul teaches in more than one place that these ceremonial things were instituted not by accident, on account of the Israelites' [μοχθοποιίαν] wrongdoing, but by a certain and defined purpose, both to foreshadow the mysteries of Christian discipline,

units.la: * Cf. note 1 in margin. ria, tum ad populum veluti sub pædagogo ad Christi usque adventum continendum, ac custodiendum. Huc accedit, quod liquido falsum esse deprehenditur, id quod nostri Διαθήκης ponunt; nimirum non fuisse quicquam de sacrificiis & aliis ritibus ante μωσαϊκοποιίαν præceptum, atq; impositum. Nam ut Abelis, Cainique, & Noachi, & Patriarcharum sacrificia, & horum circumcisionem mittam, quæ nemo dixerit sine ullo Dei mandato, sed ex mera εὐαλογίᾳ à Sanctissimis viris factitata; ut de præceptis in ipso decalogo sabbati religione nihil dicam, quam & Paulus, & cum eo omnes veteres Ecclesiæ Christianæ doctores ad cærimonias Mosaicas pertinuisse tradunt; narrat Exodi liber in ipso illo capite, quo publicati decalogi historia continetur, Moysem multo antequam vitulus conflaretur, ita populo Dei nomine præcepisse; Non facietis Deos argenteos, nec Deos aureos facietis vobis. Altare de terra facietis mihi, & offeretis super eo holocausta, & pacifica vestra, oves vestras & boves in omni loco in quo memoria fuerit nominis mei. Veniam ad te, & benedicam tibi. Hic disertissimum habes de sacrificiis quæ ἱερ-ποιήσαντων pars erant præcipua, præceptum, & quidè luculentissima benedictionis promissione sancitum. Ergo falsum est quod οἱ Διατάγεις sibi persuadent, non fuisse ullo praecepto imposita Israëlitis τὰ ἐπεισαντα ante μοχοποιίαν, falsi autem nihil vel docuerunt, vel docere potuerunt Apostoli. Non sunt igitur οἱ Διαλαγεις Apostoli. Illi quidem hanc objectionem viderunt; sed quam solvere non poterant, eam boni viri impudentissimo mendacio eluserunt. Fingunt enim Moysem ista, quae recitavimus, non simpliciter, sed hypothetice, ita dixisse; ἐὰν ὁ ποιήσης μοι Θυσιαστήριον, ἐκ γῆς ποιήσεις μοι αὐτο, καὶ εἰπε (inquiunt) ποίησον, ἀλλ' ἐὰν ποιήσης· ἐκ ἀνάγκης πεπείθηκεν, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ἐπιτρέπειν ἀπε ἐλευθέρα. Non dixit Fac, sed si feceris. Non imposuit necessitatem, sed potestati utpote liberae, permisit. Imo, inquam, non dixit, Si feceris, sed dixit, fac; adeoque non velut rem mediam eorum potestati liberam permisit, sed velut ex praecepto necessariam jussit. Testes sunt omnes Moysis Hebraei, Samaritani, Arabici, Graeci, Latini codices; testes omnes Moysis Chaldaeae, aliique paraphrases. Fateor in sequenti versiculo hypothetice locutum Moysem; Quod si (inquit) altare lapideum feceris mihi, non aedificabis illud de sectis lapidibus. Sed hoc de ratione conficiendi lapidei altaris praeceptum nemo non videt longe aliud ab eo esse, quod recitant οἱ Διατάγεις, de altari simri simpliciter faciendo, & quidem ex terra. Hoc, ut & holocaustorum ac pacificorum oblationem absolutè Moyses præcepit; illud alterum de lapidibus non sectis, non nisi conditionaliter; si ex lapidibus altare facere placuerit, non fiat ex sectis lapidibus. Ergo οἱ Διαθηκαι mendacii manifesti sunt. Viderit Bovius, an sit suorum Apostolorum mentiri, & Moysi, imo Deo aliud quam quod dixit, affingere. Nos Christi Apostolos sapientes ac verecundos, veracissimosq; tum in omnibus, tum praesertim in divinis esse scimus; eoque censemus iis τῶν Διαλαγέων opus tribui sine insigni contumelia non posse. Quod si hæc Photius numeravit inter illas ὑβρεις quas ἐκ τοῦ Δευτερονομίου jecisse arguebantur οἱ Διαθηκαι, ille quidem falso speravit eas facile dissolvi posse.
units.tr: (Cf. the marginal note 1.) ...tia, and also to keep the people, as if under a tutor, until the coming of Christ, and to guard them. Moreover, it is clearly shown to be false what our opponents [nostri Διαθήκης] maintain, namely that nothing about sacrifices and other rites was commanded or imposed before the Mosaic legislation [μωσαϊκοποιίαν]. For I say nothing of the sacrifices of Abel, Cain, Noah and the patriarchs, nor of their circumcision, which no one would call done without any command of God, but which holy men practised from pure piety [εὐαλογίᾳ]. I say nothing of the precepts in the Decalogue itself concerning the observance of the Sabbath, which Paul, and with him all the ancient teachers of the Christian Church, hold to have belonged to the Mosaic ceremonies. The book of Exodus, in the very chapter where the story of the published Decalogue is told, relates that Moses, long before the calf was made, gave this order to the people in God's name: "You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold. You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall offer upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where my name is remembered. I will come to you and bless you." Here you have a most explicit precept concerning sacrifices, which were the principal part of the sacred rites, and it is confirmed by a most plain promise of blessing. Therefore it is false what the Constitutions [οἱ Διατάγεις] persuade themselves, that before the making of the calf nothing was imposed on the Israelites by any precept [τὰ ἐπεισαντα], and the Apostles could neither have taught nor have been able to teach anything false. The Constitutions, then, are not the work of the Apostles. Those men did see this objection, but what they could not solve, they wiped away with the most shameless lie. For they pretend that Moses did not say these words I have quoted simply, but hypothetically, as follows: "If you make me an altar, you shall make it of earth for me," and they say (they claim) "Make it," but "if you make it": he did not command by necessity, but left it to their power, as free, to act as they wished [ἐὰν ὁ ποιήσης μοι Θυσιαστήριον, ἐκ γῆς ποιήσεις μοι αὐτο, καὶ εἰπε ποίησον, ἀλλ' ἐὰν ποιήσης· ἐκ ἀνάγκης πεπείθηκεν, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ἐπιτρέπειν ἀπε ἐλευθέρα]. He did not say, Make it, but if you make it. He did not impose necessity, but left it to the power of a free agent. Nay, I say, he did not say, If you make it, but he said, Make it; and so he did not leave it to their choice, as a thing indifferent and free, but commanded it as something necessary by precept. All the Hebrew, Samaritan, Arabic, Greek and Latin copies of Moses bear witness to this; all the Chaldee paraphrases of Moses, and the others, bear witness too. I grant that in the next verse Moses spoke hypothetically: "If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones." But everyone sees that this precept about the manner of making a stone altar is quite different from what the Constitutions quote, about simply making an altar of earth. This, like the command that Moses gave absolutely for burnt offerings and peace offerings, is an absolute command; that other one about stones not hewn is only conditional: if it pleases you to make an altar of stones, let it not be made of hewn stones. Therefore the Testaments [οἱ Διαθηκαι] are manifestly lying. Let Bovius consider whether it is the habit of his Apostles to lie, and to attribute to Moses, indeed to God, something other than what he said. We know the Apostles of Christ to be wise, modest, and most truthful in all things, and especially in divine matters; and so we judge that the work of the Constitutions cannot be ascribed to them without a notable insult. But if Photius counted these things among those insults [ὑβρεις] which the Testaments were charged with throwing out from Deuteronomy, he certainly hoped in vain that they could be easily dissolved.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: Arg. XV. Quod Constitutionum disciplina in baptismi & Eucharistiæ administratione, item in pœnitentiæ distributione, in Episcopi ætate, in basilicarum structura, synaxeosque ordine, ab Apostolorum ævo aliena est; pleraque diu post eorum mortem inventa.
units.tr: Arg. XV. That the discipline of the Constitutions, in the administration of baptism and the Eucharist, likewise in the distribution of repentance, in the age of the bishop, in the building of churches and the order of the synaxis, is alien to the age of the Apostles; most of it was devised long after their death.

units.la: ATQUE hæc quidem de dogmatis dicta sunto. Nunc ad disciplinas veniamus, in quibus neque minor cernitur horum Διαζάγεων à veris Christi Apostolis, quam in superioribus, diversitas. Primo illud in baptismo occurrit, quod Διαζάγεις ita praecipiant; πρὸ ῆ τὸ βαπτίσματος, νηστεύσατω ὁ βαπτιζόμενος, Iejunet autem ante baptismum is qui baptizatur. Item, ὁ ῆ εἰς Χριστὸν θάνατον μυσάμενος, πρότερον ὀφείλει νηστεῦσαι, ἢ τότε βαπτίσασθαι. Qui vero in mortem Christi baptizatur, debet prius jejunare, deinde baptizari; idq; praepostera sane subtilitate ex eo probant, quod Christus postquam à Ioanne baptizatus est, totos quadraginta dies jejunaverit, ἵνα ὑμῖν ὑπογραμμὸν παραδῷ, ut nobis exemplar praeberet. Quod si verum esset, nemo non videt consequens fore, ut non ante, quod isti sciscunt, sed post baptismum jejunetur. Neque argumentatio, quae inepta, ac ridicula est, scilicet, neque ipsius disciplinae lex, Apostolorum est; quos nusquam legimus ad jejunium, eos quos baptizabant, compulisse. Mitto Aethiopis exemplum, statim à Philippo tinctu; cujus iter caussari quis posset prohibuisse, ne ea maceratione ad baptismum praepararetur. Sed quid Petro facient, qui & tribus hominum millibus baptismum illico sine ulla jejunii mora repraesentavit, & Cornelium cum tota familia, nullo indicto jejunio, simul atque vere credere sensu, ex{a}templo aqua salutari tinxit? Neque aliter Philippus, qui Samaritanos credentes sta-tim baptizavit. Neque vel Lydiæ purpura-riæ vel Philippensis carceris custodi, vel Crispo, & aliis Corinthiis, vel Ioannis discipulis, vel cuiquam alii indictum à Paulo ad baptismum rite suscipiendum jejunium legimus. Nondum ergo Pauli & Apostolorum cæterorum temporibus obtinebat illa multo iis recentior jejunii ad baptismum solennem ac legitimum disciplina, quam hic nostri Διαζηγεῖς, ex sui scilicet sæculi more, constituunt.
units.tr: These things are enough about doctrines. Now let us come to disciplines, in which the difference between these Constitutions and the true Apostles of Christ is no less evident than in the earlier matters. First, this appears in baptism, where the Constitutions prescribe as follows: "Before baptism, let the one being baptized fast" [πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, νηστευσάτω ὁ βαπτιζόμενος]. Likewise: "The one who is baptized into the death of Christ must fast first, and only then be baptized" [ὁ δὲ εἰς Χριστὸν θάνατον βαπτισάμενος, πρότερον ὀφείλει νηστεῦσαι, ἢ τότε βαπτίσασθαι]. Whoever is baptized into the death of Christ ought to fast first, and then be baptized; and they prove this with a truly backward subtlety, from the fact that Christ, after he was baptized by John, fasted for forty whole days, in order to give us an example [ἵνα ὑμῖν ὑπογραμμὸν παραδῷ]. But even if this were true, anyone can see that the consequence would not be that fasting comes before baptism, as they decree, but after it. Nor is the argument itself, which is foolish and ridiculous, a rule of discipline from the Apostles; we never read that the Apostles compelled those they baptized to fast. I say nothing of the Ethiopian, baptized at once by Philip; one could allege that the journey prevented him from being prepared for baptism by such a regimen. But what will they do with Peter, who administered baptism at once, without any delay for fasting, to three thousand people, and who baptized Cornelius with his whole household, with no fast enjoined, as soon as they truly believed in their hearts? Philip did the same, baptizing the Samaritans immediately when they believed. Nor do we read that a fast was enjoined by Paul for the proper reception of baptism on Lydia the seller of purple, or on the jailer at Philippi, or on Crispus and the other Corinthians, or on the disciples of John, or on anyone else. Therefore in the time of Paul and the other Apostles that discipline of a fast before solemn and lawful baptism did not yet prevail; it is much later, and our present Constitutors establish it according to the custom of their own age.

units.la: Neque mihi quisquam persuaserit Apostolorum esse illud horum de baptizato præceptum; ἐχὶ αὐτὸς ἔν σωματοθαυων τῆ Χριστῷ, ἐὰν σωνηγερθεὶς, ςνπίτω· προσευχέσθω ἡ ἀνατολὰς, Ipse igitur commortuus Christo, & confusicitatus stet, Precetur vero versus Orientem. Alibi omnes quoque fideles, qui liturgiæ Ecclesiasticæ adsunt, jubent precari, εἰς ἀνατολὰς κατανοήσαντες, in orientem spectantes. Quasi scilicet Deus, ad quem unum animos nostros in spiritu & veritate convertendos Christus docuit, in Eoa magis, quam in Occidentali, aut Australi cœlorum plaga habitet. Iste vero sunt sequentium sæculorum περιοχὴ, quibus homines ex suo ingenio omnem fere Apostolorum disciplinam obruerunt. Cyrillus à Bo-
units.tr: Nor will anyone persuade me that this precept of theirs about the baptized comes from the Apostles: "Let him therefore, having died with Christ and been buried with him, stand; and let him pray toward the East" [αὐτὸς οὖν συνθανὼν τῷ Χριστῷ, ἐὰν συνηγερθεὶς, στήτω· προσευχέσθω πρὸς ἀνατολάς]. Elsewhere they also order all the faithful who attend the Church's liturgy to pray, "looking toward the East" [εἰς ἀνατολὰς κατανοήσαντες]. As if God, to whom Christ taught that our minds must be turned in spirit and truth, dwelt more in the eastern region of the heavens than in the western or southern! These are the inventions of later centuries, by which men, according to their own disposition, nearly overwhelmed the whole discipline of the Apostles. Cyril of Bo-

units.la: {a} Act. 8. 12. {b} Act. 16. 15. 33. {c} Act. 18. {d} Act. 19. 5. {e} l. 7. c. 46. {f} l. 2. c. 57. p. 380. d. {g} In hunc locum. à Bovio hic laudatus, id quarto, quo vixit, sæculo, inter cæteras baptismi cærimonias obtinuisse fidem facit; ab Apostolis, de quibus quæritur, institutum fuisse, nequaquam probat.
units.tr: {a} Acts 8:12. {b} Acts 16:15, 33. {c} Acts 18. {d} Acts 19:5. {e} Book 7, ch. 46. {f} Book 2, ch. 57, p. 380 d. {g} On this passage: the Bovius cited here shows that in the fourth century, in which he lived, this practice held among the other ceremonies of baptism; he does not at all prove that it was instituted by the Apostles, which is the question at issue.

units.la: Sunt ejusdem furfuris, quæ sequuntur in Eucharistia celebranda disciplinæ. ἐυξά-μεν& (inquiunt oi Διαταγεὶς) καθ' ἑαυτὸν ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἅμα τοῖς ἱερεῦσι, καὶ λαμπρὰν ἐσθῆτα μετενδύς, &c. εἰπάτω. Igitur Episcopus precationem silentio una cum sacerdotibus faciens, & splendidam vestem indutus, &c. dicat. Qui temporum Apostolicorum historiam, & Apostolorum studia, ac mores ex veris didicerit, is haud facile credet, vel ex illius Ecclesiæ disciplina fuisse, ut Episcopus in veste splendida liturgiam faceret, vel id diserte præcipiendum ac jubendum putasse aut curavisse Apostolos. Sed audi grave imprimis, & Apostolica mente dignum decretum; Δύο ὁ διάκονοι ἐξ ἑκατέρων τῶν μερῶν τὸ θυσιαστηρίου κατεχέτωσαν ἐξ ὑμένων λεπτῶν ῥιπίδιον, ἢ πτερῶν ταῶν, ἢ ὀθόνης, ἢ ῥῆμα ἀποσοβείτωσαν τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ἐπιζῳμένων ζῷων, ὅπως ἂν μὴ ἐγχίπτωσιν εἰς τὰ κύπελλα. Duo vero diaconi ex utraque parte altaris teneant flabella ex tenuibus membranis, aut ex pennis pavonis, aut ex linteo, ut parva animalia volitantia abigant, ne in pocula incidant. cidant. Tantum scilicet Apostolis a refua otii fuit, ut istas minutias, vel, fi verum dicendum est, ineptias sibi curandas existi-maverint! Nemo id, nisi ineptus, sibi per-suaderi patietur.
units.tr: Of the same chaff are the disciplines that follow for the celebration of the Eucharist. "Let the high priest pray silently by himself, together with the priests, and, having put on a splendid vestment," etc. [εὐξάσθω καθ' ἑαυτὸν ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἅμα τοῖς ἱερεῦσι, καὶ λαμπρὰν ἐσθῆτα μεταενδύς, εἰπάτω]. Therefore let the bishop, making the prayer in silence together with the priests and dressed in a splendid garment, etc. say [the words]. Anyone who has learned the history of the Apostolic times, and the aims and manners of the Apostles, from the true sources will hardly believe that it was the discipline of that Church for the bishop to celebrate the liturgy in a splendid vestment, or that the Apostles thought or took care to command and enjoin this explicitly. But hear a weighty decree, worthy above all of the Apostolic mind: "Let two deacons, on each side of the altar, hold fans made of thin membranes, or of peacock feathers, or of linen, or of a rag, and drive away the small flying creatures, so that they do not fall into the cups." [Δύο οἱ διάκονοι ἐξ ἑκατέρων τῶν μερῶν τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου κατεχέτωσαν ἐξ ὑμένων λεπτῶν ῥιπίδιον, ἢ πτερῶν ταῶν, ἢ ὀθονίου, ἢ ῥάκους, ἀποσοβείτωσαν τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ἐπιζῴων ζῷα, ὅπως ἂν μὴ ἐγχίπτωσιν εἰς τὰ κύπελλα.] Thus, it seems, the Apostles had so much leisure that they thought these trifles, or, if the truth is to be told, these silly details, worth attending to! No one, unless he is a fool, will allow himself to be persuaded of this. fall in.

units.la: Jam vero & ea catechumenorum, poe-nitentium & energumenorum in diversos ordines diftinction, quae in Constitutionum libris clare, perspicueque passim cernitur, fatis arguit earum scriptorem diu post A-postolorum tempora vixisse. Illam enim disciplinae partem, neque primorum tem-porum conditio ferebat, saevientibus fere persecutionibus, & ordinatos, pacatosque conventus prohibentibus; neq; sane a Ju-ftino, & Irenaeo uspiam memoratam legi-mus. Eam invenit ac inchoavit tertii pri-mo saeculi Ecclesia; expolivit & perfecit quarti industria, cum & Christianorum, & hominum ad fidem ac baptismum acce-dentium auctior multitudo, proindeque & peccantium major quam antea numerus, certum in illis quidem constituendis, his vero tum castigandis, tum purgandis ordi-nem requirerent. Tum coepti Ecclesiae ho-mines in quasdam catechumenorum, poe-nitentium, ac fidelium veluti acies diftri-bui, ex quibus toti coetus constabant. Sin-gulis attributa sua in publicis conventibus loca, ac velut suae in castris sedes; sua seorsim divisa munia ; suaeque quasi destinatæ liturgiæ, & ministrorum operæ. Cumque altissimus esset eorum gradus, quibus Eucharistiam, Sanctissimum Ecclesiasticæ communionis pignus sumere, & veluti ad Domini mensam sedere fas erat, placuit totam hujus mysterii celebrationem, à catechumenorum, & pœnitentium oculis submovere; ut ex ipso arcano major & rei ipsi reverentia, & hominibus cupido ejus potiundæ accederet. Itaque institutum, ut antequam ministri eam sacrorum partem inchoarent, voce Diaconi, catechumeni, ac pœnitentes mature dimitterentur; solis ut vocabant fidelibus manere liceret. Unde illæ posteriorum sæculorum scriptoribus passim usurpatæ catechumenorum & fidelium diversæ missæ. Sed ne ea fortasse auribus catechumeni perciperent, quæ eorum oculis negabantur, hoc quoque secuti sunt eorundem temporum antistites, ut parce de sacris Eucharistiæ & aliorum sacramentorum symbolis coram vulgo loquerentur; &, si quando aliqua cogeret necessitas, res quibusdam verborum ambagibus ac involucris ita occultarent, ut nisi ab initiatis intelligi non possent; ut ex Chrysostomi, Augustini, & aliorum Patrum homiliis constat, qui vel sub finem quarti, vel sub initia quinti sæculi floruerunt. Hæc autem ApoApostolorum, & proximorum discipulorum temporibus non fuisse in usu, & Albaspineus, & Petavius, & caeteri antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae peritissimi viri confitentur, & vero res ipsa clamat. Nam Justino sane omnium fere Scriptorum, quos Ecclesiasticos habemus, vetustissimo nulla religio fuit Eucharistiae mysterium in publico Apologetico edere; quod observat Albaspineus, ex eoque conficit, primi saeculi (christianos sua lubentes mysteria enunciasse. Fateor & primo Apostolorum, & proximo discipulorum Apostolicorum saeculo eruditos institutosque fuisse ab Ecclesiae ministris catechumenos; neque siqui ex fidelibus deliquissent, eos acta poenitentia reconciliatos ab iisdem nego. Sed quod pauci tum erant, prae iis quos sequentia tempora invexerunt, nihil ea (ut sic dicant) pompa, nihil eo ordine, ac modo qui postea servari coepit, tunc quidem opus erat. Atqui nostri (quod dicere caeperant) Διάταξις totum illum novae hujus disciplinae ordinem non minus clare commemorant, ac describunt, quam ipsi quinti saeculi scriptores. Extat apud eos catechumenorum missa, sive liturgia; in qua primum Diaconus ex edito loco clamat, Μήτις τῶν ἀκροωμένων, μήτις τῶν ἀπίστων, Ne quis audientium, nequis infidelium adsit; ubi (quod notannotandum est) duas catechumenorum classes exhibet; infimam audientium, quos una cum infidelibus dimittit; alteram provectiorum, & baptismo propiorum, quos adesse & precari jubet ἐὐξασθε οἱ κατηχούμενοι, Orate catechumeni, Tum capita inclinantibus benedicit Episcopus solenni prece; qua peracta dimittit eos Diaconus , προελθετε οἱ κατηχούμενοι ἐν εἰρήνῃ, Exite catechumeni in pace. Egressis catechumenis Energumenos Diaconus adesse animis, precarique jubet, eosdemque solenni benedictione ab antistite sanctificatos simili formula dimittit, προελθέτε οἱ ἐνεργούμενοι, Exite energumeni. Tum ὑπὲρ τῶν φωτιζομένων id est pro competentibus (qui ultimus & summus erat catechumenorum gradus) precantur; quibus dimissis, compellantur οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ, poenitentes, & post acceptam ab episcopo benedictionem, dimittuntur, Ἀπολύεσθε οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ, Exite, qui in poenitentia estis. Tum post eorum egressum Diaconus, Μὴ τις τῶν μὴ δυναμένων προελθέτω. ὅσοι πιστοὶ, κλίνωμεν γόνυ. Nemo eorum, quibus non licet, exeat. Omnes fideles, flectamus genu. Atque hinc longo ordine peragitur omnis fidelium (hoc est eorum, quibus Eucharistiam sumere licebat) liturgia. Hanc totius liturgiae adeo multiplicem disciplinam, ante tertiu quartumve
units.tr: Now the division of catechumens, penitents and energumens into different orders, which appears clearly and plainly throughout the books of the Constitutions, sufficiently shows that their author lived long after the times of the Apostles. For the condition of the earliest times did not allow that part of the discipline, since persecutions raged nearly everywhere and prevented settled and peaceful assemblies; nor do we read of it anywhere in Justin or Irenaeus. The Church of the third century found and began it; the diligence of the fourth polished and perfected it, when the greater multitude of Christians and of men coming to the faith and to baptism, and therefore also a greater number of sinners than before, required a fixed order, both for arranging the former and for disciplining and purging the latter. Then the men of the Church began to be distributed into certain companies, as it were battle-lines, of catechumens, penitents and faithful, out of which the whole congregations were composed. To each was assigned its own place in the public assemblies, like a fixed seat in a camp; each had its own separate duties, and its own liturgy and service of ministers. And since the rank of those who were permitted to receive the Eucharist, the most holy pledge of ecclesiastical communion, and to sit, as it were, at the Lord's table, was the highest, it was decided to withdraw the whole celebration of this mystery from the eyes of the catechumens and penitents, so that from this very secrecy both greater reverence for the thing itself and a desire among men to obtain it might arise. Hence it was instituted that, before the ministers began that part of the sacred rite, the catechumens and penitents should be dismissed in good time by the voice of the deacon, and that only the faithful, as they were called, might remain. Hence those separate Masses of catechumens and faithful that were commonly mentioned by writers of later centuries. But lest the catechumens perhaps hear with their ears what was denied to their eyes, the bishops of those times also followed this practice: that they spoke sparingly about the sacred symbols of the Eucharist and of the other sacraments before the common people; and, if some necessity ever compelled them, they concealed the matter by such verbal circumlocutions and veils that it could not be understood except by the initiated. This is clear from the homilies of Chrysostom, Augustine and other Fathers, who flourished either at the end of the fourth or at the beginning of the fifth century. That these things were not in use in the times of the Apostles and their immediate disciples, both Albaspinaeus and Petavius, and the other men most skilled in ecclesiastical antiquity, confess; and the thing itself cries out. For Justin, who is perhaps the most ancient of nearly all the writers we have among the ecclesiastical authors, had no scruple about setting out the mystery of the Eucharist in his public Apology; Albaspinaeus observes this and concludes from it that in the first century Christians were willing to make their mysteries known. I grant that in the first and in the next Apostolic century catechumens were taught and instructed by the ministers of the Church, and that I deny not that those of the faithful who had sinned were reconciled by them after the due performance of repentance. But since there were few of them at that time, compared with those whom the following times brought in, there was then no need of that pomp, as they might say, nor of that order and manner which afterwards began to be observed. Yet our authors, as they had begun to say, describe and record that whole new order of discipline no less clearly than the writers of the fifth century themselves. There exists among them the Mass, or liturgy, of the catechumens; in which first the deacon cries from a raised place, "Let none of the hearers, let none of the unbelievers, be present" [Μήτις τῶν ἀκροωμένων, μήτις τῶν ἀπίστων]; where (as must be noted) he presents two classes of catechumens: the lowest, of hearers, whom he dismisses together with the unbelievers; and the other of those more advanced and nearer to baptism, whom he bids to be present and to pray [ἐὐξασθε οἱ κατηχούμενοι, Pray, catechumens]. Then the bishop, with the bowed heads, blesses them with a solemn prayer; when this is finished, the deacon dismisses them [προελθέτε οἱ κατηχούμενοι ἐν εἰρήνῃ, Go forth, catechumens, in peace]. When the catechumens have gone out, the deacon bids the energumens to be present, to pray, and, having been sanctified by the bishop with a solemn blessing, he dismisses them in a like form [προελθέτε οἱ ἐνεργούμενοι, Go forth, energumens]. Then they pray for the enlightened, that is, for the competentes, who were the last and highest rank of catechumens; when these have been dismissed, those in repentance are summoned [οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ, the penitents], and after receiving the blessing from the bishop they are dismissed [Ἀπολύεσθε οἱ ἐν μετανοίᾳ, Go forth, you who are in repentance]. Then, after their going out, the deacon says: [Μὴ τις τῶν μὴ δυναμένων προελθέτω. ὅσοι πιστοί, κλίνωμεν γόνυ.] "Let none of those who are not permitted go out. All the faithful, let us bend the knee." And from this point the whole liturgy of the faithful (that is, of those who were allowed to receive the Eucharist) proceeds in a long order. That this whole manifold discipline of the liturgy was instituted, or came into use, before the third or fourth century is far from the truth; for those who set it out so clearly must necessarily have been other than the Apostles and men of Apostolic times.

units.la: Vide etiam l. 2. c. 57. p. 889. d. tumve fæculum institutam, aut usitatam fuisse, à vero alienum est; ut qui hæc ita enucleate tradunt, eos alios,quam Apostolos, & Apostolicos fuisse necesse sit.
units.tr: That these things were first instituted or came into use only in the third or fourth century is far from the truth. Those who set them out in such detail must therefore have been other than the Apostles, or at least Apostolic men.

units.la: Eodem pertinet, quod fidelem à catechumeno tanto spatio disterminant, ut illum ne domi quidem, cum hoc precari fas putent, πιςτὸς μὴ κατηχημένε μήτε κατ' οἶκον προσεύχεσθω. ὁ γὰρ δίκαιον τ μεμυημένον μὴ τὰ ἀμυήτε συμμολυνῶσθαι. Fidelis ne domi quidem precetur cum catechumeno. Non enim justum est, ut initiatus cum non initiato inquinetur. Quasi vero credibile sit quenquam eorum precibus pollui, qui nondum quidem tincti; cæterum pietatis, & baptismi candidati ad Christi communionem contendunt, & jam spe, voto, atque animo Christiani sunt. Ejusdem abollæ est illud quoque decretum, quo ex sequentium sæculorum usu & more catechumenos nocte Paschali baptizari sciscunt; Illud item, quo statim baptizari sciscunt, siquis imprudens Eucharistiam gustarit; εἰ δέ τις κατ' ἀγνοιαν μεταλάβοι, τοῦτον τάχιον ποιήσαντες μυήσατε, ὅπως μὴ καταφρονήτης ἐξέλθοι. Siquis autem per ignorantiam sumpserit, cum cito elementis fidei imbuite, & baptizate, ne exeat contemptor. Ad hunc quoque censum refero, quod orationem Dominicam ter quotidie à quibusvis fideli-bus
units.tr: To the same purpose belongs the way they separate the believer from the catechumen by so great an interval that they think a believer may not even pray at home with a catechumen: "A believer should not pray at home with a catechumen, for it is not right that one who has been initiated be defiled with one who has not" [πιστὸς μὴ κατηχημένε μήτε κατ' οἶκον προσεύχεσθω. ὁ γὰρ δίκαιον τ μεμυημένον μὴ τὰ ἀμυήτε συμμολυνῶσθαι]. As if anyone could credibly be polluted by the prayers of those who are not yet baptized but who press on in piety and the desire for baptism towards communion with Christ, and who already are Christians in hope, in wish and in mind! Of the same kind is the decree by which, according to the custom and practice of later centuries, they ordain that catechumens be baptized on the Paschal night. Likewise is that by which they ordain that anyone who has unknowingly tasted the Eucharist be baptized at once: "But if anyone has partaken through ignorance, instruct him quickly and baptize him, lest he go out as a despiser" [εἰ δέ τις κατ' ἀγνοιαν μεταλάβοι, τοῦτον τάχιον ποιήσαντες μυήσατε, ὅπως μὴ καταφρονήτης ἐξέλθοι]. To this same category I also refer their command that the Lord's Prayer be recited three times a day by all the faithful.

units.la: a l. 8. c. 34. extr. — Fidelis ne domi quidem precetur cum catechumeno.
units.tr: a Book 8, ch. 34, near the end. A believer should not even pray at home with a catechumen.

units.la: b l. 5. c. 19. init. — Siquis autem per ignorantiam sumpserit.
units.tr: b Book 5, ch. 19, near the beginning. And if anyone has partaken through ignorance.

units.la: c l. 7. c. 26. extr. bus recitari jubent; τὰς δὲ ἡμέρας ὑτὼ προσ-εὐχέσθε, Ad hunc modum ter precamini sin-gulis diebus. Plane ex poetæ illius disciplina, qui ita canit.
units.tr: c Book 7, ch. 26, near the end. ...they order it to be recited; "Pray in this way three times each day" [τὰς δὲ ἡμέρας τρὶς οὕτω προσεύχεσθε]. Clearly this comes from the discipline of that poet who sings thus.

units.la: — Numero Deus impare gaudet.
units.tr: — God delights in an odd number.

units.la: Unde & illud fortassis manavit, quod alibi decernunt Episcopum à tribus Episcopis ordinari; certe non minus quam a duobus, ἐὰν ὁ ὑπὸ ἑνὸς χειροτονηθῇ ἐπίσκοπος, καὶ Δαιρεῖσθω καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ ὁ χειροτονήσας αὐτόν, Sin vero aliquis ab uno Episcopo ordinatus fuerit, tum is, qui ordinatus est, tum is qui ordinavit, deponatur. Ista omnia, ut tertii quartique sæculi moribus nonnulla jam πτειηχγεία, superstitiosulaque morositate infuscatis convenire confiteor; sic à gravitate, simplicitateque Apostolorum procul esse contendo; proindeque frustra iis, falsoque ab impostore afficta.
units.tr: Perhaps from the same source comes also their rule elsewhere that a bishop be ordained by three bishops; at any rate, by not fewer than two: "But if a bishop is ordained by one, then both he and the one who ordained him are to be deposed" [ἐὰν ὁ ὑπὸ ἑνὸς χειροτονηθῇ ἐπίσκοπος, καὶ Δαιρεῖσθω καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ ὁ χειροτονήσας αὐτόν]. I admit that all these things agree with the customs of the third and fourth centuries, which had already begun to be somewhat tainted with superstitious fussiness, but I maintain that they are far removed from the gravity and simplicity of the Apostles, and therefore are vainly and falsely ascribed to them by an impostor.

units.la: Illud vero quis credat quod boni Διάκο-γεῖς affirmant se à Christo audivisse τ' ποι-μένα τ' καθιςάμενον ἐπίσκοπον εἰς τὰς ἐκκλησίας ἐν πάσῃ παροικίᾳ δεῖν ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἐλάττονα ἐτῶν πεντήκοντα. Oportere eum qui pastor est & Episcopus in Ecclesiis totius parœcia constitutus, non minorem natu esse, quam annorum quinquaginta? Hæc vero lex absurdissima est; neque vel Pontificum & sacerdotum Iudaicorum, neque ipsius Christi, cui ea affingitur, exemplo, neque ulla denique ratione nititur.
units.tr: But who could believe what the so-called good deacons affirm, that they heard from Christ that the bishop, who is the shepherd and is set over the churches throughout each parish, must not be younger than fifty years of age [τὸν ποιμένα τὸν καθεζόμενον ἐπίσκοπον εἰς τὰς ἐκκλησίας ἐν πάσῃ παροικίᾳ δεῖν ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἐλάττονα ἐτῶν πεντήκοντα]? This law is utterly absurd. It rests on the example neither of the Jewish priests and high priests, nor of Christ himself, to whom it is falsely attributed, nor on any reason whatever.

units.la: Iam & hoc quoque ab Apostolorum tum ævo tum moribus abhorret, quod alicubi finguntur sane impudenter, de basilicarum & collectarum forma otiose, ac suaviter præcipientes ; ϰαὶ πρῶτον μὲν (inquiunt) ὁ οἰκῷ ἔγω ἐπιμελητής, κατ' ἀνατολὰς τετραμμένῳ, ἐξ ἑκατέρων τῶν μερῶν τὰ πασοφόρια πρὸς ἀνατολὴν, ὡς εοικε νῦν. πείθω ἡ μέσῳ ὁ τῆς ἐπισκόπης ἥρον. παρ' ἑκάτερα ἡ αὐτὴ καθέζεσθω τὸ πρεσβυτέριον, οἱ διάκονοι περιεστάθωσαν ἐυσταλεῖς ᾗ πλέον ἑ-ξῆς.
units.tr: Moreover, this too is wholly out of keeping with the age and manners of the Apostles: in certain places, with considerable effrontery, they invent instructions on the form of the basilicas and assemblies, laying them down at leisure and with a pleasing air. "And first" (they say) "let the steward of the house face east, with the side chambers on either side toward the east, as now seems fitting [καὶ πρῶτον μὲν ὁ οἰκῷ ἔγω ἐπιμελητής, κατ' ἀνατολὰς τετραμμένῳ, ἐξ ἑκατέρων τῶν μερῶν τὰ πασοφόρια πρὸς ἀνατολὴν, ὡς εοικε νῦν]. Let the bishop's throne be placed in the middle, and let the presbytery sit on either side of it; let the deacons stand around, girt up and ready, in their many garments."

units.la: Ac primum quidem sit ædes oblonga, Orientem versus, navi similis; utrinque Pastophoria in Orientem. Sit solium Episcopi in medio positum; & ex utroque ejus latere sedeat presbyterium; adstent Diaconi succincti & expediti sint multa veste.
units.tr: Let the building first be oblong, facing east, like a ship; with side chambers on both sides toward the east. Let the bishop's throne be set in the middle, and on each side of it let the presbytery sit; let the deacons stand by, girt up and ready, in their long garments.

units.la: Hæccine vero sunt Apostolicorum temporum? Atqui ne basilicas quidem, vel ædes sacras ullas tum fuisse crediderim. Certe ex novi instrumenti libris non discimus aliquas fuisse. Illud quidem satis constat, si fuerunt aliquæ, non fuisse tam operosè, quam hæ describuntur, structas, ornatasque; neque, tam accurate dispositas in Ecclesiæ consessu ministeria. Apparet istos, qui tam suaviter hic nugantur, deliciari, & otio atque opibus circumfluere; quod Apostolis postolis & ejusdem memoriæ Christianis minime convenit. Quibus adeo neque id convenit, quod velut in summa pace versantibus Christianis omnibus præcipere finguntur, εἰς τὸ ἐκκλησίαν ἐνδελεχίζειν ὀρ-θῶς ἡμέρας, καὶ μὴ ἀπο-λείπεσθαι τὸ σύνολον, ἀλλὰ συνέρχεσθαι δι-πλῶς, frequentare quotidie Ecclesiam mane & vespere, neque omnino abesse sed assiduè convenire. Hoc vero ne ipsi quidem adversarii, quanquam externis istis multo plus, quam satis est, addicti, ita morose à suis exegerint; etiam in iis locis, ubi & Ecclesiarum, & ministrorum, & cæterorum omnium maxima est copia. Ac de his quidem hæc satis.
units.tr: Are these the customs of the Apostolic times? Indeed, I should not believe that there were any basilicas or sacred buildings at all in that age. Certainly we do not learn from the books of the New Testament that there were any. It is quite clear that if there were any, they were not built and adorned with the elaborate care described here, nor were the ministries arranged in the assembly of the Church with such precision. It appears that these men, who trifle so charmingly here, live in luxury and abound in leisure and wealth, which by no means suits Apostles and Christians of the same period. Nor does it suit them that they pretend to command all Christians, who were living in the greatest peace, to attend the church daily, "and not to be absent at all, but to meet twice" [εἰς τὸ ἐκκλησίαν ἐνδελεχίζειν ὀρθῶς ἡμέρας, καὶ μὴ ἀπολείπεσθαι τὸ σύνολον, ἀλλὰ συνέρχεσθαι διπλῶς], that is, to frequent the church every day, morning and evening, and never to be absent, but to assemble constantly. Yet even their opponents, though much more devoted to external things than is enough, have not so strictly exacted this from their own people, even in those places where there is the greatest abundance of churches, ministers and everything else. But enough on these matters.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Arg. XVI Constitutiones multa continere ab Apostolorum historia abhorrentia: ut 1. quod Stephanum Paulo in Apostolorum collegium allecto adesse viventem faciunt. 2. quod Iacobum Zebedæi diu post suam mortem superfuisse. 3. Cæteros itẽ Apostolos omnes vixisse cum Clemens esset Rom. Episc. cum conditus est N. T. canon, cum dicata sunt iis festa, absurdissime fingant.
units.tr: Argument 16: The Constitutions contain many things that conflict with the history of the Apostles. (1) They make Stephen, who was enrolled among the Apostles after Paul, still alive. (2) They make James the son of Zebedee survive long after his death. (3) They absurdly pretend that all the other Apostles were still alive when Clement was bishop of Rome, when the canon of the New Testament was closed, and when festivals were dedicated to them.

units.la: UNC exsequenda sunt quæ Διαταξεις in historia non uno modo peccant; unde & certissimum & evidentissimum ducitur illius καταλογίας κοπλαςίας argumentum, cujus eos Photius suis jam temporibus accusatos fuisse tradit. Primo ex divino Actuum Apostolicorum libro constat Paulum nonnisi post Stephani Diaconi necem fuisse à Christo ad Apostolatum vocatum; utpote qui & in Dominum furens eorum testium qui Martyrem lapidaverunt, vestimenta servabat; & post id tempus adhuc minas & caedem in discipulos spirans cum litteris Principis sacerdotum Damascum ad vinciendos fideles profectus narratur. Tanta vero est impostoris, qui Constitutiones consarcinavit, impudentia, ut hunc ipsum Stephanum cum Paulo jam Apostolo, & reliquis una congregatum, praeclaras hac διαταξεις scribentem & ad Ecclesias mittentem inducat, his verbis quae jam supra ex octavo libro recitata sunt: Nos igitur duodecim Apostoli Domini, qui una sumus, has vobis {Constitutiones de omni Ecclesiastica forma indicimus, praesente Paulo vase electionis, & coapostolo nostro, & Iacobo Episcopo, ac reliquis Presbyteris, & septem Diaconis: quorum ut notum est, unus fuit Stephanus. Imo tantus est istius fabulatoris stupor, ut hunc ipsum Stephanum, quem nunc una cum ceteris sex Diaconis his condendis Constitutionibus adesse praesentem facit, alibi & quidem in eadem illa octava operis parte, pro Christo, antequam hæ constitutiones fierent, mortuum esse memoret. Ipsos enim illos Apostolos, quibus eum præsentem, unaque cum illis hæc decernentem facit, ita de eo loquentes hoc loco inducit a; ὃς τοῦτ-τον τῷ Θεοσέβειαν τῇ πίστει ἐνεδείξατο, καὶ τῷ εἰς τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἀγα- πῶ, ὡς ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ δῦναι ἐτῷ ψυχῇ πρὸςτῶν ψευδοχτόνων Ἰουδαίων λίθοις βληθείς, qui adeo pietatem erga Deum fide declaravit, & charitatem in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, ut pro eo animam suam daret à Iudæis Christi interfectoribus lapidatione confectus. Fuit-ne unquam ullius scriptoris similis istius cæcitas, ac φρενοβλάβεια, ut aliquem cum iis ipsis præsentem ac loquentem inducat, qui eum mortuum narrent? Sed non in uno Stephano peccavit impostor. Ecce & aliud monstrum non minus horrendum. Iacobum Zebedæi filium Ioannis fratrem ex divina Lucæ authoritate certum est ab Herode gladio interfectum esse, antequam Concilium illud Hierosolymis ab Apostolis habitum esset, cujus historia Actuum capite decimo quinto extat, & quidem annis (ut putat Baronius) sep-tem. Idem tamen ille Iacobus apud nostrum Διαζυγίαν una cum cæteris Apostolis congregatus totam illius Concilii sep-temptem annis post mortem suam habiti histo-riam narrat a; & quod etiam prodigiofius est collegis diu post illius Concilii tempora Constitutiones istas condentibus ac mittentibus adest. Nam Concilii illius Hierofolymitani narrationem exsequuti, Propter quæ (inquiunt b) & ipsi nunc in unum congregati Petrus, & Andreas, Iacobus & Ioannes filii Zebedæi, Philippus & Bartholomæus, Thomas & Matthæus, Iacobus Alphæi, &c. scripsimus vobis Catholicam hanc doctrinam. Huc etiam pertinet quod Jacobum ipsi ἀπόστολος alibi martyrium fecille memorant. Martyres enim in honore apud nos esse præcipiunt; ὡς καὶ παρ' ὑμῖν (inquiunt c) τετίμηνται ὁ μακάριος Ἰάκωβος ὁ ἐπίσκοπος; καὶ ὁ ἅγιος ἡμῶν σωσθάνιον Στέφανος, ut & apud nos honorati sunt beatus Iacobus Episcopus, & sanctus noster condiaconus Stephanus. Sive Alphæi, sive Zebedæi Iacobum intelligant, perinde est. Ambo enim isti diserte affirmantes alibi inducuntur se condendis, mittendisque Constitutionibus adfuisse d; quorum tamen alterum iisdem hic jam martyrio functum fuisse narrant, antequam hæc conderentur, atque mitterentur. Ita inverecundissimo, atque imperitissimo impostori mortuos vivis conjungere, præterita futuraque miscere, mortuos resuscitare, tempora turbare, ludus ac locus fuit.
units.tr: Now the errors of the Diataxeis in matters of history must be examined. From them we draw the most certain and evident proof of that fabrication of falsehood, which Photius tells us was already charged against them in his own time. First, it is clear from the divine Book of the Acts of the Apostles that Paul was called to the apostolate by Christ only after the death of Stephen the deacon. For he was raging against the Lord, and was keeping the clothes of the witnesses who stoned the martyr. And after that time, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples, he is said to have set out for Damascus with letters from the high priest to bind the faithful. Yet such is the impudence of the impostor who stitched together the Constitutions, that he introduces this very Stephen, already gathered with Paul now an Apostle and with the others, writing these excellent Diataxeis and sending them to the Churches, in the words already quoted above from the eighth book: We therefore, the twelve Apostles of the Lord, who are together, declare to you these Constitutions concerning every ecclesiastical form, with Paul, the chosen vessel, present, and our fellow-apostle, and James the bishop, and the rest of the elders, and the seven deacons: of whom, as is known, one was Stephen. Indeed the stupidity of this fabulist is so great that the same Stephen, whom he now makes present together with the other six deacons in drawing up these Constitutions, he elsewhere, and indeed in that same eighth part of the work, mentions as dead for Christ before these constitutions were made. For those same Apostles, in whose presence and with whom he makes him decreeing these things, he introduces speaking of him in this passage a; who so declared his godliness by faith, and his love for our Lord Jesus Christ, that he gave his soul for him, struck down with stones by the Jews, the murderers of Christ. Has any writer ever been so blind and so φρενοβλάβεια, as to introduce someone present and speaking with those very men, who narrate that he is dead? But the impostor did not err only in the case of Stephen. Behold another monster no less horrible. It is certain from the divine authority of Luke that James, the son of Zebedee and brother of John, was killed by the sword of Herod before that council held at Jerusalem by the Apostles, whose history is found in chapter fifteen of the Acts, and indeed (as Baronius thinks) seven years before. Yet that same James, in our author, gathered with the other Apostles, narrates the whole history of that council held seven years after his death a; and what is even more prodigious, he is present with his colleagues, who drew up and sent these Constitutions long after the time of that council. For, following the account of the Council of Jerusalem, they say b: For which reasons we, now gathered together, Peter and Andrew, James and John the sons of Zebedee, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, etc., have written to you this Catholic doctrine. To this also belongs what they elsewhere record, that James, the Apostle, suffered martyrdom. For they order that martyrs be held in honour among us; as (they say c) among you the blessed James the bishop has been honoured, and our holy fellow-deacon Stephen; so also among us are honoured the blessed James the bishop and the holy Stephen. Whether they mean James the son of Alphaeus or the son of Zebedee makes no difference. For both of them are elsewhere introduced as clearly affirming that they were present at drawing up and sending the Constitutions d; yet they narrate that the one was already dead by martyrdom before these were drawn up and sent. Thus to join the dead to the living, to mix the past with the future, to raise the dead, to confound the times, was a game and a field for that most shameless and most ignorant impostor.

units.la: Neque vero in his stetit nebulonis post homines natos impudentissimi protervia. Nam & Apostolis Christi tredecim, adeoque & Iacobo Zebedaei filio, congregatis una adesse facit Clementem civem, & Episcopum Romanum. Ajunt enim se suas istas Constitutiones διαταγὰς ὑπὸ τῶν συλλειτουργῶν Κλήμεντος τὰ πιστότατα καὶ μονώτατα τέκνα ἐν Κυρίῳ, per Clementem comministrum suum, fidelissimumque ac carissimum Filium. Atqui falsum est, & ab omni veri specie alienum Clementem istum ante annum Domini 44. quo Jacobus Zebedaei interfectus est, ad Christi fidem conversum fuisse: nedum ut jam eo tempore Apostolorum συλλειτουργὸς fuerit.
units.tr: Nor did the shameless wantonness of this scoundrel, the most impudent who ever lived, stop there. For he makes Clement, a citizen and bishop of Rome, present and gathered together with the thirteen Apostles of Christ, and so also with James the son of Zebedee. For they say that their Constitutions were sent by Clement, their fellow-minister, their most faithful and beloved son in the Lord. Yet it is false, and far removed from every appearance of truth, that this Clement was converted to the faith of Christ before the year of the Lord 44, when James the son of Zebedee was put to death; much less that at that time he was already a fellow-minister of the Apostles.

units.la: Sed & boni isti, Christi scilicet XIII Apostoli, de libris in Ecclesia legendis ita praecipiunt ; μὴ τοῦτο (inquiunt) αἱ προφῆται αἱ ἡμέτεραι ἀναγινωσκέσθωσαν, καὶ ἐπιστολαὶ Παύλου τοῦ συνεργοῦ ἡμῶν. Tum; Καὶ μὴ ταῦτα διδάσκω, ἢ περισσότερα ἀναγινωσκέτω τὰ Εὐαγγέλια ἃ ἐγὼ Ματθαῖος καὶ Ἰωάννης παρεδώκαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ ἃ οἱ συνεργοὶ Παύλου παρεκάλεσαν ὑμῖν Λουκᾶς καὶ Μάρκος. Deinde Acta nostra legantur. Item Epistolae Pauli cooperarii nostri &c. Postea diaconus, aut presbyter Evangelia angelia legat, qua ego Matthæus & Joannes tradidimus vobis, & qua Pauli cooperarii Marcus & Lucas acceperunt, & reliquerunt vobis. Hæc illi. Jam, ut cætera mittam novi Testamenti hic ab istis memorata volumina, illud quidem constat Evangelium à Joanne, postquam ex infula Patmo, in quam Domitiano imperante relegatus erat, à Nerva Domitiani successore revocatus effet, (hoc est anno Domini 97) scriptum fuisse; ut ex Irenæo, & Athanafio, & Hippolito Portuenfi, & Epiphanio docet Baronius; quo tempore non modo Jacobum Zebedæi Filium, quem sub Claudio, a. D. 42. passum, Paulumque, & Petrum, quos sub Nerone ante a. D. 70. extinctos nemo dubitat, sed & reliquos omnes præter unum Joannem, Apostolos variis mortibus ac locis consumptos fuisse certa fides est. Cum ergo nostri Διαθηκης iis temporibus & vixerint, & congregati fuerint, quibus Joannis Evangelium editum erat, Apostoli vero Iesu Christi diu ante quam illud Evangelium à Ioanne ederetur, omnes præter Ioannem viverein terris desierint; clarum est fieri nequaquam posse, ut Διαθηκης Christi Apostoli vere sint; nisi eosdem homines (quo nihil neque dici, neque fingi abfurdius potest) mortuos simul ac superstites, in terris versantes, & in cœlis regnantes statuas.
units.tr: But these good men, namely the thirteen Apostles of Christ, also give the following instructions about the books to be read in the Church: Let our prophets (they say) be read, and the epistles of Paul our fellow-worker. Then: And let him not teach these things, or let him read more of the Gospels which I, Matthew and John, have handed down to you, and which the fellow-workers of Paul, Luke and Mark, urged upon you. Then let our Acts be read. Likewise the Epistles of Paul our fellow-worker, etc. Afterwards let the deacon or the elder read the Gospels which I, Matthew and John, have delivered to you, and which Mark and Luke, the fellow-workers of Paul, received and left to you. So they. Now, to pass over the other books of the New Testament they mention here, it is certain that the Gospel of John was written after he had been recalled from the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished under Domitian, by Nerva, Domitian's successor (that is, in the year of the Lord 97), as Baronius teaches from Irenaeus, Athanasius, Hippolytus of Portus, and Epiphanius. At that time it is a firm and certain fact that not only James the son of Zebedee, who (no one doubts) suffered under Claudius in the year 42, and Paul and Peter, who were killed under Nero before the year 70, but also all the other Apostles except John had perished by various deaths and in various places. Since, then, our Diathekai lived and gathered at those times when the Gospel of John had been published, while the Apostles of Jesus Christ had all ceased to live on earth, except John, long before that Gospel was published by John, it is clear that the Diathekai cannot in any way be truly the work of the Apostles of Christ, unless we suppose these men (than which nothing more absurd can be said or invented) to be at once dead and surviving, dwelling on earth and reigning in heaven.

units.la: Quid quod nostri Διαταγεὶς eos ipsos, quos se esse impudenter mentiuntur Christi Apostolos, illo tempore quo hæc scribebant, mortuos jam omnes fuisse, haud obscurè sed tantùmnon diserte confitentur? Sic enim de festis præcipientes decernunt; Τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἀγγείτωσαν. διδάσκαλοι γὰρ ὑμῶν εἰς Χριστὸν κατέγνωσαν, καὶ πνεύματι ὑμᾶς ἠξίωσαν. In diebus Apostolorum ferientur, Magistri enim vestri in Christum fuerunt, vosque spiritus sanctiparticipes fecerunt. Dies Apostolorum natalitios intelligit, id est ex Ecclesiæ sensu atque usu, eosdies, quibus Apostoli sæculo quidem ac terris denati sunt, æternitati autem & cælo nati & hinc in beatas sedes traslati: Ergo cum hæc scripta sunt, jam omnes Apostoli ultimum illum eundemque beatissimum vitæ suæ diem obierant; ut nonnisi impudentissimè hæc scripsisse dici queant. Vix refelli meretur frigida Bovii çavillatio, qui hæc ita accipi vult, quasi Apostoli ipsi suis festis viventes multum ante prospexerint, quam mortem obirent. Incredibile non est (inquit) eos suum exitum in Dei gloriam, & fidei propagatione futurum pospicientes voluisse, ut iis diebus fideles in commemorandis eorum certaminibus
units.tr: Moreover, do not our Diataxeis openly, though not quite expressly, admit that those very men whom they falsely claim to be the Apostles of Christ were all already dead at the time when they were writing? For in giving instructions about the festivals they decree thus: Let the days of the Apostles be celebrated. For your teachers were condemned for Christ, and made you worthy of the Holy Spirit. Let the days of the Apostles be kept, for your teachers were for Christ, and they made you partakers of the Holy Spirit. By the days of the Apostles he means their birthdays, that is, in the sense and custom of the Church, those days on which the Apostles were indeed born to the world and to earth, but were born to eternity and heaven, and from here were carried into blessed seats. Therefore, when these things were written, all the Apostles had already completed that last and most blessed day of their life; so that these things can be said to have been written only most shamelessly. Scarcely worth refuting is the cold quibble of Bovius, who wants this to be understood as if the Apostles, while still living, foresaw long before their death that their festivals would be kept. It is not unbelievable (he says) that, looking forward to their departure for the glory of God and the spread of the faith, they wished that on those days the faithful should be occupied in commemorating their struggles

units.la: a L.8.c. 33. extr. Dies Apostolorum, natalitios: fide Ecclesiae. bus, & Christi nomine celebrando essent occupati. Itane vero Bovi? Credibile tibi videtur ut sanctissimi viri, quorum summa erat & modestia & humilitas, sibi ipsis anniversaria festa, vivi mortuis decernerent? Profer vero alicujus sancti, ac martyris exemplum, qui talia sibi ipsi adhuc vivus decerni, ac in honorem sui nominis peragi olim a posteris edixerit? Quod si nullum reperis, si hunc typhum a cujusvis sancti humilitate abhorrere fateri cogeris; patere nos quaesso de Christi Apostolis, omnis humilitatis ac virtutis magistris reverentius sentire, quam ut in eorum mentes talem immodestiam cadere potuisse credamus.
units.tr: a L.8.c. 33. extr. Days of the Apostles, their birthday feasts: on the testimony of the Church. were busy celebrating them in the name of Christ. Is that really so, Bovius? Do you think it credible that these most holy men, whose chief marks were modesty and humility, decreed anniversary feasts for themselves while still alive, to be kept for the dead? Come now, produce one example of any saint or martyr who, while still living, ordered such honours to be decreed for himself and celebrated in his name by posterity. If you find none, and you are forced to admit that such pride is abhorrent to the humility of any saint, then allow us, I beg you, to think of the Apostles of Christ, the masters of all humility and virtue, with more reverence than to believe that such immodesty could have crept into their minds.

units.la: Sed neque tuum hoc commentum tuorum Διαζυγίων verbis convenit. Nam si quod tu iis pro tua libidine affingis, id ipsum in animo habeant; cur id non sunt elocuti? cur mentem his aut aliis consimilibus verbis non aperuerunt, Ii dies, quibus posthac moriemur, sacri posteris funto; neque quisquam iis Christianus opus ullum facito? Nemo enim non videt id, quod tu vis, sic omnino eloquendum fuisse. Tui vero Διαζυγεῖς, Bovi, plane aliter loquuntur: In diebus (inquit) Apostolorum feriantor. Cur dixerunt, non nostris, quod ex tuo sensu rectum erat, sed Apostolorum? Nimirum sentiebant absurdum esse, ut, qui viuunt, iidem dem mortis suæ diem festum indicerent. Eo coactus est impostor abiecta Apostolorum persona, quibus ista non convenint, ipse de iis in tertia, non in prima persona loqui, & Apostolorum dies dicere, quos omnes intelligunt dies quibus Apostoli mortui sunt, significari; non autem dies nostros quos ita ab ipsis Apostolis in propria persona commemoratos nemo intellexisset. Huc accedit, quod verbis sequentibus clarissime significant istos, quorum dies observari volunt, Apostolos, jam esse mortuos. Hi enim (inquiunt) vestri in Christum magistri fuerunt.
