Qui ita loquuntur, vixisse illos, suisseque, hoc est vivere, esseque desiisse, plane liquidoque testantur. Ergo, cum hæc decreta sunt, dubitandum non est quin jam mortui essent Apostoli; quin adeo quivis potius, quam ipsi, hæc decreverint, ac scripserint.
units.tr: But your invention does not agree even with the words of your Diazygia [Διαζυγίων]. For if they had in mind what you, at your whim, attribute to them, why did they not say so? Why did they not make their intention known in words like these: Let the days on which we shall afterwards die be kept holy by posterity, and let no Christian do any work on them? Everyone sees that, if this were what you claim, it should have been expressed in exactly this way. But your Diazygeis [Διαζυγεῖς], Bovius, speak quite differently: In the days (he says) of the Apostles let there be rest. Why did they say of the Apostles, and not of ours, which would have been correct according to your meaning? Clearly they felt it would be absurd for men who are still alive to appoint a feast day for their own death. That is why the impostor, dropping the persona of the Apostles, to whom such words do not belong, speaks of them himself in the third person rather than the first, and says the days of the Apostles, which everyone understands to mean the days on which the Apostles died, and not our days, which no one would have understood as recorded by the Apostles themselves speaking in their own person. Moreover, the words that follow make it very clear that the Apostles whose days they want observed are already dead. For they say: Those men were your teachers in Christ. Those who speak in this way plainly and clearly testify that those men have lived, have been, that is, have lived and ceased to be. Therefore, when these decrees were made, there is no doubt that the Apostles were already dead; indeed, anyone rather than the Apostles themselves must have decreed and written them.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Arg. XVII. Constitutiones Ebionæos & alios hæreticos post Apostolorum mortem exortos, Apostolis coævos, Clementem Petro vivo Romæ sedisse Episcopum, & alia prodigiosa fabulantur.
units.tr: Argument XVII. The Constitutions make the Ebionites and other heretics, who arose after the death of the Apostles, contemporaries of the Apostles. They also make Clement sit as bishop at Rome while Peter was still alive, and they tell other prodigious fables.

units.la: Huc alia accedunt certissima καταλογίας argumenta. Primo enim Ebionæos οἱ Διδαχεῖς mentiuntur suo tempore cæpisse; οἱ ἀφ᾽
units.tr: Other most certain arguments from chronology (καταλογίας) also come into play. First, the Constitutions falsely claim that the Ebionites began in their own time; the Greek reads, "those who [have appeared] in our time" [οἱ ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν].

units.la: ἐφ' ἡμῶν (inquiunt) νῦν φανέντες Ἐβιωναῖοι, τ υἱον τς θεῦ ‹ιλὸν ἄνθρωπον εἶναι βυλόμενοι, ἐξ ἡδονῆς ἀνδρὸς, καὶ συμπλοκῆς Ἰωσὴφ καὶ Μαρίας αὐτὸν γεννῶντες, Qui nunc nostro tempore exorti sunt Ebionai, qui Filium Dei nudum hominem esse volunt, ex voluptate viri, & ex Iosephi ac Mariæ conjunctione eum generantes. Atqui Epiphanius (quod est etiam à Baronio b observatum) initium Ebionæorum cœpisse tradit μετὰ τὴν τῶν Ἱεροσολυμῶν ἁλωσιν, post Hierosolymitanæ urbis excidium, (id est, post annum Domini 70) quo tempore non Iacobum modo, sed & Petrum & Paulum, aliosque aliquot ex Apostolis vivere in terris desiisse, omnes consentiunt. Non sunt ergo Iacobus, Petrus & Paulus nostri Ἀιαθήκης, quique se ipsos esse profitentur, apertissime mentiuntur.
units.tr: The Constitutions say: "The Ebionites who have now appeared in our time, wishing the Son of God to be a mere man, begotten from the pleasure of a man and the union of Joseph and Mary" [ἐφ' ἡμῶν νῦν φανέντες Ἐβιωναῖοι, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον εἶναι βουλόμενοι, ἐξ ἡδονῆς ἀνδρὸς καὶ συμπλοκῆς Ἰωσὴφ καὶ Μαρίας αὐτὸν γεννῶντες]. Yet Epiphanius (as b Baronius also observed) says that the Ebionites began after the capture of Jerusalem [μετὰ τὴν τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων ἅλωσιν], that is, after the year of the Lord 70. At that time, all agree, not only James but also Peter and Paul and several other Apostles had ceased to live on earth. So James, Peter and Paul, who call themselves "ours" and profess to be the Apostles, lie most plainly.

units.la: Tum iidem ajunt se Iacobo in Hierosolymitano episcopatu Symeonem Cleopæ suffecisse; Symeoni Judam Iacobi filium ; Περὶ ὃ τὴν ὑφ' ἡμῶν χειροτονηθέντων ἐπισκόπων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐστιν ἐκ Ἱεροσολύμων Ἰάκωβος ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδελφὸς, ὃ τελευτήσαντος Συμεὼν ὁ τοῦ Κλεόπα· μετ' ὃν τρίτος Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰακώβου. Καισαρείας δὲ τῆς παλαιστίνης πρότερον μὲν Ζακχαῖος ὁ ποτὲ τελώνης, μετὰ ὃν Κορνήλιος, καὶ τρίτος Θεόφιλος. De Episcopis piscopis vero, qui à nobis, dum viximus, ordinati sunt, certiores vos facimus, hos esse; Jacobum Hierosolymorum fratrem Domini, quo mortuo secundus fuit Symeon Cleopa, post hunc tertius Judas Jacobi. (Cæsarea vero Palæstina Zacchæum, qui olim publicanus fuerat, postquem Cornelius; tertiusque Theophilus. Atqui teste Petro Helloixio Jesuita, constat Clementem obiisse ante Symeonem Cleopa, & ante Theophilum Cæsarea Palæstina Episcopum. Ergo crassissimi mendacii manifesti sunt nostri Διαταγεῖς, qui, quo tempore hæc scribunt, superesse adhuc faciunt non modo Clementem , non modo Petrum & Paulum, annis plusquam 25. ante Clementem mortuos; sed & (quod insaniæ ac stultitiæ prodigium est) ipsum quoque illum Jacobum, cujus hoc loco obitum diserte ipsi commemorant.
units.tr: Then the same writers say that Simeon son of Cleopas succeeded James in the bishopric of Jerusalem, and that Judas, the son of James, succeeded Simeon [Περὶ δὲ τῶν ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν χειροτονηθέντων ἐπισκόπων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ἡμῶν γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐστὶν ἐκ Ἱεροσολύμων Ἰάκωβος ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδελφός, οὗ τελευτήσαντος Συμεὼν ὁ τοῦ Κλεόπα, μεθ᾽ ὃν τρίτος Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰακώβου]. Concerning the bishops: "Concerning the bishops who were ordained by us during our lifetime, we inform you that James, the brother of the Lord, is from Jerusalem; when he died, Simeon son of Cleopas succeeded him, and third after him was Judas son of James. At Caesarea in Palestine, first Zacchaeus, who was once a tax collector, then Cornelius, and third Theophilus." But according to Peter Halloix the Jesuit, it is established that Clement died before Simeon Cleopas and before Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. So our Constitutions are manifestly guilty of the grossest lie. At the time they are written, they make not only Clement, and not only Peter and Paul (who died more than twenty-five years before Clement) still alive, but also, a monstrous prodigy of madness and folly, that very James whose death they expressly mention here.

units.la: Ejusdem stuporis est, quod Clementem nostri Διαταγεῖς Petro vivente jam Romanum fuisse Episcopum fingunt; quem, tamen omnes Petro mortuo in illo Episcopatu, & quidem non immediate, sed post Linum omnes, plurimi ac fere omnes, etiam post Linum & Cletum, successisse consentiunt. Sic enim illi Petrum loquentem inducunt; ὁ μέντοι Σίμων ἐμοὶ Πέτρῳ πρῶτον ἐν Καισαρείᾳ τῇ Στρατῶνος συντυχῶν μοι ἐπειϱᾶτο διαςϱέφειν τ λόγον τῆς Θεῦ συμ-παϱόντων μοι τῆς ἱεϱῶν τέκνων Ζακχαῖε τ πο-τε τελῶνε καὶ Βαρνάβα ⸗ καὶ Νικήτα καὶ Ακύλα ἀδελφῶν Κλήμεντ῾ τῆς Ρωμαίων ἐπισκόπε τε καὶ πολίτε. At Simon cum me primum convenisset in Cæsarea Stratonis, &c. conabatur verbum Dei pervertere, cum essent mecum sancti filii Zacchæus olim publicanus, & Barnabas, & Nicetas, & Aquilas fratres Clementis Episcopi & civis Romani. Ex quibus liquet mentiri istum, qui hæc loquitur, dum se Petrum esse ait. Verus enim Petrus Clemente Episcopo in terris neque vixit; neque vivere potuit; cui scilicet mortuo Clemens successisse dicitur.
units.tr: Of the same stupidity is the claim that our Constitutions make Clement already bishop of Rome while Peter was alive. Yet almost all writers agree that Clement held that see after Peter's death, and not immediately, but after Linus; indeed most, almost all, agree that he succeeded after Linus and Cletus. For they introduce Peter speaking thus: "Simon, when he first met me, Peter, in Caesarea of Stratonis, tried to pervert the word of God, while there were with me the holy sons Zacchaeus, once a tax collector, and Barnabas, and Nicetas, and Aquila, brothers of Clement, bishop and citizen of Rome" [ὁ μέντοι Σίμων ἐμοὶ Πέτρῳ πρῶτον ἐν Καισαρείᾳ τῇ Στρατῶνος συντυχὼν ἐπειρᾶτο διαστρέφειν τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, συμπαρόντων μοι τῶν ἱερῶν τέκνων Ζακχαίου τοῦ ποτε τελώνου, καὶ Βαρνάβα, καὶ Νικήτα, καὶ Ἀκύλα ἀδελφῶν, Κλήμεντος τῆς Ῥωμαίων ἐπισκόπου τε καὶ πολίτου]. From these words it is clear that the man who speaks them, while saying he is Peter, is lying. For the true Peter neither lived, nor could have lived, with Clement as bishop on earth, since Clement is said to have succeeded him after his death.

units.la: Præterea boni illi nostri Διδάσκαλοι multos hæreticos memorant post Apostolorum mortem exortos; nominatim autem Marcum, Basilidem, & Saturnilum, εἶτα (inquiunt) καὶ ἕτεροι ἑτέρων κατηρξαν ἐκτόπων δογμάτων, Κηνθ, καὶ Μάρκ, & Μέ-νανδρ, καὶ Βασιλείδης, καὶ Σατυρνῖλ. Deinde alii aliorum dogmatum absurdorum authores extiterunt Cerinthus, Marcus, Menander, Basilides & Saturnilus. Jam vero constat inprimis ex Irenæo omnes istos hæreticos post Clementis Romani, adeoque & post Apostolorum mortem exortos esse. Is enim disertissime scriptum reliquit Clementis epistolam ad Corinthios
units.tr: Moreover, those good teachers of ours mention many heretics who arose after the death of the Apostles, naming in particular Marcus, Basilides and Saturninus: "Then others, one after another, began other absurd doctrines: Cerinthus, Marcus, Menander, Basilides and Saturninus" [εἶτα ἕτεροι ἑτέρων κατῆρξαν ἐκτόπων δογμάτων: Κήνθος, καὶ Μάρκος, καὶ Μένανδρος, καὶ Βασιλείδης, καὶ Σατορνῖλος]. Now it is established, first of all from Irenaeus, that all these heretics arose after Clement of Rome, and therefore after the death of the Apostles. For he wrote most explicitly that Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians

units.la: {a} L. 6. c. 8. in. vetustiorem esse illis haereticis, qui tunc docebant alterum Deum super Demiurgum; quibus verbis, ut omnes vident, significat vixisse Clementem antequam haeretici illi sua venena spargere coepissent. Deinde singillatim quoque demonstrari potest unumquemque haereticorum, quos hic nominatim memorant Διαταγεῖς, post Apostolorum & Clementis fata exortos esse. Nam Basilidem Alexandriae, Saturnilum Antiochiae a Menandro Simonis successore exortos, ἀμφίσημον ὡσαύτως καὶ Δινέφαλον ὀφιώδη τινὰ προσλθόντων δύο αὐτῶν, duarum haeresium authores, alterum in Syria, in Aegypto alterum, sub Adriano, impietatis suae officinam constituisse tradit in quarto historiarum Eusebius; idemque Basilidem iis ipsis temporibus anno Domini 136. in altero, quod Chronicon est, opere exhibet. Sic quoque Theodoretus de utroque verba faciens, ἀμφω ὁ (inquit) ἦσαν Ἀδριανοῦ τῆς Καίσαρος ἐγένοντο, Ambo autem Adriani Caesaris tempore fuerunt. Eusebio vero & Theodoreto multo vetustior Clemens Alexandrinus scribit περὶ τῆς Ἀδριανοῦ τῆς βασιλέως χρόνους γεγονέναι τῆς τὰς αἱρέσεις ἐπινοήσαντας, circa tempora Adriani Imperatoris fuisse, qui haereses excogitarunt, & pervenisse μέχρι γῆς τῆς Αντωνίνῳ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας τῆς ἡλικίας, καθάπερ ὁ Βασιλείδης (inquit) quit) καὶ Γλαυκίαν ἐπιγέφηται διδάσκαλον, ὡς ἀνχύσαν αὐτοῖ, τ Πέτρου ἑρμηνέα, usque ad atatem Antonini natu majoris, sicut Basi-lides (inquit) etiamsi Glauciam sibi adscri-bat magistrum, ut ipsi gloriantur, qui fuit Petri interpres. Antoninus autem Pius (is enim est quem πρεσβύτερον Clemens vocat) Hadriano mortuo v i. Idus Jul. successit a. D. 138. & ad a. D. 161. imperavit. Sub eo ebulliit omnis Gnosticorum colluvies a Saturnilo & Basilide quidem exorta, a Secundo vero, Epiphane, Valentino & aliis diversis modis propagata. Marcum vero, a quo Marcosii, Epiphanius tradit Secundo, Epiphani, Ptolemaeo, & Valentino successisse, proindeque post a. D. 143. (quo erupit Valentinus a) vixisse. Cum ergo neque Joannes, qui Apostolorum ultimus perfuit, neque Clemens Romanus, nisi fortasse unum annum, aut alterum, ultra primum Christianismi saeculum (quod a. D. 100. concluditur) vitam produxerint; fieri non potest, ut vel Apostoli vel Clemens fuerint nostri illi Διάταγεις; quibus, ut liquet, etiam de nomine cogniti fuerunt haeretici post annum secundi saeculi 36. & 43. exorti.
units.tr: {a} Book 6, ch. 8, beginning: is older than those heretics who then taught another God above the Demiurge. By these words, as everyone sees, he means that Clement lived before those heretics began to spread their poisons. Then each of the heretics whom the Constitutions name individually can be shown to have arisen after the deaths of the Apostles and Clement. Eusebius, in the fourth book of his History, reports that Basilides arose at Alexandria, and Saturninus at Antioch, from Menander, Simon's successor; the two were authors of two heresies, one in Syria and the other in Egypt, and under Hadrian they set up the workshop of their impiety. The same Eusebius, in the other work, which is the Chronicle, places Basilides in those very times, in the year of the Lord 136. Theodoret too, speaking of both, says: "Both lived in the time of Hadrian Caesar" [ἀμφω δὲ ... Ἀδριανοῦ τοῦ Καίσαρος ἐγένοντο]. But Clement of Alexandria, much older than Eusebius and Theodoret, writes that those who devised the heresies lived around the time of the Emperor Hadrian, and that they reached down to the age of Antoninus the elder, "just as Basilides, even though he ascribed Glaucias to himself as his teacher, as they boast, who was Peter's interpreter." Antoninus Pius (for he is the one Clement calls "the elder") succeeded Hadrian, who died on 10 July, in the year 138, and reigned until 161. Under him the whole rabble of Gnostics broke out. It arose from Saturninus and Basilides, but was spread in various ways by Secundus, Epiphanes, Valentinus and others. Marcus, from whom the Marcosians took their name, Epiphanius tells us, succeeded Secundus, Epiphanes, Ptolemy and Valentinus, and so lived after the year 143, when Valentinus broke out. Since neither John, who outlived the other Apostles, nor Clement of Rome, except perhaps a year or two, extended life beyond the first century of Christianity (which ends in the year 100), it cannot be that either the Apostles or Clement were the authors of our Constitutions. Clearly the heretics known even by name arose after the years 136 and 143 of the second century.

units.la: Arg. XVIII. Sibyllinos versus diu post Apostolorum mortem editos citant, & Romanos principes, veluti jam Apostolorum temporibus Christianos, mentiuntur Constitutiones. Bovii & Turriani κηρυγμα refellitur ac praecluditur.
units.tr: Argument: The Constitutions cite Sibylline verses that were published long after the Apostles' death, and falsely make the Roman emperors Christians already in the Apostles' own time. The declaration of Bovius and Turrianus is refuted and shut down.

units.la: MDipsum evidenter ex eo probatur, quod iidem Διαθηκης versus ex Sibyllino opere decem ad probandam resurrectionem recitant; eodemque loco ad id quoque argumentum Phoenicis historiam narrant . At carmina illa, quae Sibyllarum nomine circumferuntur, clarum certumque est, Antonino Pio & Marco Aurelio imperantibus (hoc est annis post omnium Apostolorum mortem minimum 38) ficta primum, & in lucem edita fuisse. Itaque Clemens Romanus cujus mors in annum Christi centesimum incidit, affert quidem Phoenicis narrationem ad confirmandum resurrectionis mysterium: Sibyllinorum vero versuum nullus meminit; quod ipsius scilicet aetate nondum natum esset illud Sibyllis postea affictum opus. Quod (ut obiter id quoque nunc dicam) certum argumentum est, neque Clementi agnitas fuisse iistas Apostolorum Constitutiones, nedum ut earum rum ipse vel author, vel gerulus aut lator fuerit; quas si cognitas habuisset, causa dici non potest, cur qui e duobus resurrectionis apud eas allatis argumentis, alterum de phoenice scilicet memoravit, alterum e Sibyllino opere petitium, omiserit.
units.tr: This is clearly proved from the fact that the same Constitutions cite ten verses from the Sibylline work to prove the resurrection, and in the same place they tell the story of the Phoenix for the same argument. It is clear and certain, however, that those poems circulated under the name of the Sibyls were first composed and published while Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius were emperors, that is, at least 38 years after the death of all the Apostles. So Clement of Rome, whose death falls in the hundredth year of Christ, does bring in the story of the Phoenix to confirm the mystery of the resurrection, but he mentions none of the Sibylline verses, evidently because that work, later fabricated under the Sibyls' name, did not yet exist in his day. This (to say it in passing here too) is a sure sign that Clement did not know these Apostolic Constitutions, let alone that he was their author, bearer or publisher. For if he had known them, no reason can be given why he would have mentioned one of the two arguments for the resurrection brought forward in them, the Phoenix, and left out the other, the one taken from the Sibylline work.

units.la: Quid, quod nostri Διαθηκης partim innuunt, partim clare profitentur, Romanos Caesares eo, quo ipsi haec scripserunt, tempore Christianos fuisse? Hoc quidem innuunt, cum episcopum Regibus praesse affirmant iis verbis, quae jam supra recitavimus. Dei (inquiunt a) formam vel exemplar apud homines habet, eo quod omnibus hominibus, sacerdotibus, regibus, magistratibus, &c. praesit. Ista stulte ac ridicule dicta sunt, nisi tu cum dicerentur βασιλεὺς & ἄρχοντες, hoc est, Imperatores & praefecti, sive magistratus fuerint, quibus praeessent episcopi Christiani. Qui enim βασιλέων καὶ ἀρχόντων ἄρχειν, Principibus & praefectis praesse, dici potest, qui nullos, quos regat, habet sibi subjectos neque reges, neque praefectos? Nullos autem reges praefectosve regunt Episcopi nisi Christianos; nullis praesunt, nisi Christianis. Ergo Principes, Praefectosque Christianos fuisse necesse est, cum isti haec ita scripserunt. Sed quid est argumentis opus? Ipsi ita esse, clare diserteque in alia operis parte profitentur;
units.tr: Moreover, our Constitutions partly hint at, and partly openly declare, that the Roman emperors were Christians at the time when they themselves were writing. They hint at it when they say that the bishop presides over kings, in the words we have already quoted above: God (they say) has a form or pattern among men, because he presides over all men, priests, kings, magistrates, etc. These things would be said foolishly and ridiculously, unless, when they were said, the words "kings [βασιλεὺς] and rulers [ἄρχοντες]" meant emperors and prefects, or whatever magistrates the Christian bishops presided over. For how can one who has no kings or prefects under him, whom he might rule, be said to preside over kings and rulers? But bishops rule over no kings or prefects except Christian ones, and they preside over no others than Christians. Therefore the emperors and prefects must have been Christians when these men wrote this. But why do we need arguments? They themselves declare plainly and explicitly that this is so, in another part of the work:

units.la: a) L. c. 21. tentur: ὑ μόνον ϑ (inquiunt a) τ τῆς δικαιο- σύνης νόμον δὲ ἡμῶν ἐπιδεικνυσθαι βάλει (ὁ Θεὸς) ἀλλὰ καὶ δὴ Ῥωμαίων εὐδόκησεν αὐτὸν φαινεσθαι καὶ λάμπειν. Καὶ γὰρ ἔτοι σιγιν- ταντες ἔπι τ Κυέλον, καὶ πολυθείας ἀπέςησαν καὶ ἀδικίας· καὶ τῆς ἀγαθῆς ἀποδέχουϑ, καὶ τῆς φαύλης κολάζεσϑαι. Ἰουδαίως ὁ ὑποφόρως ἔ- χεσι, καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις δικαιώμασιν ἐν ἐωσι κε- χρῆσϑαι.
units.tr: a) Loc. cit. c. 21. "God (they say) wishes not only that the law of righteousness shine through us, but he also was pleased that it should appear and shine through the Romans [οὐ μόνον τῆς δικαιοσύνης νόμον δι᾽ ἡμῶν ἐπιδείκνυσθαι βούλεται ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ Ῥωμαίων εὐδόκησεν αὐτὸν φαίνεσθαι καὶ λάμπειν]. For they, having come to believe in the Lord, have turned away from the multitude of gods and from injustice, and they approve the good and punish the wicked. The Jews, however, they hold as tributaries, and they permit them to use their own laws [Ἰουδαίως ὑποφόρως ἔχουσι, καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις δικαιώμασιν ἐᾶσι χρῆσθαι]."

units.la: Nec vero vult (Deus) ut per nos tantum lex justitia eniteat, sed voluit ut per Romanos quoq; luceret, ac splenderet. Nam & ipsi in Dominum Iesum crediderunt, & a Deorum multitudine, atque ab injustitia abscesserunt, bonosque probant, & pravos puniunt: Iudaeos vero vectigales habent, & eos legibus suis uti non sinunt. Vides istius, qui hoc scripsit, seculo Romanos in Christum credidisse, & eos, quibus vectigales erant Iudaei, a Deorum multitudine abscessisse. Hoc autem factum non est ante annum quarti saeculi 12. cum Imperator Constantinus, Paganico errore abjecto, Christi Domini fidem professus est: quo vero tempore vivebant Apostoli, summa erat Romanorum a Christo aversio, summus in Christianos furor, summus Deorum & idololatriae amor. Ergo qui haec ita scribunt Διαταγεῖς, ii Apostoli non sunt, sed homines minimum 212. annis post Apostolorum mortem viventes. Quo loco non possum sum fatis mirari impostoris, qui hanc fabulam fecit, ingenium, adeo non modo improbus & nequam fuit, qui sua Apostolis affingere ausus est, sed etiam insulsus & vecors, qui quæ fingit, tam crassè tamq; imperite fingit, ea quæ nemo nescit tantis à fe temporum intervallis divisa, impudentia nescio, an stultitia majori,conjungens. Viderunt Διατάξεων amasii, Bovius & Turrianus, rei absurditatem; & pro sua quisque virili, idoli fui turpitudinem fi non purgare, certè occultare atque obumbrare conati sunt. Noli putare (inquit ad posteriorem hunc locum Bovius) universum populum Romanum eo tempore Christi fidem amplexum fuisse: sed cum multi effent in urbe Christiani, jamque religio effet celebris, praesertim fi ab ea (ut legitur) Tiberius non abhorruit; propterea hanc rem extollens Clemens, inquit Romanos, receptâ Christiana pietate, ab idolorum cultu discessisse. Sed iste nobis de more imponit. Nullum est schema, nullus color, quo possit ista Pseudodiatageos de Apostolorum temporibus dicta oratio à mendacio & quidem crassissimo purgari. Multi erant, inquit Bovius, in urbe Christiani. Imo paucissimi erant Christiani præ Paganorum multitudine. Neque quisquam, ut opinor, dubitaverit, multo plures hodie in Gallia, vel in Polonia nia reperiri Protestantes, quam olim Romę Christianos, Apostolorum temporibus. Nemo tamen sanus idcirco dixerit, de tota gente in genere loquens, Gallos vel Polonos à Pontifice Romano defecisse, & Protestantium sacra recepisse. Qui sic loquitur, is vel de universa gente, vel certe de majori ejus parte intelligit. Neque tu mihi Bovi, ullum attuleris exemplum simile huic tuorum Διαταγίων dicto: nisi forte Iesuitæ alicujus, res apud Sinenses aut Japonios suas supra verum apud ignaros audacter extollentis. Sed Iesuitis quidem ex Ignatii sui disciplina non est omnino nefas mentiri; Apostolis ex Magistri sui Euangelio non idem licuit. Quod addis, jam tum in urbe celebrem fuisse religionem, concedo; eo effici ut Romani recte dicantur à Deorum multitudine discessisse, nego. Celebris erat, non quod eam Romanus Princeps, urbanique ac provinciales magistratus, quod significant tui Apostoli, amplecterentur ejerato Gentilismo: sed quod eam potius oppugnarent; quod eam tametsi tanta authoritate, tantisque viribus oppugnatam non vincerent. Certe & nostra (qui Protestantes sive Reformati dicimur) religio Henrici II. temporibus fuit in Gallia celebris. Tune tamen eum sapere putaveris, qui quo tempore Henricus nostros homines iniquis suspiciosuspicionibus exacerbatus ferro flamma-que insectabatur, Gallorum gentem Reformatam dixerit religionem suscepisse? Papae Romani communionem abjecisse? Nugae. Nemo sic loquitur, nisi de iis, quae vel publica Regis authoritate, vel totius gentis consensu fiunt. Quod denique de Tiberio affert Bovius, id & per se futile, & ab hac insuper causa alienum est. Futile est, inquam; Tiberius enim legitur quidem ab eo non abhorruisse, ut Christus inter Divos referretur: a Deorum multitudine, aut ab injustitia ἀπογνώσαι, dissensisse, nunquam legitur; imo hoc suum de Christo placitum legitur neque Senatui persuasisse, neque ut persuaderet, valde laborasse, aut contendisse. Sed & hoc qualecunque de caetero fuerit Tiberii consilium, ad id quidem quod nunc quaeritur, minime pertinet. Haec enim Apostoli, non imperante Tiberio, qui anno Christi 37. e vivis excesserat, sed aliis regnantibus Principibus locuti esse finguntur. Certe hoc ipso loco ajunt, Romanos Judaeis legalem cultum sic eripuisse, ut iis in Hierosolymitano solo aram ponere & sacrificare non licuerit: quae, ut quivis videt, non possunt nisi de iis temporibus accipi, quae Hierosolymitanum excidium consecuta sunt, id est annum Domini 70. Sed quo funditus subruatur Bovii cavillatio, illud praeterea est animadvertendum, quod à clarissimo reverendissimoque Vsserio vere observatum est, non de populo tantum, sed de Principibus Romanis clare, exserteque loqui Διαξῆας. Romanos enim istos, qui in Dominum crediderunt, & à Deorum multitudine discessuerunt, ac desciverunt, eos ipsos ajunt τὰς Ἰουδαίως ὑποφόρως ἔχειν, vectigales ac tributa sibi pensitantes Iudaeos habuisse, tum eos patriis legibus uti non fuisse; quae neque populo, neque ipsis populi inferioribus magistratibus, sed solis Principibus conveniunt.
units.tr: Nor indeed does he wish, that through us alone the law of justice should shine, but he willed that it should also shine and be bright through the Romans. For they too have believed in the Lord Jesus, have turned away from the multitude of gods and from injustice, they approve the good and punish the bad; but they hold the Jews as tributaries and do not allow them to use their own laws. You see that the man who wrote this, in his own century, says that the Romans believed in Christ, and that those over whom the Jews were tributaries had turned away from the multitude of gods. But this did not happen before the fourth century, when the emperor Constantine, having cast off pagan error, professed the faith of Christ the Lord, which was at least the year 312. At the time the Apostles lived, the Romans were utterly averse to Christ, their fury against Christians was at its height, and their love of gods and idolatry was supreme. Therefore those who write these things in the Constitutions are not Apostles, but men living at least 212 years after the Apostles' death. Here I cannot sufficiently wonder at the ingenuity of the impostor who made up this fable: he was not only wicked and worthless, daring to fasten his own inventions on the Apostles, but also foolish and senseless, who invents things so crudely and so unskilfully, joining things that no one doesn't know were separated by such long intervals of time, with a boldness, or a stupidity, I know not which, the greater. The lovers of the Constitutions, Bovius and Turrianus, saw the absurdity of the matter, and each, as far as his strength allowed, tried, if not to purge, at least to conceal and cloud over the ugliness of their idol. Do not think (Bovius says, with reference to this later passage) that the whole Roman people embraced the faith of Christ at that time; but since there were many Christians in the city, and the religion was already well known, especially since Tiberius (as we read) was not averse to it, for this reason Clement, in praising the matter, says that the Romans, having received Christian piety, turned away from the worship of idols. But this man imposes on us as usual. There is no figure of speech, no colour, by which this statement of the Pseudo-Constitutions about the time of the Apostles can be cleared of falsehood, and that a very gross one. There were many, Bovius says, Christians in the city. Indeed there were very few Christians compared with the multitude of pagans. Nor, I think, would anyone doubt that today there are far more Protestants to be found in France or Poland than there once were Christians at Rome in the Apostles' time. Yet no sane person would say, speaking of the whole nation in general, that the French or the Poles have fallen away from the Roman Pontiff and received the Protestant rites. One who speaks in this way means either the whole nation or at least the greater part of it. Nor, Bovius, can you bring me any example similar to this saying of your Constitutions, unless perhaps of some Jesuit, who boldly exalts his affairs among the Chinese or Japanese beyond the truth before people who do not know better. But for the Jesuits, according to the discipline of their Ignatius, it is by no means wrong to lie; the Apostles were not permitted the same by the Gospel of their Master. As for your addition, that the religion was already well known in the city, I grant it; but that from this it follows that the Romans rightly are said to have departed from the multitude of gods, I deny. It was well known, not because the Roman prince, and the city and provincial magistrates, as your Apostles indicate, embraced it with paganism rooted out; but rather because they attacked it, and did not overcome it, although it was attacked with such great authority and such great forces. Certainly our religion too (we who are called Protestants or Reformed) was well known in France in the times of Henry II. Yet would you think sane the man who, at the time when Henry, inflamed by unjust suspicions, was persecuting our people with sword and fire, said that the Reformed nation of the French had embraced the religion, had cast off communion with the Roman Pope? Nonsense. No one speaks this way except of things done either by the public authority of the king or by the consent of the whole nation. Finally, what Bovius brings forward about Tiberius is both trifling in itself and, moreover, foreign to this cause. It is trifling, I say; for Tiberius is indeed read to have not been averse to Christ being counted among the gods; but that he dissented from the multitude of gods, or renounced injustice, is never read; indeed, his opinion about Christ is read to have neither persuaded the Senate, nor to have laboured or contended to persuade it. But whatever else Tiberius's plan may have been, it has no bearing at all on the question now at issue. For these things are said to have been spoken by the Apostles not in the reign of Tiberius, who had departed this life in the year of Christ 37, but under other princes. Indeed, in this very passage they say that the Romans took away the legal worship from the Jews to such an extent that they were not permitted to set up an altar or sacrifice on the soil of Jerusalem; which, as anyone can see, can only be understood of the times that followed the destruction of Jerusalem, that is, the year of the Lord 70. But to overthrow Bovius's quibbling utterly, it must further be noted what the most distinguished and most reverend Ussher has rightly observed: the Constitutions speak clearly and expressly not only of the people but of the Roman princes. For they say that those Romans who believed in the Lord and departed from the multitude of gods and deserted them, these very men held the Jews as tributaries, collecting tribute and taxes from them; and that they did not allow them to use their ancestral laws. These things apply neither to the people nor to the lower magistrates of the people, but only to the princes.

units.la: Ad quae illud etiam postremo accedit, quod ajunt iidem, Romanos illos, de quibus verba faciunt, τὰς ἀγαθὰς ἀποδείχεσθαι, τὰς φαύλας κολάζειν, bonos probare, pravos punire, continenterque illa de Iudaeorum gravi sub imperio Romano servitute, ac calamitate subjiciunt. Nimirum clare significant, Romanos eo testari, quam sibi cordi sit justitia, quod Christianorum quidem, utpote bonorum, sacra ac religionem constituerint: Iudaeis vero improbis, ac ultima commeritis, non modo civilem, sed & sacram & legalem potestatem sacra sua faciendi, ademerint: quae rerum sub Constantino, secutisque Christianis Principibus dispositioni ad amussim congruunt; ab Apostolorum temporibus plane penitusque abhorrent; horrent: quibus scilicet Romani & Christianos gravissimis persecutionibus urgebant, omni iis interdicta suae colendae religionis potestate, & Iudaeis contra ad annum Christi 70. tutam ac securam suorum sacrorum libertate concedebant: ut falsum, absurdumque sit dicere, Romanos tum quidem & bonos probasse, & pravos punivisse; nisi forte Bovius, & pravos Christianos, & bonos Iudaeos fuisse, somniet. Atque haec de Bovio quidem satis. Sed & ex iis concidit Turriani figmentum, qui fuisse ait a, Apostolorum temporibus Roma nobiles multos credentes, ex domo etiam ac familia Caesaris; quos judicia exercuisse, & gessisse magistratus, ut hac qua Clemens dicit facere possent, nemo (inquit) cum ratione dubitare poterit. Nam neque illud certum est, quod ille suo more confidenter ponit, multos Romae nobiles tum Christianos fuisse (non enim nobiles necessario sunt, quicunque ex domo Principis sunt, in qua multi etiam sunt & ministri & servi ignobiles) neque si tum fuerunt aliqui nobiles Christiani, eosdem ideo necesse est judicia exercuisse, & magistratus gessisse, quinimo constat, ne Tertulliani quidem temporibus, id est anno Christi 217. cum res Christiana multo quam Apostolorum saeculo major esset, atque auctior, ullum fuisse Christianum, qui magistra-
units.tr: To these arguments this last point is also added, which the same writers make: that those Romans of whom they speak rewarded the good and punished the wicked [τὰς ἀγαθὰς ἀποδείχεσθαι, τὰς φαύλας κολάζειν]. They then go on to describe the heavy servitude and calamity of the Jews under Roman rule. Clearly they mean that the Romans showed by this how much they cared for justice: they founded and protected the sacred rites and religion of the Christians, as being good people, but deprived the wicked Jews, who had deserved the worst, not only of civil power but also of the power to practise their sacred and legal rites. These arrangements, under Constantine and the Christian emperors who followed him, agree exactly with the facts, but they are entirely and utterly at odds with the times of the Apostles, and shudder at them. In those days the Romans pressed the Christians with the most severe persecutions, denying them any power to worship their religion, while on the contrary they allowed the Jews to keep their sacred rites in safety and security until the year of Christ 70. So it is false and absurd to say that the Romans at that time both approved the good and punished the wicked, unless perhaps Bovius is dreaming that the wicked Christians and the good Jews were then the ones. But this is enough about Bovius. Turrian's fiction also falls to these same arguments. He says that in the times of the Apostles there were many noble believers at Rome, even from the household and family of Caesar, who exercised judgments and held magistracies, so that they could do what Clement says; no one, he says, can reasonably doubt this. For it is not certain, as he confidently assumes in his usual way, that there were many noble Christians at Rome at that time (for not everyone from the household of a prince is noble, since such a household has many ignoble ministers and slaves too). Nor, if there were some noble Christians then, does it follow that they necessarily exercised judgments and held magistracies. Indeed it is established that not even in the time of Tertullian, that is in the year of Christ 217, when the Christian cause was much larger and more widespread than in the age of the Apostles, was there any Christian who held a magistracy.

units.la: a In explanat. Apolog. ad Const. magistratum gereret; neque si Romanos aliquot, unum, & alterum fortasse, magistratus Christianismum Apostolicis temporibus coluisse donaverimus, eo consequens est, ut universim de tota gente vere dici potuerit Romanos in Christum credidisse, & à Deorum multitudine discessisse, quod ajunt Διαθήκης. Neque postremo id verum est, quod statuit Turrianus, de solis magistratibus intellexisse τῆς Διαθήκης, cum ex superioribus pateat eos de ipsis Romanorum principibus loqui, quos nemo nescit ante à. D. 312. minime fuisse Christianos. Sed nos Turrianum quidem non miramur immanes istas, planeque prodigiosas hyperbolas facile concoquere, Ignatianæ familiæ hominem; in qua omnia supra verum extollere, ex musca elephantum facere, pro pauculis aliquot homunculis regna ac imperia tota ad Christianismum traducta jactare, postremo fingere, ac, ut simpliciter dicam, mentiri, quoties ex usu est, tam licet, quam verum dicere. Tantum eo fallitur Turrianus, quod ex suæ familiæ moribus, ac institutis de Christi Apostolis judicat, quorum plane alia fuit, quam Ignatianorum est, ratio ac disciplina. Adeo enim veraces, adeoque sancti, ac severi fuerunt, ut vel mortem ipsam mendacio præoptaverint. Ergo qui tales fuerunt, nihil eos quod verum non esset, dixisse, aut scri-psisse, pro certo statuendum est. Itaque cum liquido falsum sit, Romanos eorum temporibus in Dominum credidisse, & a Deorum multitudine discessisse; illud quoque non minus falsum esse putandum est, quod vult Turrianus, ab iis hoc volumen profectum esse, in quo id ipsum habetur.
units.tr: a In the Explanation of the Apology addressed to Constantine. Nor does it follow, even if we grant that some Romans, perhaps one or two, who held magistracies, worshipped Christianity in the Apostolic times, that it could truly be said of the whole nation in general that the Romans believed in Christ and withdrew from the multitude of gods, as they put it [Διαθήκης]. Nor, last, is it true what Turrian lays down, that the words [τῆς Διαθήκης] were meant only of the magistrates, since it is plain from what was said above that they speak of the Roman emperors themselves, whom no one doubts were not Christians at all before the year 312 after Christ. But we are not surprised that Turrian can swallow such monstrous and plainly prodigious exaggerations, being a man of the Ignatian family, in which it is the custom to inflate everything beyond the truth, to make an elephant out of a fly, to boast that whole kingdoms and empires were converted to Christianity on the strength of a few little men, and, in a word, to invent and lie whenever it suits them as readily as they tell the truth. Turrian is wrong only in this, that he judges the Apostles of Christ by the customs and institutions of his own family, whose way and discipline were entirely different from those of the Ignatians. For the Apostles were so truthful, so holy and so serious that they preferred death itself to a lie. Therefore we must hold for certain that those who were such men said or wrote nothing that was not true. Accordingly, since it is clearly false that the Romans in their times believed in the Lord and withdrew from the multitude of gods, we must think it no less false what Turrian maintains, that this volume, in which that very claim is found, came from them.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Arg. XIX. Constitutiones multa habent ab Apostolorum usu & sapientia aliena, ut quod multas ex Euangeliis Ὑηοτus citatas describunt; quod multa ex V. T. apocryphis laudant; quod Israelis etymon falsum & absurdum adducunt; Philippum Simonis baptisten, Apostolum faciunt; Iacobum fratrem Domini, Apostolum fuisse negant; quod Mariam Lazari sororem a Magdalena diversam inducunt; quod & Moysem falso, & alias Scripturas perperam citant.
units.tr: Argument XIX. The Constitutions contain many things foreign to the practice and wisdom of the Apostles: they describe many passages from the Gospels as cited as having been said [ῥηθέν]; they quote many passages from the Apocrypha of the Old Testament; they give a false and absurd etymology of Israel; they make Philip, the baptist of Simon, an Apostle; they deny that James, the brother of the Lord, was an Apostle; they introduce Mary, the sister of Lazarus, as distinct from Magdalene; and they cite Moses falsely and other Scriptures wrongly.

units.la: ED praeter haec a dogmate, a disciplina, ab historia Apostolorum aliena, alia insuper non pauca apud nostros Διαζυγίας occurrunt ab eorundem sive usu, sive sapientia abhorrentia. Principio enim illi, quod ab horum in epistolis suis, quascunque habemus, usu alienum est, multas passim easque saepe satis prolixas citant ex quatuor Euangeliorum rum codicibus φήσεις; ut illam ex Joannea, ἐξετάζετε τὰς γραφάς, Scrutamini Scriptu- ras; hanc ex Matthæo b, Beati estis cum ex- probraverint vos, & ex aliis alias. Hæc etiam ex Actuum initio, ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς ποιεῖν τε καὶ διδάσκειν, qua Christus cœpit facere & docere; unde etiam colligunt, E- piscopum primo facere, hoc est, bene & Christiane vivere; deinde & docere debere: quam in illa Lucæ verba observationem, ut bellam & scitulam esse non nego, ita Spiri- tus Sancti in eo loco menti congruam, gra- vemque & Apostolis dignam non puto; neque dubito, quin eam impostor, ut ple- raque alia, ex sequentium sæculorum au- thoribus sumpserit, apud quos illa non raro occurrit.
units.tr: Besides these things, which are foreign to the doctrine, the discipline and the history of the Apostles, not a few other things occur among our writers, the Διαζυγίας ("Diazygias" or "Constitutions"), which are at odds with the practice and wisdom of the same Apostles. First, since it is foreign to the practice of these men in the epistles we have, the Constitutions everywhere cite many sayings [φήσεις] from the codices of the four Gospels, often at quite considerable length. For example, that one from John, "Search the Scriptures" [ἐξετάζετε τὰς γραφάς], and that one from Matthew, "Blessed are you when they revile you", and others from others. Also from the beginning of the Acts, "what Jesus began both to do and to teach" [ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς ποιεῖν τε καὶ διδάσκειν], which they also use to infer that a bishop must first do, that is, live well and as a Christian, and then also teach. I do not deny that this observation on the words of Luke is neat and pretty, but I do not think it is in keeping with the mind of the Holy Spirit in that place, nor weighty nor worthy of the Apostles. Nor do I doubt that the impostor, as in many other things, took it from authors of later centuries, among whom it occurs not infrequently.

units.la: Sed neque illud Apostolicum est, quod hi διαθῆκαι eos libros qui sunt Apocryphi, ut Susannæ c, & Iudithæ d, & Baruchi e, & Ecclesiastici f volumina laudant, eorumque sententiis & authoritate nituntur: quod nusquam veri Domini Apostoli fecerunt in certis & indubitatis ipsorum libris.
units.tr: But it is also not apostolic that these διαθῆκαι ("Constitutions") praise the books that are Apocryphal, such as the volumes of Susanna, Judith, Baruch and Ecclesiasticus, and rely on their sayings and authority; the true Lord's Apostles never did this in their own certain and undoubted books.

units.la: Est & hoc ab Apostolorum more alienum, quod Principes, à quibus persecutionem Ecclesia patiebatur, eos isti διαθῆκαι tyrannos, voce invidiosa & infami, alicubi appellant g.
units.tr: It is also foreign to the custom of the Apostles that these διαθῆκαι somewhere call the princes by whom the Church suffered persecution tyrants, a hateful and infamous word.

units.la: Nescio an & illud Apostolorum gravitatem, tatem, & concordiam satis deceat, quod isti postquam in superioribus libris plurima velut uno omnes ore unaque sententia constituerunt; libro repente octavo singuli, ut Ioannes a verbi gratia solus, tum Philippus, tum alii suo quisque nomine sua quædam seorsum decernentes inducuntur: quod non alia de causa factum ab impostore credederim, quam ut illa orationis varietate nonnihil recreetur lectoris animus, præcedentium si forte prolixitate ac uniformitate fessus. Nam illa, quæ isti singuli constituunt, si bona sunt, & Christo, atque Ecclesia digna; cur non, ut cætera, decernuntur ab universis, præsertim in unum simul locum congregatis? Sin mala sunt, & levia Ecclesiaeque nequaquam necessaria, ea vero ne a singulis quidem, haud magis profecto, quam ab universis decerni decuit.
units.tr: I am not sure that it also befits the dignity, consistency and harmony of the Apostles that, after they have all agreed, as with one mouth and one mind, on very many things in the earlier books, suddenly in the eighth book each of them is introduced separately, John alone for instance, then Philip, and then others each in his own name, decreeing certain things on their own. I would believe that the impostor did this for no other reason than that the reader's mind might be somewhat refreshed by this variety of style, if perhaps he was weary from the length and uniformity of what came before. For if the things these men decree individually are good and worthy of Christ and the Church, why are they not, as the rest are, decreed by all together, especially when gathered together in one place? But if they are bad, and trivial and by no means necessary to the Church, then they should not have been decreed even by individuals, no more surely than by all together.

units.la: Ab eximia vero Apostolorum sapientia illud primo abhorret, quod nomen Israel isti sic interpretantur b, quasi idem esset quod ὁ ὁρῶν Θεόν, Deum videns, quo etymo usque adeo gavisi sunt, ut id duobus locis ponere eos non piguerit. Atqui aliud esse Israelis etymon, nos docet ipse Dominus, qui profitetur id nominis se Iacobo imposuisse c, quod adversus Deum fortis fuisset, eique in luctam quodammodo prævaluisset: quo etiam respicit Oseas, cum de Iacobo ait a,In fortitudine sua directus est cum An- gelo, & invaluit ad Angelum, & conforta- tus est.Et sane congruunt huic etymo voces Ebraeæ. שור enim est dominari, principem esse, אל vero Deus: ut sit Israel idem quod princeps cum Deo, sive ἀρχων πρὸς θεὸν, ut vertebat Symmachus, vel ἐνισχύ-σας μετὰ θεῦ, qui invaluit, aut confortatus est cum Deo, ut Theodotion. Etymon vero Διαταγέων, ὀρῶν θεὸν, a vocibus Ebraeis alienum est. Nisi igitur Apostolos & linguae sanctae ignaros, & sacris Dei ipsius oraculis adversatos fuisse statuamus, necessario fatendum est, non esse Apostolos hos Bovianos Διαταγέας. Sed illi scilicet, ut multa alia, ita & falsum hoc etymon, quod secuti sunt, habent a Patribus tertii saeculi, qui aliqua vocabulorum similitudine decepti, quod ראה ruah Hebraicè sit videre, Israelem per incogitantiam eo retulerunt, putaruntque idem esse, quod ὀρῶν θεὸν, Deum videns, & litteras duas ש quae initio nominis Israel occurrunt, exististimarunt esse ex nomine ש'א vir detruncatas, unde tandem totum hoc etymon sic effinxerunt, ut sit Israel ὁ ἀνὴρ ὀρῶν θεὸν, vir videns Deum. Neque mirum est, istorum authoritatem τοῖς Διαταγεῦσι imposuisse, cum omnes paene Ecclesiasticos in eundem errorem olim abripuerit; ut ex Hieronymo discimus, scimus, qui ad hoc etymon refellendum{s}e accingens, ait, id omnium pane sermone detritum fuisse, atque ita locum totum, vere sane,ac fortiter concludit: Quamvis igitur grandis authoritatis sint, & eloquentia, & ipsorum umbra nos opprimat, qui Israel virum, sive mentem videntem Deum transtulerunt, nos magis Scriptura, & Angeli vel Dei, qui ipsum Israel vocavit, authoritate ducimur, quam cujuslibet eloquentia facularis.
units.tr: Indeed, from the outstanding wisdom of the Apostles, this first departs: that these men interpret the name Israel in such a way as if it meant the same as ὁ ὁρῶν Θεόν, "seeing God", an etymology they were so pleased with that they did not mind putting it in two places. Yet the Lord himself teaches us that the etymology of Israel is different, for he declares that he gave Jacob this name because he had been strong against God and had somewhat prevailed over him in wrestling. Hosea also alludes to this when he says of Jacob: "In his strength he had power with the Angel, and prevailed over the Angel, and was strengthened." And indeed the Hebrew words agree with this etymology: the Hebrew word for to rule [שור] means to dominate, to be a prince, and the word for God [אל]. So Israel means the same as a prince with God, or ἄρχων πρὸς θεόν, as Symmachus translated it, or ἐνισχύσας μετὰ θεοῦ, "he who prevailed" or "was strengthened with God", as Theodotion has it. But the etymology ὁρῶν θεόν, "seeing God", is foreign to the Hebrew words. Unless we suppose that the Apostles were ignorant of the holy tongue and opposed to the holy oracles of God himself, we must necessarily admit that these Bovian Constitution-writers were not Apostles. But they, of course, like many other things, have this false etymology, which they followed, from the Fathers of the third century, who, deceived by some similarity of words, since the Hebrew for to see is ruah [ראה], carelessly referred Israel to it, and thought it was the same as ὁρῶν θεόν, "seeing God". They also supposed that the two letters ש which occur at the beginning of the name Israel were cut off from the word ish [איש], meaning man, and so at last they shaped the whole etymology so that Israel would be ὁ ἀνὴρ ὁρῶν θεόν, "the man seeing God". Nor is it surprising that their authority imposed on the Constitution-writers, since it once drew almost all the ecclesiastical writers into the same error. We learn this from Jerome, who, setting himself to refute this etymology, says that it had been worn down on almost everyone's tongue, and so concludes the whole passage, truly and forcefully: "Although, therefore, they are of great authority and eloquence, and the shadow of them oppresses us, those who rendered Israel as 'a man seeing God', or 'a mind seeing God', we are led rather by the authority of Scripture and of the Angel, or of God who called him Israel, than by the eloquence of any worldly man."

units.la: Sed & haec quae sequuntur, etiam longius ab Apostolorum sapientia ac veracitate discedunt. Quale illud est a Bellarmino notatum, quod ajunt oi Διαξηγεις Philippum Hvinα ὁ Φιλιππος (inquiunt) ὁ σωματος ἡμῶν τῆς τῆς Θεοῦ δόσει, καὶ τῆ τῆς πνεύματος αὐτῆς ἐνεργεία, δυνάμεις ἰαμάτων ἐπιτέλει ἐν Σαμαρία Quando vero Philippus coapostolus noster Dei munere & Spiritus sancti operatione miracula sanitatum in Samaria faciebat, &c. Id vero (inquit Bellarminus ) manifeste falsum est. Philippum enim illum ex Actis liquet, non Apostolum, sed Diaconum fuisse. Ac illi quidem Apostolatum, ut Philippo gratis falsoque tribuunt, qui Diaconus fuit; ita & Iacobo Domini fratri, aeque falso ac contumeliose eripiunt. Enumeratis enim omnibus Christi Apostolis, hunc insuper extra eorum numerum ita adiiciunt a : Ἰάκωβός τε ὁ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀδελφός, καὶ Ἱεροσολύμων ἐπίσκοπος, & Iacobus frater Domini, idemque Hierosolymitanus episcopus. Et alibi eundem scribunt ab Apostolis ordinatum fuisse Hierosolymorum Episcopum; & Clementi Romae, Euodio Antiochiae, Zacchaeo Caesareae Episcopis, aliisque ejusdem ordinis accensent. Boviani vero Διαζυγεις duo hic ponunt: prius quidem, Iacobum fratrem Domini non fuisse Apostolum, sed Episcopum duntaxat Hierosolymitanum ab Apostolis ordinatum. Posterius vero, quod ex priori necessario consequitur, Iacobum illum fratrem Domini, alium esse a Jacobo Alphaei, qui ab Euangelistis inter XII. Christi Apostolos diserte nominatur: proindeque non duos tantum, sed tres esse Iacobos in Scripturis divinis memoratos inter primarios Christi discipulos; Jacobum Zebedaei filium Joannis fratrem, Iacobum Alphaei, utrumque Apostolum; Iacobum denique Domini fratrem non Apostolum, sed Episcopum Hierosolymitanum. Haec autem omnia falsa esse, & ex scripturis liquet, & apud doctissimos adversariorum confessum est. Jacobum enim Domini fratrem eundem quoque Apostolum
units.tr: But also what follows departs even further from the wisdom and truthfulness of the Apostles. Such is that which Bellarmine has noted, that the Διαζυγεῖς say: "Now Philip (they say), our fellow Apostle, by the gift of God and the working of his Spirit, performed miracles of healing in Samaria" [Φίλιππος δὲ ὁ συναπόστολος ἡμῶν τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ δόσει καὶ τῇ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ, δυνάμεις ἰαμάτων ἐπιτελεῖ ἐν Σαμαρίᾳ]. Bellarmine says: "This is manifestly false." For it is clear from the Acts that Philip was not an Apostle but a Deacon. And so these men give the Apostleship, freely and falsely, to Philip, who was a Deacon; and in the same way, equally falsely and contemptuously, they take it from James, the brother of the Lord. For after listing all the Apostles of Christ, they add this one beyond their number: "James the brother of the Lord, and bishop of Jerusalem" [Ἰάκωβός τε ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδελφός, καὶ Ἱεροσολύμων ἐπίσκοπος]. And elsewhere they write that he was ordained by the Apostles as bishop of Jerusalem, and they count among the same order Clement at Rome, Evodius at Antioch and Zacchaeus at Caesarea. But the Bovian Διαζυγεῖς here put forward two things: first, that James the brother of the Lord was not an Apostle, but only bishop of Jerusalem, ordained by the Apostles. Second, which necessarily follows from the first, that this James the brother of the Lord is other than James the son of Alphaeus, who is expressly named by the Evangelists among the twelve Apostles of Christ; and therefore that there are not only two but three Jameses mentioned in the divine Scriptures among the chief disciples of Christ: James the son of Zebedee, brother of John, and James the son of Alphaeus, both Apostles; and finally James the brother of the Lord, not an Apostle but bishop of Jerusalem. But that all these things are false is clear from the Scriptures, and it has been acknowledged by the most learned of our opponents. For Paul plainly says that James the brother of the Lord was also an Apostle, when, relating that he went to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and that he stayed with him fifteen days, he immediately adds: "But I saw none of the other Apostles, except James the brother of the Lord."

units.la: postolum postolorum fuisse diserte ait Paulus, dum narrans se Hierosolymam Petri visendi gratia venisse, seque apud eum diebus quindecim mansisse, continuo haec addit, Alium autem Apostolorum vidi neminem, nisi Jacobum fratrem Domini. Neque quicquam valet putida Bovii vitilitigatio, cavillantis eum a Paulo Apostolum ampliori vocabulo dici, quomodo & alii Apostoli nominantur praeter duodecim, quotquot scilicet ad propagandum Euangelium missi sunt. Fateor, Apostoli nomen interdum latius sic sumi: ita hoc loco sumendum, nego. Obstat Pauli oratio. Non enim simpliciter negat, Se ullum Apostolum vidisse, sed negat se ἕτερον τῶν Ἀποστόλων alium Apostolorum vidisse. Illud autem ἕτερον alium, evidentissime refertur ad Petrum, de quo in antecedente versiculo haec scripserat : Veni Hierosolymam videre Petrum, & mansi apud eum diebus quindecim. Cum ergo nunc subiicit, Alium autem Apostolorum vidi neminem, significat se alium a Petro Apostolum vidisse neminem, praeter unum Iacobum. Ergo Apostolos ejus ordinis intelligit, cujus erat visus a se Petrus. Non erat autem ex illo Apostolorum censu Petrus, qui minus proprie & latius sumpto vocabulo ita dicuntur, sed ἐκ τῶν duodecim. Itaque ex hoc τῶν duodecim ordine fuisse Jacobum necesse est, quem Paulus scilicet unum, præter Petrum, eximit ex ejus ordinis viris, quos non viserat. Tum huic Bovii commento repugnat Pauli in eo loco consilium. Se enim tuetur ab invidorum obtrectationibus, qui ejus authoritatem ideo elevabant, quod non una cum cæteris Apostolis, sed post eos vocatus esset; contendebantque, non esse eum antecedentibus Apostolis æquiparandum. Apostolos autem isti, non Bovianos minorum gentium Apostolos intelligebant (quibus Paulum æquiparari neque ulla fuit, neque esse potuit invidia) sed τὰς duodecim. Paulus vero, ut suum ministerium asserat, magnifice quidem, sed tamen verissime prædicat, se nullius mortalis, sed unius Christi missione atque instructione euangelizavisse gentibus; tantumque abesse, ut ab aliis Apostolis in eam provinciam missus fuerit, ut etiam antequam vel eos vidisset, tres annos totos id munus gesserit. Neque (inquit a) veni ad antecessores meos Apostolos. Hic, ut omnes vident, τὰς duodecim intelligit (neque enim illi alii minuti Bovii Apostoli, Pauli antecessores fuerunt) Atque hoc loco id occupat Paulus, quod objici poterat, ipsum tamen Hierosolymam ad Apostolos (illos scilicet duodecim) venisse. Concedit, se venisse. Negat, se venisse initio: quod omnino faciendum erat, si eorum vel missione, vel instructione nitebatur ejus praedicatio: venisse ait post totum elapsum triennium. Negat, venisse ad emendicandam, aut quaerendam eorum authoritatem. Venisse ait τὸ ἱστορῆσαι Πέτρον, ad invisendum Petrum. Denique negat, se omnes eos vidisse; (qui tamen omnino congregandi omnes fuerant, si ideo ad ipsos venisset, ut authoritatem vel munus ab illis acciperet) Vidisse tantum ait unum Petrum, & praeter eum, neminem nisi Jacobum. Ex quibus jam sole clarius est, omnem hic Paulo sermonem esse περὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων, insulse adeo, ac praeter omnem rationem eos Apostolos, (quorum censu hic Iacobus includitur) alios intelligi, quam τῆς ἀποστολικῆς. Sed & in sequenti capite idem clarissime docet Paulus. Ait enim hunc Iacobum (neque enim quisquam dubitat, quin de eodem illo loquatur, quem fratrem Domini appellaverat a) hunc (inquam) Jacobum τοῖς duodecim, imo praecipuis, ac primariis τῶν duodecim accenseт; & quidem ejus nomen primo loco ante Petri, Ioannisque nomina nuncupans. Cum cognovissent (inquit b) gratiam, quae data est mihi, Iacobus, & Cephas, & Ioannes, qui videntur columnae esse. Hunc, nisi & ipse majorum gentium (ut sic dicam) Apostolus fuisset, nunquam prose{ß}to Paulus Petro & Ioanni adjunxisset, ne id (quod sane fecit) dicam, anteposuisset; nunquam eum & duos istos columnas videri dixisset; quo clarissime significat, tres illos viros duodecim Apostolorum principes ac coryphæos ab omnibus habitos esse, in quos pæne totum Apostolici collegii Ecclesiæque onus recumbebat. Jacobum autem istum, nisi & ipse unus ex duodecim fuisset, quis sanæ mentis putaverit tali loco, ac numero vulgo à Christianis illius ævi habitum fuisse? ut exceptis si forte Cepha & Joanne, reliquis decem, non dicam (quod tamen indignandum esset) æquaretur, sed (quod omnino est intolerabile) etiam anteferretur? Sed nihil necesse est, absurdissimam Bovii cavillationem pluribus refellere, quam Bellarminus ac Baronius ipsi refutant. Ille quidem, dum interea, quæ in Constitutionibus posita abhorrere videntur à veritate, hoc diserte numerat a, quod Jacobum fratrem Domini non velint esse Apostolum ex duodecim. Hic vero, dum præfatus quosdam Jacobum extra numerum duodenarium Apostolorum imprudenter ni-mis constituere, eorum sententiam mox ex Hieronymo oppugnat, hæcque postremo addit: Sed an non plus satis Paulus Apostolus monstrat, Jacobum fratrem Domini unum ex duodecim fuisse, cum scribens ad
units.tr: Paul clearly says that this same James was also an Apostle of the Apostles. Relating that he went to Jerusalem to visit Peter and stayed with him fifteen days, he at once adds: But other of the Apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother. Bovius's foul quibbling is worth nothing here, when he carps that Paul uses "Apostle" in a wider sense, just as other Apostles are named beyond the twelve, that is, all who were sent out to spread the Gospel. I grant that the word "Apostle" is sometimes taken so broadly, but that it should be so taken here I deny. Paul's sentence stands in the way. He does not simply say that he saw no Apostle, but that he saw no other [ἕτερον] of the Apostles [τῶν Ἀποστόλων]. And that "other" [ἕτερον] clearly refers to Peter, of whom he had written in the preceding verse: I came to Jerusalem to see Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days. So when he now adds, But other of the Apostles saw I none, he means that he saw no Apostle other than Peter except James alone. He therefore means the Apostles of the same rank as Peter, whom he had seen. Peter did not belong to that body of "Apostles" taken in the looser and wider sense, but to the twelve [ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα]. It follows that James too must have belonged to this order of the twelve, since Paul, apart from Peter, excepts him alone from the men of that order whom he had not visited. Moreover, Paul's purpose in that passage refutes Bovius's fancy. He defends himself against the slanders of those who belittled his authority because he had been called not together with the other Apostles but after them, and who insisted that he was not to be put on a level with the Apostles who went before. But those men understood by "Apostles" not Bovius's Apostles of the lesser nations (with whom no one could have envied Paul's equality, nor could there have been any such envy) but the twelve [τὰς δώδεκα]. Paul, asserting his ministry, proclaims magnificently yet most truly that he preached the Gospel to the nations by the sending and instruction not of any mortal, but of Christ alone. So far was he from being sent into that province by the other Apostles that he discharged that office for three whole years even before he had seen them. Nor, he says, did I go up to those who were Apostles before me. Here, as everyone sees, he means the twelve, for those other petty Apostles of Bovius were not Paul's predecessors. In this passage Paul also takes up the objection that might be raised, namely that he too came to Jerusalem to the Apostles (that is, the twelve). He concedes that he came. He denies that he came at the start, which he certainly ought to have done if his preaching rested on their sending or instruction; he says he came after the whole three years had passed. He denies that he came to beg for or seek their authority. He says he came to visit Peter [τὸ ἱστορῆσαι Πέτρον]. Finally, he denies that he saw all of them, though they would all have had to be gathered together if he had come to them to receive authority or office. He says he saw only Peter, and besides him no one except James. From this it is now clearer than the sun that Paul's whole discourse here is concerning the Apostles [περὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων], and it is absurd and contrary to all reason to understand by those Apostles, in whose number James is included here, others than the apostolic [τῆς ἀποστολικῆς] men. Paul teaches the same most clearly in the following chapter. He says that this James (for no one doubts it is the same man whom he had called the Lord's brother) is reckoned among the twelve [τοῖς δώδεκα], indeed among their principal and chief men [τῶν δώδεκα], and he names him first, before Peter and John. When they had known the grace that was given to me, James, and Cephas, and John, who seem to be pillars. Unless he too had been one of the greater Apostles (so to speak), Paul would never have joined him with Peter and John, still less (which he certainly did) put him before them, nor would he have said that these two seemed to be pillars. He clearly signifies that those three men were regarded by all as the chief and leaders of the twelve Apostles, on whom almost the whole burden of the apostolic college and the Church rested. But who of sound mind would think that this James, unless he too were one of the twelve, was held by the Christians of that age in such a place and rank that he would be equated, apart perhaps from Cephas and John, with the remaining ten? I will not say (though that would be outrageous) but, which is utterly intolerable, that he would even be ranked above them? There is no need to refute this most absurd quibble of Bovius at length, since Bellarmine and Baronius themselves refute it. The former, while listing what in the Constitutions seems to depart from the truth, expressly names this: that they do not want James the Lord's brother to be one of the twelve Apostles. The latter, after saying that some have imprudently placed James too far outside the number of the twelve Apostles, at once attacks their opinion from Jerome, and finally adds: But does not Paul the Apostle show quite enough that James the brother of the Lord was one of the twelve, when writing

units.tr: a Book "On Ecclesiastical Writers", under Clement.
b A.D. 44, sections 36, 37.

units.la: Galatas ait, Alium Apostolorum vidi ne-minem, nisi Jacobum fratrem Domini? Eusebius a item ex Clemente Alexandrino nonnisi duos Iacobos fuisse tradit, dum sic ait; Duos item Iacobos fuisse ferunt; unum cognomento Justum, qui de templi fastigio praeceps dejectus fullonis vecte caesus occubuit: alterum, qui capite abscisso migravit e vita. Hactenus Baronius; qui & illud obiter solvit, quod est a Bovio objectum, sensisse quosdam Patres, Iacobum fratrem Domini non fuisse unum ex duodecim Apostolis; Satis (inquit b) ad ejus sententiae confutationem esse videtur, sunde est deducta, repetatur origo. Ex rejectis enim illis Clementis nomine scriptis Recognitionum libris de tribus Iacobis authoritas semel summpta, in nonnullos est inconsultissime propagata. Haec quidem praeclare Baronius; Illud minus recte, quod Constitutionum auctorem negat in eadem de tribus Iacobis sententia fuisse, vel id haberi posse ex capite 59. libri secundi. Nam ut hunc ex secundo libro locum, de quo vitilitigat Baronius, mittam, clara est Διαταγῆων in sexto illo quod supra laudavimus, operis volumine sententia. Istic enim in Apostolorum censu locant primo Iacobum, Zebedaei filium; tum & Iacobum Alphaei; ac denique extra Apostolorum censum, Iacobum Domini fratrem, fratrem, & Hierosolymorum Episcopum; Iacobum Alphæi (ut liquet) à Iacobo Domini fratre distinguentes. Sic etiam libro octavo a: Ἐπὶ Μωσέως μὲν γὰρ τῆς θεοφιλεστάτης ἀρχιερεὺς κατεστάθησαν, καὶ ἱερεῖς καὶ Λευῖται. ὑπὸ τῆς σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, ἡμεῖς οἱ δικαιότεροι Ἀπόστολοι, ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, ἐγὼ Ἰάκωβος, ἐγὼ Κλήμης. A Moyse namque qui fuit Deo carissimus, constituti sunt Pontifices, sacerdotes, & Levitæ; à Christo autem Salvatore nostro nos tredecim Apostoli, ab Apostolis vero ego Jacobus, & ego Clemens. Non potuit apertius à Christi Apostolis hunc Iacobum Episcopum, hoc est Domini fratrem, distinguere. Sed Baronio quidem aliud agenti, neque de his Constitutionum locis (ut par erat) cogitanti, hoc quicquid est erroris excidisse videtur.
units.tr: to the Galatians he says, Other of the Apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother? Eusebius, also citing Clement of Alexandria, likewise reports that there were only two Jameses, saying: They also say there were two Jameses: one, surnamed the Just, who was thrown down headlong from the pinnacle of the Temple and died, beaten with a fuller's club; the other, who was beheaded and departed this life. So far Baronius, who also solves in passing the objection Bovius raises, that some Fathers thought James the Lord's brother was not one of the twelve Apostles. It seems sufficient (he says) to refute that opinion to trace where it came from. For from the rejected books of the Recognitions written under Clement's name, the authority on three Jameses was once taken, and it was spread very rashly among some. Baronius says these things admirably. Less correct is his denial that the author of the Constitutions held the same view about three Jameses, or that this can be gathered from chapter 59 of the second book. For, to pass over that passage of the second book which Baronius quibbles about, the view of the Constitutions is clear in the sixth book, which we quoted above. There they place James son of Zebedee first in the census of the Apostles, then James of Alphaeus, and finally, outside the census of the Apostles, James the Lord's brother and bishop of Jerusalem, clearly distinguishing James of Alphaeus from James the Lord's brother. So also in book eight: From Moses, who was most beloved of God, high priests, priests and Levites were appointed; by our Saviour Christ, we the twelve Apostles; and by the Apostles, I James and I Clement. [Ἐπὶ Μωσέως μὲν γὰρ τῆς θεοφιλεστάτης ἀρχιερεὺς κατεστάθησαν, καὶ ἱερεῖς καὶ Λευῖται. ὑπὸ τῆς σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, ἡμεῖς οἱ δικαιότεροι Ἀπόστολοι, ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, ἐγὼ Ἰάκωβος, ἐγὼ Κλήμης.] He could not have distinguished this James the bishop, that is the Lord's brother, from Christ's Apostles more plainly. But Baronius, intent on other matters and not considering (as he ought) these passages of the Constitutions, seems to have let slip whatever error there is here.

units.la: Huc etiam illud pertinet, quod iidem Διαταγεῖς Mariam Lazari sororem aliam faciunt à Maria Magdalene b: σωλῶν γὰρ ἡμῖν (inquiunt) ἥτε μήτης τῆς Κυρίου, ἢ αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτῆς, ἔτι ἡ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή, καὶ Μαρία ἡ Ἰακώβου, καὶ Μάρθα, καὶ Μαρία αἱ ἀδελφαὶ Λαζάρου· Σαλώμη καὶ ἕτεραί τινες. Erat enim nobiscum mater Domini, & sorores ejus; praterea Maria Magdalena, & Maria Iacobi, ac Martha & Maria Sorores Lazari, & Salome & alia quadam. quaedam. Atqui attestatione Ioannis Euangelistae (inquit Baronius a) imo Christi, apertissime constat, unam eandemque personam fuisse Mariam Lazari & Martha sororem cum Maria Magdalena. Nam cum in Bethania eadem soror Lazari unxisset pedes Iesu, ac Iudas ob eam causam ei esset infensus, ipse Iesus, furentis discipuli audaciam reprimens, dixit b, Sinite illam, ut in diem sepulturae meae servet illud. Caeterum eandem ipsam, qua ad unguendum corpus Iesu paratum unguentum ad sepulcrum attulit, Marcus Euangelista c fuisse Mariam Magdalenam affirmat, qua cum Maria Iacobi & Salome id officii exhibuerit; cumq; nec aliqua apud eum vel aliios Euangelistas habeatur mentio de Maria sorore Lazari ad illud munus praestandum a Domino praemonstrata, cognosci perfacile potest, unam eandemque fuisse Mariam, qua utramque obierit functionem. Haec-nus Baronius. Eadem Bellarminum d monuerunt, ut inter ea, quae abhorrere a veritate videntur, hoc quoque diserte poneret, quod est in Constitutionibus, distinguit Mariam Magdalenam, a sorore Lazari l. 3. c. 6. Ergo cum ex his omnibus pateat, & Jacobum fratrem Domini, Apostolum fuisse; & Apostolum non fuisse eum Philippum, qui Samaritanos baptizavit; vit; ac denique, ut vult Baronius, Mariam Lazari sororem eandem esse cum Maria Magdalene; apparet, Christi Apostolos, quibus notissimæ erant hæ tres personæ, esse non posse τὰς Bovii Διαβολίας, qui contra evidentem rerum ex novo Testamento veritatem, primum quidem & tertium negant; secundum vero affirmant.
units.tr: This also bears on the fact that the same Constitutions make Mary, the sister of Lazarus, a different person from Mary Magdalene: "For there were with us the mother of the Lord and her sisters, and besides, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Martha, and Mary the sisters of Lazarus, and Salome, and certain others" [ὅτι σωλῶν γὰρ ἡμῖν ἥτε μήτης τῆς Κυρίου, ἢ αἱ ἀδελφαὶ αὐτῆς, ἔτι ἡ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή, καὶ Μαρία ἡ Ἰακώβου, καὶ Μάρθα, καὶ Μαρία αἱ ἀδελφαὶ Λαζάρου· Σαλώμη καὶ ἕτεραί τινες]. Yet, as Baronius says, it is most clearly established by the testimony of the evangelist John, indeed of Christ himself, that Mary the sister of Lazarus and Martha was one and the same person as Mary Magdalene. For when that same sister of Lazarus had anointed the feet of Jesus at Bethany, and Judas was angry with her on that account, Jesus himself, checking the boldness of the raving disciple, said: "Let her alone, that she may keep this for the day of my burial." Moreover, Mark the evangelist affirms that the very same woman who brought ointment to the sepulchre to anoint the prepared body of Jesus was Mary Magdalene, who performed that office with Mary the mother of James and Salome. And since neither Mark nor the other evangelists mention any Mary, sister of Lazarus, foreshown by the Lord for that duty, it can very easily be recognised that it was one and the same Mary who discharged both functions. So far Baronius. The same considerations warned Bellarmine, so that among the things which seem far from the truth he also explicitly set down this point, which stands in the Constitutions: "He distinguishes Mary Magdalene from the sister of Lazarus," book 3, chapter 6. Therefore, since all this makes plain both that James the brother of the Lord was an apostle, and that Philip, who baptised the Samaritans, was not an apostle, and finally, as Baronius wishes, that Mary the sister of Lazarus is the same as Mary Magdalene, it appears that the apostles of Christ, to whom these three persons were very well known, cannot have written the lies of this Bovius [τὰς Bovii Διαβολίας], who, against the plain truth of the New Testament, deny the first and the third and affirm the second.

units.la: Sunt & illa Διαλογίων a perspecta Apostolorum veracitate aliena, quod affirmant, & Mosem vetare legem extra Judææ terminos legi, & librum Baruch a Iudæis legi; Ἀπαγορεύει a γὰρ αὐτοῖς (Ἰουδαίοις) ὁ θεὸς Μωσ- σῆς καὶ Συσιαςήειον ἔξω Ἱερουσαλήμ ἱςᾶν. ἐ τὸν νόμον ἔξω τῶν ὅρων τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἀναγινώσκειν. Siquidem vetat eos divinus Moses & aram extra Hierusalem collocare, & legem extra Iudæa terminos legere. Item alibi de Iudeis b: Καὶ γὰρ ἐ νῦν Ἀκάτῃ ἡμ- νὸς Γορπιαίας σωαζοῤῥοιζόμενοι τὰς ὀρλωὺς Ἱε- ερμίας ἀναγινώσκεσαι, &c. καὶ τὸν Βαρὺχ, ἐν ᾧ γέγραπται, ἔτι ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ λογιζόμενος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν, &c. Siquidem & nunc decimo die mensis noni, quem Gorpiæum vocant, Iudæi in unum locum congregati, Lamentationes Hieremiæ legunt, &c. Item Baruch, in quo scriptum est, Hic Deus noster, Non reputabitur alius ad eum. Attamen qui utrumque liquido falsum est. Nam neque in Moysis libris ulla extat de non legenda
units.tr: There are also in the Dialogues [Διαλογίων] points alien to the well-known truthfulness of the apostles: they affirm that Moses forbade the law to be read outside the bounds of Judaea, and that the book of Baruch was read by the Jews. For "God, through Moses, forbade them [the Jews] to set up an altar outside Jerusalem, and to read the law outside the borders of Judaea" [ἀπαγορεύει γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς Μωσῆς καὶ Συσιαςήειον ἔξω Ἱερουσαλήμ ἱςᾶν, ἐ τὸν νόμον ἔξω τῶν ὅρων τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἀναγινώσκειν]. Indeed the divine Moses forbids them to place an altar outside Jerusalem, and to read the law outside the borders of Judaea. Elsewhere, speaking of the Jews, the same writer says: "For even now on the tenth day of the ninth month, which they call Gorpiaeus, the Jews gather in one place and read the Lamentations of Jeremiah, etc., and Baruch, in which it is written, 'This is our God, no other shall be reckoned beside him'" [Καὶ γὰρ ἐ νῦν Ἀκάτῃ ἡμνὸς Γορπιαίας σωαζοῤῥοιζόμενοι τὰς ὀρλωὺς Ἱερεμίας ἀναγινώσκεσαι, κ.τ.λ. καὶ τὸν Βαρὺχ, ἐν ᾧ γέγραπται, Οὗτος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, οὐ λογισθήσεται ἕτερος πρὸς αὐτόν, κ.τ.λ.]. Both statements are plainly false.

units.la: a L. 6. c. 24. med.; b L. 5. c. 20. init.; c Baruch. 3. genda extra Iudæam lege interdictio, neque qui ara & sacrificiis nunc ex lege carent in dispersionibus suis Iudæi, iidem legis lectione carent: neque librum illum Baruch à Constitutionibus memoratum vel mense Gorpiæo, vel alio in synagogis legunt, qui scilicet neque hebraice scriptus extat, neque est aut fuit unquam in canonem sacrarum Scripturarum à Iudæis relatus, vel pro divino habitus. Nisi ergo Christi Apostolos apertissime mentitos esse statuamus, necessario negandum est, eos ista scripsisse.
units.tr: (a) Book 6, ch. 24, middle; (b) book 5, ch. 20, beginning; (c) Baruch 3. There is no prohibition in the books of Moses against reading the law outside Judaea; nor do the Jews now scattered abroad, who lack altar and sacrifices as the law requires, therefore lack the reading of the law. Nor do they read in their synagogues, in the month of Gorpiaeus or at any other time, that book of Baruch mentioned by the Constitutions. It is, moreover, neither extant in Hebrew, nor is it, or has it ever been, reckoned by the Jews among the canon of the sacred Scriptures, or regarded as divine. Unless, therefore, we are to hold that the apostles of Christ lied most openly, we must necessarily deny that they wrote these things.

units.la: Deniq; & hoc ab Apostolis alienum est, quod Bovii Διαταγεὶς in citandis Scripturis haud semel peccant. Verbi gratia, ex I. 2. Reg. recitant τὸν Αβεδαδὰν sive Αβδα-δὰν Abedadam hæc dixisse a, ὅτι ἐγὼ μοί φησί μέγας ἐν Δαβὶδ, ὅτι κληρονομία ἐν γῇ Ἰσραὴλ, Non est mihi (inquit) pars in David, neque hæreditas in filio Iesse. Indeque paulo ante dixerant, illum Abedadam fuę in Davidem rebellionis pœnas dedisse, ὅτι γὰρ Ἀβεσαλὼμ ἐμείνασαν ἀτιμωρήσιοι, Non enim Absalom, & Abedada impuniti remanserunt. Hoc autem in altero Regum volumine b,non de Abedada (qui neque istic, neque alibi in sacris, quod sciam, libris ullus est) sed de Seba, filio Bochri, narrantur. Sed hæc Διαταγεὶς à Pseudo-ignatio c, ut & alia plurima, habent; à quo
units.tr: Finally, it is also foreign to the apostles that the Constitutions [Διαταγεῖς] err more than once in quoting Scripture. For example, from the first book of Kings (2 Sam.) they recite that Abedadan [τὸν Αβεδαδὰν], or Abdadan, Abedadam, said: "For I have no portion [μοί φησί μέγας] in David, and no inheritance [κληρονομία] in the land of Israel; I have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse." And they had said shortly before that this Abedadam paid the penalty for rebellion against David: "For neither Absalom nor Abedada remained unpunished" [ὅτι γὰρ Ἀβεσαλὼμ ἐμείνασαν ἀτιμωρήσιοι]. But in the second book of Kings these things are related not of Abedada (who, so far as I know, is not found in the sacred books either there or elsewhere), but of Sheba, the son of Bichri. These errors the Constitutions have from the pseudo-Ignatius, as they do many others; from whom

units.la: & quidem in eodem argumento, fictitius ille Abedadan memoratur: Ἀβεδδαδὰν ὡ-σαύτως (inquit) τῆς κεφαλῆς ἀφαιρεῖται. Abeddadan similiter capite truncatus est ob similem causam; nimirum ob rebellionem in principem.
units.tr: and indeed, in the same passage, that fictitious "Abedadan" is mentioned: "Abeddadan likewise [ὡσαύτως] was beheaded," he says, "for a similar cause," namely, for rebellion against the prince.

units.la: Sic iidem Διαταγεῖς Concilii Apostilici historiam ex capite Actuum decimo-quinto memorantes, fingunt, Apostolos ob turbas de lege servanda primum Hierosolymis congregatos fuisse: Antiochenos inde fratres, quorum Ecclesia eadem de causa turbabatur, cognita Apostolorum congregatione, Hierosolymam misisse: γενομένης ἓν σάσεως καὶ ζητήσεως ἐκ ολίγης, οἱ ἐν Αντιοχείᾳ ἀδελφοὶ γνόντες, ὅτι σωμελπλύθαμεν πάντες περὶ τούτου ζητήσαντες, ἐξαπέστειλαν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀνδρας πιστοὺς, καὶ τῶν χαρφῶν εἰδήμονας, μαθεῖν περὶ τοῦ ζητήματος τούτου. Cum igitur dissensio esset, & non parva quaestio haberetur, Antiochenses fratres, ubi cognoverunt, nos omnes ad hujus quaestionis disquisitionem convenisse, miserunt ad nos viros fideles, & scripturarum peritos, ut de hac quaestione intelligerent. Haec illi. Lucas vero longe aliter rem narrat. Non enim, (quod isti ajunt) primo convenisse dicit Hierosolymis Apostolos, tum Antiochenos fratres, cum eos convenisse rescivissent, legatos ad eos misisse: sed plane contra testatur, cum Antiocheni ob turbas apud se exortas, Paulum & alios nonnullos Hierosolymam ad Apostolos & presbyteros sciscitatum super hac quæstione misissent, missiq; eo pervenissent, & Antiochenorum statum, ac desideria expósuissent, tum demum, eamque ipsam ob causam, convenisse Apostolos & seniores, videre de verbo hoc, id est, ut dispicerent de hoc negotio. Ex quibus liquet, falsa & inania esse, quæ Διαταγὴς fabulantur. Neque verior est Jacobo ab istis in eadem narratione affícta interdicti de sanguine & suffocato ratio; inde petita, quod hæc etiam ante legem à Moyse latam piis divinitus fuerint vetita; ἀπὸ τῆς πάλαι γενομένης τοῖς πρὸ τῆς νόμου φυσικοῖς, Ἐνώς, Ἐνώχ, Νῶε, Μελχισεδὲκ, Ἰὼβ, καὶ εἴτις τοιοῦτο ἐγένετο, qua quidem etiam antiquis sancita fuerant, qui ante legem secundum naturam vivebant, ut Enos, Enoch, Noachus, Melchisedec, Iob, & siquis alius hujusmodi fuit. Atqui nihil istorum apud Lucam verus Iacobus.
