Neque sane ea causa fuit, cur Apostoli interdictum illud tulerint: quæ si vera esset, abstinentia à sanguine, & suffocato, utpote à naturali lege profecta, perpetua æternaque esse deberet: quod non est, ipsis consentientibus adversariis. Illi vero hanc abstinentiam ad tempus tantummodo prædo præceperunt, ad cavendum Iudæorum scandalum, quod & ab Augustino jampridem fuse præclareque demonstratum est, & nunc ab omnibus probatur. Qui ergo divinis historiis hæc de suo falsa, & Apostolorum menti adversantia impudenter assuunt, ii profecto fieri nequaquam potest, ut vere sint Apostoli. Huc quoque postremo pertinet, quod illa velut à Christo dicta ex Johannis Euangelio citant a ; ἐὰν μή τις βαπτισθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος, ὁ μὴ εἰσελθῇ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν. Nisi quis baptizatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu Sancto, non ingredietur in regnum cœlorum: quæ nemo non videt esse ab iis interpolata, substituto verbo baptizatus fuerit, pro eo, quod est apud Joannem, γεννηθῇ, natus vel genitus fuerit; Sic enim habet notissimus apud Joannem locus b; ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος, ὁ δύναται εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Nisi quis fuerit genitus ex aqua & Spiritu, non poterit introire in regnum Dei.
units.tr: So also the same Constitutions, recounting the history of the apostolic council from the fifteenth chapter of Acts, invent that the apostles first met at Jerusalem because of disturbances about keeping the law; that the brethren of Antioch, whose church was troubled for the same reason, on learning of the assembly of the apostles, sent men to Jerusalem: "When therefore there was dissension and no small question, the brethren at Antioch, learning that we had all assembled to examine this matter, sent to us faithful men, skilled in the Scriptures, to learn about this question" [γενομένης ἓν σάσεως καὶ ζητήσεως ἐκ ολίγης, οἱ ἐν Αντιοχείᾳ ἀδελφοὶ γνόντες, ὅτι σωμελπλύθαμεν πάντες περὶ τούτου ζητήσαντες, ἐξαπέστειλαν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀνδρας πιστοὺς, καὶ τῶν χαρφῶν εἰδήμονας, μαθεῖν περὶ τοῦ ζητήματος τούτου]. Thus they. But Luke tells the matter quite differently. For he does not say, as these men claim, that the apostles first assembled at Jerusalem, and that then the brethren of Antioch, having learned that they had gathered, sent envoys to them. On the contrary, he plainly testifies that when the Antiochenes, because of disturbances arising among them, had sent Paul and some others to Jerusalem to inquire of the apostles and elders about this question, and when these men had arrived there and set forth the state and wishes of the Antiochenes, then at last, and for that very reason, the apostles and elders came together, "to see concerning this matter," that is, "to consider this business." From these things it is clear that what the Constitutions fable is false and empty. Nor is the reason which these men, in the same narrative, falsely attach to James for the prohibition concerning "blood and what is strangled" more accurate, namely, that these things had been forbidden by God even before the law given through Moses, to the pious: "for they had been sanctioned of old even for those who lived before the law according to nature, such as Enos, Enoch, Noah, Melchizedek, Job, and whoever else was of this kind" [ἀπὸ τῆς πάλαι γενομένης τοῖς πρὸ τῆς νόμου φυσικοῖς, Ἐνώς, Ἐνώχ, Νῶε, Μελχισεδὲκ, Ἰὼβ, καὶ εἴτις τοιοῦτο ἐγένετο]. Yet the true James says nothing of these things in Luke. Nor was that the reason why the apostles issued that prohibition. If it were true, abstinence from blood and from what is strangled, as proceeding from natural law, ought to be perpetual and eternal; which it is not, even by the consent of our adversaries. Those apostles indeed prescribed this abstinence only for a time, to avoid giving offence to the Jews, as Augustine long ago showed fully and clearly, and as all now accept. Therefore those who impudently attach to the divine histories these falsehoods of their own, which are contrary to the mind of the apostles, certainly cannot be apostles at all. Finally, this also belongs here: that the Constitutions cite from the Gospel of John, as if spoken by Christ, the words: "Unless anyone is baptised [ἐὰν μή τις βαπτισθῇ] of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven" [ὁ μὴ εἰσελθῇ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν]: Unless someone is baptised with water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven. No one fails to see that these words have been altered by them, the word "baptised" being substituted for what stands in John, "born" [γεννηθῇ], born or begotten. For the well-known passage in John reads thus: "Unless someone is born [ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ] of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" [ὁ δύναται εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ]: Unless someone has been born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

units.la: a Ioh. 3. 5.
units.tr: a John 3.5.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Fuse refelluntur σοφὰ Bovii & Turriani Φαρμακα, quibus frustra conantur Constitutiones hīs absurdis liberare, nescio quam sermonis ideam comminiscentes, in qua vera falsaque, vetera & recentia permiscere, fabulari denique ac mentiri, & quidvis sine flagitio fingere liceat.
units.tr: The clever [σοφὰ] drugs [Φαρμακα] of Bovius and Turrianus are thoroughly refuted. With them they vainly try to free the Constitutions from these absurdities, inventing some notion of discourse (I know not what) in which it is allowed to mix true and false, old and new, in short to tell tales and lie, and to invent whatever one likes without disgrace.

units.la: ÆC autem omnia, quæ ex Apostolorum persona dicta, longe, ut quivis videt, absurdissima ac stultissima sunt, Bovius & Turrianus ut aliquo pacto molliant, inprimis statuunt, non ipsos Apostolos, sed Clementem Romanum hos Constitutionum libros scripsisse. Tum huic fundamento illud deinde superstruunt, Clementem Apostolos induxisse loquentes, ut sit totum opus quodammodo dramaticum. Sic enim Bovius Hac auctoritate praditi Apostoli, ut divinum cultum constituerent, & Euangelicas leges stabilirent, post Domini ascensionem, fidelium cætu in ordines distributo, singulis ordinibus officia, & propriam vivendi normam dederunt: sacra, cæremonias, preces, jejunia, ritus, solennia omnia instituerunt, fidem, hoc est, credendi legem, pro ratione temporum explicaverunt. Hæc vero omnia Apostoli in Ecclesiis, in quibus Euangelium nunciaverant, runt, voce ac verbis tradiderunt, Hęc ita fabulatus, Has igitur (inquit) traditiones, quæ nullis litterarum monumentis ab Apostolis commendatæ sunt, sed sermone & non scripta institutione ad Ecclesias pervenerunt, collegit in unum Clemens Pauli familiaris ac comes, atque iis octo libris digessit. De ipsa vero operis ratione infra, pagina abhinc 20. sic disserit; Quod attinet ad genus sermonum, cum Clemens disciplinam ex Apostolorum sermonibus excerptam, atque fidelibus traditam, in Ecclesiis vellet esse perpetuam, eam iis octo libris est complexus, in quibus, suppressa sua persona, omnem sermonem tribuit Apostolis, putans, opinor, majorem authoritatem habituram orationem, si quæ ab ipsis præcepta accepisset, ea Apostolos ipsos facere exponentes. Dixi autem, eum suum nomen suppressisse, propterea quod ex propria persona non est præfatus, quanquam se aliquando faciat ex cœtu loquentium unum, socium Apostolorum, & in rebus agendis administrum. Ex quo intelligitur, hujusmodi scribendi genus esse quasi mistum ex dialogo, & ex eo genere, in quo perpetuo orationis cursu res narrantur, quod Διηγηματικὸν vocant. Nam ex ea parte, qua loquentes inducuntur, videtur dialogi similitudinem habere; quatenus sermones non habentur inter ipsos loquentes, sed à principrincipio in Apostolorum personam instituta oratio eandem formam conservat, quasi ipsi Apostoli hos libros conscripserint, potest in fusum illud & perpetuum genus referri. His ita constitutis, Bovius de suo illo sermonum genere, partim ex dialogo, partim ex diexodico conflato, quod Clementi in his Constitutionibus tribuit, multa exsequitur mirabilia.Huic enim ex ea methodo, quam tenuit, vult licuisse acta, instituta-que Apostolorum, non ex temporum, quo ea acciderunt, ordine narrare, sed interdum, pro rerum, quas tractat, ingenio, ultima ante prima, superiora post inferiora. Sed & illud vult ei ex eadem ratione licuisse, fingere Apostolos in unum locum congregatos ea perscripsisse, quae tamen revera nunquam ipsi omnes uno tempore, atque in unum locum convenientes praeceperunt, sed diversis temporibus, separatim. Haec ille; quorum plane gemina sunt, quae habet Turrianus: Constitutiones Apostolorum scriptas esse factis personis. Clementem in hisce libris constituendi, & loquendi, quae in eis continentur, partes Apostolis, quibus convenire, & a quibus profecta esse scribat, dedisse; licet nunquam inter se locuti essent, neque scripsissent, ut eos loquentes & scribentes facit. Hunc enim morem habere Dialogum. Hactenus isti. Me vero virorum doctorum miseret ac pudet in dealbando Æthiope, & exornando, atque expoliendo stultissimi pariter ac impudentissimi hominis dramate, nequicquam ingenio suo abutentium,operamque ludentium. Illud mitto, quod principio, sane suaviter, & ex una animi sui libidine, fingunt omnes, qui his libris explicati habentur, ritus, omnia sacra, jejunia, preces, ac caremonias, Apostolos in eis Ecclesiis, voce ac verbis tradidisse, in quibus Euangelium annunciaverunt. Id vero quam non modo temere, sed & falso, ac inverecunde, dicatur, & ex iis quæ hactenus disputavimus, patet: & patebit etiam multo clarius ex his, quæ mox adjecturi sumus. Quin ne illud quidem certum est, quod ponit Bovius, aliquid Apostolos iis Ecclesiis, quas ædificabant, voce tradidisse, quod non sit in Novi Testamenti libris perscriptum. Neque plane & ex omni parte verum est, quod tertio loco additur, Constitutionum authorem eas traditiones colligere, quæ nullis litterarum monumentis ab Apostolis commendatæ erant, sed sermone, & non scripta institutione ad Ecclesias pervenerant. Iste enim pseud-apostolus omnia ἔγγραφα & ἄγγραφα nullo discrimine convasat. Nam plurima habet & ad fidem, & ad ritus, disciplinamque pertinentia, quæ aut plane eadem, vel leviter tantum immutata in veris Apostolorum monumentis leguntur. Sed his missis ad rem venio. Ac illud quidem imprimis Bovio, Turrianoque libens concedo, quod & partim jam invictis argumentis probatum est, & mox non infirmioribus, ut spero, demonstrabitur, has sane Constitutiones nunquam scripsisse Christi Domini Apostolos, nunquam in octo hos libros degessisse, nunquam ita inter se locutos esse aut scripsisse, ut eos iste planus loquentes, scribentesque facit; nunquam denique in unum locum uno tempore convenisse, ut haec praeciperent. Rem totam merum drama, & quidem non bellum, neque facetum, sed absurdum, ac insulsum esse fateor; in quo istum, quisquis est, ineptum sane & ineruditum ludionem, Apostolos loquentes induxisse ideo cum Bovio putaverim, quod majorem authoritatem habituram orationem speraret exeorum persona institutam. Caetera vero, quae Bovius & Turrianus ponunt, nego.
units.tr: All the things said in the person of the Apostles are, as anyone can see, far the most absurd and foolish. So Bovius and Turrianus, to soften them in some way, first maintain that the Apostles themselves did not write these books of the Constitutions, but Clement of Rome did. Then they build on this foundation the claim that Clement introduced the Apostles as speakers, so that the whole work is in a sense dramatic. Bovius says: Invested with this authority, the Apostles, in order to establish the divine worship and fix the laws of the Gospel, after the Lord's ascension distributed the assembly of the faithful into orders, and gave each order its duties and its own rule of living. They instituted the sacred rites, ceremonies, prayers, fasts, customs, and all solemnities, and they explained the faith, that is, the rule of belief, according to the needs of the times. All these things the Apostles handed down by voice and word in the churches in which they had proclaimed the Gospel. Having thus spun his tale, he goes on: "These traditions, then (he says), which were not commended by the Apostles in any written records, but came to the churches by word of mouth and unwritten instruction, were gathered together by Clement, the companion and fellow-traveller of Paul, and arranged in these eight books." On the plan of the work itself, he speaks further on, on page 20 from here, as follows: As for the kind of discourse, since Clement wished the discipline drawn from the Apostles' words and handed down to the faithful to be perpetual in the churches, he comprised it in these eight books, in which, having suppressed his own person, he attributes all the speech to the Apostles, thinking, I suppose, that a discourse would carry greater authority if it set forth as the Apostles' own what he had received as their precepts. I have said that he suppressed his own name, because he does not speak in his own person, although at times he makes himself one of the company of speakers, a fellow of the Apostles and an assistant in their business. From this it is understood that this kind of writing is a sort of mixture of dialogue and that kind in which things are narrated in a continuous flow of speech, which the Greeks call diegematic. For insofar as speakers are introduced, it seems to have a resemblance to dialogue; but insofar as the speeches are not held between the speakers themselves, and the discourse, set up from the beginning in the person of the Apostles, keeps the same form, as if the Apostles themselves had written these books, it can be referred to that fluid and continuous kind. With these matters so settled, Bovius, concerning his own kind of speech, partly dialogue and partly diegematic, which he attributes to Clement in these Constitutions, works out many marvellous points. For he wishes that Clement, by the method he followed, was permitted to narrate the deeds and institutions of the Apostles not in the order of the times when they happened, but sometimes, according to the nature of the matters he treats, the last before the first and the later before the earlier. But he also wishes that, on the same principle, Clement was allowed to pretend that the Apostles, gathered into one place, wrote down these things, which in truth they never all taught together at one time and in one place, but at different times and separately. So much for him. Turrianus's statements are exactly twins of these: The Constitutions of the Apostles are written under fictitious persons. Clement, in these books, in setting out and speaking the things contained in them, gave to the Apostles the parts that suit them and from whom he writes they proceeded, although they never spoke among themselves or wrote, as he makes them speak and write. For this is the custom of dialogue. So far they. But I pity and am ashamed of learned men who spend their effort, and their wit, in whitewashing the Ethiopian and adorning and polishing the drama of a man equally foolish and shameless, and who play with their labour to no purpose. I pass over the fact that all who are held to have explained these books assume at the outset, quite pleasantly and from the mere desire of their own minds, that the rites, all the sacred things, fasts, prayers, and ceremonies were handed down by the Apostles by voice and word in those churches in which they had preached the Gospel. That this is said not only rashly but also falsely and shamelessly is plain from what we have argued so far, and it will be plainer still from what we are about to add. Indeed, it is not even certain what Bovius asserts, that the Apostles handed down by voice to the churches they founded something that is not written in the books of the New Testament. Nor is it altogether and in every part true what is added in the third place, that the author of the Constitutions gathered those traditions which were not commended by the Apostles in any written records, but came to the churches by word and unwritten instruction. For this pseudo-apostle lumps together all written and unwritten matter without any distinction. Indeed he has very many things pertaining both to faith and to rites and discipline, which are read either exactly the same, or only slightly changed, in the true monuments of the Apostles. But setting these aside, I come to the matter. And first of all I willingly grant to Bovius and Turrianus this point, which has partly been proved by unanswerable arguments already, and will soon, I hope, be shown by no weaker ones: that the Apostles of Christ the Lord never wrote these Constitutions, never arranged them into these eight books, never spoke or wrote to one another in such a way as this smooth speaker and writer makes them, and never at last gathered in one place at one time to give these precepts. I confess that the whole thing is a mere drama, and not a witty or elegant one, but absurd and insipid. In it, I would suppose with Bovius that the man, whoever he is, who introduced the Apostles as speakers was a foolish and unlearned player, who hoped that a discourse set up in their person would have greater authority. The rest of what Bovius and Turrianus put forward, I deny.

units.la: Ac primo illud, quod, ut impostoris facinus defendant, statuunt, id, quod secutus est, scribendi genus licitum, ac laudatum esse.
units.tr: And first, that which they lay down in order to defend the impostor's deed, namely that the kind of writing he followed is lawful and praised.

units.la: Tum, quod assumit Bovius, in hoc genere licere rerum ac temporum ordinem perturbare, & facere, ut ea velut gesta ii narrent, qui, dum gererentur, vel nondum erant, vel jam mortui erant ; ac denique illud quod tertio uterque affirmant, Clementem, Pauli comitem, hujus dramatis authorem esse. Nam quod ad primum attinet, laudatos scriptores fateor viros in Dialogis ea inter se colloquentes fecisse, quæ ipsi fortasse vel nunquam omnino, vel certe non iis verbis, neque eo ordine, ac modo, locuti erant, quo eos loqui faciunt ; qualiter apud Græcos quidem Plato, Plutarchus, alii ; apud Latinos, Cicero, & multi alii, quos enumerare, longum est, Dialogos instituerunt. Sed primo illud non abs re, ut mihi quidem videtur, quæri potest, an ut illis Socratem, Gorgiam, Alcibiadem, Crassum, Antonium, Cottam, & cæteros de rebus vel philosophicis, vel oratoriis disputantes fingere licuit ; ita & huic nostro artifici, eos sermones habentes Apostolos inducere licuerit, quos nunquam habuerunt? Nam & his quam illis multo majorem deberi reverentiam constat, & longe gravius esse periculum, si ea pro Apostolicis habeantur, quæ non sunt Apostolorum, quam si pro Socraticis, vel Antonianis, quæ nunquam Socratis, vel Antonii fuerunt. Non ergo si Platonem, aut Marcum Tullium in Socrate, & Antonio, & cæteris, quorum personas in dialogis assumunt, impune ludere fas fuit, eo consequens est, ut nostro impostori idem in Apostolos licuerit, quorum sacrosanctum esse apud omnes Christianos nomen decet. Huc & illud accedit, quod nihil est inter utrorumque facta simile. Nam Platonis,& Ciceronis,& aliorum, quæ sunt de hoc genere orationes, eas ad dialogorum speciem pertinere manifestum est, in quibus plures inter se probabiliter colloquuntur: nostrorum vero Διαλογίων sermo plane abnormis est, & inusitatus. Dialogus quidem non est;in quo nullæ sunt scilicet personarum in colloquendo vices; jugis est ac perpetua, vel omnium utplurimum uno consensu, vel interdum singulorum de Ecclesiæ rebus decernentium oratio. Neque ipse Bovius ausus est dialogicum hoc opus profiteri. Dixit esse quasi mistum ex dialogo, & eo genere quod diexodicum appellatur. Sed quod Bovii pace dictum sit, nihil nostris Constitutionibus cum Dialogo commune est. Dialogus enim, quod vel nomen sonat, duorum est vel plurium inter se colloquentium per vices recurrens atque alternans oratio; quale in istis Constitutionibus nihil occurrit. Sed, inquit Bovius, ex ea parte, qua loquentes, nimirum Apostoli, inducuntur, videtur hoc opus Dialogi similitudinem habere. Fateret, si inter se loquentes, ut apud Platonem, & Ciceronem, & ex divinis scriptoribus ribus apud Iobum personæ inducerentur. Nunc qualem nobis Bovius dialogum fingit, in quo nulli quidem inter se colloquuntur, nulli interrogant, nulli respondent; sed virorum de rebus Ecclesiasticis apud Christianos leges ferentium scripta oratio perpetuo quodam cursu fertur? plane ut vel grandis aliqua Epistola ab absentibus ad absentes data, vel certe, ut legum codex ad subditos à principibus, aut à senatoribus scriptus, missusque? Desinat ergo Bovius suos nobis Dialogos obtrudere. Nihil ad Διαλογίας dialogus, vel dialogi leges. Totum eorum opus mere διάλογικον est, nulla Dialogi mistura temperatum; quod à capite ad calcem uno tenore decurrit; nulla personarum inter se colloquentium varietate distinctum. Id tantum in oratione disciminis cernitur, quod cum omnes Apostoli simul semelque uno velut ore plerumque, & in longe maxima operis parte loquentes fingantur, est interdum ubi singuli, veluti tacentibus reliquis, erumpunt,& soli aliquantisper verba faciunt, non apud cæteros collegas, ut cum iis colloqui dici aut videri possint, sed apud eosdem (Christianos scilicet, quotquot sunt, vel episcopos, vel homines) ad quos directa erat initio omnium oratio. Itaque quod iis locis occurrit, Et ego Petrus, Et ego Iacobus cobus constituo, &c. inepte quidem, ac præter laudatorum scriptorum usum, & consuetudinem dictum fateor; ad dialogi vero formam accedere, nego. Cum enim Apostoli universi hæc loquentes scribentesque jam ab initio operis inducti fuerint, eam orationis formam servari ad extremum decebat, & quæ quorundam propria, ac singularia erant, ea ipsa ab universis, quibus non erant incognita, pro instituta sermonis ratione narrari, hoc vel alio simili modo; Ita quoque unus ex nobis Petrus, vel Iacobus, &c. constituit: pro quo, sed inepte, solam Petri, Iacobi, & aliorum similiter personam in medium universorum sermonem velut subito irrumpentem, & omnem orationis œconomiam stolide, ac præter decori leges, perturbantem scriptor facit, ut quivis facile animadvertet, qui hæc Constitutionum loca diligenter inspexerit. Nobis satis est, quod simile istorum exemplum neque ex sacris, neque ex profanis authoribus, qui quidem laudati sint, afferri ullum potest. Ista ergo est, non quod vult Bovius, dialogi mistura, sed crassa, ac inexcusabilis ineruditi scriptoris ἁμαρτία. Huc & alterum accedit, ingens ac præcipuum hujus scriptoris a Dialogorum authoribus discrimen; quod hi quidem, etsi aliquid fingant, nulli tamen men impofturam faciunt ; hic vero fraudis, ac doli mali manifestus tenetur. Nam qui Dialogos cum laude instituunt, ii personam suam non occultant , sed aperte in ipso statim limine edunt , ac profitentur. Vel enim narrant, ac præsantur, quæ occasio, quisve casus eos, quos colloqui faciunt, in unum locum coëgerit, & in eos, quos illis tribuunt, sermones induxerit ; ut Cicero in Oratore , & in Bruto, & alii multi fecerunt: vel certè præscripto operi nomine suo testantur, se totius dramatis authores esse ; quod Plato in plerisque Dialogis, & alii cumplures secuti sunt, ita ut nemo vere possit queri, sibi verba data fuisse; nemo jure dubitare queat, an opus, quod obtruditur , ab uno aliquo eorum, qui colloquentes inducuntur, scriptum fuerit. Itaque nemo hactenus repertus est, qui vel leviter suspicatus sit, aut à Socrate , aut à Crasso scriptos esse eos Dialogos, qui apud Platonem , & Ciceronem extant, & in quibus illi loquentes inducuntur. Nostrarum Constitutionum parens plane aliter se gessit. Nam neque narrat,uspiam, cur, quave ex occasione Apostolos hæc una congregatos loqui faciat ; neque nomen suum operi ut authoris, præscripsit;neque denique vel suæ,vel alterius,præterquam Apostolorum & sociorum , personæ sonæ notitiam ullam in aliqua operis parte edidit; unde dici queat, non ipsos Apostolos, sed alium aliquem hos libros compo- suisse. Nam & Apostoli toto passim opere se hæc, non decernere modo, & constituere, sed etiam scribere, atque ad episcopos, cæterosque Christianos mittere affirmant; & titulus operis in ipso statim limine, Apostolorum nomen præfert, Clementis vero nomen, quod nunc in titulo legitur, & additum videtur ab alia, quam ab authoris, manu, (de quo mox pluribus dicendum erit) neque suadet, Clementem operis scriptorem fuisse. Sic enim habet titulus; Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος τῆς Ρωμαίων ἐπισκόπου τε καὶ πολίτου. Constitutiones sanctorum Apostolorum per Clementem Romanum episcopum & civem. Jam vero, cum hi Διαταγεῖς in ipso opere diserte narrent, se sua hanc καθολικὴν διδασκαλίαν διαπεμφθεῖσαν διὰ τὸ Κλήμεντος, mississe per Clementem comministrum suum, apparet, illa in titulo verba διὰ Κλήμεντος, per Clementem, (siquidem ab ipso authore scripta fuisse placeat) significare Constitutiones per Clementem non scriptas (quod volunt Bovius & Turrianus) sed missas fuisse, quod diserte memorant ipsi Διαταγεῖς. Neque sane negari potest, quin præpositio διὰ multo sepius in hoc sensu sumatur, quam in illo. Nam quam quis defert epistolam, vel constitutionem, ea ἀν' αὐτῶ πέμπτεσθαι, per eum mitti, & vulgo & recte dicitur; quam autem quis ipse scribit, ea ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, ab eo potius, quam ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, per eum, scripta dicitur. Ergo neque hic adhibitum Clementis nomen certo prodit authorem operis fuisse Clementem: illud potius innuit, missum quidem fuisse ac delatum per Clementem, non autem ab eo scriptum; omninoque videtur, quisquis hoc opus condidit, id voluisse, idque conatus ac molitus esse, ut crederent homines, sua illa ab Apostolis vere scripta fuisse ac missa. Itaque qui in Constitutiones has incidunt, eos necesse est statuere, vel eas ab Apostolis vere esse scriptas, vel certe ab aliquo impostore per summam & inexpiabilem fraudem Apostolis affictas, ac suppositas. Frustra ergo Bovius, frustra Turrianus, ad Dialogorum leges confugiunt, in quibus nullum est fraudi, & impostura praesidium. Per has enim leges personas inter se probabiliter colloquentes inducere licet; tuum partum alteri supponere, tuoque operi alterius nomen praescribere non licet. Illud elegantie est, hoc fraudis: illud ingenii, hoc impostura: illud etiam boni, ac honesti viri fecerint; hoc nemo nisi planus.
units.tr: Then there is what Bovius assumes: that in this kind of writing it is permissible to disturb the order of things and times, and to have people narrate as things done those events that either had not yet happened, or had already passed away, while they were being done. Finally, there is the third point on which both affirm that Clement, the companion of Paul, is the author of this drama. As to the first point, I grant that the writers praised have made men in their Dialogues converse with one another in ways that perhaps they never spoke at all, or certainly not in those words, in that order, or in that manner in which the authors make them speak. Among the Greeks Plato, Plutarch and others did this, and among the Latins Cicero and many others, too many to list, composed Dialogues. But first, it can not unreasonably be asked, as it seems to me, whether it was lawful for this author of ours to introduce the Apostles holding conversations they never held, just as it was lawful for those writers to imagine Socrates, Gorgias, Alcibiades, Crassus, Antonius, Cotta and the rest disputing about philosophical or oratorical matters. For it is agreed that far greater reverence is owed to the Apostles than to these others, and the danger is far more serious if things that are not the Apostles' are taken as Apostolic, than if things that were never Socrates' or Antonius' are taken as theirs. So it does not follow, because Plato or Marcus Tullius was allowed to play with impunity with Socrates, Antonius and the others whose persons they assume in their dialogues, that the same license is granted to our impostor with the Apostles, whose name ought to be held sacrosanct by all Christians. To this must be added that there is nothing similar between the two kinds of composition. For it is clear that the speeches of Plato, Cicero and others of this kind belong to the form of dialogue, in which several persons converse with one another in a plausible way. But the discourse of our Dialogues is utterly irregular and unusual. It is not a dialogue, in which there is of course an alternation of speakers in conversation; it is a continuous and unbroken speech, delivered sometimes by all of them with one accord, or sometimes by individuals who decide matters concerning the affairs of the Church. Bovius himself has not dared to profess that this work is dialogic. He says it is a kind of mixture of dialogue and the kind called diexodicum. But, with all respect to Bovius, nothing in our Constitutions has anything in common with dialogue. For a dialogue, as even the name suggests, is a speech of two or more persons conversing with one another, recurring and alternating in turn; and nothing of this sort occurs in these Constitutions. But, says Bovius, from the part in which the speakers, namely the Apostles, are introduced, this work seems to have a likeness to dialogue. He would have a point if they were introduced conversing with one another, as in Plato, Cicero, and among the divine writers, the persons in Job. But what sort of dialogue is Bovius imagining for us, in which no one converses with anyone, no one asks questions, no one answers, but the written discourse of men who lay down laws about ecclesiastical matters among Christians flows on in one continuous course? Plainly like a long letter sent from absent persons to absent persons, or certainly like a code of laws written and sent by princes or senators to their subjects. Let Bovius therefore stop obtruding his dialogues on us. The rules of dialogue have nothing to do with these Dialogues. Their whole work is purely dialogic [διάλογικον], not tempered by any mixture of dialogue; it runs from beginning to end in one unbroken tenor, and is not broken up by any variety of persons conversing with one another. The only difference visible in the discourse is this: since all the Apostles are generally represented as speaking at once and together, with one voice, and for by far the greater part of the work, there are occasionally places where individuals break in, as if the rest were silent, and speak alone for a while, not to their other colleagues, so that they could be said or seen to converse with them, but to the same audience to whom the whole speech was addressed from the beginning (Christians, that is, whether bishops or ordinary people). So, as for the places where it occurs, And I Peter, And I James, ordain, and so on, I admit that this is said awkwardly and contrary to the usage and custom of the writers praised; but I deny that it approaches the form of dialogue. For since all the Apostles were introduced from the beginning of the work as speaking and writing these things, that form of discourse ought to have been maintained to the end, and the things peculiar and individual to certain of them should have been related by all, to whom they were not unknown, in keeping with the plan of the discourse, in this or some similar manner: Thus also one of us, Peter, or James, etc., ordains. Instead, and awkwardly, the writer makes the person of Peter, James and others alone suddenly burst into the middle of the speech of all, and stupidly disturbs the whole economy of the discourse, contrary to the laws of propriety, as anyone who carefully examines these passages of the Constitutions will easily notice. It is enough for us that no similar example of this can be brought from either sacred or profane authors who are praised. So this is not, as Bovius wants, a mixture of dialogue, but the gross and inexcusable error [ἁμαρτία] of an unlearned writer. To this must be added another great and chief difference between this writer and the authors of Dialogues. Those authors, though they invent something, do not practise deception on anyone; but this writer is plainly held guilty of fraud and wicked trickery. For those who write Dialogues well do not conceal their own person, but openly declare and profess it at the very threshold. Either they explain and set forth what occasion or chance gathered those they make converse into one place, and led them to the speeches they assign to them, as Cicero did in the Orator and the Brutus, and many others did; or at least they attest on the title page, under their own name, that they are the authors of the whole drama, as Plato did in most of his Dialogues, and as several others followed, so that no one can truly complain that words were put into his mouth, and no one can rightly doubt whether the work foisted on him was written by one of those who are introduced conversing. Thus no one has yet been found who even slightly suspected that the Dialogues which exist in Plato and Cicero, and in which those men are introduced speaking, were written by Socrates or Crassus. But the parent of our Constitutions has behaved quite differently. For he nowhere relates why or on what occasion he makes the Apostles speak here gathered together; nor did he prescribe his own name to the work as its author; nor finally did he give any information in any part of the work about his own person, or that of anyone else except the Apostles and their associates, from which it could be said that these books were composed not by the Apostles themselves but by some other person. For the Apostles, throughout the whole work, affirm that they not only decree and ordain these things but also write them and send them to the bishops and other Christians; and the title of the work, right at the threshold, bears the name of the Apostles. But the name of Clement, which is now read in the title and seems to have been added by a hand other than the author's (about which more will be said shortly), does not suggest that Clement was the writer of the work. For the title reads: The Constitutions of the holy Apostles through Clement, bishop and citizen of Rome [Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος τῆς Ρωμαίων ἐπισκόπου τε καὶ πολίτου]. Now since these Constitutions expressly state within the work itself that they sent this universal teaching through Clement, their fellow-minister [καθολικὴν διδασκαλίαν διαπεμφθεῖσαν διὰ τὸ Κλήμεντος], it is clear that the words through Clement in the title (if it is agreed that they were written by the author himself) signify that the Constitutions were not written through Clement (as Bovius and Turrianus want) but were sent through him, which the Constitutions themselves expressly mention. Nor can it be denied that the preposition διά is used far more often in this sense than in that. For a letter or constitution that someone carries is commonly and correctly said to be sent by him [ἀν' αὐτῶ πέμπτεσθαι, per eum mitti]; but what someone writes himself is said to be written by him [ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, ab eo], rather than through him [ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, per eum]. Therefore the name of Clement used here does not certainly show that Clement was the author of the work; it rather hints that it was indeed sent and delivered through Clement, but not written by him. And in general it seems that whoever composed this work intended, and strove and laboured, to make people believe that these things had truly been written and sent by the Apostles. Therefore those who come upon these Constitutions must necessarily conclude either that they were truly written by the Apostles, or that they were feigned and foisted upon the Apostles by some impostor, through a supreme and inexpiable fraud. In vain, then, do Bovius and Turrianus flee to the rules of dialogue, in which there is no protection for fraud and imposture. For by these rules it is permitted to introduce persons who converse with one another in a plausible way; but it is not permitted to pass off one's own offspring as another's, or to prescribe another's name to one's own work. The former is a matter of eloquence, the latter of fraud; the former of talent, the latter of imposture; the former may be done even by good and honest men, but the latter by no one except a plain forger.

units.la: Jam neque illud verius est, quod secundo loco statuit Bovius, huic scriptori persuum illud ex dialogo & Διεξοδικῷ mistū sermonis genus, licuisse rerum ac temporum ordinem miscere ac perturbare. Hoc quidem strenue factum à Constitutionum parente, & fateor, & supra probavi, & Bovius ipse concedit. Id in ullo, sive dialogico, ac dramatico, sive diexodico, sive ex utraque specie mixto, sive alio denique sermonis genere licere, salsissimum est, & siquis hujusmodi aliquid usurpavit, perperam ac praeter rectas scribendi leges, usurpavit. Noster Ἀλεξάνδρων faber Jacobum, verbi gratia, Hierosolymorum episcopum, loquentem facit, quo tempore certum est eum fuisse mortuum: Apostolos de Ioannis Evangelio praecipientes inducit, quod scriptum fuisse, cum unus ex Apostolis superesset Ioannes, omnes consentiunt: multa alia, ut ostendimus, Apostolis tribuit ab eorum vel aetate & memoria, vel moribus & ingenio, vel cognitione & sapientia abhorrentia. Proferat Bovius, si potest, vel unum sive Dialogorum, sive alterius operis authorem, cui talia impune, ac citra reprehensionem mentiri concessum fuerit. Cicero quidem, & Plato, & alii, quotquot sunt, Dialogorum probati laudatique scriptores, nemo nescit quantopere ab hoc peccato sibi caverint, quamque studiose omnia ad veri speciem effinxerint, nihil personis, quas colloqui faciunt, uspiam tribuerint, quod esset ab eorū, vel moribus & institutis, vel etiam (quod longe turpissimum est) ætate atque temporibus alienum. Ne Poëtis quidem ipsis, quorum maxima est in hoc genere potestas, quisquam id concesserit, quod Bovius suo fabulatori vindicat. Notum est illud summi & poëtæ, & Critici a:
units.tr: Nor is the second point that Bovius makes any more accurate, namely that this writer was free to mix and disorder the sequence of events and times in his mixed style of dialogue and narrative [Διεξοδικῷ]. The Constitutions' author did indeed do this boldly; I admit it, I have already shown it above, and Bovius himself concedes it. But that such a liberty is allowed in any kind of writing, whether dialogue, drama, narrative, a mixture of these, or any other genre, is most absurd. Anyone who has taken it has done so wrongly and against the sound rules of writing. Our Alexandrian craftsman [Ἀλεξάνδρων] makes James, for instance, bishop of Jerusalem, speak at a time when it is certain he was dead. He introduces the Apostles giving instructions about John's Gospel, which everyone agrees was written when John was the only Apostle still alive. He assigns many other things to the Apostles that, as we have shown, clash with their age and memory, their character and temperament, their knowledge and wisdom. Let Bovius produce, if he can, a single author of dialogues or of any other work who was permitted to lie like this without blame or rebuke. Cicero, Plato and all the other approved and praised writers of dialogue, as everyone knows, took great care to avoid this fault. They shaped everything to look like truth, and they never attributed to the persons they made speak anything that was foreign to their character, customs and institutions, or, what is far more disgraceful, to their age and times. Not even the poets, who have the greatest licence in this kind of writing, have been granted what Bovius claims for his fabulist. The saying of that great poet and critic is well known:

units.la: - - Pictoribus atque poëtis Quælibet audendi semper fuit æqua potestas.
units.tr: "Painters and poets have always had an equal power to dare whatever they please."

units.la: Sed non ut placidis coëant immitia, non ut Serpentes avibus geminentur, tigribus agni.
units.tr: "But not so that savage things may mingle with gentle ones, that serpents may be paired with birds, lambs with tigers."

units.la: Itaque ne Virgilius quidem impune tulit, quod Palinurum portus Velinos nominantem induxerit; cum Velia oppidum, à quo portus Velinus dictus est, diu post Palinuri ævum in agro Lucano conditum, & eo nomine appellatum sit. Id enim, ut est apud Gellium b, reprehendit Hyginus; & merito quidem, ut videtur. Neque id illi Grammatico placuisse arbitror, quod idem, tametsi summus, ac cætera laudatissimus author, Æneam suum cum Didone Pœna faciat viventem ac versantem; quam nonnisi trecentis post Æneæ tempora annis vixisse clarum est. Quod si ne Poëtis quidem ista conceduntur, quanto minus rerum Christianarum, & quidem Apostolicarum Scriptori licet omnem temporum rationem spernere? eaque Apostolos velut facta diserte ac nominatim memorantes inducere, quae post eorum mortem contigerunt? Plane ergo concidit nova illa, ac inaudita Bovii methodus, qua ille immanem suarum Διαταγῶν parenti potestatem concedit quidvis pro arbitrio fingendi, ac mentiendi. Nulla ratione, nulla juris vel aequi specie, nullo denique, nisi peccantium, exemplo nititur prodigiosa illa methodus: ut necesse sit, qui eam usurpat, τῶν Διδαγῶν architectum, non modo, quod concedit Bovius, Dialogistam, & ποιητὴν, sive fictorem; sed etiam mendosum, pessimumque ποιητὴν fuisse; qui res à se invicem alienas conjunxit ac miscuit, impudentia nescio an imperitia, inscitiaque majori. Sed hoc loco operae pretium est aliud Turriani commentum obiter refellere; qui, ut à suo Διδαγῶν scriptore turpissimae κακοπλαςίας crimen depellat, ait a, eum ἀποστόλις, quos loquentes inducit, annumerare secundum idioma Scripturae, Jacobum occisum, & Stephanum lapidatum, qui τῇ γνώμῃ & secundum spiritum praesentes fuerunt. Hanc enim doctrinam Catholicam, ab Apostolis praedicatam, quam Clemens litteris mandavit,
units.tr: So even Virgil did not get away unpunished for making Palinurus name the "Velian harbour," when the town of Velia, from which the Velian harbour took its name, was founded in the land of Lucania long after Palinurus' time and was called by that name. Hyginus, as Gellius reports, criticised this, and rightly so, it seems. I do not think that grammarian was pleased either by the fact that the same author, though a great and most praised writer, makes his Aeneas live and move about with Dido of Carthage, who is clearly known to have lived only three hundred years after Aeneas' time. If the poets are not allowed even these things, how much less is a writer of Christian matters, and especially of Apostolic ones, permitted to disregard all chronology and to introduce the Apostles as explicitly naming and recounting events that happened after their death? So that new and unheard-of method of Bovius plainly collapses, the method by which he grants the parent of his monstrous Constitutions [Διαταγῶν] the power to invent and lie about whatever he likes. That monstrous method rests on no reason, no appearance of law or equity, and finally on no example except that of wrongdoers. So whoever uses it must make the architect of the Constitutions [Διδαγῶν] not only, as Bovius concedes, a dialogist and a poet, or maker of fictions, but also a bad and most wicked poet, who joined and mixed things foreign to each other, through a greater degree of impudence, or ignorance, or unskilfulness, I know not which. But at this point it is worth briefly refuting another invention of Turrianus. To clear his author of the charge of most shameful bad workmanship, Turrianus says that the Apostles whom the author introduces as speaking are counted among them in the sense of Scripture's idiom: James, who was killed, and Stephen, who was stoned, who were present "in mind" and "according to the Spirit." For this Catholic teaching, preached by the Apostles and committed to writing by Clement,

units.la: a Explan. in l. 8. Const. t. 4. vit, & has Constitutiones, Iacobum quoque fratrem Ioannis, & Stephanum, Spiritu cum reliquis congregatos sanxisse. Sed primo inauditum est, quę in terris geruntur, ea à mortuis quoque gesta dici, quod ista eorum spiritus scilicet probare quoque putentur. Et si talia recte dicantur, omnino, quod ait Reveredissimus noster Usserius , eadem quoque ratione, affirmare potuit Constitutionum author, non Baptistam modo, & Symeonem senem, sed etiam Ieremiam & Ezechielem, & Esaiam, & Mosem, & omnes Dei Prophetas, una cum Apostolis convenire, & his Διδαχαῖς condendis ac scribendis adsuisse; quod Turrianus fortasse, quo est stomacho, haud ægre concoxerit; cæterorum, nescio an ullus sit admissurus. Absit vero, ut hoc sermonis portentum Scripturæ idioma esse concedamus. Fateor, Paulum ad Corinthios ita scribere b; Ego quidem absens corpore, præsens autem Spiritu, jam judicavi ut præsens, eum qui sic operatus est, in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, tradere huiusmodi Satanæ. Eundem memini ad Colossenses quoque hæc scripsisse c; Etsi corpore absens sum, sed spiritu vobiscum sum, gaudens & videns ordinem vestrum, & firmamentum ejus, quæ in Christo est, fidei vestræ. Sed hæc quid ad Turriani glossam faciant, ciant, vel quid τῶν Διαταγίων sententiam juvent, quidve cum ea commune habeant, non video. Paulus, qui haec dicit, in vivis erat, quo tempore illa scripsit; Iacobus & Stephanus cum haec dixisse finguntur, jampridem erant mortui. Quod Paulus scribit, id ipsi notissimum, compertissimumque erat, se scilicet spiritu cum iis, ad quos scribebat, praesentem fuisse. Quod scribit impostor, Iacobum & Sthephanum Apostolis ista scribentibus, saltem spiritu adfuisse, hoc est, animo & cogitatione, id nequeipsi, neque ulli mortalium notum esse potuit. Denique Paulus diserte dicit, quo sensu, quove modo & Corinthiis & Colossensibus adfuerit, corpore (inquit) absens, spiritu praesens. Siccine etiam apud nostrum Διαταγία Iacobus ac Stephanus? Ille vero omnia plane aliter. Neque eorum praesentiam, cujusmodi fuerit, corporis ne, an spiritus, tantum definit, neque omnino vel corporis eorum, vel spiritus meminit, sed suos Apostolos simpliciter ita loqui facit a: Ἡμεῖς νῦν δι᾽ ἀ τὸ αὐτὸ γενόμενοι Πέτρος καὶ Ἀνδρέας, Ἰάκωβος καὶ Ἰωάννης οἱ Ζεβεδαίου, &c. ἅμα πάντες καὶ ὅτι τὸ αὐτὸ γενόμενοι, ἐγκαλοῦμεν ὑμῖν, &c. Nos nunc in unum congregati Petrus & Andreas, Iacobus & Ioannes filii Zebedaei, &c. una omnes in unum locum congregati, scripsimus vobis, &c. Vides, ut Ioan-
units.tr: (footnote: Explan. in l. 8. Const. t. 4.) ... and these Constitutions declare that James, the brother of John, and Stephen, gathered together with the rest in the Spirit, sanctioned them. But first, it is unheard of to say that things done on earth were also done by the dead, on the supposition that their spirits are evidently thought to approve them as well. And if such things were rightly said, then, as our most reverend Ussher says, the author of the Constitutions could by the same reasoning affirm that not only the Baptist and old Simeon, but also Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Moses and all the prophets of God came together with the Apostles and took part in composing and writing these Teachings [Διδαχαῖς]. Turrianus, perhaps, with his stomach, would have digested this without difficulty, but I do not know whether any of the others would admit it. Far be it from us to concede that this monstrous piece of talk is Scriptural idiom. I admit that Paul writes thus to the Corinthians: "For I, indeed absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, him who has done such a thing, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan." I remember that he also wrote this to the Colossians: "For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and beholding your order and the steadfastness of your faith in Christ." But I do not see what these words have to do with Turrianus' gloss, or what they support in the opinion of the Constitutions [Διαταγίων], or what they have in common with it. Paul, who writes these things, was alive at the time he wrote them. James and Stephen are pretended to have said these things long after they were dead. What Paul writes was perfectly well known and certain to him, namely that he was present in spirit with those to whom he was writing. What the impostor writes, that James and Stephen were present in spirit while the Apostles were writing these things, that is, in mind and thought, could be known neither to them nor to any mortal. Finally, Paul plainly says in what sense, and in what manner, he was present with both the Corinthians and the Colossians: "absent in body," he says, "present in spirit." Is that how James and Stephen are present in our Constitutions? By no means. He does not even define what kind of presence theirs was, whether of body or of spirit, nor does he mention their body or spirit at all. He simply makes his Apostles speak thus: "We now, Peter and Andrew, James and John the sons of Zebedee, etc., all together, and because we have come together into one, we write to you, etc." [Ἡμεῖς νῦν ... ἐγκαλοῦμεν ὑμῖν]. "We, Peter and Andrew, James and John the sons of Zebedee, now gathered together, etc., all of us gathered together in one place, have written to you, etc." You see how

units.la: a L. b.c. 14. in. Ioannem Zebedæi filium, hoc tempore his condendis, scribendisque Constitutionibus adfuisse dicant, non spiritu solo, sed veroró caeteros etiam corpore (quod omnino distinguendum erat, si ea istorum mens erat, quam fuisse vult Turrianus) sed simpliciter, una & eadem dictione se omnes Apostolos, interque eos Joannem, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ γενέσθαι ac ἁθροίζεσθαι in unum convenisse, scripsisseque dicant. Ergo cum non aliter de Joanne quam de caeteris, sed de utrisque eodem omnino vocabulo eadem dicant, necesse est, velle istos, aut ipsum quoque Jacobum corpore una cum caeteris praesentem adfuisse, aut certe neque caeteros corpore, sed omnes spiritu tantum congregatos fuisse: qui profecto miserabilis, & antehac, quod sciam, inauditus conventus est. Eadem est alterius quoque loci ratio, in quo praeter Iacobum Joannis fratrem, Diaconos quoque septem, adeoque & Stephanum, qui eorum unus erat, in hoc conventu praesentes adfuisse narrant;
units.tr: (footnote: L. b.c. 14.) they say that John the son of Zebedee was present for the composing and writing of these Constitutions at this time, not in spirit alone, but truly in body, as the others were too (which would have had to be distinguished, if their intention was what Turrianus wants it to be). But simply, in one and the same expression, they say that all the Apostles, and John among them, "came together" and "were gathered" [ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ γενέσθαι, ἁθροίζεσθαι] into one place and wrote. Therefore, since they do not speak of John differently from the others, but say the same things of both in the same words, these men must mean either that James too was present in body together with the others, or else that none of them were gathered in body, but all only in spirit. The second would be a wretched assembly, and, so far as I know, never heard of before. The reasoning is the same for another passage as well, in which they relate that, besides James the brother of John, the seven deacons too were present at this assembly, and therefore Stephen, who was one of them;

units.la: a Nos igitur 12. Apostoli una consistentes divinas has nostras de omni Ecclesiastica forma constitutiones vobis pracipimus; nobiscum quoque praesentibus & vase electionis Paulo, coapostolo nostro, & Iacobo Episcopo, ac reliquis presbyteris, & SEPTEM Diaconis. Clarum est, vel etiam septem Diaco-
units.tr: a "Therefore we, the twelve Apostles, gathered together, command you these our divine constitutions concerning every ecclesiastical form, with us also present: Paul, the chosen vessel, our fellow apostle, and James the bishop, and the other elders, and the seven deacons." It is clear that the seven

units.la: Diaconos corpore præsentes intelligi, vel cæteros certe solo & ipsos spiritu convenisse significari; quæ quam sint absurda omnes vident. Nihil ergo Turrianus in Scripturæ phrasi habet præsidii, cujus ille idioma impudenter hoc esse vult, quod non esse nunc constat. Huc & illud accedit, quod ea interdum loquuntur isti Διάκο-νες, quæ fidelium vita functorum, ut Martyrum (quales Iacobus & Stephanus fuerunt) spiritibus minime conveniunt. Verbi gratia hæreticos alicubi memorantes, hæc addunt continuo a; ὧν τῆς ἀπάτης ῥύσεταί ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν, quorum fraude liberabit nos Deus per Iesum Christum, qui est spes nostra. Ista vero omnes intelligunt; non consummatorum spirituum, sed fidelium adhuc in sæculo decertantium verba esse. Qui hæc ergo una cum cæteris Apostolis ita loquentes inducuntur Iacobus & Stephanus, ii non spiritus carne soluti, cœloque recepti, sed homines adhuc hic in certamine positi esse finguntur: quo fit, ut Turriani de eorum secundum spiritum, & τῷ γνώμῳ solam præsentia, χρησφύγετον nullum hic habere locum possit.
units.tr: Deacons must be understood to be present in body, or else the rest must be taken to have assembled in spirit alone; and everyone sees how absurd these are. Turrianus therefore has no support in the phrasing of Scripture, which he shamelessly insists is an idiom, though it is now plain that it is not. Add to this that these Διάκονες [Diakones] sometimes say things that do not suit the spirits of the faithful who have departed this life, such as the spirits of martyrs (as James and Stephen were). For example, when they mention heretics somewhere, they immediately add a: "from whose deceit God will deliver us through Jesus Christ, who is our hope" [ὧν τῆς ἀπάτης ῥύσεταί ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν]. Everyone understands that these are the words not of perfected spirits but of believers still contending in this world. Therefore, those who are introduced as speaking these things along with the other Apostles, James and Stephen, are feigned to be not spirits freed from the flesh and received into heaven, but men still placed here in the struggle. Hence Turrianus's claim about their presence according to the spirit alone, "in judgment" [τῷ γνώμῳ], cannot find here any "refuge" [χρησφύγετον].

units.la: CAPUT XIX.
units.tr: CAPUT XIX.

units.la: Contra Bovium & Turrianum probatur, non fuisse Clementem Romanum Constitutionum scriptorem.
units.tr: Against Bovius and Turrianus it is shown that Clement of Rome was not the writer of the Constitutions.

units.la: DENIQUE illud quoque aperte falsum est, quod tertio loco Bovius & Turrianus ponunt, Clementem esse horum librorum authorem. Ipsæ quidem Constitutiones reclamant; in quibus, non Clemens, sed Apostoli non semel affirmant, se eas scripsisse a: Omnes una & in unum congregati scripsimus vobis Catholicam hanc doctrinam: Item b, Nos XII. Apostoli una consistentes divinas has nostras de omni Ecclesiastica forma Constitutiones vobis præcipimus. Clementis vero meminerunt quidem, sed velut ejus, non à quo scriptæ sunt, sed per quem missæ sunt hæ Constitutiones. Sic enim alibi loquuntur iidem Apostoli c: Κατα-λιπόντες ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπισκόποις ἐ λοιποῖς ἐ-ρευσι τῶν τῷ καθολικῷ διδασκαλίαν ἀ-ξίως καὶ δικαίως εἰς μνημόσυνον ἐπιςτει-γμὰ τοῖς πεπιςτευκόσι θεῷ, διαπεμψάμενοι δι᾽ τῆς συλλειτουργῶ ἡμῶν Κλήμεντ, τῆ πιςότατα, καὶ ὁμοψύχῳ τέκνῳ ἡμῶν ἐν Κυείῳ, ἅμα ἐ Βαρνάβα, καὶ Τιμοθέῳ τῷ ποθεινοτάτῳ υἱῷ, καὶ Μάρκῳ τῷ γνησίῳ, σὺν οἷς καὶ Τίτον ὑμῖν γνωρίζο-
units.tr: Finally, it is also plainly false what Bovius and Turrianus put third, that Clement is the author of these books. The Constitutions themselves object to it. In them the Apostles, not Clement, affirm more than once that they wrote them: All of us, gathered together into one, have written to you this Catholic doctrine: likewise We, the twelve Apostles, standing together, enjoin upon you these our divine Constitutions concerning every ecclesiastical order. They do mention Clement, but as the one through whom these Constitutions were sent, not the one by whom they were written. The same Apostles speak in this way elsewhere: Leaving to you bishops, and through the rest of the elders, the teaching of the Catholic faith, worthily and justly, as a memorial for those who have believed God, sending it through our fellow-worker Clement, most faithful and like-minded child of ours in Cyprus, together with Barnabas and Timothy our most beloved son and Mark the genuine one, with whom we also make Titus known to you [Κατα-λιπόντες ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπισκόποις καὶ διὰ τῶν λοιπῶν πρεσβυτέρων τὴν τοῦ καθολικοῦ διδασκαλίαν ἀξίως καὶ δικαίως εἰς μνημόσυνον ἐπιστείλαντες τοῖς πεπιστευκόσι θεῷ, διαπεμψάμενοι διὰ τοῦ συλλειτουργοῦ ἡμῶν Κλήμεντος, τοῦ πιστοτάτου καὶ ὁμοψύχου τέκνου ἡμῶν ἐν Κυρίῳ, ἅμα Βαρνάβα καὶ Τιμοθέῳ τῷ ποθεινοτάτῳ υἱῷ καὶ Μάρκῳ τῷ γνησίῳ, σὺν οἷς καὶ Τίτον ὑμῖν γνωρίζο-].

units.la: {a} L.6.c.14. γνωσίζομεν καὶ Λυκᾶν, Ἰάσονά τε καὶ Λύκιον, & Σωσίπατρον. Vobis Episcopis, & reliquis sacerdotibus hanc doctrinam Catholicam digne ac juste reliquimus, ut memineritis fulcire ac roborare eos, qui Deo crediderunt. Quam quidem doctrinam misimus vobis per fidelissimum comministrum nostrum, ac filium carissimum Clementem: una cum Barnaba, & Timotheo filio optatissimo, & cum sincero Marco; cum quibus notos vobis esse volumus Titum, Lucam, Jasonem, & Lucium & Sosipatrum. Unde liquet quod libro octavo Clemens praesens ac loquens sed paucissima, nimirum haec tantum verba, καὶ ἐγὼ Κλήμης, Et ego Clemens constitutus sum ab Apostolis Episcopus; id inquam, efficere quidem, ut ipse quoque Clemens Apostolis haec constituentibus adfuerit: verum non tanquam una cum iis decernens ac scribens, sed tanquam ea quae Apostoli scripserint, accepturus, atque delaturus ad episcopos & sacerdotes Christianae Ecclesiae. Est & alius locus, in quo Petrus Clementis honorifice meminit, narrans, eum sibi olim cum Simone pro fidei veritate certanti adfuisse. Ergo necesse est, vel istos διαταγῆς impudenter mentiri; vel certe ruere, quod a Bovio & Turriano statuitur. Illi enim, quod hi negant, exserte ajunt, Apostolos Constitutiones ipsos scripsisse; psisse ; qui eas, non scripsisse, sed ab Apostolis scriptas, missasq; accepisse ad Episcopos sacerdotes perferendas, testantur. Ex quibus conficitur, quod habet titulus, Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Αποστόλων, id sic esse, accipiendum, ut sint hæ Constitutiones ab Apostolis, non modo statutæ ac decretæ, sed etiam scriptæ, missæque: eo referenda esse, (quod nuper monuimus) verba illa sequentia sʃ̈ε Κλήμεντ@, ut iis significetur, Constitutiones fuisse non à Clemente scriptas, quod frustra volunt adversarii, sed per Clementem missas; quod diserte narrant Διαταγεὶς. Quanquam ego quidem vehementer dubito, an hæc verba olim habuerit libri ἐπιγραφὴ. Epiphanius quidem, quoties Constitutionum meminit (eas autem, quarum meminit, Turrianus & Bovius easdem cum nostris esse volunt) nunquam Clementinas vocat, sed nude, simpliciterque Αποστόλων Διαταξεις a, & sæpius in singulari numero Διάταξιν b, Apostolorum Constitutiones, sive Constitutionem. Est & ubi tradit librum ita vocari c: Ἀλλὰ ἐὰν οἱ Ἀπόστολοι (inquit) φασιν ἐν τῇ Διατάξει τῇ καλουμένῃ. Quin & Apostoli in eo libro, qui vocatur Constitutio, ajunt Dei stirpem ac vineam esse Ecclesiam. De Clemente, ne unum quidem verbum facit. Sic Athanasius τῷ Διδαχῇ Αποστόλων, quam Bovius quoque
units.tr: {a} L.6.c.14. we make known also Lucanus, Jason and Lucius, and Sosipater. [γνωσίζομεν καὶ Λυκᾶν, Ἰάσονά τε καὶ Λύκιον, καὶ Σωσίπατρον.] We have left this Catholic teaching to you bishops and the other priests, worthily and justly, so that you may remember to strengthen and confirm those who have believed God. This teaching we have sent to you through our most faithful fellow-minister and dearest son Clement, together with Barnabas and Timothy, our most beloved son, and the sincere Mark; with whom we wish Titus, Luke, Jason, and Lucius and Sosipater to be known to you. Hence it is clear that in the eighth book Clement is present and speaks, but only in the very few words, namely, And I, Clement, am appointed bishop by the Apostles [καὶ ἐγὼ Κλήμης]. This, I say, indeed shows that Clement himself was present when the Apostles were laying down these things; yet not as one who decreed and wrote them together with them, but as one who was to receive what the Apostles had written and carry it to the bishops and priests of the Christian Church. There is also another passage in which Peter mentions Clement with honour, relating that he had once been with him, Simon, when they were contending for the truth of the faith. Therefore it is necessary either that these Constitutions [Διαταγαί] lie shamelessly, or certainly that the position laid down by Bovius and Turrianus falls. For they, while these deny it, plainly say that the Apostles themselves wrote the Constitutions; [by Clement (ὑπὸ Κλήμεντος)] the Constitutions themselves declare that the Apostles did not write them but had them written, and received them as sent to be carried to the bishops and priests. From these things it follows that what the title says, Constitutions of the holy Apostles [Διαταγαὶ τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων], is to be understood as meaning that these Constitutions were not only decreed and ordained by the Apostles, but also written and sent by them. To this (as we lately remarked) refers the following phrase, by Clement [ὑπὸ Κλήμεντος], so as to signify that the Constitutions were not written by Clement, as the opponents wrongly wish, but sent through Clement; which the title itself plainly states. Although I greatly doubt whether these words were ever in the inscription of the book. Epiphanius, whenever he mentions the Constitutions (and those he mentions, Turrianus and Bovius want to be the same as ours), never calls them Clementine, but simply and plainly Constitutions of the Apostles [Αποστόλων Διαταξεις], and more often in the singular Constitution [Διάταξιν], the Constitutions of the Apostles, or the Constitution. He also says in one place that the book is called thus: But if the Apostles (he says) speak in the Constitution which is called [Ἀλλὰ ἐὰν οἱ Ἀπόστολοι φασιν ἐν τῇ Διατάξει τῇ καλουμένῃ]. Indeed the Apostles also say, in that book which is called the Constitution, that the Church is the stock and vineyard of God. Of Clement he does not say a single word. So Athanasius calls the Teaching of the Apostles [τῇ Διδαχῇ Ἀποστόλων], which Bovius also

units.la: que suarum Constitutionum volumen esse vult, ⲉApostolorum simpliciter vocat, nunquam Clementis; quin & eam à Clementinis, ut supra diximus, diserte distinguit. Eadem est Eusebii ratio, qui Διδαχὰς Ἀποστόλων, quas memorat, Ἀποστόλων simpliciter, non autem & Clementis, vel per Clementem vocat. Itaque & ex ipso libro constat, authoris, quisquis ille fuerit, hoc consilium, hancque mentem, ac voluntatem fuisse, ut suum hoc opus haberetur, non pro suo, non pro Clementis, vel cujusquam alterius sive Episcopi, sive presbyteri, sed pro Apostolorum vero, ac genuino, & ab ipsis instituto, conscriptoque, vel certe dictato opere; & ex Epiphanio & Athanasio apparet, prima illius operis rudimenta Apostolorum duntaxat, non autem & Clementis nomen praetulisse. Ego enim ex ea sive Διδαχῇ, quam Eusebius & Athanasius memorant, sive Διατάξει, quam refert Epiphanius, sive (quod fortasse verius) ex utraque varie aucta, mutata atque interpolata, nostras Constitutiones tandem exiisse, facile crediderim; & solo Apostolorum nomine, quod illae unum praeferebant, initio inscriptas fuisse. Mox illa ὑπὸ Κλήμεντος addita, ut Constitutionum tanto major esset authoritas, quae & ab Apostolis scriptae, & per Clementem, notissimum ac sanctissimum simum Martyrem, perlatæ essent. Inde factum, ut hominum partim innocenti errore, partim fortasse & dolo, illa ςἰ Κλήμεντος perperam interpretantium, jactatum primo, mox vulgatum fuerit, illas Constitutiones à Clemente Apostolorum nomine scriptas fuisse. Gelasius quidem, quod supra observavimus, hoc opus, quod perperam cum Petri Itinerario confundit, S. Clementis libros octo vocari, ait. Canon vero eorum, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, ultimus eas Clementi tribuit; Αἱ Διαταγαὶ (inquit) ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐπισκόποις δὶ ἡμῶν Κλήμεντος ἐν ὀκτὼ βιβλίοις προσπεφωνημέναι. Constitutiones vobis Episcopis per me Clementem in octo libris nuncupatæ. Hunc autem canonem post Gelasii tempora factum inde constat, quod Gelasio paulo junior Dionysius, cognomento Exiguus, inter Apostolorum, quos exhibet, canones neque hunc habet, neque alios proxime præcedentes 34. quibus Græcorum codex auctior est, quam Latinorum. Jam Trullani Patres eadem quoque secuti videntur, qui has Constitutiones, quo loco adulteratas esse tradunt, ideoque inter apocrypha relegant, vocant τὰς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ςἰ Κλήμεντος Διδαχὰς. Recentiores commemorare nihil necesse est; quibus istorum authoritas facile idem persuasit. Sed illi quidem sive
units.tr: The same holds for the collection of their Constitutions. The author calls it simply Apostolic, never Clement's, and indeed he expressly distinguishes it from the Clementine writings, as we said above. Eusebius follows the same practice: the Teachings of the Apostles that he mentions he calls simply of the Apostles, and not of Clement or through Clement. So it is clear from the book itself that the author, whoever he was, intended and wished that this work be regarded as his own, not as Clement's or anyone else's, whether bishop or presbyter, but as genuinely the Apostles', written, or at least dictated, by them and drawn up at their direction. Epiphanius and Athanasius also show that the first beginnings of that work bore only the name of the Apostles, not also that of Clement. For I can easily believe that our Constitutions finally came out of the Teaching that Eusebius and Athanasius mention, or the Ordinance that Epiphanius reports, or (what is perhaps more likely) out of both, variously enlarged, altered and interpolated; and that at first they were titled with the name of the Apostles alone, which they put forward as one. Afterwards the words by Clement were added, so that the Constitutions might have greater authority, as being both written by the Apostles and conveyed through Clement, the most famous and most holy martyr. Hence it came about that, partly through innocent error and perhaps partly through deceit of people wrongly interpreting the phrase through Clement, it was first bandied about and then spread that these Constitutions had been written by Clement in the name of the Apostles. Gelasius indeed, as we noted above, although he wrongly confuses this work with the Itinerary of Peter, says that it is called the eight books of St. Clement. The canon of those books called Apostolic, the last of them, ascribes them to Clement: The Ordinances (it says) addressed to you bishops through me Clement in eight books. That this canon was made after Gelasius' time is clear from the fact that Dionysius, surnamed the Little, a little younger than Gelasius, neither includes this canon nor the 34 immediately preceding ones among the Apostolic canons he sets forth; the Greek collection is fuller than the Latin in these. The Trullan Fathers too seem to have followed the same view. They say that these Constitutions were corrupted at a certain point, and therefore they relegate them among the apocryphal writings, calling them the Teachings of the Apostles and of Clement. There is no need to mention more recent writers, whom the authority of these men easily persuaded in the same way. But both older and newer writers go against the mind of the author himself, who, as we have lately shown, wishes his work to be regarded everywhere as books truly written and sent by the Apostles.

units.la: vetustiores, sive recentiores contra scriptoris ipsius mentem eunt; qui, ut nuper demonstravimus, hoc opus suum ubique pro libris vere ab Apostolis scriptis, missisque haberi vult. Itaque si libri pro veracibus admittuntur, necesse est, istorum, qui eos Clementi tribuunt, opinionem concidere: ex operis vero ipsius verbis, cui de se major, quam cuivis alii, fides habenda est, statuendum erit, eos libros, non à Clemente, sed ab Apostolis fuisse scriptos, missos, atque editos. Sin pertendas ab Apostolis non esse scriptos, illud denique tibi nobiscum necessario confitendum est, eorum authorem virum fuisse, non modo mendacem, sed & insigniter impudentem, qui opus suum Christi apostolis ausus est suppo-nere, atque affingere. Unde evidentissime consequitur, quod nos defendimus, istum Constitutionum scriptorem, quisquis de cætero fuerit, Clementem certe non esse, virum optimum, ac sanctissimum, & à turpissimis impudentiæ, mendaciique, ac imposturæ criminibus, quorum iste manifestus est, vehementer alienum.
units.tr: So if the books are admitted as genuine, the opinion of those who attribute them to Clement must fall. From the words of the work itself, to which more credit must be given about itself than to anyone else, it must be concluded that these books were written, sent and published by the Apostles, not by Clement. But if you insist that they were not written by the Apostles, then you must finally confess with us that their author was a man not only lying but remarkably shameless, who dared to put forward and fabricate his work under the name of Christ's Apostles. From this it follows most clearly, as we maintain, that the writer of these Constitutions, whoever he otherwise was, was certainly not Clement, an excellent and most holy man, and that he was far removed from the most shameful charges of impudence, lying and imposture, of which that writer is manifestly guilty.

units.la: Idem quoque validissime probant pleraque eorum, quæ supra attulimus. Clementem enim Apostolorum familiarem, quique eorum mores, instituta, actus & tempora non minus quam sua, nota, ac comcomperta habebat, quis crediderit Apo-stolis ea tribuisse, quæ ab eorum vel dog-mate, vel disciplina, vel historia abhor-rent? Itaque cum supra fuse demonstratum sit, multa Apostolis hujusmodi ab isto Con-stitutionum scriptore tribui, atque affin-gi; eadem quoque opera confectum est, i-stum scriptorem alium fuisse, quam Cle-mentem, nequid de veteris memoriæ au-thoribus dicam; quorum nemo est ad an-num Christi 494. qui has Constitutiones vel inter Clementis opera recensuerit, vel eas uspiam Clementi tribuerit: cum tamen ii quæ Clementis esse sciebant, & sæpe commemoraverint, & vero plurimi, ut par erat, fecerint: quod quia in prima operis parte demonstravimus, nihil hic necesse est eadem repetendo confirmare.
units.tr: The same conclusion is also very strongly supported by most of what we have cited above. Who would believe that Clement, a close companion of the Apostles, who knew their manners, institutions, acts and times as well as his own, ascribed to them things that clash with their doctrine, their discipline and their history? Since it has been shown at length above that this author of the Constitutions attributes and fabricates many such things for the Apostles, it follows at the same time that this writer was someone other than Clement. I say nothing of the early writers, none of whom, down to the year of Christ 494, listed these Constitutions among Clement's works or ascribed them to him anywhere, although those who did know what was Clement's often cited his works, and most of them did so as they should have. Because we demonstrated this in the first part of the work, there is no need to repeat it here and confirm it again.

units.la: Huc & illud accedit, quod ex ea, quæ vere Clementis est, ad Corinthios epi-stola, apparet, diversum esse à Constitu-tionum authore Clementem. Cum enim ambo phænicis avis historiam tradant, pla-ne aliter, atque aliter eam narrant a; quod & jam supra observavimus. Atqui non est credibile, unum & eundem virum, qui qui-dem gravis sit ac sanctus, rem eandem di-versis, ac contrariis modis narrare. Non est ergo idem & epistolæ ad Corinthios, & Constitutionum author. Epistolæ ve-
units.tr: To this is added the following: the epistle of Clement that is truly his, the one to the Corinthians, shows that Clement was a different man from the author of the Constitutions. Both relate the story of the phoenix bird, but they tell it in plainly different ways a, as we have already noted above. Yet it is not credible that one and the same man, who is serious and holy, would relate the same thing in different and contrary ways. So the author of the epistle to the Corinthians and the author of the Constitutions are not the same. The epistle to the Corinthians is by a certain and undoubted writer, Clement. Therefore the same Clement cannot be the author of the Constitutions.

units.la: a Confer ep. 2. Clem. ad Cor. p. 34. extr.; 35. cum l. 5.; Const. c. 6. p. 919. ro ad Corinthios certus, atque indubita-tus scriptor est Clemens. Ergo Constitutionum idem Clemens author esse non potest.
units.tr: Compare the Second Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, p. 34 at the end; p. 35 with l. 5; and the Constitutions c. 6, p. 919. The Clement of the epistle to the Corinthians is a certain and undoubted writer. Therefore the same Clement cannot be the author of the Constitutions.

units.la: Hæc & illud accedit, quod eam, quæ vere Clementis est, ad Corinthios epi-stola, appareat, eam verum esse a Constitu-tionum auctore Clementem. Cum enim simbo-phanicis suis militantibus traditum, pla-que alteri eam tribuunt, quod & iam supra observavimus. Aequum est credere unam & eandem virum, qui qui-dem gravis fit ac lucius, rem eandem di-versis, ac continuo modo narrare. Non ergo idem & e Constitutionum auctor. Epistolæ vc-
units.tr: To this is also added that the epistle to the Corinthians, which is truly Clement's, shows that Clement is not the author of the Constitutions. For since their own partisans hand the Constitutions down and assign them to another, as we have already observed above, it is fair to believe that one and the same man, who is serious and wise, relates the same matter in a consistent manner and not in different ways. Therefore the author of the Constitutions is not the same as the author of the epistle.

units.la: JOANNIS DALLÆI DE PSEUDEPIGRAPHICIS APOSTOLICIS LIBER II. CAP. I.
units.tr: John Daillé, On the Apostolic Pseudepigrapha, Book II, Chapter I.

units.la: Argumentum I. Constitutiones à nullo veterum, qui primis Christianismi sæculis floruerunt, memorari. Argument. II. Constitutiones ipsi Clementi, qui earum author fuisse fingitur, ignotas fuisse.
units.tr: Argument I. The Constitutions are mentioned by none of the ancient writers who flourished in the first centuries of Christianity. Argument II. The Constitutions were unknown to Clement himself, to whom they are falsely said to be attributed.

units.la: ATque ita hactenus Constitutiones cum Apostolorum, quorum se esse ipsæ mentiuntur, dogmatis, & libris, & temporibus, & ingenio contendimus & comparavimus; ex eaque comparatione planum fecimus, id opus neque Apostolorum ipsorum, neque Clementis Romani esse. Quod tamen si ad frangendam omnem librorum istorum authoritatem, eosque inter apocryphos, fictitios, atque impostorum fœtus relegandos, satis esse merito videri possit: age tamen, ne quid omnino superfit ea de re dubii, eosdem nunc libros cum Ecclesiæ, & ejus quæ tribus primis à Christo nato sæculis in terris floruit, & ejus quæ deinceps ad nos usque priori successit, moribus, institutis, atque historiis comparemus; videamusque an Constitutionum opus ad primorum & sequentium temporum ingenium conlineet. Ita enim certissime explorari posse arbitror, quid de toto hoc opere statuendum sit.
units.tr: Thus far we have compared and weighed the Constitutions against the doctrines, books, times and character of the Apostles whose names they claim. From that comparison we have made it plain that this work belongs neither to the Apostles themselves nor to Clement of Rome. Yet even if this seemed sufficient to break down all authority of these books and to relegate them among the apocryphal, fictitious and impostors' products, let us nonetheless, so that no doubt on the matter remains at all, now compare these same books with the morals, institutions and history of the Church: both of that Church which flourished on earth during the first three centuries after Christ's birth, and of the Church that afterwards came down to us. Let us see whether the work of the Constitutions fits the spirit of the first times and of those that followed. I think that in this way we can most certainly determine what must be decided about this whole work.

units.la: Quo loco illud inprimis, de quo nemo Christianus dubitat, cogitandum est; quotquot habemus vel ipsorum Apostolorum, vel virorum Apostolicorum monumenta, ea nos à primis, vetustissimisque habere Christianismi sæculis. Ea enim & Apostoli, virique Apostolici suis discipulis tradebant, & hi maxima cum cura studioque ac reverentia & accipiebant, & servabant. Neque ullus hodie est primorum Christi ministrorum, vel in Scripturarum canone, vel extra canonem, certus, ac minime controversus liber, quem non constet jam secundo, tertioque Ecclesiæ Christianæ sæculo & extitisse, & pro vero vel Apostolorum, vel Apostolicorum virorum fœtu à compluribus illius memoriæ Christianis habitum fuisse. Id, quia clarum & apud omnes confessum est, pluribus persequi supersedeo. Itaque si quæ nobis nunc obtruduntur vel Apostolorum, vel Clementis nomine Constitutiones, eorum authorum, quiquibus inscribuntur, vere sint; nemo dubitaverit, quin eæ primorum illorum sæculorum Christianis cognitissimæ fuerint; quorum scilicet fidei ab authoribus traditæ, ac commendatæ esse dicuntur. Jam vero cognitas iis fuisse, neque scimus, neque profecto scire possumus; quique id affirmant, ii temere, ex sola animi sui libidine, non ex ulla certa ratione, vel ex probabili saltem argumento, id totum, quantumcunque est, affirmant. Nam certos quidem & indubitatos vel Apostolorum, vel Apostolicorum virorum, quos legimus, libros, primis illis Christianis cognitos, eoque loco ac numero, quo par est, habitos fuisse, scimus, quod eorum, qui proxime post Apostolos vixerunt, quique his deinceps successerunt, omnes, quæ supersunt, orationes, ac disputationes plenæ sint istorum librorum nominibus, ac sententiis. Clemens, Justinus, Irenæus, alter Clemens, Tertullianus, & cæteri, qui Dei gratia extant illorum temporum scriptores, libros istos semper in ore habent; eorum authoritatem, quoties ea ad rem, quam agunt, pertinet, nunquam omittunt; ex eorum denique sensibus, sententiis, ac verbis pœne omnem sermone ita contexunt, ut quicquid erat Apostolicum, id omne non tantum cognovisse, & animo suspexisse, sed etiam memoriter tenuisse, atque in numerato habuisse videan-tur; neque id mihi quisquam negabit, qui in primorum, à me nuper memoratorum, scriptorum monumentis versatus fuerit. Sed qui Apostolica ita familiaria habebant, in omnique passim sermone usurpabant, ii ne semel quidem Constitutionum istarum meminerunt, vel aliquid ex iis nominatim unquam recitant. Neque ullum nobis ex tribus prioribus Christianismi sæculis, verum ac indubitatum scriptorem adversarii proferre possunt, qui has sive Apostolorum, sive Clementis διαταξεις laudaverit, memoraverit, innuerit. Ac eam quidem epistolam, quæ ad Corinthios, tametsi neque ab Apostolis, neque ex Apostolorum persona, sed à Clemente Ecclesiæ Romanæ nomine scripta fuit, disertissimè memorant illorum temporum scriptores, Irenæus , Clemens Alexandrinus , Origenes , & ex ea non pauca recitant. Constitutionum, quæ vel ab Apostolis ipsis, vel certe à Clemente Apostolorum jussu, & nomine scriptæ dicuntur; & multo prolixiores, atque uberiores, omnem pæne Ecclesiasticam materiam complectuntur, ne semel quidem meminerunt. Quod ergo ajunt adversarii, eas illius memoriæ Christianis cognitas fuisse, id, ut liquet, totum est incertum ac dubium, neque ulla ratione ne, aut veri specie nititur, Idque unum ad evertendâ iltorum librorum authoritatem satis est.
