Non enim nos decet alia pro Apostolicis habere, quam quæ certo ac evidenter ab Apoltolis profecta esle novimus. Ab Apostolis autem profecta neque constat, neque sane constare potest, nisi quæ primis Ecclesiæ temporibus cognita fuisse certum est. Ergo cum exploratum & compertum neque sit, neque vere esse possit, primos illos Christianos iltas Διατάξεις cognitas habuisse: illud quoque, quod inde consequitur, necessario tenendum est, neminem certo scire eas ab Apostolis esse profectas; temereque adeo ac stulte facere, & in aere, vel in arena fidem suam ædificare, qui his libris eam, quam Bovius & Turrianus volunt, authoritatem tribuunt.
units.tr: Here we must first consider what no Christian doubts: whatever writings we have, whether of the Apostles themselves or of the men of Apostolic times, we have them from the earliest and most ancient centuries of Christianity. For the Apostles and the Apostolic men handed these down to their disciples, and those disciples received and preserved them with the greatest care, zeal and reverence. Nor is there today any book of the first ministers of Christ, whether within the canon of Scripture or outside it, that is certain and not at all disputed, which is not known to have existed already in the second and third centuries of the Christian Church, and to have been regarded as genuine work of the Apostles or of Apostolic men by many Christians of that time. Since this is clear and admitted by all, I pass over spending more words on it. Therefore, if the Constitutions now thrust upon us under the names of the Apostles or of Clement are truly by the authors to whom they are ascribed, no one will doubt that they were very well known to Christians of those first centuries, whose faith they are said to have been handed down and commended by their authors. But that they were known to them we neither know nor indeed can know; and those who affirm it do so rashly, from the mere pleasure of their own minds and not from any sure reasoning, nor even from some probable argument. For we do know that the books of Apostles or Apostolic men which we read were certain and undoubted, were known to those first Christians, and were held in the place and esteem they deserve, because all the writings that survive from those who lived closest after the Apostles, and from those who succeeded them, are full of the names and sentiments of these books. Clement, Justin, Irenaeus, the other Clement, Tertullian, and the rest of the writers of those times whom God be thanked we still have, always have these books on their lips. They never omit to cite their authority whenever it bears on the matter they are handling. Finally, from their meanings, opinions and words they weave almost their whole discourse in such a way that whatever was Apostolic seems not only to have been known and revered by them, but also to have been held in memory and at hand. No one who has been conversant with the writings of those early authors, which I have recently mentioned, will deny me this. But those who had Apostolic writings so familiar, and used them everywhere in all their speech, never once mention those Constitutions, nor ever cite anything from them by name. Nor can our opponents produce for us a single true and undoubted writer from the three earlier centuries of Christianity who has praised, mentioned or even hinted at these Constitutions, whether called Apostolic or Clementine [διαταξεις]. Indeed, the writers of that period, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Origen, most clearly mention that Epistle to the Corinthians, although it was written not by the Apostles nor in their person but by Clement in the name of the Church of Rome, and they quote not a few passages from it. But the Constitutions, which are said to have been written either by the Apostles themselves or at least by Clement at the command and in the name of the Apostles, and which are much longer and fuller, embracing almost all ecclesiastical matter, they never mention even once. So what our opponents say, that these were known to Christians of that time, is entirely uncertain and doubtful, rests on no reason and no semblance of truth, and this alone is enough to overthrow the authority of those books. For we ought not to hold as Apostolic anything except what we know with certainty and clear evidence came from the Apostles. But that they came from the Apostles is neither established nor indeed can be established, unless it is certain that they were known in the first times of the Church. Therefore, since it has not been shown, and cannot truly be shown, that those first Christians had those [Διατάξεις] known to them, the conclusion that follows must also necessarily be held: no one knows for certain that they came from the Apostles. Those who attribute to these books the authority that Bovius and Turrianus want to give them rashly and foolishly build their faith on air or on sand.

units.la: Sed quid dixi, incertum esse, an trium post Christi in terris natales sæculorum scriptoribus cognitæ fuerint Bovianæ Διατάξεις? Imò certum est, non fuisse cognitas; idque ex iis, quæ disputare instituimus, clarissimum, ut spero, fiet. Principio illud inde, ut mihi quidem videtur, elucet, quod ex Chrysostomo, idoneo ac omni exceptione majoritefte, constet, Natalis Dominici diem ignotum diu fuisse in Orientali Ecclesia, neque in ea ante a. D. 370. celebrari publica, solenniq; festivitate cæ-pisse. pisse. Is enim in ea oratione quam de hoc argumento scripsit,quamque Antiochiæ , antequam ad episcopatum vocatus esset, habitam fuisse, certum est, de Dominico natali hæc tradit : ἄπω ἀνιατὸν ἕξιν ἐτ@, ἐξ ὧ ἀνάλη ἡμῖν αὐτη ἡ ἡμέρα γεγέννηται, Nondum decimus annus est, ex quo hic ipse dies nobis innotuit; Item , πρὸς ἡμᾶς νομιζόμενα νῦν, καὶ ἐπὶ πολλῶν ἐτῶν. Nunc ad nos demum, non ante multos annos transmissus. Jam ex ipsa oratione constat, annum illum, eum ipsum fuisse, quo à Chrysostomo habitæ erant adversus Iudæos homiliæ. Has autem ab eo habitas post suscEptum diaconatum (id est post a. D. 380.) demonstravit Blondellus nosster. Fac hanc homiliam primo diaconatus anno à Chrysostomo dictam; inde fiet, decimo ante hunc anno (id est æræ Christianæ 370.) Antiochiæ, in qua hæc pronunciavit Chrysostomus, adeoque & in tota Orientis dicecesi, cujus Antiochia metropolis fuit, cognosci, celebrarique cœpisse natalem Christi diem. Ergo totis eo anno anterioribus 369 annis ignota, inusitataque in Oriente fuit Dominici Natalis festivitas. Ignota autem iis esse non potest, quibus Boviani Διαζύγεις noti sunt; qui eam scilicet verbis difertissimis celebrari præcipiunt τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν ἑορτῶν φυλάσ-σειν.
units.tr: But why have I said it is uncertain whether the Bovian Constitutions [Διατάξεις] were known to the writers of the three centuries after Christ's birth? Rather, it is certain that they were not known; and this will, I hope, become very clear from what we have set out to discuss. First, it seems to me, it shines forth from this: it is established from Chrysostom, a witness of sound judgement and beyond all exception, that the birthday of the Lord was for a long time unknown in the Eastern Church, and that it did not begin to be celebrated there publicly and with solemn festivity before A.D. 370. For in the sermon he wrote on this subject, which is certainly known to have been delivered at Antioch before he was called to the episcopate, he says this about the Lord's birthday: [οὔπω δέκατον ἔτος ἐστίν, ἐξ οὗ ἡμῖν αὕτη ἡ ἡμέρα γνώριμος γεγένηται] "It is not yet ten years since this very day became known to us"; likewise [πρὸς ἡμᾶς ... νῦν, οὐ πρὸ πολλῶν ἐτῶν] "Now at last it has come to us, not many years ago." Indeed, the sermon itself shows that this year was the very year in which Chrysostom delivered his homilies against the Jews. That these were delivered by him after he took up the diaconate (that is, after A.D. 380) was demonstrated by our Blondel. Suppose this homily was delivered by Chrysostom in the first year of his diaconate; then it follows that ten years before this, that is in the Christian era 370, the birthday of Christ began to be known and celebrated at Antioch, where Chrysostom delivered these words, and so throughout the whole diocese of the East, of which Antioch was the metropolis. Therefore the festival of the Lord's Nativity was unknown and unused in the East for all the 369 years before that. It cannot have been unknown to those who know the Bovian Constitutions, since they in the clearest words command that feast days be kept [τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν ἑορτῶν φυλάσσειν].

units.la: g τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν ἑορτῶν φυλάσσειν, σιτε, ἀδελφοὶ, ἐ πρῶτλω γε τὸ γνέθλιον, ἥτις ὑμῖν ἐπιτελείσθω εἰκάδι πέμπτῃ τῶ ἐννά-τῳ μηνὸς, Dies festos agitate, Fratres; ac primum quidem diem natalis, qui vige-simo quinto die mensis noni celebretur. Ergo hos Διαταγὰς totis tribus primis saeculis, duobusque quarti saeculi trientibus (ad annum scilicet Domini 370.) omnibus Orientalis dioecesis Christianis ignotos fuisse, clarum ex his, perspicuumque est.
units.tr: "Keep the feast days, brethren; and first of all the birthday, which is to be celebrated for you on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month" [τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν ἑορτῶν φυλάσσειν, ἀδελφοί, ἐπὶ πρῶτον μὲν τὸ γενέθλιον, ἥτις ὑμῖν ἐπιτελείσθω εἰκάδι πέμπτῃ τοῦ ἐνάτου μηνός]. Therefore it is clear and plain from these words that these Constitutions were unknown to all Christians of the Eastern diocese throughout the first three centuries and the two-thirds of the fourth century (namely, down to the year of the Lord 370).

units.la: Sed & in Alexandrina dioecesi pariter quoque ad a. D. 246. eosdem ignotos fuisse, patet ex Hieronymo; Alexandria (inquit a) à Marco Evangelista usque ad Heraclam, & Dionysium Episcopos, presbyteri semper unum ex se electum in excelsiori gradu collocatum Episcopum nominabant, quomodo si exercitus Imperatorem faciat; aut Diaconi eligant de se, quem industrium noverint, & Archidiaconum vocent. Atquiista à nostris Διαταγαῖς abhorrent; quę Episcopum omnem à tribus, minimum à duobus, episcopis ordinari volunt b; ab uno ordinatum deponunt; nedum ut à solis presbyteris evectum ferant. Ergo necesse est, ad Dionysium usque (id est a. D. 246.) ignotas fuisse Alexandriae Διαταγάς. Sed jam singulos illorum temporum scriptores videamus.
units.tr: But also in the Alexandrian diocese, likewise, it is clear from Jerome that these (the Constitutions) were unknown up to the year of the Lord 246: Alexandria (he says), from the Evangelist Mark down to Heraclas and Dionysius, bishops, always had the presbyters choose one of their own, set him in a higher rank, and call him bishop, just as if an army were making its own emperor; or the deacons choose from among themselves whomever they know to be diligent, and call him archdeacon. But these things are at odds with our Constitutions [Διαταγαί], which want every bishop ordained by three bishops, or at least two; they depose one ordained by a single bishop, much less do they allow one raised up by presbyters alone. Therefore the Constitutions must have been unknown in Alexandria up to Dionysius (that is, to the year 246). But now let us look at the writers of each of those times.

units.la: Primus ac vetustissimus omnium post Apostolos
units.tr: The first and most ancient of all after the Apostles

units.la: Apostolos scriptorum est hic ipse Clemens, quem homines maleferiati Constitutionum parentem esse inepte, ac sane impudenter volunt. Atqui illi viro ne cognitas quidem eas fuisse, ex ejus, quae extat, vera ad Corinthios epistola manifestum est. Mitto, quod nuper dixi, alia istum de phoenice narraturum fuisse, quam quae narrat, si authores ejus historiae, quae apud Διαταγὰς extat, habuisset Apostolos; a quibus scilicet vel latum unguem discedere nefas putasset, qui tamen non modo ab istorum narratione discedit, sed rem plane aliter, ac contra, quam hi instituunt, exsequitur. Tradit enim eam avem in Arabia mori, quam Διαταγὰς in Ægypto sponte incendi & in cinerem redigi fabulantur. Mitto & illud, quod supra quoque attigi, Clementem non omisisse hoc loco, quo resurrectionis veritatem confirmat, adhibitos in eodem argumento a Constitutionum scriptore , Sibyllae versus; quibus nihil dici poterat in eam rem clarius. Omisit scilicet, quod & ipsos, & Διαταγὰς, qui eos recitant, utrosque pariter nescire. Ad alia venio. Clemens in tota illa Epistola Corinthios objurgat, in dissidia & seditionem ex plebis in praepositos suos irreverentia, contemptuque ac rebellione delapsos; non ob-scure scure queritur quosdam ἐ δικαίως ἀποβαλέ-σθη τῆς λειτουργίας, injustè sacro ministeriodejectos esse: & mox; ὁρῶμεν γὰρ (inquitb) ὅ-τι ἐνίας ὑμεῖς μετηγάγετε καλῶς πολιτευομέ-νας ἐκ τῆς ἀμέμπτως αὐτοῖς τετιμημένης λειτουργίας. Videmus enim vos nonnullos præclare conversantes à ministerio, quod inculpate ab ipsis colebatur, transtulisse, sive exegisse. Ait c) Corinthiorum Ecclesiam, ἐν ἡ δύο πρόσωπα ςασιάζειν πρὸς τὸς πρεσβυ-τέρους, propter unam, & alteram personam contra presbyteros seditionem movere. Hic certe locus erat, quo afferri inprimis decebat illas, quas supra recitavimus, Apostolorum scilicet & Episcoporum summo in subditas plebes imperio Διατάξεις. Sed nihil horum Clemens d. Jubet Corinthios scripturas consulere, ex iis observare e, justos nunquam à sanctis, sed semper ab impiis rejectos, ac persecutionem passos. Ex scripturis f affert, debere nos Sanctis κολλᾶσθαι, adhaerescere, nosque ipsos adjungere. Affert & ista unum esse Deum, & unum Christum, & unum spiritum, unam vocationem, unum Christi corpus; scandalorum ex Euangelio poenas recitat. Iubet Corinthios scriptam olim à Paulo ad ipsos, jam tum quoque tumultuantes, epistolam, in manus sumere, & quae ab Apostolo in similí argumento dicta erant, perpendere : Caritatis, humilitatisque Christianæ officia ac laudes exsequitur; dissensionumac seditionum mala deplorat ; eos, qui peccaverant, ad pœnitentiam hortatur; monet ut se præpositis, à quibus dicesserant modeste subjiciant; ὑμεῖς ἂν (inquit ) οἱ τὰ καταβολὴ τῆς σάσεως ποιήσαντες, ὑποτασσόμενοι τοῖς προεστῶσι, καὶ παιδευθέντες εἰς μετάνοιαν. Vos igitur qui prima fundamenta seditionis jecistis, subditi estote presbyteris, & in pœnitentiam erudimini. Præclare quidem hæc Clemens. Sed nemo negaverit, multo in eam rem, quam agit, disertiora, efficacioraque esse illa nostrorum Διαταγέων scita; oportere Episcopum subjectis imperare, non autem ipsi subditos; item e Episcopos plebis sua Reges esse, principes, dynastas, deos terrenos, & cætera ejusdem generis. Inprimis vero hæc quanto sacerdotium regno præstat, tanto graviores pœnas debere, qui audet vel nutu oculorum huic adversari, ac contra tendere, quam qui regno. Tum sequentia, quibus sui hujus decreti veritatem ex Absalomi, & Abedaddæ, & Dathanis & & Coritarum gravissimis ob seditionem pœnis affirmat. Nihil intelligit, qui Clementem non intelligit, ista suo illi argumento adeo commoda, ac opportuna allaturum fuisse, si ea ab Apostolis diserte ita decreta, constitutaque sciviset. Ille autem nullius istorum meminit. Ergo neque istorum quicquam habebat cognitum.
units.tr: The first of the Apostolic writers is Clement himself, whom wicked men foolishly, and quite shamelessly, want to be the parent of the Constitutions. Yet it is plain from his genuine letter to the Corinthians that he did not even know them. I pass over what I said a little earlier, that he would have told a different story about the phoenix than he does, if he had had the Apostles as authors of that history which stands in the Constitutions; from whom, surely, he would have thought it wrong to depart by so much as a hair's breadth. Yet he not only departs from their account, but treats the matter quite differently, and even the opposite way, from what they lay down. For he says that this bird dies in Arabia, whereas the Constitutions fabulously say that in Egypt it burns itself up of its own accord and is reduced to ashes. I also pass over what I touched on above, that Clement did not leave out, at the point where he confirms the truth of the resurrection, the verses of the Sibyl which the author of the Constitutions brings in on the same subject; nothing could be said more clearly for that purpose. Clearly he omitted them because he did not know them, nor did the Constitutions, which quote them, know them either. But I come to other matters. Clement, throughout that whole letter, rebukes the Corinthians for the dissensions and sedition that arose from the people's disrespect, contempt and rebellion against their leaders. He plainly complains that certain men were unjustly removed from the ministry [ἀδίκως ἀποβληθῆναι τῆς λειτουργίας], and soon after: For we see (he says) that you have transferred some who were conducting themselves well out of the ministry which had been honoured blamelessly by them [ὁρῶμεν γὰρ ὅτι ἐνίους ὑμεῖς μετήγαγετε καλῶς πολιτευομένους ἐκ τῆς ἀμέμπτως αὐτοῖς τετιμημένης λειτουργίας]. He says that the Corinthian church, in which two persons stirred up sedition against the presbyters [ἐν ᾗ δύο πρόσωπα στασιάζειν πρὸς τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους], that is, on account of one or two individuals, set up a rebellion against the presbyters. Here surely was the place where it was especially fitting to cite those commands of the Constitutions which we quoted above, the Apostles' and bishops' supreme authority over subject people. But Clement says nothing of this. He bids the Corinthians consult the Scriptures and learn from them that the righteous were never rejected by the holy, but always by the wicked, and suffered persecution. From the Scriptures he says we ought to cleave [κολλᾶσθαι], adhere to the holy and join ourselves to them. He also states that there is one God, one Christ, one Spirit, one calling, one body of Christ; he recounts the penalties for offences from the Gospel. He bids the Corinthians take up the letter once written to them by Paul, when they were already then causing a tumult, and weigh what the Apostle said on a similar matter. He pursues the duties and praises of Christian love and humility; he laments the evils of dissension and sedition; he exhorts those who had sinned to repentance; he advises them to submit modestly to the leaders from whom they had withdrawn: You, then (he says) who laid the foundation of the sedition, be subject to the presbyters, and be instructed to repentance [ὑμεῖς οὖν οἱ τὸν καταβολὴν τῆς στάσεως ποιήσαντες, ὑποτάγητε τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις καὶ παιδευθέντες εἰς μετάνοιαν]. Clement certainly writes these things well. But no one will deny that the decrees of our Constitutions are far more explicit and effective for the purpose he is pursuing: that the bishop ought to command his subjects, not himself be subject to them; likewise that the bishops are kings, princes, dynasts and earthly gods over their own people, and other things of the same kind. Above all, these: that the more the priesthood excels the kingdom, the heavier the penalties ought to be for one who dares to oppose it even by a nod of the eyes, and to strive against it, than for one who does so against the kingdom. Then follow the passages in which he confirms the truth of this decree from the most severe punishments inflicted for sedition on Absalom, Abedda, Dathan and the Korahites. No one who does not understand Clement can fail to understand that he would have brought forward these things, so suitable and apt for his argument, if he had known them to have been stated and laid down in so many words by the Apostles. But he mentions none of them. Therefore he did not know any of them.

units.la: Quid quod nonnulla habet, quæ apertissime cum nostrorum Διαξάγιῶν scitis pugnant? Hi enim multitudini, sive plebi nullum plane jus in præpositos concedunt; & grande nefas putant, episcopos non modo ἀρχεῖσθαι parere multitudini; sed vel à laico aliter, quam per mediatorem & interpretem adiri. Clemens a ab hac spiritus elatione adeo abest, ut eum in cœlum ferat, qui Ecclesiæ multitudini obsequitur, sponteque ministerio abire, quam contra ejus jussa, ac voluntatem niti mavult. Quis (inquit b) inter vos generosus est? qui misericors & caritate plenus? Ille dicat; Si propter me seditio, contentio, schismata, ecce abscedo; abeo, quo volueritis, ἡμῖν ποιῶ τὰ προσταχθέντα ὑπὸ τῆς πλήθους, & FACIO QVÆ A PLEBE MANDANTUR. Hunc, quem Clemens velut generosissimum Christi servum laudat, Διαταγὴς velut ignavum juris episcopalis proditorem exsecratus esset, eique suum illud occinuisset c, ἀρχὴν σε χεῖρ τῶν ὑπηκόων, ἃ μὲν χρὴ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἀρχεῖσθαι. Non fuit ergo Clementi pro Apostolo cognitus ὁ Διατάκτης; nedum ut ipse Clemens fuerit.
units.tr: What of the fact that he has some things which flatly contradict the decrees of our Constitutions? For these grant the multitude, or the people, no authority at all over their leaders, and think it a great sin that bishops should not only be bound to obey the multitude, but should be approached by a layman in any way other than through a mediator and interpreter. Clement is so far from this kind of arrogance that he praises to the skies the man who submits to the church's multitude and prefers to withdraw from the ministry of his own accord rather than struggle against its commands and will. Who among you (he says) is noble? Who is merciful and full of love? Let him say: If through me there is sedition, contention, schism, behold, I withdraw; I go wherever you wish; I do what is commanded by the multitude [ἐγὼ ποιῶ τὰ προσταχθέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους], and I DO WHAT IS ORDERED BY THE PEOPLE. The Constitutions would have cursed this man, whom Clement praises as the most noble servant of Christ, as a cowardly betrayer of episcopal right, and would have sung to him their own refrain: You must rule over your subjects, not be ruled by them. So the Constitutions' lawgiver was not known to Clement as an Apostle, much less was Clement himself their author.

units.la: Sed & Clemens in eadem epistola de Apostolis sic loquitur, Κατὰ χώρας ἓν ᾧ πό-λεις Λεῖς originally printed Greek: λεῖς ηπςύοντες καθῖςανον τὰς ἀπαρχὰς αὐ- τῶν δοκιμάσαντες τῷ πνεύματι, εἰς ἐπισκόπως καὶ διακόνως τῶν μελλόντων πιστεύειν. Per regiones igitur & urbes verbum praedicantes, primitias eorum spiritu probantes, Episcopos & Diaconos eorum, qui credituri erant, constituebant. Solos, ut vides, episcopos, & diaconos memorat; & episcopos, ut li- quet, eosdem intelligit, quos & Paulus a in loco simili πρεσβυτέρως vocat, & ipse postea subinde eodem quoque nomine censet. Nostri vero Διαταγεῖς b episcopos, presbyteros, ac diaconos, & à se oppidatim institutos narrant, & quidem, ut nomine, sic etiam re inter se distinctos; & de iis instituendis, ordinandisque plures leges ferunt. Nequid de subdiaconis dicam, & lectoribus & cantoribus, & ostiariis, quos isti anxie commemorant; Clemens ne nominavit quidem, cum rei, quam agit, interesset, totum illum hierarchiæ ordinem referri, siquidem is tunc temporis in Ecclesia obtinebat.
units.tr: But Clement also speaks in the same letter about the Apostles in this way: Preaching therefore through the countries and cities, they appointed their firstfruits, having tested them by the Spirit, as bishops and deacons of those who were going to believe [Κατὰ χώρας οὖν καὶ πόλεις κηρύσσοντες καθίστανον τὰς ἀπαρχὰς αὐτῶν δοκιμάσαντες τῷ πνεύματι, εἰς ἐπισκόπους καὶ διακόνους τῶν μελλόντων πιστεύειν]. As you see, he mentions only bishops and deacons; and by bishops, as is clear, he means the same men whom Paul in a similar passage calls presbyters [πρεσβυτέρους], and whom Clement himself afterwards repeatedly calls by that same name. But our Constitutions [Διαταγαί] describe bishops, presbyters and deacons, all instituted by the Apostles town by town, and distinguished from one another in name as well as in function; and they lay down many laws about appointing and ordaining them. Not to mention subdeacons, readers, cantors and doorkeepers, whom they anxiously record; Clement did not even name them, although it would have been relevant to his purpose to mention that whole order of the hierarchy, since it was then in force in the Church.

units.la: Denique cum nostri Διαταγεῖς Episcopum, quod supra demonstravimus, magno supra presbyterorum ordinem intervallo evehant; ab eoq; omnem Ecclesiæ cujusque unitatem, velut à capite, pendere statuant; Clemens cujusquam istiusmodi ministri, qui caeterorum princeps esset, quique vel à Corinthiis seditiosis spretus, vel à tota Ecclesia colendus esset, mentionem plane nullam fecit ; nullum in singulari numero episcopum, cujus à multitudine authoritas laesa, juraque violata fuerint, in tota epistola nominat; nullum unum, ad quem plebem revocet, cuique ceteras omnes Ecclesiae partes subjectas esse velit. Semper in numero plurium πρεσβυτέρους presbyteros, appellat, in quos turbatum erat, quibusq; singulos fideles subjici vult, πρὸς τὰς πρεσβυτέρας (inquit) ςαπάζετε, contra presby-teros seditionem movetis; μόνον τὸ ποιμνίον τῆ Χριστῷ εἰρωνέυετω τῶν καθιςαμένων πρεσβυτέρων, Solum Christi ovile cum con-stitutis presbyteris in pace degat. ὑποτάγητε τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις, Subditi estote presby-teris. Ὡς προηγυμένως ἡμῶν αἰδεσθῶμεν, τὰς πρεσβυτέρας ἡμῶν τιμήσωμεν, τὰς νέας παιδεύσωμεν. Praepositos nostros revereamur, Seniores inter nos honoremus. Juvenes erudiamus. Ex his vel caecus videt, etiam tum Ecclesias communi presbyterorum consilio rectas, gubernatasque fuisse; neque cujusquam in eorum consessu praecelluisse in caeteros potestatem. Clementi ergo ignotos fuisse necesse est istos τῶν Διαταγῶν Apostolos, quorum tempore, & quidem ex ipsorum decreto, episcopus hierarches erat, totiusque presbyterii princeps, cujusq; velut
units.tr: Finally, whereas our Constitutions, as we have shown above, raise the bishop far above the order of presbyters, and hold that the unity of each church depends on him as on its head; Clement makes no mention at all of any such minister who would be the chief of the rest, and who might be either despised by the seditious Corinthians or revered by the whole Church. In the whole letter he names no single bishop in the singular, whose authority was violated by the multitude and whose rights were trampled; he names no one individual to whom he would recall the people, and to whom he wishes all the other parts of the Church to be subject. Always, in the plural, he calls them presbyters [πρεσβυτέρους], against whom the disorder had arisen, and to whom he wants individual believers to be subject: Do you (he says) rise up against the presbyters? Let the flock of Christ alone be at peace with the presbyters who have been appointed [μόνον τὸ ποίμνιον τῷ Χριστῷ εἰρηνευέτω μετὰ τῶν καθεστώτων πρεσβυτέρων]; Be subject to the presbyters [ὑποτάγητε τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις]; Let us therefore revere our leaders, honour our elders, instruct the young. [τοὺς προηγουμένους ἡμῶν αἰδεσθῶμεν, τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους ἡμῶν τιμήσωμεν, τοὺς νέους παιδεύσωμεν]. From these things even a blind man can see that even then the churches were ruled and governed by the common counsel of the presbyters, and that no one stood out among them with power over the rest. It is therefore necessary that those Apostles of the Constitutions were unknown to Clement; in whose time, and indeed by their own decree, the bishop was the hierarch, the prince of the whole presbytery, and the presbyters were nothing more than counsellors, like the subjects of some lord or king.

units.la: a p. 62. velut dynastæ aut regis, presbyteri nihil aliud erant, quam Consiliarii.
units.tr: p. 62. Like a ruler's or king's advisers, the presbyters were nothing more than counsellors.

units.la: Sed neque illud omiserim, quod cum totum epistolæ argumentum poscçeret ac flagitaret Ecclesiæ præpositos magnificis atque honorificis inprimis vocabulis appellari, Clemens nunquam eos aliter vocat, quam presbyteros, episcopos si forte, & προηγεμένας præpositos. Ιερέων & ἀρχιερέων, sacerdotum ac Pontificum nominibus, quæ & multo digniora, honestioraque, & nostris Διαταγὴν oppido familiaria sunt, in totum abstinuit. Sed nihil necesse est, quæ de hoc genere observari possent, ea omnia commemorare. Hæc satis, ut arbitror, demonstrant nullos Clementi, nullos ejusdem temporis (id est exeuntis primi à Christo nato sæculi, secundique ineuntis) Christianis cognitos fuisse Bovii Διαταγῆς.
units.tr: But I should not omit this either. Although the whole argument of the letter called for the leaders of the Church to be addressed above all by grand and honourable titles, Clement never calls them anything but presbyters, bishops if perhaps, and leaders [προηγεμένας], presidents [præpositos], priests [Ιερέων]. He has entirely avoided the names high priests [ἀρχιερέων], priests and pontiffs, which are both far worthier and more honourable, and very familiar in our Constitutions [Διαταγὴν]. There is no need to recount everything that could be noted about this kind of thing. These points, I think, sufficiently show that Clement, and no one else of his time (that is, of the end of the first century after Christ's birth and the beginning of the second), knew the Constitutions [Διαταγῆς] of Bovius.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Argum. III. Constitutiones Justino a. D. 165. Romæ martyrio functo, ignotas, invisas & inauditas fuisse. Argum. IV. ut & Athenagoræ Athen.
units.tr: Argument III. That the Constitutions were unknown, unseen and unheard of to Justin, who suffered martyrdom at Rome in the year of Christ 165. Argument IV. As also to Athenagoras of Athens.

units.la: X secundi sæculi scriptoribus primus est Iustinus, qui Anno Christi 165. Romæ pro fide à Rustico præside secuti percusus martymartyrium fecit. Egregia extant ejus opera, quibuscum quisquis Constitutiones diligenter comparaverit, facile intelliget, eas sanctissimo Martyri, adeoque & illius ævi Christianis fuisse incognitas. Quod enim Διαζυγείς sciscunt sabbati diem, velut creationis μνημόσυνον, à Christianis observandum esse, ac feriandum, neque jejunio funestandum, ab eo Iustinus tantum abest, ut sabbatum ubique inter Christi cruce abolita Moysis cæremonialia computet, ac ne ab ipsis quidem Patriarchis, qui vel ante vel post diluvium ad Moysem usque vixerunt, observatum fuisse constanter defendat . Sed & diserte testatur à sui temporis Christianis non fuisse observata sabbata τοῦτο δεῖν ὁ ἀπορεῖν ἀξιόν ἐστιν, ὅτι τοιαῦτα ὑπομένοντες, οὐχὶ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα, ὧν νῦν ζητοῦμεν, φυλάσσομεν. Hoc ipsum est consternatione animi dignum, quod talia perferentes, non etiam alia omnia, de quibus nunc quærimus, servemus. Illa autem omnia de quibus quærebatur, sunt πειτομὴ σαρκικὴ καὶ σάββατα καὶ αἱ ὀρταὶ, circumcisio carnalis, & sabbata &, & festa. Et alibi supra docuerat, novam legem indicere sabbatum quoddam perpetuum c; σαββατίζειν ὑμᾶς ὁ καινὸς νόμος ... πάντως ἐθέλει. Quibus verbis aperte significat, sabbati die nihil nobis præstandum incumbere, quod non idem cæteris quoque diebus præstandum sit. Nondum ergo novum illud nostrum Διαζωγέων mandatum Iustino, & cæteris Christianis innotuerat, quo sabbato præ aliis hebdomadis diebus quies, & a jejunio immunitas decernitur.
units.tr: Among the writers of the second century, the first is Justin, who suffered martyrdom at Rome in the year of Christ 165, struck down for the faith by the prefect Rusticus. His outstanding works survive. Whoever carefully compares them with the Constitutions will easily understand that the Constitutions were unknown to that most holy martyr, and so to the Christians of his age. For Justin is so far from counting the Sabbath, which the Constitutions teach is to be observed and kept by Christians as a memorial of creation, neither to be spent in fasting, among the ceremonial laws of Moses abolished everywhere by the cross of Christ, or from firmly maintaining that it was not kept even by the patriarchs, who lived before or after the flood until Moses, that he even states plainly that Christians of his own time did not observe the Sabbaths. "This is indeed a matter for astonishment, that while enduring such things, we do not also keep all the other things about which we now inquire" [τοῦτο δὲ ἀπορεῖν ἄξιόν ἐστιν, ὅτι τοιαῦτα ὑπομένοντες, οὐχὶ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα, ὧν νῦν ζητοῦμεν, φυλάσσομεν]. "All those things were carnal circumcision, Sabbaths and festivals" [περιτομὴ σαρκικὴ καὶ σάββατα καὶ αἱ ἑορταί]. Elsewhere he had taught that the new law bids you keep a sort of perpetual Sabbath ["σαββατίζειν ὑμᾶς ὁ καινὸς νόμος ... πάντως ἐθέλει"]. By these words he clearly signifies that nothing is laid on us to perform on the Sabbath that is not equally to be performed on the other days. So that new commandment of our Constitutions, by which rest and exemption from fasting are decreed for the Sabbath above the other days of the week, had not yet become known to Justin or to the other Christians.

units.la: Idem quoque facile deprehendemus, si quæ Iustinus de baptismo & synaxibus Christianorum, tradit, ea cum Διαζωγέων disciplina contenderimus. Illic summa simplicitas veris Apostolorum libris consentanea elucet; hic omnia ritibus & cæremoniis humanis infuscata. Baptismus quidem Iustino ita describitur, ut nihil aliud præter aquam in eo requirat; oleum & chrisma sive unguentum, quod adhibent Διαζωγεῖς, nullus memoret. In nomine (inquit) rerum cunctarum parentis, & Domini Dei, & Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi, & Spiritus Sancti suscipiunt quod in aqua est lavacrum. Tum Iustinus totum Eucharistiæ mysterium Paganis (eos enim alloquitur c) nude ac simpliciter pandit; quod nostri Διαζωγεῖς non a Paganorum modo, sed & a Catechumenorum oculis, atque auribus summa cura summovent; quod certo argumento, vel ipso fatente Albaspineo d, est, nonesse istos hujus arcani Διαζωγέας veros Christi Apostolos; quorum cum instituta & Iustinus
units.tr: We shall easily detect the same thing if we set what Justin hands down about baptism and the Christian assemblies for the Eucharist beside the discipline of the Constitutions. There the utmost simplicity shines forth, agreeing with the true books of the Apostles; here everything is smeared over with human rites and ceremonies. Justin describes baptism so that he requires nothing in it but water; no one mentions oil, chrism or ointment, which the Constitutions use. "In the name," he says, "of the Father and Lord God of all things, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they receive the washing that is in water." Then Justin sets out the whole mystery of the Eucharist plainly and simply to pagans (for it is to them that he is speaking), whereas our Constitutions, with the greatest care, keep it from the eyes and ears not only of pagans but also of catechumens. By this sure sign, as even Albaspinaeus admits, those men were not the true Apostles of Christ who gave this secret teaching; and whose institutions, if they had truly been theirs, the Christians of that time, including Justin, would surely have kept with care, and would certainly have kept this too.

units.la: c Ibid. p. 76. l. 30. & seqq. d l. 1. observ. 13 nus⸝ & qui tum erant Christiani accurate servarent, hoc utique etiam servassent, si vere eorum fuisset.
units.tr: c Ibid. p. 76. l. 30. & seqq. d l. 1. observ. 13 ...and the Christians who were then living would have kept this too, had it truly been theirs.

units.la: Mox non alterius diei meminit, quo tunc Christianorum conventus fierent, præter unum solis diem, id est Dominicum a: τῇ τῶ ἡλίͅ λεγομένῃ ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κ᾿ πόλεις ἢ ἀγρὸς μενόντων ὅπη τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευ-σις γίνεσθ᾿. Solis, qui dicitur, die omnium qui vel in oppidis, vel rure degunt, in eundem locum conventus fit. Conventus, quos sabbato Διαταγὴς b indicunt, nullus memorat; nedum ut quod hi jubent, quotidie mane & vespere Christianos in Ecclesiam ventitasse tradat. De domo illa, in quam conveniebant, an oblonga, quod morose præcipiunt Διαταγὴς, an rotunda, vel quadrata fuerit, deque cæteris ejusdem generis vanis, nihil dicit.
units.tr: Then he mentions no day other than the one day of the sun, that is, the Lord's Day, on which Christian assemblies were held. "On the day called after the sun, all who dwell in the cities or in the countryside gather in one place" [τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου λεγομένῃ ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγροὺς μενόντων ὅπη τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευσις γίνεται]. He mentions no assemblies on the Sabbath, which the Constitutions appoint; much less does he say that Christians came to the church every morning and evening, as these command. About the house in which they gathered, whether it was oblong, as the Constitutions fussily prescribe, or round or square, and about other such trifles of the same kind, he says nothing.

units.la: Quo loco id etiam obiter observandum, corpus & sanguinem Domini, quod sequentibus sæculis pro Eucharistiæ nomine vulgo apud Christianos usurpatum est, nusquam Iustino eo sensu accipi. Hoc sacramentum ille ubique vel Εὐχαριστίαν simpliciter dicit, atq; ita vocari diserte tradit c, καὶ ἡ τροφὴ αὕτη (inquit) καλεῖται παρ᾿ ἡμῖν εὐχαριστία, Alimentum hoc apud nos vocatur eucharistia; vel etiam explicatius d τὸν ἄρτον τῆς εὐχαριστίας, καὶ τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐ-χαριστίας χαρισίας nominat, id est panem & poculum Eucharistia; vel, ut habet alibi ἀρτῳ εὐχαρ-ιστίαν τὸ ἄρτον καὶ τὸ ποτήριον, panis & poculi eucharistiam, vel βευχαριστηθέν ἄρτον καὶ οἶνον, καὶ ὕδωρ, panem, vinum & aquam eucharistia sacra, vel eodem sensu τὸ δὲ εὐχῆς εὐχαριστηθέισαν τροφὴν, alimentum Eucharistica prece sanctificatum.
units.tr: Here it is also worth observing in passing that "the body and blood of the Lord", which in later centuries was commonly used among Christians as the name for the Eucharist, is nowhere understood by Justin in that sense. He everywhere calls this sacrament simply the Eucharist, and expressly says that it is so called: "This food," he says, "is called among us the Eucharist" [καὶ ἡ τροφὴ αὕτη καλεῖται παρ᾿ ἡμῖν εὐχαριστία]. Or, more fully, he names it "the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of the Eucharist" [τὸν ἄρτον τῆς εὐχαριστίας, καὶ τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐχαριστίας], that is, "bread and cup of the Eucharist"; or, as he has it elsewhere, "the Eucharist of the bread and the cup" [ἄρτῳ εὐχαριστίαν τὸ ἄρτον καὶ τὸ ποτήριον], or "bread, wine and water consecrated by the Eucharist" [εὐχαριστηθέν ἄρτον καὶ οἶνον, καὶ ὕδωρ], or in the same sense "food sanctified by the Eucharistic prayer" [τὸ δὲ εὐχῆς εὐχαριστηθέισαν τροφήν].

units.la: Nomina vero haec corpus & sanguis Christi nunquam, quod sciam, simpliciter sic posita usurpat, ut Eucharistiam significet; quod tamen est τοῖς Διαταγμένοις, ut supra diximus, familiare. Ergo isti non Iustini, sed inferioribus Iustino saeculis, quorum haec fuit usitata locutio, vixerunt.
units.tr: Yet these words, "body and blood of Christ", I have never known him to use simply in that way, to signify the Eucharist; and yet this is, as we said above, familiar to the Constitutions. Therefore those men did not live in Justin's time, but in the centuries after Justin, whose usage this was.

units.la: Eo quoque pertinet, quod Tryphoni haereticos Christianos obiicienti, Iustinus d confitetur quidem multos esse hujusmodi, quales etiam nominatim memorat Μαρκιωνίτας (id est, vel Marcionitas, ut reddit interpres, vel fortasse Marcosios) Valculinianos, Basilidianos, Saturnilianos; sed respondet primo, id a Domino Christo fuisse praedictum; quo loco haec Christi ex Euangelio e recitat, Multi venient in nomine meo, &c. Cavete a pseudoprophetis, &c. Tum protestatur se suosque, id est veri nominis Christianos, nihil cum eis commune habere; neque enim eos Christi doctrinam sequi, quantumvis ejus sibi nomen men asciscant. Hic vero, ut omnes vident, Apostolorum si quod disertum erat contra istos hæreticos dictum, commemorandum ac recitandum erat. Nullum autem recitat Iustinus. Ergo neque istos Διαθηκαι Bovii Apostolos cognitos habebat; apud quos scilicet difertissima extat contra illos ipsos hæreticos sententia a; ex quibus Marcum, Basilidem, & Saturnilium etiam nominatim memorant.
units.tr: To the same point belongs the fact that when Justin objects to Trypho that there are heretical Christians, he admits indeed that there are many of this kind, whom he names expressly: the Marcionites (that is, either Marcionites, as the translator renders it, or perhaps Marcosians), Valentinians, Basilideans and Saturnilians. But he answers, first, that this was foretold by the Lord Christ, and at this point he recites the words of Christ from the Gospel: "Many will come in my name", etc., and "Beware of false prophets", etc. Then he declares that he and his people, that is, Christians of the true name, have nothing in common with them; for they do not follow Christ's teaching, however much they claim his name for themselves. Here, as everyone sees, if any Apostolic passage had been plainly said against those heretics, it ought to have been mentioned and recited. But Justin recites none. Therefore he did not know those Apostles of Bovius' Constitutions either, among whom there survives a most explicit opinion against those very heretics, and who name Marcus, Basilides and Saturninus by name.

units.la: Huc & illud postremo accedit, quod Διαθηκεις mortuorum resurrectionem, Christique adventum cum ultimo universorum judicio clarissime difertissimeque continuant b; quod nullum, ut omnes vident, millenario Christi & Sanctorum in terris ante judicium regno locum relinquit. Atqui Iustinus c illud mille annorum regnum & ipse credit, & quotquot tum erant recta per omnia sententia (christiani, eos id ipsum quoque credere affirmat. Quis vero id eos credituros fuisse putet, si eos libros habuissent, proque Apostolicis censuissent, in quibus id delirium clarissime, ut dixi, evertitur? Sed hæc de Iustino satis.
units.tr: To this there is finally added the fact that the Constitutions teach the resurrection of the dead and the coming of Christ with the last judgement of all most clearly and most explicitly; and this, as everyone sees, leaves no place for the millennial reign of Christ and the saints on earth before the judgement. Yet Justin himself believes in that thousand-year kingdom, and he affirms that all the Christians of his time, being right in every opinion, believed the same. Who would think they would have believed it, if they had possessed those books and had regarded them as Apostolic, in which that delirium is most clearly overthrown, as I have said? But enough about Justin.

units.la: Athenagoræ, qui ejus æqualis fuisse prohibetur, nonnulla opuscula extant; e quibus multis modis id ipsum confirmari potest. Ego unum tantum adducam. Is scriptor cætera quidem præclarus, in con-jugium jugium iniquior est: sic enim habet a,ἢ οἵος τις ἑτέχθη, μένειν, ἢ ἐφ' ἑνὶ γάμῳ· ὁ γὰρ ἀνὴρ ... τῆς ἐπιγενῆς ... μοιχεία. Vel qualis natus est, quisque maneat, vel unicis nuptiis copuletur. Secunda enim honestum quoddam adulterium sunt. Haec ille nunquam ita vel sensisset, si nostrorum Διαθηκῶν eam, quam supra recitavimus, constitutionem Apostolicam agnovisset; in qua & secundae nuptiae clarissime conceduntur, imo neque tertiae plane damnantur; quartae tantum (quamquam & hoc ipsum falso & praeter Apostolicum dogma) suggilantur, velut προφανὴς πορνεία, manifesta scortatio.
units.tr: Some small works of Athenagoras, who is said to have been Justin's contemporary, survive; from many of these the same point can be confirmed in many ways. I shall adduce only one. That writer, otherwise distinguished, is rather unfair towards marriage; for he says: "Either let each one remain as he was born, or be joined in a single marriage; for the man who ... after ... is an adulterer. Either remain as one was born, or be united in one marriage. For second marriages are a certain honourable adultery." He would never have thought this, had he recognised that Apostolic Constitution which we recited above, in which second marriages are most clearly permitted, and indeed third marriages are not plainly condemned; only fourth marriages (although this too is false and contrary to the Apostolic doctrine) are branded as "manifest fornication" [προφανὴς πορνεία].

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Arg. V. Constitutiones Irenaeum a.D. 197. mortuum, nescivisse, & multa eorum dogmata vel ignorasse, vel etiam pulsasse; idque ex veris vivi monumentis fuse demonstratur.
units.tr: Argument V. That Irenaeus, who died in 197, did not know the Constitutions and either was ignorant of or actually contradicted many of their doctrines; this is shown at length from the genuine works of the living man.

units.la: UNC ad Irenaeum veniamus, quem martyrium fecisse alii anno Christi 206. volunt; Blondellus nostrer a.198. Is vel unus satis est ad id, quod instituimus, probandum. Nam cum in praeclaro illo opere, quod contra haereticos, tum alios, tum etiam Cerinthianos, Marcosios, Menandrianos, Basilidianos, Saturnianos Saturnilianos à nostris Διαλαγέων nominatim memoratos & refutatos scripsit, omnia undique ex Apostolorum, & Apostolicorum virorum monumentis ac traditionibus, quæ suo illi argumento congruebant, magna cura collegerit, nihil plane de nostris Constitutionibus habet ; qui tamen unus liber plura contra illas hæreses diserta continet, quam ullus Apostolorum ab Irenæo laudatus. Quædam tantum exempli caussa ponam ; Nam omnia annotare & longum esset, & pœne supervacaneum.
units.tr: Now let us come to Irenaeus, whom some think suffered martyrdom in the year of Christ 206, though our Blondel places it in 198. He alone is enough to prove what we have set out to show. In that famous work against the heretics, he collected with great care, from the writings and traditions of the Apostles and apostolic men, everything that suited his argument. He wrote against the Cerinthians, the Marcosians, the Menandrians, the Basilidians, and the Saturnians (Saturnilians), whom our authors name and refute. Yet he says nothing at all about our Constitutions. That single book contains more clear statements against those heresies than any Apostle whom Irenaeus cites. I will give only a few examples, since to note everything would be long and nearly superfluous.

units.la: Irenæus ergo Apostolorum doctrinam ab hæreticorum deliriis alienam fuisse, ex ipsorum Apostolorum, & scripturis, & traditionibus fuse probat. Cur Διαλαγέων, quibus nihil est in hoc genere disertius, si eos Apostolicos norat, nullus meminit ? Refert quodam loco eam, de qua diximus, Clementis ad Corinthios epistolam ; ex qua probat & Apostolos tradidisse, & Clementem accepisse, docuisseq;, unum Deum omnipotentem, factorem cæli & terræ, plasmatorem hominis, qui induxerit cataclysmum, & advocaverit Abraham, qui eduxerit populum de terra Ægypti, qui collocutus sit Moysi, qui legem disposuerit, & Prophetas miserit, qui ignem præparaverit Diabolo & Angelis ejus. Sed quid ille in istis tempus terit ? Cur non ex nostris Con-
units.tr: Irenaeus therefore proves at length, from the Apostles' own writings and traditions, that the Apostles' teaching was far from the delusions of the heretics. Why does he never mention the Dialexes, which say nothing clearer on this subject, if he knew them as Apostolic? In one place he cites that letter of Clement to the Corinthians which we have discussed, and from it he shows that the Apostles taught, and Clement received and taught, "one almighty God, maker of heaven and earth, former of man, who brought the flood, who called Abraham, who led the people out of the land of Egypt, who spoke with Moses, who ordained the law, and sent the Prophets, who prepared fire for the Devil and his Angels." But why does he waste time on these points? Why does he not cite from our Constitutions the passage where the Apostles clearly condemn by name the heretics who blaspheme the providence or creation of God?

units.la: al.3.c.3. Constitutionibus diserte ab Apostolis damnatos refert haereticos a τὰς βλασφημίας τὰς θεὸς τὴν πρόνοιαν, ἢ τὴν δημιουργίαν, Dei providentiam, vel creationem blasphemantes? Cur non de innumerabilibus aliqua profert loca, in quibus Διαθηκῆς Christi Domini Patri & mundi creationem, & omnem veteris testamenti oeconomiam, legisque Mosaicae promulgationem, & Prophetarum missionem clarissime tribuunt b? Ac, ut caetera mittam, cur non illum saltem locum recitat, in quo isti ipsos illos, quos Irenæus tam operose refellit haereticos, διαρρήδην ac nominatim proscribunt, eorumq; dogmata liquido sugillant c, εἶτα ἕτεροι ἑτέρων καλουμένων ἐντόπων δογμάτων Κηνυθ, καὶ Μάρκ, καὶ Μεναρδ, ὁ Βασιλείδης, καὶ Σατορνίλ; Ita compendio tota haec disputatio transfigi poterat. Sed ille scilicet haec, quae qua erat sapientia, loco tam necessario non fuerat, si ea habuisset, omisurus, ideo praetermisit, quod nondum ejus aevo nati essent posthumi, seriqueillí Bovii Apostoli.
units.tr: a ... those who blaspheme God's providence or creation (al. 3. c. 3.)? Why does he not quote any of the countless passages where they plainly ascribe to the Father of Christ the creation of the world, the whole economy of the Old Testament, the giving of the Mosaic law, and the sending of the Prophets? b And, to pass over the rest, why does he not at least recite the passage where they expressly and by name condemn those very heretics whom Irenaeus refutes so laboriously, and plainly brand their doctrines c: "Then others, of the so-called doctrines, Cerinthus, and Marcus, and Menander, Basilides, and Saturninus" [εἶτα ἕτεροι ἑτέρων καλουμένων ἐντόπων δογμάτων Κηνθ, καὶ Μάρκ, καὶ Μεναρδ, ὁ Βασιλείδης, καὶ Σατορνίλ]? In this way the whole dispute could have been settled briefly. But he would certainly not have left out these things, which were of such necessary importance and which he would have used if he had known them. He passed them over because the spurious ones had not yet been born in his time, nor that Bovius of the Apostles.

units.la: Neque omittendum est, quod hic tradit de Clementis epistola Irenæus, quam diserte ait d, vetustiorem esse his, qui nunc (inquit) falso docent, & alterum Deum super Demiurgum, & factorem horum omnium quae sunt, commentantur. At qui antiquissimas esse volunt Διαλόξεις, ii huic ipsi Clementi eas tribuunt; epistolæq; adeo ad Corinthios sorores germanas statuunt. Jam cum Romæ episcopus esset Clemens, quo tempore illam epistolam Romanæ Ecclesiæ nomine ad Corinthios dedit, cumque non plures, quam novem ad summum annos episcopus fuerit, omnino necesse est, Constitutionum libros, si ii vere Clementis sint, vel ante editam ad Corinthios epistolam, vel certe paucis annis, id est non pluribus quam octo, post eam conscriptos fuisse. Ex quibus evidenter sequitur, ipsas quoque Διαλόξεις, si Clementis sunt, esse iisdem hæreticis ex Irenæo vetustiores. Atqui esse non vetustiores, sed recentiores, constat, quæ scilicet illos ipsos hæreticos, veluti jam exortos memorant. Ergo fieri non potest, ut vere Clementis sint nostræ illæ Constitutiones.
units.tr: Nor should we pass over what Irenaeus says here about Clement's letter. He clearly says it is older than those who now falsely teach and invent "another God above the Demiurge and the maker of all these things." Yet those who want the Dialexes to be the most ancient works assign them to Clement himself, and so make them sisters of the letter to the Corinthians. Now Clement was bishop of Rome when he sent that letter in the name of the Roman Church to the Corinthians, and he was bishop for no more than about nine years at most. It follows necessarily that, if the books of the Constitutions really are Clement's, they were written either before the letter to the Corinthians or within a few years after it, that is, not more than eight years later. From this it clearly follows that the Dialexes too, if they are Clement's, are older than the very heretics Irenaeus names. But it is certain that they are not older but more recent, since they speak of those heretics as already risen. Therefore it cannot be that our Constitutions are really Clement's.

units.la: Narrat idem Irenæus a, audivisse aliquos a Polycarpo, Joannem Domini discipulum in Epheso, euntem lavari, cum vidisset intus Cerinthum, exiliisse de balneo non lotum, se timere dicentem, ne balneum concideret, cum intus esset Cerinthus. Cur istis non addidit, quod Clemens in Constitutionibus tradidit, Apostolos Cerinthum istum nominatim inter eos hæreticos censuisse, qui καλῆξαν ἐντόπων δογμάτων?
units.tr: The same Irenaeus a relates that some people heard from Polycarp that John, the disciple of the Lord, once went to bathe at Ephesus, and when he saw Cerinthus inside, he leapt out of the bath unwashed, saying he feared the bath-house would collapse while Cerinthus was in it. Why did he not add to this what Clement in the Constitutions records, that the Apostles named this Cerinthus among those heretics who [καλουμένων ἐντόπων δογμάτων] are condemned?

units.la: Ita & quo loco contra Ebionæos, & Nicolaïtas disputat, quæ in Constitutionibus habentur adversus istos disertissima, omnino ea attulisset, si cognita habuisset. Quod deiftis tacet, hoc ipso clamat, se ea plane nescivisse.
units.tr: Likewise, where he argues against the Ebionites and the Nicolaitans, he would certainly have brought in the most explicit passages against them from the Constitutions, if he had known them. What he keeps silent about, he thereby proclaims loudly: that he plainly did not know them.

units.la: Sed & Irenæi, præter insigne illud adversus hæreses opus, extat apud Eusebium nobilis ad Victorem epistolæ egregium fragmentum, e quo vel meridiano sole clarius est, nullas tum (id est paulo ante finē secundi sæculi) apud Christianos fuisse Bovianas Apostolorum Διατάξεις.
units.tr: Besides his famous work against the heresies, there survives in Eusebius an excellent fragment of Irenaeus's noted letter to Victor. From it, clearer than the midday sun, it is plain that at that time (that is, shortly before the end of the second century) there were no Apostolic Constitutions of Bovius [Διατάξεις] among Christians.

units.la: Primo id validissime probat ipsum epistolæ argumentum. Est enim scripta de quæstione Paschali, quæ tum eo usque exarsit, ut Victor, Romæ Episcopus, Asiæ Ecclesias excommunicandas putaret, quod eæ Pascha decima quarta Luna una cum Judæis præcise celebrarent, aliter quam ipse, & reliquus Christianorum orbis. Neque id inter Ecclesias discriminis eo primum tempore natum erat. Fuisse jam antea ait Irenæus sub Aniceto, & Pio, & Hygino, & Telesphoro, & Xysto, & Sotere, Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ut Irenæus loquitur, presbyteris. At si tum extitisset Bovianæ Constitutiones, nullus futurus erat isti controversiæ locus, in quibus scilicet ea secundum Romanos non minus clare, diserteque, que, quam ab ipso Victore definita est his verbis : Δεῖ ἓν ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοὶ, τῆς τῶ Χρι- στῶ τιμίῳ ἐξηγορασμένης αἵματι, τὰς ἡμέ- ρας τῶ πάσχα ἀνεικβῶς ποιεῖσθαι μὴ πάσης ἐπιμελείας μὴ τροπῳ ισημιεινῳ· ὅπως μὴ ὡς τῷ ἑνιαυτῷ ἑνὸς πάθήματος μνείαν ποιῆσε· ἀλλὰ ἅπαξ τῷ ἔτους τῷ ἅπαξ ἀποθανόντῳ· μηκέτι ὁ παραληφθέντες μὴ Ἰουδαίων ἑορτάζειν· ὑδημία γὰρ κοινωνία ἡμῖν νῦν πρὸς αὐτούς· πεπλάνηνται γάρ, ὧ αὐτῷ τῷ ψήφον, ὡ νομίζουσιν ἐπιτελεῖν· ὅπως πανσ- χόθεν ὡσὶ πεπλανημένοι, ἡ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀπεχοινισμένοι. ὑμεῖς ὁ φυλάσσετε ἀνεικβῶς τῷ ἰσημέριον τροπῷ ἐαυτῆς, ὡς ὅτι Δυ- σγρὸς. ἐπιτηρῶντες ἕως εἰκάδῳ πρῶτης σε- λήνης, ὅπως μὴ ἐν ἑτέρᾳ ἑβδομάδι ἐμπέσοι ἡ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτη τῆς σελήνης· ἡ πλά- νης γενομένης ἀγνοίᾳ δὲ τῷ ἑνιαυτῷ ἐπιτελέ- σωμεν τὸ πάσχα· ἡ ἐν ἄλλῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἑορτάσω- μεν τῷ τῆς Κυ-ρ-ι-α-κ-ῆ-ς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ ἀναστάσιμον ἡ- μέραν, ἀλλ' ἐν Κυριακῇ μόνῃ. Oportet ergo, fratres, ut qui pretioso Christi sanguine redempti estis, dies festos Pascha accurate, & omni diligentia post aequinoctium celebretis, ut neque unius passionis bis per annum memoriam renovetis, sed potius semel quotannis semel item mortui memoriam celebretis; neque amplius cum Iudaeis tempus celebrandi Pascha observetis. Nulla enim nobis nunc cum eis communio est. Falluntur namque in ipso etiam calculo, & ratiocinatione, quam existimant se absolvere, ut ex omni parte à veritate abstracti sint. Vos vero observate diligenter conversione verni æquinoctii, quæ incidit in vigesimum secundum diem mensis duodecimi, qui appellatur Dystros, & notate usque ad vigesimam primam Lunam, ne in aliam hebdomadam incidat Luna quarta decima, & per errorem bis uno eodemque anno Pascha agitemus, aut diem resurrectionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, alio die, praterquam Dominico, tantum celebremus. Hæc Boviani Apostoli. Mitto, quod supra observatum est, aliam extare apud Epiphanium ipsam quoque velut Apostolorum Διάταξιν, qua plane contra quam hic, pascha Christiani cum iudæis observare iubentur; quæ tametsi & ipsa spuria falsaque sit, quod suo loco demonstravimus, clarissime tamen docet, istam, quæ cum ea adversa fronte pugnat, novellam esse, ac priori recentiorem, & post Epiphaniana tempora à maleferiatis hominibus, ejecta illa superiore, quę Iudæis favet, Constitutionum codici insertam. Mitto, quod ipsa Constitutio, ut ait ac fatetur Bovius a, se prodit, & tantum non voces emittens, clamat se novam esse. Ait enim æquinoctium fieri 22. Dystri mensis, hoc est Martii: perspicuum est autem Christi tem-
units.tr: First, the subject of the letter itself proves this most strongly. It was written about the Paschal question, which at that time had become so heated that Victor, bishop of Rome, thought the churches of Asia should be excommunicated, because they celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon together with the Jews, unlike himself and the rest of the Christian world. Nor was this difference between the churches a new thing at that time. Irenaeus says it had existed earlier, under Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, Xystus, and Soter, the presbyters of the Roman Church, as Irenaeus calls them. But if the Constitutions of Bovius had existed at that time, there would have been no room for this controversy, since in them the matter is settled according to the Romans no less clearly and explicitly than Victor himself defined it in these words: [Δεῖ ἐν ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ τιμίῳ ἐξηγορασμένης αἵματι, τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ πάσχα ἀκριβῶς ποιεῖσθαι μετὰ πάσης ἐπιμελείας μετὰ τὴν ἰσημερινὴν τροπήν· ὅπως μὴ ὡς τὸ ἔτος ἑνὸς πάθους μνείαν ποιῆσαι, ἀλλ' ἅπαξ τοῦ ἔτους τὸν ἅπαξ ἀποθανόντα· μηκέτι ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων ἑορτάζειν· ἡμῖν γὰρ νῦν πρὸς αὐτοὺς οὐδεμία κοινωνία· πεπλάνηνται γὰρ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ψήφῳ, ἐν ᾗ νομίζουσιν ἐπιτελεῖν· ὅπως πάντοθεν ὦσι πεπλανημένοι, ἡ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀπεστερημένοι. ὑμεῖς δὲ φυλάσσετε ἀκριβῶς τὴν ἰσημερινὴν τροπὴν ἐπὶ ἑαυτῆς, ὡς ὅτι δυσγρὸς ἐπιτηρῶντες ἕως εἰκάδος πρώτης σελήνης, ὅπως μὴ ἐν ἑτέρᾳ ἑβδομάδι ἐμπέσῃ ἡ τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτη τῆς σελήνης· ἢ τῆς πλάνης γενομένης ἀγνοίᾳ τοῦ ἔτους ἐπιτελέσωμεν τὸ πάσχα· ἢ ἐν ἄλλῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἑορτάσωμεν τὴν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἀναστάσιμον ἡμέραν, ἀλλ' ἐν Κυριακῇ μόνῃ.] "It is necessary, therefore, brothers, that you who have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ keep the days of the Passover carefully and with all diligence after the equinox, so that we do not make remembrance of one passion twice in a year, but once in the year, of him who died once; and that we no longer keep the feast with the Jews, for we now have no fellowship with them. For they have gone astray, in the very reckoning by which they think they celebrate it, so that they are altogether led astray, deprived of the truth. But you keep the turning of the spring equinox carefully, as the one that is in itself, watching until the twenty-second day of the first moon, so that the fourteenth day of the moon does not fall in another week; and if through error we keep the Passover in ignorance of the year, or celebrate the day of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ on another day, except on the Lord's day alone." That is what the Bovian Apostles say. I pass over what was noted above: another Constitution is found in Epiphanius, likewise under the name of the Apostles, which orders the Christian Passover to be kept with the Jews, plainly contrary to this one. Although that too is spurious and false, as we showed in its proper place, it nonetheless most clearly teaches that this one, which fights against it head-on, is newer than the earlier one, and that after the time of Epiphanius, by wicked men, the older one, which favours the Jews, was thrown out and this one inserted into the body of the Constitutions. I also pass over the fact that the Constitution itself, as Bovius says and admits a, betrays itself, and almost cries out by its own voice that it is new. For it says the equinox falls on the 22nd of Dystros, that is, March; yet it is clear that in the time of Christ the equinox was on 25 March; and in the time of Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, who lived under the emperor Probus in the year 280, the time of the equinox had moved back three days, and the sun entering Aries made the spring equinox on the eleventh day before the Kalends...

units.la: a Ad Const. Apost. l. 5. c. 18. sti tempore æquinoctium fuisse 25. Martii; tempore vero Anatolii Laodiceni Episcopi, qui vixit Probo imperante a. D. 280. æquinoctii tempus retrocesserat tribus diebus, Solque arietem ingrediens faciebat æquinoctium vernum x i. Kal. Apriles, hoc est 22. Martii; quod narrat Eusebius in Eccles. Hist. l. 7. Hactenus Bovius. Haec, inquam, in praesentia quidem mitto. Illud unum ajo, si haec Apostolorum Constitutio Aniceti, Pii, Hygini, Telesphori, Xysti, Soteris, & Victoris ævo Christianis cognita fuisset, viros sanctissimos Polycarpum, Thraseam, Sagarim, Papirium, Melitonem, Polycratem, & cæteros Asianos, Apostolici nominis observantissimos, nunquam violaturos fuisse tam claram, tamque disertam legem, Pascha contra quam illa decernit, una cum Judæis celebrantes.
units.tr: Ad Const. Apost. l. 5. c. 18. At the time of Christ, the equinox fell on 25 March; but in the time of Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, who lived under the emperor Probus in the year of our Lord 280, the equinox had moved back three days, and the sun entering Aries made the spring equinox on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that is, 22 March, as Eusebius relates in Ecclesiastical History, book 7. So far Bovius. I set these points aside for the present. I say only this: if this Apostolic Constitution had been known to Christians in the time of Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, Xystus, Soter and Victor, the most holy men Polycarp, Thraseas, Sagaris, Papirius, Melito, Polycrates and the other Asian bishops, who were most careful observers of the apostolic name, would never have violated so clear and so explicit a law by celebrating the Passover against what it decrees, together with the Jews.

units.la: Quod ita instituerunt, eo ipso clamant nihil se scivisse ab Apostolis in contrariam partem decretum. Sed nihil est argumentis opus. Polycarpus, quo viro, post Apostolos, quorum familiaris fuit, vix ullus apud Christianos unquam fuit, sanctior ac divinior Aniceto affirmat apud Irenæum in hac ipsa epistola a Ioannem Domini nostri discipulum, & reliquos, quibuscum versatus erat, Apostolos, ita ut Asiani observabant, Pascha celebrasse, id est cum Judæis
units.tr: By acting as they did, they proclaim that they knew of no decree from the Apostles to the contrary. But there is no need of arguments. Polycarp, than whom after the Apostles, whose companion he was, scarcely anyone among Christians has ever been holier or more divine, affirms in this very letter, as quoted by Irenaeus, that John, the disciple of our Lord, and the other apostles with whom he lived, celebrated the Passover in the manner the Asians observed, that is, with the Jews.
