units.tr: R

units.la: Idem quoq; postea affirmavit ad Victorem scribens Asianorum princeps, veneranda canitie, sanctissimisque moribus senex Polycrates; qui commemoratis Joanne & aliis non paucis veteris memoriæ viris, partim Apostolis, partim Apostolicis, {a}ἕτοι πάντες (inquit) ἀϊτήγησαν τὸ ἡμέραν τ̃ς τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτης τῆ πάσχα κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον. Hi omnes observarunt diem Lunæ decimaquartæ Paschatis secundum Euangelium. Omnino necesse est, vel mentitos esse de Apostolis Polycarpum, ac Polycratem (quod nemo, nisi à Christo alienus, & furens dixerit) vel certe falsos esse ac fictitios nostros illos Bovii Διατηρίας, qui Apostolos de pascha plane contra, quam ipsi observabant, decernentes faciunt. Sed etiamsi Polycarpum ac Polycratem causæ suæ studio abreptos falso ista de Apostolis jactasse dixeris (quod vel suspicari de talibus viris nefas arbitror) illud quidem certe negari non potest, eorum hac in parte adversarios, Anicetum, & Victorem, & cæteros omnes, præter Asianos, illam Apostolorum pro suo usu ac ritu factam constitutionem, si ea tum cognita fuisset, in medium fuisse allaturos. Atqui neque eam, neque aliud ullum Apostolorum, quod quidem scriptum exaret, mandatum in tota hac causa adhibuisse unquam leguntur. Irenæus Anicetum, quo minus ad contrarium Polycarpi usum concederet, nihil aliud caussatum esse memorat, nisi unam suorum antecessorum consuetudinem, ὥτε μὲν ὁ Πολύκαρπος (inquit a) τὸν Ἀνίκητον ἐπεισε τηρεῖν, λίγοντα τὰ συνήθεια τῶν πρὸ αὐτῶ πρεσβυτέρων ὀφείλειν κατέχειν. Neque Polycarpus Aniceto persuasit, ut consuetudinem Asiaticam observaret; quippe qui diceret, morem presbyterorum, qui ante se fuerant, debere retineri. Neque Eusebius, qui haec narrat, contendentes ulla lege scripta, ullove praecepto in hac controversia nixos fuisse ait; sed diversam utrosque traditionem obtendisse b; Asianos quidem pascha luna decimaquarta ὡς ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀρχαιολέγας, velut ex antiquiori traditione, celebrandum esse pugnantes; alios diversum morem, qui etiam (inquit) ad hodiernam diem obtinuit, ex Apostolica traditione observantes. Ergo fatendum est, nullam tum in Ecclesia extitisse Apostolorum scriptam hac de re legem; Constitutionumque adeo nostrarum codicem, in quo ea lex disertissime habetur, illius memoriae Christianis plane, penitusque ignotum fuisse.
units.tr: Likewise, the leader of the Asians, Polycrates, an old man of venerable grey hair and most holy character, afterwards affirmed the same in writing to Victor. Recalling John and not a few other men of ancient memory, some apostles and some apostolic men, he says: "All these (he says) kept the fourteenth day of the moon for the Passover, according to the Gospel." [ἕτοι πάντες ἀϊτήγησαν τὸ ἡμέραν τ̃ς τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτης τῆ πάσχα κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον]. It is absolutely necessary either that Polycarp and Polycrates lied about the Apostles (which no one would say except one estranged from Christ and out of his mind), or else that those Bovian Διατηρίαι of ours, which make the Apostles decree about the Passover in a way plainly opposed to what these men observed, are false and fictitious. But even if you say that Polycarp and Polycrates, carried away by zeal for their cause, falsely boasted these things about the Apostles (which I think it wicked even to suspect of such men), it certainly cannot be denied that their opponents on this point, Anicetus, Victor and all the others except the Asians, would have brought forward that apostolic constitution in the open, if it had then been known. Yet we read that in this whole controversy they never appealed to it, nor to any other written command of the Apostles. Irenaeus records that Anicetus, in order not to yield to Polycarp's contrary practice, alleged nothing except the custom of his predecessors: for Polycarp (he says) persuaded Anicetus to keep the custom, saying that the custom of the elders who had gone before him ought to be retained. Nor does Eusebius, who relates this, say that either side relied on any written law or precept in this dispute; rather, he says, each side put forward a different tradition: the Asians, contending that the Passover should be kept on the fourteenth day of the moon, as from an older tradition [ὡς ἐκ παραδόσεως ἀρχαιολέγας]; the others, observing a different custom, which (he says) has held even to this day, from apostolic tradition. Therefore it must be admitted that at that time no written law of the Apostles on this matter existed in the Church; and so the collection of our Constitutions, in which that law is stated most explicitly, was entirely and utterly unknown to Christians of that age.

units.la: Quod ipsum etiam aliter nos docet in illa epistola Irenaeus. Ait enim non suo modo tempore c, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολὺ πρότερον, sed & multo prius, diversam apud Christianos stianos fuisse jejunii antepaschalis formam sive speciem; Alios enim putasse oportere se unum diem jejunare; alios, duos; alios vero, etiam plures: fuisse & qui horis diurnis, noƐturnisque quadraginta diem illum suum esurialem metirentur. Jam illud primo plane est incredibile,hujusmodi apud illorum temporum Christianos extituram fuisse jejunii varietatem, si iis cognitæ fuissent, & pro Apostolicis habitæ nostræ Διαταξεις. Hæ enim omnem ante paschalis illius jejunii rationem adeo exserte accurateque definiunt, ut nemo de eorum, qui eam decreverunt, sensu dubitare possit a. Ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῶ πάσχα (inquiunt) νηστεύετε, ἀρχόμενοι ἀπὸ σαββάτου μέχρι τῆς παρασκευῆς καὶ σάββατα ἐξ ἡμέρας, &c. τῶ μέντοι παρασκευῶ καὶ τὸ σάββατον ὁλόκληρον νηστεύσατε, οἷς δύναμις πρόσεστι τοιαύτη, μηδενὸς γινομένοι μέγις ἀλεκτοροφωνίας νυκτός. εἰ δέ τις ἀδυνατεῖ τὰς δύο σωμάτιν ὁμῶς, φυλαξάτω καὶ τὸ σάββατον. Jejunate diebus paschæ incipientes à secunda feria usque ad sextam, & Sabbatum sex diebus, &c. Sexta tamen feria & Sabbato ex toto manete jejuni, qui ita firmis viribus estis, ut ferre possitis, nihil prorsus gustantes usque ad noƐturnum galli cantum. Siquis vero propter imbecillitatem utrumque diem conjungere non potuerit, saltem sab batum servet. servet. Legis rationem inde petunt, quod his diebus ablatus fuerit sponsus ; tum, διὸ παραινοῦμεν καὶ ὑμῖν νηστεύειν ταύτας (ἡμέρας) ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐνηστεύσαμεν ἐν τῷ ἀναλημφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἀφ' ἡμῶν, μέχρις ἐσπέρας. Quamobrem vos hortamur, ut his (diebus) jejunetis, (sicut & nos jejunavimus cum ablatus fuit nobis) usque ad vesperam. Reliquis vero ante sextam feriam diebus, edite hora nona, vel vespere, vel sicut quisque valet. Sabbato autem usque ad galli cantum. Atque hanc suam de jejunio, festoque Paschali legem paulo post perpetuam esse jubent: καὶ τοῦτο ὑμῖν ἐγω νόμιμον αἰώνιον ἑως τῆς σωτηρίας τῶν αἰώνων, μέχρις ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ Κύριος. Sit hoc vobis legitimum sempiternum usque ad consummationem saeculi, donec veniat Dominus. Haec illi, sane severe ac graviter. Atqui & suo tempore, & anterioribus etiam temporibus longe aliter à Christianis factum tradit Irenaeus. Primo testatur, non fuisse unam apud omnes illius jejunii rationem; quae tamen & una esse debuerat, & procul dubio una futura erat, si haec ab Apostolis, communibus universorum magistris, lex scripta fuisset. Tum varias illas, quae tunc obtinebant, jejunii rationes hujusmodi recensGet, quae paene omnes ab hac, quae una solaque apud omnes valere debuerat, discrepant. pant. Nam & quos uno die,& quos duobus jejunafse ait,ii plurimum à nostrorum Δια- τάξεων regula, qui sex jejunari volebant, discedebant;& qui pluribus diebus,quam duobus jejunafse dicuntur,probabile est,plerosque nonfex,quod volunt Boviani Apostoli, sed tribus fi forte, quatuorve, aut quinque jejunaffe. Denique qui sex præcise diebus jejunaverint nulli diserte ab Irenæo memorantur. Tum & illud, quod ab omnibus, quorum vires id ferunt, Διαζῆς requirunt solidum sextæ feriæ , sabbatique, hoc est 40. horarum jejunium, non omnes, sed pauci quidam præstitisse ab Irenæo narrantur. Nullam ergo isti ab Apostolis hac de re latam legem norant; quam fi novissent aliquam , omnes eam communi consensu observaturos fuisse,nihil est quod dubitemus. Ea enim erat Christianorum per ea tempora pietas, is in res divinas, atque apostolicas amor, ut plane fit incredibile legem illam,fi Apostolica foret,ita secure spretam contemptamque fuisse, ut, à plerisque vulgo violaretur; à paucissimis , & (quantum quidem ex Irenæo constare potest) fortasse à nemine servaretur. Irenæus quidem certe, cui Apostolica nulla lex ignota esse potuit, commune hoc vel omnium, vel pœne omnium flagitium narrans denotaffet, fi flagitium effet; adjecifset præter institutum Apostolorum ita diversimode jejunari; legem ipsam Apostolicam recitasset, vel saltem memorasset. At nihil ille hujusmodi. Quin & illam diversitatem, hoc est (si Bovianos Διαφωνίας audimus) manifestam gravemque Apostolicæ legis transgressionem, adeo non damnat, ut etiam laudet; neque cujusquam ritum reprehendat, aut repudiet; sed bene factum censeat, quod omnes impune suo diversi modo, suaque ratione, salva interim fide & pace εἰρηνεύομεν πρὸς ἀλλήλους (inquit) χρὴ ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας τὸ ὁμόνοιαν τῆς πίστεως σωίζηται. pacem inter nos retinemus, variaque ac discrepans jejunii ratio concordiam fidei plurimum commendat. Itane vero Irenæe? Tune a quoquam eos turbari, aut rejici nefas putas, qui proculcata Apostolorum authoritate, non sex, quod illi diserte præcipiunt, sed unum tantum, aut alterum diem jejunio colendum ante pascha existimant? Absit, ut sanctissimum Martyrem ita nihili fecisse arbitremur Apostolorum decreta. Quid ergo est? Nimirum quas tu mihi, Bovi, edis Apostolorum leges, ex Irenæi temporibus nullæ fuerunt; quas jam tum fuisse obtinere non potes, nisi & eadem opera impios fuisse omnes illius memoriæ Christianos, & ipsum quoque Irenæum vel impium, um, vel certe nimis crassum fuisse statuas. Tuas nisi hac lege Constitutiones tenere non potes. Nos quidem, qui & illorum temporum Christianos optimos, maximeque (ut sic dicam) Apostolicos, & Irenaeum longe praestantissimum, sapientissimumque Episcopum fuisse scimus, Constitutiones illas tuas, quae cum istorum pietate & sapientia consistere non queunt, libentes dimittimus, nothasque & sequioribus saeculis natas esse, confitemur. Quod ipsum clarissime confirmat Irenaeus, dum illam jejunandi diversitatem non ex praecepti Apostolici contemptu, aut negligentia (quod omnino & verum erat, & dici debuerat, si qua Apostolorum de hujus jejunii ratione lex erat) sed a non satis accurata simplicis & privatae quodammodo consuetudinis observatione exortam esse docet. Ex quo liquet, non ex praecepto, aut lege, sed ex usu ac consuetudine, invaluisse apud Christianos antepaschale illud jejunium; eoque mentiri impostorem, qui suam de eo Ἀιά-ψευδῶ impudenter Apostolis affinxit.
units.tr: Irenaeus teaches us the same thing in another way in that letter. For he says that, not only in his own time but also much earlier [ἀλλὰ καὶ πολὺ πρότερον], there was among Christians a different form or kind of fasting before the Passover. Some thought that one day ought to be fasted; some two; others even more days; and there were some who measured out that forty-day fast by day and night hours. Now, first of all, it is quite incredible that such a variety of fasting would have arisen among Christians of that time if our Διαταξεῖς, regarded as apostolic, had been known to them. For these define the whole manner of the pre-Passover fast so explicitly and precisely that no one who considers it can doubt what its authors meant [a]. [Ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῷ πάσχα (inquiunt) νηστεύετε, ἀρχόμενοι ἀπὸ σαββάτου μέχρι τῆς παρασκευῆς καὶ σάββατα ἐξ ἡμέρας, &c.] Fast during the days of Passover, beginning from the second day of the week up to the sixth day, and six days on the Sabbath, &c. But on the sixth day and on the Sabbath, keep the fast entire, you who have the strength for it, tasting nothing until the crowing of the cock at night. If anyone cannot keep both days alike, let him at least keep the Sabbath. They give the reason for the law: that the bridegroom was taken away on these days. Then: [διὸ παραινοῦμεν καὶ ὑμῖν νηστεύειν ταύτας (ἡμέρας) ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐνηστεύσαμεν ἐν τῷ ἀναλημφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἀφ' ἡμῶν, μέχρις ἑσπέρας.] Therefore we exhort you to fast these (days) as we also fasted when he was taken from us, until evening. On the other days, before the sixth day, they say, eat at the ninth hour, or in the evening, or as each is able. But on the Sabbath, until the crowing of the cock. And they order this rule about the fast and the Paschal feast to be perpetual: [καὶ τοῦτο ὑμῖν ἔγω νόμιμον αἰώνιον ἕως τῆς συντελείας τῶν αἰώνων, μέχρις ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ Κύριος.] Let this be for you a lawful rule everlasting, until the consummation of the age, until the Lord comes. These are their words, certainly severe and grave. Yet Irenaeus reports that in his own time, and even in earlier times, Christians acted in a quite different way. First, he testifies that there was not one manner of that fast among all; yet there ought to have been one, and undoubtedly would have been one, if this had been a written law from the Apostles, the common teachers of all. Then he lists the various practices of fasting that prevailed at that time, almost all of which differ from this one rule, which ought to have been the single and only rule among all. For those who said they fasted one day, and those who said two, departed widely from the rule of our Διαταξεῖς, which wished six days to be fasted; and as for those who are said to have fasted for more than two days, it is likely that most fasted not six, as the Bovian Apostles want, but perhaps three, four or five. Finally, those who fasted exactly six days are not explicitly mentioned by Irenaeus at all. Moreover, Irenaeus does not say that all who were able required the full solid fast of the sixth day and the Sabbath, that is, forty hours; only a few, not all, are said to have kept it. There was therefore no law from the Apostles on this matter known to them; for if they had known of any, all would undoubtedly have observed it by common consent. For such was the piety of Christians in those times, and such their love of divine and apostolic things, that it is wholly incredible that such a law, if it were apostolic, would have been so safely despised and scorned that it was commonly violated by most, and kept by very few, and (as far as can be gathered from Irenaeus) perhaps by no one. Irenaeus, certainly, to whom no apostolic law could have been unknown, would have condemned this common sin, or nearly universal sin, if it were a sin, in narrating it; he would have added that it was against the Apostles' ordinance to fast in such diverse ways; he would have recited the apostolic law itself, or at least mentioned it. But he does nothing of the kind. Indeed, he does not condemn that diversity, which (if we hear the Bovian Διαφωνίαι) is a manifest and grave transgression of the apostolic law; rather he praises it, and he reproves or rejects no one's practice. He thinks it good that all, each in his own way and by his own reasoning, were able to act without punishment, while keeping faith and peace: [εἰρηνεύομεν πρὸς ἀλλήλους (inquit) χρὴ ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας τὸ ὁμόνοιαν τῆς πίστεως σώζεσθαι.] We keep peace with one another, he says; the disagreement of the fast ought to preserve the concord of faith. The varied and discordant manner of fasting greatly commends the agreement of faith. Is that really so, Irenaeus? Do you think it wrong for anyone to be troubled or rejected who, having trampled underfoot the authority of the Apostles, thinks that one or at most two days, and not six, which they expressly prescribe, should be kept with fasting before Easter? Far be it from us to think that so holy a martyr made so little of the decrees of the Apostles. What then is the answer? Plainly, Bovius, the laws of the Apostles that you put forward did not exist in the time of Irenaeus; and you cannot show that they were then in force, unless you at the same time declare all the Christians of that age to have been impious, and Irenaeus himself either impious or at least exceedingly dull. You cannot keep your Constitutions except on this condition. For our part, who know that the Christians of those times were the best and, if I may so put it, most apostolic, and that Irenaeus was a far more outstanding and wiser bishop, we gladly dismiss those Constitutions of yours, which cannot agree with the piety and wisdom of those men, and we confess that they are spurious and were born in later ages. Irenaeus confirms this most clearly when he teaches that this diversity of fasting arose not from contempt or neglect of an apostolic precept (which would certainly have been both true and worth saying, if there had been any apostolic law on the manner of this fast), but from a not sufficiently careful observance of a simple and somewhat private custom. From this it is clear that the pre-Passover fast became established among Christians not from a precept or law but from use and custom; and therefore the impostor who shamelessly attributed his own Ἀιάψευδῶ about it to the Apostles is lying.

units.la: Arg. VI. Ex apocrypha Barnabæ epistola ductum; quo clarissime demonstratur, Constitutiones alicujus impostoris opus esse.
units.tr: Argument VI. Drawn from the apocryphal Epistle of Barnabas, which most clearly shows that the Constitutions are the work of some impostor.

units.la: SED antequam ultra progredior, ex apocrypha Barnabæ epistola aliquid observandum est; ex quo deprehendi potest, nihil minus esse, quam Apostolos, τὰς Bovii Διαταγίας. Eam enim epistolam ante secundi saeculi finem Barnabæ suppositam, affictamque fuisse inde clarissime perspicitur, quod Clemens Alexandrinus in Stromateon opere, quod paulo post annum Domini 194. scriptum constat, non pauca passim ex illa laudavit. Iam in illa Barnabæ epistola haec verba de filiis mortis leguntur: a, ὑ κολλώμενοι ἀγαθῷ, ὑ κείμεν δικαία χήρα τῇ ὀρφανῷ προσέχοντες, ἀγρυπνοῦντες ὑπὲρ εἰς φόβον Θεοῦ, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὸ πονηρὸν· ὧν μακρὰν ἐ πόρρω πραύτης, καὶ ὑπομονή· ἀγαπῶντες μάταια, διώκοντες ἀνταπόδομα, οὐκ ἐλεοῦντες πτωχόν, ὑ πονοῦντες ὅτι τῷ καταπονουμένῳ, ἐυχερεῖς ἐν καταλαλιᾷ, ὑ γινώσκοντες τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτὰς, φονεῖς τέκνων, φθορεῖς πλάσματος Θεοῦ, ἀποστρεφόμενοι τὸν ἐνδεόμενον, καταπονοῦντες τὸν θλιβόμενον, πλουσίων παράκλητ, πενήτων ἄνομοι κριταί, παντοπαρτητοί. Non adhaerentes
units.tr: But before I go further, something must be noted from the apocryphal Epistle of Barnabas, from which it can be grasped that the Apostles are the least likely authors of the Constitutions of Bovius [τὰς Bovii Διαταγίας]. For it is quite clear that this epistle was forged under the name of Barnabas before the end of the second century, since Clement of Alexandria, in his Stromata, which is known to have been written shortly after the year of the Lord 194, quotes it often. Now in that epistle of Barnabas these words about the sons of death are read: "not cleaving to what is good, nor watching for the righteous widow and the orphan, nor attending to the fear of God, but to what is evil, from whom meekness and patience are far away; loving vain things, pursuing rewards, not pitying the poor, not labouring for the oppressed, ready and quick to slander, not knowing their Maker, murderers of children, corruptors of God's creature, turning away from the needy, oppressing the afflicted, advocates of the rich, unjust judges of the poor, sinners in all things."

units.la: a ep. pane extr. p. 252 edit. Is. Vossii. rentes bono, justo judicio vidua & orpha-no minime adtendentes, vigilantes non ad timorem Dei, sed ad malum, a quibus longe absunt mansuetudo & vigilantia, diligentes vana, vindicta amatores, non miserentes egeno, non laborantes ad levandum oppressum, ad detractionem prompti & faciles, non cognoscentes factorem suum, liberorum homicida, corruptores creaturæ Dei, se ab indigente avertentes, opprimentes oppressum, divitum advocati, pauperum iniqui judices, per omnia peccatores. Haec-tenus Pseudo-Barnabas. Non est ovum ovo similius, quam illis Barnabæ hæc nostrorum Διδαχὴ in eorundem hominum descriptione.
units.tr: (Vossius's Latin rendering, from the end of the epistle, p. 252 of the edition of Isaac Vossius: "...adhering to the good; not attending to the just judgment of the widow and orphan; watching not for the fear of God but for evil, from whom mildness and watchfulness are far off; loving vanities, lovers of revenge, not having mercy on the needy, not labouring to relieve the oppressed, prompt and easy to detract, not knowing their Maker, murderers of children, corrupters of God's creature, turning away from the one in need, oppressing the oppressed, advocates of the rich, unjust judges of the poor, sinners in every way.") Thus far the pseudo-Barnabas. The description of these men in the Teaching [Διδαχή] of our people is not more like one egg to another than it is to these words of Barnabas.

units.la: οἱ ἀγαθῷ ... Greek text as printed, beginning with οἱ, "ἀγαθῷ"; "κείσει δίκαια· ἀγρυπνοῦσιν εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ πονηρόν, ὧν μακρὰν πραότης καὶ ὑπομονή. μάταια ἀγαπῶντες, διώκοντες ἀνταπόδομα, μὴ ἐλεοῦντες πλούσιον, ἐπὶ πονοῦντες ὃν καταπονουμένῳ, ἐπιγινώσκοντες τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτούς, φονεῖς τέκνων, φθορεῖς πλάσματος Θεοῦ, ἀποστρεφόμενοι ἐνδεόμενον, καταπονοῦντες θλιβόμενον, πλουσίων παρακλητοί, πενήτων ὑπερόπται, πανταμάρτητοι."
units.tr: οἱ ... [The Greek of the passage, as printed, with the same words: "μὴ κολλώμενοι ἀγαθῷ, μὴ κρίσει δικαίᾳ χήρᾳ καὶ ὀρφανῷ προσέχοντες, ἀγρυπνοῦντες οὐκ εἰς φόβον Θεοῦ, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ πονηρόν, ὧν μακρὰν πραότης καὶ ὑπομονή· μάταια ἀγαπῶντες, διώκοντες ἀνταπόδομα, οὐκ ἐλεοῦντες πένητα, οὐ πονοῦντες εἰς τὸ ἀνορθῶσαι καταπονούμενον, εὐχερεῖς εἰς καταλαλιάν, μὴ γινώσκοντες τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτούς, φονεῖς τέκνων, φθορεῖς πλάσματος Θεοῦ, ἀποστρεφόμενοι τὸν ἐνδεόμενον, καταπονοῦντες τὸν θλιβόμενον, πλουσίων παράκλητοι, πενήτων ἄνομοι κριταί, παντοπαράβατοι."]

units.la: Omnia, paucissimis voculis exceptis, eadem, quæ Barnabæ: ut altera ex alteris descripta fuisse necesse sit. Non descripsisse autem pseudo-Barnabam ex Apostolorum constitutionibus manifestum est. Hæc enim si in-de de mutuatus esshet, haud dubie Apostolos, verborum scilicet authores, nominatim laudasset, illa, quæ in citandis sacris scriptoribus solennia sunt, addidisset, ut ajunt Apostoli, vel, ut loquuntur in suis Constitutionibus Apostoli, vel aliquid simile. Non fecit. Non est ergo dubitandum, istius pseudo-Barnabæ ævo, id est secundo Christianismi sæculo jam adulto, nullas adhuc extitisse Bovianas Apostolorum Διαταγάς. Sed & hinc clarum certumque, τῆς Διαθήκης illa nuper descripta verba ex pseudo-Barnabæ apocryphis sumpsisse; quod cum à verorum Apostolorum & ingenio, & ævo alienum sit, omnino necesse est, impostorem fuisse, qui talia Apostolis affinxit.
units.tr: Almost all of it, with very few words excepted, is the same as in Barnabas, so that one of the two must necessarily have been copied from the other. That the pseudo-Barnabas did not copy from the Constitutions of the Apostles is plain. For if he had borrowed them from there, he would undoubtedly have named the Apostles, the actual authors of the words, and would have added the formulas customary in citing the sacred writers, such as "as the Apostles say" or "as the Apostles speak in their Constitutions," or something similar. He did not do this. There can therefore be no doubt that in the time of this pseudo-Barnabas, that is, in the second century of Christianity when it was already well grown, the Constitutions of Bovius under the Apostles' name did not yet exist. And from this it is also clear and certain that the words lately quoted from the Covenant [τῆς Διαθήκης] were taken from the apocryphal writings of pseudo-Barnabas. Since this is foreign both to the genius and to the age of the true Apostles, it is wholly necessary that the one who attributed such things to the Apostles was an impostor.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Arg. VII. Constitutiones Clementi Alexandrino f. ipse ignotas. Arg. VIII. Neque eas vel scivisse, vel probasse Tertullianum. Ex eo clarissime confici, nullas adhuc tertio isto sæculo ineunte extitisse Apostolorum Constitutiones.
units.tr: Argument 7. Clement of Alexandria himself did not know the Constitutions. Argument 8. Tertullian neither knew them nor approved of them. From this it is most clearly concluded that no Apostolic Constitutions yet existed at the beginning of this third century.

units.la: ATQUE hæc de secundo Christianismi sæculo. Sed neque tertio cognitas fuisse Bovianas Διαταξεις ex omnibus, qui toto eo tempore vixerunt, scriptoribus, clarum est; quoquorum nemo est, qui eas memoraverit. Primus ex iis prodeat Clemens Alexandrinus; qui secundo saeculo exeunte florere coepit, tertiique initia attigit. Stromateon enim opus scripsit paulo post Commodi necem, hoc est paulo post annum D. 192. Is cum omni sacra & exotica eruditione ad miraculum abundaret, praeclara illa ingenii sui monumenta, quae sane reliquit non pauca, solet multis divinorum Christianorum, philosophorum, etiam haereticorum scriptorum litteris, ac testimoniis variegare. Quin & ipse non raro apocrypha, ut Barnabae epistolam, & alia usurpat. Clementis quidem certe epistolam ad Corinthios veram, ac γνησίαν, multis subinde locis laudat, & satis prolixas ex ea φωνὰς describit. Cur non & Διδαχὴ, siquas ejusdem authoris norat, aliquo loco memorat? cum tam multa passim tractet, quae ex eo libro vel probari, vel ornari, & illustrari poterant? Verbi gratia, in Paedagogo multus est, ut promiscua utriusque; sexus balnea damnet, reique foeditatem ac turpitudinem demonstret. Ac in eo sermone Hesiodum, Graecum poetam, usurpavit; utque ostenderet, quam sit periculosum nuda mulierum corpora aspicere, illud Christi ex Euangelio attulit, Qui inspexit τὴν γυναῖκα ... curiosius, jam peccavit. Obsecro te, cur tali in loco hæc ex Constitutionibus a disertissima omisit? πεῖπατῶν ἡ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ καὶ λέσασθαι βυλόμενον, χρήσῃ βαλλανείῳ ἀνδρείῳ, ἵνα μὴ ᾖ τὸ ἐπιδεικνυ- σαί σε σῶμα ἐν ἀχήμῳ ἀποκαλύφει γυναι- ξίν, ἢ διδάσκαλος ἦσαν οὐχ ἀρμόζουσαν ἀνδρά- σιν, ἢ σὺ παγιδεύουσης, ἢ παγιδεύσῃς ἑαυ- τὴν τὰς ἐτῶς ἐυαλώτας γυναῖκας. Φυλάσσε ἕν τὰ τοιαῦτα. Cum in foro deambulas, & lavare vis, utere balneo virorum, ne, quia corpus nudum mulieribus turpiter ostenderis, aut quod non decet viros spectaveris, vel illaqueeris, vel illaqueES fœminas, quasi facile capiuntur. Cave igitur ab hujusmodi rebus. Qui Clementis morem, scribendique rationem norit, non dubitabit, quin ista hic fuerit commemoraturus, si ea scivisset. Qui ejusdem πολυμάθειαν ac multijugam eruditionem perspectam habuerit, is nunquam credet, ignotas ei fuisse Apostolorum Διαταξεις, siquæ eo sæculo extiterunt. Ergo quod hanc ῥῆσιν tali loco omittit, eo fatetur se Διαταξεις nescivisse; quod nescivit, eo probatur, nullas tum apud Christianos fuisse.
units.tr: So much for the second century. That the Constitutions of Boyius were also unknown in the third century is clear from all the writers who lived throughout that time, and none of them mentions them. The first of these to come forward is Clement of Alexandria, who began to flourish at the close of the second century and reached the beginning of the third. He wrote his work the Stromata shortly after the death of Commodus, that is, shortly after A.D. 192. Although he abounded wonderfully in all sacred and foreign learning, he is accustomed to embellish the splendid monuments of his genius, of which he left not a few, with the writings and testimonies of many divine Christian writers, of philosophers, and even of heretics. Indeed, he himself not rarely makes use of apocryphal works, such as the Epistle of Barnabas and others. He certainly often praises the genuine Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, and describes quite lengthy passages [φωνάς] from it. Why does he never mention the Didache in any passage, if he knew any work of that author? He treats so many matters everywhere that could have been proved, adorned and illustrated from that book. For example, in the Paedagogus he argues at length that promiscuous bathing of both sexes is to be condemned, and he shows how foul and shameful it is. In that discourse he cites Hesiod, the Greek poet, and to show how dangerous it is to gaze upon the naked bodies of women, he brings forward that saying of Christ from the Gospel: "Whoever looks at the woman [τὴν γυναῖκα] too curiously has already sinned." I beg you, why in such a place did he omit these most eloquent words from the Constitutions? "Walking in the marketplace and wishing to bathe, use the men's bath [χρῆσαι βαλανείῳ ἀνδρείῳ], lest by displaying your body in an indecent uncovering to women you either become a teacher of what is not fitting for men, or you ensnare them, or you ensnare the women who are otherwise captured. Guard yourself against such things [Φυλάσσου οὖν τὰ τοιαῦτα]." [Greek: περιπατῶν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ καὶ λούεσθαι βουλόμενον, χρῆσαι βαλανείῳ ἀνδρείῳ, ἵνα μὴ ᾖ τὸ ἐπιδεικνύειν σε σῶμα ἐν ἀσχήμονι ἀποκαλύψει γυναιξίν, ἢ διδάσκαλος ἦσθα οὐχ ἁρμόζουσαν ἀνδράσιν, ἢ σὺ παγιδεύσῃς, ἢ παγιδεύσῃ ἑαυτὴν τὰς ἑτέρως ἁλισκομένας γυναῖκας. Φυλάσσου οὖν τὰ τοιαῦτα.] Anyone who knows Clement's habit and manner of writing will not doubt that he would have mentioned this here, had he known it. Anyone who has observed his great learning and wide-ranging erudition will never believe that the Apostolic Constitutions were unknown to him, if any existed in that century. Therefore, because he omits this saying in such a place, he confesses that he did not know the Constitutions; and because he did not know them, it is proved that none existed among Christians at that time.

units.la: Nunc ad Tertullianum, Clementis æqualem, veniamus; qui & ipse unus ad conficiendum, profligandumq; totum illud fictitium Διαταγῶν opus satis esse potest. Is enim, non modo eas (quas, cum fuerit erudi-
units.tr: Now let us come to Tertullian, a contemporary of Clement, who alone is enough to refute and overthrow that whole fictitious work of the Constitutions. For he, not only (since he was most learned, he could not have been ignorant of them, had there been any) never mentioned them anywhere,

units.la: eruditissimus, ignorare, si fuissent aliquæ, non potuit) nusquam memoravit; sed etiam plurima passim vel ipse sentit, ac docet, vel sensisse, docuisseque ejus temporis Catholicos Christianos testatur, quæ cum istorum Διαθηκῶν scitis nullo modo consistere queunt. Pauca de multis proferam. Ille, quod & ab Augustino, & quidem non sine admiratione atque indignatione, observatum est, & ex ipsius Tertulliani de Anima commentario perspicuum est, sensit, animam nostram corpoream esse.
units.tr: but he also repeatedly sets out, or testifies that the Catholic Christians of his time set out, teachings which cannot in any way be reconciled with the doctrines of those Constitutions. I will offer a few of many. He held, as Augustine also observed, and not without wonder and indignation, and as is clear from Tertullian's own commentary on the soul, that our soul is corporeal.

units.la: Nostri vero Διαθηκεῖς illustrissimo loco, hoc est in ipsa prædicationis doctrinæque suæ ἐξηγήσει, ac synopsi, ψυχὴν inquiunt b) ἀσώματον ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ ἀθάνατον ὁμολογοῦμεν. Animam in nobis confitemur incorpoream, & immortalem. Quis Tertullianum vel tam imperitum fuisse crediderit, ut Apostolorum, siquæ suo tempore extitissent, Constitutiones nesciverit; vel tam impudentem, ut contra disertissimam Apostolorum professionem contrariam ipse sententiam & sequi, & apud homines Christianos palam edere, ac defendere sustinuerit? Quin & diversam, hoc est τῶν Διαθηκῶν sententiam, vulgo tribuit, & veluti plebeium errorem dimittit; Simplicior quisque fautor (inquit) sententia nostra putabit, carnem etiam idcirco repræsentandam esse judicio,
units.tr: Yet our Constitutionists, in the most prominent place, that is, in the very explanation and summary of their preaching and teaching, say: "We confess the soul [ψυχήν] within us to be incorporeal and immortal [ἀσώματον ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ ἀθάνατον ὁμολογοῦμεν]." b) We confess the soul within us to be incorporeal and immortal. Who would believe Tertullian to have been so ignorant that he did not know the Constitutions of the Apostles, if any had existed in his time; or so shameless that, against the most explicit profession of the Apostles, he would dare to hold the opposite opinion himself, to publish it openly among Christian people, and to defend it? Indeed, he commonly ascribes to the opposite view, that is, to the opinion of the Constitutions, and dismisses it as a plebeian error: Every simpler supporter of our view (he says) will think that the flesh too must for this reason be presented at judgement,

units.la: {b} l. 6. c. 11. c. judicio, quia aliter anima non capiat passionem tormenti, seu refrigerii, utpote incorporalis; Hoc enim VULGUS existimat. Nos autem animam corporalem, & hic profitemur, & in suo volumine probamus a, habentem proprium genus substantiae, soliditatis, per quam quid & sentire, & pati possit, Tum statim se concedere ait,animam habere corpulentiam propriam. Nemo mihi persuaserit, Tertullianum, quod Apostolicum esse sciret dogma, id non modo rejecturum, sed & contemptim aspernaturum, vulgoque imputaturum fuisse. Et si eam fuisse finxeris viri inverecundiam, ut Apostolicae sententiae tam arroganter oppedere qui verit: illud certe non negabis, eum quo erat in disputando acumine, hinc redundantem ex Apostolorum nomine invidiam aliqua arte fuisse declinaturum, & eorum verba commode interpretaturum. Qui philosophorum contra hoc suum dogma & authoritatem & rationes adeo non sprevitb,ut etiam fuse ac diligenter expenderit, atque solverit, certe solvere conatus sit; ejus profecto non fuit Apostolorum, si quod erat contra se in hoc argumento vel in speciem dictum, contemnere, maxime quo loco ex ipsorum libris animae (ut loquitur) corporalitatem astruere contendit. Ille vero c nullam sibi ipsi vel hic vel alibi Apostolorum
units.tr: {b} book 6, ch. 11. "...to judgment, because otherwise the soul would not feel the suffering of torment or of refreshment, being incorporeal. For this is what the common people think. But we profess here, and prove in our own volume, that the soul is corporeal, having its own kind of substance, solidity, through which it can both feel and suffer something." Then he at once concedes, saying, the soul has its own bodily substance. No one will persuade me that Tertullian, if he had known this to be an Apostolic dogma, would not only have rejected it but also scorned it and imputed it to the common people. And even if you imagine such shamelessness in the man that he would so arrogantly oppose an Apostolic opinion, you will surely not deny that, with his keenness in disputation, he would have avoided the odium that would have overflowed from the name of the Apostles by some skill, and would have interpreted their words aptly. He who did not despise the authority and arguments of the philosophers against this his own dogma, but even examined and resolved them at length and with care, and at least tried to resolve them, would not have been one to disregard the Apostles, if something said against him on this question seemed to come from them, especially in the place where he strives to establish from their own books the corporeality (as he calls it) of the soul. But he nowhere, either here or elsewhere, objects any Apostolic constitution to himself.

units.la: ΔΙΑΤΑΞΙΝ Διάθεζιν objicit. Quid ergo est? Nempe nondum eo sæculo orti erant Boviani Apostoli; quos si scivisset Tertullianus, haud dubie vel secuturus erat, vel certe confuturus. Neutrum fecit. Nullos ergo hujus quidem commatis Apostolos cognitos habuit. Idem quoque ad Faustum Regensem, quinti sæculi scriptorem, observari posset; quia &animam &Angelos substantia corporea esse docet. Atque hæc quidem obiter. Sed ad rem. Cum nostri Διαθῆκης infantes baptizari jubeant, βαπτίζετε δὲ ὑμῶν τὰ νήπια, baptizate pueros vestros infantes; Tertullianus plane contra, baptismum in ævum maturius differri vult; Itaque (inquit) pro cujusque personæ conditione, ac dispositione, etiam ætate, cunctatio baptismi utilior est; præcipue tamen circa PARVULOS. Mox; Quid festinat innocens ætas ad remissionem peccatorum? Cautius agetur in secularibus, ut cui substantia terrena non creditur, decima credatur. Norint petere salutem, ut petenti dedisse videaris. Quo & illa, quæ hic continuat, pertinent; Non minore de causa innupti quoque procrastinandi, in quibus tentatio præparata est, tam virginibus per maturitatem, quam viduis per vacationem, donec aut nubant, aut continentia corroborentur. Vel eo prosunt hi, maximi alioqui scriptoris, errores, ut intelligas
units.tr: What then is the case? Namely, the Boyian Apostles had not yet arisen in that century; had Tertullian known them, he would undoubtedly either have followed them or at least have confuted them. He did neither. Therefore he had no knowledge of Apostles of this kind at all. The same could also be observed concerning Faustus of Riez, a writer of the fifth century, since he teaches that both the soul and the angels are of corporeal substance. But these things in passing. But to the point. Since our Covenants command that infants be baptized, "baptize your infant children" [βαπτίζετε δὲ ὑμῶν τὰ νήπια, baptize your children, infants]; Tertullian, on the contrary, wants baptism to be deferred to a later age: "Therefore (he says), according to the condition and disposition of each person, and also his age, delay of baptism is more useful; especially, however, in the case of LITTLE CHILDREN." Soon after: "Why does innocent age hasten to the forgiveness of sins? Caution will be exercised in worldly matters, so that the one to whom earthly substance is not entrusted is entrusted with the tithe. Let them learn to seek salvation, so that you may seem to have given to one who asks." To this also belongs what he goes on to say: "For no less reason the unmarried too are to be put off, in whom temptation is prepared, both virgins because of their maturity and widows because of their idleness, until either they marry or they are strengthened in continence." These errors of an otherwise very great writer are of this profit, that you may understand

units.la: a ep. ad Ben. Paul. T. 3. bibl pp. p. 40. d. e.
units.tr: a Epistle to Benedict Paul, vol. 3, Bibl. PP., p. 40 d, e.

units.la: b Const. l. 6. c. 15.
units.tr: b Const. bk 6, ch. 15.

units.la: c L. de bapt. c. 18. telligas nondum Διαβάπτισμα tum extitisse; qui scilicet si extitissent, proque Apostolis habiti essent, Tertullianum his opinionibus, sane incommodis, liberaturi erant. Sed & haec ex eodem de Baptismo opere ostenduntᵗ Tertulliano ignotas fuisse Bovii Apostolos. Nam si eos norat, cur laicis, quam illi plane penitusque adimunt, baptizandi potestatem hic liberalissime concedit? Etiam (inquit ) laicis jus est, quod enim ex aequo accipitur, ex aequo dari potest, nisi aut episcopi, jam aut presbyteri aut diaconi vocantur discentes. Domini sermo non debet abscondi ab ullo. Proinde & baptismus, aeque Dei census, ab omnibus exerceri potest. Tantum laicos monet, ut verecunde ac modeste, propter Ecclesiae honorem, nec nisi in necessitatibus, utantur. Quin & multo etiam vehementius Διαβάπτισμα nostros alibi pulsat Tertullianus. Cum enim unum hoc sit de capitalibus eorum edictis , Non permittimus laico ullum ex operibus sacerdotalibus facere, ut sacrificium, aut baptismum; Septimius plane contra, & utrumque hoc & caetera omnia, est ubi & quando concedit laico; Ubi (inquit ) Ecclesiastici ordinis non est confessus, & offers, & tinguis, & sacerdos es tibi solus. Atque ita factum fuisse in Euangelicae praedicationis primordiis, author est Hilarius
units.tr: c On Baptism, ch. 18. understand that the Constitutions had not yet appeared at that time; for if they had appeared and had been regarded as Apostolic, they would have freed Tertullian from these opinions, which are indeed inconvenient. But these things also show, from the same work On Baptism, that the Apostles of Boyius were unknown to Tertullian. For if he knew them, why does he here so very generously grant to laymen the power of baptizing, a power which they [the Constitutions] take away entirely and completely? "Even (he says) laymen have the right, for what is received on equal terms can be given on equal terms, unless bishops, or presbyters, or deacons are called by those who are learning. The word of the Lord ought not to be hidden from anyone. Accordingly, baptism too, being God's gift equally to all, can be administered by all." He only advises laymen to use it modestly and moderately, out of respect for the honour of the Church, and only in cases of necessity. Indeed, Tertullian elsewhere attacks our opponents' view of baptism even more vehemently. For since this is one of their chief edicts: "We do not permit a layman to perform any of the priestly functions, such as sacrifice or baptism"; Septimius, on the contrary, grants to a layman both this and all the other things, wherever and whenever: "Where (he says) there is no ecclesiastical order, if you offer, and baptize, and are yourself the sole priest." And that this was so done in the first beginnings of evangelical preaching is attested by Hilary

units.la: Diaconus in Commentariis, qui falso Ambrosio tribuuntur; Omnibus (inquit) inter initia concessum est & Euangelizare, & baptizare, & scripturas in Ecclesia explanare. Quæ profecto nunquam iste ita scripsisset, si nostras Constitutiones & legisset, & pro Apostolicis habuisset.
units.tr: The deacon in the Commentaries, which are falsely ascribed to Ambrose, says: "At the beginning it was permitted to all to evangelize, to baptize, and to expound the Scriptures in the Church." He would surely never have written this if he had read our Constitutions and regarded them as Apostolic.

units.la: Idem Tertullianus æque ac Justinus, Chiliastarum quoque delirium, non obscure, quod supra diximus, à Bovianis Apostolis confossum, secutus est.
units.tr: The same Tertullian, like Justin, also followed the Chiliasts' delusion, which, as we said above, the Bovian Apostles have not obscurely run through.

units.la: Sed idem clarissime, disertissimeque negat, Apostolorum vel manu, vel nomine atque authoritate scriptas fuisse Bovianas Διαλάξεις, dum multas in his voluminibus perspicue aperteque & præceptas, & litteris mandatas observationes, ipse sine ullius Scripturæ instrumento, solius traditionis titulo, & exinde consuetudinis patrocinio haberi, vindicarique ait. Quales hæ sunt, quas recenseт, aquam ad baptismum adituri (inquit) contestamur nos renunciare diabolo, & pompis, & angelis ejus; Item, oblationes pro defunctis, pro natalitiis annua die facimus. Die Dominico jejunium nefas ducimus; & Eadem immunitate à die Pasche ad Pentecoste usque gaudemus. Hos omnes ritus plane ἀγράφως esse, solaque traditione ac consuetudine sine ullius scriptura instrumento receptos fuisse, atque invaluisse docet Tertullianus. Id vero liquido falsum est, si Apostolorum vere sunt Bovianæ Διατάξεις; in quarum libro septimo primum illud de baptizandi contestatione disertissime perscriptum legitur a; Καὶ ὅταν ἡ πρὸς αὐτὸ λοιπὸν τὸ βαπτισθῆναι ὁ κλη--χη-θεὶς, μαν-θανέτω τὰ περὶ τῆς ἀποταγῆς τῆς διαβόλου. (cum in eo de catero erit catechumenus, ut jam jam baptizetur, discat ea, quæ de renuntiando diabolo habentur. Tum ipsa recitatur renuntiationis formula b; Ἀποτάσσομαι τῷ Σα-τανᾷ, καὶ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῇ πομπῇ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῇ λατρείᾳ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ, &c. Renuntio Satanæ, & operibus ejus, & pompis ejus, & cultui ejus, & Angelis ejus. Alterum de oblationibus anniversariis pro defunctorum natalitiis, haud obscurius scriptum invenitur c; Ἐνιάυσια ὑπὲρ μνείας αὐτῶν (τῶν κοιμηθέντων) καὶ διδόσθω ἐν τῇ ὑπαρχόντων αὐτῶν πένητων εἰς τὴν ἀνάμνησιν αὐτῶν. Item anno exacto pro memoria ipsius (defuncti) & ex bonis ejus detur pauperibus ad recordationem ejusdem. Tertium de dominici, & totius Pentecostes à jejunio immunitate scripserant quoque Boviani Διαταγεῖς. d Εὐ-χῶ ἁμαρτίας ἔσαι ὁ τῶν Κυριακῶν νηστευόντων ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεως ἔσαν, ἢ τῶν Πεντηκοστῶν, Reus peccati erit, qui Dominico die jejunaverit, cum is sit resurrectionis dies, aut qui Pentecoste. Si hæc vel ab Apostolis, ut præferunt ipsi libri, vel certe (quod Bovius mavult) à Clemente Apostolico, Apostolis authoribus, scripta sunt; si (quod decernit canon Apostolorum ultimus) libris novi Testamenti canonicis accensenda sunt; qui factum est, ut Tertullianus eas, quæ istic perscriptæ sunt, observationes sine ullius scripturæ instrumento haberi, vindicarique dixerit? mox ullam earum extare negaverit Scripturarum legem? Harum (inquit) & aliarum hujusmodi disciplinarum si legem expositules scripturarum, nullam invenies? Qui factum, ut eas Solius traditionis titulo, & exinde consuetudinis patrocinio stare scripserit? Itane vero? Atqui præter traditionem, luculenta erat, & quidem ἐγγραφῷ istarum disciplinarum, si Bovio credimus, ex libris vel Apostolorum ipsorum, vel certe Apostolici Clementis, probatio. Nos vero de his Tertulliano credere justius est, quam Bovio. Cum ergo neget Tertullianus illas observationes ullo Scriptura instrumento, ulla scripturæ lege, alio denique, quam unius traditionis titulo niti; necessario confitendum est, nullos adhuc illo tempore Apostolos, nullum Clementem suas de istis leges scripsisse; quæ adeo horum nomine scripta nunc leguntur, ea post Tertullianum, non ab Apostolis, vel à Clemente, qui centum ante eum annis mortui omnes erant, sed ab impostore aliquo scripta, editaque fuisse. Id vero ex hoc ipso Tertulliani loco aliter quoque confirmatur. Nam ille quandam suo ævo solennem in baptismo disciplinam commemorat, cujus nulla est apud Διαθηκας mentio. Inde (id est ex aqua baptismali) suscepti, lactis (inquit) & mellis concordiam prægustamus; exque ea die lavacro quotidiano per totam hebdomadem abstinemus. Nempe iis temporibus vixerunt Διαθηγεις, quibus illa lactis, mellisque prægustatio, Tertulliani ævo usitata, observari desierat.
units.tr: But the same author most clearly and emphatically denies that the Bovian Διατάξεις were written by the hand, or in the name and authority, of the Apostles. He says that many observances in these volumes, plainly and openly prescribed and committed to writing, are held and defended without the warrant of any Scripture, on the title of tradition alone, and thence on the patronage of custom. Such are those he lists: When we are about to approach the water of baptism, we testify that we renounce the devil, and his pomps, and his angels. Likewise, we make offerings for the dead on the annual day of their birth. We count fasting on the Lord's day unlawful, and we rejoice in the same exemption from fasting from Easter to Pentecost. Tertullian teaches that all these rites are wholly unwritten [ἀγράφως], and were received and grew strong through tradition and custom alone, without the warrant of any written Scripture. But this is plainly false, if the Bovian Διατάξεις are truly the Apostles'. In their seventh book the first of these, the testimony made at baptism, is set down most explicitly. "And when the one who has been called is finally about to be baptized, let him learn the things concerning the renunciation of the devil" [Καὶ ὅταν ἡ πρὸς αὐτὸ λοιπὸν τὸ βαπτισθῆναι ὁ κλη--χη-θεὶς, μαν-θανέτω τὰ περὶ τῆς ἀποταγῆς τῆς διαβόλου]. (That is, when the catechumen is about to be baptized at once, he should learn what is said about renouncing the devil.) Then the very formula of renunciation is recited: "I renounce Satan, and his works, and his pomp, and his service, and his angels, etc." [Ἀποτάσσομαι τῷ Σα-τανᾷ, καὶ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῇ πομπῇ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῇ λατρείᾳ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ, &c.] (I renounce Satan, and his works, and his pomps, and his cult, and his angels.) The second, concerning anniversary offerings for the birthdays of the dead, is found written no less plainly: "Let there be a yearly offering for the memory of them who have fallen asleep, and let it be given, from their possessions, to the poor in remembrance of them" [Ἐνιάυσια ὑπὲρ μνείας αὐτῶν (τῶν κοιμηθέντων) καὶ διδόσθω ἐν τῇ ὑπαρχόντων αὐτῶν πένητων εἰς τὴν ἀνάμνησιν αὐτῶν]. Likewise: "when a year has passed, for the memory of the same (deceased), let something be given to the poor from his goods in remembrance of him." The third, on exemption from fasting on the Lord's days and throughout the whole of Pentecost, was also written by the Bovian Διαταγεῖς: "He will be guilty of sin who fasts on the Lord's days, which are days of resurrection, or on the days of Pentecost" [Εὐ-χῶ ἁμαρτίας ἔσαι ὁ τῶν Κυριακῶν νηστευόντων ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεως ἔσαν, ἢ τῶν Πεντηκοστῶν]. If these things were written either by the Apostles, as the books themselves claim, or at least (as Bovius prefers) by Clement the Apostolic, with the Apostles as authors; if they are to be counted among the canonical books of the New Testament, as the last canon of the Apostles decrees: how is it that Tertullian said that the observances written there are held and defended without the warrant of any Scripture? And how did he afterwards deny that any law of Scripture exists for them? "If you examine the law of the Scriptures for these and other disciplines of this kind," he says, "you will find none." How did he come to write that they stand on the title of tradition alone and thence on the patronage of custom? Really? Yet, if we believe Bovius, besides tradition there was clear proof in writing for these disciplines, from books either of the Apostles themselves or at least of the Apostolic Clement. But it is more right for us to believe Tertullian than Bovius here. Since, therefore, Tertullian denies that those observances rest on any warrant of Scripture or any law of Scripture, but on nothing other than the title of tradition alone, it must necessarily be confessed that at that time no Apostles and no Clement had yet written laws about these matters. The writings that are now read under their names were written and published after Tertullian, not by the Apostles or by Clement, who had all been dead for a hundred years before him, but by some impostor. This is confirmed in another way from this very passage of Tertullian. For he recalls a custom in baptism that was solemn in his own age, and of which there is no mention in the Διαθηκαι: "Having been taken up from the water (that is, from baptismal water), we taste a mixture of milk and honey; and from that day we abstain from daily washing for the whole week." Certainly the Διαθηγεις lived at a time when that tasting of milk and honey, usual in Tertullian's age, had ceased to be observed.

units.la: Jam & illud clarissime arguit nullas Tertulliani temporibus extitisse Bovianas Apostolorum διαταγας, quod vir acerrimus, ac diligentissimus, disputandique mirabilis artifex, earum authoritatem neque Marcioni, aut Valentinianis, neque Praxeæ in luculentissimis quæ adversus eos edidit, operibus usquam opponit. Marcion, ut notum est, Christi Patrem negabat universi conditorem, vel Mosaicæ legis authorem fuisse: Eadem delirabant Valentiniani. Tertullianus quinque contra Marcionem volumina, unum contra Valentinianos scripsit; egregium utrumque opus, ac illud præsertim prius; in quo nihil omittit quo Marcionis impudentia frangi posset; omnes Scripturas, traditiones, & rationes, omnia argumentorum genera, stupenda diligentia, parique acumine, evolvens, investigans, eruens, ac edisserens. Solas Δια- λήξεις, quæ unæ contra Marcionis, & Valentinianorum insaniam difertissimæ sunt, eorumque prodigiosum dogma exserte, totidemque verbis evertunt, ac refutant, in neutra disputatione usquam adhibet. Quid de ejus cum Praxea, diversi generis hæretico, conflictu dicam, qui & ipse egregium unum volumen totum occupat? Ille quidem de Scripturis nihil reliquit intactum, quo Christum alium a Patre esse, contra Praxeam, utrumque in unam personam impie ac imperite miscentem & confundentem, asserat atque vindicet. Nostros Ἀπολογητὰς qui Filium a Patre ubique ita diserte distinguunt, ut etiam interdum ultra, quam quod satis est, progredi videantur, nunquam tamen adversus Praxeam advocat; nullum in tali causa testimonium istis Christi Apostolis denunciat. Eos praeterit; neque in hunc magis, quam in Marcionem, paria, quamquam diversa, furentem excitat. Si alius esset disputator, tantum flagitium in ejus socordiam, vel oblivionem conferri fortasse paterer. De Tertulliano, nemo, cui vel leviter notus ille fuerit, quicquam hujusmodi unquam suspicabitur. Quid ergo est? Nimirum Tertullianus, quæ nondum suo tempore extabant, quę non nisi diu post ejus fata natæ sunt Constitutiones, eas quantumvis acer, ac diligens vel perspicere, vel è futuri temporis tenebris eruere non potuit. Nihil mirum est, quod quæ non erant, minimè animadverterit. Cæterum nodum hunc, nisi eas nondum tunc fuisse concesseris, nunquam expedies. Huc quoque pertinet, quod cum alibi a mulieres à conferendo baptismo longissime idem submoveat; Διδασκαλιῶν disertissimam in eam rem sententiam nullus in eo loco memoravit.
units.tr: Now this also clearly proves that there were no Bovian Apostolic διαταγαι in Tertullian's times: that this most keen and diligent man, a wonderful master of disputation, nowhere in his most splendid works against Marcion, or the Valentinians, or Praxeas, sets their authority against them. Marcion, as is well known, denied that the Father of Christ was the maker of the universe or the author of the Mosaic law; the Valentinians raved in the same way. Tertullian wrote five volumes against Marcion and one against the Valentinians, both excellent works, especially the first, in which he omits nothing by which Marcion's impudence could be broken: rolling out, searching, bringing to light and expounding all the Scriptures, traditions and arguments, all kinds of proofs, with astonishing diligence and equal sharpness. Yet he never uses in either dispute the Διαλήξεις alone, which are most eloquent against the madness of Marcion and the Valentinians, and which expressly and in just as many words overthrow and refute their monstrous doctrine. What shall I say of his conflict with Praxeas, a heretic of a different kind, which also fills an entire excellent volume? He left nothing untouched in the Scriptures by which to assert and vindicate that Christ is other than the Father, against Praxeas, who impiously and ignorantly mixed and confused the two in one person. Our Apologists, who distinguish the Son from the Father so clearly everywhere that they sometimes seem to go further than is necessary, he never calls upon against Praxeas; in such a cause he cites no testimony from those Apostles of Christ. He passes them over, and in this case he does not stir up those same Apostles against Praxeas any more than against Marcion, who raged in a similar though different way. If another writer had done this, I might perhaps allow such a disgrace to be ascribed to his carelessness or forgetfulness. But nobody who knows Tertullian even slightly would ever suspect anything of the kind of him. What then is the explanation? Surely that Tertullian, however keen and diligent, could not discern, or drag out of the darkness of a later time, the Constitutions which were not yet in existence in his day and which were born only long after his death. It is no wonder that he did not notice what did not exist. Moreover, you will never untie this knot unless you grant that they did not yet exist at that time. This also bears on the point that, although elsewhere he entirely excludes women from conferring baptism, he mentions no most explicit opinion in the Διδασκαλιῶν on that matter in that place.

units.la: Quid quod non in his modo, sed & in aliis quoque causis eadem semper cernitur Tertulliani stultitia, idemque stupor? præsens, paratumque Bovianorum Apostolorum præsidium ubique constantissime fastidientis? Nam & alibi c dum adversus Catholicos stata Montani jejunia, serasque & ad vesperam dilatas escas, denique & Xerophagias magno molimine defendit, nullum de Bovii Apostolis, qui Montani in hac causa pene toti sunt, verbum fecit; de tam multis eorum pro Montano sententiis nullam attulit. Extat ejus adversus Psychicos (quo nomine Catholicos invidiose appellat) de jejuniis liber, in quo id inprimis probare
units.tr: What of the fact that the same Tertullian foolishness, and the same stupor, is seen not only in these cases but also in others? Always, with the ready and prepared protection of the Bovian Apostles at hand, he is constantly disdainful of it everywhere. For elsewhere, when he defends with great effort against the Catholics the fixed fasts of Montanus, and late evening meals delayed until dusk, and finally the Xerophagies, he says nothing of the Bovian Apostles, who are almost entirely on Montanus' side in this matter; he brings forward none of their many opinions in Montanus' favour. There survives his book against the Psychics (the name by which he spitefully calls the Catholics) on fasts, in which he chiefly tries to prove

units.la: c l. de jejun. adversus Psych. probare laborat jeiuniorum, etiam apud Christianos licitam esse νομοθετῶν, hoc est, nobis adhuc sub novo testamento stata ex praecepto, certaque lege jejunia obeunda esse. Montanum enim, quem defendit, Catholici ideo praesertim damnabant, quod jejuniorum leges Christianis imposuisset; Hic est (inquit de Montano Apollonius) ὁ Διδάξας λύσεις γαμῶν, ὁ νηστείας νομοθετήσας, qui matrimoniorum solutiones docuit; hic, qui de jejuniis leges tulit. Tertullianus ergo, ut sua illa lege certa praecepta jejunia constituat, colligit de Scripturis jejunii laudes, fructum, exempla Apostolorum; quod unice quaerebatur, quodque unum ad definiendam quaestionem satis erat, nullas usquam memorat jeiuniorum leges. Ergo nullas, quas afferret, habuit. Neque enim credibile est tam acutum, tamque diligentem disputatorem, qui etiam longinqua petit, tam praesens causae firmamentum neglecturum fuisse, si quod habuisset. Iam vero si tunc extitissent Bovianae διδαχαί, leges jejuniorum plurimas habuisset, in quibus nemo nescit plurimas extare; quales illae sunt, quas passim in iis libris legimus; de jejuniis antepaschalis hebdomadis, quadragesimae, quartae sextaque feriarum, unius post Pentecosten hebdomadis. Haec quidem Boviani Apostoli lege non minus certa, accurataque præcipiunt, quam sua olim Montanus, quæcunque tandem illa fuerunt. Quæ cum Tertullianus in tota hac disputatione alto silentio transmiserit, necessario dicenda si extitissent; clarum est nullos tum extitisse Constitutionum libros in quibus hæc extant. Iam neque de xerophagiis hoc est aridis cibis pulsatus, (quod velut novum affectati officii nomen & proximum Ethnicæ superstitioni in Montano denotabatur) ullam affert A-postolorum de hoc disciplinæ genere legem; quæ tamen, si tum extabant Bovianæ Constitutiones, in promptu erat. Xerophagiam enim exserte jubent, qui in iis loquuntur Apostoli. Totis sex diebus (qui scilicet Pascha proxime antecedunt) solo pane, & sale, & oleribus, & sola in potum aqua utimini. Hoc vero victu ne Montanicus quidem siccior aut avidior fuit. Imo clarum est ipsissimam hanc esse Montani xerophagiam. Cur Catholici reprehendebant quod erat Apostolicum? Cur quod reprehendebatur, id Tertullianus, si Apostolicum verefuit, Apostolicum fuisse non respondet? Cur ad Apostolorum tabulas, id est ad Constitutionum codicem, non provocat? Nisi & impudentes Catholicos, & hebetem Tertullianum finxeris, (quod utrumque procul à vero est) necessario fatendum est nullas
units.tr: In his book on fasting against the Psychics (his name for the Catholics), he labours to prove that fasts are lawful even among Christians as legislated [νομοθετῶν], that is, that under the New Testament fixed fasts must still be kept by precept and under a certain law. The Catholics condemned Montanus, whom Tertullian defends, mainly because Montanus had imposed laws of fasting on Christians. Apollonius says of Montanus: "This is the one who taught the dissolving of marriages [ὁ Διδάξας λύσεις γαμῶν], who legislated fasts [ὁ νηστείας νομοθετήσας]; this is the man who passed laws about fasting." Tertullian, then, in order to establish fixed precepts of fasting by his own law, gathers from Scripture the praises of fasting, its fruits and the examples of the Apostles. That was the only thing in question, and that alone was enough to settle the matter, yet he nowhere mentions any laws of fasting. Therefore he had none to offer. Nor is it credible that so sharp and diligent a disputant, who reaches for distant things, would have neglected the firm support of his own case if he had possessed one. Indeed, if the Bovian Teachings [διδαχαί] had existed at that time, he would have had very many laws of fasting, since no one doubts that very many are extant in those books, such as those we read everywhere in them about the fasts of the week before Passover, of Lent, of the fourth and sixth days of the week, and of the one week after Pentecost. The Bovian Apostles lay these down with no less certainty and exactness than Montanus once laid down his own laws, whatever they were. Since Tertullian passes over all this in silence throughout the whole discussion, though it would have had to be mentioned had these existed, it is clear that at that time there were no books of Constitutions in which these things are found. Again, he brings forward no law of the Apostles about xerophagies, that is, dry foods (a term which, as a sort of new name for an affected duty and close to Gentile superstition, was used to denounce Montanus). Yet if the Bovian Constitutions had existed then, such a law would have been at hand. For the Apostles in those books plainly command xerophagy: "For the whole six days (that is, those immediately before Passover) use only bread, salt, vegetables and water for drink." Yet not even a Montanist would have been more abstemious or more eager than this diet. Indeed it is clear that this is exactly Montanus's xerophagy. Why did the Catholics find fault with what was Apostolic? Why, if it was truly Apostolic, does Tertullian not answer that it was Apostolic? Why does he not appeal to the tablets of the Apostles, that is, to the code of the Constitutions? Unless you imagine the Catholics shameless and Tertullian dull-witted (both of which are far from the truth), it must be admitted that these Apostolic tablets which Bovius now publishes did not exist at that time.

units.la: {b} l. 5. Const. c. 18. nullas tum fuisse has, quas nunc Bovius edit, Apostolorum tabulas.
units.tr: {b} Book 5 of the Constitutions, chapter 18. Nor did these tablets, which Bovius now publishes, exist at that time as Apostolic writings.

units.la: Sed hoc ipsum multo etiam clarius, certiusque confirmat Catholicorum illius memoriae, à Bovianorum Apostolorum Scitis plane diversum dogma. Illi Christianis jejunandum esse concedunt a; ex imperio, vel sub lege praecepti jejunandum negant; jejunari voluntâ ex arbitrio, pro temporibus & causis unuscujusque; & siquae sit sollicitudinis Ecclesiasticae causa, licere episcopis universae plebi mandare jejunium. Boviani vero Apostoli omnia illa, quae nuper memoravimus b, antepaschalia, quadragesimae, unius post Pentecosten hebdomadis jejunia, non ex arbitrio singulorum, sed ex certa, exsertaque lege, non ex occurrentis necessitatis occasione interdum, sed perpetuo ex certo, statoque officio obiri praecipiunt.
units.tr: But this is confirmed far more clearly and certainly by the teaching of those Catholics of that age, which is plainly different from the doctrine of the Bovian Apostles. They concede that Christians ought to fast, but deny that fasting is to be done by command or under the force of a precept. They hold that fasting is to be undertaken voluntarily and at one's own discretion, according to the times and causes of each person; and that if the care of the Church requires it, bishops may order the whole people to fast. The Bovian Apostles, however, prescribe all those fasts which we have just mentioned (b): the fasts of the week before Passover, of Lent, and of the one week after Pentecost. They enjoin these not at the discretion of individuals, but by a fixed and express law; not occasionally, as the need of the moment arises, but perpetually, as a settled and fixed duty.

units.la: Tum illi Tertullianicorum temporum Catholici diserte negant d, Apostolos ullum aliud impositum jugum certorum, & in commune omnibus obeundorum jejuniorum. Quorum verborum (ut alibi demonstravimus) sensus est, abolitis legalibus & Propheticis vetustatibus, quarum in proximo meminerunt, nullum aliud pro remoto illo jejuniorum legalium onere, jugum certorum (qualia erant legalia) jejuniorum ab Apostolis Christianorum cervicibus impositum esse. Sed etsi, quod pertendunt adversa-rii, nullum aliud jugum imposuisse Apostolos, sic interpreteris, ut Catholici significent, praeter illos dies quibus ablatus est sponsus, nullos alios certis & in commune omnibus obeundis jejuniis dies determinasse Apostolos; nihilominus constabit Boviaanos Apostolos ab illius memoriae Catholicis non fuisse pro Christi Apostolis habitos, vel agnitos. Boviani enim Διαλαγεῖς non modo dies illos duos, quibus ablatus est sponsus, hoc est sextam feriam, & sabbatum antepaschale, sed & alios quatuor proxime praecedentes dies, & quadragesimam totam, & unam post Pentecosten hebdomaden, & omnium totius anni hebdomadum quartam, sextamque ferias, jejuniis (ut diximus) determinant. Ergo fieri non potest, ut illos Catholici illorum temporum pro veris Christi Apostolis agnoverint; quos plane contra, quam Διαταγίας, ajunt vel nulla omnino, vel certe nulla praeter biduiantepaschalis jejunia certa, & in commune omnibus obeunda praecepisse, legeque lata decrevisse. Tertio, ex eodem Tertulliani opere liquet (quod a clarissimo Rigaltio de Africana Ecclesia observatum est) nullu evo Tertulliani apud Catholicos integrum sive solidum jejunium commune ac publicum fuisse, nisi Dominica die: quae vero certis per reliquum annum diebus usi-tata erant, ea spontanea, seu privata, & propria cuique pro sua religione fuisse. At Boviani Apostoli omnibus omnino Christianis reliqua totius anni non minus quam paschatis ϛαυξωσίμα jejunia præcipiunt, lataque lege imponunt. Quarto hoc ipsum Paschatis ϛαυξωσίμα jejunium, commune quidem, & quasi publicum, (ut alibi loquitur Tertullianus adhuc Catholicus) apud Christianos tum fuisse constat; cœterum usu & consuetudine non præcepto & lege stetisse: & ex supra memoratis Irenæi & Apollonii verbis, & ex omni Catholicorum apud Tertullianum de jejuniis causa, apparet. Apud Bovianos vero Διαζυγίας id ipsum antepaschale jejunium, certa lege exserte præceptum est. Denique cum isti, quod supra ostendimus, omnes omnino Christianos sex diebus antepaschalibus jejunare præcipiant, ex Irenæo b & Tertulliano c liquet istorum temporum Catholicos plærosq; uno tantum,& altero die jejunasse;& qui pluribus diebus jejunarunt,eos, ut cum Tertulliano dicam, differenter, & ex arbitrio, non ex imperio jejunasse. Quinto, Xerophagias Boviani, ut nuper diximus, Διαζυγεις non modo probant, ac commendant, sed etiam præcipiunt, atque impe-rant; quas illorum temporum Catholici damna-
units.tr: Then those Catholics of Tertullian's time expressly deny (d) that the Apostles imposed any other yoke of fixed fasts to be observed by all in common. The sense of these words (as I have shown elsewhere) is this: after the legal and prophetic ancient customs, which they mentioned just before, were set aside, no other yoke of fixed fasts (such as the legal ones were) was laid by the Apostles on the necks of Christians in place of that removed burden of legal fasts. But even if we interpret the adversaries' claim, that the Apostles imposed no other yoke, to mean what the Catholics intended, namely that, apart from "the days when the bridegroom was taken away," the Apostles determined no other days for fasts to be observed in common and by fixed rule by all; still it will be evident that the Bovian Apostles were not regarded, or acknowledged, as Christ's Apostles by the Catholics of that age. For the Bovian Diataxeis determine fasts not only on those two days "when the bridegroom was taken away," that is Friday and the Saturday before Easter, but also on the four days immediately preceding, on the whole of Lent, on the one week after Pentecost, and on the fourth and sixth days of every week of the whole year. Therefore it cannot be that the Catholics of that age acknowledged these men as true Apostles of Christ, whom, on the contrary, they say either commanded no fixed fasts to be kept in common by all by law, or certainly commanded none except the two days of fasting before Easter, and so decreed nothing by law. Thirdly, it is clear from the same work of Tertullian (as the most distinguished Rigaltius has observed concerning the African Church) that in Tertullian's age no whole or solid fast was common and public among the Catholics except on the Lord's Day; what was customary on certain days through the rest of the year was voluntary or private, and belonged to each person according to his own devotion. But the Bovian Apostles prescribe and impose by law, upon all Christians without exception, fasts on all the remaining days of the year, no less than the fast of Passover. Fourthly, it is established that this very fast of the week before Passover was then common, and as it were public, among Christians (as Tertullian, still a Catholic, says elsewhere); but it stood by custom and practice, not by precept and law; and this appears from the words of Irenaeus and Apollonius cited above, and from all the Catholic arguments about fasting in Tertullian. But among the Bovians this same pre-Easter fast is expressly commanded by a fixed law. Finally, since these men, as we have shown above, enjoin all Christians without exception to fast on the six days before Passover, it is clear from Irenaeus (b) and Tertullian (c) that the Catholics of that time mostly fasted on only one or two days; and those who fasted on several days, to use Tertullian's words, fasted "by choice and at their own discretion, not by command."
