units.tr: {a} Book on Prayer, chapter 14.

units.la: b apud Eusseb. hist. l. 5. c. 26.
units.tr: b In Eusebius, Church History, book 5, chapter 26.

units.la: c de jejun. c. 14.
units.tr: c On Fasting, chapter 14.

units.la: bant, velut novum affectati officii nomen, & proximum ethnicæ Superstitioni; & iis castimoniis comparabant, quæ Apim, Isidem, & magnam Matrem certorum ediliorum exceptione apud Paganos purificabant.
units.tr: Fifthly, the Bovian Xerophagies, as we have just said, the Diataxeis not only approve and commend but also prescribe and command; the Catholics of that age condemned these as "a new name for an affected duty" and "close to Gentile superstition," and compared them with those purifications which among the pagans were performed with the exception of certain days for Isis, Apis and the Great Mother.

units.la: Tantumque abeo aberant, ut id disciplinæ genus positum ab Apostolis fuisse putarent, ut etiam Montanistas, qui Xerophagias illas præcipiebant, jam olim à Paulo prænotatos fuisse dicerent, quo loco eos detestatur, qui sicut nubere prohibeant, ita jubeant cibis abstinere à Deo conditis huicque velut superstitiosæ abstinentiæ objicerent fidem in Christo esse liberam, ac ne Iudaicæ quidem legi abstinentiam quorundam ciborum debere, semel ab Apostolo in totum macellum admissam. Catholicos ergo istorum temporum (id est secundi sæculi exeuntis, tertiineuntis) clarum, manifestumque est pro Christi Apostolis neque habuisse, neque agnovisse illos Bovii Διαταγίας, quorum scilicet leges, præceptaque, ac disciplinas nescierunt, vel si sciverunt (quod non est verisimile) certe contempserunt, ac proculcarunt, & à verorum Apostolorum doctrina alienas esse censuerunt.
units.tr: So far were they from thinking that this kind of discipline had been laid down by the Apostles, that they even said the Montanists, who prescribed those xerophagies, had long ago been marked out by Paul. In that passage he condemns "those who forbid marriage, and likewise command abstinence from foods which God created," and against this kind of supposedly superstitious abstinence they objected that "faith in Christ is free, and that not even the Jewish law requires abstinence from certain foods, a thing the Apostle once allowed in the whole meat market." It is therefore clear and manifest that the Catholics of that time (that is, toward the end of the second century and the beginning of the third) neither held nor acknowledged as Christ's Apostles those Diataxeis of Bovius, whose laws, precepts and disciplines they evidently did not know; or, if they did know them (which is not likely), they certainly despised and trampled them underfoot, and judged them alien to the teaching of the true Apostles.

units.la: Sed & hoc quoque ex eodem Tertulliani contra Psychicos opere observandum est, quod quodam loco, ut crimen repercutiat, quo Montanistæ à Catholicis ob certorum torum dierum religiosam obseruationem Galaticari dicebantura, omnes dies moro-se colligit, quorum erat aliqua apud ipsos Catholicos in religione obseruatio, Pa-scha, quinquaginta exinde ad Pentecostes dies, quartam sextamque ferias stationibus dicatas, etiam jejuniis parasceuem, & sab-batum ipsum antepaschale. Rogo te cur non & Natalem Domini, & Apostolorum, Martyrumque dies hic commemoraverit? Cur non inprimis quadraginta quadrage-simalis jejunii dies in medium attulerit, multo decentius atque opportunius memorandos, quam quinquaginta Pentecostes dies, non moerori & jejuniis (de quibus Montano cum Ecclesiaiis erat) sed laetitiae atque exultationi determinatos? Huic quaestioni unum est quod respondeas; tacuisse ista Tertullianum, quod ea nondum apud Christianos in usum recepta essent. Unde porro constat neque Διαζυγίας, qui ista omnia praecipiunt b, Christi esse Apostolos; qui si essent, jam tum in usu futura erant, quaecunque sunt ab iis praecepta. Sed & ex hoc ipso Tertulliani libro aliter etiam demonstratur nondum apud Catholicos tunc temporis in usu fuisse quadragesimam.
units.tr: But this too must be noted from the same work of Tertullian against the Psychici: in one place, to turn the charge back on them, he lists every day on which the Montanists were called "Galaticari" by the Catholics because of their scrupulous observance of certain days. Among these were observances that the Catholics themselves kept in their religion: Pascha, the fifty days from there to Pentecost, the fourth and sixth days of the week given to stations, and the fasts of Parasceve and of the Sabbath before Easter. I ask you, why did he not also mention the day of the Lord's Nativity, and the days of the Apostles and Martyrs? Why did he not, above all, bring forward the forty days of the Lenten fast, which were far more fitting and appropriate to recall than the fifty days of Pentecost, which were set apart not for mourning and fasting (the things Montanus shared with the Church) but for joy and exultation? There is one answer to this question: Tertullian kept silent about these things because they were not yet received into use among Christians. And from this it further follows that those Διαταγαί which prescribe all these things were not written by the Apostles of Christ. If they had been, what they prescribe would already have been in use. But this same book of Tertullian also shows in another way that the Lenten fast was not yet in use among the Catholics at that time.

units.la: Is enim difertissime scribit c Montanistas duas in anno hebdomadas Xerophagiarum, nec totas, exceptis scilicet sabbatis, & dominicis, minicis, minicis, obtulisse Deo. Itaque si jam tum obtinebat apud Catholicos quadragesima, sequetur,eos multo plures Xerophagiarum dies observavisse, quam Montanistas: (Illi enim ex his rationibus quadraginta;hi vero non plures, quam decem, observarunt.) multo adeo majorem apud Catholicos, quam apud Montanistas, fuisse ciborum interdictionem; quod quam stultum, absurdumque,quam ab omni veteri historia alienum sit,etiam pueri norunt. Ergo,ut quod certum est, constet; ut scilicet fuerit major ciborum apud Montanistas, quam apud Catholicos interdictio; pluresque Xerophagiæ, omnino necesse est,hos toto anno pauciores, quam decem dies abstinuisse à certis cibis, quos non rejiciebant, sed differebant; quod illi scilicet dies non plures quam decem observarent. Dies vero si pauciores, quam decem, hujusmodi abstinentiæ Catholici determinarunt, nondum ergo illi quadragesimam observarunt; neque adeo Διαζηγέας, qui eam exserte praecipiunt, pro sui Christi Apostolis habuerunt.
units.tr: For he writes most plainly that the Montanists offered to God "two weeks of xerophagies in the year, not whole weeks, of course, but excluding the Sabbaths and the Lord's Days." So if the Lenten fast already prevailed among the Catholics, it would follow that they observed many more xerophagy days than the Montanists. (The Montanists, on these reckonings, observed forty; the others observed no more than ten.) It would follow that the prohibition of foods was far greater among the Catholics than among the Montanists. How foolish and absurd this is, and how alien to all ancient history, even children know. So, to establish what is certain: since the prohibition of foods was greater among the Montanists than among the Catholics, and their xerophagies were more numerous, it must necessarily be that the Catholics abstained from certain foods on fewer than ten days in the whole year. They did not reject these foods but postponed them, and so they observed no more than ten such days. If the Catholics set fewer than ten days for this kind of abstinence, then they had not yet observed the Lenten fast, and therefore the Διαταγεῖς, who expressly prescribe it, were not regarded as Apostles of Christ.

units.la: ὑμῖν φυλακτέα ἡ νηστεία ἡ τεσαρακοστὴ, μνημεῖον περιέχουσα τῆς Κυρίου πολιτείας καὶ νομοθεσίας, Servandum vobis est jejunium quadragesima, quod vitae Christi & legis latae recordationem continet.
units.tr: "The fast of forty days must be kept by you, since it keeps the memory of the life and the law given by the Lord." [ἡ νηστεία ἡ τεσσαρακοστή, μνημεῖον περιέχουσα τῆς Κυρίου πολιτείας καὶ νομοθεσίας]

units.la: Sed & ex alia Tertulliani nobili cum Catholicis controversia idem quoque elucet. Decreverat Romanus, certe Catholicus, Episcopus admittendos per poenitentiam ad reconciliationem moechos, & fornicatores, poenitentiaque functis dimittendum ab Ecclesiae ministris crimen. Hoc decretum, ut novum, atque insolens, ut iniquum & a scripturis alienum, impotenter invadit Tertullianus, mirisque modis vexat ac dilacerat, denique id toto neque modico volumine oppugnat, quod de Pudicitia inscripsit. Pertendit nefas esse, moechis ab Ecclesia concedi ullum inter suae reconciliationis candidatos locum; ullam paenitentia quantumvis accurata functis, communionem. Quaecunque ex Scripturis Apostolicis suo iussu, certe immani, & a veri specie abhorrenti dogmati objiciebantur, studiose colligit, & quatenus quidem in ipso est, solvit. Διατάξεων Bovianarum non magis quam ipsius Bovii meminit. Atqui in iis non uno loco difertissime & explosum, ac damnatum cernitur Tertullianicum illud dogma & constitutum illud, quod Septimius oppugnat, Catholicorum decretum.
units.tr: The same thing also appears from another famous controversy of Tertullian with the Catholics. The Roman bishop, certainly a Catholic, had decreed that adulterers and fornicators should be admitted to reconciliation through repentance, and that the sin should be dismissed by the ministers of the Church once they had completed penance. Tertullian attacks this decree, as new, strange, unjust and foreign to the Scriptures, with fierce vehemence and bitter abuse, and finally assails it in a whole and no small volume, which he entitled On Modesty. He contends that it is wrong for the Church to grant adulterers any place among the candidates for its reconciliation, or any communion after penance, however careful. He diligently gathers together whatever passages of the Apostolic Scriptures could be brought against this monstrous dogma, which he judges to be remote from the appearance of truth, and so far as he can, he answers them. Yet he makes no mention of the Διαταγαί, any more than of Bovius himself. And yet in those writings, in more than one place, that Tertullianic dogma, and that decree of the Catholics which Septimius attacks, are seen to be most plainly rejected and condemned.

units.la: Κρίνε α ἂν ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, μετὰ ἐξουσίας ὡς ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ τὰς μετανοοῦντας προσλαμβάνε. Indica igitur, o Episcope, cum potestate, tanquam Deus; Sed poenitentes recipe. Mox; Peccatorem inquiunt cum misericordia, & com& commiseratione & susceptione allice; promissa ei salute, si mores mutet, & peccatorum poeniteat. Poenitentem vero castigando recipe, memor Domini, cum dixit, gaudium esse in coelo super uno peccatore poenitentiam agente. Sin vero poenitentem non receperis, objicis eum insidiatoribus. Et paulo posta; Recipe ergo poenitentem nihil adubitans. Neque obstent tibi, aut ab hoc officio retardent, qui inhumane ajunt, non oportere talium convictu contaminari, neque communem cum eis habere sermonem.
units.tr: "Judge whatever you judge, O bishop, with authority, as God does, but receive the penitents." [Κρῖνε ἃ ἂν κρίνῃς, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, μετὰ ἐξουσίας ὡς ὁ Θεός, ἀλλὰ τοὺς μετανοοῦντας πρόσλαμβάνε.] Soon after: "They say: with mercy and compassion and welcome, invite the sinner, having promised him salvation if he changes his ways and repents of his sins. But receive the penitent with correction, mindful of the Lord when he said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner repenting. But if you do not receive the penitent, you give him over to the plotters." And a little later: "Receive the penitent then without doubt. Let not those stand in your way, or delay you from this duty, who inhumanly say that one should not be defiled by the company of such people, nor have common conversation with them."

units.la: Istos vero qui peccatores repellebant, multis confutant; Tum ita concludunt b; Oportet igitur vos qui haec auditis, eos qui delinquerunt hortari & ad poenitentiam impellere, ac bona spe esse facere; neque suspicari debetis, quasi participes eorum, quae ipsi commiserant, efficiamini, quod eos diligatis. Recipite ergo libenter ac laeti poenitentes, & judicate cum misericordia, ac miseratione peccantes. Et paulo post; Sic, inquam, ut dixi, recipite, ut & populus moneatur, & is, qui peccavit, non prorsus intereat. Idem agunt capite sequenti, & ordinem, quo peccator ab episcopo examinari, poenitentiamque suscipere debeat, liquido praescribunt, ac denique haec subjiciunt c; ὅτως ἂν τὴν ἡμᾶς ςέον ὃς ποιεῖν, τὰς ἐφ' ἁμαρτίας λέγοντας μετανοεῖν, ἀφορίζειν τὸν
units.tr: They refute at length those who reject sinners. Then they conclude thus: "You who hear these things ought therefore to exhort those who have offended, to urge them to repentance, and to give them good hope. Nor should you suspect that you become partakers of what they committed, merely because you love them. Receive therefore the penitents gladly and joyfully, and judge sinners with mercy and compassion." And a little later: "Thus, I say, as I have said, receive them, so that the people may be warned, and so that the one who has sinned may not be utterly lost." The same writers do the same in the following chapter, and they clearly prescribe the order by which a sinner ought to be examined by the bishop and receive penance. Finally they add these words: [Greek follows]
{a} Ibid. {c} 14.

units.la: {c} Ibid. c. 16. extr. χρόνον ὠφεισμένον κ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς ἁμαρ-τήματος. ἐπειτα μετανοοῦντας προσλαμβάνε-σθαι ὡς πατρὶς ὑμᾶς. Sic igitur vos facere oportet; eos scilicet, qui se ajunt pœnitere, quod peccaverint ejicere vel separare ab Ecclesia definito certoque tempore, secun-dum proportionem peccati; postea vero re-cipere pœnitentes, ut Patres Filios. Alibi quoque fusius de variis pro peccatorum va-rietate imponendis reo pœnitentiis agunt. Illa quoque in eandem rem sunt disertissi-ma; ubi converso ad unumquemque Epi-scopum sermone; τὰς ὁ (inquiunt) ἡμαςλη-κοῖς νυθέτει, καὶ ςιβῶν ἐν τῇ νηςεία, ἐν τῇ ἀφέσει ἐλάφρωον, καὶ προσκλαύσαντα εἰσδέχε, πάσης τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὑπὲρ αὐτῶ ςεομένης, καὶ χειροθετήσας αὐτὸν, ἐκλοιπον εἶναι ἐν τῷ ποιμνίῳ. Lapsos vero mone, & jejunio pre-mens, leva remissione, & eum qui luxit re-cipe cuncta Ecclesia pro eo deprecante, & manus ei imponens sine eum de cætero in Ec-clesia esse. Hic habes peccatoris προσκλαυ-σιν, & Ecclesiæ pro eo deprecationem; & ejusdem postremo reconciliationem post peractam pœnitentiam per manuum impo-sitionem ab Episcopo suscep tam; quibus, ut ex ipso Tertulliano videre est, ordo ille omnis continetur, quo Catholicus, cujus decretum impugnat, Episcopus mœchos & fornicatores data pœnitentia reconcilia-ri præ-
units.tr: {c} Ibid. c. 16. extr. [οὕτως ἂν ... τὸν χρόνον ὡρισμένον καὶ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς ἁμαρτήματος· ἔπειτα μετανοοῦντας προσλαμβάνεσθαι ὡς πατέρας υἱούς.] "Thus you ought to act: those who say that they repent of the sins they have committed, cut off or separate from the Church for a defined and certain time, in proportion to the sin; afterwards receive the penitents as fathers receive their sons." Elsewhere too they treat at greater length of the various penances to be imposed on the guilty according to the variety of sins. Those passages are also most explicit on the same point, where, speaking to each bishop, they say: "Admonish the lapsed, and let him be lightened in the fast by remission, and receive the one who has wept, while the whole Church prays for him, and lay hands on him, and let him be in the flock from then on." Here you have the sinner's weeping, the Church's prayer on his behalf, and finally his reconciliation after completed penance by the bishop's laying on of hands. From these, as may be seen from Tertullian himself, the whole order is contained by which the Catholic bishop, whose decree he attacks, had prescribed that adulterers and fornicators be reconciled after penance was given.

units.la: b Ibid. c. 48. ri præceperat. Sed & alibi, quod supra diximus, pœnitentium in Ecclesia ordinem ab aliis distinguunt, & quibus illi verbis tum ab Episcopo benedicantur, tum à Diacono dimittantur, postremoq; peracta pœnitentia communionem recipiant, & alia id genus eodem spectantia, clare enarrant.
units.tr: b Ibid. c. 48. had prescribed. But elsewhere too, as we said above, they distinguish the order of penitents in the Church from the others, and tell clearly with what words they are then blessed by the bishop and then dismissed by the deacon, and at last, when penance is complete, receive communion, and they describe other things of this kind bearing on the same point.

units.la: Nihil necesse est cætera describere, quæ plurima passim in eandem sententiam habent Boviani Διαταγεις; quę omnia si Tertulliani temporibus in Ecclesia extitissent, proque Apostolicis agnita fuissent; primo neque necesse erat Catholicum illum episcopum, quem Tertullianus petit, pœnitentiæ ordinem tam disertis, tamque multis ipsorum Apostolorum verbis constitutum novo decreto figere. Sed neque verisimile est vel Montanum, vel Tertullianum tam luculenta Apostolorum authoritate firmatum institutum oppugnaturos, ac eversuros fuisse. Illud quidem nemo negaverit, hæc si Christiani pro Apostolicis tum habuissent, ea Catholicos quidem in hac disputatione, velut firmissima, ac invicta causæ suæ præsidia haud dubie allaturos fuisse; Tertullianum vero, præcipuum in iis vel solvendis, vel certe secandis, operam positurum fuisse. Atqui cum in cæteris, quæ & ipsa sane haud infirma è scripturis Catholici afferebant, explicandis toto hoc libro sudaverit, de istis τῶν Διαθηκῶν dictis ne unum quidem verbum fecit. Unde apparet, neque à Catholicis quicquam ei fuisse ex his libris objectum. Quin & has Διαταξεις usque adeo nescivit Tertullianus, ut in quasdam earum hypotheses recta incurrat. Verbi gratia Διαθηκης passim Episcopo potestatem tribuunt peccata fidelibus lapsis remittendi; ut & ex iis, quae nuper descripsimus, liquet, & ex his disertis eorum verbis a; γνώσεζε οὖν, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, τὸ ἀξίωμά σου, ὅτι ὡς τὸ ἀσφαλὲς ἐκλησίας ἐκκλησίαν, ἵνα ... τὸ λύειν. Agnosce igitur Episcope dignitatem tuam, quod potestas, ut ligandi, sic etiam solvendi tibi obtigit. Haec vero Tertullianus liquido refutat b, & Episcopos, non potestatem delictorum dimittendorum, sed solius disciplinae officia sortitos, κληρώσασθαι contendit. Quis hominem tantum ea, quae Apostolica sciret, ita praefracte ac invererecunde dejecturum fuisse crediderit? Scripturam quidem Pastoris sibi in hac ipsa causa à Catholicis objectam libere repellit, & inter apocrypha amandat c: Cederem tibi, inquit, si Scriptura Pastoris, quae sola moechos amat, divino instrumento meruisset incidi, si non ab omni Concilio Ecclesiarum, etiam vestrarum, inter apocrypha, & falsa judicaretur, adultera & ipsa, & inde & inde patrona sociorum. Saltem simile quid de Constitutionibus dixisset, ubi earum sententiam aperte explodit; siquidem eas novisset, & Apostolis tribui scivisset. Nunc cum earum in hac causa nullus meminit, satis ostendit, ne extitisse quidem tum ullas, nedum ut pro Apostolicis vel apud Catholicos, vel apud hæreticos habitæ fuerint.
units.tr: There is no need to describe the rest, of which the Boviani Διαταγαί contain very many passages to the same effect. If all these things had existed in the Church in Tertullian's time, and had been recognised as Apostolic, then in the first place there would have been no need for that Catholic bishop, whom Tertullian attacks, to establish the order of penance by a new decree, when it was laid down so plainly, and in so many words of the Apostles themselves. Nor is it likely that either Montanus or Tertullian would have attacked and overturned an institution confirmed by such clear Apostolic authority. No one would deny that, if the Christians had then regarded these writings as Apostolic, the Catholics would undoubtedly have brought them forward in this dispute as the firmest and unconquerable defences of their cause, and Tertullian would have taken great pains to solve them, or at least to cut them down. Yet although in dealing with the other arguments, which the Catholics did bring from Scripture and which were by no means weak, he laboured throughout this whole book, he did not say a single word about those sayings of the "Covenants" [τῶν Διαθηκῶν]. From this it appears that the Catholics did not object anything to him from these books. Indeed, Tertullian was so ignorant of these Διαταξεις that he runs straight into some of their hypotheses. For example, the "Covenants" everywhere grant the bishop power to remit sins to the lapsed faithful, as is clear both from what we have just described and from these plain words of theirs: "Know therefore, O bishop, your dignity, that power, as of binding, so also of loosing, has been given to you." But Tertullian plainly refutes this, and contends that the bishops were allotted only the duties of discipline, and not the power of forgiving sins. Who could believe that a man who knew these things as Apostolic would have rejected them so stubbornly and so irreverently? Indeed, in this very case he freely rejects the Pastor's writing which the Catholics brought against him, and consigns it to the Apocrypha: "I would yield to you," he says, "if the writing of the Pastor, which alone loves adulterers, had deserved to be included in the divine instrument, if it were not judged by every council of the Churches, even yours, to be among the apocryphal and false writings, adulterous itself, and therefore a patron of its companions." At least he would have said something similar about the Constitutions, where he openly explodes their opinion, if he had known them and known that they were attributed to the Apostles. But since no one mentions them in this case, it shows sufficiently that they did not then exist at all, let alone that they were regarded as Apostolic either by the Catholics or by the heretics.

units.la: Aliud præterea ex eodem Tertulliani opere observandum est, quod multo etiam evidentius conficit, nullas istis temporibus Christianis fuisse Bovianas Apostolorum Constitutiones. Nimirum tametsi mœchos & fornicatores ad pœnitentiam, indeque ad communionem admittendos decreverit Catholicus ille à Tertulliano exagitatus Episcopus; multosque alios idem vel tunc vel proxime insecutis temporibus factitasse ex Africanæ Ecclesiæ scriptoribus constet a; illud tamen certum est, & fuisse alias Catholicorum Ecclesias, quæ & tunc & diu postea, mœchos à pœnitentia & communione excluserint; & ipsos illos qui mœchos tunc admittere coeperunt, eosdem antea exclusisse, & cum mœchos primum admiserunt, tamen etiam tum homicidas & apostatas ab omni reconciliationis Ecclesiasticæ spe submovisse. Id ex tota Tertulliani disputatione clarum est, in qua hoc veluti abfurdiffi-mum objicit, quod pacem cum adulteris promittant, eandem homicidis & in ido-lolatriam lapsis negent. Hinc est (inquit) quod neque idololatriæ neque sanguini pax ab Ecclesiis redditur. Tum idololatras & homicidas sic facit loqui; Igitur aut nec illis (mœchis) aut etiam nobis pœnitentiæ subsidia convenient. Aut detinemus eam (mœchiam) aut sequimur. & cætera sane (tametsi in pessima causa) longe facundissima. Cyprianus ita tunc fuisse ipse quoque testatur. Et eum ipsum quem Tertullianus defendit, in omnes gravius peccantes rigorem, in Hispanienfi Ecclesia, etiam ultra tertium sæculum mansisse, Eliberitani canones, & Pacianus satis fatentur. Quæ quia fuse ac diligenter ab Albaspineo demonstrata sunt, & nunc ab omnibus accuratis Christianarum antiquitatum indagatoribus, conceduntur, ea pluribus probare supersedeo. Jam nemo non vidit cum hac Catholicorum per illa sæcula adversus peccatores severitate, ac rigore pugnare ea quæ nuper ex Constitutionibus attulimus; in quibus ὁι Διαζαγεῖς quorumvis peccatorum reos ad pœnitentiam cum veniæ & reconciliationis Ecclesiasticæ spe non modo admittunt, sed etiam invitant ac provocant. Quin & negatores, in quos præcipræcipuus, maximeque diuturnus fuit Catholicorum rigor, ipsos tamen ad pœnitentiam, indeque ad veniam admittendos docent allato Petri exemplo, quem Christus ἀρνησάμενον αὐτὸν ὀξ᾽ ὁ ἐπ᾽ ἀντείτον, καὶ ἐξ μετανοίας ἐξιλεωσάμενον ἢ προσκλαύσαν-τα πίστεως προσήνατο, cum ipsum tertio ob metum negasset, postquam per pœnitentiam placavit Deum, & amare flevit, recepit, & Pastorem suarum pecudum fecit. A- libi etiam difertius; μείζων ἐιδωλολατρείας ἐν ἐστιν ἁμαρτία. εἰς Θεὸν γὰρ ἐστὶ ὑσεβεία, ἀλλ᾽ ὁμως καὶ αὐτὴ ὀξ᾽ γνώσεως μετανοίας συν-ηχώρηθη. Nullum majus peccatum est, quam idolorum cultus. Est enim impietas in Deum; tamen per veram pœnitentiam remissum est. Imo si quis paulo diligentius expenderit ea quæ nostri Διαταγεῖς passim contra crudeles quosdam disputant, qui fidelem semel in peccata lapsum, pæniten-tia, veniæque spe excludunt; facile intelliget illos, quos tam sæpe, tamque graviter perstringunt, non alios fuisse, vel esse posse, quam Montanistas. & eundem postea rigorem secutos Novatianos; quibus omnia, quæ in illos à Constitutionibus dicta sunt, sane ad amussim conveniunt; ὁ τὸν ἐπιςρέφοντα μὴ προσδεχόμενον (inquiunt) φονεὺς τῷ ἀδελφῷ ἐστι, καὶ αἷμα ἐκχέει, ὡς Κάιν Ἀβελ τῷ ἀδελφῷ. Qui se conconvertentem non recipit, fratris sui interfector est, & sanguinem ejus fundit, sicut Cain Abelis fratris sui. Sic alibi tradunt a, istos caussatos esse nolle se peccatorum convitiu ac communione contaminari. Omnia Novatianis congruunt; ut vel ex Cypriano apparet, qui eos dixisse tradit c, alterius peccato alterum inquinari, & idolatriam delinquentis ad non delinquentem transfire; & hunc ille eorum errorem plane ut hoc loco Διαζυγίς, ex his scripturae dictis confutat d, Justitia justi super eum erit, & scelus scelerati super eum erit. Non morientur patres pro filiis, & filii non morientur pro Patribus. Unusquisque in peccato suo moritur. Cum ergo veteres illi Tertullianicorum temporum Catholici eundem illum disciplinae adversus peccatores vel omnes, vel certe plerosque rigorem servaverint atque exercuerint, quem tantopere, tam saepe, tamque diserte improbant ac refutant nostri Διαζυγίς, vel caecus videt, non fuisse illis temporibus pro Apostolicis habitas, quae nunc extant, eorum Constitutiones: sed, quod clare hinc intelligitur, diu postea scriptas atque editas, cum jam mitigata esset prisana severitas, cumque qui eam mordicus retinendam contendebant Montanistae ac Novatiani, Ecclesia ejecti, pro schismaticis smaticis apud Christianos haberentur. Hęc vidit Albaspineus ; & inter cætera , quibus Constitutionum novitatem argui ac revinci tradit a, pœnitentiam quoq;, hoc est adulterorum , sicariorum , & idololatrarum receptionem recenset ; quæ clare dilucideque in his libris explicata & constituta est,cum tamen eam constet tertio sæculo summa contentione disputatam ac exagitatam fuisse, in Ecclesiæ adversus Montanistas & Novatianos certaminibus. At si (Constitutiones istæ (inquit) ab Apostolis probata, sancitaque fuissent, quis existimet ea in dubium fuisse revocanda, quæ ab Apostolis decreta, sancitaque fuissent ? An adeo ignorantes erant illius ætatis Patres, ut, si extitissent illi Apostolorum canones, eos continuo non produxissent ? Hæc Albaspineus; ex quibus liquido id sequitur , quod ibidem paulò ante ab eo scriptum nos jam supra alibi memoravimus, imperitum censendum, siquis esset qui D. Clementis Constitutiones Apostolorum authoritate sancitas , publicatasque certo affirmaret.
units.tr: Another point to note from the same work of Tertullian makes the case even more clearly: in those times there were no Bovian Constitutions of the Apostles among Christians. It is true that the Catholic bishop whom Tertullian attacked decided that adulterers and fornicators should be admitted to repentance and then to communion, and the writers of the African Church show that he and many others did the same either then or in the years immediately following a. Yet it is certain that other Catholic churches, both then and for a long time afterwards, excluded adulterers from repentance and communion. Moreover, those very people who then began to admit adulterers had earlier excluded them, and even when they first admitted adulterers, they still shut out murderers and apostates from every hope of ecclesiastical reconciliation. This is clear from the whole of Tertullian's discussion, in which he objects, as something most absurd, that they promise peace to adulterers and deny it to murderers and those who have fallen into idolatry. Hence it is (he says) that peace is given by the churches neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed. Then he makes the idolaters and murderers speak thus: So either the adulterers should not be given the aids of repentance, or neither should we. Either we keep the adultery, or we follow it. The rest of his argument, though in a very bad cause, is certainly most eloquent. Cyprian himself testifies that this was the situation at that time. The canons of Elvira and Pacian fully confirm that the same severity toward all who sinned gravely, which Tertullian defended, remained in the Spanish church even beyond the third century. Since Albaspinaeus has demonstrated these matters at length and with care, and since all careful investigators of Christian antiquity now grant them, I will not spend more time proving them. Now everyone sees that the things we recently quoted from the Constitutions conflict with this severity of the Catholics toward sinners during those centuries. In those Constitutions the Διαταγαί [Diatagai] not only admit, but even invite and summon to repentance, with the hope of pardon and ecclesiastical reconciliation, the guilty of any sins whatever. Indeed, they teach that even those who denied the faith, against whom the Catholics were especially and most lastingly rigorous, are to be admitted to repentance and thence to pardon, citing the example of Peter, whom Christ received after he had denied Him three times out of fear, once he had appeased God through repentance and wept bitterly; He made him the shepherd of His flock. Christ received him, after he had denied him three times for fear, once he had appeased God through repentance and wept bitterly, and made him the pastor of his sheep. Elsewhere they say even more plainly: There is no sin greater than idolatry. For it is impiety against God; yet even this has been forgiven through true repentance. Indeed, if anyone weighs more carefully what our Διαταγαί argue here and there against certain cruel people, who shut out from repentance and the hope of pardon a faithful man who has fallen into sin once, he will easily understand that those whom they so often and so severely attack were none other, or could be none other, than the Montanists, and afterwards the Novatians, who followed the same rigor. Everything said against them in the Constitutions fits them exactly. They say: He who does not receive the one who turns back is a murderer of his brother and sheds his blood, as Cain did to Abel his brother. So they are said elsewhere to have professed that they did not want to be defiled by the reproach and communion of sinners . Everything agrees with the Novatians, as is clear even from Cyprian, who reports that they said one man is polluted by another's sin, and the idolatry of the offender passes over to the one who has not offended c. This error Cyprian refutes, as our Διαταγαί do here, with the words of Scripture: The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. The fathers shall not die for the children, nor the children die for the fathers. Each one dies for his own sin d. Therefore, since those ancient Catholics of Tertullian's time kept and practised either all or at least most of the same rigor against sinners, which our Διαταγαί so greatly, so often, and so clearly condemn and refute, even a blind man can see that the Constitutions which now exist were not regarded as Apostolic in those times. Rather, as is clearly understood from this, they were written and published much later, when the former severity had already been softened, and when the Montanists and Novatians, who stubbornly insisted on keeping it, had been cast out of the Church and were regarded among Christians as schismatics. Albaspinaeus saw this. Among the other arguments by which he claims and proves the novelty of the Constitutions, he lists the reception of penitents too, that is, of adulterers, murderers and idolaters, which is clearly and plainly explained and laid down in these books, although it is certain that in the third century it was disputed and debated with great contention in the Church's struggles against the Montanists and Novatians. But, he says, if these Constitutions had been approved and sanctioned by the Apostles, who would think that matters decreed and sanctioned by the Apostles could have been called into doubt? Or were the Fathers of that age so ignorant that, if those canons of the Apostles had existed, they would not have produced them at once? These are Albaspinaeus's words. From them it clearly follows what he wrote a little earlier in the same place, which I have already mentioned above elsewhere: that anyone who confidently asserts that the Constitutions of Clement were sanctioned and published with the authority of the Apostles must be judged inexperienced.

units.tr: Argument 9: the Constitutions were unknown to Origen. Argument 10: it is most clearly shown that the Constitutions were not seen by Cyprian, nor by the whole Church as it then was. Argument 11: they were also unknown to Dionysius (Argument 12) and to Peter, bishops of Alexandria.

units.la: Rrꝛter has de jejuniis, & pœnitentia, alia quoque Tertulliano de monogamia cum Catholicis lis fuit, quam & ipsam uno seorsim volumine tractavit. Qua in causa cum ipse ex Montani disciplina secundas nuptias illicitas, juxta adulterium judicaret; Catholici, ut licitas ex Scripturis defenderent; omnino in hac disputatione locum suum, siquidem cognita tum fuisset, habitura erat illa nostrorum Διαταγῶν definitio, quam supra recitavimus; eo magis, quod ambigua & inter utrumque dogma suspensa ac pœne anceps, habet, quod utrisque licuit in suam sententiam trahere.
units.tr: Besides these matters concerning fasting and repentance, Tertullian also had a dispute with the Catholics about monogamy, which he treated in a separate volume. In that controversy, since he himself judged second marriages unlawful and equal to adultery, following the discipline of Montanus, the Catholics defended them as lawful from the Scriptures. In this dispute our definition from the Constitutions, which we quoted above, would certainly have had its place, if it had then been known. It would have been all the more useful because it is ambiguous and hangs between the two opinions, almost doubtful, so that each side could bend it to its own view.

units.la: Nam Tertulliano quidem favet, quod ajunt Διαταγεῖς τῷ μονογαμίαν τῇ νόμον γινομένῳ, δικαίαν ὡς ἂν τῇ γνώμῃ Θεῦ ὑπάρχειν, unas nuptias secundum legem peractas, justas esse, utpote secundum Dei sententiam; item quod paulo post de Genesi huc afferunt, runt, Deum in creatione unam uxorem dedisse uni viro; denique quod ibidem etiam pronunciant tertias nuptias intemperantiae esse indicium; quartas vero, & supra, manifestam esse scortationem. Catholicis vero illud favere videtur, quod dum secundas nuptias post promissionem ( continentiae scilicet ) παρᾶνομον reminiquam ac sceleratam esse statuunt, diserte negant injustas esse δι᾽ τὸ συμάφεαν propter conjunctionem ipsam; injustas δι᾽ τὸ ψεῦδος propter mendacium solum esse concedant; eoque secundas nuptias culpae per se ipsas expertes esse scisGunt; certe scisGere videntur. Cum ergo in pauculis istorum verbis fuerint, & quae Tertulliano, & quae ipsis etiam in altera parte Catholicis in speciem faveant, ne dubites quin utrique hoc Διαταγῶν decretum in hac causa pro se quisque allaturi fuerint; si quidem ii pro Apostolis habiti, agnitique essent. Nunc cum neutros adeo probabile argumentum usurpasse ex tota Tertulliani disputatione clarum sit, ne dubites utrisque juxta ignotos fuisse Bovii nostri Διαθήκης.
units.tr: For it does favour Tertullian, when the Constitutions say that marriage contracted once, according to the law, is just, as being in accordance with the judgement of God, as they say in Greek, "monogamy, which is made according to law, is righteous as being in the mind of God" [μονογαμίαν ... δικαίαν]. Likewise, when they later cite from Genesis that God gave one wife to one man in creation. Finally, in the same place they declare that a third marriage is a sign of intemperance, and a fourth, or anything beyond, is plainly fornication. But the Catholics seem to be favoured by this: while the Constitutions declare that a second marriage after the promise (of continence, that is) is a lawless and wicked thing [παρᾶνομον], they plainly deny that second marriages are unjust because of the union itself [δι᾽ τὸ συμάφεαν], and they grant that they are unjust because of the lie [δι᾽ τὸ ψεῦδος] alone. Thus they make second marriages free of blame in themselves; at least they seem to do so. Since, then, a few of their words support both Tertullian and the Catholics on the other side, you may be sure that each side would have brought this Constitutions' ruling forward in this controversy in its own favour, if these writings had been recognised as Apostolic. But since it is clear that neither side drew any convincing argument from them throughout Tertullian's whole discussion, you may be sure that our Bovius's Διαθήκη [Diathēkē] was unknown to both.

units.la: Sed neque id omiserim, quod a Rever. Usserio est observatum, Christianorum illius saeculi hanc esse de Regis supra caeteros omnes mortales ὑπερογῆ apud Tertullianum confessionem; Colimus Imperatore, ut homi-
units.tr: Nor will I omit what the Reverend Ussher has observed: that in Tertullian there is this confession of the Christians of that age, that the Emperor is honoured above all other mortals, "We honour the Emperor in such a way as a man is honoured by God, second to God, and inferior only to God. He himself would wish this, for thus he is greater than all, while he is less than the one true God alone."

units.la: b Ad Scap. c. 2. ut hominem a Deo secundum, & quicquid est a Deo consecutum, & solo Deo minorem. Hoc & ipse volet. Sic enim omnibus major est, dum solo vero Deo minor est. Quorum & ista ex praestantissimo ejusdem opere gemina sunt a: Imperatores (inquit) sentiunt eum esse Deum solum, in cujus solius potestate sunt, a quo sunt secundi, POST QUEM PRIMI, ante omnes & super omnes Deos. Quidni? cum super omnes homines, qui utique vivunt, & mortuis antistant. Ita quidem Tertullianici temporis Christiani. Longe alia Διατάξεων fides; qui locis, quos supra discripsimus, rotunde profitentur, Episcopum Imperatore majorem; πάντων ἀνθρώπων, nominatim τῶν βασιλέων ἄρχειν, & c rege tanto esse majorem, quanto anima corpore praestantior est. Non itaque si istos audis, a Deo secundus; post Deum primus, Solo Deo minor Imperator, quod credebant illi Christiani, Episcopo foli haec elogia conveniunt; post quem, non secundus, sed tertius si forte a Deo imperator, neque solo Deo, sed & episcopo minor, neque omnibus major; quo scilicet praeter Deum, & Episcopus insuper major. Ergo vel qui illa ita credebant ac confitebantur secundi, tertiique saeculi Christiani, non fuerunt Apostolici; vel si fuerunt, certe qui haec sic docent Διαταγεὶς, ii non sunt ἀποστόλοι. Illud nemo, nisi insanus, dixerit; Hoc igitur omnino, quod nos defendimus, tenendum est. Atque haec de Tertulliano satis.
units.tr: b To Scapula, ch. 2. As a man is second to God, and whatever has been obtained from God, and less than God alone. He himself would wish this. For thus he is greater than all, while he is less than the one true God alone. Of the same author's excellent work, these two passages are also twins: a: The emperors (he says) acknowledge that he alone is God, in whose sole power they are, by whom they are second, AFTER WHOM FIRST, before and above all gods. Why not? For he is over all men, who certainly live, and stands before the dead. That was indeed the belief of the Christians of Tertullian's time. The faith of the Constitutions is quite different. In the passages we noted above, they plainly profess that the bishop is greater than the emperor, that he rules over all men [πάντων ἀνθρώπων], and specifically over kings [τῶν βασιλέων], and that he is as much greater than a king as the soul is more excellent than the body. Therefore, if you listen to them, the emperor is not second to God, first after God, inferior only to God, as those Christians believed. Such praises belong to the bishop alone. After him the emperor is not second but third, if he is by chance God's emperor; he is not inferior to God alone but also to the bishop; and he is not greater than all, since besides God the bishop is also greater. So either those Christians of the second and third centuries who so believed and confessed these things were not Apostolic, or, if they were, those who teach these things in the Constitutions are not Apostles. No one but a madman would say the latter. So this, which we defend, must be held without doubt. And so much for Tertullian.

units.la: Sequitur Origenes, a. D. 185. natus, 254. mortuus, tertii adeo saeculi pene totus. Is vero notas sibi fuisse Apostolorum Constitutiones eo negat, quod earum in tam multis, quae ex innumerabili librorum ejus multitudine supersunt, monumentis, nunquam meminit; tametsi & ipse Clementis Alexandrini, praeceptoris ac decessoris sui, more, omne librorum genus, etiam apocryphos, ut Recognitionem Petri citare & in disputationibus adhibere miscere soleat; Clementis vero, (quem Constitutionum parentem Bovius & Turrianus esse volunt) eam, quae vere ipsius, est ad Corinthios epistolam diserte alicubi memoret. Sed & in Origenis, non secus ac in Tertulliani libris, multa haud dubie cum Constitutionibus pugnantia, reperiet, qui illos accurate cum his comparaverit. Nos unum tantum exempli gratia annotabimus (neque enim de omnibus omnia observare necesse est) Origenes in eximio contra Celsum opere, quod circa a. D. 239. scriptum videtur, de festis disputans, tum alia multa, tum hoc inprimis observandum habet, quod Christianorum dies festos non alios recenrecenset, quam Dominicum, Parasceven, pascha, & pentecosten. Nostri vero Διάλα- γεις, quod supra demonstravimus, præter hos dies, etiam Natalem Christi, & Epiphaniam, & Ascensionem, & Apostolorum natalitios, à Christianis celebrari exserte præcipiunt. Origenis ergo temporibus nondum Christianis Apostoli erant οἱ Διάλαξεις à quibus scilicet instituta, præceptaque festa illi Apostolicorum institutorum observantissimi, nullo loco aut numero habebant.
units.tr: Origen follows; he was born in 185 and died in 254, and is almost entirely of the third century. He denies that the Apostolic Constitutions were known to him, because he never mentions them in the many writings that survive from his countless books. Yet, following the custom of Clement of Alexandria, his teacher and predecessor, he is accustomed to cite every kind of book, even apocryphal ones such as the Recognitions of Peter, and to use them in his disputations. Clement, whom Bovius and Turrianus wish to be the parent of the Constitutions, clearly mentions somewhere the epistle to the Corinthians which is truly his. But anyone who compares Origen's books carefully with the Constitutions will find many things in them that certainly clash with the Constitutions, just as in Tertullian's books. I will note only one as an example, since it is not necessary to observe everything about all of them. In his outstanding work against Celsus, which seems to have been written around 239, Origen discusses feasts, and among other things he notes especially this: that he lists no Christian feast days other than the Lord's Day, Preparation, Passover, and Pentecost. But our Constitutions, as we showed above, expressly command that the Christians also celebrate, besides these days, the birthday of Christ, Epiphany, Ascension, and the birthdays of the Apostles. So in Origen's time the Apostles, to whom the Constitutions were attributed, were not yet regarded as the Constitutions' authors, and those feasts, which he would have kept with great care if they had been ordained by Apostolic institutions, held no place or number for him.

units.la: De Cypriano Origenis æquali (nam & ipse quatuor post hunc extinctum annis martyrio consummatus est) plura dicenda sunt; quos is magna pars fuerit duarum nobilissimarum quæstionum, quæ in Christianorum Ecclesiis, maxime Carthagine & Romæ per ea tempora exortæ, plurimumque agitatæ sunt. Prior fuit de eorum, qui in idololatriam lapsi essent, pœnitentia ac reconciliatione. Cum enim multi in persecutione septima, quæ sub Decio a. D. 249. cœpit, suppliciorum metu lapsi, inde gravi sceleris pœnitentia ducti reconciliari Deo, atque Ecclesiæ vehementer expeterent, Episcopi, inprimis Cyprianus Carthaginis, Cornelius Romę temporum necessitati succumbentes, de pristina severitate, quæ omnem hujusmodi peccatoribus in EcclesiEcclesiam reditum negabat, aliquid remittendum censuerunt, lapsosque ad pœnitentiam, indeque ad pacem admittendos. Sed ut priori de mœchis admittendis indulgentiæ Tertullianus & Montanistæ intercesserant; ita nunc huic in negatores clementiæ Novatianus & alii vehementer obstiterunt; à quibus Novatianorum schisma, quod diu postea mansit, tunc primum exortum est. Quin & ex ipsis Catholicis nonnullos nova hæc in lapsos lenitas conturbavit; e quibus episcopus Antonianus unus fuisse videtur, ad quem extat luculentissima Cypriani de toto hoc negotio epistola. Jam nullas tum apud Christianos extitisse Bovianas Constitutiones, tam ex his patet, quam ex iis, quę nuper ad Tertullianum de mœchorum pœnitentia & pace diximus.Cum enim Boviani Διδαχαὶ disertissime, ut ostendimus, quosvis lapsos ad pœnitentiam ab Ecclesiĕ præpositis recipi jubeant; si eorum Constitutiones tunc temporis extitissent, & pro Apostolicis habitę essent; nihil erat,ut quivis videt, cur sacrificatis & libellaticis tamdiu pax præsracte negaretur: nihil, cur de eorum caussa toties à Cypriano, Cleroque Romano dies ampliaretur, ejusq; judicium in id tempus differretur, quo reddita pace convenire in unum episcopi, matureque de re deliberare possent; nihil erat, quod data deta deinceps opportunitate convenirent, decretumque de recipiendis certo ordine lapsis novum conderent; nihil erat, quod Novatianus & schismatici reclamarent, & invidiam decreti authoribus facerent; nihil erat, quod Antonianus, & alii Catholici id decretum, velut novum & inusitatum, mirarentur; nihil denique, cur Cyprianus in illis quidem frangendis, & compescendis; his vero placandis tantopere laboraret. Res tota, utpote disertissima Apostolorum lege constituta, plana erat atque expedita. Ac siqui vel improbi obloquerentur, vel infirmi dubitarent, omnis eorum vel contentio vel dubitatio uno verbo aut frangi, aut componi poterat; allata scilicet in medium τῶν Διαταγέων authoritate. Sed hos quidem Cyprianus, quorum clarae sunt de hac quaestione voces, clara ac diserta contra Montanistas & Novatianos & quotquot sunt ejusdem instituti, velut in crudeles, & inhumanos, & ab omni Dei bonitate ac lenitate alienos carnifices, testimonia, hos inquam Cyprianus in omni hac disputatione, quae sane apud eum satis prolixa extat, nullos plane memorat (neque alius veterum quisquam, quod sciam, horum authoritatem contra Catharos adhibuit) totam vero hanc causam ex Scripturis, quae in notro canone habentur, fuse, docteque ac graviter agit . Alte-
units.tr: Something more must be said about Cyprian, Origen's contemporary (for he too was crowned with martyrdom four years after Origen's death). He was a major figure in two most noteworthy questions which arose and were very much debated in the Christian churches, especially at Carthage and Rome, at that time. The first concerned the repentance and reconciliation of those who had fallen into idolatry. For when many, fearing punishment in the seventh persecution, which began under Decius in 249, had lapsed, and then, moved by deep sorrow for their sin, earnestly desired to be reconciled to God and to the Church, the bishops, above all Cyprian at Carthage and Cornelius at Rome, yielding to the needs of the time, decided that something should be relaxed from the former severity, which denied any return to the Church for such sinners, and that the lapsed should be admitted to repentance and thence to peace. But just as Tertullian and the Montanists had opposed the earlier indulgence toward admitting adulterers, so now Novatian and others strongly resisted this new clemency toward those who denied it. From them the schism of the Novatians, which long remained afterwards, first arose at that time. Indeed, this new leniency toward the lapsed troubled some even among the Catholics themselves; of these, Bishop Antonian seems to have been one, to whom there survives Cyprian's most illuminating letter on this whole affair. Now that there were then no Bovian Constitutions among the Christians is clear both from this and from what we have just said about Tertullian's treatment of the repentance and peace of adulterers. For if the Bovian Teachings [Διδαχαί], as we have shown, most clearly order that all the lapsed be received to repentance by the presiding ministers of the Church, and if their Constitutions had existed at that time and been regarded as Apostolic, there was no reason, as anyone can see, why peace should have been so obstinately refused to the sacrificers and the libellatics. There was no reason why Cyprian and the Roman clergy should have so often postponed the decision about their case, deferring judgement until the time when peace could be restored and the bishops could meet together and deliberate on the matter with due care. There was no reason why, when the opportunity was given, they should meet and draw up a new decree on receiving the lapsed in a fixed order. There was no reason for Novatian and the schismatics to protest and to bring odium upon the authors of the decree, nor for Antonian and other Catholics to marvel at that decree as new and unusual. Finally, there was no reason for Cyprian to labour so hard to break and restrain the one side and to appease the other. The whole matter, being settled by the most explicit law of the Apostles, would have been plain and straightforward. And if any wicked men had objected, or any weak men had doubted, their whole contention or doubt could have been broken or settled with a single word, namely by bringing forward the authority of the Constitutions [τῶν Διαταγῶν]. But Cyprian, whose clear words on this question survive, in which he speaks plainly and eloquently against the Montanists, the Novatians, and all who belong to their party, calling them cruel, inhuman butchers, alien to all the goodness and gentleness of God, does not mention these witnesses at all in this whole discussion, which indeed survives in his writings in a fairly lengthy form. (Nor, as far as I know, did any other of the ancients use their authority against the Cathari.) Instead he treats this whole question fully, learnedly, and seriously from the Scriptures that are held in our canon. The other...

units.la: Altera controversia ipfiusCypriani a & Afrorum, & aliorum non paucorum fuit contra Stephanum, Romæ episcopum, collatum ab hæreticis baptismum pro nullo habendum, eosque adeo, qui ab hæreticis tincti fuerant, rebaptizandos esse contendentium. Extat Afrorum Episcoporum Lxxxvii. Carthagine habita, Cypriano præside, ea de re Synodus: extant complures Cypriani b, una Firmiliani c, Cæsareæ in Cappadocia nominatiffimi antistitis, de eodem argumento epistolæ. Omnes illam de rebaptizandis hæreticis sententiam magno molimine, Afri quidem ex Solis Scripturis, Firmilianus d etiam ex provinciæ fuę consuetudine ac traditione, confirmant; nullam nostrorum Διαλαγίων in tota disputatione mentionem faciunt. Atqui hi, quod supra luculentiffime demonstravimus, ipsi quoq; idem de hæreticorum baptismo sentiunt. Si extabant illis temporibus, proque Apostolicis habebantur Bovianę Διαταξεις primum rogo, cur Stephanus, Apostolicus scilicet Papa, contra diserta Apostolorum præcepta definivit valere hæreticorum baptisma? Omnino necesse est, vel Apostolicum non fuisse Stephanum, (quod nunquam concedent adversarii) vel Apostolos certe (quod nos defendimus) nequaquam esse Boyianos Διαλαγίας. Tum & illud quæro; Cur Cyprianus, cur Afri, cur Firmilianus, tam in rem suam disertam, tamque evidentem Apostolorum, si sciverunt, διά-ταξιν omiserunt? cur alia causæ suæ præsidia e longinquo petunt? hoc quod & præsens, & ineluctabile erat, neglexerunt; Negat Firmilianus quemquam esse tam stultum, qui credat Apostolos tradidisse, quod contendebat Stephanus. Unde liquet, affirmasse Stephanum id quod ipse docebat (valere scilicet hæreticorum baptismum) à Christi Apostolis fuisse traditum. Id vero sine summa impudentia affirmare (si Apostolicæ quidem sunt Bovii διαταξεις) non potuit. Nisi ergo benedictum illum Papam feceris impudentem, pertendere, Bovi, non potes, Apostolos esse tuos Διατάγιας.
units.tr: The second controversy, between Cyprian a and the Africans, and not a few others, was with Stephen, bishop of Rome. They maintained that baptism conferred by heretics was to be regarded as nothing, and that those who had been baptized by heretics must be baptized again. There survives the record of the synod of eighty-seven African bishops held at Carthage under Cyprian's presidency on this matter. There survive several letters of Cyprian b, and one letter of Firmilian c, the most renowned bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, on the same subject. All of them defend the view about rebaptizing heretics with great effort: the Africans from Scripture alone, and Firmilian d also from the custom and tradition of his province. In the whole dispute none of them mentions our Constitutions [Διατάξεων]. Yet these men, as we have shown most clearly above, themselves held the same view about heretics' baptism. If the Bovian Constitutions existed in those times and were regarded as Apostolic, I ask first: why did Stephen, the Apostolic Pope, define, against the express precepts of the Apostles, that heretics' baptism is valid? Either Stephen was not Apostolic, which the opponents will never concede, or the Apostles were not the authors of the Bovian Constitutions, which is what we maintain. I ask this too: if they knew of the Apostles' ordinance [διάταξιν], so explicit and so plainly bearing on their case, why did Cyprian, the Africans and Firmilian leave it out? Why do they seek other defences of their cause from far away, and neglect this one, which was both at hand and unavoidable? Firmilian denies that anyone is so foolish as to believe that the Apostles handed down what Stephen contended. From this it is clear that Stephen asserted that what he himself taught, namely that heretics' baptism is valid, had been handed down by the Apostles of Christ. Yet he could not have asserted this without the greatest shamelessness, if the Bovian ordinances really are Apostolic. Unless you make that blessed Pope out to be shameless, Bovius, you cannot maintain that the Apostles are yours [Διατάγιας].

units.la: Sed & qui Papam urbis mentiri dicit Firmilianus, & quidem adeo crasse, ut ei nemo nisi stultus creditur fit, is profecto debuit demonstrare, id à se merito fieri. Demonstrare autem nullo negotio potuit, si eas, quas nunc habemus Apostolicas Bovii διαταξεις, ipse quoque in promptu habuit, in quibus scilicet Apostoli, non modo id, quod affirmabat Stephanus, nusquam tradunt, sed id insuper, quod ipse quidem negabat ac refutabat, Cyprianus vero & Afri, ejus in hac causa adversarii, affirmabant, clare, liquidoque docent, ajunt, instituunt. stituunt, ac præcipiunt. Atqui neque hoc loco Firmilianus, neque alibi usquam, quod dixi, vel ipse, vel Cyprianus, vel Afri de nostris Διαξήχυσι ullum verbum faciunt. Quin etiam concedit Cyprianus, traditionem de non rebaptizandis hæreticis invaluisse; eamque non aliter quam ex Dominicis Scripturis refellere instituit; plane imprudenter, ne dicam stulte, si erat ad manum contraria Apostolorum traditio, disertis verbis vel ab Apostolis ipsis, vel certe à Clemente descripta; quem Stephano, uni ex ejus posteris atque successoribus, in hac disputatione opponi dignum, necessariumque erat, si quid tum extabat Clementis nomine vulgatum, quod Stephani sententiæ opponi posset. Ergo & Stephani ipsius, & Cypriani, cæterorumque in hac causa factum invicto argumento est, nullas istis temporibus extitisse Bovianas Apostolorum διατάξεις. Id vidit, & confessus est Albaspineus a, qui inter cætera ex quibus hujus voluminis novitas deprehenditur, illam tertio hoc sæculo agitatam de hæreticorum baptismo disputationem nominatim recenset.
units.tr: But suppose Firmilian says that the Pope of the city lies, and so crudely that no one but a fool would believe him. He ought to have shown that he was right to say so. He could have shown this without any trouble, if he had had at hand those Apostolic Constitutions of Bovius which we now possess. In them the Apostles not only nowhere hand down what Stephen asserted, but moreover teach, declare, institute and command clearly and plainly what Stephen denied and refuted, and what Cyprian and the Africans, his opponents in this matter, affirmed. Yet neither here nor anywhere else do Firmilian, Cyprian or the Africans say a word about our [Διαταξεις]. Moreover Cyprian concedes that the tradition of not rebaptizing heretics had prevailed, and he undertook to refute it only from the Lord's Scriptures. That was very imprudent, not to say foolish, if a contrary tradition of the Apostles was at hand, set down in express words either by the Apostles themselves or at least by Clement. Clement was fit and necessary to oppose to Stephen, one of his successors, in this dispute, if anything circulated under Clement's name could have been set against Stephen's opinion. So the conduct of Stephen himself, of Cyprian and of the others in this matter is an invincible argument that no Bovian Constitutions of the Apostles existed in those times. Albaspinaeus a saw this and confessed it. Among the other things by which the novelty of this volume is detected, he specifically lists that dispute about heretics' baptism, which was debated in this third century.

units.la: Jam & ex Dionysio Alexandrino Episcopo, qui Cypriano annos aliquot superfuit, earundem διατάξεων novitas non minus aperte colligitur. Is enim testatur, suo quidem tempore jam in usu fuisse, ut sex diebus ante Pascha jejunaretur; caeterum varium ac multiplex fuisse id jejunium, libereque ac diverse à diversis observatum; alios a sex illos dies jejunasse totos, alios duos; alios tres; alios quatuor; alios ne unum quidem. Atqui cum tota hujus antepaschalis jejunii ratio accuratissime fuerit in Constitutionibus, ut supra ostendimus, definita; profecto si eae tum extitissent, proque Apostolicis habitae fuissent, nullum haec diversitas locum in Ecclesia habitura erat. Certe eos, qui aliter jejunabant, quam Διδαγὴς praecipiunt, obiter Dionysius reprehendisset, & ad Apostolicam normam revocasset; quod nequaquam fecit. Ad haec constat ex eadem Dionysii epistola, de hora, qua solvendum est illud antepaschale jejunium, tunc dubitatum esse. Sic enim Basilidem, à quo erat ea de re consultus, affatur b: Τι-νὰς μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν λέγειν φὴς, ὅτι χρὴ τοῦτο ποιεῖν πρὸς τὸ ἀλειτουργοφωνίαν. τινὰς δ᾽ ὅτι ἀφ᾽ ἑσπέρας χρὴ· οἱ μὲν γὰρ δὲ ἐν Ρώμῃ ἀδελφοί, ὡς φασι, περιμένουσι τ᾽ ἀλέκτορα. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ τῶν ἐνθάδε αὐτα ἐλέγεις, ὅτι τάχιον. Aliis enim aliquos fratres dicere, quod oportet hoc in galli cantu facere; alios autem, quod id fit faciendum vespere. Qui enim Roma sunt fratres, ut ajunt, gallum expectant. De iis autem, qui hic sunt, dixisti, quod citius; nimirum mirum jejunium solvunt. Hæcille. Atqui si tum extabant Bovianorum Apostolorum Constitutiones, nulla inprimis causa fuit, cur hac de re quisquam Christianus dubitaret. Illi enim accuratissime, disertissimeque non uno in loco eam definiunt; ἀπονη-σεῦσαι ὁ (inquiunt) προσέταξεν (ὁ χρεί-σὸς) τῇ ἱβδόμῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἀλέκτορος φωνήσαντος. Iejunium vero solvere praecepit (Christus) septima die post galli cantum. Iterum ali-bi b:τὸ μέντοι παρασκευὴν, ἡ τὸ σάββατον ὀ-λόκληρον νηστεύσατε, οἷς δύναμις προσέστι τοιαύτη, μηδενὸς γευόμενοι μέχρις ἀλεκτοροφωνίας νυκτός. Sextaferia & sabbato ex toto manete jejuni, quibuscunque adsunt vires, nihil prorsus gustantes usque ad nocturnum galli cantum. Denique paulo post clarissime c; ἐν ἥ λοιπαῖς τ προ τ παρασκευῆς ἐν-νάτῳ ὥρᾳ ἢ ἐσπέρᾳ ἔκας ἐδιέτω ἡ ὅπως ἄνθις δύναιτο· τῷ ὃ σαββάτῳ μέχρις ἀλεκτοροφωνίας παραλείποντες, ἀπονης ἴζητε ἐπιφωνήσης μιᾶς σαββάτων, ἥτις ἔστι Κυριακὴ, ἀπὸ ἐσπέ-ρας ἕως ἀλεκτοροφωνίας ἀγρυπνοῦντες. Reliquis vero diebus ante sextam feriam, edite hora nona, verspere, aut pro ratione virium, ut quis potest; Sabbato autem usque ad galli cantum jejunium producite, & illucescente una sabbatorum, qui est dies Dominicus pervigilantes à vespera usque ad galli cantum. Hæc illi; quæ si Dionysii temporibus extabant,si pro veris Apostolorum vocibus habebantur;quis non videt, Christianorum, qui tum vivebant, nemini fas fuisse dubitare, an ante galli cantum solvendum esset illud sabbati antepaschalis jejunium, cum eo ipso temporis articulo solvendum exserte & Apostoli isti præcipiant, & ab ipso Christo Domino præceptum fuisse affirment ? Ac ut Christianorum vulgo rem ab Apostolis definitam in dubium vocare licuerit, Basilidi quidem certe non licuit. Fuit enim is Episcopus, & quidem, ut est apud Eusebium a, Pentapolitanus. Ergo si nostræ tum Διαταξεις extitissent, neque Basilidi quisquam negotium de solvendi hujus jejunii hora facessivisset, neque ipse Basilides Dionysium consuluisset de re, quam ab Apostolis definitam ignorare non potuisset. Dubitarunt autem multi, & ante galli cantum jejunium solvendum dixerunt Pentapolitani, & Basilides ipse rem dignam putavit, de qua Dionysium consuleret. Ergo necesse est, nullos tum fuisse Christianorum vel vulgo, vel Clero, cognitos Bovii Apostolos. Sed cæteros quidem, etiam Basilidem, tametsi Episcopum, & quidem, ut eum salutat Dionysius, λογιώτατον sapientissimum, mittamus; Dionysium vero, virum (quod ex Eusebianæ historiæ libris sexto septimoque abunde constat) illius memoriæ præstantissimum, atque in omnibus Ecclesiasticis rebus longe eruditissimum, quis bonos illos Bovii Apostolos ignoraturum fuisse putet, si ii jam tum extabant? Ignorasse autem ex iis, quæ Basilidi respondet, clarum est. Nam si eos scivisset, quid responsurus fuerit vel puer divinaverit: nimirum & eorum, quorum sententiam refert Basilides, & ipsius Basilidis, insciitiam castigasset, qui de re Christi & Apostolorum authoritate definita ambigerent, veluti quærentes an sol meridie luceret; Tum ipsas illas Apostolorum, quas nuper repræsentavimus diataxes, recitavisset. Ille vero istorum nihil, imo omnia plane aliter. Primo enim præfatur, horam solvendi jejunii accurate definire, a id τῷ Δύσκολον ἐξ σφαλέςτερον ἐξ, difficile esse, & anceps atque lubricum. Tum multis exsequitur, obscurum esse, vixque ac ne vix quidem ex Evangelio explorari posse, quo præcise tempore punctô Christus de mortuis resurrexerit; denique concludit, reprehendendos sibi videri, qui jejunium nimium mature ante mediam noctem solvunt; laudandos qui diutissime perseverant ad quartam vigiliam; minime pulsandos aut turbandos, qui medio inter hæc duo extrema tempore vel pro animi sui sententia, vel pro virium modo, jejunare desinunt. Hæc ille ad quæquæstionem à Basilide propositam; quæ, ut vere post clarissime. Seldenum ait reve-rend. Usserius a, unquam ita dicturus fuit, si eas, quibus nos beavit Bovius, Apostolorum Constitutiones habuisset; ex quibus scilicet, tot missis ambagibus, totam quæstionem uno verbo decidere promptum erat; solvendum esse gallicinio jejunium ex Christi & Apostolorum lege. Sed neque illa video, quî possint cum nostrorum Διαζυγίων scitis conciliari, quæ decernit in eadem epistola Dionysius b. Hic enim mulieres τὰς ἐν ἀφιδρῳ nefas esse putat vel τῆ τριπλίζη τῆ ἁγία προσελθεῖν, ad sacram mensam accedere, vel τὸ σῶμα τοῦ & τὸ αἷμα τοῦ & χεῖρας προσάψασθαι, corpus & sanguinem Domini attingere; idque ita clarum, atque obvium esse arbitratur, ut etiam supervacaneum esse dicat, quærere, an mulieres sic affectas deceat εἰς τὸν οἶκον εἰσελθεῖν τοῦ Θεοῦ, Domum Dei ingredi; Itaque concludit, εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων ὁ μὴ πάντη καθαρὸς ἡ ψυχῇ & σώματι, προσελθεῖν κωλυθήσεται, Ad sancta sanctorum, qui non anima & corpore purus est, accedere prohibebitur. Hac vero pene Iudaica superstitione Dionysium nostri Διαζυγίης liberassent, si in eos incidisset, qui præclarè sanè ac fortiter (neque enim hac laude fraudandi sunt) de re hac tota ta philosophantur; ὥτε νόμιμος (inquiunt a) μίξις, ὥτε λέχος, ὥτε αἵματος φορά, ἡ ὀνείρωξις μιᾶναι ζωὰ) ἀνθρώπῳ φύσιν, ἢ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα χωρίσαι, ἡ μόνη ἀσέβεια καὶ παρανομία. Neque enim legitimus concubitus, neque partus, neque sanguinis fluxio, neque genitalis seminis per somnium excretio, naturam hominis polluere possunt, aut Spiritum Sanctum separare, praeterquam sola impietas, & actio à lege aliena; moxque iterum idem docent sola in Deum impietate, iniquitateque, & adversus proximum injustitiâ, furto, adulterio, scortatione, animam inquinari. Itaque mulieri ita praecipiunt: Διὸ τῶν ματαίων ἀπόχθ λόγων, ὦ γυνή, ἐξ ἴσω μεμνημένη πάντοτε Θεὸν τὸν σε δημιουργήσαντα, καὶ προσεύχου τούτῳ· ἔστι γάρ σε ὁ τῶν ὅλων κύριος, ᾗ μελέτα τὰς αὐτοῦ νόμους, μηδὲν παρατηρουμένη· μὴ καθαρσιν φυσικῶν, μὴ μίξιν νόμιμον, μὴ τοκετὸν, ἢ ἀποβολῶ. Quocirca abstine, mulier, a vanis sermonibus, Deinque conditoris tui jugiter memor esto: & eum precare, qui & tuus & universi Dominus est. Meditare ejus legem; nihil istorum observans, non purgationem naturalem, non concubitum legitimum, non partum, aut abortum. Haec si Apostolica scivisset Dionysius, non videtur mulierem naturali illo profluvio laborantem vel Ecclesia, quæ domus est orationis, vel Christi mensa, quæ Eucharistiæ sacramentum est, repulsurus, ac exclusurus.
units.tr: Moreover, the novelty of these same διατάξεις is no less clearly shown from Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, who survived Cyprian by some years. He testifies that in his own time it was already the custom to fast for six days before Easter, but that this fast was varied and manifold, and that people observed it freely and in different ways: some fasted all six days, some two, some three, some four, and some not even one. Yet the whole scheme of this pre-Paschal fast is defined with the greatest precision in the Constitutions, as we showed above. Surely, if those Constitutions had then existed and had been regarded as Apostolic, this diversity could have had no place in the Church. Dionysius certainly would have rebuked in passing those who fasted otherwise than the Teaching [Διδαχή] prescribes, and would have recalled them to the Apostolic rule. He did nothing of the kind. Further, it is clear from the same letter of Dionysius that doubt then existed about the hour at which this pre-Paschal fast was to be broken. He addresses Basilides, who had consulted him on the matter, in these words: "For you say that some of the brothers hold that it must be done at cock-crow [ἀλειτουργοφωνία]; others that it must be done in the evening. For the brothers at Rome, as they say, wait for the cock to crow. But those here, you say, do it earlier; that is, they break their strange fast." So far Dionysius. Yet if the Constitutions of the Apostles of Bovius had then existed, there was above all no reason why any Christian should have doubted this matter. For they define it most exactly and most plainly, in more than one place: "The Lord commanded that the fast be broken on the seventh day, when the cock has crowed." And again elsewhere: "On the Preparation [Friday] and the Sabbath, fast entirely, as far as your strength allows, tasting nothing until the cock crows at night." Finally, a little later, most clearly: "On the other days before the Preparation, eat at the ninth hour or in the evening, or as each can, according to his strength; but on the Sabbath, fast until the cock crows; and as one of the Sabbaths dawns, which is the Lord's Day, keep vigil from evening until the cock crows." These are their words. If these words had existed in Dionysius's time and had been held to be the true words of the Apostles, who could fail to see that no Christian of that time could have had any right to doubt whether the Sabbath pre-Paschal fast ought to be broken before the cock crowed, when those same Apostles expressly order it to be broken at that very moment of time, and affirm that it had been commanded by Christ the Lord himself? And even if ordinary Christians might have been allowed to call into question what the Apostles had settled, Basilides at least was certainly not allowed to do so. For he was a bishop, and, as Eusebius reports, Bishop of the Pentapolis. Therefore, if our Διαταξεις had existed then, no one would have raised for Basilides any question about the hour of breaking this fast, and Basilides himself would not have consulted Dionysius on a matter which, defined by the Apostles, he could not have failed to know. But many doubted, and the people of the Pentapolis said that the fast must be broken before the cock crowed, and Basilides himself thought the matter worth putting to Dionysius. It is therefore necessary that the Apostles of Bovius were then known neither to ordinary Christians nor to the clergy. But let us pass over the others, even Basilides, though he was a bishop, and, as Dionysius greets him, "most learned [λογιώτατος]." Who would suppose that Dionysius, a man (as is abundantly clear from the sixth and seventh books of Eusebius's history) of outstanding memory and by far the most learned in all ecclesiastical affairs, would have been ignorant of those good Apostles of Bovius, if they already existed? That he was in fact ignorant is clear from what he replies to Basilides. For had he known them, even a child could guess what he would have answered: he would have rebuked both the opinion which Basilides reports and Basilides' own ignorance, since they doubted a matter settled by the authority of Christ and the Apostles, as if asking whether the sun shines at noon. Then he would have quoted those very Apostolic ordinances which we have just set before the reader. But he does none of this; on the contrary, he does everything quite differently. First, he declares that it is difficult to fix exactly the hour for breaking the fast, and that the matter is doubtful and slippery [δύσκολον, ἀσφαλέστερον]. Then he argues at length that it is obscure, and can scarcely, or hardly at all, be ascertained from the Gospel, at what precise moment Christ rose from the dead. Finally he concludes that those seem to him to be blamed who break the fast too early, before midnight; that those are to be praised who persevere to the fourth watch; and that those who, between these two extremes, stop fasting at a time of their own judgment or according to their strength are by no means to be harassed or disturbed. This is what he says in answer to the question put by Basilides. Venerable Ussher, as Selden says, would never have spoken thus if he had possessed those Apostolic Constitutions which Bovius has given us. For with them, clearly, all the tangled arguments could have been set aside, and the whole question settled in a single word: the fast is to be broken at cock-crow, by the law of Christ and the Apostles. Nor do I see how the Dionysian decrees which he lays down in the same letter can be reconciled with the rules of our Διαζυγίων. For he thinks it unlawful for women in their menstrual state to approach the holy table [τὴν τράπεζαν τὴν ἁγίαν], or to touch the body and blood of the Lord; and he holds this to be so plain and obvious that he says it is superfluous even to ask whether such women may enter the house of God. Accordingly he concludes that one who is not wholly pure in soul and body will be prevented from approaching the holy of holies. Yet Dionysius would have freed our Διαζυγίης from this almost Jewish superstition, had he fallen in with those who speak most nobly and bravely on this whole subject (for they too deserve this praise): "Neither lawful intercourse, nor childbirth, nor a flow of blood, nor the emission of seed in a dream can defile the nature of man or separate the Holy Spirit, but only impiety and transgression of the law." Then they teach again that the soul is defiled by impiety alone against God, and by injustice against neighbours, by theft, adultery, and fornication. So they give the following instruction to a woman: "Therefore, woman, refrain from vain words, and remember always the God who made you, and pray to him; for he is the Lord of all, and meditate on his law, observing none of these things: neither natural purgation, nor lawful intercourse, nor childbirth, nor miscarriage." If Dionysius had known these Apostolic words, he would not, it seems, have turned away and shut out a woman suffering from that natural flow, whether from the Church, which is a house of prayer, or from the table of Christ, which is the sacrament of the Eucharist.

units.la: Atque hæc de Dionysio Alexandrino satis. Petrus, ejusdem Ecclesiæ præsul, qui Theonæ, circa a. D. 300. successit, neque ipse, ut videtur, Bovianas Constitutiones habuit cognitas. Quod enim ab his, ut supra demonstravimus, scripta lege præceptum est, quartę sextæque serię jejunium, id illeuni non scriptæ traditioni acceptum refert ; ἐκ ἐγκαλέσει τις ὑμῖν (inquit a) παραδεδομένοις τετράδα καὶ παρασκευὴν, ἓν ἃς καὶ νηστεύειν ὑμῖν ἐν παρασκευὴν ἐυλόγως παραγγέλλουσι. Non reprehendet nos quispiam quartam & sextam feriam observantes, in quibus nobis jejunare secundum traditionem præceptum est. Dixisset haud dubie, non quod ait ex traditione jussos esse nos duabus illis feriis jejunare, sed Apostolos domini id diserte præcepisse; si cognitos habuisset, & Apostolos censuisset Bovianos Διδα-χὰς. Itidemque, quam statim subjicit duplicis hujus jejunii rationem ex hoc eorundem codice, in quo ea pæne totidem verbis expressa extat, repetivisset, si hunc eorum codicem legisset. Ait enim nobis jejunare ex traditione præceptum esse, τῶν μὲν τετράδα καὶ τὸ γενόμενον συμβάλλον δὴ τῇ προσδοκίᾳ τῶν Κυρίου ὑπὸ ἱδιαίων. τὸν δὲ παρασκευὴν ἐγκλιτικῶς ϱασιλευλὼ δ͂ξ τὸ πεπονθέναι αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, Feria quidem quarta propter initum a Iudaeis consilium de proditione Domini; Sexta vero feria, eo quod pro nobis passus sit. Hæc utraque ratio diserte neque semel, a nostris Constitutionibus allata est. τετράδα ⸌(inquiunt a) ⸍ παρασκευὴν προσέταξεν ἡμῖν vn-ειν. τὴν μὲν δ͂ξ τὴν προσδοκίαν, τὴν δ͂ξ τὸ πάθος. Quarta vero feria, & sexta jussit (Christus) nos jejunare; illa quidem propter traditionem, hac vero propter passionem. Iterum alibi; Jejunate (inquiunt b) quarta sextaque feria; ὅτι τῇ μὲν τετράδι ἡ ἡμέρα ἐξήλθεν ἢ κῆ τῆς Κυρίου, Ἰησᾶ χρήματα ἐπαγγελλόμενος τὴν προσδοκίαν. τὴν δὲ παρασκευήν, ὅτι ἔπαθεν ὁ Κύριος ἐν αὐτῇ πάθος τὸ δ͂ξ σταυρῷ ὑπὸ Ποντίῳ Πιλάτῳ. Quoniam quarta quidem judicium in Dominum pronunciatum est, postquam Judas proditionem pecunia promiserat; sexta vero feria; quoniam eadem Dominus passus est mortem in cruce sub Pontio Pilato. Cur ergo hic rationem eam adhibens Petrus, vel Apostolos, vel certe Clementem Constitutionum (ut volunt) authorem, non laudat? non nominat? quos, ut quivis videt, laudari, ac nominari, ipsius, quam Petrus agit, causæ intererat, quo scilicet ei, quam a reprehensione vindicat, observationi suæ constaret authoritas? Nihil aliud vere appositeque positeque respondefile, nisi hoc unum; Petrum ab Apostolis scripto traditam vel observationem, vel observationis rationem nescivisse; non adeo hunc, quo utraque continetur, codicem scivisse. Iam cum istorum, quae apud Petrum legimus, verborum gemina sint, quae apud Διδαχὴν extant; cumque hinc appareat, illum ab his ea minime mutuatum esse; omnino consequens est, ut hos ab illo eadem, non quidem mutuatos, sed furatos esse dicamus; proindeq; post Petri Alexandrini tempora, id est post tertii à Christo nato saeculi exitum, vixisse.
units.tr: So much for Dionysius of Alexandria. Peter, bishop of the same Church, who succeeded Theonas around the year 300 after Christ, does not seem to have known the Bovian Constitutions either. The fasting on Wednesday and Friday, which, as we have shown above, is prescribed in the written law, he attributes to an unwritten tradition. He says: "No one will find fault with you for observing the fourth and sixth days, on which you are bidden by tradition to fast" [οὐκ ἐγκαλέσει τις ὑμῖν παρατηροῦντας τετράδα καὶ παρασκευήν, ἐν αἷς καὶ νηστεύειν ὑμῖν ἐκ παραδόσεως παραγγέλλουσι]. Without doubt he would have said that the Apostles of the Lord had expressly commanded this, and not merely that we were bidden by tradition to fast on those two days, if he had known the Bovian Constitutions and had judged them to be the work of the Apostles. Likewise, when he immediately gives the reason for this double fast, taken from the same book, where it stands almost word for word, he would have repeated it had he read that book. He says that we are bidden by tradition to fast, on the fourth day because of the counsel of the Jews concerning the Lord's expectation of betrayal [τὴν μὲν τετράδα διὰ τὸ γενόμενον συμβούλιον τῶν Ἰουδαίων περὶ τῆς προδοσίας τοῦ Κυρίου], and on the sixth day because he suffered for us [τὴν δὲ παρασκευὴν διὰ τὸ πεπονθέναι αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν]. Both reasons are stated plainly, and more than once, in our Constitutions. "(Christ), say they, ordered us to fast on Wednesday and Friday [τετράδα καὶ παρασκευὴν προσέταξεν ἡμῖν νηστεύειν]: the one for the betrayal, the other for the passion [τὴν μὲν διὰ τὴν παράδοσιν, τὴν δὲ διὰ τὸ πάθος]." And again elsewhere: "Fast on Wednesday and Friday, because on the Wednesday the judgment against the Lord went forth, when Judas promised money for the betrayal; and on the Friday, because the Lord suffered on that day the passion on the cross under Pontius Pilate [ὅτι τῇ μὲν τετράδι ἡ κρίσις ἐξήλθεν κατὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, Ἰούδα χρήματα ἐπαγγειλαμένου τὴν προδοσίαν· τὴν δὲ παρασκευήν, ὅτι ἔπαθεν ὁ Κύριος ἐν αὐτῇ πάθος τὸ ἐπὶ σταυροῦ ὑπὸ Ποντίου Πιλάτου]." Why then does Peter, when giving this reason, not cite or name the Apostles, or at least Clement, whom they say is the author of the Constitutions? Anyone can see that it was in the interest of his own cause, which he defends against criticism, that these authorities should be named and cited, so that the observance he upholds would rest on authority. Nothing else can be truly and appositely answered except this one thing: Peter did not know either the observance, or the reason for it, as handed down in writing by the Apostles; nor did he know that book in which both are contained. Since the words of these passages that we read in Peter are the same as those found in the Didache, and since it is clear from this that he did not borrow them from it, it follows entirely that we should say that the author of the Constitutions took them from Peter, not borrowed but stolen, and that he therefore lived after the time of Peter of Alexandria, that is, after the close of the third century from the birth of Christ.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Arg. XIII. Constitutiones ignotas fuisse Patribus Eliberitanis, & Nicaenis. Ex his concluditur, nondum eas extitisse quarto ineunte saeculo; quod ipsum insuper tribus novis argumentis demonstratur.
