units.tr: Argument XIII. The Constitutions were unknown to the Fathers of Elvira and of Nicaea. From this it is concluded that they did not yet exist at the beginning of the fourth century; and this is further demonstrated by three new arguments.

units.la: SEd, neque Bovii Apostolos agnoscebant Eliberitani Patres, quarti saeculi anno quinto. Hi enim & multos peccatores, ut eos, qui post fidem baptismi salutaris adulta aetate ad templum idololatraturi accesserint & fecerint, aliosque item non pacuos, in perpetuum a veniae & communionis spe excludunt, & omni sabbato jejunandum esse decernunt; quod utrumque est, ut ex supra dictis liquet, à Διαταγῶν scitis alienum.
units.tr: But neither did the Fathers of Elvira, in the fifth year of the fourth century, recognise the Apostles of Bovius. For they exclude from the hope of pardon and of communion for ever many sinners: those who, having received the faith of saving baptism, went to the temple in adult age and offered idol worship, and likewise others not a few; and they decree that fasting is to be kept every Sabbath. Both of these, as is clear from what was said above, are foreign to the decrees of the Constitutions [Διαταγαί].

units.la: Jam & Nicaenos quoque Patres, anno ejusdem saeculi 25. Apostolicas Bovii Διαθήκης nescivisse, perspicuum est. Constat enim eos sive Apostolorum scripturis, sive etiam Ecclesiastica traditione ea confirmare, quae vel illarum, vel hujus authoritate nituntur; ut ex canonibus secundo, sexto, septimo apparet; in quibus Apostolicam scripturam, Ecclesiae Romanae morem, & antiquam traditionem laudant. Unde apparet, eos Διαθηκῶν quoque authoritatem allaturos fuisse, si eas Apostolicas scivissent, cum aliquid decernunt, quod iis congruere deprehenditur. Atqui nusquam id fecerunt, neque ubi Episcopum à tribus minimum Episcopis ordinari a, neque ubi laicos, qui sub Licinio negaverant, ad poenitentiam & pacem admitti, neque ubi homines a Paulianistis haereticis venientes rebaptizari praecipiunt, quae, ut liquet, omnia disertis Διαταγῶν regulis, sive legibus conveniunt; quas quia non semel supra exhibuimus, hic repetere non placet. Quid, quod Διαθήκης, non modo quo loco memorandi erant, tacent, sed etiam eorum decreta evertunt? Dum enim Paulianistarum nominatim baptismum infirmant, eo caeterorum haereticorum admittunt, quorum dispar fuit ab illis ratio. At Boviani Apostoli nullius haeretici baptismum valere censent. Ergo quos ita aperte pulsant, pro veris Apostolis nequaquam habuerunt Nicaeni illi Patres.
units.tr: Moreover, it is plain that the Fathers of Nicaea too, in the twenty-fifth year of the same century, did not know the Apostolic Covenants [Διαθῆκαι] of Bovius. For it is established that they confirmed by the writings of the Apostles, or even by ecclesiastical tradition, those things which rest on the authority of either; as appears from the second, sixth and seventh canons, in which they praise Apostolic Scripture, the custom of the Church of Rome, and ancient tradition. Hence it is evident that they would have brought forward the authority of the Covenants as well, had they known them to be Apostolic, whenever they decreed something that is found to agree with them. Yet they never did so: neither where they order that a bishop be ordained by at least three bishops, nor where they admit to repentance and peace laymen who had denied the faith under Licinius, nor where they order that people coming from the heretical Paulianists be rebaptised. All of these, as is clear, agree with the explicit rules or laws of the Constitutions; since we have set these out more than once above, we do not wish to repeat them here. What of the fact that the Covenants are not only silent where they ought to have been mentioned, but actually overturn the decrees of the Nicene Fathers? For while they explicitly weaken the baptism of the Paulianists, they admit the others, whose case was different from theirs, to baptism. But the Bovian Apostles judge that the baptism of no heretic is valid. Therefore those Nicene Fathers by no means held as true Apostles those whom these Apostles so openly oppose.

units.la: Ad superiora, tria insuper accedant argumenta, quibus liquido probatur, totis illis tribus primis Christianismi saeculis ignotas fuisse Apostolicas Bovii Constitutiones. Primum ducitur a decimis & primitiis, quas Διακονίας a Ecclesiae ministris accuratissime ab omnibus & singulis Christianis solvi praecipiunt; quod toto illo primitivae Ecclesiae tempore inauditum, ne nunc quidem a Graecis fit, vel ab Aethiopibus ipsis; quibus quantumvis in canonem relati Διακονίας, nondum hoc in Clericos officium persuadere potuerunt. Soli Latini decimarum jus apud suos constituerunt; quod maxime sub domus Carolinae principibus obtinuisse videtur. Valafridus quidem Strabo b, scriptor noni saeculi, quo loco de decimis agit, easque deberi probare studet, nullum alium in hanc rem vel laudat, vel nominat veteris Ecclesiae authorem, praeter Augustinum, quem anno quinti saeculi 30. denatum constat; & a cujus authoritate illud decimarum jus in occidente maxime invaluisse videtur. Sed neque in tam multis Synodorum sub Carolina domo apud nos habitarum hac de re canonibus, atque sanctionibus uspiam cernitur adhibita Constitutionum Apostolicarum authoritas. Ex quibus clarum est, neque veteribus trium priorum saeculorum Christianis cognitos fuisse Apostolos Bovii, neque episcopis Carolinorum temporum, id est noni saeculi. Illi enim decimas suis clericis solvissent, si Apostolos istos notos habuisent; quod nequaquam eos fecisse ex omnium vetustissimorum scriptorum silentio deprehenditur. Hi vero eorum de solvendis decimis decreta, disertasque leges in medium attulisent, quo loco id negotium maximo cum studio constituunt; si quas Apostolorum hujusmodi leges scivisent; quod (ut dixi) nusquam omnino fecisse cernuntur.
units.tr: To what has been said, let three further arguments be added, by which it is clearly proved that throughout all those first three centuries of Christianity the Apostolic Constitutions of Bovius were unknown. The first is drawn from tithes and first-fruits, which the Constitutions [Διακονίαι] most carefully order to be paid by all and each of the Christians to the ministers of the Church. This was unheard of throughout that whole period of the primitive Church, and it is not even now practised by the Greeks, or even by the Ethiopians themselves; although the Constitutions, however much they were admitted into the canon, have not been able to persuade them of this duty for the clergy. Only the Latins established the right of tithes among their people, which seems chiefly to have prevailed under the princes of the house of Charlemagne. Indeed Walafrid Strabo, a writer of the ninth century, when he treats of tithes at the place where he seeks to prove that they are due, cites or names no other author of the ancient Church on this matter except Augustine, who is known to have died in the thirtieth year of the fifth century, and from whose authority that right of tithes seems chiefly to have grown strong in the West. But in the many canons and sanctions on this matter of the synods held among us under the house of Charlemagne, the authority of the Apostolic Constitutions is nowhere to be seen being used. From these things it is clear that the Apostles of Bovius were known neither to the ancient Christians of the first three centuries nor to the bishops of the time of Charlemagne, that is, of the ninth century. For they would have paid tithes to their clergy had they known those Apostles; and that they did not do so is established by the silence of all the most ancient writers. Those bishops, however, would have brought forward the decrees on paying tithes and the express laws of the Apostles on the subject, at the place where they establish this matter with the greatest zeal, had they known any such laws of the Apostles; which, as I have said, they are nowhere seen to have done at all.

units.la: Alterum argumentum inde sumitur, quod Διαζυγίς a Episcopo tribunal ac forum quoddam, judiciaque certa die, feria scilicet secunda, exercenda attribuunt; cum potestate de singulorum litibus, ac controversiis cognoscendi, ac decernendi. Denique rem totam sic describunt, ut planum sit, nihil aliud eos intellexisse, quam quod multis post Apostolos temporibus Principum Christianorum benignitate atque authoritate Episcopis indultum fuit; quod cum neque verisimile sit sub Paganis Principibus, Chri-
units.tr: A second argument is drawn from this: the Constitutions [Διατάξεις] assign to the bishop a tribunal and a court of his own, with judicial sittings on a fixed day, namely the second day of the week, and with power to hear and decide the disputes and controversies of individuals. In short, they describe the whole matter in such a way that it is plain they understood nothing other than what was granted to bishops many centuries after the Apostles, through the kindness and authority of Christian rulers. Since this is not likely to have happened under pagan emperors, who were hostile to the Christian name, the very laws and decrees of the Caesars to whom it is attributed sufficiently show that it was new. It would surely be most absurd to regard as Apostolic, or as men of the Apostolic age, those who record and establish this so explicitly and so plainly.

units.la: a L. 2. c. 47. Christiano nomini infensis, locum habuisse; & novum esse ipsæ Cæsarum, quibus id conceditur, leges ac sanctiones satis per se prodant; absurdissimum profecto fuerit, qui hoc ipsum tam diserte tamque perspicue commemorant, ac constituunt, eos vel pro Apostolicis, vel pro Apostolicorum temporum hominibus habere.
units.tr: a L. 2. c. 47. Those laws and decrees of the Caesars, who were hostile to the Christian name, show of themselves that the matter was novel and had no place under such rulers. It would surely be most absurd for those who record and establish this so clearly and openly to regard them as either Apostolic or men of the Apostolic age.

units.la: Tertium postremo argumentum inde habetur, quod locupletissimus testis Chrysostomus a affirmat, Antiochenos ante Nicænæ synodi tempora Paschale jejunium aliter observasse; tandem 300. & amplius Patrum (id est Nicænorum) authoritati cessisse. Ergo tota illa orientis diœcesis, cum Antiochia metropoli, veterem Asianorum morem in Paschate celebrando servavit ad Nicænam synodum. Atqui morem difertissime Διαςαυρῶν damnatum, quis tantam tamque excellentem Ecclesiam præoptaturam fuisse crediderit, si iistos Διαςαυρῖας vel ipsa notos pro Apostolicis habuisset, vel ab aliis Christianorum Ecclesiis tali loco ac numero haberi scivisset?
units.tr: Finally, a third argument is drawn from this: the most weighty witness, Chrysostom, affirms that the Antiochenes had observed the Paschal fast differently before the time of the Nicene synod, and that at last they yielded to the authority of more than 300 Fathers (that is, the Nicenes). Therefore that whole eastern diocese, with Antioch as its metropolis, kept the ancient custom of the Asians in celebrating Easter up to the Nicene synod. Yet who would believe that so great and so excellent a Church would have preferred a custom most plainly condemned as that of the Diastaurites [Διαςαυρῶν], if it had regarded those men as Apostolic, or had known that other Christian churches held them in such esteem and in such numbers?

units.la: Atque ita ex his quæ hactenus disputavimus patet, totis trecentis & viginti quinque à Christo in terris nato annis nullas Christianis hominibus auditas cognitasve fuisse Bovianas Apostolorum Διατάξεις, neque ex omni illa memoria quemquam vel unum proferunt, vel proferre possunt Bovius Turrianusve, qui earum vero meminerit, aut sibi eas vel per somnium agnitas fuisse significaverit. Id vero ad convellendum, penitusque evertendum illum, quem ipsæ sibi tribuunt, & hi aliique concedunt, Apostolatum satis superque est. Nam si primis tribus Christianismi sæculis Apostolicæ non fuerunt Bovianæ istæ Διά-ξηαι, nemo non videt, nulla sequentium temporum vel authoritate vel industria fieri eas Apostolicas posse. Ut enim quod factum est, infectum fieri nequit; ita quod factum non est, id ut factum fuerit, nulla vi fieri potest. Atque hic inprimis valere illud debet quod vulgo dicitur, qua ab initio non valuerunt, ea tractu temporis convalescere non posse. Apostolicas autem non fuisse tribus illis primis sæculis, quas Bovius nobis nunc exhibet, Διαθηκας, clarissime, validissimeque hactenus firmavimus. Non est ergo deinceps metuendum, ne illæ aliquando Apostolicæ fiant.
units.tr: And so from what we have argued so far it is clear that throughout the whole three hundred and twenty-five years since Christ was born on earth, the Bovian Apostolic Constitutions [Διατάξεις] were neither heard of nor known by Christian people; and from all that memory neither Bovius nor Turrianus can produce, or is able to produce, even one man who remembered them, or who indicated that they had been recognised by him, even in a dream. But to overthrow and utterly undo that apostleship which they claim for them, and which these and others concede, this is quite enough and more. For if these Bovian Constitutions [Διά-ξηαι] were not Apostolic in the first three centuries of Christianity, no one fails to see that they cannot be made Apostolic by the authority or the diligence of any later times. For just as what has been done cannot be undone, so what has not been done cannot be made to have been done by any force. And here above all that saying ought to hold good which is commonly quoted: what did not hold good from the beginning cannot gain strength with the passage of time. That the Covenants which Bovius now sets before us were not Apostolic in those first three centuries, we have so far established most clearly and most firmly. There is therefore no need from now on to fear that they will ever become Apostolic.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Arg. XVI I. Quod & Ariani & Catholici quarti sæculi Constitutiones nesciverunt. Arg. XVIII. Laodiceni Patres eas ignorarunt. Arg. XIX. Et Basilius Cæsar. Arcudii stropha confutatur.
units.tr: Arg. XVII. That the Arians and the Catholics of the fourth century did not know the Constitutions. Arg. XVIII. The Laodicean Fathers were ignorant of them. Arg. XIX. And Basil of Caesarea. The quibble of Arcudius is refuted.

units.la: Ideamus tamen, quæ de iis fuerit sequentium temporum fides; sed breviter; non distincte neque enucleate, quo ordine superiora fæcula emensi sumus, sed ϰῷ πλάτος, & universim, diversos ætatum gradus percurrendo.
units.tr: Let us nonetheless see what the belief of later times was concerning them; but briefly, not in detail or with exact elucidation, in the order in which we went through the earlier centuries, but in broad outline, running through the different stages of the ages.

units.la: Principio notas non fuisse proximis post synodum Nicænam temporibus Constitutiones Bovianas ex eo satis constare potest, quod cum plurima habeant, ut supra demonstravimus, Arianæ & Macedonianæ in Christum ac spiritum Sanctum blasphemiæ non tantum in speciem faventia, sed aperte congruentia, nihil tamen ex iis Arianos, aut Macedonianos ad erroris sui patrocinium adhibuisse, vel laudasse discimus ex plurimis, quæ toto quarto sæculo, deincepsque conscriptæ adhuc extant: adversus illos hæreticos disputationibus.
units.tr: First, it can be fairly established that the Bovian Constitutions were not known in the period immediately after the Council of Nicaea. For although they contain many things, as we showed above, which not only seem to favour but plainly agree with the blasphemies of the Arians and Macedonians against Christ and the Holy Spirit, we nevertheless learn from the many writings from the whole of the fourth century and later, still extant, which were written against those heretics, that the Arians or Macedonians never used anything from them to defend their error, nor did they cite them.

units.la: Ex Athanasio quidem constat, Arianos Dionysii Alexandrini multa securius dicta in rem suam torsisse; in quibus explicandis, solvendisque multus est Athanasius. Quanto magis illi Apostolorum Constitutiones, si quae tum, quales nunc hodie habemus, extitissent, in hac causa adhibituri erant? Nullas autem adhibuisse vel Athanasii silentium docet. Qui enim de unius Dionysii dictis epistolam, eamque prolixam, & sane accuratam ac eruditam scripsit Athanasius; quanto diligentius ac studiosius siqua ex Apostolis jactassent Ariani, ea colleturus, expensurusque, ac pro virili sua explicaturus erat? Non fecit; neque in tam multis ejus contra Arianos, copiosis ac uberibus disputationibus in quibus omnes eorum machinas, omnia ex divinis humanisque vel scripturis, vel rebus argumenta proponit, ac solvit, ulla uspiam cernitur Apostolicarum Constitutionum facta vel levissima mentio. Ergo nullas tum quidem neque Ariani, neq; Athanasius norant; quae scilicet si extitissent ullae, earum authoritatem & illi objecturi, & hic objectam memoraturus erat. Atque hinc evidenter confirmatur, quod nos supra diximus, aliisque etiam argumentis probavimus, non Boviarum Διατάξεων codicem, sed alium aliquem, & ipsum quoque apocryphum librum fuisse illam Eusebio, Athanasioque memoratam Apostolorum doctrinam.
units.tr: From Athanasius it is clear that the Arians twisted to their own purpose many statements of Dionysius of Alexandria which had been made too carelessly, and Athanasius labours long in explaining and resolving them. How much more would the Arians have brought forward the Constitutions of the Apostles, if such had existed then in the form we have them today, in this controversy? That they used none of them is shown by the silence of Athanasius. For Athanasius wrote a long, certainly careful and learned letter about the words of Dionysius alone. How much more diligently and eagerly would he have gathered and weighed whatever the Arians had alleged from the Apostles, and explained it to the best of his ability? He did not do so. In so many of his copious and rich disputations against the Arians, in which he sets out and resolves all their devices and all the arguments from divine and human writings and from facts, there is nowhere any even slight mention of the Apostolic Constitutions. Therefore neither the Arians nor Athanasius knew any at that time; for had any existed, they would have brought forward their authority, and he would have mentioned it as an objection. And from this it is clearly confirmed, as we said above and proved by other arguments, that the book which Eusebius and Athanasius mention as the teaching of the Apostles was not the Bovian code of the Διατάξεις, but some other, and itself an apocryphal book.

units.la: Jam & aliorum Patrum eadem ratio est, qui cum Arianis confligentes caetera eorum ex Scripturis, vel ex priorum Ecclesiae hominum libris sophismata memorant: Deusurpata ab iis Διατάγιων aliqua authoritate nihil dicunt. Id in Basilio, qui anno quarti saeculi 78. denatus est, nominatim observari potest. Is enim a & Dionysii illius, quem Athanasius quoque, ut diceba-mus, ab Arianis in hac causa adhibitum fuisse testem refert, & Gregorii item Neocaesariensis, quaedam incautius dicta recitat, & excusat. In Διαζηγιῶν vero Arianicis ut videtur Macedonianisque venenis infectas voces, nullum usquam orthodoxis antidotum praebet. Quid-ni, cum multo speciosius, eoque nocentius esset Apostolorum, quam vel Dionysii, vel Gregorii nomine propinatum venenum? Nimirum nulli tunc erant Boviani illi Apostoli; quorum nomen, & voces, vel arripere Ariani, vel timere Catholici possent.
units.tr: The same is true of the other Fathers as well. When they contend with the Arians, they mention their other sophisms drawn from Scripture or from the books of earlier churchmen, but say nothing of any authority usurped from the Constitutions [Διαταγῶν]. This can be observed by name in Basil, who died in the year 378 of the fourth century. For he recites and excuses some rashly spoken words of that Dionysius whom Athanasius also, as we said, reports was used by the Arians as a witness in this matter, and likewise of Gregory of Neocaesarea. But in the Constitutions, whose words seem tainted with Arian and Macedonian poisons, he offers no antidote to orthodox readers anywhere. Why not, when the poison given in the name of the Apostles would have been far more specious and therefore more harmful than that given in the name of Dionysius or Gregory? Clearly there were then no such Bovian Apostles, whose name and words the Arians could have seized or the Catholics feared.

units.la: Id quoque in causa fuit, cur Laodiceni Patres circa annum D.365. nullam horum mentionem fecerint, quo loco vetant, ne quisquam vir Christianus in balneo cum mulieribus lavetur; tametsi hoc decretum τῆς Διαζηγιῶν authoritate confirmari & liceret, si tum extitissent Boviane eorum Constitutiones, & vero operae pretium effet. Sed & Laodiceni multo etiam clarius, difertiusque negant, sibi notos fuisse istos Bovii Apostolos; dum severe vetant quod hi praecipiunt, sabbati otium, anathemateque id ipsum feriunt, quod hi non modo concedunt, sed etiam jubent. Διαταγὴν legem supra recitavimus. Quę vero Laodicenorum est, ea ita habet: Οὐ δεῖ χειςιανὸς Ἰουδαΐζειν καὶ ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ σχο-λάζειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτὰς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ, τὴν δὲ Κυριακὴν τιμῶντας, εἰ δὲ σχολάζειν ὡς χειςιανοὶ. εἰ δὲ εὑρεθεῖεν Ἰουδαΐζοντες, ἔστωσαν ἀνάθεμα παρὰ Χριστῷ. Non oportet Christianos Iudaizare, & in sabbato otiari, sed eos ipso illo die operari; diem autem Dominicum praeferentes otiari, si modo possint, ut Christianos. Quod si inventi fuerint Judaizantes, sint anathema apud Christum.
units.tr: This also was the reason why the Laodicean Fathers, about the year 365, made no mention of them in the place where they forbid any Christian man to bathe with women. Yet they could have confirmed this decree by the authority of the Constitutions, if those Bovian Constitutions had then existed and been worth the trouble. But the Laodiceans deny even more clearly and plainly that these Bovian Apostles were known to them, since they severely forbid what these prescribe, a sabbath rest, and curse that very thing which these not only permit but even command. We quoted the law of the Constitutions above. The canon of the Laodiceans reads as follows: "Christians ought not to Judaize and rest on the Sabbath, but to work on that day, honouring the Lord's day; and if they can, to rest as Christians. But if they are found Judaizing, let them be anathema from Christ" [Οὐ δεῖ χριστιανὸς Ἰουδαΐζειν καὶ ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ σχολάζειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ἡμέρᾳ, τὴν δὲ Κυριακὴν τιμῶντας, εἰ δὲ σχολάζειν ὡς χριστιανοί. εἰ δὲ εὑρεθεῖεν Ἰουδαΐζοντες, ἔστωσαν ἀνάθεμα παρὰ Χριστῷ].

units.la: Neque pluris Basilius, vir eorundem temporum, toto orbe Christiano notissimus, Bovianorum Apostolorum authoritatem fecit. Nam hi quidem librorum τῆς ἔξωθεν omnium lectione Christianis interdicunt; τῆς ἐνδικῶν βιβλίων πάντων ἀπέχεσθαι (inquiunt) τί γάρ σοι καὶ ἀλλοτρίοις λόγοις ἢ νόμοις ἢ ψευδοπροφήταις, ἃ δὴ καὶ παραγγέλλει τῆς πίστεως τὰς ἐλαφρὰς. Abstine ab omnibus libris Gentilium. Quid enim tibi cum alienis sermonibus, aut legibus, aut falsis prophetis, quae quidem homines leves à fide recta detorquent? Basilius ab hac istorum severitate usque adeo abfuit, ut etiam orationem, sane praeclaram, hoc lemmate scripserit a, πρὸς τὰς νέας, ὅπως ἂν ἐξ Ἑλληνικῶν ὠφελοῖντο λόγων, ad juniores, quomodo ex Gentilium libris doctrinisque utilitatem capere possint. Multa apud amicum & familiarem ejus Gregorium (virum usque adeo probatum, ut etiam Theologi cognomentum apud veteres nactus sit) Multa, inquam, apud eum similia occurrunt, e quibus hoc unum ob suavitatem & elegantiam ponere placuit. Monet ita legendos Ethnicos scriptores, ut orationis quidem jucunditate & pulchritudine fruamur; caeterum sparsam in iis idololatriae vanitatem caveamus; sic locum concludens b; — ὥσπερ ἐξ ἑνὸς φυτοῦ Καὶ τὰς ἀκανθας φεύγε, ἐκ ῥόδων ἄνθη. — Ab una ut, atque eadem plantula Spinis relictis floridas rosas lege.
units.tr: Nor did Basil, a man of the same period and known throughout the Christian world, give any more weight to the authority of the Bovian Apostles. For these forbid Christians to read any of the books of the outsiders, saying: "Abstain from all the books of the Gentiles; for what have you to do with foreign discourses, or laws, or false prophets, who indeed turn light men away from the true faith?" Basil was so far from this severity of theirs that he wrote, under the title "To the young, how they may profit from the Greek discourses", for juniors, how they may derive advantage from the books and teachings of the Gentiles. Many similar things occur in his friend and intimate Gregory, a man so esteemed that the ancients gave him the surname of Theologian. I will quote from him one which I like for its sweetness and elegance. He advises that the pagan writers be read in such a way that we enjoy the charm and beauty of their style, but guard against the vanity of idolatry scattered through them; and he concludes the passage thus: "Just as from one plant, avoid the thorns and take the flowers from the roses" [ὥσπερ ἐξ ἑνὸς φυτοῦ καὶ τὰς ἀκανθας φεῦγε, ἐκ ῥόδων ἄνθη]. That is, pluck the flowery roses from the single little plant and leave the thorns.

units.la: Neq; hic audiendę Bovii excusationes c; confirmata religione, cum jam homines nonfierent, sed nascerentur Christiani, minus periculi fuisse à librorum exoticorum lectione metuendum; eoque & liberiorem eorum legendorum consuetudinem fuisse.
units.tr: Nor are the excuses of Bovius to be heard here, that since religion was by then firmly established, and men were no longer made Christians but born Christians, there was less danger to be feared from reading foreign books, and therefore a freer custom of reading them.

units.la: Nam neque Basilii ætate sic erat contra Paganos firmata religio, ut nihil esset ab eorum libris periculi; quod vel Iuliani desertoris exemplum demonstrat, quem illa lectio iis ipsis temporibus evertit, magna Ecclesiæ clade, magno Paganismi commodo; neque si vel confirmatissima tum fuisset religio, eo decebat Basilium latam ab Apostolis legem ita exserte, præfracteque violare; suamque illam temeritatem ne uno quidem verbo purgare, vel excusare, aut scandalum, quod ex hac disciplinæ diversitate existere necesse est, mollire, & occupare. Nihil enim istorum fecit; neque profecto necesse fuit; quod scilicet nulla tum esset in Ecclesia Apostolorum de vitanda librorum Ethnicorum lectione cognita lex; à qua sibi Basilius librorum istorum lectionem concedens ac commendans meteuerit.
units.tr: For in Basil's time the religion was not so firmly established against the pagans that there was no danger from their books. The example of the apostate Julian shows this, whom that reading turned away in those very times, to the great loss of the Church and the great advantage of paganism. And even if religion had then been most firmly established, Basil ought not to have so openly and stubbornly violated a law given by the Apostles, nor to have excused that rashness by a single word, nor to have softened and removed the scandal which must arise from this difference in discipline. Yet he did none of these things, nor was it indeed necessary, since evidently no law forbidding the reading of pagan books was known in the Church of the Apostles, a law from which Basil, by permitting and recommending the reading of those books, could have been freed.

units.la: Huc accedit, quod Basilius in alio opere exserte negat, scripto ullo tradita esse quædam eorum, quæ in Constitutionibus scripta leguntur; Τῷ τύπῳ (inquit) ςαυρῷ τὰς εἰς τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἠλπι- κότας καταση-μαίνεσθαι τὶς ὁ δὲ γράμμα-τῷ διδάξας· τὸ προς ἀναλολὰς τετραφθαι τῇ τῶν προσευχῶν ποιον ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς γράμ-μα; τὰ δ ἐπικλήσεως ῥήματα ὅπ τῇ ἀνα- δεíξει τῶ ἀρτῷ ἡ εὐχαριστίας ἢ τῷ ποτηρίῳ ὁ ἐυλο-
units.tr: Add to this that Basil, in another work, plainly denies that some of the things written in the Constitutions were handed down in any writing: "Who," he says, "taught us by a written word to mark with the sign of the cross those who have placed their hope in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ? Who taught us by writing to turn to the East in prayer? What written words of invocation do we use when the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing are made? Who of the saints left these to us in writing?" [Τῷ τύπῳ τοῦ σταυροῦ τοὺς εἰς τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἠλπικότας καταση­μαίνεσθαι τίς ὁ διδάξας; ... τὰ δὲ ἐπικλήσεως ῥήματα ἐπὶ τῇ ἀναδείξει τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας ἢ τῷ ποτηρίῳ τῆς εὐλογίας, τίς τῶν ἁγίων ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν καταλέλοιπεν;]

units.la: a L.de Sp. S.c. 27. T. 1. p. 351. d. ἐυλογίας, τίς τῶν ἁγίων ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν καταλέλοιπεν; Ut signo crucis eos qui spem collocarunt in Christum signemus, quis scripto docuit? Ut ad Orientem versi precemur, qua nos docuit scriptura? Invocationis verba cum conficitur panis Eucharistia, & poculum benedictionis, quis sanctorum in scripto nobis reliquit? Mox; εὐλογοῦμεν τὸ ὕδωρ (inquit a) τὸ βαπτισμαλος, & τὸ ἔλαιον τῆς χεῖσεως, & προσέτι αυτὸν τὸν βαπτι-ζόμενον, ὑπὸ ποιῶν ἐγγράφων; ἐκ ὑπὸ τῆς σιω-πωμένης, καὶ μυστικῆς παραδόσεως; τί ὃ αυ-τῷ τῆ ἐλαίᾳ ἢ χεῖσιν, τίς λόγος γεγραμμένος ἐδίδαξε; τὸ ὃ τρὶς βαπτίζεσθαι τ᾽ ἀν-θρωπον, πόθεν; ἀλλὰ ὃ ὅσα περὶ τὸ βάπτι-σμα ἀποτάσσεσθαι τῷ Σατανᾷ ἢ τοῖς ἀγγέ-λοις αὐτοῦ, ἐκ ποίας ἔγγραφης; ἐκ ἐκ τῆ ἀ-δημοσιεύτῳ ταύτης, καὶ ἀπορρήτῳ διδασκα-λίας, ὧν ἐν ἀπολυτρομυμένῳ & ἀπειλεγά-σῳ σιγῇ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν ἐφύλαξαν; Consecramus autem aquam baptismatis, & oleum unctionis, praeterea ipsum qui baptismum accipit, ex quibus scriptis? nonne ex tacita, arcanaque traditione? Ipsam porro olei inunctionem qui sermo scripto proditus docuit? Jam ter immergi hominem, unde? reliqua item, quae fiunt in baptismo, veluti renuntiare Satanae, & Angelis ejus, ex qua scriptura habemus? annon ex arcana hac, minimeque publicata traditione? an-non
units.tr: a L. de Sp. S. c. 27. T. 1. p. 351. d. "We bless the water of baptism," he says, "and the oil of anointing, and moreover the person who is baptized; from what written sources? Is it not from the silent and mystical tradition? What written word taught the anointing with oil itself? From where comes the threefold immersion of the man? But whatever is done in baptism, such as renouncing Satan and his angels, from what written source do we have it? Is it not from this unpublished and secret teaching, which our fathers preserved in a silence that is inviolable and undisturbed?" [εὐλογοῦμεν τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ βαπτισμάτος, καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον τῆς χρίσεως, καὶ προσέτι αὐτὸν τὸν βαπτιζόμενον, ὑπὸ ποίων ἐγγράφων; οὐχὶ ὑπὸ τῆς σιωπωμένης, καὶ μυστικῆς παραδόσεως;]

units.la: non ex doctrina, quam Patres nostri quieto, minimeque curioso silentio fervarunt? At-qui si trinam immersionem exceperis, quam in Canonibus Apostolorum a legi, in Con-stitutionibus (quod meminerim) non legi, caetera omnia, nimirum & crucis b typo ob- signatos fideles, & inter precandum conver- sionem ad solis ortus c, & invocationis in Eucharistia confectione verba d, & aquae baptismatis e, oleique f, & ipsius baptizan- di benedictionem g, & ex oleo inunctio- nem h, & abrenunciationem i; omnia, in-quam Boviani Διαταγεῖς difertissimis, con-ceptissimisque verbis scripserunt. Loca e l. 7. c. annotasse satis est; recitare, nihil necesse est, pleraque jam in superioribus descri-pta, & apud omnes confessa. Itaque si isti Constitutionum libri jam tum extabant, h l. 3. c. quis non videt Basilium, rogantem quis ista scripto tradiderit? quae & ipse & omnes ab Apostolis, vel certe eorum nomine à Clemente scripta sciebant, non modo invere-cundum, sed etiam stultum, ac ridiculum esse? Atqui Basilium omnes veteres recentioresque confitentur, quod & ipsa ejus monumenta clarissime demonstrant, virum fuisse verecundum inprimis, & gravem, & sapientem, & veracem. Ergo omnino necesse est, ignotas & ipsi, & adversariis cum quibus disputabat, & caeteris il-lius lius ævi Christianis fuisse Bovii nostri Δια-τάξεις; in quibus scilicet ista disertissime vel ab Apostolis vel à Clemente scripta sunt, quæ Basilius ab ullo sanctorum scripta, litterisve mandata tam sæpe tamque fortiter negat. Arcudius, tametsi horum librorum veritatem in medio relinquat, atque de iis non nisi dubitanter loquatur, hoc tamen ab iis telum depellere conatur, sed vano & irrito molimine. Respondet enim Basilium, & alios aliquot Patres, quorum similes extant de hoc argumento voces, dicere a has traditiones esse minime scriptas, quia revera non sunt scripta in divinis litteris, non quia non sunt scripta in aliis libris. Nam Apostoli (inquit) qui canonicam scripturam condere poterant, nihil de iis scripserunt sed ore tenus tradiderunt. Patres vero tantum τῷ Διαπνεύστῳ γραφῷ per excellentiam ἔγγραφον nominant; quam in primo genere, & ut ita dicam, primo gradu certitudinis collocant; Catera, quæ non sunt ex numero τῶν κανονιζομένων βιβλίων in canonem sacrorum librorum acceptorum, ad rationem Scripturæ ἄγραφα esse testantur. Sed hæc Arcudii solutio nihil valet; quod ut liquido intelligatur, inprimis observandum est, duobus modis dici posse observationem aliquam esse scriptam. Idenim significat eam ab aliquo vel scripta lege fuisse præceptam, (qui proprius est & usitatus horum verborum sensus) vel tantum in scripto libro commemoratam. Vel significat, ejus observandæ legem scriptam extare, litterisque mandatam haberi, vel ejus mentionem in Scripto aliquo facta esse. Non nego posteriori hoc sensu etiam eas quæ proprie dicuntur traditiones, scriptas dici posse; sic ut intelligas earum meminisse scriptorem aliquem; qualiter verbi gratia contestationem illam, qua baptizandus se diabolo & pompis ejus renunciare profitebatur, commemorant & Tertullianus a,& hoc ipso loco Basilius; , sed velut jam antea non ullo scripto præcepto institutam, sed sola voce traditam, indeque à Christianis observatam referentes. Priori vero sensu, quo scriptam de re aliqua observanda legem extare significatur, nego ullam proprie sic intellectam traditionem scriptam dici posse, aut ab ullo unquam probato scriptore dictam esse. Traditio enim sic accepta ea est, de qua nulla lex scripta est, quæque voce tantum privatim ac sigillatim deposita; non litteris, quæ publicæ sunt & omnium communes, mandata. Traditio quippe stricte proprieque accepto vocabulo, doctrina vel observatio est ἀγράφος; rectèque ei oppo-nitur, nitur, quæ est ἐγγραφος. Iam vero clarum est, Basilium non posteriori, sed priori sensu negare scriptas esse eas, quas memorat, traditiones. Significat nimirum neminem de iis observandis legem scripsisse: neminem eas scripta aliqua διατάξει instituisse, ac præcepisse; fortasse non significat nullum scriptorem vllam earum memorasse; quod si diceret, falsum diceret, cum Tertullianum quasdam ex iis memorasse constet; quanquam id ipsum cum Basilius homo Græcus ignoraret, fieri profecto potest, ut utroque sensu scriptas esse negaverit istas observationes. Nimirum putabat fortassis neminem Christianorum, qui ad illa tempora scripserant, earum usquam mentionem fecisse. Verum utcunque sit, illud quidem quod diximus certum est, intelligere Basilium nullam extare scriptam de istis observandis legem; sola eas muta, & ἀγράφῳ traditione acceptas apud Christianos invaluisse; neque unquam, ut opinor, quisquam aliter, vel alia mente negavit aliquam traditionem scriptam esse. neque hujus phraseos posteriori illo, quem finximus & donavimus sensu, ullum exemplum afferri posse crediderim. Itaque necessario concedendum est, Basilium non hoc posteriori sensu, qui est insolens, & inusitatus, sed priori, qui communis est, & usitatus. tatus, negasse illas quas refert, observationes, scriptas esse. Atqui hoc sensu non potuit negare eas scriptas esse, si verae sunt Bovianae constitutiones; in quibus scilicet de iis observandis diserte extant scriptae, literisque mandatae leges. Ergo nisi Basilium (quod absurdissimum est) inverecunde praeter animi sui sententiam, publicamque fidem mentitum esse dicas, necessario confitendum est, nullas ei vel fama cognitas fuisse Constitutiones istas; in quibus scriptae sunt illarum observationum leges, quas ipse uspiam scriptas unquam fuisse negat. Non enim, ut Tertullianus, & Basilius, sic quoque διατάξεων author memorat, ista a Christianis observari, & in usu apud eos esse, traditione, non autem scripto, accepta. Nihil apud istum simile. Ille vero ista instituit, διατάξει, decernit, sciscit, sancit; ut ab omnibus observentur edicit, ac praecipit; instituere se & litteris mandare, atque ad omnes scripta mittere clare, ac saepius profitetur; ut quae ita apud eum scripta, mandataque leguntur, ea ἄγραφα id est non scripta dici, censerive, nisi falso, stulteque, ac ridicule nequeant. Quod vero pertendit Arcudius ἄγραφα haec dici a Basilio, quod eorum leges, non quidem nullis plane cujusquam literis mandatae essent, sed quod in iis libris, qui
units.tr: Is it not from the doctrine that our Fathers kept with quiet and most incurious silence? Yet if you except the threefold immersion, which I read in the Canons of the Apostles but (as I recall) do not read in the Constitutions, all the rest, namely the faithful sealed with the sign of the cross, turning toward the rising of the sun in prayer, the words of invocation in the consecration of the Eucharist, the water of baptism, the oil, the blessing of the one who baptizes, the anointing with oil, and the renunciation, all of these, I say, the Constitutions of Bovius describe in the most eloquent and carefully chosen words. It is enough to note the places in book 7, ch.; there is no need to recite them, since most have already been described above and are acknowledged by all. So if these books of the Constitutions already existed at that time, who does not see that it would be not only shameless but also foolish and ridiculous to say, as Basil does in book 3, ch., "Who handed these down in writing?", when he and everyone else knew that these things were written by the Apostles, or at least in their name by Clement? Yet all writers, ancient and recent, admit that Basil was a man above all modest, serious, wise and truthful, as his own works most clearly show. It is therefore entirely necessary that Bovius's Ordinances [Διατάξεις] were unknown both to Basil himself, and to the opponents with whom he was disputing, and to the other Christians of his age. In them, clearly, these things are stated most eloquently as written either by the Apostles or by Clement, whereas Basil so often and so vehemently denies that these things were written or committed to letters by any of the saints. Arcudius, although he leaves the truth of these books open and speaks of them only doubtfully, nevertheless tries to ward off this weapon, but with a vain and fruitless effort. For he replies that Basil and some other Fathers, whose similar statements on this subject survive, say that these traditions are "not written at all, because they are not in fact written in the divine letters, not because they are not written in other books. For the Apostles (he says), who could compose the canonical Scripture, wrote nothing about them but handed them down by word of mouth. The Fathers, however, call Scripture, by excellence, 'the written' [ἔγγραφον], which they place in the first kind and, as I may say, first degree of certainty; the rest, which are not among the books received as the canon of sacred writings, they testify to be 'unwritten' [ἄγραφα] in the manner of Scripture." But this solution of Arcudius is worth nothing. To understand this clearly, we must first observe that a practice can be called "written" in two ways. Either it was prescribed by someone in a written law (which is the proper and usual sense of these words), or it is merely recorded in a written book. Or it means that a written law for observing it exists and is held in writing, or that some mention of it has been made in some writing. I do not deny that, in this latter sense, even those things properly called traditions can be called "written", so that you understand that some writer recalls them, as for example Tertullian recalls that declaration by which the one to be baptized professed that he renounced the devil and his pomps, and Basil himself does in this very passage; but they report these things as having been observed by Christians, not as instituted by any written precept beforehand, but handed down by voice alone. In the former sense, however, in which it is meant that a written law about some practice to be observed exists, I deny that any tradition understood in this way can properly be called a "written tradition", or has ever been called so by any approved writer. For a tradition accepted in this sense is one for which no written law exists, and which has been deposited only by voice, privately and individually, not committed to letters, which are public and common to all. Strictly and properly speaking, a tradition is a doctrine or observance that is "unwritten" [ἄγραφος], and it is rightly opposed to what is "written" [ἔγγραφος]. Now it is clear that Basil denies that the traditions he mentions are written not in the latter sense but in the former. He means, of course, that no one wrote a law about observing them; that no one instituted and prescribed them by any written ordinance [διατάξις]. Perhaps he does not mean that no writer ever mentioned any of them; if he said that, he would be saying something false, since it is established that Tertullian mentioned some of them. Yet even though Basil, being a Greek, may not have known this, it is quite possible that he denied these observances were written in either sense. Perhaps he thought that none of the Christians who wrote in those times had made any mention of them anywhere. However that may be, what we have said is certain: Basil understood that no written law about these observances exists; they were received among Christians as silent and unwritten tradition, and I suppose no one has ever denied that a tradition was written in any other sense or with any other intention. Nor, I think, can any example be brought forward of this phrase in the latter sense, which I have invented and attributed to him. It must therefore necessarily be conceded that Basil denied that the observances he reports were "written" not in that latter sense, which is strange and unusual, but in the former, which is common and usual. But in this sense he could not have denied that they were written, if Bovius's Constitutions are genuine, since in them the laws about observing these things are expressly written and committed to letters. Therefore, unless you say (which is most absurd) that Basil shamelessly lied against his own opinion and the public faith, it must necessarily be admitted that these Constitutions, in which the laws of those observances are written, were not known to him even by report, although he elsewhere denies that those observances were ever written. For this author, unlike Tertullian and Basil, does not record that these practices were observed by Christians and in use among them, received by tradition and not by writing. There is nothing like this in him. Rather, he establishes these things by ordinance [διατάξει], decrees, enacts and sanctions them; he orders and prescribes that they be observed by all; and he clearly and repeatedly declares that he sets them down and commits them to writing and sends them in writing to everyone. Therefore, those things which are read as written and committed to writing in his work cannot be called or considered "unwritten" [ἄγραφα], that is, "not written", except falsely, foolishly and ridiculously. As for Arcudius's claim that these things are called "unwritten" by Basil because their laws were not indeed committed to any writing at all, but because they are not noted or mentioned in those books of the New Testament which are held to be divinely inspired [Θεόπνευστοι] in the canon, that is plainly futile and frivolous.

units.la: divini & Θεόπνευςτοι in Novi Testamenti canone habentur, nusquam scriptæ vel commemoratæ deprehendantur, id inquam plane futile est, ac frivolum. Negat enim Basilius ista, de quibus loquitur, quemquam δια γραμμάτως scripto docuisse; negat ullum sanctorum ἐγγραφως καταλελοιπέναι, scripto tradita reliquisse; negat ab ullis ἐγγράφοις litteris, sive scriptis haberi; negat ea ullo ἐγγεγραμμένῳ λόγῳ, scripto, litterisve mandato sermone docta, sive tradita esse; haberi ait ἐκ τῆς ἀπορρήτου ἀδημοσιεύτου & ἀπορρήτως διδασκαλίας ex non publicata, arcanaque doctrina, sive institutione, aut traditione; ait ἐκ ἀπολυπραγμονήτῳ ἀπεριεργάστῳ σιγῇ φυλαχθῆναι, quieto minimeque curioso silentio à Patribus servata. Ex quibus vel cæcus videt eam, qua ista accepta erant, traditionem, Basilium non quibusdam; sed quibusvis litteris; non canonicis, sed omnibus omnino libris opponere. Ista vero, si Boviani Constitutiones veræ sunt, & ἐξ γραμμάτος erant tradita, & ἐγγράφως ab aliquibus sanctis relicta, & ἐγγεγραμμένῳ λόγῳ mandata, & aliter quam ἐκ τῆς ἀδημοσιεύτως ἡ ἀπορρήτως διδασκαλίας habebantur, & aliter quam in silentio observabantur; quę scilicet jam inde ab initio sive ab ipsis Apostolis (ut narrat Constitutionum codex) sive (quod malunt lunt adversarii) à Clemente Apostolorum familiari, litteris mandata, & in codice scripto vulgata ac publicata. Quod enim hos Constitutionum libros Apostolorum canon a ἀημοσιεύειν ἐπὶ πάντων publicare, seu vulgare opud omnes vetat, id, ut optime observavit Albaspineus, est à posteriori aevo, quo illa arcana μυστικὰ esse caperunt; cum antea Apostolicis & proximis temporibus nulla Christianis religio esset sua omnia palam habere, & apud omnes edere. Caeterum authoris, qui Constitutiones fecit, mentem hanc fuisse, ut libri illi vulgarentur, ac publicarentur, vel illud satis docet, quod & in ipso limine omnes Christianos salutat, & ad eos universos suum hoc opus mittit, ac (ut vulgo loquimur) dirigit b, πάντας τὰς ἐξ ἐθνῶν πιστεύσαντας εἰς τ Κύριον, ad omnes qui ex Gentibus in Dominum crediderant; quodque non episcopos modo, & clericos, sed & laicos, & ipsas etiam mulieres c interdum recta alloquitur. Stare ergo non potest Arcudii commentum. Quin imo si bene rem reputes, quod ille concedit, nunquam fuisse iStas Διαθῆκας in librorum sacrorum canonem relatas, id ipsum inquam nothas, fictitiasque eas esse docet; quae, quod supra diximus, si vere Apostolorum essent, haud dubie in canonem cum reliquis eorum libris relatæ fuissent. Neque si vere sunt, causa dici potest, cur eæ à canone potius exclusæ sint, quàm Marci aut Lucæ Euangelia. Sed redeo ad Basilium, de cujus mente nunc quidem satis constat.
units.tr: For Basil denies that anyone taught these things, of which he speaks, "by writing" [δια γραμμάτων]; he denies that any of the saints "left them in writing" [ἐγγράφως καταλελοιπέναι], that is, handed down in writing; he denies that they are held "in written letters" [ἐγγράφοις γράμμασιν], or in writing; he denies that they were taught or handed down "by a written word" [ἐγγεγραμμένῳ λόγῳ], that is, by a word committed to letters. He says they are held to come "from the secret, unpublished" [ἐκ τῆς ἀπορρήτου ἀδημοσιεύτου] and "secret teaching" [ἀπορρήτως διδασκαλίας], that is, from unpublished and arcane doctrine or institution or tradition. He says they were kept "with quiet and incurious silence" [ἐν ἀπολυπραγμονήτῳ ἀπεριεργάστῳ σιγῇ], "kept in silence by the Fathers". From these things even a blind man sees that Basil opposes the tradition from which these things were received not to "certain" letters but to "any" letters, not to "canonical" books but to all books whatsoever. But if Bovius's Constitutions are genuine, and these things were handed down "by writing" [ἐκ γραμμάτων], and were left "in writing" [ἐγγράφως] by certain saints, and were committed to a "written word" [ἐγγεγραμμένῳ λόγῳ], and were regarded as something other than "from the unpublished or secret teaching", and were observed otherwise than in silence, then they were from the very beginning, either from the Apostles themselves (as the codex of the Constitutions relates) or (as our opponents prefer) from Clement, the familiar companion of the Apostles, committed to letters and published and made known in a written codex. For the canon of the Apostles, which forbids these books of the Constitutions to be published "among all" [ἀημοσιεύειν ἐπὶ πάντων], that is, to be made public or spread "among all", belongs, as Albaspinaeus rightly observed, to a later age, when those secrets began to be regarded as mysteries; for in the Apostolic and nearby times, no Christian scruple prevented them from having everything openly and publishing it among all. Moreover, that the intention of the author of the Constitutions was that those books should be spread and made public is sufficiently shown by the fact that he greets all Christians at the very threshold and sends this work of his to all of them, and (as we commonly say) addresses it to them, "to all who from the Gentiles believed in the Lord" [πάντας τὰς ἐξ ἐθνῶν πιστεύσαντας εἰς τὸν Κύριον], "to all who from the Gentiles had believed in the Lord"; and that he sometimes speaks directly not only to bishops and clergy but also to laymen and even to women. Arcudius's invention therefore cannot stand. Indeed, if you consider the matter carefully, what he concedes, that these Covenants [Διαθῆκαι] were never included in the canon of sacred books, itself shows, I say, that they are spurious and fictitious. For if, as I said above, they were truly the Apostles', they would undoubtedly have been included in the canon along with their other books. Nor, if they are genuine, can any reason be given why they were excluded from the canon rather than the Gospels of Mark or Luke. But I return to Basil, whose mind is now quite clear enough.

units.la: Enimvero ex eodem illo ejus opere apparet, incognitas ei fuisse Bovianas Apostolorum Διαταγαὶ. Ipse enim præfatur, sibi hujus scribendi operis causam fuisse, quod nonnulli eam δοξολογίαν reprehenderent, qua publice in Ecclesia sic erat usus, ut interdum diceret a, δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ τῷ Υἱῷ σὺν τῷ Πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ, Gloria Deo ac Patri cum Filio, & cum Spiritu Sancto. Contendebant autem illi non aliter dicendum fuisse, quam, Gloria Deo per Filium in Spiritu Sancto. Illam ergo priorem doxologiæ formulam tuetur toto illo libro Basilius; multaque & ad rem ipsam, & ad voces singulas pertinentia ex scripturis disserit; Ipsam autem itainstitutam, expressamque glorificandi formulam ex traditione esse ait. Ac primo fuse defendit, de Filio recte ita dici, Gloria Patri καὶ τῷ Υἱῷ cum Filio; & particulâ καὶ hoc modo ex traditione usos passim affirmat sinceros Christianos. Tum latè demonstrat, Spiritum quoque licere adhibita illa particula σῳ ita glorificare, ut dicatur, Gloria Patri cum Filio, vel & Filio σῳ cum Spiritu Sancto; idque, ut & illud de Filio prius, ex traditione apud Christianos usitatum esse affirmat. Iam quisquis Constitutiones non oscitanter legerit, confitebitur earum, siquidem tum extabant, mentionem à Basilio in hac disputatione sine flagitio omitti non potuisse. Nam quod ad prius illud de Filii glorificatione pertinet, ea plurima suppeditant Basilianæ sententiæ argumenta; in quibus scilicet partim hanc ipsam Filii Doξολογίαν legimus, quam Basilius defendit; in qua dicitur Gloria Patri μῆ τῷ ψ̄ cum Filio. Posterioris vero de Spiritu, ut de eo dicatur σῳ τῷ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ cum Spiritu Sancto, nullum (quod memini-rim) extat in Constitutionibus exemplum, quæ solent hic ad illud alterum usurpare; ἐν τῷ πνεύματι in Spiritu Sancto, vel certe particulam ἡ, & Gloria Patri & Filio & Spiritui Sancto. (Constitutiones si norat Basilius, cur vel illa fastidit, vel hæc dissimulat? Illis quidem nihil afferre poterat clarius, atque illustrius ad eorum compescendam insaniam, qui Patrem cum Filio glorificandum negabant. Erant enim hæ Διατάξεις, si Bovio credimus, certæ incorruptæque Apostolicæ traditionis
units.tr: Indeed, it is clear from that same work of his that Basil did not know the Bovian Diataxeis of the Apostles [Διαταγαὶ]. He himself says in his preface that the reason for writing this work was that some people found fault with the doxology [δοξολογίαν] which he used publicly in the Church, saying sometimes, Glory to the Father, and to the Son, with the Holy Spirit [δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ τῷ Υἱῷ σὺν τῷ Πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ], Glory to God and the Father with the Son, and with the Holy Spirit. Those men, however, contended that it ought to have been said only in this way: Glory to God through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Basil therefore defends that first form of doxology throughout that whole book, and he argues at length from Scripture both about the thing itself and about the individual words. He says that the form of glorifying itself, as it was set down and expressed, comes from tradition. First he argues at length that it is right to say of the Son, Glory to the Father and with the Son, and he affirms that sound Christians everywhere used the particle and [καὶ] in this way from tradition. Then he shows at length that the Spirit too may be glorified with that same particle with [σύν], so that one says Glory to the Father with the Son, or with the Son and with the Holy Spirit; and he affirms that this too, like the earlier point about the Son, was in common use among Christians by tradition. Now, anyone who has read the Constitutions with attention will admit that, if they were then in existence, Basil could not have omitted mention of them in this discussion without a serious lapse. For as regards the first point, about the glorification of the Son, they supply very many arguments for Basil's view; in them we read partly this very doxology of the Son which Basil defends, in which it is said Glory to the Father with the Son. But as for the second point, that the Spirit should be spoken of as with the Holy Spirit, I recall no example of this in the Constitutions, which are wont to use the other form here: in the Holy Spirit, or certainly the particle and, Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. (If Basil knew the Constitutions, why did he either disdain that part or pass over this?) Certainly nothing could have been clearer or more striking to him for repressing the madness of those who denied that the Father was to be glorified with the Son. For these Διατάξεις, if we believe Bovius, were the sure and uncorrupted witnesses and guardians of Apostolic tradition.

units.la: Y testes, ac custodes. Sed quod eædem in Spiritu, vel, & Spiritui sæpe dicunt; cum Spiritu, nunquam; idꝰ speciosum Basilii adversariis argumentum prębebat; quod proinde commemorari, solvique debuit; sine crimine omitti non potuit. Certe si tum extabat Διατάξεων liber, nimium secure, ac pene ridicule ista à Basilio dicta sunt a, λέξιν (συν) dictiunculam cum à Patribus venisse, traditione scilicet ἀγράφῳ acceptam. Fac enim Constitutiones tum extitisse; Nonne eas Basilio objecisset adversarius Apostolicæ traditionis testes? quæ non ut ille, cum Spiritu, sed in Spiritu, vel & spiritui semper usurpant in doxologiis? Cum ergo altum in utramque partem de his Constitutionibus silentium sit apud Basilium, ne dubites nullas tum extitisse; quas scriptor gravissimus si fuissent aliquæ, tali loco omnino commemoraturus fuit.
units.tr: Witnesses and guardians. But that these same Constitutions often say in the Spirit, or and to the Spirit, and never with the Spirit: this gave Basil's opponents a plausible argument, which therefore ought to have been mentioned and answered, and could not be passed over without fault. Certainly, if the book of the Diataxeis then existed, Basil spoke far too carelessly, and almost ridiculously, when he said that this little word with [σύν] had come down from the Fathers, received by unwritten tradition [ἀγράφῳ]. For suppose the Constitutions had then existed: would not his adversaries have objected to Basil that the witnesses of Apostolic tradition never use with the Spirit, but always in the Spirit, or and to the Spirit, in their doxologies? Since, therefore, there is such a deep silence about these Constitutions on both sides in Basil, do not doubt that none existed then; for so grave a writer would certainly have mentioned them, had there been any, in such a place.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Arg. X X. Ex diversa sabbatarii jejunii observatione Constitutiones quinti saeculi initio fuisse adhuc Christianis ignotas.
units.tr: Argument XX. From the differing observance of the Sabbath fast, the Constitutions were still unknown to Christians at the beginning of the fifth century.

units.la: ID ipsum vero certissime deprehendes, si eorum, qui quarto saeculo jam praecipiti, & sequentibus vixerunt, tum instituta, tum opiniones cum nostris illis Boviano-rum Apostolorum Διαταγαῖς comparaveris. In primis enim cum illi sabbato, nisi uno (hoc est antepaschali) quemquam Christianum jejunare non semel vetent, eumque diem ab omnibus laetum festumque, instar dominici agitari praecipiant , constat ex Augustino & aliis sabbato in ipsa urbe Roma, vivente Ambrosio (hoc est ante a. D. 397) jejunari solenne fuisse, eundemque usum paucos etiam Occidentales, praeter Romanos, servasse; Ambrosium vero & Augustinum, tametsi ipsi aliter facitarent, sabbati tamen jejunatores nequaquam damnasse, sed ut in re media, ac libera pro earum Ecclesiarum, ad quas appuleris, & in quibus versaris, more vel jejunandum, vel prandendum judicasse; Eademque Hieronymi est hac de re sententia, qui Lucinio de sabbati jejunio quaerenti,
units.tr: You will discover this very thing most certainly if you compare our Constitutions of the Bovian Apostles [Διαταγαῖς] with the practices and opinions of those who lived in the fourth century, when it was already falling, and in the centuries after it. For those Constitutions forbid any Christian to fast on the Sabbath, except the one Sabbath before Easter, and they order that this day be kept joyful and festive by all, like the Lord's Day. It is established from Augustine and others that, while Ambrose was alive, in the city of Rome itself (that is, before AD 397), fasting on the Sabbath was customary, and that a few Western churches besides the Roman ones kept the same practice. Ambrose and Augustine, although they themselves acted otherwise, nevertheless never condemned those who fasted on the Sabbath. Instead they judged it a matter indifferent and free, so that one should either fast or not fast according to the custom of the churches to which one came and among which one lived. Jerome held the same opinion on this question. When Lucinius asked him about fasting on the Sabbath,

units.la: a Const. l. 7. c. 2. — b Ep. 86. quae est ad Casulan. & ep. 19. — c Cassian. de inst. coenob. l. 3. c. 10. Socrat. l. 5. c. 2. (al. 21.) renti, Unaquaque (inquit) provincia abundet in sensu suo & praecepta majorum leges Apostolicas arbitretur. Item; Sed ego te illud breviter admonendum puto, traditiones Ecclesiasticas (praesertim quae fidei non officiant) ita observandas, ut a Majoribus traditae sunt, nec aliorum consuetudinem aliorum contrario more subverti. Quin & Romae fuit quidam sabbatarii jejunii usque adeo acer, & immodestus zelotes, ut scripta disputatione contenderit illo die necessario jejunandum esse, & qui aliter facerent, eos verbis saevis & contumeliosis damnaret. Extat Augustini contra illum urbicum sabbatari jejunii defensorem insignis ad Calulanum epistola; in qua inter caetera hoc liquido statuit, certo sciri non posse, an ab Apostolis institutum fuerit, ut sabbato vel jejunetur, vel prandeatur; siqueea de re ex suo quisque more, atque usu certent, interminabilem fore istam contentionem, generantem lites, nec finientem quaestiones. Denique Innocentius Romae Episcopus a.D.416. Sabbato jejunandum decernit, idque evidentissima ratione demonstrari putat; Sabbatum negat praetermitti debere (absque jejunio scilicet) idque praetermittere dementis esse ait. Atque is usus deinceps apud Latinam Ecclesiam obtinuit, hodieque in tota
units.tr: a Const. l. 7. c. 2. — b Ep. 86. which is to Casulanus, and ep. 19. — c Cassian, On the Institutes of the Cenobites, l. 3. c. 10; Socrates l. 5. c. 2 (al. 21.) he answered: "Let each province abound in its own sense, and regard the precepts of its elders as Apostolic laws." Again: "But I think I should briefly remind you that ecclesiastical traditions (especially those which do not harm faith) are to be observed as they were handed down by our forefathers, and that the custom of others should not be overturned by the contrary practice of others." Indeed there was once at Rome a certain zealot for the Sabbath fast, so fierce and intemperate that he argued in a written disputation that one must fast on that day of necessity, and he condemned those who acted otherwise with harsh and insulting words. There survives Augustine's notable letter to Casulanus, written against that city advocate of the Sabbath fast. In it, among other things, he clearly states that it cannot be known for certain whether it was instituted by the Apostles that one should either fast or dine on the Sabbath. If each person contends about this matter according to his own custom and practice, he says, "that contention will be endless, generating quarrels and never ending questions." Finally, Innocent, Bishop of Rome, in AD 416 decrees that one must fast on the Sabbath, and he thinks this is shown by the clearest reasoning. He denies that the Sabbath ought to be passed over (that is, without a fast), and he says that to pass it over in that way is the act of madmen. This practice thereafter prevailed in the Latin Church and is still held throughout the whole communion of the Roman Pope.

units.la: a Ep. 28. b Ep. 86. c Ibid. T. Aug. 2. 147. a. d Ep. 1. quae est ad Decent. c.4. tota Romani Papæ communione obtinet. Ergo illæ quæ nunc obtruduntur Apostolorum nomine dictæ Constitutiones, ignotæ toto illo tempore erant, & Romanæ Ecclesiæ, occidentalibusque illis ab Augustino commemoratis, & Ambrosioipsi, & urbico disputatori, & Augustino, & Hieronymo, & Innocentio. Nam sabbati jejunium si ab Apostolis vetitum scivisent; neque vel Roma, vel aliæ illæ Ecclesiæ usurpassent, neque pro re media, & ex singulorum locorum consuetudine vel omittenda, vel observanda sensissent Ambrosius, Augustinus, & Hieronymus; neque denique urbicus vel disputator anonymus, vel antistes Innocentius eo die necessario jejunandum definivissent. Quid, quod Hieronymus hanc sabbati observationem, inter traditiones Ecclesiasticas censet à majoribus traditas (non ergo ab Apostolis) & quidem hujusmodi, quarum authoritas contrariis aliorum moribus fraudi esse non debeat? Apostolicarum vero traditionum longe majorem esse dignitatem nemo non videt. Quod vero ait Augustinus litem esse interminabilem utrum sit sabbati observatio ab Apostolis constituta, nec ne, eo, inquam, apertissime negat Apostolos esse Bovii Διαζυγίας; ex quibus scilicet clare facileque deciditur tota illa lis? Sed
units.tr: a Ep. 28. b Ep. 86. c Ibid. Augustine, vol. 2, p. 147 a. d Ep. 1, which is to Decentius, c. 4. Throughout the whole communion of the Roman Pope. Therefore those Constitutions which are now thrust forward under the name of the Apostles were unknown during all that time, to the Roman Church, to those Western churches Augustine mentions, to Ambrose himself, to the city disputant, to Augustine, to Jerome, and to Innocent. For if they had known that the Sabbath fast had been forbidden by the Apostles, neither Rome nor those other churches would have practised it. Nor would Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome have judged it a matter indifferent, to be omitted or observed according to the custom of each place. Nor would the city advocate, the anonymous disputant, or the bishop Innocent have decreed that on that day one must fast of necessity. Moreover, Jerome counts this observance of the Sabbath among "ecclesiastical traditions handed down by our forefathers" (therefore not by the Apostles), and indeed of such a kind that their authority ought not to be harmed by the contrary customs of others. Yet no one fails to see that the apostolic traditions have far greater dignity. As for Augustine's statement that the question is an endless one, whether the observance of the Sabbath was instituted by the Apostles or not, by that very fact, I say, he most plainly denies that the Apostles wrote Bovius's Διαζυγίας [separations]. Would not that whole dispute be clearly and easily settled by them? But

units.la: Y & eo fatetur istos sibi fuisse incognitos, quod hanc ipsorum de sabbato Διαταξεων urbico illi difputatori nusquam objicit; qua tamen una omnis ejus insolentia multo validius fracta effet, quam caeteris omnibus Augustini epicheremalis. Denique fi Apostoli sunt Boviani Διαταγεις, Apostolicus non est Innocentius, qui quod hi decernunt, exserte ipse refigit, dementisque esse pronunciat id facere, quod illi omnino fieri volunt, ac praecipiunt. Sed nihil necesse est hic quidem immorari diutius, cum adversarii nobiscum negent Apostolicam esse illam de sabbati a jejunio immunitate Διαταξιν, Nulla est (inquit Petavius) ab Apostolis edita sanctio, qua jejunium ea die prohiberetur; ut Augustinus asserit ep. 118. ubi in rebus hujusmodi negat quicquam esse vel Scripturae sanctae authoritate, vel universalis Ecclesiae traditione determinatum. Qua quidem praescriptione tanquam spurius & alienus Canon ille rejicitur, qui inter Apostolicos 68. numeratur, &c. Nec melioris notae sunt quae in Apostolicis Constitutionibus leguntur l. 7. c. 24. ubi τα σαββατα και τας νηστειας εορτazeιν praecipit. Quod ab Apostolis toti Ecclesiae nunquam esse praescriptum, sanctissimorum Patrum consensus approbavit. Hactenus Petavius; Caeteri ri adversarii idem de hac διατάξει sentiunt. Nos caetera exsequamur.
units.tr: And by this he confesses that those writings were unknown to them, since he never brings this Constitution of the Sabbath [Διαταξεων] against that city disputant. Yet by this one point all his insolence would have been broken far more forcefully than by all the other arguments of Augustine's epicheirema. Finally, if the Bovian Constitutions [Διαταγεις] are the work of the Apostles, then Innocent was not an apostolic man. He openly rejects what they decree, and he declares that those who do what they absolutely wish and command to be done are madmen. But there is no need to dwell on this longer here, since our adversaries deny with us that the exemption from the Sabbath fast is an apostolic Constitution [Διαταξιν]. "There is no sanction issued by the Apostles," says Petavius, "that forbade fasting on that day; as Augustine asserts in ep. 118, where he denies that anything in such matters is determined either by the authority of Holy Scripture or by the universal tradition of the Church. That canon which is numbered among the Apostolic ones as the 68th is rejected by this very objection as spurious and foreign. Nor are those things of better quality which are read in the Apostolic Constitutions, book 7, c. 24, where they order that the Sabbaths and the fasts be kept as feasts [τα σαββατα και τας νηστειας εορτάζειν]. That the Apostles never prescribed this to the whole Church has been approved by the consensus of the most holy Fathers." So far Petavius. The rest of our adversaries think the same about this Constitution [διατάξει]. Let us proceed with the remaining matters.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAP. X.

units.la: Arg. XXI. Ex jejuniorum diebus certis affixorum ratione deprehendi certo Constitutiones vel nescivisse, vel certe nihili fecisse Hieronymum, Victorem, Augustinum, Socratem, Nicephorum, Bernonem, Chrysostomum, Cassianum, Isidorum, Rabanum, totam Latinorum Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Arg. XXI. From the fixed days of the fasts assigned by the Constitutions, it is clear that Jerome, Victor, Augustine, Socrates, Nicephorus, Berno, Chrysostom, Cassian, Isidore, Rabanus and the whole Latin Church either did not know of them or at least made no account of them.

units.la: EX superioribus notum est Διατάξεις certos, statosque dies, jejuniis determinasse, ut quartam sextamque ferias, ut quadragesimam, &c. At multi sunt inter veteris Ecclesiae scriptores, qui stata illa certorum dierum jejunia ab Apostolis instituta fuisse in genere negent. Hieronymus, qui anno quinti saeculi 20. in Domino obdormivit, Jejunia (inquit a) & congregationes inter dies propter eos a viris PRUDENTIBUS constitutos, qui magis saeculo vacant quam Deo. Cur a viris prudentibus, cur non a B. Apostolis constituta dixit jejunia, si Apostolos eorum vere Authores fuisse credidit?
units.tr: We have already noted that the Διατάξεις fix certain and set days for fasting, such as the fourth and sixth days of the week and Lent, etc. But many of the ancient Church's writers deny that these fixed fasts were instituted by the Apostles at all. Jerome, who fell asleep in the Lord in the twentieth year of the fifth century, says: Fasts and assemblies on certain days were appointed by PRUDENT men, who are more concerned with the world than with God. Why did he say the fasts were appointed by prudent men, and not by the blessed Apostles, if he believed the Apostles were their true authors?

units.la: Victor Antiochenus, qui centum annis post Juliani necem vixisse ex eo deprehenditur, quod Cyrillum Alex. laudet, idem dem docet, dum Christum prædicen-tem inducit Christianos ab Apostolis ad jejunia nulla legis necessitate adaƈtum iri, eosque virtutis amore, liberaque volun-tatis eleƈtione, non legis coaƈtione jejuna-turos; Stata vero, definitaque quæ post-ea obtinuerunt jejunia, ut quadragefi-male, ea propter ignavos & negligen-tes indućta esse.
units.tr: Victor of Antioch, who is shown to have lived a hundred years after the death of Julian because he praises Cyril of Alexandria, teaches the same thing. When he introduces Christ foretelling that the Christians would be led by the Apostles to fasts with no necessity of law, and that they would fast out of love of virtue and by free choice of the will, not by compulsion of law, he says that the fixed and defined fasts which later prevailed, such as Lent, were introduced because of the idle and negligent.

units.la: Augustinus eadem sequitur, Quibus (inquit b) diebus non oporteat jejunare,& quibus oporteat, præcepto Domini, vel Apostolorum, non invenio definitum. Huic quidem certe nulli fuerunt cogniti Boviani Apostoli; qui nihil disertius, quam jejunandi, & non jejunandi tem-pora præceperunt.
units.tr: Augustine follows the same view: On what days one should not fast, and on what days one should, I do not find defined by a precept of the Lord or of the Apostles. Certainly the Bovian Apostles were unknown to him, since they prescribed nothing more explicitly than times of fasting and times of not fasting.

units.la: Sic etiam Socrates, vetus Ecclesiasticæ historiæ scriptor, de jejuniis & abstinen-tiis verba faciens, ὡδεὶς (inquit c) ταῦτα ἐγγεγραφὸν ἔχει δεῖξαι παραγγέλμα. Nemo de hoc præceptum litterarum mo-numentis proditum potest ostendere. Ergo nulli tum erant Bovii διαθηκαὶ, apud quos ἐγγεγραφα extant, & quidem disertissima, de toto jejunandi negotio παραγγέλματα. Tum; περὶ τούτων τῆς ἐκάςου γνώμης, ἡ προαιρέσεως ἐπέτρεψαν οἱ Ἀπόςολοι. De hoc Apostoli uniuscujusque sententiæ, & arbitrio permiserunt. Non sunt ergo Apo-stoli stoli οἱ Διάταξεις, qui horum nihil cu-jusquam arbitrio permittent, omnia certis legibus in perpetuum definita tradunt.
units.tr: So too Socrates, an ancient writer of ecclesiastical history, speaking of fasts and abstinences, says: No one can show a command about these things written down [οὐδεὶς ταῦτα ἐγγεγραμμένον ἔχει δεῖξαι παράγγελμα]. No one can point to a precept handed down in written records. Therefore at that time there were no Bovian constitutions [διαθῆκαι] in which such written and very explicit commands about the whole business of fasting are found. Then he adds: Concerning these things the Apostles left it to the judgment or choice of each one [περὶ τούτων τῆς ἑκάστου γνώμης, ἢ προαιρέσεως ἐπέτρεψαν οἱ Ἀπόστολοι]. The Apostles, therefore, left this to the opinion and choice of each person. So the Apostles are not the authors of the Διατάξεις, which leave none of these matters to anyone's choice and hand down everything fixed in perpetuity by certain rules.

units.la: Eandem sententiam pæne iisdem verbis expressit Nicephorus Callistus, vir saeculi quarti decimi; unde liquet quam nulla fuerit Διαταγῶν, etiam apud infimæ Græciæ eruditos, authoritas.
units.tr: Nicephorus Callistus, a man of the fourteenth century, expressed almost the same opinion in nearly the same words. From this it is clear how little authority the Διαταγαί had, even among the learned of lower Greece.

units.la: Apud Latinos idem quoque sæculo undecimo ineunte senserat Berno, Abbas Augiensis, qui pleraque in Constitutionibus præcepta jejunia, ut quadragesimam, &c. censet inter consuetudines Ecclesiasticas à Sanctis Patribus (non ergo ab Apostolis) infra canonica regula terminos constitutos.
units.tr: Among the Latins, Berno, Abbot of Reichenau, had likewise held the same view at the beginning of the eleventh century. He thought that most of the precepts about fasting in the Constitutions, such as Lent, etc., were among the ecclesiastical customs established by the holy Fathers (not, therefore, by the Apostles), and fixed within the limits of canonical rule.

units.la: Sed sunt etiam ex omnium pæne sæculorum scriptoribus multi & quidem insignes, qui quædam apud Διαταγίας præcepta jejunia negant ab Apostoilis instituta. Quadragesimæ quidem jejunium, quod omnium est nobilissimum, quodque in Constitutitionibus exserte præcipitur, non ab Apostolis, sed à Patribus, non per se, neque ex primo religionis consilio, sed ex occasione propter multorum in percipienda Eucharistiæ socordiam, ac irreverentiam, institutum fuisse docet, qui sæculi quarti exitum, quinti initia vidit Chrysostomus a; σωμεισ̔ὀτες οι πελεγες ἢ βλαβλιω ἢ γενομένῳ ἐν τῇ ἡμελημένης προσοδῷ, σωμελ- λοντες ἐτύπωσαν ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα νη- στείας. Cum intelligerent Patres, quantum ex neglecto (ad sacra mysteria) accessu detrimenti caperetur, convenientes, quadraginta dies jejunii designarunt ac definiverunt.
units.tr: But there are also, from almost all centuries, many and very distinguished writers who deny that certain fasts prescribed in the Διαταγαί were instituted by the Apostles. Lent, indeed, the most noble of all fasts, which is expressly prescribed in the Constitutions, was not instituted by the Apostles but by the Fathers, not of its own accord or from the first plan of religion, but on the occasion of the many people's carelessness and irreverence in receiving the Eucharist. So teaches Chrysostom, who saw the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century: When the Fathers perceived how much harm came from the neglected approach (to the sacred mysteries), they gathered together and fixed forty days of fasting [συνιόντες οἱ πατέρες ἢ βλέποντες ἢ γινόμενον ἐν τῇ ἡμελημένῃ προσόδῳ, συνελθόντες ἔταξαν ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα νηστείας].

units.la: Augustinus quoque quadragesimæ institutum, dum usui & consuetudini tribuit, Apostolis abstulit; Ut quadraginta (inquit b) illi dies ante Pascha observantur, Ecclesia consuetudo roboravit; sic etiam ut octo dies neophytorum distinguantur à cateris, id est, ut octavus primo concinat.
units.tr: Augustine too, when he ascribes the institution of Lent to use and custom, takes it away from the Apostles: That those forty days before Easter are observed, the custom of the Church has strengthened; so too that the eight days of the newly baptized are distinguished from the others, that is, that the eighth day is chosen first.

units.la: Cassianus, qui seculi quinti anno 40. floruit, Chrysostomum sequitur, docens c, quadragesima observantiam, quandiu Ecclesia primitivæ perfectio inviolata permansit, penitus non fuisse; postea corruptis hominum moribus universis sacerdotibus placuisse, ut eos ad opus sanctum canonice jejuniorum indictione revocarent.
units.tr: Cassian, who flourished in the fortieth year of the fifth century, follows Chrysostom, teaching that the observance of Lent was not at all in place as long as the perfection of the primitive Church remained unbroken; later, when the morals of men were corrupted, it pleased all the priests to recall them to the holy work by a canonical appointment of fasts.

units.la: Isidorus Hispalensis d, & Rabanus Maurus e, ille septimi sæculi a. 36. hic noni 56. denati, Cassiani & sententiam, & ipsa verba tenuerunt, ut videre est in iis, quæ de quadragesimæ institutione scripserunt. runt. Rupertus Tuitiensis eadem duodecimo saeculo ultra initia jam provecto, sensit, scripsitque non Apostolica, sed Ecclesiastica disciplina quadragesimale institutum tribuens, Telesphorumque urbis Episcopum à B. Petro septimum, ejus authorem edens. Idem & in ultima temporum foece, jam inchoato saeculo Christianismi 16. Ioannes Major nobilis scholasticus, prodit, Legitur (inquit b) quod Telesphorus Papa jejunium quadragesimale imposuit. Sed hi quidem Latini.
units.tr: Isidore of Seville, who died in the thirty-sixth year of the seventh century, and Rabanus Maurus, who died in the fifty-sixth year of the ninth, held Cassian's opinion and even his very words, as can be seen from what they wrote about the institution of Lent. Rupert of Deutz, in the twelfth century, already well advanced beyond its beginnings, likewise thought and wrote that the Lenten institution derives not from Apostolic but from ecclesiastical discipline, naming Telesphorus, bishop of the city, the seventh from blessed Peter, as its author. In the very last period of time, at the beginning of the sixteenth century of Christianity, John Major, a noted scholastic, also states: It is read that Pope Telesphorus imposed the Lenten fast. But these are Latins.

units.la: E Graecis non est dubitandum, quin eadem fuerit & Socratis c, & Nicephori Callisti d sententia; qui pascha ipsum, à quo omnis quadragesimae ratio pendet, negant, ut mox audiemus, ab Apostolis institutum. Atque hi quidem hactenus.
units.tr: Among the Greeks there is no doubt that the opinion of Socrates and of Nicephorus Callistus was the same. They deny that Easter itself, on which the whole reasoning of Lent depends, was instituted by the Apostles, as we shall hear shortly. So much for these.

units.la: Iam cum in Constitutionibus Apostoli inducantur, & quadragesimam; & multa alia insuper jejunia diserte, nominatim qui instituentes; nemo non videt fieri non posse, ut qui vel quadragesimale in specie jejunium, vel ullum in genere certi temporis jejunium ab Apostolis institutum esse negat, idem ille (si quidem sapit) Constitutionum codicem, in quo aliud clarissime traditur, pro vero vel Apostolorum, vel Clementis opere habeat. Cum ergo nuper memorati scriptores Hieronymus nimus Presbyter, Victor Antiochiæ, Chrysostomus Constantinopolis, Augustinus Hipponis, Isidorus Hispalis, Rabanus Moguntiæ episcopi; cum Cassianus, Berna, & Rupertus Abbates; cum Socrates, & Nicephorus historiæ scriptores; Ioannes Major Scholæ Romanæ Theologus, omnes, vel jejunium ullum, vel certe quadragesimale ab Apostolis institutum fuisse negent; omnino necesse est neminem eorum Διαταξεις Boccianas pro vero vel Apostolorum vel Clementis opere habuisse.
