Denique cum nulla sit ratio, cur suspicemur illos viros, plærosque maximi apud omnes Christianos nominis, librum aliquem ab ea Ecclesia, in qua ii vivebant, pro vero agnitum ac celebratum, vel nesciusse ipsos, vel cognitum reprobasse; hinc quoq; concludendum est neq; in Orientali Ecclesia, in qua Victor, & Chrysostomus, & Nicephorus, & Socrates; neque in Occidentali, in qua Hieronymus, & Cassianus, & Isidorus; neque in Australi, in qua Augustinus; neque in Boreali in qua Berno, Rabanus, Rupertus, & Major floruerunt, quarto, quintoq;, septimo, nono, undecimo, duodecimo, decimoquarto, decimoquinto sæculis (quibus illi omnes vixerunt) pro veris vel Apostolorum, vel Clementis libris habitas fuisse, quas nunc nobis Bovius & Turrianus obtrudunt suorum Apostolorum διαταξεις.
units.tr: Now, since the Apostles are introduced in the Constitutions as prescribing Lent, and many other fasts expressly and by name, with the persons who instituted them, no one can fail to see that whoever denies that a Lenten fast in particular, or any fast of a certain season in general, was instituted by the Apostles cannot (if he has any sense) regard that codex of Constitutions, in which the contrary is most clearly taught, as the genuine work of the Apostles or of Clement. Since therefore the writers just mentioned (Jerome, presbyter of Rome; Victor of Antioch; Chrysostom of Constantinople; Augustine of Hippo; Isidore of Seville; Rabanus, bishop of Mainz; Cassian, Berno and Rupert, abbots; Socrates and Nicephorus, historians; John Major, theologian of the Roman school) all deny that any fast, or at least a Lenten fast, was instituted by the Apostles, it is absolutely necessary that none of them regarded the Bovian Διατάξεις as the genuine work of the Apostles or of Clement. Finally, since there is no reason to suspect that those men, most of them of the greatest name among all Christians, either did not know a book that was accepted and held as genuine in the Church in which they lived, or knew it and rejected it, we must conclude also that these books were not regarded as genuine works of the Apostles or of Clement, neither in the Eastern Church, where Victor, Chrysostom, Nicephorus and Socrates flourished, nor in the Western, where Jerome, Cassian and Isidore flourished, nor in the Southern, where Augustine lived, nor in the Northern, where Berno, Rabanus, Rupert and Major flourished, in the fourth, fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth and fifteenth centuries (in which all of them lived). These are the books which Bovius and Turrianus now thrust upon us as the Διαταξεις of their Apostles.

units.la: Idem & quidem aliquanto luculentius ostendit ipsa Ecclesiæ in hoc jejuniorum negotio praxis. Primo enim Διαταγεις sic alicubi præcipiunt ; μὴ ὣν τὸ ἑορτάσαι ὑμας τῷ πεντηκοστῷ, ἑορτάσατε μίαν ἑβδομάδα, καὶ μετ' ἐκεῖνο νηστεύσατε μίαν. δίκαιον γὰρ ἐυφραντηναι ὅτι τῇ ἐν Θεῷ σωτηρίᾳ· καὶ νηστεῦσαι μὴ τῷ ἀνισον. Post agitatos festos Pentecostes dies, unam hebdomadam festam quoque agite; & post illam unam item jejunate. Æquum enim est tum lætitiam de dono Dei capere; tum post relaxationem, rursum jejunare. Vides, ut non proximam, sed alteram post Pentecostèn, hebdomaden totam jejunio determinent. Atqui illius jejunii nullum, quod sciam, apparet neque in veteris, neque in recentis Ecclesiæ praxi vestigium; nedum ut ab universa id observatum fuerit; fuisset autem si ab Apostolis institutum esse Christiani, maxime veteres, credidissent.
units.tr: The practice of the Church itself in this matter of fasting shows the same thing, and does so rather more clearly. For the Διαταγαί prescribe it in this way somewhere: Therefore, after the Pentecost festival, do not keep the feast for one week only; keep a festal week, and after that fast for one week. For it is right to rejoice in the salvation that is in God, and to fast, but not in an unequal way [μὴ οὖν τὸ ἑορτάσαι ὑμᾶς τῇ πεντηκοστῇ, ἑορτάσατε μίαν ἑβδομάδα, καὶ μετὰ ἐκεῖνο νηστεύσατε μίαν. δίκαιον γὰρ εὐφραίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῇ ἐν Θεῷ σωτηρίᾳ, καὶ νηστεῦσαι μὴ τῷ ἀνίσῳ]. You see how they fix a whole week of fasting not for the week immediately after Pentecost but for the second week after it. Yet, so far as I know, no trace of such a fast appears in the practice of the ancient or of the more recent Church, much less that it was observed by the whole Church; yet it would have been, if Christians, especially the ancient ones, had believed it to have been instituted by the Apostles.

units.la: De Sabbati à jejunio immunitate, quam Διαταγεις quidem decernunt, Latina vero omnis Ecclesia inde ab Innocentii temporibus abrogavit, supra diximus. An scilicet istos Apostolos credidit Ecclesia Latina, quæ quo ii die jejunare nefas putant, eo ipso non jejunare nefas esse decrevit?
units.tr: I have already said above that the immunity from fasting on the Sabbath, which the Constitutions [Διαταγεῖς] decree, has been abrogated by the whole Latin Church since the time of Innocent. Did the Latin Church then believe those Apostles, when it decreed that it is wrong not to fast on the very days on which those Apostles forbid fasting, and that for that reason it is wrong to abstain from fasting?

units.la: Sed & eadem feriæ quartæ determinatum ab illis jejunium, jam pridem antiquavit; eoque confessa est se Διαταξεις pro spuriis, ac non Apostolicis habere. Quod enim ajunt nonnulli translatum è quarta feria in sabbatum jejunium, id inquam, si isti Διαταγεις revera Apostoli sunt, Latinorum crimen non minuit, sed geminat; quibus non fuit satis jejunium ex ea feria, cui ab Apostolis scilicet affixum erat, movere, nisi insuper & in eam id transferrent, quam illi diserte jusserant ab omni jejunio esse immunem.
units.tr: The fast which the same Constitutions prescribe on Wednesday also was abolished long ago, and so the Latin Church has admitted that it regards the Constitutions as spurious and not Apostolic. For as for what some say, that the fast was transferred from Wednesday to Saturday, if these Constitutions really are Apostolic, that does not diminish the offence of the Latins but doubles it. It was not enough for them to move the fast away from the day to which, as it was evidently fixed by the Apostles, it had been attached; they must also transfer it to the day which the Apostles had expressly ordered to be free from all fasting.

units.la: Neque vero in uno quartæ feriæ jejunio violata sunt à Latinis Διαταγὲων decreta. Ut hanc impositio jejunandi officio liberarunt; ita vicissim alia tempora perpetua immunitate per Διαταγίας gaudentia, jejuniis (ut sic dicam) oppresserunt ac funestarunt. Nam illi quidem totos à Pascha te ad pentecosten quinquaginta dies ita festos esse decernunt, ut si quis hoc tempore jejunet, eum peccati reum pronuncient; ἔνοχος ἁμαρτίας ἔσται (inquiunt a) ὁ τὴν νη-στείαν τῶν ἡμερῶν ἀναστάσεως ἔσαν, ἢ τῆς πεντηκοστῆς, ἢ ὅλως ἡμέρων ἑορτῆς Κυρίου καταφρῶν. Reus peccati erit, qui Dominico die jejunauerit, cum sit dies Resurrectionis, aut Pentecostes, ut qui denique ullum diem Domini festum in moestitia egerit. Hanc Διαταξιν
units.tr: Nor indeed have the Latins violated the decrees of the Constitutions only in the one matter of the Wednesday fast. Just as they freed one day from the obligation of fasting, so in turn they have burdened, so to speak, and spoiled with fasts other times which the Constitutions keep in perpetual immunity. For those Constitutions decree that the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost are so festive that if anyone fasts during this time they pronounce him guilty of sin. They say: he will be guilty of sin [ἔνοχος ἁμαρτίας ἔσται] who despises the fasting of the days of the Resurrection, or of Pentecost, or indeed of any day of the Lord's festival. He will be guilty of sin who fasts on the Lord's day, since it is the day of the Resurrection, or of Pentecost, or who in general spends any festal day of the Lord in mourning. This Constitution [Διαταξιν]

units.la: a L. 5. const. c. 20. extr. Διαζξιν primo jam pridem violavit, ac proculcavit, anno circiter 470. Manuertus, Viennensis apud nos Episcopus, in media pentecostes intercurrentes Rogatio- num (ut vocant) dies tristibus jejunandi officiis moestificans; exindeq; omnis Gal- liarū Ecclesia idem institutum probans 4. Synodicisque decretis confirmans; ac po- stremo tota fere Latinorum Ecclesia idem exemplum sequens. Sed & sextam feriam, & Sabbatum Latina jam dudum Ecclesia jejuniis celebrat in Pentecoste, non mi- nus quam in aliis anni tempestatibus; in sabbato bis rea; quod scilicet a jejunio per illas hebdomadas duplici ratione & propter ipsius diei, & propter Pentecostes, in quam incurrit, religionem ex Διαζγεων decreto immunem, jejunio & quidem necesario ac legitimo temerare non dubitat. Siccine Latini de Apostolorum decretis ludunt? Absit. Quid ergo est? Res ipsa loquitur nunquam eos vel agnovisse vel certe pro Christi Apostolis habuisse Bovianos istos Pentecosteae a jejunio immunitatis institutores; quos si eo loco ac numero censuisent, homines eorum observantissimi, quaecunque Apostolica arbitrabantur, nunquam latas ab illis leges tam secure contemnisset. Sed & siquis apud Gregorium nostrum eum jejuniorum ordinem consideret, quæ per anni circulum observanda olim disposuit Perpetuus Turronensis Episcopus, circa a. D. 470. facile intelliget nullo tum apud nos loco, aut numero fuisse τὴς Διαζυγίας ; quorum scilicet nullam Perpetuus rationem in illa sua dispositione habuit. Quin & alia non pauca à Διαζυγίων decretis in jejuniis veteris Ecclesiæ abhorrentia deprehendi fortasse possent, siquis in id negotium paulo attentius incumberet. Nos & ad alia properamus, & hæc quæ diximus, satis esse arbitramur.
units.tr: was first violated and trampled underfoot long ago, about the year 470, by Mamertus, bishop of Vienne in our country (see L. 5. const. c. 20.), who made the days of the so-called Rogations, which fall in the middle of Pentecost, sad with mournful fasting; from there the whole Church of Gaul, approving the same practice, confirmed it by synodical decrees, and finally nearly the whole Latin Church followed the same example. Moreover, the Latin Church has long since celebrated the sixth day and Saturday with fasts during Pentecost, no less than in other seasons of the year, and it observes Saturday with fasting twice over. That is, although the Constitutions have exempted the Pentecost weeks from fasting, both on account of the sanctity of the day itself and because of Pentecost, into which it falls, the Church does not hesitate to violate that immunity by necessary and lawful fasting. Do the Latins thus make a joke of the decrees of the Apostles? Far from it. What then is the case? The thing itself speaks: they never either recognised those authors of the Pentecost immunity from fasting or at any rate regarded them as Apostles of Christ. If they had esteemed them in that rank and number, these men, most scrupulous in observing whatever they thought Apostolic, would never so confidently have despised laws laid down by them. Moreover, if anyone examines in our Gregory the order of fasts which Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, about the year 470, laid down to be observed through the yearly cycle, he will readily understand that at that time there was no place or account for these Constitutions among us; Perpetuus, of course, took no account of them in that arrangement. Indeed, if anyone were to apply himself to this business a little more carefully, many other things in the fasts of the early Church, at odds with the decrees of the Constitutions, could perhaps be detected. But we are hastening on to other matters, and we think that what we have said is enough.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Arg. XXII. Et festorum ratione itidem deprehenditur Constitutiones nullius pretii fuisse apud Socratem, Nicephorum, apud Latinam & Gracam Ecclesiam, imprimis apud Gregorium Magnum.
units.tr: Argument XXII. The same is detected from the matter of feasts: the Constitutions were of no account with Socrates, with Nicephorus, in the Latin and Greek Church, and above all with Gregory the Great.

units.la: Eniamus ergo ad festos dies; ex quibus non minus, quam exjejuniis, clarissime patefiet, ignotos fuisse veteri Ecclesiæ Bovii Apostolos. Mitto, quæ de Natali Domini in priorum quatuor sæculorum Ecclesia surpa observavimus. Sed istos sane Apostolos etiam multos sequentium temporum porum scriptores, aut nescivisse, aut contempsisse, proque impostoribus habuisse, inde liquet, primo, quod cum hi multa festa Christianis accuratè observanda præcipiant, quidam ex illis, plane contra festa, quæ postea coluerunt Christiani, ea ab Apostolis instituta fuisse negant. Secundo ex eo quod quædam festa nominatim in Constitutionibus præcepta omnes fere veteres, recentesque Christiani vel negligunt, vel etiam damnant. Ac nulla quidem festa ab Apostolis instituta, ne ipso quidem Paschate excepto, aperte sentiunt Socrates & Nicephorus Callistus.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the festal days, from which it will be no less clearly seen than from the fasts that the Bovian Apostles were unknown to the ancient Church. I pass over what we have already noted about the Nativity of the Lord in the Church of the first four centuries. That many writers of later times either did not know these Apostles, or despised them and held them to be impostors, is plain from the following. First, while these Constitutions prescribe many feasts to be observed carefully by Christians, some of those writers, directly against the feasts which Christians afterwards kept, deny that these were instituted by the Apostles. Second, almost all ancient and modern Christians either neglect or even condemn certain feasts that the Constitutions name expressly. Indeed Socrates and Nicephorus Callistus plainly hold that no feast at all was instituted by the Apostles, not even Easter excepted.

units.la: Illius quidem hæc sunt verba a; τῶ ἑορτῶ τῶ πάσχα, ἡμῖν τὰς ἄλλας ἑορτὰς οἱ ἀνθρωποι διὰ τὸ ἀνιέσθαι τῆς πόνων ἐν αὐταῖς, ἕκασοι κατὰ χώρας, ὡς ἐβουλήθησαν τῷ μνήμῳ τῆς σωτηριώδους πάθους ἐξ ἔθους τινὸς ἐπιτέλεσαν· ὁ δὲ νόμῳ τοῦτο παραφυλάττειν ὁ Σωτὴρ ἢ οἱ Ἀπόστολοι ἡμῖν παρήγγειλαν. Festum Pascha, & alia festa homines propter laborum in ijs relaxationem singulis per loca, ut voluerunt, salutaris passionis memoriam, ex consuetudine quadam celebrarunt. Neque enim lege ea observare jusserunt Servator, vel Apostoli. Mox ex consuetudine ortam Paschæ observationem iterum dicit; διὰ τὸ μηδένα τῶν Ἀποστόλων, ὡς ἔφλω, μηδενὶ νενομοθετηκέναι περὶ αὐτῆς, propterea quod quod nemo Apostolorum, ut dixi, cuiquam leges de ea tulit. Nicephori eadem fuit sententia; ὃ πάντως νόμῳ τινὶ Σωτῆρα ἢ τὰς μαθητὰς τὸ τὸ παραφυλάττειν ὀείσασθ᾽, Neque Servatorem, vel ejus discipulos lege ulla id observandum esse statuisse; nimirum, τὸ πάσχα, καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς τῶν ἑορτῶν, pascha & reliqua festa; ut ex superioribus verbis liquet. Mox ita concludit; ὡς ἐνδηλον εἰ τὸ μηδένα τῆς Ἀποστόλων μηδὲν τι περὶ ταύτης νομοθετῆσαι τῆς ἑορτῆς, Ut satis manifestum sit neminem Apostolorum de festo hoc (Paschali scilicet) ulla lege quicquam constituisse. Hæc illi. Non jam quæro recte-ne an secus ita sentiant. Hoc unum ajo, nunquam Socratem, nunquam Nicephorum ita scripturos vel opinaturos fuisse, si Bovianas Διατάξεις legissent, proque Apostolicis habuissent; in quibus scilicet & de Pascha te, & de aliis festis leges extant disertissimæ, de quibus illi negant ullas ab Apostolis latas leges; quin & manifestum esse ajunt, nullas ab iis esse latas. Quod quanti sit & quam incredibilis stuporis nemo non videt; si quidem eos Apostolicas censuisse nostras Bovii Διατάξεις statuas.
units.tr: Socrates' words are these: "The festival of Easter, and the other festivals, men celebrated in each place as they wished, from a certain custom, in order to be relieved of their labours on those days, in memory of the saving passion; but the Saviour or the Apostles did not command us to observe this by law" [τῆς ἑορτῆς τοῦ πάσχα ... ἐξ ἔθους τινός ... ὁ δὲ νόμῳ τοῦτο παραφυλάττειν ὁ Σωτὴρ ἢ οἱ Ἀπόστολοι ἡμῖν παρήγγειλαν]. Soon after, he again says that the observance of Easter arose from custom, "because none of the Apostles, as I said, enacted any law concerning it" [διὰ τὸ μηδένα τῶν Ἀποστόλων μηδενὶ νενομοθετηκέναι περὶ αὐτῆς]. Nicephorus held the same opinion: that neither the Saviour nor his disciples had decreed by any law that this should be observed [οὐδὲ τὸν Σωτῆρα ἢ τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ νόμῳ τινὶ ... ὀρίσασθαι], namely the Pascha and the rest of the festivals, as is clear from the words above. Then he concludes: "so that it is manifest that none of the Apostles enacted any law about this festival" [ὡς ἐνδηλον ... μηδένα τῶν Ἀποστόλων μηδὲν τι περὶ ταύτης νομοθετῆσαι τῆς ἑορτῆς]. So far they. I do not now ask whether they are right or wrong in this view. I say only this: Socrates and Nicephorus would never have written or thought thus had they read the Bovian Diatáxeis and held them to be apostolic. In those Constitutions there are most explicit laws both about Easter and about the other feasts, and yet these men deny that the Apostles made any laws, and even say it is manifest that none were made. How great a thing this is, and how incredible a stupidity, no one fails to see, if indeed you suppose that they considered our Bovian Diatáxeis to be apostolic.

units.la: Sed non soli Socrates & Nicephorus Bovianorum Apostolorum de festis decreta pulsarunt. Sunt quædam ab iis instituta festa, quæ omnis contempsit, imo & damnavit Ecclesia. Certe quæ de sabbato una cum dominico die celebrando decernunt, post Laodicenam synodum, cujus supra decretum huic istorum Διαταξει tota diametro adversum retulimus, & Latina pariter, & Græca Ecclesia constantissime ad hanc diem improbant. Neque quisquam est Christianorum (si Æthiopes exceperis) qui sabbatum ea quam Διαταγεις præcipiunt, religione celebrandum putet. Gregorius qui Romanæ Ecclesiæ septimo sæculo ineunte præerat, hunc sabbati cultum atrocissime denotat; Pervenit ad me (inquit) quosdam perversi spiritus homines, prava inter vos aliqua, & sanctæ fidei adversa seminasse, ita ut die sabbati aliquid operari prohiberent. Quos quid aliud nisi Antichristi prædicatores dixerim? Qui veniens diem sabbatum, atque Dominicum ab omni facit opere custodiri. I nunc Bovi, & tuos Διαταγίας Christi Apostolos jacta, quos Gregorius tuus habet pro Antichristi prædicatoribus; qui scilicet illud ipsum quod ille tanta cum indignatione refutat, difertissimis verbis statuunt; Σάββατον (inquiunt b) & Κυριακὴν ὀγολαζέσθωσαν. Item c; τὸ σάββατον μέντοι ἡ τῆς Κυριακῆς ἑορτάζετε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν δημιουργίας ἐστὶν ὑπόμνημα, ἡ δὲ ἀναστάσεως. Sed & totius
units.tr: But it was not only Socrates and Nicephorus who struck at the decrees of the Bovian Apostles concerning feasts. There are some feasts they instituted which the whole Church has despised, nay, condemned. Certainly, as to what they decree about keeping the Sabbath together with the Lord's day, the Latin and the Greek Church alike, after the Laodicean synod, whose decree against this Diatáxis of theirs we cited above, have constantly disapproved it down to this day. Nor is there any Christian (if you except the Ethiopians) who thinks the Sabbath should be kept with the religious observance that the Diatáxeis prescribe. Gregory, who presided over the Roman Church at the beginning of the seventh century, most bitterly denounces this observance of the Sabbath: "Men of a perverse spirit have come to me (he says), who have sown among you certain wicked things, contrary to the holy faith, so that they forbid any work to be done on the Sabbath day. What else should I call them but preachers of Antichrist? For he who comes makes the Sabbath and the Lord's day kept free from all work." Go now, Bovius, and boast of your Christ's Apostles, whom your Gregory counts as preachers of Antichrist; for they, of course, lay down in the plainest words the very thing which he refutes with such indignation: "Let the Sabbath and the Lord's day be kept as feasts" [Σάββατον καὶ Κυριακὴν ἑορταζέσθωσαν]. Likewise: "You keep the Sabbath together with the Lord's day as a festival, because the one is a memorial of creation, the other of the resurrection" [τὸ σάββατον μέντοι ... ἡ τῆς Κυριακῆς ἑορτάζετε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν δημιουργίας ἐστὶν ὑπόμνημα, ἡ δὲ ἀναστάσεως]. But the constant practice of the whole Church from Gregory's time onward, as I have said, confesses that its judgment on this Diatáxis is similar, and that nothing is less fitting than to regard the Apostles as its authors.
