units.la: c L. 8. c. 33. init.; c L. 7. c. 24. tius Ecclesiæ à Gregorii temporibus con- stans, ut dixi, praxis, simile ejus esse de hoc Diataxi judicium fatetur; nihil adeo minus quam Apostolos censendos illius authores.
units.tr: c L. 8. c. 33. init.; c L. 7. c. 24. The constant practice of the whole Church from Gregory's times onward, as I have said, likewise confesses that its judgement on this Diataxis is of the same kind: by no means are the Apostles to be considered its authors.

units.la: Jam & illam, quæ proxime Pentecosten sequitur, hebdomadam, quam festam totam agitari decernunt οι Διαταγεις, μὴ ἐν τὸ ἐορταζειν ὑμᾶς τῶν πεντηκοστῶν, ἑορτάσατε μίαν ἑβδομάδα, illam, inquam, festam hebdomadam, quæ vel antiqua, vel recens norit Ecclesia, equidem nescio. Hoc scio, hanc istorum Diataxin in Romanæ sedis communione usque adeo contemni, ut illos ipsos dies, quos Διαταγεὶς festos agitari scisci-unt, illa jam a multis sæculis ad hunc usque diem solenni legitimoque jejunio dicaverit. In hanc enim ipsam hebdomadam (ut notum est) incidit unum ex iis jejuniis, quæ vulgo quatuor temporum vocantur; quæ adversarii non tantum a Leonis, sed & à Callisti P. R. ꝙvo (idest ab a. D. 224.) repetunt; ut, si hæc stat eorum hypothesis, omnino necesse sit, omnem jam inde à tertio Christi sæculo ad nostra usque tempora Romanam Ecclesiam istos Διαταγὰς pro impostoribus habuisse; quæ scilicet jejunandum iis diebus præscripsit, quos isti lætos, festosque agitari jusserant. Sed de illius quidem Pentecosten costen excipientis hebdomadis præcepta ab istis festivitate, ut de proxime sequentis jejunio, altum apud veteres silentium; ut vere meritoque scripserit Reverendis. Userius nostera, se qui alterius mentionem fecerit antiquorum neminem memi-nisse.
units.tr: Next, as to the week that immediately follows Pentecost, which the Diataxis decrees should be kept entirely as a festival ["οἱ Διαταγεῖς, μὴ ἐν τὸ ἑορτάζειν ὑμᾶς τῶν πεντηκοστῶν, ἑορτάσατε μίαν ἑβδομάδα"], I truly do not know whether that festal week is known to the ancient or to the recent Church. This I do know: in communion with the Roman see this Diataxis of theirs is so utterly despised that the very days which the Diataxis-writers have ordered to be kept as festivals have for many centuries, down to the present day, been set apart by the Church for a solemn and lawful fast. For into this very week (as is well known) falls one of those fasts commonly called the Ember Days, which our opponents trace back not only to Leo but also to Callistus, the Roman bishop (that is, to the year 224 A.D.). So if their hypothesis holds, it must necessarily follow that from the third century of Christ down to our own times the Roman Church has regarded those Diataxeis as impostors, since it prescribed fasting on the very days which they had ordered to be kept joyful and festive. But concerning the observance of that festal week following Pentecost, as concerning the fast of the week that closely follows it, there is a deep silence among the ancients; so that the most reverend Ussher, our countryman, rightly and justly wrote that no one among the ancient writers who mentioned the other remembers it.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Arg. XXIII. Nihili fecisse Constitutiones omnis pene memoriæ Christianos Græcos Latinosque, probatur ex Laicorum baptismo pene ab omnibus recepto. Arg. XXIV. Constitutiones sprevisse Hieronymum & alios plurimos in judicio de Episcopatu. Et (Arg. XXV.) Augustinum, de Mediatore, de Juda, de Magdalena. Baronii ea de re verba.
units.tr: Argument XXIII. That almost all Christians, Greek and Latin, have held the Constitutions in no regard, is shown from the practice of lay baptism, received by almost everyone. Argument XXIV. That Jerome and very many others despised the Constitutions in their judgment on the episcopate. And (Argument XXV.) that Augustine did so on the Mediator, on Judas, and on Mary Magdalene. Baronius's words on this matter.

units.la: ATQUE hæc quidem de jejuniorum, festorumque disciplina satis sunt. Nunc ad cætera pergamus. Boviani Διατάξεις, quod etiam est à Bellarmino inter eorum errores notatum, prohibent absolute, ne laici baptizent. Nam mulierem quidem baptizare ἐπισφαλὲς, μᾶλλον ὁ παράνομον καὶ ἀσεβὲς, periculosum esse, imo illegitimum & impium pronunciant . Tum; ἀλλ' ἐτέλαι-νοῖς ἐπιτρέπομεν (inquiunt ) ποιεῖν τι ἐργα-τικῶν ἔργων· οἷον θυσίαν, ἢ βάπτισμα. Imo neque laico permittimus facere aliquod opus sacersacerdotale, ut sacrificium, aut baptismum. Denique, ΑΛΛ' ὕτι (inquiunt *) τοῖς λοιποῖς κληρικοῖς, ἢ ψάλταις, ἢ πυλωροῖς, ἢ ὑπηρέταις ἢ μόνοις ἐπισκόποις καὶ πρεσβυτέροις, ἐξυπηρετουμένων αὐτοῖς τῶν διακόνων· οἱ δὲ τολμῶντες τοῦτο, τῷ Κοιτῶν ὑποίσει ἡ δίκη.
units.tr: These remarks on the discipline of fasts and feasts are enough. Now let us proceed to other matters. The Constitutions of Bovius, which Bellarmine also lists among their errors, absolutely forbid laymen to baptize. They declare that baptizing a woman is dangerous [ἐπισφαλὲς], or rather unlawful [παράνομον] and impious [ἀσεβὲς], indeed illegitimate and impious. Then they say: "But we permit the laity [ἐτέλαινοῖς] to do none of the priestly works, such as sacrifice or baptism [θυσίαν, ἢ βάπτισμα]." Indeed we do not permit a layman to perform any priestly act, such as sacrifice or baptism. Finally: "But to the remaining clergy, or to the psalmists, or the doorkeepers, or the attendants, or only to the bishops and presbyters, with the deacons serving them; but those who dare to do this shall undergo the punishment of the Coritae [τῷ Κοιτῶν ὑποίσει ἡ δίκη]."

units.la: Imo neq; reliquis clericis potestatem baptizandi facimus, ut lectoribus, cantoribus, janitoribus, aut ministris, nisi tantum episcopis, & presbyteris, ministrantibus Diaconis. Qui vero hoc ausi fuerint, poenas coritarum pendent. Non jam quæro, rectum ne sit, an secus hoc istorum decretum. Hoc unum nunc contendo, id pro Apostolico nequaquam ab iis haberi, qui sentiunt, & Diaconis & laicis fidelibus interdum, imo sæpe licere baptizare, ut Tertullianus a; ut Eliberitani Patres, quorum hac de re disertus habetur canon b; ut Hieronymus c, cujus hæc sunt verba, Baptizare si necessitas cogat, scimus etiam licere laicis: ut Augustinus d: ut Gelasius e; ut Isidorus f; ut Lombardus g; ut Florentini Patres; quorum nihil necesse est in re clara confessaque loca describere. Romana quidem, quæ hodie est omnis Ecclesia non modo editis disputationibus, sed ipsa quotidiana praxi profitetur ac defendit, & clericis omnibus, & laicis, seu viris, seu fœminis, quin & Paganis, hominibusque non baptizatis baptizandi jus aliquod quibus-dam temporibus esse; baptismumque ab iis tum collatum valere, modo adfuerit materia, forma, & intentio debita. Quis vero istos omnes in eam sententiam ituros fuisse putaverit, si Bovii Διαταγὴς qui il-lam periculosam παράνομον, impiam Coritarum supplicis dignam pronunciant, vere Christi Apostolos fuisse existimavisent?
units.tr: Indeed we do not grant the power of baptizing to the other clergy either, such as readers, cantors, doorkeepers, or ministers, but only to bishops and presbyters, with deacons assisting. Those who dare to do so shall pay the penalty of the Coritae. I am not now asking whether this decree of theirs is right or wrong. I contend only this: that it is by no means regarded as apostolic by those who hold that deacons and lay believers may sometimes, indeed often, baptize. So Tertullian holds [a]; so the Fathers of Elvira, whose canon on this point is clear [b]; so Jerome [c], whose words are: "We know that laymen are also permitted to baptize if necessity compels"; so Augustine [d]; so Gelasius [e]; so Isidore [f]; so Lombard [g]; so the Fathers of Florence. There is no need to list places for a matter so clear and agreed. The Roman Church, which today is the whole Church, professes and defends this not only in published disputations but in its daily practice: that all clergy, laymen, men or women, even pagans and unbaptized persons, have at certain times some right to baptize, and that baptism conferred by them is valid provided that matter, form and due intention are present. Who would have thought that all these men would have agreed with this view, if they had truly believed the Constitutions of Bovius, which call that practice "dangerous," "unlawful," "impious," and "worthy of the punishment of the Coritae," to have been written by the true apostles of Christ?

units.la: Adhæc Διαταγὲς (quod nos supra fuse demonstravimus) magnum, latumque esse volunt presbyterorum, & episcoporum discrimen, idque ipsis eorum nominibus ostendi volunt; ac ut alia taceam, solis episcopis jus ministros ordinandi concedunt, neque vere episcopum censent, nisi qui a tribus, minimum a duobus episcopis ordinatus fuerit. Jam ista Hieronymum pro Apostolicis scitis minime habuisse clarum est, cujus nota est huic e diametro oppo-sita sententia, eundem esse presbyterum & episcopum; & Apostolorum temporibus eosdem fuisse Episcopos & presbyteros: illos magis Ecclesiæ consuetudine, quam dispositionis Dominicæ veritate presbyteris majores esse factos; hos ex Ecclesiæ consuetudine ei, qui sibi præpositus est, esse subjectos; nulloque discrimine a Paulo & cæteris Apostolis pro re eadem usurpari utrumque vocabulum. Eadem quoque secutos &
units.tr: Moreover, the Constitutions (which we demonstrated at length above) want the difference between presbyters and bishops to be great and wide, and they wish this to be shown by their very names. To pass over other points: they grant to bishops alone the right of ordaining ministers, and they do not regard anyone as a true bishop unless he has been ordained by at least three bishops, or at least two. Now it is clear that Jerome did not hold these rules as apostolic. His well-known opinion is the direct opposite: that a presbyter and a bishop are the same; that in the times of the Apostles bishops and presbyters were the same; that the former were made superior to presbyters by the custom of the Church rather than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement; and that the latter are subject, by the custom of the Church, to the one set over them. He held that Paul and the other Apostles used both words for the same thing without any distinction. The same view was also held by

units.la: Hilarium Diaconum a in Commentariis (qui vulgo, sed perperam Ambrosii nomine censentur)& Chrysostomum b, & Augustinum c, & Isidorum Hispalensem d, & Amalarium e, & Haimonem Halberstadensem f, & Rabanum Maurum g, & Hincmarum Rhemensem h, & ex locis in margine annotatis constat, & nuper fuse demonstravit ὁ πολυμαθέστατος Blondellus noster in Apologia Hieronymi de Episcopis; ut alios non paucos mittam, quos itidem de episcopis & presbyteris sensisse, & Blondellus probavit, & iis, quos commemoravi, partim quarti quintiq; partim septimi & noni saeculorum scriptoribus; Apostoli non fuerint Boviani Διατάξεις
units.tr: Hilary the Deacon [a], in his Commentaries (which are commonly, but wrongly, ascribed to Ambrose); by Chrysostom [b], by Augustine [c], by Isidore of Seville [d], by Amalarius [e], by Haimo of Halberstadt [f], by Rabanus Maurus [g], and by Hincmar of Reims [h]. This is clear from the passages noted in the margin, and our very learned Blondel has recently demonstrated it at length in his Apology for Jerome concerning Bishops. To pass over many others whom Blondel has shown to have held the same view about bishops and presbyters, some of them writers of the fourth and fifth centuries, others of the seventh and ninth: the Apostles were not the authors of the Constitutions of Bovius.

units.la: De Augustino idc ex eo videre est, quod Parmenianum Donatistam graviter quodam loco reprehendit, quod Mediatorem posuisset Episcopum inter populum & Deum; hasque voces vir sanctissimus ita exhorruit, ita ab omnium Piorum animo, auribus, atque usu alienas esse putat, ut si quis vel Apostolus se pro ovibus sibi creditis Mediatorem apud Deum esse profiteretur, quis (inquit i) eum ferret bonorum, atque fidelium Christianorum? Quis sicut Apostolum Christi, & non sicut Antichristum intueretur? Moxque pluribus suam istam sententiam firmat. Homines (inquit) omnes Christiani invicem se commendant orationibus suis. Pro quo autem nullus interpellat, sed ipse pro omnibus hic unus verusque Mediator est. Subjicitque Paulum, quanquam sub capite praecipuum membrum, non tamen mediatorem se facere inter populum & Deum, sed rogare ut pro se orent invicem omnia membra corporis Christi. Nam si (inquit) esset Mediator Paulus, essent utique & caeteri coapostoli ejus, ac sic multi Mediatores essent, nec ipsi Paulo constaret ratio, qua dixerat, Unus enim Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Jesus. Haec ille. Atque nihil erat, quod indignaretur, nihil quod sic paratragoediaret, si Bovii Apostolos notos habuisset; qui plane eadem, eodemque modo dicunt, quo Parmenianus; Sic enim Episcopos alloquuntur ; ὑμεῖς τοῖς ἐν ὑμῖν λαϊκοῖς ἐστε προφῆται, ἀρχοντες καὶ ἡγούμενοι, ὡς βασιλεῖς, οἱ μεσῖται Θεοῦ τῆς πίστεως αὐτῶν. Vos estis vestris laicis Prophetae, principes, duces, Reges, MEDIATORES Dei, & fidelium ejus, Mox eadem ad laicos ; ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, ἔτος λόγε διάκονος, γνώσεως φύλαξ, μεσίτης θεοῦ καὶ ὑμῶν. Qui Episcopus est, hic est Minister verbi, scientiae custos, MEDIATOR Dei & vestrum. Profecto Augustinus istos, vel nun- a l. 2. c. 25. p. 752. c. b Ibid. c. 26. init. quam legerat, vel si legerat, non sicut Apostolos Christi, sed sicut Antichristos hac in parte intuitus erat. Huc etiam pertinet, quod idem Augustinus, dum Tertulliani de animae corpulentia sententiam (quod non semel facita) castigat,ac refellit, nusquam nostrorum Διαζηγέων diserta illa in eam rem, quae supra exhibuimus, verba adfert, haud dubie non omissurus, nisi ea nescivisset. Idemque de Claudiano Mamerti Viennensis fratre, dictum puta; qui circa quinti saeculi finem ex professo defendens adversus Faustli Regensis errorem animam esse incorpoream, idque multis, subtilissime sane atque acutissime conficiens disertissimam Apostolorum professionem c, Animam in nobis incorpoream confitemur, sine flagitio praetermittere non poterat, si quid hujusmodi vere ab Apostolis dictum scivisset, aut sensisset; maxime qui in eodem opusculo suae huic sententiae firmamenta, etiam apud homines, & saeculi, ut Philosophos; & Ecclesiae, ut Patres, conquirat; Gregorium Nazianzenum, Ambrosium, Augustinum, in rem suam laudans d.
units.tr: That Augustine did not hold these rules can be seen from the fact that he rebukes Parmenian the Donatist severely in one place, because Parmenian had called the bishop a mediator between the people and God. That holy man so shrank from these words, and thought them so foreign to the mind, ears and practice of all the pious, that he says: if anyone, even an Apostle, professed that he was a mediator with God on behalf of the sheep entrusted to him, who (he asks) of good and faithful Christians would bear it? Who would look on him as an Apostle of Christ and not as Antichrist? He then confirms his opinion at length: "All Christians (he says) commend one another to their prayers. But for whom does no one intercede, while he himself is the one true Mediator for all." He adds that Paul, though a chief member under the Head, did not make himself a mediator between the people and God, but asked that all the members of Christ's body pray for him in turn. "For if (he says) Paul were a mediator, his fellow Apostles would also be mediators, and so there would be many mediators; nor would the reasoning of Paul himself stand, when he said: 'For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'" So he wrote. And there would have been nothing to rouse his indignation, nothing to make him so theatrical, if he had known the Apostles of Bovius; for they say exactly the same things in exactly the same way as Parmenian. They address bishops thus: "You are prophets to the laity among you, rulers and leaders, like kings, the mediators [μεσῖται] of God for their faith." Then they say the same to the laity: "The bishop, who is the minister of the Word, the keeper of knowledge, is the mediator [μεσίτης] of God and of you." You are prophets, rulers, leaders and kings to your laity, the mediators of God and of their faith. The bishop is the minister of the word, the keeper of knowledge, the mediator of God and of you. Surely Augustine, either before he had read these words or, if he had read them, regarded such men in this respect not as Apostles of Christ but as Antichrists. To this also belongs the fact that Augustine, when he censures and refutes Tertullian's opinion on the corporeality of the soul (which he does more than once [a]), never quotes those clear words of our Constitutions which we set out above on this point; he would undoubtedly not have omitted them, if he had not known them. The same may be said of Claudian Mamertus, brother of the bishop of Vienne. Near the end of the fifth century, defending in set form against the error of Faustus of Riez that the soul is incorporeal, and proving this very subtly and acutely with many arguments, he could not have passed over without disgrace the clearest confession of the Apostles, "We confess the soul within us to be incorporeal" [c], if he had known or thought that anything of this kind had truly been said by the Apostles. This is especially so because in the same little work he gathers support for his view both from men of the world, such as the philosophers, and from the Church, such as the Fathers, praising Gregory Nazianzen, Ambrose and Augustine for his purpose [d].

units.la: Praeterea Judam negant οἱ Δαζηγεῖς Eucharistiae sacramentum a Christo una cum reliquis Apostolis accepisse. Παρακλῆς ὁ ἡμῶν (inquiunt de Christo e) τὰ ἀντίτυπα μυστήρια μυστήεια τῆς τιμῆς σώματος αὐτῶ καὶ αἵματος, Ἰσσα μὴ συμπαρόντος ἡμῖν, ἐξῆλθεν εἰς τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν. Cum autem tradidis-set nobis (Iesus) antitypa mysteria pretiosi corporis & sanguinis sui, absente Juda, egressus est in montem Oliveti. Augustini vero constans est sententia a Iudam sacramentum Dominici corporis & sanguinis una cum caeteris Apostolis accepisse. Ergo fieri nequit, ut Διαθήκης pro Apostolis habuerit Augustinus. Eademque est aliorum non paucorum Patrum ratio, qui idem hac de re cum Augustino senserunt, ut Chrysostomus b, Hieronymus c, Leo d, alii; Itemque recentiorum ex adversariorum partibus, qui una cum iis Iudam sacrae Domini caenae & interfuisse, & communicasse volunt; ut Jansenius Gandavensis e, Vitriacus f, Estius g, & caeteri fere omnes. Istos omnes vel nullam Christi Apostolis fidem habuisse fatendum est; vel istos Bovii Διαθήκης aut nescivisse (quod de veteribus verius puto) aut certe si scierunt, pro Apostolis, Apostolicisve viris minime habuisse.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Constitutions [οἱ Διαταγεῖς] deny that Judas received the sacrament of the Eucharist from Christ together with the other Apostles. They say of Christ [e]: "When our Lord had given to us [the Apostles] the antitypal mysteries [τὰ ἀντίτυπα μυστήρια] of the precious body and blood, Judas being absent, he went out to the Mount of Olives." When Jesus had delivered to us the antitypes of the mysteries of his precious body and blood, Judas being absent, he went out to the Mount of Olives. But Augustine holds firmly [a] that Judas received the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood together with the other Apostles. So it cannot be that Augustine regarded the Constitutions as from the Apostles. The same view is held by many other Fathers who agree with Augustine on this matter, such as Chrysostom [b], Jerome [c], Leo [d], and others. Likewise, among recent writers on the opposing side, who insist that Judas both was present at the Lord's Supper and communicated there: Jansen of Ghent [e], Vitriacus [f], Estius [g], and nearly all the rest. We must either say that all these men had no faith in the Apostles of Christ, or that they did not know the Constitutions of Bovius (which I think is more likely for the ancients), or, if they did know them, that they certainly did not regard them as from the Apostles or from apostolic men.

units.la: Huc accedit quod Augustinus interdum dubitat h, an Maria quae pedes Domini unxit unguento & tersit capillis suis, quos laverat
units.tr: Moreover, Augustine sometimes doubts whether Mary, who anointed the Lord's feet with ointment and wiped them with her hair, which she had washed with her tears, is the sister of Lazarus, and he inclines to believe that she is; at other times he even affirms that she is the same woman.

units.la: c Concord. c. 130.132. f hist. occid. c. ult. g In Ioa. 13. 26. Luc. 7. Ioan. 11. h In Ioan. tract. 49. laverat lacrymis, ipsa sit soror Lazari, eoque propendet ut esse credat; interdum etiam eandem esse affirmat. At cum Ἀιάχ- ῥ eandem esse negent, aperteque Magdalenam a Lazari sorore (quod supra diximus) distinguant; nihil erat, cur Augustinus (si eos pro veris Apostolis habebat) non modo affirmaret, utramque mulierem eandem fuisse, sed etiam cur dubitaret ⁊ quin altera ab altera diversa sit.
units.tr: c Concord. c. 130.132. f hist. occid. c. ult. g In Ioa. 13. 26. Luc. 7. Ioan. 11. h In Ioan. tract. 49. But since they deny that she is the same, and clearly distinguish Magdalene from Lazarus's sister (as we said above), there was no reason why Augustine, if he regarded them as true Apostles, should not only affirm that the two women were one, but also doubt whether the one is not different from the other.

units.la: Quid? quod, si Baronio credimus, non Augustinus modo, sed & Ambrosius, & Hieronymus, & Gregorius, & Beda, & multi alii Patres, idem quoque senserunt; scilicet illam mulierem diversis Magdalenæ, sororisque Lazari nominibus insignem, unam eandemque revera fuisse? Quo loco verba Baronii usurpare satis est;
units.tr: What then? If we believe Baronius, not only Augustine but also Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory, Bede, and many other Fathers held the same view, namely that the woman who is distinguished by the names Magdalene and Lazarus's sister was in fact one and the same person? On this point it is enough to quote Baronius's own words:

units.la: Sane quidem (inquit d) si hæc (de distinctione Magdalenæ a Maria Lazari sorore vel ab Apostolis, vel) à Clemente dicta sunt; quomodo ea latere potuerunt tot antiquos Patres, qui ea de rescripserunt, cum præsertim tanti authoris præcipua fuerit authoritas in Ecclesia? adeo ut licet ejus epistola ad Corinthios scripta penitus exciderit, tamen quod sæpius citata reperiatur, pane revivisset integra in fragmentis e. Certe cuilibet adjudicata causa fuisset, qui authoritate Clementis id demonstrare
units.tr: "Certainly (he says d), if these things (about the distinction between Magdalene and Mary, Lazarus's sister, or the Apostles) were said by Clement, how could they have escaped so many ancient Fathers, who wrote on them, especially since the authority of so great an author was pre-eminent in the Church? So much so that although his epistle to the Corinthians has been entirely lost, yet because it is found cited so often, it would have been revived whole in fragments. Certainly anyone could have won his case who could have demonstrated this by the authority of Clement."

units.la: e nostra memoria toto corpore revixit ex manuscripto Theclæ codice, excusa o-nii strare potuisset. Atqui hac à Clemente dicta, eodem teste Baronio, antiquos illos omnes Patres latuerunt; Ergo, eodem assentiente, fieri non potest, ut verè Clementis sit illud Διαθηκῶν volumen, in quo verba illa leguntur. Cui argumento & hoc alterum addamus; Qui Clementis authoritate in hac de duplici illa Maria quæstione nituntur, iis, Baronio judice, adjudicanda est causa. Non tamen vel hodie iis causa apud Ecclesiam Romanam adjudicatur, qui Δια-θηκης authoritate in hac controversia nituntur; ergo vel iniqua & injusta est Romana Ecclesia, vel sane Clementis authoritate non nituntur, qui his Διαθηκης Boviani dictis nituntur. Nituntur autem authoritate Clementis, si vere Clemens est ὁ Διαθηκὴς, Ergo Διαθηκὴς Clemens non est, vel ipsa Romæ Ecclesia judice; quicquid contra tendant Bovius & Turrianus: Romana enim Ecclesia diversas illas fuisse mulieres ex Διαθηκῶς authoritate probantibus causam hanc adeo non adjudicat, ut etiam in diversam eorum partem, qui unam mulierem fuisse volunt, manifeste propendeat; quod ex ipso Baronio Maldonato b, & cæteris pene omnibus istarum partium Theologis patet.
units.tr: e "In our own time it was revived in its entire body from the manuscript codex of Thecla, printed..." Yet, on Baronius's own testimony, all those ancient Fathers were ignorant of "these things said by Clement." Therefore, with his agreement too, it cannot be that the Diathēkē [Διαθήκη] in which those words are read is truly Clement's. To this argument let us add another: those who rest their case in this question of the two Marys on the authority of Clement ought, by Baronius's judgment, to win it. Yet even today the Roman Church does not give judgment for those who rest on the authority of the Diathēkē in this controversy. Therefore either the Roman Church is unjust and unfair, or else those who rest on the sayings of Bovius's Diathēkē do not rest on the authority of Clement at all. They rest on the authority of Clement, if Clement is truly the author of the Diathēkē; therefore, by the Roman Church's own judgment, the Diathēkē is not Clement's, whatever Bovius and Turrianus may contend. For the Roman Church, when those who appeal to the authority of the Diathēkē maintain that the women were different, does not give judgment for their cause; rather, it manifestly inclines to the opposite side, namely of those who hold that there was one woman. This is clear from Baronius himself, from Maldonatus b, and from almost all the theologians of that party.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Arg. XXVI. Constitutiones vel nescierunt vel contempserunt & Gregorius M. & ejus discipulus Augustinus, & Beda, & plurimi liturgiæ interpretes etiam infimorum temporum.
units.tr: Argument XXVI. The Constitutions were either unknown to or disregarded by both Gregory the Great and his disciple Augustine, and by Bede, and by very many writers on the liturgy, even those of the lowest times.

units.la: Neque vero novum est, quod Ecclesia Romana istas Diataxes aut ɴescit, aut contemnit, quas ipsis Gregorii I. temporibus apparet nullo loco apud eam fuisse. Augustinum enim in Britanniam à Gregorio missum, verum ab eruditione, & sanctitate, & à Zeto in rem Romanam inter paucos eo sæculo commendatum non latuissent hæ constitutiones, si quo in nomine & honore apud illam sedem tum fuissent. Atqui Augustino ignotas fuisse ex iis patet, de quibus iste Gregorium contulit; à quo inter cætera quærit a, an prægnans mulier debeat baptizari? aut postquam genuerit, post quantum tempus possit Ecclesiam intrare? aut si menstrua consuetudine tenetur, an Ecclesiam intrare ei liceat? aut sacra communionis sacramenta percipere? aut vir sua conjugi permixtus, priusquam lavetur aqua, si Ecclesiam possit intrare? vel etiam ad mysterium communionis
units.tr: Nor is it new that the Roman Church either does not know these Constitutions or despises them, since it is clear that in the time of Gregory I they had no standing anywhere among them. For Augustine, sent by Gregory into Britain, and commended to the Roman cause by his learning and holiness, and by Zeto, among the few of that age, would not have missed these Constitutions if they had held any name or honour with that See at the time. Yet it is clear from the matters on which he consulted Gregory that they were unknown to Augustine. Among other things he asks a, whether a pregnant woman ought to be baptized? Or, after she has given birth, after how long she may enter the Church? Or, if she is subject to her monthly course, whether it is lawful for her to enter the Church, or to receive the sacred sacraments of communion? Or whether a man who has lain with his wife may enter the Church before he has washed in water? Or even approach the mystery of communion?

units.la: Apud Bedam hist. Eccl. l. 1. c. 7. T. 3. Bed. p. 21. in. nionis sacra accedere? Atqui de his & aliis id genus clara, disertaque lex apud nostros Διαθηκῶν extat a, quam & alibi recitavimus; Neque legitimus concubitus, neque partus, neque sanguinis fluxio, neque genitalis feminis per somnium excretio naturam hominis pollnere possunt, aut spiritum sanctum separare, praterquam sola impietas, & actio à lege interdicta. Hęc si scivisset, si Apostolica censuisset ille Anglorum Apostolus, nunquam profecto suum magistrum de negotio jam pridem ab Apostolis, & Clemente definito obtundendum putasset. Vel si ( quod non est credibile) ea erat hominis in Ecclesiæ suæ rebus ignorantia, ut etiam ejus leges nesciret; Gregorius quidem certe non erat ei hoc loco defuturus; Apostolorum illi decreta, quibus hæ quæstiones jam pridem definitæ erant, hoc loco recitaturus erat.Atqui ne ipse quidem in suo ad Augustini quæsita responso ullam Διαθηκῶν legem memorat; Et cum sic respondeat, ut quædam ab illa abhorrentia, quædam ei consentanea pronuntiet, neque hæc legis ab iis latę authoritate confirmat, neque illa ab ea vindicat. Nam quod negat b menstruam consuetudinem mulieribus culpam ullam esse, nostrorum Διαθηκῶν scitis, ut liquet, convenit; Quod vero vetat virum uxore usum, nisi aqua lotum' Ecclesiam intrare; vel lotum statim intrare; id omnes vident ab eorum disciplina esse alienum. Quin & haec diserta habet, Quamvis (inquit) de hac re diversa hominum nationes diversa sentiant, atque alia custodire videantur, Romanorum tamen semper ab antiquioribus usus fuit, post admixtionem propria conjugis, & lavacri purificationem quaerere, & ab ingressu Ecclesia paululum reverenter abstinere. Haec vero ille, quae cum Διαξάτων sententia pugnant, nunquam ab antiquioribus Romanorum repetivisset, si Clementem, antiquissimum Romanorum episcopum, Διαξέως authorem, scriptoremque esse scivisset, Itaque concludendum est, & Augustinum & Gregorium nostros Διαξάς vel nescivisse, vel certe nihili fecisse.
units.tr: (Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 7; vol. 3 of Bede, p. 21, near the beginning.) ...approach the sacred communion? Yet on these and similar matters our own Constitutions contain a clear and explicit law, which I have also quoted elsewhere: Neither lawful intercourse, nor childbirth, nor a flow of blood, nor the emission of seed in a dream can defile the nature of a man or drive away the Holy Spirit, except impiety and an act forbidden by the law alone. Had Augustine, the Apostle of the English, known this, or had he judged these to be apostolic, he would certainly never have thought that his master ought to be troubled about a matter long since settled by the Apostles and by Clement. Or if (which is not credible) the man was so ignorant of the affairs of his own Church that he did not know its laws, Gregory at least would not have failed him at this point; he would have recited the decrees of the Apostles, by which these questions had long been decided. Yet Gregory himself, in his reply to Augustine's questions, mentions no law of the Constitutions at all. And in answering he gives some rulings that are at odds with them and others that agree with them, and he confirms neither kind by any authority of that law, nor claims the one kind from it. For his denial that a woman's monthly course is any fault agrees, as is plain, with the teaching of our Constitutions. But his prohibition of a man entering the Church after intercourse with his own wife, unless he has washed in water, or entering immediately after washing, is plainly alien to their discipline. Indeed he also says this explicitly: Although different nations hold different views on this matter, and seem to observe different customs, nevertheless it has always been the custom of the Romans, from earlier times, to seek purification after union with one's own wife and after washing, and to keep a little reverently away from entering the Church. Yet he would never have appealed to the earlier Romans for these rulings, which conflict with the teaching of the Constitutions, if he had known that Clement, the most ancient bishop of the Romans, was the author and writer of the Constitutions. So we must conclude that Augustine and Gregory either did not know our Constitutions or certainly made no account of them.

units.la: Neque dum illi ex suis tenebris vel anno Domini 664. emerserant; ut ex eo apparet, quod cum Beda a aliquot Britannorum Scotorumque cum Anglis Romanisque de Pascha te dissidentium colloquia describat, nusquam memoret ad hanc decidendam litem in medium allatam Constitutionum authoritatem, Colmannus pro Scotis majorum traditionem, & Joannis Apostoli usum obtendit;
units.tr: Nor had they yet emerged from their darkness even in the year of the Lord 664. This is clear from the fact that Bede, describing the conferences of some Britons and Scots who differed from the English and Romans about Easter, never mentions that the authority of the Constitutions was brought forward to settle the dispute. Colman, for the Scots, pleads the tradition of their elders and the practice of the Apostle John;

units.la: a Ibid.c. 25.p.76. 77.78.c. 26. Vid. & 1.4. cpi-stolam Colfridi p.141. Vuilfrid pro Anglis Romæ, & reliqui (præter unum Britonum & Pictonum angulum) Christiani orbis consuetudinem, Petrique Apostoli institutum objicit; multaque alia, vana pleraque & incerta, utrique jactant. Διαταγὲων decretum, quod omnem hanc quæstionem ad unguem definit, nullus vel Vuilfrid, vel alius memorat. Ne ergo dubitaveris, quin ignotus istis fuerit τῶν Διατα-γέων codex.
units.tr: Ibid., chapter 25, pp. 76–78; chapter 26. See also the letter of Ceolfrid, p. 141. Wilfrid, for the English at Rome, and the rest (except a corner of the Britons and Picts), object the custom of the whole Christian world and the institution of the Apostle Peter; and they both throw out many other things, mostly vain and uncertain. Neither Wilfrid nor anyone else mentions the decree of the Constitutions [Διαταγῶν], which settles this whole question exactly. So do not doubt that the codex of the Constitutions [τῶν Διαταγῶν] was unknown to them.

units.la: Sed & hinc videre est, quam nihili nostras Constitutiones Latini fecerint. Constans est apud eos & jam inde à Gregorio I. ab omnibus fere, qui Liturgica scripserunt, diserte expressa sententia, simplicissimum fuisse Apostolicis temporibus eucharistiæ ritum. Gregorius quidem tradit, morem Apostolorum fuisse, ut ad ipsam solummodo orationem Dominicam oblationis hostiam consecrarent; precemque illam, quæ super oblationem dicitur, à Scholastico compositam esse ait. Alcuinus , qui sub Carolo Magno, circa octavi sæculi exitum, noni initia floruit, in missa tres tantum modo orationes in initio fidei prolatas fuisse scripsit. Amalarius, solam benedictionem Episcoporum, aut presbyterorum ad benedicendum panem & vinum, quo reficeretur populus ad animarum salutem, sine cantoribus, & lectoribus, & cæteris, quæ ibi agunter tur, satis esse, sicut (inquit) primævis temporibus fiebat apud Apostolos. Rabanus quoque ait a, quod Christus benedictione, & gratiarum actione corporis & sanguinis sui sacramenta dedicavit, exinde Apostolos imitatos fecisse, & successores suos facere docuisse; neque initio morem istum cantandi fuisse, qui nunc (inquit) in Ecclesia ante sacrificium celebratur: moxque docet quæ à quibus fuerint addita. Id ipsum multo accuratius exsequuntur Valafridus Strabo, & Rupertus Tuitiensis, viri suo quisque sæculo doctissimi; ille nono, hic duodecimo. Strabonis autem hæc sunt inprimis verba b; Quod nunc (inquit) agimus multiplici orationum, cantilenarum, & consecrationum officio, totum hoc Apostoli, & post ipsos proximus (ut creditur) orationibus & commemoratione passionis Dominicæ, agebant simpliciter. Mox; Relatio majorum est, ita primis temporibus missas fieri solitas, sicut modo in parasceve Paschæ (in quo die apud Romanos missæ non aguntur) communicationem facere solemus, id est præmissa oratione Dominica, & sicut ipse Dominus nos ter præcepit, commemoratione Passionis ejus adhibita, eos corpori Dominico communicasse & sanguini, quos ratio permittebat. Proficiente dehinc religione amplius aucta sunt à Christi cultoribus ribus officia missarum, &c. quod aliqui sequentium Apostolis fuerint scientia, vel religiositate majores, sed quia illi maxime curabant ab infidelitate ad fidem, à tenebris homines ad lucem vocare & in veritate stabiles reddere ipsa facilitate religionis melius, quod volebant, rudibus persuadere potuerunt. Rupertus vero Tuitiensis suam hanc dissertationem ita orditur; Olim non tanto exteriori apparatu decoris Missarum solennia celebrabantur; nec ab uno quolibet omnis religiosi obsequii gloria consummata & perpolita est. Idem multis ante Rupertum annis docuerat Berno Abbas; idque allatis, quæ nuper recitavimus, Gregorii verbis affirmaverat b; missæq; & canonem ipsum, & cætera paulatim à diversis suam singulis veluti symbolam conferentibus, aucta, ornataque, & expolita fuisse. Ac idem quoque tradit Micrologus ejusdem sæculi, id est undecimi scriptor c; & Radulphus item Tungrensis, qui cum multa in hanc rem vana afferat, illud tamen rotunde fatetur d; Ab initio cum adhuc novilla esset Ecclesia, Apostolos cum sanctificatione crucis & oratione Dominica, prout in quibusdam scripturis veteribus reperitur, & in quotidianis vestibus, & ligneis calicibus celebrasse. Author item ejus libri, qui Gemma Animæ inscribitur, Apostolos los ait a,super panem & vinum verba, qua Dominus dixit, & Dominicam orationem dixisse; quæ verba apud Hugonem de Sto. Victore ipsissima leguntur . Hæc eadem multi alii tradunt; omnia falsa, stulta, & ridicula, si supponas iis cognitas fuisse, & pro Apostolicis habita Bovianas Constitutiones; in quibus ipsi Apostoli totam Eucharistiæ liturgiam ita plene, atque affatim & multiplici precum sacrarum varietate, & tanto rituum atque cæremoniarum apparatu, & ea ministrorum copia, & eo vestium, cæterorumque externorum splendore instruxerunt, exornarunt, atque excoluerunt, ut posterorum diligentiæ, vel nihil, vel certe perpauca reliqua fecerint.
units.tr: But from this too one can see how little the Latins made of our Constitutions. Since the time of Gregory I, almost all who wrote on the liturgy have held, and firmly stated, that the rite of the Eucharist in apostolic times was most simple. Gregory indeed teaches that it was the custom of the Apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering by the Lord's Prayer alone, and he says that the prayer said over the offering was composed by a scholastic. Alcuin, who flourished under Charlemagne, around the end of the eighth century and the beginning of the ninth, wrote that in the Mass only three prayers were said at the beginning of the faith. Amalarius held that the blessing of the bishops or presbyters alone, to bless the bread and wine by which the people are refreshed for the salvation of their souls, without the singers, readers and the rest of what is done there, was enough, as (he says) it was in the earliest times among the Apostles. Rabanus also says that Christ dedicated the sacraments of his body and blood by blessing and thanksgiving, that the Apostles then imitated this, and taught their successors to do the same; and that at first there was no such custom of singing as is now celebrated in the Church before the sacrifice; and he goes on at once to teach what was added, and by whom. Valafrid Strabo and Rupert of Deutz, men most learned in their own centuries, treat the matter much more carefully, the former in the ninth and the latter in the twelfth century. The main words of Strabo are these: "What we now do with the many-fold office of prayers, chants and consecrations, the Apostles and those closest after them (as is believed) did in simplicity, with prayers and remembrance of the Lord's passion." Soon after: "It is the tradition of our elders that in the earliest times Masses were customarily celebrated as we now usually make communion on Good Friday (on which day Masses are not said among the Romans), that is, with the Lord's Prayer said first, and, as the Lord himself commanded us three times, with the remembrance of his Passion added, they communicated in the body and blood of the Lord those whom reason allowed. Then, as religion advanced, the offices of the Masses were increased by the worshippers of Christ, etc. Some of the later ones may have been more learned or more pious than the Apostles, but since the Apostles were most concerned to call men from unbelief to faith and from darkness to light, and to make them steadfast in the truth, they could more easily persuade the untutored of what they wished through the very simplicity of their religion." Rupert of Deutz begins his discourse thus: "Formerly the solemnities of the Mass were celebrated without such great outward display of splendour; nor was the whole glory of religious worship completed and polished by any one person." Berno the Abbot had taught the same many years before Rupert, and, citing the words of Gregory that we have just quoted, had affirmed that the Masses, and the canon itself and the rest, were gradually enlarged, adorned and polished by different people each contributing their share. The same is also handed down by the Micrologus of the same age, that is, a writer of the eleventh century; and likewise by Radulph of Tongres, who, though he asserts much that is vain on this matter, nevertheless plainly confesses this: "From the beginning, when the Church was still young, the Apostles celebrated with the sanctification of the cross and the Lord's Prayer, as is found in certain old writings, and with everyday garments and wooden chalices." The author also of the book called Gemma Animae says that the Apostles, over the bread and wine, said the words which the Lord spoke, and the Lord's Prayer; and these very words are read in Hugh of Saint-Victor. Many others hand down the same things. All of them are false, foolish and ridiculous, if you suppose that the Bovian Constitutions, which they regarded as apostolic, were known to them. In those Constitutions the Apostles themselves furnished, adorned and cultivated the whole liturgy of the Eucharist so fully and abundantly, with such manifold variety of sacred prayers, with such a great display of rites and ceremonies, with so many ministers, and with such splendour of vestments and other outward things, that the diligence of later generations left either nothing or very little to add.

units.la: Nemo certe negaverit, magno in id studio incubuisse, qui & duos diaconos operanti sacerdoti astare, cum pavonaceis caudis, muscaque prætervolantes abigere jusserunt; quæ diligentia usque adeo delicata est, ut ne nostro quidem hoc sæculo à Romanis hominibus, quantumvis ad omnem elegantiam expolitis, in suis Sacris, quod sciam adhibeatur. Itaque & Gregorium, & cæteros, quos memoravimus, necesse est Bovii <bl>Διαζυγίας</bl> vel omnino nescivisse, vel certe pro impostoribus habuisse; quibus scilicet nullam habuerunt fidem; putaruntque omnem illam orationum, cæremoniamoniarumque pompam, quam Boviani Διαθηκης Apostolis authoribus tribuunt, nihil habuisse cum Apostolorum simplicitate, atque parsimonia commune.
units.tr: No one will deny that those who devoted such great zeal to this had two deacons stand beside the officiating priest with peacock-feather fans, ordered to drive away the flies that flew past. This fastidiousness is so refined that, as far as I know, it is not used even in our own age in the sacred rites of Roman men, however polished they are in every elegance. It must therefore be that Gregory and the others we have mentioned either knew nothing at all of the Bovian Constitutions [Διαθήκης], or at least regarded them as impostors, to whom they accordingly gave no credence. They thought that all that pomp of prayers and ceremonies, which the Bovians attribute to the Apostles as authors of the Constitutions [Διαθήκης], had nothing in common with the simplicity and frugality of the Apostles.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Arg. XXVII. Valafrido Straboni ignota Constitutiones. Arg. XXVIII. Imo & toti Latinorum Ecclesia, quae duo earum de Exorcistis & inferioribus ordinibus decreta jampridem violat.
units.tr: Argument XXVII. The Constitutions were unknown to Valafridus Strabo. Argument XXVIII. Indeed, they also violate the whole Latin Church, which long ago broke with the two decrees of theirs concerning exorcists and the lower orders.

units.la: AC quando in istorum Liturgiae interpretum mentionem incidi, illud quoque praeter haec obiter annotare nō pigebit, Valafridum Strabonem, quam sibi incognitae fuerint Διαλάξεις eo insuper fateri, quod scribit, primis temporibus, illis solummodo baptismi gratiam dari solitam, qui & corporis & mentis integritate jam ad hoc pervenerant, ut scire & intelligere possent, quid emolumenti in baptismo consequendum, quid confitendum atque credendum; quid postremo renatis in Christo esset servandum; postea augescente divina religionis diligentia, cum intellexissent, peccato originali infectam esse totam hominum naturam, sana fidei sectatores statuisse parvulos baptizari in remissionem peccatorum; idem etiam
units.tr: And since I have come to the mention of these interpreters of the Liturgy, I will not hesitate to note in passing also this: that Valafridus Strabo, however unknown to him the Constitutions were, admits as much in what he writes: in the earliest times, grace of baptism was given only to those who had already reached the wholeness of body and mind to know and understand what advantage was to be gained from baptism, what was to be confessed and believed, and, finally, what was to be kept by those reborn in Christ; afterwards, as the diligence of divine religion grew, when they had understood that the whole nature of man was infected by original sin, the sound followers of the faith decided that infants should be baptized for the remission of sins; he also says the same thing.

units.la: am aita,primo simpliciter in fluviis vel son-tibus baptizatos fuisse credentes; inde cre-scente processu temporum religionis honore, & institutionum Ecclesiasticarum usque ad plenitudinem decus crevisse, & hujus mysti-ci lavacri gradatim per temporum aug-menta in majus celebrationem crevisse; addidisse enim alios chrismatis unctionem; quam ex veteri sumptam consuetudine ne-mo, qui dubitet, cum primis temporibus im-positione manuum baptismum confirmari soleret, &c. Alios addidisse exorci-smos, alios consecrationem fontis, &c.
units.tr: a, at first, that believers had been baptized simply in rivers or springs; then, as time advanced and the honour of religion grew, and the ecclesiastical institutions increased in dignity to their fullness, the celebration of this mystical washing gradually grew larger as the ages went on. For others added the anointing with chrism, which no one who doubts that in the earliest times baptism was usually confirmed by the laying on of hands would think was taken from the old custom, and so on. Others added exorcisms, others the consecration of the font, and so on.

units.la: Idem denique docetb,multa post revelatio-nem Euangelii tempora transisse, antequam ita ordinarentur quarundam per diem, & noctem horarum solennia, sicuti nunc ha-bentur. Haec ille nunquam ita scripsisset, si Bovianas Διατάξεις legisset, proque ve-ris habuisset; in quibus scilicet ipsos Apo-stolos audiisset difertissime jubentes & par-vulos baptizari, & chrismate tinctos o-mnes inungi, & exorcizari, & fontem benedici, & horas canonicas certo, statoque ordine precationibus obire, ευχάς επιτελεῖτε ὡρᾷς τρίτῃ ὥρᾳ, καὶ ἕκτῃ, καὶ ἐννάτῃ, καὶ ἑσπέρᾳ, καὶ ἀλεκτοροφωνίᾳ. Precationes facite mane, tertia hora, ac sex-ta, & nona, & vespere, & gallicinio.
units.tr: Finally, he teaches the same thing: b, many centuries passed after the revelation of the Gospel before the solemn hours of certain days and nights were arranged in the way they are now observed. He would never have written this if he had read the Boviani Constitutions and held them to be true. In them he would have heard the Apostles themselves most plainly commanding that infants be baptized, that all who were anointed with chrism be anointed, that they be exorcised, that the font be blessed, and that the canonical hours be kept in prayer at fixed and set times: [εὐχὰς ἐπιτελεῖτε ὥρᾳ τρίτῃ, καὶ ἕκτῃ, καὶ ἐνάτῃ, καὶ ἑσπέρᾳ, καὶ ἀλεκτοροφωνίᾳ] Perform prayers at the third hour, and the sixth, and the ninth, and evening, and cockcrow.

units.la: Denique (ut sit finis) duae sunt in Διατάξεων τάγμα. {τ}ταγέων Bovianorum volumine Constitutio-nes, etiam à Bellarmino inter errores notatæ, quæ liquido demonstrant, eos neque apud veterem, neque apud recentem Latinorum Ecclesiam pro Apostolis, Apostolicisve viris vel olim habitos fuisse, vel nunc haberi.
units.tr: Lastly (to bring this to an end), there are two Constitutions in the Boviani volume of the Constitutions, which Bellarmine also marked among the errors. They clearly show that these were neither regarded as the work of the Apostles, or of apostolic men, in the ancient Latin Church, nor are they so regarded now.

units.la: Prior constitutio decernit subdiaconis, lectoribus, & Diaconissis manus dum ordinantur, imponi; ὑποδιάκονον χειροτονῶν ὢ ἐπίσκοπε, ἐπιθήσεις ἐπ' αὐτῆς τὰς χεῖρας, Cum hypodiaconum ordinas Episcope, manus ei impones. Ἀναγνώστην c προχείεισαι, ἐπιθεὶς αὐτῷ τὴν χεῖρα. Lectorem elige, vel constitue, manum ei imponens. Περὶ δ d διακονίσσης Βαρθολομαῖος διατάσσομαι, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, ἐπιθήσεις αὐτῇ τὰς χεῖρας. De Diaconissa vero ego Bartholomæus constituo, ut manus ei, Episcope, imponas. Altera constitutio negat Exorcistam ordinari; ἐποχείσης δ χειροτονεῖται· ἐυνοίας δ' ἐκ τοῦ ἐπαδλον, ὁ χάειτο Θεῖ δ' ἀξ Χεὶς ἐπιφοίτησει τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι. Exorcista non fit ordinatione. Spontanea enim benevolentia est hoc certamen, & gratia Dei per Christum, superventione Spiritus Sancti. Cum his duobus Ἰῶν Διαλαγέων Bovianorum decretis pugnant primo Carthaginensis Concilii quarti a. D. 398. congregati, canones f: Subdiaconus, cum ordinatur, quia manus impositionem non accipit, patinam de Episcopi manu accipiat vacuam, & calicem vacuum. (Multo vero etiam minus vel Lector, vel Diaconisse ulla manus impositione ordinantur.) Tum a Exorcista cum ordinatur, accipiat de manu Episcopi libellum; & quae sequuntur. Sed & secundo ipsa, etiam hodierna Romanae Ecclesiae doctrina, ac praxis, (in qua notum est & exorcistas ordinari, & subdiaconis & aliis minorum, ut vocant, ordinum ministris nequaquam manus in ordinatione imponi) his Diatagmon decretis non minus adversatur. Ergo vel Apostolica neque fuit olim Africana quarti saeculi Ecclesia, neque est hodie Romana; vel istae certe Bovianae Διαταξεις Apostolicae non sunt censendae.
units.tr: The first Constitution orders that hands be laid on subdeacons, lectors and deaconesses when they are ordained: [ὑποδιάκονον χειροτονῶν, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, ἐπιθήσεις ἐπ' αὐτοῦ τὰς χεῖρας] When you ordain a subdeacon, bishop, you shall lay your hands on him. [ἀναγνώστην προχειρισάμενος, ἐπιθεὶς αὐτῷ τὴν χεῖρα] Choose or appoint a lector, laying your hand on him. [Περὶ δὲ διακονίσσης Βαρθολομαῖος διατάσσομαι, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, ἐπιθήσεις αὐτῇ τὰς χεῖρας] Concerning the deaconess, I, Bartholomew, give order, bishop, that you lay your hands on her. The other Constitution denies that an exorcist is ordained: [ἐξορκιστὴς οὐ χειροτονεῖται· ἐκ προαιρέσεως δὲ ἐκ τοῦ ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι, ὁ χάρισμα θεοῦ διὰ Χριστοῦ, ἐπιφοιτήσει τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος] An exorcist is not made by ordination. It is a contest undertaken from spontaneous goodwill, and the grace of God through Christ by the coming of the Holy Spirit. These two decrees of the Boviani Constitutions are opposed, first, by the canons of the Fourth Council of Carthage, assembled in the year of our Lord 398: A subdeacon, when he is ordained, because he does not receive the imposition of hands, shall receive from the bishop's hand an empty paten and an empty chalice. (Much less are lectors or deaconesses ordained by any imposition of hands.) Then, an exorcist, when he is ordained, shall receive a book from the bishop's hand; and what follows. But, secondly, the very doctrine and practice of the Roman Church even today (in which it is well known that exorcists are ordained, and that the hands are by no means laid on subdeacons and the other ministers of the so-called lesser orders in their ordination) is no less opposed to these decrees of the Diatagma. Therefore either the African Church of the fourth century was not apostolic, nor is the Roman Church today; or else those Boviani Constitutions cannot be considered apostolic at all.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Refellitur putida, frivolaque Trullanorum Patrum, & multorum recentium exceptio, Constitutiones haereticorum fraude, manuque corruptas fuisse caussantium.
units.tr: The foolish and flimsy objection of the Trullan Fathers, and of many recent writers, who claim that the Constitutions were corrupted by the fraud and hand of heretics, is refuted.

units.la: MULTA alia ejusdem generis ex quorumvis Christianismi saeculorum scriptoribus observari, & ad demonstrandam Constitutionum novitatem afferri possent. Sed haec, ut nobis quidem videtur, satis sunt.
units.tr: Many other things of the same kind could be observed in the writings of any centuries of Christianity and brought forward to show the novelty of the Constitutions. But these, as it seems to us, are enough.

units.la: Verum antequam manum de tabula, breviter expendendum est, quod jactari solet, corruptos fuisse Ἰῶν Διαταξεων codices. Trullani Patres jam olim (a. D. 691.) scripserunt a, ὅτι Ἰαΐς Ἰῶν Ἀποστόλων διὰ Κλήμεντος διατάξεισ πάλαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἑτεροδόξων ὅπι λύ-μη τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, νοθα τινὰ καὶ ξένα τῆς εὐ-σεβείας παρεγνεγέθησαν, τὸ ἐυπρεπὲς καλῶν θείων δογμάτων ἀμαυρώσαντα, Apostolorum per Clementem (constitutionibus jam olim ab heterodoxis ad labem Ecclesiæ aspergendam adulterina quaedam, & à pietate aliena assuta, & intermixta fuisse, divinorum nobis decretorum elegantiam, ac decoram speciem obscurantia. Hæc illi; quæ ad ea Constitutionum loca pertinere videntur, quæ Arianicam impietatem spirant; quorum nos specimen supra exhibuimus. Bovius, & alii Διαταξεων patroni, quia & ii ipsi, qui opus inter apocrypha censent, Baronius, Bellarminus, alii, eo quoque interdum confugiunt, ut quæ ex eo volumine sibi objiciuntur, ea dicant non esse authoris γνήσια, sed ab alia manu per fraudem codici inserta. Ita Bovius eam de Paschate Διάταξιν, quæ libri quinti capite vel decimonono (ut habet Turrianica editio) vel decimo-octavo (ut habet Boviana) extat, totam expungendam putat b; In hoc caput b (inquit) nihil jam annotandum est, sed id totum potius delendum, ut nothum ac novum. Ita aliam Διάταξιν, in qua sabbatum à jejunio immune esse debere statuitur, & Baronius & Bellarminus, & ipse etiam Petavius, à Græcis vel effictam, vel certe in suum sensum corruptam fuisse volunt. Denique ad hanc velut sacram anchoram confugiunt, quoties aliquid objicitur, quod nulla techna, nullo commento solvi, aut explicari potest. Ego vero, si qua occurreret in manuscriptis codicibus lectionis in iis locis diversitas, facile iis concederem, aliquid in iis ex caussæ studio vel à Græcis vel ab aliis factum mutatum. Nunc cum summo omnes codices consensu ea ipsa, quæ isti expungi cupiunt, integra, ac illibata pariter exhibeant; summæ, nec ferendæ est impudentiæ ea quidem, quæ causæ tuæ nihil officiunt, authoris esse velle; quæ vero tibi adversantur, ea notha ac aliena esse contendere. Quod si id tibi juris in veterum libros lumis, frustra tecum ex iis disputabitur. Nihil in tota hac disputatione certi super erit. Quod enim tu de his locis Græcos pulsas, illi te itidem de iis accusabunt, quæ ex Latinis pro Sabbati jejunio afferre soles. Caussabuntur ea antiquis scriptoribus ex caussæ studio falso fuisse affecta. Atque ita in fumos abibit omnis veterum librorum fides, mutuis disputantium aliorum in alios calu-
units.tr: Yet before I lift my hand from the tablet, it must be briefly considered what is commonly bandied about, that the codices of the Constitutions have been corrupted. The Trullan Fathers wrote long ago (in the year of our Lord 691) that [ὅτι ἐν ταῖς διὰ Κλήμεντος Ἀποστόλων διατάξεσιν πάλαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἑτεροδόξων εἰς λύμην τῆς Ἐκκλησίας νόθα τινὰ καὶ ξένα τῆς εὐσεβείας παρεγγεγράφθαι] that in the Constitutions of the Apostles through Clement, adulterous matter alien to piety had long ago been inserted by heterodox men to stain the Church, and had obscured the elegance and fair appearance of the divine decrees for us. So they wrote; and these words seem to refer to those passages of the Constitutions which breathe Arian impiety, of which we have given an example above. Bovius and the other defenders of the Constitutions, because even those who count the work among the apocrypha, Baronius, Bellarmine and others, sometimes take refuge in this too, say that whatever is objected to them from that volume is not the genuine work of the author, but was inserted into the codex by another hand through fraud. Thus Bovius thinks that the Constitution about Easter, which is found in the eighteenth or nineteenth chapter of the fifth book (depending on whether one has the Turrian edition or the Boviani), should be struck out entirely: In this chapter, he says, nothing more is to be noted, but rather the whole of it must be deleted, as spurious and recent. So too Baronius, Bellarmine, and Petavius himself wish that another Constitution, in which it is laid down that the Sabbath must be free from fasting, was either made up by the Greeks or at least corrupted to suit their own view. Finally, they flee to this as to a sacred anchor whenever something is objected which cannot be dissolved or explained by any art or contrivance. For my part, if any variant readings appeared in the manuscript codices in those places, I would readily grant that something there had been changed by the Greeks or others from zeal for their cause. But since all the codices agree, with one accord, in presenting intact and unimpaired those very passages which they wish to expunge, it is a supreme and intolerable impudence to claim as the author's own those things which do not hurt your cause, and to contend that those which oppose you are spurious and alien. And if you claim this right over the old books, it will be in vain to dispute with you on their basis. Nothing certain will remain in this whole dispute. For just as you drive the Greeks from these passages, they will likewise accuse you of those things which you are wont to bring from the Latins in support of the Sabbath fast. They will charge that the ancient writers were falsely affected by zeal for a cause. And thus all faith in the old books will go up in smoke, shattered and crushed by the mutual calumnies of disputants accusing one another.

units.la: Note: the line "totum potius delendum" etc. as printed. calumniis fracta, ac elisa. Huc accedit, quod nullam fere veri speciem habeat omnis hæc istorum criminatio. Trullani Patres putant, sincero Apostolicorum Constitutionum codici inspersa ab hæreticis impia quædam, quæ in iis leguntur. Arianos, ut opinor, dicunt. Sed si hoc ab Arianis factum est, cum non alio, quam causæ suæ juvandæ studio id ab iis factum fuisse dici possit; cur illi quod quidem ex veterum monumentis sciamus, nunquam usi sunt his in disputando præsidiis? Miros nobis narras impostores; qui impostnram quidem faciunt; cæterum ob quem eam faciunt, fructum, nullum ex ea percipere satagunt. Tum, siquæ in his libris Ecclesiasticæ vel fidei, vel traditioni adversantur, eorum authores Ariani censendi sunt; cur vel quo consilio illa tam multa supra à nobis denotata peccarunt, quæ nihil plane ad Arianorum adversus Catholicos causam pertinent? Si hæc labes ab Arianis est, veraces erunt libri in iis, quæ nihil ad Arium. At præter hæc innumerabilia sunt, gravissima omnis generis in istis libris peccata. Non est ergo verisimile, adulteratos ab Arianis fuisse hos libros. Potius putaverim, eos ab homine & antiquatum Ecclesiasticarum parum perito, & insuper Ariano, jam inde à principio scriptos fuisse. Pari laborat ineptia Latinorum in Græ-
units.tr: Moreover, this whole accusation of theirs has hardly any appearance of truth. The Trullan Fathers think that impious matter, which is read in them, was sprinkled by heretics into the genuine codex of the Apostolic Constitutions. They mean the Arians, I suppose. But if this was done by the Arians, since it can be said to have been done by them for no other reason than zeal to help their own cause, why have they never used these defences in disputation, so far as we know from the monuments of the ancients? You tell us of strange impostors, who do indeed make the forgery, but strive to gain no fruit from it on whose account they make it. Then, if any passages in these books are opposed to the faith or to the tradition of the Church, their authors are to be counted as Arians; but why, or with what design, did those many things we have noted above go wrong, which have nothing at all to do with the Arian cause against the Catholics? If this blemish comes from the Arians, the books will be trustworthy in those things which have nothing to do with Arius. But besides these there are innumerable, most serious errors of every kind in these books. It is not likely, therefore, that these books were adulterated by the Arians. I would rather suppose that they were written from the beginning by a man ignorant of ecclesiastical antiquity, and moreover an Arian. The Latins labour under the same absurdity in regard to the Greeks-

units.la: Græcos calumnia. Græci enim, si libros istos vitiassent, ea tantum parte vitiassent, quę ad ipsorum adversus Latinos controversias spectat; cætera sincera, & à labe omni pura mansissent. Nunc longe aliter res habet; Nam & illa quæ Græcis in hac causa favent, paucissima sunt, & cætera, quæ nihil ad privatas Græcorum opiniones pertinent, contaminatissima sunt, & innumeris mendaciis, atque erroribus plena, quod ex iis quæ supra disputavimus, satis jam constare arbitror. Sed utcunque sese res habeat, de ea nobis quidem non est vehementer laborandum. Neque enim si vel ab Arianis, quæ Trullani denotant, vel à Græcis, quæ Latini, ea in Constitutionum codicem de suo præter sinceram primi scriptoris editionem infulta fuisse concesserimus, eo fiet, ut Apostolorum, vel Clementis vere fuerit primo scriptus ac editus Constitutionum codex; quia scilicet præter ista à Trullanis, Latinisque denotata alia sunt in iis libris pœne innumerabilia novitatis argumenta. Quo factum est, ut ipsi illi Baronius, Bellarminus, ac Petavius, qui fraudis hujus Græcos arcessunt, nihilofecius tamen de toto Διατάξεων opere graviter dubitent; imo ne dubitent quidem, quin id Apocryphum sit, falsoque vel Apostolis, vel Clementi suppositum. Denique si bene repureputes, hæc ipsa Trullanorum, Latinorumque exceptio evidentissime conficit,nihil minus quam Apostolicas, Clementinasve esse has Constitutiones. Illos enim utrosque (Trullanos, inquam, Patres, Latinosque Scriptores) aliquid sincero Constitutionum codici ab aliena manu additum, causantes, pariter convenio. Rogo, ut codicem aliquem Græcum, Latinumve edant, ac proferant, sincerum, à quo ista absint, quæ additicia, ac adulterina esse contendunt? Illi vero nullum proferre possunt; rotundeque adeo confitentur, nullos Constitutionum codices impias adulteratorum manus effugisse; omnes eorum fraude corruptos fuisse, ac vitiatos. Cum vero clarum, manifestumque sit, non alios vel ab hæreticis, vel à schismaticis vitiatos esse, vel vitiari potuisse Constitutionum codices, quam quos ipsi penes se, & in sua potestate habebant; profecto horum alterum fatendum est, vel sinceros, etiam post hæreticorum & schismaticorum scelus, aliquos remansisse penes Catholicam Ecclesiam Apostolicarum Constitutionum codices, quo tempore vitium iis oblatum est. (Neque enim credibile est etiam eos ipsos, qui penes Catholicos erant, ab hæreticis & schismaticis fuisse corruptos.) Atqui Trullani Patres liquido confitentur, sinceros ros Constitutionum libros, & ab ea hæreticorum, de qua conqueruntur, labe intactos nullos fe penitus nolle; qui scilicet totum illud Διαταξεων opus ob istam labem explodunt, atque abjiciunt, quod ex veris, sincerisque codicibus emendari, ac corrigi jussissent, fiqui ipsis melioris notæ libri fuissent, quam ii, qui ab haereticis corrupti circumfereban- tur. Neque enim librum vere Apostoli- cum quisquam ideo, quod ab aliquo hæretico corruptus fit, abjiciendum putaverit; fiquis suppetat ejus sincerus ac emendatus codex. Neque Catholici, credo, Lucæ Evangelium & Pauli epistolas ideo olim abjecerunt, quod multi utriusque operis circumferrentur à Marcione vitiati, multisque modis interpolati codices. Planum ergo est, Tertullianorum Patrum temporibus nullum fuisse Constitutionum codicem, à quo ista abessent, quæ illi additicia esse putant. Jam neque nostra memoria ullus repertus est earundem Constitutionum liber manu scriptus, in quo illa, quæ nunc Latini à Græcis affuta ajunt, desiderentur; eademque in Constitutionibus jam olim ante fexcentos annos fuisse, certa inde fides est, quod ea ipsa Latinis jam tum objiceret Nicetas; quo tempore Humbertus, non quod nunc alii Latini, hæc à GræGræculorum, non ab authoris manu, esse respondebat; sed simplicius, & meliori quidem fide ipsum Constitutionum opus, ut apocryphum, & fabulosum, & à Patribus rejectum, totum respuebat. Ex his satis, ni fallor, liquet, nullum superfuisse Constitutionum codicem ab hæreticorum, & schismaticorum fraude intactum, atque illæsum. Itaque illud alterum, quod posui, necessario statuendum est, nullos penitus apud Catholicos fuisse Constitutionum Apostolicarum codices, quo illi tempore ab hæreticis, & schismaticis temerati sunt. (Si enim apud eos aliqui fuissent, ii profecto, etiam post alios codices corruptos, sinceri ac puri remansissent.) Quod si verum est, (ut sane est, & quidem necessario, si stet quod isti volunt, vitiatos fuisse Constitutionum libros) quis non ex eo ipso intelligit, nihil minus quam pro veris Apostolorum, Clementive libris habitas ab illorum temporum Catholicis fuisse Bovianas Διαταξεις? Scilicet ejus operis, quod vere illorum authorum fuisse crederet, nullum apud se Ecclesia, neque Græca, neque Latina, codicem haberet? hunc thesaurum, suæ fidei, ac curæ creditum, sic negligeret, ut eum sibi de manibus totum eripi ab inimicis, corrumpique sineret? Vos, Trullani, appello; qui ab heterodorodoxis notha quædam, & à pietate aliena huic operi admixta fuisse dicitis. Cur ista spuria, & adulterina à sinceris non secernitis? cur opus ex Ecclesiasticorum codicum fide non emendatis ac repurgatis? Nullos (inquiunt) habemus codices sinceros. Quis eos vobis, quis majoribus vestris de sinu, ac de scriniis eripuit? Siccine custoditis divinum Apostolorum à Clemente apud parentes vestros depositum fidei ac pietatis monumentum? Ubi fides? ubi pietas? ac vigilantia vestra? ut vobis librum Apostolicum hostis sic totum excusserit, ut ne unum quidem ejus exemplar sanum, ac integrum penes vos remanserit?
units.tr: The Greeks are charged with it too. If the Greeks had corrupted these books, they would have corrupted only the parts that bear on their own controversies with the Latins, and the rest would have remained sound and free of all taint. The situation is quite different. The few passages that favour the Greeks in this matter are very rare, while everything else, which has nothing to do with the Greeks' particular opinions, is thoroughly contaminated and full of countless falsehoods and errors. I think this is already sufficiently clear from what we have argued above. However the matter stands, we need not be greatly troubled about it. Even if we grant that the things the Trullan Fathers mark as Arian, or the Latins mark as Greek, were foisted into the codex of the Constitutions by someone's own hand, apart from the genuine edition of the first writer, it does not follow that the codex of the Constitutions was truly first written and published by the Apostles or by Clement. For apart from those things that the Trullans and Latins have pointed out, there are in these books almost countless other signs of novelty. This is why Baronius, Bellarmine and Petavius themselves, who blame the Greeks for this fraud, nonetheless seriously doubt the whole work of the Διατάξεις; indeed they do not even doubt that it is apocryphal and falsely attributed to the Apostles or to Clement. Finally, if we weigh the matter properly, this very exception taken by the Trullans and the Latins proves most clearly that these Constitutions are by no means Apostolic or Clementine. For both parties (I mean the Trullan Fathers and the Latin writers) agree in alleging that something was added by a foreign hand to the genuine codex of the Constitutions. I ask them to produce and publish some Greek or Latin codex, genuine, from which those things they claim are supplementary and adulterated are absent. They cannot produce one. Indeed they flatly confess that no codex of the Constitutions escaped the impious hands of the corrupters, and that all of them were corrupted and spoiled by fraud. But since it is clear and manifest that the codices of the Constitutions were corrupted, or could have been corrupted, by heretics or schismatics only if they were in the possession of those same people, one of two things must be admitted: either some genuine codices of the Apostolic Constitutions remained with the Catholic Church even after the crime of the heretics and schismatics, at the time when the damage was done to them (for it is not credible that even those codices which were in Catholic hands were corrupted by heretics and schismatics), or... Yet the Trullan Fathers plainly confess that they do not wish to have any genuine books of the Constitutions, untouched by that heretical taint of which they complain. They reject and cast aside that whole work of the Διαταξεων because of that taint, though they would have ordered it to be emended and corrected from genuine and sound codices, if they had had books of better quality than those that were handed about corrupted by heretics. For no one would think that a book truly Apostolic should be thrown away merely because some heretic has corrupted it, provided a genuine and emended codex of it is available. Nor, I believe, did Catholics ever reject the Gospel of Luke and the epistles of Paul on the ground that many codices of both works, adulterated by Marcion, were in circulation and interpolated in many ways. It is plain, then, that in the time of the Tertullian Fathers there was no codex of the Constitutions free of those additions which the Latins think spurious. Nor in our own memory has any manuscript copy of these same Constitutions been found in which the things the Latins now say were added by the Greeks are absent. And that these things were already in the Constitutions six hundred years ago is certain from the fact that Nicetas already objected them to the Latins; at that time Humbert did not reply, as some Latins do now, that these things were from a Greek hand and not from the author's; rather, more simply and with better faith, he rejected the whole work of the Constitutions as apocryphal, fabulous, and rejected by the Fathers. From this, unless I am mistaken, it is sufficiently clear that no codex of the Constitutions survived untouched and unharmed by the fraud of heretics and schismatics. Therefore the other alternative that I put forward must necessarily be affirmed: that among the Catholics at that time there were no codices of the Apostolic Constitutions at all which the heretics and schismatics had violated. (For if there had been any among them, those would surely have remained sound and pure even after the other codices were corrupted.) And if this is true (as it certainly is, and indeed necessarily so, if what those men want holds, that the books of the Constitutions were corrupted), who does not understand from this very fact that the Bovian Διαταξεις were by no means regarded by the Catholics of those times as the true books of the Apostles or of Clement? For would the Church, Greek or Latin, have no codex of a work it believed to be truly by those authors? Would it so neglect this treasure, entrusted to its faith and care, as to let it be snatched entirely from its hands by enemies and corrupted? I appeal to you, Trullan Fathers, who say that certain spurious and alien-to-piety matters were mixed into this work by heterodox men. Why do you not separate those spurious and adulterated things from the genuine? Why do you not emend and purge the work by the testimony of the ecclesiastical codices? You say, "We have no genuine codices." Who tore them from your bosom and from your cabinets, from you or from your forebears? Is this how you guard the divine monument of faith and piety, deposited by Clement with your ancestors as the Apostles' work? Where is your faithfulness? Where is your piety, and your vigilance? Did the enemy shake the Apostolic book out of your hands so completely that not even one sound and whole copy of it remained with you?

units.la: Atqui longe alia fuit Ecclesiæ veteris in eos, quos vere Apostolicos fuisse scimus, libros cura, ac providentia. Sæpe illos hæretici vitiarunt, mutilarunt, auxerunt, interpolarunt, suisque zizaniis impleverunt; nunquam ita penitus in sacros illos codices grassati sunt, ut non aliqua semper exstiterint apud Ecclesiam integra, atque illæsa divinorum librorum exemplaria. Absit, ut quæ hos tam studiose, tamque sollicite puros atque incorruptos servavit, ac vobis tradidit, eam nos Ecclesiam existimemus in alios, siquos nosset veros Apostolorum vel Apostolici Clementis partus, ita futuram fuisse negligentem, ut eos ab exteris Omnes rapi, ac violari sineret; vobis neunum quidem eorum exemplar verum, ac sincerum relinqueret. Hæc, si ipsa quoque vel Apostolica, vel Clementina vere effent, vetus Ecclesia & custodiisset accurate, & ad posteros fideliter propagaffet, neque ulla hæreticorum fraus effecisset, quominus sacrum hoc peculium apud vos à majoribus depositum nunc quoque maneret. Hoc ipsum, quod vos vultis corruptos esse omnes omnino Constitutionum codices, liquido arguit, non fuisse eas vel ab Apostolis, & Clemente Ecclesiæ ab initio traditas, vel ab Ecclesia eo loco, atque numero habitas. Nihil enim eorum, quæ hujus census sunt, vetus Ecclesia aut interire, aut sic in universum deformari, ac corrumpi passa est. Ac ne id fiat, & ad Dei providentiam, & ad hominum salutem, atque ædificationem pertinet. Eadem ratio adversus similia caussantes Latinos militat; & quidem eo validius, quod cum Clemens, Romæ Episcopus, Constitutionum scriptor fuisse dicatur, Romanæ quam ullius alterius Ecclesiæ majorem esse decuit curam, ac sollicitudinem in eo πειμηλίῳ asservando, tuendoque, ac custodiendo, quod ab uno ex primis, sanctissimisque ejus antistitibus apud ipsam depositum, ipsius quodammodo proprium peculiareque erat.
units.tr: But the care and providence of the ancient Church toward those books which we know to have been truly Apostolic was quite different. Heretics often corrupted, mutilated, enlarged, interpolated and filled those books with their own tares; yet they never raged so thoroughly against those sacred codices that there did not always remain with the Church some whole and unharmed copies of the divine books. Far be it from us to think that the Church which kept these books so carefully and so diligently pure and uncorrupted, and handed them down to you, would have been so careless about any other books, if it had known them to be genuine productions of the Apostles or of the Apostolic Clement, that it would have allowed them to be seized and violated by outsiders, leaving you not even one true and sound copy of them. If these books too were truly either Apostolic or Clementine, the ancient Church would have guarded them accurately and handed them on faithfully to posterity, and no fraud of heretics would have prevented this sacred treasure, deposited with you by your forebears, from remaining with you even now. The very fact that you want all the codices of the Constitutions to have been wholly corrupted clearly shows that they were neither handed down to the Church from the beginning by the Apostles and Clement, nor regarded by the Church as having that rank and number. For the ancient Church never allowed anything of this kind either to perish, or to be so entirely deformed and corrupted. And that this should not happen pertains both to the providence of God and to the salvation and edification of men. The same argument tells against the Latins, who make similar objections; and it does so all the more forcefully because, since Clement is said to have been the writer of the Constitutions while bishop of Rome, the Roman Church ought to have shown greater care and concern than any other Church in preserving, safeguarding and keeping this treasure [κειμηλίῳ], which was in a sense its own and peculiar possession, since it had been deposited there by one of its earliest and most holy bishops.

units.la: {§} Ms. text as printed. erat. Quod cum non fecerit, sed a fchif-maticis totum invadi, ac occupari ita passa sit, ut ne unum quidem exemplar ab eorum manibus illæsum defenderit; apparet, totum opus quam nihili fecerit, quam non Apostolicum censuerit. Certe id usque adeo despexit, ut ne Latine quidem ab aliquo suorum hominum verti olim justerit, aut sategerit; Ac ne unum quidem id volumen apud nos aliud, quam Græcum extaret, nisi Bovius, & Turrianus Latine nudius tertius edendum putassent. Ita quæ adversarii de operis hujus corruptione afferunt, ea ipsa nostram de ejus novitate sententiam clare, liquidoque confirmant.
units.tr: Ms. text as printed. erat. Since he did not do this, but allowed the schismatics to seize and occupy the whole thing in such a way that he did not preserve even a single copy unharmed from their hands, it is clear how little he valued the whole work and how little he judged it to be apostolic. Certainly he so despised it that he never ordered or took care to have it translated into Latin by any of his own people; and there would not even be that volume among us in any form other than Greek, had Bovius and Turrianus not thought fit to publish it in Latin only the other day. Thus the very things the opponents bring forward about the corruption of this work clearly confirm our opinion about its novelty.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Excutitur ac confutatur absurda, & inanis Albaspinei de Constitutionibus conjectura, sive potius deliratio.
units.tr: The absurd and empty conjecture of Albaspineus about the Constitutions is examined and refuted, or rather, his raving.

units.la: Itaque nullus nunc amplius superest locus dubitandi, quin vere, meritoque & nostri homines & adversariorum coryphæi Baronius, Bellarminus, Petavius, aliique, Bovianarum Constitutionum libros octo apocryphos esse censuerint; non ab Apostolis, quod libri ipsi mentiuntur, non à Clemente, quod præ se ferre operis titulus videtur, sed ab alio aliquo Apostolorum, & Clementis nomine multis post eos mortuos temporibus scriptos atque concinnatos fuisse.
units.tr: So there is now no longer any room for doubt that Baronius, Bellarmine, Petavius and others, both our own people and the leading champions of our opponents, were right and justified in judging the eight books of the Constitutions of Bovius to be apocryphal. They were not written by the Apostles, as the books themselves falsely claim, nor by Clement, as the title of the work seems to suggest.
