Rather, they were written and put together under the name of some one of the Apostles and of Clement by someone who lived many centuries after them.

units.la: Sed & ex superioribus liquido patet, salsissimum id esse, quod scribit Albaspineus nemini dubium esse debere, quin probus juxta & antiquus sit Constitutionum liber; certoque se affirmare posse, trecentis primis annis eo Ecclesiam Graecam, tanquam ritriali & Pontificali usam esse, quique eas attentius legerit, judicaturum, additas decursu temporum primis novas, quemadmodum & novae leges, ac Constitutiones in regimine Ecclesiae, novis occasionibus enatis, facta sunt.
units.tr: But it is also clear from what was said above that what Albaspineus writes is most absurd: that no one should doubt that the Constitutions are an honest and ancient book; that he can affirm with certainty that for the first three hundred years the Greek Church used it as its ritual and pontifical, and that whoever reads it more carefully will judge that new things were added over time, just as new laws and constitutions in the governance of the Church have been made as new occasions arose.

units.la: Quis vero illum crederet ita de iis ipsis Constitutionibus censurum, quas paulo ante negaverat Apostolorum authoritate sanctitas publicatasque? etiam velut imperitos sugillans, qui aliud de his affirmarent? An ergo probus huic Episcopo is liber videtur, qui mendaciis scatet? qui se Apostolicum aut Clementinum esse profitetur, cum neque Apostolicus sit, neque Clementinus? qui tempora miscet? totamque Apostolicae historiae seriem foedissime perturbat? qui sanctissimis Apostolis impias Arianorum Macedonianorumque voces affingit? qui inaudita festa, jejuniaque in Ecclesiam inducit? & alia hujus generis sexcenta peccat? cat? Si probi sunt hujus farinæ libri, haud e-quidem scio, qui nam mali ac improbi libri censendi sint. De libri ævo, quod addit, fateor non esse nuper natum, antiquum si dicit, ante quartum, quintumve sæculum scriptum, atque editum non assentior; & multa supra dixi, quæ aliud suadent. Quod vero certo affirmare se posse ait Albaspineus, eo libro tanquam rituali & Pontificali trecentis primis annis usam esse Græcam Ecclesiam, id inquam ego quidem non capio. Si enim (quod ille nunc ait) verum est, profecto necesse est, eum librum jam ab initio trium illorum sæculorum, scriptum, editumque fuisse ab Apostolis; (Neque enim fieri potest, ut Græcorum Rituale fuerit id volumen, quod nondum scriptum, nondum editum erat) Atqui ipse Albaspineus nuper negabat eas, quæ hoc libro habentur Constitutiones, ὑπὸ Apostolorum authoritate sancitas fuisse. Ergone Græca Ecclesia pro rituali Pontificalique, ipso Apostolorum ævo habebat Constitutiones, Apostolorum authoritate neque sancitas, neque publicatas? Ista mihi non videntur cohærere. Neque conjicere possum, quænam illa sint argumenta, quibus Albaspineus certo se affirmare posse ait, hunc librum trecentis primis annis Ecclesia Græca pro rituali fuisse. Nos vero supra fuse, liquidoque demonstra-
units.tr: Who would believe that he would pass such judgment on those very Constitutions, which he had just denied were sanctioned by the authority of the Apostles and published, even mocking as unskilled those who said otherwise? Is that book really sound in the Bishop's eyes, when it is full of lies? It claims to be Apostolic or Clementine, though it is neither Apostolic nor Clementine. It confuses the times and wrecks the whole sequence of Apostolic history in the most shameful way. It puts impious utterances of the Arians and Macedonians into the mouths of the most holy Apostles, introduces unheard-of feasts and fasts into the Church, and commits six hundred other errors of this kind. If books of this sort are sound, I really do not know what books should be called bad and wicked. As for the age of the book, which he adds, I admit it is not recently written, but I do not agree that it was written and published before the fourth or fifth century if he calls it ancient, and I have said much above that points the other way. But when Albaspineus says that he can affirm with certainty that the Greek Church used that book as a ritual and pontifical for the first three hundred years, I, for my part, do not grasp it. For if (as he now says) this is true, then the book must surely have been written and published by the Apostles from the very beginning of those three centuries (for the volume that was not yet written or published cannot have been the Greeks' ritual). Yet Albaspineus himself recently denied that the Constitutions contained in this book were sanctioned [ὑπὸ] by the authority of the Apostles. So did the Greek Church, in the Apostles' own age, have as its ritual and pontifical Constitutions that were neither sanctioned nor published by Apostolic authority? These claims do not seem consistent to me. Nor can I guess what arguments Albaspineus has in mind when he says he can affirm with certainty that the Greek Church used this book as a ritual for the first three centuries. We, however, have above fully and clearly demonstrated

units.la: monstravimus, multa esse in hoc libro de jejuniis, de festis, de aliis plurimis decreta Græcis Christianis partim primo, ac secundo, partim etiam toto tertio sæculo; imo etiam sequentibus ad nostram memoriam temporibus inusitata. Illud quidem scire pervelim, cujusnam sæculi Ecclesia apud Græcos institutum ab hoc suo scilicet Rituali sabbati festum observaverit? aut proximam post Pentecosten hebdomadem festam celebraverit, ex hoc suo Pontificali? ut alia mittam non pauca, quæ licet sequentia sæcula observaverint, primis tamen tribus nullo fuisse in usu constat? Denique quod ait Albaspineus, qui hos libros attentius legerit, eum judicaturum additas decursu temporum primis novas constitutiones, quemadmodum nova leges in regimine Ecclesiæ, novis occasionibus enatis, facta sunt; id, inquam, nulla necessaria atque evidenti ratione vel probat, vel probare potest. Fateor, quod ille ait esse verissimum, novas in Ecclesia leges pro re nata, interdum etiam abs re, factas, & antiquis additas esse; eoque Ecclesiasticam & fidem & disciplinam e simplicissima, qualis ab Apostolis tradita erat, paulatim evasisse multiplicem, ac immensam, novis illis ex variis occasionibus enatis legibus, decretis ac institutis auctam. Id quoque, quod ille pa-riter
units.tr: many things in this book concerning fasts, feasts and many other decrees, which the Greek Christians adopted partly in the first and second centuries and partly even throughout the third; indeed, some of them were unusual even in the times up to our own memory. I would very much like to know which century's Church among the Greeks observed the Sabbath feast as instituted in this ritual of theirs, or celebrated the week after Pentecost as a feast according to this pontifical of theirs? To pass over many other things, which, although later centuries observed them, it is well established were not in use at all in the first three. Finally, as for what Albaspineus says, that whoever reads these books more carefully will judge that new constitutions were added over time, just as new laws were made in the government of the Church as new occasions arose, I say that this neither proves nor can prove anything by any necessary and evident reasoning. I admit what he says is quite true: new laws were made in the Church as the need of the moment required, sometimes even without reason, and were added to the old ones; and so the Church's faith and discipline gradually grew from the utmost simplicity in which they had been handed down by the Apostles into something manifold and immense, increased by those new laws, decrees and institutions that arose from various occasions.

units.la: * Cf. marginal asterisk at "facta sunt" in the text. riter statuit, non tantum confiteor, sed etiam exosculor,ambabusque ulnis amplector, quæ in codice Boviano hodie leguntur leges, eas non unius ejufdemque sæculi esse, sed diversorum temporum; alias antiquissimas; alias antiquas; alias novas; alias etiam novis recentiores; ut quæ hactenus disputavimus attentius intuenti liquebit. Cæterum ex his id sequi nego, quod inde Albafpineus judicare nos jubet; nempe novas antiquis leges, prout in sæculorum decursu fiebant, ita & in hoc ipsum Διαταγῶν volumen variis temporibus relatas fuisse; sic, ut is liber jam ab initio fuerit quidem, sed brevis; mox fecundo verbi gratia sæculo, tertioque item & quarto subinde adjectis pro temporum ordine novis, quæ recens factæ erant, legibus, auctior in hanc, qua nunc hodie est, molem tandem creverit. Nihil nos cogit de Διαταγῶν volumine ita judicare. Cur non potius censebimus, quod res est, operis quidem authorem simul, semelque in volumen suum conjecisse omnes eas constitutiones, quæ nunc in eo leguntur; sed authorem illum, quisquis est, impostorem fuisse, qui cum ipse post jam constitutam in Ecclesia multo maximam illarum legum, quas memorat, partem, (id est fequioribus fæculis, quarto fortasse, aut quinto) viveret, quo præfentis tis Ecclesiæ decretis plus ponderis, atque authoritatis adderet, finxit eas ab Apostolis ipsis decerni? Ut siquis hodie Jesuitarum librum ederet, in quo Apostolos faceret loquentes, omniaq; Ecclesiæ Romanæ instituta, ac dogmata, etiam multis post Apostolicam ætatem sæculis nata, etiam nupera, docentes ac decernentes. Non negO, quod affert Albaspineus, Græcos uno eodemque volumine, cui nomen est, Codex canonum Ecclesiæ universalis, omnes tum antiquos, tum recentes, ad sua tempora, diversarum synodorum canones, sub eodem numerorum ordine, complexos esse. Et si similis esset Constitutionum liber; si nudas diataxes per numeros dispositas haberet; si eas nullis certis personis tribueret; si nihil narraret; faterer, id quod de eo nos judicare vult Albaspineus, non absurde de hujusmodi libro opinaturos. Nunc vero Διαταξεων plane alia ratio, ac forma est. Nam in iis Apostoli in unum congregati finguntur ista decreta plurima in commune omnes, aliqua seorsim singuli facientes, scribentes, ad Ecclesias universas per Clementem mittentes. Hujus generis volumen non capit illa successiva aliarum, quam quas ab initio habebat, cum primum scriptum est, legum additamenta. Et si quis libro ita instituto, sequentibus tem-poribus poribus adjecit, is planus atque impostor fuit; æque ac primus operis author. Certe nullam in Constitutionibus legimus earum legum, quas post quartum fæculum, quinque initia factas fuisse constat. Nimirum videbant illorum temporum homines, librum numeris suis omnibus absolutum, neque debere, neque citra fraudem & impostturam posse novis additamentis augeri.
units.tr: I not only grant, but also embrace with both arms, what he likewise lays down: that the laws now read in the Bovian codex are not all of one and the same century but of different times, some very ancient, some ancient, some new, and some even more recent than the new ones; as our discussion so far will make clear to anyone who looks at it closely. But I deny that what Albaspineus then urges us to conclude follows from this: namely, that just as new laws were added to the old ones as they were made over the course of the centuries, so too in this very volume of the Διαταγῶν [Diatagon] new laws were brought in at various times, so that the book was indeed there from the beginning but short; then, with new laws added in the second century, for example, and likewise in the third and fourth as they were made, it finally grew into the bulk it has today. Nothing compels us to judge the Διαταγῶν [Diatagon] volume in this way. Why should we not rather hold what is the case: that the author of the work, whoever he was, put into his volume all the constitutions now read in it at one time, but that this author was an impostor who, while living long after these laws had already been established in the Church (that is, in later centuries, perhaps the fourth or fifth), invented that they were decreed by the Apostles themselves, in order to lend greater weight and authority to the decrees of the present Church? It would be as if someone today published a book of the Jesuits in which he made the Apostles speak, and had them teach and decree all the institutions and doctrines of the Roman Church, including those born many centuries after the Apostolic age, even recent ones. I do not deny what Albaspineus reports, that the Greeks, in one volume called the Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church, gathered under a single numerical order all the canons of various synods, both ancient and recent, down to their own times. And if the Constitutions book were similar to that, if it had bare diataxeis arranged by number, if it attributed them to no definite persons, and if it told no story, I would concede that those who judged it as Albaspineus wishes us to judge it would not be unreasonable in their opinion. But as it is, the Διαταξεων [Diataxeon] has a quite different plan and form. For in it the Apostles are imagined as gathered together, making and writing many of these decrees together as a body, and some separately one by one, and sending them through Clement to all the Churches. A volume of this kind does not admit the later additions of laws, other than those it had from the beginning, when it was first written. And if anyone, after this book had been constructed in this way, added to it in later times, he was a fraud and an impostor, just as the original author of the work was. Certainly we read in the Constitutions no laws of the kind that are known to have begun after the fourth century. Clearly the men of those times saw that a book complete in all its parts should not be enlarged with new additions, and that this could not be done without deceit and imposture.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De authore ac tempore Constitutionum non plane liquere. Nihil cogere ut ante Nicænam synodum prodiisse; multa suadere, ut diu post eam publicatas credamus. Conclusio totius disputationis.
units.tr: The author and the time of the Constitutions are not plainly clear. Nothing compels us to think the book appeared before the Council of Nicaea; much suggests that it was published long after it. Conclusion of the whole discussion.

units.la: {Q}UOD si quæras, à quibus viris quove nominatim tempore scriptus, consarcinatusque ea, qua nunc est, forma fuerit Constitutionum liber; primo respondeo, nihil esse quod ea de re vehementius laboremus. Satis est, quod librum fictitium, atque supposititium, falsoque sive Apostolis, sive Clementi adscriptum, adhæc pessimæ inter apocryphos notæ, mendaciorum atque errorum plenum esse deprehendimus. Ut nummum qui scit esse adulterinum, satis habet eum rejicere, ac repudiare; Quando, ubi, à quo cusus, signatusque fuerit, quærendum rendum non putat. Id vero præterquam quod quæsitu supervacaneum, adhæc inventu difficile est; quod quæ homines mentiuntur, ea furtim, ac in tenebris plerumque moliuntur; ut non sit facile eorum originem, diemque (ut sic dicam) natalem investigare. Si tamen, ut in re obscura, conjecturas & argumenta admittere libet, illud inprimis pro certo constitui posse mihi videtur, fuisse hoc opus ante finem quinti sæculi scriptum atque editum. Primo enim cum multa habeat, tertio quartoque sæculis in Ecclesiæ mores, ac disciplinam inventa, nihil eorum, quantum memini, exhibet, quæ post quintum sæculum de novo inducta sunt; nullam imaginum uspiam mentionem facit; nullam reliquorum, quæ prioribus temporibus inusitata, istis frequentari cœpere. Huc accedit, quod illos octo Clementis libros, quos à Gelasio Romano episcopo in suo Concilio a. D. 494. memoratos, damnatosque, & inter apocrypha rejectos fuisse supra diximus, verisimillimum est, eos ipsos esse Διατάξεων libros, quos nuper ediderunt Bovius, ac Turrianus. Certe ita sensit olim Humbertus Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinalis, a. D. 1050. quod fuit à nobis in prima parte hujus operis observatum. Sed & ex iis quæ supra sunt à nobis disputata, non minus clarum rum, minusve certum esse videtur, non fuisse istos libros ante Synodi Nicaenae tempora, hoc est ante a. D. 325. scriptos editosve. Quod cum multa, quae nihil opus est repetere, probent, tum illud inter caetera evidenter arguit, quod hoc opus scriptum fuerit cum jam Christiani essent Romanorum Caesares: Ut illud mittam, quod eorum, qui ante Synodum vixerant, scriptorum nullus est, qui hujus operis vel tenuissimam notitiam prae se ferat. Quod enim a viris doctissimis, ac praestantissimis de Tertulliano ac Dionysio Alexandrino affertur, (quasi ipsorum temporibus, hoc est ante a. D. 204. & 208. Constitutiones istae extarent) id, inquam, perquam infirmum est. Ac Tertulliano quidem quam ignotae essent Bovianae illae nostrae Διατάξεις, nos supra neque paucis, neque obscuris rationibus ita probavimus, ut iis expensis neminem repugnaturum arbitremur.
units.tr: If you ask by which men, or at what time by name, this book of the Constitutions was written and put together in its present form, my first answer is that there is nothing about which we need to labour more earnestly. It is enough that we have found the book to be fictitious and spurious, falsely ascribed either to the Apostles or to Clement, and, besides, of the worst class among the Apocrypha, full of lies and errors. Someone who knows a coin to be counterfeit is content to reject and refuse it, and does not think it necessary to ask when, where, and by whom it was struck and stamped. Such an inquiry is not only superfluous but also hard to carry out, because what men invent they usually contrive in secret and in the dark, so that their origin and, as one might say, their birthday are not easy to trace. Still, since in an obscure matter we may admit conjectures and arguments, it seems to me that this can be established first of all as certain: this work was written and published before the end of the fifth century. For, although it contains many things that were introduced into the customs and discipline of the Church in the third and fourth centuries, as far as I remember it presents nothing that was newly brought in after the fifth century. It nowhere mentions images, and it makes no mention of the other things that began to be practised frequently in later times though they were unusual in earlier ages. Add to this that those eight books of Clement, which we said above were cited, condemned, and rejected among the apocryphal writings by Gelasius, bishop of Rome, in his council in the year 494, are very probably the same books as the Διατάξεις that Bovius and Turrianus lately published. Certainly Humbert, cardinal of the Roman Church, thought so long ago, in the year 1050, as we observed in the first part of this work. But also, from what we have argued above, it seems no less clear and certain that these books did not exist, written or published, before the time of the Council of Nicaea, that is, before the year 325. Although many things, which there is no need to repeat, prove this, one argument among others clearly shows it: this work was written when the Roman emperors were already Christians. To pass over the fact that none of the writers who lived before the Council gives even the slightest hint of knowing this work. As for what very learned and eminent men bring forward about Tertullian and Dionysius of Alexandria, as if these Constitutions existed in their times, that is, before the years 204 and 208, I say that it is very weak. As for Tertullian, how unknown those Bovian Διατάξεις of ours were to him, we have proved above with not a few and not obscure reasons, so that, once they are weighed, I do not think anyone will dispute it.

units.la: Sed viri doctissimi, post Turrianum putant, Διαδοχῆς de Phoenice libro operis quinto sententiam a Tertulliano his verbis in libro de resurrectione expressam fuisse a; Animalis est res & vita obnoxia, & morti; illum dico alitem Orientis peculiarem, de singularitate famosum, de posteritate monstruosum; qui semetipsum lubenter funerans renovat, natali fine decedens, atque succedens.
units.tr: But very learned men, following Turrianus, think that Tertullian expressed in the fifth book of the work, on the Phoenix, the opinion which he gives in his book on the resurrection in these words: a A living creature is a thing subject to death; I mean that unique bird of the East, famous for being alone, wondrous for its descendants, which, joyfully burying itself, renews itself, dying at its natural end and succeeding itself.

units.la: a De resurr. car. c. 15. succedens, iterum phœnix, ubi jam nemo; iterum ipse, qui non jam; alius, idem. Quid expressius, atque signatius in hanc causam? aut cui alii rei tale documentum? Hæc Tertullianus. In quibus phœnicis historiam audio; nullos Apostolos, nullum Clementem audio. Sed (inquis) unde hęc de phœnice habet, si non à Constitutionibus habet? Quid? Si me nescire respondero: an ideo, quod hæc unde habeat, nescimus, eo fiet, ut ex Constitutionum codice ea habuerit? Sed res clara est.
units.tr: a On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 15. Succeeding itself: again the phoenix, where no one is now; again himself, who is no longer himself; another, yet the same. What could be more explicit and more pointed for this cause? Or what other thing gives such proof? So Tertullian. In these words I hear the history of the phoenix; I hear of no Apostles, no Clement. But you will say: whence does he have this about the phoenix, if not from the Constitutions? What then? If I answer that I do not know, will it follow that, because we do not know where he got it, he got it from the code of the Constitutions? But the matter is clear.

units.la: Historiam ipsam, etiamsi nullas Apostolorum Constitutiones legisset, nescire profecto non potuit, cujus pleni sunt veterum Paganorum libri; quam totam non solum accurate, sed etiam ambitiose scripserunt & Herodotus olim, & postea Plinius, & Tacitus, & utroque vetustior Seneca, Latinorum nobilissimi; nequid de Mela, & Solino, & aliis dicam. Ab his Tertullianus habere potuit; imo habuit, quæ de Phœnice narrat. Quanquam & de Christianis nonnemo fuit, à quo ei hæc discere licuerat, scilicet epistolæ ad Corinthios omnibus illorum temporum Christianis cognitissimæ scriptor Clemens; ut nihil necesse sit Constitutiones jam tum extitisse, è quibus hæc disceret; quæ (ut liquet) & à Paganis, & à Christianis nis haurire licebat ; quanquam equidem eum ad Paganorum potius, quam ad Clementis narrationem hoc loco respexisse crediderim. Sed Phoenicem (inquis) à Paganis Tertullianus habuerit, phoenicis certe ad resurrectionem probandam usum à Paganis, qui resurrectionem nesciebant, nō habuit Διαλαγίως exemplo, qui hanc historiā eodem refert, habuit. Quasi vero Tertulliano, viro acutissimo, ac sagacissimo, & ad miraculum erudito, quam Διαλεκτι homini, ut apparet, crasso, & ad prodigium stulto, difficilius fuerit, quod de phoenice apud Naturæ Scriptores reperiebat, id ad resurrectionis argumentum transferre. Atqui res ipsa eo per se ducit; neque ullum est tam mediocre ingenium, cui promptum non sit id statim odorari. Quanquam & si Tertullianum adeo hebetem fuisse fingamus, ut id per se & suo marte deprehendere non quiverit, ne sic quidem sequetur, necesse fuisse extare Διατάξεις, à quibus doceretur eam historiam ad resurrectionem referre. Praesto enim aderat alius, qui moneret, scilicet author epistolae ad Corinthios Clemens ; Ea enim, & tum, ut omnes fatentur, extabat, & hanc de phoenice narrationem ipsa quoque ad confirmandam resurrectionis nostrae fidem adhibet. Sed Clementem mittamus. Tertullianus
units.tr: The story itself, even if he had read no Constitutions of the Apostles, he certainly could not have failed to know, since the books of the ancient pagans are full of it. Herodotus once, and afterwards Pliny, and Tacitus, and Seneca, who is older than both and the most noble of the Latin writers, all wrote about it fully and with great care and even with flourish; not to mention Mela, and Solinus, and others. From these Tertullian could have had, indeed did have, what he tells about the phoenix. Yet there was also one among the Christians from whom he could have learned it, namely Clement, the writer of the epistle to the Corinthians, which was best known to all the Christians of those times. So there is no need to suppose that the Constitutions already existed from which he learned this; it was possible to draw it, as is clear, from pagans as well as Christians, although I rather think that in this passage he looked to the pagan accounts rather than to Clement's. But, you will say, Tertullian had the phoenix from the pagans; certainly the use of the phoenix to prove the resurrection did not come from pagans who did not know the resurrection. Yet Lactantius, who relates the same story, had it to this end. As if it were more difficult for Tertullian, a most acute and sagacious man, and wonderfully learned, than for Lactantius, a man evidently dull and foolish to a marvel, to transfer to the argument for the resurrection what he found about the phoenix in the writings of the natural historians. But the thing itself leads there by its own nature, and there is no talent so mediocre that it fails to sniff it out at once. Yet even if we imagine Tertullian to have been so dull that he could not perceive this by himself and by his own effort, it still would not follow that the Διατάξεις had to exist to teach him to refer that story to the resurrection. For another was at hand to advise him, namely Clement, the author of the epistle to the Corinthians; for that epistle, as all admit, was then in existence, and it too uses this story of the phoenix to confirm our faith in the resurrection. But let us leave Clement aside. Tertullian

units.la: Note: marginal and Greek words are transcribed as printed where legible; see notes. lianus enim ipse profitetur longe alium sibi fuisse hujus cogitationis authorem; Nempe Psalmographum; Deus etiam (inquit) Scripturis suis, & florebit enim, inquit, ut phoenix; id est de morte, de funere, uti credas de ignibus quoq; substantiam corporis exigi posse. Hæc ex psalmis petita constat; in quibus quod græce apud lxx. legitur ὁ ϑικαιος ὡς φοίνιξ ἀνθήσει, Septimius de phoenice ave sumpsit, nominis φοίνιξ ambiguo sponte deceptus, quod ex Hebraeo omnis ambiguitatis experte חמר palmam arborem hic esse certum est, non avem. Sed Tertullianus vel imprudens, vel (quod potius reor) volens de ave sumpsit, ut ingeniose ad argumentum sibi propositum infleCteret; quales interdum lusus, etiam apud Patres, occurrunt. Ambrosio quidem, & ipsi quoque, sive similis error, sive Tertulliani authoritas, Phoenicem avem in Scripturis divinis memoratam esse persuasit. Nulla ergo nobis est ex hoc Tertulliani loco necessitas id confiteri, quod ab omni veri specie alienissimum est; jam octavo tertii saeculi anno extitisse Apostolis suppositas Διαταγὰς.
units.tr: For Tertullian himself declares that the thought came to him from quite another author: namely the Psalmist. "God also," he says, "in his Scriptures," and "he will flourish, he says, like the phoenix"; that is, concerning death and burial, so that you may believe that the substance of the body can be drawn out even from the fires. It is plain that this is taken from the Psalms, where in the Septuagint the Greek reads ὁ δίκαιος ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀνθήσει [ho dikaios hōs phoinix anthēsei, "the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree"]. Septimius took the bird phoenix from this, being led by the ambiguity of the word φοῖνιξ, which in the Hebrew, free of all ambiguity, is clearly here the palm tree [תָּמָר, tamar], not a bird. But Tertullian took it from the bird either through carelessness or, as I rather suppose, deliberately, so that he could bend it cleverly to the argument he had set himself; such plays on words occur sometimes even among the Fathers. Certainly for Ambrose, and for others too, either a similar error or the authority of Tertullian persuaded them that the phoenix, a bird, is mentioned in the divine Scriptures. There is therefore no necessity for us, from this passage of Tertullian, to admit what is most alien to every appearance of truth: that the Apostolic Διαταγαί, falsely ascribed to the Apostles, existed already in the eighth year of the third century.

units.la: Neque vero anno ejusdem saeculi 64. extitisse eas persuadet Dionysii Alexandrini locus; quem virum & ipsum quoque ex veris, certisq; supra demonstravimus Constitutiostitutionum librum nescivisse. Is apud Eu-sebium de visione quaedam sibi divinitus oblata verba faciens, haec, fateor, habet a; a-πεδξάμεν τὸ ὄραμα, ὡς ἀποστολικὴ φωνὴ συνταξίχον τῇ λεγόμενη πρὸς τὰς διωατωτέρας, γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται. Acceptavi visionem hanc, tanquam Apostolica voci conformem, sic ad potentiores dicenti, Estote probati trapezitae. Haec verba, quae in nullo quidem ex canonicis N. Test. scriptoribus, expressa leguntur, apud Διαθήκας vero totidem litteris atque apicibus descripta extant, putant viri illi doctissimi Dionysium ex horum libris sumpsisse, & ἀποστολικῶν φωνῶν dixisse, quod Apostolorum nomen Diataxes praeferrent. Sed haec ratio nos non cogit, ut concedamus haec verba ex Constitutionibus citasse Dionysium. Primo enim, ut ante & vere observavit Reverendissimus Vsserius c, Διαθήκης haec verba, non tanquam sua pronunciant, ut eorum proprie voces dici possint, sed velut ex Scriptura petita afferunt, quod ex ipsa eorum oratione patet. τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν (inquiunt) ἐπιτρέπει κρίνειν μόνοις. ὅτι εἴρηται αὐτοῖς, κείμενα δίκαια κεῖνται, ἢ πάλιν, γίνεσθε τραπεζῖται δόκιμοι. Solis sacerdotibus judicare permissum est, quia dictum est eis, Iustum judicium judicate; & rursus, Estote probi trapezitae. Vt ergo illud, iustum judicium
units.tr: Nor does the passage of Dionysius of Alexandria persuade us that they existed in the sixty-fourth year of the same century; we have shown above, from certain and true evidence, that this man too did not know the book of the Constitutions. In Eusebius, speaking of a certain vision divinely offered to him, he says these words, I admit: a "I accepted the vision as agreeing with an apostolic voice that speaks to the more powerful: Be approved money-changers" [ἀπεδεξάμην τὸ ὅραμα, ὡς ἀποστολικῇ φωνῇ συνταξάμενον τῇ λεγομένῃ πρὸς τοὺς δυνατωτέρους, Γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται]. Those most learned men think that Dionysius took these words from the books of the Διαθῆκαι, and that he called them apostolic voices because those books bore the name of the Apostles. These words are not read as expressed in any of the canonical writers of the New Testament, but are found written in exactly the same letters and characters in the Constitutions. But this reasoning does not compel us to grant that Dionysius quoted these words from the Constitutions. For, first, as the most reverend Ussher rightly observed before, they do not present these words as their own, so that they can properly be called their own expressions, but adduce them as taken from Scripture, as is clear from their own speech. "Judgment," they say, "is permitted to the priests alone, because it was said to them, Judge righteous judgment [Κρίνατε δίκαια κρίματα]; and again, Be approved money-changers. Solis sacerdotibus judicare permissum est, quia dictum est eis, Iustum iudicium iudicate; et rursus, Estote probi trapezitae." So just as "righteous judgment"

units.la: * Hist. l. 7. c. 3. gr. edit. → note at left margin, reference marks as printed. judicium judicate; Ita & hoc, Estote probi trapezitæ, è scriptura citant; utrumque non pro suo, sed pro Scriptura dicto usurpant. Ac illud quidem, quamvis nusquam fortasse in scripturis expressum sit his ipsis verbis, κρίμα δίκαιον κρίνατε, tamen pro scriptura dicto habent, quod res ipsa in multis Scripturarum locis a præcepta reperiatur; maxime apud Ioannem b, ubi Dominus hæc, quæ ad Διαταγὴν verba proxime accedunt, loquitur, μὴ κρίνετε κατ' ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε, Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judicium judicate. Eadem est alterius dicti ratio, estote probi trapezitæ. Nimirum etiamsi ipsa verba totidem syllabis expressa nusquam in Scripturis legantur, id tamen pro Scripturæ dicto habuerunt Διαζυγεῖς, quod sensus iis verbis expressus in sacris Scripturis inveniatur. Neque ii soli sic senserunt. Fuerunt multi patres in eadem sententia. Ut verbi gratia Clemens Alexandrinus, Dionysiii civis, & conterraneus, sed eo haud paucis annis vetustior c, εἰκότως ἀρα & ἡ γραφὴ τοιούτους τινὰς ἡμᾶς Διαλεκτικὰς ἴτως ἐθέλεσα γενέσθαι, παραινεῖ· γίνεσθε ὁ δόχιμοι τραπεζῖται· τὰ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες. Merito ergo & Scriptura, tales nos esse volens Dialecticos, sic hortatur, Estote autem probi trapezitæ, alia quidem reprobantes, quod vero bonum est, retinentes. Ut ergo Clemens, sic & Dionysius hanc sententiam, non pro Διαταγῶν (quos utrique ignotos fuisse supra demonstravimus) sed pro Scriptura dicto habuerunt. Ac Dionysius quidem dum eam sententiam vocem ⸂Αποστολικὰν⸃ nominat, in Paulum digitum intendit, cujus haec sunt scilicet apud Clementem, τὰ μὴ ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες, quae fere totidem verbis in priore ad Thessalonicenses epistola etiam in nostris hodie codicibus leguntur, πάντα δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε. Ergo ex Clementis, Dionysiique locis inter se comparatis patet, utrumque scriptorem, dum haec citant, Paulum in animo habuisse. Idem quoque Basilii verba confirmant, qui uno infra Dionysium saeculo vixit. Is enim alicubi eandem sententiam ita usurpat; ὡς δοκιμάζων τραπεζίτης, τὸ μὲν δόκιμον κατέξει, ὁ δὲ πονηρὸς ἀφίξει. Ut bonus trapezita, quod bonum fuerit retinebit, & ab omni specie mali abstinebit. Verba ultima ab omni specie mali abstinebit, ostendunt Basilium ad Paulum respexisse, apud quem haec eadem nuper citatis verbis continuantur, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε, ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ ἀπέχεσθε. His Clementis Basiliique locis tertium Eusebii addit Rev. Ussherius ex Apologia pologia Origenis, Ab his qui Origenis libros legunt, istud penitus putant exclusum esse mandatum, quo probabiles jubentur effici trapezita, scientes, quod bonum est retinere, ab omni autem specie mali se abstinere. Dubitari non potest, quin Eusebius, æque ac Clemens, & Basilius ad Paulum respiciat, cujus totam illam in priore ad Thessalonicenses ρῆσιν recitat. Fronto quidem Ducæus, nobilis Iesuita, ea de re non dubitavit, qui ad illum Basilii locum habet. Qua sequuntur, ut bonus trapezita &c. alludunt ad illud Apostoli 1. Thessal. 5.21. πάντα δοκιμάζοντες, &c. Eodemque refert illa Gregorii Nazianzeni, sane appositissimè;
units.tr: * Hist. l. 7. c. 3. gr. edit. → note at left margin, reference marks as printed. judicium judicate. Likewise they quote this, Estote probi trapezitæ, from Scripture; they use both expressions not as their own words but as sayings of Scripture. Now the first, κρίμα δίκαιον κρίνατε (judge a just judgment), though perhaps nowhere in Scripture expressed in these exact words, they still regard as a saying of Scripture, because the thing itself is commanded in many passages of Scripture, above all in John b, where the Lord speaks words that come close to those of the Διαταγὴ: μὴ κρίνετε κατ' ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε (Judge not according to appearance, but judge a just judgment). The reasoning is the same for the other saying, estote probi trapezitæ. Indeed, even if these words, with the same syllables, are nowhere read in the Scriptures, the Διαζυγεῖς [Constitutions] still held it to be a saying of Scripture, because the sense expressed in these words is found in the holy Scriptures. Nor were they alone in this view. There were many Fathers of the same opinion. For example Clement of Alexandria, a citizen and fellow countryman of Dionysius, but a few years older than he c, says: εἰκότως ἄρα καὶ ἡ γραφὴ τοιούτους τινὰς ἡμᾶς διαλεκτικοὺς ἐθέλουσα γενέσθαι, παραινεῖ· γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται· τὰ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες. Rightly, therefore, Scripture, wishing us to become such skilled judges, exhorts us: Be approved money-changers, rejecting the bad but holding fast to what is good. So, as Clement, so also Dionysius held this sentiment to be a saying not of the Διαταγῶν (whom we have shown above to have been unknown to both) but of Scripture. Dionysius, when he calls this sentiment an Apostolic word, points his finger at Paul, whose words are evidently in Clement: τὰ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες, which are almost word for word read in the first epistle to the Thessalonians, even in our codices today: πάντα δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε (Prove all things; hold fast what is good). Therefore, from a comparison of the passages of Clement and Dionysius, it is plain that both writers, in quoting these words, had Paul in mind. The words of Basil also confirm this, who lived about one century after Dionysius. For he somewhere uses the same sentiment in this way: ὡς δοκιμάζων τραπεζίτης, τὸ μὲν δόκιμον κατέξει, ὁ δὲ πονηρὸς ἀφίξει, like an approving money-changer, he will keep what is approved and reject the bad; as a good money-changer, he will retain what is good and abstain from every appearance of evil. The final words, "abstain from every appearance of evil," show that Basil had Paul in view, in whose writing these same words are continued in the passage just cited: τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε, ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ ἀπέχεσθε. To these passages of Clement and Basil, Rev. Ussher adds a third from Eusebius, taken from the Apology of Origen: "Those who read the books of Origen think that this command, by which the approvable are bidden to become money-changers, knowing that what is good is to be retained and that one must abstain from every appearance of evil, has been wholly excluded." It cannot be doubted that Eusebius, like Clement and Basil, has Paul in view, whose whole saying in the first epistle to the Thessalonians he recites. Fronto Ducaeus, a noble Jesuit, did not doubt this matter, who on the passage of Basil remarks that the words ut bonus trapezita etc. allude to that saying of the Apostle, 1 Thess. 5:21, πάντα δοκιμάζοντες, etc. To the same point he refers those words of Gregory Nazianzen, most fittingly:

units.la: ὥσπερ ευφυὴς Ἀγγυροχωμων, εἴ τι μὴ καλὸν ἡ χυ Ἀπιυλήγυ δ᾽ ἂν μή σε ποιεῖ βελτίω. — quisquis es bonus mensarius, Siquid probandum est, accipe, ac per qua nequis Probitatis aliquid consequi, cuncta improba.
units.tr: ὥσπερ εὐφυὴς ἀργυρομέτρης, εἴ τι μὴ καλὸν ἡ χρυσὸς ἀπολήγει, δ᾽ ἂν μὴ σε ποιῇ βελτίω. — Whoever you are, a good money-changer: if anything is not good, reject it; accept whatever is worthy of approval, and reject everything that does not make you better.

units.la: Non dubitavit eruditissimus, atq; optimus Sylburgius noster, qui in notis ad locum Clementis nuper descriptum, Allusio (inquit d) est, ad dictum Pauli 1. Thess. 5. Ex his nemo non videt, nihil esse necesse ad Διαζαγέας confugere, vel concedere eos istorum Patrum temporibus jam extitisse, quo hæc eorum verba defendantur. Apparet enim scriptores istos, Clementem, inquam, Dionysium, Eusebium, Basilium, Gregorium, ad Paulum Apostolum respicere, atque hæc velut ex ejus 1. epistola ad Thessalonicenses sumpta, ductaque habere; de nostris Constitutionibus non cogitasse. Idque etiam ex eo clarissime confirmatur, quod cum præter hos alii quoque sint Patres, qui hæc verba memorant, nemo eorum est, qui ea τοῖς Διαθήκαις tribuat, aut eos ista recitans vel levissime innuat. Origenes quidem prior; postea etiam Hieronymus, non Apostolis, ut Dionysius, sed Christo ea verba diserte tribuunt; Qui ea Διαθήκαις tribuerit, ex veteribus nemo est. Origenes ; Quid aliud sunt numismata, quam divini sermones, imaginem magni Regis impressam habentes, qui considerantur a mensariis probatis, gnaris dividendi probata ab improbatis, qua mentiuntur se esse probata, & servantibus illud Jesu mandatum, Estote probi trapezitæ; & Pauli doctrinam dicentis, Omnia probantes, quod bonum est tenentes, ab omni specie mala abstinentes vos. Hieronymus plane itidem; Siquis autem (inquit ) contraria sationis immurmurat, quare eorum explanationationes legam, quorum dogmatibus non ac-quiesco, Sciat me illud Apostoli libenter audire, Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete; & Salvatoris verba dicentis, Estote probati numularii; ut siquis nummus adulter est, & figuram Caesaris non habet, nec signatus est moneta publica, reprobetur. Qui autem Christi faciem claro praefert lumine, in cordis nostri marsupium recondatur. Origenem & Hieronymum sequutus Cassianus (à Rev. Ufferio a nostro ipse quoque laudatus) Christo, non Apostolo, eadem verba tribuit, quo loco nos jubet cogitationes nostras sagaci discretione discutere, ut (inquit b) efficiamur secundum praeceptum Domini probabiles trapezitae. Mox, postquam trapezitarum munus, actusque descripsit; Quae omnia (inquit) nos quoque debere spiritualiter observare Euangelicus sermo sub hujus nominis demonstrat exemplo. Idem in sequenti volumine illam hic à se tractatam sententiam commemorans. Euangelicam probatam vocat, qua jubemur (inquit) fieri probabiles trapezitae. Sunt & alia Patrum loca, in quibus ii ad hęc quidem verba manifeste alludunt; an vero ea ex scripturis citent, non dicunt; qualis est ille Hieronymi locus, Omni (inquit c) studio legenda nobis Scripturae sunt, & in lege Domini meditandum die, ac noEte, ut probati trapezitæ sciamus, quis num-mus probus sit, quis adulter. Alia similia ex Basilia in caput Isaiæ quintum, ex Ambrosio in Lucæ proœmium, denique ex ejusdem Hieronymi & Apologia adversus Ruffinum, & Commentario in Epistolam ad Philemonem, repræsentat eruditissimus Croius noster. Nostrum non est, hic quidem excutere quomodo Christi sit hæc sententia, quæ in nullo nostrorum Euangeliorum abeo pronunciata invenitur. Videat qui volet eruditorum de hac quæstione opiniones; tum apud Alardum Gazæum, tum apud nostrum in recentissimo opere Crojum; quorum alii, ut Ciaconius, hæc verba in Euangelio secundum Hebræos extitisse, indeque a Clemente & Origene petita esse volunt; alii, in quorum numero ipse Alardus fuisse videtur, putant, hæc quidem in nullo libro scripto extitisse, sed tamen vocali jam inde ab Apostolis traditione accepta fuisse; qualiter illud, quod nullus Euangelistarum descripsit, Beatius est dare quam accipere, Paulus Apostolus in Actibus Domini Jesu verbum esse dicit; ut Patres hanc sententiam Christo ideo tribuisse statuantur, non quod eam a Domino totidem verbis expressam, vel in ullis scripturis legissent, vel ulla traditione accepissent; sed quod eam sibi viderentur ex quibusdam parabolicis in Euangelio positis Domini sermonibus, haud absurde concludere; quales isti sunt, apud Matthaeum a quidem, Oportuit te committere pecuniam meam numulariis, sive trapezitis; apud Lucam b vero hi, in quibus Crojus noster praecipue pedem figit, ἀπαγ-ματαιώσαντε, ἕως ἔρχομαι, Negotiamini, dum venio. Haec, inquam, & alia nunc mitto. Nam ad praesens institutum satis est attendisse hanc celeberrimam in veteri illa Ecclesia sententiam, esto probi trapezitae, Patres, non Constitutionum auctori (quod nemo eorum prodit) sed Scriptur is canonicis constanter acceptam ferre; plane, ut ipsos Διαθηκας, quo loco eam memorant; in eo tantum, caetera concordes, discrepare, quod eam alii Apostolis, ut Dionysius, alii Christo Servatori, ut Origenes, & Hieronymus, tribuunt. Ac horum quidem est difficilior, & impeditior ratio. Dionysii vero nostri, qui hanc sententiam φονλῶ Αποστολικῶ vocat, & Clementis, qui ejusdem Pauli ad Thesalonicenses verba continuavit, multo facilior, atque explicatior ratio est. Omnino enim videntur ad Paulinum illum locum respexisse, ac dum eum ex memoria, non ex codice, recitant, Pauli quidem sensum edidisse; verba ipsa (quod ex memoria aliquid pronuntiantibus contin-gere solet) non usque adeo accurate ex-presserit. Cum enim Paulus ita dixerit, πάντα δοκιμάζετε, Clemens hoc quod Paulus proprie ac sine figura expressit, improprie ac figurate, adhibita elegantissima, & in Scripturis obvia similitudine, ita elocutus est, γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται. Nam si recte rem putas, idem uterque sensus est, Omnia probare, & probum trapezitam esse. Verba tantum alia atque alia sunt. Sequentia vero apud Paulum, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε, Clemens etiam illustravit, Supplens alteram, quae ab Apostolo omissa est, antithesis partem, hoc modo; τὰ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες. Duobus quippe iisdem probi trapezitae officium continetur; ut ea quidem, quae non sunt proba, abjiciat atque repudiet; quae vero proba sunt, ea retineat. Dionysius Clementis, Scriptoris vernaculi, venustate, ut videtur, delectatus, Paulinum praeceptum, non ipsius Apostoli propriis, sed Clementis figuratis verbis expressum, quod memoriae ob elegantiam (ut fit) tenacius inhaeserat, simpliciter, ac secure reddidi, γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται. Haec omnino longe mihi facillima, atque expeditissima hujus sententiae ratio videtur; nisi forte quis (quod neq; ipsum absurdum est) suspicietur, cum aliquis eruditus, ad exornandam Pauli sententiam, πάντᾳ δοκιμάζετε, hæc in codicis sui margine e regione ejus scripsisset, γίνεσθε δόκιμοι ταμιεῖται, vel Clementem ipsum, vel alium, qui hæc ita scripta legisset, levi memoriæ errore, vel quod in margine erat, simpliciter posuisse, vel id una cum verbis ipsis Paulinis immiscuisse; Cæteros Patres (quod iis sæpe in aliis contingit) viri authoritate deceptos, idem sequutos esse; Ex quo fortasse & illud accidit, ut errore latius serpente, quod hi Paulo tribuerant, id alii deinceps & Christo Servatori altero memoriæ lapsu tribuerint; Unde illa postremo extiterit Origenis, & Hieronymi hallucinatio, qui unius illius sententiæ eam quidem partem quæ verbis non Paulinis expressa est, Christo tribuerint; cætera, in quibus Pauli verba extant, ipsi Paulo rediderint. Sed hæc quidem de Dionysio plus satis.
units.tr: The most learned and excellent Sylburg, our friend, did not hesitate. In his notes on the passage of Clement quoted above he says: It is an allusion to the saying of Paul in 1 Thess. 5. Anyone can see from this that there is no need to take refuge in the Diataxes [Διαταξεις], or to grant that they already existed in the time of those Fathers, in order to defend these words. It is clear that these writers, I mean Clement, Dionysius, Eusebius, Basil and Gregory, were looking to the Apostle Paul and had taken these words as if drawn from his first epistle to the Thessalonians. They were not thinking of our Constitutions. This is also made very clear by the fact that, although other Fathers besides these also cite these words, none of them attributes them to the Constitutions [τοῖς Διαθήκαις], nor even slightly hints at them when quoting them. Origen came first. Later Jerome too attributes these words plainly not to the Apostles, as Dionysius does, but to Christ. Among the ancients, no one has attributed them to the Constitutions. Origen: What else are coins than divine words, bearing the image of the great King stamped upon them, which are examined by approved money-changers, who know how to separate the approved from the disapproved, who are not deceived by what pretends to be approved, and who keep the command of Jesus: Be approved money-changers; and the teaching of Paul saying, Prove all things, hold fast that which is good, abstain from every appearance of evil. Jerome likewise: If anyone (he says) grumbles against me on the ground that I read the explanations of those whose doctrines I do not accept, let him know that I gladly listen to that saying of the Apostle, Prove all things, hold fast that which is good, and to the words of the Saviour saying, Be approved money-changers; so that if any coin is counterfeit, and does not bear the image of Caesar, and is not stamped with the public mint, it is rejected. But whoever bears the face of Christ in clear light, let him be stored in the purse of our heart. Following Origen and Jerome, Cassian (whom our Ussher also praises) attributes the same words to Christ, not to the Apostle, where he bids us examine our thoughts with a keen discernment, so that (he says) we may become, according to the precept of the Lord, approved money-changers. Soon after, having described the office and work of money-changers, he says: The gospel saying shows under the example of this name that all these things ought to be observed by us also in a spiritual way. In the following book, recalling the same sentence which he treats there, he says: He calls it the gospel approved saying, by which we are ordered (he says) to become approved money-changers. There are also other passages of the Fathers in which they clearly allude to these words; but whether they cite them from Scripture they do not say. Such is that passage of Jerome: The Scriptures (he says) are to be read by us with all zeal, and we must meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, so that, as approved money-changers, we may know which coin is genuine and which is counterfeit. Our most learned Crusius sets out other similar sayings from Basil on the fifth chapter of Isaiah, from Ambrose on the preface to Luke, and finally from Jerome's own Apology against Rufinus and his commentary on the Epistle to Philemon. It is not our task here to examine how this saying is Christ's, since it is not found pronounced in that way in any of our Gospels. Let whoever wishes see the opinions of learned men on this question, both in Alardus Gazaeus and in our Crusius in his most recent work. Some of them, such as Ciaconius, want these words to have existed in the Gospel according to the Hebrews and to have been derived from it by Clement and Origen. Others, among whom Alardus himself seems to have been, think that these words were never in any written book, but were nonetheless received from an oral tradition going back to the Apostles, in the way that Paul the Apostle says of the words of the Lord Jesus, It is more blessed to give than to receive, which none of the evangelists recorded. So the Fathers are thought to have attributed this saying to Christ not because they had read it expressed by the Lord in just these words in any writings, or had received it by any tradition, but because they seemed to conclude it, not absurdly, from certain parabolic sayings of the Lord set down in the Gospel. Such are these: in Matthew, You ought to have committed my money to the bankers, or money-changers; and in Luke, the ones on which our Crusius especially takes his stand: Trade [ἀπαγματαιώσαντε], until I come [ἕως ἔρχομαι]. I set these aside, I say, along with other matters. For it is enough for our present purpose to have observed that this very famous saying in the ancient Church, Be approved money-changers, is carried constantly by the Fathers not to the author of the Constitutions (which none of them reports) but to the canonical Scriptures. Plainly, they differ from the Constitutions themselves where they cite it, and agree with them in everything else, in this only: that some attribute it to the Apostles, as Dionysius does, while others attribute it to Christ the Saviour, as Origen and Jerome do. The reasoning behind the latter is more difficult and intricate. But the reasoning concerning our Dionysius, who calls this saying the Apostolic word [φονλῶ Αποστολικῶ], and concerning Clement, who continued the words of Paul's epistle to the Thessalonians, is much easier and more straightforward. For they evidently looked to that Pauline passage, and, since they quote it from memory and not from a manuscript, they set out the sense of Paul but did not express his very words so exactly; this commonly happens to those who recite something from memory. For when Paul said πάντα δοκιμάζετε [prove all things], Clement expressed in an improper and figurative way what Paul had expressed properly and without figure, using a most elegant comparison, familiar from the Scriptures, and spoke thus: γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται [be approved money-changers]. If you consider the matter rightly, both expressions carry the same sense, to prove all things and to be an approved money-changer. Only the words are different. Clement also clarified what follows in Paul, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε [hold fast that which is good], supplying the other half of the antithesis, which the Apostle omitted, in this way: τὰ μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες [rejecting the one, holding fast the good]. For the office of an approved money-changer consists of these two things: he throws away and rejects what is not genuine, and keeps what is genuine. Dionysius, who was delighted, as it seems, by the charm of Clement, a writer in the vernacular, simply and confidently reproduced the Pauline precept, not in the Apostle's own proper words but in Clement's figurative expression, which had stuck in his memory more tenaciously because of its elegance, as usually happens: γίνεσθε δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται. This seems to me by far the easiest and most straightforward explanation of this saying, unless perhaps someone suspects (which is not absurd either) that some learned man, wishing to adorn Paul's saying πάντα δοκιμάζετε, had written beside it in the margin of his manuscript γίνεσθε δόκιμοι ταμιεῖται, and that Clement himself, or someone else who had read these words so written, through a slight lapse of memory, or because it was in the margin, simply put them in, or mixed them in with the Pauline words themselves; and that the other Fathers, as often happens with them in other matters, were deceived by the authority of the man and followed him. From this perhaps it also came about that, as the error spread more widely, what these men had attributed to Paul was then attributed by others to Christ the Saviour through a second lapse of memory. Hence finally arose the mistake of Origen and Jerome, who attributed to Christ that part of this one saying which is expressed in words not Paul's, while they assigned to Paul himself the rest, in which Paul's words stand. But this is enough about Dionysius.

units.la: Jam cum nihil suadeat, ut Diataxes vel Tertulliani, vel Dionysii temporibus extitisse putemus, plurima vero fateri cogant eas & ipsis, & sequentium etiam temporum scriptoribus ignotas fuisse; ut in superioribus fuse demonstravimus; illud denique, quod nuper diximus, relinquitur ut eas pro certo habeamus non fuisse ante Synodi Nicænæ tempora editas, vel scriptas. Sed neque toto quarto sæculo, quintove adulto innotuisse hinc apparet, quod eæ neq; Eusebio, neque Hieronymo, neque Gennadio, diligentissimis authorum Christianorum, etiam apocryphorum, scriptoribus memoratæ sint; ut supra ostendimus. Ex quibus denique veri mihi simillimum videtur, ut quinto jam inclinato sæculo ab impostore factæ, ac in eum quem videmus, modum digestæ, compositæque fuerint; eodemq; tempore & ab eodem fortasse authore ordinata, atque edita fuerit ea, quæ extat, Canonum (ut vocant) Apostolicorum collectio. Quod si (ut sane videtur) verum est, haud diu fefellit impostura. Utrumque enim opus ejusdem illius sæculi, quo infaustis avibus editum erat, anno 94 à Gelasio, ut ostendimus, totaque, cui ille præerat, Romana 70 episcoporum Synodo, damnatum, & inter Apocrypha rejectum est; qua sententia, veluti quodam fulmine, prostratæ confractæque Diataxes, mirandum non est, quod nunquam postea apud Latinos ad Bovii Turrianique tempora, caput erexerint, ullumve in eorum Ecclesia nomen habuerint.
units.tr: Since nothing suggests that the Diataxes existed in the time of Tertullian or Dionysius, and since many considerations force us to admit that they were unknown both to those writers and to writers of later times, as we showed at length above, what remains, as we said recently, is that we must hold for certain that they were not published or written before the time of the Council of Nicaea. Nor does it appear that they became known during the whole fourth century or even in the early fifth, since neither Eusebius, nor Jerome, nor Gennadius, the most diligent of Christian writers, even of apocryphal ones, mentions them, as we showed above. From all this it seems to me most likely that, as the fifth century was already drawing to a close, they were made by an impostor and put together in the form we see, and that at the same time, and perhaps by the same author, the collection of so-called Apostolic Canons that now exists was arranged and published. If this is true (as indeed it seems to be), the imposture did not deceive for long. For both works, which had been published under unlucky auspices in that same century, were condemned in the year 94 by Gelasius, as we have shown, together with the whole Roman synod of seventy bishops over which he presided, and were rejected among the Apocrypha. By that judgment the Diataxes were, as if struck by a thunderbolt, laid low and broken, so it is no wonder that they never afterwards raised their head among the Latins, down to the times of Bovius and Turrianus, nor had any standing in their Church.

units.la: Materiam Impostor, ex qua adulterinum opus, pingui sane Minerva, effinxit, partim ex Scripturis, partim ex Ecclesiasticis vel cis vel libris, vel etiam ritibus ac disciplinis suo tempore obtinentibus mutuatus est; quæ omnia homo stultissimus, rudisque mentiendi artifex, magna quidem temeritate atque imperitia, nullo vero vel ingenio, vel judicio confudit ac permiscuit. Ac cum jam ante editi tunc extarent, apocryphi duo ejusdem fere argumenti libelli, alter ante Athanasium & Eusebium (id est ante a. D. 316.) hoc titulo Διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων; alter vero, ante Epiphanium (id est annum D. 370.) hoc lemmate, Διαλάξεις τῶν Ἀποστόλων, crediderim impostorem ex utroque; plurima in suum opus transfudisse.
units.tr: The impostor, who certainly produced his spurious work with a rather crude skill, borrowed his material partly from Scripture and partly from ecclesiastical customs, books, rites and disciplines prevailing in his own time. This most foolish man, a clumsy craftsman of lies, with great rashness and ignorance but no talent or judgment, jumbled and mixed all of it together. And since two apocryphal little books of much the same subject were already in circulation at that time, one before Athanasius and Eusebius (that is, before the year 316 A.D.), under the title Teaching of the Apostles [Διδαχὴ τῶν Ἀποστόλων], and the other before Epiphanius (that is, around the year 370 A.D.), under the heading Ordinances of the Apostles [Διατάξεις τῶν Ἀποστόλων], I believe the impostor transferred a great deal from both into his own work.

units.la: Nam ut unum idemque opus cum illis sit, quod Bovius & Turrianus cupiunt, res, ratioque & veterum, qui priora duo volumina memorant, testimonia, atq; authoritas, non sinunt; quod quia fuse supra demonstravimus, nihil necesse est hoc loco repetere.
units.tr: For the reports and testimonies of the ancients, who mention the first two volumes, together with the subject matter, the reasoning and the authority, do not allow that one and the same work should be these books and the one Bovius and Turrianus desire. Since I have shown this at length above, there is no need to repeat it here.

units.la: Sed tametsi hoc nostrum Bovianarum Διατάξεων opus diversum esse & ab Eusebiana, Athanasianaque Διδαχῇ, & ab Epiphaniana Διατάξει contendam; illud tamen libens confiteor, ex utroque opere plurima impostorem in suum vel mutuo sumpta, vel, ut verius dicam, furto ablata videri transfudisse. Nam ille ipsum primo unius titulum suæ farragini prærscripsit, eam quoque Διατάξεις Ἀποστόλων, vocans, & aliquas etiam
units.tr: But although I maintain that this work of ours, the Diataxes of Bovius, is different both from the Eusebian and Athanasian Didache, and from the Epiphanian Diataxis, I gladly concede this: it seems that the impostor transferred into his own compilation a great many things taken from both works, either borrowed or, to put it more truly, stolen. For he first prefixed to his hodgepodge the title of the one, calling it also Ordinances of the Apostles [Διατάξεις Ἀποστόλων], and he also used some of its

units.la: ejusdem sententias usurpavit, ut ex Epipha-nio didicimus; hanc, verbi gratia, Θεὸς φυτεία ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, ἡσ̔ ἀμπελῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκλεκτός, & quædam contra nimium barbæ & capillorum cultum, & alia de quartæ, sextæque feriæ perpetuo, nisi in Pentecoste, jejunio, deque antepaschalis hebdomadis Xerophagiis decreta; quæ in Epiphaniana Διατάξει memorata apud Bovii quoque Apostolos leguntur. Alterius vero operis nomen, si non ipsum, certe aliud ejus geminum, nempe Διδασκαλίας (quod quantulo à Διδαχῇ differt?) sibi quoque haud raro nostri Διαθῆκης assumunt; ut in ipso statim lumine, Ἀνάστασι Διδασκαλίαν ἠχῶν. Alibi, πάντες δὴ τὸ αὐτὸ γενόμενοι ἐγραψαμεν ὑμῖν τῶ καθολικῶ ταύτῃ Διδασκαλίαν. Neque dubito, quin præter titulum, multa quoque alia ex illa Athanasiana Apostolorum Διδαχῇ noster impostor furatus sit; quæ facile, si extaret ipsum Διδαχῆς opus, deprehenderentur. Quod vero tum Διδαχῇ hæc, tum illa Epiphaniana Διαθῆκις interciderint, hanc ipsam causam fuisse arbitror; quod scilicet cum recentior hic noster Διαθηκῶς ex iis plurima, ac fere omnia in opus suum transcripsisset, supervacaneum esse visum est seorsim edita retinere, quæ ille uno eodemque opere plenius ac fusius complecti sategerat.
units.tr: sayings, as we have learned from Epiphanius. For example, this one: "The Catholic Church is God's planting, his chosen vineyard" [Θεὸς φυτεία ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, ἧς ἀμπελῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκλεκτός], and certain rules against excessive cultivation of beard and hair, and others about the perpetual fast on Wednesday and Friday, except at Pentecost, and about the Xerophagies in the week before Easter. These are recorded in the Epiphanian Diataxis, and are also read under the name of Bovius' Apostles. As for the title of the other work, if not the work itself then at least its twin, namely Teachings [Διδασκαλίαι] (how far does this differ from Didache?), our author often assumes it for himself as well, as in the very first line: "Anastasi ... Didaskalian ēchōn." Elsewhere: "All of us, having become of one mind, wrote to you this Teaching for the universal Church" [πάντες δὴ τὸ αὐτὸ γενόμενοι ἐγράψαμεν ὑμῖν τῷ καθολικῷ ταύτῃ Διδασκαλίαν]. I do not doubt that, besides the title, our impostor also stole many other things from that Athanasian Teaching of the Apostles, which could easily be detected if the work of the Didache itself survived. And I think the same reason explains why both this Didache and the Epiphanian Diataxis have perished: since our more recent author had transcribed much, indeed almost everything, from them into his own work, it seemed superfluous to keep them separately published, when he had striven to embrace them in one work, more fully and at greater length.

units.la: Sed praeterquam, quod planum atque impostorem fuisse horum librorum scriptorem insolentissime abeo sumpta, pessime vero atque imperitissime gesta Apostolorum persona arguit; haereticum insuper, Arianaque labe infectum fuisse, ex iis, quae supra disputavimus, apparet; ut vix ullum aliud sit apocryphum opus, quod sic undique & ab omni parte laboret, ut Bovianae Διατάξεις.
units.tr: Besides the fact that the author of these books was obviously a fraud, shown by his most insolent assumption of the Apostles' persona, and by the wretched and most ignorant way he carried it out, it also appears from what we have argued above that he was tainted with heresy and the Arian stain. So there is hardly any other apocryphal work that is so flawed on every side and in every part as the Diataxes of Bovius.

units.la: Atque haec quidem sunt, quae nos de iis dicenda putavimus. Suos sibi Apostolos Bovius. Turrianusque, & siqui alii sint fabularum avidi, habeant. Nobis satis sunt, qui & veteri, & recentiori Ecclesiae satis fuerunt, veri Domini Christi Apostoli, in Θεοπνεύστοις Scripturis quaecunque sunt ad salutem consequendam necessaria, plane, pleneque docentes: nulla vel in moribus fraude, vel in doctrina labe maculosi; nulli Christianorum saeculo, nulli climati, aut ignoti, aut suspecti; sed ab omnibus semper Catholicis Graecis, Latinisque pro canonicis nostrae fidei ac religionis magistris, atque authoribus habiti cultique.
units.tr: These are the things we thought should be said about them. Let Bovius and Turrianus, and any others who are fond of fables, have their own Apostles. For us it is enough that the true Apostles of the Lord Christ, who were sufficient for the ancient Church and for the more recent, teach plainly and fully in the God-breathed Scriptures whatever is necessary for obtaining salvation; they are stained neither by fraud in morals nor by corruption in doctrine; they are unknown or suspect to no century, no region; and they have always been held and honoured by all Catholics, Greek and Latin, as the canonical masters and authors of our faith and religion.

units.la: JOANNIS DALLÆI DE PSEUDEPIGRAPHICIS APOSTOLICIS LIBER III.
units.tr: JOANNES DALLÆUS, ON THE APOSTOLIC PSEUDEPIGRAPHA, BOOK III.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Canonibus, qui Apostolici dicuntur, seorsim disputandum esse. Diversa de iis Latinorum recentiorum judicia. Bellarmini 50 tantum admittentis; Baronii alios 33 praeter hos probantis. Turriani 85 defendentis una cum Graecis.
units.tr: That the so-called Canons of the Apostles must be discussed separately. The differing judgments of recent Latin writers on them: Bellarmine admits only 50; Baronius approves 33 others besides these; Turrianus defends all 85 together with the Greeks.

units.la: VERSIS superiore disputatione Constitutionibus una quoq; concidunt. Apostolorum canones, extrema scilicet pars libri octavi Constitutionum, ut ait diserte Turrianus a, utque in sua editione exhibet, in qua post hæc ultima capitis quadragesimi-sexti verba, Itaque & Philippus & Ananias non se ipsos elegerunt, sed a Christo Pontifice & Deo, cum quo nemo comparari potest, electi sunt, continuo sequuntur Canones (ut praefert titulus) Ecclesiastici; hoc est omnes illi, qui vulgo dicuntur Apostolorum. Ac ut intelligas, eos superioris operis partem esse; qui in superioribus libris loquentes inducti erant Apostoli, sive Διαταγαὶ, iidem post explicitos omnes canonas, tandem perorant, & opus ita concludunt;
units.tr: With the previous disputation on the Constitutions concluded, these fall together as well. The Canons of the Apostles, namely the final part of the eighth book of the Constitutions, as Turrianus a plainly says, and as he presents it in his edition, is followed directly, after the last words of chapter forty-six, And so Philip and Ananias did not choose themselves, but were chosen by Christ, the High Priest and God, with whom no one can be compared, by the ecclesiastical Canons (as the title announces). That is, all those which are commonly called of the Apostles. So that you may understand that they are part of the earlier work, the Apostles who speak in the earlier books, or the Diatagai, after setting out all the canons, at last bring their address to a close and conclude the work in this way:

units.la: Ταῦτα δὲ ἐκ κανόνων διατεταχθῶ ὑμῖν παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων, μων, ὢ ἐπίσκοποι, ὑμεῖς ὁ ἐμμένοντες αὐ-τοῖς σωθήσεσθε, καὶ ἱερωσύνῃ ἔξετε. Hæc nos vobis, Episcopi, constituimus. Vos vero in eis perseverantes, salvi eritis, & pa-cem habebitis; non obedientes vero punie-mini; & quæ sequuntur longiuscula. At-que eo fortasse factum est, ut hæreticus quidem, sed tamen vetus imperfecti in Matthæum operis Author totum Constí-tutionum opus à partis nomine Canones Apostolorum nuncupaverit, Quomodo au-tem (inquita) quodam sacerdotes ex homi-nibus ordinantur, manifeste in libro octavo Canonum Apostolorum dicitur; Qui autem ex hominibus ordinatus est, quantum ad Deum, non est Diaconus aut Sacerdos; qui locus non in Canonibus proprie dictis, sed in capite secundo libri octavi Constí-tutionum iisdem pene verbis extat. Ita-que cum eversò, ac dissipato toto sive integro corpore, quæ erant ejus partes consistere amplius non possint; nos, qui totum Constitutionum opus nothum, ac fictitium esse idoneis, ac luculentis argu-mentis demonstravimus, nihil necesse videtur in Canonibus convellendis ac re-futandis immorari, quorum scilicet au-thoritas eo, cujus pars sunt, opere e-versò abunde labefactata, ac prostrataest.
units.tr: These things have been ordered for you from the canons by the holy apostles [Ταῦτα δὲ ἐκ κανόνων διατεταχθῶ ὑμῖν παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων ἀποστόλων], O bishops: you who abide in them will be saved and will have the priesthood [ὦ ἐπίσκοποι, ὑμεῖς οἱ ἐμμένοντες αὐτοῖς σωθήσεσθε, καὶ ἱερωσύνῃ ἕξετε]. We have laid these down for you, bishops. If you persevere in them you will be saved and will have peace; if you do not obey, you will be punished; and what follows is rather long. Perhaps this is why the author of the unfinished commentary on Matthew, a heretic but an ancient one, called the whole work of the Constitutions by the name of one part, Canons of the Apostles. For he says: How priests are ordained from among men is plainly stated in the eighth book of the Canons of the Apostles: he who is ordained from among men, so far as God is concerned, is not a deacon or a priest. This passage is found, in nearly the same words, not in the Canons properly so called, but in the second chapter of the eighth book of the Constitutions. Therefore, since the whole body has been overthrown and dissipated, its parts can no longer stand. We, who have shown by sound and clear arguments that the whole work of the Constitutions is spurious and fictitious, seem to have no need to linger on overturning and refuting the Canons. Their authority, since the work of which they are part has been overthrown, has been more than sufficiently weakened and laid low.

units.la: Sed quamquam ita se se res habere vide-tur, tur, sunt tamen non contemnendae rationes, quae nos operae pretium facturos suadent, si de Canonibus istis seorsim, ac proprie disputemus. Primo enim Bellarminus & alii non pauci, qui Constitutionum vel nullam, vel certe perexiguam esse authoritatem concedunt, pugnant tamen iidem Canones istos magna ex parte vere Apostolicos esse. Quo factum est, ut in ultima Conciliorum editione quae a.D.1636. Lutetiae Parisiorum in lucem exiit Canones quidem isti in ipso limine exhibiti fuerint; Constitutiones vero nullum in toto opere locum invenerint. Huc accedit, quod siquis rem accuratius expenderit, fortasse non immerito dubitaverit, an jam inde ab initio, & ex primi Constitutionum confarcinatoris mente Canones istius operis pars fuerint. Nam cum absurdum sit, & supervacaneum eadem in eodem opere saepius statuere ac definire, pauca in Canonibus occurrunt, quae non clarissime fuerint in Constitutionibus decreta. Tum ultimus Canon a tantum non clamare videtur diversum a Canonibus esse Constitutionum opus. In eo enim canone Constitutiones in sacros novi foederis libros una cum Euangeliis & Actibus Apostolorum referuntur. Adhaec vetat idem canon apud omnes divulgari, quae sunt in Constitutionibus mystica;
units.tr: But although the matter appears to stand thus, there are nonetheless considerations, not to be despised, which suggest it is worth our while to deal with these Canons separately and on their own. First, Bellarmine and many others who concede that the Constitutions have either no authority or certainly very little, nonetheless contend that these Canons are for the most part truly Apostolic. The result is that in the latest edition of the Councils, published at Paris in 1636, these Canons were indeed set out right at the threshold, whereas the Constitutions found no place anywhere in the whole work. In addition, anyone who weighs the matter more carefully may reasonably doubt whether, from the very beginning and in the mind of the first compiler of the Constitutions, the Canons were part of that work. For since it is absurd and superfluous to decree and define the same things several times in the same work, few things occur in the Canons that were not most clearly decreed in the Constitutions. Then the last Canon seems almost to cry out that the work of the Constitutions is different from the Canons. For in that canon the Constitutions are listed among the sacred books of the New Covenant, together with the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. Besides, the same canon forbids that those things which are mystical in the Constitutions be divulged to all.

units.la: a Can. 84. al. 85. stica ; Id vero , quod supra monuimus, cum ipsorum Διαθηκῶν mente pugnare videtur ; qui sua omnia omnibus Christianis inscribunt , non solum viris , sed etiam mulieribus , quas non semel nominatim alloquuntur. Præterea Canonum à Constitutionibus diversum opus fuisse videtur Gelasii temporibus, hoc est a.D.494. Nam Gelasius postquam Clementis libros octo, id est, ut Humberto quidem Cardinali olim visum est , ac nobis nunc videtur , hos ipsos, quos habemus Constitutionum libros, in apocryphorum censum rejecit , postea itidem librum Canonum Apostolicorum Apocryphum esse pronunciat a; supervacaneo , ut quivis videt, labore, si librorum octo pars erant Canones. Denique ne ipsis quidem Photii temporibus videntur Canones Constitutionum pars habiti fuisse, Is enim utriusque operis in eodem quidem capitulo meminit , atque utrumque in eodem codice sibi visum, ac lectum fuisse ; cæterum alterum alterius partem fuisse satis evidenter negat. Scribit enim à se lectos duos codices, quorum b prior(inquit c) inscribitur Constitutiones Apostolorum μὴ κλήμεντος, cum Clemente, ἐν ᾧ καὶ οἱ τῆς συνοδικῶν κανόνων τῷ ἀφορισματι τῆς Ἀποστόλων κανόνες ἐπιγεγραφόμενοι περιέχοντας, In quo & ii qui inscribunscribuninscribuntur Apostolorum canones una cum synodicorum canonum collectione continentur. Nemo non videt haec addi nihil fuisse necesse, si Constitutionum ipsi canones pars erant; ut illud taceam, quod Photius his verbis Canones Apostolorum Collectioni illi canonum, potius quam Constitutionibus accenset. Ex his vero propius videri posset diversis temporibus, neque ab uno authore consarcinatum utrumque opus; ac prius quidem effictas fuisse Constitutiones; postea collectos atque editos seorsim Canones; tandem impostori alicui placuisse utrumque opus in unum conflari; a cujus manu & exemplari propagati fuerint ii codices, quos Turrianus exhibuit, addito, ut fucus fieret, illo de quo nuper diximus, Canonum epilogo. Neque quod in contrariam partem attulimus imperfecti in Matthaeum scriptoris testimonium, multum valere videtur. Quid enim prohibet, quominus dicamus, eum Canones Apostolorum dixisse pro Constitutionibus? Certe adeo exiguum est διαταξεως & κανόν in hoc argumento discrimen, ut facile ei fuerit alterum pro altero usurpare. Sed utcumque fit (neque enim res ejus momenti est quae pluribus disceptari debeat) illud quidem cerne apparet, nos neque Bellarmino, neque aliis eadem sequentibus satisfacere posse, nisi ipsos seorsim Apostolorum, qui dicuntur Canones nothos, ac suppositicios esse propria ac peculiari opera demonstraverimus.
units.tr: a Can. 84, al. 85. This, however, as we noted above, seems to conflict with the intention of the Diathekai themselves, which address all their words to all Christians, not only men but also women, whom they more than once address by name. Moreover, the Canons appear to have been a work distinct from the Constitutions in the time of Gelasius, that is, in 494. For Gelasius, after rejecting among the apocryphal writings the eight books of Clement, that is (as Cardinal Humbert once thought, and as we now think) these very books of the Constitutions which we have, afterwards likewise declares the book of the Apostolic Canons to be apocryphal; a superfluous labour, as anyone can see, if the Canons were part of the eight books. Finally, not even in the time of Photius do the Canons seem to have been regarded as part of the Constitutions. For he mentions both works in the same chapter, and says that he saw and read both in the same codex, but he plainly denies that one was part of the other. For he writes that he read two codices, of which the first, b he says, c is entitled Constitutions of the Apostles, with Clement, in which the Apostolic Canons, which are entitled [as an appendix] to the collection of synodal canons, are also contained. Everyone sees that these additions would have been unnecessary if the Canons were themselves part of the Constitutions. To say nothing of the fact that Photius, in these words, counts the Apostolic Canons among that collection of canons rather than among the Constitutions. From these facts it may seem more likely that the two works were produced at different times and not by one author; that the Constitutions were fabricated first, the Canons were later collected and published separately, and finally some impostor thought fit to join the two works into one. From his hand and copy, the codices which Turrianus produced would have been propagated, with the addition, to make a show, of that epilogue of the Canons which we mentioned just now. Nor does the testimony of the author of the unfinished commentary on Matthew, which we brought forward on the other side, seem to carry much weight. For what prevents us from saying that he used Canons of the Apostles to mean the Constitutions? Certainly the difference between diataxis [διαταξις] and canon [κανών] in this matter is so slight that it would have been easy for him to use one for the other. But however that may be (for the matter is not of such weight as to need lengthy debate), this much is clear: we cannot satisfy Bellarmine and others who follow him unless we demonstrate, by a separate and particular labour, that the so-called Canons of the Apostles are spurious and supposititious.

units.la: Age ergo, & hanc quoque seorsim partem inspiciamus. Ac ut tota disputatio eodem, quo superior, ordine decurrat; primo quidem videamus, quid adversariæ, hoc est Romanæ communionis Theologi de Canonum Apostolicorum codice sentiant; tum quid veteres Græcæ, Latinæque Ecclesiæ homines de eo litteris mandatum reliquerint; quibus peractis demonstrandum denique erit nothos esse istos Canones, & Apostolis non modo falso, sed etiam impudenter affictos.
units.tr: Come, then, let us examine this part separately as well. So that the whole discussion may run in the same order as the previous one, let us first see what the theologians of the opposing side, that is, of the Roman communion, think of the body of the Apostolic Canons; then what the ancient men of the Greek and Latin Church have left in writing about them; and when these things are done, it will finally be necessary to show that these Canons are spurious and have been fabricated under the name of the Apostles, not only falsely but also shamelessly.

units.la: Adversarii (quod omnium fere qui contra verum nituntur fatum est) non uno eodemque omnes modo de Canonibus sentiunt. Turrianus, ut erat immani stomacho, nullo, aut perexiguo vel pudore, vel judicio, omnes Apostolorum canones pro veris, ac genuinis agnoscit, libroque singulari Apostolicam iis authoritatem adversus Magdeburgenses centuriatores vindicavit; cujus insaniam secutus est Lambertus quidam Gruterus in præfatione Clementis. Bellarminus paulo modestius quinquaginta duntaxat priores legitimos esse censet; reliquos qui sunt 35. vel, ut alii numerant, tra.
units.tr: The adversaries (as is almost the fate of all who strive against the truth) do not all think of the Canons in one and the same way. Turrianus, with a monstrous stomach and little or no shame or judgment, acknowledges all the Apostolic canons as true and genuine, and in a single book defended their Apostolic authority against the Magdeburg Centuriators. Lambert Gruter, a certain man, followed his madness in the preface to Clement. Bellarmine, somewhat more moderately, judges only the first fifty to be legitimate; the remaining ones, which are 35 or, as others count them, 34-

units.la: a L. pro can. Ap. b Edit. Col. a. 1569. c L. de Script. Eccl. in Clem. §. At contra.
