units.tr: a Book for the canons of the Apostles. b Cologne edition, 1569. c Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, under Clement, §. "At contra."

units.la: 34. non esse legitimos, quamvis a Gracis recipiantur. Baronius in eadem est opinione; quam multis rationibus firmat, qua quidem parte illis 35. postremis canonibus authoritatem adimit, & tamen, quod mireris, Turriani, qui hos non minus, quam priores quinquaginta tuetur, scriptam pro his omnibus defensionem fortissimam vocet. Poffevinus Jesuita, Bellarminum quoque sequitur; ut alios qui sunt in eadem sententia nunc mittam. Binius, vero istis haud paulo liberalior est. Is enim praeterquam quod priorum quinquaginta authoritatem certam ac indubitatam esse vult, caeteros insuper (hoc est 35. postremos, duobus tantum demptis, nimirum sexagesimo quinto, & octogesimo quarto, sive, ut alii numerant, quinto) jure meritoque inter authenticos haberi posse ac debere scribit; cum tamen, quod sane mirabile est, confitentur, eos a Gelasio Romae episcopo inter Apocrypha recenseri. Ita ex Binio nihil vetat, quin pro authenticis habeantur, quae Romani Papae apocrypha esse judicarunt. Jam de canonum scriptore non magis, quam de numero atq; authoritate adversarii consentiunt. Omnes quidem pariter concedunt, non fuisse eos ab Apostolis conscriptos; quod non est oscitanter observandum. Turrianus; Quis unquam ex Catholicis (inquit) scriptos
units.tr: 34. that they are not legitimate, although they are received by the Greeks. Baronius holds the same opinion and supports it with many arguments, which in fact take away the authority of those last 35 canons. Yet, strangely, Turrianus, who defends these no less than the earlier fifty, calls the written defence of all of them very strong. The Jesuit Possevinus follows Bellarmine too, not to mention others who share this view. Binius is considerably more generous than these. Besides holding that the first fifty have certain and undoubted authority, he writes that the others (that is, the last 35, minus only two, namely the sixty-fifth and the eighty-fourth, or the fifth, as others count) can and ought rightly and justly to be regarded as authentic. Yet they admit, which is truly remarkable, that Gelasius, bishop of Rome, listed them among the Apocrypha. So, according to Binius, nothing prevents those things that the Roman Pope judged to be apocryphal from being regarded as authentic. Now, concerning the author of the canons, the opponents agree no more than they do about their number and authority. All of them alike concede that they were not written by the Apostles, and this should not be overlooked. Turrianus says: Which of the Catholics has ever said that they were written

units.la: b Ibid. §. 12. c Appar. verbo Clemens. d Not. in tit. Can. T. 1. Concil. p. 17. b.
units.tr: b Ibid. §. 12. c Apparatus, under the word Clemens. d Notes on the title of the Canons, Tom. 1 of the Councils, p. 17 b.

units.la: dPr.Can. c. 1. p. 1. rf. scriptos ab Apostolis dixit? Baronius ait, incertum esse ab ipsis Apostolis esse conscriptos; ac ne ipsum quidem Turrianum hoc contendere notat. Sic Binius; Quoniam (inquit) author eorum alius ignoratur, Apostolica traditione ad nos dimanasse recte creduntur. Sed ubi definiendum est, a quo nominatim scripti fuerint illi Canones, tum vero Romani Theologi in diversa abeunt.
units.tr: d Preface to the Canons, c. 1, p. 1. written by the Apostles? Baronius says it is uncertain whether they were written by the Apostles themselves, and he observes that Turrianus himself does not maintain this. Binius likewise says: Since their author is unknown, they are rightly believed to have come down to us by Apostolic tradition. But when it must be decided by whom those canons were precisely written, the Roman theologians go in different directions.

units.la: Turrianus quidem, fortissimus eorum defensor, vult omnes a Clemente Romano Apostolorum discipulo litteris mandatos in eam, quam hodie habemus, formam. Quin etiam, ut erat magnus fabularum artifex, & homo ex fumo lucem dare promptus, omnem eorum originem tam clare, tamque confidenter nobis narrat, quam si iis condendis ipse oculatus testis affuisset. Nam cum legisset apud Ἰουδαϊκας Apostolos Hierosolymis multos dies post decretum de legalibus factum remansisse , conquirentes una omnes quae ad communem utilitatem, & correctionem pertinerent; cumque postea apud Sophronium Hierosolytanum episcopum, in homilia (ut quidem ipse affirmat; eam enim ille unus vidit) de agone Petri & Pauli invenisset, Petrum & Paulum diebus illis quindecim, quibus una in sacra urbe fuerunt, canones & constitutiones fecisse; homo ingeniosus ex his hariolatus est, canones hos suos ab Apostolis una congregatis Hierosolymæ post illud de legalium cessatione decretum constitutos quidem fuisse ac traditos; postea vero à Clemente eorum discipulo litteris mandatos. En tibi veros Canonum natales. Hierosolyma locus est, in quo lucem ii primum viderunt. Si consulem requiris, Turriano authore, scito editos Anno Domini quidem xlv. Claudii vero Augusti 6o. P. Valerio Asiatico II. Cos In hoc enim tempus incidit illud Apostolorum de legalium cessatione memoratum à Turriano decretum. Binius, qui canones omnes, duobus exceptis, authenticos esse Turriano assentitur, de eorum scriptore aliud sensit. Primo enim ipsorum illorum quinquaginta, quos & ipse & alii adversarii maxime certos atque indubitatos esse volunt, quis vere scriptor fuerit, in ambiguo relinquit, quos scilicet Apostolica traditione ad nos dimanasse ideo recte credi putat, quod author eorum alius ignoretur. De cæteris triginta tribus, quos ipse quoque una cum Turriano probat, dubitat Sint-ne illi ex hoc Apostolicorum canonum codice à Pontificibus, Conciliis, ac Patribus accepti, an potius ex ipsorum sententiis in hunc codicem translati. Ita tota pene hæc causa ex Binio dunio dubia, atque incerta est. Sed Gabrie-lis Albaspinei, Aurelianensis Episcopi, multum ab his omnibus diversa est de Canonibus sententia. Primo enim pronun-ciat a, imperitos censendos, qui Canones istos Apostolorum authoritate sancitos, publicatosque certo affirment; quibus verbis & Turrianum, & ipsum etiam Bellarminum, ac Baronium suos, aliosque pene omnes Romanæ scholæ Theologos, qui de hoc argumento scripserunt, imperitia, & quidem, ut demonstrabimus, merito arguit. Tum hos Canones ab antiquitate Apostolicos appellatos esse existimant. Nam (inquit) cum eorum aliquot ab Apostolorum successoribus, qui teste Tertulliano de præscriptionibus Apostolici viri nominabantur, facti essent, Apostolicorum primum canones; deinde nonnullorum Latinorum ignorantia, aliquot litterarum detractione Apostolorum dicti sunt. Et apud Græcos quoque res ita processisse videtur. Aucti sunt postea, cum illis adjuncti essent, & eodem volumine comprehensi Græcæ Ecclesiæ canones.
units.tr: Turrianus, the most vigorous defender of them, holds that all of them were committed to writing by Clement of Rome, a disciple of the Apostles, in the form we have today. Indeed, since he was a great maker of fables and a man ready to make light out of smoke, he tells us the whole origin of them so clearly and so confidently, as if he had been an eyewitness present when they were composed. For when he had read in the Judaic writings [Ἰουδαϊκας] that the Apostles remained at Jerusalem for many days after the decree concerning the legal observances was made, gathering together all things that pertained to the common benefit and correction; and when afterwards he had found in a homily of Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem (as he himself claims, for he alone saw it), concerning the contest of Peter and Paul, that Peter and Paul in those fifteen days, while they were together in the holy city, made canons and constitutions, this clever man divined from these things that the canons were indeed drawn up and handed down by the Apostles, gathered together at Jerusalem after that decree on the cessation of legal observances, and afterwards committed to writing by Clement, their disciple. Behold the true birth of the canons: Jerusalem is the place where they first saw the light. If you ask for the consul, on Turrianus' authority you should know they were published in the year of the Lord 45, in the sixth year of Claudius Augustus, when P. Valerius Asiaticus was consul for the second time. For it was at this time that, as Turrianus recounts, that Apostolic decree on the cessation of legal observances occurred. Binius, who agrees with Turrianus that all the canons, except two, are authentic, thought otherwise about their writer. For first, concerning those very fifty which he and other opponents want to be most certain and undoubted, he leaves open who truly wrote them, holding that they are rightly believed to have come down to us by Apostolic tradition simply because their author is unknown. Concerning the other thirty-three, which he too approves along with Turrianus, he doubts whether they were received by Popes, Councils, and Fathers from this codex of Apostolic canons, or rather were translated into this codex from their opinions. Thus almost this whole matter is doubtful and uncertain, even from Binius' own account. But the opinion of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, differs greatly from all of these concerning the canons. For first he pronounces that those are to be considered unskilled who assert with certainty that those canons were sanctioned and published by the authority of the Apostles. By these words he charges Turrianus, Bellarmine, and Baronius, along with nearly all the Roman school's theologians who have written on this subject, with lack of skill, and indeed, as we shall demonstrate, rightly so. Then they think these canons were called Apostolic by antiquity. For (he says) since some of them were made by successors of the Apostles, who, as Tertullian says in the book On Prescription, were called apostolic men, they were first called Apostolic canons; then, through the ignorance of some Latins and the omission of a few letters, they were called of the Apostles. And it seems the matter went the same way among the Greeks too. They were afterwards enlarged, when the canons of the Greek Church were added to them and included in the same volume.

units.la: Hæ sunt, quantum quidem observare potui, adversariorum de Canonibus Apostolicis sententiæ; quarum ipsa diversitas arguit, quam anceps, quamque dubium, atque incertum sit totum hoc istorum Canonum nonum negotium, quorum authoritatem qui confirmare, ac constituere cupiunt, ii ipsi cogantur tamen varias, ac inter se pugnantes ea de re opiniones sequi.
units.tr: These are, so far as I have been able to observe, the opinions of the opponents concerning the Apostolic canons. Their very disagreement shows how uncertain, how doubtful, and how unsettled this whole business of those canons is, and those who want to confirm and establish their authority are themselves compelled to follow various opinions on the matter that contradict one another.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Graecorum de Canonibus sententia in Trullano Concilio promulgata, omnes 85. veros & Apostolicos esse. Latinos veteres ab a. D. 520. plerosque 50. canones Apost. admisisse, non tamen pro plane authenticis habuisse.
units.tr: The Greek view of the canons, promulgated at the Council in Trullo, is that all 85 are genuine and Apostolic. The older Latins, from the year 520 AD, mostly admitted about 50 of the Apostolic canons, but did not regard them as wholly authentic.

units.la: ED nunc videamus, quid de Canonibus istis ii Christiani senserint, qui superioribus retro ante haec ultima tempora saeculis vixerunt. Illud inprimis certum, atque confessum est apud universam Graecorum Ecclesiam jam inde a mille & paulo amplius annis perpetuo ac constanter pro Apostolicis habitos fuisse non modo quinquaginta quos Bellarminus & alii Latini admittunt, sed omnino octoginta quinque illos canones, quos Graeci codices exhibent, quosque a suis ad schismaticos hac in parte deficiens Turrianus defendit. Id vero constat ex Zonara, Balsamone, & caeteris juris Ecclesiastici Graecis interpretibus. Unus Photius, dubitasse videtur. Certe non dissimulavit dubios quibusdam videri, dum in
units.tr: Let us now see what those Christians thought of these canons who lived in the centuries before these last times. First, it is certain and agreed that across the whole Greek Church, for more than a thousand years, not only the fifty that Bellarmine and other Latins admit, but all eighty-five canons found in the Greek manuscripts, have been constantly and uniformly regarded as Apostolic. Turrianus, who falls short on this point, defends this view against the schismatics of his own side. This is clear from Zonaras, Balsamon, and the other Greek interpreters of canon law. Only Photius seems to have doubted. He certainly did not hide that some canons seemed doubtful to him, for in the preface to his Nomocanon he writes

units.la: ED: initial capital E of "Ed" printed as decorative woodcut initial S. in Proœmio sui Nomocanonis (quod, ut observavit Rever. Usserius a, in editione ea praeterminssum est, quae adjuncta habet Balsamonis scholia) scribit, se non alios modo canones comparavisse, ἀλλὰ τὰς λεγομένας τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, εἴ ϰαὶ τινὲς αὐτὰς ἀμφιβόλως διά τινας αἰτίας ἡγήσαντο, sed etiam eos, qui sanctorum Apostolorum esse dicuntur, licet aliqui quasdam ob causas dubia eos authoritatis esse existimaverint. Quamquam, ne quid dissimulem, Latinos fortasse, non Graecos his verbis notavit Photius. Ipse quidem in tota passim Nomocanone Apostolicos omnes nullo cum aliis Ecclesiasticis discrimine, velut authenticos, & receptos laudat. Sed & multis ante Photium annis Trullana, quae ab omnibus Graecis admittitur, Synodus b exeunte 7. saeculo ita diserte decreverat: Ἐδόξε ϰ τοῦτο τῇ ἁγίᾳ ταύτῃ συνόδῳ, ϰαλλίσϰα τε ϰ ἀπηδαιοῦσθαι, ὡς μένειν ἢ ὑπὸ τῶν νῦν βεβαίως ϰ ἀσφαλεῖς πρὸς ψυχῶν θεραπείαν, ϰ ἰατρείαν παθῶν τῶν ὑπὸ τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν ἁγίων ϰ ἐνδόξων Ἀποστόλων διδοόμενα πέντε ϰανόνας. Hoc quoque huic Sancta Synodo pulcherrime & honestissime placuit, ut deinceps ad animarum medelam, & perturbationum curationem firmi, stabilesque maneant; qui ab iis, qui nos praecesserunt, sanctis & gloriosis Apostolis traditi sunt, octoginta quinquinque Canones. Quin & annis ante hanc Synodum circiter centum & quinquaginta Justinianus Augustus hos Apostolorum canones prolixe commendaverat in constitutione ad Epiphanium CP. Patriarcham ita scribens; Recte (inquit a) atque congruenter omnia agerentur, si ipsum rei initium gratum Deo esset; quod quidem certe futurum credimus, si sacri illi canones diligenter observentur, quos nunquam satis laudati, adoratione digni, & qui ipsi Filium Dei conspexerunt, illique ministrarunt Apostoli nobis reliquerunt, ac Sancti Patres custodierunt & interpretati sunt. Hactenus Justinianus; a quo hos ipsos, quos nunc habemus. 85. canones intelligi inde constare a Rev. Vsserio didicimus; primo quod totidem in Nomocanonem ab ipso Justiniano confirmatum, & eidem illi Epiphanio commendatum relatos fuisse fides sit ex Arabico illius codicis interprete, qui in Oxoniensi Bibliotheca habetur, a Thoma Roe ex Oriente allatus, & donatus; secundo quod eosdem quoque canones 85. alter Nomocanon exhibeat iisdem temporibus, non a Theodoreto Cyrensi (quod perperam praeferunt nonnulla exemplaria) sed a Ioanne Epiphanienfi Scholastico concinnatus; eodem inquam illo Ioanne, qui Eutychio C P. Eiscopo circa suprema Iustiniani niani Augusti tempora suffectus est. Hæc fuerunt Ecclesiæ Græcæ, quæ jam inde à Iustiniani imperio (hoc est à sexto Christianismi jam adulto sæculo) ad nostram memoriam extitit, de illis 85. Apostolorum (ut vulgo appellantur) canonibus judicia. Ioannes Damasceni singularis est, neque ab ullo alio Græco (quod sciam) probata sententia; qui divinos novi Testamenti libros recensens, his annumerat istos Canones; sic canonem suum claudens a; Παῦλε Ἀποστόλε ἐπιστολαὶ Διαταξαμένη. Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννε εὐαγγελίςῤ. Κανόνες τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων Κλήμεντος. Pauli Apostoli epistolæ xiv. Apocalypsis Ioannis Euangelistæ. Canones sanctorum Apostolorum per Clementem.
units.tr: Indeed, in the preface to his Nomocanon (which, as the Reverend Ussher a has noted, is omitted from the edition that has Balsamon's scholia attached) he writes that he had consulted not only the other canons but also those that are said to be of the holy Apostles, though some have judged them doubtful in authority for certain reasons: ἀλλὰ τὰς λεγομένας τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, εἴ ϰαὶ τινὲς αὐτὰς ἀμφιβόλως διά τινας αἰτίας ἡγήσαντο. Still, to be honest, Photius may have made this remark about the Latins rather than the Greeks. Throughout his Nomocanon, however, he cites all the Apostolic canons without any distinction from the other ecclesiastical canons, as authentic and received. Moreover, many years before Photius, the Council in Trullo, which all Greeks accept b, had decreed at the end of the seventh century in plain terms: Ἐδόξε ϰ τοῦτο τῇ ἁγίᾳ ταύτῃ συνόδῳ, ϰαλλίσϰα τε ϰ ἀπηδαιοῦσθαι, ὡς μένειν ἢ ὑπὸ τῶν νῦν βεβαίως ϰ ἀσφαλεῖς πρὸς ψυχῶν θεραπείαν, ϰ ἰατρείαν παθῶν τῶν ὑπὸ τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν ἁγίων ϰ ἐνδόξων Ἀποστόλων διδοόμενα πέντε ϰανόνας. This also pleased this holy Synod most excellently and honourably: that the eighty-five canons handed down by the holy and glorious Apostles, who went before us, should remain firm and stable from now on, for the healing of souls and the cure of passions. Indeed, about a hundred and fifty years before this Synod, the Emperor Justinian had warmly commended these Apostolic canons in a constitution addressed to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople, writing thus: "Everything would rightly and fittingly be done (he says a) if the very beginning of the matter were pleasing to God; and this we surely believe will be so, if those holy canons are diligently observed, which the Apostles, who saw the Son of God and served him, have left us, worthy of endless praise and worship, and which the holy Fathers have kept and interpreted." So far Justinian. From this passage, the Reverend Ussher taught us that these very 85 canons we now have are meant. First, because the fact that the same number were incorporated into the Nomocanon, confirmed by Justinian himself and commended to that same Epiphanius, is attested by the Arabic translator of that manuscript, which is in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, brought from the East and given by Thomas Roe. Second, because another Nomocanon from the same period also contains the same 85 canons, compiled not by Theodoret of Cyrus (as some copies wrongly state) but by John the Scholastic of Epiphania; the same John, I say, who succeeded Eutychius, Bishop of Constantinople, near the end of the reign of the Emperor Justinian. These were the judgements of the Greek Church about the 85 canons of the Apostles, as they are commonly called, from the time of Justinian's reign (that is, from the sixth century of the now-mature Christianity) down to our own memory. John of Damascus holds a singular view, and, as far as I know, no other Greek has approved it. In listing the divine books of the New Testament, he counts these canons among them, closing his catalogue thus: Παῦλε Ἀποστόλε ἐπιστολαὶ Διαταξαμένη. Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννε εὐαγγελίςῤ. Κανόνες τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων Κλήμεντος. "The fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul. The Apocalypse of John the Evangelist. The Canons of the holy Apostles, through Clement."

units.la: Latinorum longe alia ratio est. Illi enim toto illo tempore, quod à Iustiniano ad proximum avorum nostrorum sæculum fluxit, habuerunt & ipsi Canones Apostolorum; sed neque numero, neque authoritate Græcis pares. Nam apud eos quinquaginta duntaxat fuerunt; cum essent apud Græcos, ut diximus, 85. Tum ipsi illi quinquaginta, tametsi à Latinis toto illo tempore aliquantum usurpati, nullius tamen, quod sciam, generalis Synodi, apud eos authoritate confirmati ac promulgati sunt, (Trullanos quippe canones nones neque nunc recipit, neque olim unquam admisit Romana Ecclesia.) Hanc fuisse Latinorum omnium de Canonibus iistis opinionem patet primo ex Gratiano qui suam juris canonici rhapsodiam circa annum Domini 1150. concinnasse perhibetur. Is enim haec nomine Leonis IX. P. R. contra epistolam Nicetae Abbatis, in suum decretum retulit; Clementis librum id est Petri Apostoli itinerarium, & Apostolorum Canones numerant Patres inter Apocrypha, exceptis capitulis quinquaginta, quae decreverunt orthodoxae fidei adjungenda. Quo loco observandum est ista, non Leonis, ut imprudens putavit Gratianus, sed Humberti Cardinalis verba esse; quae nos in superiori de Constitutionibus disputatione descripsimus. Sed utcunque sit, cum ea pro Pontificis sui sententia habuerit Gratianus, cumque Humbertum ex suae Ecclesiae sensu eascripsisse, palam sit; non est dubitandum, quin Latini & duodecimo seculo quo vixit Gratianus, & undecimo, quo floruit Humbertus, quinquaginta quidem priores canones pro legitimis, triginta vero quinque posteriores pro spuriis, & apocryphis habuerint. Eodem quoque pertinere merito judicavit Bellarminus , haec Urbani II. (qui a D. 1088. Romae sedit) apud eundem Gratianum verba, Sciendum vero, quod Canonum Apostolorum authoritate Orientalis, & ex parte Romana utitur Ecclesia. Significat nimirum, Græcos Apostolorum dictos canones omnes plane, penitusque admittere; Latinos eorum duntaxat partem; hoc est quinquaginta tantum, non autem 85. Sic etiam Isidorus Mercator, qui post a. D. 800. vixit, tametsi, insignis alioqui impostor, & fœcundus apocryphorum parens, non est tamen ausus suę tarragini plures quam quinquaginta Apostolorum canones inserere, hæc Collectioni suæ præfatus, ut ea ex vetutissimo codice emendata exhibet Baronius b; Denique propter eorum authoritatem cæteris Conciliis præposuimus Canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum (licet à quibusdam Apocryphi dicantur) quoniam plures eos recipiunt, & sancti Patres eorum sententias synodali authoritate roboravere, & inter canonicas posuere constitutiones. Atque Isidoricæ hujus præfationis (quod non putavi negligendum) diserte a. D. 870. meminit Hincmarus in eo opere, quod LV. capitum dicitur. Locum, quia ex eo Baroniana emendatio liquido confirmatur, adscribere placuit c; In cujus, collectionis scilicet) præfatione idem (inquit c) Isidorus dicit de Apostolorum canonibus, quod à quibusquibusdam dicantur apocryphi, & plures eos recipiant, & sancti Patres eorum sententias synodali authoritate roboraverunt, & inter canonicas constitutiones posuerunt; quod de quibusdam sententiis verum est, sicut alibi in hoc opusculo potes legere. Postremo his omnibus multo anterior Dionysius Exiguus, initio sexti saeculi, cum codici Canonum Ecclesiasticorum suo Apostolicos quoque canonas praeponendos putasset, eos non plures, quam quinquaginta exhibuit; ut apparet, tum ex Indice canonum, qui in eo codice continentur; Lutetiae, a. D. 1609. ex manuscripto Nicolai Fabri edito; tum ex ipso codice ibidem a. D. 1628. ex Bibliotheca Clar. Iustelli publicato. Eorum autem Canonum, quos Dionysiacus codex repraesentat, ultimus sub numero quinquagesimo sic habet; Siquis Episcopus, aut presbyter non trinam merfionem unius mysterii celebret, sed semel mergat in baptismate, quod dari videtur in Domini morte, deponatur. Non enim dixit nobis Dominus in morte mea baptizate, sed, Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Jam in hanc Dionysiacam collectionem evidentissime pertinent illa Leonis quarti P. R. in epistola a. D. 849. ad Britanniae episcopos data, & a Gratiano in decretum relata, & à Turriano in hac disputatione laudata; De libellis & commentariis aliorum non convenit aliquem judicare, & sanctorum Conciliorum Canones relinquere, vel decretalium regulas, id est quae habentur apud nos simul cum illis in canone, & quibus in omnibus Ecclesiasticis utemur judiciis, id est Apostolorum, Nicaenorum, Ancyranorum, Neocaesariensium, Gangrensium, Antiochensium, Laodicensium, Cathedonensium, Sardicensium, Carthaginensium, Africanensium; & cum illis regulae praesulum Romanorum Sylvestri, Siricii, Innocentii, Zosimi, Coelestini, Leonis, Gelasii, Hilarii, Symmachi, Simplicii.
units.tr: The Latins' reasoning was quite different. For throughout the whole period from Justinian to the next-to-last century of our ancestors, they too possessed the Canons of the Apostles, but these were not equal to the Greek ones either in number or in authority. For they had only fifty, whereas the Greeks, as we have said, had 85. Moreover, even those fifty, though used to some extent by the Latins throughout that whole period, were, so far as I know, never confirmed and promulgated by the authority of any general Council among them (for the Roman Church neither now receives the canons of Trullo nor ever admitted them). That this was the opinion of all the Latins about these canons is clear, first, from Gratian, who is said to have compiled his rhapsody of canon law around the year of the Lord 1150. For he carried into his decree, under the name of Pope Leo IX, these words against the letter of Abbot Nicetas: "The Fathers count the Book of Clement, that is the itinerary of the Apostle Peter, and the Canons of the Apostles, among the Apocrypha, except for fifty chapters, which they decreed should be added to orthodox faith." Here it must be noted that these words are not Leo's, as Gratian unwisely thought, but those of Cardinal Humbert; we set them out in our earlier discussion of the Constitutions. But however that may be, since Gratian held these words to be the opinion of his Pontiff, and it is plain that he copied Humbert according to the sense of his own Church, there is no doubt that the Latins, both in the twelfth century when Gratian lived and in the eleventh century when Humbert flourished, regarded the first fifty canons as legitimate and the last thirty-five as spurious and apocryphal. Bellarmine rightly judged that the following words of Pope Urban II (who sat at Rome from 1088), also in Gratian, belong to the same point: "It must be known that the Eastern Church uses the authority of the Canons of the Apostles, and the Roman Church does so in part." This plainly means that the Greeks fully and completely admit all the canons called Apostolic, while the Latins admit only a part of them, that is, only fifty and not 85. So too Isidore Mercator, who lived after the year 800, although otherwise a notorious impostor and a prolific parent of forgeries, did not dare to insert more than fifty Apostolic canons into his collection, as he prefaced it, and as Baronius presents it, corrected from a very old manuscript: "Finally, because of their authority, we have placed before the other Councils the canons called Apostolic (though some call them apocryphal), since many accept them, the holy Fathers confirmed their judgements with synodal authority, and they placed them among the canonical constitutions." Hincmar, in the work called the Book of Fifty-Five Chapters, expressly recalls the preface of this Isidore in the year 870, and I thought it not worth neglecting. Since the Baronian correction is clearly confirmed by his words, I have chosen to quote the passage c: "In the preface of that collection (says c), Isidore says the same about the Canons of the Apostles, that some call them apocryphal, that many accept them, that the holy Fathers have confirmed their judgements with synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions; which is true of certain judgements, as you may read elsewhere in this little work." Finally, long before all these, Dionysius Exiguus, at the beginning of the sixth century, when he thought that the Apostolic canons should also be placed before the code of his ecclesiastical canons, presented no more than fifty of them. This is clear both from the index of canons contained in that code, published at Paris in 1609 from the manuscript of Nicolas Fabri, and from the code itself, published in 1628 from the library of the distinguished Justellus. The last of the canons which the Dionysian code presents, under number fifty, reads thus: "If any bishop or presbyter does not celebrate the trine immersion of the one mystery, but dips only once in baptism, which seems to be given in the death of the Lord, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say to us, 'Baptize in my death,' but 'Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.'" Now the following words of Pope Leo IV, in his letter of 849 to the bishops of Britain, plainly pertain to this Dionysian collection; Gratian placed them in his decree, and Turrianus cites them in this dispute: "It is not fitting to judge about the libels and commentaries of others, or to leave aside the canons of the holy Councils, or the rules of the decretals, that is, those which we have among us together with those in the canon, and which we use in all ecclesiastical judgements, namely the Apostles', the Nicene, the Ancyrene, the Neocaesarean, the Gangrene, the Antiochene, the Laodicean, the Chalcedonian, the Sardican, the Carthaginian, the African; and with them the rules of the Roman prelates Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Simplicius."

units.la: Priori parte totidem capitum canones nominat, quot habentur in Dionysii codice; nisi quod GPnae. primae synodi canones omittit, quos tres Dionysius exhibet; ut non sit dubitandum, quin Apostolorum eosdem canones intelligat, quos repraesentat Dionysius, hoc est quinquaginta, non plures. Ex posteriori vero hujus Leoninae sententiae parte, Turrianus (ut hoc obiter dicam si judicii, vel pudoris micam habuisset, intelligere poterat, nullo adhuc tum in pretio apud Romanam sedem fuisse stramineas illas priorum Romae ad Sylvestrum usque episcoporum a pseudo-Isidoro ipsis illis (ut videtur) temporibus conficonfictas epistolas, quas ipse impetu, ac loquacitate, nescio an stultitia & amentia majore totis quatuor libris procacissime defendere ausus est. Sed redeo ad Canones Apostolorum, quos (ut ex superioribus apparet) non plures, quam quinquaginta omnis Latinorum Ecclesia totis his undecim saeculis cognitos habuit; donec avorum nostrorum memoria turpiter a suis descisens Turrianus, & in Graecorum schismaticorum castra impudenter transiens, triginta quinque illos, nunquam antehac in Occidente agnitos, canones superioribus quinquaginta adjiciendos, & Apostolica authoritate donandos assereret.
units.tr: In the first part he names as many canons as are found in Dionysius's collection, except that he leaves out the canons of the First Synod, which Dionysius gives as three. So there is no doubt that he means the Apostles' canons that Dionysius presents, that is fifty, and no more. As for the latter part of this statement by Leo, Turrianus (let me say this in passing, since if he had any judgment or a crumb of shame he could have understood it) ought to have recognised that those straw-stuffed letters of the earlier bishops of Rome, down to Sylvester, forged by the pseudo-Isidore at what seems to be the same period, were then held in no esteem at the Roman see. Turrianus has dared, with great impudence, to defend them through four whole books, with a rashness and garrulity, and I do not know whether it was greater folly or madness. But to return to the Canons of the Apostles: as is clear from what precedes, the whole Latin Church throughout these eleven centuries knew and held no more than fifty. Then, in the memory of our grandfathers, Turrianus shamefully deserted his own side, passed shamelessly into the camp of the schismatic Greeks, and asserted that those thirty-five canons, never before recognised in the West, should be added to the fifty above and endowed with apostolic authority.

units.la: Iam Apostolorum Canones Latini, ut pauciores numero, ita & authoritate multo inferiores, quam Graeci habuere. Hi, quod nuper audivimus, suos illos 85. & a sanctis gloriosisque Apostolis relictos, ac traditos esse, & firmos stabilesque manere in generali synodo a decreverunt; Quin & eos Graecorum nonnemo libris scripturarum canonicis annumerare ausus est b. Latini veteres de suis quinquaginta omnia multo modestiora. Nam Hincmarus Remensis magni apud nos nominis Episcopus (quem Turrianus c pro consueta sapientia Germanicae nationis praesulem eo ipso loco facit, quo Remensem dixerat) is, inquam;
units.tr: Now the Latin Apostolic Canons, being fewer in number, also have much less authority than the Greeks gave theirs. The Greeks, as we have lately heard, decreed that their 85 canons were handed down and delivered by the holy and glorious Apostles, and that they remain firm and stable in a general synod a. Indeed, one of the Greeks has even dared to count them among the canonical books of Scripture b. The older Latins were far more modest about their fifty. For Hincmar of Reims, a bishop of great name among us (whom Turrianus, with his usual learning, makes a German prelate in the very place where he had called him the bishop of Reims), this Hincmar, I say,

units.la: a Trull. can. 2. — b Damasc. l. 4. de fid. c. 18. — c L. pro can. c. 15. p. 48, verf. quam, Hincmarus in opere quinque & quinquaginta capitum, quod a. D. 870. adversus Hincmarum nepotem, Laudunen-sem episcopum, elucubravit, Canones i-stos negat ab Apostolis scriptos; Caeterum iidem (inquit a) canones, qui vocantur A-postolorum, non ab Apostolis conscripti esse creduntur; idque ipse ex eo probat, quod praeter quinque, quas enumerat Synodos, nullam aliam Apostoli habuisse legentur, in qua istos Canones condiderint. Sed & in eos laudat Gelasii catalogum, qui nullam eorum inter libros ab Ecclesia Catholica receptos mentionem fecit. In iis vero ait quaedam esse receptibilia, quaedam etiam non secunda, de quibus (inquit b) quaedam assumpta sunt in Conciliis, quaedam etiam a maximis, & praecipua authoritatis viris, in suis opusculis, sicut & de apocryphis, assumpta fuisse, legimus, quoniam in quibusdam ad instructionem valent. Et ideo, sicut majorum traditione didicimus, seorsum ante Concilia in canonum libris ad instructionem, & propter vulgatam eorum famam ponuntur. Vides, ut ab Apostolis conditos negat; ut ab authenticis Ecclesiae regulis excludat; ut non per omnia recipiendos doceat; ut in Canonum libris seorsim ante Concilia (veluti in codice Dionysiaco) poni, non ob authoritatem, sed ad instru-ctionem
units.tr: a Trull. can. 2. — b Damasc. l. 4. de fid. c. 18. — c L. pro can. c. 15. p. 48, verf. quam. In his work of fifty-five chapters, which he composed in 870 against his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon, Hincmar denies that these canons were written by the Apostles. Moreover, these same canons (he says a) which are called the canons of the Apostles are not believed to have been written by the Apostles; and he proves this from the fact that, apart from the five synods he lists, we read of no other synod that the Apostles held, at which they could have drawn up these canons. He also cites the catalogue of Gelasius, which makes no mention of them among the books received by the Catholic Church. In that catalogue, he says, some things are receivable, and some are not of the second rank, of which (he says b) some have been adopted in councils, and some also have been taken up, as we read, by the greatest and most authoritative men in their own writings, as also with the apocryphal books, since in some respects they are useful for instruction. And therefore, as we have learned from the tradition of our elders, they are placed separately before the councils, in the books of canons, for instruction, and because of their widespread reputation. You see how he denies that they were composed by the Apostles; how he excludes them from the authentic rules of the Church; how he teaches that they are not to be received in every respect; and how they are placed separately before the councils in books of canons (as in the Dionysian collection), not on account of their authority but for instruction,

units.la: b Ibid. p. 473. ctionem, & propter famam. De eorum vero origine sic sentit, non fuisse constitutos Conciliorum Episcopalium authoritate, sed a primis temporibus traditione viritim Apostolicorum virorum fuisse mentibus commendatos; & partim verbis, partim sensu, ac sparsim diversis quorundam epistolis pro qualitate causarum, & personarum, ac temporum inditos, atque exinde antequam Episcopi Concilia libere inciperent celebrare, a devotis quibusque collectos. Denique totum hunc de istis Canonibus sermonem concludit a; Quapropter (inquit) in lectione illorum sequenda est cautela ab eodem S. Gelasio pramonita; Cum hac (inquit) ad Catholicorum manus advenerint, B. Pauli Apostoli b pracedat sententia, qua dicit, Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. Eat nunc Turrianus, & suum nobis Igmarum (sic enim hunc scriptorem appellat) objectet. Ille vero hanc, ut liquet, Canonum collectionem eadem cum cautela legendam, qua leguntur apocrypha, nunquam dixisset, si Apostolicam, aut Clementinam putasset. Certe neque ille de variis capitulis Ecclesiasticis liber, cujus decimum octavum caput laudat Turrianus, neque ullus ex iis tribus, quae idem inde describit locis, extat in iis Hincmari operibus, quae nuper in duos grandes Tomos digesta, publicavit Sirmondus, doctissi-mus, ac diligentissimus Jesuita; quo fit credibile Turrianum (cujus quale sit ingenium, quam audax, quam fabularum avidum non semel dicendum est) haec vel Hincmaro ipsum prudentem scientemque affinxisse, vel certe ex falsis, & interpolatis codicibus descripsisse. Huc accedit, quod & ipsa illa, quae velut ex Hincmaro adfert, Canonum Apostolicorum librum non obscure jugulant.Haec enim habet tertius velut ex Hincmaro a Turriano descriptus locus; Ait Apostolus, Omnia probate, Quae bona sunt, tenete. Ergo juxta eundem Apostolum utrumque debemus, & librum de canonibus Apostolorum APOCRYPHUM REPUDIARE; & capitula, siqua in illo ad veritatem pertinentia inveniantur, non reprobare, illa, inquam, minime reprobare, quae sancti Patres pro authenticis receperunt; imo quorum authoritate suas sanctiones piissime firmaverunt. Haec Turrianicus ipse Hincmarus de hoc Apostolicorum Canonum libro; quem repudiat quidem, velut apocryphum, non sic tamen, ut abjicienda putet, quaecunque in eo leguntur. Omnia probari vult ex Pauli & Gelasii sententia; (quod & noster, id est verus, Hincmarus dixit) & teneri, quae recta; explodi, quae aliena deprehensa fuerint. Atqui nullus est usque adeo apocryphus liber, in quo non idem quoque fit adhibendum temperamentum. Multa enim vel in ipsis haereticorum libris posita legi, quae ad veritatem pertineant, non adeo refutanda, sed suscipienda, & Gelasius jampridem monuit, & omnes sciunt ac confitentur. Ergo dubitari non debet, quin hunc librum ab Ecclesiasticorum censu alienum existimaverit Hincmarus. Sed & multo, quam Hincmarus, tristius atque atrocius de his jampridem Canonibus decreverat Isidorus, non ille noni saeculi tenebrio, de quo paulo ante diximus, sed clarissimus Hispalis antistes, quem anno septimi saeculi sexto & tricesimo mortuum constat. Ejus autem ea de re verba, & a Gratiano in Decretum relata, & teste Antonio Augustino longe doctissimo viro, in omnibus veteribus libris Hispania Conciliorum inventa, ita habent; (canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, sed quia eosdem nec sedes Apostolica recepit, nec sancti Patres illis assensum praebuerunt, pro eo quod ab haereticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositi dignoscuntur; quamvis in eis utilia inveniantur, tamen ab authoritate canonica, atque Apostolica, eorum gesta constat esse remota, atque inter apocrypha deputata. Hactenus Hispalensis Isidorus; rus; plane contra sentiens, quam ille alter Isidorus, cujus verba Gratianus quoque, sed mendosa recitat (nos supra à Baronio emaculata exhibuimus) Gratianus vero, ut notavit Antonius Augustinus b, non distinxit varietatem horum scriptorum ut debuit, cum contraria dicerent. Hic enim Mercator hos Canones probat, quos ille (Hispalensis scilicet Isidorus) rejecerat. Hoc vero dicto, Isidorus, ceu quodam ictu fulminis, omnem Graecanicorum canonum authoritatem prostravit, atque confregit; omnes Turiani, Baroniique ac Bellarmini pro iis machinas, atque conatus disjecit, ac dissipavit. Quos enim hi ab Apostolis conditos ac promulgatos, & à Clemente conscriptos fuisse volunt canonas, hic eos ab haereticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositos esse liquido pronuntiat; Quos illi à Romae episcopis, & à veteribus Theologis pro sacrosanctis Ecclesiae regulis semper agnitos fuisse pertinaciter contendunt, eos Isidorus vel à sede Apostolica receptos, vel à patribus probatos disertissime negat; quos denique illi pro legitimis ac canonicis semper in Ecclesia habitos fuisse ajunt, hic contra affirmat, inter apocrypha deputatos, & ab authoritate Canonica, atque Apostolica remotos fuisse. Unde certo certius est, quicquid est istorum Apostolicorum Canonum, nonum ; ullam adhuc publicam inter omnes Christianos authoritatem circa septimi saeculi initia habuisse; & Justiniani, & Joannis Nomocanonem, in quem isti primum canones jam adulto sexto saeculo fuerant relati, nondum ineunte septimo saeculo vel Isidoro, vel nostris Latinis cognitum fuisse.
units.tr: b Ibid. p. 473. for instruction and because of their reputation. As to their origin, he thinks they were not established by the authority of episcopal councils, but were commended to the minds of individuals from the earliest times by the tradition of the apostolic men; and that, partly in words, partly in sense, and scattered through the various letters of certain men, they were set down according to the nature of the causes, the persons and the times, and afterwards, before bishops began to hold councils freely, were gathered together by various devout people. Finally he concludes his whole discussion of these canons thus: Therefore (he says) caution must be observed in reading them, as St Gelasius admonished. When these have come into the hands of Catholics, let the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul go before them, in which he says, Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Let Turrianus now go and object to us his "Igmarus" (for so he calls this writer). Clearly, Hincmar would never have said that this collection of canons is to be read with the same caution with which the apocryphal books are read, had he thought it Apostolic or Clementine. Certainly neither that book of miscellaneous ecclesiastical chapters, whose eighteenth chapter Turrianus cites, nor any of the three passages which he describes from it, is found in those works of Hincmar which Sirmond, a most learned and diligent Jesuit, has lately published in two large volumes. So it is credible that Turrianus (whose character, and how bold and how fond of fables he is, must be said more than once) either invented these words for Hincmar himself, knowing full well what he was doing, or at least copied them from false and interpolated manuscripts. Add to this that the very passages he brings forward as from Hincmar openly undermine the book of Apostolic Canons. For the third passage, which Turrianus copied as from Hincmar, says this: The Apostle says, Prove all things; hold fast what is good. Therefore, according to the same Apostle, we ought both to reject as apocryphal the book of the Canons of the Apostles, and not to condemn whatever in it is found to pertain to the truth; I say, by no means to condemn those chapters which the holy Fathers have received as authentic, indeed by whose authority they most devoutly confirmed their own decrees. This is what Turrianus's own Hincmar says about this book of Apostolic Canons. He rejects it indeed as apocryphal, yet not so as to think that everything read in it should be cast away. He wants everything to be proved by the sentence of Paul and of Gelasius (as our Hincmar, that is the true one, also said), and what is right to be held, and what is found to be foreign to be rejected. Yet there is no apocryphal book so entirely bad that the same moderation should not be applied to it. For many things that are found in the books of heretics too, and which pertain to the truth, are not to be refuted but received; Gelasius warned of this long ago, and everyone knows and admits it. Therefore it should not be doubted that Hincmar judged this book to be outside the reckoning of the Church. But Isidore had decreed far more harshly and savagely about these same canons long before Hincmar. This was not that obscure writer of the ninth century of whom we spoke a little earlier, but the most distinguished bishop of Seville, who is known to have died in the thirty-sixth year of the seventh century. His words on this matter, which Gratian also quoted in the Decretum, and which, according to Antonius Augustinus, a most learned man, are found in all the old books of Spanish councils, read thus: (The canons which are called those of the Apostles, but since neither the apostolic see has received them, nor the holy Fathers given their assent to them, because they are known to have been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles; although useful things are found in them, nevertheless their deeds are clearly removed from canonical and apostolic authority, and are reckoned among the apocrypha.) So far Isidore of Seville, plainly thinking the opposite of that other Isidore, whose words Gratian also quotes, though in a corrupt form (we have given them above, corrected, from Baronius). Gratian, however, as Antonius Augustinus observed, did not distinguish the variety of these writers as he ought to have, since they said contrary things. For Mercator approves these canons, which the other (namely Isidore of Seville) had rejected. By this one statement, Isidore, as with a kind of thunderbolt, overthrew and shattered all the authority of the Greek canons, and scattered and dispersed all the machinery and efforts of Turrianus, Baronius and Bellarmine on their behalf. For where these men insist that the canons were composed and promulgated by the Apostles and written down by Clement, he plainly declares that they were composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles. Where those men stubbornly maintain that they were always recognised in the Church as sacred rules by the bishops of Rome and the ancient theologians, Isidore emphatically denies that they were received by the apostolic see or approved by the Fathers. And where those men say they were always held in the Church as legitimate and canonical, he affirms on the contrary that they were reckoned among the apocrypha and removed from canonical and apostolic authority. Hence it is more certain than certain that whatever these Apostolic Canons are, they had no public authority among all Christians at the beginning of the seventh century; and that the Nomocanon of Justinian and John, into which these canons had first been carried in the sixth century, was not yet known, at the beginning of the seventh century, either to Isidore or to our Latins.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Gelasium E. R. cum Romana Synodo a. D. 494. omnes omnino Apostolorum canones velut apocryphos repudiasse; & in eadem sententia Isidorum Hispal. a. D. 620. fuisse. Turriani, Bellarmini, & Baronii diversa quidem, sed omnes inanes & inverecunda ad Gelasii decretum glossa atque exceptiones fuse refelluntur.
units.tr: Gelasius of Rome, with the Roman synod in AD 494, rejected all the canons of the Apostles entirely as apocryphal, and Isidore of Seville in AD 620 held the same view. The varied but all empty and shameless glosses and exceptions of Turrianus, Bellarmine and Baronius against Gelasius' decree are thoroughly refuted.

units.la: QUOD vero negat Isidorus istos Canones à Romana sede receptos, quod eos ait inter apocrypha deputatos, id utrumque quam vere dixerit, luculentissime testatur Synodi Romanae, anno D. 494. Gelasio praesidE habitae de libris Canonicis, Ecclesiasticis, & Apocryphis decretum Nam inprimis (quod ab Hincmaro nuper observatum fuisse audivimus) in priori decreti parte, qua post sacros utriusque foederis libros, alia Ecclesiastica monumenta, nimirum mirum Synodorum Nicenæ, CPæ. Ephesinæ, Chalcedonensis decreta, Sanctorum Patrum, ut Cypriani, Basilii, Athanasii, Cyrilli, Chrysostomi, Theophili & aliorum opuscula memorantur, nulla plane fit istorum canonum mentio; quos tamen si recepti fuissent, & pro Apostolicis habiti, nemo non videt, vel Scripturis divinis accensendos, vel certe statim post eos, primo ante alia omnia loco, collocandos fuisse. Tum in altera decreti parte a, quæ notitiam continet eorum, quæ ab hæreticis, sive schismaticis conscripta vel prædicata sunt, quaque nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Romana Ecclesia, in ea inquam parte dissertissimis verbis nominantur Apostolorum canones b; Liber Canonum Apostolorum apocryphus. Hæc Gelasii Synodus; quibus nihil clarius, aut luculentius dici potest. Eo ergo, ut liquet, respexit Isidorus, dum Canones ab hæreticis compositos, & à canonica & Apostolica authoritate remotos, & inter apocrypha deputatos dixit; & à sede Apostolica receptos negavit. Eadem diserte, quod nuper dicebamus, laudavit Hincmarus c; Sed & B. (inquit) Gelasius in Catalogo, qui libri ab Ecclesia Catholica recipiantur descripto; authenticis Scripturis, & Nicænæ, Constantinopolitanæ, ac Ephesinæ, Chaloecdonensis quoque Synodi, & aliis Concilijs à sanctis Patribus institutis, & Orthodoxorum opusculis, atque decretalibus epistolis Apostolicæ Sedis Pontificum, aliisque scripturis discrete commemoratis, de his Apostolorum Canonibus penitus tacuit; sed nec inter apocrypha eos misit, Hactenus Hincmarus, cujus ultima illa verba, sed nec inter apocrypha eos misit, vel memoriæ lapsu imprudenti exciderunt; vel certe mendosa sunt, & restituto verbo omisit, pro eo, quod in codicibus vulgatis legitur misit, corrigenda; ut ita scripserit Hincmarus, sed nec inter apocrypha eos omisit. Nam Gelasius quidem, quin eos Canones inter apocrypha miserit, hoc est relegarit, & rejecerit, vel ex illius sæculi idiotismo, posuerit ac collocaverit, nemo dubitare potest, qui nuper à nobis recitatum Gelasii decretum legerit. Quin & ipse Hincmarus (apud Turrianum quidem certe) in illo, quem nuper memoravimus, de variis capitulis Ecclesiasticis libro diserte affirmat, Canones Apostolorum à Gelasio in apocryphorum classem rejectos; Sciendum autem (inquit ) quod B. Gelasius Papa librum, qui de Canonibus Apostolorum apud Græcos inscribitur, pro apocrypho deputavit, cui & nos contradicere non debemus, quia hoc cum sine causa fecisse non credimus. Sed & ad hanc ad hanc quoque Gelasii sententiam perti- nere videtur,quod Dionysius Exiguus cum in Canonum collectione sua hos quoque Apostolorum Canones praeter veterū morem inserendos putasset, Stephanum Episcopum, ad quem opus mittit, ita monitum in praefatione voluit ; In principio itaque (inquit) canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum de Graco transtulimus ; quibus quia plurimi consensum non praebuere facilem, hoc ipsum vestram noluimus ignorare sanctitatem ; quamvis postea constituta Pontificum ex ipsis Canonibus assumpta esse videantur. Nimirum ignorare non potuit vir Gelasii aevo proximus, ac pene ejus par, (hic enim exeunte quinto, Dionysius ineunte sexto saeculo floruit) Latinos, quorum erat inquilinus, istorum Canonum librum paulo ante in Synodo Romana inter apocrypha rejecisse. Sed homo ortu, ac natu, cultuque ac eruditione exterus a se impetrare non potuit, quin vernaculos gentis suę Canones, nondum Latina lingua ad illa tempora ornatos, Romanis, apud quos vivebat, communicaret; ac ne eorum animos nova hac merce offenderet, invidiam, qua eos flagrare intelligebat, lenire inprimis modesta hac praefatione studuit; non dissimulans quidem rejectos a plurimis, sed tamen eos tacite purgans, aut certe excusans, sans, dum ait ex ipsis assumpta fuisse Pontificum constituta. Ego vero putaverim non ex canonum collectione sua decreta Pontifices, sed ex Pontificum constitutis suos canones assumpsisse primum eorum collectorem. Atque ita quidem Dionysius. Ferrandus vero Diaconus Carthaginiensis, qui iisdem propemodum temporibus, id est paulo post sexti saeculi initia, Canonum Ecclesiasticorum breviarium confecit, intra terminos Patrum se continuit; & Apostolorum Canones in sua illa collectione praetermisit; plane ex Gelasii disciplina. Sed Dionysiaca ob elegantiam, & ordinem veteris codicis aemulum; adhaec ob insigne viri meritum placuerunt; & eam, de qua diximus, Canonibus Apostolicis gratiam apud Latinorum plerosque paulatim conciliarunt; ita tamen, ut manerent non obscura veteris in eos odii vestigia. Nam & in Cresconiana collectione Baronius a,& in Vigornienfi a Dunstano collato canonum vetustissimo codice Ussperius b praefixum extare hunc titulum memorant, ex Dionysii (ut liquet) ad Stephanum epistola, ductum, ac desumptum; Incipiunt Ecclesiastica regula Sanctorum Apostolorum, prolata per Clementem Ecclesiae Romanae Pontificem; qua ex Graecis exemplaribus in ordine primo ponuntur; Quibus quamplurimi quidem
units.tr: That Isidore denies these canons were received by the Roman see, and says they were counted among the apocrypha, the most splendid evidence that both claims were true is the decree of the Roman synod held under Gelasius in AD 494 on the canonical, ecclesiastical and apocryphal books. First, in the earlier part of the decree, where after the sacred books of both covenants other ecclesiastical writings are listed, namely the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, and the works of the holy Fathers such as Cyprian, Basil, Athanasius, Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophilus and others, there is no mention at all of these canons. Yet if they had been received and regarded as apostolic, anyone can see they would have been placed either among the divine Scriptures or at least directly after them, first of all, before everything else. Then in the other part of the decree, a which contains a list of what has been written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics, and which the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church by no means receives, in that part, I say, the canons of the Apostles are named in the most explicit words: b The book of the Canons of the Apostles, apocryphal. This is the synod of Gelasius, and nothing clearer or more plainly stated can be said. Isidore therefore, as is evident, had this in view when he said the canons were composed by heretics, removed from canonical and apostolic authority, and counted among the apocrypha, and denied they were received by the Apostolic see. Hincmarus c praised the same thing explicitly, as we said just now: But (he says) Gelasius too, in the catalogue describing which books are received by the Catholic Church, mentioned the authentic Scriptures, the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon too, and other councils instituted by the holy Fathers, and the writings of the orthodox, and the decretal letters of the Popes of the Apostolic See, and other writings, separately listed, and he said nothing at all about these canons of the Apostles; nor did he put them among the apocrypha. So far Hincmarus. His last words, nor did he put them among the apocrypha, either slipped out through a careless lapse of memory, or else the text is faulty and must be corrected by restoring the word omisit (left out) in place of the misit (put) read in the printed editions, so that Hincmarus wrote nor did he leave them out among the apocrypha. That Gelasius did in fact put them among the apocrypha, that is, relegated and rejected them, or, in the idiom of that age, placed and classed them there, no one who has read the decree of Gelasius which we quoted just now can doubt. Indeed Hincmarus himself (at least as Turrianus cites him) plainly affirms in that book, On various ecclesiastical chapters, which we mentioned just now, that the canons of the Apostles were rejected by Gelasius into the class of apocrypha: Moreover, it should be known (he says) that Blessed Pope Gelasius counted as apocryphal the book which among the Greeks is entitled the Canons of the Apostles, and we too ought not to contradict this, since we do not believe he did it without cause. But the letter of Dionysius Exiguus to Bishop Stephen also seems to belong to this same opinion of Gelasius. When Dionysius, in his own collection of canons, thought these canons of the Apostles ought to be inserted, contrary to the older custom, he wanted Stephen, to whom he sends the work, to be warned in the preface: At the beginning, therefore (he says) we have translated the canons which are called those of the Apostles from the Greek; since many have not given them easy assent, we did not wish your holiness to be ignorant of this very thing; although later the constitutions of the Popes seem to have been taken from these same canons. Surely a man so close in age to Gelasius, and nearly his equal (for he flourished at the end of the fifth and the beginning of the sixth century), could not have been ignorant that the Latins, whose guest he was, had shortly before rejected the book of these canons among the apocrypha in the Roman synod. But a man foreign by birth, upbringing, culture and learning, could not bring himself not to share with the Romans, among whom he lived, the canons of his own people's language, which had not yet been adorned in Latin in those times; and so that he might not offend their feelings with this new merchandise, he took pains above all to soften the ill will which he understood they burned with, by this modest preface, not concealing indeed that they were rejected by many, but still quietly excusing them or at least defending them, when he says that the constitutions of the Popes were taken from them. I, however, would think that it was not from his own collection of decrees that the Popes took their constitutions, but rather that this collector first took his canons from the constitutions of the Popes. So far Dionysius. Ferrandus the deacon of Carthage, who at nearly the same time, that is shortly after the beginning of the sixth century, compiled an abridgment of the ecclesiastical canons, kept within the limits of the Fathers and passed over the canons of the Apostles in his collection, plainly following the discipline of Gelasius. But the work of Dionysius pleased because of its elegance and its order, rivalling the older codex, and also because of the outstanding merit of the man; and gradually it won for these canons of the Apostles that favour among most Latins of which we have spoken, yet in such a way that traces of the old hostility toward them remained visible. For in the Cresconian collection Baronius, and in the Worcester codex of the most ancient canons collated by Dunstan, Ussher, as they report, found this title prefixed, clearly taken and derived from the letter of Dionysius to Stephen: Here begin the ecclesiastical rules of the holy Apostles, set forth through Clement, Pope of the Church of Rome; which are placed first in order from the Greek copies; to which very many indeed

units.la: a a. D. 102. §. 10. — b Diffed. de Ign. c. 6. p. 37. dem consensum non prabuere facilem; & tamen postea quadam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis Canonibus assumpta esse videntur. Atque ex his, quae hactenus diximus, constat, quae Latinorum veterum a quinti saeculi supremis fuerint de Canonibus, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, judicia. Primo, ab iis rejecti sunt, ac inter apocrypha relegati; mox authore Dionysio, viro Graeco cultu, Scytha ortu, ac quibusdam recepti & Canonum collectionibus inserti, sed (ut ait Hincmarus) ad instructionem, & ob famam, ab aliis, ut Isidoro, haud segniter reprobati; tandem a Leone quarto, a. D. 849. admissi; ita tamen, ut nunquam plane obliteratus sit, qui iis a principio adhaesit haereticae originis laevus rumor. Siquid ergo Romani sanguinis adversariis nostris inesset, ii nobiscum hac in causa dextras jungerent; & invectam a Graecis peregrinam hanc mercem ex suis terminis ejicerent, ac inter apocrypha ex veteri Gelasii laudatissimi apud eos Pontificis scito ablegarent. Sed eorum animos sic corrupit causae quam adversus nos agunt, quamque ex his fictitiis ac apocryphis canonibus nonnihil juvari posse sperant, studium, ut antiquiorum immemores, veterisque in Graecos schismaticos odii obliti, nihil non malint, quam Gelasii decreto obsequi. Itaque quo firma, fartaq; ac tecta maneat eorum, quæ attulimus, veritas, ac nequis istis superfit color, quo suam deinceps & in antiquissimos Patres contumaciam, & ad schismaticos Græcos hac in parte defectionem excusent, nunc operæ pretium est eorum, tum ad Gelasii decretum, tum ad Ifidori sententiam effugia considerare, atque præcludere. Illi vero, ut quos magnum aliquod discrimen repente opprimit, in diversa de more abeunt. Turrianus ex suo, chimærarum ac prodigiorum feracissimo ingenio, librum nobis procudit a inauditum, à Prifcillianiftis sub nomine Apostolorum edi-tum, cui titulus fuerit, Liber Canonum Apostolicorum, vel plane à suo 85. canonum codice diversum; vel certe pluribus una cum veris canonibus, permixtis fœcibus, ac venenis scatentem. Hunc à Gelasio damnari; hunc ab Ifidoro denotari, acerbissimisque verbis reprobari respondet; non vero suum, quem purum, atque illimem, & ab hæretica manu intactum esse contendit. Ac ut musteo, & futili commento aliquam addat speciem, Leonis verba recitat de falsis atque apocryphis Prifcillianiftarum scripturis conquerentis, feque testantis b multos corruptissimos eorum codices, qui canonici titulantur, invenisse; & apocryphas scripturas commemorantis, quæ sub nominibus Apostolorum, postolorum, multarum habent seminarium falsitatum. Addit Clementem in Consti-tutionibus prodidissea, fuisse jam tum scri-ptos libros pestiferos nomine Apostolorum; quin & editos fuisse Moysis, & Esaiæ, &c. apocryphos libros. An igitur (inquit) quia erat inter istos prophetia quædam nomine Esaiæ apocrypha, & quidam liber apocryphus psalmorum; idcirco apocryphus sit liber psalmorum David? & apocrypha omnis prophetia Esaiæ? Ego vero confiteor, hęc ex illo nequaquam sequi; & si ad id exemplum dixisset Gelasius extare apud hęreticos quédam librum apocryphum, qui dicatur Canonum Apostolorum liber; ipse vero inter Ecclesiasticos alium ejusdem tituli commemorasset; concederem equidem, siquis inde argumentaretur omnes Apostolorum dictos canones falsos esse & apocryphos, eum inquam concederem stulte ac perperam ratiocinari. Nunc vero res plane aliter habet. Nullum Gelasius toto decreto memorat legitimum, atque Ecclesiasticum Canonum Apostolicorum librum; nullum hoc titulo ante Gelasium ullus prodidit veterum Patrum. Omnino primus est ex omni antiquitate hic Gelasii locus in quo liber Canonum Apostolicorum nominatus reperiatur. Ergo clarum est, nullum ei visum, aut cognitum fuisse librum hujus nominis legitimum atque Ecclesiasticum. Et quod hinc sequitur, ergo delirat Turrianus, qui res toto genere dissimiles, veluti similes, ineptissime inter se comparat, ac exæquat. Tum edat nobis, si potest, aliquem ex omni Christianorum historia librum, hoc titulo inscriptum, Canones Apostolici, præter eum ipsum, de quo nunc quærimus, vel 85. canones (ut ipse cum schismaticis Græculis mavult) vel certe 50. (ut Dionysius & alii exhibent) continentem. Leo refert, se invenisse corruptissimos Priscillianistarum codices, qui canonici titularentur; Commemorant apocryphas Scripturas, quæ sub nominibus Apostolorum multarum haberent testimonium falsitatum. Audio; sed neque Leo, neque quisquam veterum librum hujus tituli, Canones Apostolorum, præter hunc ipsum Turrianicum nominavit. Ergo hunc ipsum Gelasius intellexit, non alium. Leo canonicos titulari, item sub Apostolorum nominibus circumferri eos hæreticorum libros ait, qui vel Euangeliorum, vel aliorum librorum vere canonicorum, vel alicujus ex Apostolis, nomen præferebant; quædam etiam vera, ut facilius deciperent, continebant, venenis subdole infuperfa; cujus generis erant illa hic ab ipso Gelasio memorata Thaddæi, Matthiæ, Petri, Iacobi, Barnabæ, Thomæ, Bartholomei, lomęi, & Andreæ nominibus Euangelia; item ea, quæ falsavisse dicitur Lucianus; item Sortes Apostolorum, & actus Theclæ & Pauli; & cęteræ ejusdem census quisquiliæ. Tertio fac (quod non est) fuisse tum temporis duos Apostolicorum canonum codices; unum verum, legitimum, & Ecclesiasticum; alterum corruptum, apocryphum, & hæreticum; cæterum ejusdem utrumque nominis ac tituli; qualiter duo Lucæ codices Tertulliani tempore extabant; unus verus, ac γνήσιος, falsus alter, à Marcione interpolatus. Certe si hæc ita habuerint, nemo non videt Gelasium, quem damnat, falsum Apostolicorum canonum codicem, ab altero, quem probatum voluit, necessario distinguere debuisse; atque ita decernere; Liber, qui falso à Priscilllianistis canonum Apostolicorum dicitur, apocryphus; ut siquis Marcionicum Lucæ Euangelium rejicere velit, ei necessario dicendum erit, Lucæ, quod dicitur, à Marcione interpolatum Euangelium, apocryphum; non autem simpliciter & absolute, Liber Euangelii Lucæ, vel secundum Lucam apocryphus. Hoc vero nemo Catholicus dixerit; quo clarum est, non Marcionicum, sed ipsum, quod apud omnes dicitur, Lucæ Euangelium significari. Jam vero non illo, sed hoc modo, pure ac simpliciter locutus est Gelasius, Liber (inquit) Canonum Apstolicorum apocryphus. Ergo necesse est, ejus verba de illo libro accipi, qui vulgo ac communiter eo nomine circumferebatur; hoc est de eo ipso, quem defendit Turrianus. Si quis diversus, verus, ac γνήσιος extabat, apparet Gelasium stultissime locutum esse, & ineptissimæ orationis ambiguo catholica cum hæreticis, vera cum falsis, genuina cum spuriis, canonica denique cum apocryphis eadem condemnatione perperam involvisse; quod quidem de Gelasio neque nobis, neque cuiquam cordato Turrianus persuaserit. Neque sane ante istum natum, aliter Gelasii verba quisquam intellexerat, aut illos Priscillianistarum Apostolicos canones, in uno hujus Jesuitæ cerebro natos, norat. Dionysius quidem, quibus Apostolorum canonibus plurimos scribit consensum non præbuisse facilem, eos non nescio quos Priscillianistarum, aut aliorum hæreticorum, sed hos ipsos, quos de græco ipse transtulit, canones intelligit; hoc est Turrianicos. Et Crisconianus Baronii, & Vigornien-sis Ussherii codex illos plane eosdem exhibent; quibus quam plurimos nequaquam aliensos esse confitentur. Neque de Priscillianistis, quos Turrianus, (ut Sabini solebant) ex sua libidine somniavit, sed de ipsis Græcorum, quos ille defendit canonibus Apostolicis accipit Humbertus eos Apostolorum canonas, quos Patres inter Apocrypha numeraverant. Idenim teste ac judice Turriano, ad Gelasianum de libro Apostolicorum Canonum decretum pertinet. Ergo si is sibi constare velit, agnoscat necesse est Humbertum quos vocat apocryphos libros & canones pari sententia Sanctorum Patrum repudiatos, eos ipsos intelligere, qui à Gelasio damnati erant. Jam vero clarum est, Humbertum loqui de canonibus, non Priscillianistarum de quibus ne per somnium quidem unquam cogitavit, sed Græcorum. Hos enim objiciebat Nicetas; ut apparet, tum ex eo, quod cum esset Græcus, non alios cognitos habuit Apostolorum canones, quam quos Trullana Synodus, cujus & ipse meminit, confirmaverat; tum ex eo ipso canone, quem nominatim afferta. Is enim ille ipse est, qui etiam hodie in Græco Apostolicorum canonum codice sexagesimus quintus, aliis 64. (ut numerat Nicetas) his verbis expressus legitur; εἴτις κληρικὸς ἐυρεθῇ τὼ νυεταικῶ ἡμέραν νηςευών, ἢ τὸ σάββατον, πλὼ τᾶ ἑνὸς μόνᾳ, καθαιρείσθω· εἰ ὁ λαϊκὸς, ἀφορίζεσθω. Si quis inventus fuerit, Dominicam diem jejunans, aut Sabbatum, praeter unum solum, deponatur. Si autem laicus, sequestretur. Ad hanc objectionem respondens Humbertus Hoc (inquit, id est Sabbato nunquam jejunandum) afferere conaris ex apocryphis libris, & Canonibus pari sententia Sanctorum Patrum repudiatis. Ergo ex Humberto, Patrum (id est, assentiente Turriano, Gelasii & Synodi Romanae) sententia repudiati erant Apostolici, non Priscillianistarum, sed Graecorum, adeoque ipsius Turriani canones. Et quod mox addit Humbertus, Canones Apostolorum numerari (a Gelasio scilicet & Synodo Romana) inter apocrypha, id pariter de Graecorum, adeoque & Turriani canonibus, necessario intelligendum est; exceptis tantum quinquaginta illis capitulis, quae ait Patres decrevisse regulis orthodoxis adjungenda. Neque de aliis sumpsit juris Pontificii interpres, ac collector Gratianus. Audi quaeso, Turriane. Apostolorum (inquit b) Canones, qui per Clementem T. R. (sicut quidam afferunt) dicuntur esse translati, sunt quinquaginta. Hos non recipiendos, sed inter apocrypha deputatos scribit Isidorus, dicens; Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum; & caetera nuper a nobis descripta. Qui per Clementem translati dicuntur, & sub quinquaginta numeris dispositi apud Latinos habentur, Apostolorum canones, ii non Priscillianistici, sed ipsi illi sunt canones, quos & Trullana Synodus consecravit, & Turrianus nunc defendit. Atqui Gratiano quidem authore, ac interprete quos Isidorus scribit non recipiendos, sed inter apocrypha deputatos esse, hi ipsi sunt Apostolorum canones quinquaginta, per Clementem (ut creditur) translati; Ergo quos Isidorus, adeoque & Gelasius, inter apocrypha deputant, ii canones, non Priscillianistici sunt, aut ulli alii imaginarii, sed ipsi illi, quos Turrianus nunc defendit, olim a Patribus Trullanis receptos ac confirmatos. Idem est, quod paulo ante exhibuimus, eruditissimi, ac in his litteris facile principis viri Antonii Augustini Tarraconensis Archiepiscopi judicium; qui quos Canonas Isidorus Mercator probat eosdem Hispalensem Isidorum rejecisse affirmat. Non autem Priscillianisticos opinor, sed Dionysiacos, & Turrianicos probavit Mercator; Ergo & hos ipsos, non autem illos, velit nolit Turrianus, rejecerat Hispalensis Isidorus, judice quidem Antonio Augustino, omnibus Jesuitis in hoc disciplinarum genere potiori. Sed hic Turriano res ridicula, ac jocosa accidit. Nam usque adeo vaecors fuit, ut ad eundem lapidem impegerit, ad quem Gratianum impegisse notavit Antonius; sibi nimirum persuasit homo omnium qui sunt, aut fue-runt, suo quidem judicio sapientissimus, unum eundemque esse Isidorum, & illum qui probat, & illum, qui rejicit Apostolorum canones apud Gratianum. Itaque in Magdeburgenses vir gravis plenis buccis detonat a, quod scilicet quem in rejicien-dis canonibus ducem secuti sunt Isidorum, eundem in iis approbandis minime sequantur, eosque in ipsum illum, quem strinxerant gladium, ut novos Amalecitas irruere jubet, & suo pugione confossos perire. Quis non hominis amentiam, ac cæcitatem rideat? Tu vero deliras, vel ut melius dicam, furis, Turriane; qui Mercatoris istius tui, hominis nihili, gladium Isidori Hispalensis esse putas. Hic Isidorus gladium quidem in te, ac in tuos Canones formidabilem stringit; nobis nullo mucrone minatur, qui canones una cum ipso tuos ab Apostolica authoritate semovemus. Mercatori vero tuo nihil præter nomen, cum Isidoro commune est. Tu, si lubet, nobilis impostoris merces tibi habe. Nos ejus authoritatem, neque pertimescimus, neque tibi invidemus. Quanquam sane neque ille tecum stat in hoc quidem articulo. Nam & quinquaginta tantum numerat Canones, non ut tu cum schismaticis Græcis 85. & hos ipsos, quos numerat, non autem quod tu vis, Priscillianistas, à quibusdam apocryphos dici, confitetur. Ex illis quibusdam unus, ut liquet, fuit Gelasius; quocum nulla, credo, invidia est quemquam eadem de canonibus tuis sentire. Sed satis verborum consumpsimus in refellendo futili vanissimi hominis commento; quod adeo absurdum omnibus visum est, ut neminem unquam, ne ex ipsis quidem Turriani Symmistis Jesuitis habuerit sectatorem.
units.tr: a A.D. 102, §10. — b Dissertation on Ignatius, ch. 6, p. 37. did not readily give their assent; yet afterwards certain decrees of the Popes seem to have been taken from these very canons. From what I have said so far, it is clear what the judgements of the Latin writers of the earlier centuries, up to the end of the fifth, were concerning the canons called Apostolic. First, they were rejected by them and relegated among the apocrypha. Then, through the author Dionysius, a man of Greek culture and Scythian birth, some of them were received and inserted into collections of canons; but (as Hincmar says) they were admitted for instruction and for their reputation, while others, such as Isidore, did not hesitate to reject them. Finally, under Leo IV in the year 849 they were admitted, yet in such a way that the uneasy rumour that clung to them from the beginning, of heretical origin, was never wholly wiped out. If there were anything of Roman blood in our opponents, they would join us in this matter, and would cast out this foreign merchandise imported by the Greeks from their borders, and would relegate it among the apocrypha by the old decree of Gelasius, the Pope most praised among them. But the zeal of the case they are pleading against us has so corrupted their minds, and their hope that these fictitious and apocryphal canons may give some help against us, that, forgetting the older writers and the old hatred of the schismatic Greeks, they prefer anything rather than obey the decree of Gelasius. Therefore, so that the truth of what we have brought forward may remain firm, solid and secure, and so that no pretext may remain for them to excuse their present obstinacy against the most ancient Fathers and their defection from the schismatic Greeks in this matter, it is now worth our while to consider and to close off the escape routes they have, both from the decree of Gelasius and from the opinion of Isidore. Those men, as is their habit when some great danger suddenly oppresses them, run off in different directions. Turrianus, from his own mind, the most fertile of chimeras and prodigies, forged for us a an unheard-of book, published by the Priscillianists under the name of the Apostles, with the title Liber Canonum Apostolicorum, either wholly different from his codex of eighty-five canons, or at any rate full of many falsehoods and poisons mixed in with the true canons. He answers that this book was condemned by Gelasius and denounced by Isidore, and rejected with the harshest words; but his own book, which he maintains is pure, spotless, and untouched by heretical hand, is not that one. And to give some appearance to his mouldy and futile invention, he quotes the words of Leo, who complains of the false and apocryphal writings of the Priscillianists, and testifies b that he had found many very corrupt codices of theirs, which are called canonical; and he mentions apocryphal scriptures, which under the names of the Apostles, a seed-bed of many falsehoods, [contain]. He adds that Clement in the Constitutions had already reported a that pernicious books under the name of the Apostles had already been written at that time; indeed that apocryphal books of Moses and Isaiah, and so on, had been published. Is it therefore (he says) because among those there was a certain prophecy under the name of Isaiah that was apocryphal, and a certain apocryphal book of the Psalms, that the book of David's Psalms is apocryphal? And is every prophecy of Isaiah apocryphal? I for my part confess that this does not follow at all from those premises. And if Gelasius had said, by way of example, that among the heretics there existed a certain apocryphal book called Book of the Canons of the Apostles, while he himself had mentioned another book of the same title among the ecclesiastical books, I would certainly grant that anyone who argued from this that all the so-called canons of the Apostles canons were false and apocryphal, I would grant, I say, reasons foolishly and wrongly. But now the matter stands quite otherwise. Gelasius mentions no genuine and ecclesiastical Book of the Canons of the Apostles anywhere in the whole decree; and none of the ancient Fathers has mentioned such a book under this title before Gelasius. In the whole of antiquity, this passage of Gelasius is the first in which a book called the Book of the Canons of the Apostles is found. Therefore it is clear that he had never seen or known a book of this name that was genuine and ecclesiastical. And from this it follows that Turrianus is raving, who most absurdly compares and equates things utterly unlike as if they were alike. Let him then produce for us, if he can, from the whole history of the Christians, any book inscribed with this title, Apostolic Canons, apart from the very one about which we are now inquiring, containing either eighty-five canons (as he prefers with the schismatic Greeklings) or at least fifty (as Dionysius and others present). Leo reports that he found very corrupt codices of the Priscillianists, which were called canonical; they mention apocryphal Scriptures, which under the names of the Apostles had much evidence of falsehood. I hear this; but neither Leo nor any of the ancients named a book of this title, Canons of the Apostles, apart from this very one of Turrianus. Therefore Gelasius meant this very one, and no other. Leo says that those heretical books were called canonical, and likewise circulated under the names of the Apostles, which bore the name either of the Gospels, or of other truly canonical books, or of one of the Apostles; some also contained true material, so that they might deceive more easily, with poison craftily poured in. Of this kind were those Gospels under the names of Thaddeus, Matthias, Peter, James, Barnabas, Thomas, Bartholomew, Philip, and Andrew, mentioned here by Gelasius himself; likewise those which Lucian is said to have falsified; likewise the Lots of the Apostles, the Acts of Thecla and of Paul, and other trifles of the same stamp. Thirdly, suppose (though it is not so) that at that time there existed two codices of the Apostolic canons, one true, legitimate and ecclesiastical, the other corrupt, apocryphal and heretical, both of the same name and title; just as in Tertullian's time two codices of Luke existed, one true and genuine, the other false, interpolated by Marcion. Certainly, if things were so, no one can fail to see that Gelasius, who condemns the false codex of the Apostolic canons, must necessarily have distinguished it from the other, which he wished to be approved, and so have decreed: The book which is falsely called the canons of the Apostles by the Priscillianists is apocryphal; just as, if someone wished to reject Marcion's Gospel of Luke, he would necessarily have to say, the Gospel of Luke, which is said to have been interpolated by Marcion, is apocryphal, and not simply and absolutely, The Gospel book of Luke, or the Gospel according to Luke, is apocryphal. No Catholic would say this; so it is clear that not Marcion's Gospel but the Gospel of Luke which is acknowledged by all is meant. Now Gelasius did not speak in that way, but in this way, purely and simply: The Book of the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal. Therefore his words must necessarily be taken of that book which was commonly and generally circulated under that name; that is, of the very one Turrianus defends. If another, true and genuine, existed, it appears that Gelasius spoke most foolishly, and by the ambiguity of a most inept expression confusedly involved the Catholic with the heretical, the true with the false, the genuine with the spurious, and finally the canonical with the apocryphal under the same condemnation; and this indeed neither we nor anyone of sound mind will be persuaded by Turrianus to believe of Gelasius. Nor indeed did anyone understand the words of Gelasius in any other way before this man was born, nor did anyone know those Apostolic canons of the Priscillianists, which were born in the single brain of this Jesuit.
