Dionysius, indeed, when he writes that very many of the Apostolic canons did not readily give their assent, means by these not some canons of the Priscillianists or of other heretics, but these very canons which he himself translated from the Greek; that is, Turrianus's canons. And the codex of Cresconius in Baronius, and the codex of Worcester in Ussher, exhibit exactly the same canons; and they confess that these are by no means unfamiliar to very many. Nor does Humbert understand by the canons of the Apostles those of the Priscillianists, whom Turrianus (as the Sabines used to do) dreamed up from his own wanton fancy, but the canons of the Greeks themselves, which Turrianus defends, which the Fathers had numbered among the apocrypha. For, by the testimony and judgement of Turrianus himself, this pertains to the Gelasian decree concerning the book of the Apostolic Canons. Therefore, if he wishes to be consistent with himself, he must acknowledge that the canons which Humbert calls apocryphal books and canons rejected by an equal judgement of the holy Fathers are those very canons which were condemned by Gelasius. Now it is clear that Humbert is speaking of the canons not of the Priscillianists, of whom he never even dreamed, but of the Greeks. For Nicetas was objecting these; as appears both from the fact that, being a Greek, he knew no Apostolic canons other than those which the Synod of Trullo, of which he himself also makes mention, had confirmed; and from that very canon which he quotes by name. For this is the very canon which is still read today in the Greek codex of the Apostolic canons as the sixty-fifth (by the other numbering, sixty-four, as Nicetas counts it), expressed in these words: [Εἴτις κληρικὸς εὑρεθῇ τὴν κυριακὴν ἡμέραν νηστεύων ἢ τὸ σάββατον, πλὴν τοῦ ἑνὸς μόνου, καθαιρείσθω· εἰ δὲ λαϊκός, ἀφορίζεσθω.] If any cleric is found fasting on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except only one, let him be deposed. But if a layman, let him be excommunicated. Replying to this objection, Humbert says: This (he says, namely, that one must never fast on the Sabbath) you try to assert from apocryphal books and canons rejected by an equal judgement of the holy Fathers. Therefore, according to Humbert, the Apostolic canons had been rejected by the judgement of the Fathers (that is, with Turrianus agreeing, of Gelasius and the Roman Synod), not of the Priscillianists but of the Greeks, and thus the canons of Turrianus himself. And what Humbert adds immediately, that the canons of the Apostles are numbered (by Gelasius, of course, and the Roman Synod) among the apocrypha, must necessarily be understood equally of the canons of the Greeks, and so of Turrianus's canons; with the sole exception of those fifty chapters which he says the Fathers decreed should be added to the orthodox rules. Nor did the interpreter and compiler of papal law, Gratian, take his statements from any other source. Listen, I beg you, Turrianus. The Canons of the Apostles (he says b), which are said to have been translated through Clement (as some assert), are fifty in number. Isidore writes that these are not to be received, but are reckoned among the apocrypha, saying: The canons which are called the Apostles' and the other things recently described by us. Those which are said to have been translated through Clement, and are held among the Latins as arranged under fifty numbers, are the Apostolic canons; these are not the Priscillianist canons, but those very canons which the Synod of Trullo also consecrated, and which Turrianus now defends. And indeed, on the authority and according to the interpretation of Gratian, those which Isidore writes are not to be received but are reckoned among the apocrypha are these very fifty Apostolic canons, translated (as is believed) through Clement. Therefore the ones which Isidore, and so Gelasius, reckon among the apocrypha are not the Priscillianist canons, nor any other imaginary ones, but those very canons which Turrianus now defends, once received and confirmed by the Trullan Fathers. It is the same judgement that I produced a little earlier, that of the most learned man, and in these matters easily the first, Antonio Agustín, Archbishop of Tarragona; who affirms that the same canons which Isidore Mercator approves were rejected by Isidore of Seville. Mercator, however, approved not the Priscillianist canons, I think, but the Dionysian and Turrianic ones. Therefore it was these very canons, not those, that Isidore of Seville rejected, whether Turrianus likes it or not, on the judgement of Antonio Agustín, the most powerful of all Jesuits in this kind of learning. But here something ridiculous and laughable happens to Turrianus. For he was so senseless that he ran against the same stone against which Antonio observed that Gratian had run. Indeed, the man, the wisest of all who are or have been in his own judgement, persuaded himself that Isidore is one and the same, both he who approves and he who rejects the Apostolic canons in Gratian. Hence the grave man thunders against the Magdeburg Centuriators with full cheeks, because, namely, those whom they followed as leader in rejecting the canons, that same Isidore, they do not at all follow in approving them; and he orders them, like new Amalekites, to rush upon that very sword which they had drawn, and to perish pierced by their own dagger. Who would not laugh at the madness and blindness of the man? You are raving, or to put it better, you are frenzied, Turrianus; you who think the sword of your Mercator, a worthless man, is the sword of Isidore of Seville. This Isidore indeed brandishes a formidable sword against you and your canons; he threatens us with no point, we who together with him remove your canons from Apostolic authority. But your Mercator has nothing in common with Isidore except the name. You may keep, if you like, the wares of your noble impostor. We neither fear his authority nor envy you it. Although, to be sure, not even he agrees with you on this point. For he counts only fifty canons, not eighty-five as you do with the schismatic Greeks; and he admits that these very canons which he counts, not those which you want, are said by some to be apocryphal, namely the Priscillianists. Of those some, clearly one was Gelasius; and I believe there is no quarrel between him and anyone who holds the same view of your canons. But we have spent enough words in refuting the futile invention of this most vain man, which seemed so absurd to everyone that he never found a follower, not even among Turrianus's own Jesuit associates.

units.la: Venio ad alterum, quod Bellarmini est, effugium. Is cum quaedam partim falsa, partim inania attulisset a, quibus effici videtur legitimos esse Apostolorum canones, & ex alia parte Gelasii decretum objecisset, quo canonum Apostolicorum liber pronunciatur apocryphus; Hæc (inquit) conciliari possunt, si dicamus Canones legitimos esse solum quinquaginta priores; reliquos non esse legitimos, quamvis à Græcis recipiantur. Tum multa affert, & quidem ea fere, quæ nos supra descripsimus, quibus probatur, canones Apostolorum esse solum quinquaginta. Hæc autem iste ab Humberto Cardinali mutuatus est, qui a. D. 1050. eadem his verbis scripserat, quæ nos supra jam recitavimus; Apostolorum canones numerant Patres inter apocrypha; exceptis capitulis quinquaginta, quæ decreverunt orthodoxæ fidei tractatores ad-jungenda. jungenda. Ego vero inprimis fareor, quod tanto conatu probare studet Bellarminus, quinquaginta solum & in Dionysii, & in cæterorum antiquis codicibus Latinis canones reperiri. Quid hoc faciat ad solvendam difficultatem ex Gelasii decreto objectam, non video. Non fuerunt (inquis) plures quam quinquaginta Apostolorum canones apud veteres Latinos. Esto, inquam. Quid tum postea ? Ergo (inquis) hos quinquaginta non tangit Gelasii fulmen; sed quosdam tantum alios, numero triginta quinque, a Græcis vel hæreticis superadditos. Atqui, inquam, Gelasius decernit apocryphum esse librum Canonum Apostolorum. Tui illi quinquaginta vel eum librum conficiunt, vel certe ejus pars sunt, & quidem major. Ergo & ipsos apocryphos esse decrevit Gelalius; Qui si in animo id, quod tu vis, habuisset, triginta tantum & quinque postremos a nescio quibus hereticis additos ferire, tuis vero, qui supersunt, quinquaginta parcere; alios profecto ab alliis distinxisset; non, quod fecit, indiscrete, ac simpliciter librum canonum Apostolicorum ad apocrypha amandasset. Humbertus ait, Patres decrevisse quinquaginta capitula orthodoxæ fidei adjungenda. Quæro, qui Patres, & quo loco hoc decreverint ! Gelasius quidem ab Ecclesiasticis clesiasticis regulis ad apocrypha amandat canones Apostolorum. Ex his nuspiam quinquaginta excipit; nuspiam eos orthodoxis regulis adjungit. Quid sequentium temporum Patres fecerint, ipse & Bellarminus viderint. Nos scimus, neque Gelasium, neque ullos ante eum Græcos Latinosve Patres quicquam hujusmodi de canonibus istis quinquaginta decrevisse. Quod ii tandem apud Latinos recepti sint, id una Dionysii Exigui temeritas fecit, qui primus hoc 50. Canonum auctario Ecclesiasticarum regularum codicem auxit. Itaque somnia sunt, quæ nobis & Humbertus, & Bellarminus de suis illis 50. canonibus narrant; ex sola eorum libidine, caussaque studio orta. Nos vero, ut istorum vanitas clarius elucescat, veteres interrogemus, quinam sint ii Apostolorum canones, quos multi olim rejecerunt. Primus omnium, ac Gelasio proximus occurrit ipse ille Dionysius, qui suæ collectioni 50. Apostolorum canones præposuit. Ille narrat, plurimos Apostolorum canonibus consensum non præbuisse facilem. Quibus? Iis (inquit) quos de græco transtulimus, quosque in principio ante regulas Nicænæ Synodi locavimus. Atqui nullus illos triginta quinque posteriores, sed solus quinquaginta priores transtulit, & in suo codice recenrecensuit. Ergo hos ipsos quinquaginta, plurimi olim rejecerunt. Eadem, ut supra audivimus, loquuntur veteres canonum praefationes Crefconianæ, & Vigornienfi collectionibus praefixæ. Ipse quinetiam, peffimæ alioqui fidei Mercator, fatetur tamen eos ipsos Apostolorum Canones, quos ipse cæteris conciliis præposuit à quibusdam apocryphos dici. Atqui non alios ipse, quam hos ipsos quinquaginta, pro quibus pugnat Bellarminus, Conciliis in sua collectione præposuit, & quidem à Dionysio Exiguo translatos. Ergo hi ipsi, non alii, à quibusdam veterum apocryphi dicti sunt. Quod si quæras, quibus-nam Canones, qui vocantur Apostolorum, apocryphi dictifint, non alios reperies apud veteres illos, qui hoc eos elogio ornarint, quam Gelasium, & 70. Synodi Romanæ Patres, & secundum hos Hispalensem Isidorum. Ergo isti cum librum Canonum Apostolorum apocryphum esse pronuntiant, hos ipsos quinquaginta Canones intelligunt. Eadem quoque est Hincmari Remensis ratio. Is docet, & ratione confirmat a, quod supra demonstravimus, Canones, qui vocantur Apostolorum, ab Apostolis neque conscriptos, neque editos ac promulgatos fuisse. Ait in iis quædam esse receptibilia, quædam etiam non servanda; ideo legendos cum illa Apostoli in Apocryphorum lectione ex Gelasio adhibenda cautela, Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete; Deniq; scribit Gelasium in Catalogo librorum, qui ab Ecclesia Catholica recipiuntur, de his Apostolorum Canonibus penitus tacuisse. Si queris, de quibusnam Apostolorum Canonibus haec omnia dicat, respondet a disertisime se de iis loqui, qui seorsum ante Concilia in Canonum libris ad instructionem, & propter vulgatam eorum famam ponuntur.
units.tr: I come now to the other evasion, which is Bellarmine's. He brought forward some arguments, partly false and partly empty, by which he seems to prove that the canons of the Apostles are genuine. On the other side he objected the decree of Gelasius, by which the book of the Apostolic canons is pronounced apocryphal. These things (he says) can be reconciled, if we say that only the first fifty canons are genuine, and the rest are not genuine, although they are received by the Greeks. Then he offers much, and for the most part the same things that we set out above, by which he proves that the canons of the Apostles are only fifty. But Bellarmine took these things from Cardinal Humbert, who in the year 1050 had written the same things in the words that we have already quoted above: The Fathers number the Apostles' canons among the apocrypha, except the fifty chapters, which the teachers of orthodox faith decreed should be added. I, indeed, first admit what Bellarmine so eagerly tries to prove, that only fifty canons are found in the ancient Latin codices of Dionysius and of the others. I do not see what this has to do with resolving the difficulty raised from the decree of Gelasius. "There were not (you say) more than fifty canons of the Apostles among the ancient Latins." Granted, I say. What follows from that? "Therefore (you say) the thunderbolt of Gelasius does not strike these fifty, but only certain others, thirty-five in number, added by the Greeks or by heretics." But, I say, Gelasius decrees that the book of the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal. Your fifty either make up that book, or are certainly part of it, and indeed the greater part. Therefore Gelasius decreed that these also are apocryphal. If he had intended what you want, to strike only the last thirty-five, added by I know not what heretics, and to spare your remaining fifty, he would surely have distinguished one group from the other. He would not, as he did, have indiscriminately and simply consigned the book of the Apostolic canons to the apocrypha. Humbert says that the Fathers decreed that fifty chapters should be added to orthodox faith. I ask which Fathers, and in what place, they decreed this! Gelasius, indeed, consigns the canons of the Apostles to the apocrypha, apart from the ecclesiastical rules. He excludes no fifty from this anywhere, and he attaches none of them to the orthodox rules anywhere. What the Fathers of later times did, Bellarmine and he himself may see. We know that neither Gelasius nor any Greek or Latin Father before him decreed anything of this kind about those fifty canons. That they were later received among the Latins was caused by the rashness of Dionysius Exiguus alone, who first enlarged the code of ecclesiastical rules with this appendix of fifty canons. So the things that Humbert and Bellarmine tell us about their fifty canons are dreams, arising only from their own whim and zeal for a cause. But we, so that the vanity of these men may shine more clearly, will ask the ancients which are those canons of the Apostles that many once rejected. The first of all, and nearest to Gelasius, is that same Dionysius, who placed fifty canons of the Apostles before his collection. He tells us that very many did not give easy assent to the canons of the Apostles. To which? (He says) to those which we have translated from the Greek, and which we placed at the beginning, before the rules of the Synod of Nicaea. But he translated not those last thirty-five, but only the first fifty, and he listed them in his code. Therefore very many once rejected these very fifty. The same things, as we heard above, are said by the old prefaces to the canons, prefixed to the Cresconian and Vigorniensian collections. Even Mercator, otherwise a most wicked man in faith, confesses nevertheless that the very canons of the Apostles, which he himself placed before the other councils, are called apocryphal by some. But he placed before the Councils in his collection none other than these very fifty, for which Bellarmine fights, and indeed translated by Dionysius Exiguus. Therefore these very ones, and not others, were called apocryphal by some of the ancients. And if you ask which canons, called those of the Apostles, were called apocryphal, you will find among those ancients who gave them this designation none other than Gelasius, the seventy Fathers of the Roman Synod, and following them, Isidore of Seville. Therefore when these men pronounce the book of the Canons of the Apostles apocryphal, they understand these very fifty canons. The reasoning of Hincmar of Reims is the same. He teaches, and confirms by argument, a, what we demonstrated above, that the canons called of the Apostles were neither written nor published and promulgated by the Apostles. He says that some of them are acceptable, and some are also not to be observed; therefore they should be read with that caution, to be employed with Gelasius in reading the Apocrypha, Prove all things, hold fast that which is good. Finally, he writes that Gelasius in the Catalogue of books received by the Catholic Church had completely passed over these canons of the Apostles in silence. If you ask about which canons of the Apostles he says all these things, he answers very plainly that he speaks of those which are placed separately before the Councils in the books of canons, for instruction and on account of their widespread fame.

units.la: Jam ex Dionysio Exiguo, & Pseudo-Isidoro Mercatore patet, non alios illis temporibus in Latinis Canonum libris ante Concilia positos fuisse Apostolorum Canones, quam hos ipsos quinquaginta, de quibus litigat Bellarminus. Ergo hi ipsi sunt, quos a catalogo receptorum in Ecclesia librorum exclusit Gelasius; quosque cum cautela, velut dubios, legendos putat Hincmarus. Neq; Isidori Hispalensis alia mens fuit; dum Canones Apostolorum negat a sede Apostolica receptos; dum ait eos ab haereticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositos. Plane istos quinquaginta intelligit; Neque enim alii, quam hi, in Latinis Conciliorum libris habebantur; ad quos in omnibus Hispaniae veteribus codicibus inventum fuisse hanc Isidori annotationem testatur vir gragravissimus Antonius Angustinus. Quod si nobis hoc credere nolit Bellarminus, credat saltem Gratiano suo, cujus hæ sunt jam à nobis nuper recitatę voces; Apostolorum Canones, &c. sunt quinquaginta. Hos non recipiendos, sed inter apocrypha deputatos, Isidorus scribit. Non potuit disertius frigidam Bellarmini cavillatiunculam refutare, ad 35. postremos Canones torquentis, quæ hic clamat de his ipsis quinquaginta dicta esse. Denique idem quoque agnovit ac docuit celeberrimus, ac doctissimus Archiepiscopus Antonius Augustinus, dum scribit, Mercatorem probare hos Canones, quos Isidorus rejecerat. Probavit autem Mercator quinquaginta Apostolorum Canones; Ergo & hos quinquaginta rejecerat Isidorus. Jam illud clarum atque confessum est Isidorum, dum negat sedem Apostolicam Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, recepisse, vel Patres iis assensum præbuisse, Gelasium Romæ Episcopum, & 70. Romanæ Synodi Patres, decretumque ab iis de libro Canonum Apostolorum factum in animo habuisse. Ergo Isidoro judice, hos ipsos, quos Latini habent quinquaginta, damnavit Gelasius. Quod ipsum ex iis omnibus liquido colligitur, quos nuper scripsisse diximus vel plurimos, vel quamplurimos his Canonibus Apostolorum (quinquaginta quaginta scilicet) consensum non praebuisse, vel apocryphos eos dixisse, vel in catalogo librorum Ecclesiasticorum tacuisse. Rogo, quinam isti fuerint, qui hos 50. Canones rejecerunt. Nulli alii ex omnibus Latinis ante Isidorum & Dionysium reperientur quicquam hujusmodi de Apostolicis Canonibus statuisse, praeter Gelasium, Synodique Romanae 70. Patres. Ergo necesse est, vel hos, Apostolorum quinquaginta Canones damnasse, vel certe falso ac temere Dionysium & caeteros collectionum authores scripsisse, Canonibus istis quinquaginta vel multos, vel quosdam intercessisse. Nam si, quod vult Bellarminus, Gelasius triginta quinque postremos duntaxat damnavit, falsum est, quinquaginta priores a plurimis, vel a quibusdam damnatos, quos nulli damnasse reperiuntur, siquidem eos Gelasius, & 70. Patres Romanae Synodi intactos reliquerunt. At certum est ex Dionysio & caeteris, hos etiam quinquaginta rejectos fuisse & explosos; Ergo necesse est eos ipsos Gelasium damnasse, cum librum Canonum Apostolorum apocryphum esse pronuntiavit. Neque sine summa impudentia hoc a nobis flagitare poterit Bellarminus, ut ipsi potius, quam Dionysio, & caeteris collectoribus de rebus, quae eorum memoria gerebantur, credamus, damus. Itaque claris & invictis rationibus demonstratum est, Gelasii de Apostolorum Canonibus decretum hos ipsos priores quinquaginta canones damnare, ac in apocryphorum censum amandare; non autem 35. postremos, (quod praeter omnem & rerum ipsarum rationem, & veterum Latinae Ecclesiae scriptorum fidem contendit Bellarminus.) Quinimo recte & accurate rem expendenti omnino apparebit anno illo quinti saeculi 94. quo Gelasianum de apocryphis decretum conditum fuisse constat, solos quinquaginta priores Apostolorum, qui dicuntur, Canones in rerum natura extitisse, necdum iis temporibus consarcinatos fuisse illos 35. Canones, qui paulo post Gelasii fata, emersisse, & a Graecis, harum quisquiliarum avidis, excepti, & quinquaginta prioribus additi fuisse videntur, & a Justiniano, & Ioanne ex Scholastficis in nomocanonem mox relati. Cujus rei hoc clarum, ut mihi quidem videtur, & evidens argumentum habeo, quod Dionysius Exiguus, qui viginti aut triginta post Gelasium annis Romae vivebat, non plures quam quinquaginta priores Apostolorum Canones in suo Codice Conciliis praepo-suerit. Nulla enim ratio est, cur hos triginta quinque canones, quibus nunc auctior est Graecorum, quam Dionysii & Latinorum tinorum ex eo codex, praetermiserit, si ii jam tum apud Christianos extabant. Tur-{a}rianus quidem rotunde alicubi fatetur a, exceptis quinquaginta prioribus Apostolorum Canonibus, cæteros (id est illos 35. reliquos) tardius ad Latinos, quam ad Græcos pervenisse; hos enim eos a Clemente Romano grace scriptos prius accepisse. Idem alibi ait illis temporibus (hoc est Gelasianis & anterioribus etiam sæculis) non plura, quam quinquaginta capitula Latinos habuisse. Sed hæc Turriani hypothesis, ut illius viri pleraque, & absurdissima per se est, & causam Bellarmini jugulat, & ad solvendam quam proposui rationem est inutilis. Absurdissima est. Fac enim Clementem Romæ Episcopum, 85. illos Apostolorum canones, jam ab initio Christianis (quod vult Turrianus) conscripsisse, & eo quo nunc habentur, ordine digessisse, ac edidisse; quis crediderit optimum ac sapientissimum episcopum hunc potissimum, planeque necessarium (si qua Turriano fides) thesaurum Græcis quidem procul remotis totum tradidisse? Romanis vero, & civibus, & omnibus suis invidisse; nec nisi mutilum ac magna sui parte truncatum dedisse? Tum si erant a principio 85. canones, cur quæso, qui eos Latine vertit, quinqua-
units.tr: Now from Dionysius Exiguus and the Pseudo-Isidore Mercator it is clear that in those times the Latin books of canons placed before the Councils contained no other canons of the Apostles than these very fifty about which Bellarmine disputes. Therefore these are the very ones which Gelasius excluded from the catalogue of books received in the Church, and which Hincmar thinks should be read with caution, as doubtful. Nor was the mind of Isidore of Seville any different, when he denies that the canons of the Apostles were received by the apostolic see, and when he says that they were composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles. Plainly he means these fifty; for no others than these were held in the Latin books of the Councils. That this note of Isidore was found in all the old Spanish codices is attested by the most grave man Antonius Augustinus. But if Bellarmine is unwilling to believe us in this, let him at least believe his own Gratian, whose words, quoted by us just now, are these: The canons of the Apostles, etc., are fifty. Isidore writes that these are not to be received, but are reckoned among the apocrypha. He could not have refuted more plainly the cold little cavil of Bellarmine, who twists it to the last thirty-five canons, when what is said here was said of these very fifty. Finally, the most famous and most learned Archbishop Antonius Augustinus also acknowledged and taught the same thing, when he writes that Mercator approved these canons which Isidore had rejected. Now Mercator approved the fifty canons of the Apostles; therefore Isidore also had rejected these fifty. And it is clear and admitted that Isidore, when he denies that the see of the Apostles received the canons which are called of the Apostles, or that the Fathers gave assent to them, had in mind Gelasius, bishop of Rome, and the seventy Fathers of the Roman Synod, and the decree that they made about the book of the Canons of the Apostles. Therefore, in Isidore's judgment, Gelasius condemned these very fifty that the Latins have. This is clearly gathered from all those writers whom we said above wrote either very many or very many did not give assent to these Canons of the Apostles (that is, fifty), or called them apocryphal, or passed them over in silence in the catalogue of ecclesiastical books. I ask who those were that rejected these fifty canons. No others among all the Latins before Isidore and Dionysius will be found to have decided anything of this kind about the Apostolic canons, except Gelasius and the seventy Fathers of the Roman Synod. Therefore it is necessary either that these fifty canons of the Apostles were condemned, or certainly that Dionysius and the other authors of the collections wrote falsely and rashly, and that many or some objected to those fifty canons. For if, as Bellarmine wants, Gelasius condemned only the last thirty-five, it is false that the first fifty were condemned by very many or by some, whom no one is found to have condemned, since Gelasius and the seventy Fathers of the Roman Synod left them untouched. But it is certain, from Dionysius and the others, that these fifty also were rejected and cast out. Therefore it is necessary that Gelasius condemned these very ones when he pronounced the book of the Canons of the Apostles apocryphal. Nor, without the greatest impudence, can Bellarmine demand this of us: that we should believe him rather than Dionysius and the other collectors about matters that were in their memory. Thus it has been demonstrated by clear and unconquered reasons that the decree of Gelasius about the canons of the Apostles condemns these very first fifty canons and consigns them to the number of the apocrypha, and not the last thirty-five, as Bellarmine maintains, contrary to all reason of the matters themselves and to the testimony of the old writers of the Latin Church. Indeed, anyone who weighs the matter rightly and accurately will clearly see that in the year 494, in which the Gelasian decree on the apocrypha is known to have been issued, only the first fifty canons of the so-called Apostles existed, and that those thirty-five canons had not yet been patched together in those times. They seem to have emerged a little after the death of Gelasius, to have been taken up by the Greeks, who were fond of these trifles, and added to the first fifty, and soon afterwards were carried into the nomocanon by Justinian and John of Scholasticus. Of this, as it seems to me, I have a clear and evident proof: that Dionysius Exiguus, who lived at Rome twenty or thirty years after Gelasius, placed before the Councils in his code no more than the first fifty canons of the Apostles. For there is no reason why he would have omitted these thirty-five canons, with which the Greek code, and from it the Latin ones, is now enlarged, if they were already then in existence among Christians. Turrianus indeed openly admits somewhere that, apart from the first fifty canons of the Apostles, the rest (that is, those other thirty-five) reached the Latins later than the Greeks; for they had received them earlier as written in Greek by Clement of Rome. He says elsewhere that in those times (that is, in the times of Gelasius and even earlier centuries) the Latins had no more than fifty chapters. But this hypothesis of Turrianus, like most of that man's, is in itself most absurd, and it both cuts the throat of Bellarmine's cause and is useless for solving the reasoning I proposed. It is most absurd. For suppose that Clement, bishop of Rome, wrote those eighty-five canons of the Apostles for Christians from the beginning (as Turrianus wants), and arranged and published them in the order in which they are now held. Who would believe that this most excellent and wisest bishop gave the whole treasure, especially and plainly necessary (if Turrianus is to be trusted), to the Greeks, far away, and begrudged it to the Romans, and to his own citizens, and gave it only mutilated and cut down in a great part of itself? Then, if there were eighty-five canons from the beginning, why, I ask, did he who translated them into Latin leave out... fifty...

units.tr: For the canons, chap. 28, p. 101, verso.

units.la: {b} Ibid. c. 15. p. 48. versa. quinquaginta duntaxat vertit? cæteros Græcis totos reliquit? Ista sane Turriani fommia non cohærent. Sed & eadem Bellarminianam conciliationem jugulant. Si enim sæculo quinto non plures erant apud Latinos, quam quinquaginta Apostolorum canones (quod statuit bonus Turrianus) clarum est Gelasium, non illos triginta quinque postremos, quod ait Bellarminus, ut pote sibi, & cæteris Latinis ignotos, sed hos ipsos priores quinquaginta damnaffe; nisi (quod ftultiffimum est) dicamus illum episcopum cum Romana Synodo canones quidem sibi ignotos diserte damnaffe; deiis, qui Latini erant, & sibi cogniti ac familiares, nihil decrevifle. Neque postremo hæc Turriani hypothesis præfentem nodum solvit. Fingamus enim, quod Turrianus somniat, nimirum ineunte sexto sæculo, quo tempore vixit Dionysius, jam apud Græcos quidem extitisse 35. illos Apostolorum canones, Latinis vero eosdem incognitos fuisse; Non ideo confeceris,eos Dionysio quoque pariter incognitos fuisse. Is enim non Latinis tantum, sed & Græcis litteris apprime fuit exercultus, & in omni utriusque linguæ doctrina Ecclesiastica verfatiffimus; quod ex Caffiodoro , eorundem temporum scriptore, & Beda , & aliis notum est; ut tali
units.tr: {b} Ibid., c. 15, p. 48, verso. Did he translate only fifty? Did he leave the rest to the Greeks entire? Those are surely Turrian's dreams, and they do not hang together. They also undermine Bellarmine's reconciliation. For if in the fifth century there were no more than fifty Apostolic canons among the Latins (which good Turrian maintains), it is clear that Gelasius condemned not those last thirty-five, as Bellarmine says, since they were unknown to him and to other Latins, but these very first fifty. Unless (what is most foolish) we say that this bishop, together with the Roman synod, explicitly condemned canons unknown to him, while deciding nothing about those that were Latin and known and familiar to him. Finally, this hypothesis of Turrian does not solve the present knot. Suppose, as Turrian dreams, that at the beginning of the sixth century, when Dionysius lived, those thirty-five Apostolic canons already existed among the Greeks but were unknown to the Latins. It does not follow that they were equally unknown to Dionysius. For he was thoroughly trained not only in Latin but also in Greek letters, and was very well versed in all the ecclesiastical learning of both languages. This is known from Cassiodorus, a writer of the same period, and from Bede and others. So such a man could not have been ignorant of those thirty-five Apostolic canons, if they had existed among the Greeks.

units.la: a Divin. lect.c.13. b De rat. temp. c. 45. c Vid.Bar. von. a.D. 527. §. 67. & seqq. Item a.D.102. §. 14. tali viro ignoti esse non potuerint, siqui apud Græcos fuissent hi 35. Apostolorum Canones. Adhæc ipse testatur se, quos exhibet Apostolorum canones, de Græco transtulisse a. Cum ergo codex, ex quo eos legit & transtulit, Græcus esset, is omnino ex Turriani hypothesi 85. canones continebat, non autem 50. duntaxat. Vult enim Turrianus eo jam numero apud Græcos fuisse Apostolorum Canones. Itaque dici non potest Dionysium illos triginta quinque postremos ideo non convertisse, quod eos, licet extantes, notos tamen minime habuerit; qui ut ex his liquet, si apud Græcos extitissent ulli, Dionysium nequaquam latere potuissent. Si dicas Dionysium, licet probe cognitos, ideo tamen prætermisisse, quod sciret ipsos à Latinis, quibus hanc operam destinabat, non haberi legitimos; primo mirabile est, planeque incredibile eum hoc, siquid hujusmodi erat, dissimulasse ac penitus tacuisse in præfatione ad Stephanum. Siquid enim hujusmodi fuisset, omnino res ipsa poscebat, ut lectorem de eo moneret; ne scilicet codicis sui tanta à græco diversitas quemquam offenderet. Qui Stephanum monendum putavit suis illis quinquaginta canonibus plurimos consensum non præbuisse facilem; quanto magis hoc, si verum
units.tr: a Divin. lect. c. 13. b De rat. temp. c. 45. c See Baron. ad a. D. 527, §. 67 and following; likewise ad a. D. 102, §. 14. Moreover, he himself testifies that the Apostolic canons which he presents were translated from the Greek. Since the codex from which he read and translated them was therefore Greek, it must, on Turrian's hypothesis, have contained eighty-five canons, not merely fifty. For Turrian holds that the Apostolic canons already existed among the Greeks in that number. So it cannot be said that Dionysius omitted those last thirty-five because, although they existed, he had little knowledge of them. As is clear from what has been said, if any of them had existed among the Greeks, Dionysius could by no means have failed to know them. If you say that Dionysius, although he knew them well, passed them over because he knew that the Latins, for whom he intended this work, did not regard them as genuine, then first, it is remarkable and quite incredible that he would have concealed this and kept silent about it entirely in his preface to Stephen. For if there had been anything of this kind, the matter itself demanded that he warn the reader about it, so that the great difference of his codex from the Greek would not offend anyone. If he thought Stephen ought to be warned that the fifty canons would not easily win the agreement of many, how much more would he have explained this, if it were true? Yet he did not.

units.la: a ep. ad Steph. rum erat, enarrasset; Ille vero non fecit. Huc accedit, quod canones illi triginta quinque, Turriano quidem judice, omnes, Baronio a vero ac Binio b authoribus propemodum omnes legitimi sunt, ac authentici (Hi enim illos omnes eo loco ac numero habent duobus tantum exceptis, scilicet 65. aliis 66. & ultimo) Ergo nihil obstabat, quominus Dionysius, vel omnes 35. ex Turriano, vel certe 33. ex Baronio & Binio, duobus (quod facile fuit) vel omissis, vel atro carbone notatis, suae collectioni adderet. Atqui ne unum quidem istorum 35. posuit, sed solos quinquaginta priores exhibuit. Ex his ergo concludendum est, istos triginta quinque postremos, nullos adhuc tunc temporis in rerum natura extitisse; qui si extitissent scilicet, Dionysio agniti, etiam in hac collectione inserti essent. Illos Dionysius quod omittit, eo sibi fatetur ignotos; Quod autem ignotos sibi fuisse arguit, hoc ipso ne extitisse quidem eos demonstrat. Idque ipsum vi veritatis victus, haud obscure prodidit his verbis Baronius c; Qui primus (inquit) e Graco sermone Canones Apostolicos in Latinum vertit, accuratissimus atque fidissimus interpres Dionysius, Graecus author, & inter Latinos magna cum laude diu versatus, quinquaginta tantum reperit. Iam
units.tr: a Letter to Stephen. Add to this that those thirty-five canons, on Turrian's judgment, are all genuine and authentic, and on the authority of Baronius and Binius almost all are (for they place all of them in that position and number, with only two exceptions, namely 65, the other 66, and the last). Therefore nothing stood in the way of Dionysius adding to his collection either all thirty-five, as Turrian would have it, or at least the thirty-three of Baronius and Binius, with two omitted or marked with a black mark, which was easy to do. Yet he did not include even one of those thirty-five, but presented only the first fifty. From this we must conclude that those last thirty-five did not yet exist in nature at that time. For if they had existed, they would certainly have been known to Dionysius and would have been inserted in this collection too. That Dionysius omits them shows that they were unknown to him; but what proves they were unknown to him shows at the same time that they did not even exist. Baronius, overcome by the force of truth, revealed this plainly in these words: "The first to translate the Apostolic canons from Greek into Latin, the most accurate and trustworthy translator Dionysius, a Greek author who for a long time was held in great esteem among the Latins, found only fifty." Now,

units.la: Canones Apostolorum, cum non plures, quam quinquaginta, Dionysii tempore exti-terint, fieri non potest, ut auctiores Ge-lasii, quiDionysio anterior fuit, ævo fue-rint. Unde postremo ineluctabili necessi-tate sequitur, ut quem Gelasius apocry-phum pronunciat Apostolicorum canonum librum, is idem ille fuerit canonum quin-quaginta codex, quem & Dionysius olim translulit, & nunc defendit Bellarminus ; non autem illa Græcanica triginta quinque canonum lacinia, qui ne Dionysii quidem tempore ulli extabant, nedum ut Gelasio cogniti fuerint.
units.tr: since the Apostolic canons, in the time of Dionysius, existed in no more than fifty, it cannot be that the longer ones were in circulation in the age of Gelasius, who was earlier than Dionysius. Hence, by an inescapable necessity, it follows that the book of Apostolic canons which Gelasius pronounced apocryphal was that same codex of fifty canons which Dionysius once translated and which Bellarmine now defends; and not that Greek patchwork of thirty-five canons, which did not exist in the time of Dionysius at all, much less were known to Gelasius.

units.la: His rationibus subactus Baronius, hoc quidem quod nos demonstravimus confi-tetur, librum scilicet Canonum Apostoli-corum a Gelasio inter apocryphos numera-tum, ipsum esse Dionysiacum quinqua-ginta canonum codicem ; sed alio effugio elabi, Gelasianumque fulmen a suo Pal-ladio depellere conatur. Fingit enim hunc librum ideo apocryphum a Gelasio dici, quod non sit in sensu divinorum Novi Te-stamenti librorum; non autem sic, ut in-telligatur ex librorum Ecclesiasticorum albo exclusus, atque expunctus. Isti ca-nones ea (inquit) ratione, quod cum A-postolorum nomine censerentur, non essent in canone librorum novi Testamenti, me-rito rito fum apocryphorum cenfura fignati ; quod vero a Sanctis Patribus privatim, & a facris Synodis publice funt recepti, merito authentici dici debent. Sed longe ineptiffimam, ac impudentiffimam glos- fam refellit ipfe multis modis Gelafius ; ac primo quidem eo quod in fuo illo Sy- nodico decreto, non fimpliciter divino- rum & Θεοπνεύςων librorum, fed eorum etiam, quos Romana Ecclefia fufcipi non prohibebat, canonem ac breviarium tra- dit ; in quo adeo poft recenfitas priore (ut decebat) loco ipfas utriufque foederis divinas Scripturas, deinceps enumerat cae- teras ab Ecclefia, licet non eodem honoris gradu, probatas ac fufceptas Conciliorum & virorum Ecclefiafticorum litteras, ac chartas ; ut Nicaenae, CPae. Ephefinae, & Chalcedonenfis fynodorum canones, ut Cypriani, Gregorii, Bafilii, Athanafii, Cyrilli, Chryfoftomi, Theophili, Hila- rii, Ambrofii, Auguftini, Hieronymi, Profperi, & aliorum opufcula. His ex ad- verfo fubnectit notitiam eorum librorum, qui non recipiuntur ; in qua collocat Ari- minenfem fynodum, Itinerarium Petri, oSto Clementis libros, Actus Andreae, Thomae, Petri, & Philippi, Euangelia Thaddaei, Matthiae, Petri, Jacobi minoris, Barnabae, Thomae, Bartholomaei, Andreæ, libros de infantia Salvatoris, item de ejus nativitate, & de Maria, & obstetrice, & cæteros, quos enumerare longum est. Itaque tres sunt, ut quivis videt, in hoc Gelasiano decreto librorum ordines. Primus, divinos ac Θεοπνεύστως complectitur. Alter non divinos quidem, neque proprie Θεοπνεύστως, probatos tamen & receptos & laudatos, & in usu Ecclesiæ positos. Tertius vero rejectos ac improbatos continet, & duorum priorum ordinum libris oppositos, id est, neque divinos, neque Ecclesiasticos. Jam vel cæcus viderit Gelasium, Apostolorum canones, si, quod somniat Baronius, de iis sensisset, debuisse in secundo ordine, & quidem in ipsis statim principiis collocare; unacum Synodorum probatarum regulis, & orthodoxorum ac Catholicorum hominum litteris; quæ licet non divinæ, neque Θεοπνευστοι sint, sunt tamen, ac habentur, ut illeait, authenticæ. Atqui id non fecit Gelasius. Canonum Apostolicorum librorum, non in secunda classe, ubi ex Baronii figmento legitimus erat ejus locus, sed in tertia censuit; quę eorum librorum est, qui plane nullam neque divinam, ut Scripturę, neque Ecclesiasticam, ut Concilia & scripta Catholicorum probata, authoritatem habent. Ergo Gelasius Apostolorum
units.tr: Overcome by these arguments, Baronius admits what we have demonstrated, namely that the book of the Canons of the Apostles which Gelasius numbered among the apocryphal books is the very codex of fifty canons used by Dionysius. But he tries to escape by another route, and seeks to turn aside the Gelasian thunderbolt by his Palladius. He imagines that this book is called apocryphal by Gelasius for the reason that, since they bore the name of the Apostles, they were not in the canon of the books of the New Testament, and so they were rightly marked with the censure of the apocryphal; but not in the sense that they were excluded and struck from the roll of ecclesiastical books. Yet what was approved by the holy Fathers privately and received publicly by the sacred synods ought rightly to be called authentic. But Gelasius himself refutes this very foolish and impudent gloss in many ways. First, because in his synodical decree he hands down a list and breviary not merely of the divine and theopneustic [θεόπνευστος] books, but also of those which the Roman Church did not forbid to be received. In it, after listing first, as was fitting, the divine Scriptures of both covenants, he then enumerates the other writings of councils and ecclesiastical men, which the Church has approved and received, though not with the same degree of honour: the canons of the synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, the works of Cyprian, Gregory, Basil, Athanasius, Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophilus, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Prosper and others. Opposite these, he adds a notice of those books which are not received, in which he places the synod of Ariminum, the Itinerary of Peter, the eight books of Clement, the Acts of Andrew, Thomas, Peter and Philip, the Gospels of Thaddeus, Matthias, Peter, James the Less, Barnabas, Thomas, Bartholomew and Andrew, the books on the infancy of the Saviour, likewise on his nativity, on Mary and the midwife, and the others, which would take too long to list. So there are, as anyone can see, three orders of books in this Gelasian decree. The first embraces the divine and theopneustic [θεόπνευστος] books. The second contains books that are not divine, nor properly theopneustic, yet are approved, received, praised and in use in the Church. The third contains rejected and disapproved books, opposed to the books of the two former orders, that is, neither divine nor ecclesiastical. Now even a blind man can see that if Gelasius had thought of the Apostolic canons as Baronius dreams, he ought to have placed them in the second order, and indeed right at its beginning, together with the rules of approved synods and the writings of orthodox and Catholic men; which, though not divine nor theopneustic [θεόπνευστος], are nevertheless, as he puts it, authentic and held to be so. But Gelasius did not do this. He placed the book of the Apostolic canons not in the second class, where by Baronius's fiction its proper place would have been, but in the third, which contains books that have plainly no authority, neither divine, like the Scriptures, nor ecclesiastical, like the approved councils and writings of Catholic men. Therefore Gelasius did not merely decide that the Apostolic canons

units.la: Gg lorum Canones decrevit, non modo divinos non esse, quod concedit Baronius, sed ne Ecclesiasticos quidem vel authenticos haberi, quod iste pertendit. Sed quid opus est argumentis? Ipse Gelasius clara voce clamat a mente sua plane penitusque alienam fuisse, quam Baronius comminiscitur, Glossam. Is enim postquam secundi ordinis opera percensuit; Catera, qua ab haereticis (inquit) sicce scismaticis conscripta, vel praedicata sunt, nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia, e quibus pauca, qua ad memoriam venerunt, & a Catholicis vitanda sunt, credimus esse subdenda. Tum continuo subdit; In primis Ariminensem Synodum, &c. item itinerarium nomine Petri Apostoli, quod appellatur Sancti Clementis libri octo, & post multa ejusdem ordinis continenter recensita, Liber (inquit) Canonum Apostolicorum apocryphus. Ergo etiam hic liber, judice Gelasio, ab haereticis, sive scismaticis conscriptus est; Etiam hic liber a Catholicis vitandus; Etiam hunc librum nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia. Dic mihi Baroni; etiam-ne ab haereticis sive scismaticis conscriptos libros; etiam-ne a Catholicis vitandos; etiam-ne nullatenus ab Ecclesia Catholica receptos, pro authenticis & Ecclesiasticis sticis habendos putas? Me quidé tuæ pudet ac piget inverecundię, qui Canones istos talibus stigmatis à Gelasio inustos, ac compunctos, ab eodem pro authenticis habitos contendis. Sed nondum finis est. Recensitis enim illis tertii ordinis libris, in quibus est, ut diximus, Apostolicorum canonum codex, ita tandem concludit Gelasius; Hæc ( adeoque & canones Apostolorum paulo ante cum cæteris memoratos ) hæc, inquit, & cætera his similia, quæ Simon Magus, &c. nec non & omnes hæretici eorumque discipuli sive scismatici docuerunt, vel conscripserunt, quorum nomina minime retinentur, non solum repudiata, verum etiam ab omni Romana Catholico Apostolica Ecclesia eliminata, atque cum suis authoribus, authorumque sequacibus sub anathematis indissolubili vinculo in æternum confitemur esse damnata.
units.tr: Gelasius condemned the canons of the Apostles, and he did not merely deny that they are divine, which Baronius concedes; he also did not regard them as ecclesiastical or authentic, which Baronius contends. But why do we need arguments? Gelasius himself clearly declares that the gloss Baronius invents was wholly and entirely foreign to his mind. After going through the works of the second order, he says: "The rest, which were written or preached by heretics or schismatics, the Catholic and Apostolic Church does not receive at all. Of these, we believe that the few which have come to our memory, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be listed." He then immediately adds: "First, the Synod of Ariminum, etc.; likewise the itinerary under the name of the Apostle Peter, which is called the eight books of Saint Clement." And after many works of the same order are listed in succession, he says: "The book of the Canons of the Apostles, apocryphal." So, in Gelasius's judgment, this book too was written by heretics or schismatics; this book too is to be avoided by Catholics; this book too is not received at all by the Catholic and Apostolic Church. Tell me, Baronius: do you think that books written by heretics or schismatics, books to be avoided by Catholics, books not received at all by the Catholic Church, should be held authentic and ecclesiastical? I am ashamed and grieved by your shamelessness, since you insist that these canons, branded and pricked in this way by Gelasius, were held authentic by him. But the matter is not yet finished. For after listing those books of the third order, in which, as we have said, the code of the Apostolic canons is found, Gelasius finally concludes thus (and so the canons of the Apostles, mentioned a little earlier along with the others): "These, and other things like them, which Simon Magus, etc., and likewise all heretics and their disciples or schismatics have taught or written, whose names are in no way preserved, we confess are not only rejected but also expelled from the whole Roman, Catholic and Apostolic Church, and, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, condemned forever under the indissoluble bond of anathema."

units.la: En quales nobis Baronius fingat libros authenticos! ab hæreticis quidem, vel à scismaticis conscriptos, ab Ecclesia vero Romana non solum repudiatos, verum etiam eliminatos, & in æternum damnatos! Hæc enim velit nolit Baronius, etiam in librum Canonum Apostolicorum congerit Gelasius; qui in horum, de quibus ista dicit, numero disertissime ab ipso commemoratus legitur. Postremo ipsum apocryphi vocabulum, bulum, quo usus est Gelasius, Baronianum commentum apertissime conficit. Hæc sunt Gelasii verba, Liber canonum Apostolicorum apocryphus. Vult Baronius apocryphum librum hic dici, qui Apostolicum nomen præferens, non est tamen certo ab Apostolis conscriptus, neque adeo divinus, tametsi alioqui sit authenticus, atque Ecclesiasticus. Concedam; si Gelasius id vocabulum, quod in hoc decreto bis & sexagies posuit, vel semel eo sensu sumpserit, Ille vero in tota hac sententia constanter apocryphum dicit, id quod à publica Ecclesiasticæ authoritatis luce remotum inter rejecta, damnataque delitescit, neque ab Ecclesia suscipitur, aut probatur. Ita cum in proximo dicit Gelasius, Liber, qui appellatur Sortes Apostolorum, apocryphus; Liber, qui appellatur Laus Apostolorum, apocryphus; Liber Physiologus, qui ab hæreticis conscriptus est, & B. Ambrosii nomine signatus, apocryphus; nemo est usque adeo Baronianus, qui ista non eo ipso, quem demonstravimus, sensu, apocrypha dici fateatur; ac, ut semel dicam, nunquam aliter toto hoc opusculo usurpatum est apocryphi vocabulum. Quod usque adeo manifestum est, ut etiam à Bellarmino diserte fuerit observatum; ubi ille edisserens, quo sensu apocryphi cryphi vocabulum usurpare soleant scriptores Ecclesiastici, Interdum (inquit a) vocant apocryphos libros eos, qui errores admixtos habent. Sic utitur hac voce Origenes homilia 1. in Cantico, Hieronymus in epistola ad Latam de institutione Filiæ, & Augustinus l. 15. de Civitate Dei, c. 23. Quam significationem secutus Gelasius in decreto de libris Ecclesiasticis, eos libros vocat Apocryphos, qui sunt editi ab authoribus hæreticis, vel certe suspectis. Sed & præter ipsum Gelasium ac Bellarminum, omnes insuper, de quibus diximus, veteris & Gelasiana tempora proxime consecutæ memoriæ scriptores, hanc Baronianæ frontis duritiem frangunt. Inprimis Isidorus docet, quo sensu Gelasius apocryphum Canonum Apostolorum codicem dixerit, dum ad ejus decretum, ut liquet & Turrianus fatetur, respiciens scribit, istos canones nec sedem Apostolicam recepisse, nec sanctos Patres illis assensum præbuisse, & ab authoritate canonica, atque Apostolica removisse, atque inter apocrypha deputasse, pro eo quod ab hæreticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositi dignoscuntur. Obsecro tuam fidem, Baroni; siccine excipiuntur libri, qui licet non divini, authentici tamen sunt, atque Ecclesiastici? Neque aliter recentior Isidorus rus Mercator intellexit, dum profitetur, se Apostolorum Canones in sua syllogę descri- psisse, licet (inquit) à quibusdam apocry- phi dicantur. Nemo non videt istum sen- sisse apocryphos ab illis quibusdam dici, nul- lius Ecclesiastica authoritatis. Si enim istos putasset apocryphos canones eo sensu dixisse, quem vult Baronius, pro non divinis, vel non canonicis scriptura libris; nihil erat, quod eorum sententiam vel suo consilio, vel aliorum plurium, qui eos recipiebant, opinioni opponeret; cum neque vel ipse, vel hi plures divinam authoritatem Cano- nibus tribuerent; neque vero illi, si nihil aliud quam Θεοπνευστος esse eos negassent, intercessuri fuerint, quominus inter alios canones, licet non divinos, Ecclesiasticos tamen, censerentur. Sed & ipse à Baro- nio tantopere laudatus Dionysius, & prae- sationis author, quam in Crescoiana col- lectione à se visam describit idem Baroni- us, eadem quoque docent, dum uterque narrant suis istis Canonibus plurimos con- sensum non prabuisse facilem; hoc est, ut li- quet, aliter de iis, quam se, sensisse. Illi vero non aliter quam ipsi, de Canonibus sentiebant, si eos à Scripturarum divina- rum duntaxat, non etiam Ecclesiasticarum canone rejecisset. Nam eos neque qui regulis Ecclesiasticis accensent, Dionyfius, Crefconius, alii in Scripturarum Ϛεοπνευςων censu habent; à quo usque adeo abest ipse qui eorum sententiam sequitur ac defendit Baronius, ut Damnascenum, qui eos libris divinae Scripturae Canonicis post Apocalypsin accenset, graviter reprehendat, idque eum inconsulte nimis fecisse dicat. Iam & ipse quoque Gratianus a, hęc eodem modo accepit, dum id quod ait Isidorus, inter apocryphos deputari Canones Apostolorum, opponit τῷ recipi, scilicet inter Ecclesiasticas regulas, & τῷ servari, ut apparet ex duobus primis canonibus distinctionis decimae sextae. Sed & Humbertus Cardinalis, & qui eum sequitur, alter Cardinalis Bellarminus, dum ajunt, Patres Apostolorum canones numerasse inter apocrypha, clarissime significant, istos canones, non (quod unus omnibus somniavit Baronius) ex Scripturarum divinarum alio, sed (quod nos volumus) ab Ecclesiasticorum librorum & canonum censu à Patribus remotos fuisse; ut; vel hæc exceptio, quam addunt, demonstrat, exceptis capitulis quinquaginta, quae decreverunt orthodoxae fidei, vel ut rectius legit Baronius b, regulis orthodoxiae adjunEgenda. Quibuscum Antonius quoque Augustinus à nobis supra memoratus indubitato sentit, dum Isidorum scribit canones.
units.tr: See what sort of authentic books Baronius invents for us! Written indeed by heretics or schismatics, and not only rejected by the Roman Church but also expelled and condemned forever! For, whether Baronius likes it or not, Gelasius places even the book of the Canons of the Apostles among these, and it is read that he mentions it most clearly in the number of those of whom he speaks. Finally, the very word apocryphal, which Gelasius used, plainly refutes the Baronian fiction. These are Gelasius's words: "The book of the Canons of the Apostles, apocryphal." Baronius wants an apocryphal book here to mean one which, bearing an apostolic name, was not certainly written by the Apostles and so is not divine, although otherwise it is authentic and ecclesiastical. I grant this, if Gelasius used that word, which he employed in this decree some sixty-two times, even once in that sense. But he consistently calls apocryphal in this whole passage that which, removed from the public light of ecclesiastical authority, lies hidden among the rejected and condemned books, and is not received or approved by the Church. Thus, when Gelasius says a little earlier, "The book which is called the Lots of the Apostles, apocryphal; the book which is called the Praise of the Apostles, apocryphal; the Physiologus book, which was written by heretics and bears the name of Saint Ambrose, apocryphal," no one is so Baronian as to deny that these are called apocryphal in exactly the sense we have shown. To say it once for all: the word apocryphal is never used in any other sense throughout this little work. This is so manifest that Bellarmine also observed it expressly, when he set out in what sense ecclesiastical writers are accustomed to use the word apocryphal. "Sometimes" (he says) "they call apocryphal those books which contain mixed-in errors. Origen uses this word thus in Homily 1 on the Song of Songs, Jerome in his letter to Laeta on the education of a daughter, and Augustine in book 15 of The City of God, chapter 23. Following this meaning, Gelasius in his decree on ecclesiastical books calls apocryphal those books which were issued by heretical authors, or at least suspect." But besides Gelasius himself and Bellarmine, all the other writers of whom we have spoken, both the ancient ones and those of the memory of the time immediately following Gelasius, break this hardness of Baronius's brow. First of all, Isidore teaches in what sense Gelasius called the code of the Canons of the Apostles apocryphal, since he writes with reference to Gelasius's decree (as Turrianus, too, admits): "These canons neither the Apostolic See received, nor did the holy Fathers give their assent to them; they removed them from canonical and apostolic authority and assigned them among the apocrypha, because they are recognized as composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles." I beg you, Baronius, in good faith: are books which, though not divine, are nonetheless authentic and ecclesiastical, excluded in this way? Nor did the more recent Isidore Mercator understand it otherwise, when he declares that he has described the Canons of the Apostles in his collection, although (he says) they are called apocryphal by some. Everyone sees that he meant that they are called apocryphal by certain persons, of no ecclesiastical authority. For if he had thought that the canons were called apocryphal in the sense Baronius wants, that is, not divine or not canonical scripture books, there would have been no reason for him to oppose their opinion either by his own judgment or by that of many others who received them. For neither he himself nor those many others attributed divine authority to the Canons; nor, if they had denied only that they are inspired by God [Θεοπνευστος], would they have objected to their being counted among other canons, not divine but nevertheless ecclesiastical. But also Dionysius, so greatly praised by Baronius, and the author of the preface which Baronius himself describes as seen in the Cresconian collection, teach the same things, since both report that many people did not readily give their consent to these canons of theirs; that is, as is clear, they thought differently about them. Yet those people did not think about the canons otherwise than these men did, if the canons had been excluded only from the canon of divine Scriptures and not also from the ecclesiastical canon. For Dionysius and Crescon, and others, do not count those who reckon them among the ecclesiastical rules as inspired by God [Θεοπνευστος] in the Scriptures. From this, Baronius, who follows and defends their opinion, is so far removed that he sharply rebukes Damascene, who counts them among the canonical books of divine Scripture after the Apocalypse, and says that he did this too rashly. Moreover, Gratian too understood these things in the same way, when he set against what Isidore says, that the Canons of the Apostles are counted among the apocrypha, both being received [τῷ recipi], namely among the ecclesiastical rules, and being observed [τῷ servari], as appears from the first two canons of Distinction 16. Also Cardinal Humbert, and the Cardinal Bellarmine who follows him, when they say that the Fathers numbered the canons of the Apostles among the apocrypha, clearly indicate that these canons were removed by the Fathers not from the list of divine Scriptures (as Baronius alone dreamed to all), but from the list of ecclesiastical books and canons (as we maintain). This is shown by the exception they add, except for fifty chapters which decree the orthodox faith, or, as Baronius reads it more correctly, to be added to the rules of orthodoxy. With them, Antonius Augustinus, whom we have mentioned above, indubitably agrees, when he writes of Isidore's canons.

units.la: b Append. ad Tom. II. p. 1004. nones rejecisse, quos probavit Mercator. Hinc enim apparet canones inter apocry‐pha deputare (quod Isidorus & Gelasius fecerunt) huic nihil aliud esse, quam eos ex regularum Ecclesiasticarum censu, in quem a Mercatore admissi, receptique sunt, rejicere ac summovere. Sed jam satis confutata sunt tria adversariorum commenta, Turrianicum, Bellarminianum, & Baronianum; dissimilia quidem, sed tamen paria, & quae cum inter se pugnent, ejusdem tamen sunt amentiae, atque inverecundiae; sic ut difficile sit definire; cui haec laurea debeatur; nisi forte quis indignum putet Turriano eam eripi, adeo multarum in hoc genere palmarum gladiatori, ut vix quisquam cum eo sive veterum, sive recentiorum, comparari hac in parte possit. Is autem adversus tantam Gelasiani decreti lucem quaedam offundit, levia quidem illa, ut solet, & inania, sed quae tamen disjicere ac dispellere ideo operaepretium est, quod ea quoque Baronius non putaverit asper‐nanda.
units.tr: b Append. ad Tom. II. p. 1004. ...nones rejecisse, quos probavit Mercator. For from this it appears that to count the canons among the apocrypha (which Isidore and Gelasius did) amounts to nothing else than rejecting and removing them from the rank of ecclesiastical rules into which Mercator admitted and received them. But the three inventions of our opponents, the Turrianic, the Bellarminian and the Baronian, have already been sufficiently refuted: they are unlike one another, yet equal, and though they clash among themselves they spring from the same madness and shamelessness. So that it is hard to decide to whom this laurel should go, unless perhaps someone thinks it unworthy to snatch it from Turrianus, so many palms has he won as a gladiator in this kind of contest, so that scarcely anyone, of the ancients or of the moderns, can be compared with him in this respect. He, however, casts certain shadows over the great light of the Gelasian decree: those things are trivial, as is his habit, and empty, yet they are worth refuting and dispelling, because Baronius too did not think they should be despised.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: Solvuntur, quæ Turrianus Gelasiana sententia objicit, & quibus probare nititur, Gelasium canones Apostolicos pro veris agnovisse.
units.tr: Their objections from Gelasius are answered, in which Turrianus tries to prove that Gelasius recognised the Apostolic Canons as genuine, and the points on which he relies are refuted.

units.la: PRincipio ergo objicit, hunc ipsum Gelasium multa in suis epistolis, ac decretis ex Apostolicorum canonum libro laudare, ac velut Ecclesiasticas regulas afferre. Quo loco primo hæc recitat a ex prima, mihi nona, epistola b; De his autem, qui se ipsos abscindunt, paterni canones evidenter sequenda posuerunt, quorum tenorem sufficiat indidisse; Dicunt enim talia perpetrantes, mox ut agniti fuerint, à munere clericali debere eos secludi; quod modis omnibus custodire nos convenit; quia fas esse nulli suppeditat, quicquam præter illa, quæ memorabilis forma decrevit, censere. Tum ejusdem c hæc contra Simoniacos describit; Quos vero constituerit sacram mercatos esse pretio dignitatem, convictos oportet arceri, non sine periculo talia perpetrantes; Quia dantem & accipientem damnatio Simonis, quam sacra lectio testatur, involuit. Tertio & hæc ex eodem Gelasio recitat; Quisquis propria desertor Ecclesiæ nullis extantibus causis ad aliam putaverit transeundum, temereque susceptus fuerit, & promotus, reverendorum canonum vel ipse, vel receptor ejus atque promotor constituta non effugiet, qua de hujusmodi praesumptionibus praefixere servanda. Quarto & ista ejusdem Pontificis adjungit; Majorum veneranda constituta pronuntiant hujusmodi (peccatores) etiam si forte surrepserint, tam qui ante peccaverunt, detectos oportere repelli, quam sacra professionis oblitos, prævaricatoresque sancti propositi procul dubio submovendos. Deinde ex alio ejusdem epistola haec habet; Sed quid miremur Ecclesiarum principes ista negligere, quos sicut a multis audivimus contra canones omnia gerere, & contra Apostolicam disciplinam passim cuncta miscere, manifestum est, non servatis regulis ordinare. Haec ille; in quibus cum ne uno quidem verbo libri Canonum Apostolorum facta fuerit mentio, equidem frontem hominis mirari satis non queo, qui hinc se confecturum putavit, ut Gelasius, quem librum in 70. Episcoporum Synodo disertissimo damnavit, eum ipse pro authentico, vereque Apostolico habuerit. Primo locus Gelasii secundus contra Simoniacos nullum omnino canonem laudat, neque Apostolicum, neque Ealesiasticum. Tantum Simonis damnationem memorat, quam sacra (inquit) lectio Actuum scilicet Apostolicorum, ut notum est, est, testatur. Quintus vero locus canones simpliciter nominat, Ecclesiasticos scilicet; non ex libro illo canonum Apostolicorum petitos. Ait & contra disciplinam Apostolicam facere eos, qui passim cuncta miscent; quia scilicet Paulus Apostolus jubet omnia in Ecclesia εὐσχημόνως τάξιν honeste & secundum ordinem geri; in priore ad Corinthios epistola a. Fateor primo loco paternos canones, & memorabilem formam afferri contra eos, qui se ipsos abscindunt. Sed nihil necesse est, ut hoc unde sumpserit intelligamus, ad apocryphos canones confugere. Ecce enim in ipso Nicaenae Synodi limine occurrit canon, haec de eunuchis, quae ait Gelasius, exserte praecipiens. Sic quae tertio loco contra clericos proprias Ecclesias deferentes, & alienas invadentes ex reverendis canonibus citantur, ea inquam in Nicaenis regulis sub numero 15. & 16. clarissimis verbis expressa leguntur. Denique in eadem augustissima Synodo reperiuntur numero 9. & 10. quae quarto loco ex Venerandis majorum constitutis contra peccatores surrepentes laudat Gelasius. Ergo nulla hinc arte confici potest Gelasium librum Apostolicorum Canonum laudasse vel probasse. Nullo enim invidia erat haec eum ex Nicaena Synodo citare, ejusque decreta vocare paternos canones, memorabilem formam, reveren-
units.tr: First, then, he objects that this same Gelasius, in many of his letters and decrees, quotes from the book of the Apostolic canons and cites them as ecclesiastical rules. In this place he first recites these words a from his first letter, which by my count is the ninth b: "Concerning those who mutilate themselves, our fathers' canons have plainly laid down what is to be followed. It is enough to have set down their substance. For they say that those who commit such acts must be removed from clerical office as soon as they are known, which we ought to observe in every way, since it is not lawful for anyone to judge anything beyond what that memorable form has decreed." Then from the same c he describes this against the Simoniacs: "Those who have bought holy office for a price, once convicted, must be kept away, not without danger to those who commit such things, since the condemnation of Simon, which holy reading attests, has involved both the giver and the receiver." Third, he also recites this from the same Gelasius: "Whoever, a deserter of his own church, with no lawful causes existing, thinks he must pass to another, and is rashly received and promoted, shall not escape the reverend canons which have been laid down to be observed concerning such presumptions, whether he himself, or the one who received him and promoted him." Fourth, he adds this of the same pontiff: The venerable established decrees of our elders pronounce that such sinners, even if they have crept in by chance, must be repelled once detected, both those who sinned before and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and prevaricated against holy purpose must without doubt be removed. Then from another letter of the same he has this: But why should we wonder that the leaders of the churches neglect these things? As we have heard from many, they act contrary to the canons and throw everything into confusion against apostolic discipline; it is plain that they ordain without observing the rules. So he writes. Since not even one word of the book of the Apostolic Canons is mentioned in these passages, I truly cannot marvel enough at the man's brazenness, who thought he could establish from them that Gelasius, who condemned that book so eloquently in the Synod of seventy bishops, had himself held it to be authentic and truly apostolic. First, the second passage of Gelasius against the Simoniacs cites no canon at all, neither apostolic nor ecclesiastical. It mentions only Simon's condemnation, which "holy reading," namely the Acts of the Apostles as is well known, attests. The fifth passage names canons simply, meaning ecclesiastical ones, not drawn from that book of Apostolic canons. He also says that those who throw everything into confusion act against apostolic discipline, since the Apostle Paul bids that all things in the Church be done decently and in order [εὐσχημόνως τάξιν] in his first letter to the Corinthians a. I grant that in the first passage the canons of our fathers and the memorable form are cited against those who mutilate themselves. But there is no need to flee to apocryphal canons to discover where he took this. For at the very threshold of the Nicene Synod there is a canon concerning eunuchs, which Gelasius mentions, expressly commanding it. Likewise, the things cited in the third place from the reverend canons against clerics who carry off their own churches and invade others are, I say, stated in the clearest words in the Nicene rules, numbers 15 and 16. Finally, in that same most august synod are found numbers 9 and 10, which Gelasius cites in the fourth place from the venerable constitutions of our elders against sinners who creep in. Therefore it cannot be shown by any art that Gelasius cited or approved the book of the Apostolic Canons. There was no reason for him to draw these things from the Nicene Synod and call its decrees paternal canons, a memorable form, reverend canons,

units.la: a 1. Cor. 14. 40. reverendos canones, & veneranda majorum statuta. Quinimo hæc elogia Nicænis, quam Apostolicis decretis multo & melius conveniunt & frequentius à Patribus tribuuntur; qui quæ ab Apostolis habent Apostolica & divina oracula ac præcepta potius vocare solent, quam paternos canones, aut majorum statuta. Quod vero Turrianus Nicænos Patres hæc ipsa, quæ eos decernere non neget, contendit ex suo Canonum Apostolicorum libro habuisse, id mox suo loco demonstrabimus futile esse, ac ridiculum. Unde liquet, quantopere seque & lectores suos fallat Baronius, dum scribit facile esse pervidere ex compluribus locis à Turriano collectis (hoc est iis ipsis, quos modo repræsentavimus) Gelasium sæpe videri mutuatum testimonium & authoritatem ex iis, quæ in Apostolorum canonibus habentur. Nusquam id fecit Gelasius, nusquam id eum fecisse probavit Turrianus.
units.tr: a 1. Cor. 14. 40. reverend canons and the venerable constitutions of our elders. Indeed these epithets suit the Nicene decrees far better and more fittingly than the Apostolic ones, and the Fathers give them far more often. They usually call what they have from the Apostles apostolic and divine oracles and precepts, rather than paternal canons or constitutions of the elders. As for Turrianus's claim that the Nicene Fathers took these very things, which he does not deny they decreed, from his book of the Apostolic Canons, I will show in its proper place that this is futile and ridiculous. From this it is clear how greatly Baronius deceives both himself and his readers when he writes that it is easy to see from several passages collected by Turrianus (that is, the very ones we have presented) that Gelasius often seems to have borrowed testimony and authority from what is found in the Apostolic canons. Gelasius never did this, and Turrianus never proved that he did.

units.la: Non sunt minus vana, quæ idem Jesuita secundo loco objicit, Gelasius (inquit) inter authentica scripta retulit epistolas decretales, quas beatissimi Papæ diversis temporibus ab urbe Romana pro diversorum Patrum consultatione dederunt venerabiliter recipiendas. At (inquit) ex iis est epistola Zephyrini, in qua continetur 70. sententias Apostolos cum aliis quamplurimis Episcopis præfixisse, fixisse, & servandas censuisse. Ergo qui hanc epistolam probavit Gelasius, Apostolorum sententias, quas ille laudat tanquam authenticas, non potuit non probare. Illæ autem sententiæ, hi ipsi sunt Apostolorum canones, quos exhibet Turrianus; Ergo & eos ipsos velut authenticos probavit Gelasius. Turrianus quidem ita argumentatur; sive potius restim & arenam nectit; Ergo vero fateor, Gelasium Decretales Romanorum episcoporum epistolas inter orthodoxorum opuscula recipere ac recensere. Zephyrini, quam affert Turrianus epistolam, unam ex his epistolis, quas Gelasius recipit, fuisse nego. Quæ vero fuerint illæ à Gelasio probatæ episcoporum Romanorum epistolæ, non ex meis, aut Turriani somniis, sed ex authentica Leonis quarti epistola, qui & ipse summus istorum Pontifex fuit, & octingentis annis ante nos vixit, edo ac doceo. Is enim, quod supra me jam dixisse memini, ad episcopos Britanniæ scribens, quæ fuerint illæ decretales præsulum Romanorum regulæ; quę apud sedem Romanam in Canone habebantur, & quibus in Ecclesiasticis negotiis utebantur istius sedis Episcopi, disertissime ac nominatim demonstravit; nempe Sylvestri, Siricii, Innocentii, Zosimi, Cælestini, & Leonis epistolæ; inter quas cum nullam ponat Ze-
units.tr: What the same Jesuit objects in the second place is no less empty. "Gelasius," he says, "listed among authentic writings the decretal letters which the most blessed popes gave at various times from the city of Rome, to be received with reverence, for the consultation of various Fathers. But (he says) among these is the letter of Zephyrinus, in which it is contained that the Apostles, together with many other bishors, set down seventy sentences, and resolved that they were to be observed." Therefore whoever approved this letter, Gelasius, could not but approve the apostolic sentences which he praises as authentic. Those sentences are the very Apostolic canons which Turrianus sets out. Therefore Gelasius also approved those very canons as authentic. Turrianus does argue in this way, or rather he spins a rope of sand. I admit that Gelasius accepts and reviews the decretal letters of the Roman bishops among the writings of the orthodox. That the letter of Zephyrinus which Turrianus cites is one of the letters Gelasius accepts, I deny. Which letters of the Roman bishops Gelasius approved, I teach and show not from my own dreams or Turrianus's, but from the authentic letter of Leo IV, who was himself a supreme pontiff of that see and lived eight hundred years before us. For he, as I recall saying above, writing to the bishops of Britain, most clearly and by name set out which decretal rules of the Roman prelates were held in the canon at the Roman see and used in ecclesiastical affairs by the bishops of that see: namely the letters of Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Caelestine, and Leo. Among these, since he includes no letter of Zephy-

units.la: Zephyrini decretalem, frustra est Turrianus, qui eam Gelasio cognitam & probatam somniat. Id ipsum confirmo ex ea collestione, quam Adrianus Romæ itidem episcopus a. D. 787. Carolo regi ad usum Occidentalium Ecclesiarum obtulit; quamque Nicolaus Papa (odicem Canonum vocat. Ea enim collestio præter Conciliorum Orientalium & Africanorum canones, non alia Pontificum decreta continebat, quam eorum qui à Siricio ad Gregorium juniorem sederunt; ut narrat Sirmondus b, æq; quidem ac Turrianus Jesuita, sed eruditione, candoreque ac fide, non Turriano modo, sed & quovis ejusdem ordinis, potior, ac præstantior. Ergo ex his patet, ne annis quidem Domini 707.& 858. quibus vixerunt Adrianus & Nicolaus, ullam extitisse inter Romanorum episcoporum decretales Zephyrini epistolam; nedum ut ea jam inter eas fuerit, quas habebat ac probabat Gelasius, annis ante hos trecentis & amplius. Itaq; nihil ad Gelasium quicquid bonus ille Zephyrinus in straminea sua epistola delirat. Quæcunque vero pro ea constituenda in hoc ipso opere attulit Turrianus ea accurate dissolvit doctissimus Blondellus noster; ipsamque & cæteras ejusdem commatis priorum urbis præsulum ad Siricium usque Latinas epistolas, ita plane, liquidoque
units.tr: rinus as a decretal, Turrianus is in vain, dreaming that it was known and approved by Gelasius. I confirm this from that collection which Hadrian, likewise bishop of Rome, offered to King Charles in the year 787 for use in the Western churches, and which Pope Nicholas calls the Codex of Canons. For that collection, besides the canons of the Eastern and African councils, contained no other papal decrees than those of the popes who held the see from Siricius to Gregory the Younger, as Sirmond b relates. He is as much a Jesuit as Turrianus, but in learning, candour and fidelity he is superior to Turrianus, and more outstanding than any of that order. Therefore it is plain from these facts that in the years of the Lord 787 and 858, in which Hadrian and Nicholas lived, there was no letter of Zephyrinus among the decretals of the Roman bishops; much less was it already among those which Gelasius had and approved, more than three hundred years before. So whatever that good Zephyrinus raves in his straw letter has nothing to do with Gelasius. As for whatever arguments Turrianus brought in this very work to establish it, our most learned Blondel has accurately dissolved them, and he has demonstrated the letter itself, along with the other Latin letters of the early prelates of the city down to Siricius, so plainly and clearly

units.la: c In epist. decret. confutatione. In Zepharin ep.p.237. doque demonstravit post a. D. 800. à nequissimo & imperitissimo impostore fuisse confictas ; ut ne ex ipsis quidem adversariis quisquam in eum totis his viginti annis, à quo scilicet ipsius liber lucem vidit, pro epistolis certator surrexerit. Cum itaque & ex Blondelli demonstrationibus, & ex multorum celeberrimorum atque praestantissimorum etiam Romanae communionis virorum testimonio constet, nihili esse etjam Zephyrini, ac frustra & malis avibus à Turriano allatam & defensam epistolam, non est necesse, nos diligentius quaerere, quid istepseudo-Zephyrinus sibi velit, cum ait septuaginta Apostolos sententias praefixisse, cum aliis quamplurimis Episcopis servandas censuisse ; & quaenam sint Apostolorum septuaginta illae sententiae, quas apud caeteros omnes Christianos inauditas unus hic impostor blaterat; quasque Turrianus hos suos Apostolorum Canones esse vult, tristique ac ridiculo labore sudat, ut qui sunt 85. ii possint non plures esse quam 70. magno conatu magnas nugas agens. Blondellus quidem noster vero propius esse existimat, impostorem significare sententias quas Adrianus I. R.P. a.D. 785. indict. q. 13. Kal. Oct. in gratiam Ingelramni Melensium Episcopi collegisse dicitur ex Graecis & Latinis canonibus nibus & Synodis Romanis, atque decretis praesulum ac principum Romanorum; quod eae scilicet duae ac septuaginta fuerint, & ab hoc spuriarum decretalium parente, plurimum usurpatae deprehendantur. Fortasse simplicius fuerit cum Usserio nostro locum mendosum pronunciare, & proseptuaginta sententiis, quinquaginta scribere. In pseudo-Zephyrini (inquit ille ) commentitia ad Siciliae episcopos epistola, & Hincmarus Remensis olim, & nos hodie legimus, Septuaginta Apostoli sententias praefixerunt, vel sexaginta, ut citant Ivo, Decr. p. 4. ac. 107. author Pannomia. l. 2. c. 105. & Gratianus d. 16. c. 2. ubi cum non fine caussa suspicatus fuerit Bellarminus vitio librariorum erratum esse in numero, eum errorem (si quis tamen authorem tam futilem emendatione dignum censuerit) non melius quam ex Gregorii presbyteri citatione sanari posse censuerim, qui in Polycarpi fuit. 3. c. 20. neque septuaginta, neque sexaginta hic haberi, sed quinquaginta tantum; quemadmodum ad dictum Gratiani locum Romani correctores annotarunt.
