Haec Usserius; quae si, ut verisimillima sunt, ita esse videantur, fatebor equidem quinquaginta pseudo-Zephyrinianas Apostolorum sententias ipsissimos esse Apostolorum a Dionysio primum, Romae Latine publicatos catos quinquaginta canones; Hinc sequi, ut Zephyrino vel Gelasio noti fuerint, nego: quod annis scilicet post verum Zephyrinum sexcentis, post Gelasium vero trecentis, vixerit pseudo-Isidorus Mercator, Zephyrinianae epistolae verus ac indubitatus parens. Quin imo non modo rerum veritati, sed & ipsius Turriani rationibus adversatur, quod nunc iste pugnat, Zephyrino cognitos fuisse hos 85. Apostolorum canones. Nam ipse quod supra dixi-mus, statuit exceptis quinquaginta prioribus Apostolorum canonibus, reliquos 35. tardius ad Latinos, quam ad Graecos pervenisse; neque Latinos plura, quam quinquaginta capitula, diu habuisse. At si, quod nunc idem, suorum immemor, contendit, Zephyrino, qui ab a.D. 197. ad 217. Romae sedit, omnes illi 85. canones cogniti fuerunt; concidet, quod idem alibi vult non plura, quam 50. eorum capitula, Latinos initio habuisse; quinimo hac ratione fiet, ut Apostolorum canones ad Latinos multo ante quam ad Graecos pervenerint; apud quos (ut postea demonstrabitur) plane nulla occurit istorum 85. canonum ante sextum saeculum adultum mentio. Sed haec de lata Pseudo-Zephyrini epistola plus satis.
units.tr: In the Refutation of the Decretal Letters, on the letter of Zephyrinus, p. 237: and he showed that it was fabricated after AD 800 by a most wicked and most unskilled impostor. For this reason not even one of the adversaries themselves has come forward in all these twenty years, since the book first saw the light, to champion the letters. Since it is established, both from Blondel's demonstrations and from the testimony of many most renowned and eminent men, even of the Roman communion, that the letter of Zephyrinus is worth nothing, and that Turrianus brought it forward and defended it in vain and to his own misfortune, there is no need for us to inquire more closely what this pseudo-Zephyrinus means when he says that the seventy Apostles prefixed sentences, which they wished to be observed along with very many other bishops. Nor need we ask what those seventy sentences of the Apostles are, which this one impostor babbles about as unheard of among all other Christians, and which Turrianus wants to be his Canons of the Apostles, sweating over them with a sad and ridiculous labour, so that the eighty-five might be no more than seventy, achieving great trifles with great effort. Our Blondel, however, thinks it more likely that the impostor means the sentences which Adrian I, Roman pontiff, is said to have collected in AD 785, in the thirteenth indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, for the favour of Ingelram, bishop of Meaux, from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman prelates and rulers. He reasons that these were evidently the seventy-two, and that they are found to have been much used by this parent of the spurious decretals. Perhaps it would be simpler, with our Usher, to declare the passage corrupt and to write fifty in place of seventy. "In the pseudo-Zephyrinus letter to the bishops of Sicily, which is fabricated (he says), both Hincmar of Reims formerly and we today read: 'The seventy Apostles prefixed sentences,' or sixty, as Ivo, Decr. p. 4, c. 107, and the author of the Pannomia, book 2, c. 105, and Gratian, d. 16, c. 2, cite it." Since Bellarmine suspected, not without reason, that the number had been mistaken through the error of scribes, I think that error (if anyone thinks such a trifling author deserves correction) can be remedied no better than by the citation of Gregory the presbyter, who was in Polycarp, book 3, c. 20. There neither seventy nor sixty is found, but only fifty; as the Roman correctors noted on the passage of Gratian. So Usher. If these things are as very probable as they seem, I will freely admit that the fifty pseudo-Zephyrinian sentences of the Apostles are the very fifty canons of the Apostles that Dionysius first published in Latin at Rome. But I deny that it follows that they were known to Zephyrinus or Gelasius; for the pseudo-Isidore Mercator, the true and undoubted parent of the Zephyrinian letter, lived six hundred years after the real Zephyrinus and more than three hundred after Gelasius. Moreover, this claim, that the eighty-five canons of the Apostles were known to Zephyrinus, contradicts not only the facts but also Turrianus's own reasoning. For he himself, as I said above, holds that apart from the first fifty canons of the Apostles, the remaining thirty-five reached the Latins later than the Greeks, and that the Latins for a long time had no more than fifty chapters. But if, as he now contends, forgetful of his own words, all those eighty-five canons were known to Zephyrinus, who sat at Rome from AD 197 to 217, then what he says elsewhere, that at first the Latins had only fifty of their chapters, will fall; indeed, by this reasoning it would follow that the canons of the Apostles reached the Latins much earlier than the Greeks, among whom (as will be shown later) there is clearly no mention of these eighty-five canons before the sixth century was well advanced. But enough about the letter of pseudo-Zephyrinus.

units.la: Jam ergo profligatis quaecunque ad hunc locum à Turriano, Bellarminoque & Baronio objecta, vel excogitata sunt, firmum ac verum stat Gelasii in Romana 70. episcoporum Synodo decretum, Liber Canonum Apostolicorum apocryphus. Unde clarum certumque fit primo Dionysium Exiguum quinquaginta Apostolorum Canones à se in græcis exemplaribus inventos, temere acinscite & præter disertissimam Episcopi, Conciliique Romani sententiam Ecclesiastico codici primum omnium inseruisse; multo pejus, atque periculosius paulo post peccasse Justinianum, & Joannem ex Scholasticis, qui eundem canonum Apostolicorum librum, & quidem triginta quinque capitulis auctiorem, in publicum Nomocanonem retulerunt; gravissime omnium peccasse Damascenum, qui non modo falsos ac nuperos, sed etiam à Papa & Concilio Romano damnatos canones divinis libris per intolerabilem, planeque sacrilegam audaciam exæquavit; peccasse & Trullanos Patres, qui eundem librum firmare & authoritate summa donare non dubitarunt, eodemque in flagitio hæreret reliquos omnes Græcos, qui hujus Synodi placita sequuntur; errasse postremo Leonem I v. & Nicolaum I. & cæteros Latinos, quotquot Dionysiacæ collectionis specie decepti, adversus sacra canitie veneranda Gelasii & majorum statuta, ac contra luculentissimam Isidori Hispalensis admonitionem, damnatos, qui Apostolorum dicuntur, canones, inter Ecclesiasticas regulas habere ac recensere ausi sunt. Horum omnium quotcunque, ac quanticunq; de caetero sint, authoritatem omnem obterit antiquius Gelasii, Romanaeque Synodi decretum; neq; ullis posterorum sententiis convalescere possunt, quae jam tot ante saeculis legitimo, ac canonico, non Romani modo Praesulis, & quidem ejus, qui inter sapientissimos habetur, sed & Romanae, & quidem LXX. Episcoporum Synodi, statuto convulsa & ex Ecclesiae Catholicae finibus exterminata fuerunt. Hoc ego Romanae veteris Ecclesiae decretum omnibus recentiorum scitis, ac disputationibus oppono; hoc unum plurisfacio, quam & Trullanae Synodi, & Graeculorum omnium canones & psephismata. Neq; satis mirari possum degenerem Turriani & aliorum ignaviam, qui in tota hac causa Romani nominis dignitate foedissime prodita, unius Scythae nugas, & Graecorum levitatem sui Gelasii, suaeque Synodi authoritati anteponunt. Ac illis quidem, si moribus, quos jactant, Romanis vere essent, haec ad contemnendos, & ad Apocrypha relegandos quotquot dicuntur, Canones, satis esse deberent. Nobis vero, qui non Paparum, neque omnino ullorum hominum, nominibus vel authoritate, sed uno vero nitimur, nondum sunt ista satis. Itaque ne praeter nostrum institutum, moremque solam hominis authoritatem secuti videamur, ostendendum est, rectum verumque fuisse Gelasii, quod amplectimur, de libro Canonum Apostolicorum judicium. Quod ut praestemus, inprimis amolienda sunt Bellarmini, ac Turriani Sophismata, quibus illi contra sui ipsorum Pontificis sententiam conficere conantur, vere Apostolicos esse, quos ille damnavit, canones; Tum veris, solidisque argumentis demonstrandum erit, eos, quos ipsi defendunt, quosque Gelasius ex Ecclesia proscripsit, Canones, neque ab Apostolis editos, neque à Clemente Romano litteris mandatos, sed ab impostore nescio quo aliquot post Apostolorum tempora saeculis consarcinatos fuisse.
units.tr: Now, therefore, having disposed of whatever objections or inventions Turrianus, Bellarmine and Baronius have brought against this point, the decree of Gelasius at the Roman synod of seventy bishops stands firm and true: The Liber Canonum Apostolicorum is apocryphal. From this it becomes clear and certain, first, that Dionysius Exiguus, rashly and without warrant, and against the most explicit judgment of the bishop and the Roman council, was the first of all to insert the fifty canons of the Apostles, which he had found in Greek copies, into the ecclesiastical collection. Much worse and more dangerously, shortly afterwards, Justinian and John the Scholastic sinned, who brought this same book of canons of the Apostles, and indeed enlarged by thirty-five chapters, into the public Nomocanon. Damascene sinned most gravely of all, who by an intolerable and plainly sacrilegious audacity placed on a level with the divine books canons that were not only false and recent but had even been condemned by the Pope and the Roman council. The Trullan Fathers also sinned, who did not hesitate to confirm this book and to endow it with the highest authority, and all the other Greeks who follow the decisions of this synod remain in the same disgrace. Finally, Leo IV and Nicholas I, and all the other Latins who, deceived by the appearance of the Dionysian collection and against the venerable and sacred antiquity of Gelasius and the statutes of our forefathers, and against the most evident admonition of Isidore of Seville, dared to count among the ecclesiastical rules the canons that are called those of the Apostles, though they were condemned, erred. Whatever the number and quality of these men's other claims, the authority of the older decree of Gelasius and of the Roman synod overthrows them all; nor can they gain strength from the opinions of later men, which were already overturned, by a lawful and canonical judgment, so many centuries before, not only by a Roman prelate, and indeed one counted among the wisest, but by a Roman synod of seventy bishops, and were cast out of the bounds of the Catholic Church. I set this decree of the ancient Roman Church against all the opinions and disputes of more recent times; I value this one decision above the canons and decrees of the Trullan synod and of all the Greeklings. Nor can I sufficiently wonder at the degenerate cowardice of Turrianus and others, who in this whole matter, shamefully betraying the dignity of the Roman name, prefer the trifles of one Scythian and the lightness of the Greeks to the authority of their own Gelasius and his synod. For them, if they were truly Romans in the manner they boast, this would be enough to despise and to relegate to the apocrypha all the books that are called Canons. But for us, who rely not on the names or authority of popes, nor of any men at all, but on the one true (ground), this is not yet enough. Therefore, lest we seem to have followed merely human authority, contrary to our purpose and custom, it must be shown that Gelasius's judgment on the book of the Canons of the Apostles, which we embrace, is right and true. To do this, first the sophisms of Bellarmine and Turrianus must be removed, by which they try to prove, against the opinion of their own Pontiff, that the canons he condemned are truly apostolic; then, by true and solid arguments, it must be shown that the canons they defend, and which Gelasius expelled from the Church, were neither issued by the Apostles nor committed to writing by Clement of Rome, but were patched together by some impostor or other, some centuries after the times of the Apostles.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Solvuntur ac refelluntur qua pro Canonibus Apo- stolicis contra Gelasii decretum attulit Bellar- minus ex Tertulliano, Athanasio, & Da- masceno.
units.tr: The arguments that Bellarmine brought from Tertullian, Athanasius and Damascene in defence of the Apostolic Canons against the decree of Gelasius are answered and refuted.

units.la: AC cum Bellarmino quidem res paucis transigetur, quod quae hic pro Canonibus attulit, ea & pauca sint, & levia, & à Reve-rer. Usserio jam luculente confutata. Primo ergo Tertullianus (inquit) in libro adversus Praxeam scribit Canones Apostolorum esse nobis per manus traditos. Idipsum & ante Bellarminum affirmaverat Sixtus Senensis in libro secundo Bibliothecæ; & post Bellarminum repetivit Possevinus c; falso omnes, temereque, ac in-verecunde, ut observat noster Usserius d. Haec enim Tertullianus, quae ei nullo pudore affinguntur, neque in libro adversus Praxeam, neque usquam alibi, scripsisse deprehenditur. Nos vero certis ac indubitatis argumentis paulo post demonstrabimus, Tertulliano plane fuisse incognitos illos Apostolorum sive Dionysiacos, sive Turrianicos Graecanicosque canones. Ergo vana est prima Bellarmini ratio; quae non Tertulliani testimonio, sed Sixti Seti Senensis vel mendacio, vel certe somnio nititur. Secunda non est firmior (quam idem quoque Sixtus Bellarmino, æque ac priorem dictavit) inde ducta, quod Athanasius (ut isti quidem affirmant) in Synopsi canones istos inter hagiographa numeret. Respondeo, nullam in tota Synopsi Canonum Apostolicorum, ne levissimam quidem, occurrere mentionem. Fateor Athanasium ainter ... ea novi Testamenti scripta, quibus contradicitur, una cum Petri, Johannisque, & Thomæ periodis, sive itinerariis, Thomaque Evangelio, τὰ Κλημέντια, Clementina quoque reponere. Quod si Sixtus & Bellarminus contendant Clementinorum nomine Apostolorum Canones significare, primo id probare debuerant, non, quod fecerunt, velut certum & indubitatum sumere. Nos enim negamus τὰ Κλημέντια Athanasio esse Canones Apostolorum. Nam istos canones à Clemente conscriptos esse non modo clarum certumve non est, sed est insuper evidentissime falsum; quod postea suo loco demonstrabitur. Si quæras, quid sint illa τὰ Κλημέντια, nihil mihi quidem verisimilius occurrit, quam ut hoc nomine significarit Athanasius, illa Clementis nomine paulo ante Eusebii tempora, conficta ac vulvulgata πολυετῆ καὶ μακρὰ συγγράμματα, Πέτρᾳ δὲ καὶ Ἀππίωνος διαλόγες περιέχοντα, verbosa & prolixa scripta, Petri & Appionis colloquia, sermonesque complectentia; quae Eusebius a, & ex eo Hieronymus, memorant, ac veluti spuria, nuperque nata, explodunt ac refutant. Hujus enim libri argumentum plane cum iis omnibus congruit, quae eodem ordine ab Athanasio censentur, ac memorantur Petri, Joannisque itinerariis, & Thomae Euangelio. Caeterum cave putes ista, quaecunque tandem sint, Κλημέντια, ab Athanasio inter libros hagiographos (quod Sixtus & Bellarmiuus inverecundissime affirmant) in Synopsi numerari. Nam si hagiographa sunt, quaecunque illic Athanasius nuncupat, τὰ τῆς νέας διαθήκης ἀντιλεγόμενα, profecto necesse erit pro libris hagiographis haberi Petri ac Thomae circuitus, & Euangelium secundum Thomam, libros, ut notum est, damnatissimos, pessimisque ac deterrimi inter ipsos apocryphos furfuris; quod nescio an Sixtus, & Bellarminus admissuri sint; hoc scio, nunquam eos cuiquam cordato persuasuros, ut infelices librorum istorum quisquilias inter novi testamenti hagiographa censeant. Sequeretur tantum eos libros Athanasium eodem loco, ac numero censendos existimasse,
units.tr: I shall deal with Bellarmine briefly, since what he has brought forward for the Canons is both slight and thin, and has already been thoroughly refuted by the Reverend Ussher. First, he says, Tertullian in his book against Praxeas writes that the Canons of the Apostles have been handed down to us. Sixtus of Siena had already asserted the same thing before Bellarmine, in the second book of his Bibliotheca, and after Bellarmine Possevinus repeated it. They are all wrong, and rashly and shamelessly so, as our Ussher observes. For Tertullian is not found to have written these things, which are shamelessly attributed to him, either in the book against Praxeas or anywhere else. I shall show soon, by sure and indubitable arguments, that those Apostolic canons, whether the Dionysian, the Turrian or the Greek, were entirely unknown to Tertullian. So Bellarmine's first argument is empty. It rests not on Tertullian's testimony but on the lie, or at any rate the dream, of Sixtus of Siena. The second argument, which Sixtus dictated to Bellarmine just as he did the first, is no firmer. It is drawn from the claim that Athanasius, as these men maintain, counts these canons among the sacred writings in his Synopsis. I reply that there is not the faintest mention of the Apostolic Canons anywhere in the whole Synopsis. I grant that Athanasius, among the ... writings of the New Testament that are disputed, also places, together with the Itineraries of Peter, John and Thomas, and the Gospel of Thomas, the Clementine writings [τὰ Κλημέντια]. But if Sixtus and Bellarmine maintain that by the name of the Clementines the Canons of the Apostles are meant, they ought first to have proved this, not, as they have done, take it for granted as certain and beyond doubt. For we deny that τὰ Κλημέντια are the Canons of the Apostles in Athanasius. That these canons were written by Clement is not merely unclear and uncertain; it is plainly false, as will be shown in its proper place later. If you ask what those τὰ Κλημέντια are, nothing seems to me more probable than that by this name Athanasius meant those long and extended writings, invented and published under Clement's name shortly before the time of Eusebius, containing the dialogues of Peter and Appion [πολυετῆ καὶ μακρὰ συγγράμματα, Πέτρου δὲ καὶ Ἀππίωνος διαλόγους περιέχοντα], which Eusebius, and after him Jerome, mention and reject and expose as spurious and recently produced. For the subject of that book agrees entirely with all the works that Athanasius lists in the same order: the Itineraries of Peter and John, and the Gospel of Thomas. But beware of thinking that these Clementines, whatever they are, are counted by Athanasius among the sacred books in his Synopsis, as Sixtus and Bellarmine shamelessly assert. For if all the works that Athanasius names among the disputed books of the New Testament [τὰ τῆς νέας διαθήκης ἀντιλεγόμενα] are sacred books, then it must follow that the Itineraries of Peter and Thomas, and the Gospel according to Thomas must be regarded as sacred books too: books which, as is well known, are most condemned, the worst and most wretched dregs among the apocryphal rubbish. I do not know whether Sixtus and Bellarmine will concede this; I do know that they will never persuade any sensible person to count the wretched trifles of these books among the sacred writings of the New Testament. It would only follow that Athanasius thought those books should be counted in the same place and in the same number

units.la: quo Petri & Joannis & Thomæ circuitus, & Euangelium secundum Thomam censentur. Atqui hæc inter apocrypha omnis semper censuit Ecclesia. Ergo & inter apocrypha ablegandos esse Apostolorum Canones (quod ipsum est Gelasii de iis judicium) ex Athanasio sequeretur, siquidem is hoc loco eorum (quod nullus fecit) meminisset.
units.tr: as the Itineraries of Peter, John and Thomas, and the Gospel according to Thomas, are counted. But the Church has always counted these among the apocrypha. So it would follow from Athanasius, if he had mentioned the Canons of the Apostles in this place (which nobody has ever done), that they too must be relegated to the apocrypha, which is exactly Gelasius's judgment about them.

units.la: Tertia Bellarmini ratio inde ducitur, quod Synodus Trullana capite secundo recipit Canones Apostolorum octoginta quinque. Ego vero fateor id fuisse Trullanæ Synodi de his Canonibus judicium. Nego ejus Synodi authoritatem valere. Primo eam summis viribus omnes Latini impugnant, ac refutant, intolerabilisque superbiæ accusant, quod leges ipsis Romanis dicere ausa sit; quo nullum apud istos est dirius, aut capitalius nefas. Tum ipse, qui eam objicit, Bellarminus & quidem hoc ipso loco contemnit. Cum enim ea Apostolorum canones admittat 85. Bellarminus non plures, quam quinquaginta, habet pro legitimis. Adhæc si ratio antiquitatis habenda est (& in his præsertim, ubi de facto quæritur, habendam omnes consentiunt) Trullani Patres annis ducentis Gelasiorecentiores sunt. Sin authoritas quæritur, quin Roma Constantinopoli, GelaGelasius Romanorumque Patrum Synodus, Græculorum hominum Synodo, nullo præsente, nullo annuente vel probante Papa habitâ, multis partibus major, potiorque sit, nemo adversariorum negabit.
units.tr: Bellarmine's third argument is drawn from the fact that the Synod of Trullo, in its second canon, accepts the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles. I grant that this was the judgment of the Synod of Trullo about these canons. I deny that the authority of that Synod is valid. First, all the Latins attack and refute it with the utmost force, and accuse it of intolerable arrogance in daring to prescribe laws to the Romans themselves, and among them there is no more dreadful or capital crime. Then Bellarmine himself, who brings this objection, despises it even in this very place. For although the Synod admits eighty-five canons of the Apostles, Bellarmine holds no more than fifty to be genuine. Besides, if the consideration of antiquity is to be taken into account (and everyone agrees that it must be, especially in matters of fact), the Fathers of Trullo are two hundred years more recent than Gelasius. But if authority is what is being asked about, no opponent will deny that Rome is far greater and more powerful than Constantinople; that the decree of Gelasius and the synod of the Roman Fathers, held without any Greek presence and without the approval or consent of the Pope, is in many respects greater and weightier than a synod of Greek men.

units.la: Denique affert Bellarminus Damascenum. Sanctus (inquit) Ioannes Damascenus l. 4. de fide orthodoxa c. 18. videtur Canones Apostolorum ponere inter Sacras Scripturas. Ego vero miror, cur iste scripserit videri Damascenum Canones sacris Scripturis accensere; quasi scilicet non quidem eos revera scripturis annumeret, sed duntaxat annumerare videatur. Atqui clamant diserta ipsius verba, quæ nos supra descripsimus, hanc ejus apertam, liquidamque esse sententiam, ut Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum in divinarum ac Θεοπνεύστων Scripturarum canone censeantur, atque habeantur; quam hominis cæcitatem, atque temeritatem ne ipse quidem Baronius potuit vel dissimulare, vel intactam prætermittere; inconsulte nimis ab eo factum dictitans, quod Canones divinæ Scripturæ libris post Apocalypsin accensere non dubitaverit. Desinat ergo Bellarminus id Damasceni judicium objicere, quod & ejus collega Baronius improvidum, inconsultumque pronuntiat, & ipse eo satis damnat, quod id neque sequitur aut probat,neque integrum vere ac aperte proponere hoc loco ausus est. Adhæc quid de his Canonibus somniaverit Damascenus, nihil ad Gelasium, qui annis ducentis ante eum vixit. Si viros spectes, æquum fuit Damascenum Gelasii, juniorem senioris, monachum Episcopi, & quidem summi, judicio cedere, neque ulla ratione purgari vel excusari potest, quod quos Canones sapientissimus, ut ferunt, Theologus, primæ sedis Episcopus, totiusque Ecclesiæ, ut volunt, rector una cum septuaginta antistitibus ante ducentos annos in apocryphorum classem rejecerat, eos ipsos homo novus, nulla in Ecclesia dignitate fungens, novo & hactenus apud Christianos inaudito facinore divinis sanctissimarum Scripturarum libris æquiparare, atque accensere ausus sit. Sin res ipsa, caussaque sola spectetur, sole meridiano clarius est, rationes fuisse & plurimas & gravissimas, cur istos Canones veluti spurios, & apocryphos reje-cerit Gelasius; nullas penitus fuisse, cur eosdem in sacrum καθολικῶν canonem referret Damascenus; ut ex iis, quæ postea, disputabimus, apparebit. Atque hæc quidem ad Bellarmini objectiones satis.
units.tr: Finally, Bellarmine brings forward Damascene. Saint John Damascene (he says) in book 4 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 18, seems to place the Canons of the Apostles among the Holy Scriptures. I am surprised that he wrote that Damascene seems to reckon the Canons among the sacred Scriptures, as if Damascene did not really count them among the Scriptures but only seemed to do so. Yet his own plain words, which I quoted above, proclaim that his open and clear opinion is that the so-called Canons of the Apostles are to be counted and held in the canon of the divine and God-breathed [Θεοπνεύστων] Scriptures. Not even Baronius could dissimulate or pass over this man's blindness and rashness without comment; he keeps saying that it was done too much without consideration by him, in that he did not hesitate to count the Canons among the books of divine Scripture after the Apocalypse. Let Bellarmine therefore stop objecting to the judgment of Damascene, which his colleague Baronius pronounces rash and ill-considered, and which Bellarmine himself condemns enough by the fact that it neither follows from nor proves his point, and that he has not dared to set it out here whole and openly. Besides, whatever Damascene dreamed about these Canons has nothing to do with Gelasius, who lived two hundred years before him. If you look at the men, it was right that Damascene, a younger man yielding to an older, a monk yielding to a bishop, and indeed a bishop of the highest rank, should defer to Gelasius's judgment; and it cannot be defended or excused in any way that a man new to the Church, holding no dignity in it, should with an unprecedented deed, unheard of among Christians until now, dare to set equal to the divine books of the most holy Scriptures, and to count among them, those very Canons which the most wise theologian, as they say, bishop of the first see, and ruler of the whole Church, as they claim, had rejected two hundred years earlier with seventy bishops, as spurious and apocryphal. But if the matter itself and its cause alone are examined, it is clearer than the noonday sun that Gelasius had many and very weighty reasons for rejecting these Canons as spurious and apocryphal, and that Damascene had no reason at all for placing them in the sacred catholic [καθολικῶν] canon, as will appear from what we shall discuss later. So much for Bellarmine's objections.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Solvuntur quæ Turrianus pro Canonibus ex Paulo Apostolo objicit, contra decretum Gelasii.
units.tr: The objections that Turrianus raises from the Apostle Paul in favour of his Canons, against the decree of Gelasius, are answered.

units.la: URRIANUS majori mole pro suis Canonibus pugnat; omnem antiquitatem jam inde ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus, suis excitam sedibus advocat; veros, falsosque, receptos & apocryphos scriptores in unum cogit; adhæc suis dissertationibus, vanis plerumque & paralogisticis, omnia miscet; denique per fas, & nefas Apostolicam canonibus authoritatem vindicare molitur. Piget quidem, ac tædet ineptissimam vanissimi hominis disputationem refellere. Sed quid facias? Devorandum est hoc tedium; aliter deerunt, qui inania hujus Pyrgopolinicis somnia proinvictis demonstrationibus jactent.
units.tr: Turrianus fights for his Canons with a great mass of material. He calls up all antiquity from the very times of the Apostles, roused from its seats. He gathers together true and false writers, accepted and apocryphal alike. Besides this, he mixes everything up in his own discourses, which are for the most part empty and fallacious. In short, by right and by wrong he labours to vindicate apostolic authority for the Canons. I am indeed vexed and wearied at having to refute the most inept discourse of this most vain man. But what can one do? This tedium must be swallowed, or there will be people who boast of this Pyrgopolinices' empty dreams as if they were proved by unanswerable demonstrations.

units.la: Principio homo ingeniosus suos Canones apud ipsum Paulum reperit; Quod enim Apostolus alicubi Corinthiis præcipit ut omnia honeste, & secundum ordinem apud ipsos fiant; quod idem Timotheum jubet recte tractare, ὀρθοτομεῖν verbum veritatis; & ad eundem scribit certo quodam modo in domo Dei, quæ est Ecclesia, conversandum esse, quod idem nos hortatur, ut in eadem regula permaneamus a; quod denique Corinthiis pollicetur, se apud eos omnia, cum venerit, dispositurum, sive ordinaturum; ex his, inquam, Turrianus b colligit certum quendam ordinem jam tum fuisse ab Apostolis constitutum, certam quandam fixam regulam ad verbum tractandum; positas certas leges, ex quarum praescripto, & Timotheus & caeteri versari in Ecclesia debuerint; certum comparatum canonem, in quo constanter haerendum, atque decurrendum sit; certas denique διαταξεις sive constitutiones editas ad regendam Ecclesiam. Jam vero hos ex Paulo exsculptos ordines, has Ecclesiasticae conversationis, Euangelicaeque tractationis normas, hunc nostri cursus canonem; has denique Diataxes ipsissimos esse suos Apostolorum Canones vaticinatur Turrianus. Quin & magno, ac insano hujus negotii amore incensus, ac prae nimio animi ardore tantum non furens edicit, omnem nos Apostolis sapientiae ac caritatis laudem erepturos, nisi hoc ipsi assentiamur; quod scilicet negare c canones Ecclesiasticos Sanctorum Apostolorum, quos habemus, nihil aliud sit, quam velle, Sanctos Apostolos in nulla, dum viverent, sollicitudine fuisse futura post obitum suum gubernationis, & statu omnium Ecclesiarum,
units.tr: First, this clever man finds his canons in Paul himself. The Apostle, in one place, instructs the Corinthians that everything among them should be done decently and in order. He bids Timothy to handle rightly [ὀρθοτομεῖν] the word of truth, and writes to him that one must conduct oneself in a certain way in the house of God, which is the Church. He also urges us, in the same passage, to remain in the same rule. Finally, he promises the Corinthians that when he comes he will set in order and arrange everything among them. From these passages, I say, Turrianus gathers that a certain order was already established by the Apostles at that time, a certain fixed rule for handling the word; that fixed laws were laid down, by whose prescription both Timothy and the others ought to conduct themselves in the Church; that a settled canon was drawn up, in which one must constantly stand and proceed; and, lastly, that set ordinances [διαταξεις] were issued for governing the Church. Moreover, Turrianus prophesies that these orders, these norms of ecclesiastical conduct and gospel practice, this canon of our course, and finally these ordinances, are the very canons of the Apostles themselves, extracted from Paul. Indeed, so inflamed by a great and mad love of this business, and so furious with his excess of zeal, he declares that we shall rob the Apostles of all praise for wisdom and charity unless we assent to this: namely, that to deny that the ecclesiastical canons of the holy Apostles which we have are anything other than to claim that the holy Apostles, while they lived, had no concern for the government and condition of all the Churches after their death,

units.la: a 1. Tim. 3. Phil. 3. b Turr. pro can. c. 16. p. 52. & fusius c. 26. & c. 21. p. 72. c c. 26. p. 95. recte. tum, nullamque eos curam habuisse relin- quendi Ecclesiis sanctas inposterum consue- tudines. Haec illę; ad quae nihil necesse est, quatuor illa Pauli loca excutere nunc, & interpretari accuratius. Paucis respon- deo, concedere nos, quod ex iis conclu- dit Turrianus, Apostolos Christianis sanctissimum ordinem, absolutissimam normam, regulam certissimam, diataxes denique sapientissimas, tum ad totius vitæ, tum ad Ecclesiasticorum ministerio- rum regimen, ac directionem tradidisse. Hunc Apostolicum ordinem, hanc regu- lam ac normam, has denique diataxes ea canonum collectione contineri, quam ob- trudit Turrianus, negamus; idque, in quo totius controversiæ cardo vertitur, proba- re iste debuit, non sumere; quod nihil a- liud est, quam id ipsum quod est ἐν ἀρχῇ, petere, ac postulare. Quod vero ait nisi hoc constituatur, Apostolis sapientiam, & Ecclesiæ curam, ac sollicitudinem eripi, id quoque inepte ac ridicule sumit, quod non nescit à nobis negari. Quasi vero Gelasius eo de Apostolis male sensisse putandus sit, quod istos Apostolicos ut sal- so dicuntur canones Apostolis abjudicatos in apocryphorum censum misit! Certe ipsa hodierna Romæ Ecclesia magnam il- lam, quam in iis Turrianus contineri putat, sapientiam usque adeo contemnit, ut paucissimos observet, teste Michaële Medina, cujus haec sunt verba; Ex 84. Apostolicis Canonibus, quos Clemens Romanus Pontifex & eorundem discipulus in unum coegit, vix sex aut octo Latina Ecclesia nunc observat. Apostolorum autem veras diataxes, non ex hac straminea collectione, sed ex divinis ipsorum libris, atque epistolis petendas esse existimamus; quibus plenissime continentur omnia tum ad singulorum vitam bene beateque instituendam, tum ad Ecclesiam universam sapienter, feliciterque gubernandam necessaria.
units.tr: a 1 Tim. 3; Phil. 3. b Turr. pro can. c. 16, p. 52; and more fully c. 26, c. 21, p. 72. c c. 26, p. 95, rightly. And so, that they had no care for leaving holy customs to the Churches for the future. So far he. To these claims there is no need to examine those four passages of Paul now and interpret them more carefully. I answer briefly: we grant what Turrianus concludes from them, that the Apostles handed down to Christians a most holy order, a most complete norm, a most certain rule, and, finally, most wise ordinances, for the governing both of the whole of life and of the ministry of the Church. But that this Apostolic order, this rule and norm, and these ordinances are contained in that collection of canons which Turrianus thrusts upon us, we deny. And this, on which the whole hinge of the controversy turns, he ought to have proved rather than assumed. To assume it is nothing other than to beg the very point in question [ἐν ἀρχῇ]. As for his claim that, unless this is established, wisdom is taken from the Apostles and care and concern for the Church are taken away, he also argues foolishly and ridiculously, assuming what he knows we deny. As if Gelasius should be thought to have had a poor opinion of the Apostles because he placed those so-called Apostolic canons, which are falsely attributed to the Apostles, among the apocryphal writings! Certainly the Church of Rome today itself so despises that great wisdom which Turrianus thinks is contained in them, that it observes very few of them, as Michael Medina testifies, whose words are these: Of the 84 Apostolic Canons, which Clement the Roman Pontiff and his disciple gathered into one, the Latin Church now observes scarcely six or eight. But we hold that the true ordinances of the Apostles are to be sought not from this straw-like collection but from their divine books and epistles, in which are most fully contained all things necessary both for establishing the life of each individual well and happily, and for governing the whole Church wisely and prosperously.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Defenditur decretum Gelasii contra alias Turriani ex Patribus objectiones. Ac primo rejiciuntur, quae ille ex Apocryphis adduxit, ut ex Anacleti, Alexandri, Julii, &c. urbis episcoporum straminetis epistolis; ex Nicaenis Canonibus Arabicis; ex fictitia Hieronymi ad Damasum epistola, & ex Pseudo-Dionysio.
units.tr: The decree of Gelasius is defended against Turrian's other objections drawn from the Fathers. First, those he brought from the Apocrypha are rejected: the flimsy letters of the bishops of the city, Anacletus, Alexander, Julius, and the rest; the Arabic Nicene Canons; the fictitious letter of Jerome to Damasus; and Pseudo-Dionysius.

units.la: ED missis Apostolorum litteris (in quibus praeter hunc Turrianum, nemo hactenus ex omnis memoriae Christianis istos Canones vel reperit, vel quaesivit) caeteros ChristiaChristianæ religionis veteres scriprores videamus. Quo loco inprimis ex testium legitimorum censu expungendi sunt quotquot Turrianus aspurios, & falsi nomi-nis authores in hanc causam nulla verecundia induxit. Hujus generis sunt primo omnes vetustissimi Ecclesiæ Romanæ ante Siricium Episcopi Anacletus b, Alexander *, Julius c, Eleutherius d, Marcellus e, Fabianus f, Eusebius g, Anicetus h, Calixtus i, Lucius k, Eutychianus l. Horum enim, quæ à Turriano in Canonum gratiam adducuntur Epistolæ Decretales, totis prioribus pene novem Christianismi sæculis, etjam in ipsa urbe Roma, ignotæ, inauditæque, nono demum sæculo prodierunt, & tam multa, tamque insignia præferunt falsimoniæ argumenta, ut nemo fere hodie, ne in ipsa quidem Romæ communione paulo eruditior vivat, qui aliquam infaustis illis & male confictis opusculis auctoritatem tribuat. Neque nos necesse est in confodiendis istis Decretalibus immorari; quas eruditissimus Blondellus noster proprio ac singulari opere copiosissime atque accuratissime impugnavit, ac profligavit, sigillatim confutatis iis omnibus, quæ pro illis Turrianus totis quatuor verbosissimis libris attulerat; clarissimeque ostendit, eas omnes epistolas ex ejusdem impostoris officina circa noni sæculi initia prodiisse; quo tempore cum jam dudum apud Latinos extarent quinto ineunte sæculo à Dionysio Exiguo publicati Apostolorum Canones, mirum non est, quod cogniti fuerint impostori sub primorum urbis episcoporum larva delitescenti, & ab eo pro consueta væcordia alienis personis inepte, absurdeque, ac præter temporum genium, aptati ac commodati.
units.tr: Having set aside the letters of the Apostles (in which, apart from this Turrian, no one from the whole memory of Christians has either found or sought these canons), let us look at the other ancient writers of the Christian religion. Here, above all, must be struck from the roll of legitimate witnesses all those whom Turrian, with no shame, has brought into this case as spurious authors under false names. Of this kind, first, are all the most ancient bishops of the Roman Church before Siricius: Anacletus b, Alexander *, Julius c, Eleutherius d, Marcellus e, Fabian f, Eusebius g, Anicetus h, Callixtus i, Lucius k, Eutychian l. Their letters, which Turrian adduces in favour of the canons as Decretal Epistles, were unknown and unheard of throughout almost the first nine centuries of Christianity, even in the city of Rome itself, and appeared only in the ninth century. They display so many and such striking marks of forgery that scarcely anyone today, even among the more learned within the communion of Rome itself, gives any authority to those unlucky and badly fabricated little works. Nor is it necessary for us to linger over digging up these Decretals. Our most learned Blondel has attacked and overthrown them most fully and accurately in his own separate work, refuting point by point everything that Turrian had brought forward for them in his four very wordy books. He has most clearly shown that all these letters came out of the workshop of the same impostor around the beginning of the ninth century. At that time the Apostolic Canons, published for the Latins by Dionysius Exiguus at the beginning of the fifth century, had long been extant. It is no wonder, then, that they became known to the impostor, who hid behind the mask of the first bishops of the city, and that he, with his usual foolishness, fitted and applied them clumsily and absurdly to persons not their own, and contrary to the spirit of the times.

units.la: 2. Iam eversa illarum epistolarum authoritate una quoque corruit fictitius ille B. Petri ad populum in Clementis ordinatione sermo, unde Turrianus suis Canonibus testimonium alicubi petivita. Non enim alio fundamento totus hic Petri sermo nititur, quam Clementinæ ad Iacobum epistolæ, in qua is narratur, testimonio. Illa vero Clementis epistola, licet aliis vetustior, una tamen est ex iis, quas spurias, & primis Romæ episcopis affictas atque suppositas fuisse demonstravit noster Blondellus b, & ex ipsis adversariis nobilissimi, ac eruditissimi quique, Turrecremata c, Cusanus d, Driedo e, Espencæus f, Baronius g, Bellarminus h, Perronius i, Binius k, Possevinus l, hujus nominatim Clementinæ epistolæ fidem, vel plane penitusque negant, vel certe vehementer dubiam biam, ac suspectam habent, ut videre est, apud Blondellum a. Quamquam ne si vera quidem ac legitima esset haec epistola, Canonum Apostolicorum authoritatem hilum affirmaret. Quid enim Petrum dixisse narrat fictitius ille Clemens b ? Ipsi (inquit, id est Clementi) trado a Domino mihi traditam potestatem ligandi & solvendi, ut de omnibus quibuscunque decreverit in terris, hoc decretum sit & in coelis. Ligabit enim quod oportet ligari, & solvet quod expedit solvi, tanquam qui ad liquidum Ecclesia regulam noverit. Obsecro tuam fidem, quid haec ad Turrianicos canones? Imo, inquit Turrianus, haec Ecclesia regula ipsissima est Canonum 85. syllogé. Ego vero, mi homo, tibi hoc affirmanti non credo. Clemens quidem nihil ait. Tuum est, non Clementis, totum hoc testimonium. Sed Turrianum suscepti negotii studium ita dementavit, ut absque hac sua Canonum farragine Ecclesiam regula caritturam, sublatoque omni ordine ac regimine pessum ituram non dubitet. Itaque quoties regulam, aut canonem, aut diataxin, aut normam, aut diorthosin audit, toties suam illam sapientissimam farraginem somniat. Nos quibus integri, & ab his praestigiis liberi sunt sensus, Ecclesia regulam Dei Scripturam intelligimus, omnium actuum
units.tr: 2. Now that the authority of those letters is overthrown, that fictitious sermon of St Peter to the people at the ordination of Clement collapses with it, the sermon from which Turrian seeks testimony somewhere for his canons. For this whole sermon of Peter rests on no other foundation than the testimony of the Clementine letter to James, in which it is narrated. That Clementine letter, though older than the others, is nevertheless one of those which our Blondel b has shown to be spurious, forged, and foisted upon the first bishops of Rome. Even the most noble and learned of the adversaries themselves, Turrecremata c, Cusanus d, Driedo e, Espencaeus f, Baronius g, Bellarmine h, Perron i, Binius k, Possevinus l, either altogether and utterly deny the credibility of this very Clementine letter, or at least hold it highly doubtful and suspect, as may be seen in Blondel a. Yet even if this letter were true and genuine, it would not confirm the authority of the Apostolic Canons in the slightest. For what does that fictitious Clement b say Peter said? "To him (that is, to Clement) I hand over the power, given to me by the Lord, of binding and loosing, so that whatever he decrees on earth concerning anything whatsoever, this decree shall also be in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound, and loose what it is expedient to loose, as one who has known the rule of the Church clearly." I beg your good faith, what has this to do with Turrian's canons? "Indeed," says Turrian, "this Church rule is the very collection of the 85 Canons." But I, my friend, do not believe you when you assert this. Clement says nothing of the kind. This whole testimony is yours, not Clement's. But zeal for the business he has undertaken has so maddened Turrian that he does not doubt that without this farrago of his canons the Church would lack a rule, and would go to ruin with all order and government abolished. And so whenever he hears rule, or canon, or arrangement, or norm, or correction, he dreams of that most wise farrago of his. We, whose senses are sound and free of these tricks, understand by the rule of the Church the Scripture of God, the most complete norm of all ecclesiastical acts;

units.la: {a} p. 26. {b} Clem. ep. 1. paulo post init. actuum Ecclesiasticorum absolutissimam normam; qua quæcunque accurate, & pro eo ac decet utetur Ecclesia, nullos profecto desiderabit Turriani, vel aliorum impostorum canones.
units.tr: {a} p. 26. {b} Clem. ep. 1, shortly after the beginning. of ecclesiastical acts; which the Church, using it accurately and as is fitting, will surely not lack any canons of Turrian or of other impostors.

units.la: 3 Pertinet etiam ad hoc genus id testimonium, quod Turrianus a pro Canonibus ex Canone Nicæno 56. affert, quo affirmatur sanctos Apostolos constituisse, ne sacerdos curas sæculares suscipiat, neque lucris usuræ studeat, neque sit ei cum Judaïs societas, neque cum eis prandeat, aut potet. Sane istis congruunt quæ in Turriana sylloge canonibus sexto, quadragesimo quarto, & septuagesimo leguntur: ut eo omnino respexisse videatur quisquis est illius, qui pro Nicæno obtruditur, canonis author. Sed cum ex perpetuo totius veteris Ecclesiæ consensu, omnibusque Græcorum, & Latinorum qua manuscriptis, qua excusis exemplaribus constet non plures, quam viginti canones edidisse Nicænam Synodum, apparet istos, qui nuper ab hoc ipso Turriano, & ab Alphonso Pisano Iesuitis, numero 8o. publicati sunt, & ex Arabico Alexandrini nescio cujus Patriarchæ scrinio in hunc nostrum orbem primum invecti, nothos esse ac spurios ab impostore aliquo recentioris memoriæ, vel in Arabiæ desertis, vel in Ægypti latebris tebris procul Nicæa conditos, ac consarcinatos. Itaque prohibet natalium obscuritas, atque infelicitas, quominus isti canones in hac testium quarti, quintique sæculi luce consistere vel possint, vel debeant.
units.tr: 3. To this class also belongs the testimony that Turrian a brings forward for the canons from Nicene Canon 56, where it is affirmed that the holy Apostles ordained that a priest should not take up secular cares, nor pursue usury for gain, nor have fellowship with the Jews, nor eat or drink with them. Indeed these things agree with what is read in Turrian's collection in canons six, forty-four, and seventy, so that whoever was the author of the canon foisted on the Nicene Council seems to have had these in view. But since it is established by the perpetual consensus of the whole ancient Church, and by all Greek and Latin copies, both manuscript and printed, that the Nicene Synod issued no more than twenty canons, it appears that those published lately by Turrian himself and by the Jesuit Alfonso Pisano, numbering eighty, and first brought into our world from the Arabic chest of I know not what Patriarch of Alexandria, are bastard and spurious. They were put together and patched up by some impostor of more recent memory, either in the deserts of Arabia or in the hiding places of Egypt, far from Nicaea. Thus the obscurity and unhappiness of their origin prevent these canons from being able, or from being obliged, to stand in the light of witnesses of the fourth and fifth centuries.

units.la: 4. Sed & in hoc apocryphorum testium censu merito collocanda est illa jam olim à Gratiano inauspicata laudata Hieronymi ad Damasum epistola, ex qua hæc pro suis Canonibus recitat Turrianus a; Quod autem beatitudo tua quæsivit, utrum usus decimarum & oblationum sæcularibus provenire possit, novit tua sanctitas omnino non recta licere, protestantibus hoc divinis authoritatibus paternorum Canonum. Hactenus Gratianus. Sed hæc epistola spuria est, & ab Hieronymi ingenio plane aliena; neque ulla earum epistolarum, quæ ab eo ad Damasum scriptæ extant, aut uspiam alibi in omnibus, quæ habemus, Hieronymi operibus hæc verba leguntur; quod & ipsi Gregoriani Gratianei decreti correctores ad hunc ejus locum annotarunt, Pars (inquit) hujus capitis citatur ex B. Hieronymo, in cujus qua extant, scriptis nihil hujusmodi inventum est. Sane eam, quæ circumfertur Hieronymi ad Damasum de oblationibus altaris epistolam, ex qua hæc verba desumpta esse probabile est (tametsi hodie nulla in ea legantur) notham esse, & indignam, quæ tanto viro tribuatur, monuit,& probavit Bellarminus {a}4; idemque de illa judicium est & Mariani Victoris, & Erasmi. Quamquam ne illud quidem liquet, quod audacter de more fingit Turrianus, hunc quiquis fuit, scriptorem per paternos canones Apostolicos significasse. Verisimilius est Episcoporum & Synodorum veterum canones eo nomine intellexisse, quorum authoritatem divinam dixit, quod ea eximia sit, & maximi in rebus hujusmodi ponderis. Nam ne ipse quidem Turrianus suorum Canonum authoritatem divinam, proprie, strictéque sumpto vocabulo esse dixerit, quos Θεοπνεύστους non esse confitetur; neque in divinarum litterarum canone censendos contendit.
units.tr: 4. But also in this census of apocryphal witnesses there is rightly placed that letter of Jerome to Damasus, long ago launched and praised by Gratian, from which Turrian a recites these words for his canons: "As to what your blessedness asked, whether the use of tithes and offerings can pass to secular persons, your holiness knows that it is by no means lawful, the divine authorities of the paternal canons testifying to this." Thus far Gratian. But this letter is spurious and wholly alien to Jerome's genius. None of the letters that he wrote to Damasus that are extant, nor any of these words, is read anywhere else in all the works of Jerome that we have. The Gregorian correctors of Gratian's decree themselves noted this on the passage: "Part of this chapter (they say) is cited from St Jerome, in whose extant writings nothing of the kind has been found." Certainly that letter of Jerome to Damasus about altar offerings that circulates, from which these words were probably taken (although today none of them is read in it), Bellarmine {a} 4 warned and proved to be spurious and unworthy of being ascribed to so great a man. The judgment of Marianus Victor and of Erasmus is the same. Yet it is not clear even that which Turrian boldly and customarily invents, that this writer by paternal canons meant the Apostolic canons. It is more likely that he understood by that name the canons of bishops and of ancient synods, whose authority he called divine because it is outstanding and of the greatest weight in matters of this kind. For not even Turrian himself would say that the authority of his own canons is divine in the proper and strict sense of the word, since he confesses they are not God-breathed [Θεοπνεύστους] and does not contend that they are to be counted in the canon of the divine writings.

units.la: 5. Denique in eandem spuriorum & apocryphorum scriptorum classem relegandus quoque est Dionysius Pseud-Areopagites, cujus quædam ex epistola ad Demophilum describit Turrianus {b}. Quamquam ne illa quidem, quæ illinc citat, quicquam ejus causam juvant. Is enim scriptor ὅρως τῆς ἱεραρχίας, definitiones & constitutiones memorat quidem, & νομοθεσίαν ἱεραρχικὴν, hoc est hierarchicam legum constitutionem; unde merito concludas, Ecclesiam regula aliqua fuisse gubernatam, ejusque res certo ordine, certaque lege administratas; (quod nemo negat.) Editam vero fuisse vel ab Apostolis, vel à Clemente Romano hanc, quam obtrudit Turrianus. 85. vel ut alii malunt, 50. duntaxat canonum farragi-nem, neque hic, neque uspiam alibi dicit fi-ctus ille Dionysius. Sed nihil opus est e-jus authoris verba accuratius expendere, quem multa clarissima argumenta aliquot saeculis vero Dionysio recentiorem esse coarguunt, quemque anno Domini 532. ab haereticis objectum Catholici aper-tissime rejecerunt, atque exploserunt, ut testatur Innocentius Maroniae Episco-pus, epistola ad Thomam presbyterum , in qua illam Catholicorum cum Severia-nis haereticis Constantinopoli habitam collationem narrat.
units.tr: 5. Finally, the pseudo-Dionysius, the so-called Areopagite, must also be relegated to this same class of spurious and apocryphal writings. Turrianus describes some passages from his letter to Demophilus {b}. Yet even those passages he cites from it do nothing to help his cause. This writer does mention definitions and constitutions (ὅρος τῆς ἱεραρχίας), and a hierarchical legislation [νομοθεσίαν ἱεραρχικὴν], that is, a hierarchical constitution of laws. From this one may rightly conclude that the Church was governed by some rule and that its affairs were administered in a fixed order and by a fixed law, which nobody denies. But that this collection, which Turrianus thrusts upon us, of 85 canons, or as others prefer, of only 50, was published either by the Apostles or by Clement of Rome, that fictitious Dionysius nowhere says, neither here nor anywhere else. There is no need, however, to weigh his words more carefully. Many very clear arguments prove that he lived several centuries after the true Dionysius, and the Catholics openly rejected and refuted him when the heretics objected to him in the year of the Lord 532, as Innocent, Bishop of Maronia, testifies in his letter to the presbyter Thomas, in which he narrates that conference of the Catholics with the Severian heretics held at Constantinople.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII.

units.la: Quam stulta atque absurda sit omnis Turriani ex veteribus hac in causa disputatio. Expen-duntur ac refelluntur sigillatim, quae ille ex Origene, & Cypriano, & ex Synodis Nicaena, Antiochena, & Gangrensi attulit; & ostenditur quis verus sit locorum sensus.
units.tr: How foolish and absurd is all of Turrianus' argument from the ancients in this matter. What he brought forward from Origen, Cyprian, and the Synods of Nicaea, Antioch and Gangra is weighed and refuted one by one, and the true sense of the passages is shown.

units.la: IS ergo ex legitimo testium censu rejectis nothis, & falsi nominis authoribus, ad veros, sinceros-que veniamus; quos Turrianus nus nullo, quod quidem aliequi potuerim ordine, credo prout singuli in buccam, vel in mentem veniebant, perturbatissime in hanc caussam induxit. Nos à vetustioribus exorsi omnes profuorum quemque temporum ratione audiemus. Quamquam sane audiri eos vix operæpretium est ; adeo sunt ab hac causa aliena, quæcunque isti loquuntur. Hoc enim inprimis de universis, qui quidem ante Gelasium vixerunt, confirmare possum, neminem esse eorum, qui istius, quam Turrianus probandam suscipit, Apostolicorum canonum farraginis mentionem diserte, liquidoque fecerit.
units.tr: SO, having rejected the spurious and the authors of the false name from the lawful roll of witnesses, let us come to the genuine and sincere ones. Turrianus introduced these into this cause in a most confused manner, with no order (though I could have arranged them in some order), apparently as each one came into his mouth or mind. We shall begin with the most ancient and hear each one in the order of his time. Yet it is hardly worth the effort to hear them at all, so alien to this cause is everything they say. I can affirm this above all about all who lived before Gelasius: there is none of them who clearly and expressly mentioned that hodgepodge of Apostolic canons which Turrianus undertakes to prove.

units.la: Sed siquis veterum vel Apostolos ex certo canone Ecclesiam rexisse, regendamve tradidisse dixerit, siquis Apostolorum decreto, vel regulas nominaverit, siquis eorum aliquid, quæ in Pseud-Apostolicis canonibus continentur, memoraverit, nosster in ista statim involat, & inani rerum specie deceptus, stimulante, judicium que, quod per se alioqui exiguum fuisse videtur, perturbante nimio caussæ studio, ea suis istis Canonibus accipit. Hæc omnino sunt Turriani in hac disputatione artes; hæc μεθοδεία, quæ tam multis authoribus pro peßima, ac complorata caussa, testimonium extorsit. Sed hæc quidem disputandi ratio, quam futilis sit, quam-que que inepta, omnes vident. Quis enim negat, vel Apostolos certa quadam regula Ecclesiam administrasse? vel ex iis, quæ in pseudo-apostolicis canonibus habentur, non pauca jam quidem in Ecclesiæ usu fuisse? Apostolos quidem sapienter, ac summa cum ratione omnia gubernasse & ipsi eorum divini libri clamant, & omnes Christiani confitentur. Planum vero istum, quem Turrianicam hanc canonum 85. syllogen sub quinti sæculi finem, sextique initia consarcinasse putamus, nemo usque adeo bardum, aut stupidum fuisse censet, ut non multa ex iis, quæ suo tempore in Ecclesia observabantur, suæ isti farragini ad fucum faciendum immiscere vel noluerit, vel non potuerit. Itaque non siquid Apostolos in Ecclesia constituisse, aut à veteribus olim servatum fuisse demonstretur, eo probatum quoque fuerit veram esse ac genuinam quam defendit Turrianus, Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen. Sed jam singula testimonia, hæc in genere prefati, audiamus, ac expendamus.
units.tr: But if anyone among the ancients says that the Apostles governed the Church by a fixed canon, or handed down that it should be governed so, if anyone names decrees of the Apostles or rules, or mentions any of the things contained in the pseudo-Apostolic canons, our author immediately pounces on it. Deceived by a empty appearance of things, and goaded and confused by his excessive zeal for the cause, which in itself seems to have been of little weight, he takes such passages as support for his canons. These are altogether Turrianus' tricks in this dispute; this is the method which has extorted testimony from so many authors for a thoroughly bad and desperate cause. But everyone sees how futile and how inept this way of arguing is. For who denies that even the Apostles governed the Church by some fixed rule? Or that many of the things contained in the pseudo-Apostolic canons were already in use in the Church? That the Apostles governed all things wisely and with the greatest reason, both their own divine books proclaim and all Christians confess. But that this compiler of the 85 canons, whom we suppose to have stitched together his Turrianic collection at the end of the fifth century and the beginning of the sixth, was so dull or stupid that he did not wish or could not mix into his patchwork, to make it look genuine, many things observed in the Church in his own time, no one believes. Therefore, even if it were shown that the Apostles established something in the Church, or that it was once kept by the ancients, it would not thereby be proved that the Apostolic canons defended by Turrianus, this collection, are true and genuine. But now let us hear and weigh the individual testimonies, after these general remarks.

units.la: Primum esto Origenis; ex quo Turrianus quædam citat, in quibus ille ait Christianos à muneribus reipublicæ gerendis abstinere, non quod communis vitæ ministeria fugiant, sed quod servent se divinio-ri, ri, ac magis necessario ministerio Ecclesiæ Dei ad salutem hominum. Sed ex eodem refert, fideles lapsos perac-ta legitima pœ-nitentia in Ecclesiæ quidem communio-nem admissos fuisse; non tamen ad sacrum ministerium promotos. Tum canones A-postolorum recitat sextum, sexagesimum primum, & octogesimum primum, qui-bus cavetur, ne Ecclesiæ ministri curas mundi, vel populares administratio-nes suscipiant; item canonem quinquagesi-mum primum, & octogesimum, quibus edicitur, ut lapsi pœnitentes recipiantur, ita tamen, ne ad Episcopatum promoveantur, priusquam documentum vitæ suæ præbeant. Hæc ille; quibus succinens Binius pari inverecundia scribit canonem Apostolorum 51. ab Origene 1. 3. contra Celsum, citatum esse. Ego respondeo ex Origenis dictis recte concludi, triplicem illum morem in Ecclesiæ usu jam fuisse Origenis temporibus, id est tertio Chri-stianismi sæculo jam adulto. Ideo in usu fuisse, quod Turrianica Apostolicorum canonum sylloge, (cujus Origenes non magis, quam regulæ Loyoliticæ meminit) aliquod hujusmodi præcepisset, vel Origenicæ memoriæ Christianis nota esset, nulla est Dialectica, quæ hinc extun-dere possit. Verius est, cum hæc esset an-tiquâ tiqua Ecclesiæ Christianæ consuetudo, ex ea impostorem suos illos à Turriano commemoratos Canones effinxisse, callideque Apostolis suppositisse; ratum sehac antiquitatis objecta specie facilius latere, atque incautis hominibus imponere posse.
units.tr: First let Origen's come. Turrianus cites some passages from him in which he says that Christians abstain from holding civil offices, not because they shun the duties of common life, but because they keep themselves for the more divine and more necessary ministry of the Church for the salvation of men. But from the same passage Origen reports that the fallen faithful, after legitimate repentance, were admitted to communion in the Church, yet were not promoted to the sacred ministry. Then Turrianus cites the sixth, sixty-first and eighty-first canons of the Apostles, by which it is provided that ministers of the Church must not take up worldly cares or civil administrations; likewise the fifty-first and eightieth canons, which order that the fallen who repent be received, yet on condition that they not be promoted to the episcopate until they have given proof of their life. So he says, and Binius, echoing him with equal shamelessness, writes that the Apostolic canon 51 is cited by Origen in book 3 against Celsus. I answer that from Origen's words it is rightly concluded that this threefold custom already existed in the Church in Origen's time, that is, in the third century of Christianity, now grown up. But that it was in use because the Turrianic collection of Apostolic canons (which Origen mentions no more than he mentions the rule of Loyola) had prescribed something of this kind, or because it was known to the Christians of Origen's time, there is no dialectic that can deduce this. It is more likely that, since this was an ancient custom of the Christian Church, that impostor drew his canons, which Turrianus recalls, from it and cunningly attributed them to the Apostles, because under this appearance of antiquity they could more easily lie hidden and deceive unwary people.

units.la: Ejusdem farinæ est, quod Turrianus ex Cypriano, Origenis fere æquali, huc torquendum putavit. Laudat Cornelium Cyprianus, quod Fœlicissimum à se & aliis Africæ episcopis abstentum & condemnatum ipse quoque rejecisset. Item ibidem Pseudo-episcopos narrat foris sibi conventicula constituisse. Ergo (inquit Turrianus) jam tum erat hæc in Ecclesia regula, ne vel ab uno episcopo rejecti ab aliis susciperentur, vel cuiquam liceret seorsim, sive separatim ab Ecclesia collectas facere, quod utrumque est Apostolorum canone 32. & 31. vetitum. Respondeo, utrumque verum esse; sed ex utroque nequaquam sequi, ut vel Cypriano cognita fuerit, vel jam tum extiterit à Gelasio damnata, à Turriano defensa Apostolicorum canonum sylloge. Quasi vero nemo præter fictitios istos Apostolos Ecclesiam id docere potuerit, quod & rectæ rationi, & Scripturis divinis consentaneum est; ut scilicet fraterna inter se concor-
units.tr: Of the same kind is what Turrianus thought he could twist to this purpose from Cyprian, who was almost contemporary with Origen. Cyprian praises Cornelius because he himself also rejected and condemned Felicissimus, who had been excommunicated by him and by other bishops of Africa. Likewise, in the same place, he tells that the pseudo-bishops set up private meetings for themselves outside. Therefore (says Turrianus) this was already the rule in the Church, that those rejected by one bishop should not be received by others, and that no one should be allowed to form a separate assembly apart from the Church, both of which are forbidden by the Apostolic canons 32 and 31. I answer that both are true, but that from neither does it follow that the Apostolic canon collection defended by Turrianus was known to Cyprian, or already existed then, condemned later by Gelasius. As if no one except those fictitious Apostles could teach the Church what agrees with right reason and with the divine Scriptures, namely that all Christ's ministers should unite in brotherly harmony in Church administration,

units.la: concordia in Ecclesiastica administratione omnes Christi Ministri conspirent; neve extra legitimorum Pastorum caulam, quisquam Dominicas oves colligat. Non hoc a tuis Apostolis, Turriane, Cornelius, Cyprianusque didicerant; sed ab ipsis potius tui illi post eos jam dudum mortuos nati Apostolii id hauserunt atque expresserunt.
units.tr: and that no one should gather the Lord's sheep outside the fold of lawful ministers. Cornelius and Cyprian did not learn this from your Apostles, Turrianus; rather, those your Apostolic writers, born long after them and long since dead, drew it from them and copied it.

units.la: Idem est Jesuitæ alusus in iis, quæ ex Synodis quarto sæculo habitis adfert. Patres (inquit) Nicæni statuunt, siquis sei-psum exciderit, ne in clerum admittatur.
units.tr: The same Jesuit's trick is found in what he brings from the synods held in the fourth century. The Fathers of Nicaea (he says) decree that if anyone has castrated himself, he must not be admitted to the clergy.

units.la: Quos vero barbari, aut Domini castravenerunt, si inveniuntur alias digni, tales ad clerum τὸν κανόνα regulam suscipere. Idem autem in Canonum Apostolicorum syllogge decernitur; canonibus 20. 21. & 22. Ergo cognita fuit Nicænis Patribus hæc sylloge; & quam memorant regulam, ea nihil aliud significat, quam ipsos illos Apostolorum canones. Ego vero hoc ex illo sequi nego. Illud quidem hinc haberi fateor, fuisse jam ante Nicenæ Synodi tempora aliquam in Ecclesia regulam; ex qua hæc ita administrarentur; Eam regulam ab ipsis Apostolis ita diserte constitutam fuisse, vel a Clemente litteris mandatam, & in istam, quam Turrianus defendit, syllogen relatam; nego hinc, nego ex ullo veteri quatuor priorum seculorum scriptore, confici, vel colligi posse. Certe ex iis quę deOrigene narratEusebius apparet istud sui ipsius exsecandi facinus jam tum apud Christianos invidiosum fuisse. Refert enim Demetrium Alexandriae Episcopum, id Origeni objectasse, eosque simul, qui illum presbyterum creavissent, criminibus involvere conatum esse. De tribus illis Canonibus Apostolicis nihil dicit; quos siqui tunc hujusmodi extitisent, non est verisimile vel Origenem tam absurdo facinore violaturum, vel Demetrium in tali causa praetermissurum fuisse. Vero proprius videtur ex ea Origenici facti occasione vetitum ab Ecclesiasticis praepositis, nequis tale quid pietatis specie, vel illius viri exemplo, auderet; & siquis auderet, is a sacris submoveretur; eamque deinceps regulam & apud Ecclesias obtinuisse; & a Nicaenis Patribus hoc loco intelligi. Cum enim & a praeceptain divinis litteris humanitate, & sanctimonia & ab ipso communi naturae sensu plurimum abhorreat haec in seipsum saevities; non facile crediderim ullam latam in eos, qui tale quid audent, legem ante editum ab aliquo talis saevitiae exemplum. Nam cur quaeso divinassent Apostoli futuros olim, qui suis ipsi genitalibus manus violentas inferrent? Id autem Apostolicis temporibus quemquam Chri-stianum designasse, nulla tradidit Ecclesiæ historia. Non ergo Apostolorum tempo-ribus, sed secutis sæculis, ex Origenici facti occasione, decreta, constitutaque, & inde ad Nicænos Patres propagata videtur illa regula, quam ipsi hoc loco memorant.
units.tr: But those whom barbarians or their masters have castrated, if they are found otherwise worthy, such persons are to be received into the clergy according to the rule [τὸν κανόνα]. The same is decreed in the Apostolic canon collection, in canons 20, 21 and 22. Therefore this collection was known to the Nicene Fathers, and the rule they mention means nothing other than those very Apostolic canons. I deny that this follows from that. I admit that this much can be held: that even before the time of the Nicene Synod there was some rule in the Church by which these matters were administered. But that this rule was expressly laid down by the Apostles themselves, or committed to writing by Clement and included in that collection which Turrianus defends, I deny; this cannot be inferred or gathered from any ancient writer of the first four centuries. Certainly from what Eusebius relates about Origen it appears that this self-mutilation was already an odious act among Christians. For he reports that Demetrius, Bishop of Alexandria, objected this to Origen, and tried to implicate in the charges those who had made him a presbyter. He says nothing about those three Apostolic canons; if any such had existed then, it is not likely that Origen would have violated them by so absurd a deed, or that Demetrius would have passed them over in such a case. It seems more likely that on the occasion of Origen's deed the Church leaders forbade anyone to dare such a thing under the appearance of piety or by that man's example, and that whoever dared would be removed from the sacred office; that this rule then prevailed in the Churches, and that the Nicene Fathers mean this here. For since such savagery against oneself is wholly abhorrent from the precepts of divine letters, from humanity and holiness, and from the common sense of nature itself, I could hardly believe that any law was enacted against those who dare such a thing before some example of such savagery had been given by someone. For why, I ask, would the Apostles have foreseen that there would one day be people who would lay violent hands on their own genitals? Church history tells us of no Christian who did this in Apostolic times. Therefore that rule which they themselves mention here seems to have been decreed and established not in the Apostolic times but in the following centuries, on the occasion of Origen's deed, and from there handed down to the Nicene Fathers.

units.la: Eadem fere cæterorum ratio est, quæ ex Nicæna Synodo colligit Turrianus. Ait Synodus multa facta esse adversus Ecclesiasticam regulam; verbi gratia, quod homines ex Gentili vita nuper accedentes ad fidem, brevique tempore instructi, mox ad lavacrum spirituale perducerentur, simulque ad Episcopatum, vel ad presbyterium promoverentur. Regulam Ecclesiæ, præter quam ista fierent, Turrianus decernit canonem esse suæ collectionis 8o. quo ista à Synodo commemorata vetantur. Sed hoc non jubendum erat, sed probandum.
units.tr: The reasoning of the others is nearly the same, and Turrian draws it from the Nicene Synod. The Synod says that many things were done contrary to the ecclesiastical rule. For example, men who had recently come from heathen life to the faith, and were instructed for only a short time, were soon brought to the spiritual laver and at once promoted to the episcopate or the presbytery. Turrian lays down that the rule of the Church, apart from which these things were done, is canon 8 of his collection, by which the Synod's examples are forbidden. But this should not be commanded; it should be proved.

units.la: Ego vero multo (ut mihi quidem videtur) probabilius non significari à Patribus Apostolicam regulam ex eo argumentor, quod hanc Ecclesiæ simpliciter vocant. Cur enim Apostolicæ nomen ei regulæ invidissent, quam Apostolicam scivissent? Quamquam & Apostolicam dici eam regulam, quam violatam conqueruntur Patres, nihil sane vetabat, etiamsi nullam tum extitisse Turrianicam syllogen, quod verum est, statuamus. tuamus. Imo ipsi Patres Apostolicam esse diserte probant; ex Apostolicorum dogmatum codice, non Turrianico, sed nostro, Tempore (inquiunt) opus est ei, qui baptizatur, & post baptismum probatione quamplurima. Manifesta est enim Apostolica Scriptura, qua dicit a;Non neophytum, ne in superbiam elatus, in judicium incidat, & in laqueum Diaboli. Cur non potius Turriane tuum illum 8o. canonem, qui disertissimus est,& totidem verbis conceptus, non laudarunt Patres; Nimirum eum illi nondum cognitum habebant.
units.tr: For my part, I argue much more probably (as it seems to me, at least) that the Fathers did not mean the apostolic rule, from the fact that they simply call it of the Church. For why would they have begrudged the name apostolic to a rule which they knew to be apostolic? Yet nothing prevented that rule which the Fathers complain was violated from also being called apostolic, even if we grant that Turrian's collection did not yet exist at that time, which is true. Indeed the Fathers themselves plainly prove that it is apostolic, not from Turrian's code of apostolic doctrines but from ours: Time (they say) is needed for the one who is baptized, and after baptism a great deal of testing. For the apostolic Scripture is plain, which says: "Not a novice, lest being puffed up with pride he fall into judgement and into the snare of the devil." Why, then, did the Fathers not rather praise your canon 8, Turrian, which is most explicit and worded in exactly the same terms? Clearly they did not yet know it.

units.la: Sequitur sextus ejusdem Synodi canon; quo praecipitur, ut antiqua consuetudines vigeant, τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἐτη κρατείτω. Antiquas consuetudines Turrianus contendit canones esse suorum Apostolorum tricesimum quartum & tricesimum quintum. Quo argumento? Quia (inquit) Synodus Constantinopolitana, quae Nicaena hic statuit, repetens jubet secundum canones Episcopum Alexandria, qua in Ægypto sunt gubernare, & Episcopum Orientis qua sunt in Oriente. Sed Turrianus solens delirat. Nicaeni Patres distinctionem dioecesēon, & singulorum in suos metropolitarum jus consuetudinem vocant, quia nimirum tacito hominum usu, atque consensu id totum, quantumcunque, est jus in Ecclesia paula,paulatim obtinuerat; nullo diserto vel Apostolorum, vel Synodorum praecedentium praecepto (quo ipso plane evertuntur duoilli Turrianici Apostolorum canones) Constantinopolitani vero Patres idem illud jus, non jam ex consuetudine duntaxat, sed secundum Canones valere ajunt; quia scilicet ad consuetudinem accesserat Nicaenorum Patrum canon; quo antiquae illae consuetudines confirmatae, publicaque veluti lege sancitae erant. Synodus enim CP. (quod omnes norunt) a. D. 381. hoc est annis 56. post Nicaenam habita est.
units.tr: Next comes the sixth canon of the same Synod, which orders that ancient customs prevail [τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἔθη κρατείτω]. Turrian contends that the ancient customs are the thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth canons of his Apostles. On what ground? Because (he says) the Synod of Constantinople, which repeats what the Nicene Synod decreed here, orders that the bishop of Alexandria govern the regions of Egypt, and the bishop of the East the regions of the East, according to the canons. But Turrian raves as usual. The Nicene Fathers call the division of dioceses, and each metropolitan's right over his own province, a custom, because clearly this whole right, whatever its extent, had gradually obtained in the Church through the silent practice and consent of men, with no explicit precept of the Apostles or of earlier synods behind it (and by this very fact Turrian's two apostolic canons are plainly overturned). But the Fathers of Constantinople say that the same right is valid not merely from custom but according to the canons, because clearly a canon of the Nicene Fathers had been added to the custom, by which those ancient customs were confirmed and sanctioned as by public law. For the Synod of Constantinople (as all know) was held in A.D. 381, that is, fifty-six years after the Nicene.

units.la: Sed affert etiam Turrianus, quod in eodem Nicaenae Synodi sexto canone habetur de electionis decreto κατὰ κανόνα ἐκκλησιαστικὸν, secundum Ecclesiasticam regulam comprobato. Hic & quidem vehementer nos urget, rogans identidem, quae sit illa Ecclesiastica regula, jam ante Nicaenae Synodi tempora in electionibus Episcoporum observari solita? Et quia nos putat nihil habere, quod respondeamus, ait ipse eam haberi in octavo libro Constitutionum capite quarto. Verum nos de canonibus nunc quidem agimus. Constitutiones Apostolorum Turrianicas nullas Nicaenae Synodi temporibus extitisse, unde superiori disputatione probavimus. Neque nos sane ut vel ad eas, vel ad Canones Apostolorum confugiamus, cogunt Turriani acres licet, ac vehementes interrogationes. Satis est ad Nicænorum Patrum sententiam explicandam statuere, jam tum fuisse certum aliquem ac legitimum morem, quo ministrorum electiones rite instituerentur, partim ex Sacræ Scripturæ, partim ex rectæ rationis luce haustum; ab omnibus approbatum & usurpatum; hunc fuisse Ecclesiasticum electionum canonem. An is autem lege aliqua scripta explicatus, litterisque mandatus, an vero communi, publicoque tametsi tacito, omnium usu, ac consensu receptus fuerit, nihil ad Synodi mentem interest; nedum ut à Clemente Turriano in Constitutionibus traditum fuisse necesse sit.
units.tr: But Turrian also brings forward that in the sixth canon of the same Nicene Synod there is a decision about elections, approved according to the ecclesiastical canon [κατὰ κανόνα ἐκκλησιαστικὸν], according to the ecclesiastical rule. Here he presses us hard, asking again and again what that ecclesiastical rule was which was customarily observed in the elections of bishops even before the time of the Nicene Synod. And because he thinks we have nothing to answer, he says that he himself has it in the eighth book of the Constitutions, chapter four. But we are now speaking of canons. We have already proved in the earlier discussion that Turrian's Constitutions of the Apostles did not exist in the times of the Nicene Synod. Nor are we forced, by Turrian's fierce and vehement questions, to take refuge in them or in the Canons of the Apostles. It is enough, in order to explain the mind of the Nicene Fathers, to affirm that even then there was a certain established and lawful custom by which the elections of ministers were properly conducted, drawn partly from Holy Scripture and partly from the light of right reason; approved and practised by all; and that this was the ecclesiastical canon of elections. Whether this law was set out in some written form and committed to writing, or was received by the common and public, though silent, practice and consent of all, makes no difference to the mind of the Synod, much less does it follow that it must have been handed down by Clement Turrian in the Constitutions.

units.la: Atque hic ipse publicus Ecclesiæ illorum temporum usus, apud omnes receptus, canon est, præter quem paulo post queruntur Patres in quibusdam partibus consuetudinem hanc inveniri, ut de civitate ad civitatem transferantur episcopi, presbyterique, ac diaconi. Fateor similia præcipere Turrianicos Apostolos canone 14. Nicænos ab istis Apostolis sua sumpsisse Zonaras homo Græcus, putat; Putat & Græcorum Schismaticorum hac in parte sectator Turrianus. Ego rectius puto, ut planus Turrianicorum Apostolorum parens, sua à Nicænis sumserit; post quos eum vixisse & censeo, & post hoc, si Deus dederit, demonstrabo. Nunc satis est ostendisse, nihil esse in his Nicænorum Patrum verbis, quod Zonarae & Turriani opinioni faveat.
units.tr: And this very public custom of the Church of those times, received by all, is the canon, apart from which the Fathers complain a little later that in some regions this custom is found, that bishops, presbyters and deacons are transferred from city to city. I admit that Turrian's Apostles order similar things in canon 14. Zonaras, a Greek, thinks that the Nicene Fathers took their decrees from those Apostles; and Turrian, a follower of the Greek schismatics in this matter, thinks so too. I think more rightly, as the plain father of the Turrian Apostles, that he took his own material from the Nicene Fathers; and I also think he lived after them, and, God willing, I will demonstrate this later. For now it is enough to have shown that there is nothing in these words of the Nicene Fathers which favours the opinion of Zonaras and Turrian.
