units.la: Ad eundem denique publici Ecclesiae moris, ususque canonem pertinet, quod ajunt iidem Patres a, τὸν καινοτομηγορεύειν τῆς ὑπὸ ἐλέγων ἀποβλήτους ὑπὸ ἑτέρων μὴ προσίεσθαι, canonem vetare, ne ab his abjecti ab aliis recipiantur. Quanquam & hujus moris, absque quo consistere nequit Ecclesiae pax, atque concordia, in vetustiorum etiam Patrum scriptis documentis extabant vestigia; qualia sunt, quae nuper ex B. Cypriano à Turriano allata audivimus; ut nihil necesse sit ad 12. & 32. Turrianicorum Apostolorum canones confugere, qui quae istic praecipiunt huic Nicæno decreto similia, ex Nicæna scilicet & Antiochena Synodis furati sunt, suisque stramineis Apostolis aptarunt.
units.tr: Finally, to the same canon of public custom and usage of the Church belongs what the same Fathers say: the canon forbids that those cast out by some be received by others [μὴ προσίεσθαι]. Although traces of this custom, without which the peace and concord of the Church cannot stand, are found also in the writings of the more ancient Fathers, such as those which we lately heard Turrian quote from Blessed Cyprian. So there is no need to take refuge in canons 12 and 32 of Turrian's Apostles, which order things similar to this Nicene decree; they plainly stole them from the Nicene and Antiochene Synods, and fitted them to their straw-stuffed Apostles.

units.la: Eodem quoque modo intelligenda sunt multa illa, quae Turrianus ex Antrochena Synodo huc convasanda putavit. Ait Synodus quisquis ex clero cum excommunicatis communicat, eum Ecclefia regulam confundere. Eadem Episcopum, qui alterius parœciæ clericum à suo Episcopo depositum receperit, affirmat παρακαλύειν τὰς θεσμὰς τὰς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς, constituta sive jura Ecclesiastica dissolvere. Iubet eadem Synodus a Metropolitam honore præcellere, & nihil amplius prater eum cæteros Episcopos agere, secundum antiquam (inquit b) à Patribus nostris regulam constitutam. Eadem memorat τὸν θεσμὸν τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν, constitutum, sive jus Ecclesiasticum, quo continetur c,oportere non aliter fieri Episcopi cujusque Ecclesiæ electionem, & ordinationem, nisi cum Synodo & judicio Episcoporum provinciæ. Alibi quoque scisicit d, episcopum manere in Ecclesia quam à Deo sortitus est secundum ὅρον decretum, sive terminum prius ea de re editum. Et quod eadem mox ait e, καλῶς ἔχειν recte habere, ut quæ sunt Ecclesiæ, debeant cum omni bona conscientia servari. Turrianus ista accipit, ac si dictum esset, rectè constitutum esse aliquo majorum decreto. Jam quæ Antiocheni Patres ad regulam Ecclesiæ, ad constituta Ecclesiastica, ad regulam antiquam à Patribus constitutam, ad decretum prius ea de re editum, referunt, ea inquam decreta, sanciteque in iis Apostolorum canonibus reperiuntur, quos exhibent Græci, quos-que que defendit Turrianus; ut deprehendet quisquis ista comparaverit cum canonibus 9. 15. 17. 34. 74. 14. 41. Græcanicæ Turrianicæque collectionis. Ergo liquere putat Turrianus, suam hanc collectionem jam tum fuisse Ecclesiæ cognitam; imo regulam ipsam Ecclesiæ fuisse. Ego respondeo, ut supra, ex his tantum legitime concludi posse, ea, quæ sex istis à Turriano citatis Antiochenis canonibus continentur, jam ante illam Synodum in usu Ecclesiastico fuisse, à superioris memoriæ sive synodis, sive Episcopis constituta. Non fieri, ut ista Turrianica velut Apostolicorum canonum collectio tunc extiterit; quæ si vel Antiochenis, vel aliis ejusdem sæculi Patribus cognita fuisset, causa dici non poterat, cur non interdum eam, ubi occasio incidebat, vel Apostolorum, vel certe Clementis nomine, vel sub numeris, quibus ea distinguitur, diserte laudaverint; quod neque hi, neque alii istorum temporum fecisse uspiam deprehenduntur. Sed urget nos more suo homo acutissimus, Dicant nobis (inquit) qui hic Canones Apostolorum citari negant, cujus Synodi antegresse, aut quorum Patrum canones antiqui hic vocentur, aut vocari possint? Si nullos alios reperire possunt, annon convincuntur citari hic Canones Apostolorum? Mihi vero, ut semel ostendam puerilis paralogifmi, in quo iste tantopere fe jactat, vanitatem, ipse nunc vicissim conveniendus quoque est, & interrogandus Turrianus. Synodi Nicænæ Canone xiii. hæc sunt verba; De his qui ad exitum veniunt, ὁ παλαιὸς καὶ κανονικὸς νόμος, lex antiqua, regularisque sive canonica servabitur, ita ut si quis egreditur e corpore, ultimo & necessario viatico minime privetur. Hæc Nicæni Patres. Nunc te, Turriane, appello, Dic nobis, sodes, quo loco antiqua illa, regularisque lex in Apostolicis tuis Canonibus habeatur? Recita eam, quæso, ex tuo codice. Numerum ede, sub quo disposita est. At non facies; nisi Apostolicum codicem nobis ex alicujus Arabiæ angulis hoc tuo, nostroque auctiorem ac locupletiorem promas. In hoc enim certe, quem tu Latinis repudiatis à Græcis magistris accepisti, 85. canonum codice, nulla plane extat illa Nicænis memorata vetus, ac canonica Ecclesiæ lex. Sed neque ex omni hac quę ad nos pervenit, veterum monimentorum copia, ullum vel Concilium, vel Patrum proferre potes, à quo hæc lex ante Nicænam Synodum lata fuerit. Ergo tibi, velis nolis, confitendum est, aliquam etiam legem veterem, & canonicam, Nicænorum tempore Patrum fuisse, quæ tamen men neque in tuo Apostolico codice, neque in ullo alio vetustiori Nicæna Synodo monumento monstrari possit. Adhæc eadem Nicæna Synodus negat vel regulam vel consuetudinem tradidisse, ut quod in quibusdam locis fiebat, presbyteris gratiam sacra communionis diaconi porrigerent. Ergo inquam, etiam ante Nicænam Synodum extabat regula, obtinebat consuetudo, ne diaconi id facerent. Hic rursus Turrianum convenio; Eam regulam nobis ille vel in suo Apostolico codice, vel apud aliquam Synodum Nicæna vetustiorem legat; vel si nullam invenit, illud certe confiteatur, quod nos volumus, fuisse etiam ante illa tempora, quasdam in Ecclesia regulas, ac consuetudines, quæ neque in suo codice, neque in aliis, quæ extant, Nicæna Synodo anterioribus monumentis leguntur. Jam Ancyrani Patres a τὸν προ-τέρου ὅρον, antiquam, interprete Dionysio, definitionem, sive regulam prohibuisse ajunt, ne mulieres, quæ fornicatæ fœtus in utero perimerent, ante vitæ exitum communionem acciperent. Et Neocæsariensis Synodus affirmat b. septem esse debere diaconos in unaquaque Ecclesia κατὰ τὸν καινὸν, juxta regulam. Ostendat nobis Turrianus vel in Apostolico suo codice, vel in aliquo duobus iis Synodis vetustiori-
units.tr: In the same way must be understood those many things which Turrian thought could be dragged here from the Synod of Antioch. The Synod says whoever of the clergy communicates with the excommunicated, he confounds the rule of the Church. The same Synod affirms that a bishop who receives a clergyman of another parish deposed by his own bishop [παρακαλύειν τὰς θεσμὰς τὰς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς] dissolves the ecclesiastical constitutions or laws. The same Synod orders that the metropolitan excel in honour, and do nothing beyond the other bishops, according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers. It mentions the same ecclesiastical constitution [τὸν θεσμὸν τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν], or ecclesiastical law, by which it is laid down that the election and ordination of each church's bishop ought not to be done otherwise than with the synod and judgement of the bishops of the province. Elsewhere too it decrees that a bishop should remain in the church which he has obtained from God according to the decree [ὅρον], or the term previously published on that matter. And what the same Synod says soon after, that it is right [καλῶς ἔχειν] that what belongs to the Church should be kept with all good conscience. Turrian takes these words as if it had been said that something was rightly established by a decree of our forebears. Now the decrees to which the Antiochene Fathers refer as the rule of the Church, the ecclesiastical constitutions, the ancient rule established by the Fathers, and the decree previously published on that matter, are, I say, found in those apostolic canons which the Greeks put forward and which Turrian defends; as anyone will discover who compares them with canons 9, 15, 17, 34, 74, 14 and 41 of the Greek and Turrian collection. So Turrian thinks it is clear that his collection was already known to the Church at that time; indeed that it was itself the rule of the Church. I reply, as above, that from these things it can be legitimately concluded only that what is contained in the six Antiochene canons cited by Turrian was already in ecclesiastical use before that Synod, established by earlier memorable synods or bishops. It does not follow that Turrian's collection, as a collection of apostolic canons, then existed. If it had been known to the Antiochene or other Fathers of the same century, there was no reason why they did not sometimes cite it explicitly where the occasion arose, either under the name of the Apostles, or certainly of Clement, or under the numbers by which it is distinguished; and this is not found to have been done anywhere by them or by others of those times. But that most sharp-witted man, in his usual way, presses us: Let them tell us (he says) those who deny that the canons of the Apostles are cited here, what earlier synod, or what ancient canons of which Fathers, are or can be called here? If they cannot find any others, are they not convicted of citing here the canons of the Apostles? But to show once and for all the childishness of this paralogism, in which he boasts so greatly, it is Turrian himself who now must in turn be confronted and questioned. The words of canon 13 of the Nicene Synod are these: As for those who are at the point of death, the ancient and canonical law [ὁ παλαιὸς καὶ κανονικὸς νόμος] , the old and regular law, shall be observed, so that if anyone is departing from the body, he is not to be deprived of the last and necessary viaticum. So say the Nicene Fathers. Now, Turrian, I ask you: please tell us, in which place of your Apostolic canons is that ancient and regular law found? Recite it, I beg you, from your own code. Give the number under which it is arranged. But you will not do so, unless you bring forth for us an Apostolic code, from some corner of Arabia, larger and richer than yours and ours. For certainly in that code of eighty-five canons which you received from Greek masters, rejecting the Latin ones, there is no trace at all of that ancient and canonical law of the Church mentioned by the Nicene Fathers. Nor, out of all this store of ancient monuments which has come down to us, can you produce any council or any Fathers by whom this law was enacted before the Nicene Synod. So you must, whether you like it or not, confess that there was also some ancient and canonical law in the time of the Nicene Fathers, which nevertheless cannot be shown either in your Apostolic code or in any other monument older than the Nicene Synod. Moreover the same Nicene Synod denies that any rule or custom had been handed down that deacons should give the Eucharist to presbyters, which in certain places was done. Therefore, I say, even before the Nicene Synod there existed a rule, and a custom prevailed, that deacons should not do this. Here again I challenge Turrian: let him read out that rule to us either from his Apostolic code or from some synod older than Nicaea; or, if he finds none, let him at least confess what we maintain, that even before those times there were certain rules and customs in the Church, which are read neither in his code nor in other earlier monuments extant before the Nicene Synod. Now the Fathers of Ancyra say that they forbade, by the former decree [τὸν προτέρου ὅρον], that is, the ancient definition or rule (in Dionysius's translation), that women who had committed fornication and destroyed the foetus in the womb should receive communion before the end of their life. And the Synod of Neocaesarea affirms that there ought to be seven deacons in every church, according to the rule [κατὰ τὸν καινὸν]. Let Turrian show us either in his Apostolic code or in some monument of one of those two synods older than these, both of these rules. But he will find neither anywhere. Therefore it must necessarily be confessed that even before the times of those two synods, that is before A.D. 314, there existed in the Church some rules, of which no mention is found in those monuments of their times that survive. And…

units.la: ri moñ monumento, utramque hanc regulam. Atqui neutram uspiam reperiet. Ergo necessario confitendum, etiam ante utriusque Synodi tempora, id est ante a.D. 314. extitisse aliquas in Ecclesia regulas, quarum nulla invenitur in iis, quæ eorum temporum supersunt, monumentis mentio. Atque ex his jam ut opinor, omnes vident, quam frustra nos Turrianus suis interrogationibus urgeat. Iubet nos edere vel Concilia, vel Patres, quorum eæ regulę fuerint, quæ vel à Nicænis, vel ab Antiochenis Patribus memorantur, & antiquæ interdum appellantur. Confitemur, nulla nunc extare anteriora istis Synodis monumenta, in quibus hæ regulæ appareant. Ille concludit, eas ergo ex suo Apostolicorum Canonum codice fuisse à Synodis citatas. Negamus eum bene ac legitime concludere; cum ex iis quæ nuper diximus, appareat & à Nicænis, & ab Ancyranis, & à Neocæsariensibus Patribus leges, ac regulas antiquas commemorari, quę cum in nullo vetustiorum temporum monumento nunc cernantur, non tamen à Patribus ex codice Apostolicorum canonum citatæ sunt, vel citari potuerunt, in quo scilicet nullæ sunt. Res vero clara est & expedita; quamquē ipse Turrianus, nisi eum caussæ studium excæcasset, casset, facile videre potuit. Non omnia quæ in usu fuerunt antiquę illius Ecclefię, Apostoli nominatim, diserteque vel in aliquo codice, vel etiam una voce tradiderant. Multa ipsa rerum, temporumque, & causarum emergentium ratio suggessit, & persuasit, longo post usu confirmata; Non pauca invexit, vel Synodorum, vel etiam singulorum Episcoporum sententia, atque authoritas, quæ ex una vel provincia, vel parœcia, in qua primum orta erant, in vicinas postea, inde in alias, aliasque latius sese paulatim effuderunt; quod eorum institutio rationi consentanea videretur. Nam & iis quæ Nicænam Synodum antecesserunt temporibus multas apud Christianos habitas fuisse locales Synodos, multa à Synodis, multa à singulis Episcopis de disciplina, ac vitibus Ecclesiæ decreta, ac constituta fuisse, nemo adeo stultus est, vel rerum antiquarum impe-ritus, qui nesciat. Extat adhuc multarum hujusmodi Synodorum clara memoria; ut Orientalium, & Asiaticarum de Pafchatis controversia, Africanarum & Romanarum de hæreticorum baptismo, Antiochenæ contra Paulum Samofatenum. Nonnullarum etiam canones extant, ut Eliberitanæ in Hispania, ut Ancyranæ in Galatia, quas constat ante Nicænam habitas bitas esse : idemque de Laodicena (sed falso, ac temere) sibi persuadent Baronius, & Binius. Jam & Episcoporum quorundam itidem quoque supersunt canones, ac decreta, ut Gregorii Thaumaturgi (si tamen vera sunt, quæ ejus nomine circumferuntur) ut Dionysii, ut Petri, utriusque Alexandrini; qui omnes longe ante Nicænam Synodum vixerunt. Zephyrini quidem Romani Episcopi, quin canon fuerit de admittendis ad pœnitentiam fornicatoribus, nemo dubitat; tametsi ipse canon interciderit. Cætera de hoc genere mitto. Res enim apud omnes in confesso est. Quas ergo nobis leges, regulas, Definitiones, constitutiones Patrum, vel Ecclesiæ memorat Nicæna, & Antiochena, & siqua alia Synodus, eæ erant, quæ tum in Ecclesiæ regimine obtinebant, vel tacito (ut dixi) omnium consensu receptæ, quales eas præsertim fuisse credibile est, quas ⟨Syriac⟩ consuetudines vocant; vel quæ alicujus sive Synodi, sive etiam Episcopi, decreto præceptæ, ac sancitæ, vel in una provincia, vel in pluribus, vel etiam in omnibus observabantur. Quod si extarent omnia veterum ante Nicænam Synodum vel Conciliorum, vel Episcoporum decreta, ac constituta, facilius nobis effet singularum istarum regula- rum origines, authoresque demonstrare. Nunc cum veterum istorum monumen- torum pars longe maxima, partim tem- porum, partim etiam hominum injuria a- bolita interciderit, plane inique nobiscum agit Turrianus, dum hanc nobis legem dicit, atque statuit, ut nisi Synodum, aut Episcopum nominatim edamus, cu- jus authoritate decretæ, constitutæque fuerunt istæ à Nicænis & Antiochenis commemoratæ regulæ, eas cogamur confiteri è suo illo Apostolicorum scili- cet canonum codice fuisse citatas. Facile enim, ut quivis videt, fieri potest, ut his idem, quod illis aliis, quas ex Ni- cæno, Ancyranoque & Neocæsarienfi, Conciliis attulimus, acciderit; nimirum ut ea perierint vel Synodorum, vel Pa- trum acta, atque codices, ex quibus à veteribus citabantur; ut jam luce meri- diana clarius fit, nullam Turrianicas ero- tefes vim habere ad id, quod nos ne- gamus, probandum, scilicet fuisse jam tum in Ecclesia hunc, qui nunc obtru- ditur, Canonum Apostolicorum co- dicem.
units.tr: ...ri, with no monument surviving, both of these rules. Yet Turrianus will find neither anywhere. So we must necessarily confess that, even before the times of both those Synods, that is before A.D. 314, there were some rules in the Church, and no mention of them is found in the records of those times that survive. And from this, as I think, everyone now sees how vainly Turrianus presses us with his questions. He bids us produce either Councils or Fathers under whose authority those rules were issued, which are mentioned by the Nicene or the Antiochene Fathers and are sometimes called ancient. We admit that no records earlier than those Synods survive in which these rules appear. He concludes that they must therefore have been cited by the Synods from his codex of the Apostolic Canons. We deny that he concludes this well and rightly. For from what we have just said, it appears that the Nicene, Ancyrene and Neocaesarean Fathers mention laws and ancient rules, which, although they are not now found in any monument of earlier times, were nonetheless not cited by the Fathers from a codex of the Apostolic Canons, or could not have been, since such a codex contains none of them. The matter is in fact clear and simple, though Turrianus himself could easily have seen it had his zeal for his cause not blinded him. The Apostles did not, by name and in plain words, hand down everything that was in use in that ancient Church, either in some codex or even by a single pronouncement. Many things were suggested and commended by the very nature of things, times, and emerging circumstances, and were confirmed by long use. Not a few were introduced by the opinion and authority of Synods or even of individual bishops, which spread gradually from the one province or parish where they first arose into neighbouring regions, then into others, and wider still, because their institution seemed reasonable. For no one is so foolish, or so ignorant of ancient history, as not to know that in the times before the Nicene Synod there were many local Synods among Christians, and that many decrees and constitutions about the discipline and manners of the Church were made by Synods and by individual bishops. There is still a clear record of many such Synods, such as the controversy about Easter among the Eastern and Asian churches, the African and Roman controversy about the baptism of heretics, and the Antiochene Synod against Paul of Samosata. Canons of some of them survive, such as those of Elvira in Spain and of Ancyra in Galatia, which are known to have been held before the Nicene Synod; Baronius and Binius persuade themselves that the same is true of Laodicea, though wrongly and rashly. Moreover, there also survive canons and decrees of certain bishops, such as those of Gregory Thaumaturgus (if indeed the things circulated under his name are genuine), of Dionysius, of Peter, and of the two Alexandrians, all of whom lived long before the Nicene Synod. That Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, issued a canon about admitting fornicators to repentance, no one doubts, although that canon has perished. I pass over other things of this kind, for the matter is granted by all. Therefore, the laws, rules, definitions and constitutions of the Fathers or the Church that the Nicene and Antiochene and any other Synod mention were those which then held sway in the government of the Church, either received by the tacit consent of all (as I said), which kind it is especially credible were those which they call customs, or ordained and sanctioned by the decree of some Synod or even of a bishop, and observed either in one province, or in several, or even in all. If all the decrees and constitutions of Councils or bishops before the Nicene Synod survived, it would be easier for us to show the origins and authors of each of these rules. But now, since by far the greatest part of these ancient monuments has perished, abolished partly by the injury of time and partly by the injury of men, Turrianus treats us most unjustly when he lays down this rule for us, that unless we name the Synod or bishop by whose authority those rules mentioned by the Nicene and Antiochene Fathers were decreed and established, we must be forced to confess that they were cited from his codex of the Apostolic Canons. For, as anyone can see, it can easily happen that these rules met the same fate as the others we have brought forward from the Nicene, Ancyrene and Neocaesarean Councils, namely that the acts of the Synods or Fathers and the codices from which the ancients cited them have perished. As is clearer than noonday light, Turrianus's questions have no force to prove what we deny, namely that this codex of Apostolic Canons, which is now thrust upon us, already existed in the Church at that time.

units.la: Atque idem quoque dictum velim ad ea, quæ Turrianus plane ejusdem generis ex Synodo Gangrenfi laudat a, τὰς ἐκκλησιαςς
units.tr: And I would wish the same to be said of those things which Turrianus, in quite the same way, quotes from the Synod of Gangra, [τὰς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς]

units.la: a Turr. c. 14. p. 42. versa. {ecclesiasticas} ἐκκλησιαστικὰς κανόνας, Ecclesiasticas regu-las, commendante sanctas scripturas, a Canonibus & Apostolicas traditiones. Fuisse jam ante Gangrensem Synodum suas Ecclesiae regulas, suas Scripturas, Apostolicasque traditiones, apud omnes in confesso est. Quaeritur, num eae Ecclesiae regulae ab Apostolis traditae, à Clemente scriptae & in codicem relatae essent, hunc ipsum pro quo nunc pugnat Turrianus. Ea vero de re ne ἀγῷ quidem dicunt Patres Gangrenses.
units.tr: a Turr. c. 14. p. 42. turned: the ecclesiastical rules [ἐκκλησιαστικὰς κανόνας], commending the holy Scriptures and the Canons and Apostolic traditions. That before the Synod of Gangra there were already their own Church rules, their own Scriptures and Apostolic traditions, is granted by all. The question is whether those Church rules, handed down by the Apostles, written down by Clement and brought together into a codex, were that very codex for which Turrianus now contends. On this matter the Fathers of Gangra do not even give a hint.

units.la: CAPUT IX,
units.tr: CHAPTER IX

units.la: Diluuntur, quae Turrianus ex Africanis Synodis, item ex Athanasio, Basilio, & Epiphanio pro suis Canonibus stulte & inverecunde obtrudit.
units.tr: Refuted: what Turrianus, from the African synods, and likewise from Athanasius, Basil and Epiphanius, foolishly and shamelessly thrusts forward in support of his canons.

units.la: ED & Africanarum Synodorum eadem mens est, dum disciplinam Ecclesiasticam ordinem & a Patribus & a majoribus servatum , formam antiquam statuta ex antiquorum sententia, memorant, ac commendant, observariaque praecipiunt. His enim nominibus, quae apud suam Ecclesiam in usu erant, vel à vetustis Synodis constituta, vel à majoribus nuda, & simplici traditione accepta, pta, significant. Hæc ipsa in Apostolicorum canonum eo, qui nunc circumfertur, codice digesta fuisse, & ex eo citata, Turriani somnium est, cujus neque vota, neque vestigium in Africanorum Patrum Synodis cernitur. Fateor, unum extare, & à Turriano objici locum, cujus alia ratio est, quo Afri sancientes Episcoporum, presbyterorum, & diaconorum ab omni mulierum, etiam conjugum, usu continentiam, ajunt b, id Apostolos docuisse, & ipsam servavisse antiquitatem. Appa-ret enim istos putasse, non majores, vel Episcoporum synodos duntaxat, sed ipsos etiam Christi Apostolos hanc sacrorum hominum continentiam præcepisse. Nimirum sibi persuaserant, vel extare in divinis novi fœderis libris antiqua hujus legis documenta, eoque fortasse numero habebant illum Pauli locum c, ut quo tradit, Episcopum inter cæteras dotes continentem esse decere; vel Apostolos ἐγκράτειαν, viva voce, extra Scripturas hoc præceptum suis discipulis dedisse. Non jam disputo, jure-ne ita senserint (alio pertinet ista disputatio) certe ita eos sensisse fateri videtur hæc ipsorum oratio. Nam quod vult eos Turrianus dad quintum suæ farraginis canonem respexisse, id ab omni veri specie alienum, quin & pe-ne ridine ridiculum est. Canon sic habet, Episcopus, vel presbyter, vel Diaconus uxorem suam ne ejiciat religionis praetextu. Obsecro tuam fidem, nonne ludibrium debebit siquis isto canone doceri, ac praecipi contenderit, ut Episcopus, & presbyter, & diaconus ab uxorum usu abstineant? Atqui plane contrais videtur vetare, atque interdicere, ne eas a sua consuetudine semoveant. Sed esto; ne jubeat canon homines sacros uxoribus suis conjugalis thori fidem ac consortium servare; Illud quidem certum, planumque est, non interdicere iis uxorum usum. Quid enim stultius dici potest, aut infantius, quam ei, quem omni uxoris usu arcere, atque semovere vis, edicere, gravibusq; verbis interminari, ne ullius rei obtentu uxore ejiciat? Frustra rogat Turrianus, cur hoc magis sacris hominibus vetetur, quam laicis. Nam & laicis eandem esse latam legem, quis dubitet: quod autem clerici (ut vocant) de hoc in uxores officio proprie moneantur, ratio in promptu est, & ea quidem a Canone expressa. His nimirum religionis & rerum sacrarum ministerium speciem aliquam praebet, quam suo ab uxoribus secessui obtendant? Laicis vero non suppetit idem color. Innocentius certa, Afrorum istorum aequalis, hunc Turrianicum canonem, vel ApostoApostolicum nesciebat, vel episcoporum & presbyterorum ab uxoribus continentiam jubere non putabat; qui hanc causam agens divinarum litterarum disciplinam, hoc est Levitici quædam loca, Pauli item ex epistolis quædam testimonia, ac in primis Siricii antecessoris sui monita ad eam confirmandam citati hujus Turrianici canonis non meminit. Quin & eos clericos, ad quos Siricii epistola non pervenerat, venia dignos pronunciat; quam nulli meriti essent, si Apostolicus jam tum extitisset in universali Ecclesia de sacerdotum continentia canon.
units.tr: The mind of the African synods is the same too, when they speak of and commend the ecclesiastical discipline and order observed by the Fathers and the elders, the ancient form, statutes drawn from the opinion of the ancients, and enjoin that they be kept. For by these names, which were in use in their own church, they mean either what had been established by early synods, or what was received from their elders as bare and simple tradition. That these things were arranged in the code of the Apostolic canons, now circulating, and were cited from it, is a dream of Turrianus, for neither the wish nor any trace of it is seen in the synods of the African Fathers. I admit that there is one passage, which Turrianus objects, and its case is different: where the Africans, decreeing that bishops, presbyters and deacons must abstain from all use of women, even of their wives, say that this the Apostles taught, and that antiquity itself observed it. For it is clear that they thought not only the elders or the synods of bishops, but the Apostles of Christ themselves, had prescribed this continence of holy men. Doubtless they were persuaded either that ancient documents of this law were to be found in the divine books of the New Covenant, and so they counted in that number the words of Paul, where he says that a bishop ought to be continent among his other gifts; or that the Apostles had given this precept to their disciples by word of mouth, outside Scripture, under the name of self-control. I do not now dispute whether they judged rightly (that question belongs elsewhere); certainly their own words seem to confess that this is what they thought. For that Turrianus claims they had in view the fifth canon of his medley is far from any appearance of truth, and is almost laughable. The canon reads: A bishop, or presbyter, or deacon shall not cast out his wife under the pretext of religion. I beg your good faith: would it not be a mockery if anyone insisted that this canon teaches and prescribes that bishop, presbyter and deacon abstain from the use of their wives? Yet it seems plainly to forbid and prohibit that they remove them from their company. But grant it: suppose the canon does not command holy men to keep the faith and fellowship of the marriage bed with their wives. This at least is certain and plain, that it does not forbid them the use of their wives. For what can be said more foolish or more childish than to order, with heavy words and threats, a man whom you wish to keep away and remove from all use of his wife, that he shall not cast out his wife on any pretext? Turrianus vainly asks why this is forbidden to sacred men more than to laymen. For that the same law was passed for laymen, who would doubt it? But that clergy (as they are called) are admonished specifically about this duty toward their wives, the reason is at hand, and the canon itself expresses it: for to them the ministry of religion and sacred things offers a certain pretext, under which they may withdraw from their wives. Laymen, however, have no such colour. Innocent, a certain contemporary of these Africans, either did not know this Turrianic canon, or Apostolic one, or did not think that it ordered bishops and presbyters to be continent from their wives; for, pleading this cause, he cites the discipline of the divine letters, that is, certain places of Leviticus, likewise certain testimonies from the epistles of Paul, and above all the admonitions of his predecessor Siricius for confirming it, and does not mention this canon of Turrianus. Indeed he pronounces worthy of pardon those clergy to whom Siricius's letter had not come; they would be worthy of no pardon if an Apostolic canon on the continence of priests had already existed in the universal Church.

units.la: Atque hæc de quarti sæculi Synodis. Ex Patribus eorundem temporum non argumentatur felicius Turrianus. Athanasium inprimis laudat quod Georgius Cappadox jussu Comitis per vim in Alexandrinam Ecclesiam episcopus immissus esset, id contra priscos canones Ecclesiasticos factum fuisse affirmantem, eosque canones non nunc datos Ecclesiis scribentem, quin potius pulcre ac firme a Patribus nostris traditos. Vides, quos canones dicat; a Patribus scilicet, hoc est ab Episcopis, vel Synodis constitutos, non ab Apostolis, quod vult Turrianus. Nam a Domini quidem discipulis, non hos canones, sed fidem ait in nos derivatam esse. Jam vero non de fide, sed de canonibus quaeritur.
units.tr: So much for the synods of the fourth century. Turrianus argues no more successfully from the Fathers of the same times. He praises Athanasius above all, because George the Cappadocian was thrust by force into the Alexandrian church as bishop by order of the Count, Athanasius affirming that this was done against the ancient ecclesiastical canons, and writing that those canons were not given to the churches just now, but rather were handed down beautifully and firmly by our Fathers. You see which canons he means: those, namely, established by the Fathers, that is, by bishops or synods, not by the Apostles, as Turrianus wishes. For he says that the faith, not these canons, was derived to us from the disciples of the Lord. Now, however, the question is not about faith but about canons.

units.la: aBasilii eadem est ratio, qui antiquum canonem esse ait b,ut lapsi ex gradu,ex ministerio quidem sacro ejiciantur; communione vero nequaquam priventur. Concedo hunc canonem antiquum fuisse. A Clemente scriptum, & in Turrianicum codicem relatum, hinc ulla machina confici posse nego. Imo de canone Turrianicae sylloges 24. (Dionysio 25.) quo haec refert Turrianus, non cogitasse Basilium manifestum est. Sic enim ille; Arbitror secutos esse illos primos legem illam, Non vindicabis bis id in ipsum: quae omnino frigide, ac inepte diceret, si de canonis Turrianici authoribus diceret. Hi enim suo illi canoni diserte ac nominatim hanc rationem addunt, Dicit enim Scriptura, Non vindicabis bis in ipsum. Magnam Turriani inverecundiam fuisse necesse est, qui illa Basilii ad suos canones torquere ausus est. Ejusdem est amentiae, quod idem cex suae syllogescanone 49. Basilium hausisse vult illam, quam memorat, de trina in baptismo mersione traditionem. Nihil hujusmodi Basilius; Contra de iis, quas isto loco recensetDe traditionibus quaerit d, τίς τῆς ἀγίων ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν καταλέλοιπεν; Quis Sanctorum scripto nobis eas reliquit? Stulte pro-
units.tr: Basil's reasoning is the same, who says that the following is an ancient canon: that the lapsed, who fall from their rank, are expelled from sacred ministry, but are by no means deprived of communion. I grant that this canon was ancient. That from it some engine can be built, showing that it was written by Clement and put into the Turrianic code, I deny. Indeed it is clear that Basil did not think of the twenty-fourth canon of the Turrianic collection (twenty-fifth in Dionysius), to which Turrianus refers this. For he says: I think those first men followed that law, and I shall not claim the same thing against him. That would be a very cold and foolish thing to say if he were speaking of the authors of the Turrianic canon. For those men expressly and by name add to their canon this reason: For Scripture says, You shall not muzzle the ox. It must be great shamelessness in Turrianus to dare to twist Basil's words to suit his canons. Of the same madness is his claim that the same man drew, from canon forty-nine of his collection, the tradition he mentions about the threefold immersion in baptism. Basil says nothing of the kind; on the contrary, concerning those traditions which he recounts in that place, he asks d, τίς τῆς ἀγίων ἐγγράφως ἡμῖν καταλέλοιπεν; Who of the saints has left them to us in writing? Foolishly, and (as anyone can see) impudently, would he have said this if Clement, a most holy man and contemporary of the Apostles, had committed them to writing and put them into a public and authentic code.

units.la: d Bas. de Sp. f. c. 27. te profecto (ut quivis videt) & impudenter, si eas Clemens vir sanctissimus, & Apostolorum aequalis litteris mandatas in publicum, & authenticum codicem retulerat. Jam quod Turrianus addit, suae fargraginis Canones alibi a Basilio in primo suo de haereticorum, & schismaticorum canone, item in canone. 12. de digamis, citari, id quam falso, ac inverecunde dictum sit, vel inspectus Basilii codex docet; in quo neque Apostolorum, neque Clementis, neque ullius omnino sylloges ulla vel tenuissima occurrit mentio. Tantum canones nominantur, qui scilicet in Ecclesiae illius usu erant. Quod vero quae istic decernit Basilius ex Ecclesiae suae instituto in Turrianicae farraginis canonibus 40. 50. & 17. propemodum eadem praecipiuntur; hoc inquam, non magis probat Ecclesiam sua a Turrianico legislatore accepisse, quam hunc sua ab illa esse furatum; quod nos verum esse defendimus.
units.tr: d Bas. de Sp. f. c. 27. As for what Turrianus adds, that the canons of his medley are cited elsewhere by Basil, in his first canon on heretics and schismatics, and likewise in canon 12 on digamists, how falsely and shamelessly this is said, even a glance at Basil's text shows; in it no mention, not even the slightest, occurs of the Apostles, of Clement, or of any collection at all. Only canons are named, which of course were in use in that church. And that the things Basil decrees there, from the custom of his own church, are almost the same as those enjoined in the canons 40, 50 and 17 of Turrianus's medley, this, I say, proves no more that his church received them from the Turrianic lawgiver than that he stole them from it; which we maintain is the truth.

units.la: Denique quod postremo loco adfert Turrianus Epiphanii testimonium, id pluribus persequi aut explicare nihil necesse est; quod de eo satis multa in superiori disputatione, ad quam pertinet, dixerimus. Est enim de Constitutionibus, non autem de Canonibus Apostolorum. Constitutiones porro Apostolorum Epiphanianas a nostris, id est Turrianicis, alias fuisse, & rebus ipsis, & adversariorum eruditissimo- tum testimonio, demonstravimus. Quod veroin suis illis Epiphanius ait, πᾶσαν κα- νονικὴν τάξιν, omnem canonicum ordinem contineri, id significat, non, quod velle videtur Turrianus, 85. canonum syllogen in ultima operis parte haberi, sed, ut li- quet, eum ipsum ordinem, quo canonice tunc administrabatur Ecclesia, in iis libris traditum, atque expressum fuisse. Hæc o- mnino sunt, quæ ex quatuor prioribus Christianismi sæculis attulit Turrianus; ex quibus jam constare arbitror, nullum toto illo tempore scriptorem occurrere, qui testetur, quod iste defendit, fuisse vel ab Apostolis conditam, vel à Clemente Ro- mano scriptam eam canonum 85. farragi- nem, quam ipse à recentioribus Græcis acceptam nobis obtrudit.
units.tr: Finally, as to the testimony of Epiphanius which Turrianus brings forward last, there is no need to pursue or explain it at length, since we have said much about it in the earlier discussion to which it belongs. For it concerns the Constitutions, not the Canons of the Apostles. We have shown, both from the facts themselves and from the testimony of the most learned of our opponents, that the Apostolic Constitutions of Epiphanius were other than our Turrianic ones. And what Epiphanius says in those books, that πᾶσαν κανονικὴν τάξιν, the whole canonical order, is contained in them, means, as is plain, not, as Turrianus seems to wish, that a collection of eighty-five canons is held in the last part of the work, but that the very order by which the Church was then canonically governed was set out and expressed in those books. These are all the things Turrianus has brought from the first four centuries of Christianity; from them I think it is now established that in all that time no writer is found who bears witness that what he defends was either founded by the Apostles or written by Clement of Rome, that medley of eighty-five canons which he himself, having received it from recent Greeks, thrusts upon us.

units.la: Expenduntur quae non minori impudentia ex quinti saeculi Patribus, Innocentio, Ephesina & Chalcedonensis Synodorum Patribus; adhaec ex Cyrillo, & Leone, pro suis Canonibus furens Turrianus convasavit.
units.tr: The points are weighed which the raging Turrianus, with no less shamelessness, has patched together from the fifth-century Fathers: Innocent, and the Fathers of the Synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon; and besides these from Cyril and Leo, in support of his canons.

units.la: UNC ad quintum saeculum, quae praecipiti vixit, ac floruit Gelasius, veniamus. Primus, quem ex hoc saeculo testem citat Turrianus, Innocentius est Romae Episcopus in Epistola ad Victricium Rotomagensem, a. D. 404. data. Sed in hoc Iesuita eosdem, quos in superioribus, ludos facit. Neque enim vel unum extat in tota illa epistola vel de Clementina Sylloge, vel de canonibus Apostolicis verbum. Illud quidem fateor, in tredecim illis capitulis, quae continet epistola, nonnulla esse, quae in Canonibus itidem Apostolorum Turrianicis praecipiuntur; quae scilicet quod essent in communi Ecclesiarum usu, impostor in suam farraginem retulit, ut publica authoritas speciem aliquam mendacio concilaret. Sed haec Innocentius nusquam dicit, vel in libro Apostolicorum Canonum extare, vel inde a se descripta esse; quod non erat ille praetermissurus, siquem Clementinum mentinum agnovisset codicem, in quo ista haberentur. Hoc enim imprimis pertinebat ad authoritatem iis apud Victricium, & caeteros conciliandam, quibus hunc suum librum insinuari cupiebat Innocentius. Certe cum capite primo decernit, Episcopum extra Metropolitani conscientiam non esse ordinandum, Synodum Nicaenam, quae illud idem canone quarto praecipit, nequaquam putavit omittendam;Hoc enim (inquit a) & in Synodo Nicaena constitutum est, atque definitum. Quo loco ridiculus est Turrianus, particulam & vexans, quasi significet praeter Apostolos, hoc etiam Patres Nicaenos definivisse. Atqui Apostolorum nullus meminerat Innocentius. Manifestum est quid velit; non se solum ita decernere, vel sui temporis Ecclesias, vel singulos Episcopos; Synodum etiam Nicaenam, cujus maxima erat apud omnes authoritas, idem constituisse. Capite secundo Nicaenam itidem Synodum nominatim laudat Innocentius; & quidem semel, atque iterum. Idem facit capite septimo. Qui Nicaenos canones tam diligenter, ubi incidit occasio, citat, cur is, quaesto, nusquam nominat Apostolicos, multo majoris (si ulli erant vere Apostolici) & authoritatis & antiquitatis, cum eaipsa commemorat ac
units.tr: Now let us come to the fifth century, in which Gelasius lived and flourished in the decline of the age. The first witness from this century whom Turrianus cites is Innocent, bishop of Rome, in his letter to Victricius of Rouen, dated in the year of our Lord 404. But here the Jesuit plays the same games as before. For there is not a single word in that whole letter about the Clementine Sylloge or the Apostolic Canons. I admit this much: among the thirteen chapters the letter contains, some are likewise prescribed in Turrian's Apostolic Canons. Since these were in common use in the Churches, the impostor put them into his hodgepodge, so that public authority might lend some appearance to the lie. But Innocent nowhere says that these are found in a book of Apostolic Canons, or that he took them from there. He would not have omitted this if he had known of that Clementine codex in which these things were contained, for it would above all have helped win authority with Victricius and the others to whom Innocent wished his book to be recommended. Certainly, when in chapter one he decrees that a bishop is not to be ordained without the knowledge of the Metropolitan, he did not think the Synod of Nicaea should be left out, since it prescribes the same thing in canon four: For this (he says) has also been established and defined in the Synod of Nicaea. Here Turrianus is ridiculous, twisting the particle "also" as if it meant that the Nicene Fathers had defined this besides the Apostles. Yet Innocent mentions no apostle at all. What he means is clear: he is saying that he does not decree this alone, whether for the Churches of his own time or for individual bishops; the Synod of Nicaea, whose authority was greatest with everyone, had laid down the same thing. In chapter two Innocent also names the Synod of Nicaea expressly, and indeed more than once. He does the same in chapter seven. Since he cites the Nicene canons so diligently wherever the occasion arises, why does he never name the Apostolic canons, which, if any were truly Apostolic, were of far greater authority and antiquity, when he recalls and decrees the same things?

units.la: decernit, quæ erant in illis definita, ut ver-bi gratia capitibus primo, secundo, tertio, quinto, sexto, &c. quibus eadem definit, quæ jam erant in Apostolicis canonibus, primo, sexagesimo primo, tricesimo quarto, tricesimo sexto, duodecimo, &c. si Turriano quidem credimus definita? Ratio in promptu est; Nimirum canones Nicænos, quos citaret, cognitos habuit Innocentius; Apostolicos, quos laudaret, nullos plane norat; quos, siquos, novisset, non minus, quam Nicænos, nominatim laudaturus erat. Sed Turrianus tamen contra calcitrat; & præter manifestam rerum rationem contendit, Innocentium hæc, quæ in illa epistola decernit, ex sua Apostolicorum canonum Sylloge desumpsisse. Quod ut probet, hæc recitat, quæ præfatur Innocentius; Non quo nova præcepta aliqua imperentur, sed ea quæ per desidiam aliquorum neglecta sunt, ab omnibus observari cupiamus; quæ tamen Apostolica, & Patrum traditione sunt constituta. Scriptum est enim namque ad Thessalonicenses, Paulo monente b, State ac tenete traditiones nostras, quas tradidi vobis, sive per verbum, sive per epistolam. Hactenus Innocentius; ex quibus, quod primo colligit Turrianus, ego id equidem libens concedo, putasse nimirum Innocentium, ista
units.tr: and decrees those things which were defined in those canons, as in chapters one, two, three, five, six, and so on, by which he lays down the same things that were already in the Apostolic canons, in chapters one, sixty-one, thirty-four, thirty-six, twelve, and so on, if we believe Turrianus that they were defined there. The reason is at hand: Innocent undoubtedly knew the Nicene canons, which he cites; the Apostolic canons, which he would have praised had he known them, he plainly did not know. Had he known any, he would have named them no less than the Nicene ones. But Turrianus nevertheless kicks back, and against the plain logic of the matter he contends that Innocent took the things he decrees in that letter from Turrian's Sylloge of Apostolic canons. To prove this he recites what Innocent prefaces: Not that some new precepts are to be imposed, but we wish that those things which have been neglected through the carelessness of some be observed by all; which nevertheless have been established by Apostolic and patristic tradition. For it is written to the Thessalonians, Paul admonishing: Stand and hold the traditions which I delivered to you, whether by word or by letter. So far Innocent. From these words, what Turrianus first infers I readily grant: that Innocent thought these things he decrees in this letter had already been handed down to Christians by the Apostles themselves, whether by living voice or in writing.

units.la: a Thess. 2. 14. ista quæ deinceps in hac epistola decernit, fuisse jam ab ipsis Apostolis, sive viva voce, sive etiam scripto Christianis tradita. Et ipse sane istorum quædam ex divinis Scripturis confirmare conatur; ut ex Levitico, quod capite quarto de uxore clerici virgine decernit; ex Paulo, quod capite sexto, de digamis à sacris ordinibus arcendis; ex Moyse & ex Paulo, quæ capite nono de sacerdotum & diaconorum ab uxoribus continentia præcipit; ex eodem denique Paulo, quæ capite decimo tertio statuit de virginibus non velatis, quæ neglecto proposito nubunt. Cætera, quæ nullo allato Scripturarum testimonio definit, omnino videtur censuisse ipsa quoque ab Apostolis tradita; sed viva voce. Quod vero ex his concludit Turrianus, nos recte concludi negamus; Cum partim istorum (inquit) in canonibus Apostolorum contineantur, qui sunt traditiones eorum per sermonem, consequens est, non ignorasse eum hos Apostolorum canones, id est has eorum traditiones, tametsi in ipsis capitulis istos ipsos canones Apostolorum non semper citet, neque nominet, nec enim opus erat. Respondeo, Turrianum vel in ambiguo ludere, vel nihil concludere. Si enim intelligit, non ignorasse Innocentium, id est existimasse hæc ab Apostolis fuisse viva voce tradita, id quidem concedo. Sed iste nos ludit; neque id quod quaeritur, concludit. Non enim simpliciter quaeritur, an ista Innocentius aliqua in genere ratione ab Apostolis tradita fuisse putaverit. Quaeritur, an ista in Clementina Apostolicorum canonum sylloge, in Ecclesia tunc nota, scripta fuisse sciverit; quod, ut liquet, minime concludit Turrianus. Finge enim animo, Turriane, quod nos quidem verissimum esse & credimus, & postea demonstrabimus, nullam quinto ineunte saeculo extitisse. Clementinam illam, tuam scilicet 8 5. Apostolicorum canonum syllogen; An ideo putabis, Innocentium non potuisse aliunde discere ista pauca quae commemorat ac decernit ab Apostolis fuisse tradita? Nulla-ne extabant superiorum vel Synodorum, vel Patrum monumenta, ex quibus id ipsum accipere, atque haurire potuerit? Ipse Ecclesiae usus, quem, quod ejus initia nulla videbat, antiquissimum fuisse suspicabatur, nonne ei persuadere potuit haec fuisse Apostolica? Tui quidem ita tradunt, vulgatam hanc esse Sanctorum Patrum regulam, quorum author alius ignoratur, ea Apostolica traditione ad nos dimanasse, recte credi. Ergo etiamsi nulla extitisset Innocentianis temporibus Clementina Canonum sylloge (& sane nulla
units.tr: a 2 Thess. 2. 14. Indeed Innocent himself tries to confirm some of these points from the divine Scriptures: from Leviticus, which in chapter four decrees about a virgin wife of a cleric; from Paul, which in chapter six concerns excluding digamists from sacred orders; from Moses and from Paul, which in chapter nine prescribes the continence of priests and deacons from their wives; and finally from the same Paul, which in chapter thirteen lays down concerning unveiled virgins who marry after neglecting their vow. The rest, which he decrees without citing any testimony of Scripture, he seems wholly to have judged were likewise handed down by the Apostles, but by living voice. But what Turrianus concludes from these, we deny is rightly concluded. Since some of these (he says) are contained in the Apostolic canons, which are their traditions by word, it follows that he was not ignorant of these Apostolic canons, that is, of these their traditions, although in these very chapters he does not always cite or name these Apostolic canons, for there was no need. I answer that Turrianus either plays on an ambiguity or concludes nothing. For if he means that Innocent was not ignorant, that is, that he thought these things had been handed down by the Apostles by living voice, that I indeed concede. But he mocks us and does not conclude what is in question. For the question is not simply whether Innocent thought these things had been handed down by the Apostles in some general way. The question is whether he knew these things to be written in the Clementine Sylloge of Apostolic canons, which was known in the Church at that time; and as is clear, Turrianus in no way concludes this. Imagine, Turrianus, what we both believe to be most true, and will demonstrate afterwards: that no such Clementine collection, your "Sylloge of the Apostolic canons," existed at the beginning of the fifth century. Would you then think that Innocent could not have learned from elsewhere that those few things he recalls and decrees were handed down by the Apostles? Did no monuments of earlier synods or Fathers survive from which he could receive and draw that very thing? Could not the usage of the Church itself, which he supposed to be most ancient since he saw no beginnings of it, have persuaded him that these were Apostolic? Your own people indeed teach that this is the common rule of the holy Fathers, whose author is unknown, that it has flowed down to us from Apostolic tradition, and that this is rightly believed. Therefore, even if there had been no Clementine collection of canons in Innocent's time (and indeed none existed)

units.la: a Binius annot. in titul. Can. Ap. T. I. Conc. p. 17. A. tradunt ... nulla extitit) etiamsi omnia alia ante a-- -ditemporis monumenta plane penitusque intercidissent, potuit tamen Innocentius ex aurea illa scilicet tuorum regula recte credere, quorum alium authorem ignora-bat, ea adse, suosque Apostolica traditio-nedimanasse. Quid? quod Hieronymus eorundem homo temporum, hanc omni-bus provincialibus potestatem concedit, ut quod à suis parentibus apud se quisque constitutum reperiunt, id pro Apostolico habeant? Unaquaque provincia (inquit) abundet in sensu suo, & praecepta majorum leges APOSTOLICAS arbitretur. Hac quidem lege licuit Innocentio ista omnia, quae decernit, eo ipso pro Apostolicis traditionibus censere, quod ea Romae usitata, & à majoribus praecepta reperiret. Huc accedebat, quae Romanis jam olim penitus animo infixa est, de suae sedis, ac disciplinae excellentia opinio; ut nihil apud se quantum vis leve sit, quod non jactent Apostolicum esse; utque Romanum & Apostolicum aequipollere existimentt. Non jam disputo, recte ne, an secus, ita instituant; neque discutio quae Apostolica traditione haberi scribit Innocentius, ea ne vere sint Apostolica; Hoc unum obiter dicam, qui Nicaenae synodo sive imprudens, sive er-
units.tr: a Binius, note on the title of the Apostolic Canons, in volume 1 of the Councils, p. 17 A, says they relate ... none existed. Even if all other monuments of earlier times had utterly perished, Innocent could still rightly believe, from that golden rule of yours, of whose author he knew nothing, that these had flowed down to him and his people from Apostolic tradition. And what of it? Does not Jerome, a man of these same times, grant to every provincial this power, that each may hold as Apostolic whatever he finds established among his own forebears? Let each province abound in its own sense, and regard the precepts of its elders as Apostolic laws. By this law Innocent was free to judge all those things he decrees to be Apostolic traditions, simply because he found them in use at Rome and handed down by the elders. Added to this was the opinion, long since fixed deeply in the minds of the Romans, of the excellence of their see and discipline: so that nothing among them, however trivial, is not boasted to be Apostolic, and they think the Roman and the Apostolic to be equivalent. I am not now disputing whether they establish these things rightly or otherwise, nor do I examine whether the things Innocent writes are held by Apostolic tradition are truly Apostolic. This one thing I will say in passing: whoever, either unwittingly or in error, departs from the Nicene synod

units.la: {a} Ep. 28. ad Lucin. T.1. Hier. jam sciens, volensque, hoc decretum affingit majores causas ad sedem Apostolicam, (id est Romanam) post episcopale (id est metropoliticum) judicium esse referendas (quod nusquam a Nicaena Synodo factum constat) qui hoc inquam Nicaenis tribuit, eum profecto nequaquam absurdum est, quaedam Apostolis itidem vel per errorem, vel etiam ex suae sedis, suarumque rerum studio tribuisse, quae vere non sunt Apostolorum. Sed hoc inquam nos nunc quidem minime agimus.
units.tr: Jerome, Ep. 28 ad Lucin., tom. 1. Knowingly and deliberately, he attributes to the Nicene fathers this decree: that the greater causes are to be referred to the Apostolic See (that is, the Roman) after the episcopal (that is, metropolitan) judgment, which is nowhere recorded as having been done by the Nicene Synod. I say that whoever ascribes this to the Nicenes is certainly not absurd in supposing that he has likewise attributed to the Apostles, either through error or even from zeal for his own see and his own interests, some things that are not truly the Apostles'. But I am by no means dealing with that now.

units.la: Id unum nobis in praesentia satis est, quod cum tam multae aliae sint rationes quibus Innocentius eo induci potuerit, ut ista, quae in hac epistola decernit, Apostolica traditione constituta fuisse scripserit, frustra, inepteque argumentari Turrianum, qui quod ille ista Apostolica traditione constituta esse scripserit, eo conficit, Clementinam illam suam Apostolicorum Canonum Syllogen jam tum extitisse, ipsique Innocentio probe cognitam fuisse. Quod postremo idem negat opus fuisse citari istos Apostolorum canones, miror equidem cur id neget. Quaeso enim annon opus erat Innocentium, quae Victricio, quae caeteris Gallis Victricio vicinis Episcopis persuadere, atque utenda tradere cupiebat, ea diligenter confirmare? re ? Si hoc nihil necesse fuisse putavit, cur ergo tam studiose è Scripturis, Nicæ-nisque canonibus arripit, quæcunque ad rem suam facere existimavit? At si jam tum in publicæ Ecclesiæ luce ab omnibus receptus extabat Clementinus iste 85. Canonum codex, apparet, nihil omnino ad ista, quæ decernit Innocentius, commendanda, nihil ad Apostolicam originem atque institutionem iis vindicandam aptius, atque efficacius afferri potuisse, quam hujus codicis authoritatem. Ergo nisi quæ sunt ad causam probandam omnium aptissima, maximeque necessaria, ea ipsa afferre nihil opus esse statuat Turrianus, non video cur istos canones ab Innocentio citari neget opus fuisse. Nullus tamen eos citavit, vir alioqui frugi, & rerum suarum inprimis diligens, ac studiosus. Ergo ex hac ejus epistola, non modo non sequitur, quod stulte nullaque ratione vult Turrianus, cognitam ipsi fuisse Clementinam canonum syllogen; sed plane contra, quod nos defendimus, evidenter conficitur, nullum ei hujus furfuris notum fuisse Clementis, vel Apostolorum librum.
units.tr: This one point is enough for us at present. Innocent could have been led by many other reasons to write that the things he decrees in this letter were established by Apostolic tradition. Turrianus argues in vain and foolishly when he infers from Innocent's words that the Clementine collection of Apostolic Canons already existed and was well known to Innocent himself. Turrianus also denies that there was any need to cite those canons of the Apostles, and I wonder why he denies it. For I ask, was it not necessary for Innocent to firmly confirm, with care, the things he wished to persuade Victricius and the other Gallic bishops near Victricius to accept and hand down for use? If he thought this was not necessary at all, why did he so eagerly seize from the Scriptures and the Nicene canons whatever he judged would serve his purpose? But if this Clementine code of 85 canons was already then in the light of the public Church, received by all, it is clear that nothing more apt or effective could have been brought forward to commend what Innocent decrees, or to claim for it an Apostolic origin and institution, than the authority of this code. Therefore, unless Turrianus lays down that only what is most apt and most necessary for proving the case should be brought forward, I do not see why he denies that Innocent needed to cite those canons. Yet no one cited them, although Innocent was otherwise a sound man and especially careful and diligent in his own affairs. Therefore from this letter it does not follow, as Turrianus foolishly and without any reason maintains, that the Clementine collection of canons was known to him. On the contrary, as we maintain, it is plainly shown that this rubbish, whether attributed to Clement or to the Apostles, was not known to him at all.

units.la: Pertinet ad ejusdem quinti sæculi annum 31. Ephesinæ Synodi laudatum à Turriano testimonium. Ajunt (inquit) Ephesini Patres præter canones Apostolorum esse, versa.
units.tr: To the same year of the fifth century, the year 431, belongs the testimony of the Synod of Ephesus that Turrianus cites. testimonium The Ephesian Fathers, he says, state that the matter lies outside the canons of the Apostles.

units.la: a c. 13. p. 36. recta. & c. 14, p. 39. quod Episcopus Antiochia in provinciis Cypri ordinationes faciebat a. Ergo jam tum notus erat Apostolicorum Canonum Clementinus codex; in quo scilicet diserte vetitum legimus b, ne Episcopus audeat extra suos fines facere ordinationes in urbibus & pagis non ei subjectis. Ego vero respondeo, Latinam Ephesinæ Synodi editionem loco illo citato nihil de Apostolis habere: Rem hanc (inquit) quæ præter Ecclesiasticas Constitutiones, & Sanctorum Patrum canones innovatur, & omnium libertatem attingit, annunciavit piissimus Episcopus Rheginus; & quæ sequuntur. Non Apostolorum, ut callide, temereque & falso supponit Turrianus, sed Sanctorum Patrum canones dicit. Græcus codex vetus Canonum universalis Ecclesiæ Lutetiæ a. D. 1610. editus, eandem lectionem exhibet ç; τράγματα τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς διατάξεως, τῆς κανόνας τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων καινοτομουμένου, καὶ τῶν πάντων ἐλευθερίας ἀποτέμνου προσηγγέιλεν ὁ θεοφιλέστατος σωσπιστικοπῆς Ρηγίνων. Eandem exhibent Romana Concilio-rum a. 1608. Colonien-sis a. 1618. Parisiensis denique a. 1636. græcolatinę editiones d. Itaque nihil ad Apostolicos canones hæc Ephesinorum Patrum verba. Patrum canones dicunt; hoc est Episcoporum & Synodorum superiorum decreta, ac con-
units.tr: (a) Chapter 13, page 36, correctly, and chapter 14, page 39, that the Bishop of Antioch was making ordinations in the provinces of Cyprus. Therefore, he argues, the Clementine codex of the Apostolic Canons was already known by then; in it, we read, it is expressly forbidden for a bishop to dare to make ordinations outside his own borders, in cities and villages not subject to him. But I reply that the Latin edition of the Ephesian Synod says nothing about the Apostles in the passage cited: "This matter (it says), which is being innovated beyond the ecclesiastical constitutions and the canons of the holy Fathers, and which touches the freedom of all, was announced by the most pious Bishop of Rhegium"; and what follows. It does not say "of the Apostles", as Turrianus cunningly, rashly and falsely puts it, but "the canons of the holy Fathers". The old Greek codex of the Universal Canons, published at Paris in 1610, gives the same reading: [τράγματα τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς διατάξεως, τῆς κανόνας τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων καινοτομουμένου, καὶ τῶν πάντων ἐλευθερίας ἀποτέμνου προσηγγέιλεν ὁ θεοφιλέστατος σωσπιστικοπῆς Ρηγίνων]. The Roman edition of the Councils of 1608, the Cologne edition of 1618, and finally the Greek-Latin Paris edition of 1636 give the same. So these words of the Ephesian Fathers have nothing to do with the Apostolic canons. They say "canons of the Fathers", that is, the decrees of earlier bishops and synods, and their constitutions.

units.la: e Ex versione Latina, ut alias. constitutiones; Videntur autem ad Antiochenum Canonem 13. digitum intendere; Μηδένα ἐπίσκοπον τολμᾶν ἀφ' ἑτέρας ἐπαρχίας εἰς ἑτέραν μεταβαίνειν, καὶ χειροτονεῖν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ τινὰς εἰς προαγωγὴν λειτουργίας. Eum Dionysius in codice numero 91. his verbis expressum repraesentat; Nullus Episcopus ex alia provincia audeat ad aliam transgredi, & ad promotionem ministerii aliquos in Ecclesiis ordinare. Sed & similia decernuntur à Patribus Constantinopolitanis canone secundo; quorum Synodus hanc Ephesinam annis propemodum quinquaginta antecesserat. Nihil ergo necesse est ad ullos Apostolorum Canones, nedum ad Turrianicos, confugere, ut haec Ephesinae Synodi verba intelligamus. Quam vero eorum lectionem Turrianus obtrudit, substituto ἀποστόλων, pro Πατέρων, nomine quamquam nuper commemorate Conciliorum graeco-latinae editiones exhibent quidem, sed in margine duntaxat, non autem in ipso Synodi corpore, ea inquam à Graecis suae Apostolicorum canonum farragini favent-tibus effecta, & excogitata videtur; quorum nos fraudibus non tenemur, & in veteri Latina versione, publicisque Conciliorum codicibus libentes conquiescimus.
units.tr: (e) From the Latin version, as elsewhere. They seem, however, to point their finger at Antiochene Canon 13: [Μηδένα ἐπίσκοπον τολμᾶν ἀφ' ἑτέρας ἐπαρχίας εἰς ἑτέραν μεταβαίνειν, καὶ χειροτονεῖν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ τινὰς εἰς προαγωγὴν λειτουργίας]. Dionysius, in code number 91, renders it in these words: "No bishop from one province should dare to pass into another, and to ordain persons in churches for advancement to the ministry." Similar things are also decreed by the Fathers of Constantinople in canon 2, whose synod had preceded this Ephesian one by almost fifty years. Therefore there is no need to flee to any Apostolic canons, much less Turrianus' canons, to understand these words of the Ephesian Synod. As for the reading Turrianus forces on us, with ἀποστόλων substituted for Πατέρων, the Greek-Latin editions of the Councils I mentioned recently do indeed exhibit it, but only in the margin, not in the body of the Synod itself. This reading, I say, seems to have been produced and devised by Greeks favouring their hodgepodge of Apostolic canons. We are not bound by their frauds, and we gladly rest in the old Latin version and the public codices of the Councils.

units.la: Cyrilli vero nomen, qui in Ephesina
units.tr: Turrianus also vainly mixes in here the name of Cyril, who presided over the Ephesian Synod.

units.la: Synodo præfuit, frustra quoque hic miscet Turrianus. Cyrillus (inquit) 10. homilia ἑορταστικὴ, celebrationem Paschæ, ut nunc celebrat Ecclesia, secundum traditionem Apostolicam fieri dicit. Ille vero in illa quidem decima homilia, nihil hujusmodi dicit, neque aliud de festo Paschæ habet, quam hæc b(quæ quam sint ab istis Turrianicis aliena, omnes vident) ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀπαντᾷ λαμπρῶν ὕτως ἐπιτελεῖμεν τὸν ἑορτὸν, Ob hæc omnia merito festivitatis tam insignis solennia celebramus, non nobis ipsis adhuc viventes, ut habeatur in sacris litteris, sed ei a quo omnes redempti sumus, Christo. Tum etiamsi Pascha secundum traditionem Apostolicam fieri diceret Cyrillus; quid hoc ad Clementinam Canonum collectionem? Certe eorum verborum non alius esset, vel esse posset sensus, nisi hic unus, tradidisse scilicet Apostolos, id quod Christiani celebrant, Paschæ festum. Id vero tradere Apostoli aliter vel alibi potuerunt, quam in Clementino codice? Quot vero, quamque multæ sunt pro Apostolicis habitæ traditiones, quarum nulla extat in istis sictitiis Canonibus mentio? Etiam tradidisse Apostoli dicuntur, quæcunque Christianis viva voce observanda mandarunt, etiamsi nulla de iis littera, vel in Clementino, tino , vel in ullo alio codice scripta sit.
units.tr: Cyril, he says, in his tenth festal homily, states that the celebration of Easter, as the Church now celebrates it, is made according to Apostolic tradition. But in that tenth homily he says nothing of the kind, nor has he anything about the festival of Easter other than these words (how far these are from Turrianus' claims, everyone can see): [ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀπαντᾷ λαμπρῶν ὕτως ἐπιτελεῖμεν τὸν ἑορτὸν]: "For all these reasons we celebrate the solemnities of so remarkable a festival, not living any longer for ourselves, so that it may be recorded in the sacred letters, but for Christ, by whom we have all been redeemed." Yet even if Cyril said that Easter is made according to Apostolic tradition, what has this to do with the Clementine collection of canons? Surely the sense of those words could be none other than this: that the Apostles handed down the feast of Easter, which Christians celebrate. But could the Apostles have handed this down in some other way or place than in the Clementine code? And how many, and how many, traditions are held to be Apostolic, of which not one is mentioned in those fictitious canons! The Apostles are said to have handed down whatever they commanded Christians to observe by word of mouth, even if nothing about it is written in the Clementine code or in any other.

units.la: Ex quinto sæculo præter hos, de quibus diximus testes citat Turrianus a Patres Chalcedonenses b, & Leonem, qui ad a. D. 451. pertinent. Ex Chalcedonensi Concilio refert τὰς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς θεσμὰς id est (Dionysio interprete) præter Ecclesiastica statuta facere eos Episcopos, qui Principum authoritate interpolita sedibus suis metropoleωn honorem quærebant. Turrianus hariolatur illa statuta Ecclesiastica esse suorum Apostolorum canones 30um. & 34um. Ego quod iste nullo argumento pronuntiat, pari facilitate rejicio. Statuta Ecclesiastica quid sint, nemo nescit. An illa Ecclesiæ statuta ex canonibus Clementinis habuerint Patres ex eorum verbis non liquet, & frustra vaticinatur Turrianus; cum illi Clementini Canones apud omnem antiquitatem sint inauditi. Balsamo quidem ad hunc Chalcedonensem canonem adire nos jubet, non Apostolicos, sed Nicænos Constantinopolitanosque canones; id est canones primæ Synodi sextum, septimumque, & secundæ secundum. Sed & ad Apostolorum suorum canonem 40. trahit Turrianus de jusdem synodi Chalcedonensis canonem 22. quo vetatur, ne Clerici in res mortui Episcopi involent; quia scilicet eadem quoque ille alter decernit. Ego ad synodi nodi Antiochenæ canonem referendum ajo, quem Turrianus ipse fatetur, paria præcipere. Ratio manifesta est; quod istius quidem Turriani Apostolorum codicis nulla neque in Chalcedonensi Synodo, neque in superioribus retro monumentis ulla extat mentio; Antiochenæ regulæ & omnibus notissimæ erant, & sunt ab ipsis Chalcedonensibus Patribus disertissime, neque semel ex codice Ecclesiæ universalis citatæ. Neq; valet, quod objicit Turrianus, τὰς παλαιὰς κανόνας antiquos canones eos à Chalcedonensibus dici, à quibus id, quod ipsi statuunt, decretum erat. Quę enim, quæso, invidia erat canones Synodiante 110. annos Antiochiæ habitæ τὰς παλαιὰς veteres, sive antiquos dici?
units.tr: Besides the witnesses of whom we have spoken, Turrianus cites from the fifth century a the Fathers of Chalcedon b and Leo, who belong to the year 451. From the Chalcedonian Council he cites the phrase [τὰς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς θεσμὰς], that is (in Dionysius' translation) "beyond ecclesiastical statutes", where those bishops are condemned who, by the interposed authority of princes, sought the honour of metropolitan status for their sees. Turrianus guesses that those "ecclesiastical statutes" are his Apostolic canons 30 and 34. I reject this with equal ease, since he asserts it without any argument. What ecclesiastical statutes are, no one fails to know. Whether the Fathers had those statutes of the Church from the Clementine canons is not clear from their words, and Turrianus prophesies in vain, since those Clementine canons were unheard of throughout all antiquity. Balsamo indeed bids us go to this Chalcedonian canon, but not to the Apostolic canons; rather to the canons of Nicaea and Constantinople, that is, canons six and seven of the first synod and canon two of the second. Turrianus also draws to his Apostolic canon 40 the canon 22 of the same Synod of Chalcedon, which forbids clerics to lay hands on the goods of a deceased bishop, because, of course, that other canon decrees the same. I say it should be referred to the canon of the Synod of Antioch, which Turrianus himself admits prescribes the same things. The reason is plain. No mention at all of Turrianus' Apostolic code exists in the Synod of Chalcedon or in earlier records, whereas the rules of Antioch were well known to all, and were cited quite explicitly by the Chalcedonian Fathers themselves, and not just once, from the code of the universal Church. Nor does it help that Turrianus objects that the Chalcedonians called "the ancient canons" [τὰς παλαιὰς κανόνας] those by which what they decreed had been settled. For what, I ask, was the offence in calling the canons of the Synod of Antioch, held 110 years earlier, "the ancient" [τὰς παλαιὰς], or old?

units.la: Neque firmiora sunt, quæ Turrianus ex Leone pro Clementinis canonibus objicit; quale illud est, quod Leo sine dubio ait ex Apostolica traditione descendere eam Ecclesiæ consuetudinem, qua presbyteri, & diaconi, criminis alicujus rei citra impositionem manuum, privata seorsim peracta pœnitentia Deo reconciliarentur. Id Turrianus ad canonem suorum Apostolorum 22. refert; Frustra. Nam Leo ipse ratio-nem, cur id sentiat, ex Apostolica traditione descendere, edisserens, non illum Clementini codicis canonem 22. adfert, quod & decebat, & facillimum erat, si eo respe-rissét ; sed locum quendam è divinis scripturis,hunc nimirum a,Sacerdos, si pec- caverit, quis orabit pro eo ? Verba Leonis sunt ; quod sine dubio ex Apostolica traditione descendit, secundum quod scriptum est ; Sacerdos, si peccaverit, quis orabit pro eo ? Unde hujusmodi lapsis ad promerendum misericordiam Dei, privata est expetenda secessio, ubi illis satisfactio, si fuerit digna, sit etiam fructuosa. Hæc Leo; hunc ab Apostolis unum esse inde argumentaris, quod divinis litteris esset consentaneus. Quid vero istis ambagibus opus fuit, si à Clemente, viro Apostolico, litteris mandatæ Apostolorum voces, in eam rem disertissimæ, ab omnibus in publico Ecclesiæ codice legebantur ? Itaque docet allatus Leonis locus, Clementinum codicem nullum illis temporibus potius, quam aliquem extitisse.
units.tr: Nor are the arguments Turrianus draws from Leo in support of the Clementine canons any stronger. Take his statement that the custom by which presbyters and deacons, for some crime, are reconciled to God through private penance performed apart, without the imposition of hands, sine dubio descends from Apostolic tradition. Turrianus refers this to canon 22 of the Apostolic canons. In vain. Leo himself, explaining why he holds this view, descends from Apostolic tradition, does not cite canon 22 of the Clementine collection, though he ought to have done so and could easily have done so if he had found it there. Instead he cites a passage from the divine Scriptures, namely this: "If a priest sins, who will pray for him?" Leo's words are: "which without doubt descends from Apostolic tradition, according to what is written: If a priest sins, who will pray for him? Hence for such fallen men, to obtain the mercy of God, a private withdrawal is to be sought, where satisfaction, if it is worthy, may also be fruitful." So says Leo. You argue from this that it is one of the Apostles' rules because it agrees with the divine writings. But what need was there for such circumlocution, if the words of the Apostles, written down for this very purpose and most plainly stated, had been read by everyone in the public codex of the Church, through Clement, a man of Apostolic times? The passage of Leo just quoted therefore shows that no Clementine codex existed in those times, or at least not one of that kind.

units.la: Alter Leonis locus extat epistola prima, in qua præfatus nos & Apostolo docente & divina præceptione didicisse, & canonum regulis, qualis unicuique sacerdotum & diaconorum natalium honestas, & morum esse debeat ; subjungit ; Constat ad sacerdotium pervenisse viduarum maritos, quosdam etiam, quibus fuerint numerosa conjugia, & ad omnem licentiam vita liberior, ad ad Sacrum ordinem passim patefactis aditi‐bus fuisse permissos, contra illam B. Apo‐stoli a vocem, qua talibus reclamat, dicens, Unius uxoris virum : Et contra illud anti‐qua legis præceptum b, quo dicitur, & ca‐vetur, Sacerdos virginem uxorem acci‐piat, non viduam, non repudiatam. Turrianus c istas canonum à Leone tertio loco memoratas regulas dejerat esse suos Clementini codicis canones 17. & 18. Qui pote, inquam? Leo tria proponit diver‐sa documenta, è quibus discimus, qualis esse debeat sacerdotibus & diaconis natalium & morum honestas. Ad primum caput Apostoli locum refert, ex c. 3. prioris ad Timotheum epistolæ : ad secundum, descriptum è Levitico locum : ad tertium pertinent canones Ecclesiastici, quos quia omnibus notos sciebat, ideo nullos citat, sed tacite tantum præsuppo‐nit (ut vulgo loquimur) Ergo Apostoli‐cam doctrinam, qua primum probatio‐num caput continetur, clare & enucleate à canonum regulis, quæ tertium proba‐tionum caput complectuntur, distinguit, perperam, ac stulte, ut quivis videt, si & canonum regulæ Apostolica doctrina sunt. Nam si ita est, quod in istis regulis disci‐mus, Apostolo docente discimus. Ergo si sa‐pit Turrianus, deliravit Leo. Sed cui u‐terque terque notus fuerit, illum potius desipuisse censebit; qui tamen, qua est pectoris fœ-cunditate, hanc fuisse Leonis mentem (quæ si fuit, Leo deliraverit) ita probare instituit, Leo(inquit a)alibi rem eandem agens, scribit eos, qui secundas nuptias inierunt, vel viduarum se conjugio sociarunt, nec Apostolicam, neque legalem authoritatem sacerdotium obtinere pracipere. Quam hic (inquit Turrianus) Apostolicam authoritatem dicit, in loco superiori regulas canonum dixerat. Hoc quidem jubet Turrianus. Nos, quia nulla ratione jubet, non assentimur. Apostolicam authoritatem idem esse Leoni, quod in superiori loco Apostolum docentem, & res & oratio, & Leo ipse loquitur, qui eandem Pauli sententiam, quam in prima epistola laudaverat; hic quoque describit b ex priore ad Timotheum epistola petitam, & ex ea conficit, neque qui plures uxores, neque qui unam, sed viduam, duxerit, episcopum fieri licere; eodemque, ut supra, torquet Leviticum decretum, ut virginem sacerdos accipiat. Ergo Apostolica, quæ Leoni dicitur, authoritas, ea Pauli est in priore ad Timotheum sententia, ipso teste Leone; nihil adeo commune habet cum Clementino canonum codice.
units.tr: Another passage of Leo is found in his first letter, where, after prefacing that "we have learned both from the Apostle teaching and from divine precept, and from the rules of the canons, what the birth and morals of each of the priests and deacons ought to be," he adds: "It is established that husbands of widows, some also who had numerous marriages, and men of freer life in every licence, have been admitted to the priesthood, the approaches to the sacred order being thrown open everywhere," contrary to that voice of the blessed Apostle, which rejects such men, saying, "the husband of one wife"; and contrary to that precept of the ancient law, which says and forbids: "let the priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not a repudiated woman." Turrianus solemnly declares that these rules, which Leo mentions in the third place as canons, are his Clementine canons 17 and 18. How can that be, I ask? Leo sets out three different proofs, from which we learn what the birth and morals of priests and deacons ought to be. For the first he refers to the Apostle, in chapter 3 of the first letter to Timothy; for the second, to a passage taken from Leviticus; and the third concerns the ecclesiastical canons, which, since he knew they were known to all, he does not cite but only tacitly presupposes, as we commonly say. Therefore he clearly and explicitly distinguishes the Apostolic doctrine, which contains the first head of proof, from the rules of the canons, which make up the third head. He does this wrongly and foolishly, as anyone can see, if the rules of the canons are also Apostolic doctrine. For if that is so, what we learn from those rules we learn from the Apostle teaching. So if Turrianus is wise, Leo has gone mad. But whoever knows both will judge rather that he himself has lost his senses; yet Turrianus, with that fertility of mind he has, sets out to prove that this was Leo's meaning (and if it was, Leo was out of his mind) in this way: "Leo," he says, "dealing with the same matter elsewhere, writes that those who have entered second marriages, or joined themselves to the marriage of widows, may obtain neither the Apostolic nor the legal authority of the priesthood." This Apostolic authority, Turrianus says, is what in the earlier passage he called the rules of the canons. This is what Turrianus commands us to believe. We do not assent, because he gives no reason for it. That Apostolic authority means for Leo the same as the Apostle teaching in the earlier passage, both the matter and the wording show, and Leo himself speaks thus; he repeats the same sentence of Paul which he had praised in the first letter, here too drawing it from the first letter to Timothy, and from it concludes that neither one who has had several wives nor one who has married a widow may be made a bishop; and in the same way, as above, he applies the decree of Leviticus that the priest should take a virgin. Therefore the Apostolic authority of which Leo speaks is, on Leo's own testimony, the opinion of Paul in the first letter to Timothy; it has nothing so much in common with the Clementine codex of canons.

units.la: Tertio Leonis ista ddescribit Turrianus, in quibus is metropolitanos decernit secundum sanctorum Patrum Canones Spiritu Dei conditos, & totius mundi reverentia consecratos, jus tradita sibi antiquitus dignitatis intemeratum habere. Turrianus suos Clementinos canones hic, ut ubique somniat; stulte quidem ille, & absque ratione, ut solet. Qui enim mundi reverentia consecratos Leo diceret, quos ne uni quidem ex mundo Christiano ante Leonem & ipsius Leonis tempore, cognitos fuisse probari potest?
