Hoc elogium Nicaenis Canonibus convenit; iisque a Leone hic tribui nemo, quod reor, ante vatem Turrianum dubitavit. Ipsa Nicaenae Synodi verba se a Leone respici clamant in 6. canone, quo constituuntur metropolitanorum jura, & privilegia Ecclesiarum nominantur, quae hic Leo optime interpretatur jura tradita antiquitus dignitatis. Ergo neque in hoc Leonis loco quicquam Clementinis Turriani canonibus vel feritur, vel metitur.
units.tr: Thirdly, Turrianus describes this passage of Leo, in which he decrees that the metropolitans, "according to the canons of the holy Fathers, framed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, should keep the dignity handed down to them from ancient times inviolate." Here Turrianus, as everywhere, dreams of his Clementine canons; foolishly, indeed, and without reason, as is his habit. For how could Leo speak of canons consecrated by the reverence of the world, when it cannot be shown that they were known even to the Christian world, either before Leo or in Leo's own time? This description suits the Nicene canons, and I think no one before the prophet Turrianus has doubted that Leo here attributes them to these. The very words of the Nicene Synod cry out that Leo is looking at its sixth canon, in which the rights of metropolitans are established and called privileges of the churches; and Leo interprets these excellently as rights handed down from ancient times of dignity. Therefore in this passage of Leo nothing is either aimed at or measured by Turrianus's Clementine canons.

units.la: Ad eandem Nicaenam Synodum pertinet quartus locus, in quo Leo scribit a, Sanctos Patres salubriter ordinasse, ut bini conventus per annos singulos habeantur, in quibus de omnibus querelis, quae inter diversos Ecclesiae ordines nasci adsolent, judicetur. Disertus est Nicaenorum Patrum in eam rem & notissimus canon quintus {a}. Turrianus mavult de Clementino 37. accipi. Non miror. Sed hic, non quid vellit, sed quid probet, spectamus. Hinc autem nullus probat, Clementinum codicem Leoni fuisse cognitum; imo ne hoc quidem hactenus demonstravit, Leonis temporibus extitisse illum codicem. Quî ergo nos credere vult, Leonem ex eo codice hæc sua sumpsisse, quem ne nunc quidem nos docuit Leone vivo, in rerum natura extitisse? Sed etsi jam tunc extitisset, Leonique cognitus fuisset, non ideo tamen crederem, ad eum hoc loco respexisse Leonem: qui, si eum in animo habuisset, omnino dicturus erat vel Apostolos, vel certe Clementem id ordinasse, quod ipse decernit. Nunc Sanctos Patres cum dicat, verbis eo sensu passim obviis, clarum est non Apostolos, sed Nicænæ Synodi Episcopos significari. Nam ut Sanctos Patres id ordinasse dicas, quod Domini Apostolos ordinasse significare vis, non concedit communis Ecclesiæ loquendi usus; quæ solet in re hujusmodi Patres Apostolis tacite opponere; ut Patres fere semper intelligantur, cæteri, præter Apostolos, veteris Ecclesiæ Christianæ doctores. At (inquit Turrianus {b}) sunt & Apostoli, patres; Fateor; sed tamen qui Patres sunt Apostoli, simpliciter Patres dici non solent; sed honorificentiori vocabulo, vel Apostoli, vel, quod addit Turrianus, Patres Patrum, distinctionis gratia. Non sunt nauci, quae idem blaterat, vt suos Apostolos hic a Leone intelligi vincat. Non Nicaena (inquit) Synodus hoc ipsa primum ordinavit, ut Concilia bis in anno fierent; sed jam olim antiquo canone, id est Apostolico salutariter ordinatum roboravit. Immo inquam, neque id ullo ante Nicaenum decretum canone constitutum fuisse appareret, neque si antiquiori canone decretum fuisse constaret, ideo constaret id decretum antiquius fuisse Apostolicum; neque denique si vel hoc Apostolicum fuisset, eo fieret, ut Turrianico canonum sylloge, Apostolica vel Clementina censenda esset. Nam neque ad Clementinam hanc syllogen pertinere statim necesse est, quaecunque a veteribus habita sunt pro Apostolicis, neque Apostolica fuisse, quaecunque de rebus Ecclesiasticis ante Synodum Nicaenam constituta sunt in Ecclesia; neque, quod primum erat, aliquem de Synodis bis in anno habendis Nicaeno anterius decretum fecisse demonstratur. Futile enim est quod argutatur Turrianus, Nicaenos Patres his verbis, καλῶς ἔχειν εἰδῆναι ἐκάστῳ ἐνιαυτῷ καὶ ἐκάστῳ ἐπαγγελίαν ἡς τῆς ἔτους ἐτὰς σωνόδους γίνεσθαι, significare non novum esse, sed antiquum hoc decretum. Iste vero de more suo nobis narrat somnia, Nicæni Patres nullum veterem canonem vel nominant, vel innuunt. Tantum statuunt, ut bis in anno provinciales habeantur Synodi; bene habere visum est, hoc est, placuit, ut quotannis in singulis provinciis bis fiant Synodi. Et rationem, cur id placuisset, dixerant, ut de singulorum episcoporum latis in subditos sententiis decenter inquiratur. Neque alia Patrum Antiochenorum mens, quos huc advocat Turrianus; ἃ καλῶς ἔχειν εἶναι ὤξε (inquiunt a) μὴ πλείονος συνέλευσεως καὶ ἐπισκέψεως ὑμῶν πάντων τῶν ἐπισκόπων, κ̄ τὸ αὐτὸ συγκεχωρημένων ἐν τῆς Ἀντιοχείας ἐκ διαφόρων ἐπαρχιῶν, ἐν τῷ ὑμετέραν γνώσιν ἀνενεγκάμεν. Quæ bene habere visa sunt, cum majore consideratione, & dijudicatione nostrum Episcoporum simul omnium Antiochiæ ex diversis provinciis in unum collectorum, in vestram notitiam retulimus. Hactenus illi; significantes se, quæ sibi singulis recte habere videbantur, hoc est, quæ sibi singulis placebant, ea in commune collecta, diligenterque considerata, & accuratiori, quam antea judicio, communicatis inter se sententiis, expensa, atque examinata, edere ac publicare,
units.tr: The fourth passage belongs to the same Nicene Synod, in which Leo writes that "the holy Fathers wisely ordained that two assemblies be held each year, in which all complaints that customarily arise among the different orders of the Church should be judged." The fifth canon of the Nicene Fathers, which is clear and very well known for this purpose, deals with it. Turrianus prefers that it be taken to refer to Clementine canon 37. I am not surprised. But here we look not at what he wishes but at what he proves. Yet he proves nothing from this, that the Clementine codex was known to Leo; indeed, he has not even shown so far that this codex existed in Leo's time. How then does he want us to believe that Leo took these things of his from that codex, which not even now has he shown to have existed while Leo was alive? But even if it had existed already at that time, and had been known to Leo, I would still not believe that Leo was looking at it in this passage. For if he had had it in mind, he would certainly have said either that the Apostles, or at least that Clement, had ordained what he himself decrees. As it is, since he says holy Fathers, in words that are everywhere used in that sense, it is clear that not the Apostles but the bishops of the Nicene Synod are meant. For to say that the holy Fathers ordained what you wish to signify that the Lord's Apostles ordained is not allowed by the common usage of the Church, which in matters of this kind is accustomed to set the Fathers tacitly against the Apostles, so that by Fathers are generally understood all the teachers of the early Christian Church apart from the Apostles. But, says Turrianus, there are also Apostles who are fathers. I grant it; yet those who are Apostles are not commonly called simply Fathers, but by a more honourable name, either Apostles, or, as Turrianus adds, Fathers of the Fathers, for the sake of distinction. What he babbles to win the point that Leo here understands his Apostles is worth nothing. "The Nicene Synod," he says, "did not itself first ordain this, that Councils be held twice a year; but long ago, by an ancient canon, that is, by an Apostolic decree, it wisely ordained and confirmed it." Nay, I reply: it does not appear that this was established by any canon before the Nicene decree, nor, if it were shown that it was decreed by an earlier canon, would it therefore be established that this decree was more ancient, or Apostolic; nor finally, even if this too were Apostolic, would it follow that it should be counted among the Apostolic or Clementine canons of Turrianus's collection. For it is not at once necessary that whatever the ancients held to be Apostolic belongs to that Clementine collection, nor that whatever was established in the Church concerning ecclesiastical matters before the Nicene Synod was Apostolic; nor is it demonstrated, which is the first point, that anyone before Nicaea made a decree about holding Synods twice a year. For Turrianus's quibbling is trifling, that the Nicene Fathers, by these words, "it is well to know that each year and each ... Synods are held" [καλῶς ἔχειν εἰδῆναι ἐκάστῳ ἐνιαυτῷ], meant that this decree was not new but ancient. Turrianus, in his usual way, tells us dreams: the Nicene Fathers name or hint at no ancient canon at all. They merely establish that provincial Synods be held twice a year; it seemed good, that is, it pleased, that Synods be held twice a year in each province. And they had given the reason why it pleased them: that the sentences passed by individual bishops against their subjects might be examined fittingly. Nor is the mind of the Antiochene Fathers, whom Turrianus calls in here, any different. "Those things," they say [ἃ καλῶς ἔχειν εἶναι ὤξε], "which seemed well to us, after a fuller assembly and examination of all of you bishops, agreed upon by the bishops gathered at Antioch from different provinces, we have brought to your notice." Thus far they; signifying that what seemed right to them individually, that is, what pleased each of them, had been brought together in common, carefully considered, and weighed by a more accurate judgement than before, with their opinions shared among themselves, and examined, and that they were then issued and published,

units.la: his suis scilicet canonibus explicata, ac sancita. An autem ista, quæ edunt, ab aliis ante se decreta ac constituta essent, nec ne, non definiunt; non significant; nihil denique in alterutram partem statuunt, vel dicunt. Quamquam, ut hoc obiter dicam, neque plane cum illa Antiochenorum oratione convenit superior Nicænorum sermo. Hi enim simpliciter dicunt, καλῶς ἔχειν ἐδόξε συνόδους γίνεσθαι, quod aliud significare non potest, nisi sibi placuisse bene habere visum esse, ut Synodi fiant; id est se decernere, & ex animi sui sententia constituere, ut Synodi fiant. Antiocheni paulo aliter. Non enim hæc simpliciter, ut Nicæni, ajunt, sibi bene habere videri, ut hoc vel illud fiat; sed aliud præterea verbum addunt, nimirum, ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ γνώμῃ ἀναλωσόμεθα. Quæ nobis præclare habere visa sunt, ea in vestram notitiam retulimus. Si sic dixissent Nicæni, Quod bene habere visum est, id decernimus, aut promulgamus, fortasse haberet aliquid coloris Turrianica glossa. Nunc cum simpliciter dixerint, καλῶς ἔχειν ἐδόξε συνόδους γίνεσθαι, nulla vel rationis umbra est, cur ista verba aliud significare suspiceris, quam quod diximus, nimirum Patres ex animi sui sententia decernere, ac constituere, ut Synodi bis fiant. Vt jam satis pateat, quam vana ridiculaque sit Turriani jactantia, negantis licere ullo modo dubitare, quin Leo sanctos, quos ait, Patres Apostolos intelligi voluerit.
units.tr: by these, namely his own canons, explained and sanctioned. Whether the things they publish had been decreed and established by others before them, they do not define, do not indicate, and in short state or say nothing either way. Yet, to add this in passing, the earlier words of the Nicenes do not quite agree with the speech of the Antiochenes. The Nicenes simply say it seemed good that synods should be held [καλῶς ἔχειν ἐδόξε συνόδους γίνεσθαι], which can mean nothing else than that it pleased them to think it good that synods be held; that is, they decree, and establish by their own judgment, that synods be held. The Antiochenes speak somewhat differently. They do not simply say, as the Nicenes do, that it seemed good to them that this or that be done; they add another phrase besides, namely we shall spend [ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ γνώμῃ ἀναλωσόμεθα] on your judgment. What seemed to us to be excellent we have reported to your notice. If the Nicenes had said, "What seemed good we decree or promulgate," the Turrianic gloss might have some colour. But since they simply said it seemed good that synods be held [καλῶς ἔχειν ἐδόξε συνόδους γίνεσθαι], there is not even a shadow of reason why you should suspect these words to mean anything other than what we have said: namely, that the Fathers decree and establish, by their own judgment, that synods be held. So that it may now be plain enough how empty and ridiculous is the boasting of Turrian, who denies that it is allowed in any way to doubt that Leo meant by the holy ones, as he says, the Fathers, the Apostles.

units.la: Hactenus Turrianicas pro Clementinis Canonibus hariolationes verius, quàm argumentationes, excusssimus; pauculis quibusdam de quadragesimae ritu exceptis, quae in sequenti disputationis parte refellentur opportunius. Atque ex his liquet, in omnibus, quae extant, priorum quinque Christianismi saeculorum monumentis nullum plane locum occurrere, in quo vel Clementinae istius Canonum (ut appellantur) Apostolicorum Sylloges diserta fiat mentio, vel aliquid contineatur, ex quo valide, ac legitime demonstrari possit, eam jam tum extitisse, & illorum temporum Christianis cognitam fuisse. Vnde & illud clarum, certumque fit, quod demonstrandum suceperamus, nihil caussae fuisse, cur dubitaret Gelasius, illum Canonum Apostolicorum librum in apocryphorum censum (quod fecit) rejicere atque amandare. Caetera, quae magno, sed vano labore Turrianus ex posterioribus Gelasii saeculo temporibus, plurima congerit, mittimus; qualia sunt quae ex quinque sexta a, septimaque b, & octava b, imo & Tridentina b Synodis describit; item ex Parisiensi
units.tr: Thus far we have shaken out the Turrianic guesses, rather than arguments, offered for the Clementine Canons, except for a few things about the ritual of Lent, which will be refuted more fittingly in the following part of the disputation. And from these things it is clear that in all the surviving monuments of the first five centuries of Christianity there occurs no place at all where this Clementine collection of the so-called Canons of the Apostles is explicitly mentioned, or where anything is contained from which it could be validly and lawfully shown that it already existed at that time and was known to the Christians of those times. Hence it is also clear and certain what we undertook to demonstrate: that there was no reason why Gelasius should hesitate to reject and relegate that book of the Apostolic Canons to the number of the apocrypha, which he did. The rest, which Turrian heaps up with great but vain labour from the times later than Gelasius, we set aside: such as what he describes from the Fifth, Sixth a, Seventh b, and Eighth b Councils, indeed even the Tridentine b Synod; likewise from the Parisian

units.la: a Turr.c. 15.
units.tr: a Turrian, ch. 15.

units.la: Parisiensi Concilio , & Romano sub Gregorio VII. & Tribvrienfi; denique ex Iustiniano, Damasceno, Tarasio, Photio, Bonifacio Moguntino, Nicolao I. Gregorio 9. Leone 4. Ioanne 8. & Nicephoro Multa quidem & in his peccavit; quae si in hominem stylum strinxissem, arguerem. Nunc cum non proprie in Turrianum, sed de Canonibus illis Apostolicis disputemus, nihil necesse est, ea persequi, quae ad hanc, quam agimus, causam non pertinent. Iam illa omnia quae modo memoravimus, cum authorum sint Gelasio recentiorum, nullum operae pretium fecerit, qui ea ad Clementinam canonum syllogen referenda vel esse, vel non esse probaverit. Nos enim jam in priori operis parte confessi sumus, secutis post Gelasium temporibus Canonum Apostolicorum farraginem, & apud Latinos emersisse a Dionysio publicatam, & apud Graecos in Nomocanonem relatam esse, 35. canonibus, quam apud Latinos, auctiorem; deinceps apud Graecos maturius, Trullanae Synodi authoritate confirmatam fuisse; sed & apud Latinos, licet serius, in usum tamen ac notitiam omnium paulatim tandem venisse; quo loco ex his ipsis, quae Turrianus affert, nonnulla, quantum institutio nostro satis esse videbatur, nos quo-que que attulimus. Horum vero omnium, utpote recentiorum; sententia nihil decreto Gelasii praejudicii afferre potest; qui & ipse judicandi authoritatem, & quidem, si adversariis credimus, summam, atque ἀνυπεύθυνον habuit, & fuit sapientissimus, & istis universis antiquior, neque solus sed ex 70. Patrum in Synodum, cui ipse praerat, collectorum, sententia ita judicavit.
units.tr: Council, and the Roman under Gregory VII, and the Tribur; finally from Justinian, Damascene, Tarasius, Photius, Boniface of Mainz, Nicholas I, Gregory IX, Leo IV, John VIII, and Nicephorus. He indeed erred in many things in these too; if I had turned my pen against the man, I would have accused him. But since we are disputing not properly against Turrian but about those Apostolic Canons, there is no need to pursue those things which do not pertain to the cause we are pursuing. Now, all those things which we have just mentioned, since they are the writings of authors more recent than Gelasius, will be of no use to anyone who would prove that they do or do not refer to the Clementine collection of canons. For we have already confessed, in the earlier part of this work, that after Gelasius's time a medley of the Apostolic Canons emerged, published among the Latins by Dionysius, and among the Greeks was brought into the Nomocanon, with thirty-five canons, which was fuller among the Latins; and afterwards among the Greeks, rather earlier, it was confirmed by the authority of the Synod of Trullo; and also among the Latins, though later, it gradually came at last into the use and knowledge of all. In this place we also brought forward some of those things which Turrian cites, as far as our purpose seemed to require. Now the opinion of all these, being more recent, can bring no prejudice to the decree of Gelasius, who also himself had authority to judge, and indeed, if we believe our opponents, the highest and unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνον], and he was most wise, and older than all of them; and he judged thus not alone but by the opinion of the seventy Fathers gathered into the Synod over which he himself presided.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Asseritur & constituitur Gelasii de Apost. Canon. decretum. Disputationis ordo proponitur, quae in partes tres distribuitur. I Pars, qua demonstratur syllogen 35. canonum ex 85. postremorum, neque Apostolorum, neque Clementis, neque vetustissimorum post Apostolos Patrum esse. I. Arg. sumptum ex testimonio omnium (praeter unum Turrianum) Latinorum.
units.tr: The decree of Gelasius concerning the Apostolic Canons is asserted and established. The order of the disputation is set out, which is divided into three parts. Part I, which shows that the collection of thirty-five canons from the last eighty-five is neither of the Apostles, nor of Clement, nor of the most ancient Fathers after the Apostles. First argument, taken from the testimony of all the Latins (except Turrian alone).

units.la: SED ut Gelasium recte & ex vero, illos alios Gelasio posteriores sive Graecos, sive Latinos homines, perperam, falsoque, ac inscite judicasse appareat, jam postremo, non ex nostris somniis, aut hariolationibus, sed ex certis, atque evidentibus argumentis demonstrandum est, illam Apostolicorum canonum farraginem, quam ille apocrypham hi authenticam esse decreverunt, verunt, revera falsam, ac fictitiam esse, neque ab Apostolis editam, neque à Clemente, sapientissimo eorum discipulo collectam, sed ab ignoto tenebrione multis post Apostolorum & Clementis mortem temporibus consarcinatam, & impudenter Apostolis affictam fuisse. Ac quoniam non una est adversariorum sententia, aliis quinquaginta duntaxat, aliis vero 85. canonibus constare eam, cui Apostolicam authoritatem asserunt, collectionem defendentibus; nos primo loco ea explicabimus, quibus triginta quinque postremorum canonum refellitur authoritas, quos Turrianus, & pauci ex Latinis una cum omnibus Graecis probant; secundo loco prioris quinquaginta canones, quos utraque pars Apostolicos esse reconciliatis animis affirmant, confutabimus propriis ac peculiaribus argumentis: tertio denique, eoque postremo loco ea exsequemur, quae utramque in commune opinionem simul, ac semel labefactant, totumque sive 85. sive 50. tantum Canonum Apostolicorum codicem, nullo discrimine pulsant, atque evertunt. Caeterum, quod quibus ostenditur Apostolicae Canonum sylloges novitas, pleraque eadem sint cum iis, quae supra ad Constitutionum authoritatem confodiendam attulimus, nobis in tota hac disputationis parte brevioribus esse licebit; quod plurima eorum, ex quibus sententia nostra demonstratur, jam ante satis confirmata, atque explicata fuerint.
units.tr: But so that it may appear that Gelasius judged rightly and in accordance with the truth, and that those men who came after him, whether Greeks or Latins, judged wrongly, falsely, and unskilfully, it must now be demonstrated, not from our dreams or guesses but from certain and evident arguments, that that medley of Apostolic canons, which he decreed to be apocryphal and they decreed to be authentic, is in truth false and fictitious: that it was neither published by the Apostles nor collected by Clement, their most wise disciple, but was patched together by some unknown scribbler many years after the deaths of the Apostles and Clement, and was shamelessly fastened upon the Apostles. And since the opinion of our opponents is not one, some holding that it consists of only fifty canons, others of eighty-five, defending the collection to which they assert Apostolic authority, we shall first set out those things by which the authority of the last thirty-five canons, which Turrian and a few Latins approve together with all the Greeks, is refuted; second, we shall confute with our own particular arguments the first fifty canons, which both parties agree are Apostolic; third and last, we shall set out those things which shake both opinions together at once and strike and overthrow the whole code of Apostolic Canons, whether eighty-five or only fifty, without any distinction. Moreover, since the novelty of the Apostolic collection is shown by many things which are the same as those we brought forward above to overthrow the authority of the Constitutions, we may be brief in this whole part of the disputation, because most of the things by which our opinion is demonstrated have already been sufficiently confirmed and explained.

units.la: I. Ut ergo ab eo, quod primo loco constituimus, ordiamur, non fuisse vel ab Apostolis editam, vel à B. Clemente litteris mandatam, & in unum cum reliquis Apostolicis (quos vocant) canonibus corpus relatam horum 35. postremorum canonum syllogen, testantur primo contra Turrianum & Græcos viri ex ipsa Latinorum Ecclesia celeberrimi, tum recentes, tum veteres non pauci: Recentes Bellarminus, ac Baronius, maximæ inter adversarios dignitatis, ac famæ, Turriano nullo non nomine anteponendi, quorum extant hanc in rem disertæ supra à nobis laudatæ sententiæ, atque disputationes ex professo contra Turrianicum errorem susceptæ; eorumque tanto major hac in parte ratio habenda est, quod cum post Turrianum scripserint, hominis, cui alioqui plurimum favebant, cujusque fortissimam pro Canonibus defensionem vocant, opinionem deserere, etiam post lectas & excussas eas omnes rationes, quibus ille nititur, & in contrariam partem concedere, vi veritatis victi, coacti sint. Sed & eandem fuisse veterum Latinorum, quotquot canones Apostolorum aliquos admiserunt, de his postremis 35. sententiam, ex iis, quę nuper disputavimus, ita clarum certumque est, ut ne ipse quidem Turrianus contra hiscere possit. Nam, ut à novissimis incipiam, Romanorum Canonistarum, qui his quadringentis proximis retro annis vixerunt, omnis schola non plures, quam quinquaginta Apostolorum canones agnovit; quique ad hunc numerum adjicerentur, eos Gratiano duce ac authore, constantissime explosit, veluti à Leone IX. Romæ Episcopo, ex sua, & antiquorum Patrum authoritate damnatos; ut ex ea sententia apparet, quam illius Pontificis nomine laudatam & à Gratiano in jus Pontificium relatam, supra exhibuimus, disertissime affirmantem, canones Apostolorum (exceptis capitulis quinquaginta) Patres inter apocrypha numerare a. Idem quoque haud dubie sensit is ipse Humbertus, cujus hæc revera verba sunt, quę à Gratiano, Leoni IX. velut authentica, & publicam Romanæ Ecclesiæ sententiam continentia, tribuuntur; ut supra diximus. Is autem Humbertus a. D. 1050. floruit, inter principes Ecclesiasticæ dignitatis viros clarus, Sylvæ candidæ Card. Episcopus, tanti apud
units.tr: I. Therefore, to begin with what we set out first: that this collection of the last thirty-five canons was neither published by the Apostles nor committed to writing by blessed Clement and brought together into one body with the rest of the so-called Apostolic canons, is attested first against Turrian and the Greeks by men most celebrated in the Latin Church itself, both recent and not a few ancient. Among the recent are Bellarmine and Baronius, of the greatest dignity and fame among our opponents, to be preferred to Turrian in every way, whose clear opinions on this matter, cited above by us, and whose disputations undertaken expressly against the Turrianic error, still survive; and their witness must be held the greater in this matter because, although they wrote after Turrian, and although they were otherwise greatly favourable to him, whose "most strong defence" of the Canons they call it, they were compelled, overcome by the force of truth, to abandon his opinion and yield to the contrary side, even after reading and examining all the arguments on which he relies. But also that the opinion of the older Latins, all who admitted some of the Apostolic canons, concerning these last thirty-five was the same, is so clear and certain from those things which we lately disputed that not even Turrian himself can gainsay it. For, to begin with the most recent, the whole school of Roman canonists who lived in the four hundred years just past recognised no more than fifty canons of the Apostles; and those who were added to this number were most constantly rejected by Gratian as leader and authority, as condemned at Rome by Leo IX, bishop of Rome, on the authority of his own and of the ancient Fathers; as appears from that opinion, cited under that Pontiff's name and brought by Gratian into the Pontifical law, which we set out above, affirming most plainly that the Fathers count the canons of the Apostles, except the fifty chapters, among the apocrypha a. The same, beyond doubt, was also the opinion of that very Humbert, whose words these really are, which are attributed by Gratian to Leo IX as authentic and expressing the public opinion of the Roman Church, as we said above. This Humbert flourished in A.D. 1050, famous among the leading men of ecclesiastical dignity, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida, of so great weight with Baronius that he thought the whole of his disputation against the Greeks, written by himself when he was sent as legate to the Emperor of the East at Constantinople, should be appended, annotated, to volume XI in the Appendix to the work.

units.la: a d. 16. c. Clementis. apud Baronium pretii, ut totam ejus contra Græcos disputationem ab ipso scriptam, cum Constantinopolim ad Imperatorem Orientis missus esset legatus, xr. tomo Annotatis subjiciendam in operis Appendice exististimaverit. Neque contra hunc valet putidum Turriani effugium, ignotos ei fuisse hos, quos ipse defendit, 35. græcorum canones. Hi enim ipsi (quod supra demonstravimus) ei a Niceta objecti erant: quos tamen rotunde ac sine ambagibus inter apocrypha a Patribus numeratos esse respondet. Cum autem Humbertus talis, tantusque vir fuerit, ad hæc Romanæ sedi in omnibus addictissimus, nulli dubium esse debet, quin Latinæ totius Ecclesiæ fuerit ea, quam ipse de Canonibus sequitur, sententia. Idipsum Bellarminus a Urbani 2. P. R. testimonio, quod supra exhibuimus, confirmat, quem ait dicere Canones Apostolorum ex toto a Græcis, ex parte a Latinis recipi. Iam & Isodorus Mercator, cujus nono seculo facta collectio apud Latinos obtinuit, diuque regnavit, idem quoque sensisse ex eo apertissime deprehenditur, quod non plures, quam 50 Apostolorum canones memoraverit; cæteros 35. utique non omissurus, si putasset legitimos. Sed quid alios memoro? Antiquissimusipse, celeberrimusque juris Ecclesiastici a-
units.tr: ...to have thought it worth adding, in the Appendix to the volume, the whole of his disputation against the Greeks, which he wrote himself when he was sent as legate to the Emperor of the East at Constantinople (d. 16. c. Clementis). Nor does the foolish evasion of Turrianus hold against him, that the thirty-five Greek canons he defends were unknown to him. For these very canons (as we have shown above) were objected to him by Nicetas, and he answers plainly and without hedging that the Fathers numbered them among the apocrypha. Since Humbert was such a man, and so great a man, and so entirely devoted to the Roman see in all things, there ought to be no doubt that the opinion he follows about the canons was that of the whole Latin Church. Bellarmine confirms this by the testimony of Pope Urban II, which we set out above, whom he says to have stated that the canons of the Apostles are received entirely by the Greeks, and in part by the Latins. Indeed Isidore Mercator, whose collection made in the ninth century prevailed among the Latins and reigned for a long time, is most clearly shown to have held the same view by the fact that he recorded no more than fifty canons of the Apostles; he would certainly not have left out the other thirty-five had he thought them genuine. But why do I cite others? The most ancient and most celebrated of the Latin writers on ecclesiastical law...

units.la: a L. de Script. Eccl. in Clem. pud Latinos rhapsodus Dionysius, sexti vir sæculi, quos primus omnium in Ecclesia publicavit Apostolorum cananes, eos quinquaginta, non plures, edidit: ut ex ejus etiamnum superstite codice, constat. Ille ergo reliquos 35. (siquidem ii jam tum extabant, quod non est verisimile) reprobavit, & à censu Apostolicorum canonum alienos esse judicavit; idque viri judicium, ut cæteros taceam, secuti sunt & Cresconius Afer, qui neque ipse plures quam quinquaginta Apostolorum Canones in sua Canonum Concordia novit, & Adrianus primus urbis Episcopus a. D. 787. qui eum Carolo Magno ad usum Ecclesiarum Occidentalium codicem donavit, in quo hi ipsi Dionysiaci 50. Apostolorum canones, non plures, continebantur, ut ex iis conficitur, quæ Iesuitarum eruditissimus, ac candidissimus Sirmondus Notis in Galliæ nostræ Concilia narrat ad a D. 787 a. Quibus Leonem quoque adjungi decet b, hujus nominis Romæ Episcopum; qui cum codicem, quem describeret, Ecclesiasticum Dionysiacum clarissime intelligat, quos in eo collocat Apostolorum canones, non alios profecto quam Dionysiacos, id est quinquaginta, non plures, significasse putandus est. Denique, ut rem in pauca contraham, ex omnibus Latinis, qui ab a. D. 525. quo fa-eta sta fuisse creditur Dionysiaca collectio, ad Turriani tempora, id est ad a. D. 1573. vixerunt, ne unus quidem fuit, qui illos triginta quinque canones Græcanicos, probaverit, & qui authenticam eorum syl-logen censuerit. Si vel unum protulerit Turrianus, non recuso, quin causam vin-cat. Quo major atque inexcusabilior cen-senda est audacissimi hominis temeritas, qui Latinus Latinorum unus omnium, recentissimus antiquissimorum, monachus Episcoporum & Paparum sententiam deserere, atque infestis siquis palam ag-gredi, atque impugnare, non dubitavit; effecturumque se speravit, ut quæ jam undecim totis sæculis apud suos steterat, ea pro unius Jesuitæ libidine caderet.
units.tr: ...Dionysius, a man of the sixth century, who first of all published the Apostolic canons among the Latins, gave only fifty, no more, as is clear from his codex, which survives to this day (L. de Script. Eccl. in Clem.). He therefore rejected the remaining thirty-five (if indeed they then existed, which is not likely) and judged them foreign to the authority of the Apostolic canons. Others followed this man's judgement, not to mention the rest: Cresconius of Africa, who in his Concordance of Canons likewise knew no more than fifty Apostolic canons; and Hadrian I, bishop of the city, who in 787 gave Charlemagne a codex for the use of the Western churches, which contained these same fifty Dionysian canons and no more, as the most learned and most upright Jesuit Sirmond relates in his notes on the Councils of our Gaul at the year 787. To these should be added Leo, bishop of Rome of that name, who, since he clearly understood the Dionysian ecclesiastical codex that he was copying, must be thought to have meant by the Apostolic canons he placed in it none other than the Dionysian ones, that is, fifty and no more. Finally, to sum up briefly: of all the Latins who lived from 525, when the Dionysian collection is believed to have been made, down to the time of Turrianus, that is to 1573, there was not even one who approved those thirty-five Greek canons and regarded their collection as authentic. If Turrianus can produce even one, I do not object that he wins the case. All the greater and less excusable must be judged the rashness of this most audacious man, a Latin unique among Latins, the most recent of the most ancient, a monk, who did not hesitate to desert the opinion of bishops and popes, to attack it openly and assail it with hostility, and who hoped to bring it about that what had stood among his own people for eleven whole centuries should fall at the whim of a single Jesuit.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Arg. II. contra Syllogen 35. canonum, ex I. ejusdem canone ductum. Arg. III. IV. & V. ex can. 9. 12. & 15. ducta explicantur, & a Turriani strophis vindicantur.
units.tr: Argument II against the collection of the thirty-five canons, drawn from canon I of the same. Arguments III, IV and V, drawn from canons 9, 12 and 15, are explained and defended against Turrianus's stratagems.

units.la: SED res ipsæ Latinorum a Turriani furore sententiam satis defendunt, veriorem-que esse ostendunt. Nam ipsa 35. canonum sylloge si paulo accuratius interrogetur, respondebit se neque ue ab Apostolis editam, neque a Clemente Romano litteris mandatam fuisse.
units.tr: BUT the matter itself defends the Latins' view against Turrianus's fury well enough, and shows it to be the truer. For if the collection of the thirty-five canons is questioned a little more carefully, it will answer that it was neither issued by the Apostles nor committed to writing by Clement of Rome.

units.la: Primo reclamat, qui in ipso limine occurrit primus horum triginta quinque (hoc est Græcanicorum quinquagesimus primus) canon. ἔιτις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος τὸν ἐπιςῤῥέφοντα ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἢ πρὸσδέχεται, ἀλλ' ἀποβάλλεται, καθαιρέω, ὅτι λυπεῖ χρῖςτὸν τὸν ἐπόντα, χαρᾷ γίνεται ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι. Siquis Episcopus, vel presbyter (vel Diaconus) eum, qui à peccatis convertitur, non recipit, sed ejicit, deponatur, quoniam Christum molestia afficit, qui dixit, Gaudium est in cœlo propter unum peccatorem pœnitentiam agentem. Cui canoni jungendus quoque est ejusdem sententiæ sexagesimus primus, edicens, ut clericus negator, si pœnitentiam egerit, recipiatur, ut laïcus. Hunc utrumque merito novum pronunciat Albaspineus, quod is controversias dirimat sequutis post Apostolos sæculis natas. (canon (inquit b) qui de admittendis ad pœnitentiam lapsis factus est, certe ante Cyprianum (id est ante a. D. 250.) sancitus esse non potuit, cum alius esset Ecclesiæ (antea) usus, & illa demum tempestate admittendos esse lapsos decretum sit. Hæc ille vere sane, ac sapienter. Primo enim constat, idque ab ipso Albaspineo
units.tr: First, the very first of these thirty-five (that is, the fifty-first of the Greek canons) raises an objection at the threshold: If any bishop or presbyter does not receive one who turns back from sin, but casts him out, let him be deposed, since he grieves Christ who said, There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. [Εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος τὸν ἐπιστρέφοντα ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας οὐ προσδέχεται, ἀλλ' ἀποβάλλεται, καθαιρείσθω, ὅτι λυπεῖ Χριστὸν τὸν εἰπόντα, Χαρὰ γίνεται ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι.] To this canon should also be joined the sixty-first of the same tenor, which orders that a clergyman who has denied the faith, if he has repented, be received as a layman is. Albaspineus rightly pronounces both of these new, since they settle controversies that arose after the Apostles, in the centuries that followed. (The canon, he says, which was made concerning the admission to repentance of the lapsed, could certainly not have been sanctioned before Cyprian (that is, before the year 250), since the earlier usage of the Church was different, and only in that later age was it decreed that the lapsed be admitted.) He speaks truly and wisely in this. For first it is established, and by Albaspineus himself most brilliantly demonstrated, and now received and acknowledged by all learned men, as he says, and as we taught more fully above, that before the time of Tertullian and Cyprian himself there was a usage of the Church other than what these canons prescribe.

units.la: b Ioan. 3. Albaspineo luculentissime demonstratum est, & nunc apud omnes eruditos receptum, ac confessum est, quod hic ait Albaspineus, & nos supra fusius docuimus, olim, hoc est ante Tertulliani, & ipsius Cypriani tempora, alium fuisse Ecclesiae usum, quam qui his Canonibus praecipitur. Nam & in ipsa urbe Roma ante Zephyrini decretum, & in Hispania etiam diu post illa tempora, fuisse liquet eum disciplinae rigorem, ut lapsis pax & communio negaretur. Sed & post admissos Zephyrini decreto fornicatores, constat tamen ex Tertulliano pristinam severitatem in idololatras, & homicidas fuisse servatam, ut ii ab omni spe Ecclesiasticae reconciliationis excluderentur; & ex Cypriano denique discimus, hunc in idololatras rigorem non ante ejus aevum, hoc est ante a. D. 254. remissum, ac relaxatum fuisse; quae omnia, quod latius in priore hujus operis parte explicata sint, nihil hic necesse est diligentius persequi. Iam vero, quis crediderit, tot sanctissimas Ecclesias, Romanam, Carthaginensem, Hispanicam, alias, hac disciplinae severitate usuras fuisse, ut peccatores conversos non receptura, sed (quod fecerunt) ejectura fuerint, si id ipsum ab Apostolis difertissimo canone damnatum fuisse fcivillent; hoc certe nemo negare potest, Catholicos, cum fornicatores primo, mox & idololatras ad poenitentiam, indeque ad pacem admitterent, cumque de priori indulgentia à Montanistis, de posteriori à Novatianis pulsarentur, omnino hos Apostolorum canones in hac causa adhibituros, atque laudaturos inprimis fuisse; quibus scilicet hæc ipsorum in lapsos levitas contra Montani, & Novatiani inhumanitatem, aperttissime constituitur. Atqui Catholicos, neque in priori contra Montanum certamine, neque in posteriori contra Novatianum, canones istos usurpasse, vel memorasse, constat & ex Tertulliani libro de Pudicitia, & ex Cypriani plurimis hac de controversia scriptis opusculis, maxime vero ex epistola ad Antonianum. Sed hæc, quia cum de Constitutionibus ageremus, fusius executi sumus, nihil necesse est hoc loco repetere; eadem enim omnino Canonum istorum, quæ Constitutionum, hac in parte ratio est. Hoc tantum obiter monebo, hinc clarissime refelli Turriani de Zephyrino Episcopo somnium; cui ille notissimos fuisse vult 85. Apostolorum canones, & sub septuaginta sententiarum nomine memoratos, ac commendatos. Nam si id verum esset, eorum authoritate Zephyrinus
units.tr: b Ioan. 3. For both in the city of Rome itself before the decree of Zephyrinus, and in Spain long after those times, it is clear that such severity of discipline prevailed that peace and communion were denied to the lapsed. Yet even after Zephyrinus's decree admitted fornicators, it is evident from Tertullian that the earlier severity was kept toward idolaters and murderers, so that these were excluded from every hope of ecclesiastical reconciliation; and finally we learn from Cyprian that this rigour toward idolaters was not relaxed or softened before his own age, that is, before the year 254. Since all these things have been explained more fully in the first part of this work, there is no need here to pursue them in more detail. Now who would believe that so many most holy churches, the Roman, the Carthaginian, the Spanish, and others, would have practised such severity of discipline as not to receive converted sinners, but (as they did) to cast them out, if they had known that this very thing had been condemned by the Apostles in a most explicit canon? This at least no one can deny: the Catholics, when they first admitted fornicators to repentance, and afterwards idolaters too, and so to peace, and when they were attacked for the former indulgence by the Montanists and for the latter by the Novatianists, would certainly have used these canons of the Apostles in this dispute and would especially have praised them; for by these canons their own leniency toward the lapsed would plainly have been set against the harshness of Montanus and Novatian. But it is established, both from Tertullian's book On Modesty and from the many small works of Cyprian written on this controversy, and most of all from his letter to Antonianus, that the Catholics used or even mentioned these canons neither in the earlier conflict against Montanus nor in the later one against Novatian. But these points have been treated at length when we dealt with the Constitutions, and there is no need to repeat them here; for the reasoning about these canons in this respect is entirely the same as about the Constitutions. I will only note in passing that Turrianus's dream about Bishop Zephyrinus is clearly refuted by this. He wants the eighty-five Apostolic canons to have been well known to him, and cited and commended under the name of the Seventy Sentences. For if that were true, by their authority Zephyrinus...

units.la: Zephyrinus ad constituendum suum illud de mœchis recipiendis decretum usus esset; imo nullum aliud ea de re decretum fecisset; tantum quod ab Apostolis factum, à Clemente suo antecessore litteris mandatum erat, promulgasset ac renovasset. Atqui ex Tertulliano constat, non modo iltorum nihil fecisse Zephyrinum, sed & insuper hunc qui ipsi notus fuisse fingitur, Apostolorum canonem quadamtenus violasse: dum idololatras & homicidas ipse non minus quam Montanus, vel Tertullianus, rejiceret.
units.tr: Zephyrinus would have used them to establish his own decree on receiving adulterers; indeed, he would have made no other decree on that matter at all. He would merely have promulgated and renewed what the Apostles had done and what his predecessor Clement had enjoined by letter. But it is clear from Tertullian that Zephyrinus not only did nothing of the kind, but also in some measure violated the Apostolic canon that this man is pretended to have known, since he himself rejected idolaters and murderers no less than Montanus or Tertullian did.

units.la: III. Sed & canon nonus supra quinquagesimum ostendit hanc syllogen post Apostolorum tempora factam esse. Is enim vetat in Ecclesia publicari τὰ ψευδεπιγραφα τῶν ἀσεβῶν βιβλία, falso inscriptos impiorum libros; edita ab hæreticis sub ementitis Apostolorum & discipulorum nominibus Euangelia, acta, itineraria &, alia ejusdem farinæ opuscula clarissime denotans; quæ nondum ipsis Apostolorum temporibus nata, postea emerserunt. Quod enim Binius hæc verba ad eos libros refert, de quibus ψευδοδιδασκαλίαι l. 1. Const. c. 7. (aliis 6.) id inquam consistere non potest. Nam quos significant Διαταγεῖς, ii erant libri Paganorum, τῶν ἐξωτικῶν βιβλίων πάντων ἀπέχε (inquit) & quos statim memorant pseudoprophetas iidem Ethnicorum vates erant. Quos vero canon vetat libros; ii sunt haereticorum; ut apparet, tum ex eo, quod Pseudoprophetas vocat, tum ex eo quod a quibusdam in Ecclesia publicari eos significat, quorum neutrum Paganorum libris convenit.
units.tr: III. But the ninth canon after the fiftieth also shows that this collection was made after the time of the Apostles. It forbids that the spurious books of the impious [τὰ ψευδεπίγραφα τῶν ἀσεβῶν βιβλία] be published in the Church, books falsely ascribed to the impious, clearly denoting the Gospels, Acts, Itineraries and other little works of the same stamp that heretics issued under the false names of the Apostles and their disciples, and which emerged later, not yet in the very times of the Apostles. For Binius's reference of these words to the books concerning which the false teachings [ψευδοδιδασκαλίαι] appear in Book 1 of the Constitutions, chapter 7 (or 6 in others), cannot stand, I say. For the books that the Constitutions [Διαταγεῖς] refer to were the books of the pagans, since it says, "abstain from all external books" [τῶν ἐξωτικῶν βιβλίων πάντων ἀπέχε], and the ones it mentions immediately afterwards, the false prophets, were the same soothsayers of the heathen. But the books the canon forbids are those of heretics, as is evident both from the fact that it calls them false prophets and from the fact that it signifies that they are published in the Church by some people, neither of which applies to the books of the pagans.

units.la: IV. Quarto idem demonstrat allata in 62. canone interdicti suffocatorum, & morticinorum esus ratio; τοῦτο γὰρ (inquit) ὁ νόμος ἀπεῖπεν, Hoc enim lex prohibuit.
units.tr: IV. Fourthly, the same is shown by the reason given in canon 62 for the prohibition on eating what is strangled and what has died of itself: "For this (it says) the law forbade" [τοῦτο γὰρ ὁ νόμος ἀπεῖπεν].

units.la: Veri Apostoli hujusmodi rebus vesci Christianos vetuerunt ad vitandum Iudaeorum scandalum; non ob legis ipsius authoritatem, quam hac in parte a Christo Domino abrogatam luculentissime passim docent. Tantumque abeo abest Paulus , ut quamquam ob hujusmodi simpliciter esum vel deponi vel segregari jubeat, (quod inhumanus & vere Iudaicus canon sancit) ut solo excepto scandali casu, libere quemvis, pura que conscientia, etiam idolothytis (quorum non minor, quam suffocatorum erat religio) vesci posse docent.
units.tr: The true Apostles forbade Christians to eat such things in order to avoid giving offence to the Jews, not on account of the authority of the law itself, which they teach very clearly throughout was abrogated in this respect by Christ the Lord. And Paul is so far from ordering that anyone be deposed or segregated for merely eating such things (which the inhuman and truly Jewish canon decrees) that he teaches that, except in the case of scandal alone, anyone may freely eat with a pure conscience, even meat sacrificed to idols (whose religious scruple was no less than that of meat strangled or dead).

units.la: Ergo neque hic Apostolicus canon est, neque vel Apostolica, vel Clementina ea sylloge, in qua eum insertum legimus.
units.tr: Therefore this is neither an Apostolic canon, nor is that collection, whether Apostolic or Clementine, in which we read it inserted.

units.la: V. Sed id ipsum multo etiam clarius evincit, qui paulo post sequitur canon 15. supra quinquagesimum; ἐπὶς κλησικὸς ἐυρέθη εὐχέσθη τῇ Κυριακῇ ἡμέραν νηστεύων, ἢ τὸ σάββατον, πλὴν τῆς ἑνὸς μόνης, καθαιρείσθω· εἰ δὲ λαϊκὸς, ἀφοριζέσθω. Siquis Clericus inventus fuerit die Dominico jejunare vel sabbato, praterquam uno solo, deponatur; Sin autem laicus segregetur. Non esse hunc canonem Apostolicum; ita pugnat Baronius a; Quomodo quaso (inquit) tot tamque disertos antiquos Patres, qui de jejunio sabbati instituerunt disputationem, canon ille praeteriit, ut à nemine citatus reperiatur? Vel quonam pacto obsecro, Romana Ecclesia contra omnium Apostolorum canonem sabbati jejunium suscepisset, vel eorum Episcopus Clemens, id fieri permisisset, qui quod statuissent Apostoli, & ipse scripsisset, perquam optime sciret? Vel quomodo extraditione Petri & Pauli Apostolorum Principum, ejusmodi diei sabbati jejunii sibi vendicare est solita eadem Ecclesia observantiam, quam Apostolorum canoni penitus adversari nosset? Hactenus Baronius, quocum & Bellarminus *,& Possevinusb,& Biniusc,& Petaviusd, & cæteri, ni fallor, omnes, uno excepto Turriano, & recentiores & vetustiores Latini consentiunt. Petavii verba de sabbati jejunio supra recitavimus; hunc canonem velut spurium & alienum diserte rejicentis; negantisque fieri potuisse, ut is ab Apostolis communi decreto constitueretur ex illa, quam Augustini esse demonstrat, præscriptione, neque Scripturæ, authoritate, neque universalis Ecclesiæ traditione determinatum esse, sabbato-ne jejunare deceat, an prandere, sed ejus, in qua veriseris Ecclesiæ, consuetudini obtemperandum esse. Hæc illi. Sed ut frangatur singularis Turriani impudentia, qui solus inter suos hunc etiam canonem contendit vere esse Apostolicum, breviter hoc loco repetenda sunt; quæ de jejuniorum, & dierum certorum natura, atque ingenio, deque sabbato, & dominico nominatim & ex Apostolorum veris libris, & ex veterum monumentis in priori operis parte contra pseudodiataxes diximus. Primo enim ex Paulo demonstravimus de diebus, nominatim de sabbatis nefas esse judicari Christianum. Non est ergo iste Paulus, non est Apostolorum (qui omnes cum Paulo consentiebant) quisquam, qui & clericos & laicos, id est omnes Christianos, de sabbato judicat; Vtillud mittam, quod ex eodem Paulo istic quoque attulimus, nos si manducaverimus nequaquam idcirco abundaturos, hoc est nihilo plus consecuturos, quam si abstinuerimus; quod (ut liquet) recta cum isto canone pugnat, qui sabbato vel dominico jejunantem deponit, aut segregat; manducantem, Ecclesiæ communione, gradus honore frui decernit. Secundo, ibi- dem ex Tertulliano a probavimus, quod die Dominico jejunare nefas duceretur, id nulla scripta lege, solius traditionis titu-lo, & inde consuetudinis patrocinio stetis-se; quod liquido falsum est, si ille ritus facto ab Apostolis canone, à Clemente conscripto sub gravissima poena constitutus, sancitusque erat. Tertio, & illud quoque ex Hieronymo demonstravimus, constare ex Actis & Paulum, & qui cum eo erant, die dominica jejunasse. Quis crediderit sanctissimum virum idipsum admisisse, quod & ipse & caeteri Apostoli scilicet depositione in clerico, segregatione in laico dignum judicarant? Quarto, ex Augustino, Cassiano, Innocentio & aliis plurimis ostendimus, omnibus sabbatis Romae & paucis aliis Occidentis locis jejunari solenne fuisse; eumque usum & Urbicum quemdam disputatorem apertissime, & Innocentium ipsum haud obscure necessarium existimasse. Qui factum, ut homines Catholici tam enormiter ab Apostolica lege desciverint? ut Innocentius Apostolicus Apostolicum canonem; & quidem à Clemente Romano descriptum, ita contumeliose pulsaverit? Quinto, diximus contra Urbicum illum sabbatarium jejunatorem ex professo scripsisse Augustinum, ac illud jejunium, licet non putaverit necesario servandum, liberum tamen, & si cui libuerit, citra noxam usurpandum fuisse. Qui factum, ut vir tantus eum innoxium pronuntiet, quem Apostoli vel gradu suo dejici, vel communione privari jusserant? Qui factum, ut in tali causa Apostolicam hanc scilicet regulam, ne semel quidem objecerit adversario, vel omnino memoraverit? Denique ex eodem Augustino recitavimus, non inveniri definitum praecepto Domini vel Apostolorum, quibus diebus non oporteat jejunare, quo nihil vel stultius, vel impudentius dici poterit, si Apostolorum vere est hic canon, quo disertissime definitur neque sabbato, neque dominica die jejunandum. Atque ex his patet, Apostolicum esse non posse hunc de sabbati a jejunio immunitate canonem. Nunc breviter Turriano satisfaciamus, qui & ratione & antiquitate & omnibus suis invitis Apostolicum esse pugnat. Primo id probat libro Constitutionum quinto, & septimo. Διαταγῶν testimonium satis supra demonstravimus nullam habere vim; qui & ipsi scilicet spurii sunt, & novi, falsique nominis scriptores. Secundo Ignatium citat, cujus haec verba circumferuntur c, Εἴτις ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ ἡ σάββατον νηστεύει (πλὴν ἑνὸς σαββάτῳ) βάτ᾽ τὸ πάσχα ) ἐτ᾽ χειςοκτόν᾽ ἐςί, Quicunque Dominicam, aut Sabbatum jejunaverit, (praeter unum Sabbatum Paschæ) ipse est Christi interfector. Nihil hic necesse est ea persequi, quæ Petavius, & alii adversarii ad hanc objectionem solvendam afferre solent, vana pleraque, & sola istorum suspicione nixa. Breviter respondeo hunc Ignatium non magis fide dignum esse, quam eos, quorum testis adducitur, Apostolos. Est enim & ipse spurius & fictitius, ac personatus Ignatius; sanctissimi Martyris nihil habens præter nudum nomen, quod impostor istius ad Philippenses epistolæ parens, ad agendam suam fabulam impudenter assumpsit. Nam nequid jam de cæteris dicam Ignatii nomen præferentibus epistolis, quas viri docti veras & genuinas esse, sed frustra, ut mihi quidem videtur, contendunt, illam certe quæ ad Philippenses scripta extat, & ea quæ recitavimus verba continet, antiquis Patribus ignotam fuisse ex eo satis constat, quod neque ejus Eusebius, vel Hieronymus, usquam meminerunt, qui Ignatii res gestas & opera diligentissime exsequuntur; neque veterum ante sextum sæculum, qui Ignatii epistolas sæpe laudant, quisquam aliquid ex hac citasse reperiatur. Ut alia nunc mittam falsimoniæ ex iisipsis, quæ epistola continet, ducta argumenta (de quibus videat, qui volet Rev. Usserium a) hoc certe, quod ipse scriptor tam, atroci sententia quasi Christi interfectores, eos percellit, qui vel sabbato, vel die dominico jejunaverint, hoc inquam unum, etiamsi nihil aliud esset, clarissime docet, istum nihil minus esse, quam Ignatium, neque eum veteribus, ut Augustino, Innocentio, aliis, pro Ignatio unquam habitum. Sed omnem superat impudentiam, quod Turrianus, non hos modo falsos, & personatos scriptores, sed etiam ipsum Augustinum suo huic Apostolico canoni testem adducit; Canonem (inquit) 64. (aliis 65.) de non jejunando sabbato; & dominico, Apostolorum esse, testimonio est, non solum Ignatius, & Clemens, sed etiam B. Augustinus in Epistola, quam ad Casulanum scripsit, contra Urbicum Ecclesias Orientis accusantem, quæ sabbato non jejunant. Hæc ille quæ quia fronte scripserit, vel id satis ostendit, quod à nobis nuper descriptum in ipsa illa ad Casulanum epistola profitetur Augustinus se quibus diebus non oportet jejunare, & quibus oportet, præcepta Domini, vel Apostolorum, non invenire definitum. Potuit-ne clarius, vel difertius testari, non esse huic Apostolorum, quem Turrianus defendefendit, canonem? Ille quidem, fateor, & Orientis, & alias etiam plurimas Ecclesias, imo omnes (Romana, & paucis aliis exceptis) sabbatum à jejunio immunes servantes à stultissimi Vrbici disputatoris calumniis defendit; sed earum morem ab Apostolico aliquo decreto fluxisse nusquam dicit; quinimo rem totam libera esse observationis pugnat, varie vel usurpandam, vel omittendam pro eorum locorum, in quibus degimus, ratione. Atque hoc loco obiter castigandus venit Turrianus, qui quod ait Tertullianus de iis, qui Saturni diem otio & victui decernebant, non Iudaico tamen ritu, perperam ac inepte de Christianis Orientis accipit die sabbati non jejunantibus. Totius vero loci genius, ac series ostendit, Tertullianum non de Christianis, sed de Paganis quibusdam intelligere, qui & ipsi, licet à Judaismo alieni, sabbata nihilo secius religiose colebant. Æque (inquit a) si diem solis latitiæ indulgemus alia longe ratione, quam religione solis, secundo loco ab eis sumus, qui diem Saturni otio & victui decernunt, exorbitantes & ipsi ab Iudaico more, quem ignorant. Eos enim de quibus hæc dicit, non fuisse Christianos liquet; plane ut Persas, quos proxime superioribus verbis memoraverat; Alii (inquit; plane humanius, & verisimilius Solem credunt Deum nostrum. Ad Persas si forte deputabimur, licet solem non in linteo depictum adoremus, habentes ipsum utique in suo clypeo, id est in ipso illo orbe, e quo nobis lucet. Sed, ut ad sabbati a jejunio immunitatem redeamus, Turrianus nequicquam conatus eam Apostolico canone decretam asserere, postremo ad id respondet, quod & Baronius, & nos supra objecimus; scilicet contempti Christi, violataeque Apostolorum authoritatis manifestam esse Romam, quae sabbatis jejunat, si id ab Apostolis vere interdictum fuit. Hanc (inquit) consuetudinem sabbato non jejunandi Apostoli non in commune cunctis fidelibus tradiderunt, sed Ecclesiis Orientis, non solum propter Simonianos inde ortos, qui mundum, a cujus creatione sabbato Deus requievit, opus ejus esse negabant, sed quod jam per spiritum praecognoscerent, futuros quoque esse in illis locis haereticos alios Manichaeos, Eustathianos, Marcionistas, Lampetianos, & Messalianos, qui in Paphlagonia apparuerunt; hos enim scribit Anastasius Antiochenus Patriarcha, solutos secundum dogma suum sabbato, & die Dominico jejunare. Sed haec mera sunt Turriani commenta, ex causse studio conficta. Primo enim ipse Canonis author neque que hic, neque usquam alibi prodit hanc fuisse institutæ sabbati à jejunio immunitatis rationem. Secundo, neque quisquam veterum, (qui multi illius ritus meminerunt) aliquid hujusmodi de eo tradidisse reperitur. Et Diatageis ipsi non alio hoc sabbati privilegium referunt, quam ad creationis memoriam, ut unam errandi occasionem habuisse videantur Mosaicum de sabbato feriando præceptum quod cum in Decalogo extare viderent, moralis legis breviario, id quoque ad nos pertinere putaverint. Itaque sabbato, non solum non jejunare, sed etiam otiari præceperunt.
units.tr: V. But this is shown even more clearly by the canon that follows shortly after, the fifteenth beyond the fiftieth: If any cleric is found fasting on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except only the one, let him be deposed; but if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated. [Εἴ τις κληρικὸς εὑρεθῇ τῇ Κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ νηστεύων ἢ τὸ σάββατον, πλὴν τῆς ἑνὸς μόνης, καθαιρείσθω· εἰ δὲ λαϊκός, ἀφοριζέσθω.] That this canon is not Apostolic is maintained by Baronius a: Why, I ask, (he says) did that canon pass over so many and such eloquent ancient Fathers, who debated the fasting on the Sabbath, so that it is never found cited by anyone? Or, I beg you, how could the Roman Church have adopted the fasting on the Sabbath against the canon of all the Apostles, or how could its bishop Clement have permitted it, when he, who wrote down what the Apostles had decreed, would have known it perfectly well? Or how, by the tradition of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the same Church has come to claim for itself the observance of a Sabbath fast, which it knew to be entirely opposed to the canon of the Apostles? Thus Baronius. With him agree, as far as I know, all the recent and older Latin writers: Bellarmine, Possevinus, Binius, Petavius d, and the rest, with the single exception of Turrianus. We have already quoted Petavius's words on Sabbath fasting, where he expressly rejects this canon as spurious and foreign, and denies that it could have been established by the Apostles by common decree. By that prescription, which he shows to be Augustine's, he holds that the question whether it is fitting to fast or to dine on the Sabbath is determined neither by the authority of Scripture nor by the universal tradition of the Church, but that one must obey the custom of the Church in which one truly lives. So much for him. But to break the singular impudence of Turrianus, who alone among his people insists that this canon too is truly Apostolic, the following points must be briefly repeated here, which we set out in the earlier part of our work against the pseudo-diatassēs, concerning the nature and character of fasts and of certain days, and concerning the Sabbath and the Lord's day by name, both from the genuine books of the Apostles and from the monuments of the ancients. First, we showed from Paul that it is wrong to judge a Christian about days, and about Sabbaths in particular. So this is not Paul, nor is it any of the Apostles (all of whom agreed with Paul), who passes judgment on the Sabbath for both clerics and laymen, that is, for all Christians. I shall pass over what we also quoted there from the same Paul: that if we eat we shall in no way be the better for it, that is, we shall gain nothing more than if we abstain. This (as is plain) directly contradicts that canon, which deposes or excommunicates the one who fasts on the Sabbath or the Lord's day, and decrees that the one who eats shall enjoy communion with the Church and the honour of his rank. Second, in the same place we showed from Tertullian a that to fast on the Lord's day was regarded as wrong, and that this rested on no written law, only on the title of tradition and so on the patronage of custom. This is plainly false if that practice had been established by a canon of the Apostles, written down by Clement, and sanctioned under the most severe penalty. Third, we also showed from Jerome that it is clear from the Acts that both Paul and those who were with him fasted on the Lord's day. Who could believe that so holy a man would have permitted the very thing which he himself and the other Apostles had judged worthy of deposition in a cleric and excommunication in a layman? Fourth, from Augustine, Cassian, Innocent and many others we showed that fasting on every Sabbath was customary at Rome and in a few other places in the West, and that both a certain Urbicus, a debater, and Innocent himself openly and not obscurely considered this practice necessary. How did it happen that Catholic men so grossly departed from the Apostolic law? How did Innocent, an Apostolic man, so contemptuously assail an Apostolic canon, and indeed one written down by Clement of Rome? Fifth, we pointed out that Augustine wrote expressly against that Urbicus, the Sabbath faster, and that although he did not think that fast was to be kept as necessary, it was nevertheless free, and might be practised without harm by whoever wished. How did it happen that so great a man pronounced harmless one whom the Apostles had ordered to be deprived of his rank or cut off from communion? How did it happen that in such a case he never once objected to his opponent this Apostolic rule, nor even mentioned it at all? Finally, from the same Augustine we quoted that there is no precept of the Lord or of the Apostles defining on which days one should not fast; nothing could be said more foolish or more shameless than this, if this canon were truly Apostolic, since it most expressly defines that one must fast neither on the Sabbath nor on the Lord's day. From these points it is plain that this canon on exemption from fasting on the Sabbath cannot be Apostolic. Now let us briefly answer Turrianus, who, against reason, antiquity and all his own witnesses, insists that it is Apostolic. First, he proves this from the fifth and seventh books of the Constitutions. We have already shown sufficiently above that the testimony of the Diatageis has no force, since they are themselves spurious, and written by writers of recent and false name. Second, he cites Ignatius, whose words are circulated as follows: Whoever fasts on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except the one Sabbath of Easter, is a murderer of Christ. [Εἴ τις ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ ἢ σάββατον νηστεύει (πλὴν ἑνὸς σαββάτου τοῦ πάσχα) ἢ τὴν κυριακήν, χριστοκτόνος ἐστί.] There is no need here to pursue what Petavius and other opponents usually bring forward to answer this objection; most of it is empty and rests only on their own conjecture. I answer briefly that this Ignatius is no more worthy of trust than the Apostles whose witness is alleged. For he himself is spurious and fictitious, a masked Ignatius, having nothing of the holy martyr except the bare name, which the impostor who wrote the epistle to the Philippians shamelessly took up in order to carry on his own fable. For, to say nothing further of the other epistles that bear Ignatius's name, which learned men contend (but in vain, as it seems to me) are true and genuine, it is quite certain from this fact that the epistle which is extant as written to the Philippians, and which contains the words we have quoted, was unknown to the ancient Fathers: neither Eusebius nor Jerome, who most carefully go through the deeds and writings of Ignatius, ever mention it anywhere, and no one among the ancients before the sixth century, who often praise the epistles of Ignatius, is found to have cited anything from it. To leave aside the other arguments for its falsity drawn from the contents of the epistle (on which let anyone who wishes consult the Reverend Ussher a), this one thing, at least, clearly shows that this writer is anything but Ignatius: that he strikes down with such a savage sentence, as though they were murderers of Christ, those who fast on the Sabbath or on the Lord's day; and that the ancients, such as Augustine and Innocent and others, never regarded him as Ignatius. But Turrianus surpasses all shamelessness in bringing forward as a witness for this Apostolic canon not only these false and masked writers, but even Augustine himself. The canon (he says) 64 (in others 65) concerning not fasting on the Sabbath and on the Lord's day is Apostolic; the testimony is not only that of Ignatius and Clement, but also of Blessed Augustine in the epistle which he wrote to Casulanus, against Urbicus, who accused the Churches of the East, which do not fast on the Sabbath. That he wrote this with a straight face is shown well enough by the fact that Augustine, as we recently set out, professes in that very epistle to Casulanus that he does not find defined by precept of the Lord or of the Apostles on which days one ought not to fast, and on which one ought. Could he have borne witness more clearly or more expressly that this is not a canon of the Apostles, which Turrianus defends? Augustine indeed, I admit, defends from the slanders of that most foolish debater Urbicus both the Eastern Churches and many others, nay all (except the Roman and a few others), who keep the Sabbath free from fasting; but he nowhere says that their custom flowed from any Apostolic decree. On the contrary, he holds that the whole matter is free to be observed, and may be used or omitted, as the practice of the places in which we live may require. And here, in passing, Turrianus deserves to be rebuked, since he takes what Tertullian says of those who assigned the day of Saturn to leisure and to food, yet not in the Jewish manner, as referring wrongly and foolishly to Christians of the East who do not fast on the Sabbath. But the whole drift and sequence of the passage shows that Tertullian is speaking not of Christians but of certain pagans, who, though alien to Judaism, nonetheless kept their Sabbaths no less religiously. In the same way (he says) if we indulge the day of the sun for joy by a far different reason than the religion of the sun, we are in the second place from those who assign the day of Saturn to leisure and food, going astray themselves from the Jewish custom, which they do not know. That those of whom he speaks were not Christians is plain, just as with the Persians whom he had mentioned in the words immediately before: Others (he says), more humanely and more plausibly, believe the sun to be our God. If by chance we shall be reckoned among the Persians, although we do not worship the sun painted on linen, since we have it indeed on our shield, that is, in that very orb from which it shines upon us. But to return to the exemption from fasting on the Sabbath: Turrianus, having vainly tried to assert that it was decreed by an Apostolic canon, finally replies to what both Baronius and we have objected above, namely that if it was truly forbidden by the Apostles, then Rome, which fasts on Sabbaths, is manifestly guilty of contempt for Christ and of violating the authority of the Apostles. The Apostles (he says) did not hand down this custom of not fasting on the Sabbath to all the faithful in common, but to the Churches of the East; not only on account of the Simonians who arose from there, who denied that the world, from whose creation God rested on the Sabbath, was his work, but because they already foreknew by the Spirit that there would be in those regions other heretics, the Manichaeans, Eustathians, Marcionites, Lampetians and Messalians, who appeared in Paphlagonia; for Anastasius, the Patriarch of Antioch, writes that these, following their own doctrine, were loosed from the Sabbath and fasted on the Lord's day. But these are the mere inventions of Turrianus, fabricated for the sake of his cause. For first, the author of the canon himself neither states here nor anywhere else that this was the reason for establishing the Sabbath's exemption from fasting. Second, none of the ancients, who mention that rite often, is found to have handed down anything of this kind about it. And the Diatageis themselves refer this privilege of the Sabbath to nothing other than the memory of creation, so that they seem to have had a single occasion for error: since they saw in the Decalogue the Mosaic precept about keeping the Sabbath as a rest, they thought it also pertained to us as part of the summary of the moral law. Thus they commanded that on the Sabbath one should not only not fast, but also keep leisure.

units.la: Tertio, sunt ex veteribus, ut urbicus apud Augustinum disputator, & omnes in genere Romani apud Cassianum, qui diserte testantur, Apostolos nihili fecisse hanc à Turriano allatam hujus decreti rationem. Ii enim ajebant Petrum, cum ipso illo Simone, cujus hæresim Turrianus somniat fuisse interdicti sabbatarii jejunii occasionem; Petrum, inquam, ajebant cum illo Apostata certaturum, jejunium in ipsum illum diem & in præsens indixisse; & in posterum ut idem servaretur, instituisse; nedum, ut ob Simonem (quod gratis fingit Turrianus) refugiendum sabbati jejunium putaverit. Quarto, quamcunque statuas hujus præcepti occasionem, ipsum quidem præceptum à Canonum, & Constitutionum authoribus omnibus omnino Christianis poni, & quidem gravi pœna sancitum, patet. Quod enim solis Orientalibus datum vaticinatur Turrianus, id unde quæso habet? Nullum hujus distinctionis vel in Canonibus, vel in Constitutionibus apparet vestigium. Omnia in diversum eunt. Nam Constitutiones (quarum canones Turrianus partem esse vult) ad omnes omniho Christianos è Gentibus vocatos dirigantur; Apostoli & presbyteri (inquiunt a) omnibus, qui e genti-bus in Dominum Jesum credidistis, gratia vobis & pax ab omnipotente Deo per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum in agnitione ejus multiplicetur. Iis canones isti figunt quos alloquuntur; Omnes de gentibus fideles alloquuntur, Ergo & omnibus fidelibus canones istos figunt; adeoque & Romanis, nisi forte somniet Turrianus solos in Oriente fideles fuisse; Romæ & in Occidente nullos fuisse fideles, vel nullos saltem è Gentibus conversos. Sed & canonum author perorans omnibus Episcopis, adeoque & Occidentalibus, sua decreta commendat; Hæc vero de regulis (inquit) constituta sint vobis per nos, o Episcopi. Vos autem obtemperantes, salua-bimini & pacem habebitis. Iste Romę antistitem, tistiteum, vel Episcopum non censuit, vel si censuit, suis certe canonibus æque ac cæteros, subjecit. Denique nulla ratio est, cum cæteri omnes canones omnibus Christianis positi sint, cur hic unus ad solos Orientales pertineat; qui una cum cæteris, eodem ordine, eadem ratione, nullo omnino discrimine, positus legitur. Quod si Occidentales ejus jugum à se excogitatis nescio quibus ratiunculis, impune amoliri fas est, licebit & Orientalibus, vel Australibus, aut Borealibus Christianis aliorum canonum obsequium, ex caussis eadem ratione, eodemque jure excogitatis detrectare. Imo solvetur ac ruet omnis omnium divinarum, humanarumque legum authoritas, si semel admittantur hujusmodi cavillationes: ut in caussas præcipientis inquirant subditi, neque ad se legem, quantumvis generalem, pertinere putent, nisi & quam commenti sunt ejus caussam, ea ad se pertineat. Itaque si vere (quod vult Turrianus) Apostolorum est hic canon, causa dici non potest, cur quæ quod hic decernit, tot jam sæcula contemnit, ac violat Roma, non gradu, ac communione Ecclesiastica excidisse, planeque ab Apostolicis Christianis aliena & esse, & fuisse jam olim censeatur. Non potest minori mercede Turrianus suorum canonum authoritatem constituere. Quod optime viderunt Baronius, & Petavius, qui cum simili hujus effugio ad Ignatianam Philippensibus solis scriptam epistolam (quanquam & hic quoque, temere, ac frustra) usi sunt, non sunt ausi in Apostolicum canonem, omnibus, ut liquet, Christianis positum idem moliri; omissaque frigida cavillatione rotunde, quod res est, confessi sunt, nimirum falsum esse, & falso Apostolis affictum hunc canonem; ejus adeo authoritate minime teneri Romam. Postremo, ut hunc locum concludam, etiamsi id Turriano, quod gratis, ac praeter omnem rationem postulat, donaverimus; nimirum eam fuisse suorum Legislatorum mentem, ut in iis duntaxat locis vigeret hic eorum canon, in quibus haeretici esse nt qui mundum hunc a vero & summo Deo conditum negarent, ne sic quidem Romam liberaverit. Constat enim in ea ipsa urbe & Simonem, & Marcionem, & Manichaeos ab eo commemoratos, venena sua sparsisse sedesque & domicilia quaesivisse atque habuisse; omniaque fere tetra, ac sordida eo confluxisse, ut ne hoc quidem caussificari posset Turrianus, quominus Romam suam turpiter in Apostolos rebellasse fateatur; si hic quidem Apostolorum est, qui ab ea tot jam saecula secure violatur, tur, ac conculcatur canon. Quod cum ne ipsi quidem Græci de antiquioribus Romanis dicturi sint, necessario denique fatendum est, quorumvis potius esse, quam Apostolorum, Turrianicum illum canonem. Sed explosa, ac confutata Turriani cavillatione, superest, ut paucis Bellarmini conjecturam a refellamus; qui falsatum à Græcis posterioribus hunc canonem hariolatur, inserto sabbati nomine, cum initio solius diei dominicæ jejunium hoc decreto prohiberetur. Concederem, si extaret aliquis vel inter Græcos, vel inter ipsos Latinos codex, in quo hujus diversitatis aliqua vel umbra cerneretur. Nunc cum omnes & scripti & excusi libri summo consensu sabbati æque ac dominici nomen præferant; cum idem omnes Constitutionum codices exhibeant; cum Humbertus idem jam a. D. 1050. in hoc sibi à Niceta totidem, quot nunc legitur verbis objecto canone fuisse testetur, neque de lectione conqueratur; aut Græcos insimulet; cum Trullani b Patres a. D. 569. de Latinis expostulent sabbato jejunantibus τὸ παραδόθεισαν ἐκκλησιαστικὴν ἀκολουθίαν, prater traditam Ecclesiasticam consequentiam, quod non potest alio, quam ad hunc canonem, similemque Apostolicam διάταξιν referri; cum denique LatinoLatinorum ante hæc tempora nemo Græcis de vitiata hnjus canonis lectione litem intenderit; nemo recentiorum aliam, quam hanc ipsam Græcorum, nemoraverit, apparet sabbati vocabulum jam inde à principio in hoc canone scriptum fuisse, neque unquam aliter lectum fuisse quam nunc legitur; & hanc Bellarmino conjecturam de uno causæ studio, cui plurimum indulget, in mentem venisse; cujus licentiæ exemplum si cæteri inmitentur, ut nobis quod in veterum monumentis non placet, id velut à Græcis, Latinisve additum, expungere nulla codicum authoritate, nullaque ratione allata, liceat; nemo non videt, actum esse de omni veterum librorum fide. Atque hæc de 65. canone satis.
units.tr: Third, there are the ancients, such as the citizen disputant in Augustine and all the Romans in general in Cassian, who expressly testify that the Apostles had nothing to do with the reason for this decree that Turrianus brings forward. They said that Peter, when he was about to contend with that same Simon, whose heresy Turrianus dreams was the occasion for the prohibition of the Sabbath fast, proclaimed a fast for that very day and for the present, and then ordered that it be kept in future. Surely they did not think that the Sabbath fast ought to be avoided because of Simon, as Turrianus invents without any warrant. Fourth, whatever cause you assign to this precept, it is plain that the precept itself is laid down by all the authors of the Canons and Constitutions, all of them Christians without exception, and that it is enacted under a serious penalty. For where does Turrianus get his claim that it was given only to the Orientals? There is no trace of this distinction either in the Canons or in the Constitutions. Everything points the other way. The Constitutions (of which Turrianus wants the Canons to be a part) are addressed to all Christians called from the Gentiles: "The Apostles and elders" (they say a) "to all of you who from the Gentiles have believed in the Lord Jesus, grace and peace be multiplied to you from almighty God through our Lord Jesus Christ in the knowledge of him." These canons are laid upon those whom they address. They address all the faithful from the Gentiles; therefore these canons are laid upon all the faithful, and so upon the Romans too, unless perhaps Turrianus dreams that only the faithful in the East existed, and that there were no faithful at Rome or in the West, or at least none converted from the Gentiles. But the author of the canons, in concluding, also commends his decrees to all the bishops, and so to the Western bishops as well: "These things, O bishops, are laid down for you by us as rules. Obeying them, you will be saved and will have peace." He did not regard the bishop of Rome, whether as pontiff or bishop, as one of these, or if he did, he certainly made him subject to his canons like the rest. Finally, since all the other canons are laid upon all Christians, there is no reason why this one alone should pertain only to the Orientals, when it is read in the same order, on the same footing, and without any distinction at all alongside the others. If it is lawful for Western Christians to throw off its yoke, on the strength of I know not what little reasons of their own invention, the Orientals, or Christians of the South or North, will also be free to refuse obedience to the other canons, for causes devised on the same principle and by the same right. Indeed, the authority of all divine and human laws will be dissolved and collapse once such quibbles are admitted, so that subjects inquire into the reasons for a command and do not consider a law, however general, to apply to them unless the cause they have invented applies to them. Therefore, if this canon is truly of the Apostles (as Turrianus wishes), no reason can be given why Rome, which for so many centuries has despised and violated what it decrees, should not be thought to have fallen from grade and from ecclesiastical communion, and to be, and to have long been, alien to the Apostolic Christians. Turrianus cannot establish the authority of his canons at a lower price. Baronius and Petavius saw this well. When they used a similar escape for the Ignatian letter written to the Philippians alone (though here too rashly and in vain), they did not dare to attempt the same thing against an Apostolic canon, which clearly binds all Christians. Dropping the cold quibble, they plainly confessed what was the case: that this canon is false and falsely attributed to the Apostles, and so Rome is in no way bound by its authority. Lastly, to conclude this point: even if we grant Turrianus what he asks without warrant and against all reason, namely that it was the intention of his legislators that this canon should hold force only in places where there were heretics who denied that this world was created by the true and supreme God, even so he will not free Rome.
