For it is established that in that very city Simon, Marcion and the Manichaeans, whom he mentions, spread their poisons and sought and held their seats and dwellings; and nearly every foul and filthy thing flowed together there. So Turrianus could not even make the excuse that Rome has shamefully rebelled against the Apostles, if this is indeed an Apostolic canon, which for so many centuries has been violated and trampled underfoot there with impunity. Since not even the Greeks themselves will say this about the older Romans, it must finally be admitted that the canon of Turrianus belongs to anyone rather than to the Apostles. But with Turrianus's quibble exploded and refuted, what remains is to refute briefly the conjecture of Bellarmine a, who guesses that this canon was falsified by the later Greeks, by inserting the word Sabbath, since at first this decree forbade a fast on the Lord's day alone. I would concede this if there existed any manuscript, either among the Greeks or among the Latins themselves, in which some trace or shadow of such a variation could be seen. But now all printed and written books alike carry the name of the Sabbath as well as the Lord's day with unanimous agreement; all the manuscripts of the Constitutions show the same. Humbert, already in the year 1050, testifies that this canon was objected to him by Nicetas in the same number of words as it is read now, and he does not complain about the reading or accuse the Greeks. The Trullan Fathers in the year 569 complain of the Latins who fast on the Sabbath, saying that they break "the ecclesiastical order handed down" [τὸ παραδόθεισαν ἐκκλησιαστικὴν ἀκολουθίαν], "the ecclesiastical custom handed down", which can only refer to this canon and the similar Apostolic "ordinance" [διάταξιν]. Finally, before these times no Latin ever brought a dispute against the Greeks over a corrupted reading of this canon, and no later writer mentioned any other reading than this very one of the Greeks. It appears that the word Sabbath has been written in this canon from the beginning, and was never read otherwise than it is read now. Bellarmine's conjecture came to mind from a single zeal for his cause, to which he gives himself up too much. If others were to follow this example of licence, so that whatever pleases us less in the monuments of the ancients could be struck out as if added by Greeks or Latins, with no authority from manuscripts and no reason given, then no one can fail to see that the trustworthiness of all the old books would be at an end. So much for the 65th canon.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Arg. VI. contra 35. canones, ex iis quae de quadragesima & jejuniis decernit canon 18. Turriani objecta & glossa refelluntur. Aperitur insignis ejus hallucinatio de Psychicis, & Tertulliano. Arg. VII. VIII. IX. X. ex canonibus 21. 22. 30. 34. ducta. Immanis canonis huius 34. absurditas, & par in ea defendenda Turriani impudentia. Concluditur disputationis prima pars, quae instituta erat contra 35. canones postremos.
units.tr: Argument VI against the 35 canons: the objections of Turrianus concerning the Lenten fast and the fasts, from canon 18, are refuted, along with his gloss. His striking error about the Psychici and Tertullian is exposed. Arguments VII, VIII, IX and X are drawn from canons 21, 22, 30 and 34. The monstrous absurdity of canon 34, and Turrianus's matching impudence in defending it, are shown. The first part of the dispute, which was directed against the last 35 canons, is concluded.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: IAM neque fieri potest, ut Apostolorum fuerit, qui in proximo sequitur, decimus octavus supra quinquagesimum canon. εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ἀναγνώστης, ἢ ψάλτης, τὸ ἁγίαν τεσσαρακοστὸν τῶ πάσχα, ἢ τελεάδα, ἢ παρασκευὴν, ὑνηστεύοι, καθαιρείσθω, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ δι᾽ ἀδύνειαν σωματικὴν ἐμποδίζοιτο, εἰ ἢ λαϊκὸς εἴη, ἀφορισθέσθω, Siquis Episcopus, vel presbyter, vel diaconus, vel lector, vel cantor, sanctam Pascha quadragesimam non jejunat, vel quartum diem, vel parasceven (praeterquam si propter imbecillitatem corporalem impediatur) deponatur; si sit autem laicus, segregetur. Hic certe canon Apostolorum inquam esse non potest; qui quadragesimæ, quartæque & sextæ feriæ jejunia sub gravissima pœna præcipit, quæ veri Apostoli neque præceperunt unquam, neque vero præcepisse à veteribus plerisque Patribus crediti sunt; quod utrumque, quia in superioribus clarissime tum ex vera ac indubitata Apostolorum doctrina, tum ex certis veterum monumentis demonstratum fit, nihil hic repetere necesse est. Quaedam tantum in Turrianum, quæ istic omnimus, sunt observanda; quale illud est inprimis, quod Psychicos à Tertulliano oppugnatos vir minime malus nostros fuisse ait a;suum adeo fuisse hac in parte fatetur Psychicorum oppugnatorem Tertullianum. Nos vero, ô bone, Psychicorum istorum non pudet, neque sane Tertullianum, qua adversus eos pugnat, tibi, ac tuis invidemus. Nam quod tu quidem tantus antiquitatis helluo, nescitis, omnes vero etiam hodie pueri sciunt, & Psychici illi, quos tu nobis relinquis, ii veri illius ævi Catholici fuerunt, & quem tu adoptas Tertullianum, is hac in parte hæreticus Montanista fuit. Itaque per te quidem & Catholici nos sumus; & tui Romani Montanistæ in hac causa sunt; quod certe verissimum est, idque à te, quamvis inscio ac imprudente, præter animi tui sent entiam dictum, nos libentes accipimus. Quod si, ut tu vis, canon ille quem defendis, Tertullianicum dogma decrevit, Psychicorum sententiam damnavit; negare profecto non potes, quin ab ipsis Apostolis alienus sit; nisi in canonum tuorum gratiam Christi Domini Apostolos & Montanistas fuisse affirmes, & Catholicos fuisse neges. Secundo. Quod idem Turrianus a ait Hieronymum dicere, nos quadragesimam secundum Apostolorum traditionem jejunare, in eo observandum est, istum & lectoribus imponere, neque quaestionem concludere. Non enim, quod iste fingit, simpliciter ait Hieronymus b, nos secundum Apostolorum traditionem quadragesimam jejunare, sed unam nam quadragesimam. Nos (inquit) unam quadragesimam secundum traditionem Apostolorum, toto anno, tempore nobis congruo jejunamus; Illi (nimirum Montanistae) tres in anno faciunt quadragesimas, quasi tres passi sint Salvatores. Non hoc vult, quod putat Turrianus, institutum fuisse, & lato canone decretum ab Apostolis, ut quadragesimam Christiani celebrent (quod quam falsum sit, & non modo a veritate, sed & ab omnium fere veterum sententia alienum, & alias fuse proprio opere, & supra nuper, satis demonstravimus) sed vult, quod unam tantum sui temporis
units.tr: Nor can it be that the eighteenth canon after the fiftieth, which follows next, belongs to the Apostles: "If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, reader, or cantor does not fast during the holy forty days of Pascha, or on the fourth day, or on the Preparation (unless he is prevented by bodily weakness), let him be deposed; if he is a layman, let him be cut off." [εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ἀναγνώστης, ἢ ψάλτης, τὸ ἁγίαν τεσσαρακοστὸν τῶ πάσχα, ἢ τελεάδα, ἢ παρασκευὴν, ὑνηστεύοι, καθαιρείσθω, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ δι᾽ ἀδύνειαν σωματικὴν ἐμποδίζοιτο, εἰ ἢ λαϊκὸς εἴη, ἀφορισθέσθω] I say that this canon cannot be of the Apostles. It prescribes, under the gravest penalty, the fasts of Lent, of the fourth day and of the sixth day, which the true Apostles never enjoined, and which most of the ancient Fathers are not believed to have enjoined either. Since both points have been demonstrated very clearly above, both from the true and undoubted doctrine of the Apostles and from certain ancient records, there is no need to repeat them here. Only a few points against Turrianus, which I shall pass over here, need to be noted. Chief among them is this: he says that the Psychici, whom Tertullian attacked, were a most honest man's our people, and yet he confesses that Tertullian, the opponent of the Psychici, was his own in this respect. But we, my good sir, are not ashamed of those Psychici, nor do we begrudge you and yours Tertullian, insofar as he fights against them. For you, a great glutton for antiquity, do not know what even children today know: those Psychici whom you leave to us were the true Catholics of that age, while Tertullian, whom you adopt, was in this respect a heretical Montanist. So through you we are indeed the Catholics, and your Romans are the Montanists in this matter. This is certainly most true, and we gladly accept it, since you have said it, though unwittingly and carelessly, against your own opinion. But if, as you wish, that canon which you defend has decreed the Tertullianist dogma and condemned the view of the Psychici, you certainly cannot deny that it is alien to the Apostles themselves, unless you claim that the Apostles of Christ the Lord and the Montanists were the same, and deny that they were Catholics, all for the sake of your canons. Second: where Turrianus says that Jerome said we fast Lent according to the tradition of the Apostles, it must be noted that he deceives his readers and does not settle the question. For Jerome does not simply say, as he pretends, we fast Lent according to the tradition of the Apostles; he says one Lent: "We (he says) keep one Lent according to the tradition of the Apostles, fasting in the proper season throughout the year; they (that is, the Montanists) make three Lents in the year, as if the Saviour had suffered three times." He does not mean, as Turrianus thinks, that it was instituted and decreed by the Apostles, by a general canon, that Christians should celebrate Lent (how false this is, and how far it is not only from the truth but from the opinion of almost all the ancients, we have demonstrated fully elsewhere in our own work and above, recently enough). Rather, he means that the observance of one Lent a year, which was the custom of his time, agreed with the tradition of the Apostles, who indeed hand down that only one Saviour suffered once for us; and that the practice of the Montanists, who made three Lents every year, departed from this and was alien to it, because it is established from the books of the Apostles that not three but only one Saviour suffered.

units.la: a c,21.p. 68.versa. b Ep. ad Marcellam adv. Mont. T. 2. Hier. sol. 36. L. poris Christiani in anno quadragesimam observabant, id Apostolorum traditioni congruere, qui scilicet unum tantum Salvatorem pro nobis semel passum tradant; ab iis Montanistarum institutum, qui tres quotannis quadragesimas faciebant, discedere, atque alienum esse: quod scilicet non tres, sed unum tantum salvatorem ex Apostolorum libris passum esse constet. Sed ista & alia ejusdem generis nihil nunc quidem necesse est operosius explicare. Esto enim, quod frustra contendit Turrianus, Hieronymus, & pauci si forte alii veteres quadragesimam ab Apostolis institutam fuisse crediderint. Non ideo sequitur, & hoc quoque eos sensisse, hunc, quem nunc obtrudit Turrianus, de quadragesima canonem, ab Apostolis editum, a Clemente scriptum fuisse; cujus neque apud illos, neque apud alios veteres, ulla omnino fit mentio. Quidni potius sensisse eos dixero, non hoc, vel ullo alio scripto canone, sed viva tantum voce traditam fuisse ab Apostolis quadragesimam? Contra vero hunc antiquitati ignotum fuisse canonem recte ex eo concluditur, quod & vetustissimi quadragesimam minime observaverint, tribus prioribus Christianismi saeculis, & qui saeculorum sequentium Patres plurimi quadragesimam, licet suo aevo usitatam, ab Apostolis tamen instituta negaverint; neque enim horum alterum cum illo canone consistere potest. Utrumque autem supra satis confirmatum est. In jejunio vero quartæ feriæ, cujus hic canon eandem esse religionem decernit, omnes vident, ab ejus authoritate jamdudum aperte defscivisse Romanam ipsam Ecclesiam; quæ facto hoc suo palam negat, Apostolicum esse hoc decretum: quod scilicet Apostolicum censere non potest, nisi se fateatur non Apostolicam; qua de re etiam supra, quantum satis est, suo loco ad Constitutiones diximus; & frigidam Binii & aliorum exceptionem, confutavimus, qui quartæ feriæ jejunium in sabbatum translatum esse cavillantur.
units.tr: a See c. 21, p. 68, reverse. b Letter to Marcella against the Montanists, Jerome, vol. 2, sol. 36, L. Christians in the year observed Lent, and this agreed with the tradition of the Apostles, which holds that a single Saviour suffered once for us, and departed from and was alien to the institution of the Montanists, who made three Lents each year: because it is established that from the books of the Apostles not three, but only one Saviour, suffered. But there is no need now to explain these and other points of the same kind in greater detail. Grant that Jerome, and perhaps a few other ancients, believed that Lent was instituted by the Apostles, as Turrianus vainly contends. It does not follow that they also thought that this canon on Lent, which Turrianus now forces upon us, was issued by the Apostles and written by Clement; no mention of it whatever is found among them or among any other ancients. Why should I not rather say that they meant that Lent was handed down by the Apostles not by this or any other written canon, but by living voice alone? On the contrary, it is rightly concluded from this that the canon was unknown to antiquity, because the most ancient Christians did not observe Lent at all during the first three centuries, and many of the later Fathers denied that Lent, though used in their own age, was instituted by the Apostles; for neither of these can stand with that canon. Both points have been sufficiently confirmed above. As for the fast of the fourth day, whose observance this canon likewise commands, everyone sees that the Roman Church itself has long since openly departed from its authority, and by this very fact openly denies that this decree is Apostolic. Clearly it cannot judge it Apostolic unless it confesses that it is not itself Apostolic; on this matter we have also spoken, as far as necessary, in the proper place above, on the Constitutions, and we have refuted the flimsy objection of Binius and others, who cavil that the fast of the fourth day was transferred to the Sabbath.

units.la: VII. Ad canones redeo; in quorum 71. quod decernitur, Segregandum, siquis vel clericus, vel laicus ceram, vel oleum à sancta Ecclesia abstulerit: ab Apostolicis quoque temporibus abhorret.
units.tr: VII. I return to the canons. In canon 71 it is decreed: "Let anyone, whether cleric or layman, who has taken wax or oil from the holy Church, be cut off." This too is repugnant to the times of the Apostles.

units.la: Neque enim ex omni novi fœderis instrumento apparet, aliud in Ecclesia oleum beato illo sæculo floruisse, vel in pretio fuisse, præter illud Spiritus sancti mysticum, quo Deus Christum, & ex eo homines cælestis gratiæ consortes perfundit, atque inungit; vel alias ceras, quam quæ igne sacro, ac spirituali incensæ tenebras bras hujus sæculi sanctorum exemplorum radiis illuminant.
units.tr: For from the whole instrument of the New Covenant it does not appear that any other oil flourished in the Church in that blessed age, or was held in esteem, except that mystical anointing of the Holy Spirit with which God anoints and pours out Christ, and through him men, partakers of heavenly grace; nor any other wax than that which, kindled by the sacred and spiritual fire, lights the darkness of this age with the rays of holy examples.

units.la: VIII. Ejusdem est farinæ, quod mox in sequenti canone in eos decernitur a, qui vas aureum, vel argenteum, vel velum sanctificatum, in suum usum converterint. Vel hæc loquuntur, istos canones secutis sæculis fuisse conditos; cum sacras ædes, & pretiosam supellectilem & reliquam pompam Christianorum copiæ in usum apud nos invexissent. Apostolorum ævo tanta erat nostrorum simplicitas, atque parsimonia, & frugalitas, adhæc tenuitas, tantæque à persecutorum odiis ac furore angustiæ, ut iis indulgere non licuerit. Certe, quod jam supra me dixisse memini, ne ædes quidem sacras in illis initiis habuisse Christianos verisimile est; nedum ut velis, aureisque & argenteis vasis instructas habuisse eos crediderim.
units.tr: VIII. Of the same kind is what is decreed in the following canon against those who have converted a golden or silver vessel, or a sanctified veil, to their own use. These words suggest either that these canons were composed in later centuries, when, with the Christians' wealth, they had brought sacred buildings, costly furnishings and the rest of Christian pomp into use among us; or that in the Apostles' age our people were so simple, so sparing, so frugal, and so poor, and so straitened by the hatred and fury of the persecutors, that such indulgences were not permitted. Certainly, as I recall having said above, it is likely that Christians in those beginnings did not even have church buildings, much less that I would believe they had them furnished with gold and silver vessels and veils.

units.la: IX. Æque abhorret à temporibus Apostolorum, quod canone 8o. statuitur, ὅτι ὁ χρὴ ἐπίσκοπον ἢ πρεσβύτερον καθιέναι ἑαυτὸν εἰς δημοσίας διοικήσεις, non oportere Episcopum vel presbyterium se ipsum ad publicas administrationes demittere; & quod mox ejusdem ingenii canone 82. subjicitur, ut deponatur Episcopus, presbyter, & diaconus σρατείᾳ σχολάζων, ἢ βιαλόμενος ἀμφότερα κατέχειν, Ῥωμαϊκῶ ἀρχῇ χλως, χ ἱεράτικῶ ὰιολωσιν, exercitui vacans, & utraq; obtinere volens, Romanum scilicet magistratum, & sacerdotalem administra-tionem. Quasi vero Apostolis verendum fuerit, ne Christiani, quos Pagani vix aere & luce communi frui patiebantur, nedum ut eos ad publicas dignitates admitterent, sacerdotium una cum Romano magistratu obtinere vellent! Quis non videt haec se-cutis saeculis decreta, cum immutatis Principum, & populorum animis, Christianis hominibus & Ecclesiae, & reipublicae mu-nera, ac dignitates paterent?
units.tr: IX. Equally foreign to the times of the Apostles is what is laid down in canon 80: that a bishop or presbyter ought not to lower himself to public administrations [ὅτι ὁ χρὴ ἐπίσκοπον ἢ πρεσβύτερον καθιέναι ἑαυτὸν εἰς δημοσίας διοικήσεις]; and what is added right after, in the same spirit, in canon 82: that a bishop, presbyter or deacon who is devoted to the army [στρατείᾳ σχολάζων], or who wishes to hold both [βουλόμενος ἀμφότερα κατέχειν], the Roman magistracy [Ῥωμαϊκῶ ἀρχῇ] and the priestly administration [ἱεράτικῶ διοικήσει], is to be deposed. As if the Apostles had had to fear that Christians, whom the Pagans scarcely allowed to enjoy the air and common light, far less admitted them to public offices, would wish to hold the priesthood together with the Roman magistracy! Who does not see that these decrees belong to later centuries, when, with the minds of princes and peoples changed, the offices and dignities both of the Church and of the commonwealth lay open to Christian men?

units.la: X. Superest Canon de scripturis 84. ex quo alii duos faciunt, his verbis expressus;
units.tr: X. There remains the canon concerning Scripture (84), from which some make two, expressed in these words:

units.la: Sint vobis omnibus Clericis & laicis libri venerandi & sancti; Veteris quidem testamenti, Moses quinque, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numeri, Deuteronomium; Iesu Nave unus. Iudicum unus. Ruth unus. Regnorum IV. Paralipomenon, id est derelictorum libri dierum, duo. ἐσδρας ἓν, Hester unus. Maccabaeorum tres. Iob unus. Psalterium unus. Salomonis tres, Proverbia, Ecclesiastes, Cantica Canticorum. Prophetarum XII. unus. Esaiae unus. Ieremiae unus. Ezechiel unus. Daniel unus. Extrinsecus autem a vobis intelligatur, debere vestros adolescentes discere Sapientiam eruditissimi Sirach. Nostra autem, id est, novi Testamenti Euangelia quatuor, Matthaei, Marci, Lucae, Ioannis. Pauli epistola quatuordecim. Petri, epistola duae. Ioannis, tres. Iacobi, una. Iudae, una. Clementis Epistolae duae, & Constitutiones vobis Episcopis per me Clementem in octo libris editae (quae non sunt omnibus divulgandae, propter ea, quae sunt in eis mystica) & Actus nostri Apostolorum. Ille vero canon clara voce clamat se nihil minus esse, quam Apostolicum, dum & in sacrum veteris Testamenti canonem tria Maccabaica volumina, & in novi, Constitutionum (ut appellat) Clementinarum libros octo, & alia praeter verum, & communem, constantemque, qua veteris, qua recentis Ecclesiae consensum, refert. Ac primum quidem, quod Maccabaeorum priores duos libros canonicis accenset, eo, fatente ipso Turriano, Eusebii, Athanasii, Gregorii Nazianzeni, Amphilochii Iconiensis, sed & (quod res ipsa demonstrat) Cyrilli Hierosolymitani, Epiphanii, Ioannis Damasceni, Hilarii, Philastrii, Ruffini, Hieronymi, & aliorum sententiam pulsat, qui totam Maccabaeorum scripturam vel tacite vel etiam diserte in apocryphorum numero censent. Ergo necesse est, omnes isthos veterum saeculorum homines hunc canonem vel
units.tr: Let there be for you all, clergy and laity, books venerable and holy. Of the Old Testament: Moses's five, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy; Joshua son of Nun, one; Judges, one; Ruth, one; Kings, four; Paralipomenon, that is, the books of the things left behind of the days, two; Esdras, one [ἐσδρας ἓν]; Esther, one; Maccabees, three; Job, one; the Psalter, one; Solomon's three: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs; the Twelve Prophets, one; Isaiah, one; Jeremiah, one; Ezekiel, one; Daniel, one. Let it be understood, moreover, as outside these, that your young people ought to learn the Wisdom of the most learned Sirach. But our books, that is, of the New Testament: the four Gospels, of Matthew, Mark, Luke, John; the fourteen epistles of Paul; Peter's two; John's three; James, one; Jude, one; the two epistles of Clement, and the Constitutions, edited for you bishops by me, Clement, in eight books (which are not to be published to all, because of the mystical matters in them), and our Acts of the Apostles. That canon clearly proclaims that it is nothing less than Apostolic, since it reports into the sacred canon of the Old Testament three Maccabean volumes, and into the New the eight books of the Constitutions (as it calls them) of Clement, and other things beyond the true, common and constant consensus of both the older and the recent Church. And first, indeed, that it counts the first two books of the Maccabees among the canonical books, Turrianus himself admitting it, it strikes against the opinion of Eusebius, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Amphilochius of Iconium, but also (as the thing itself shows) of Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius, John of Damascus, Hilary, Philastrius, Rufinus, Jerome and others, who judge the whole Maccabean writing to be among the apocrypha, either tacitly or even expressly. Therefore it is necessary that all these men of the older centuries must either have been wholly ignorant of this canon, or

units.la: {a} In hunc locum. vel omnino nescivisse, vel certe non Apostolicum, sed spurium; ac fictitium censuisse. Quis enim credat viros sapientia & pietate insignes, quod ab Apostolis Domini definitum scivissent, id relicturos fuisse, & in diversa ituros? Secundo, non ab horum modo, sed & ab omnium omnino Ecclesiasticorum hominum sententia abhorret, quod canon praeter duo priora (quae nonnulli admiserunt) etiam tertium Maccabaicum volumen, quod nemo in divinorum librorum catalogum retulit, pro canonico habendum decernit. Quo loco sese prodit immanis Turriani impudentia; qui contra omnium saeculorum fidem, contra utriusque Ecclesiae veteris, recentisque, Graecae, & Romanae, denique contra ipsam Tridentinae Synodi authoritatem homo confidentissimus hanc istius Canonis de Maccabaico tertio volumine sententiam tueri ac propugnare audet; & ad objectam tot tantorumque testium nubem respondet, fieri potuisse, ut hic liber a principio quidem canonicus fuerit, dubitatum tamen aliquando de eo sit, idque in causa fuisse, & adhuc fortassis esse, cur inter libros canonicos non numeretur; nam & aliquando dubitatum fuisse, utrum Apocalypsis esset Ioannis, ac proinde canonicus liber, cum tamen a principio canonicus liber, & sui authoris, authoris, id est Apostoli Ioannis fuisset. Sed nihil inter ista simile. Nam de apocalypsi ita aliquando à nonnullis dubitatum est, ut fuerint semper alii, & quidem complures qui librum Ioannis esse confiterentur; ut ex Eusebio *, & aliis patet. Hunc Maccabaicum tertium ex omni Christiani- smi memoria, qui in canonem sacrum retulerit, nemo praeter stramineos istos Apostolos, & Turrianum eorum praeconem, repertus est. Quod enim Eusebium, & Theodoretum, in suas patres trahit Turrianus, id pro solita audacia, atque vaesania facit. Nimirum quod uterque historias quasdam in eo libro contineri dixerit, id homo amens sic accipit, quasi librum in Theopneustων canone censuissent. Itaque ex hujus Theologi novis decretis, historiarum scriptores quisquis citat, pro divinis habet: & hoc judice Livium, Josephum, Philonem, Herodotum, Varronem, Sanchoniatonem, & alios innumerabiles saeculares vel eruditionis vel antiquitatis authores pro canonicis & divinis scriptoribus habuerunt quotquot Patres eorum authoritate in libris suis usi sunt, Origenes, Tertullianus, Augustinus, aliique paene omnes. Secundo hoc inter duo ista, quae homo sapientissimus inter se comparat, discriminis intercedit, quod de divina Apocalypseos authoritate nullum veteres in Apostolorum veris ac geminis (si Turriano credimus) canonibus decretum inveniebant; Maccabaicum tertium disertissime in canonem sacrum relatum legebant, ut mirandum non sit, quod de priore nonnulli dubitaverint; de posteriori non modo mirabile, sed plane incredibile sit, quemquam dubitasse, siquidem hic in Ecclesia Turrianicus canon extabat. Atqui de illo tertio Maccabaico volumine, non modo unus aliquis, quod dixi; non modo aliquot, ut de Apocalypsi, dubitarunt; omnis de eo Ecclesia dubitavit; imo ne dubitavit quidem, sed ex sacris divinorum librorum scriniis, quo id Turrianicorum Apostolorum temeritas magno sacrilegio intulerat, dereptum in apocryphorum censu constantissime semper aut reposuit, aut reliquit. Itaque necessario confitendum est, omni antiquae Ecclesiae hos Turriani Apostolos plane ignotos fuisse; quos si cognovissent, proque veris Apostolis habuissent, nunquam eorum de Scripturarum canone sententiam ita aperte abjecissent, ac oppugnasset. Tertio. Sed & hunc falso Apostolis affictum esse canonem inde clarissime elucet, quod Clementinas Constitutiones in divinorum librorum censu, per intolerabilem impudentiam am, collocat; quæ cum novæ sint, neque ante quartum sæculum consarcinatæ, adhæc fictitiæ, & erroribus omne genus scatentes, ut superiori disputatione invictis argumentis demonstratum est, fieri profecto non potest, ut vel Apostolis cognitæ, vel divinitus traditæ ac inspiratæ fuerint. Quo accedit constans, ac luculentum totius Ecclesiæ testimonium, quæ octo illos Διαταξεων libros in Scripturarum canonem, neque olim reperit, neque nunc admittit. Quinimo ne suis quidem Græcis hic canon persuadere potuit, ut eas tali loco, ac numero haberent, ut ex ipsa Trullana Synodo patet; quæ cum Canones authenticos esse decernat, Constitutionum tamen librum ad sequiora & apocrypha amandat. Quo satis produnt boni illi Trullani Patres, quam vertiginosus esset is, quo ducebantur, spiritus, qui eas constitutiones rejiciendas putant, quarum summam divinamque authoritatem Canones illi sanciunt, quos ipsi veluti vera, atque authentica Apostolorum decreta, amplecti se ac venerari ibidem profitentur. Quid est ex uno eodemque ore, & frigidum, & calidum flare, si hoc non est. Sed non est hæc una Trullanę Synodi contradictio. Ergo cum omnis Ecclesia hoc Constitutionum Clementinarum opus extra Scripturarum { }rum divinarum censum hactenus habuerit; quod in eo diserte numerat Turrianicus canon; omnino necesse vel non esse hunc Apostolicum, vel certe nullam ad hæc tempora in terris fuisse Christianorum Ecclesiam Apostolicam; exceptis si forte unis Æthiopibus, qui & hos ipsi libros cum Turrianico canone divinis novi fœderis Scripturis æquiparare atque accensere feruntur. Quarto. Illud etiam & ab Apostolica veritate, & a totius Ecclesiæ fide palam abhorret, quod in eodem canone duæ Clementis epistolæ in eodem Scripturarum divini fœderis catalogo recensentur: quas pro sacris & θεοπνεύστοις neque vetus neque recentior unquam Ecclesia agnovit. Ac priorem quidem veteris magni faciebant; ut ex Eusebio, & Hieronymo discimus; non sic tamen, ut ab ullo unquam Patre in canone divinorum librorum collocata sit. Posteriorem vero, quam & ipsam Apostoli scilicet, canonicam esse decernunt, veteres non modo Scripturis non accensuerunt, sed & spuriam, fictitiamque esse judicarunt , & ipso Clementis nomine indignam; nedum ut divinitus inspiratam, cum istis Turrianicis, sane hac in parte mirificis, planeque peregrinis & inusitatis legislatoribus, putaverint. Quinto. Id etiam hujus canonis falsitatem abunde coarguit, quod Scriptura-rum rum nostrarum catalogum texens, neq; Ef-dram in veteri Testamento collocat, neque Apocalypsin Græcorum quorundam, qui de ea olim dubitarunt, errorem, ut liquet, secutus in novo memorat. Neque valet eorum exceptio, qui respondent, ideo omissam à canone Apocalypsin, quod, quo tempore scriptus est à Clemente canon, nondum effet edita. Nam Apocalypsin à Ioanne ante Euangelium scriptam esse, plurimi, gra-viffimique authores testantur, inquit Bellarminus , hanc ipsam istorum refponfionem refellens. At in isto Canone Ioannis Euangelium nominatim memoratur. Ergo quo tempore canon scriptus est, jam scriptam, editamque fuisse à Ioanne Apocalypsin necesse est. Itaque qui eam licet extantem, in Scripturarum nostrarum censu omittit, is profecto nullus Apostolorum esse potuit; quos quæ vere divinæ sunt Scripturæ minime omnium latuit. Sexto. Romanam quidem Ecclesiam jamdudum hunc canonem Apostolicum nescire, præter superiora, id etiam docet, quod & librum Syrachidis, quem canon diserte ἐν τοῖς ἔξω-θεν, in exoticis, five iis quæ extra scripturas sunt, censet, & libros Tobiæ, Iudith, Ecclesiastici, quos idem canon indictos præ-termittit, ipsa jampridem pro canonicis habet; ut patet ex Innocentii , Gelafiiq; decretis, & novissimo Tridentinæ Synodi canone Ergo vel Apostolica non est Ecclesia Romana, vel Turriano (si hoc abominatur) confitendum est, non esse Apostolicum, quem hactenus defendit canonem. Septimo. Hinc etiam liquet omni antiquitati ignotum, adeoque neque Apostolicum esse hunc canonem, quod eum neque Eusebius b, qui ab aliquot Patribus, ut à Melitone Sardensi & ab Origene traditos divinæ scripturæ canones exhibet, neque Athanasius, neque Hieronymus, neque (ut uno verbo dicam) quisquam alius veterum memorasse deprehenditur, tot, tamque multis ac illustribus locis, quibus sive de universæ scripturæ libris, sive de hujus, aut illius sigillatim authoritate quæritur. Quis enim tales viros talibus locis & caussis hunc, si notum habuissent, Apostolicumque censuissent, canonem prætermissuros crediderit, qui siquis hujus generis tum fuisset, solus obtinere, solus in tota hac de libris sacris controversia normæ, regulæque certissimæ vicem obtinere debuerat, ut nullum extra eos, quos commemorat libros, divinum habere, nullum ex iis, quos recenseт, non divinum haberi, nefas esset. Octavo denique, pugnant quædam eorum, quæ continet canon, cum Turriani hypothesibus. sibus. Hic enim (quod supra diximus) statuit Apostolos Hierosolymis congregatos statim post factum de legalium cessatione decretum, id est a. D. 45. præclaros istos 85. canones constituisse, atque edidisse, à Clemente postea conscribendos. At in hoc ipso ultimo eorum canone memorat & actus suos, id est Apostolorum, & omnes Pauli Petrique & Jacobi Epistolas, & quatuor Euangelia, quorum omnium vix credibile est quicquam adhuc eo anno (D. 45,) scriptum fuisse. Sed ut de cæteris taceam, Euangelium certe Joannis quinquaginta fere annis post illud tempus conscriptum, editumque supremis ipsius Joannis temporibus, cum præter eum nemo Apostolorum superesset, constans est & ab antiquissimis temporibus ad nos usque ducta fama. Quo ergo pudore inducuntur Apostoli opus post quinquaginta demum annos nascitu-rum, in canonem Ecclesiæ referentes? Profecto non modo Apostolos non fuisse, qui ista ita decreverunt, necesse est; sed & insuper valde bardum, ac crassum fuisse eum, qui Apostolos cum simulandos assumpsisset, ne eos quidem facere potuerit ad rerum, ac temporum, quæ simulat, rationem loquentes. Atque harum quidem rationum tanta, tamque evidens vis est, ut præter unum Turrianum, cujus invicta est, & inexsuperabilis pertinacia, cæteri omnes adversarii hunc canonem totum apocryphum & surreptitium esse confiteantur, & iis fere argumentis, quæ nos attulimus, probent Bellarminus a, Binius b, Baronius c, alii d. Baronii disputationem exempli & speciminis causa describere satis erit; Quod ad novissimum (inquit) illum canonem spectat, quo libri canonici recensentur; Ecquis unquam antiquorum Latinorum, atque Græcorum adnumerare inter canonicos libros præsumpsisset Apocalypsin, quam sciisset in Apostolorum canone prætermissam, qui vel saltem causam aliquam ejusmodi silentii non adduxisset? Certe quidem sancto Hieronymo authore superius demonstratum est, à Latinis omnibus & antiquioribus Græcis æque fuisse receptam? Vel quid est, quod cum de his frequens inter Patres oborta sit controversia, nemo penitus reperiatur, qui ejusmodi Apostolorum canonis vel saltem obiter meminerit? Tum illam exceptionem, de Apocalypsi nondum, quo tempore conditus est canon, cognita, futilem & inanem tergiversationem vocat, eamque eadem, qua nos supra usi ex Bellarmino sumus, ratione refellit; moxque hæc subjicit; Quod item (inquit) ad eundem spurium
units.tr: {a} On this passage. Either they knew nothing of it at all, or, at the least, they judged it not Apostolic but spurious and made up. For who would believe that men distinguished by wisdom and piety, if they had known it was defined by the Lord's Apostles, would have abandoned it and gone off in different directions? Secondly, the canon dissents not only from the opinion of these men but from that of all churchmen without exception, in decreeing that besides the two earlier books (which some have admitted) the third Maccabean volume too, which no one has ever placed in the catalogue of the divine books, is to be held canonical. Here the monstrous impudence of Turrianus shows itself. Against the faith of every age, against the faith of both the ancient and the recent Church, Greek and Roman alike, and finally against the very authority of the Synod of Trent, this most overconfident man dares to uphold and defend the view of this canon concerning the third Maccabean volume. To the cloud of so many and so great witnesses that has been set against him, he replies: it may have happened that this book was canonical from the beginning, yet at some time doubt was raised about it, and this was the cause, and perhaps still is, why it is not numbered among the canonical books; for doubt was also at one time raised whether the Apocalypse was John's, and therefore a canonical book, although it was canonical from the beginning and was the work of its author, that is, of the Apostle John. But there is nothing similar between these cases. For concerning the Apocalypse, doubt was indeed raised at one time by some, yet there were always others, and indeed many, who confessed it to be the book of John, as is clear from Eusebius and others. Of this third Maccabean volume, no one at all, from the whole memory of Christianity, has been found to have placed it in the sacred canon, except those straw-stuffed Apostles and Turrianus, their herald. For the fact that Turrianus drags Eusebius and Theodoret into his own camp is done with his usual audacity and madness. Surely, because both said that certain histories are contained in that book, this madman takes it as though they had judged the book to belong to the divinely inspired canon. Thus, by the new decrees of this theologian, whoever cites any writer of histories holds him to be divine. And by his judgment, Livy, Josephus, Philo, Herodotus, Varro, Sanchuniathon, and countless other secular authors of learning or antiquity have been regarded as canonical and divine writers, as many as the Fathers used in their books on their authority: Origen, Tertullian, Augustine, and almost all the others. Secondly, between these two things, which this most wise man sets against each other, there lies this difference: that concerning the divine authority of the Apocalypse the ancients found no decree in the true and twin canons of the Apostles (if we believe Turrianus); but they read that the third Maccabean book was most plainly reported in the sacred canon. So it is not surprising that some doubted the former; but that anyone should have doubted the latter is not only remarkable but quite incredible, since this Turrianic canon stood in the Church. Yet concerning that third Maccabean volume, not merely one man, as I have said, nor several, as with the Apocalypse, doubted; the whole Church doubted. Nay, it did not even doubt, but, when the rashness of the Turrianic Apostles had carried it off as a great sacrilege from the sacred chests of the divine books, it always most steadfastly either put it back or left it among the apocrypha. Therefore it must necessarily be confessed that these Turrianic Apostles were wholly unknown to all the ancient Church; for had they known them and held them to be true Apostles, they would never have so openly rejected and attacked their opinion about the canon of the Scriptures. Thirdly. But that this canon was falsely attributed to the Apostles is also most clearly evident from the fact that, with intolerable impudence, it places the Clementine Constitutions in the catalogue of the divine books; and since these are recent, compiled no earlier than the fourth century, and moreover made up and teeming with errors of every kind, as has been shown by invincible arguments in the earlier disputation, it certainly cannot be that they were known to the Apostles or handed down and inspired by God. To this is added the constant and manifest testimony of the whole Church, which neither formerly found those eight books of the Διαταξεων [Diataxeis] in the canon of the Scriptures, nor admits them now. Indeed, this canon could not even persuade its own Greeks to hold them in such a place and rank, as is clear from the Synod of Trullo itself; which, while it decrees that the Canons are authentic, nevertheless relegates the book of Constitutions to the lesser and apocryphal ones. By this the good Fathers of Trullo show plainly how giddy was the spirit that led them, since they think those Constitutions to be rejected, whose supreme and divine authority those same Canons sanction, and which they themselves in that very place profess to embrace and venerate as the true and authentic decrees of the Apostles. What is it to blow both hot and cold from one and the same mouth, if this is not? Yet this contradiction of the Synod of Trullo is not the only one. Therefore, since the whole Church has hitherto held this work of the Clementine Constitutions outside the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, while the Turrianic canon expressly numbers it among them, it must necessarily follow either that this canon is not Apostolic, or that there was no Apostolic Christian Church on earth down to these times, except perhaps the Ethiopians, if indeed they too are said to put these books on a level with the divine Scriptures of the New Covenant and to reckon them among them. Fourth. That also, both from Apostolic truth and from the faith of the whole Church, plainly departs: that in the same canon two epistles of Clement are listed in the same catalogue of the divine Scriptures of the covenant, which neither the ancient nor the more recent Church ever acknowledged as sacred and divinely inspired. Indeed the ancients held the former in high regard, as we learn from Eusebius and Jerome; yet not so as to have it placed by any Father among the canon of the divine books. As for the latter, which they decree to be canonical, namely the Apostles' own, the ancients not only did not count it among the Scriptures, but judged it spurious and made up, and unworthy even of Clement's name, let alone to be thought divinely inspired, since it came from these Turrianic lawgivers, certainly wonderful in this part, and entirely strange and unusual. Fifth. This canon is also abundantly convicted of falsity by the fact that, in drawing up the catalogue of our Scriptures, it neither places Ezra in the Old Testament, nor mentions the Apocalypse in the New, evidently following the error of certain Greeks who once doubted it. Nor does their objection avail, who answer that the Apocalypse was omitted from the canon because it was not yet published at the time when the canon was written by Clement. For very many and most weighty authors testify, says Bellarmine, refuting this very reply of theirs, that the Apocalypse was written by John before the Gospel. But in this canon the Gospel of John is mentioned by name. Therefore at the time the canon was written, the Apocalypse must already have been written and published by John. So whoever, though it was extant, omits it from the catalogue of our Scriptures, certainly could not have been any of the Apostles, who least of all were ignorant of which Scriptures are truly divine. Sixth. That this canon has long been unknown to the Roman Church as an Apostolic one is taught, besides the above, by this: that the Church of Rome has for a long time held as canonical both the book of Jesus the son of Sirach, which the canon expressly counts among the exotic books, that is, those outside the Scriptures, and the books of Tobit, Judith and Ecclesiasticus, which the same canon passes over unmentioned; as is clear from the decrees of Innocent and Gelasius and from the most recent canon of the Synod of Trent. Therefore either the Roman Church is not Apostolic, or (if Turrianus abhors this) it must be confessed that the canon he has so far defended is not Apostolic. Seventh. It is also clear from this that this canon was unknown to all antiquity and therefore is not even Apostolic: neither Eusebius, who sets out the canons of the divine Scripture handed down by several Fathers, such as Melito of Sardis and Origen, nor Athanasius, nor Jerome, nor (to say it in one word) any other of the ancients is found to have mentioned it, in so many and such famous passages, in which the question is raised about the books of the whole Scripture, or about the authority of this or that book individually. For who would believe that such men, in such passages and in such causes, would have omitted this canon, if they had known it and judged it Apostolic? If any canon of this kind had existed, it alone should have held sway in the whole of this controversy about the sacred books, and should have served as the most certain norm and rule, so that it would have been wrong to hold anything divine outside those books it mentions, or to hold anything not divine among those it lists. Eighth and finally, some of the things it contains clash with the hypotheses of Turrianus. For he holds (as we said above) that the Apostles, gathered at Jerusalem immediately after the decree concerning the cessation of the legal observances, that is in the year 45 A.D., established and published these famous eighty-five canons, to be written down afterwards by Clement. Yet in this very last of their canons it mentions both the Acts of the Apostles, that is, of the Apostles, and all the Epistles of Paul, Peter and James, and the four Gospels, of which it is scarcely credible that anything had yet been written in that year (45 A.D.). But to pass over the rest, it is certain and a constant report handed down from the most ancient times to us that the Gospel of John was written about fifty years after that time, and published in John's last days, when no Apostle survived except him. With what shame, then, are the Apostles introduced as enacting in the canon of the Church a work that was to come into being only fifty years later? Surely it must follow not only that the men who decreed these things were not Apostles, but also that the one who took upon himself to counterfeit Apostles was so clumsy and gross that he could not even make them speak in keeping with the circumstances and the times he was pretending. And the force of these arguments is so great and so evident that, except for Turrianus, whose obstinacy is unconquerable and beyond overcoming, all the other opponents admit that this whole canon is apocryphal and surreptitious, and Bellarmine, Binius, Baronius and others prove it by nearly the same arguments that we have brought forward. It will be enough to set out Baronius's discussion as an example and sample: As for that latest canon (he says), in which the canonical books are listed, who of the ancient Latins or Greeks would have presumed to count the Apocalypse among the canonical books, if he had known it to have been omitted from the Canon of the Apostles, and had not at least offered some reason for such silence? Surely it has been shown above, on the authority of Saint Jerome, that it was received by all the Latins and equally by the older Greeks? Or what is it that, although this question arose frequently among the Fathers, no one at all is found who even briefly mentioned such a canon of the Apostles? Then he calls that objection, that the Apocalypse was not yet known at the time the canon was composed, a futile and empty evasion, and refutes it by the same reasoning we used above from Bellarmine; and immediately he adds these words: Likewise (he says), as to that same spurious

units.la: a l. 1. de Binio, a 20. b in c. Ap. 84. T. 1. Conc. p. 23. c a. D. 102. §. 15. & 16. d Lindan. Panopl. l. 3. c. 3. spurium canonem spectat, taceo in praesentiarum dicere de sacris libris veteris Testamenti, ut Esdrae, Iudith, Tobiae, Sapientiae, & Ecclesiastici, qui omnes in eo canone omittuntur. Caeterum quis aequo animo ferat, ut eodem canone inter canonicos libros octo libri Constitutionum Clementis, & duae ejus epistolae recensitae habeantur? Quis unquam tam Graecorum, quam Latinorum Scriptorum, aut quaenam ex sacris Synodis, tam in Oriente, quam in Occidente antiquitus celebratis, quae texuerunt catalogum canonicorum librorum, inter eos adnumeravit Constitutiones Clementis? Noverunt eas quidem, & complures easdem sunt venerati (id quatenus verum sit, nos supra ostendimus) sed nequaquam ejus aestimationis esse quisquam illorum putavit, ut inter canonicas eas Scripturas adnumeraret. Praeteriissent-ne si Apostolorum hoc monuisset authoritas, & Clementis universalis Ecclesiae Episcopi chirographum consignasset? At qui nomine sexta Synodi fertur canon, (quod noscetur, magni esse periculi omnes canones illos 85. aeque probari) sic se illos probare dicit, ut tamen inter libros Canonicos non recipiendas tradat Constitutiones Clementis, quod ab haereticis fuerint adulterata. Hactenus de ultimo canone Baronius; idemque que, ut diximus, de eo sentit, qui numeratur 65. Cæteros, quod eos Ecclesia probasse (ut quidem affirmat) noscatur, valere quidem & authenticos esse censet; sic tamen, ut constare neget, an sint Apostolici; quod in aliis antiquitatis monumentis ita posita reperiantur, quæ ab iis decernuntur, ut in dubium æque revocari possit, illa-ne ex his canonibus accepta fuerint, an contra, in eos aliunde translata. Cum ergo tam multa in illis 35. canonibus habeantur, vel ab ævo, vel à disciplina, vel à fide Apostolorum, Apostolicorumque virorum aliena, conclusum esto eam, quæ à Græcis, Turrianoque eorum discipulo, nobis obtruditur, horum syllogen falsam, spuriamque esse; neque ab Apostolis conditam, in Ecclesia promulgatam, neque à Clemente Romano conscriptam ac digestam.
units.tr: a l. 1. de Binio, a 20. b in c. Ap. 84. T. 1. Conc. p. 23. c a. D. 102. §. 15. & 16. d Lindan. Panopl. l. 3. c. 3. As to the spurious canon, I will for the present say nothing about the sacred books of the Old Testament, such as Esdras, Judith, Tobit, Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, all of which are omitted in that canon. But who could bear calmly that the eight books of the Constitutions of Clement and his two epistles are listed among the canonical books in the same canon? Has any Greek or Latin writer ever done this, or any of the holy synods, whether in the East or the West, that were held in antiquity and drew up catalogues of canonical books? Certainly they knew these Constitutions, and many have revered them (how far that is true we have shown above), but none of them thought they were of such authority as to count them among the canonical Scriptures. Would they have passed over this in silence if the authority of the Apostles had enjoined it, and if Clement, bishop of the universal Church, had set his hand to it? But the canon that is cited under the name of the Sixth Synod (and it is well known that it is dangerous to approve all those 85 canons alike) says it approves them in such a way that it nevertheless hands down that the Constitutions of Clement are not to be received among the canonical books, because they were corrupted by heretics. So far Baronius on the last canon, and he holds the same view, as we have said, of the one numbered 65: that the Church has approved them (as he indeed affirms) is known, and so he thinks they are valid and authentic; yet he denies that it is established whether they are Apostolic. For in other monuments of antiquity the things decreed are set down in such a way that it can equally be doubted whether those things were taken from these canons or, on the contrary, were transferred into them from elsewhere. Since, then, so many things are contained in those 35 canons that are either of a later age or foreign to the discipline or the faith of the Apostles and apostolic men, let it be concluded that the collection which is forced upon us by the Greeks and by Turrianus, their disciple, is false and spurious, and was neither founded by the Apostles, nor promulgated in the Church, nor written down and arranged by Clement of Rome.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Altera pars disputationis contra 50. priores Apostolica sylloges canones. Demonstratur, eos quoque falsos, atque apocryphos esse. I. arg. ex Isidori Hispalensis & aliorum Latinorum veterum, & Hincmari nominatim testimonio. Arg. II. ex canone de Episcopis. Arg. III. ex canone 4. Arg. IV. ex 3. can. de incensa.
units.tr: The second part of the dispute against the first fifty canons of the Apostolic collection. It is shown that these also are false and apocryphal. I. Argument from the testimony of Isidore of Seville and other Latin ancients, and Hincmar by name. Argument II from the canon on bishops. Argument III from canon 4. Argument IV from canon 3 on incense.

units.la: ONTRA Turrianum & Graecos hactenus pro Latinis pugnavimus. Nunc major surgit certaminis moles contra recentiores Latinos, Graecosque, pro Gelasio, & Synodo Romana. Illi enim omnes conjunctis in unum viribus, Apostolorum esse defendunt, quem Gelasius apocryphum pronunciavit quinquaginta Apostolicorum canonum codicem. Nobis praeter ipsam rerum veritatem, ac lucem, quae una satis esse poterat, in hoc certamine adsunt, manusque amicas consociant, primo plurimi illi, sexti ineuntis saeculi homines, quos ipse Dionysius ingenue fatetur suis istis quinquaginta canonibus consensit non praebuisse facilem; tum ex proximo saeculo Hispalensis episcopus Isidorus πολλῶν ἀνεξίος ἄλλων, qui, quod in superioribus demonstratum est, hos ipsos canones negat ab Apostolica sede receptos; negat à Sanctis Patribus probatos; ast ab haereticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositos, adeoque à canonica, atque Apostolica authoritate remotos, & inter Apocrypha deputatos. Ad hunc talem, tantumque virum accedunt illi quamplurimi, quos Cresconiani codicis laudata à Baronio, eademque Vigorien sis libri ab Usserio memorata praefatio narrat his ipsis canonibus consensum non praebuisse facilem. Accedit postremo & Hincmarus celeberrimus noni saeculi jam vergentis praesul, cujus illa sunt a supra à nobis descripta; hos canones non credi ab Apostolis esse conscripatos; quaedam in iis esse non servanda; eos duntaxat ad instructionem, & propter vulgatam famam seorsum ante Concilia in Canonum libris poni; caeterum sic legendos, ut sequamur cautelam à Gelasio de apocryphis praemonitam, cum haec ad catholicorum manus advenerint, B. Pauli Apostoli praecedat sententia, qua dicit, Omnia probate; quod bonum est, retinete.
units.tr: Against Turrianus and the Greeks we have so far fought on behalf of the Latins. Now a greater struggle arises against the more recent Latins and Greeks, on behalf of Gelasius and the Roman Synod. For all of them, joining their forces together, defend as the work of the Apostles the collection of fifty Apostolic canons which Gelasius pronounced apocryphal. On our side, besides the truth of the matter itself and its light, which alone might have been enough, there come into this contest and join hands with us, first those many men of the beginning of the sixth century, whom Dionysius himself frankly admits did not readily give their assent to these fifty canons of his; then, from the following century, Isidore, bishop of Seville, far superior to many others [πολλῶν ἀνεξίος ἄλλων], who, as has been shown above, denies that these very canons were received by the Apostolic see; denies that they were approved by the holy Fathers; but says they were composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, and so removed from canonical and Apostolic authority, and counted among the Apocrypha. To this man, so great, there join those very many whom the praise of the Codex Cresconius recorded by Baronius, and the preface of the Vigorian book noted by Ussher, tell did not readily give their assent to these same canons. Last of all there joins Hincmar, the most celebrated prelate of the ninth century, now drawing to its close, whose words are those a which we have quoted above: that these canons are not believed to have been composed by the Apostles; that some things in them are not to be observed; that they are placed apart before the councils in the books of canons only for instruction, and because of popular report; and that they are to be read in such a way that we follow the caution given by Gelasius concerning apocryphal writings, when these have come into the hands of Catholics, the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul goes before, by which he says, Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

units.la: II. Horum ergo, quam sequimur, sententiam, allatis certissimis rerum ipsarum argumentis, firmemus, ac constituamus. Principio, quod in ipso statim collectionis limine occurrit , ut episcopus à duobus, aut tribus Episcopis ordinetur, id inquam ab Apostolicis temporibus alienum est; quibus ex Paulo constat à presbyteris solitas imponi manus. Quod autem Binius a in illo Pauli loco, presbyterum vult intelligi trium, aut plurium Episcoporum coetum, in quo unus, metropolitanus nimirum, ordinat, reliqui duo, aut plures ordinanti assistunt simulque cum eo super caput ordinandi manus imponunt, eo inquam, splendide nobis illudit, omnem vocabulorum vim ac sensum pro sua libidine ad causam, quam agit, contorquens, atque commutans. Nam presbyterium, quod ait Paulus, omnes vident presbyterorum esse coetum. Presbyteri vocem ita nude positam episcoporum, qui nunc dicuntur, coetum cum suo metropolitano collectum significare, Binianum est somnium, apud homines hactenus inauditum. Scio, qui sunt Paulo presbyteri, eosdem ipsi quoque Episcopos esse, ac dici, & vicissim. An vero Paulino ipso tempore, istorum ministrorum, qui nullo discrimine presbyteri episcopique dicebantur, duo diversi, ut vel nunc apud adversarios, vel ut olim apud tertii saeculi Christianos, essent gradus atque ordines re ipsa, consessu, authoritate, atque ordinatione inter se distincti, atque divisi, ait quidem, ut intelligo, Binius; sed non probat, neque sane unquam probabit. Nos de re ipsa nunc dicere supersedemus. Hoc unum dicimus, ipsam istius, qui hunc canonem scripsit, orationem prodere, non fuisse eum Apostolum. Episcopus (inquit a) a duobus, vel tribus Episcopis ordinetur. Tum continenter; Presbyter (inquit) ab uno Episcopo ordinetur, & diaconus, & reliqui clerici. Nemo non videt hunc velle, Episcopos ab Episcopis, non autem a presbyteris ordinari; presbyteros contra non a presbyteris sed ab episcopis; & quidem hoc discrimine, ut presbiterum ab uno Episcopo, Episcopum non nisi a pluribus Episcopis, ordinari liceat. Atqui pugnat, etiam fatente Binio, totum hoc orationis genus cum Apostolici sermonis usu. Nam si (quod Binius concedit, quodque certissimum ac verissimum est) in Apostolico sermone presbyteri & episcopi vocabula pro duobus illis ministrorum, quos isti fingunt jam tum extitisse, ordinibus nullo discrimine sumebantur, ut presbyterum qui diceret, tam primi, id est summi, quam secundi ordinis hominem significaret; & vicissim, qui Episcopum nominaret, non minus secundi atque inferioris, quam primi ordinis ministrum designaret; nemo non videt nihil ineptius aut stultius dici posse, quam quod ait noster Canonista. Episcopus (inquit) a duobus vel tribus Episcopis ordinetur. Hæc verba ex concesso at-que que indubitato Apostolici sermonis usu, tam significant secundi ordinis ministrum, quem nunc solum, presbyterum vocant, à duobus aut tribus episcopis ordinari debere, quam primi ordinis ministrum, qui & ipse episcopus nunc solus dicitur. Item tam significant hæc verba debere istum, de quo loquuntur, à duobus, tribusve secundi ordinis ordinari, quam à duobus, tribusve primi. Sed & illa quæ sequuntur, ut presbyter ab uno Episcopo ordinetur, ex Apostolico itidem stilo, primi æque ac secundi ordinis ministros à primi æque ac secundi ordinis ministro uno ordinari debere significant. Hac vero oratione, quid vel animo fingi possit stultius, perturbatius, ac infulsius, equidem non video; quæ nullum scilicet proprium, ac genuinum sensum habet; omnia de quibus loquitur, in incerto, atque ambiguo relinquit; nihil veri ac certi definit. Plane ac siquis nunc canones hos duos his verbis apud adversarios figeret; Ecclesia minister ordinetur ab Ecclesia ministris duobus, aut tribus; Ecclesia vero minister ab uno Ecclesia ministro ordinetur; quibus, ut omnes vident, nihil potest dici putidius. Cum ergo nihil Apostoli, nisi sapientissime, divineque locuti sint; cumque hæc oratio verbis, ex quibus contexitur, sensu, quo ea usurpare solebant Apostoli, sumptis, plane delira, & quovis etiam mediocri ingenio indigna sit; omnino necesse est, velit nolit Binius, fateri, hunc utrumque canonem, quomodo hic legitur, Apostolicum non esse. Nimirum res clamat, eum iis temporibus fuisse conditum, ac conscriptum, quibus presbyteri, & episcopi vocabula inter se distinguebantur, suamque alterum ab altero divisam significationem in vulgari Ecclesiæ usu habebat. Hunc vero istorum vocabulorum proprium ac divisum usum Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ tempori minime convenire vel ipse agnoscit Binius. Non sunt ergo hi canones Apostolico tempore conditi; nedum ut ab ipsis Apostolis editi ac promulgati fuerint. Idemque etiam ostendunt illi clerici quos præter episcopos, presbyteros & Diaconos memorat secundus canon. Apostolis enim non alios legimus cognitos fuisse clericos, quam episcopos, sive presbyteros & Diaconos.
units.tr: II. Therefore, let us confirm and establish the opinion of these men, which we follow, by the most certain arguments drawn from the matters themselves. In the first place, what meets us at the very threshold of the collection, that a bishop is ordained by two or three bishops, this, I say, is foreign to Apostolic times, when it is clear from Paul that hands were customarily laid on by the presbyters. As for Binius wanting, in that passage of Paul, presbytery to be understood as a gathering of three or more bishops, in which one, namely the metropolitan, ordains, while the other two, or more, assist the one ordaining and together with him lay their hands on the head of the one being ordained, this, I say, splendidly mocks us, twisting and altering the whole force and sense of the words to suit the cause he is pursuing. For that presbytery which Paul speaks of, everyone sees is a gathering of presbyters. That the word presbyters, placed thus bare, should signify a gathering of those who are now called bishops, assembled with their metropolitan, is a Binian dream, unheard of among men until now. I know that those who are presbyters in Paul are also themselves bishops, and are called so, and conversely. But whether in Paul's own time there were, in the strict sense, two different grades and orders of these ministers, who were called presbyters and bishops without any distinction, distinct and separated from one another in rank, assembly, authority and ordination, as there are now among our opponents, or as there were once among Christians of the third century, Binius says so, as I understand it, but does not prove it, and indeed never will. We shall now pass over saying anything about the matter itself. We say only this: the very wording of the man who wrote this canon betrays that he was not an Apostle. A bishop (he says) is ordained by two or three bishops. Then immediately: A presbyter (he says) is ordained by one bishop, and a deacon, and the other clerics. Everyone sees that he means bishops to be ordained by bishops, but not by presbyters; and presbyters, on the contrary, not by presbyters but by bishops; and indeed with this distinction, that a presbyter may be ordained by one bishop, but a bishop only by several bishops. Yet this whole manner of speaking clashes, even by Binius's own admission, with the Apostolic usage of speech. For if (as Binius concedes, and as is most certain and true) in Apostolic speech the words presbyter and bishop were used without distinction for those two orders of ministers which these men imagine already existed at that time, so that whoever said presbyter signified a man of the first, that is the highest, as well as of the second order; and conversely, whoever named bishop designated a minister of the second and lower order no less than of the first; then everyone sees that nothing more absurd or foolish can be said than what our canonist says: A bishop (he says) is ordained by two or three bishops. These words, according to the admitted and undoubted Apostolic usage, signify equally that a minister of the second order, whom now alone they call presbyter, must be ordained by two or three bishops, and that a minister of the first order, who himself now alone is called bishop, must be so ordained. Likewise these words signify equally that the one of whom they speak ought to be ordained by two or three of the second order as by two or three of the first. And the words that follow, that a presbyter is ordained by one bishop, in the same Apostolic style signify that ministers of the first and of the second order alike ought to be ordained by one minister of the first or of the second order. Indeed, I do not see what could be imagined more foolish, more confused, or more insipid than this manner of speech, which has no proper and genuine sense; it leaves everything it speaks of in doubt and ambiguity, and defines nothing true or certain. Just as if someone were now to fix these two canons among our opponents in these words: A minister of the Church is ordained by two or three ministers of the Church; but a minister of the Church is ordained by one minister of the Church; nothing, as everyone sees, could be said more putrid. Since therefore the Apostles spoke nothing except most wisely and divinely; and since this manner of speech, with its words taken in the sense in which the Apostles were accustomed to use them, is plainly silly and unworthy of even a mediocre mind, it is absolutely necessary, whether Binius likes it or not, that he admit that this pair of canons, as it is read here, is not Apostolic. Indeed the thing itself cries out that it was composed and written at a time when the words presbyter and bishop were distinguished from one another, and when each had its own separate meaning in the common usage of the Church. But that this proper and separate usage of these words is by no means suited to the Apostolic age, Binius himself acknowledges. Therefore these canons were not composed in Apostolic times, much less were they issued and promulgated by the Apostles themselves. The same is also shown by those clerics whom the second canon mentions besides bishops, presbyters and deacons. For we read that the Apostles knew no clerics other than bishops, or presbyters, and deacons.

units.la: III. Neque cum Apostolorum vel dogmate, ævo congruit, quod quarto canone jubentur fructuum primitiæ Episcopo & clericis solvi, & in eorum ædes comportari. Id enim ad legem Mosaïcam cæremonialem pertinet; quam veri Apostoli Dominica morte abrogatam docent; nedum ut aliquam ejus partem à fidelibus observari præcipiant.
units.tr: III. Nor does it agree with the doctrine or the age of the Apostles that by the fourth canon the first-fruits of the produce are commanded to be paid to the bishop and the clerics, and brought into their houses. For this pertains to the ceremonial law of Moses, which the true Apostles teach was abrogated by the death of the Lord, much less do they command that any part of it be observed by the faithful.

units.la: IV. Sed & ab Apostolis alienum est quod hic noster Canonista a paulo antesignificaverit, suo tempore offerri solitum in Ecclesia <bl>θυμίαμα τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἁγίας προσφορᾶς</bl>, incensum tempore sanctæ oblationis.
units.tr: IV. But it is also foreign to the Apostles that this canonist of ours, around Paul's time, mentions incense being customarily offered in the Church at the time of the holy oblation, [θυμίαμα τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἁγίας προσφορᾶς].

units.la: Atqui ne Tertulliani quidem ævo (hoc est anno post Apostolos minimum centesimo) usitatum apud Christianos thymiama fuit in religionis sacris. Testis ipse, quo loco nostros purgat à Paganorum criminatione, qui eos infructuosos esse in negotiis diceritabant. Thura plane (inquit b) non emimus. Si Arabia queruntur, scient Sabæi pluris & cariorisfuas merces Christianis sepeliendis profligari, quam Diis fumigandis. Clare fatetur, nullum apud suos, nisi ad mortuos funerandos, usum aromatum hujusmodi fuisse. Quod si & in sacra thuris, vel odorifieri aliquid expensum fuisset, id ad placandos Sabæos non minus profecto memorasset, quam quod ad sepeliendos mortuos erogabatur.
units.tr: Yet not even in Tertullian's day (that is, at least a hundred years after the Apostles) was incense in use among Christians in the sacred rites. Tertullian himself is a witness, in the passage where he clears our people of the charge of the Pagans, who used to say that they were unproductive in business. "Indeed, we do not buy frankincense," he says. "If the Arabians complain, the Sabaeans will know that their wares are sold off for the burial of Christians at a higher and dearer price than for the fumigation of the gods." He plainly admits that among his people there was no use of such spices except for the burial of the dead. And if any money had been spent on incense or on sweet-smelling things in the sacred rites, he would certainly have mentioned it, in order to appease the Sabaeans, no less than what was spent on burying the dead.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Arg. V. ex can. 7. de Pascha cum Iudais non celebrando. Arg. VI. ex can 8. de Clericis non communicantibus. Arg. VII. ex can. 9. de fidelibus post oblationem non communicantibus. Refelluntur Bellarmini & Binii cavillationes.
units.tr: Argument 5, from canon 7, on not celebrating Easter with the Jews. Argument 6, from canon 8, on clergy who do not communicate. Argument 7, from canon 9, on the faithful who do not communicate after the oblation. The cavils of Bellarmine and Binius are refuted.

units.la: IAM ex canone septimo a res multo etiam clarior est: εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος (inquit) ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος τῶν ἁγίων τὰ ἡμέραν πρὸ τῆς ἐαυτῶν ἱερωσύνης μὴ Ἰουδαίων ἐπιτελέσει, καθαιρείσθω. Siquis Episcopus, vel presbyter, vel Diaconus sanctum Pascha diem ante vernale aequinoctium cum Iudaeis celebraverit, abjiciatur, sive deponatur. Si fabulosis niti vellem, objicerem (quod est ab Epiphanio traditum) plane contra statuisse Apostolos, uti cum Judaeis pascha celebraretur. Sed ut fatear quod res est, neutrum Apostolos decrevisse reor. Eo certe prodest ista fabulatorum inter se diversitas, ut neutros verum dixisse appareat. Nos supra abunde demonstravimus, nunquam hoc, quod praecipit hic canon, decrevisse veros Christi Apostolos, nunquam hoc ab Apostolis decretum credidisse, vel scivisse veterem Ecclesiam; quippe quae id ipsum, quod hic sub depositionis poena vetatur, diu in multis, iisque sanctissimis parœciis, imo dioecesibus Asiæ, Orientis, & Syriarum servavit. Idemque ex eo etiam docuimus, quod qui aliter Pascha celebrant, nunquam eos hunc canonem in hac causa protulisse, vel leviter commemorasse, vel quicquam ea de re à Clemente scriptum laudasse, legimus. Quæ quoniam fusissime exsecuti sumus, nihil necesse est in iis immorari, neque item Turriani a vanissimam ad hæc, & impudentissimam vitilitigationem persequi, ac refellere; cujus omnia fundamenta satis superque sunt à nobis in illa superiori disputatione subversa. Addam tantum iis, quæ istic dicta sunt, insigne unius recentioris Iesuitæ b testimonium; difertissime confitentis præter Ioannem & Asianos, ipsum etiam Petrum Antiochia Pascha observasse Luna XIV. & Euodium item ejus successorem, & Ignatium, & Heronem, clarissimos martyres; omnesque alios Episcopos istorum successores, usque ad Nicænum Concilium per annos circiter trecentos. Ad id vero, quod contra ex epistola Ignatii ad Philippenses objicitur, à sanctissimo martyre pronuntiari κοινωνὸν τῶν ἀποκτεινάντων τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν eorum qui Christum & Apostolos interfecerunt, communicatorem, si quis cum Iudaïs Pascha
units.tr: Now from the seventh canon the matter is clearer still: "If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon celebrates the holy Passover with the Jews on a day before the vernal equinox, let him be cast out, or deposed" [εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος τῶν ἁγίων τὰ ἡμέραν πρὸ τῆς ἐαυτῶν ἱερωσύνης μὴ Ἰουδαίων ἐπιτελέσει, καθαιρείσθω]. If I wished to rely on fables, I would object (as Epiphanius has handed down) that the Apostles plainly decreed the opposite, that the Passover should be celebrated with the Jews. But to confess how things stand, I think the Apostles decreed neither. The very disagreement among these fabulists serves at least to show that neither side told the truth. We have shown above at length that the true apostles of Christ never decreed what this canon commands, and that the ancient Church never believed or knew that the Apostles had decreed it. For that Church itself kept for a long time, in many and most holy parishes, indeed in dioceses of Asia, the East and Syria, the very practice which here is forbidden under penalty of deposition. We have taught the same also from this, that those who keep Easter otherwise never, as we read, brought forward this canon in their cause, nor even lightly mentioned it, nor praised anything Clement wrote about the matter. Since we have set these things out very fully, there is no need to linger on them, nor likewise to pursue and refute the most vain and shameless wrangling of Turrianus on these points, all the foundations of which have been more than sufficiently overturned by us in that earlier disputation. To what has been said there I will add only the notable testimony of one recent Jesuit, who most openly admits that, besides John and the Asians, Peter himself at Antioch also kept Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, and likewise Euodius his successor, and Ignatius, and Heron, most famous martyrs; and all the other bishops, their successors, down to the Council of Nicaea, for about three hundred years. As for the objection drawn against this from the epistle of Ignatius to the Philippians, that the most holy martyr pronounces a communicant [κοινωνὸν τῶν ἀποκτεινάντων τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν] of those who killed Christ and the Apostles, if anyone keeps the Pascha with the Jews

units.la: a c.7.p. 19. verf.
units.tr: a Canon 7, p. 19, verso.

units.la: b Petr. Halloix. illustr. Eccl. Orient. script. T. 2. Notat. ad c. 2. 11. vitæ S. Irenæi & T. 1. in vita Ignat. c. 22. 26. Pascha egerit, aut solennia dierum festorum eorum susceperit; ad id, inquam, Jesuita iste respondet his verbis ab Ignatio damnari, non qui Luna 14. eodem, quo Judæi die pascha celebrant; sed qui in eadem mensa cum Judæis Judaïce agnum edebant, aut ejus partes ad se missas manducabant. Hæc ille: inepte quidem, ac inscite, ut pluribus est à R. Usserio demonstratum; sed tamen ita, ut satis ostendat, quam stultum sit & inverecundum id opinari, quod defendit Turrrianus; nimirum vel Apostolos, vel Ignatium, vel Clementem, vel quemquam denique sanctissimorum virorum, qui eo tempore vixerunt, nefas putasse pascha eadem cum Judæis die, id est Luna 14. celebrare; Sane perabsurdum esset (inquit Iesuita) tam graviter denotare id quod tam multi sancti viri ea ipsa in ætate qua hoc proferebat Ignatius (atque inter alios ipse S. Polycarpus) facitabant. Neutiquam profecto istud fecit mitissimus Ignatius; neutiquam fecit: imo ne cogitavit, ne somniavit quidem. Si hoc, ut ille verisimè asseverat, non fecit Ignatius; certe neque fecerunt, qui Ignatio haudquaquam inclementiores erant Apostoli. Quid ergo est? Nimirum, qui ita atrociter in quartadecimanos Paschæ celebratores detonant, ut eos vel gradu Ecclesiastico co dejiciant, vel ad Iudæorum communionem ablegent, ii inquam, neque Apostoli sunt, neque Ignatius; sed impostores post Nicænam demum Synodum viventes, qui quod fere apud omnes Christianos suo sæculo observarin Paschæ celebratione videbant, semel sublata perillius Synodi authoritatem pristina ritus diversitate, id inquam & Apostolis & Ignatio, ut alia passim non pauca, non minus stulte, quam impudenter more suo affixerunt.
units.tr: b Petrus Halloix, Illustrium Ecclesiae Orientalis scriptorum, vol. 2, notes on chapter 2, 11 of the life of St Irenaeus, and vol. 1, in the life of Ignatius, chapters 22 and 26. "Keeps the Pascha, or takes up the solemnities of their festal days": to this, I say, this Jesuit replies in these words, that Ignatius condemns not those who celebrate the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon on the same day as the Jews, "but those who at the same table with the Jews ate the lamb in the Jewish manner, or ate the portions sent to them." So he says. He is foolish and ignorant here, as has been shown at length by R. Usher; yet his answer sufficiently shows how foolish and shameless it is to hold what Turrianus defends, namely that either the Apostles, or Ignatius, or Clement, or indeed any of the most holy men who lived at that time, thought it wrong to celebrate the Passover on the same day as the Jews, that is, on the fourteenth day of the moon. "Certainly it would be most absurd (says the Jesuit) to brand so severely what so many holy men in that very age in which Ignatius wrote (and among them St Polycarp himself) were doing." The most gentle Ignatius certainly never did this; never did it, indeed did not even think of it or dream of it. If Ignatius, as this man confidently asserts, did not do it, then certainly neither did the Apostles, who were by no means harsher than Ignatius. What then is the truth? Clearly those who thunder so savagely against the quartodeciman celebrants of Pascha, as to cast them down from their ecclesiastical rank or banish them from communion with the Jews, are neither Apostles nor Ignatius. They were impostors living only after the Nicene Synod, who, seeing that nearly all Christians of their age kept Easter in one way, and once the authority of that Synod had removed the former diversity of rite, attached this to the Apostles and to Ignatius, as they do with many other things here and there, no less foolishly than shamelessly, after their custom.

units.la: VI. Iam octavum, nonumque canones Romana certe Ecclesia quos abrogavit, Apostolicos non esse eo ipso confessa est.
units.tr: VI. Now the eighth and ninth canons, which the Roman Church has certainly abrogated, she has by that very act confessed not to be Apostolic.

units.la: Quis enim eam, quod ab Apostolis Domini præceptum, sanctitatemque esse putaret, neglecturam, violaturamque fuisse crediderit? Ac de octavo quidem canone, quo clerici qui facta oblatione non communicaverint, nisi causam rationabilem dixerint, communione privantur, præter ipsam hodiernam Romanorum praxin, diserte fatetur Binius; Totum hoc decretum (inquit) non divino, sed humano jure constitutum, jam contraria consuetudine est abrogatum.
units.tr: For who would believe that she would neglect or violate what she considered a precept and a holy rule of the Lord's Apostles? Concerning the eighth canon, by which clergy who do not communicate after the oblation are deprived of communion unless they give a reasonable cause, Binius plainly admits, apart from the present practice of the Romans, that "this whole decree was established not by divine but by human law, and has already been abrogated by contrary custom."

units.la: VII. De nono vero, qui Dionysio decimus, multo etiam manifestior res est. Canon sic habet, interprete Dionysio: Omnes
units.tr: VII. Concerning the ninth canon, which is the tenth in Dionysius, the matter is even clearer still. The canon reads, in the translation of Dionysius: All

units.la: Omnes fideles, qui ingrediuntur Ecclesiam, & Scripturas audiunt, non autem perseverant in Oratione, nec sanctam communionem percipiunt, velut inquietudines Ecclesiæ commoventes, convenit communiuniane privari. Hoc quam accurate in Ecclesia Romana observetur, nemo non videt; in qua sacram Eucharistiam non aliius plerumque sumit, nisi qui confecit. Fideles presbyterum sacra facientem spectare, satis habent. Quod ait Bellarminus , jam ipsis Ambrosii, Chrysostomique temporibus, id est 4. sæculo exeunte, Græcos non nisi post annum communicare solitos; id, inquam, si verum est (quod nunc non discutio) confirmat, Græcam illorum temporum Ecclesiam hos canones vel nescivisse penitus, vel eos certe pro Apostolicis nequaquam habuisse; quam scilicet incredibile est tam secure violaturam fuisse, si quid ab Apostolis, & quidem sub gravissima pœna decretum, sancitumque putasset. Iam quod Binius & Bellarminus & alii cavillantur, octavum canonem jubere, ut clerici communicent, non quidem semper, quoties sacræ intersunt synaxi, sed solennibus tantum diebus, quibus sacrificanti in missa solenniter ministrant, & altari assistunt; id inquam, merum istorum commentum est, quod cum difertissimis canonis verbis recta pugnat. Siquis Episcopus (inquit) aut presbyter, aut Diaconus, vel quilibet ex sacerdotali catalogo, facta oblatione non communicaverit, aut causam dicat, &c. aut communione privetur. Nihil de diebus solennibus; nihil de altaris ministerio. In genere quisquis ex sacro ordine Synaxi interfuerit, neque communicaverit, causam dicere jubet; si probabilem non dixerit, communione privari. Nihil fictitius Anacletus Binium contra clara disertaque canonis verba juvat, ut si hoc Apostolorum decretum est, negari non possit, quin & excommunicationis rei sint omnes hodierni Romanarum partium episcopi, presbyteri, aut diaconi, & ipsa Ecclesia Romana, quae hunc tantum Apostolicae authoritatis contemptum fert & probat, Apostolicae nomine indigna censeatur. Non sunt meliora quae de canone 9. (Dion 10) subjicit Binius. Duplex (inquit) est expositio hujus canonis.
