Prima est Concilii Antiocheni capite 2. non excommunicari vel damnari eos, qui simpliciter & absolute, extra legitima & constituta certa tempora non communicant; sed eos duntaxat, qui certa de causa, nimirum ob aliquam superstitionem, aut pravam opinionem, Scripturas quidem audiunt, sacram autem communionem aversantur. versentur. Quid istis facias, qui quasi cum stipitibus, aut cæcis surdisque ac mutis animalibus agunt, omnia pro libidine immutant, ac pervertunt, nosque vetant ipsa illa sentire, quæ & videmus, & audimus? Damnat canon πάντας τὺς εἰσιόντας πιςτὺς, omnes fideles, qui ingrediuntur Ecclesiam, & scripturas audiunt, non autem perseverant in Oratione, necfanctam communionem percipiunt. Non damnantur (inquit Binius) qui extra legitima & constituta tempora non communicant; Certe, inquam, ut fiquis, quo tempore sacrum non fit, pomeridianis exempli causa horis non communicet. Sed hoc non vult Binius. Vult non damnari, nisi qui Paschæ die, tribusve aut quatuor ad summum toto anno diebus festis non communicaverit; Quotquot (his exceptis temporibus) sacræ fynaxi adsunt, neque communicant tamen, eos ab hoc canone tangi, vel pulsari negat. Atqui omnes fideles ferit canon, qui ingrediuntur Ecclesiam, & scripturas audiunt; neque tamen communicant. Ergo vel tuæ, Bini, Ecclesiæ nisi statutis illis tuis temporibus non sunt, neque fideles tui, nisi hi diebus solis, fideles sunt; vel certe etiam istos tuos damnat canon, dum quibusvis temporibus ita sacris intersunt, ut non communicent. Obsecro tuam fidem; tuam frontem appello. Vestri illi homines, quos sacris vestris interesse, inde nulla recepta hostia discedere quotidie video, sunt-ne fideles? Tu quidem, ut opinor, non negabis. Sunt-ne ingressi Ecclesiam? Ne hoc quidem abnuere potes. Quid? Scriptu-ras-ne audierunt? Certe inquam; nisi tu eos surdos fuisse finxeris. Ultimum superest quod ait canon; illi non percepta communione discesserunt? Hoc vero etiam annuis. Ergo velis nolis, confitendum est, etiam istos tuos Canonem segregandos jubere. Par est de causa, quam Binius hariolatur, inverecundia. Non (inquit) damnantur, qui simpliciter abstinent, sed qui ob aliquam superstitionem, aut pravam opinionem, scripturas quidem audiunt; sacram autem communionem aversantur. Os impudens! Quam vero superstitionem, quam opinionis pravitatem, quos communionem aversantes narras? Atqui de istis ne unum quidem μὺ posuit Canon. Simpliciter, absoluteque de his omnibus fidelibus loquitur, qui Ecclesiam ingressi, Scripturisque auditis, non permanent in oratione, nec sanctam communionem percipiunt, quod etiam facere possunt, imo quotidie faciunt, qui neque ulla superstitione, aut prava opinione laborant, neque Christi Sacramentum aversantur. Ergo & hos percellit canon. Antiochenum canonem frustra advocat Binius. Primo enim quis nos ex hoc Apostolicum interpretari jussit? Patres quidem Antiocheni nihil de hoc, nihil de ullo Apostolorum canone, memorant; ut summa sit istorum inverecundia, qui hanc suam stultissimam atque impudentissimam glossam, Concilii Antiocheni expositionem appellare non dubitant: quasi scilicet ea Synodus hunc Apostolicum canonem ex professo interpretata sit, quem ne nominavit quidem. Tum nihil plane Antiocheni de superstitione, aut prava opinione (Ista mera Binii commenta sunt) Tantum eorum, quos damnant, crimen discribentes ajunt, illos ἀποσχίζεσθαι τὴν μετάληψιν τῆς εὐχαριστίας κατά τινα ἀταξίαν, aversari participationem sanctae Eucharistiae per quandam inordinationem (si nobis fas sit ita loqui) id est per quendam ordinis vel contemptum, vel certe neglectum. Quod ipsum, aut certe simile quid ille noster Apostolicus canon, iis quoque, quos damnat, impingit; Ait enim eos ἀτάξιαν ἐμποιεῖν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, perturbationem, & inordinationem, sive confusionem, vel (ut ait Dionysius) inquietudinem Ecclesiae commovere. Ut non tam notet quo animo hi Eucharistiam vitent, quam quid ex hoc eorum facto consequatur; (quae fortasse & ipsa est Antiochenae Synodi mens) Nimirum faciunt isti in Ecclesia ἀταξίαν. Ergo hanc in Ecclesia τάξιν, hunc ordinem esse volunt, ac decernunt nostri Canonistae, ut quisquis sacrae Eucharistiae, dum ea celebratur, interest fidelis, is communionem sanctam percipiat. Itaque si hi Canonistae vere sunt Apostoli, causa dici non potest, cur non Romana Ecclesia (quae totum illum ab his Canonistis constitutum ordinem, foedissime contemnit, & ab omnibus violari patitur) ab Apostolorum regulis discivisse, Apostolicaque nomen perdidisse censenda sit. Altera huius canonis expositio Gentiani Herveti est, hic segregari fingentis, non qui Ecclesiam ingressi scripturisque auditis non communicant, sed qui ante peractum a ministro sacrum discedunt. Sed hanc ipse Binius vix probare audet. Merito. Nam quod Graece est παρα μένειν τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ παραλήψει, id Latine esse perseverare in Oratione & sanctam communionem percipere, & verba ipsa clamant, & testatur Dionysius, antiquissimus & eruditissimus interpres, qui haec verba ita plane, ut diximus, reddidit; & demonstrat ille ipse Antiochenus canon, quo veram huius Apostolici expositionem contineri affirmabat Binius.
units.tr: All the faithful who enter the Church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere in prayer, nor receive the holy communion, stirring up unrest in the Church, ought to be deprived of communion. How strictly this is observed in the Roman Church, no one fails to see; there the holy Eucharist is for the most part received by no one except the celebrant. The faithful are content to watch the presbyter perform the sacred rite. As for Bellarmine's claim that already in the times of Ambrose and Chrysostom, that is at the end of the fourth century, the Greeks used to communicate only once a year: if that is true (which I do not now examine), it confirms that the Greek Church of those times either knew nothing of these canons or certainly did not regard them as Apostolic. For it is hardly credible that they would have violated so casually something that they thought had been decreed and sanctioned by the Apostles, and that under the most severe penalty. Now as to what Binius, Bellarmine and others cavil, that the eighth canon orders the clergy to communicate, not indeed every time they attend the sacred synaxis, but only on solemn days, when they minister solemnly at the sacrifice of the Mass and assist at the altar: I say this is pure invention of theirs, and it fights directly against the most explicit words of the canon. If any bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, or anyone from the sacerdotal list, having made the offering, does not communicate, let him give a reason, etc., or let him be deprived of communion. Nothing about solemn days; nothing about the ministry of the altar. In general, whoever of the sacred order has been present at the synaxis and has not communicated is ordered to give a reason; if he gives no probable reason, he is to be deprived of communion. Anacletus helps Binius nothing against the plain and explicit words of the canon. So if this is an Apostolic decree, it cannot be denied that all the present-day bishops, presbyters and deacons of the Roman party are liable to excommunication, and that the Roman Church itself, which bears and approves this contempt for Apostolic authority, should be judged unworthy of the name Apostolic. What Binius adds about canon 9 (Dionysius' 10) is no better. There are two explanations of this canon, he says. The first is that of the Council of Antioch, chapter 2: that those are not excommunicated or condemned who simply and absolutely, outside the lawful and fixed set times, do not communicate; but only those who, for some definite cause, namely on account of some superstition or a perverse opinion, hear the Scriptures but shun the holy communion. What can one do with people who deal with the matter as though with blocks of wood, or with blind, deaf and dumb animals, who change and pervert everything at their pleasure, and forbid us to think what we both see and hear? The canon condemns all the faithful who enter the Church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere in prayer, nor receive the holy communion. They are not condemned, says Binius, who do not communicate outside the lawful and fixed times. Certainly, I reply, as when someone does not communicate at a time when no sacrament is celebrated, say in the afternoon hours. But Binius does not mean this. He means that no one is condemned except one who has not communicated on Easter Day, or at most on three or four festival days in the whole year; and he denies that all who, apart from those times, attend the sacred synaxis and yet do not communicate are touched or struck by this canon. Yet the canon strikes all the faithful who enter the Church and hear the Scriptures, and yet do not communicate. Therefore, Binius, either your Churches exist only at those set times, and your faithful are faithful only on those days, or else this canon condemns even those of yours who attend the sacred rites at any time without communicating. I appeal to your good faith, I appeal to your forehead. Those men of yours, whom I see every day attending your sacred rites and leaving without receiving any host, are they faithful? You will not, I think, deny it. Have they entered the Church? You cannot deny even this. What then? Have they heard the Scriptures? Certainly, I say; unless you pretend they were deaf. The last thing the canon says is that they left without receiving communion. This too you admit. Therefore, willy-nilly, it must be confessed that the canon orders even your people to be separated. The defence Binius conjectures for this cause is of the same shamelessness. Those are not condemned, he says, who simply abstain, but those who, on account of some superstition or perverse opinion, hear the Scriptures but shun the holy communion. Impudent mouth! What superstition, what perversity of opinion, what shunners of communion are you describing? Yet the canon does not contain a single not about such people. It speaks simply and absolutely of all these faithful who have entered the Church, and having heard the Scriptures, do not persevere in prayer, nor receive the holy communion; and they can do this, indeed they do it every day, though they are troubled by no superstition or perverse opinion, and do not shun the Sacrament of Christ. So the canon strikes these too. Binius calls on the Antiochene canon in vain. For first, who ordered us to interpret this Apostolic canon by that one? The Fathers of Antioch say nothing about this, nothing about any canon of the Apostles; so great is the shamelessness of those who do not hesitate to call their most foolish and impudent gloss the explanation of the Council of Antioch, as though that Synod had professedly interpreted this Apostolic canon, which it did not even mention. Then the Antiochenes say nothing at all about superstition or perverse opinion (these are mere inventions of Binius). They merely describe the crime of those they condemn, saying that they ἀποσχίζεσθαι τὴν μετάληψιν τῆς εὐχαριστίας κατά τινα ἀταξίαν [apart themselves from the participation in the Eucharist through a certain disorder], that is, that they stand apart from the participation of the holy Eucharist through a certain disorder (if we may speak so), that is, through a certain contempt or at least neglect of order. This same charge, or something very like it, that canon of ours from the Apostles also lays against those it condemns. For it says that they ἀτάξιαν ἐμποιεῖν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ [bring disorder into the Church], that they stir up disturbance and disorder or confusion, or, as Dionysius puts it, unrest in the Church. So it does not so much note with what mind these people avoid the Eucharist as what follows from their action (which perhaps is also the meaning of the Synod of Antioch). Clearly those people cause ἀταξία [disorder] in the Church. Therefore our canonists want this τάξις [order] in the Church, this order, and decree that whoever, being a faithful person, is present when the holy Eucharist is celebrated, should receive the holy communion. Accordingly, if these canonists are truly Apostles, no reason can be given why the Roman Church, which most foully despises the order these canonists have laid down and allows it to be violated by all, should not be judged to have departed from the rules of the Apostles and to have lost the name Apostolic. The second explanation of this canon is that of Gentian Hervet, who pretends that those are separated not who have entered the Church and heard the Scriptures but do not communicate, but those who leave before the sacred rite has been completed by the minister. But Binius himself hardly dares to approve this. Rightly so. For what in Greek is [παραμένειν τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ παραλήψει], in Latin is to persevere in prayer and to receive the holy communion; the words themselves cry this out, and Dionysius, a most ancient and learned translator, bears witness, since he rendered these words just so, as we have said; and that Antiochene canon itself, by which Binius claimed the true explanation of this Apostolic canon was contained, demonstrates it.

units.la: Is enim canon segregat τὰς μὴ κοινωνοῦντας ψυχῆς ἅμα τῷ λαῷ ἢ ἀποσχιζομένας τὸ μεταλη-ψιν τῆς εὐχαριστίας, qui non communicant in oratione cum populo, aut aver-santur participationem Eucharistiæ. Neque aliter acceperunt ipsi Græci Canonum interpretes, Balsamo, & Zonaras; Ac hujus quidem hæc sunt in hunc locum verba; καὶ οἱ λαϊκοὶ γὰρ συνεχῶς τότε μεταλαμβάνειν ἀπῄτουντο. Siquidem tum temporis etiam à Laicis exigebatur, ut assidue communicarent. Balsamonis vero illa ibidem leguntur; ὁ τὸ παρόντ᾿ κανόν᾿ διορισμὸς, δεμνύτατός ἐστιν· ἀφοείζει γὰρ τὰς ἐκκλησιάζοντας, καὶ μὴ παραμένοντας μέχρι τέλους, μηδὲ μεταλαμβάνοντας. Præsentis canonis constitutio est acerbissima: Segregat enim eos, qui in Ecclesiam conveniunt, & non ad finem usque expectant, nec communicant. Ergo nulla vi, vel arte effugere potest Binius, quin sit Romæ Ecclesia, non, quod gloriatur, Apostolica, sed plane, quod abominatur, Apostatica, siquidem hi duo vere sunt Apostolorum canones. Hoc vero, prius, quam concedant, istos equidem arbitror non stramineos modo hos canones, sed & ipsa Euangelia in dubium revocaturos.
units.tr: For this canon sets apart those who do not communicate [τὰς μὴ κοινωνοῦντας] along with the people in prayer, or who shrink from partaking of the Eucharist: those who do not join the people in prayer, or who shun taking part in the Eucharist. The Greek commentators on the canons, Balsamon and Zonaras, understood it in the same way. Zonaras, on this passage, says: For in those days the laity too were required to communicate constantly; at that time, that is, the laity were obliged to communicate regularly. Balsamon's words on the same passage read: The provision of the present canon is most severe. For it cuts off those who attend the assembly but do not remain to the end, and do not communicate. [ὁ τὸ παρόντ᾿ κανόν᾿ διορισμὸς, δεμνύτατός ἐστιν· ἀφοείζει γὰρ τὰς ἐκκλησιάζοντας, καὶ μὴ παραμένοντας μέχρι τέλους, μηδὲ μεταλαμβάνοντας.] Therefore Binius cannot by any force or skill escape the conclusion that the Roman Church is not, as it boasts, Apostolic, but plainly, as it deserves to be called, Apostate, since these two are truly canons of the Apostles. Yet before they concede this, I think they will find that these canons not only threaten to bring down straw, but will call into doubt the Gospels themselves.

units.la: Arg. VIII. ex canone 16. de clerico concubinario. Refelluntur Turriani ineptiæ.
units.tr: Argument VIII, from canon 16 on the concubinary clergyman. The follies of Turrianus are refuted.

units.la: VIII. TIDEM ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ usu & praxi discedit, quod Turriani Apostoli decernunt canone 16. (Dionysio 17.) ὁ δνοὶ γάμοις συμπλακεὶς μὴ τὸ βάπτισμα, ἢ παλλακὴν κτησάμενος, ἡ δωδεκάτη ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὁ λαὸς τὴν καταλοιπὴν τὴν ἱερατικὴν. Qui post sanctum baptismum duobus conjugiis fuit implicitus, vel habuerit concubinam, non potest esse Episcopus, vel presbyter, vel Diaconus, vel omnino ex numero sacerdotali. Primo, quod concubinarium a sacro ministrorum censu arcet, id bona Roma ducit intolerabile; cujus est hic (sane sanctissimus, meritoque inviolabilis) canon, concubinatum irregularitate non puniri. Itaque quod hic dicitur, nunc usu revocatum, & sublatum esse tradit Cavarruvias, referente Binioa. Quamquam ipse Binius concubinarium, non propter ipsum flagitium, sed tantum ratione infamia irregularem hoc canone constitui, ac declarari putat; adeoque eum tantum cujus
units.tr: VIII. Likewise, what the Turrianian Apostles decree in canon 16 (Dionysius 17) departs from the usage and practice of the Roman Church: ὁ δὶς γάμοις συμπλακεὶς μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, ἢ παλλακὴν κτησάμενος, ἡ δωδεκάτη ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὁ λαὸς τὴν καταλοιπὴν τὴν ἱερατικήν. Whoever, after holy baptism, has been entangled in two marriages, or has acquired a concubine, cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the priestly order. First, the good Romans regard as intolerable that this canon, which is certainly most holy and rightly inviolable, bars a concubinary from the sacred roll of ministers. Its rule is concubinage is not punished by irregularity. Accordingly, what is said here, Cavarruvias tells us, has now been revoked and abolished by use, as Biniusa. reports. Yet Binius himself thinks that by this canon a concubinary is declared irregular not for the disgrace itself but only by reason of infamy, and so only the one whose

units.la: a Clem. ut supra. jus publicum est, & cum magna infamia conjunctum flagitium. Sed ille quidem nobis solens illudit. Canon enim sacris ordinibus excludit, non qui ex stupris & fornicationibus, atque vagis publicisque flagitiis infamiam collegit, sed qui con-cubinam habuerit; ut nihil sit verius, quam quod rotunde fatetur in Canonicis Binio multo doctior Covarruvias, quod nunc in Romana Ecclesia sabbatum est, id ipsum esse, quod in hoc canone dictum erat. Itaque alio confugit Turrianus, & quam canon παλλακὴν vocat, id est pel-licem, vel concubinam, eam iste pro consueta audacia, non fornicariam, sed legitimo thori jure sociatam mulierem accipit, quod interdum concubinae nomen honestorum illo sensu sumptum reperiatur. Sed ille, ut alias solet, ita hic quoque frustra insanit. Nam ut Graecos interpretes mittam, qui hunc τὸν παλλακὴν ὑπεσταμένον, interpretantur b τὸν μετὰ τὸ ἅγιον βάπτισμα πορνεύσαντα, eum qui post sanctum baptisma fornicatus est; ipse quid sit sequendum, edicit, ac docet canon. Nam quem concubinam habuisse dicit, eum illi ex adverso opponit, qui conjugiis fuerit implicitus; stulte, ut quivis videt, ac praeter omnem rationem, si is conjugio & ipse legitimo implicitus fuerit. Tum si Canonista hoc, quod vult Turrianus, in animo habuisset, à sacris ordinibus arcendum dixisset, non qui concubinam, sed qui duas concubinas habuerit. Nam si (quod unus mortalium delirat Turrianus) pellex sive concubina hoc loco est legitima conjux, apparet non unam, sed qui duas habuerit concubinas, sacerdotio arcendum. Alienum enim est ab omni Romano Graecoque, ac (ut semel dicam) Ecclesiastico jure, ut qui unam tantum uxorem habuerit, is sacris ordinibus excludatur. Itaque, ut duo conjugia, sic & necessario duas concubinas dicere canon debuit, si concubina nomine legitimam conjugem intellexit. At hoc tamen nequaquam dixit; sed δυσὶ γάμοις, duobus conjugiis, τῷ παλλακῇ pellicem sive concubinam oppositit. Nimirum significat conjugium rem honestam, neminem à sacris prohibere, nisi iteratum fuerit, quod eo videatur aliqua incontinentiae significatio contineri. Concubinatus, foedae & flagitiosae rei aliam esse rationem. Eo enim vel semel pollutos, ab Ecclesiasticis cancellis excludi. Certe hanc fuisse veteris Ecclesiae (ex qua hunc canonem sumpsit impostor) sententiam, docet Synodus Neocaesariensis, gravius multans presbyterum fornicantem, quam conjugium contrahentem, Πρεσβύτερος ἐὰν γήμῃ (inquit) τῆς τάξεως αὐτοῦ. αὐτὸν μετατίθεσθαι. ἐαν ὁ πορνεύση ἡ μοιχεύση ἐξωθεῖσθαι αὐτὸν τέλεον, & ἁγιέσ αὐτὸν εἰς μετάνοιαν. Deniq; si concubina hic esset, quam vult Turrianus, conjux scilicet legitima, omnino stultum, ac supervacaneum erat hęc in canone verba addere.Satis quippe cautum est prioribus verbis, ne quis, qui duobus conjugiis implicitus fuerit, in sacerdotali catalogo esse possit. Ergo si est Apostolorum hic canon, Romanam Ecclesiam ab Apostolica regula deflectere palam est, quæ (concubinatum inter caussas irregularitatis (ut loquuntur) non habet; quem à canone eo loco ac numero haberi clarum, certumque est. Sed & eadem jam pridem discessat à priori canonis parte, qua à sacro catalogo arcetur, qui duobus post baptismum conjugiis fuerit implicitus. Ipsa enim, quod notum est, à clericatu excludit quisquis uxores duas duxerit, sive post, sive etiam ante baptismum. Ridicula est Turriani audacia, qui Canonem sic interpretatur a, quasi duobus conjugiis implicitus post baptismum, is sit, qui vel bis duxit uxorem ante baptismum, vel semel ante baptismum, & iterum post baptismum, vel bis post baptismum. Sed si ista Canonis mens fuisset, nihil necesse erat baptismi mentionem facere, cujus scilicet ratio nullum hic locum habet; cum sacris ordinibus nibus
units.tr: a Clem., as above. crime is a matter of public law and is joined with great infamy. But he mocks us, as he is wont to do. The canon excludes from the sacred orders not one who has gathered infamy from debauchery, fornication, and open vagrant vices, but one who has had a concubine. So nothing is truer than what Covarruvias, far more learned than Binius in canon law, frankly admits: what is now a dead letter in the Roman Church is itself what was stated in this canon. Turrianus therefore flees elsewhere. Since the canon calls her παλλακὴν, that is pellex or concubina, he takes her, with his usual boldness, not as a fornicatress but as a woman joined under the lawful right of marriage, since the name concubina is sometimes found used in that honourable sense. But he rages in vain here too, as he usually does. Not to mention the Greek interpreters, who render τὸν παλλακὴν ὑπεσταμένον as "the one who after holy baptism has fornicated," the canon itself prescribes and teaches what is to be followed. For the one whom it says had a concubine it sets over against the one who was entangled in marriage. That is foolish, as anyone can see, and against all reason if this one too was entangled in a lawful marriage. Moreover, if the canonist had meant what Turrianus wants, he would have said excluded from holy orders not he who had a concubine but he who had two concubines. For if (which only Turrianus of all mortals raves) pellex or concubina here is a legitima conjux, a lawful wife, it is plain that it is whoever had two, not one, who should be barred from the priesthood. For it is alien to every Roman, Greek, and (to say it once for all) ecclesiastical law that one who has had only one wife should be excluded from holy orders. So if by concubina he meant a lawful spouse, the canon ought necessarily to have said two concubines, as it says two marriages. But it did not say this at all. It set δυσὶ γάμοις, two marriages, against τῇ παλλακῇ, pellex or concubina. Plainly, marriage signifies an honourable thing, which bars no one from the sacred orders unless it has been repeated, since a repeated marriage seems to contain some sign of incontinence. Concubinage, a foul and shameful thing, has another reckoning. By it, even once defiled, a man is excluded from the ecclesiastical enclosure. This was certainly the view of the old Church, from which the impostor took this canon, as the Synod of Neocaesarea teaches, punishing a presbyter who fornicates more severely than one who contracts marriage: "A presbyter, if he marries" (it says) "is to be removed from his order; if he fornicates or commits adultery, he is to be cast out utterly and placed among penitents" (Πρεσβύτερος ἐὰν γήμῃ τῆς τάξεως αὐτοῦ μετατίθεσθαι· ἐὰν πορνεύσῃ ἢ μοιχεύσῃ, ἐξωθεῖσθαι αὐτὸν τέλεον, καὶ ἁγιέσθαι αὐτὸν εἰς μετάνοιαν). Finally, if concubina here were what Turrianus wants, namely a lawful wife, it would be utterly foolish and superfluous to add these words to the canon. For it is sufficiently guarded against by the preceding words, lest anyone who has been entangled in two marriages be found in the sacerdotal catalogue. So if this canon is Apostolic, it is plain that the Roman Church deviates from the Apostolic rule, which does not count concubinage among the causes of irregularity (as they call it). It is clear and certain that the canon holds that place and number. But that Church long ago also departed from the earlier part of the canon, by which one is barred from the sacred roll who after baptism has been entangled in two marriages. For it itself, as is well known, excludes from the clergy whoever has married two wives, whether after or even before baptism. Turrianus's boldness is ridiculous. He interprets the canon as if entangled in two marriages after baptism meant one who married twice before baptism, or once before and again after baptism, or twice after baptism.

units.la: a Vb. supr. p. 74. verf. nibus'ex hac Turrianica hypothesi tam excludatur, qui ante, quam qui post baptismum, vel unam e duabus, vel utramque duxerit. Simpliciter dicendum erat, Qui duobus conjugiis fuerit implicitus, is sacerdos esse non potest; vel si metuebat Canonista, nequis conjugium baptismum antecedens exciperet, plane occurrendum erat exceptioni hoc modo, Qui duobus conjugiis, etiam ante baptismum, vel sive post, sive ante baptismum implicitus fuerit, ne esto sacerdos. Nunc plane aliter habent Canonis verba; Ita enim posita sunt, ut hanc ipsam, quam excludi vult, Turrianus exceptionem constituant, ac confirment, ὁ δυο γάμοις ἐμπλακεὶς μὴ τὸ βάπτισμα, is (ut omnes graece periti vident) est duobus conjugiis post baptismum implicitus; ut si quis bis quidem uxorem duxerit; sed vel utramque, vel certe priorem, antequam baptizaretur, duxerit, eum praesens canon a sacro ordine minime arceat, vel excludat. Quo pertinet hujus canonis allata a Zonara ratio; quod divino scilicet lavacro sancti baptismatis abluantur omnes sordes ipsis baptizatis ante baptismum illita.
units.tr: a Vb. above, p. 74. Yet if this were the canon's meaning, there was no need to mention baptism at all, whose relevance has no place here. On this Turrianian hypothesis, one who married before baptism is excluded from holy orders just as much as one who married after it, whether he took one of the two wives or both. It should have been stated simply: Whoever has been entangled in two marriages cannot be a priest. Or if the canonist feared that someone might take the marriage preceding baptism as an exception, he should clearly have obviated that exception in this way: Whoever has been entangled in two marriages, whether after baptism or before it, or both, let him not be a priest. As it is, the words of the canon are quite different. They are so placed that they establish and confirm the very exception which Turrianus wants excluded: ὁ δὶς γάμοις ἐμπλακεὶς μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα. He (as all who know Greek see) is one entangled in two marriages after baptism. So if someone has indeed married twice, but has married both, or at least the former, before he was baptized, the present canon does not bar or exclude him at all from holy orders. To this pertains the reason for the canon given by Zonaras: that by the divine laver of holy baptism all the defilements smeared upon the baptized before baptism are washed away.

units.la: Itaque Innocentius hac, quae a sacris ordinibus excludit, digamia etiam id conjugium contineri docens, ac decernens, quod ante baptismum contractum fuerat, hunc Apostolo-
units.tr: Accordingly Innocent, teaching that the digamy which excludes from holy orders also includes that marriage which was contracted before baptism, and decreeing this, does not interpret this Apostolic

units.la: a Ep. ad Vitr. Pro tom. c. 6. Apostolicum canonem, non sane interpretatur, quod stultissime ait Turrianus, sed plane oppugnat, atque evertit; eoque ipso testatur sibi quidem Apostolicum non fuisse; quem, ut liquet, si vere Apostolicum putasset, plane aliter, quam fecit, de toto hoc negotio statuisset. Ergo neque Innocentio, neque Ecclesiae Romanae, quae ejus hac de re judicium sequitur, Apostolicus esse vel potest, vel debet hic Turrianicus canon.
units.tr: a Letter to Vitricius, Pro tom., ch. 6. canon, as Turrianus very foolishly says, but plainly opposes and overturns it. By that very fact he testifies that it was not Apostolic for him. For had he truly thought it Apostolic, he would have decided the whole matter quite differently from how he did. Therefore this Turrianian canon can be, or ought to be, Apostolic neither for Innocent nor for the Roman Church, which follows his judgment in this matter.
