units.la: Arg. IX. ex canonibus 21. 22. 23. de iis, qui se abscindunt. Arg. X. ex can, 26. 29. de iis, qui potestatis facularis favore Ecclesiae dignitates invadunt. Arg. XI. ex can. 33. de metropolitanis. Arg. XII. ex can. 49. de trina in baptismo mersione. Adversariorum cavillationes discutiuntur.
units.tr: Argument IX, from canons 21, 22 and 23, concerning those who castrate themselves. Argument X, from canons 26 and 29, concerning those who seize Church offices through the favour of secular power. Argument XI, from canon 33, concerning metropolitans. Argument XII, from canon 49, concerning threefold immersion in baptism. The cavils of the opponents are examined.

units.la: IX. ERGAMUS. Tres de Eunuchis canones a decernunt, ne qui seipsum abscidit, clericus fiat, & si factus sit, ut deponatur; laicus vero tribus annis segregetur, hac ratione allata, Est enim sui homicida, & Dei opificii hostis. Vera quidem ratio, & rectum decretum; sed tamen hujusmodi, quod non videtur ab Apostolis ipsis constitutum. Nam cum e morum vitiis, peccatorumque praecipuae singularium, & quae rarissime contingunt, exemplis nascantur ut plurimum leges; quo factum olim fuisse accepimus, ut nullum a sapientissimo licet legislatore, in parricidas supplicium constitutum esset; non est verisimile hos in rarum, absurdumque facinus canones prius in Ecclesia positos, ac promulgatos fuisse, quam ferendae hujusmodi legis occasionem dedisset editum ab aliquo hujus facinoris exemplum. Apostolicis vero temporibus, & iis, quae Apostolica proxime consecuta sunt, hujusmodi aliquid ab ullo Christiano designatum fuisse inauditum est; cum tamen ipsa rei singularitas, siquid tale contigisset, id ad posterorum memoriam propagari posceret, ac paene flagitaret. Iustinus quidem non tacet Christiani adolescentis factum, qui a Felice praefecto Augustali Alexandriae oblato libello petivit, ut sibi liceret medici opera partes illas sibimet abscindere, quod tamen non impetravit. Origenis vero, qui postea idem in se ipsum designare ausus est, factum quam sit in omnibus antiquitatis monumentis celebre, nemo nescit. Cum ergo nulla hujusmodi apud Christianos ante Iustini tempora facinotinoris extet memoria, à veri specie abhorret, ullum ab Apostolis contra eos, qui rem adeo absurdam, & à naturæ, civitatumque, ac Dei denique ipsius legibus alienam auderent, factum unquam decretum. Certe si quod factum fuisset, Justinique temporibus extitisset; primo adolescens ille Alexandrinus, cujus magna erat pietas, & insignis in pietatem zelus, non videtur unquam rem ab Apostolis disertissime, & quidem sub triennalis segregationis poena vetitam, aggressurus fuisse. Quo loco obiter detegenda est Baronii fraus, qui hoc istius adolescentis factum referens a, ait eum id propterea tentasse, quo careret omni carnis irrationali motu. Ea vero annalistæ hariolatio est; immo merum somnium, à monachalis causæ studio profectum. Nihil hujusmodi Justinus tradit, à quo uno hanc historiam habemus. Ille vero longe diversum adolescentis consilium narrat; quem ait hoc aggressum esse, ὑπὲρ τῆς πείσαι ὑμᾶς (inquit) ὅτι ἐν ἐςτιν ἡμῖν μυςήριον ἡ ἀνέδλω μίξις, ut urbis (id est Paganis) persuaderet non esse nobis mysterium promiscuam & propatulam mistionem. Tum siqui hujusmodi apud Christianos extitissent Apostolorum canones, aliquam erat eorum hoc loco mentionem facturus Justinus. Omnino enim ad ejus
units.tr: IX. Let us proceed. Three canons on eunuchs decree that anyone who has castrated himself may not become a cleric, and if he has become one, that he be deposed; a layman, however, is to be separated from the Church for three years. The reason given is: for he is a murderer of himself and an enemy of God's workmanship. The reason is true and the decree right, but it is of a kind that does not seem to have been laid down by the Apostles themselves. For laws usually arise from the vices of morals and from examples of particular sins, and especially of those that very rarely occur. We are told that this was the case in the past, when no penalty against parricides had been established even by the wisest lawgiver. So it is not likely that canons on so rare and absurd a crime were first set down and promulgated in the Church before some example of this crime had occurred to prompt the making of such a law. In Apostolic times, and in those that immediately followed the Apostles, it is unheard of that any Christian had done anything of this kind; yet the very singularity of such a thing, had it happened, would have demanded, and almost required, that it be handed down to the memory of posterity. Justin indeed does not keep silent about the deed of a Christian young man who, having presented a petition to Felix, the Augustal prefect at Alexandria, asked that he might be allowed to have those parts cut off by a physician; he did not obtain this. As for the deed of Origen, who afterwards dared to do the same to himself, how famous it is in all the monuments of antiquity no one fails to know. Since, therefore, there is no memory of any such deed among Christians before the time of Justin, it is far from the appearance of truth that any canon was ever issued by the Apostles against those who dared a thing so absurd, and so alien to nature, to the state, and indeed to the laws of God himself. Certainly, if such a deed had occurred, it would have come to light in Justin's time. First, that young Alexandrian, whose piety was great and whose zeal for piety was remarkable, does not seem ever to have undertaken a thing that the Apostles had forbidden so plainly, and indeed under the penalty of three years' separation. Here, in passing, the fraud of Baronius must be exposed. In recording this deed of the young man, he says that he attempted it so that he might be free from every irrational motion of the flesh. This is the divination of an annalist, or rather a mere dream, arising from zeal for the monastic cause. Justin reports nothing of the kind, and he is our only source for this story. Justin, indeed, gives a quite different account of the young man's purpose: he says that he undertook it in order to persuade you (he says, that is, the city, meaning the pagans) that promiscuous and open intercourse is not a mystery among us [ὑπὲρ τῆς πείσαι ὑμᾶς ὅτι ἐν ἐστιν ἡμῖν μυστήριον ἡ ἀνέδην μίξις]. Then, if any canons of the Apostles of this kind had existed among Christians, Justin would certainly have made some mention of them at this point.

units.la: a a. D. 230. §. 4. ejus consilium pertinebat, ne ex tali facinore lævum aliquid de nostræ disciplinæ inhumanitate suspicarentur Pagani, offendere id quidem facinus adolescentem juvenili animi ardore aggressum esse; sed præter Christi & Apostolorum institutum, qui tale quid audentes, adeo non laudant, ut etiam veluti sui ipsorum homicidas gravissime insectentur, pœnisque ac censuris Ecclesiasticis subjiciant. Hæc omnino commemoraturus hoc loco erat Iustinus, si fuissent a secretis Apostolis hi Dionysiaci Turrianicique canones facti, atque traditi. Atqui nihil ille hujusmodi toto eo loco dicit. Ergo nondum eos extitisse patet. Idem ex Origenis facto, qui aliquanto post, anno scilicet Domini (ut quidem conjicit Baronius) 208. se ipsum abscidit, evidenter apparet. Nam quis credat, si canones isti in publica Ecclesiæ luce extitissent, proque legibus Apostolicis habiti essent, adolescentem egregium, tantæ jam in illa ætate eruditionis, ut schola Alexandrinæ Ecclesia præesset a, id facinus aggressurum fuisse, quod sub excommunicationis vel depositionis pœna ab Apostolis prohibitum esse scivisset? Demetrius certe Episcopus, postquam id ejus factum rescivit, hominem violati Apostolici decreti manifestum, non solum muñere illo, quo in Schola fungebatur,
units.tr: a A.D. 230, §. 4. For it was part of his purpose to keep the pagans from suspecting anything harsh in the inhumanity of our discipline, and so he said that the young man had undertaken the deed in the ardour of youthful spirit; but he said this against the institution of Christ and the Apostles, who not only do not praise those who dare such things, but even sharply rebuke them as murderers of themselves and subject them to penalties and ecclesiastical censures. Justin would certainly have mentioned all this at this point, had these Dionysian and Turrianian canons been made and handed down by the Apostles in secret. But he says nothing of the kind in that whole place. Therefore it is plain that they did not yet exist. The same is evident from the deed of Origen, who, a little later, in the year of the Lord (as Baronius conjectures) 208, castrated himself. For who would believe that, if these canons had existed in the full light of the Church, and had been regarded as Apostolic laws, a young man of such distinction, already so learned at that age that he presided over the school of the Alexandrian Church, would have undertaken a deed which he knew had been forbidden by the Apostles under the penalty of excommunication or deposition? Certainly Demetrius, the bishop, after he learned of the deed, a man plainly guilty of violating an Apostolic decree, not only would have removed him from that office which he held in the School, but would also have punished him by exclusion from the communion of the Church for three years. Yet Demetrius did none of this. Indeed, as Eusebius testifies, although he greatly marvelled at this bold deed of his, he nevertheless embraced his incredible eagerness of mind and his candour of faith, and bade him at once take heart and be of good cheer, and urged and impelled him to devote himself with greater care and zeal to teaching the principles of the faith.

units.la: a Eusebius l. 6. c. 7. tur abdicasset, sed etiam Ecclesiæ communione ad triennium multasset. Atqui non modo nihil istorum fecit Demetrius; sed & insuper, teste Eusebio, tametsi hoc audax ejus factinus vehementer admiratus est, tamen incredibilem animi propensionem, & ingenuitatem fidei amplexatus, eum illico confidere, & bono animo esse jubet; & majore cura ac studio in munus fidei principia instituendi incumbere hortatur, impelcitque. Et post hæc tempora narrat idem Eusebius , Origenem illud suum docendi munus Alexandriæ magna cum laude, & hominum utilitate plures annos gessisse, & postquam honorifice à Demetrio in Arabiam ad Præsidem ejus colloquium expetentem, missus fuisset, Alexandriam reversum in eodem honore mansisse. Sed & postea, cum Demetrius mutato animo, viri gloriæ (ut quidem tradit Eusebius ) invidens, eum à Theoctisto Cæsareæ, & Alexandro Hierosolymorum, Episcopis, spectatis inprimis, & præsentibus Palæstinæ antistitibus; ad presbyteri dignitatem evectum indignaretur, & alia criminandi occasione destitutus, facti illius, quod ab ineunte ætate conscivisset, calumniam objectaret, eamque apud episcopos totius orbis, tanquam absurdissimi facinoris reum per litteras notaret; constat tamen neq; Theoctistum
units.tr: a Eusebius, book 6, chapter 7. ...had removed him from that office, but had also excluded him from the communion of the Church for three years. Yet Demetrius did none of these things. On the contrary, as Eusebius testifies, although he was greatly astonished at this bold deed of his, nevertheless, embracing his incredible readiness of mind and the sincerity of his faith, he bids him at once to take heart and be of good courage, and urges and impels him to apply himself with still greater care and zeal to teaching the principles of the faith. And Eusebius relates that after this time Origen held his teaching office at Alexandria for many years, with great praise and to the benefit of many, and that, after Demetrius honourably sent him to Arabia at the governor's request for a conference, he returned to Alexandria and remained in the same office. But afterwards Demetrius changed his mind. Envious of the man's glory (as Eusebius indeed reports), and indignant that Origen had been raised to the rank of presbyter by Theoctistus of Caesarea and Alexander of Jerusalem, bishops of the highest standing and present as leaders of Palestine, and lacking another ground for accusation, he brought up the charge of that deed which Origen had committed in his early youth, and denounced him in letters to the bishops of the whole world as guilty of a most absurd crime. Yet it is certain that neither Theoctistus

units.la: a Id. l.6. c.13. b l.6. c.7. ěistum & Alexandrum de suo in illum studio quicquam propterea remisisse, neque vel ipsos, vel alios Episcopos re intellecta, hominem de presbyterii gradu dejecisse ; ut ex omni Eusebiana de Origenis rebus, quæ amplissima est, narratione intelligimus. At quis laudatissimos, jurisque omnis Ecclesiastici scientissimos viros putet hominem in ea dignitate confirmaturos fuisse, e qua disertis Apostolorum vocibus deturbari eum scivissent ? Quid, quod annis post id tempus circiter centum, Athanasius de Leontio primum presbytero, mox & episcopo Antiocheno Arianarum partium, verba faciens, ejusque simile facinus invidiosissime exagitans, nullam tamen memorat Apostolicam contra istos legem ; sed hæc tantum habet, (inquit a) ον ὡς ἀλλὰ ...
units.tr: a Id., book 6, chapter 13. b Book 6, chapter 7. ...and Alexander bore any further ill will against him on that account, nor did they, or any other bishops, once they understood the matter, remove the man from the rank of presbyter, as we learn from the whole of Eusebius's account of Origen's affairs, which is very full. But who would think that the most celebrated men, and most learned in all Church law, would have confirmed a man in that dignity, from which they knew he ought to be thrust out by the plain words of the Apostles? What of the fact that about a hundred years after that time Athanasius, speaking of Leontius, first a presbyter and then bishop of Antioch on the Arian side, and bitterly denouncing a similar deed, nevertheless mentions no Apostolic law against such men? He says only this: [ον ὡς ἀλλὰ ...]

units.la: Λεοντιν ὁ ἀποκοπῶ ... Leontius ille castratus, quem ne ut laicum quidem ad communionem admitti oportuit, eo quod seipsum abscidit, ut libere cum Eustolio dormiret, revera quidem ejus muliere, sed quæ virgo dicitur. Nemo non videt multo fortius, ac invidiosius dicturum fuisse Athanasium, si ex Apostolico canone hanc Leontio sui facinoris mercedem deberi adjecisset. Quod non adjecit, eo fatetur, nullum sibi ea de re Apostolorum canonem fuisse cognitum. Quo ergo (inquis) canone Leontium decebat presbyterio abdicari, & laica ipsa communione multari? Nempe inquam, ex Nicaeno annis antequam Leontius presbyter fieret, aliquot condito, & ex aliquo etiam fortasse antiquiori ab Alexandrinis ex Origenici facinoris occasione, ut supra diximus, constituto. Huc denique accedit, quod Epiphanius, Athanasio junior, Valesiorum, qui seipsos abscindebant, sectam ac dogma refellens argumentis, tum a re ipsa, rectaque ratione, tum etiam ab Apostolorum, Pautique nominatim in epistolis doctrina petitis, nullam istorum canonum mentionem facit; quos, si vere Apostolici essent, in tali disputatione omittere flagitium erat; quod nihil scilicet afferri poterat in absurdum Valesiorum institutum his disertius atque potentius. Ergo non fuerunt hi canones illius saeculi (hoc est quarti) Christianis pro Apostolicis habiti, neque adeo Apostolici revera sunt; quos haud dubie, si ii Apostolici vere essent, hoc numero ac loco habituri erant & Athanasius, & Epiphanius.
units.tr: [Λεοντιν ὁ ἀποκοπῶ ...] Leontius, that castrated man, who ought not to be admitted to communion even as a layman, because he cut himself off so that he might sleep freely with Eustolius, indeed with his wife, though she is called a virgin. Everyone sees that Athanasius would have spoken far more strongly and bitterly if he had added that Leontius deserved this reward for his deed by Apostolic canon. That he did not add it shows he knew of no canon of the Apostles on this matter. By what canon, you will say, was Leontius fitting to be removed from the presbyterate and punished with exclusion even from lay communion? Indeed, I answer, by the Nicene canon, drawn up some years before Leontius became a presbyter, and perhaps also by some still earlier one, which the Alexandrians established on the occasion of Origen's deed, as we said above. Finally, to this must be added that Epiphanius, a younger contemporary of Athanasius, in refuting the sect and doctrine of the Valesians, who castrated themselves, by arguments drawn both from the nature of the matter and right reason, and also from the teaching of the Apostles and of Paul specifically in his epistles, makes no mention of any of these canons. Had they truly been Apostolic, to omit them in such a dispute would have been a scandal, since nothing could have been brought against the Valesians' practice more clearly and forcefully than them. Therefore these canons were not regarded as Apostolic by Christians of that century (that is, the fourth), nor are they in fact Apostolic; for had they truly been Apostolic, both Athanasius and Epiphanius would certainly have cited them in this number and in this place.

units.la: X. Iam neque Apostolicis temporibus congruunt canones 26. & 29. (aliis 28. & 31.) quorum ille deponi jubet episcopum, presbyterum, & diaconum, verberantem fideles qui peccant, vel infideles, injuriam facientes, & per hujusmodi perterrefacere volentem; hic vero eadem poena Episcopum multat, qui saecularibus potestatibus ipsus Ecclesiam per ipsos obtinet. Atqui non patitur temporum Apostolicorum ingenium, ut vel Christianorum episcopos verberibus in quemquam saevisse (quod diu postea, planeque sero in Ecclesiam, jam corruptis nostrorum moribus, invectum est) vel potestates saeculares, quae tum erant nobis infertissimae, quemquam suo favore ad episcopalem dignitatem vel invadendam, vel retinendam adjuvisse. Cur disertas leges Apostoli in ea peccata tulissent, quorum nulla erant, nulla probabiliter metui in eo rerum statu poterant exempla? Nimirum hae leges postea ex occasione factae sunt; cum erumpentem hominum audaciam novis, ac disertis decretis coerceri ipsa Ecclesiae salus, atque aedificatio deposceret.
units.tr: X. Moreover, the canons 26 and 29 (28 and 31 in other editions) do not agree with apostolic times. The first orders that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon be deposed if he strikes believers who sin, or unbelievers who do wrong, and tries to frighten them by such means. The second imposes the same penalty on a bishop who obtains the Church through secular powers. Yet the character of the apostolic age does not allow that Christian bishops would have raged against anyone with blows (a practice that came in long afterwards, and quite late, when the morals of our people were already corrupted), nor that secular powers, which were then most hostile to us, would have helped anyone to seize or keep the episcopal dignity by their favour. Why would the apostles have framed explicit laws against sins for which there were no instances, and for which, in that state of affairs, no examples could reasonably be feared? Clearly these laws were made later, on occasion, when the Church's own safety and upbuilding demanded that the audacity of men, breaking out, be restrained by new and explicit decrees.

units.la: XI. Canone 33. (aliis 35.) Episcoporum metropolitanorum jura constituuntur, quorum, (praeterquam quod nullum in veris, ac indubitatis Apostolorum monumentis apparet vestigium) illud etiam novitatem vitatem confirmat, quod Nicæna syno-dus hæc istorum jura & ad consuetudinem refert, & secundum eam constituit, τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἐᾶσθη κρατείτω, inquit, Antiqui mores obtineant. Nulla Apostolica vel authoritatis, vel legis meminit. Absurde profecto & inepte; si hæc jura, non mos tantum, & longus usus, factaque ex eo consuetudo, invexerat, sed Apostolorum, quæ summa est in Ecclesia, authoritas jam ab initio fixerat, ac constituerat. Nimirum ἀφ᾽ ὧ τὸ ἐν τῇ μητροπόλει πανταχόθεν συντρέχειν πάντας τὰς τὰ πράγματα ἔχοντας, eo quod in metropolim (id est primam cujusque provinciæ civitatem) undequaque concurrunt omnes negotia habentes, (ut Antiochenorum Patrum in hoc ipso argumento verba usurpem) idcirco factum est, ut paulatim aliquid Episcopo, qui illius civitatis Ecclesiam regebat, plus quam cæteris ejusdem provinciæ tribueretur; ut exempli caussa jus convocandæ ex tota provincia Synodi, & alia hujusmodi procurandi ad totius provinciæ utilitatem spe-ctantia. Inde nata Nicænis judicibus Metropolitanorum in suas provincias jura; quæ quod ex usu, & commodo Ecclesiarum esse, & ad ordinis decorum pertinere viderentur, ideo sunt Nicænæ primo, tum & clarius atque enucleatius Antiochenæ SynodoSynodorum authoritate confirmata. Qui vetustiora facit, & ab ipsis Apostolis constitui fingit hujus Dionysiacæ Sylloges author, is manifeste impostor est; rem recentioris ævi inepte atque improbe superioris memoriæ hominibus tribuens.
units.tr: XI. Canon 33 (35 in other editions) lays down the rights of metropolitan bishops. Apart from the fact that no trace of these appears in the true and undoubted monuments of the apostles, this also confirms their novelty: the Synod of Nicaea refers these rights to custom and establishes them on that basis, saying "Let the ancient customs prevail" [τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἐᾶσθη κρατείτω]. It makes no mention of any apostolic authority or law. That would be absurd and foolish indeed, if these rights had come in not merely through custom, long usage, and the practice that grew from it, but if the authority of the apostles, which is supreme in the Church, had fixed and established them from the beginning. Clearly, since all who have business gather from every side into the metropolis (that is, the chief city of each province), as I may use the words of the Antiochene Fathers on this very question, it came about that little by little more was granted to the bishop who ruled the Church of that city than to the others of the same province. For example, the right of convoking a synod from the whole province, and of managing other such matters that concern the good of the whole province. From this arose the rights of metropolitans over their provinces, which the Nicene judges established first, and which the Synod of Antioch later confirmed more clearly and fully, since they seemed to serve the use and benefit of the Churches and to belong to the good order of the Church. Therefore the author of this Dionysian collection, who makes these things older and pretends that they were instituted by the apostles themselves, is manifestly an impostor, foolishly and wickedly attributing to men of an earlier age a thing of a more recent time.

units.la: XII. Denique, ne plura huc conferam, non esse hanc vel Apostolicam, vel Clementinam Syllogen apertissime, conficit canon ejus penultimus, hoc est quadragesimus nonus, diserte præcipiens deponi vel episcopum vel presbyterum, qui sine trina in aquam mersione quemquam baptizaverit.
units.tr: XII. Finally, to add no more here: the canon next to last, that is the forty-ninth, shows most plainly that this collection is neither apostolic nor Clementine. It expressly orders that either a bishop or a presbyter be deposed if he has baptized anyone without a threefold immersion in water.

units.la: Fateor vetustissimum fuisse apud Christianos hunc morem, ut ter, qui baptizabantur, mergerentur. Sed non fuisse tamen id vel ab Apostolis traditum, vel a Clemente scriptum, luce meridiana clarius est. Nam, ut ritus ipsius ineptiam mittam mysteria nescio quę intern-ario numero pueriliter quærentis, quod a divina verorum Apostolorum gravitate, ac simplicitate longissime abest; certe ex multis non sacrarum modo litterarum, sed & ipsius Ecclesiasticæ antiquitatis documentis clarum est, ad baptismum satis esse unam vel mersionem, vel etiam aspersionem; quod, quia hac in parte confitentes ipsos adversarios habemus, nihil necesse est demonstrare. Ergo iniquus est, Apostolisque que adeo indignus hic canon, qui baptismum, una aut altera tantum mersione celebrantes damnat, omninoque trinam mersionem requirit. Annotatio, quae in hunc canonem ab aliquo vel Surio, vel Binio, vel alio hujus generis homine scripta est, ita habet; In hoc canone (inquit) directe damnatur error eorum, qui baptizabant in nomine Christi mortui pro nobis, & ad hunc ritum magis introducendum utebantur una mersione tantum. Contra hos ergo docetur invocandam Trinitatem, & additur, ter esse mergendum, tum propter consuetudinem illius temporis, tum in detestationem illius erroris. Ego vero damnari eum hoc canone fateor, qui semel tantum mergit in nomine Domini pro nobis mortui; Sed & illud contendo, quod dixi, eum quoque hic simpliciter damnari, quisquis ita baptizat, ut non ter mergat, εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος μὴ τρία βαπτίσματα μιᾶς μυήσεως ἐπιτελέσῃ. Siquis Episcopus, aut presbyter, non trinam mersionem unius mysterii celebret, &c. deponatur. Et id ipsum ipse adversarius imprudens docet. Fatetur enim id in hoc canone praecipi, quod illius temporis consuetudo ferebat. Ferebat autem antiquissimi temporis consuetudo, ut ter mergerentur quicumque baptizabantur; ut ex Tertulliano a, mil.
units.tr: I grant that it was a very ancient custom among Christians that those being baptized were immersed three times. But that this was handed down either by the apostles or written by Clement is clearer than noonday light. For, to pass over the foolishness of the rite itself, and the mysteries which some childishly seek in the number three, which are far removed from the gravity and simplicity of the true apostles, it is certainly clear from many witnesses, not only of Holy Scripture but also of ancient ecclesiastical writings, that one immersion or even one sprinkling is enough for baptism. Since in this matter we have our opponents themselves confessing it, there is no need to prove it. Therefore this canon, which condemns those who celebrate baptism with only one or two immersions and altogether requires a threefold immersion, is unfair and unworthy of the apostles. The annotation written on this canon by someone, whether Surius, Binius, or another man of this sort, reads as follows: "In this canon (he says) the error is directly condemned of those who baptized in the name of Christ who died for us, and who used only a single immersion in order to introduce this rite more widely. Against these, therefore, it is taught that the Trinity is to be invoked, and it is added that one must be immersed three times, both on account of the custom of that time and in detestation of that error." I indeed grant that this canon condemns the one who immerses only once in the name of the Lord who died for us. But I also maintain what I said: that the canon also simply condemns anyone who baptizes without immersing three times: "If any bishop or presbyter does not perform three baptisms of one initiation" [εἴτις ἐπίσκοπος ἢ πρεσβύτερος μὴ τρία βαπτίσματα μιᾶς μυήσεως ἐπιτελέσῃ]. "If any bishop or presbyter does not celebrate a threefold immersion of one mystery, etc., let him be deposed." This same adversary, without realizing it, also teaches this very thing. For he admits that what is commanded in this canon is what the custom of that time carried with it. But the custom of the most ancient time was that all who were baptized were immersed three times, as Tertullian, Basil, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and others make plain. Therefore this very thing is also commanded by this canon. As for what the canon adds, "but one baptism, which is given into the death of the Lord" [ἀλλ' ἐν βαπτισμα εἰς τὸν θάνατον τῦ Κυρίου καταδύμενον], but (it celebrates) one immersion, which is given into the death of the Lord, it does not add this as if it thought some others should be borne with who did not perform the threefold immersion at all, but rather that the single immersion they did perform was not carried out together with the others into the death of the Lord. (Nothing can be invented more alien to the mind of that canon.) But the canon adds these words because, of course, no others among Christians at that time were found who baptized into the death of the Lord except those, and none baptized otherwise than with three immersions. Then I should like to know what time our annotator understands, on account of whose custom he says these things about the threefold immersion were added? Does he mean the time of the apostles themselves? But he himself, in this very place, proves that it was done otherwise then, even from the baptism administered by Peter and the apostles in Acts 2, and indeed the matter is most clear from Scripture, in which that troublesome immersion of the baptized into the number three is nowhere found. Does he mean something other than the time of the apostles? But if he thinks so, he is bound to concede what we want: namely, that this canon was composed at a time other than the apostolic, and so by others than the apostles.

units.la: a De cor.
units.tr: a De cor.

units.la: Basilio, Ambrosio, Hieronymo, Augustino, & aliis patet. Ergo & hoc ipsum hoc canone praecipitur. Quod autem addit canon ; ἀλλ' ἐν βαπτισμα εἰς τὸν θάνατον τῦ Κυρίου καταδύμενον, sed unam mersionem (celebrat) quae datur in mortem Domini, non ideo addit, quasi alios quosdam ferendos putet, trinam quidem mersionem minime peragentes; sed eam tamen unam, quam peragebant, non una cum iis in mortem Domini peragentes. (Nihil fingi potest ab istius canonis mente alienius. Sed haec, quae dixi, verba ideo addit canon, quod nulli scilicet praeter istos in Domini mortem baptizantes apud Christianos tum reperirentur, qui baptismum aliter, quam tribus mersionibus peragerent. Tum velim scire, quodnam noster annotator tempus intelligat, propter cujus consuetudinem haec de trina mersione addita ait? Significat-ne ipsorum Apostolorum tempus? Atqui ille, & quidem hoc ipso loco, aliter tum factum, etiam ex baptismo à Petro & Apostolis Act. 2. administrato probat, & profecto res ex Scriptura clarissima est: in qua nusquam occurrit morosa illa in ternarium numerum instituta baptizatorum mersio. Intelligit-ne aliud, quam Apostolorum tempus? Atqui si ita sentit, hoc
units.tr: Basil, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and others make this clear. So the canon also prescribes this very practice. As for the words the canon adds, "but one immersion [ἀλλ' ἐν βάπτισμα εἰς τὸν θάνατον τοῦ Κυρίου καταδυόμενον] (celebrates) which is given into the death of the Lord," it does not add them as though it thought some people should be borne with who did not perform the threefold immersion at all. It adds them to say that they performed that one immersion without joining with the others in the death of the Lord. Nothing could be invented that is further from the mind of that canon. But the canon adds these words because, as far as Christians then went, there were evidently none besides those who baptized into the death of the Lord who administered baptism otherwise than by three immersions. Next, I should like to know what time our annotator means, on whose custom he says these remarks about the threefold immersion were added. Does he mean the time of the Apostles themselves? But he himself, in this very place, proves from the baptism administered by Peter and the Apostles in Acts 2 that things were otherwise then, and indeed the matter is very clear from Scripture, in which that fussy practice of immersing the baptized in a threefold number nowhere occurs. Does he mean some other time than the Apostles'? But if that is his view, he must necessarily concede this very thing that we want, namely that it was at a time other than the Apostolic one, [...]

units.la: a Basilius de Spiritu S. c.27. b l.2.de Sacr.c.7. c dial. contra Lucif. d Serm.de temp.91. & 101. e Cyrill. Hier. cat. 2. Athan. q.125. ad Ant. hocipsum, quod nos volumus, concedere eum necesse est; nimirum alio quam Apostolico tempore, adeoque & ab aliis, quam ab Apostolis, conditum fuisse hunc canonem. Tum & illud quæro, quinam isti sint in canone refutati, ac damnati, qui non trina mersione, sed unica in mortem Christi baptizabant? Profecto non alii in veteri Christianismi historia occurrunt, quam Eunomiani quidam, qui, teste Socrate a, ἐκ εἰς τλὼ τρίαδα, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸν τῆ Χρι- στῷ θάνατον, non in Trinitatem, sed in Christi mortem baptizabant, quique (ut Synodus Constantinopolitana I. docet) εἰς μίαν καταδύσιν ἐβαπτίζοντο, una mersione baptizabantur, quod utrumque ex Theodoreto quoq; discimus; qui hoc Eunomii de baptismo placitum refert μὴ χρῆ- ναι τρὶς καταδύειν τὸν βαπτιζόμενον, μηδὲ ποιεῖσθαι τὴν τρίαδα ἐπίκλησιν, ἀλλ' ἅπαξ βαπτίζειν εἰς τὸν θάνατον τῆ Χριστῷ, non oportere ter illum immergere, qui baptizatur, nec invocare Trinitatem, sed semel immergere in mortem Christi. Ad istos totum hunc Dionysiacæ sive Græcanicæ collectionis canonem 49. respicere, ac pertinere qui non intelligit, næ ille nihil intelligit. Itaque cum ii, quos recta ferit, Eunomiani Constantii principatu (hoc est post a. D. 337.) exorti sint, fieri proseȣto non potest, ut non modo Apostolis, sed etiam Clemente duobus totis & amplius sæculis recentior non fuerit, qui hunc canonem condidit. Sed & aliter ejusdem novitas deprehenditur. Hanc enim trinam, quam in baptismo decernit, mersionem, & Tertullianus, & Basilius, & Hieronymus, gravissimi viri, authores sunt sola muta, & ἀγραφῳ traditione fuisse à majoribus acceptam; nulla scripta lege, nullis literarum tabulis expressam, ut præceptam. Tertullianus a enim inter eas observationes, quas sine ullius Scripturæ instrumento, solius traditionis titulo, & exinde consuetudinis patrocinio vindicabant, & hanc nominatim censet, ter mergitamur; in baptismo scilicet. Sic Basilius b, τὸ ὃ τῆς βαπτιζομένου τὸν ἄνθρωπον, πόσων; jam ter immergi hominem, unde est? hoc est, (ut ex proximis verbis constat) ἐκ τινὸς λόγου γεγραμμένου; Ex quo sermone scripto, vel, ex quibus litteris? quod nemo non videt, impudenter queri, si extabat publicus in Ecclesia Apostolorum à Clemente scriptus canon, ex quo is ritus haustus esset. Hieronymus plane itidem, ut Tertullianus, Multa alia (inquit c) quæ per traditionem in Ecclesiis observantur, authoritatem sibi scriptæ legis usurpaverunt; veluti in lavacro ter caput mergitare. Atqui & hujus ritus tus scripta erat lex, si Apostolicus hic à Clemente scilicet scriptus canon extabat. Ergo hunc neque Tertulliano, neque Basilio, neque Hieronymo cognitum fuisse, non adeo Apostolicum esse, necesse est; qui si vere Apostolorum esset, talibus ac tantis viris ignotus esse non potuisset. Quę contra hujus demonstrationis vim nugantur Turrianus & Arcudius, qui quod scripta lege præcipitur, idipsum tamen minime scriptum esse volunt, nos in priori contra Diataxes disputatione satis confutavimus, ut eadem hic dicere nihil necesse sit. Esto ergo conclusum, neque hanc priorem Turrianicæ collectionis partem, 50. Dionysiacis constantem canonibus, verius Apostolicam esse, quam posteriorem 35. Latinis ignotos canones continentem.
units.tr: a Basilius de Spiritu S. c.27. b l.2.de Sacr.c.7. c dial. contra Lucif. d Serm.de temp.91. & 101. e Cyrill. Hier. cat. 2. Athan. q.125. ad Ant. He must concede this very point that we want: namely, that this canon was composed at a time other than the Apostolic age, and so by others than the Apostles. I also ask this: who are those people condemned and rejected in the canon for baptizing not with a threefold immersion but with a single one into the death of Christ? Certainly no others appear in the history of the early Christian church except certain Eunomians who, according to Socrates, baptized not into the Trinity, but into the death of Christ [οὐκ εἰς τὴν τριάδα, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ θάνατον], and who (as the Council of Constantinople I teaches) were baptized with one immersion [εἰς μίαν καταδύσιν ἐβαπτίζοντο]. We learn both of these from Theodoret as well, who reports this opinion of Eunomius about baptism: that one must not immerse the person being baptized three times, nor make the invocation of the Trinity, but baptize once into the death of Christ [μὴ χρῆναι τρὶς καταδύειν τὸν βαπτιζόμενον, μηδὲ ποιεῖσθαι τὴν τριάδα ἐπίκλησιν, ἀλλ' ἅπαξ βαπτίζειν εἰς τὸν θάνατον τοῦ Χριστοῦ]. That this whole canon 49 of the Dionysian or Greek collection refers and applies to them, let him understand nothing who does not see it. Therefore, since those whom this canon strikes, the Eunomians, arose under the reign of Constantius (that is, after A.D. 337), it cannot be otherwise than that the man who composed this canon was not only later than the Apostles, but was also more recent than Clement by two full centuries and more. But its novelty is also detected in another way. For Tertullian, Basil and Jerome, very weighty men, are witnesses that this threefold immersion which it prescribes in baptism was handed down by our forefathers as a tradition known only by word of mouth and unwritten [ἀγράφῳ]; it was not expressed in any written law or in tablets of letters, as a precept. For Tertullian, among those observances which they claimed without the authority of any Scripture, by the title of tradition alone, and from that the support of custom, names this one explicitly: we are dipped three times, namely in baptism. Likewise Basil: Whence comes it that a man is immersed three times? [τὸ δὲ τρὶς βαπτίζεσθαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον πόθεν;] This is, as is clear from the words that immediately follow, from some written word? [ἐκ τίνος λόγου γεγραμμένου;] From what written word, or from what letters? Anyone can see that it would be shameless to complain in this way if a public canon written by Clement, from the Apostles, existed in the Church from which this rite was drawn. Jerome, quite like Tertullian, says: Many other things which are observed in the churches by tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of written law; for example, dipping the head three times in the bath. Yet if this canon, supposedly written by Clement and handed down from the Apostles, existed, then the rite too would have had written law. Therefore it is necessary that this canon was unknown to Tertullian, Basil and Jerome, and so not truly Apostolic; for if it really belonged to the Apostles, it could not have remained unknown to such great men. The arguments by which Turrianus and Arcudius try to undo the force of this demonstration are trifling: they insist that what is prescribed by written law was nevertheless in no way written. We have sufficiently refuted this in our earlier dispute against the Diataxes, so there is no need to say the same things again here. Let it therefore be concluded that neither this first part of the Turrianic collection, consisting of the 50 Dionysian canons, is more truly Apostolic than the latter part, which contains the 35 canons unknown to the Latins.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Tertia pars disputationis, qua communibus argumentis utraque pars Apostolica Sylloges, id est tota canonum 85. Sylloge falsa ac apocrypha esse demonstratur. Arg. I. ex totius sermonis, quo scripti sunt canones, idea ductum, ab Apostolorum oratione aliena. Arg. II. ab Episcopi & presbyteri diversitate, quam statuunt can. Apostolis ignota. Arg. III. a collato ab haereticis baptismo, quem canones reprobant. Binii vitilitigationes profligantur.
units.tr: The third part of the discussion, in which both parts of the Apostolic Sylloge, that is, the whole collection of the 85 canons, are shown to be false and spurious by arguments common to both. Argument I: from the whole style of the language in which the canons are written, which is foreign to the Apostles. Argument II: from the distinction between bishop and presbyter, which the canons lay down and which was unknown to the Apostles. Argument III: from the baptism conferred by heretics, which the canons reject. The trifling objections of Binius are refuted.

units.la: TRVMQVE praeter superiora, cujusque partis propria, communibus insuper non paucis, neque contemnendis argumentis confirmatur, quae jam tertio loco veniunt explicanda.
units.tr: BOTH parts are confirmed, besides the points peculiar to each, by not a few common arguments, which are not to be despised. These now come third, to be explained.

units.la: I. Principio ipsa totius Sylloges oratio authorem prodit, nihilque eum minus, quam ex Christi Apostolis unum fuisse arguit. Nam multa vocabula usurpat, vel Sanctis Apostolis penitus inusitata, vel non eo certe sensu, quo in his Canonibus sumuntur, usurpata. Qualia sunt κληρικὸς, clericus, pro homine ministerium aliquod Ecclesiasticum exercente; καταλογὸς τῶν κληρικῶν, catalogus clericorum, ἐπίσκοπος & πρεσβύτερος. episcopus & presbyter, pro ministris diversorum ordinum, summi secundi ; ἀναγνώστης, ὁ ψάλτης, lector & cantor a; ἱερεὺς, ἱερατικὸς καταλόγος, ἱερα-τικὴ διοίκησις, sacerdos, sacerdotalis catalogus, sacerdotalis administratio b, pro presbytero, & eo, quod presbyterorum est; λαϊκὸς, laicusc, pro eo fideli, qui extra cen-sum ministrorum in Ecclesia est; Ejusdem hęc quoque sunt generis, quæ in priori syllogęs parte, hoc est Dionysiaca, leguntur, Θυσιαστήριον, altare, pro mensa Domini d; Θυσία, sacrificium, pro Eucharistiæ celebratione e, & pro eadem προσφορὰ oblatio f; πεντηκοστὴ Pentecoste g, pro toto eo tempore, quod & à Paschæ festo ad proprie dictam Pentecosten decurrit; πρῶτος ἐν ἐπισκόποις, primus inter Episcopos h, id est Metropoleos in provincia episcopus; τὰ Κυριακὰ, Dominica i, pro rebus, quas possidet Ecclesia, quas iidem canones vocant τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πράγματα, Ecclesiae res k; Υπερβέρεταῖος, October l. Hæc & alia fortasse non pauca sequentibus Christianismi sæculis usitata in eo, quo canones usurpant, sensu, constat in veris, & indubitatis, hoc est canonicis Apostolorum scripturis, nusquam sic posita occurrere. Cum ergo nulla sit ratio, cur Apostoli in canonicis decretis aliter loqui debuerint; quam in aliis, sive libris, sive epistolis suis, apparet Apostolos non esse, qui aliter scilicet
units.tr: I. First of all, the very wording of the whole Syllogue reveals its author, and shows that he was anything but one of Christ's Apostles. For it uses many terms that are either wholly unknown to the holy Apostles or, at least, not used in the sense in which these Canons employ them. Such are κληρικὸς, clergyman, for a man who exercises some ecclesiastical ministry; καταλογὸς τῶν κληρικῶν, list of the clergy; ἐπίσκοπος and πρεσβύτερος, bishop and presbyter, for ministers of different orders, the higher and the lower; ἀναγνώστης and ὁ ψάλτης, reader and cantora; ἱερεὺς, ἱερατικὸς καταλόγος, ἱερατικὴ διοίκησις, priest, priestly list, priestly administrationb, for a presbyter and for what belongs to the presbyters; λαϊκὸς, laymanc, for a believer who is outside the roll of ministers in the Church. Of the same kind are the terms read in the first part of the collection, that is, the Dionysian: Θυσιαστήριον, altar, for the Lord's tabled; Θυσία, sacrifice, for the celebration of the Eucharist, and προσφορὰ, oblation, for the same thing f; πεντηκοστὴ, Pentecostg, for the whole period that runs from the feast of Easter to what is properly called Pentecost; πρῶτος ἐν ἐπισκόποις, first among bishopsh, that is, the bishop of the metropolis in a province; τὰ Κυριακὰ, the Dominicalsi, for the property which the Church possesses, which these same canons call τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πράγματα, the affairs of the Churchk; Υπερβερεταῖος, Octoberl. It is established that these and perhaps many other terms, which were in use in the later centuries of Christianity in the sense the canons give them, do not occur anywhere in the true and undoubted Scriptures of the Apostles, that is, the canonical writings. Since there is therefore no reason why the Apostles should have spoken differently in their canonical decrees than in their other books or letters, it is clear that the Apostles were not the authors of this collection, which speaks differently from the way they speak. It is clear that, whoever its authors were, they were men of later times, and therefore impostors, who shamelessly, yet foolishly and clumsily, put the language of their own age into the mouths of the Lord's Apostles.

units.la: d c. 3. c. 30. e c. 45. (46.) c. 5. f c. 8. (9.) g c. 38. (36) h c. 33. (35) i c. 39. (al. 40) k c. 37. (39.) c. 40. (41) l c. 38. (36) licet quam Apostoli loquuntur, hujus syl-loges authores; apparet, quicunque de cæ-tero sint, homines fuisse sequentium tem-porum, adeoque impostores, qui sæculi sui sermonem Apostolis Domini inverecun-de quidem & impudenter, sed tamen stul-te ac imperite affinxerunt.
units.tr: d c. 3. c. 30. e c. 45. (46.) c. 5. f c. 8. (9.) g c. 38. (36) h c. 33. (35) i c. 39. (al. 40) k c. 37. (39.) c. 40. (41) l c. 38. (36) than the Apostles speak, the authors of this collection; it appears, whoever they were, that they were men of later times, and therefore impostors, who put the idiom of their own age into the mouths of the Lord's Apostles, shamelessly indeed, but foolishly and ignorantly.

units.la: II. Idem quoque id arguit, quod prio-rem minisRerii Ecclesiastici partem, quæ supra diaconatum est, hi Canones in duos diversos ordines episcoporum, & presby-terorum perpetuo dividunt, plurimum inter se & nomine, & jure, & statu, & au-thoritate differentes. Nam, quod jam su-pra notavimus, Episcopum non aliter, quam a duobus, tribuere Episcopis presbyte-rum non aliter, & ipsum, quam ab Epi-scopo, sed uno, ordinari scisciunt : Tum jus Episcopo tribuunt, presbyterum se-gregandi ; Omnium rerum Ecclesiasticarum curam & præfecturam eidem vindi-cant ; ei omnes presbyteros, & diaconos sic subjiciunt , ut nihil pertentare absque ipsius sententia audeant, & alibi in posteriori syllogès parte, judicari presbyterum ab Episcopis, non a presbyteris, præcipiunt. Nihil est quod in re clara, & confessa plura afferamus. Iam vero constat, neq; Apostolos hujusmodi episcopi a presbytero discrimen unquam in veris, divinisque
units.tr: II. This same point is also shown by the fact that these Canons divide the higher part of the ecclesiastical ministry, that which stands above the diaconate, into two distinct orders, bishops and presbyters, which differ greatly from one another in name, in right, in status and in authority. For, as we have already noted above, they lay down that a bishop may be ordained by two bishops only, and a presbyter by a bishop alone; then they grant the bishop the right to depose a presbyter; they claim for him the care and government of all ecclesiastical affairs; they make all presbyters and deacons so subject to him that they dare attempt nothing without his judgment; and elsewhere, in the latter part of the collection, they direct that a presbyter be judged by bishops, not by presbyters. There is no need to bring more proofs in a matter that is clear and admitted. Now it is established that neither the Apostles handed down such a distinction between bishop and presbyter in their true and divine books, nor can it be gathered from the writings of the New Testament that anyone was a presbyter or a bishop (for they use the two names interchangeably…

units.la: a c. 1, c. 2. b c. 31. (33) c c. 37. (39) d c. 38. (40) e c. 73. nisque libris tradere; neque ex Novi Testamenti litteris colligi posse, quemquam presbyterorum, sive episcoporum esse (utrumque enim nomen promiscue usurpant divini scriptores) cujus aliquod sit præ collegis authoritatis πρωτόμιον, sive præcipuū. Sed & illud constat, Hieronymum, plurésque alios ex veteribus scriptores nobilissimos sensisse, litterisque mandasse illud Episcopi supra presbyterum jus, non ab Apostolis institutum, sed Ecclesiæ tantum usu, atque decretis inductum esse, ut jam supra ad Constitutiones fusius docuimus.
units.tr: a c. 1, c. 2. b c. 31. (33) c c. 37. (39) d c. 38. (40) e c. 73. books; nor can it be gathered from the writings of the New Testament that any one of the presbyters or bishops (for the divine writers use the two names interchangeably) had any primacy [πρωτεῖον], or pre-eminence of authority over his colleagues. But it is also certain that Jerome, and several other most notable ancient writers, held and committed to writing that this right of a bishop over a presbyter was not instituted by the Apostles, but introduced only by the custom and decrees of the Church, as we have already shown more fully above in discussing the Constitutions.

units.la: Ergo neque hi canones, qui id exsertissime constituunt, ab Apostolis conditi sunt, neque eos ab Apostolis conditos sciverunt Hieronymus, & cæteri idem cum Hieronymo hac de re sentientes Patres. Neque eos priscís temporibus pro Apostolicis habuerat tota Alexandrinorum Ecclesia, in qua usque ad Dionysium (id est a. D. 246.) episcopum, teste, quod alibi diximus, Hieronymo, non, quod jubent hi canones, à duobus tribusve episcopis consecrari, sed communi presbyterorum judicio atque authoritate constitui, totiqué Ecclesiæ præponi, mos fuit.
units.tr: Therefore neither do these canons, which state this most expressly, come from the Apostles, nor did Jerome and the other Fathers who think with Jerome on this matter know them to have been composed by the Apostles. Nor did the whole Church of Alexandria in early times regard them as apostolic; in that Church, down to the bishop Dionysius (that is, A.D. 246), it was the custom, as Jerome attests, as we have said elsewhere, not for bishops to be consecrated by two or three bishops, as these canons order, but for them to be chosen by the common judgment and authority of the presbyters, and set over the whole Church.

units.la: III. Huc accedit, quod utraque collectio ministratum ab hæreticis baptismum explodit a: Ἐπίσκοπον ἢ πρεσβύτερον ...
units.tr: III. Add to this that both collections reject the baptism administered by heretics [a]: "A bishop or presbyter who receives baptism or the Eucharist from heretics..." [Ἐπίσκοπον ἢ πρεσβύτερον ...]

units.la: a c. 45. (46) κὼν ἀπξάμενον βάπτισμα, ἢ Ϭυσίαν, καθαι-ρεῖσθαι προσάγομεν. Episcopum, aut presbyterum, haereticorum suscipientem Baptisma, damnari praecipimus. Tum ἐπίσκο-πῷ ἢ πρεσβύτερῳ τὸν κατ' ἀλήθειαν ἔχοντα βάπτισμα, ἐὰν ἀνωθὲν βαπτίσῃ, ἢ τὸν μεμολυσμένον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀσεβῶν, ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσῃ, καθαιρεῖσθω, ὡς γελῶν τὸν σταυρόν. Episcopus, aut presbyter, si eum, qui secundum veritatem habuerit baptisma, denuo baptizaverit, aut pollutum ab impiis non baptizaverit, deponatur tanquam deridens crucem. Sic etiam in posteriori parte Syllogès; τὰς ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων (αἱρετικῶν) βαπτισθέντας, ἢ χειροτονηθέντας ὡς πίστας ὡς κληρικὰς εἶναι σωτήρ. Qui ab eis (haereticis) baptizati, vel ordinati sunt, ut fideles vel clerici sint, fieri non potest. Haec canones; quae si vera sunt, necesse est omnem, jam à vetustissimis temporibus, Ecclesiam in gravissimo errore versari; praesertim Romanam, quae Stephano duce, & authore, urbis circa a. D. 254. Episcopo, haereticorum baptismum valere ab illo saeculo ad hunc tempora constanter sensit; & Africanam, quae Donatistas idem cum istis canonibus de baptismo sentientes Augustini calamo, acerrime confutavit; & Nicaenam denique ipsam Synodum, quae solos ex omnibus haereticis Paulianista. [?]ianista, rebaptizandos pronunciavit. Cum ergo ipsi adversarii veram esse hanc Ecclesiae sententiam confiteantur, nisi Apostolos aliquid praeter verum decrevisse velint, omnino illud quoque concedere debent, non fuisse hos ab Apostolis conditos canones. Binii nugas nil moror, cavillantis hos canones de baptismo, non quorumvis haereticorum, sed eorum tantum esse intelligendos, qui alia forma baptizabant, quam Ecclesiastica, ut qui in tribus Patribus, seu in nomine trium principii expertium, aut trium filiorum, vel trium Paradotorum, vel qui in morte Domini baptizabant, de quibus testantur canones 49. & 50.Sed haec glossa pugnat primo cum Canonistae verbis, qui non horum aut illorum haereticorum, sed simpliciter αἱρετικῶν βάπτισμα repudiat, & fideles esse posse negat, τὰς ἐκ τῶν αἱρετικῶν βαπτιζομένας. Ergo quacunque in fidei parte laborent, si modo haeretici sint, baptisma ab iis collatum valere negat. Tum & illud Binianam glossam confodit, quod non baptismum modo, sed θυσίαν, id est eucharistiam, & χειροτονίαν ordinationem haereticorum una cum baptismo reprobat. At non concedet, puto, Binius aliquorum tantum, non autem omnium, haereticorum eucharistiam & ordinationem nullam esse & invalidam. Cum ergo & baptismi eadem sit, ex Canonistae quidem mente, ratio; omnino fatendum est, eum, non quorumdam duntaxat, sed quorumvis haereticorum baptisma reprobare, ac pro nullo censere. Huc accedit ratio, quam Canonista suo huic decreto addit, non à baptismo iniforma, sed à baptizantis persona ducta; Haereticorum (inquit a) baptisma suscipi vetamus: Quid ita? τίς γὰρ (inquit) συμφωνῆσις τῷ Χριστῷ πρὸς Βελιάλ; ἢ τίς μερὶς πιστῷ μετὰ ἀπίστου; Qua enim conventio Christi ad Belial? aut qua pars fidelis cum infideli? Vult haeretici baptisma rejici, quod haereticis nulla sit cum Christo communio ac conventio. Ergo Binio necessario fatendum est, vel ineptam, & à Canonistae consilio alienam allatam esse rationem, vel certe reprobatum esse omnium, sive quorumvis haereticorum baptismum. Neque enim Binium usque adeo insanire putaverim, ut quisquis vere haereticus est, ejus aliquam vel cum Christo conventionem, vel cum fidelibus partem esse posse defendat. Itaque cum statuat Canonista, cujus nulla est cum Christo conventio, ejus futile ac nullum (ut loquuntur) esse baptismum, profecto idem quoque necessario decrevit, omnium haereticorum invalidum ac pro nullo habendum esse baptismum; quorum scilicet omnium
units.tr: a c. 45. (46) [...] "we command that a bishop or presbyter who receives the baptism of heretics be condemned" [κὼν ἀπξάμενον βάπτισμα, ἢ Ϭυσίαν, καθαιρεῖσθαι προσάγομεν]. Then: "a bishop or presbyter who baptizes again one who truly has baptism, or who fails to baptize one defiled by the impious, let him be deposed as one who mocks the cross" [ἐπίσκοπῷ ἢ πρεσβύτερῳ τὸν κατ' ἀλήθειαν ἔχοντα βάπτισμα, ἐὰν ἀνωθὲν βαπτίσῃ, ἢ τὸν μεμολυσμένον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀσεβῶν, ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσῃ, καθαιρεῖσθω, ὡς γελῶν τὸν σταυρόν]. Likewise in the latter part of the Sylloge: "Those who have been baptized or ordained by such (heretics) cannot be made faithful or clerics" [τὰς ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων (αἱρετικῶν) βαπτισθέντας, ἢ χειροτονηθέντας ὡς πίστας ὡς κληρικὰς εἶναι σωτήρ]. These are the canons. If they are true, it must follow that the whole Church, from the most ancient times, has been in the gravest error; especially the Roman Church, which under Stephen, its leader and author, around A.D. 254, as bishop of the city, consistently held from that age down to our own times that the baptism of heretics is valid; and the African Church, which through the pen of Augustine most fiercely refuted the Donatists, who thought the same as these canons about baptism; and finally the Council of Nicaea itself, which pronounced that of all heretics only the Paulianists were to be rebaptized. Since therefore our adversaries themselves confess that this is the true opinion of the Church, unless they wish the Apostles to have decreed something contrary to the truth, they must altogether concede that these canons were not framed by the Apostles. I pay no attention to the trifles of Binius, who argues that these canons on baptism are to be understood not of any heretics whatever, but only of those who baptized in a form other than the ecclesiastical one, such as those who baptized in the names of three unbegotten principles, or of three sons, or of three paracletes, or who baptized into the death of the Lord, of whom canons 49 and 50 speak. But this gloss clashes first with the words of the canonist, who rejects not the baptism of this or that heretic, but simply the baptism of heretics [αἱρετικῶν βάπτισμα], and denies that those baptized by heretics can be faithful [τὰς ἐκ τῶν αἱρετικῶν βαπτιζομένας]. Therefore, in whatever article of faith they err, provided only they are heretics, he denies that the baptism conferred by them is valid. Moreover, the same canon also overthrows Binius's gloss, because it rejects along with baptism not only baptism but also the sacrifice [θυσίαν], that is the Eucharist, and the ordination [χειροτονίαν] of heretics. But Binius, I suppose, will not concede that the Eucharist and ordination of only some heretics, and not of all, are null and invalid. Since therefore the reason for baptism is the same, according to the mind of the canonist, we must altogether admit that he rejects and regards as nothing the baptism not of some heretics only, but of any heretics whatever. Add to this the reason that the canonist adds to his decree, drawn not from the form of baptism but from the person of the one baptizing: "We forbid the baptism of heretics to be received", he says. Why so? "For what agreement", he says, "has Christ with Belial? Or what part has the faithful with the unfaithful?" [τίς γὰρ συμφωνῆσις τῷ Χριστῷ πρὸς Βελιάλ; ἢ τίς μερὶς πιστῷ μετὰ ἀπίστου;] "For what conventio is there of Christ with Belial? Or what part has the faithful with the infidel?" He wishes the baptism of a heretic to be rejected because a heretic has no communion or agreement with Christ. Therefore Binius must necessarily admit either that a reason has been alleged that is inept and foreign to the canonist's purpose, or certainly that the baptism of all heretics, of whatever kind, has been rejected. For I should not think Binius so mad as to defend that whoever is truly a heretic can have any agreement with Christ, or any part with the faithful. And so, since the canonist declares that one who has no agreement with Christ has a futile and null (as they say) baptism, he has certainly decided also of necessity that the baptism of all heretics is invalid and to be held as nothing; for of all of them there is no agreement with Christ, nor any part with the faithful.

units.la: a c. 45. (46.) omnium nulla est vel conventio cum Christo, vel pars cum fidelibus. His insuper ea adjungenda sunt, quæ de Constitutionum sententia diximus; quam eandem esse ac canonum liquet. Neque sane aliter fieri potest, si stat Turriani hypothesis, qui idem esse defendit utrumque opus, & ab eodem authore scriptum. Atqui supra demonstravimus, Constitutiones, non quorumdam sed omnium omnino hæreticorum baptisma excludere, ac reprobare; quod quia cum universalis Ecclesiæ fide pugnat, Apostolicum censeri non potest. Neque ullos sane extitisse primis Christianismi sæculis hujusmodi canones, vel pro Apostolicis agnitos fuisse, in superiori disputatione clarissime ex eo probavimus, quod cum Cyprianus, omnesque Afri Episcopi baptismum hæreticorum præter communem Ecclesiæ fidem & praxim, pro nullo habendum, adeoque iterandum docerent, neque ipse Cyprianus in epistolis, quæ de hoc argumento plurimæ ab eo scriptæ extant, neque quisquam 87. Episcoporum, qui eandem opinionem in Synodo Carthaginensi confirmarunt, legitur in hac causa, quam sedulo petitis undequaque argumentis agunt, hos canones Apostolicos scilicet laudasse, vel memorasse, qui tamen, si extitissent ulli, in primis afferendi fuerant; utpote qui causam secundum eos plane, liquidoque decidebant. Sed neque credibile est, Stephanum urbis Episcopum illam Afrorum sententiam oppugnaturum fuisse & quidem vehementer, si eam in ullis Apostolorum canonibus extare scivisset. Idemque observari potest in Augustini contra Donatistas disputationibus; in quibus nusquam reperiuntur Donatistae, pro Cypriani, quam sequebantur, opinione ullum Apostolorum, vel Clementis canonem Augustino vel caeteris Catholicis objecisse. Ergo ne tum quidem, hoc est quinto ineunte saeculo, extabat in Ecclesia haec Apostolicorum canonum Sylloge. Quibus ratiionibus eo adductus est Albaspineus, ut haec de baptismo haereticorum decreta inter eos canones numeraret, quos Apostolica authoritate sancitos fuisse exerte negat. Si
units.tr: a c. 45. (46.) none of them has either a fellowship with Christ or a share with the faithful. To these must be added what we have said concerning the opinion of the Constitutions, which is plainly the same as that of the canons. Nor indeed can it be otherwise, if the hypothesis of Turrianus stands, who maintains that both works are the same and written by the same author. Yet above we have demonstrated that the Constitutions exclude and reject the baptism, not of some heretics but of all heretics without exception; and because this conflicts with the faith of the universal Church, it cannot be regarded as Apostolic. Nor indeed did such canons exist in the first centuries of Christianity, or were they acknowledged as Apostolic, as we have proved most clearly in the earlier discussion: since Cyprian and all the African bishops taught that the baptism of heretics, apart from the common faith and practice of the Church, was to be regarded as nothing and therefore repeated, and neither Cyprian himself in the letters, of which many written by him on this subject survive, nor any of the eighty-seven bishops who confirmed the same opinion in the Synod of Carthage, is read in this cause, which they pursue with eager arguments from every side, to have praised or mentioned these Apostolic canons, which, had any existed, should above all have been brought forward, since they would have decided the cause plainly and clearly in their favour. But neither is it credible that Stephen, bishop of the city, would have opposed that opinion of the Africans, and vehemently so, had he known it to be contained in any canons of the Apostles. The same can be observed in Augustine's disputations against the Donatists: in them nowhere do the Donatists, appealing to the opinion of Cyprian whom they followed, object to Augustine or the other Catholics any canon of the Apostles or of Clement. Therefore not even then, that is at the beginning of the fifth century, did this collection of Apostolic canons exist in the Church. For these reasons Albaspinaeus was led to number these decrees on the baptism of heretics among those canons which he expressly denies were sanctioned by Apostolic authority.

So too Possevinus expressly pronounces canon 67 concerning those baptized by heretics to be spurious, and thus false and supposititious.

Eadem quoque fuit Bellarmini incogitantia, qui cum canonem hunc 67. de baptizatis vel ordinatis ab haereticis, inter eos numeret a, ob quos posteriorem Sylloges Apostolicae partem apocryphaм esse confitetur, sui oblitus priorem, in qua idem error, ut ex superioribus constat, apertissime docetur, pugnat esse veram & authenticam. Hanc scilicet habent erroris & inverecundiae mercedem, quotquot claram veritatem oppugnant, ut sibi ipsis constare nequeant. Sed nos ad caetera pergamus.
units.tr: b In app. verbo Clemens. and he confesses that the other part of the collection, in which that canon is contained, that is the medley of the last thirty-five canons, is supposititious. Although he contends that the former part, that is the Dionysian collection of the first fifty canons, is genuine, he does so foolishly and against all reason. For since canons 45 (46) and 46 (47) on those baptized by heretics decree exactly the same as canon 67, and indeed more clearly and distinctly, with what sort of mind, I ask, do you reject the latter part of the canons as apocryphal on account of that admixed error, yet absolve the former part, in which the same error is likewise mingled, and judge it true and authentic? Bellarmine showed the same lack of thought: although he numbers this canon 67, concerning those baptized or ordained by heretics, among those for which he confesses the latter part of the Apostolic collection to be apocryphal, forgetting himself he contends that the former part, in which the same error, as is clear from what precedes, is most openly taught, is true and authentic. Such, to be sure, is the reward of error and shamelessness held by all who oppose clear truth, so that they cannot remain consistent with themselves. But let us go on to the rest.

units.la: IV. SI hęc vel tota Apostolicorum (quæ dicitur) canonum collectio, vel saltem ejus aliqua pars vere ab Apostolis edita, vereque aut ab ipsis, aut à Clemente conscripta esset; ea profecto vel tota, vel partim saltem, fuisset à veteribus quatuor priorum sæculorum Christianis in scripturarum novi Testamenti canonem relata. Nulla enim est ratio, cur quod ab Apostolis editum ac traditum esse, & vel ab ipsis, vel certe ab aliquo sancto & veraci eorum discipulo, & amanuensi conscriptum scias, id à canonicis novi fœderis libris excludas; ut à nobis alibi supra demonstratum est. Itaque secutis sæculis qui hunc istorum canonum librum vere Apostolicum fuisse putabat Damascenus, is non dubitavit eundem canonicis Scripturis accensere, vere meritoque arbitratus, quicquid Apostolicum esse constat, stat, id canonicam in Ecclesia Christiana authoritatem habere. Baronius ait Damascenum inconsulte nimis fecisse; certe inquam, qui librum non Apostolicum Apostolicis, adeoque canonicis annumeravit. Sed & Turrianus, Baroni, fortissimus ille tuus canonum defensor, & plerique omnes tui, & tu ipse, siquidem idem cum iis sentis: vos inquam, non minus inconsulte, quam Damascenus, facitis, qui, quem librum à canonicorum censu excluditis, eum tamen vere Apostolicum esse pugnatis. Ejusdem enim est stultitiæ & librum non Apostolicum Novi Testamenti canoni inserere, & Apostolicum in canonem non admittere. Prius facit Damascenus; posterius adversarii. Ergo utrorumque, quamquam dissimilis, par tamen error atque temeritas esse videtur. Nam si quod hi statuunt, vere ab Apostolis editi, vere à Clemente eorum discipulo, atque fidissimo velut amanuensi scripti sunt Canones, eos Damascenus jure meritoque in sacro canone recensuit; hoc enim ex illo necessario atque evidenter sequitur. Quo fit, ut adversarii, si bene res putetur, gravius etiam aliquanto, quam Damascenus, in hoc negotio, à vero rectoque aberrasse videantur. Hic enim in eo quidem erravit, quod hos canones Apostolorum poltolorum (quod non sunt) vere esse nulla ratione putavit; caeterum quid ex hoc semel posito consequeretur, recte vidit; nimirum augendum iis esse sacrorum & divinorum canonem, quandoquidem sunt Apostolici. Adversarii vero, utroque in loco peccarunt; dum & Apostolorum esse hos, qui obtruduntur, canones, una cum Damasceno delirantes opinati sunt; neque tamen cum eodem quos Apostolicos censent, eos in Ѕtoⲣwévᵴwv canone habendos existimarunt. Quod si Damascenus paulo acrius ac diligentius mentem contendisset, facile ei erat ex eo, quod vere statuebat, principio, errorem de canonibus suum perspicere, eoque correcto recte de toto hoc negotio sentire. Cum enim qui vere Apostolici sunt libri, eos ille vere rec-teque statuat in divinum novi Testamenti canonem esse referendos; profecto quem a nullo vetustiorum vir antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae peritus videbat in sacrum hunc canonem relatum suum Canonum Apostolicorum codicem, eum inquam debuit neque vere Apostolicum esse, censere. Nulla enim ratio est, cur Apostolorum fuisse ipse octavo demum saeculo eum librum putaret, quem veteribus, praesertim trium primorum saeculorum, Patribus ignotum fuisse; hinc clarissime concluconcluditur. Nam Damascenus, vir, ut apparet, sui saeculi eruditissimus, & in veterum monumentis versatissimus, nescire non potuit, cum plurimi extent à veteribus traditi divinarum Scripturarum canones, nullum tamen inveniri, in quo liber Canonum Apostolicorum recensetur. Id vero usque adeo clarum, certumque est, ut ne ipse quidem Turrianus, vir alioqui omnium, qui canones defendunt, longe audacissimus, atque confidentissimus, carissimam illam suam canonum Apostolicorum syllogen in divinorum librorum censu habendam esse contendat. Nimirum videbat, aliud sensisse omnes omnis retro memoriae (uno excepto Damasceno) Christianos; omnes Romanos Pontifices; omnes denique Synodos. Nullus enim est vel à Patribus, vel à Pontificibus, vel à Synodis traditus sacer divinorum librorum canon, in quo ille Apostolicorum canonum codex caeteris annumeratus inveniatur. Ergo missis jam & Damasceno, & Baronio, concludamus, non esse hunc, qui dicitur, Apostolorum librum, qui si esset scilicet, ab omnibus Christianis, praesertim vero à vetustissimis, & Apostolico aevo proximis in sacrum Scripturarum canonem haud dubie relatus esset; quod tamen à nemine sex primorum, ac ne reliquorum quorum quidem post sextum sæculorum (si unum Damascenum exceperis) factum esse satis constat.
units.tr: IV. If this collection of so-called Apostolic canons, or at least some part of it, had truly been published by the Apostles and written either by them or by Clement, then certainly the whole of it, or at least part of it, would have been received by the ancient Christians of the first four centuries into the canon of the Scriptures of the New Testament. For there is no reason why you should exclude from the canonical books of the New Covenant what you know was published and handed down by the Apostles, and written either by them or at least by some holy and truthful disciple of theirs acting as scribe, as we have shown elsewhere above. Accordingly, in the following centuries, Damascene, who thought this book of canons was truly Apostolic, did not hesitate to count it among the canonical Scriptures, rightly and justly judging that whatever is certainly Apostolic has canonical authority in the Christian Church. Baronius says that Damascene acted far too imprudently; certainly, I say, since he numbered among the Apostolic, and so among the canonical, a book that is not Apostolic. But you also, Turrianus, that most valiant defender of the canons of yours, and most of your people, and you yourself, if you agree with them: you, I say, act no less imprudently than Damascene, since you exclude from the canonical list the book you maintain to be truly Apostolic. For it is the same folly to insert into the canon of the New Testament a book that is not Apostolic, and to refuse admission to one that is. Damascene does the former; your side does the latter. So the error and rashness of both seem equal, though unlike in kind. For if what these men assert is true, that the Canons were truly published by the Apostles and truly written by Clement, their disciple and most faithful scribe, then Damascene rightly and justly listed them among the sacred canon, for this follows necessarily and plainly from that premise. Hence, if the matter is judged fairly, your side seems to have strayed from truth and right in this business rather more seriously than Damascene. He erred in thinking these canons of the Apostles (which they are not) were in any way genuine; but what would follow from that assumption he saw correctly, namely that the canon of sacred and divine books must be enlarged by them, since they are Apostolic. Your side, however, erred at both points: while raving along with Damascene that the canons thrust upon us are the Apostles', they did not think that those they judged Apostolic should be held in the canon of the Scriptures. If Damascene had applied his mind a little more sharply and diligently, it would have been easy for him, from the very principle he correctly held, to see the error about the canons and, having corrected it, to judge the whole matter rightly. For since he rightly holds that books which are truly Apostolic are truly and rightly to be included in the divine canon of the New Testament, he ought to have concluded that this codex of Apostolic Canons, which he saw was included in the sacred canon by none of the earlier writers versed in Church antiquity, was not truly Apostolic. There is no reason why he should think a book was Apostolic when it was unknown to the ancients, especially to the Fathers of the first three centuries; from this the conclusion is most clear. For Damascene, evidently the most learned man of his age and most versed in the monuments of the ancients, could not fail to know that, although many canons of the divine Scriptures handed down by the ancients survive, there is none in which the book of the Apostolic Canons is listed. This is so plain and certain that not even Turrianus, by far the boldest and most confident of all who defend the canons, claims that his beloved collection of Apostolic Canons should be counted among the divine books. Evidently he saw that all Christians of every earlier age (with the single exception of Damascene) thought otherwise; all the Roman Pontiffs; all the Synods. For no sacred canon of the divine books handed down by the Fathers, the Pontiffs or the Synods includes that codex of Apostolic Canons among the others. So, setting aside both Damascene and Baronius, let us conclude that this so-called book of the Apostles is not Apostolic. For if it were, it would undoubtedly have been included in the sacred canon of Scripture by all Christians, especially the most ancient, who were close to the Apostolic age; yet it is well established that this was done by none of the first six centuries, nor indeed by any of the later ones after the sixth (if you except Damascene alone).

units.la: V. Sed etsi negaverint adversarii (quod tamen nulla ratione negari potest) debuisse veteres hanc collectionem, si eam Apostolicam scivissent, in sacrum Novi Testamenti canonem referre; illud quidem certe minime negaverint, fuisse eam saltem à veteribus, siquidem eam novissent, in Ecclesiasticorum canonum codice inserendam, ac ante cæteros omnes collocandam; qualiter eam Dionysius, multoque post eum Isidorus Mercator in collectionibus juris Ecclesiastici suis habuisse ac censuisse cernuntur, primo scilicet statim loco ante omnes alios sive Synodorum, sive Pontificum, aut aliorum episcoporum canones. Hunc enim iis locum vindicabat tum antiquitas, tum authoritas Apostolorum; qui scilicet & primi omnium Christianorum fuerunt, & ab ipso Christo constituti sunt totius Ecclesiæ magistri, ac rectores, cum summa authoritate tum in docenda fide, tum in ordinanda disciplina; ut eorum canones, siqui revera fuissent, dubitari non posset, quin veteres magno in pretio habituri, ac primo statim loco inter regulas Ecclesiasticas, pro sua & in Dominum pietate, & in Apostolos stolos reverentia, posituri fuerint. Atqui veteres non modo non deprehenduntur, duplicem illam collectionem (id est, & Dionysiacam 50. & Turrianicam 85, canonum) eo loco ac numero habuisse, sed insuper clarissime, certissimeque inveniuntur utramque nullo plane loco, ac numero in suo canonum codice censuisse. Quod ut in clara, atque illustri luce constituatur, inprimis tenendum est, quinto saeculo ante annum D. 451. institutum fuisse a Christianis canonum Ecclesiasticorum codicem sacrum; quem odoratus eruditissimus, & celeberrimus Jurisconsultus Jacobus Leschasserius a ex quibusdam Synodi Chalcedonensis, & aliorum veterum monumentorum locis, solertissime ac feliciss ime investigavit, ac reperit; jamque antea aliquid hujusmodi olim extitisse subolfecerant & Baronius *, & Antonius Augustinus b. Nam, ut caetera loca nunc mittam, in Chalcedonensi Synodo c citantur, ac discribuntur duo quidam canones, quorum unus 95. fuisse ibidem dicitur, alter 96. Ἀεόντι@ ὁ ἐυλαβέσαται ἐπίσκοπος Μαγνησίας ἀνέγνω, Can. 95. ἐπισκέψεως Χολάζων, &c. Leontius reverendissimus Episcopus Magnesia, ex codice relegit regulam nonagesimam quintam, Siquis
units.tr: V. But even if our opponents deny (though this cannot be denied on any ground) that the ancients ought to have included this collection in the sacred canon of the New Testament had they known it to be Apostolic, they can hardly deny at least this: that if the ancients had known it, they would have inserted it in the codex of Ecclesiastical canons and placed it before all the others. This is how Dionysius, and long after him Isidore Mercator, are seen to have held and classed it in their collections of Church law: namely, in the very first place, before all the other canons, whether of Synods, Pontiffs or other bishops. For both the antiquity and the authority of the Apostles claimed this place for them, since they were the first of all Christians and were appointed by Christ himself as the teachers and rulers of the whole Church, with supreme authority both in teaching the faith and in ordering discipline. So if these canons had really been theirs, there could be no doubt that the ancients would have held them in high esteem and placed them at the very head of the Church's rules, out of their piety towards the Lord and their reverence for the Apostles. Yet the ancients are not only not found to have held that double collection (that is, the Dionysian of fifty canons and the Turrianic of eighty-five) in that place and order, but they are found, quite clearly and certainly, to have placed neither of them anywhere at all, in any number, in their codex of canons. To set this in clear and bright light, we must first hold that in the fifth century, before the year of our Lord 451, the Christians established a sacred codex of Ecclesiastical canons. The most learned and renowned jurist Jacques Leschassier, with great skill and good fortune, investigated and discovered this from certain passages of the Synod of Chalcedon and other ancient monuments; and Baronius and Antonius Augustinus had already faintly suspected that something of this kind once existed. For, to pass over other passages, in the Synod of Chalcedon two canons are cited and quoted, of which one is said to be the 95th and the other the 96th. Leontius, the most reverend bishop of Magnesia, read (Λεόντιος ὁ εὐλαβέστατος ἐπίσκοπος Μαγνησίας ἀνέγνω), Canon 95 (ἐπισκέψεως χολάζων, &c.), from the codex, the ninety-fifth rule, "If any"

Alibi quoque in eadem Synodo, cum judices canones legi jussissent, Beronicianus, Magistrianus, & Secretarius divini consistorii, ex codice dato ab Eunomio dicitur legisse CAN. VI. (omnino in hoc numero mendum est; legendumque IV. pro VI. ut mox patebit) in haec verba a, ἐπίσκοπον παροῦσαι μάλιστα μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐπαρχίᾳ ἐπισκό- των καθίσταςθαι; Episcopum oportet quidem praecipue ab omnibus episcopis provincialibus ordinari, &c. Ex his clarissime conficitur, quod & pluribus demonstravit Leschasserius, & omnes nunc sequuntur eruditi, Concilii Chalcedonensis tempore, hoc est a. D. 451. extitisse in Ecclesia corpus, sive codicem canonum perpetua numerorum serie distinctum; eo ordine, ut primum in codice locum occuparent Nicaenae Synodi Canones; inde sequerentur Ancyranae primo, tum Neocaesariensis, mox Gangrensis Synodorum canones, quos Antiocheni exciperent; coujunctim omnes sub continuatis numeris decurrentes, sic ut qui primus est Ancyrani cyrani Concilii canon, is effet hujus codicis 21. qui Neocaesarienfis primus, is 46. loco in hac collectione occurreret, atque ita deinceps primus Gangrenfis sub numero 60. Antiochenus primus sub numero 80. reperiretur. Qui enim in Synodo Chalcedonenfi Codicis ab Eunomio dati quartus (sic enim legendum est) canon dicitur, is deprehenditur Synodi Nicaenae quartus esse canon; qui vero ejusdem codicis canones in eadem Synodo dicuntur octogesimus tertius, octogesimus quartus, nonagesimus quintus, & nonagesimus sextus, eos conflat esse Antiochenae Synodi canones quartum, quintumque, decimumfextum, & decimum septimum; quibus ipsis locis evidenter occurrunt, Si Nicaenos, Ancyranos, Neocaefarienfes, Gangrenfes, & Antiochenos canones perpetua (ut dixi-mus) numerorum serie astrinxeris, ac in unum corpus vinxeris. Sunt enim (ut omnes norunt) Nicaeni quidem canones viginti; Ancyrani vero viginti quinque, Neocaefarienfes quatuordecim, Gangrenfes viginti, Antiocheni viginti quinque; qui omnes fi uno hoc ordine conjungantur, canones omnino fient quatuor, & centum; quorum hac serie dispositorum octogesimus tertius praecise erit, qui Antiocheni Concilii feorfim sumpti numeratur quartus;
units.tr: If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, etc. Elsewhere in the same synod, when the judges had ordered the canons to be read, Beronicianus, Magistrianus, and the secretary of the divine consistory are said to have read, from a copy given by Eunomius, CANON VI.
