(there is certainly an error in this number; IV should be read for VI, as will soon be clear) in these words: a, [ἐπίσκοπον παροῦσαι μάλιστα μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐπαρχίᾳ ἐπισκόπων καθίστασθαι]; A bishop ought to be ordained chiefly by all the bishops of the province, etc. From these things it is most clearly established, as Leschasserius showed in many ways and as all learned men now follow, that at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, that is, in the year of our Lord 451, there existed in the Church a body, or codex, of canons distinguished by a continuous series of numbers; in such an order that the canons of the Nicene Synod occupied the first place in the codex, followed by those of the Ancyrene synod first, then the Neocaesarean, then the canons of the Gangra synod, which the Antiochene canons followed; all running on together under continuous numbers. Thus the first canon of the Ancyrene council would be number 21 of this codex, the first of the Neocaesarean would occur in this collection as number 46, and so on, the first of Gangra would be found under number 60, and the first Antiochene under number 80. For the one whom the Synod of Chalcedon calls the fourth canon of the codex given by Eunomius (for so it must be read) is found to be the fourth canon of the Nicene Synod; and those canons of the same codex which in the same synod are called the eighty-third, eighty-fourth, ninety-fifth and ninety-sixth are plainly the canons of the Antiochene Synod, the fourth, fifth, sixteenth and seventeenth; and these places clearly correspond, if you bind the Nicene, Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Gangra and Antiochene canons into one body by a continuous series of numbers, as I have said. For there are (as all know) twenty Nicene canons; twenty-five Ancyrene; fourteen Neocaesarean; twenty Gangra; twenty-five Antiochene. If all these are joined in this one order, they make exactly one hundred and four canons; and in this arrangement the eighty-third will be precisely the one which is numbered fourth when the Antiochene council is taken separately;

units.la: Item 84. qui ejusdem Synodi est quintus; itidemque duo alii qui in Synodo Antiochena sunt 16. & 17. numeris in Synodo Chalcedonensi notatis accuratissime respondebunt. Eadem ex Chalcedonensi Synodo jampridem observaverat Hincmarus a, cujus verba non pigebit describere; Sed & actio xii. (inquit) Chalcedonensis Concilii, in qua scriptum habetur, Regula 95. de Vacante Episcopo, Et paulo post Leontius ex eodem codice legit regulam 96. de his, qui ad episcopatum vocati evitant. Quas regulas connumeratis a capite viginti capitulis Nicæni Concilii, siquis per singula consequentia Concilia ex ordine numeraverit, in Antiocheno Concilio loca præfatorum numerorum tenere inveniet. Hactenus Hincmarus. Atque hunc Synodicorum canonum ordinem omnes Græcorum, Latinorumque antiquæ collectiones exhibent; retinentque adhuc Græci Canonistæ; ut ex Zonaræ, & Balsamonis commentariis liquet. Sed & post Antiochenam Synodum, cujus a Patribus Chalcedonensibus citati sunt & descripti canones quatuor, eædem collectiones uno pariter omnes consensu exhibent Laodicenos canones, Constantinopolitanos, Ephesinos, & Chalcedonenses; ut nullum superfit dubium, quin is codex ipse ille fuerit, quem clariss. Justellus ante ante annos 27. Lutetiæ hoc titulo publicavit , Βίβλος κανόνων ἁγίων Καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας, (codex Canonum Ecclesiæ universalis) idque ipsum luculentissime confirmat codex Dionysii Exigui ab eodem ex vetustissimis manuscriptis libris a. D. 1628. ibidem editus; in quo superiores illæ omnes regulæ in unum pariter corpus collectæ sub perpetuis itidem, ut Græcè, numeris decurrunt. Videat, qui plura desiderat, Leschasserium in libello nuper memorato, & ipsum lustellum in præfationibus, quas & Codici Græco, & Dionysio Exiguo præfixit. Nobis ad rem institutam satis est, hæc delibasse, & quamquam breviter, valide tamen confirmasse. Nam cum ex his constet in veteri universalis Ecclesiæ codice anno adhuc 451. (quo habita est Chalcedonensis Synodus) primos fuisse Nicænos Canones, vel cæcus videt, Ecclesiam netum quidem ullos habuisse Apostolorum canones; quos si habuisset scilicet, haud dubie Nicænis antepositura fuerat. Idem autem ille canonum publicus & universalis codex apud Latinos quoque extabat; ut ex Dionysii ad Stephanum præfatione constat, in qua prisca regularum Ecclesiasticarum translationis diserte meminit, atque ejus confusione offensum Laurentium quemdam familiarem suum, assidua assidua cohortatione se ad easdem regulas de graco transferendas pepulisse. In hoc vero prisco Latinorum codice nullos fuisse Apostolorum canones abunde fatetur idem Dionysius, dum alia quaedam praefatus, Stephanum nominatim monet, se in principio canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, de graco transtulisse. Quod ipsum inde quoque perspicitur, quod Dionysius regulas quidem Nicaenas, Synodorumque consequentium ad Constantinopolitanam usque sub ordine numerorum, id est a primo capite usque ad 165. se digessisse profitetur, & digessit sane; Canones vero Apostolorum seorsim initio extra hunc numerorum ordinem collocavit; non ausus scilicet veterem canonicorum numerorum catenam, solas Nicaenas, & sequentium Synodorum regulas complectentem abrumpere. Sed & nullos in veteri Latina codicis translatione Apostolicos canones extitisse, ex eo videre est, quod (ut acutissime observavit Vsserius noster a) Isidorus Mercator, cum in reliquis Conciliorum Graecorum canonibus antiquam versionem retinuerit, in quinquaginta istis Apostolicis translatione Dionysii uti coactus est. Nulli nempe translati erant a veteri Latino interprete Apostolorum canones. Itaque non Latinis magis, quam Graecis,
units.tr: likewise 84, which is the fifth of the same synod; and likewise the two others in the Antiochene synod, 16 and 17, will correspond most accurately to the numbers noted in the Synod of Chalcedon. Hincmar had long ago observed the same things from the Synod of Chalcedon, and I will not hesitate to copy his words: But also the twelfth action (he says) of the Council of Chalcedon, in which is written rule 95, concerning the vacant bishop, and shortly after Leontius read from the same codex rule 96, concerning those who avoid being called to the episcopate. If you count these rules from the twentieth chapter of the Nicene Council onward, following the councils in order one by one, you will find that they hold the places of the numbers mentioned in the Antiochene council. So far Hincmar. And all the ancient collections of Greeks and Latins present this order of synodical canons; and the Greek canonists still keep it, as is clear from the commentaries of Zonaras and Balsamon. Moreover, after the Antiochene Synod, from which the Chalcedonian Fathers cited and copied four canons, the same collections all agree in presenting the Laodicene canons, the Constantinopolitan, the Ephesine and the Chalcedonian; so that there remains no doubt that this is the very codex which the most distinguished Justellus published at Paris twenty-seven years ago under this title, [Βίβλος κανόνων ἁγίων Καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας] (the book of the holy canons of the Catholic Church). The codex of Dionysius Exiguus, published by the same man in the same place in the year of our Lord 1628 from very ancient manuscripts, most brilliantly confirms this; in it all those earlier rules, collected together into one body, likewise run on under continuous numbers, as in the Greek. Whoever wants more should see Leschasserius in the little book mentioned above, and Justellus himself in the prefaces which he prefixed both to the Greek codex and to Dionysius Exiguus. For our purpose it is enough to have touched on these things, and although briefly, to have confirmed them strongly. For since it is established from these things that in the ancient codex of the universal Church, in the year 451 (when the Synod of Chalcedon was held), the Nicene canons were the first, even a blind man sees that the Church did not yet have any canons of the Apostles; for if it had, it would undoubtedly have placed them before the Nicene ones. Moreover that same public and universal codex of canons existed also among the Latins; as is clear from the preface of Dionysius to Stephen, in which he expressly mentions the old translation of the ecclesiastical rules, and says that Laurentius, a friend of his, who was offended by its confusion, had driven him by constant urging to translate those same rules from the Greek. In this ancient Latin codex, Dionysius himself abundantly admits that there were no canons of the Apostles; for when he has prefaced certain other things, he warns Stephen by name that at the beginning I translated from the Greek the canons which are called Apostolic. This is also seen from the fact that Dionysius professes that he had arranged the Nicene rules and those of the synods that followed, down to the Constantinopolitan, under an order of numbers, that is, from the first chapter to the 165th, and indeed he did arrange them; but the canons of the Apostles he placed separately at the beginning, outside this order of numbers, evidently not daring to break the old chain of canonical numbers, which embraced only the Nicene and the following synods' rules. Moreover, that there were no Apostolic canons in the old Latin translation of the codex can be seen from this, that (as our Usher most acutely observed) Isidore Mercator, although he kept the old version in the remaining canons of the Greek councils, was compelled to use the translation of Dionysius for those fifty Apostolic canons. For no Apostolic canons had been translated by the old Latin interpreter. So neither to the Latins any more than to the Greeks,

units.la: a Dissert. de Ignat. c. 6. p. 37. quarto sæculo, quintoque jam ad annum 51. adulto cogniti erant isti Apostolorum canones. Ac tametsi sexto ineunte sæculo quinquaginta Dionysiaci jam extarent, ne tum quidem inter regulas Ecclesiasticas ab omnibus admissi sunt. Nam neque iis Ferrandus Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis Diaconus locum ullum in Breviario canonum dedit, quod circa sexti sæculi principia concinnavit, atque publicavit; neque qui in Hispania a. D. 580. obiit, Martinus Bracarensis, eos vel memoravit, vel usurpavit, aut inseruit in sua illa Græcorum Canonum interpretatione, quam Collectionis Orientalium canonum nomine ad Nitigesium a. D. 572. misflam edidit. Huc & illa Gregorii Turonici a, jam ab aliis quoque observata, in Concilii Parisiensis de Pretextati caussa narratione pertinent; Ipse vero (Chilpericus) discessit, transmittens librum canonum, in quo erat quaternio NOVUS adnexus, habens Canones quasi Apostolicos continentes hæc, Episcopus in homicidio, adulterio, perjurio deprehensus à sacerdotio divellatur (quæ in canone 35. Dionysiaco, tametsi non iisdem plane verbis, leguntur.) Hinc videsillis temporibus (hoc est circiter annum D. 580. ignotos vulgo apud nos fuisse Canones istos Apostolorum Dionysiacos; {a}eos; vides eos in vetustioribus exemplaribus defuisse, ut Chilperici codici adnecti necesse fuerit NOVUM quaternionem, in quo descripti exhiberentur. Vides denique Gregorium inter suae gentis Episcopos primarium, id velut novum atque insolitum annotare, & canones istos veluti dubios, atque incertae fidei non simpliciter Apostolicos, sed quasi Apostolicos vocare. Ergo ne saeculo quidem sexto praecipiti vulgo, passimque apud nostros in regularum Ecclesiasticarum codice habebantur Apostolici illi, tametsi a Dionysio editi, quinquaginta canones. Sed & apud Hincmarum, noni saeculi scriptorem, praeter ea, quae nuper notavimus, luculentissimus est de canonum Ecclesiasticorum codice locus; in quo primo affirmat extare certos quosdam canones a, quos & Apostolica sedes, & omnes Episcopi per universum orbem a prima (inquit) sedis Pontifice usque ad illum, qui modo novissime, etiam post te (Hincmarum Laudunensem alloquitur) est ordinatus Episcopus; imo & omnis Catholica Ecclesia Canones appellant. Tum qui qualesque sint, clarius ac distertius, sigillatim haec continenter subjiciens, edisserit; quique a Nicaeno Concilio (inquit) quod PRIMUM in nostris codicibus (quos ab Apostolica sede majores nostri acceperunt) runt) sequendos per ordinem usque ad Africanum (concilium pro Canonibus recipiendis, venerandis, & observandis retinent, & Innocentius, Zosimus, Bonifacius, Coelestinus, Leo, Hilarus, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisda, Gregorius, & cateri quicque observandos canones nominant. Hactenus Hincmarus; ex quo liquet primo etiam tum (hoc est a. D. 870.) in Galliis nostris extitisse Canonum Ecclesiasticorum codicem; secundo in eo codice primo loco positos fuisse Nicaenos canones; tertio, exinde in eodem dispositos extitisse Synodorum sequentium canones usque ad Africanam; qui codex plane, ut utrumque comparanti constabit, ille ipse est, quem Graeco-Latinum publicavit clariss. Iustellus a. D. 1610. quarto eum codicem à Sede Romana in Gallias ad majores Hincmari misssam. Atque hinc apparet, cur quaternio, qui in Chilperici codice canones quasi Apostolicos continebat, novus fuerit. Nempe in codicibus vetustissimis, Roma scilicet missis, PRIMUM, teste Hincmaro, fuit Concilium Nicaenum; itaque canones istos quasi Apostolicos de novo, recentiori manu, ac opere superaddititi erant. Quinto deniq; docet nos Hincmarus, hujus codicis canones a Patribus, qui post eorum collectionem vixerunt, canones nes simpliciter vocari; item observandos canones ab iisdem nominari; quibus vocabulis supra diximus Turrianum suos illos falso Apostolicos dictos canones voluisse significari; quod quam falso, ac praeter rationem fecerit, nunc quidem nos luculentissime docet Hincmarus. Atq; ex his jam satis, ni fallor, constat totis prioribus quinque Christianismi saeculis neque apud Graecos, neque apud Latinos, in codice Ecclesiae inter publicas regulas extitisse ullam Apostolicorum canonum syllogen, sive priorem Dionysiacam, quae 50. tantum canonum est, sive posteriorem Graecanicam, quae triginta quinque capitulis auctior est.
units.tr: (a Dissertation on Ignatius, ch. 6, p. 37), in the fourth century, and already in the fifth century up to about the year 451, were those Apostolic canons known. And although in the early sixth century the fifty Dionysian canons were already in circulation, not even then were they admitted by all among the ecclesiastical rules. For neither did Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, give them any place in the breviary of canons which he put together and published around the beginning of the sixth century; nor did Martin of Braga, who died in Spain in the year 580, either mention or use them, or insert them into his own Greek canon law translation, which he published under the title of Collection of Eastern Canons, sent to Nitigisius in the year 572. To this also belongs that account of Gregory of Tours, already noticed by others, in his narrative of the case of Pretextatus at the Council of Paris: But he himself (Chilperic) departed, sending a book of canons, in which there was an attached NEW quire, containing canons as if Apostolic, which say these things: a bishop caught in murder, adultery or perjury shall be cut off from the priesthood (which in Dionysian canon 35 is read, though not in quite the same words). From this you see that in those times (that is, about the year 580) those Dionysian canons of the Apostles were generally unknown among us; you see that they were lacking in the older copies, so that it was necessary to attach a NEW quire to Chilperic's codex, in which they might be written out. You see finally that Gregory, the foremost of the bishops of his nation, notes this as something new and unusual, and calls those canons not simply Apostolic but as if Apostolic, as though doubtful and of uncertain credit. Therefore not even in the sixth century, in the common and widespread practice among our people, were those Apostolic canons, fifty in number though edited by Dionysius, held in the codex of ecclesiastical rules. Moreover, in Hincmar, a writer of the ninth century, besides what we have lately noted, there is a most illustrious passage about the codex of ecclesiastical canons; in which he first affirms that there exist certain canons which the Apostolic See, and all bishops throughout the world, from the first Pontiff of that See down to him who was most recently made bishop, even after you (he addresses Hincmar of Laon) have accepted; indeed the whole Catholic Church calls them canons. Then he sets forth clearly and distinctly, going through them one by one in continuous order, what and what kind they are; and those which, from the Nicene Council (he says), which is FIRST in our codices (which our ancestors received from the Apostolic See), are to be followed in order down to the African council (for the reception, honouring and observance of canons), and Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory, and the rest, name them canons to be observed. So far Hincmar. From this it is clear: first, that even then (that is, in the year 870) there existed in our Gaul a codex of ecclesiastical canons; second, that in that codex the Nicene canons were placed first; third, that from there the canons of the following synods, down to the African, were arranged in the same codex (which codex, as anyone comparing the two will see, is that very one which the most distinguished Justellus published in Greek and Latin in the year 1610); fourth, that this codex was sent from the Roman See into Gaul to Hincmar's ancestors. And from this it appears why the quire which contained the canons as if Apostolic in Chilperic's codex was new. Clearly, in the most ancient codices, those sent from Rome, the Nicene Council was FIRST, as Hincmar attests; so those canons as if Apostolic were added later, by a more recent hand and work. Fifth, finally, Hincmar teaches us that the canons of this codex were called simply canons by the Fathers who lived after their collection, and likewise that the same men named them canons to be observed; by which terms, as we said above, Turrianus wished to signify those canons of his which he falsely called Apostolic; how falsely and beyond reason he did this, Hincmar now very clearly shows us. And from these things, unless I am mistaken, it is now sufficiently established that throughout the first five centuries of Christianity, neither among the Greeks nor among the Latins, was there in the codex of the Church, among the public rules, any collection of Apostolic canons, whether the earlier Dionysian, which is only fifty canons, or the later Greek one, which is enlarged by thirty-five chapters.

units.la: Hoc vero luculentissimum est, atque invictissimum veritatis, quam defendimus, argumentum; quod si vel unum esset, liquido & ineluctabiliter demonstrat, neutram collectionem veteri illorum temporum Ecclesiae cognitam fuisse; neutram adeo vel ab Apostolis ipsis editam, vel a Clemente Romano scriptam; quam scilicet (si qua hujusmodi Christianorum praepositis ab illis tradita esset) vel nescivisse, vel cognitam abjecisse, & a regulis Ecclesiasticis eas, quas Apostolicas scirent, exclusisse omnes illorum quatuor & amplius saeculorum homines, neque credibile est, neque possibile.
units.tr: This, moreover, is the most striking and unanswerable argument for the truth we defend. Even if it were the only one, it would clearly and inescapably demonstrate that neither collection was known to the Church of those early times: neither one put forth by the Apostles themselves, nor one written by Clement of Rome. For it is neither credible nor possible that all the people of those four and more centuries either did not know of such a collection (if any such had been handed down to the Christian ministers by the Apostles), or, knowing of it, set it aside, and excluded from the Ecclesiastical rules those which they knew to be Apostolic.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAP. XX.

units.la: Arg. VI. inde ductum, quod omnes isti canones omnibus quatuor priorum saeculorum Christianis ignoti fuerint; ut ex eo apparet quod a nullo istorum temporum scriptore uspiam memorati reperiantur. Concluditur tota contra Canones istos disputatio.
units.tr: Argument VI, drawn from the fact that all these canons were unknown to every Christian of the first four centuries; this appears from the fact that no writer of those times is found anywhere mentioning them. The whole dispute against these canons is thereby concluded.

units.la: VI. DOSTREMO illud ipsum inde quoque evidentissime apparet, quod veteres illi primorum quatuor & amplius saeculorum Episcopi, non modo & hanc, & illam collectionem, Dionysiacam inquiam, & Graecanicam, vel in Scripturarum canonem, vel certe in regularum Ecclesiasticarum codicem (quod utrumque fieri decebat) non retulerunt, sed & insuper neutrius in ullo suorum monumentorum, quae propemodum innumerabilia superstant, mentionem uspiam fecisse reperiuntur; quod quidem quam vere affirmemus, satis eo ipso demonstravimus, quod ex omnibus Scriptorum illius aevi locis, quae sunt a Turriano, maximo antiquitatis helluone, adhaec impigerrimo & diligentissimo disputatore, in hanc causam inducta, plane nullum esse ostendimus, qui ad illam Apostolicorum canonum collectionem
units.tr: VI. Finally, it also appears most clearly from this that those ancient bishops of the first four centuries and more not only failed to include either this collection or that one, I mean the Dionysian and the Greek, either in the canon of Scripture or at least in the code of Church rules (which both ought to have been done), but are also found nowhere to have mentioned either one in any of their writings, which survive in almost countless numbers. How truly we make this assertion, we have sufficiently demonstrated by the very fact that, from all the passages of writers of that age which Turrianus, the greatest glutton for antiquity and also a most tireless and diligent disputant, has brought into this question, we have shown that there is plainly none that pertains to that collection of Apostolic canons

units.la: ctionem lectionem pertineat. Huc accedit, quod sparsim multa in illorum Patrum controversiis ac causis observavimus, in quibus quam res ipsa poscebat ac flagitabat horum Canonum fieri mentionem, ne talibus quidem locis ac temporibus factam fuisse ullam docuimus. Duo tantum iis, quæ superius diximus, ad ejusdem rei probationem addenda operæ pretium esse duximus. Unum est, quod neque Eusebius, neque Hieronymus, viri (ut notum est) eruditissimi, dum & Apostolorum & Clementis opera summa utraque diligentia recensent, & ea, quæ iis falso affingebantur, pari ἀχεῖβεία exsequuntur, acsugillant, in neutro ordine Canones ullos Apostolicos memorant. Cur eos prætervieserunt, siquos vel veros vel falsos norant? Talibus viris ignotos fuisse Apostolorum Canones, (liquidem ii vere Apostolorum, & ea, quam tantus titulus deposcit, venerations vere digni sunt) id inquam, tam ab omni rationis specie abhorret, ut in hominis sani ac sapientis mentem venire non possit. Quis enim Christiani totius orbis reverentia, ac religione consecratas (si Turriano quidem credimus) regulas, à majoribus summa fide traditas, à posteris pari cura ac studio susceptas, perpetua præteritorum sæculorum praxi sancitas, illustrissimum strissimum Apostolicæ sapientiæ monumentum, unicum Ecclesiæ thesaurum, ac peculium; quis inquam, rem adeo publicam ac salutarem nescivisse putaverit viros clarissimos, & eruditionis Ecclesiasticę suo utriumque sæculo facile principes? Sin iis notos quidem canones fuisse dicas; cæterum quos probe noverant, eos vel oblivionem, vel de industria præterMisisse; quis absurdissime, neque ulla veri specie fucato mendacio fidem habuerit? Eusebio scilicet, vel Hieronymo non venerit in mentem inter Apostolorum opera, id quod inprimis nobile erat, ac necessarium, & si non primo, certe secundo loco dicendum, commemorare? idem fuerit eorum tor-por, dum Clementis scripta recensent; cujus quidem manus nihil istis Canonibus vel præstantius, vel Ecclesiæ utilius elucubravit, siqua istis Turrianicarum partium hominibus fides. Atqui ne crassi quidem, ac pingues de vulgo scriptores tantum flagitium commiserint; sedum ut in id incidisse credamus Eusebium, aut Hieronymum. Hos vero eos confulto præterMisisse, absurdius dictu est, quam ut refelli mereatur. Quæ enim ratio viros sapientissimos id consilii capere subigebat? Versentse in omnes partes Turriani, Biniique, ac Bellarmini; Nunquam ullam afferent tam absoni, tamque absurdi facti rationem. Hoc Eusebii, hoc Hieronymi (ut cæteros taceam, quorum omnium eadem fuit oblivio) silentium omni voce clarius clamat, omnique sermone difertius loquitur nullos ab Apostolis editos, nullos à Clemente scriptos istos Canones. Alterum secundo hic loco observandum est, quod cum quatuor, istorum primorum sæculorum Patres & in Synodicis actis sæpe, & in propriis singuli operibus interdum quædam vel constituant, vel commemorent, quæ in ea, quam habemus, Apostolicorum canonum sylloge decreta quoque, ac perscripta leguntur, nullus tamen hujus generis locus occurrit, in quo veteres illi authores hujus Apostolicæ Sylloges vel verba nominatim citent, ac describant, vel saltem canonis, in quo id ipsum, quod præcipiunt, decernitur, numerum annotent. Pauca è multis exempla hic observare lubet. Ecce verbi gratia, quod in primo statim Syllogæs canone decernitur, ut Episcopus à duobus, tribusve Episcopis ordinetur; id ipsum inquam, & Synodus Nicœna a, & Arcelatensis utraque b, & Carthaginensis c 2. decernunt, & Theodoretus d memorat; sed ita ut neque illæ Synodi, neque hic scriptor idem ab Apostolis canone primo constitutum fuisse.
units.tr: ...reading. Moreover, we have observed scattered through the controversies and causes of those Fathers many places where the nature of the matter itself demanded and required mention of these canons, and we have shown that no mention was made of them even in such places and at such times. We have thought it worth adding only two points to what we have said above, to prove the same thing. The first is that neither Eusebius nor Jerome, men (as is well known) most learned, while they recount the works of the Apostles and of Clement with the greatest care, and while they examine and censure with equal diligence what was falsely attributed to them, mention any Apostolic canons in either list. Why did they pass them over, if they knew of any, whether genuine or spurious? That the Apostolic canons were unknown to such men (since, if they are truly the Apostles', they are truly worthy of the reverence that so great a title demands), I say, this is so far from every appearance of reason that it cannot enter the mind of a sane and wise man. For who would think that men so illustrious, and the foremost authorities of ecclesiastical learning in their own age, did not know of a monument so distinguished and so necessary, a rule consecrated by the reverence and religion of the whole Christian world (if we believe Turrianus), handed down by our forebears with the greatest fidelity, received by posterity with equal care and zeal, sanctioned by the continuous practice of past centuries, the unique treasure and possession of the Church? Or if you say that they did know these canons, but that they either forgot them or deliberately passed them over, who would believe so absurd a lie, one that has no semblance of truth? Did it simply not occur to Eusebius or Jerome to mention among the works of the Apostles this item, which was above all notable and necessary, and which ought to have been named, if not first, at least second? Would they have been equally dull when recounting the writings of Clement, whose hand (if we believe these partisans of Turrianus) produced nothing more excellent or more useful to the Church than these canons? Yet not even crude and common writers from the crowd would have committed such a blunder, and we cannot believe that Eusebius or Jerome fell into it. To say that they deliberately passed them over is more absurd than deserves refutation. For what reason could have moved such wise men to such a decision? Turrianus, Binius and Bellarmine may turn in every direction; they will never give a reason for so discordant and absurd a deed. This silence of Eusebius and of Jerome (to say nothing of the others, all of whom share the same oversight) cries out more clearly than any voice and speaks more eloquently than any discourse: that these canons were issued by no Apostles and written by no Clement. The second point to be observed here is that, although these four Fathers of the first centuries often, in their synodal acts and sometimes in their individual works, lay down or recall certain things which are also found decreed and written down in the collection of Apostolic canons we have, yet no passage of this kind occurs in which those ancient authors name and quote the words of this Apostolic collection, or at least note the number of the canon in which what they prescribe is decreed. Let me point out a few examples out of many. For instance, what is decreed in the very first canon of the collection, that a bishop be ordained by two or three bishops, this very thing both the Synod of Nicaea<a> and both Synods of Arles<b> and the Synod of Carthage<c> decree, and Theodoret<d> records it; yet neither those synods nor this writer say or imply that the same was laid down by the Apostles in the first canon.

units.la: a can. 4. b Syn. Arel. 1. c. 21. Secundac. 5 ccan. 21. d hist. l. 5. c. 9. fuisse vel dicant, vel innuant. Sic etiam quod eadem Apostolicorum canonum syl-loge canone 13 (14) vetat episcopum alienam parœciam invadere, id ipsum Ni-cœna quoque & Antiochena Synodus vetat: neutra Apostolicam, vel Clementinam Syllogen memorat. Eadem quoque ejus est ratio, quod Apostolico canone 14 (15) adversus presbyteros deserta sua parœcia in aliam migrantes decretum Antiochena itidem & Nicæna Synodus præcipit. Canone Apostolico 31 (33) statuitur, nequis Episcopus presbyterum vel Diaconum ab alio Episcopo segregatum suscipiat. Idem nuper memoratæ Synodi, sed nulla de Apostolis injecta mentione, præcipiunt. Sed & Antiochena eodem quoque modo vetat Episcopum extra suam parœciam ordinationes facere; quod itidem prohibet Apostolicæ syllogcs canon 34 (36) Apostolicus canon 36 (38.) duas quotannis Synodos provinciales celebrari jubet; priorem quarta Pentecostes hebdomade; alteram Hyperberetæi (id est Octobris) die duodecimo. Nicæni & Antiochheni Patres idem quoque ut fiat decernunt; nisi quod Nicæni priorem ante quadragesimam, Antiocheni itidem, ut Apostolicus canon, quarta Pentecostes hebdomade colligi volunt; & hi alteram ad decimum Hyperberetæi (non in duodecimum) indicunt, quam Nicæni simplicius, ac solutius circa tempus autumni haberi sciscunt. Apostolici canonis, neque ubi cum eo conveniunt, neque ubi ab eo discedunt, neutri meminerunt. Antiocheni ea quoque decernere reperiuntur, quæ Apostolicis canonibus 37 (39) & 39 (40) de Ecclesiasticis, & Episcopalibus rebus, utrarumque distinctione, præcipiuntur; sed nullis nominatis vel Apostolis, vel Apostolicis canonibus. Multa alia sunt in veterum libris, præsertim vero in Antiochena hac Synodo, quæ ad ea pertinent, quæ Apostolicis canonibus continentur. Rogo, cur Nicæni, cur cæteri, cur præsertim illi Antiocheni, non significent diserte, se ista ex Apostolorum syllogeClementis manu, atque authoritate tradita habere? Atqui Scripturę locum aliquem quoties usurpant, toties fere solent authorem loci edere, vel certe divinas Scripturas, aut Apostolos nominare. Cur in solis canonibus aliter instituunt? Atqui id talibus locis diserte monere, & ad Apostolorum laudem, & ad ipsorum scriptorum pietatem, & ad rerum, quas præcipiunt, authoritatem inprimis pertinebat. Scio, quid respondeat Turrianus, sæpe istos in hujusmodi locis canones, vel antiquos, vel Ecclesiasticos, & mores, & consuetudinem nominare; his autem vocabulis suæ sylloges librum ac decreta significari. Sed primo neque semper id faciunt, sed raro; neque qui antiquos aut Ecclesiasticos Canones, aut mores, & consuetudinem nominat, is statim Apostolicos Turrianicæ Sylloges canones vel significat, vel significare intelligitur. Plane contra videtur potius aliquid ab Apostolico diversum significari; hujusmodi scilicet, quod non quidem ab Apostolis decrerum fuerit, sed tamen Ecclesiæ vel more, & usu tacito, vel etiam præcepto constitutum invaluerit. Quid opus erat istis ambagibus, si Apostolis in Clementino codice hæc, quæ ipsi decernunt, decreta jam fuisse, significare Patres volebant? Cur hoc non dicunt aperte? cur non simpliciter & bona fide eloquuntur? Hoc quidem multo fuerat, ut quivis videt, ad rem aptius. Itaque postquam ista Syllogé innotuit, hoc est post sæculum sextum inchoatum, quotquot aliquid ex ea citare cupiunt, ii fere librum aperte nominant, & ea dicunt, ex quibus omnes intelligunt, eos, non Ecclesiæ, vel Patrum decreta, sed (quod multo amplius est) ipsorum Apostolorum canones, & quidem ex aliqua vel ab ipsis, vel à Clemente, vel certe ab antiquissimis facta collectione. Ita Septi-
units.tr: <a> can. 4. <b> Syn. Arel. 1, c. 21; Syn. Arel. 2, can. 21. <c> Carthage, can. 21. <d> Hist. l. 5, c. 9. Likewise, the same collection, in canon 13 (14), forbids a bishop to invade another's parish; the Synod of Nicaea and the Synod of Antioch also forbid this, but neither mentions the Apostolic or Clementine collection. The same reasoning applies to the fact that, by Apostolic canon 14 (15), the Synod of Antioch and likewise the Synod of Nicaea order that presbyters who leave their parish and move to another be punished. By Apostolic canon 31 (33) it is laid down that no bishop shall receive a presbyter or deacon who has been separated from another bishop. The Synods just mentioned order the same, but without any mention of the Apostles. The Synod of Antioch likewise forbids a bishop to perform ordinations outside his own parish, which the Apostolic collection also forbids in canon 34 (36). Apostolic canon 36 (38) orders that two provincial synods be held each year: the first in the fourth week after Pentecost, the second on the twelfth day of Hyperberetaeus (that is, October). The Fathers of Nicaea and of Antioch also decree that this be done, except that the Nicene Fathers want the first held before Lent, and the Antiochene Fathers, like the Apostolic canon, want it gathered in the fourth week after Pentecost; and the latter call the second for the tenth of Hyperberetaeus (not the twelfth), whereas the Nicene Fathers more simply and loosely decree that it be held about the time of autumn. Neither group mentions the Apostolic canon, either where they agree with it or where they depart from it. The Antiochene Fathers are also found to decree those things which the Apostolic canons 37 (39) and 39 (40) prescribe concerning ecclesiastical and episcopal matters and the distinction between the two; but they name neither the Apostles nor the Apostolic canons. There are many other points in the books of the ancients, especially in this Synod of Antioch, that pertain to what is contained in the Apostolic canons. I ask, why did the Nicene Fathers, and the others, and especially those of Antioch, not state plainly that they had these things from the Apostolic collection, handed down by the hand and authority of Clement? Yet whenever they use some passage of Scripture, they usually name its author, or at least name the divine Scriptures or the Apostles. Why do they proceed otherwise only with the canons? Surely to state this plainly in such places pertained above all to the praise of the Apostles, to the piety of the writers themselves, and to the authority of the things they prescribe. I know what Turrianus will answer: that these men often in such places name "canons," or "ancient" or "ecclesiastical" canons, and "customs" and "usage," and that by these words the book and decrees of his collection are meant. But first, they do not always do this, but rarely; and whoever names "ancient" or "ecclesiastical canons," or "customs" and "usage," does not at once signify, or is understood to signify, the Apostolic canons of Turrianus's collection. Rather, it seems plain that something different from the Apostolic is meant: something, that is, which was not indeed decreed by the Apostles, but which had become established in the Church by silent custom and practice, or even by precept. What need was there for such circumlocutions, if the Fathers wanted to signify that these things which they decree had already been decreed by the Apostles in the Clementine codex? Why do they not say this openly? Why do they not speak simply and in good faith? Surely, as anyone can see, this would have been far more suitable to the matter. Therefore, since this collection became known, that is, after the sixth century had begun, all who wish to quote anything from it name the book openly and say things by which everyone understands that they mean not the decrees of the Church or the Fathers, but (which is much more) the canons of the Apostles themselves, and indeed from some collection made either by the Apostles, or by Clement, or at least by very ancient men. Thus the Seventh-

units.la: Septima Synodus aa. D. 787. Divinos (in- quit) canones amplectimur, quod S. Apo-stoli, Spiritus S. clarissima tuba ediderunt. Et paulo post, Fiat (inquit b) secundum ca- nonem Apostolorum, qui ait, Siquis episcopus pecunia hanc dignitatem obtinuerit, aut presbyter vel Diaconus, privetur omnino communione, ut Simon Magus à me Petro. Canon autem iste est Apostolicae collectionis 28. (30) totus de verbo ad verbum descriptus. Et alibi de eo, qui bona Ecclesiae alienat, Sit (inquit c) irritum secundum canonem Apostolorum, qui ait, Omnium bonorum Ecclesiasticorum; & cætera. Recitat autem Turrianicæ collectionis canonem 37 (39) totum. Ita etiam Synodus Parisiensis sub Ludovico; In canonibus qui Apostolorum prænotantur (inquit d) titulo 41. ita legitur; tum canonem illum (qui græcis est 40. Latinis ex Dionysio 41.) ad verbum recitat. Neque secus aliter cæteri. Cur non sic quoque primorum quatuor sæculorum scriptores? è quibus, si unum dederit Turrianus, qui canones suos Apostolicos ita citaverit ut i- sti Parisienses, non pugnabo, quin triumphet. Nimirum hi quidem recentiores istam canonum syllogen norant, & vere Apostolicam putabant: Illi veteres nullam sciebant; nullam ab Apostolis
units.tr: The Seventh Synod, in the year 787, says: "We embrace the divine canons, which the holy Apostles published by the clearest trumpet of the Holy Spirit." And a little later it says: "Let it be done according to the canon of the Apostles, who says: If any bishop has obtained this dignity by money, or a presbyter or deacon, let him be wholly deprived of communion, as Simon Magus was by me, Peter." This canon is canon 28 (30) of the Apostolic collection, copied word for word in full. Elsewhere, concerning one who alienates the goods of the Church, it says: "Let it be void according to the canon of the Apostles, who says: Of all ecclesiastical goods," and so on. It quotes in full canon 37 (39) of the collection of Turrianus. So too the Synod of Paris under Louis: "In the canons which are headed with the name of the Apostles," it says, "the following is read as number 41," and then it quotes that canon (which is 40 in the Greek and 41 in Dionysius's Latin) word for word. The others do no differently. Why do the writers of the first four centuries not do likewise? If Turrianus can produce even one of them who cited his Apostolic canons as those Parisian writers did, I shall not argue against his triumph. Clearly the more recent writers knew that collection of canons and truly believed it to be Apostolic, whereas those older writers knew no such collection and did not believe that any collection had been published by the Apostles. This is the true ground of the difference. You will look in vain for another.

units.la: a c. 1. — b c. 5. — c c. 12. — d c. 15. editam credebant. Hæc vera est discrimi- nis ratio. Frustra aliam quæsieris.

Itaque cum tam multis tamque evidentibus argumentis, & cujusque partis proprиiis, & utriusque communibus, tum a rebus ipsis, tum a veterum testimonio petitis, demonstratum sit, neutram collectionem, id est, neque Dionysiacam, neque Turrianicam, vel Apostolorum esse, vel Clementis; illud postremo quod probandum susceperamus, concludendum est, Gelasium urbis Episcopum, septuaginta- que Romanæ Synodi Patres, quidquid illius libri est, qui Canonum Apostolicorum dicitur, vere sane, meritoque, ac sapienter in apocryphorum censum rejecisse; graviterque hallucinari omnes sive Græcos, sive Latinos homines, qui spreto ac conculcato venerandorum illorum Patrum judicio, illam Syllogen vel totam, vel certe priorem ejus partem, vere Apostolicam esse, inanibus recentiorum somniis, ac præjudiciis fascinati contendunt; quasi scilicet vel Trullanum Conciliabulum, vel Iesuitæ nudius tertius nati melius intelligant, qui veri sint Apostolorum libri, quam Gelasius & æquales Episcopi, qui ducentis annis ante Trullanum conventum, mille & quod excurrit ante exortum Iesuitarum parentem Ignatium, in Ecclesia floruerunt, maximaque dignitates gesserunt.
units.tr: Therefore, since it has been shown by so many and so evident arguments, both those special to each side and those common to both, drawn both from the things themselves and from the testimony of the ancients, that neither collection, that is neither the Dionysian nor the Turrianic, is either the Apostles' or Clement's, the last thing we undertook to prove must follow: Gelasius, bishop of the city, and the seventy Fathers of the Roman Synod, rightly, justly and wisely placed among the apocryphal writings whatever belongs to that book which is called the Canons of the Apostles; and all men, whether Greeks or Latins, who, scorning and trampling on the judgment of those venerable Fathers, contend that that collection, either wholly or at least its earlier part, is truly Apostolic, are gravely mistaken, bewitched by the empty dreams and prejudices of more recent writers. As if, forsooth, the Trullan conciliabulum, or the Jesuits born only the other day, understood better which books are truly the Apostles' than Gelasius and his contemporary bishops, who flourished in the Church two hundred years before the Trullan assembly, and more than a thousand years before the birth of Ignatius, the father of the Jesuits, and held the highest offices.

units.la: CAPVT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Expenditur, ac refellitur, & exploditur Albaspinei de Canonibus conjectura; diversis temporibus ab Apostolicis viris conditos, sensimque alios aliis additos, in eam, quam habemus, Syllogen, paulatim excrevisse, prater omnem rationem hariolantis. Syllogen quinto saeculo, sed jam adulto, factam ac publicatam videri.
units.tr: The conjecture of Albaspinaeus about the Canons is examined, refuted and exploded: that canons drawn up at different times by apostolic men, and gradually added one to another, grew little by little into the collection we now have, beyond all reasonable guessing. It appears that the collection was made and published in the fifth century, but already grown to maturity.

units.la: ID unum jam superesse videtur, ut Albaspinei Aurelianensis Episcopi, singularem de his Canonibus sententiam expendamus. Is enim, ut supra diximus, concedit, imo & validis rationibus probat hos Canones, quod verissimum est, & ex superioribus patet, non uno eodemque seculo omnes fuisse conditos, sed aliis alios temporibus; quosdam primo secundoque Christianismi saeculo ab Apostolicis, id est Apostolorum successoribus, quosdam, ut verbi gratia, eos, qui de admittendis ad poenitentiam lapsis, praecipiunt, tertio saeculo, Cypriani demum aevo ab aliis Episcopis; atque ita de ceteris: ac cum initio primi illi ab Apostolicis viris facti in unum collecti essent, Syllogen logen ipsam ab authorum nomine Apo-stolicorum canones appellatam fuisse : auctamque postea diversis temporibus, cum prioribus canonibus subinde alii adiiceren- tur, & eodem volumine comprehende- rentur, vetus Canonum Apostolicorum nomen, quod primæ partis proprie fuerat, penes totam Syllogen hæsisse, tametsi non omnes, sed primi tantum & vetustissimi Apostolicorum proprie essent ; alii vero à diversis vel Episcopis, vel etiam Synodis diu post primos illos conditi essent, & in hunc codicem suis quique temporibus relati ; itaque nihil aliud esse hanc canonum syllogen, quam breviarium & epitomen privatorum Conciliorum, & rerum ab Episcopis privatis sancitarum, qui Ecclesias Græcas ante Concilium Nicænum administrarunt. Cæterum ex Apostolicorum Canonibus, quod prius, veriusque fuerit Sylloges nomen, nonnullorum Latinorum ignorantia, aliquot litterarum detractione, factos, dictosque esse Apostolorum canones. Hæc viri eruditissimi, & in antiquitatibus Ecclesiasticis versatissimi sententia, prima fronte magnam præ se fert veri speciem ; sed tamen si penitus & accuratius excutiatur, deprehendetur & ipsa multa continere à vero & recto aliena. Vt autem clarius elucescat, quid sit de ea tota
units.tr: Now it only remains for us to weigh the particular opinion of Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, concerning these Canons. For he, as we said above, concedes, indeed even proves by weighty arguments, what is most true and is clear from what has gone before: that these Canons were not all composed in one and the same century, but at different times; some in the first and second centuries of Christianity by apostolic men, that is, by the successors of the apostles, and some, for example those which prescribe the admission of the lapsed to repentance, in the third century, in the age of Cyprian at last, by other bishops; and so with the rest. And when those first ones made by apostolic men had at the beginning been gathered into one, the collection itself was called "The Canons of the Apostles" from the name of its authors; and afterwards, as it was enlarged at various times, other canons being continually added to the earlier ones and included in the same volume, the old name "Canons of the Apostles", which had properly belonged to the first part, clung to the whole collection, although not all of them, but only the first and most ancient, were properly apostolic; while others, which had been drawn up long after those first ones by various bishops or even by synods, were entered in this codex each in its own time. Hence, he says, this collection of canons is nothing other than an abridgement and epitome of private councils and of decrees issued by private bishops who governed the Greek churches before the Council of Nicaea. Moreover, he says, through the ignorance of some Latins, with a few letters dropped, the name of the collection, which was first and more correct, "Apostolic Canons", was turned into and became "Canons of the Apostles." This opinion of these most learned men, who are most versed in ecclesiastical antiquities, at first sight bears a great appearance of truth; yet if it is examined thoroughly and more carefully, it will be found that it too contains many things alien to the truth and to what is right.

units.la: [Note: the typeset text is partly italic as shown; some words uncertain.] tota statuendum, hujus Sylloges, (quæ vulgo dicitur Canones Apostolorum) forma inprimis à materia (ut loquuntur in scho-lis) distinguenda est. Materiam hujus sylloges appello res ipsas, quæ in cano-nibus vel præcipiuntur, vel vetantur, sin-gulaque decreta, ex quibus coagmenta-tis, & inter se colligatis facta est sylloge. Formam vero intelligo & ipsum illum or-dinem, quo canones per numeros decur-runt, iis tanquam hamis conserti; & o-rationis totius speciem, hoc est & verba, quibus illa decreta hic expressa habentur, & personas quæ inducuntur, hæc decer-nentes, & loquentes. Hęc enim pluri-mum inter se differre nemo adeo crassus est, qui non videat; ut in juris Canonici cor-pore, quod à Gratiano compilatum de-cretum vulgo dicitur, aliud est materia, ex qua id conflatum est, scilicet Synodorum & Pontificum constituta, Patrumque sen-tentiæ; aliud forma, quam operi author indidit, illa tam multa, & ex tam variis locis, ac temporibus comportata certo in-ter se ordine disponens, ac connectens; unde totum opus Gratiani dicitur; ta-metsi pene omnia, quę continet, non Gratiani, sed longe aliorum authorum sint. Ergo, ut ad institutum veniam, si ipsam Canonum Apostolicorum mate-riam riam feorsim ab ea forma, quam in hac sylloge habet, sumptam nude, simpliciterque spectemus; fateor equidem ei propemodum convenire, quod ait Albaspineus, ejusque adeo sententiam proxime ad verum accedere, si de hac Canonum materia sic ut dixi, intelligatur. Apparet enim, plurima ac fere omnia, ex quibus hæc sylloge constat, decreta, si per se singula considerentur, variis temporibus, aliis alia sæculis, & locis, toto quatuor primorum sæculorum decursu in Ecclesia Orientali facta fuisse: idque optime demonstrant argumenta ab Albaspineo allata; inde ducta, quod multa in hac sylloge diserte constituta, decretaque legantur, quæ ad controversias, sæculis Apostolorum tempora consecutis exortas pertinent; item quod in eadem Sylloge aliquot canones inveniantur, quos ex Concilio Gangrensi desumptos esse vel ipsa lectione constet. Cui Albaspinei observationi illud quoque adjecerim, videri & ex Antiocheno Concilio desumptos non paucos hujus Apostolicæ farraginis canones, ut alteros cum alteris conferenti liquebit. Sed ne in hac quidem parte plane, penitusque in Albaspinei sententiam possum concedere, & cum eo fateri omnia, quæ in his Canonibus habentur, ex privatis Græcorum, sive Conciliorum, sive Episcoporum actis decretisque sumpta fuisse. Nam quaedam in his legimus, quae ab omnis Graecanicae Ecclesiae, praesertim ante Nicaenam Synodum doctrina sic abhorrent, ut non sit verisimile, ea unquam ab ullo Graecorum Catholicorum sive Concilio, sive Episcopo, fuisse tradita; quale est, verbi gratia, quod 84. & 85. canonibus de libris divinis decernitur. Quis enim quaeso vetustiorum, non dico Latinorum, sed & Graecorum Patrum, tertium librum Maccabaicum in sacrum veteris Testamenti, vel Clementinarum Constitutionum octo volumina in novi canonem ante hujus Syllages patrem retulerat? Hic vero error usque adeo crassus est, ut neminem Catholicorum veterum authorem habuisse videatur. Hoc quidem constat, nulla ejus in trium primorum saeculorum monumentis, quantumvis levia occurrere usquam vestigia, ut illud mittam, fieri non potuisse, ut Constitutionum Clementinarum libros quisquam ante Nicaenae Synodi tempora in canonem sacrum referret, quas scilicet nondum tunc extitisse, sed temporibus eam Synodum consecutis effectas ac consarcinatas fuisse satis, ni fallor, superiori disputatione demonstratum est. Caeterum his, & pauculis si forte aliis canonibus demptis, libens confiteor, quae in aliis plerisque omnibus decernuntur, ea ex Græcæ Ecclesiæ sive Synodicis constitutis, sive etiam episcopalibus rescriptis, adhæc moribus & ritibus observationibusque, usu ac consuetudine invectis ac confirmatis, desumpta videri. Atque hæc quidem de Canonum materia seorsim spectata. Si vero opus quale circumfertur, totum consideremus, habita ratione non materiæ modo, ex qua compositum est & conflatum, sed & formæ, ad quam effectum & concinnatum id cernitur; hic profecto ab Albaspinei sententia discedere, & in alia omnia ire cogimur. Nam si res accuratius expendatur, nihil eorum, quæ ille ponit, poterit consistere; facileque deprehenditur ista Syllogæ longe aliter, quam ille narrat, facta fuisse; ab eaque forma, quam ipse ei tribuit, plurimum abhorrere. Nam ut hic ordiar, id inprimis procul à vero esse videtur, quod ille ait hunc codicem breviarium esse, atque epitomen Ecclesiasticorum ante Nicænam Synodum apud Græcos decretorum. Si enim res ita se haberet, omnino hanc Syllogen codici canonum Ecclesiæ universalis ejus authores inseruissent; imo primo codicis loco posuissent, velut & à viris Apostolicis exortum, & ipsa antiquissimi temporis vetustate venerabile monumentum. Quale enim quæso istud est, ut qui Antiochenos canones ab authoribus parum probatis Arianisimique merito suspectis conditos, Codici Ecclesiastico inseruerunt, iidem nullum in suo codice locum iis canonibus darent, quibus totius Ecclesiasticæ antiquitatis jam inde à viris Apostolicis ad Nicæna usque tempora ductæ breviarium ac epitomen contineri scirent ? Tum si quis extitisset hujusmodi codex, cur nunquam eum diserte ac nominatim memorant Ancyrani, Nicæni, Neocæsarienses, Antiocheni, alii Patres ? cur non interdum aliquem ex istius codicis canonibus indicato, ac nominato numero, sub quo in eo positus extat, citarunt, ac laudarunt ? verbi gratia hoc modo ; decernit canon Apostolorum primus, vel tricesimus, vel quinquagesimus, &c. Sicuti à Patribus Chalcedonensibus in Codice Ecclesiæ universalis usurpatum est; quoscilicet ejus codicis canonem quartum, octogesimum tertium, quartumque, & nonagesimum quintum, sextumque his diserte numeris expressis, laudasse ac descripsisse nuper demonstravimus ? Nimirum hi quem ita laudarent Ecclesiasticum canonum codicem in promptu habebant; Illi, quem ita citarent, Apostolicum nullum habebant. Denique hunc Apostolicum codicem (si is vere tum fuisset habitus pro breviario) quis Gelasium, sapientissimum, ut ferunt, antistitem; quis Episcopos Romani Concilii septuaginta, inter apocrypha procul ab Ecclesiasticis libris rejecturos fuisse crediderit? Hæc vero nescio quibus persuasurus sit Albaspineus: mihi quidem certe non persuadet. Eadem est cæterorum, quæ cum his connexa ponit, ratio. Statuit horum Canonum codicem jam inde à principio incœptum, inchoatumque, & ex Apostolicorum virorum paucis primo decretis collectum, adjectorum postea sequentibus subinde temporibus canonum accessione paulatim auctum in eam tandem, quam videmus, speciem ac formam ante Concilii Nicæni tempus coaluisse. At huic figmento repugnat ipsa totius operis ratio. Primo enim si verum esset, quod statuit Albaspineus, canones pro ipsorum temporum, quibus singuli conditi sunt, ordine, in hæc syllogæ dispositi occurrerent; sub primis numeris, qui primi ab Apostolicis viris conditi esse dicuntur; sub sequentibus sæculis facti sunt; sub novissimis denique, qui ultima memoria constituti fuerunt. At nihil tale in tota syllogæ cernitur; nullus temporum, nullus decurrentium sæculorum ordo observatus deprehenditur; omnia promiscue, prout in mentem scriptori veniebant, in medium conjecta, confusaque, non temporibus, non rebus ipsis sed solis numerorum notis cohaerentia reperiuntur. Ecce habemus veteris Ecclesiae illum, de quo paulo ante diximus, Graecum codicem, omnino ejus formae ac rationis, cujus Apostolicam farraginem esse vult Albaspineus. In eo nemo non videt, accuratissime habitam esse temporum rationem; praecedere Nicaenae Synodi Canones, utpote vetustissimae, a. D. 325. habitae; subsequi secutis temporibus habitarum Synodorum regulas, Gangrensis eodem anno, sed post Nicaenam; Antiochenae, a. D. 341. Laodicenae, a. D. 364. Constantinopolitanae, a. D. 381. Ephesinae, a. D. 431. Chalcedonenses, a. D. 451. Ac si cubi eum ordinem ob gravem aliquam rationem violari placuit, ut in Ancyranis, & Neocaesariensibus canonibus factum est, qui Nicaenis, licet tempore anteriores, postpositi sunt in codice, de eo diligenter admonitus est lector, expositaque ratio, cur in his neglectus fuerit qui in aliis sedulo observatus est ordo. Sic enim hoc loco habet codex; Concilii Ancyrani canones 25. qui quidem priores sunt Nicaenis, sed ideo postpositi sunt propter authoritatem Synodi Oecumenicae. Ita & in canone Neocaesariensium; Concilii Neocaesariensis cæsariensis canones 14. qui quidem sunt Ancyranis posteriores, Nicænis vero antiquiores. Ergo, si ad hanc formam, quod vult Albaspineus, factus quoque fuisset Apostolicorum (ut vocant) canonum codex, dubitandum non est, quin, quem ipsa recta ratio suadebat temporum ordinem in eo concinnando collectores perinde secuturi fuerint, ac ii secuti esse cernuntur, qui codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ universalis collegerunt. Imo necessario iste temporum ordo in hoc codice servatus inveniretur, quem statuit Albaspineus, non ab uno collectore simul ac semel concinnatum, sed a pluribus diversis, quorum suo quisque tempore, alii aliis succedentes, illis, quæ a majoribus jam perscripta & collecta inveniebant, ea, quæ sua memoria in Ecclesia constituta norant, adjecerint. Atqui nihil (ut diximus) hujusmodi in hac canonum Apostolicorum syllogé deprehenditur. Ergo eam necesse est aliter, quam statuit Albaspineus, factam esse. Præterea si vera esset ejus sententia, nulla ratio dici potest, cur non fuerit in hoc codice perscriptum, atque diserte annotatum, quorum sive Conciliorum, sive Episcoporum vere sint singuli canones, ex quibus totus codex conflatus est, qualiter in omnibus Græcorum collectionibus, quæ sunt hujus generis ex diversoz diversorum authorum canonibus coagmen-tatę, factum videmus. In iis enim diserte annotatur, quorum sint authorum singulæ totius sylloges partes : hos esse Nicænæ, illos Basilii, & sic de cæteris. Fateor, a quod hoc loco ait Albaspineus, Græcos so-litos fuisse uno eodemque quasi titulo & volumine complecti, cum antiquos canones, tum recentes. Quod vero ibidem subjicit, hoc eos fecisse, nulla concilii, temporis, authorumque mentione facta, quique praecedentibus addebantur canones eos, tacito ordine numeroque, quem in conciliis, unde decerpebantur, habebant, ab iis ordinem, numerumque accepisse, quibus in illa collectione adjiciebantur; ut si jam centum canones prapositi fuissent, qui de novo addebatur, centesimus primus censeretur; parque esset in cæteris ratio; id inquam Albaspinei dictum non possum totum planeque admittere. Cætera vera sunt; illud nunquam probabit Albaspineus in hujusmodi Græcorum collectionibus nul-lam factam fuisse mentionem conciliorum, nullam authorum, à quibus conditi essent canones, qui iis continebantur; nullum unquam afferet tam absurdi ineptique atque indigesti codicis è Græcis exemplum; in quo scilicet diversorum authorum canones confusi simul, permixtique ja-ceant, ceant, nulla authorum, quorum singuli sunt, nomenclatura adhibita, inter se distincti. Neque verum est, id à Baronio aut Antonio Augustino, quod ait Albaspineus, annotatum esse; Nihil aliud utrumque annotant, nisi hoc unum, jam ante Chalcedonensem Synodum extitisse quandam communem canonum collectionem communi majorum authoritate probatam; & in ea suum locum habuisse Antiocheni Concilii canones; quod sane verissimum est, & à nobis nuper ex iis ipsis Chalcedonensis Synodi locis, ex quibus id isti subodorati sunt, luculentissime demonstratum. Hinc vero non modo non firmatur, sed clarissime etiam refellitur, ac coarguitur, quod probare studet Albaspineus. Nam illa Chalcedonensi Synodo antiquior à Baronio, & Augustino memorata collectio; illa inquam, quod paulo ante ostendimus, nihil aliud erat, quam prima ejus codicis pars, qui Lutetiæ a. D. 1610. publicatus est, hoc titulo, Codex canonum Ecclesiæ universalis, quemque olim Dionysius Exiguus Latine de novo interpretatus est ob veteris translationis confusionem. Iam vero constat tum ex Græca, tum ex Latina Dionysiaca hujus codicis editione, diserte factam fuisse in eo mentionem Concilio-rum, atque authorum, à quibus conditi sunt ii canones, quos tota collectio continet. Numeri, fateor, sub quibus apud suos quique authores extabant, mutati sunt, proque iis, quod optime observavit Albaspineus, alii notati ex ordine, ac loco, quem in communi hoc codice habent; ut, verbi gratia, qui Ancyrani Concilii primus est canon, is in hoc communi codice, censetur & indigetatur vicesimus primus, quod primo post 20. Nicænæ Synodi canones loco occurrat; & sic deinceps de cæteris res habet. Cæterum in hujus numeri capite diserte monet codex, qui sequuntur canones, eos Ancyranos esse; & Ancyranis in 45. numero explicitis, itidem docet, qui post illum 45. numerum subjiciuntur canones, eos esse Neocæsarienses; atque ita deinceps canonum authores præfixi singulis partibus tituli edunt. Si ergo ad hoc exemplum, quod statuit Albaspineus, facta esset Apostolicorum canonum collectio, tametsi numeri canonum perpetua serie à capite ad calcem decurrant, tamen additum significatumque esset singulis locis (ut in codices universalis Ecclesiæ factum est) quos quique canones authores habuissent; nihil autem in ista Sylloge tale occurrit; nihil ex quo intelligi possit vel diversos fuisse canonum authores; nedum ut inde discere liceat, quinam revera singuli authores fuerint. Ergo falsum est, eam fuisse, quam vult Albaspineus, hujus collectionis rationem. Sed quid ego, quasi res obscura sit, argumentis utor? Ipse codex, Albaspineo ita clare valideque reclamat, ut mirum sit tali viro tam alienum à re ipsa figmentum in mentem venire potuisse. Non enim qui hoc codice continentur canones, authores suos, quod ille vult, tacent; sed eos edunt, profitentur, eloquuntur, identidemque inculcant; non diversorum, quod ille pertendit, saeculorum, sed unius ejusdemque temporis homines; non denique (quod ille somniat) Apostolicos viros, non Episcopos, sive seorsim singulos, sive una in Synodis congregatos jurà dictantes; sed ipsos Domini Christi Apostolos. Mitto, quae Apostoli his Canonibus in Constitutionum Turrianicarum calce praefantur: mitto, quae post 85. hoc est ultimum canonem perorant; horum sibi canonum opus vindicantes. Ipsos canones interrogemus. Nonne canon 28. (30) contra Simoniacos, Petrum ex authorum suorum numero unum fuisse diserte testatur, adeoque Petri collegas, unaque cum iis ipsum Petrum, hoc est omnes Apostolos authores se habere docet? Sic enim de Simoniaco praecipit; καθαιρείσθω αυτος αὐτὸς καὶ χειροτονήσας, καὶ ἐκκοπτέσθω ἀπὸ κοινωνίας, ὡς Σίμων ὁ Μάγος ὑπὸ ἐμοῦ Πέτρου. dejiciatur & ipse & ordinator ejus, & a communione modis omnibus exscindatur, ut Simon Magus a me Petro. Id ipsum profitetur canon 50. (49) qui haec apud Dionysium habet; Non enim dixit NOBIS Dominus, In morte mea baptizate, sed, Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Qui hos canones condunt, aperte affirmant, se eos ipsos esse, ad quos haec verba fecit Christus, hoc est (ut omnes intelligunt) Apostolos. Quo & illud pertinet, quod canone 81. ubi de servo sermo est ad ministerii Ecclesiastici gradum idoneo, οἵ (inquiunt) καὶ ὁ ἡμέτερος Ὀνήσιμος ἐφάνη, qualis noster quoque Onesimus visus est. Clare, ut quivis videt, Onesimum Philemonis fugitivum, Pauli discipulum, intelligunt; quem ideo suum vocant. Denique nequid dubii superfit, Apostolos se diserte vocant canone ultimo, dum Actus Apostolorum, quos in divinorum librorum canonem post Clementinas Diataxes referunt, sic describunt, καὶ αἱ πράξεις ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποστόλων, & actus nostri Apostolorum. Ergo quicunque sint, qui hos canones collegerunt, eorum certe mens ea non fuit, quam fingit AlbaspiAlbafpineus ; nempe ut hæc eorum Syllo- ge pro breviario Synodicorum , epifcopa- liumque decretorum haberetur, diversis ante Nicænum Concilium temporibus conditorum. Eos longe aliud voluisse clarum certumque ex his sermonibus est, nimirum, ut hi canones vere ab Apostolis omnes conditi, atque editi crederentur; & hic, qui eos continet codex, ab ipsis Apostolis factus, digestus, conscriptusque & promulgatus censeretur. Quod enim de Clemente scriptore vel Turrianus, & Latini, vel Græci fabulantur, id ipsorum commentum est, cujus neque vota, neque vestigium in ipsis canonibus ullum cernitur. Sed homines quidlibet ex usu ac commodo suo fingere prompti, à Clemente scriptum opus audacter affirmarunt, quod ita & minus invidiosum fore, & facilius defendi posse putaverunt, quam si ab ipsa Apostolorum manu profectum diceretur. Verum illi frustra sunt. Cum enim canones ipsi Apostolos authores, atque editores profiteantur, Clementis velut scriptoris sui nusquam meminerint; profecto necesse est vel (quod nos quidem certo credimus) canones ipsos mentiri, vel, si veraces censeas, ab Apostolis ipsis, non a Clemente post Apostolorum mortem (quod volunt Turrianus & adversarii) editos, ac conscriptos scriptos fuisse. Atque ex his illud etiam patet, quam vana fit Albaspinei de Apostolicorum nomine hariolatio in Apostolorum nomen ex quadam Latinorum nonnullorū ignorantia demutato. Binio enim hæc pro libidine dictavit Albaspineus. Nullum de veteribus suæ hujus conjecturæ authorem, vel testem edit, aut edere potest. Quotquot canonum istorum meminerunt (meminerunt autem post quintum expletum sæculum plurimi) ii omnes constanter Apostolorum canones vocant, nemo plane Apostolicorum, excepto uno Albaspineo, cui nostra demum memoria id somniare libuit. Tum manifesta est nominis ex iis, quæ nuperrime diximus, ratio. Cum enim ii, qui in hac Sylloge decernentes, ac præcipientes inducuntur, se non Apostolicos, sed Apostolos ipsos esse clare, liquidoque profiteantur, eorum decreta, non Apostolicorum, (quod præter omnium veterum consensum frustra fingit Albaspineus) sed Apostolorum canones dici, censeriqve decuit ab iis quidem, qui librum, quo continentur, velut sincerum, ac veracem admiserunt. His ergo explosis ac confutatis omnibus adversariorum de Apostolicorum canonum codice sententiis, diversis quidem, sed tamen juxta falsis, unum id verum esse relinquitur, quod nos defendi-
units.tr: Before we settle what this collection is, its form must be distinguished from its matter, as the schoolmen put it. By the matter of this collection I mean the things themselves that the canons either prescribe or forbid, and the individual decrees from which the collection was put together and joined. By its form I mean the order in which the canons run through their numbers, linked together like links of a chain, and the character of the whole composition: the words in which those decrees are expressed here, and the persons who are introduced as decreeing and speaking. No one is so dull as not to see that these differ greatly. In the body of canon law that is commonly called the Decretum, compiled by Gratian, the matter is one thing, namely the enactments of synods and popes and the opinions of the Fathers, from which it is made up. The form is another, the arrangement the author gave it, putting so many things gathered from so many places and times into a fixed order and linking them together. That is why the whole work is called Gratian's, although almost everything it contains belongs not to Gratian but to many other authors. So, to come to our subject: if we look at the matter of the Canons of the Apostles simply and by itself, apart from the form they have in this collection, I admit that what Albaspineus says fits it nearly everywhere, and his opinion comes close to the truth, if it is understood of this matter alone, as I have said. For it appears that most, indeed nearly all, of the decrees from which this collection is made, if each is considered on its own, were issued at various times and places, in different centuries, over the whole course of the first four centuries in the Eastern Church. The arguments Albaspineus brings forward demonstrate this very well: that many things are expressly enacted and decreed in this collection which relate to controversies that arose after the apostolic age; and also that in the same collection some canons are found, which it is clear from the reading itself were taken from the Council of Gangra. To Albaspineus's observation I would add that not a few canons of this apostolic hodgepodge seem to have been taken from the Council of Antioch, as anyone who compares them one with another will see. Yet even in this respect I cannot wholly and entirely agree with Albaspineus, nor admit with him that everything in these canons was taken from the private acts and decrees of the Greeks, whether of councils or of bishops. For we read in them some things so completely at odds with the whole doctrine of the Greek Church, especially before the Nicene Synod, that it is not likely they were ever handed down by any Greek catholic, whether council or bishop. Such is, for example, what is decreed about the divine books in canons 84 and 85. For who, I ask, of the older writers, I do not say Latin but even Greek Fathers, ever counted the third book of the Maccabees among the sacred books of the Old Testament, or the eight volumes of the Clementine Constitutions in the canon of the New, before the time of the father of this collection? This error is so gross that it seems no Catholic writer of antiquity ever held it. It is certain that in the monuments of the first three centuries there is no trace of it anywhere, however slight; to say nothing of the fact that no one could have placed the books of the Clementine Constitutions in the sacred canon before the time of the Nicene Synod, since, as I think I have sufficiently demonstrated in the earlier discussion, those books did not yet exist, but were made and patched together in the times following that Synod. However, apart from these and perhaps a few other canons, I freely confess that what is decreed in most of the others appears to be taken from the synodal enactments of the Greek Church, or from episcopal rescripts, and also from customs, rites and observances introduced and confirmed by use and practice. This is what I have to say about the matter of the canons when considered by itself. But if we consider the work as it is circulated as a whole, taking account not only of the matter from which it is composed and put together, but also of the form to which it is seen to have been shaped and fitted, then we are indeed compelled to depart from the opinion of Albaspineus and go in quite another direction. For if the matter is weighed more carefully, none of the things he lays down can stand, and it is easily seen that this collection was made in a very different way from what he describes, and that it differs greatly from the form he assigns to it. To begin here, what he says of this codex seems far from the truth above all: that it is an abridgment and epitome of the decrees of the Church made among the Greeks before the Nicene Synod. For if that were so, the authors of the collection of canons of the universal Church would certainly have inserted this collection into their codex; indeed they would have put it first, as a monument going back to the apostolic men and venerable for the great antiquity of its time. For what sort of thing is this, I ask? Those who inserted the Antiochene canons, composed by authors of little repute and rightly suspected of Arianism, into their ecclesiastical codex, would have given no place in their codex to those canons which they knew to contain an abridgment and epitome of the whole ecclesiastical antiquity, drawn from the apostolic men down to the Nicene times! Then, if such a codex had existed, why do the Ancyrans, the Nicenes, the Neocaesareans, the Antiochenes and other Fathers never mention it expressly and by name? Why did they never cite or quote from its canons by stating the number under which each stands in it, as in this form: "The first canon of the Apostles decrees" or "the thirtieth" or "the fiftieth," and so on? This is what the Chalcedonian Fathers did with the codex of the universal Church, whose fourth, eighty-third, eighty-fourth and ninety-fifth and sixth canons, quoted and transcribed with their numbers expressly given, we have recently shown. Surely those who quoted the ecclesiastical codex of canons in this way had it at hand, while those who cited the other had no apostolic codex at all. Finally, who would believe that this apostolic codex (if it had really been regarded as an abridgment at that time) would have been rejected by Gelasius, that most wise bishop, as they say, and by the bishops of the Roman council of seventy, as apocryphal, far from the ecclesiastical books? Albaspineus may have some means of persuading us of these things, I do not know; but he certainly does not persuade me. The same reasoning applies to the other points he connects with these. He holds that the codex of these canons was begun and started from the beginning, collected at first from the few decrees of the apostolic men, and afterwards gradually increased by the addition of canons at successive times, until it took the shape and form we see before the time of the Nicene Council. But the very plan of the whole work contradicts this fiction. For first, if what Albaspineus lays down were true, the canons would appear in this collection arranged in the order of the times in which each was made: under the first numbers those said to have been first made by the apostolic men; under the following, those made in later centuries; and finally, under the last, those established in the most recent memory. But nothing like this is seen in the whole collection. No order of times, no order of successive centuries is found to have been observed. Everything is thrown together indiscriminately, as it came into the writer's mind, confused and jumbled, held together not by times nor by the subjects themselves, but only by the marks of the numbers. Here we have the Greek codex of the old Church that I spoke of a little while ago, of exactly the form and plan that Albaspineus wants his apostolic hodgepodge to be. In that codex, no one fails to see, the order of times has been most carefully kept: the Canons of the Nicene Synod come first, as the oldest, held in the year 325; the canons of later synods follow in their times: the Gangra council in the same year, but after Nicaea; Antioch in 341; Laodicea in 364; Constantinople in 381; Ephesus in 431; Chalcedon in 451. And if at any point it was thought fit to break this order for some weighty reason, as was done with the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons, which were placed after the Nicene canons though earlier in time, the reader is carefully warned, and the reason is explained why the order that was diligently observed elsewhere was neglected here. For the codex says at this point: "The twenty-five canons of the Council of Ancyra, which indeed are earlier than the Nicene, but were placed after them on account of the authority of the Ecumenical Synod." Likewise at the canons of the Neocaesareans: "The fourteen canons of the Council of Neocaesarea, which indeed are later than the Ancyran, but earlier than the Nicene." So if the apostolic (as they call them) codex of canons had been made in the form Albaspineus wants, there is no doubt that the collectors would have followed the order of times, which right reason itself suggests, just as those who gathered the codex of canons of the universal Church are seen to have followed it. Indeed, the order of times that Albaspineus supposes would necessarily be found in this codex, if it had been put together not by one compiler at one time, but by several different men, each in his own time, one succeeding another, adding to what their elders had already written down and collected the canons which they knew had been established in the Church during their own memory. But, as we have said, nothing of this kind is found in this collection of apostolic canons. Therefore it must have been made in some other way than Albaspineus supposes. Moreover, if his opinion were true, no reason could be given why this codex did not record, and expressly note, which councils or bishops really issued the individual canons from which the whole codex was assembled, as we see is done in all the Greek collections of this kind, which are put together from the canons of various authors. For in these it is expressly noted whose authorship each part of the whole collection has: these are the Nicene, those are of Basil, and so on with the rest. I grant what Albaspineus says here, that the Greeks were accustomed to embrace under one and the same title and volume both the ancient canons and the recent ones. But what he adds immediately after, that they did this without any mention of council, time or authors, and that the canons added to the preceding ones took the order and number, tacit and unstated, that they had in the councils from which they were picked, so that the order and number were received by them from the places in which they were added to that collection; for example, if a hundred canons had already been set down, the canon added next would be counted as the hundred and first, and so with the rest, this statement of Albaspineus I cannot admit as a whole and altogether. The rest is true; but Albaspineus will never prove that in such Greek collections there was no mention of councils or authors by whom the canons they contained were made; nor will he produce any example from the Greeks of so absurd, inept and disordered a codex, in which the canons of different authors lie confused and mixed together, with no naming of the authors of each to distinguish them. Nor is it true, as Albaspineus says, that Baronius or Antonius Augustinus noted this. Both of them note nothing more than this one thing: that before the Council of Chalcedon there already existed a certain common collection of canons approved by the common authority of the elders, and that the canons of the Council of Antioch had their place in it. That is certainly most true, and it has been shown very clearly by us lately from those very passages of the Chalcedonian Synod from which they had guessed it. But this does not merely fail to confirm what Albaspineus is striving to prove; it clearly refutes and convicts it. For that collection, earlier than the Chalcedonian Synod, which Baronius and Augustinus mention, was, as we have shown a little before, nothing other than the first part of that codex published at Paris in 1610 under the title Codex of the canons of the universal Church, which Dionysius Exiguus once translated anew into Latin because of the confusion in the old translation. Now it is clear from both the Greek and the Latin Dionysian edition of this codex that mention was expressly made in it of the councils and authors by whom the canons contained in the whole collection were made. The numbers under which each canon stood among its own authors have indeed been changed, and in their place, as Albaspineus rightly observed, other numbers have been given according to the order and place each has in this common codex: for example, the first canon of the Ancyran Council is in this common codex counted and marked as the twenty-first, because it occurs first after the twenty Canons of the Nicene Synod; and so on with the rest. Moreover, at the head of this number the codex expressly notes that the canons which follow are Ancyran; and after the forty-fifth number, where the Ancyran canons end, it likewise shows that the canons placed after that forty-fifth number are Neocaesarean; and so the names of the authors prefixed to the individual parts of the title announce the same thing. So if the collection of apostolic canons had been made on the model Albaspineus proposes, then, even though the numbers of the canons ran in one unbroken series from beginning to end, still it would have been added and indicated at each place (as was done in the codex of the universal Church) which authors each canon had. But nothing of this kind appears in that collection; nothing from which one could understand that the canons had different authors, much less learn who the individual authors really were. Therefore it is false that this collection was made on the plan Albaspineus proposes. But why do I argue as if the matter were obscure? The codex itself so clearly and strongly contradicts Albaspineus that it is astonishing that a man of such learning could have hit on a fiction so alien to the facts. The canons contained in this codex do not keep silent about their authors, as he claims; they state them, profess them, declare them, and again and again insist on them.
