They are not men of different centuries, as he contends, but men of one and the same time; and finally they are not (as he dreams) apostolic men, not bishops, either each singly or gathered together in synods, dictating laws, but the Apostles of the Lord Christ himself. I pass over what the Apostles say before these canons, at the end of the Turrianus constitutions, and what they add after the 85th, that is the last canon, claiming this work of canons for themselves. Let us question the canons themselves. Does not canon 28 (30), against the Simonians, expressly testify that Peter was one of their number of authors, and so teach that Peter's colleagues, and together with them Peter himself, that is all the Apostles, are their authors? For it thus prescribes concerning the Simonian: "Let him be deposed, both he himself and the one who ordained him, and let him be cut off from communion altogether, as Simon the Magician was by me, Peter" [kathairesthō... hōs Simōn ho Magos hypo emou Petrou]. Canon 50 (49) professes the same thing, which in Dionysius reads: "For the Lord did not say to US, 'Baptize in my death,' but 'Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.'" Those who compose these canons openly affirm that they themselves are the very ones to whom Christ spoke these words, that is (as everyone understands) the Apostles. To this also belongs what is said in canon 81, where the discussion is about a servant fit for the grade of ecclesiastical ministry: "Such, they say, was also OUR Onesimus" [hoi (inquiunt) kai ho hēmeteros Onēsimos ephanē]. Clearly, as anyone can see, they mean Onesimus, the runaway slave of Philemon, the disciple of Paul; and they call him theirs for that reason. Finally, lest any doubt remain, they call themselves Apostles expressly in the last canon, when they describe the Acts of the Apostles, which they place in the canon of the divine books after the Clementine Diataxeis, in this way: "and OUR acts of the Apostles" [kai hai praxeis hēmōn tōn Apostolōn], and our Apostles' acts. Therefore, whoever they were who gathered these canons, their intention certainly was not the one that Albaspineus invents, namely that this collection of theirs should be regarded as an abridgment of synodal and episcopal decrees made at various times before the Nicene Council. It is clear and certain from these words that they wanted these canons to be believed as truly made and published by the Apostles, and that this codex containing them should be considered as made, arranged, written out and promulgated by the Apostles themselves. For what the Turrianus and the Latins, or the Greeks, invent about Clement as the writer is their own fabrication, for which there is neither will nor trace in the canons themselves. But men ready to make up anything to suit their own use and advantage boldly affirmed that the work was written by Clement, believing that this would be less invidious and easier to defend than if it were said to come from the very hand of the Apostles. But they are wrong. For since the canons themselves profess the Apostles as their authors and editors, and never mention Clement as their writer, it is necessary either that the canons themselves are lying (which we most certainly believe), or, if you judge them truthful, that they were issued and written by the Apostles themselves, not by Clement after the death of the Apostles, as Turrianus and his opponents maintain. And from this it is also clear how vain is Albaspineus's guesswork that the name Apostolic was changed into the name of the Apostles through some ignorance of certain Latins. For he dictated these things at his own pleasure. He produces, and can produce, no ancient author or witness for his conjecture. Whoever has mentioned these canons (and many have mentioned them after the close of the fifth century) all consistently call them the Canons of the Apostles; no one at all calls them the Apostolic canons, except Albaspineus alone, who in our own day chose to dream it up. Then the reason for the name is clear from what we have just said. Since those who are introduced as decreeing and commanding in this collection clearly and openly profess that they are not Apostolic men but the Apostles themselves, their decrees ought to be called, and considered to be, the canons of the Apostles, not (as Albaspineus vainly invents, against the consent of all the ancients) of the Apostolic men; and this would be so for those who admit the book containing them as sincere and truthful. Therefore, with all the opinions of the opponents about the codex of the Apostolic canons now set aside and refuted, diverse indeed but all equally false, there remains one thing which is true, and which we undertake to defend.

units.la: defendimus; nimirum, librum illum, non ab Apostolis, vel à Clemente scriptum, aut editum, (quod somniat Turrianus) non ab Apostolicis viris cœptum & inchoatum, ab aliis ante Synodum Nicænam perfectum, atque adeo à pluribus authoribus consarcinatum (quod fingit Albaspineus) sed ab uno eodemque impostore, vel certe à duobus in hanc quam videmus speciem compositum, Apostolorum nomen impudentissime mentitis, ut suis decretis pondus darent. Authorem operis materiam ex iis, quæ in Ecclesia sui ævi Græca, vel omni, vel aliqua, usitata erant, furatum confitemur: eo factum esse, ut plurima in toto opere reperiantur, quæ vel Synodorum decretis, vel episcoporum authoritate, vel ipso denique hominum usu in Ecclesiam invecta, apud Christianos, vel omnes, vel quosdam quarto, quintoque sæculis obtinebant; quorum nomine temere atque inscite abusus est Turrianus, ut codicem hunc antiquissimum, imo & Apostolicum esse vinceret. Cæterum non ita vel prudentem, vel sobrium callumque fuisse impostorem, ut nulla his Ecclesiasticis peregrina, vel nova, & inusitata miscerēt; ut ex iis apparet, quæ de Maccabaicorum tertio, Clementinarumque Constitutionum octo libris in divinum canonem præter omnis Ecclesiæ sententiam relatis diximus ; item de repudiando hæreticorum quorumvis baptismo, ac de sabbati à jejunio immunitate. Unde clareconstat, Gelasium, Synodumque Romanam nequissimi impostoris fœtum merito damnasse, & erepto Apostolorum titulo, quo falso ac impudenter ornatus incedebat, in apocryphorum tenebras abjecisse; merito Isidorum eadem secutum esse, verissimeque scripsisse, quamvis in his canonibus utilia inveniantur (quæ scilicet planus ex Ecclesiæ suæ ævo vigentis usu mutuatus est) eos tamen ab hæreticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositos dignosci; quod nimirum non facile credendum sit, hominem eum Catholicum fuisse, qui vel illa falsa & ab Ecclesiæ sententia abhorrentia decernere non dubitaverit; vel etiam suo operi sanctissimum Apostolorum nomen imponere ausus sit.
units.tr: We maintain this: that the book was written and published neither by the Apostles nor by Clement (as Turrianus dreams); that it was not begun and started by apostolic men and finished by others before the Synod of Nicaea; and that it was not patched together from many authors (as Albaspinaeus imagines). Rather, it was composed in this form that we see by one and the same impostor, or certainly by two, who most shamelessly borrowed the name of the Apostles so that their decrees would carry weight. We admit that the author stole his material from what was in use in the Greek Church of his own age, either wholly or in part. The result is that many things in the whole work can be found which had been brought into the Church by synodal decrees, by the authority of bishops, or by the custom of men, and which were held by all Christians, or by some, in the fourth and fifth centuries. Turrianus has rashly and foolishly abused these things to prove that this most ancient codex is even apostolic. But the impostor was not so wise, sober, and skilful that he mixed nothing foreign, new, or unusual with these ecclesiastical matters. This appears from what we have said about the third book of the Maccabees and the eight books of the Clementine Constitutions, which were received into the divine canon against the judgment of the whole Church; likewise about rejecting the baptism of any heretics, and about the exemption of the Sabbath from fasting. From this it is clear that Gelasius and the Roman Synod rightly condemned the offspring of a most wicked impostor, stripped it of the title of the Apostles with which it falsely and impudently walked adorned, and cast it into the darkness of the apocrypha. Isidore rightly followed them and wrote most truly that although useful things are found in these canons (which he plainly borrowed from the usage of his own Church's age), yet they are recognised as composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles. Indeed, it is not easy to believe that a man was Catholic who did not hesitate to decree those false things which are repugnant to the judgment of the Church, or who dared to put the most holy name of the Apostles on his own work.

units.la: Denique si de tempore quæratur, quo pseud-apostolica illa, & apocrypha Canonum collectio facta & edita primum fuerit, apparet ex iis, quæ hactenus disputata sunt, eam neque ante quintum sæculum adultum innotuisse, & quinto exeunte jam extitisse, publicarique coeptam esse. Prius demonstrat universale omnium, qui ante a. D. 451. vixerunt, de ea silentium; quod abunde supra demonstratum est. Neque enim credibile est, nullam ejus mentionem, si extitisset, facturos fuisse Eusebium, Hieronymum, & alios illorum temporum eruditissimos scriptores, qui etiam ea, quę apocrypha judicabant, præcipue quæ Apostolis afficta erant, diligenter persequi, & refellere solent. Posterius vero ex Gelasii decreto a. D. 494. facto patet; in quo scilicet ea collectio damnata est. Ergo paucis ante illud tempus annis ab homine hæretico, Græci generis, consarcinatam fuisse probabile est, & in 50. tantum canones digestam; (neque enim plures exhibuit Dionysius, qui codicem suum annis post factum Gelasianum decretum 28. aut triginta Latine edidit) mox paucis post editum Dionysii codicem annis apud Græcos, quos benevolentiores ac clementiores experta est, quam Latinos, triginta quinque canonibus, vel ab eodem vel ab ejusdem certe spiritus impostore auctam esse; ut inde perspicitur, quod quem Iustinianus commendavit, & Ioannes Epiphaniensis in nomocanonem retulit, Apostolicum codicem, is 85. canonibus constaret, ut supra diximus. Iustinianum autem & Ioannem illum certum est paulo post a. D. 560. floruisse. Quæ vero à Iustiniani temporibus ad nostram memoriam fuerint de illa sylloge tum Græcorum, tum Latinorum judicia, supra fuse ostendimus. Sed qui, Gelasii sententiam secuti, falsum & adulterinum librum inter apocry-pha censuerunt, eos verius, quam cæteros sensisse, evidentibus invictisque, ni fallor, argumentis, satis probavimus. Atque hæc de Canonibus Apostolorum 85. dicta sunto.
units.tr: Finally, if one asks at what time this pseudo-apostolic and apocryphal collection of canons was first made and published, it appears from what has been argued so far that it was not known in its mature form before the fifth century, and that it began to be published only at the close of the fifth century. The first point is shown by the universal silence about it of all who lived before the year 451 of our Lord; this has been amply demonstrated above. For it is not credible that Eusebius, Jerome, and the other most learned writers of those times would have made no mention of it, if it had existed. They were accustomed to examine carefully, and refute, the things they judged apocryphal, especially those falsely attributed to the Apostles. The second point is clear from the decree of Gelasius made in the year 494, in which this collection was condemned. Therefore it is probable that it was put together by a heretic of Greek origin a few years before that time, and arranged in only fifty canons (for Dionysius did not present more, and he published his codex in Latin some twenty-eight or thirty years after the Gelasian decree). Soon after the publication of Dionysius's codex, within a few years, among the Greeks, who proved kinder and more lenient to it than the Latins, it was increased to thirty-five canons, either by the same man or certainly by an impostor of the same spirit. This is seen from the fact that the Apostolic codex which Justinian commended, and which John of Epiphania included in the Nomocanon, consisted of eighty-five canons, as we said above. It is certain that Justinian and that John flourished shortly after the year 560. What judgments, both of Greeks and of Latins, were passed on that collection from the times of Justinian down to our own memory, we have set out at length above. But that those who followed the opinion of Gelasius and judged this false and spurious book to be among the apocrypha thought more truly than the others, we have, unless I am mistaken, sufficiently proved by evident and unanswerable arguments. And so let these things be said about the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXII.

units.la: Altera quæstio de 9. canonibus, quos velut in Concilio Antiocheno ab Apostolis conditos obtrudit Turrianus, & ex eo Binius, ac Baronius. Totam hujus sylloges canonum Antiochenorum molem una Turriani fide niti; quæ quam sublesta sit, exemplis comprobatur.
units.tr: The second question concerns the nine canons which Turrianus foists on the Council of Antioch as if they had been enacted by the Apostles, and which Binius and Baronius follow him in. The whole mass of these Antiochene canons rests on Turrianus's word alone. How unsound that is, examples will show.

units.la: ED ecce novam nobis Apostolorum fœturam obtrudunt Baronius a, & Binius b, novos canones in Antiocheno quodam concilio editos scilicet, numero novem; de quibus quoque paucis, antequam opus concludam, disputandum est. Principio ab istis quæro, unde hos canones habeant? Baronius quidem fabulam sic orditur; Tradunt alii (inquit) Antiochiæ ab Apostolis ad sedandas controversias illic exortas, habitam esse Synodum, idque authoritate Pamphili Martyris, cujus fragmenta recitat Turrianus, sibi vendicant, qui & canones illos in compendium redactos recenset. Haec ille. Quinam illi alii sunt, quos haec tradere ait? An Lucas, an Eusebius vel Socrates, aut Theodoretus? an Sozomenus, & Euagrius, aut Ruffinus, vel historiae tripartitae author Senator Cassiodorus? a quibus & Apostolorum, & Ecclesiae deinceps Christianae historiam descriptam habemus? Atqui certissimum est, omnes istos neque de Antiochena ulla Apostolorum Synodo, neque de novem istis canonibus vel unum verbum uspiam fecisse-Quinam ergo illi alii sunt, qui hanc hi, storiam tradunt? An Iustinus vel Irenaeus vel Clemens Alexandrinus? An Tertullianus, aut Cyprianus, vel eorum Patrum quisquam, quorum opera habemus? An Latinorum aliquis, qui totis quindecim superioribus saeculis vixerunt? Atqui ne unum quidem fabulae istius authorem, vel testem edere possunt. Iam veteres Canonum Ecclesiasticorum tabulas adeamus: Codicem antiquissimum universalis Ecclesiae in Chalcedonensi Synodo laudatum, Dionysiacum circa a. D. 524. editum, Ferrandi eodem propemodum tempore factum breviarium, Cresconii Afri, Martini Bracarensis, Isidori Mercatoris, Burchardi Moguntini, Ivonis Carnotensis, Gratiani ipsius collectiones, Ioannis Epiphanienfis, Photiique Nomocanones; Zonarae, Balsamonis, aliorum Græcorum de canonico jure commentarios, omnes Synodorum Græcas, Latinasque, veteres, ac recentiores ad Binianam usq; editiones. Nusquam in his omnibus apparent novem isti Antiocheni Apostolorum à Baronio commemorati canones. Quinam ergo tandem illi alii sunt, à quibus hæc tradi ait magnus Annalium parens? Illi vero alii nulli sunt; neque ipse ullos edit, vel citat; quos non erat prætermissurus vir, etiam in nugis diligens, si quos habuisset. Nam Binium quidem non intelligit, qui, cum scriberet Baronius, nondum suam Conciliorum farraginem ediderat; quique sua hac in parte omnia, ut fere solet, à Baronio habet, eumque authorem diserte laudat. Unus supererat Turrianus, qui totius fabulæ verus, ac unicus parens. Sed illum Baronius nominat, & præter istos alios, à quibus hæc tradi dicit, seorsim censet. Nimirum Baronium pudebat confiteri nullo alio teste atque authore niti rem tantam, nisi uno Turriano, homine recentissimo, adhæc Jesuita, & inter omnes illius nominis sodales fabularum amantissimo, audacissimo, & procacissimo. Itaque ut caussæ hujus suæ inopiam obumbraret, alios eadem tradere dere finxit; sperans bonum lectorem, ta-metsi istos alios nullos videat, multos tamen, saltem aliquos esse, sibi creditururn. Ergo, ut detractis verborum inanibus fucis, id quod res est, simpliciter dicamus, nullum hujus suae temeritatis alium authorem habent Baronius, & Binius, praeter unum Turrianum; qui primus omnium totam hanc fabulam domi apud se vel natam, vel repertam, ut erat ingenio quisquiliarum & feracissimo & cupidissimo, anno demum Christianismi 1573. edidit. Sed ne putes istum haec gratis (quod non solet illa natio) mentitum, aut fabulatum; tota fabula inventa, instructa, ornata, facta, editaque est ad imaginum, quas Romanum genus impense diligit, venerationem Apostolica authoritate constituendam. Fertur enim quoddam Apostolis a Gregorio Pessinuntis Episcopo jam olim in Synodo 7. impudenter affictum de Icone Christi verbum, quod vel Turrianus, vel alius aliquis firmare, & authoritate aliqua donare operae pretium putavit. Id ut consequeretur, canones alios excitavit hujus veluti comites, pedisequos, vel anteambulones futuros; Antiochiae scenam adornavit, in qua eos conderent Apostoli; denique Turrianus tanti esse censuit illud pro suis imaginibus testimonium, ut ejus firmandi gratia fabulam ipsum facere, vel certe ab alio factam edere non piguerit. Nunc ego ab isto, ut nuper à Baronio, quæro, unde homo novus habeat, Apostolos Antiochię canones istos olim annis, ante quam ipse animum ad scribendum appelleret, mille fere & quinquentis condidisse? Respondet homo verecundissimus, se à Pamphilo martyre habere. Quæro ubi, & quando id testatus sit Pamphilus ? quibus dixerit ? in quo opere id scriptum reliquerit ? Ego (inquit) sic reperi in antiquissimo codice Græco scriptum, τὰ ἁγία ἱερομάρτυρος Παμφίλε ἐκ τῆς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων συνόδου, τυτέςιν ἐκ τῶν συνοδικῶν αὐτῶν κανόνων μέςῳ τῆς ἐυρισκέντων εἰς τὸ Ὠριγένες βιβλιοθήκῃ. Sancti hieromartyris Pamphili ex Antiochena Apostolorum Synodo, id est pars ex Synodicis ipsis canonibus inventis in Origenis Bibliotheca. Hoc unum ponit Turrianus hujus causæ fundamentum; plane, ut omnes vident, futile ac ficulneum. Principio illum ipsum codicem antiquissimum, in quo se hæc scripta reperisse dicit, nemo mortalium unquam, præter ipsum, vidit; nemo se vidisse, quantumvis magna sit passim fingendi mentiendique audacia, hactenus professus est. Neque ipse dicit, quis qualisque sit ille codex; ubi sit, & in quibus sive cryptis, sive bibliothecis tot jam saecula abditus & omnibus ignotus delitescat. Nimirum homo astutus merito veritus est, ne ex indicio, si quod ederet, mendacium proderetur, atque deprehenderetur. Nunc ei facile est tuto ac impune mentiri, visum a se librum, quem nemo coarguere poterit, quod omnes libri investigandi vias obsepserit, neque ubi sit, neque apud quos reperiri possit, docens. Ego vero, si nescirem, quae sit hominis frons, etiam simplici ejus asseveratione nonnihil commoverer. Sed aliunde didici, qua ille protervia, quaque inverecundia in fingendis, comminiscendis, ac pro libidine adulterandis veterum & scriptis, & rebus, grassari soleat. Hic enim ipse ille est Turrianus, qui vetustissimis Romae Episcopis impudentissime affictas stramineas nescio quas epistolas, ab omnibus cordatis, & eruditis, etiam Romanarum partium, scriptoribus vel plane explosas, vel certe in dubium vocatas, sollicitatasque, ipse immani, ac giganteo ausu, veras germanasque, ac geminas asserere non dubitavit. Hic est, qui Eusebium Alexandrinum in sermonibus a, Magnetem adversus Thesthenem b, Theophanem c in Symphonia veteris & novi Testamenti, & alias hujusmodi scriptorum in Ecclesiae hactenus
units.tr: And behold, they thrust upon us a new brood of Apostles: Baronius a and Binius b, who tell of nine new canons issued at a certain Council of Antioch. Before I finish this work, these too must be discussed briefly. First I ask them where they get these canons. Baronius begins his fable thus: Others relate (he says) that a Synod was held at Antioch by the Apostles to settle controversies that had arisen there, and that they claim this on the authority of the martyr Pamphilus, whose fragments Turrianus cites, and who also sets out those canons in summary form. So he says. Who are those others whom he says hand these things down? Luke? Eusebius, Socrates or Theodoret? Sozomen, Evagrius, Rufinus, or the senator Cassiodorus, author of the Tripartite History? From these writers we have the history of the Apostles and of the Christian Church after them. Yet it is quite certain that none of them has said a single word about any Apostolic Synod at Antioch, or about these nine canons. Who, then, are those others who hand down this story? Justin, Irenaeus or Clement of Alexandria? Tertullian or Cyprian, or any of the Fathers whose works we have? Any of the Latins who lived in the fifteen centuries before? Yet they cannot produce even one author or witness of that fable. Let us now turn to the old tables of ecclesiastical canons: the most ancient code of the universal Church, cited at the Council of Chalcedon; the Dionysian collection published about 524; the breviary of Ferrandus, made at about the same time; the collections of Cresconius the African, Martin of Braga, Isidore Mercator, Burchard of Mainz, Ivo of Chartres, and Gratian himself; the Nomocanons of John of Epiphania and of Photius; the commentaries on canon law of Zonaras, Balsamon and other Greeks; all the Greek and Latin Synods, old and recent, down to the edition of Binius. Nowhere in all of these do those nine Antiochene canons of the Apostles that Baronius mentions appear. Who, then, are those others from whom this great parent of the Annals says these things are handed down? In truth there are no such others. Nor does he himself produce or cite any; a man so careful even in trifles would not have passed them over had he had any. He does not understand Binius, who had not yet published his own collection of Councils when Baronius wrote, and who in this part, as usual, has everything from Baronius and expressly names him as author. Only Turrianus is left, the true and sole parent of the whole fable. But Baronius names Turrianus and counts him separately from those others from whom he says these things are handed down. Clearly Baronius was ashamed to confess that so great a matter rests on no witness or author except Turrianus alone, a very recent man, moreover a Jesuit, and among all men of that name the greatest lover of fables, the most bold and the most shameless. So, to cover the poverty of his case, he pretended that others hand down the same thing, hoping that the good reader, though he sees no such others, will still believe that there are many, or at least some. To put it simply, stripping away the empty colouring of words, Baronius and Binius have no author for their rashness other than Turrianus alone. He was the first of all to publish this whole fable, devised or found at home, a man of a mind as fertile as it was eager for trifles, in the year of Christianity 1573. But lest you think he invented this for nothing (which that nation is not wont to do), the whole fable was contrived, built up, adorned, made and published to establish, on Apostolic authority, the veneration of images, which the Roman people cherish with great zeal. For it is reported that a word about the Icon of Christ was shamelessly fabricated in the name of the Apostles long ago by Gregory, bishop of Pessinus, at the Seventh Synod; and Turrianus, or someone else, thought it worth confirming and endowing with some authority. To achieve this he brought forth other canons as its companions, attendants and forerunners; he set the scene at Antioch in which the Apostles were to issue them; and finally Turrianus judged that testimony so valuable for his images that he did not hesitate to make the story himself, or at least to publish one made by another, in order to confirm it. Now I ask this man, as I asked Baronius just now, where this newcomer gets the knowledge that the Apostles at Antioch issued those canons some fifteen hundred years ago, long before he himself turned his mind to writing? This most modest man replies that he has it from the martyr Pamphilus. I ask where and when Pamphilus attested this, to whom he said it, and in what work he left it written. "I," says Turrianus, "found it written thus in a very ancient Greek codex" [τὰ ἁγία ἱερομάρτυρος Παμφίλε ἐκ τῆς ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων συνόδου, τυτέςιν ἐκ τῶν συνοδικῶν αὐτῶν κανόνων μέςῳ τῆς ἐυρισκέντων εἰς τὸ Ὠριγένες βιβλιοθήκῃ]. The holy hieromartyr Pamphilus, from the Synod of the Apostles at Antioch, that is, part of the synodical canons themselves, found in the library of Origen. This single thing Turrianus lays down as the foundation of his case; plainly, as everyone can see, it is flimsy and worthless. In the first place, no mortal ever saw that very ancient codex, in which he says he found these things written, except himself; no one has professed to have seen it, however great the boldness of pretending and lying that prevails everywhere. Nor does he say what sort of codex it is, or where, or in which vaults or libraries it lies hidden, known to none, for so many ages. Clearly the crafty man rightly feared that, if he gave any indication, the lie would be exposed and caught. Now it is easy for him to lie safely and with impunity, saying he has seen a book that no one can refute, since he has blocked every way of searching for books and does not say where it is or among whom it can be found. For my part, if I did not know what sort of man he is, I would be somewhat moved even by his simple assertion. But I have learned elsewhere with what effrontery and what shamelessness he is wont to run riot in inventing, fabricating and at will corrupting both the writings and the affairs of the ancients. This is the very same Turrianus who, with a monstrous and gigantic audacity, did not hesitate to assert as genuine and authentic certain straw-stuffed letters, I know not what, shamelessly attributed to the most ancient bishops of Rome, which all judicious and learned writers, even those on the Roman side, have either entirely rejected or at least called into doubt and disputed. This is the man who throws at his adversaries, as so many bugbears, the spurious works of Eusebius of Alexandria a in his sermons, Magnes against Thestheus b, Theophanes c in the Symphony of the Old and New Testaments, and other such writings of unheard-of authors, to frighten the Church until now

units.la: a l. 1. pro epist. c. 21. l. 2. c. 6. & 12. 20. b Ibid. l. 1. c. 5. l. 2. c. 3. 13. l. 4. c. 7. c Ibid. l. 2. c. 18. l. 4. c. 13. nus inauditorum larvas, pro libidine effi-ctas adversariis suis, veluti totidem μορμολυκεία objicit. Ac ut cætera vel impudenter, vel inscite & imperite ab eo in his disputationibus gesta prætermittam, quorum luculentum noster Blondellus catalogum contexuit, hic inquam, illeipse Turrianus est, quem & Constitutiones, & 85. Canones Apostolis non minus inverecunde quem indocte affinxisse, nuper probavimus. Tali viro, cui vel jurato nemo sapiens crediderit, quis injurato crediderit, aliquem revera manuscriptum antiquum codicem extare, in quo ipsa illa, quæ describit, legerit? quem nemo præter ipsum legit, vidit, commemoravit? Sed etiamsi tale aliquid veteres libri continerent, non ideo tamen fieret, ut id statim pro vero habendum esset.
units.tr: a l. 1. pro epist. c. 21. l. 2. c. 6. & 12. 20. b Ibid. l. 1. c. 5. l. 2. c. 3. 13. l. 4. c. 7. c Ibid. l. 2. c. 18. l. 4. c. 13. ...unheard-of bugbears [μορμολυκεῖα] he has made up at will for his opponents. To pass over the rest, which he has done either shamelessly or clumsily and inexpertly in these disputations, and which our Blondel has set out in a full catalogue, I say that this is the same Turrianus whom we have recently shown to have fabricated the Constitutions and the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles, no less shamelessly than ignorantly. Who would believe, even on oath, that such a man had really found some ancient manuscript codex containing the very things he describes, a codex that no one but himself has read, seen or mentioned? But even if ancient books did contain such things, it would not follow that they should at once be held to be true.

units.la: Quam multa enim manuscripti, etiam antiqui codices authoribus tribuunt non suis? Magno omnino judicio in veteribus libris opus esse ad discernenda vera à falsis, omnes eruditi consentiunt. Quod si codicem illum (siquis tamen revera est hujusmodi codex, neque omnia pro sua vanitate finxit Turrianus) si inquam, codicem illum, quisquis est habueremus totum, fortasse in eo ipso deprehenderemus clara falsimoniæ argumenta; ut in aliis plurimis accidit, cidit, in quibus ipsa opera titulos saepenumero revicerunt. In isto vero Turriano codice (si quis vere est in rerum natura) tale aliquid subesse, ex quo coargui & labefactari possit ejus fides, duo faciunt, ut non modo suspicer, sed etiam prope modum credam. Prius est, quod librum ipsum Turrianus non edidit in publicam lucem, satisque habuit fragmenta quaedam ex eo describere. Alterum est, quod etiam nunc, cum tot annis a Turriani morte fluxerint, in iisdem tamen tenebris delitescit liber; neque manum adhuc invenit, quae ei jam pridem ad exitum maturo, obstetricaretur. Quis enim vel Turrianum, vel ejus socios, qui quotidie hujusmodi merces avidissime extrudunt, & vera falsaque nullo discrimine habentes, quicquid causae suae vel in speciem favet, per fas nefasque honesto antiquitatis nomine commendatum publicant; quis, inquam, eos sibi persuaserit tantum imaginum fautorem, quantus est, si verus est hic canonum Antiochenorum liber, tamdiu tenebris & umbra mortis clausum in arcanis scriniis detentuos fuisse, nisi aliquid timerent? nisi falsorum, mentitorumque natalium notas in eo aliquas animadverterent?
units.tr: For how many manuscripts, even ancient codices, ascribe to authors works that are not theirs? All learned men agree that there is need of great judgment in old books to distinguish true from false. But if we had that codex entire (if indeed there is such a codex at all, and Turrianus has not invented everything out of his own vanity), we would perhaps detect in that very codex clear arguments of forgery, as happens in very many other cases, in which the works themselves have often betrayed their titles. But that there is something in this Turrianus codex (if it really exists in nature) by which its credibility could be refuted and undermined, two things make me not only suspect it but almost believe it. The first is that Turrianus did not publish the book itself to the public light, and was content to copy out certain fragments from it. The second is that even now, though so many years have passed since Turrianus's death, the book still lies hidden in the same darkness, and has not yet found a hand to assist its long-overdue birth. For who would persuade himself that Turrianus, or his associates, who every day most eagerly put forth such wares, and who make no distinction between true and false, publishing under the honourable name of antiquity whatever favours their cause, by fair means or foul; who, I say, would persuade himself that they are such friends of images, as they are, and that if this book of the Antiochene canons is genuine, it would have been kept shut up for so long in the secret chests, buried in shadow and the darkness of death, unless they were afraid of something? Unless they had noticed in it some marks of a false and spurious origin?

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Falsos & fictitios esse hos Canones probatur, 1. ex ipso illo, qui à Turriano editur, eorum teste ac authore Pamphilo Martyre, qui librum scripsisse impudenter fingitur, contra disertam Eusebii vocem negantis, eum quicquam scripsisse. Turriani cum Ruffino germanitas. 2. idem probatur ex Eusebii de istis silentio. 3. ex eo quod & Eusebio & Origeni ipsi, in cujus bibliotheca fuisse finguntur, plane ignotos fuisse deprehendatur. 4. ex eo quod Synodus illa Apostolorum Antiochena in omni retro Ecclesia ignota fuerit. Insignis Hincmari locus. Objectus à Baronio pro illa Synodo ex Innocentio ep. 18. locus mendosus emendatur & asseritur. Gregorii Pisinuntensis Episcopi ex 7. Syn. testimonium exploditur. Peßima Patrum Syn. 7. fides.
units.tr: That these canons are false and fictitious is shown: (1) from that very document which Turrianus publishes, in which Pamphilus the Martyr, to whom it is shamelessly ascribed as author and witness of the canons, is said to have written it, though Eusebius plainly states that he wrote nothing. The kinship of Turrianus with Rufinus. (2) The same is shown from Eusebius's silence about these canons. (3) From the fact that they are found to have been wholly unknown both to Eusebius and to Origen himself, in whose library they are supposed to have been. (4) From the fact that this Antiochene Synod of the Apostles was unknown to the whole Church in earlier times. A notable passage of Hincmar. A passage of Innocent, Ep. 18, cited by Baronius in favour of that Synod, is shown to be corrupt, and is corrected and vindicated. The testimony of Gregory, Bishop of Pisinum, from the seventh Synod, is refuted. The very poor faith of the Fathers of the seventh Synod.

units.la: SED hæc ipsa tamen videamus, quæ Turrianus exhibet ex antiquissimo scilicet codice decerpta, ac delibrata fragmenta. Primo ille titulus impostorem arguit. Pamphylum enim Martyrem libri illius, quicunque tandem sit, authorem profitetur. Atqui Eusebius, Sanctissimi Martyris familiaris, cujus res gestas proprio opere exsecutus est, quem sic amavit, ac coluit, ut ab eo etiam cognomen nactus sit (ab hoc enim viro dictus est Eusebius Pamphili) ille inquam Eusebius, testis hac in causa omni exceptione major dixit Pamphilum nihil scripsisse, exceptis brevibus epistolis ad amicos. Mentitur ergo, cujuscunque authoris sit, antiquissimus Turriani codex; fingens contra Eusebii fidem, Pamphilum nescio quem librum scripsisse de Antiochenæ Synodi canonibus. Author locupletissimus Hieronymus, qui Eusebii & historiam (quam habemus, & in qua, cum non uno in loco Pamphili mentionem factam reperiamus, nihil plane invenimus ab eo scriptum) & (quos non habemus) de Pamphili vita libros viderat. Is autem retractans, quod olim à Ruffino deceptus, Pamphilum inter Christianos scriptores censuerat, Ante annos (inquit a) ferme decem, cum Dexter amicus meus, qui praefecturam administravit praetorii, me rogasset, ut authorum nostrae religionis ei indicem texerem, inter cateros tractatores posui & hunc librum à Pamphilo editum (Apologiam Origenis intelligit, Pamphili nomine à Ruffino latine publicatam) ita putans esse, ut à te, & tuis discipulis fuerat divulgatum. Sed cum ipse dicat Eusebius, Pamphilum nihil scripsisse, exceptis brevibus epistolis ad amicos; & primus liber sex voluminum illius, eadem & eisdem verbis contineat, quae sub nomine Pamphili à te ficta sunt, perspicuum est, te idcirco librum hunc disseminare voluisse, ut sub
units.tr: But let us examine these very fragments which Turrianus sets forth, plainly taken and culled from a most ancient codex. First, that title exposes the impostor. For it professes that Pamphilus the Martyr is the author of that book, whoever he may be. Yet Eusebius, the close friend of that most holy Martyr, whose deeds he recorded in his own work, and whom he so loved and esteemed that he even took his surname from him (for Eusebius was called "of Pamphilus" after this man), that same Eusebius, I say, a witness above all exception in this matter, has stated that Pamphilus wrote nothing except brief letters to friends. Therefore the most ancient codex of Turrianus, whatever its author, lies, inventing against the testimony of Eusebius that Pamphilus wrote I know not what book on the canons of the Antiochene Synod. The most learned author Jerome, who had seen both Eusebius's history (in which, though we find mention of Pamphilus in more than one place, we find nothing at all written by him) and the books on the life of Pamphilus which we no longer have, also testifies to this. Retracting his earlier view, by which he had been deceived by Rufinus and had counted Pamphilus among Christian writers, he says: About ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who administered the praetorian prefecture, asked me to compile for him an index of the writers of our religion, I included among the other authors also this book published by Pamphilus (he means the Apology for Origen, published in Latin under Pamphilus's name by Rufinus), thinking it to be as it had been published by you and your disciples. But since Eusebius himself says that Pamphilus wrote nothing except brief letters to friends, and the first book of his six volumes contains the same things, in the same words, as those which have been falsely put under Pamphilus's name by you, it is plain that you wished to spread this book so that under the persona of the Martyr you might introduce a heresy.

units.la: a l. 2. A-pol. adversus Ruffin. T. 2. Hier. sol. 8o. D. sub persona Martyris haresim introduceres.
units.tr: a Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, book 2; Jerome, vol. 2, Latin edition of 1580, p. D.

units.la: Hactenus Hieronymus: hanc Ruffini fraudem & aliis locis non semel exagitans a. In Pamphilo quod olim Ruffinus, idem nunc Turrianus audet: viri plane similes. Geminos diceres, si eodem tempore vixissent; usque adeo eadem est utriusque audacia, ac in vitiandis, adulterandisque authoribus licentia; ad haec ventosa de Graecae Latinaeque linguae cognitione jactantia. Bilinguis enim uterque fuit; & quos ubi Graeciliant Latinos diceres; ubi Latine loquuntur, Graecos. Nostri tamen vel inverecundia, vel certe stultitia major fuit. Nam Ruffinus quidem Pamphilo Origenis, cujus eum studiosissimum fuisse constabat, non absque aliqua veri specie defensionem affingebat. Nostri drama absurdissimum est, omniqué etiam fuco caret. Cui enim unquam fando auditi erant Apostolici isti canones de quibus novus Ruffinus, Turrianus, nullo nunc colore Pamphilo librum supponit? Sed bene est, quod utriusque impudentia eodem Eusebii testimonio convincitur; nihil Pamphilum scripsisse affirmantis praeter epistolas, cui isti praeter epistolas, alia nescio quae opera tribuere non erubescunt. Praeterea si, quod Turrianus fingit, canones istos in Origenis Bibliotheca reperit Pamphilus, si librum de iis scripsit; profecto fieri non potest, ut ii Eusebio ignoti fuerint, quocum Pamphilus vixit conjunctissime. Atqui canones istos Eusebio ignotos fuisse, non est obscurum. Eos enim si scivisset, in Ecclesiae historia haud dubie memorasset, in rebus Apostolorum, quas fuse, & quoad ejus fieri potuit, diligentissime exsequitur, narrasset, habitam ab iis Antiochiae Synodum; conditosque saluberrimos canones. Haec enim, ut quivis videt, admodum memorabilia, nulla causa dici potest, cur, si scivit, tacuerit. Est & alius in historia Ecclesiastica locus, in quo horum canonum mentionem fieri ab Eusebio decebat, si eos notos habuisset; nimirum ubi continetur de Paneadensibus statuis narratio; quam exsecutus Eusebius a, Θαυμαστὸν (inquit) τῆς παλαιᾶς ἐξ ἰδνῶν ἐνεργηθέντας πρὸς τὸ Σωτῆρ ἡμῶν ταῦτα πεποιηκέναι, Nihil autem mirum, eos, qui ex Gentibus erant, beneficiis a Servatore nostro affectos, haec fecisse, simulacra ei posuisse. Hic omnino, ut mirandi occasionem praeciperet, commemorandus veniebat canonum Turrianicorum octavus, diserte praecipiens pingi sive effingi τὸ θεανθρωπινὸν σῶμα τοῦ Σωτῆρος, divino-humanam Christi effigiem. At nihil hujusmodi eo loco Eusebius. Non enim nim Apostolorum præceptum, sed Ethnicorum morem adfert, velut veram istius facti causam; quod scilicet cum Ethnici Servatores, sive benefactores suos hujusmodi simulachris atque imaginibus honorare solerent, mirandum non sit eos, qui inter Ethnicos nati, atque educati erant; hunc sibi suisque inolitum morem ad honorandum Christum usurpasse. Sed extat in Synodo 7. a quædam ejusdem Eusebii ad Constantiam Constantini Augusti sororem epistola, quæ multo omnium clarissime ostendit, huic viro plane penitusque ignotos fuisse istos canones. Cum enim illa mulier Christianismum recens professa, ex Ethnico ritu, in quo antea cum viro suo Licinio, infensissimo Christianismi hoste vixerat, Christi imaginem sibi mitti ab Eusebio petivisset, ille se missurum negat; imo vel posci hujusmodi Christi effigiem nefas esse docet; cujus nempe naturam vel divinam, vel humanam, nulla mortalium ars vel exprimere vel adumbrare ullis coloribus possit. Atqui ex canonibus istis Antiochenis non modo licet, sed etiam decet, ac necesse est, Christianos sui Servatoris imaginem effingere. Ergo qui Constantiæ sic respondet Eusebius, istos Apostolorum canones plane, penitusque nescivit. Nescivisse porro incredibile est, siquidem ii Pam-
units.tr: Thus far Jerome, who on this and other occasions more than once attacked this fraud of Rufinus a. What Rufinus once did to Pamphilus, Turrianus now dares to do: the two men are entirely alike. You would call them twins, had they lived at the same time, so exactly the same is the audacity of both, and the same licence in corrupting and falsifying authors, and the same empty boasting about their knowledge of Greek and Latin. Both were bilingual, and where they write in the Greek style you would call them Latins, and where they write in Latin you would call them Greeks. Yet our man's shamelessness, or at least his stupidity, is greater. Rufinus at least defended Pamphilus's Origen, whom he was known to have admired greatly, with some appearance of truth. Our man's play is utterly absurd and does not even have a veneer. Who ever heard of those Apostolic canons, about which the new Rufinus, Turrianus, now without any pretence attributes a book to Pamphilus? But it is well that the impudence of both is refuted by the same testimony of Eusebius, who says that Pamphilus wrote nothing except letters. Yet these men are not ashamed to attribute to him, besides the letters, I know not what other works. Moreover, if, as Turrianus invents, Pamphilus found these canons in the library of Origen, and wrote a book about them, then it certainly cannot be that they were unknown to Eusebius, with whom Pamphilus lived in closest intimacy. But that these canons were unknown to Eusebius is not obscure. For had he known them, he would undoubtedly have mentioned them in his Ecclesiastical History, in the section on the deeds of the Apostles, which he treats at length and as carefully as he could, and would have related that a synod was held at Antioch by them and that they drew up most wholesome canons. For these things, as anyone can see, are very memorable, and no reason can be given why, if he knew them, he would have kept silent. There is also another passage in the Ecclesiastical History where Eusebius ought to have mentioned these canons, had he known them: namely, where the account of the statues at Paneas is given. Eusebius, following this account, says: "Nothing is strange, since those who were from the Gentiles, having been benefited by our Saviour [Σωτῆρ], did these things and set up images of him" [Θαυμαστὸν τῆς παλαιᾶς ἐξ ἰδνῶν ἐνεργηθέντας πρὸς τὸ Σωτῆρ ἡμῶν ταῦτα πεποιηκέναι]. Nothing strange, that those who came from the Gentiles, benefited by our Saviour, did these things and set up his images. Here, to give occasion for wonder, the eighth of the Turrianic canons ought to have been recalled, which expressly orders that the divine-human body of the Saviour be painted or fashioned, the divine-human likeness of Christ. But Eusebius says nothing of the kind in that place. For he does not cite a precept of the Apostles, but the custom of the Gentiles, as the true cause of that act: since the Gentiles were accustomed to honour their Saviours, or benefactors, with such statues and images, it is no wonder that those who were born and brought up among the Gentiles took over this custom, which had grown up among them, to honour Christ. But there exists in the Seventh Synod a a letter of Eusebius himself to Constantia, the sister of the Emperor Constantine, which shows most clearly of all that this man was completely and utterly ignorant of these canons. For when that woman, newly professing Christianity, asked Eusebius to send her an image of Christ, coming from the pagan practice in which she had lived before with her husband Licinius, the most hostile enemy of Christianity, he refuses to send it; indeed he teaches that it is wrong even to ask for such an image of Christ, whose nature, whether divine or human, no human art can express or sketch with any colours. But from those Antiochene canons it is not only permitted, but even fitting and necessary, for Christians to fashion the image of their Saviour. Therefore Eusebius, in answering Constantia in this way, plainly and utterly did not know those Apostolic canons. Moreover, it is incredible that he did not know them, since they were known to Pamphilus [Act. 6.] and had been described by him in some book.

units.la: a Act. 6. ii Pamphilo noti, & ab eo in aliquo libro, discripti erant. Ergo falsum est, quod ait Turrianicus codex, a Pamphilo nunquam visos, descriptosque fuisse. Sed neque verius est, quod Turrianicus codex narrat, hos canones Antiochenos in Origenis bibliotheca a Pamphilo repertos esse.
units.tr: Known to Pamphilus, and described by him in some book, these canons therefore were. So it is false that the Turrianic codex says they were never seen or described by Pamphilus. Nor is it truer what the Turrianic codex relates, that these Antiochene canons were found by Pamphilus in the library of Origen.

units.la: Id enim si verum esset, nunquam ea Origenes contra imaginum in religione usum scripsisset, quae in veris & indubitatis ejus libris leguntur; quale est, verbi gratia, quod negat a Christianis tales Deo honores exhiberi, quales a Paganorum populis solebant Diis exhiberi (hos autem honores in eo sitos esse dixerat, quod templa & simulacra iis ponerent) imo hujus generis honores daemonibus magis quam Deo congruere pronunciat; Item {Christianos homines & Judaos sibi temperare a statuis, & earum cultibus propter illud Legis, Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & ipsi soli servies; Non erunt tibi Dii alieni praeter me, & non facies tibi simulacrum, nec ullam effigiem eorum quae in coelo sunt, &c. Ita scilicet de simulacris & imaginibus scribere, qui ab Apostolis decretum sciret, ut fideles Christi effigiem, Sanctorum simulacra ex oppo sito Gentium effingant? Hanc Christianorum cum Judaeis communem causam faceret, qui ab Apostolis di-
units.tr: For if that were true, Origen would never have written against the use of images in religion what is read in his genuine and undisputed books. For example, he denies that such honours are paid to God by Christians as were customarily paid to the gods by the peoples of the pagans (and he had said that these honours consist in setting up temples and statues to them); indeed he declares that honours of this kind befit demons rather than God. Likewise he says that Christians and Jews alike refrain from statues and their worship, on account of that law: "You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him alone; you shall have no other gods before me, and you shall not make for yourself a graven image, or any likeness of those things which are in heaven," etc. Would someone who knew of the decree of the Apostles, that the faithful should fashion the image of Christ and the statues of the saints in place of the pagan practice, write about statues and images in this way? Would he make this a common cause of Christians with the Jews, he who knew the Apostles' decrees?

units.la: al. 3. contr. Celsp. 135.gr. 132. lat. — Celsus p. 135 gr., 132 lat.
units.tr: a Origen, Against Celsus, book 3, p. 135 Greek, 132 Latin. Celsus, p. 135 Greek, 132 Latin.

units.la: b l.7. p. 386. Lat. 382. — Origenes, ed. p. 386 lat., 382. lis diserte vetitum sciret, ne similes Iudaeis hac in parte fiamus? At haec scisset Origenes, si codex ille Turrianicus in eius bibliotheca extitisset. Ergo fieri non potest, ut verum sit, quod liber à Turriano visus narrat, canonum illorum codicem in Origenis bibliotheca repertum esse. Denique quod idem ille codex de Antiochena &Apostolorum Synodo narrat, id inquam, apud omnes veteris, recentisque memoriae Christianos Graecos, Latinosque incognitum, & inauditum est, & evidenter falsum. Nam si quam Apostoli Antiochiae Synodum habuissent, id vetustissimi quatuor primorum saeculorum scriptores scivissent, posterisque tradidissent; quod ab eorum nemine factum videmus. Certe ne inferioribus quidem saeculis in Ecclesia Latina notam fuisse illam Antiochenam Synodum, testis & author luculentus est Hincmarus, qui a. D. 871. ut canones illos 50. quos nuper confutavimus, demonstret non fuisse ab Apostolis conscriptos, quas Apostoli Synodos habuisse ab omni sui temporis Ecclesia credebantur, fuse his verbis exsequitur; Caeterum (inquit) iidem canones, qui vocantur Apostolorum, non ab Apostolis conscripti esse creduntur, quoniam, sicut in sacra historia legimus, & inde scriptum ob Ecclesiae sia magistris accepimus ; prima Synodus Apostolorum habita est Hierosolymis de electione duodecimi Apostolorum pro Iuda a. Secunda de electione septem diaconorum b ; tertia c de circumcisione, ne credentibus e x gentibus imponeretur ; quarta d facta est de credentibus ex Iudaeis illo tempore, ne prohiberentur, ubi necessitas exigeret, etiam legalibus ceremoniis initiari, ob devitandum scilicet eorum scandalum, qui putabant eos ista Mosaica decreta, tanquam idololatriae dogmata damnasse, quod etiam ante facere consuesse Timothei maxime circumcisione probatum est. Quintam e demum Synodum Apostolorum Patres nostri fuisse tradunt, quando secundum quod praedictum est tempus adimpletionis advenit, ut in omnem terram exiret sonus eorum, & in fines orbis terrae verba eorum, & secundum Domini dictum, Euangelium praedicaretur in toto mundo per Apostolos, quibus dixit f Ite, docete omnes gentes. Et tunc Symbolum, sicut universalis tenet Ecclesia, condiderunt, singuli singulas sententias proferentes, sicut & Leo ad Pulcheriam Augustam demonstrat g; Tum recitatis Leonis verbis, Denique (inquit) post hac nulla Synodus ab Apostolis legitur celebrata, qui fuerunt per omnem terram ad verbum fidei seminandum progredien do dispersi. dispersi. His Hincmari congruunt, quæ ex Glossa ordinaria, adeoque ex antiqua communique Ecclesiæ Latinæ fide, initio Conciliorum de quatuor ↄApostolorum conventionibus, sive conciliis fusè descripta habentur; hoc uno discrepant, quod hic quatuor tantum priora Concilia recensentur; quintum, in quo Symbolum ab Apostolis conditum ex quorundam Patrum opinione dicit Hincmarus, omittitur; non abs re, ut videtur: nam quatuor quidem priora Hierosolymis habita esse, ex divino Actuum Apostolicorum libro certa fides est; quinti nulla in sacra Historia mentio. Utcunque sit, (neque enim nunc necesse est ea de re diligentius disputare) illud quidem ex his clarum certumque est, præter hos quatuor, vel ad summum ex Hincmaro quinque nullam aliam Apostolorum Synodum jam à vetustis temporibus ad nostram memoriam Ecclesię fuisse cognitam. Hincmarus disertissime; Denique post hæc nulla Synodus ab ↄApostolis legitur celebrata. Cum ergo Synodicum Apostolorum conventum, præsertim in quo non pauca de religione decreta facta fuerint, vetus & nova omnium à Christianismi initiis sæculorum non potuerit nescire, appareret, quam antiquus Turriani liber loquitur, Antiochenam Apostolorum Synodum, eam, (quippe quam omnis hactenus ne‑scivit Ecclesia) fictitiam ac commentitiam esse. Sane rem ipsam accuratius intuenti apparebit, nullam unquam Apostolorum Synodum Antiochiae convenisse. Inprimis enim ante annum aerae Christianae 58. non convenisse ex sano Actuum libro constat; qui cum res ab Apostolis gestas ad illum usque temporis articulum exsequatur, nullam hujus conventus mentionem fecit; qui tamen si revera habitus esset, cum celeberrimus, adhaec de rebus tantis habitus fuisse dicatur, omitti praefecto sine piaculo non poterat. Iam ut post a. D. 58. (hoc est ab ascensione Christi 26.) dispersis, ut liquet, in varias, longeque inter se dissitas gentes ad praedicandum Euangelium Apostolis, pluribusque ex eorum numero fortasse jam ministerio, ac vita defunctis, habita fuerit Synodus illa Antiochena; id inquam, ab omni veri specie abhorret. Ex his porro videre est, quam temere, quamque praeter omnem rationem ad hanc suam (quae nulla unquam fuit) Antiochenam Synodum verba quaedam Innocentii I. referant Turrianus a, & Baronius b. Certe quidem (inquit Baronius) Innocentius Romanus Pontifex, in epistola ad Alexandrum Episcopum Antiochenum ejusmodi Synodi Apostolicae meminisse videtur. Verba In‑ ba Innocentii sunt de Ecclesia Antiochena, ubi (inquit a) & nomen accepit religio Christiana, & quae conventum Apostolorum apud se fieri celeberrimum meruit. Baronius legit, conventum Apostolorum apud se celeberrimum meruit, expuncto verbo fieri. Ego vero, cur sic legat nescio; & siquid sit mutandum, multo rectius ac verius voculas apud se expugnandas putaverim, quam verbum fieri, ut sic legatur locus, & quae conventum Apostolorum fieri celeberrimum meruit. Imo, hoc verum puto, neque dubito, quin ita scripserit Innocentius. Sic enim res omnis plana est, ac expedita, quae alioqui magnas & inextricabiles habet difficultates. Nam si lectio vel Baroniana, vel vulgata retineatur; obsecro tuam fidem, quis ille conventus est Apostolorum celeberrimus Antiochiae habitus? Profecto nullus in tota Ecclesiae historia occurrit, cui id nominis conveniat. Ut donem Baronio, fuisse aliquem Antiochiae Apostolorum conventum, res tamen & ratio non sinunt, ut ab Innocentio putemus celeberrimum dictum fuisse eum conventum, qui (siquis fuit) adeo celeberrimus non fuit, ut ne ab uno quidem Ecclesiae ante Innocentium scriptore memoratus sit. Nisi ergo Innocentium usque adeo desipuisse fingamus, ut celeberrimam berrimam dixerit eam Synodum, quæ apud totam Ecclesiam inaudita, ne uni quidem authori dicta, vel memorata fuit; necesse est hunc, quem celeberrimum vocat Apostolorum conventum, omnino alium ab eo esse, quem Turrianus, & Baronius ex unius, & quidem obscurissimi, & à nullo præter Turrianum, lecti vel visi codicis fide, Antiochiæ habitum contendunt. Si vero Innocentii verba sic, ut diximus, legas, omnia clara erunt. Nimirum, ille Apostolorum conventus, quem intelligit Innocentius, is ipse est, qui de causa Antiochenæ Ecclesiæ, & ejusdem rogatu, ab Apostolis habitus est Hierosolymis, cujusque & historia, & Synodica epistola ad Antiochenos, & alios Syros missa extat à Luca in Actibus a descripta. Hic vero conventus merito celeberrimus dictus est, qui & à divino authore litteris traditus, & ex eo ab omnibus Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus memoratus, & apud omnes omnis memoriæ Christianos vulgatissimus ac decantatissimus est, & apud Glossam ordinariam verissime perhibetur fuisse plenaria Conciliorum forma, postmodum à summis Pontificibus, & sanctis Patribus observata, & observanda. Sed & is conventus, licet non Antiochiæ, sed Hierosolymis habitus, ad Ecclesiæ tamen Antiochętiochenæ gloriam, quo eum refert Innocentius, evidentissime pertinet; cujus pax & voluntas scilicet, tanti Apostolis fuit, ut ad ea explicanda, de quibus scisscitatum miserant Antiocheni, omnes in unum convenire, capitibusque collatis quid verum esset, indagare, & decretum ab omnibus, qui tunc erant, Christianis observandum postulante Antiochia condere, & ei ipsi ante omnes, veluti primariæ cuidam, matricique Gentium Ecclesiæ inscribere operæ pretium esse putaverint; quo honore nullum Antiochena, nullum ulla alia Christianorum Ecclesia, majorem unquam adepta est. Hoc ergo est, quod significat Innocentius, cum ait Antiochenam Ecclesiam meminisse conventum Apostolorum celeberrimum fieri. Nimirum Ecclesia Antiochena fuit, quæ meruit, ut celeberrimus ille conventus fieret, quem Lucas ab Apostolis habitum Hierosolymis fuisse capite Actuum 15. narrat; ejusque habendi occasionem fuisse refert tum exortam apud Antiochiam controversiam, tum inde missos Paulum, & Barnabam, & alios, scisscitatum ab Apostolis, quid facto opus esset; ut omnes norunt. Nihil igitur ad fictitiam Turriani Synodum Innocentianus locus. Sicui vero religio est vulgatam lectionem sollicitare (quamquam equidem non videam, quæ religio esse debeat, duas voculas apud se à loci sententia penitus alienas exterere) fatebor equidem scripsisse hic Innocentium habitum esse, Antiochiæ Apostolorum conventum; vere & consulto scripsisse negabo; dicam (quod sæpe, maximis etiam authoribus contingit) imprudentem, & aliud agentem, ex memoriæ, non ex mentis culpa id Antiochiæ tribuisse, quod Hierosolymis convenit; eaque in re labi eo fuisse proclivius, quod totus ille conventus, tametsi non Antiochiæ, de Antiochenæ tamen Ecclesiæ causa, & quidem ipsius rogatu, ab Apostolis fuerit habitus. Sed neq; nos ab antiqua Ecclesiæ de Apostolicis Synodis sententia absterrere debet Gregorii Pisinuntensis Episcopi in Synodo septima oratio a, qui nescio quam ἀντιόχειαν συνοδὸν τῶν Ἀποστόλων apostolorum apud Antiochiam Synodum memorat. Primo enim ex omni Christianæ Ecclesiæ memoria iste unus reperitur, qui hoc affirmet; apud cæteros omnes altum de ea Synodo silentium. Imo diserte eam, ut audivimus, negant & Hincmarus, & Glossa ordinaria. Quin & ipse Anastasius Synodi interpres, de ea dubitasse videtur; dum illa Gregorii verba sic reddit: In Synodo Sanctorum Apostolorum, quæ apud Antiochiam congregata dicitur. Cur non simpliciter dixit, qua congregata est? cur praeter graeca, illud de suo addidit, congregata dicitur? Nimirum sciebat inauditam esse hanc Synodum, eoque non ausus simpliciter affirmare congregatam fuisse, rei fidem penes Gregorium relinquens, dixit, congregatam dici. Tum hic Gregorius a. D. 787. illa, quae adversarii recitant, pronuntiavit, septem pene saeculorum intervallo disiunctus, unde nam didicit hanc ab illis habitam Antiochiae Synodum? Omnino necesse est hunc, si vera certaque sunt quae dicit, ea ab aliquo veterum accepisse. Atqui nullus eorum est, qui Synodi istius meminerit. Ergo relinquitur, ut quae aliunde non didicerat, ipse finxerit; adeoque nulla in iis fide dignus sit. Adhaec unus ille fuit ex Synodi septimae Patribus; quibus ludus, ac jocus fuit apocrypha pro veris, atque authenticis in hoc imaginum negotio obtrudere, & falsos, spuriosque libros authoribus non suis affingere. Hoc iis crimen jampridem gravissime exprobavit, anno post peractam ipsam Synodum tertio, vir immortalis in Ecclesia gloriae, & ab ipsis adversariis in Sanctos relatus Carolus Magnus a; negans Chrysostomi esse, quae boni illi Patres b ejus nomine attulerant; & quas veluti veras laudabant, Christi ad Abgarum, & Abgari ad Christum stum epistolas, eas in apocryphorum censum Gelasio authore rejiciens. Quibus ad-di possunt, ac debent, ut cętera nunc mit-tam, quæ magni Athanasii nomine de Be-rytensis imaginis miraculo vel ipsi confin-xerunt, vel ab aliis confiĉta ufurparunt b; item quę veluti Basilii ex nescio qua ad Ju-lianum epistolarecitant. Ipsi adversarii hęc pene omnia rotunde confitentur. Nam & d illam Chrysostomi homiliam inter notha ejus opera Fronto Ducæus c, nobilis Je-suita, censuit, & Abgari ad Christum, Christique ad Abgarum epistolas spurias esse ac fictitias Bellarminus ex professo pro-bat, & idem e quoque libellum de passione imaginis Domini, demonstrat nequaquam esse magni Athanasii. Nihil ergo miran-dum est, quod Gregorius ex istorum a-dulteratorum numero, ipse quoque Apo-stolis Synodum Antiochenam præter ve-rum, cæterorumque omnium Patrum fi-dem ausus sit affingere. Sed istius proprie Gregorii quam sublesta sit fides, vel ex eo potest intelligi, quod qui nunc tanto stu-dio imaginum causam tuetur, is paulo ante Iconoclasta fuerat, & in Iconoclastarum Synodo sederat. Homo scilicet vanus, & religionem ex commodo pro temporum diversitate mutare solitus, cum ad deme-rendum Irenes Augustæ, impotentissimæ imagiimaginum cultricis, animum, retinendamque Episcopatus dignitatem, Iconoclastarum castra deseruisset, & imaginum defensoribus nomen dedisset, putavit mutationem suam apud novos amicos insigni aliquo facinore affirmandam, neque de ejus animo suspicio remaneret. Itaque non satis habuit Iconoclastis nuntium remittere, & Iconodulorum dogma profiteri, eorumque rationes & argumenta laudare; Ipse novi aliquid ad eam causam conferendum ratus, Apostolicam Synodum impudentia nescio an stultitia majore confinxit, & à se repertam jactavit; cui vel desultoria illa, & pro rebus ac temporibus vela contorquens levitas omnem apud probos fidem merito detrahere debet. Postremo omnem omnibus septimæ Pseudo-Synodi hominibus fidem abrogavit magnum annis post ipsam non pluribus quam septem Francofurti habitum Concilium quod trecentorum episcoporum fuisse accepimus; qui uno omnes consensu Græcam illam Pseudo-Synodum, septimæ nomen præferentem, reprobarunt. Ergo testimonii, quod in ea dixit Gregorius, nulla esse debet apud nos vis, vel authoritas. Sed quod mox iterum de eodem dicendum erit; hæc nunc quidem satis sunt ad omnem ipsi fidem in hac causa detrahendam. Cum ergo unius testis, & quidem pene sexcentis post rem de qua quæritur, nati, adhæc merito in hoc negotio suspecti, nulla haberi vel possit, vel debeat ratio, conclusum esto, quod omnis semper credidit Ecclesia, quatuor tantum, vel ad summum quinque fuisse Apostolorum Synodos; falsam adeo esse & commentitiam sextam illam, quæ dicitur Antiochena; falsum pariter & mendacem antiquum Turriani librum, qui eam impudenter Apostolis affingit.
units.tr: b l.7. p. 386. Lat. 382. — Origen, ed. p. 386 lat., 382. Did he know that it was expressly forbidden, lest we become like the Jews in this respect? But Origen would have known this if that Turrianus codex had existed in his library. Therefore it cannot be true, as the book that Turrianus saw reports, that a codex of those canons was found in Origen's library. Finally, what the same codex reports about the Antiochene and Apostolic Synod is, I say, unknown and unheard of among all Christians, Greek and Latin, of ancient and recent memory, and is evidently false. For if the Apostles had held some synod at Antioch, the most ancient writers of the first four centuries would have known of it and handed it down to posterity. We see that none of them did so. Certainly, even in the later centuries, that Antiochene synod was not known in the Latin Church. Hincmar is a clear witness and authority on this. In 871 he set out, to show that those fifty canons which we lately refuted were not written by the Apostles, which synods the Apostles were believed by the whole Church of his time to have held, and he does so at length in these words: "Moreover," he says, "those same canons, which are called of the Apostles, are not believed to have been written by the Apostles, since, as we read in sacred history, and as we have received from the teachers of the Church, the first synod of the Apostles was held at Jerusalem concerning the election of the twelfth apostle in place of Judas (a). The second was concerning the election of the seven deacons (b). The third (c) was concerning circumcision, lest it be imposed on believers from the Gentiles. The fourth (d) was held concerning believers from the Jews of that time, that, where necessity required, they should not be prevented from being initiated into the legal ceremonies, namely to avoid the scandal of those who thought that those Mosaic decrees had been condemned as doctrines of idolatry; which was also proved by Timothy's circumcision, which he had practised before. Our Fathers finally tell us of a fifth (e) synod of the Apostles, when the time of fulfilment foretold came, that their sound should go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, and, according to the Lord's word, the Gospel should be preached throughout the whole world by the Apostles, to whom he said (f) Go, teach all nations. And then they composed the creed, as the universal Church holds it, each one contributing a single sentence, as Leo also shows to Pulcheria Augusta (g)." Then, after quoting Leo's words, he adds: "Finally," he says, "after this no synod of the Apostles is read to have been celebrated, since they were scattered throughout the whole earth, going forth to sow the word of faith." These agree with Hincmar's account, which is set out at length at the beginning of the councils, from the Gloss and so from the ancient and common faith of the Latin Church, concerning the four assemblies or councils of the Apostles. They differ only in this: here only the first four councils are listed. The fifth, in which Hincmar says the creed was composed by the Apostles according to the opinion of some Fathers, is omitted, and not without reason, it seems. For that the first four were held at Jerusalem is certain faith from the divinely inspired book of the Acts of the Apostles; of a fifth there is no mention in sacred history. However that may be (for there is no need now to dispute this more carefully), this much is clear and certain from these sources: beyond these four, or at most five according to Hincmar, no other synod of the Apostles has been known to the Church from ancient times down to our memory. Hincmar says it most plainly: Finally, after this no synod of the Apostles is read to have been celebrated. Since, then, the ancient and the modern Church of all the centuries from the beginnings of Christianity could not have been ignorant of an assembly of the Apostles in synod, especially one in which not a few decrees concerning religion were made, it becomes plain that the Antiochene synod of the Apostles, of which the ancient book of Turrianus speaks, is fictitious and made up, since the whole Church until now has been ignorant of it. Indeed, anyone who looks at the matter more closely will see that no synod of the Apostles ever met at Antioch. First, it is established from the sound book of Acts that it did not meet before the year 58 of the Christian era, since that book, which relates the things done by the Apostles up to that point of time, makes no mention of such an assembly. Yet if it had really been held, since it is said to have been very famous and held concerning such great matters, it could not have been passed over without sacrilege. Now, that that Antiochene synod was held after the year 58 (that is, 26 years after Christ's ascension), when, as is clear, the Apostles were scattered among various and widely separated nations to preach the Gospel, and many of their number were perhaps already dead from ministry and life, I say, is utterly remote from any appearance of truth. Moreover, from these things it can be seen how rashly, and how contrary to all reason, Turrianus (a) and Baronius (b) refer certain words of Innocent I to this Antiochene synod of theirs, which never existed at all. "Certainly," says Baronius, "Innocent, Roman Pontiff, seems to recall such an Apostolic synod in his letter to Alexander, Bishop of Antioch." Innocent's words are about the Church of Antioch, where (he says (a)) the Christian religion also received its name, and which deserved to have the very famous assembly of the Apostles held among them. Baronius reads: deserved to have the very famous assembly of the Apostles among them, with the word held struck out. But I do not know why he reads it so. And if anything is to be changed, I would think it far more right and true to strike out the little words among them than the word held, so that the passage reads: and which deserved to have the very famous assembly of the Apostles held. Indeed, I think this is true, and I do not doubt that Innocent wrote it so. For in this way the whole matter is plain and clear, which otherwise has great and inextricable difficulties. For if either the Baronian reading or the common one is retained, I beg you, what is that most famous assembly of the Apostles said to have been held at Antioch? Surely none occurs in the whole history of the Church to which that name can apply. Even granting Baronius that there was some assembly of the Apostles at Antioch, the facts and reason still do not allow us to think that Innocent called that assembly very famous, when it (if there was one) was so far from famous that not even a single writer of the Church before Innocent mentioned it. Unless, then, we imagine Innocent to have been so foolish as to call very famous a synod which was unknown to the whole Church, and mentioned or spoken of by no single author, it must necessarily be that the assembly of the Apostles which he calls very famous is wholly different from the one which Turrianus and Baronius contend was held at Antioch, on the authority of a single codex, and that a most obscure one, which no one but Turrianus has read or seen. But if you read Innocent's words as we have said, all things will be clear. Clearly, that assembly of the Apostles which Innocent means is the very one which was held by the Apostles at Jerusalem concerning the cause of the Church of Antioch, and at its request; its history and its synodal letter to the Antiochenes and the other Syrians, described by Luke in the Acts (a), are extant. This assembly rightly deserves to be called very famous, since it was handed down in writing by the divine author, and from him was mentioned by all ecclesiastical writers, and is most widely known and celebrated among all Christians of every age; and the Gloss rightly says of it that it was the full form of a council, afterwards observed and to be observed by the supreme Pontiffs and holy Fathers. And that assembly, although held not at Antioch but at Jerusalem, clearly pertains to the glory of the Church of Antioch, to which Innocent refers it. The Apostles, it seems, so valued its peace and purpose that, to explain the matters on which the Antiochenes had sent to ask, they all came together into one place, and, with heads joined, sought out what was true, and at Antioch's request thought it worth while to settle a decree to be observed by all the Christians then living, and to inscribe it in the name of Antioch before all others, as of a primary and mother Church of the Gentiles; no Antiochene church, and no other Christian church, ever obtained a greater honour than this. Therefore this is what Innocent means when he says that the Antiochene Church remembered that the very famous assembly of the Apostles was held. Surely it was the Church of Antioch that deserved that the very famous assembly should be held, which Luke, in chapter 15 of the Acts, relates was held by the Apostles at Jerusalem; and he tells that the occasion for holding it was the controversy that had arisen at Antioch, and that Paul and Barnabas and others were sent from there to ask the Apostles what needed to be done, as everyone knows. Therefore Innocent's passage has nothing to do with the fictitious synod of Turrianus. If anyone has scruples about altering the common reading (though I do not see what scruple there should be in removing two little words wholly foreign to the sense of the passage), I will admit that Innocent here wrote that an assembly of the Apostles was held at Antioch; but I will deny that he wrote it truly and deliberately. I will say (as often happens even with the greatest authors) that he, careless and thinking of something else, attributed to Antioch from memory, not from intention, what was held at Jerusalem; and that he slipped into this error the more readily because that whole assembly, though not at Antioch, was held by the Apostles about the cause of the Antiochene Church, and indeed at its request. Nor should the opinion of the ancient Church concerning the Apostolic synods be disturbed by the speech of Gregory, Bishop of Pisinus, in the seventh synod (a), who mentions I know not what Antiochene synod of the Apostles. For, first, from the whole memory of the Christian Church this one man alone is found to affirm it; among all the others there is deep silence about that synod. Indeed Hincmar and the Gloss expressly deny it, as we have heard. Moreover, even Anastasius, the translator of the synod, seems to have doubted it, since he renders Gregory's words thus: In the synod of the holy Apostles, which is said to have been assembled at Antioch. Why did he not simply say in which it was assembled? Why, besides the Greek, did he add of his own is said? Clearly he knew that this synod was unheard of, and so, not daring to affirm simply that it had been assembled, he left the truth of the matter to Gregory and said that it was said to have been assembled. Then this Gregory, who in the year 787 pronounced those things which our opponents recite, separated by an interval of nearly seven centuries: whence did he learn that this Antiochene synod was held by them? It is quite necessary that, if what he says is true and certain, he received it from one of the ancients. Yet none of them mentions that synod. Therefore it remains that what he had not learned from elsewhere, he himself invented; and so he is not worthy of trust in these matters. Besides, he was one of the Fathers of the seventh synod, for whom it was a game and a joke to foist apocryphal writings on the public as true and authentic in this business of images, and to attribute false and spurious books to authors who were not their own. Long ago the immortal glory of the Church, Charles the Magnus, whom even their own opponents have counted among the saints, gravely reproached them for this crime, in the third year after the synod itself was held. He denied that the things which those good Fathers (b) brought forward under Chrysostom's name were his, and he rejected, as apocryphal, on the authority of Gelasius, the letters of Christ to Abgarus and of Abgarus to Christ, which they praised as genuine. To these may be added, and ought to be added (to pass over for now the rest), what they either themselves invented or took from others under the name of the great Athanasius about the miracle of the Berytus image; likewise what they cite from an epistle of Basil to Julian, I know not from where. The opponents themselves almost entirely and openly confess these things. For Fronto Ducaeus (c), a noble Jesuit, judged that Chrysostom's homily among his spurious works was not his; Bellarmine professedly proves that the letters of Abgarus to Christ and of Christ to Abgarus are spurious and fictitious; and the same author shows that the little book on the passion of the Lord's image is by no means the work of the great Athanasius. Nothing is therefore to be wondered at if Gregory, from the number of these adulterators, himself also dared to attribute to the Apostles an Antiochene synod, against the truth and the faith of all the other Fathers. But the feebleness of Gregory's own trustworthiness can be understood even from this: that the man who now defends the cause of images so zealously had shortly before been an Iconoclast, and had sat in the synod of the Iconoclasts. He was, clearly, a vain man, accustomed to change his religion for advantage according to the changing times; and when, to win the favour of Irene Augusta, a most powerful worshipper of images, and to keep his episcopal dignity, he had deserted the camp of the Iconoclasts and enrolled himself among the defenders of images, he thought his change had to be confirmed among his new friends by some striking deed, so that no suspicion of his mind would remain. So he was not content to send word to the Iconoclasts and to profess the doctrine of the Iconodules and praise their reasons and arguments. Thinking that he must contribute something new to that cause, he invented an Apostolic synod with a boldness I know not whether to call greater than his folly, and boasted that he had discovered it. Such a levity, turning its sails this way and that according to affairs and times, must rightly remove all credit from him among honest people. Lastly, a council held at Frankfurt not many more than seven years after the synod itself, which we have heard was attended by three hundred bishops, took away all trust from all the men of the seventh pseudo-synod; for with one consent they all rejected that Greek pseudo-synod which bears the name of the seventh. Therefore the testimony which Gregory gave in it ought to have no force or authority with us. But what must be said again about the same man presently is enough for now to strip him of all credit in this cause. Since, therefore, the testimony of a single witness, and one born nearly six hundred years after the matter in question, and moreover suspect in this business, can or should have no weight, let it be concluded that the Church has always believed that there were only four, or at most five, synods of the Apostles; that the so-called sixth, the Antiochene, is false and made up; and that the ancient book of Turrianus, which impudently attributes it to the Apostles, is likewise false and lying.

units.la: CAPUT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Expenduntur ipsi illi à Turriano editi Canones, & ex ineptis atque absurdis plurimis, quæ in iis deprehenduntur, demonstratur, eos falsos & fictitios esse 1. can. absurda, fingentis decretum esse, ut in Dominum credentes Christiani dicerentur. Baronii & Binii à Turriano in canonis lectione diversitas. Tum can. 2. absurditas, in circumcisione vetanda. Can. 9. prodigiosa ineptia, & immanis in depravanda Scriptura impudentia. Sed & 3. can. ineptum esse, & ridicule Apostolis affictum.
units.tr: The very canons published by Turrianus are examined, and from the many silly and absurd things found in them it is shown that they are false and fabricated. (1) The canon is absurd in claiming a decree was made that believers in the Lord should be called Christians; Turrianus differs from Baronius and Binius in reading the canon. Then canon 2 is absurd in forbidding circumcision. Canon 9 is a prodigious silliness and a monstrous impudence in corrupting Scripture. But canon 3 is also silly and ridiculously invented for the Apostles.

units.la: ED jam ipsa canonum fragmenta consideremus, à Turriano ex illo libro decerpta. Ea vero multa continent absurda, & Apostolis indigna; unde eorum falsimonia clarissime deprehenditur. Turrianus hunc canonem nonem primo loco recitat, ut credentes in Dominum Jesum, quos illius temporis homines vocabant Galilaos, Christiani deinceps vocarentur. Sed Baronius & Binius aliter canonem efferunt, nempe; Ut credentes in Dominum Jesum, quos illius temporis homines (ut habent Acta) appellabant discipulos, dicerentur Christiani. Primo hæc istorum diversitas canoni fidem abrogat; istosque arguit Babelis esse architectos, lingua dissonos, mendacii operarios. Neque enim effugere possunt, quin ipsorum alter, id est vel Turrianus, vel Baronius mentitus sit. Tum à Baronio quæro, unde hanc, quam exhibet, lectionem habeat? Nullum à se, nullum ab alio, præterquam à Turriano, visum hujus Synodi codicem memorat. Cur ergo, quod Turrianus ex uno illo codice repræsentat, mutat? Hic quidem mendacii manifestus est, captus, ut ajunt, ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ. Sed vir bonus, qui probe sciret fabulosam esse totam hanc materiam, sibi in ea pro libidine ludere jus fasque esse putavit.
