Itaque cum intelligeret, quod stolide & absurde finxerat impostor Turrianus, credentes in Dominum tempore Apostolorum vocatos fuisse Galilaos, id ob omni historiæ Ecclesiasticæ fide abhorrere; quæ nostris Galilæorum nomen narrat, non initio, sed quarto deto demum sæculo jam adulto, sub Juliano desertore, fuisse impositum ; vir Urbanus Baronius stultum & absurdum mendacium alio minus incredibili permutandum ac corrigendum existimavit. Sed non, si ex ejus usu hoc comminisci commodum fuit, ideo & licuisse putandum est. Ergo vel Baronii ipsius, Biniique judicio falsus, perperamque fictus est allatus à Turriano canon ; quem scilicet nunquam mutaturi fuissent, si rectum, verumque esse censuissent. Sed neque stare potest, quod hi pro Turrianicis verbis impudenter supponunt. Ex actis liquere concedo, & Apostolos, & Lucam credentes dixisse discipulos ; Illius temporis homines, hoc est vulgum, eo quoque vocabulo ita usos esse, ut cum discipulos simpliciter dice-rent, eos, qui in Christum crederent, intelligerent ; hoc inquam nulla Apostolorum, nulla aliorum Acta, nulla veterum monumenta docent. Id merum est Baronii somnium, ex causæ studio, atque usu natum. Tum quod utriq; narrant Apostolorum decreto Christi discipulos vocari coepisse Christianos; id inquam, à Lucæ divini scriptoris mente & verbis alienum est. Ille quidem narrat, cum Barnabas & Paulus annum totum Antiochiæ conversati turbam multam docuissent, factum esse, ut ibi pri-mum mum Christiani cognominarentur discipu-li a (unde impostor hujus fingendi canonis occasionem arripuit) caeterum id decreto Apostolorum factum esse, neque Lucas, neque quisquam, praeter hunc maleferiatum simium, litteris unquam mandavit. Neque sane quicquam hujusmodi decrevisse Apostolos verisimile est. Quid enim necesse erat, legem de eo ferre, quod per se res ipsa docebat? Haec lex vel ipsis discipulis, vel exteris facta est, Discipulis supervacanea fuit quos ipsa illa Christi religio, quam profitebantur, cujusque praecipua pars erat in Christum ipsum fides, satis per se monebat, ut se Christianos dicerent. Exteris vero, & ab Euangelio alienis, in quos nihil juris habebant Apostoli, legem fuisse latam, ridiculum dictu est. Cum ergo a virorum gravissimorum atque sanctissimorum sapientia abhorreat legem ferre vel supervacaneam, vel ridiculam, apparet Apostolos legem, quam istis affinxit crassus impostor, nunquam revera tulisse.
units.tr: Let us now consider the fragments of the canons themselves, taken from that book by Turrianus. They contain many absurdities, unworthy of the Apostles, and by these their falsehood is most clearly seen. Turrianus cites this canon, the ninth, first: that believers in the Lord Jesus, whom the men of that time called Galileans, should thereafter be called Christians. But Baronius and Binius give the canon differently, namely: that believers in the Lord Jesus, whom the men of that time (as the Acts have it) called disciples, should be called Christians. First, this difference between them undermines the credibility of the canon and shows them to be architects of Babel, speaking different languages, workers of falsehood. For they cannot escape that one of them, either Turrianus or Baronius, has lied. Then I ask Baronius where he got the reading he gives? He mentions no manuscript of this Synod seen by himself or by anyone else, except Turrianus. Why, then, does he change what Turrianus presents from that single manuscript? Here indeed he is clearly a liar, caught, as they say, in the act [ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ]. But this good man, who knew well that this whole matter is fabulous, thought he had the right and license to play with it at his pleasure. So when he understood that the impostor Turrianus had foolishly and absurdly invented that believers in the Lord were called Galileans in the time of the Apostles, a thing abhorrent to all the faith of Church history, which tells that the name of Galileans was imposed on our people not at the beginning but only in the fourth century, when it was already mature, under the apostate Julian, the learned Baronius judged that this foolish and absurd lie should be replaced and corrected by another, less incredible. But if it was convenient for him to devise this for his own purposes, it must not be thought that he had the right to do so. So the canon brought forward by Turrianus is false and fictitiously composed, by the judgement of Baronius and Binius themselves; surely they would never have changed it if they had judged it right and true. But neither can what they impudently substitute for Turrianus's words stand. I concede that from the Acts it is clear that both the Apostles and Luke called the believers disciples, and that the men of that time, that is the common people, used that same word so that when they said simply disciples they understood those who believed in Christ. But no Acts of the Apostles, no other Acts, and no ancient records teach this, I say. It is pure dream of Baronius, born of his cause and his habit. Then, as both of them relate, that by decree of the Apostles the disciples of Christ began to be called Christians*, I say this is foreign to the mind and words of Luke, the divine writer. He indeed relates that when Barnabas and Paul had lived a whole year at Antioch and taught a great crowd, it happened that there the disciples were first called Christians (and from this the impostor seized the occasion for his fabricated canon); but that this came about by a decree of the Apostles, neither Luke nor anyone else except this ill-fated ape has ever committed to writing. Nor is it at all likely that the Apostles decreed anything of the kind. For why was it necessary to make a law about what the matter itself taught by its own nature? This law was made either for the disciples or for outsiders. For the disciples it would have been superfluous, since that very religion of Christ which they professed, whose chief part was faith in Christ himself, sufficiently taught them to call themselves Christians. That a law should be passed for outsiders, who were alien to the Gospel and over whom the Apostles had no authority, is ridiculous to say. Since, then, the wisdom of the most serious and holy men shrinks from making a law that is either superfluous or ridiculous, it is clear that the Apostles never really enacted the law which the crude impostor has attributed to them.

units.la: Secundo loco, hunc Antiochenum scilicet canonem promit Turrianus; ut baptizati non jam circumciderentur more Iudaeorum, siquidem sit baptismus circumcisio non manu facta. Huic conjungendus est alius, septimo loco a Turriano & Binio memoratus, a Baronio nugarum, credo, pertaesus omissus; quo (inquit Turrianus) renova-tum, ac confirmatum est decretum Synodi Hierofolymitana, ut abstinerent Christiani a sanguine, & suffocato, & fornicatione. Sed & ejusdem farinæ est nono, eoque ultimo loco recensitus à Turriano canon, verbofiffimus & nugaciffimus; quem Latine ex Turriano describam; Ne (inquit a) Christiani a cibis abstinendo Judæos imitentur; imo vescantur suilla, cum Dominus pronuntiaverit, quæ in os intrant, non inquinare hominem, sed quæ ex ore exeunt, utpote ex corde exeuntia; Et ne fecundum litteram eos feftentur, sed spiritualiter & anagogicè vivant. Belluina enim Judaorum synagoga quidem abominatur; turpem vero vitam vivit, & improbitate tenetur constricta; sicut ait Propheta: Satu-rati sunt suilla, & reliquerunt reliquias parvulis suis. Similiter non est interdictum Christianis vesci pisce testam habente; & pisce item squamis carente. Hoc enim est fecundum spiritum pisce testaceo vesci, cum quis stupido & imprudenti corde veritatis prædicationem instar testa abjicit. Hos tres canones, ut liquet, ex Apostolorum decreto in Hierofolymitana Synodo facta, fabricatus est impostor. Quod enim primus & tertius Canones Christianos circumcisionis, & abstinentiæ à suilla, & à piscibus
units.tr: Secondly, Turrianus brings forward this Antiochene canon: that the baptized should no longer be circumcised after the manner of the Jews, since baptism is the circumcision not made with hands. To this must be joined another, which Turrianus and Binius mention seventh, and which Baronius, I suppose, weary of such trifles, has omitted: by which (says Turrianus) was renewed and confirmed the decree of the Synod of Jerusalem, that Christians should abstain from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication. But the ninth canon, mentioned by Turrianus in the last place, is of the same kind, most wordy and most trifling; I shall copy it in Latin from Turrianus: That Christians (he says) should not imitate the Jews by abstaining from foods; indeed let them eat swine's flesh, since the Lord has pronounced that what enters the mouth does not defile a man, but what comes out of the mouth, as proceeding from the heart; and let them not keep the feasts according to the letter, but live spiritually and anagogically. For the bestial synagogue of the Jews indeed abhors it, yet lives a foul life and is held bound by wickedness, as the Prophet says: They are satisfied with swine, and have left the remnants to their little ones. Likewise, it is not forbidden to Christians to eat fish that has a shell, and also fish that lacks scales. For to eat shelled fish according to the Spirit is this: when someone with a dull and careless heart casts away the preaching of the truth like a shell. That these three canons were fabricated by the impostor as the decree of the Apostles made at the Synod of Jerusalem is clear. For that the first and third canons release Christians from circumcision and from abstinence from swine and from fish that are either shelled or not scaly, from the yoke and observance, the Apostles had indeed commanded at the Synod of Jerusalem, and much better and more clearly:

units.la: a p. 93. versa. piscibus vel testaceis, vel non squamosis, jugo ac observatione solverunt, id Apostoli, & quidem multo melius, ac luculentius in Synodo Hierosolymitana praeceperant a; non esse imponendum jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos (inquiunt) portare potuimus. Tum in Synodica Epistola b; Visum est Spiritui Sancto, & nobis, nihil ultra imponere vobis oneris, quam haec necessaria, ut abstineatis vos ab immolatis simulacrorum & sanguine & suffocato, & fornicatione. His verbis, & quod habet secundus Turriani canon, de Idolothytis, sanguine, suffocato, & fornicatione vitandis diserte praecipiunt Apostoli, & quod duo reliqui canones de circumcisione & suillae piscumque esu edicunt, id satis docent, dum se profitentur nihil ultra oneris fidelibus imponere, praeter eam, quam subjiciunt, a quatuor illis nuper commemoratis abstinentiam. Nam cum his quatuor, neque circumcisio, neque a suilla carne, & a piscibus certi generis abstinentia contineatur, clarum est, utriusque observationis, ut & aliorum Mosaicorum rituum jugo, exsolutos fuisse per hoc Apostolorum decretum fideles. Cum ergo ista ab Apostolis jam antea fuissent Hierosolymis, frequentissima Synodo, luculentissimo
units.tr: a p. 93, verso. That no yoke should be laid upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we (they say) were able to bear. Then in the Synodal Letter b: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication. In these words, and in what the second canon of Turrianus contains about avoiding idol-offerings, blood, what is strangled, and fornication, the Apostles expressly prescribe; and what the two remaining canons decree about circumcision and the eating of swine and fish, they sufficiently teach, in that they profess that they impose no further burden on the faithful beyond that abstinence which they add, namely the four things just mentioned. For since circumcision, abstinence from swine's flesh, and abstinence from certain kinds of fish are not contained in these four, it is clear that the faithful were released from the yoke of both observances, as well as of the other Mosaic rites, by this decree of the Apostles. Since, then, these things had already been settled by the Apostles at Jerusalem, in a very full Synod, by a most splendid decree of great authority, and sent to the Antiochenes and the other Syrians by Barnabas and Paul and other most faithful disciples, and received by the whole multitude with great joy, and further commended and enjoined by Paul in Syria and Cilicia in all the churches everywhere, what, I ask, was the need for the same Apostles, a short time later, to decree and press these same things again in the Church of Antioch, to which they were both very well known and very dear, or to frame new canons, as if the earlier decree were either incomplete or obscure?
a Acts 15. 10.

units.la: b Ibid. 28. 29. lentissimo decreto, amplissima authoritate constituta, ad Antiochenos, & reliquos Syros per Barnabam, & Paulum, aliosq; fidelissimos discipulos missa, ab omni multitudine magno cum gaudio excepta, à Paulo insuper in Syria, Ciliciaque omnibus passim Ecclesiis commendata, atque praecepta; quid quaesso opus fuit eadem parvo post intervallo eosdem Apostolos in Antiochena Ecclesia, cui illa & notissima erant, & carissima, decernere, ac inculcare ? vel novos canones condere, quasi prius decretum vel mutilum esset, vel obscurum ? Certe siqua repetendi decreti (quae non demonstratur ulla fuisse) necessitas extitisset, ea suasisset superiorem Apostolorum constitutionem, qua nulla unquam in terris à Domini Christi ascensione, majori authoritate facta est, de integro edi, ac commendari; novos, ac numero plures ea de re, quae sapientissime, ac plenissime uno decreto constituta erat, canones fieri, nihil omnino cogebat; omnia ne fierent potius repugnabant. Novis enim legibus, veterum, si non evertitur, certe labefactatur, ac quodammodo sugillatur authoritas; quasi scilicet eae vel male fuerint, vel aliquo saltem vitio laboraverint, minusque vel plenae, vel claræ fuerint. Quae enim ab omni parte recte, sapiensapienterque constitutæ sunt, eas interpolare, ac demutare, hominis est, ut videtur, parum prudentis. Cum ergo omnium mortalium longe sapientissimi fuerint Christi Domini Apostoli, plane est incredibile eos, quam paucis ante annis divine constituerant deiftis legem, tribus his canonibus, quod mentitur impostor, voluisse commutare. Huc accedit, quod in tertio canone non pauca occurrunt ab Apostolis penitus aliena. Quale est, quod ibi legitur Christianos debere ἀναγωγικῶς πολιτεύεσθαι, anagogice conversari, vel vivere? Quis Apostolorum, quis divinorum scriptorum, imo quis homo sanæ mentis sic locutus est? Anagogice aliquid interpretari Christianorum Theologi dicunt, (quamquam ne sic quidem usquam loquuntur divini scriptores) anagogice vero conversari, qui dixerit, præter istum Turriani impostorem, scio neminem. Tum & quod statim Judæorum Synagogam κτη-νώδη belluinam vocat, id ab Apostolorum & gravitate & modestia, imo & sapientia abhorret; quod Iudæos delinire, & sibi inprimis conciliare in illis Christianismi initiis studerent, ut vel ex decreto de idolothytis, & suffocatis vitandis apparet, quod in eorum gratiam factum esse constat. Veri quidem Apostoli, capite Actorum 15. in quo idem, quod hic canon, præcipiunt, ab omni in Iudæos convitio sedulo abstinent; neque quicquam de re tota gravius dicunt, quam hoc unum, neque se, neque majores suos potuisse portare illud Mosaicorum rituum jugum. Præterea hic canon sacram scripturam & impudenter, & sane joculariter corrumpit. Hæc enim ex Prophēta citat, ἐχοῤῥτάσθησαν ὑεiῶν, καὶ ἀφῆ-καν lα καὶ αλλοῖτα τοῖς νηπίοις αὐτῶν, id est, interprete Turriano, Saturati sunt suilla, & reliquerunt reliquias parvulis suis. Hic vero impostoris stultitia an impudentia major sit, nescio. Nam cum apud Prophetam scriptum sit, Saturati sunt filiis, & diminuerunt reliquias suas parvulis suis, impostor ex eo quod in Græco legebat, ἐχοῤῥτάσθησαν υἱῶν, Saturati sunt filiis, levi litterarum mutatione, ut locum ad suillæ suæ esum inflecteret, fecit, ἐχοῤῥτάσθησαν υεiῶν, Saturati sunt suillis carnibus, quod usque adeo puerile, joculare, ac ridiculum est, ut qui hoc scripsisse Apostolos putat, eum non suillam, sed fœnum & carduos esse oporteat. Denique, nonne & Apostolico ingenio dignissima est illa præclara allegoria, qua testaceo pisce vesci secundum spiritum, idem esse ait, quod veritatis prædicationem instar testæ abjicere? Vere testaceum ἀλληγόρημα. At tibi male sit, impostor; postor ; ita non modo impudens es & nequam, sed etiam stultus & vaecors.
units.tr: b Ibid. 28. 29. Surely if there had arisen any need to repeat the decree (and none is shown to have arisen), that need would have suggested the re-publishing and commending of the earlier constitution of the Apostles, which was never made on earth since the ascension of the Lord Christ with greater authority; but nothing at all compelled them to make new canons, and more of them, about a matter already settled most wisely and fully by one decree; rather, everything opposed it being done. For by new laws the authority of the old is, if not overturned, at least weakened and in some measure disparaged, as if they had been badly made or had some defect, or were less full or less clear. For to alter and change what has been rightly and wisely established in every part seems to be the act of a man of little prudence. Since, then, the Apostles of Christ the Lord were by far the wisest of all mortals, it is quite incredible that they wished, as the impostor lies, to change for the faithful by these three canons the law which they had divinely established so few years before. Add to this that in the third canon there occur not a few things wholly alien to the Apostles. Such is what is read there, that Christians ought to live anagogically [ἀναγωγικῶς πολιτεύεσθαι], or to live anagogically. Which of the Apostles, which of the divine writers, nay, which sane man has spoken thus? Christian theologians say to interpret something anagogically (though not even so do the divine writers anywhere speak), but that anyone besides this impostor Turrianus has said to conduct oneself anagogically, I know of no one. Then also that he at once calls the Jewish synagogue bestial [κτηνώδη]: this is abhorrent to the gravity, the moderation, and indeed the wisdom of the Apostles, who in those first beginnings of Christianity took pains to win over and above all to conciliate the Jews, as is evident even from the decree about avoiding idol-offerings and what is strangled, which is known to have been made for their sake. The true Apostles, in Acts chapter 15, where they prescribe the same things as this canon, carefully abstain from every reproach against the Jews; nor do they say anything more serious about the whole matter than this one thing, that neither they nor their fathers were able to bear that yoke of the Mosaic rites. Moreover, this canon corrupts Holy Scripture both impudently and, indeed, in a jesting manner. For it cites these words from the Prophet: [ἐχορτάσθησαν υἱῶν, καὶ ἀφῆκαν λείμματα καὶ ἀλλότρια τοῖς νηπίοις αὐτῶν], that is, in Turrianus's rendering: They are satisfied with swine, and have left remnants to their little ones. Whether the impostor's stupidity or his impudence is greater here, I do not know. For since in the Prophet it is written: They are satisfied with sons, and have lessened their remnants for their little ones, the impostor, from what he read in the Greek, [ἐχορτάσθησαν υἱῶν], They are satisfied with sons, by a slight change of letters, to bend the passage to his eating of swine, made it [ἐχορτάσθησαν υεiῶν], They are satisfied with swine's flesh; a thing so childish, jesting, and ridiculous that whoever thinks the Apostles wrote this must suppose them to be not swine but hay and thistles. Finally, is that famous allegory, by which eating shelled fish according to the Spirit is said to be the same as casting away the preaching of the truth like a shell, not most worthy of Apostolic genius? Truly a shelled allegory. But woe to you, impostor; so you are not only impudent and worthless but also foolish and mad.

units.la: Quid de illo tertio canone dicam, in quo Turrianus ait cautum fuisse, ut ex omni natione, & genere ad fidem Orthodoxam admitterentur ? Quasi vero post disertum Domini Christi mandatum, oblatamque coelitus Petro visionem, & sermones de hoc argumento ultro citroque ab Apostolis habitos, & ipsa Gentium conversione repraesentatam coelestium mandatorum fidem, quisquam inter Christianos remanserit, qui dubitaret, an alicujus vel generis, vel gentis homines a Christi fide excludi deberent ! Eadem ratione licebat impostori Apostolos facere decernentes, ut in posterum jus quibusvis esset poenitentiam agere, & Deum invocare. Non enim haec illo clariora, aut in Christi disciplina notiora. Sed quia impostor inaudiverat fuisse initio aliquid inter primos discipulos ideo turbatum, quod Petrus & alii homines Ethnicos ad baptismum, & Ecclesiae communionem praeputiatos admisissent: eo putavit, bellam sibi canonis cudendi oblatam occasionem, quo, quod ab Apostolis factum sciebat, id ab omnibus fieri decerneret.
units.tr: What shall I say about that third canon, in which Turrianus says it was provided "that men of every nation and kind should be admitted to the orthodox faith"? As if, after the plain command of the Lord Christ, and the vision sent from heaven to Peter, and the discussions on this subject held back and forth among the Apostles, and the conversion of the Gentiles itself, which displayed the faith of the heavenly commands, any Christian could remain who doubted whether men of any kind or nation ought to be shut out from the faith of Christ! By the same reasoning the impostor might have had the Apostles decree that from then on anyone at all had the right to do penance and call upon God. For nothing is clearer than that, or better known in the discipline of Christ. But the impostor had heard that at the beginning there had been some disturbance among the first disciples because Peter and others had admitted uncircumcised Gentiles to baptism and to the communion of the Church; so he thought he had been offered a fine occasion to frame a canon, by which he might decree that everything be done by all which he knew the Apostles had done.

units.la: Cap. P. Liber ill. Vnusquisque hoc modo explicetur ... (marginal reference, largely illegible)
units.tr: Chap. P. Book ill. Let each be explained in this way ...

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 25.

units.la: Octavus canon expenditur, & quam falsus sit & vanus ostenditur, 1. ex ipsa lectionis triplicis varietate. 2. ex Apostolica doctrina. 3. ex vetustissimorum Patrum fide. 4. ex ipsius Synodi 7. totiusque Graeca Ecclesia de imaginibus sententia, & praxi; quo loco Binii fraus detegitur in voce σπλη, cujus etymon, & sensus explicatur. Tota de pseudepigraphis Apostolicis disputatio concluditur.
units.tr: The eighth canon is examined, and its falsity and emptiness are shown: (1) from the very diversity of the three readings; (2) from apostolic doctrine; (3) from the faith of the most ancient Fathers; (4) from the Seventh Synod itself and the view and practice of the whole Greek Church concerning images. Here Binius's fraud is exposed in the word στήλη [stēlē], whose etymology and sense are explained. The whole discussion of the apostolic pseudepigrapha is concluded.

units.la: ENIQUE octavus canon, ob quem unum caeteros omnes fictos suisse apparet, evidentissime falsus est. Idque primo arguit ipsa lectionis diversitas; Nam canon in Septimę Synodi (in qua à Gregorio Pisinuntis episcopo recitatur) antiqua translatione Latina ita legitur; Servatos non debere amplius ad idola aberrare, sed certandum esse ante columnam Dei hominisque Iesu Christi Domini nostri. In recentiori vero Anastasii Bibliothecarii versione, hominis in imaginum negotio, fidei vehementer suspecte longe aliter; Ne ultra errent hi, qui salvi fiunt, circa idola, sed pro eis imaginentur deivirilem statuam Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Denique in Turriani libro hoc modo expressus habetur; Τῆς μὴ πλανωμένης τῆς σωζομένης εἰς τὰ εἰδωλα, ἀλλὰ ἀντειἀντεικονίζειν τῷ θεανδρεικῷ ἀχράντου χει-ροποιήτου σήλῳ τῆ ἀληθινῆ θεῷ καὶ σωτῆ-ρῷ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ καὶ τῷ αὐτῷ διεφθορό-των ἀντικρὺ τῶν εἰδώλων ᾧ Ἰουδαίων, ᾧ μη-κέτι πλανᾶσθαι εἰς εἴδωλα, μηδὲ ὁμοιοῦσθαι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις. quę Latine sic exhibet Binius; Ut ne errent salvati in idola, sed pingant ex opposito divinam humanamq; manufactam impermixtam effigiem Dei veri, ac salva-toris nostri Iesu Christi ipsiusque servorum, contra idola, & Iudæos. Neque errent in idolis, neque similes fiant Iudæis. Hæ tres sunt hujus canonis, multum, ut quivis videt, diversæ, discrepantesque lectiones. Prima, omnium antiquissima, de imaginibus verbum facit nullum; tantum ait certandum esse ante columnam Domini nostri Iesu Christi; quod quid sit, difficile est dicere, nisi forte hoc velit, in conspectu Ecclesiæ, quæ Christi in terris columna est, divinæque veritatis σύλῳ, καὶ ἰσχυρωμα, fortiter contra idola, & idololatras pugnandum. Vel fortasse per σήλῳ χειρῶ crucem Dominicam intelligit; nam cruci σήλης quoque vocabulum convenire, ex iis, quæ de hujus vocis usu & etymo mox dicemus, apparebit. Secunda longe hinc abit; & pro eo, quod prior certandum esse dicebat, hæc ait imaginandum; pro ea quod illa habet, ante columnam Dei hominisque minisque Iesu Christi, hęc deivirilem Christi statuam reponit. Inter quæ quam immane sit discrimen, omnes vident. Illa certare nos jubet ante Christi columnam; quod si est, ut diximus, ante Christi vel crucem, vel Ecclesiam, verum est, & apud omnes confessum; hæc præcipit nobis imaginari statuam Christi, quod neque divinæ litterę, neque Ecclesiasticorum hominum quisquam ante sextum sæculum docuisse legitur; ut ipsam locutionis ineptiam mittam. Quis enim præter Anastasium dixit unquam imaginari statuam, ut significaret statuam facere & effingere? Illa denique Christum Deum hominemque vocat, quod sanum est; hæc imaginariam illam, sive potius imaginatam Christi statuam Deivirilem appellat; quod novum est, & in omni Ecclesia ante istum Anastasium inauditum. Ex quibus liquet, textum Græcum pessime ab Anastasio acceptum fuisse, penitusque corruptum, substituto verbo ἀντεικονίζειν (quod ipse imaginari pro idolis, sive in vicem idolorum reddidit) pro verbo ἀγωνίζεσθαι certare; quod verisimile est in primis illis codicibus extitisse, quibus usus est antiquus, qui idem simplicissimus est, interpres. Tum pro eo quod in veteri codice fuisse videtur, Θεανθρώπῳ Χριστῷ Dei hominis Christi, iste sinxit τῷ Θεανθρώπῳ. ξεανλῶ Deivirilem Christi statuam. Turrianicus impostor Anastasianas corruptelas secutus est; sed eas aliis insuper auxit; ut fere est immoderatum, & inexsaturabile mendacii & superstitionis ingenium. Cum enim Christi ςήλω statuam Anastasius simpliciter dixisset Διανδρικῶ, iste eam insuper novis elogiis cohonestat, ἀχειροποίητον, impermixtam, & χειροποίητον manufactam appellans; quod ultimum ideo adjecisse videtur, nequis quod ipse de sculpta ab artifice statua intelligit, ad aliam aliquam Christi sive statuam, sive columnam, referret. Adhæc cum Anastasius solius Dominicæ effigiei meminisset, recentior iste planus Servos quoque Christi, id est Sanctos diserte commemorandos censuit. Ac denique mercem, ut vendibiliorem faceret, novo colore à Judæorum odio, & lepida quadam antithesi ducto, commendandam, ac exornandam putavit. Anastasius dixerat, pro idolis imaginentur Deivirilem statuam Domini nostri Iesu Christi; hic præterea ista addidit, ipsiusque servorum contra idola & Iudæos. Neque errent in idolis, neque similes fiant cum Iudæis. Nos Christianos medio inter Paganos Iudæosque loco consistere vult; ut neque scilicet cum illis falsorum numinum simulacra colamus; sed neque cum his Domini & sanctorum storum imagines repudiemus. Sui ergo canonis verba inter se concilient, si possunt, Binius ac Baronius; Neque enim fieri potest, ut verum sit, quod unum non est, sed varium ac multiplex. Quod enim ait bonus Baronius hujus canonis verba concisſe & perperam traslata ab antiquo 7. Synodi interprete fuisse perfacile colligi ex Graeca editione, quam Turrianus describit; id inquam, falso ac temere, & ex uno causæ studio dictum fuisse respondeo. Imo vero ex iis, quæ nuper diximus, perfacile colligitur primo, corruptum ab Anastasio homine astuto, magno imaginum patrono, Græcæ Synodi textum, quem vetus interpres vere & simpliciter (ut solet) repræsentaverat; secundo, ipsam Anastasii fœtum novis insuper modis à recentiore illo Turriani impostore adulteratum fuisse, additis istis, quas nuper descripsimus, laciniis, quæ neque in Anastasiana translatione, neque in Græco Synodi septimæ ex ea vitiato, ut videtur, codice, comparent. Itaque cum antiquiora recentioribus, simplicia artificiosis anteferenda sint, si quos hujusmodi canones ab Apostolis Antiochiæ conditos constaret (quod quam non modo incertum, sed & falsum sit demonstravimus) hæc canonum istorum hoc loco verba ex veteris interpretis fide legenda essent; sent; & ex eo Anastasii, Turrianicique codicis corruptelæ corrigendæ, ac emendandæ; quos scilicet veteri illo septimę Synodi interprete recentiores fuisse clarum est. Sed viderint adversarii. Nos, qui canonem hunc omnino falsum ac fictitium esse putamus, neque ullam ejus lectionem Apostolorum vere esse arbitramur, ultimam illam Turrianicam, quam Baronius, tametsi præter omnem rationem, cæterarum, novissimam antiquorum normam esse vult, nunc sigillatim expendamus. Hunc ergo canonem à Turriano descriptum falso & inverecunde Apostolis tribui; primum ex iis, quibus constat, verbis probo. Nam vox Θεανδρικὸς deivirilis, quæ in eo extat, ab omni Apostolorum sermone aliena est, neque uspiam in veris eorum litteris ostendi potest. Tum idem ex rebus ipsis multo etiam luculentius demonstro. Nam quod hic canon statuit, ut Christi εἰκὼν statua fiat, id à vero Apostolorum dogmate abhorret; idque liquet primo ex veris canonicisque Apostolorum libris, in quibus nihil uspiam tale fidelibus præceptum invenimus; nusquam oppositas Paganorum simulacris Christi & servorum ejus statuas. Secundo idem ex eo probatur, quod canon Christianos Judæorum hac in parte dissimiles esse vult; id vero non modo nusquam
units.tr: Lastly, the eighth canon, by which alone all the others are shown to be forged, is most evidently false. First, the diversity of its readings proves this. In the Seventh Synod, where it is recited by Gregory, bishop of Pisinus, the canon reads in the old Latin translation: The saved ought no longer to wander after idols, but ought to contend before the pillar of God and of the man Jesus Christ our Lord. In the more recent version of Anastasius the Librarian, which is strongly suspect in the matter of images, it reads quite differently: Let those who are saved no longer err about idols, but in their place let them image the God-man statue of our Lord Jesus Christ. Finally, in Turrianus's book it is given in this form: [Τῆς μὴ πλανωμένης τῆς σωζομένης εἰς τὰ εἰδωλα, ἀλλὰ ἀντειἀντεικονίζειν τῷ θεανδρεικῷ ἀχράντου χει-ροποιήτου σήλῳ τῆ ἀληθινῆ θεῷ καὶ σωτῆ-ρῷ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ καὶ τῷ αὐτῷ διεφθορό-των ἀντικρὺ τῶν εἰδώλων ᾧ Ἰουδαίων, ᾧ μη-κέτι πλανᾶσθαι εἰς εἴδωλα, μηδὲ ὁμοιοῦσθαι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις]. Binius renders this in Latin as follows: That the saved may not err into idols, but may paint over against them the divine and human, unmixed effigy, made by no hand, of the true God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of his servants, against idols and the Jews. Let them not err into idols, nor become like the Jews. These three readings of this canon are, as anyone can see, very different and discordant. The first, which is by far the oldest, says nothing about images. It only says one must contend before the pillar of our Lord Jesus Christ. What this means is hard to say, unless perhaps it wishes us to fight strongly against idols and idolaters in the sight of the Church, which is the pillar of Christ on earth, and [σήλῳ] of divine truth and its [ἰσχυρωμα] stronghold. Or perhaps by the pillar of the cross he means the Lord's cross; for the word pillar [σήλης] also fits the cross, as will appear from what we shall say shortly about the use and etymology of this word. The second reading departs far from this. In place of the first's contend, it says imagine; in place of the first's before the pillar of God and of the man Jesus Christ, it puts a God-man statue of Christ. How immense the difference between these is, everyone sees. The first bids us contend before the pillar of Christ; if that pillar is, as we have said, either the cross or the Church before Christ, it is true and admitted by all. The second orders us to imagine a statue of Christ, which is something that neither the divine letters nor any churchman is read to have taught before the sixth century, not to mention the awkwardness of the expression itself. For who, apart from Anastasius, ever said to imagine a statue in order to mean making and fashioning a statue? Finally, the first calls Christ God and man, which is sound; the second calls that imagined, or rather imagined, statue of Christ God-man, which is a novelty and unheard of in any Church before this Anastasius. From these things it is clear that the Greek text was very badly taken up by Anastasius and thoroughly corrupted: the verb [ἀντεικονίζειν], which he rendered to image in place of idols, or in the stead of idols, was substituted for the verb [ἀγωνίζεσθαι], to contend. This is likely to have stood in those earliest manuscripts which the old translator, who is also the plainest, used. Then, in place of what seems to have stood in the old codex, [Θεανθρώπῳ Χριστῷ], to Christ the God-man, he invented [τῷ Θεανθρώπῳ], the God-man [ξεανλῶ], a God-man statue of Christ. The impostor Turrianus followed Anastasius's corruptions, but he also increased them with others, as is nearly the habit of an immoderate and insatiable nature of lying and superstition. For when Anastasius had simply said of the statue of Christ [Διανδρικῶ], this man further adorns it with new epithets, calling it [ἀχειροποίητον], unmixed, and [χειροποίητον], made by hand. He seems to have added this last because he did not want anyone to refer it to some other statue or pillar of Christ, when he means a statue sculpted by an artist. Moreover, whereas Anastasius had mentioned only the effigy of the Lord alone, this more recent plain-speaker thought that the servants of Christ, that is, the saints, should also be expressly named. And finally, to make his wares more saleable, he thought they should be commended and decorated with a novel colouring drawn from hatred of the Jews and a certain charming antithesis. Anastasius had said let them image in place of idols the God-man statue of our Lord Jesus Christ; this man additionally added, and of his servants, against idols and the Jews. Let them not err into idols, nor become like the Jews. He wants us Christians to stand in a middle position between Pagans and Jews, so that we neither worship with them the images of false deities nor reject with these people the images of the Lord and the saints. Let Binius and Baronius, then, if they can, reconcile the words of their own canon with each other. For it cannot be that what is true is one thing, while what is not one is various and manifold. As for what good Baronius says, that the words of this canon were clearly mangled and wrongly translated by the old interpreter of the Seventh Synod, as is very easily gathered from the Greek edition which Turrianus describes, I answer that this was said falsely and rashly, and out of a single zeal for the cause. Indeed, from what we have just said, it is very easily gathered, first, that the Greek text of the Synod was corrupted by Anastasius, a crafty man and a great patron of images, who had truly and plainly (as is his habit) rendered it, and secondly that Anastasius's own offspring was further adulterated in new ways by that more recent impostor Turrianus, who added those scraps which we have just described, which appear neither in Anastasius's translation nor in the Greek of the Seventh Synod, which was apparently spoiled from that translation. Therefore, since older things must be preferred to newer, and simple things to artificial ones, if it were established that such canons had been drawn up by the Apostles at Antioch (which we have shown is not only uncertain but false), the words of these canons should be read here according to the faithfulness of the old interpreter, and by that the corruptions of the codices of Anastasius and Turrianus should be corrected and emended, since it is clear that these are more recent than that old interpreter of the Seventh Synod. But let our opponents look to it. We, who think this canon is altogether false and fictitious, and who judge that no reading of it is truly the Apostles', will now examine carefully that last Turrianic reading, which Baronius, although against all reason, wants to be the newest and the norm of the older ones. First, I prove from the very words that this canon, as described by Turrianus, is falsely and shamelessly attributed to the Apostles. For the word [Θεανδρικὸς], divine-human, which is found in it, is alien to all the Apostles' language and cannot be shown anywhere in their genuine writings. Then I demonstrate the same from the things themselves, much more clearly. For what this canon lays down, that Christ's [εἰκὼν], statue, should be made, is abhorrent from the true doctrine of the Apostles. This is evident, first, from the true and canonical books of the Apostles, in which we find nothing of the kind commanded to the faithful anywhere, nor any statues of Christ and his servants set against the images of the Pagans. Secondly, the same is proved by the fact that the canon wants Christians to be unlike the Jews in this respect; and this is not only nowhere decreed by the Apostles in the divine letters, but it is also plain that it was never truly decreed at all; and then, because we read that the Jews never objected or reproached this to the Apostles, which (if it were true) no one doubts they would have brought against them before everything else, as a capital crime; and then because this…

units.la: ab Apostolis in divinis litteris decernitur, sed neque decretum revera unquam fuisse patet; tum quod hoc Iudæos nunquam Apostolis objecisse, exprobrasseque legamus, quod (si verum esset) nemo dubitat, quin ante omnia velut capitale scelus, iis objecturi fuerint; tum quod id falsum sit, & cum divina lege diserte pugnet. Cum enim Dei lex, in qua cujusquam rei simulacrum fieri prohibetur, excepta ea parte, quæ cærimonialis & politica dicitur, tam Christianorum, quam Iudæorum sit; apparet, nisi (quod stultum est) fingatur, illud de simulacris præceptum ad cærimonialem legem pertinere; eandem omnino esse Christianorum, quæ Iudæorum est, rationem. Tertio, idem quoq; validissime ex totius veteris Christianæ praxi, ac sententia demonstratur: quam quia proprio opere fuse exsecuti sumus, nihil necesse est hic pluribus explicare. In illa enim disputatione ostendimus nullas apud vetustissimos trium primorum sæculorum Christianos fuisse Christi & Sanctorum imagines; quinimo quosdam ex vetustissimis Theologis, ut Clementem, ut Tertullianum, ut ipsum illum Origenem (in cujus bibliotheca præclarum hunc canonem repertum fuisse fabulantur) eo usque processisse, ut nefas esse docerent ullam imaginem effingere. Tum & quasdam dam veterum voces recta cum isto canone pugnantes attulimus; qualis illa est Elibe-ritanorum Patrum; Placuit picturas in Ec-clesiis esse non debere, ne quod colitur, aut adoratur, in parietibus depingatur; & hæc Epiphanii, In Ecclesia Christi contra Scripturarum authoritatem est hominis pendere imaginem; quam sententiam Epiphanius ipso facto comprobavit, scisso, Anablatensis Ecclesiæ velo, quod in eo depictam vidisset imaginem quasi Christi vel sancti cujusdam. Cætera mitto, quæ in illa disputatione videat, qui volet. Absurdum autem est, planeque incredibile, sanctissimos illos viros de his ita sensuros fuisse, si Apostoli quod hic canon decernit, id revera statuissent. Sed neque verisimile est Synodum Constantinopoli a. D. 754. ex 338. Episcopis constantem una voce, concordique sententia definituruum fuisse Christum Dominum impie vel dividere, vel confundere eos, qui ejus imaginem pingunt; Item talem ejus imaginem neque ex Christi, neque ex Apostolorum, vel Patrum traditione esse habere; B. vero Virginis & Sanctorum imagines & inutiles esse, & in ipsos Sanctos contumeliosas; neque item credibile est eandem Synodum vel depositioni, vel anathematis subjecturam fuisse eos omnes, qui imagines hujusmodi vel conconstru-xisent, vel in Ecclesia, privatis-ve aedibus collocavisent, si hic Turrianicus canon vere ab Apostolis conditus, publi-catusque in Ecclesia fuisset. Quinto. Ca-rolus Magnus, cujus ore omnis loquebatur Galliarum, , ac Germaniarum Ecclesia, difertissime negat rem à Synodo septima definitam (id est imaginum causam) ab Apostolis vel ab eorum successoribus statu-tam fuisse. Sexto. Idem quoque ex eo de-prehenditur, quod eorum omnium, qui Christi & sanctorum imagines probarunt ac defenderunt, nemo unquam hunc difer-tissimum, quique si verus esset, unus ab-unde sufficeret, canonem Antiochenum in hac causa attulisse, adversariisque objeci-sse legitur, non Gregorius Magnus Sereno Massilienfi, non Damascenus, non Ger-manus, non Nicephorus Graeci suae gentis Iconoclastis, non Adrianus Carolo, non Ionas Aurelianensis Claudio, non Vala-fridus Strabo, non caeteri, qui imagines vel colendas, vel duntaxat ad ornatum, aut instructionem habendas senserunt. Vnus ex omni istorum ingenti numero reper-tus est Gregorius ille Pisinuntis Episcopus, homo ignobilis, neque uspiam, quod sciam nisi in illa 7. Synodo, cui interfuit, nomi-natus, qui peregrinum istum, totique ha-ctenus Christiano orbi indictum, & inaudi-tum tum canonem,ex nescio quibus latebris erutum in lucem primus edidit, sed & ipsū longe alium (ut diximus) ab eo, quem nunc obtrudit Turrianus. Istum vero canonem quis Gregorio Romano, quis Damascemo, & Germano, aliisque nuper memoratis viris, quorum incomparabiliter major in Ecclesia est, quam istius Pisinuntensis fama, gloria, atque authoritas, ignotum futurum fuisse putaverit, si revera esset Apostolicus? Postremo non cum Iconoclastarum modo fide pugnat iste canon, sed & ipsorum Septimae Synodi Patrum, Graecorumque ejus placita sequentium, sententiam pulsat. Nam Graeci, quod omnes sciunt, solas imagines ex coloribus pictas probant; sculptas, & eminentiam expressionum repudiant; Septima vero pariter Synodus non alias constituit, quam τὰς ἐκ χρωμάτων καὶ ἐκ ψηφίδων, ex coloribus & tesselles, id est operis (ut vocant) musivi; & Germanus similiter negat statuas aneas faciendas. Turrianici Apostoli plane contra, nullas alias vel Christi, vel sanctorum effigies commendant, quam vel sculptas, vel conflatas, ac denique stantes. Id enim significat nomen στήλη statua, quo utitur canon; omninoque perverse ac falso eam vocem Binius effigiem, multo latiori, quam decebat, vocabulo reddidit. Στήλη enim a
units.tr: It is not only that this canon is nowhere decreed by the Apostles in the divine writings; it is also clear that it was never in fact decreed at all. For we read that the Jews never threw this at the Apostles or reproached them with it, though if it were true, no one doubts they would have raised it first of all, as a capital crime. And the canon is false and flatly contradicts the divine law. For the law of God, in which the making of an image of any thing is forbidden, applies to Christians as much as to Jews, except for the part called ceremonial and political. Unless one invents something foolish, it is evident that the precept about images belongs to the ceremonial law, and that the position of Christians is altogether the same as that of the Jews. Thirdly, the same point is very strongly shown from the whole practice and opinion of the ancient Christians. Since we have set this out at length in a work of its own, there is no need to explain it at greater length here. In that discussion we showed that the most ancient Christians of the first three centuries had no images of Christ or of the saints. Indeed, some of the earliest theologians, such as Clement, Tertullian, and Origen himself (in whose library they fable that this excellent canon was discovered), went so far as to teach that it was wrong to make any image at all. We also cited some sayings of the ancients that clash directly with this canon, such as that of the Fathers of Elvira: "It has been decided that pictures should not be in churches, lest what is worshipped or adored be painted on the walls." And this saying of Epiphanius: "It is contrary to the authority of Scripture for a human image to hang in the Church of Christ." Epiphanius confirmed this opinion by his own action, when he tore the veil of the church at Anablatha, because he had seen depicted on it an image as of Christ or of some saint. I pass over the rest, which anyone who wishes may read in that discussion. It is absurd, and utterly incredible, that those most holy men would have thought as they did if the Apostles had really decreed what this canon lays down. Nor is it likely that the Synod of Constantinople in the year 754, made up of 338 bishops, would with one voice and one mind have defined that those who paint the image of Christ the Lord either divide or confuse him impiously; that such an image of him has no basis in the tradition of Christ, the Apostles, or the Fathers; and that the images of the Blessed Virgin and of the saints are useless and insulting to the saints themselves. Nor is it credible that the same synod would have subjected to deposition or anathema all those who had either made images of this kind or placed them in church or in private houses, if this Turrianic canon had truly been framed by the Apostles and published in the Church. Fifthly, Charlemagne, through whose mouth the whole Church of the Gauls and Germans spoke, most plainly denies that the matter defined by the Seventh Synod (that is, the cause of images) was ever laid down by the Apostles or by their successors. Sixthly, the same is shown by this fact: among all who approved and defended the images of Christ and the saints, no one ever cited this most express canon in the matter, which, if it were genuine, would have been enough on its own. Nor is it read that it was thrown at their opponents. Neither Gregory the Great to Serenus of Marseilles, nor Damascene, nor Germanus, nor Nicephorus to the Iconoclasts of his own nation, nor Hadrian to Charles, nor Jonas of Orléans to Claudius, nor Walafrid Strabo, nor the others who held that images were either to be venerated or at least to be kept for decoration or instruction, ever did so. Out of that vast number, only one is found: Gregory, that obscure bishop of Pisinus, a man of no note, who, so far as I know, is named nowhere except in the Seventh Synod, which he attended. He first brought into the light this foreign canon, unheard of until now throughout the Christian world, dragged out of I know not what hiding place. But he produced a canon quite different (as we have said) from the one Turrianus now puts forward. And who would have thought that this canon would have been unknown to Gregory of Rome, to Damascene and Germanus, and to the other men just mentioned, whose reputation and authority in the Church are incomparably greater than the fame, glory, and authority of that Pisinuntine, if it had really been Apostolic? Lastly, this canon conflicts not only with the faith of the Iconoclasts, but also with the opinion of the Fathers of the Seventh Synod themselves and of the Greeks who follow their decisions. For the Greeks, as everyone knows, approve only images painted in colours, and reject carved images and raised relief. The Seventh Synod likewise laid down nothing but images made from colours and from tesserae (that is, of what they call mosaic work). Germanus similarly says that bronze statues should not be made. The Apostles of Turrianus, on the contrary, recommend no images of Christ or the saints except carved, cast, or standing ones. For the word used in the canon, στήλη [stēlē], means a standing statue, and Binius has wrongly and falsely rendered it by the much wider word "effigy," more broadly than it should be. For στήλη [stēlē] comes from στῶ [stō], whence the Latin sto is derived, and I find no instance of this word being used of an image painted with a brush in colours on a flat surface. The Etymologicum Magnum: "stēlē, from stēsō [στήσω]: it signifies the stone set up at the head of a tomb; whence also stēlitēs and stēliteuō, which means to triumph." Eustathius says more subtly: "stēlē is a stone pillar, or made of stone, as the other name for the stone, lās, comes from stēlē, which is a stone set up as a sign of a man." "A straight sign from stone." He wants it to be compounded of stō and lās, stone. From this, he says, stēliteuein was also formed, meaning, by a figure of speech, to write against someone's name on a stele. Hence stēliteutikoi logoi, such as the two invective orations of Gregory Nazianzen against Julian the Augustus, the apostate, are so called. Suidas defines such a stele thus: "A stēlē is a long stone or bronze set up in a square shape, on which is written the insult to be publicized." So a stēlē is a cippus, a column of stone standing up out of the earth, such as sepulchral columns. Suidas also explains the "foundations of the stēlai" in Hemelias, and the stone that held the chariot, in the stadium, the stone "around which the charioteers turned," which Sophocles calls a stēlē. He then applies the word to columns that were either placed on tombs or raised to victors, "and they receive inscriptions" (he says). On these, of course, the victor's name, his contest, and his praise were written. In general, stēlai are columns, such as the Pillars of Hercules, which the Greeks in the same Suidas call the stēlai of Heracles. Since, then, the Apostles of Turrianus order that stēlai be made and set up for Christ and the saints, and say nothing about pictures painted with a brush on a flat surface, it is clear that they think quite differently from the Fathers of the Seventh Synod and the Greeks, who reject statues and images erected of stone, bronze, or wood, standing and solid, and admit into religious use only pictures and icons painted in colours on tablets. Hence it may be seen that this Gregory of Pisinus did not even persuade the synod he attended that this was truly a canon of the Apostles; otherwise they would undoubtedly have followed it, had they thought it Apostolic. But perhaps Gregory himself, if he had seen that Turrianic canon, would not have recognised it, since it is so different from the one he himself cites.

units.la: b In Synt. 7. Act. 4. ςῶ, unde Latinum sto factum est, neque id nominis de imagine penicillo, & coloribus in plano expresfa dictum reperitur. Etymologicum magnum, ςήλη τὸ ςῶ, ςήσω· σημαίνει ὁ τὸν ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ κείμενον τῆς τετρωτ@ λίθον· ἐξ ἧς καὶ ςηλίτης, καὶ ςηλιτεύω τὸ ςριαμβεύω· Eustathius argutius. ςήλη ὃ νυείως, ἢ ἐκ λίθων, ὡς ἄλλο τῆς ςήσω τῆς λάς ὁ λίθος, ὃ ἐκ λίθου ςηλαςῆ ἀντιςηκως ἀνδρίας. Rectum ex lapide signum. Vult componi ex ςῶ & λᾶς lapis. Unde & ipse quoque ςηλιτεύειν factum dicit, σιωπτικως τὸ ςήλαις ἐγγράφειν τὰ κατὰ τινῶν. Inde ςηλιτευτικοὶ λόγοι, quales habemus hoc ipso nomine dictas Gregorii Nazianzeni adversus Julianum Augustum desertorem orationes invectivas duas. Hujusmodi ςήλω Suidas sic definit, ςήλη λίθος ἐςιν ἡ χαλκὸς ἐπιμήκης, τετράςωνω χρῆ-ματι ἰδρύμενος, ἐν ᾗ γέγραπτῃ ἡ τὸ ςηλι-τευομένη ὕβρεις. Ergo ςήλη cippus est, columna lapis è terra extans, quales sepulcrales columnæ. Suidas Ἡμελίας quoque fundamenta ςήλας interpretatur, & λίθον κααρτῆρα, in stadio lapidem, ad quem flectebant currum auriga, à Sophocle ςήλῳ dictum docet. Tum de columnis accipit, quæ vel sepulcris imponebantur, vel victoribus erigebantur, καὶ ἐπιγράμματα (inquit) ἐπιδέχονται. Iis scilicet victoris nomen, men, & certamen, & laus inscribebatur. In genere ςῆλαι columnæ ; ut Herculis, quæ Græcis apud eundem Suidam ςῆλαι Ἡρακλείας. Cum ergo Turrianici Apostoli ςήλας Christo & sanctis fingi & poni jubeant, de imaginibus penicillo in plano expressis nihil dicant, apparet eos plane aliud sentire quam septimæ Synodi patres, & Græcos, qui signa, & statuas ex lapide, vel ære, vel ligno erectas, stantesque ac solidas reprobant; solas coloribus illusas, pictasq; tabulas, & icones in religionis usum admittunt. Unde videre est Gregorium illum Pisinuntensem ne ei quidem, cui interfuit, Synodo persuasisse hunc vere Apostolorum esse canonem; quem haud dubie secuti essent, si Apostolicum esse putassent. Sed ne ipse quidem fortasse Gregorius illum Turrianicum canonem, si vidisset, agnovisset; plane, ut ostendimus, ab eo diversum, quem ipse citat.
units.tr: In Synt. 7. Act. 4. It comes from στῶ, whence the Latin sto is derived, and this word is not found used of a picture expressed with a brush and colours on a flat surface. The Etymologicum magnum says: stele is from στῶ, στήσω [I will set up]; it signifies the stone set upright on the head of a tomb, and from it come stelites and stelitevo, meaning to triumph. Eustathius is more ingenious: a stele is either a stone pillar, or a stone set upright like a statue, from λᾶς [stone] with στῶ. A straight sign made of stone. He wishes it to be compounded of στῶ and λᾶς, stone. From this he also says that stelitevein was formed, meaning to inscribe charges against someone on a stele. Hence come stelitic speeches, such as the two invective orations of Gregory Nazianzen against Julian the Augustus and deserter, which bear this very name. Suidas defines such a stele thus: a stele is an elongated stone or bronze, set up in a square shape, on which the insult of the one being stelitevated is written. So a stele is a cippus, a column, a stone standing up out of the ground, such as sepulchral columns were. Suidas also explains [στήλας] as the bases of the stelae, and as a stone pillar; in the stadium, he teaches, the stone is called by Sophocles [στήλῳ] the stone around which charioteers turned their chariot. Then he takes it of columns, which were either placed on tombs or erected for victors, and which (he says) also received inscriptions: on them the victor's name, his contest and his praise were written. In general, steles are columns, such as the columns of Hercules, which among the Greeks in the same Suidas are called [Ἡρακλείας] steles of Heracles. Since, then, the Turrianic Apostles order steles to be fashioned and set up for Christ and the saints, and say nothing about pictures expressed with a brush on a flat surface, it appears that they think quite otherwise than the fathers of the Seventh Synod and the Greeks, who reject signs and statues erected of stone, bronze or wood, standing and solid, and admit into the religious use only tables and icons painted and adorned with colours. Hence one can see that Gregory of Pisinunte did not even persuade the Synod in which he took part that this canon was truly of the Apostles; they would doubtless have followed it, had they thought it Apostolic. But perhaps Gregory himself, had he seen that Turrianic canon, would not have recognised it, since, as we have shown, it is quite different from the one he cites.

units.la: Atque ita satis superque demonstratum est non modo Apostolicos non esse novem istos nuper à Turriano editos canones, sed ne sani quidem, aut eruditi esse authoris; in quibus, ut nunc quidem liquet, nihil pœne sani est, aut integri; omnia absurda, ab historiæ divinæ atque Ecclesiasticæ veritate, à doctrinæ sacræ rationibus, ab omnium fere Christianorum rum sententia alienajut nō modo impuden-tem, sed etiam crassum, ac stupidum fuisse oporteat, qui tales ineptias præter omnem veri speciem sanctissimis Apostolis affinge-re ausus sit. Quo fit, ut tametsi non nesci-am summam esse Turriani in his adversum nos disputationibus audaciam, atque inve-recundiam, ac non mediocrem etiam in-terdum inscitiam; vix tamen queam in ani-mum meum inducere, tam informem, absurdumq; fœtum ab eo prognatum esse, potiusque eo propendeam, ut credam im-postorem de ista recentiorum Græculorum caterva fuisse, qui dictam à Gregorio in Synodo 7. sententiam nactus, eam arri-puit, excolendamque, ac perpoliendam putavit, & ex hoc rudimento, pro captu suo (nihil enim est istis infimorum sæculo-rum Græculis nequius, imperitus, & ad omnia in litteris flagitia projectius) hanc Synodi scilicet Antiochenæ fabulam, stul-tissime, absurdissimeque instruxit, ac fecit; in quam cum incidisset Turrianus, homo omnium quisquiliarum, ineptiarum, & anilium fabularum avidissimus, carbones pro thesauro nobis venditavit, Hæc autem paulo fusius, quam fortassis necesse erat, disputare libuit, ut omnis adversariorum frangeretur impudentia. Nam si apud ho-mines candidos, sapientes, & verecundos, quales etiam in istis partibus plurimi reperiuntur, hæc caussa agatur, non dubito, quin ab ipso statim disputationis limine summovendus sit Turrianus. Cujus enim frontis est, post clausum obsignatumque jam ante quindecim pene sæculà Apostolicarum scripturarum canonem, repente nobis novos istos omnibusque antiquissimis authoribus ignotos canones obtrudere, eosque summa vi in Apostolicorum librorum censum inferre velle? Si hæc licent, nullus unquam erit Apostolici canonis finis, aut modus. Neque enim unquam deerunt procacia & inverecunda ingenia, quæ suos partus Apostolis commodent, suasque fabulas ac næniasgloriosissimo, & sanctissimo eorum nomine commendent. Atqui contra & Turriani, & Græcorum & omnium, qui fuerunt, quique erunt, impostorum audaciam, justissima hac æquissimaque præscriptione abunde cautum erit, si nullus unquam liber Apostolicus censeatur, vel pro Apostolico obtrudatur, nisi quem in Apostolicorum librorum canone diserte reposuerint, vel omnes, vel certe plurimi priorum trium sæculorum Patres; cæteri, vel à nemine primæ illius memoriæ, vel certe à paucissimis in hoc numero recensiti, aut memorati, ex Ecclesiæ finibus evestigio exterminentur, velut apocryphi, & ab hominibus vel improbis, vel otiosis infeliciter conficti. Neque quisquam sit piorum adeo stultus, aut imperitus, qui sibi ullius manuscripti codicis authoritate, vel ullius sive Turriani garrulitate, sive Montacutii pollicitatione persuaderi patia-tur, Apostolorum ea esse, quę nemo trium beatissimorum, & sanctissimis illis viris proximorum sæculorum memoraverit, nemo pro Ecclesiæ norma ac regula agnoverit. Quale enim quæso istud est, ut qui vere sint Apostolorum libri, Justinus quidem, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Origenes, Melito Sardensis, & alii eorundem temporum sanctissimi atque antiquissimi viri, vel nescierint, vel scribere litterisque mandare noluerint. Turrianus vero, & Bovius, & Montacutius, & alii nudiustertius nati, adhæc suspectæ omnes fidei, nonnulli & judicii parum sani, id optime sciverint, fidelissimeque monuerint? Sed hęc quidem de his plus satis. Qui vere pius, vereque Apostolorum amans fuerit, ille non temere, neque sine magna evidentique veterum testimoniorum authoritate quicquam pro vero Apostolorum opere suscipiet; qua authoritate, præter eos libros, quos summus Christiani orbis consensus jampridem, & ab ipsis Ecclesiæ initiis, in canonem sacrum retulit, cæteri
units.tr: And so it has been demonstrated more than enough that these nine canons recently published by Turrianus are not only not Apostolic, but do not even come from a sound or learned author. In them, as things now stand, there is almost nothing sound or whole; everything is absurd, alien to the truth of divine and ecclesiastical history, to the principles of sacred doctrine, and to the opinion of almost all Christians. One would have to think the man shameless, indeed crass and stupid, who dared to attribute such nonsense, lacking any appearance of truth, to the most holy Apostles. Hence, although I am not unaware of Turrianus's great boldness and shamelessness in his disputes with us, and at times no small ignorance, I can scarcely bring myself to believe that so shapeless and absurd an offspring was born from him. I incline rather to think that some impostor from that crowd of recent Greeklings obtained the seventh sentence cited by Gregory at the Synod, seized upon it, and thought it worth embellishing and polishing; and that from this rudiment, according to his capacity (for nothing is more wicked, more unlearned, and more abandoned in every literary crime than those Greeklings of the lowest centuries), he built up this tale of the Synod of Antioch, most foolishly and absurdly. Into this Turrianus fell, a man most greedy of every trifle, nonsense, and old wives' fable, and he sold us coals for treasure. I have chosen to discuss these matters somewhat more fully than perhaps was necessary, so that the impudence of our adversaries might be broken. For if this cause were pleaded before candid, wise, and modest men, such as are found in great numbers even on that side, I do not doubt that Turrianus would be shut out from the very threshold of the dispute. What face does a man have, when the canon of the Apostolic Scriptures has already been closed and sealed nearly fifteen centuries ago, to suddenly thrust upon us these new canons, unknown to all the most ancient authors, and to insist with all his might that they be counted among the Apostolic books? If such things were allowed, there would be no end or limit to the Apostolic canon. For bold and shameless minds will never be lacking, which will lend their own productions to the Apostles and commend their own fables and dirges under the most glorious and holy name of those men. But against the audacity of Turrianus, of the Greeks, and of all the impostors who have been and who will be, this most just and equitable rule will give ample protection: that no book be judged Apostolic, or put forward as Apostolic, unless either all or at least most of the Fathers of the first three centuries have expressly placed it in the canon of the Apostolic books. The rest, which were listed or mentioned by no one of that earliest memory, or by very few, must be driven at once out of the bounds of the Church, as apocryphal, and wretchedly fabricated by men either wicked or idle. Nor is anyone among the pious so foolish or unlearned as to allow himself to be persuaded, by the authority of any manuscript codex, or by the chattering of Turrianus, or the promise of Montacutius, that those things are Apostolic which none of the three most blessed centuries, nearest to those most holy men, has recorded, and none has acknowledged as the norm and rule of the Church. For what kind of thing is this, I ask, that the books which are truly Apostolic should have been either unknown or unwilling to be written down and committed to letters by Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Origen, Melito of Sardis, and the other most holy and most ancient men of those times, but that Turrianus, Bovius, Montacutius, and others born only the day before yesterday, all of them of suspect faith and some of unsound judgment, should have known it perfectly and reported it most faithfully? But enough of these matters. Whoever is truly pious and truly loves the Apostles will not rashly, and without great and evident testimony of the ancients, take up anything as a genuine work of the Apostles; and by that authority, apart from those books which the highest consensus of the Christian world has long since, from the very beginnings of the Church, placed in the sacred canon, the rest...
